THE
PARLIAMENTARY DEBATES:
(OFFICIAL REPORT.)
IN THE
FIRST SESSION OF THE SECOND PARLIAMENT OF NORTHERN IRELAND
APPOINTED TO MEET THE FOURTEENTH DAY OF APRIL, IN THE
FIFTEENTH YEAR OF THE REIGN OF
HIS MAJESTY
KING
GEORGE V.
FIRST SERIES-VOLUME
VI.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

---

Tuesday, 14th April, 1925.
The Parliament begun and held at the
City of Belfast, on Tuesday, the Fourthteenth day of April, in the Fifteenth Year
of the Reign of Our Sovereign Lord
George, by the Grace of God, of the United
Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and
of the British Dominions beyond the Seas,
King, Defender of the Faith, and in the
year of our Lord 1925.
On which day, at Ten Minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, being the first day of
the meeting of this Parliament, pursuant to
a Proclamation, Arthur Irwin Dasent, Esq.,
Clerk of the Parliaments of Northern
Ireland, and Major George Thomson, D.S.O.,
Second Clerk Assistant, attending in the
House, Andrew Newton Anderson, Esq.,
Clerk of the Crown, delivered to the said
Arthur Irwin Dasent a Book containing a
List of the Names of the Members returned
to serve in this Parliament.
Several of the Members repaired to their
seats.
Ꭺ message was delivered by Major T.
Dalby Hackett, D.S.O., Gentleman Usher of
the Black Rod, as followeth :-
:-
Members of the House of Commons, His
Grace the Governor of Northern Ireland
commands this Honourable House to attend
immediately in the Senate
"
Accordingly the House proceeded to
attend His Grace in the Senate.
The Clerk of the Senate was commanded
by His Grace to read the Dissolution
Proclamation.
HIS GRACE then said:-
SENATORS AND MEMBERS OF THE HOUSE OF
COMMONS OF NORTHERN IRELAND.
In the name and on behalf of His Majesty
I have to let you know that, as soon as the
Members of both Houses shall have been
sworn, the causes of His Majesty's calling
this Parliament of Northern Ireland will be
declared to you; and, it being necessary that
a Speaker of the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland should be first chosen, I
declare His Majesty's pleasure that you,
Members of the House of Commons, do proceed to the choice of a Speaker, and that you
present such person whom you shall so
choose here for His Majesty's Royal
approbation.
The House having returned,
Mrs. CHICHESTER (addressing herself
to the Clerk of the House, who, standing up,
pointed to her and then sat down): Mr.
Dasent, in compliance with the Gracious
wish of His Majesty that we should forthwith elect a Speaker I have great pleasure
in proposing:
"That the Right Honourable
William Hugh O'Neill do take the Chair
of this House as Speaker.'
Robert
A
Election of Speaker.
Election of Speaker.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mrs. Chichester]
Four years ago the privilege of proposing my
right hon. Friend to this position fell to the
lot of one (Mr. Coote) who is, alas, no longer
with us, but some of whose noble words on
that occasion I would like to recall to your
minds. He said:-
We realise the great trust we are placing
in our hon, and gallant Friend. He will be
the custodian of our honour; he will be the
guardian of our liberties; and he will be
the protector of minorities in this House,
even of individuals, and therefore he must
be a man who in our judgment has
qualities necessary for such a high and important position.
In the four years which have elapsed since
those words were spoken I think we can
claim that my right hon. Friend has proved
our judgment to have been sound. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Our trust has never
been misplaced. Our honour and our
liberties have been in safe keeping, he has
clearly demonstrated that he possessed those
qualities which were attributed to him, and
has proved that he was eminently fitted to fill
the high and important position in which we
then placed him. The position is a very high
and a very honourable one. We are perhaps
apt to forget that we as Members come here
not as individuals but as representatives of
the people of Northern Ireland. The Speaker
of this House when he is elected becomes not
only the representative but the embodiment
of the spirit of Parliament and the personification of the people. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Our honour and our dignity are his
honour and dignity. In what better hands
could we lay them than in my right hon.
Friend's?
He was the first Speaker of the first Parlianent of Northern Ireland. The annals of
our House will tell those who care to read
them how he filled that high office, and how
he led our inexperienced feet on the straight
and narrow Parliamentary path. That none
of us strayed from that path or trespassed
over much on the surrounding hard and fast
rules of Parliamentary procedure as laid
down by the Mother of Parliaments which
gave us birth, is due to his guidance, to his
patience, and also perhaps to the affection
and esteem in which we all hold him. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). For these reasons I
do not think his task. although possibly at
times a tedious one, can ever have been a
very difficult one. Yet I am convinced that
should difficulties arise. should the second
chapter of our Parliamentary history prove
less placid reading than the first, no one will
be found who would fill that position with
more dignity, more firmness, more tact and
discretion, more impartiality and greater
kindness towards those rew to Parliamentary
life than the right hon. and gallant Gentleman whom I now propose as Speaker. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: Mr. Dasent, I rise to second
the resolution to elect the Right Honourable Robert William Hugh O'Neill to
the high office of Speaker of this
House, proposed Dy the hon. Member
who has just sat down. As one of the Onposition, the first Opposition to take their
place in this House, an Opposition few in
number but destined to grow, I second the
election of the Right Honourable Hugh
O'Neill the more readily as I appreciate the
position he is likely to be in so far as we of
the Opposition are concerned. Being keen to
put our view point before this House and the
country, and being, perhaps, over zealous in
the performance of what we conceive to be
our public duty, I realize that he will have
a somewhat difficult task.
The qualifications of a Speaker ought to include tolerance, a judicial mind. unfailing
patience, and a desire to give fair play to all,
and last but not least charity-that charity
which St. Paul spoke of, that charity that
suffereth long and is kind. We realize that
a scion of that illustrious family that has
given Ulster not only the Red Hand with the
motto. "Lam Dhearg Abu," but the glorious
traditions of Owen Roe and Red Hugh
O'Neill is more likely to deal justice-evenhanded justice-to us than perhaps any other
member of the party to which he belongs.
It is the duty of the Speaker to act impartially towards every section of the House,
and it is because I believe and have no doubt
that the Right Honourable Robert William
Hugh O'Neill will act in that manner that I
have pleasure in seconding the resolution
proposed by the hon. Member for Derry.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The House then unanimously called Mr.
Hugh O'Neill to the Chair.
Mr. O'NEILL (who standing up in his
place, was received with general cheers):
I rise to submit myself to the will of the
House, and first let me thank the two hon.
Members who have in such very well chosen
language proposed and seconded my election
to the Chair of this House. I think we have
created two new Parliamentary precedents
to-day, for so far as I know, at any rate
within the ambit of the United Kingdom,
this is the first occasion on which the election
of a Speaker has ever been proposed by a
lady Member. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I think it is also the first occasion upon
which the seconding of such a motion has
ever been made in a maiden speech, and I
am sure we all most heartily congratulate the
hon. Gentleman the Member for North
Belfast (Mr. Kyle) upon the admirable way
in which he has to-day performed his difficult
Election of Speaker.
Election of Speaker.
14 APRIL 1925
duty. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The hon.
Lady, the Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester)
is, of course, already an experienced and very
able Parliamentarian, and her first speech
in this new Parliament is only what might
be expected from her on an occasion like
this. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
This House, as has been stated by the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle), will be
in many respects different from the House
which was recently dissolved. In that Parliament when it met four years ago very few
of its Members had any Parliamentary experience. In this one, on the contrary, the
great majority of the Members have Parliamentary experience and have by now considerable knowledge of the rules of this
House and of Parliament. If I may take this
opportunity of doing so, I should like to pay
the very warmest tribute that I can to the
splendid manner in which the Members of
the last House of Commons, to whatever
section they may have belonged, supported
me and brought about a state of affairs by
which the first Parliament of Northern Ireland will go down in history as having been
in every way an assembly which conducted
itself in accordance with the very highest
Parliamentary traditions. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
Now, as the hon. Member for North Belfast
(Mr. Kyle) stated, the office of Speaker contains very much more than the mere presiding over the deliberations of this House.
First of all, the Speaker is the guardian of
the rights and privileges of the House of
Commons, and although in these days that
may seem merely a method of speech, nevertheless in the long and checkered history in
which our Parliamentary institutions have
risen that aspect of the Speaker's office
played an important, indeed, I may say a
paramount, part, because in those long constitutional struggles across the water between
the House of Commons and the King, in
which the House of Commons was naturally
and properly victorious, the Speaker of the
House of Commons was the Gentleman upon
whom devolved the duty of asserting against
the Crown the rights and privileges of Parliament. In these days it is unlikely that
Parliament will be attacked from outside, but
should it be in any respect it will devolve
upon me, if I am elected to-day as your
Speaker, to defend the rights and privileges
of this House as they have been defended in
the past.
Members
we
of
are
We who are elected
Parliament should realise that
elected to a very different class of assembly
from the other electoral assemblies which
exist in our daily life, because this Parliament of Northern Ireland is supreme in
Northern Ireland upon all matters with regard to which it has power to legislate.
Parliament consists of His Majesty the King,
the Senate, and House of Commons of
Northern Ireland, and as such a Parliament
it is absolutely supreme.
The second duty of the Speaker is to take
the Chair in the proceedings of this House,
and, as has already been stated, his object
in the Chair should be, first of all, to see
that the proceedings of the House are conducted with a proper dignity and with a
proper sense of the responsibility of the
great trust which the people have reposed in us. Of course, the Speaker
must be absolutely impartial with regard to all matters within the province of
this House, and although, perhaps, in the
last House of Commons there was not that
natural, proper, and healthy clash of party
opinions which I have no doubt will exist to a
great extent in this one, still there were
occasions when possibly Members who were in
a minority at the time may have felt that impartiality in the Chair was of greatest service
to them-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)—and I
can assure the Members of this House, from
whatever quarter they have been elected or
whatever Party they represent, that they will
find in me, if I am elected to-day, one who
is determined that every Member shall have
equal rights and that there shall be no
partiality, favour, or affection in any
direction whatever. That is the foundation
of all Parliamentary procedure, and, as far
as I can do so, I will certainly ensure that
it is the foundation of the procedure in this
House.
There is one more aspect of the Speaker's
office to which I should like to refer, and that
is that he is there to help Members, and I do
hope that no hon. Members of this House,
whether they be old Members or whether
they be new Members, will hesitate to
come and see me in the Chair during the
ask
Sittings of the House and
me any
question with regard to which they have been
in doubt, because it is only by personal
conversation and through my trying to
smooth away their difficulties that they will
gradually learn the procedure of Parliament.
It is a complicated procedure. It has been
built up as the result of centuries of experience, and tradition, and precedent, and
it is impossible for any Member coming into
this House for the first time to be fully
acquainted with it. Consequently, I do hope
that all Members will have no hesitation
whatever in coming up and asking me to help
them, and I can assure them I shall always
do my very best to do so.
If this House elects me to-day as its
Speaker, I fully realise the trust which it
thereby imposes upon me. It really makes
me a trustee for itself, and I can only say
that it will be my earnest endeavour to carry
out that trust in such a way that this House
Election of Speaker.
Election of Speaker.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Speaker]
of Commons of Northern Ireland, as I
believe it has done in the past, will continue
to command the respect and the support of all
classes, parties, and creeds in our Province,
and that in those circumstances it will go on
as it has begun making history and making,
I believe, glorious history for the future of
our Province. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The House then having again unanimously called Mr. Hugh O'Neill to the
Chair, he was taken out of his place, and
conducted to the Chair by Mrs. Chichester
and Mr. Kyle.
Mr. SPEAKER-ELECT (standing on the
upper step): Before taking the Chair of this
House I wish to express to the House my
deep sense of the high honour it has conferred upon me by electing me once again as
its Speaker.
Mr. SPEAKER-ELECT sat down in the
Chair.
Then the Mace (which before lay under
the Table) was placed upon the Table by the
Serjeant-at-Arms (Brigadier-General H. G.
Young, C.I.E., D.S.O.)
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
Mr. Speaker-Elect, it is with the greatest
delight I rise to speak on behalf of all sections of the House and to congratulate you
most warmly upon being once more elected
our Speaker. I remember quite well four
years ago when you were asking for the support and the loyalty of the Members generally-that support which you are properly
entitled to in the Chair and that loyalty
which was so freely given-you also expressed
the earnest hope that in time you would
earn the affection of all Members here
present, and I can assure you that you have
amply earned the deepest affection of all of
us. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We are
proud of you as Speaker. You have added
lustre to the name that you bear and you
have also added lustre to Ulster and to
Ulster's new Parliament. You are to be
presented forthwith to his Grace the Governor, and I can only say that I sincerely
trust, whatever this new Parliament is to
bring forth, that you will find at the termination of it you have retained, and even
added to, the affection, the respect, the
esteem, and the loyalty of Members of all
sides of the House. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
This is not the time, I fully appreciate,
to say very much about what may take place
or may not take place, but I am quite sure
that Members on all sides will devote themselves to their Parliamentary work with that
close attention and with that desire to help
on the welfare of all classes of the community
that has distinguished those Members who
have served Ulster for the past four years.
In conclusion, I wish you, Mr. Speaker-Elect,
the utmost prosperity in the seat of which
you are so distinguished an occupant, and
trust that at the end of your term you will
carry away with you nothing but the fondest
remembrance of this the second administration of the Parliament of Northern Ireland.
Colonel WOODS: It is with the greatest
pleasure I rise to congratulate not you, Sir,
so much as the House on your election as
Speaker, because when I entered this House
I felt that I had practically no friends in
the House but yourself. And that feeling
was very strong when I got nothing but encouragement and help from you. I am
certain that the new Members elected to
this House will have in you as great a friend
as you have been to me. There is nothing in
anyone I have more admiration for than that
impartiality and sense of sportsmanship
which are entirely your own. It is with the
greatest pleasure I endorse the remarks of
the Prime Minister and congratulate the
Members of this House on your election.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: As a private Member for the last four years who has ploughed
a somewhat lonely furrow I would like to
join in congratulating you, Sir, and in endorsing most heartily the words that have
been used by the Prime Minister. He has
not used a word too much in praise of the
service you have rendered to this House.
It has been said that the ideal Speaker is a
man who is kind, helpful and tolerant. Those
of us who have sat in this House for the
past four years know that you possess those
three qualities in abundance. You have been
kind to Members, you have been tolerant
with some of us who have probably talked
too much, you have been very helpful to every
one of us, and we who are old Members can,
therefore, join most heartily in congratulating you to-day on having been elected for the
second time to this office. You have added
lustre and dignity to an office that is held in
high respect in every place where British
institutions are. You have been an ideal
Speaker, and I am sure that as long as you
are in the Chair this House will be the
sanctuary of Ulster's liberties. You have
not only the confidence of the Members of
this House but, I am sure, in carrying out
your task you also have their support.
The hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Kyle) in that model maiden speech which he
has just made referred you to Owen Roe
O'Neill, but I would warn you that I hope
you will pursue your own policy rather than
the policy of Owen Roe. Whatever policy
you do pursue I am sure you will have the
whole-hearted support of every hon. Member
in this House, no matter on which side he
sits. I hope that this Parliament will be a
pleasant and prosperous one not only for you
but for hon. Members.

Election of Speaker.

Mr. G. HENDERSON: Mr. Speaker-Elect, I
assume the privilege of saying a few words
of congratulation to you on your election to
your very high office, and of supporting what
has been so well said by the Prime Minister.
I feel sure that your name, your personality,
and your attainments will add adornment to
this House and will eminently qualify you for
filling your exalted position. I feel sure also
that in committing into your hands the
honour and dignity of this House the House
is committing them into safe hands, into wise
hands, and into experienced hands. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I just wish to say
also that, from what I know of you, I am
quite satisfied that in conducting the business of this House you will know no person,
you will be strictly impartial, there will be
the greatest sense of fair play, and every hon.
Member of the House will get the fullest opportunity, inside the rules of the House, for
expressing his opinions. Probably it is an
added pleasure that you are a County Antrim
man, representing County Antrim, and, while
they say that comparisons are odious, I think
it is not unfitting that the premier county
should supply the man for such a high position. I have great pleasure indeed in supporting what has been said in congratulating
you on your appointment to this very high
office, and I feel sure, as a Member who has
no Parliamentary experience, that if I have
to depend upon your kindness, your clemency,
or, indeed-to use the stronger word which
the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Kyle) has used-upon your charity, they will
be extended to me. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).

SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are returned for two or more places in any part of
Northern Ireland do make their Election for
which of the places they will serve, within
one week after it shall appear that there is
no question upon the Return for that place;
and if anything shall come in question touching the Return or Election of any Member,
he is to withdraw during the time the
matter is in debate; and that all Members
returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath been elected or returned a Member of this House or endeavoured so to be,
by Bribery, or any other corrupt practices,
this House will proceed with the utmost
severity against all such persons as shall
have been wilfully concerned in such Bribery
or other corrupt practices.
West Belfast and South Belfast.-
Lieutenant-Colonel Philip James Woods,
C.M.G., D.S.O., returned as a Member for
West Belfast and South Belfast, stated that
he elected to sit for West Belfast.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath been tampering with any
Witness in respect of his evidence to be given
to this House, or any Committee thereof,
or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured
to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence, the same is declared
to be a high crime or misdemeanour; and
this House will proceed with the utmost
severity against such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath given false evidence in any case
before this House, or any Committee thereof,
this House will proceed with the utmost
severity against such offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary do take care that,
during the Session of Parliament, the passages through the streets leading to this
House be kept free and open, and that no
obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members to and from this House,
and that no disorder be allowed in the precincts of or in the passages leading to this
House, during the Sitting of Parliament,
and that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant-at-Arms
attending this House do communicate this
Order to the Commissioner of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS AND RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings and
Records of this House be printed, being first
perused by Mr. Speaker; and that he do
appoint the printing thereof; and that no
person but such as he shall appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered: That a Committee of Privileges
be appointed.

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report to the
House that the House has this day attended
in the Senate to hear the Speech of his
Grace, the Governor, on behalf of the
King's Speech.
Debate on Address.
15 APRIL 1925
Crown, to both Houses of Parliament; of
which I have for greater accuracy obtained
a copy. The speech is as follows:-
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I feel confident that the new Parliament
now inaugurated will conduct with wisdom
and moderation the important matters entrusted to its control.
My Government recognises that the
most important and urgent subjects with
which it is faced are the state of our
Industries and the problem of Unemployment. Every effort will be made to encourage agriculture, to aid industry and
commerce through the operation of the
Loans Guarantee Acts and, in association
with Local Authorities, through schemes
of public utility, to find useful employment for our people.
You will be asked to authorise the provision of seed potatoes in certain districts
where necessitous circumstances prevail.
A Bill will be introduced this Session
continuing the principle of the Rent Restriction Act, but amending it in certain
directions.
A Bill will be laid before you to provide
for the better administration of the
Drainage Acts. A Committee established
to examine this subject has made suggestions, which will be embodied in the
Bill, investing Local Authorities with
certain powers and providing more elastic
machinery to cope with the problem of
the destructive flooding of our agricultural
lands in various districts For more than
a century this has exercised the minds of
the best engineers and the phenomenal
rainfall of the last three years has emphasised the urgency of seeking some
palliative.
A Bill will be introduced to make provision for the improvement of mining
facilities.
A Bill will be laid before you to make
provision for granting moderate Compassionate Pensions or Gratuities to
persons, or the widows and children of
persons who have rendered distinguished
service in the field of science, literature
or the arts, or who have rendered exceptionally meritorious service in a public
capacity.
Amongst other measures which will
engage your attention are a Bill dealing
with the Preservation of Ancient Monuments, a Bill to establish a Pharmaceutical Society for Northern Ireland, a Bill to
prevent the sale in our State of inferior
brands of condensed and dried milk, and
a Jury Bill, which is being prepared in
pursuance of the findings drawn up by the
recent Commission.
Members of the House of Commons.
Estimates for the public services will be
laid before you in due course. I am glad
to learn that the general financial position
is sound, but nevertheless it is recognised
that economical administration is
essential for the well-being of Northern Ireland, and every effort will be made to reduce public expenditure to the lowest
possible limit consistent with efficiency.
Members of the Senate and House
of Commons.
My Ministers recognising the importtance of the provision of electric power in
the industrial areas of Northern Ireland,
are giving this question close attention.
They are also giving careful consideration
to the valuable recommendations of the
Development Commission on afforestation,
harbours and other matters.
Your labours upon these and all other
matters I humbly commend to the blessing of Almighty God.
Debate on the Address.
Dr. MORRISON (in morning dress): I beg
to move
"That an humble Address be presented
to His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland, as followeth :--
Your Grace,
We. His Majesty's most dutiful and loyal
Subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland
in Parliament assembled, beg leave to offer
our humble thanks to your Grace for the
Speech which your Grace has addressed to
both Houses of Parliament."
The policy of the Government as outlined
in the Speech is wise, and I think non contentious. Agricultural and industrial
depression with the accompanying sequelæ
of unemployment and a heavy load of taxation
entailing great suffering and poverty to
many of our people are specially noted, and
helpful action and sympathetic consideration
are promised to meet these abnormal conditions. The provision of seed potatoes for
necessitous districts, and the continuance of
the Rent Restriction Act, redress for the
grievances of Jurors, moderate pensions for
outstanding individuals or their dependants,
the total annual sum to be fixed by this
House, and a Drainage Bill are subjects that
all of us will think necessary and useful. We
are glad to have a promise of economical
administration and an effort to reduce ex-
Debate on Address.
Debate on Address.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
.
[Dr. Morrison.]
penditure to the lowest limit consistent with
efficiency. This will gladden the heart of
every rate-payer.
I confess to a dread of the cost, and from
past experience a doubt as to the utility
of costly schemes of drainage, and for
my own part I hope the Government will
go slowly in these cases; but an enabling
Bill for County Councils and loans at a low
rate of interest, repayment to be a charge
on the rates of those benefited, would, I
think, be sufficient in these days of financial
stringency. The field of action mentioned
in the Speech covers many important subjects that will be fully discussed when the
Bills come before the House, but I am certain we are going on lines that will satisfy
the public.
It is difficult to face the conditions in the
agricultural interests to-day without a feeling of extreme depression. The constant
rain for two seasons has practically crippled
the farmers. This season has opened badly,
the land is again saturated with water and
spring work cannot be done in the fields,
the agricultural labourer has also suffered
severely, and I trust that farmers will avail
themselves heartily of the measures introduced by the Ministry for the improvement
of Agricultural Development-to the end that
we may cope successfully with foreign
competition. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I stress the first paragraph in His Grace
the Governor's speech "I feel confident that
the new Parliament now inaugurated will
conduct with wisdom and moderation the im
portant matters committed to its control."
I am sure everyone in this House echoes that
wish.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I detest
bitterness and abuse, in the act, in the
spirit, in the consequences, and most of all
in the example. There has been too much of
it in Ireland North and South. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The strongest force in our
social and national life is working, it may be
slowly but steadily, on these lines of wisdom
and moderation. It has always been so.
You see it in primitive man, the family growing into the tribe or clan, the tribe or clan
growing into the race or nation, on lines of
wisdom and moderation.
In the slow but certain process of evolution Great Britain emerges from struggling
factions into a harmonious, homogeneous island, through wisdom and moderation. This
Island Empire plants colonies and dominions,
and commonwealths, all over the world, and
by wisdom and moderation nurses them into
prosperous states who are daughters in their
mother's house, while mistresses in their own.
The dominating force in this phenomenon,
that obliterates distance, and divisions of
race, and religion, and colour and class, is
community of interests, mutual advantage,
in a word, national well-being. In no part
of His Majesty's dominions is this bond so
obviously compelling as in the relations of
Ireland to the Empire, and between Northern Ireland and the Free State. The Prime
Minister has on more than one occasion defined our relation to the Free State. Invariably he has used the language of wisdom
and moderation and never once did I hear an
offensive remark in any speech. He is recognised as a statesman with reasonable, moderate views who although always firm, does
not make the mistake of being insulting or
offensive. My own opinion is if we follow
the example of the Prime Minister we can
face the future with an easy mind, in the
sure and certain hope that if we earnestly
try-in the wise words of His Grace the
Governor-with wisdom and moderation, we
shall solve all the difficulties that lie before us
and bring contentment and prosperity to
all sections of our people. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Mr. ELLIOTT (in morning dress): I rise
to second the Motion which has been proposed by my hon. Friend the Member for the
University (Dr. Morrison). In doing so may
I as one altogether unaccustomed to Parliamentary procedure crave the indulgence of
this Honourable House-an indulgence which
I believe has never been denied to any
Member, especially to one who like myself
addresses the House for the first time? The
honour which has been conferred on me
I do not take as altogether a personal one,
but rather as a compliment to the Border
Counties of Fermanagh and Tyrone which
I have the honour to represent. The recent
visit of the Prime Minister to these Border
Counties was very much appreciated by the
loyal inhabitants residing there, bringing to
them as it did the reassuring message of the
loyal co-operation and support of the Prime
Minister and Government of Northern
Ireland in defence of any portion of their
territory in danger of being detached from
the jurisdiction of Northern Ireland and included in the Irish Free State. These
sentiments have been re-echoed by the
loyalists of these two counties who have returned my three Colleagues and myself as
their representatives, pledged as the Prime
Minister is to "not an inch," with very much
increased figures over the figures of the
General Election for Northern Ireland in
1921. If the Boundary Commission is still in
existence I hope it will take full cognisance
of these facts, because the election which has
just taken place was altogether a Boundary
election.
As agriculture is the staple industry of
Northern Ireland I am glad to see that in the
Gracions Speech delivered from the Throne
a very prominent place has been given to it,
Debate on Address.
Debate on Address.

15 APRIL 1925
and that legislation for its encouragement is
promised. No person except some one like
myself closely associated with and deeply
interested in agriculture can have any idea of
the depression that exists throughout the
entire farming community at the present
time. This is no doubt due in a great
measure to the continual rain of the past
two seasons, and other circumstances over
which perhaps the Government of Northern
Ireland had little or no control, and while
recognising the fact that something has
already been done to help agriculture,
particularly the grant in relief of rates on
hope the Governagricultural land, which I
ment will be able to make a permanent one,
I trust any legislation that may be effected
during the present Parliament will be such
as will be shorn to a great extent of the
usual officialdom and proverbial red tape,
and that it will not be necessary to employ
an additional number of Inspectors and
other officials to carry it out. What we want
is something practical to help and encourage
the farmers. I think something practical
might be done along the lines of having the
railway and steamboat rates reduced to a
level that would enable Irish farmers to put
their produce on the English and Scottish
markets as cheaply as the German, Dutch and
Danish farmers can.
It is all very well to tell the farmers to
plant immune varieties of potatoes and even
get their hens to lay bigger eggs, but what
is the use of this all if we cannot help them
to find a market for their produce at a price
that will at least show a reasonable return
on the amount of money expended in production? Might I suggest to my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Agriculture that he
should gather around him from the different
counties of Northern Ireland a number of
practical, not theoretical, farmers who know
where the shoe pinches and who would, I
think, be able to guide and act as an
advisory council to him so that legislation
dealing with this important industry might
be such as would stimulate and encourage
the farmers throughout the length
breadth of Northern Ireland. The Governand
ment propose to give seed potatoes in
necessitous cases, I hope they will also see
their way to give seed oats where required.
I would also like to see the Government
give their subsidy for the building of houses
to agriculturists as well as to town dwellers.
It is a rather unfair disadvantage to the
farmer that he is debarred from receiving
the Government subsidy simply because he
is not a townsman. As the agricultural
labourer is an important asset to this industry I hope the Government will encourage
rural district councils to build labourers'
cottages where required, and also urban
councils in provincial towns to build more
Better
houses for the industrial workers.
houses make better workmen. We cannot
expect our workers, either agricultural or
industrial, to give of their best unless their
housing conditions are very much improved.
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I am glad to see that
drainage is to be dealt with during the
present Parliament. No person could travel
through the counties of Northern Ireland
without seeing the immediate necessity for
a very comprehensive drainage scheme or
schemes. Thousands of acres of our best
agricultural lands have been almost continually under floods for the past twelve
months and thousands of pounds worth of
crops have been lost by the farmers of
Northern Ireland owing to flooding. I hope
that something immediate may be done to
remedy this and that some schemes may be
put in hands during the present summer
season with this end in view.
Unemployment is, I am sorry to say, still
very prevalent. I recognise that the Government of Northern Ireland have already done
a great deal to relieve unemployment. My
right hon. Friend the Minister of Labour
has never been known to turn a deaf ear to
any genuine scheme put before him in this
direction and I have no reason to think he
will be less sympathetic during the life of
the present Parliament. Perhaps the proposed drainage legislation will give my right
hon. Friend an opportunity of still further
helping in this direction. As one of the
representatives for the constituency of Fermanagh and Tyrone in which the coalfields
of Northern Ireland are situated I welcome
any legislation that would stimulate an industry which has already done a great deal
both to help our industries and give employment, and I am glad to bear testimony to
the good work already done by Sir Samuel
Kelly, himself an Ulsterman-(hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-in developing the mining industry.
It is also encouraging to me and it will
be to those whom I represent in this House
to know that a Jury Bill is shortly to be
introduced. This Bill will, I hope, remove
the grievances from which jury men and
women have suffered, and I hope that due
provision will be made in that Bill for the
payment of travelling and reasonable hotel
expenses to those who are called to serve in
the capacity of jury men. After all, it is
only reasonable that any man called to serve
his country as a jury man should be paid his
out-of-pocket expenses, seeing that his own
business has to be neglected while he is so
serving. Proper provision should also be
made in all our Court Houses for the comfort of jury men. In too many of them we
find there is not even standing room for
the jurors.

Debate on Address.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Elliott]
There are a number of other Bills outlined in the Gracious Speech from the Throne
which I need not here enumerate but which
I hope will be for the good of the people of
Northern Ireland. Perhaps the paragraph
in the Gracious Speech dealing with economy
will find most acceptance with our people.
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I am glad to see that in
every Government department the strictest
economy is to be enforced. I have heard it
stated over and over again that all our Government departments are already very much
over-staffed with a very much over-paid and
a very much under-worked lot of officials.
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Mr. ELLIOTT: It is re-assuring to hear
that the Government intends to apply the
"Geddes axe" which will if carried out

the taxpayers at ease.
In conclusion, may I say that I hope when
the present Parliament comes to be dissolved
we may all be able to look back at our record
of work done with satisfaction and that we
may have the gratification of knowing that
we have at least done something to make
Northern Ireland one of the brightest spots
in the King's Dominions? (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
The PRIME MINISTER: It is my pleasing duty, in the first place, to tender my
personal, and I am sure our collective congratulations to the mover and seconder who
have just sat down. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Of course our old friend the hon.
Member for the University (Dr. Morrison)
is a skilled hand at debate and has had considerable Parliamentary experience, and we
always listen to his words of wisdom with
that attention which they deserve. He will,
perhaps, pardon me if under the circumstances
meed
my
of praise is chiefly
bestowed upon the new hon. Member (Mr.
Elliott) who has broken the ice for the first
time to-day, and who has in a most admirable, concise, and well-chosen speech carried
out the duties of seconder in a way which
reflects the greatest credit upon himself personally and the county from which he comes.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) He is evidently of Tyrone stock, because my experience of that county is that its representatives
in this House are never weary and never
backward in opening their mouths as wide as
possible where the public purse is concerned,
and he has on this occasion I think risen to
the very best heights in that regard. However, I can assure him that the Government's
duty will be to exercise the same caution in
balancing such financial means as are at our
disposal between the claims of the great commercial centres of Ulster and the still greater
claims of the agricultural community. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) As his experience
in this House becomes longer and wider he
will recognise that there is a criss-cross of
crying out, on the one hand, for strict
economy and, on the other hand, there are
constant and ever-recurring deputations to
the Government asking them not so much to
economise as to meet their particular claims
which in their view are in the forefront of
the important points that have to be dealt
with in Ulster. I can assure the House that
we will do our very utmost in that respect to
maintain the scales evenly between town and
country, so that the whole area of Northern
Ireland may benefit to the greatest possible
extent from the limited financial resources to
our hand.
Before I venture upon a very few remarks
I would like to pay a tribute to the late Mr.
McKeown (Hon. Members: Hear, hear)--who
was so able and so respected an hon. Member
of this House. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I think he is the third Member whom we
have lost since we were established in 1921,
and I can only say that his association with
myself endeared him to me. It was a case
of affection right through the period for
which he undertook the work of Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministries of Commerce
and Education. I am sure those hon. Members who served during the same period will
always remember his sterling worth, his
open, patent honesty, his indefatigable
zeal on behalf of his country, and the
able manner in which he discharged
his Departmental duties. We regret his
passing extremely. I was more grieved
than I can say to know that at the
very time when he was on his death bed there
were reports-it is true they were across the
Channel-that he had parted from the Government because of some difference of opinion
over the Education Act. I think that has
been effectively cleared up. To the very last
he was with us in sentiment, he was with
us to the letter in regard to every step that
was taken in connection with that Measure.
I can only say that this House pays him
tribute, a tribute that he deserves as an hon.
Member who discharged his duties in a most
effective way. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I would like to preface my further remarks
by emphasising what has fallen from the
hon. Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone
(Mr. Elliott) that the cause of the election
was the Border question. I held the election
as all who are present will realise, because I
felt convinced that, although in the year 1921
the people of the Border counties had almost
exhausted themselves in showing their desire
to remain in Northern Ireland and not to be
transferred to the Free State, it was possible
for them to do still better, and that that

part of the directions to the Boundary Commission relating to the ascertaining of the
wishes of the people could be supplied by
the people themselves through an election
constitutionally for this House better than
in any other manner. I take no credit for
the fact that I was fully justified in asking
for a response to that appeal. The men on
the Border played the most manly part--
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear) and I think
that even abroad it has not been thoroughly
understood how satisfactory the result has
been from the position of Northern Ireland.
In 1921 the Loyalist figures-that is those
voting to remain in Northern Ireland-were
149,666. In 1925, the election which is just
over, it mounted up to 152,089. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I am referring of course
to the Border counties and the City of Derry.
The Republican and Nationalist figures in
1921 were 113,334 and at the last election
103,573-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-a reduction apparently of the desire of the Republicans and Nationalists to go into the
Free State of 48,516. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The Loyalist majority, therefore, was
increased during the four years 1921-1925 by
12.184, and I hold that that is conclusive evidence for the Border Commission that those
counties have no desire to break their connection with this Parliamentary institution,
or with Great Britain and the Empire.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
My next words will be with regard to some
of those questions that were raised by hon.
Members during the election and by certain
hon. Members since the election. I hope at
this starting off point of the new adminis
tration I am not going to say one provocative
word if it can be avoided. I would like to
see our proceedings started with new Members in our midst in such a way as will augur
well for the future, and that we should all
put ourselves in the position of representatives of the people desirous of doing our
best for them. Hon. Members attacked the
Government because we paid hon. Members
salaries. This is a democratic community.
In practically every part of the world-certainly
every part of the world that
I know of-wherever there is a
Parliamentary institution it is now
the custom that Members should be
paid. If only those who are wealthy enough
to give their time, to give their means to
represent their constituencies in an assembly
of this sort, if only they were qualified to
sit in this House everybody would instantly
recognise that we did not represent the
democracy of Ulster. (Hon Members: hear,
hear.) Therefore, I think that the modest
sum which is granted annually, not in the
form of a salary but in the form of meeting
the expenses to which hon. Members are
put, is a very wise and judicious move on
the part not alone of the Goevrnment but of
The second point to which I would like to
refer is the charge that there are too many
members of the Government here, that is
to say that there is a larger number of
Ministers than is requisite and necessary for
a small state like Ulster. We have gone
through all this before. The Parliament of
Northern Ireland was thrown on us against
our own desire. but having accepted the
responsibility of governing Ulster we had
to place our house in such order that
we could carry on the various departments in
the manner in which Ulster demanded that
they should be carried on, in practically the
same way in which the Imperial Parliament
is carried on in order that there should be
no criticism of any of the Departments as to
their work. The charge is made that we have
too many. Out of curiosity I took up the
figures dealing with New Zealand this morning. Our estimated population in 1922 was
1,284,000. The population of New Zealand.
taking the census of 1921, was 1,320,000-almost analagous. Our paid Ministers are six
in number. In New Zealand they are twelve
in number. Our paid Under-Secretaries are
six in number, and in New Zealand they are
something like thirty-eight, although I am
not quite certain, and I have not had time
to find out, whether those thirty-eight are
necessarily Members of Parliament or not-
I rather fancy they are not. However, the
fact remains that we have here to deal
only with those actually in the Cabinetexactly half the number that there are in
New Zealand.

very fact that railways are not entirely

does
not suit to shift on immediately to another, but in case

state this, if independent testimony is required that in the course of the deliberations

sufficient to allay any suspicion or feeling
that there may be in the country.
I think it was the hon. Member opposite
(Mr. Thomas Henderson) who said that I
would find him buzzing round my head like
a busy bee. As a matter of fact the busy
bees have been buzzing round the heads of
six gentlemen, Under-Secretaries in the
Government and not round my head, and I
want to make it perfectly plain that those
Under-Secretaries are necessary, and I will
tell you why. Outside the question of
Ministers' responsibility, there is
an
enormous amount of work attached to each
office. I am not going through any of the
offices in detail. I take them all. I know
that those gentlemen have received their
salaries, and ought to have earned the thanks
of Ulster for the way in which they have
discharged their duties. But is it
to be said that Members in this
House are not to be trained up
in order to help Ulster in future years?
Are we merely to have Ministers who come
and go? Are we to have it said that a
Minister, when he is off for a month's
holiday, or it may be longer, has no one to
leave in his place who understands the
Department? Are we to have it said that
because he is ill for a month, or it may be
two months, there is no one in the House
who understands the Department and can
answer for him? Is it to be said when one
wants to put his hand upon a new Minister
for any reason that one is not able to pick

the administrative duties attached to the
office in which he has served as Parliamentary Secretary? No, Sir. I am going to
stick up for the Parliamentary Secretaries.
I think they are a necessary institution in this
House, and I think they have done their
work remarkably well. I have seen my hon.
Friend here (Mr. Gordon) going to one place
and another, explaining the Unemployment
Insurance Acts, and encouraging the people
with regard to the Local Employment Committees. I have seen him travelling about,
I have heard him speaking in this House with
an intimate knowledge of everything connected with Unemployment Insurance and
other labour questions, and I would say this
House would suffer if we had to go back to
the bad old system of having government in
Ulster by one Home Secretary or one Chief
Secretary or whatever you care to call him,
and being in reality dependent not upon Ministers and Under-Secretaries, but dependent
entirely upon the officials who run the various Departments. I remember very well indeed in the Imperial House when it was
suggested to one of the Ministers that the
gallery occupied by the various heads of Departments on important nights for debate
should be given up to the public because
they would much prefer to see the Ministers
thoroughly understanding their own jobs and
not always having to run to and fro to what
is called "Under the Gallery," in order to get
this piece of information, or that piece of
information, or guidance as to what
steps they should take. I think we are very
modest in asking the House to supply us with
six of these gentlemen to help us along in the
arduous duty we have to perform. I think
we are moderate, and I think they are
necessary for the good conduct of the Government.

below what is imposed by the Chancellor of
the Exchequer in Great Britain, because ]
intend to stick by the pledge to the working
classes of this country that any balance
that we have would be placed upon the Estimates with a view to finding suitable work
for those who are walking our streets unemployed.
Now I made a somewhat tedious and dull
speech a short time ago on the subject of
economy, and I would just like to amplify

misconception as to what economy in the
Government means. We have not yet
stabilised our financial relations with Great
Britain. That is one of the anxieties that we
are still faced with.

Debate on Address.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
The PRIME MINISTER: Let us take the
paper that I have just quoted as being a standard for our Parliamentary and Government
institutions, approved of by the British
Government as satisfactory, and we
materially reduce the sum. I do not object to
materially reducing it, but I do object to reducing it at the cost of efficiency. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Efficiency must come
first. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I believe
we have got efficiency, but I want the House
to understand that if the cost is reduced
below what it is at the present time and
efficiency imperilled-my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Pollock) will be able to tell you better
than I can--I am not certain that that saving
will not revert to the British Government
through having to go in increased contributions from Northern Ireland to their
Treasury and will not be available for distribution in another form inside the Six
Counties area. Therefore, I hope that it will
be clear to hon. Members, that although
charges are easy to throw out carelessly, we
want to get an equilibrium that will be recognised for all time-not merely for a short
period such as is suggested by the British
Government-as the standard year of expenditure on which Ulster may calculate and
on which her contributions are to be based.
If we get that eventually stabilised out of
the British Government, then we will be in
a position to see exactly where we stand with
regard to all the services we have to meet
in Northern Ireland.
There is no use my hiding from this House
the fact that our first and most serious consideration is the Unemployment Insurance
Fund. That hangs round our neck. I do not
regret for one moment the Government's
courageous and bold attitude towards carrying on and seeing that our poor fellows in
the streets are treated on level terms
with those in Great Britain. I am sure
there is not a Member of this House who
regrets the risk that we ran in carrying that
on although we did discover very rapidly
that we were an uneconomic unit so far as
unemployment insurance is concerned. I can
only say that one of the greatest wonders to
me in my Parliamentary career was that when
the late Labour Government was in power
in England and was approached by my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) and by myself to
rectify what was a provable injustice to trade
unionists in the city of Belfast and in Ulster
generally, and when we begged and implored
them to make that injustice right they did
not take a step to do it.
Mr. KYLE: What was the injustice?
The PRIME MINISTER: The injustice was
that when Northern Ireland was granted
this Parliament and the Unemployment
Insurance Fund was divided between Great
Britain and Northern Ireland we were given
over the Fund in a state which must
have been known to the authorities on the
other side to be uneconomic and unable by
the same contributions from the working
classes to give the same benefits or to be able
in any reasonable time whatever to show a
balance on the right side. That was the injustice. This injustice was pointed out to the
Minister of Labour for the late Labour
Government, to the Prime Minister, to
the Chancellor of the Exchequer and to the
Financial Secretary to the Treasury in the
clearest possible manner, and I did think that
the Labour Government then in power would
have seen to it that we were made right in this
matter. However, I am not unhopeful that
we may be able yet to come to some understanding with the British Government whereby the two things that should never have been
separated may be once more united. Even if
we accept the responsibility on our shoulders
of the debt that has been in the meantime
piling up against us, I believe taking a long
view for the working classes and for the
credit of our community it would be better
to do that than to carry on in the way we
are doing to-day with the certainty that
sooner or later we are bound to ask them
either to pay a higher contribution for the
same benefits or else to pay the same contribution and accept less benefits. As I have
said in this House before when that day
comes I will step out of this Chair. I always
said that when Ulster accepted Home Rule
for herself she did so on the understanding
that the standard of living of the peoplenot the living of the classes only but the
living of all the people inside our domainshould be in no way lessened from the
standard maintained in Great Britain, and
that we are justly entitled to have this very
serious matter made right. I am not unhopeful. My right hon. Friends are working
away as usual like giants on behalf of the
working classes.
It will have been observed by the Manifesto
that I issued to the Loyalists of the Province
that the aim of the Government is to have
as little as possible of what I shall call provocative or contentious legislation during
this administration. I want the House and I
with
want the Government to get on
business. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I
want the people to settle down and do all
they can to develop the resources that lie at
their hands. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The Government want to do everything in
their power to help them, and to help every
lame dog over the stile. My hon. Friend who
seconded the Address (Mr. Elliott) covered
Along
a great deal of the ground.
that
ground we hope to go. We hope to be able to
help all these things, some more, some less.
Debate on Address.
Debate on Address.
15 APRIL 1925
The only limit to our generosity is our purse.
It is no use holding out all sorts of promises
to the people. We want to deal with hard
facts and say we have so much money in our
pockets for the coming year, and we propose
to place before the House how that money can
best be spent and let it be criticised. That
is the reason why we are anxious to do away
as much as possible with contentious legislation so that we can get on with the development of our Province.
It is only honest for me in the presence of
the new Members to say, so that there shall
be no misunderstanding in the future, that so
far as the Government is concerned and as
far as I am concerned the question of going
into the Free State, the question of Bolshevism, Communism, and Socialism, or the
question of altering the Education Act except
with the proviso I mentioned in my manifesto, or of opening the public houses on
Sunday, or a renewal of the bonafide traveller-these, I wish to say in this House, are
outside practical politics. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I stand by those statements and
I intend to stand by them. We are a united
Cabinet and a united Government. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I would like to say
on the other hand that if the new Members
in this House will lend to its debates useful
contributions along the lines of how best they
can help the people, how they can ameliorate
the sufferings of the working classes during
these terribly hard times, what can be done
to assist the people in the country, a matter
which has become a burning question, what
can be done to help the tenant farmers who
are in great difficulties with regard to their
crops, many of which were destroyed, and
who have practically nowhere to turn to to
make good what occurred during the past
two years-with regard to any of these matters that are deep down in the hearts of the
people I say to the Members who will contribute to assist us in the solution of these
weighty matters that they will be doing a
service to their country, and that service to
their country we expect and demand. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. KYLE: I would like to add my congratulations to the proposer and seconder of
the motion before the House, particularly to
the seconder on the very wide range of subjects which he covered. I hope I may crave
the indulgence of the House if I may transgress any established Parliamentary rules in
the carrying on of this debate. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) In his Grace's Speech the
state of our industries is mentioned. One
would have expected that a spokesman on
behalf of the Government would have told
us what they intend to do in order to try
and get back the trade that we have lost. I
refer to our engineering and shipbuilding
trades. One would have expected also something to be said in regard to the deplorable
condition of the linen trade in which I am
especially interested. One would have expected that some attempt at least would have
been made to reduce the bank rate in Northern Ireland to an equal basis to the bank
rate in London to enable some of our business men who may have overdrafts-and I
understand that is the position of a great
many of them to-day (Hon. Members: Hear,
hearto lessen their burden and also enable
them to carry on their industry on more successful lines than they can at the present
time. They suffer from the fact that the
bank rate in Northern Ireland is one per
cent. higher than on the other side. Now
that we have got a Government with an Opposition we hope we shall get some of the
advantages of helping capital in our Northern province. I think that this problem
is linked up to a very large degree
with the problem of unemployment, which
will be dealt with in a special Amendment
from these Benches moved by one of my
colleagues. I think most persons will agree
that the problem of the bank rate has something at least to do with the question of
unemployment, and it deserves the very
serious consideration of the Government. I

I interrupted the Prime Minister during
his speech to know why he said the Labour
Government had treated our people here
badly. Our Government here took up office
in 1921. The Labour Government in Great
Britain was not then in power; it did not
come into power until November, 1923. It
was in office eight months with a minority,
and it governed the British Empire better
than any other Administration, Liberal or
Tory, that has ever sat in the British House
of Commons, and it is not good enough to
blame the Labour Government for something for which a Conservative Government
or a Coalition Government were responsible.
Who fixed the figure of £7,920,000 for Ulster?
It was not the Labour Government. No, it
was the friends of hon. Members who sit
opposite who fixed that figure. We know
now, we knew then that such an exorbitant
figure could not be paid, and it will not be
paid, I hope.
The Imperial Minister of Labour in reply
to a question the other day said that the
Government-the present Conservative Government-were not prepared to do the
things that our Prime Minister has blamed
the Labour Government for not doing when
they were in office. I just wanted to correct
him as far as that is concerned, and I think
it is necessary and desirable that it should
be done at the earliest possible moment.
I was very pleased to hear the hon. Member
for Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr. Elliott)

Although I represent North Belfast I do not

of workpeople-

Colonel WOODS: I wish with the greatest
possible pleasure to congratulate the hon.
Member for the University (Dr. Morrison)
on the way in which he moved this Address,
and the hon. Member for Fermanagh and
Tyrone (Mr. Elliott) on the very excellent

speeches we have heard to-day rather raise

been. I would like to point out that, so far
as my information goes, the hon. Member for
Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Elliott) in common with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr.
Kyle) have not quite understood the Loans
Guarantee Act. As such I think it has not
been advertised sufficiently, and, therefore,
has not been taken advantage of to the extent it should have been. If it were more
widely known it would be of a great deal more
use to the community.
The hon. Member for Fermanagh and
Tyrone (Mr. Elliott) also made a remark
regarding Sir Samuel Kelly and the coalmining at Coalisland. I would like to ask
the Government to bring their influence to
bear on the same gentleman to have his ships
built in Belfast instead of in Glasgow or
elsewhere.
I am sorry the Prime Minister has gone
because he referred in his speech, I think indirectly, to some things that might have been
said during the election campaign. He called
it a Border election. I can assure him and
this House that, so far as the Border is concerned, the independent Unionists stand
four square with the Prime Minister on that
question. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) There
cannot be any doubt about that. Then again
he referred to the salaries of hon. Members of
this House. It was salaries I think that were
quoted from my platform and not expenses.
The salaries referred to of course meant those
mainly paid to gentlemen holding more or
less sinecure appointments at such a rate
that, when worked out by people who care
for figures more than the hon. Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Kyle), came to something
like £5 per minute in some cases for working
time. That, of course, is ridiculous, and I
consider that gentlemen holding what should
be honorary positions in this House should
accept a small honorarium, or you could call
it slightly heavier expenses than the ordinary
Member. That they should be paid an
exorbitant figure, at the same rate as they are
paid in the Imperial House, is rather ridiculous for the size of this House where there
are only 52 hon. Members as against 600 odd.

I may say that I know of at least one case
where the right hon. Gentleman, a Minister
of the Government, returned his emoluments,
I believe. I think I have that on pretty good
authority, and he deserves credit, and I hope
his example will be followed by various others
who can do so.
The Prime Minister referred to the independent Unionists in particular as disturbing
public opinion. I do not know that I need
say anything to justify myself as far
as that is concerned, because I was a
sitting Member of this House, and deliberate opposition was offered to me by
the Government although they knew
I was a Unionist. That was not disturbing
public opinion on my part; it lies entirely at
the door of the Government themselves. If
they wish to disturb public opinion they are
quite welcome to do so. I am sorry that
the Prime Minister referred to the unemployed persons who might take over the jobs
of Parliamentary Secretaries in this House.
He referred to them as being unemployed,
possibly with some discredit to themselves.
That was the impression I gained. Well,
I do not think that the Prime Minister
should kick the poor lame dog that he
referred to, but rather that he should help
him over the stile. I would like to refer also
to his remarks to the effect that the finances
of Ulster are not stabilised yet, and that the
matter is occasioning him very great anxiety.
If that is the case, and if the real meaning
of the Government is to enforce economy in
the administration of this State, may I ask
why a gentleman was put at the head of the
Ministry of Finance who could not possibly
have any experience of financial matters, and
why his particular work is passed on to one
of the permanent staff? When the gentleman
of the permanent staff objected, I suppose,
his salary was raised by £400, while the
gentleman who was put into the job of head
of the Civil Service is paid at the same rate
as the gentleman who vacated the office.
Mr. POLLOCK: No, sir.
Colonel WOODS: I stand corrected, if
that is not so, but that is the understanding
outside. May I pay a tribute to the Minister
of Labour, to whom I spoke over a year ago
regarding the risk of the Unemployment
Fund not being met by the British Government. I know that he was trying then, and
trying very strenuously, to have the matter
adjusted, and I am only sorry to think that
he has not succeeded. I agree very largely
with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr.
Kyle) regarding the bank rate in Belfast.
I do not understand why it should not be
at the same rate as in Britain. On the
Rent Restriction Act, of course, he was
talking absolute sense; there is not a fault
to be found with what he said. I congratulate him most heartily upon what he
did say on that subject, but he forgot to
mention that we could do with a little off
the Entertainment Tax, of which we here
pay 25 per cent. more than is paid in England. If these things are all done I think
that the Government can pat themselves on
the back, and really go to the people with
open minds and honest hearts. Perhaps
they will not be accused the next time of
jobbery, if they carry out these things. I
hope not.

More important perhaps than the King's

or whether there is not in a
fashion, without dragging in other

Drainage, and things of that sort. I am not

The second point I would like to put to the
Minister is in regard to drainage. We have
been told this Government was going to drain
the country dry-I do not mean in the liquor

this century-old question of flooding in

I am also keenly interested to know something

With regard to compassionate pensions, I

I do hope that the opening words of

splendid spirit in which to enter on the

speech of the Prime Minister, who has not

followers by indulging in abusive language
He has not used a single provocative word,

possibly could, if returned, to try to reduce
this unemployment. Therefore, I hold it
is the duty of every Member of the House
to do all he possibly can to assist the
Government, because all the brains of the
House are not possessed by the members of
the Government. Let us try and assist the
Government to grapple with this great and
growing problem.
We have heard and read a great deal lately
about the question of expenditure. I rather
fancy that some of the critics on this question
are very sore not because there is a great deal
of expenditure in Northern Ireland-I am
afraid it is rather a personal matter with
Some of them because they feel that they are
not in office. We cannot all be Cabinet
Ministers, and we ought to try as far as
possible to assist the Government in doing
the right thing. If we see Cabinet Ministers
making mistakes we ought to point out those
mistakes, and I am sure they will not be beyond taking advice from hon. Members.
I would like to take this opportunity of
congratulating the Financial Secretary (Mr.
Barbour) on his promotion as a Member of
the Cabinet. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
We are very fortunate in having a gentleman
like him in this House, and I am quite
certain he is worth far more than the salary
he will receive for this particular job. If we
had more business men like him it would be
well for this Parliament, for this city, and
for Northern Ireland generally. Many
changes have taken place in this House owing
to the recent elections, but the new Members
will find that the old Members are just as
keen and as anxious to promote the welfare,
prosperity and happiness of the people as
they are. We have all confidence in our
Prime Minister. He is nothing if not straight
and above board, and the Members of the
Opposition will find him a true friend of
Ulster. He has no axe to grind. His one
object is to help industry, create employment,
and bring about peace and concord. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. T. HENDERSON: I may say first of
all that I am a little bit nervous. One of the

to my smiling. In other words, I am like the
old lady, who was singing at a village concert

the song, "I wonder will he miss me." She

Reference is made in the Speech to seed

pay a living wage to their employees. I came

the handsome sum of 78 a week.
I hope and trust that the Government

to their employees. If we are going to

important that the employers of Ulster

the employers in Ulster are starting factories
in other parts of the world. We do not want

Ulster. There are thousands and thousands

With regard to the question of drainage,
those of us who have had the honour of
going to Portadown know the necessity that
exists for such a scheme being started at
once. Why was it not started in the past?
Extensive crops have been destroyed, and yet
both the Imperial Government and the
Ulster Government presented closed eyes to
the state of affairs that existed in that particular part of Ulster and took no action. I
am glad the present Government are going to
take action. and I hope and trust that the

Some hon. Members have spoken of families

there is one lady Member in the House (Mrs.

as far as the mothers of Ulster are concerned.
As to the matter of ancient monuments, I
am more concerned with the living monuments at the present time. We should really
deal with the living monuments who are now
suffering great hardships. The question of
ancient monuments should take a minor
part in the deliberations of this House.
I come now to the ruthless expenditure
of the Government, the question of which
will be raised when the Estimates are submitted to the House. You had a glaring
example of it to-day. The streets were
lined by troops and policemen shivering
to death. There is no necessity for all
that mock display. There is no necessity
for this Parliament, of which we are proud
to be Members, trying to imitate the
Mother Imperial Parliament. We should
cut out all this ruthless expenditure
because, after all, what happened to-day?
The streets were lined with troops. The

necessity for it.

I am sorry I have taken up your time, but

The hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.

Britain orders that will keep our yards

That is the answer to my hon. Friend (Mr.

The hon. Member for West Belfast (Sir
Robert Lynn) was also curious on the subject
of the drainage measure outlined in the
King's Speech. I am sure the House will not
expect me now to go into all the particulars
of a Measure which will be before us in a
few days. I can say generally that the object
of the Measure is to enable local authorities
to exercise control over the farming interests
in order that water-courses and drains
should be relieved of the stoppages which have
contributed so much to the internal flooding
of the country. Farmers who do not keep
their lands properly drained, or who permit
their water-courses to be stopped up do far
more damage than they apprehend generally
over the country, because they hold the water
in the soil, and not only sour the land, but
actually produce a state of things that puts
a considerable area of land out of good and
sound cultivation. This little Measure will
have the object, as a preliminary step, of
enabling county authorities to deal with this
matter of arterial drainage, but I am not sure
whether my hon. Friend had in his mind
the question of a large central drainage
scheme. I think the hon. Member who spoke
Jast did think of the conditions in Portadown.
That is clearly a matter for a large central
scheme of drainage. But may I remind not
only my hon. Friend from West Belfast (Sir
Robert Lynn), but other hon. Gentlemen who
spoke, that for the last hundred years the
most distinguished engineers in the country
have directed their attention to the solution
of this very grave problem. So late as
twenty or thirty years ago, one of the most
important and distinguished engineers of the
time, Sir Alexander Binnie, surveyed the
whole of Lough Neagh and all the rivers that
contribute to the waters of Lough Neagh.
The curious result of these engineering investigations is that hardly two of them agree
as to the proper method of solving the
problem. I can assure hon. Members that it
cannot be done by the waving of a magic
wand. The fact of the matter is that the
outlet of Lough Neagh does not seem to be
sufficient to allow the large volume of water
entering it to get freely to the sea, and until
that can be cured I do not think there is
likely to be any really radical cure on that
great central question of flooding. Even I,
who am a layman and do not pretend to any
engineering knowledge, have taken sufficient
interest in the subject to have had engineers
with me on two or three occasions surveying
the whole of that outlet to endeavour to discover whether by some radical method the
problem could be solved at least to the extent
of relieving Lough Neagh of such a measure
of surplus water as would mitigate the flooding which takes place round its shoresflooding which is very serious. I saw 5,000
acres of good, arable land rendered practically
valueless by flooding. That is the one great
economic problem, I may say, that faces the
Government of Northern Ireland at present,
and I can assure hon. Members that they
certainly are not failing in their duty so far
as giving attention to this matter is concerned.
The points referred to by my hon.
Friend, the Member for West Belfast (Sir

will be dealt with by legislation, but they are

are important in theraselves, but they do not
offer any difficulty or develop anything that
is controversial. Pit props and such
like general matters relating to mining
are all that are contemplated in
this little Measure. This is something
in the nature of a summary
of the
matters that have been referred to by

I put figures before the Government of

going to put a burden of £1,700,000 more on
the unbought tenants before their loans were
redeemed than this bargain come to in Dublin in 1918. The Government say they will
give a grant of six months' rent, estimated at
about £160,000 or £170,000, and they say that
squares the account. We have got to pay
£1,700,000 more according to their own figures,
and we get six months' rent forgiven. That
is estimated at £170,000. I feel this House
should give an expression of opinion even at
the eleventh hour that this Bill should be
amended in order to give fair play to these
28,000 tenants. I think I am right in saying
that but for this cause I would probably never
have been a Member of this House. We did
challenge the Government in Co. Antrim on
this question in regard to their attitude, and
I say the decision has been against the
Government.
There are other means by which agriculture
can also be encouraged, and one of them is
this: I think the Government are scarcely
considering the question of transport, and it
is too bad that we should be so heavily handicapped by our transport costing so much as
compared with the cost of the transport of
goods coming from the Continent and other
places. While we appreciate the grant of
£128,000 given by the Government in relief of
rates we have to recognise the fact that even
with this rates at the present time are a
desperately serious matter in rural areas.
This increase is largely due to the expenditure
that is necessitated on our trunk roads by the
very heavy motor traffic which they are
asked to carry. These roads are being remade, and if we are going to have this heavy
motor traffic that is necessary because the
old roads cannot carry this traffic, I feel that
the time has come when the Government
should produce a scheme, if it is necessary to
re-make these roads, whereby they would take
over the entire upkeep of trunk roads as
Government expenditure. The Government
would be quite justified in borrowing a sufficient sum to remake our roads if it is found
that they cannot carry the heavy motor
traffic. I feel that it is unfair to ask the
farmers in the rural areas to meet the
tremendous taxes for roads which they do not
need, and in fact which they cannot use. Why
in the vicinity of Belfast I am informed that
the farmers in a great many instances have to
make a detour off the main roads because the
horses cannot walk on the surfaces. I feel
that those are two lines along which the
Government could usefully legislate, by taking
steps to reduce transport rates, and by taking
over the trunk roads, and, if necessary, getting a loan to remake them to carry the heavy
traffic passing over them.
We hear a good deal of talk about "Back
to the land," but it is my experience that
once people get off the land it is a desperately hard job to get them back again. There
should be some very special effort at the
present time to keep the people on the land
who are on it, and every facility and encour-

"Go on.") With regard to the question of

With regard to the Jury Bill, I certainly
