15 APRIL 1925
In the 1921 election we understood that
there was to be no contentious legislation
produced with regard to licensing matters.
Again we have heard the same words. How
are we to know what contentious legislation
may not again be introduced? I went to my
constituents in East Belfast and with no
uncertain voice I placed before them what
was the principal plank in my platform.
I received from my constituents in East
Belfast 20,000 votes for my policy-20,000 out
of 33,000. That, I think, is a sufficient
mandate for me to come here to-day and to
ask the Prime Minister and the Cabinet to
reconsider the decision that was taken before
the election. I think that it will really be
necessary for the Cabinet to reconsider the
matter. I will not press this home at the
moment. I will leave it to sink into the
memories of the Cabinet. Let them think it
over, and perhaps in more congenial times
when the opening of a fresh Parliament is
got over, and considering the fact that some
of their members who voted for the Act are
not here any longer, they may reconsider
their position, and I will be able at a near
date to carry to my constituents the fact that
we are going at any rate to get an amendment
of the Licensing Act.
I am not at all anxious, as some of my
teetotal friends try to make us believe, that
we should go back to the days when publichouses were open to eleven o'clock on Sunday
night. Recently I was reading not exactly a
history but rather a minute hook of the
Association to which I have the honour to
belong, and in that minute book away back
in 1872 I found that there was a considerable
amount of trouble in those days because the
public-houses were going to be closed at
eleven o'clock on Sunday night. I know that
we are living in different times to those days.
I know that no one has temperance at heart
more than the Association to which I have
the honour to belong. I say that any parts
of the Bill of any value at all were the parts
suggested by my Association. The poteen
portion which was brought into the Finance
Act was suggested by my Association. I also
refer to the methylated spirits portion. I
saw recently in the Press where there were
only so many arrests for drunkenness on
Sunday during the six months prior to the
passing of the Act and only so many arrests
after the passing of the Act, but no
account is taken of the methylated spirit
drinking that went on. Do we not all know
that if it had not been for the passing of that
Bill in relation to methylated spirits we
could scarcely tell what the conditions might
be to-day? We know dens still exist in Belfast
to-day where methylated spirits are consumed.
On Sunday mornings you will see men going
to places that I am afraid the police should
be looking after better. I see it, and it has
been pointed out to some of the temperance
people, but no action seems to have been
taken. I suggest to the Minister of Home
Affairs that there are dens in the centre of
the city where methylated spirits are being
consumed on Sundays to an enormous extent.

The temperance people evidently are very
much afraid that I am going to be assaulted
because the Prime Minister has decided that
there is going to be no Amendment of the
Act. Already in the Press I find that one of
friends of the temperance party
advising me to leave home and
disappear out of the constituency in

whether he would like to see me assaulted
or not, but I know this that I do not intend
to disappear from my constituency and I do
not intend to disappear from this House. I
will continuously raise my voice until such
times as we get an Amending Act, for an
Amending Act we will get no matter how long
it may be. The people are demanding it;
the people will have it. The Sunday trains
that are leaving Belfast and going into the
Free State carry hard-earned money that
never comes back. We have trains going
to Dundalk, Warrenpoint, and Omeath.
We find that the money which is being
drained out of the country never comes
back to us here, and all because a few
faddists want to keep people in leadingstrings. They want to tie them to their
mothers' apron-strings. They tell the men
who can build ships and make linen, and
the women, too, that they are not to have
any freedom whatever. They do not know
what is good for them, but if some of you
had come with me to my election meetings
you would have seen women pat me on the
back, and say, "Go on, our brothers and our
husbands demand their freedom and their
rights, and we hope you will be successful.”
I will not detain you any longer, and I
will not speak to any other part of the
King's Speech. I simply want to say I am
in thorough sympathy with my hon. Friend,
the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Kyle)
when he speaks of the Rent Restriction Act,
of widows' pensions, and of old age
pensions. We wish to see the people of
Northern Ireland on exactly the same footing as their brothers and sisters in England, and I see no reason why the people of
Northern Ireland should be penalised for
their thrift. I will not speak any longer
on this matter.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Cooper]
Government this year should be deferred.
In County Fermanagh and in County
Tyrone many of the smaller farmers have
lost what beasts they had on their lands
through fluke. Numbers of cows and sheep
have died, and the people at the present
moment are not able to pay the annuity. A
lot of them have lost all their stock, and
have no money to re-stock their lands, and
it is a question that the Government must
either grant them loans at a small rate of
interest or defer these annuities. They
do not want a gift of the annuities, they
merely wish them deferred for twelve months
and added on to the end of the term. A lot
of these people have appealed to the Government and the only answer they have got up
to the present is a civil bill. Several of them
have been decreed and costs have been added,
and the Government will find that all those
decrees will be returned marked "no goods."
It has come to a point with numbers of them
that time must be given or their farms must
be sold. I would very strongly appeal to the
Minister to defer payment of these annuities
even if only for six months, because if the
people are allowed to put in their crops and
take them out again, the probability is that
at the end of this year they may have some
money. At the present time they are quite
unable to pay. My colleague in Tyrone and
Fermanagh (Mr. Elliott) made certain statements which might have been made by me if
I had not spoken after he did. However, I
really hope the Minister of Finance will do
something in this matter as it is really very
pressing.

Question again proposed.
Old Age Pensions.
"
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move, at the end
of the Address, to add the words, but
regret that no mention is made in the
Gracious Speech of any contemplated
Amendment to the Old Age Pensions Act
during the present Session, so as to remove
the thrift disqualification clauses, and to
reduce the pensionable age to 60 years."
I rise to move this Amendment to the
Address, because I feel that in the Gracious
Speech there has been a wanton neglect of
the interests of the aged poor of the Six
Counties. I may not be able to give their
case all the assistance that it deserves, but
as a young Member of this honourable House
I will endeavour to place before the House
my views in regard to the conditions under
which the Old Age Pensioners of the Six
Counties live. We have often been told
throughout the country-aye, and even in
this House I have heard it stated, although
I am a very young Member of it-that the
standard of living of the people shall not be
lessened in any way by reason of the
existence of Home Rule in the Six Counties.
Now, I say that the privileges of the Old
Age Pensioners in the Six Counties have
been lessened. They have been lessened by
reason of the fact that we as a legislative
assembly have not put into operation the

sad to think that the last Government lived

and there is no one entitled to so much respect from myself as the grey-haired old
woman or old man. It is therefore my

I come now to the old-age pension as it
stands under the Old Age Pensions Act, and
I think if my memory serves me aright--
and I am quoting from memory now-that
when the Bill was passing through the
House of Lords the opposition at that particular time--and by the way it was, I think,
a Tory opposition-held that the Old Age
Pensions Act, would become a demoralising
Act, that it would tend towards doing away
with the thrifty habits of the working-class
people. Well, now I think those arguments
have turned out unsound, and I am pleased
to know they have been unsound. To-day
we find the same opposition in this House
and I do not know yet; I may be presumptuous in saying something in which
perhaps I may be disappointed-but I hope
the Government in this House will recognise
that it is their duty to encourage thrifty
habits among the people. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) If you discourage thrift I do
not know where you might be in a very few
years. I am sure there is not an hon.
Member sitting in this House to-day who
would feel satisfied if a Bill was passed
through this House to deny him the
right of enjoying his hard earnings, the
fruit of his thrifty habits. Well, I would
encourage any man to put a little bit away
for a rainy day. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I would encourage him because I feel
that by encouraging men to be spend-thrifts
you are going to come to an end which none
in this House would like to see coming to
our present Ulster Province. I remember, 1
think it was in the British House of
Commons,
when the Bill was being discussed-it was on June 25-Sir Laming
Worthington Evans said, "If a man has subscribed to a friendly society or has saved

pension is an anti-social act." I am sure

ત
We in the past in Northern Ireland have
been looked upon as a very industrious race.
I have heard it repeatedly said to me, "You
think of nothing but work." Work has been
the battle-cry of the Northerner from his
earliest boyhood until his old age. Well
perhaps we have been working and working
very hard, and at the end of our years of
hard work we cannot see very much to
maintain us in our old age. Now that is the
case, and if our hard work has accumulated a little savings for the people of
Northern Ireland I cannot see why their
efforts in that field should now be penalised
by their being denied the right to pensions
at the age as stated in the Act. I would
claim that this amendment is a justifiable
one as far as thrift is concerned, and proceed
to the matter of drawing the age line at 60.
I would just like to give a comparison
that I have running through my mind.

engaged.

Northern Ireland workers have the shipbuilding, they have the linen, and they have
agriculture. I say these are three industries
that tend to wear the worker down more
than any other industry that I could
mention at the moment within the confines
of the Ulster Government. For that reason
I would ask the House to reduce the age
from the present standing of 70 years to 60

Britain that the age is too high at the

Province we claim that we lead in many

Government of the country will the people
of the country realise that it is a government of the people. Then at election times
I am sure they will not forget the works of

I would tend towards going out not alone

It gives me the greatest pleasure to move

that the ultimate result of our labours here

The MINISTER OF FINANCE
Pollock): Ithink possibly I had better intervene
at this stage in order that the position of the
Government inay be made clear. We approach
this matter with the fullest sympathy for
those persons for whom the mover and
seconder of the Amendment and those who
followed them entertain equal sympathy, but
neither the mover nor the seconder, nor anyone who followed, not even the hon. Member
for West Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn), who is
more familiar with the conditions of our
finances than probably any of the others who
have spoken, has taken into account the extent of the necessities of our Province, or the
ability of the Government to provide the
money. I doubt very much whether any of
the hon. Gentlemen who have spoken have
any idea of the additional cost involved in
this scheme. To carry out the policy which
has been adopted in Great Britain would involve an expenditure of £350,000 a year on
this Province. I have no definite figures in
regard to the cost of the latter part of the
Amendment, but in consultation with my
advisers I think if I estimated it at half a
million of money I would be within the
mark. In other words, to carry out the
programme outlined by the two hon. Members
would cost the Province £850,000 a year-to
carry out the entire scheme..
Now I said at the beginning that I have
the utmost sympathy personally with the inclusion of those persons who have saved some
little money and who should not be debarred
from the advantages of the pensions scheme
if the money is available for such a provision.
But the Government had to make up its
mind whether, on the one hand, all the unemployment relief schemes should be dropped,
whether the full course of our educational
scheme could be carried out, or whether the
grant in relief of rates to the agricultural
community should be dropped. In the present
condition of our finances, when no definite
arrangement has been made with the Imperial
Government in regard to our position in
relation to expenditure of this character, no

Minister of Finance could think of plunging
the Province into debt to the extent of
£350,000 a year, which would be the cost of
the first part of the scheme only, until he
knew with some definiteness what his resources were.
It is a very easy thing, and also a very
popular thing, no doubt, for hon. Members
to stand up in this House and say that old
people over sixty years of age should be provided for with Government money and
maintained. It may be that it is not only a
popular scheme, but it may be also a fair
and an equitable scheme-I do not decry that
or deny it, not at all-but, as I said yesterday,
this whole question of the provision of public
relief is, as it were, in the melting pot. At
the present time the British Government is
considering how and to what extent all forms
of public relief can be amalgamated. Assuming that such a measure were adopted on the
other side, when a general scheme of contributory public relief would be adopted, all
the arrangements that we make here would
have to be transformed, and it would of
course naturally be expected that we would
follow the British practice. We have stated
from time to time here that it was our policy
to conform to all British measures of public
relief, and it is the intention of this Government to follow that practice when we have the
money available. But I put it to hon.
Members from every point of view, from the
point of view of the extent of the Province, of
the necessity of feeding such a large number
of people, the numbers of whom I hesitate
even standing at this Table here to give, they
are so appalling, from this point of view I
appeal to hon. Members whether the Government should be tied to an immediate adoption
of this scheme when they have it in view,
assuming that all their financial arrangements
are completed with the other side, and have
the money to do it, that we shall distinctly
follow the practice of the British Government.
There is also another difficulty in relation
to Great Britain, and that is that the
numbers of old people who would be eligible
for the old-age pension are greater per
thousand in Northern Ireland than in Great
Britain, so that the British Government,
I am quite convinced, would not recognize
our claim that we should get credit for the
whole of the expenditure that would be
necessary. Another thing I wish to point
out is that the British scheme, if adopted
not affect or benefit the
here, would
present old-age pensioners to the extent of

Debate on Address-
Public Expenditure.
16 APRIL 1925
Public Expenditure.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I beg to move as an
Amendment to the Address, at end add:
"But humbly regret that no reference
is made to the burden of taxation which has
had the effect of raising prices, increasing
the cost of living, hampering industry, and
reducing employment, and call upon the
Government to make such economies as will
result in a considerable reduction in public
expenditure."
On rising to move this Amendment that
stands in my name on this paper, I wish with
your permission, and with the permission of
the House, to do something I have never done
in my lifetime before, either in Parliament,
in the Press, or on the platform, and that is
to make a personal explanation. I make that
personal explanation because of a particularly
offensive remark that was made yesterday by
the Member for North Belfast (Mr. Grant). In
dealing with this question of reducing expenditure he referred not by name, but in a manner
that nobody could misunderstand, to myself,
and said the reason why I acted as I did was
because of some personal feeling I had, and
because I had not been included in the
Cabinet. Well, I want to say, and say it at
once, that never in my lifetime did I seek to
get into any Cabinet, either in Ireland or in
Great Britain, nor did I ever seek to enter
any Ministry, but four years ago the Prime
Minister was good enough to offer me in turn
two important offices in the Northern
Ministry, and I declined them, not because I had any lack of faith
confidence in the Prime Minister, because I
never had that, but for the simple reason I
felt that as the editor of an important paper
I could not conscientiously discharge my
duties, and at the same time be a Member of
the Government. I have got the feeling-it
may be old-fashioned--that a journalist to do
his duty faithfully to the public must be as
free of entanglements as a judge himself.
or
I am sorry to have to make this personal
explanation, but I want to nail down this
statement at the very beginning. I want to
go a step further to make it clear and say
that there was some confidential correspondence that I sent to the Prime Minister at the
time, and if he in his wisdom thinks it should
be published he has my liberty and permission
to do so. If it is published it will make it
quite clear and I am sure the Prime Minister
will agree that there is no justification whatever for the charge that has been levelled
against me that I am dealing with this
question out of any personal motive. I want
to see the business of this House conducted
on a higher plane and free from all persona-
I
lities. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
remember, I think, at the second or third
sitting of the House, that the Prime Minister
himself said he wanted the Members of the
House and his followers--and there were only
his followers in the House at the time-to be
absolutely frank in their discussions. I refuse
to believe that we have reached the stage
when loyalty to the Prime Minister, when
loyalty to the Party-and I am loyal to the
Prime Minister and loyal to the Party-(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-is to be measured by
the number of relatives that you happen to
get into fat jobs in the Government.
I pass from that, and I will deal now
with the more important question as to
whether there has been excessive expenditure or not. The Prime Minister in his
speech yesterday-and in many respects it
was an interesting speech-was rather
illogical in dealing with this question of
expenditure, because in the first place he
said that Cabinet Ministers were really so
overworked that it was necessary for them
to have Under-Secretaries to help them, and
then in reply, evidently to some critic
during the election-I do not know whomhe proceeded to point out that it was
necessary that the men we get into the
Cabinet and I do not disagree with himshould be men of wide experience, men who
were carrying on large businesses like the
three right hon. Gentlemen sitting next to
him now. I agree with him in that, but we
cannot have it both ways. Then there was
the other question that we must train our
Under Secretaries at the expense of the taxto become Cabinet
payers
Ministers. I
understood we had got a perfect Cabinet, and
sometimes I agree we have, and yet I think
the Prime Minister himself is the only member of that Cabinet who ever served as an
Under Secretary, so that that point may be
wiped aside.
But we come now to the question of whether
really our Government is extravagant or
whether it is not. As a result of some controversy that is going on I went to the trouble
the other day of looking up the last audited
accounts of this House which were ordered to

year, and that if we are able to make economies in any direction we shall get credit
for those economies so far as we are concerned as a Government. I trust that when
the Colwyn Committee's findings are published we will find that the future of Ulster
is secure on a firm and sure foundation from
the financial standpoint and that we will go
forward to develop our resources and do the
best we can from every standpoint for the
people over whom we have jurisdiction.
I know political gratitude is a very pe
culiar commodity, and sometimes the work
of men who have spent themselves in the
services of a Government is not fully appre
ciated until long years after they are gone.
I want before I sit down, if I never have
another opportunity of doing it, to say that
I do not think this House or the people of
the Six Counties have ever fully understood
or appreciated the marvellous work that was
done during the last four or five years in
carrying on our Government so efficiently
and so well. They have no full appreciation
of the great work done by the Minister of
Finance for the Six Counties. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) He has tided us over
every difficulty, he has assisted every worthy
and deserving object, and we find ourselves
to-day in a position of which every one of
us ought to be proud.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Hear, hear. So we
are.
Public Expenditure. 96

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: We have carried on and done our work efficiently and
well without a penny of debt, and in addition fulfilled our obligations to the Mother
of Parliaments which established us here
four years ago. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. KYLE: I rise to support the Amendment proposed by the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn). If there is one
thing more than another that was stressed
during the election in the city of Belfast it
was the question of expenditure and the
necessity for economy in administration. I
do not intend to weary the House with many
of the stories that were told from election
platforms, but I just want to recount one
little incident that took place shortly after
the Northern Government was established.
A young man was working in Dublin Castle,
in one of the departments there.
sent for by one of the offices being set up
under the Northern Parliament. He considered the telegram very carefully. He
said to his workmates in the office, "What
do you think about it?" Finally, after consulting with them he made up his mind that
he would not like to come North. He went
home and consulted his wife. She, like his
workmates, also thought that, having
a
He was
decent home where they were, they
would not like to change. However, to get
out of the difficulty and not to leave a bad
impression with the department which sent
for him, his wife suggested, "Oh, ask for half
as much more than you know they will give
you and they will not take you." Accordingly he sent back word to say that he would
be prepared to come up to Belfast if they gave
him just half as much more than he expected
to get. The result was that the Northern
Government Department immediately wired
him to come up at once. He is to-day serving
the Northern Government, and I am sure
serving it quite well. That is an example, I
think, of perhaps avoidable expense in some
things.
One appreciates the difficulties in which the
Government were at the time of their formation. They had to man their offices. They
had to man their Departments, but I think
the hon. Member for West Belfast (Sir Robert
Lynn) is quite justified, in view of the
election contest from which we have just
emerged, in pressing this matter, and I hope
he will press it to a division of the House
in order to urge the most rigid economy as
far as our Northern administration is concerned.
Mr. POLLOCK: My hon. Friend from
Derry (Sir Robert Anderson) entered into
such an exhaustive defence of the Government's position in relation to expenditure,
and so effectively dealt with the points submitted by the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Sir Robert Lynn) that it has rendered my

Lynn) in regard to the comparison which he
undertook to make between different foreign
countries and our own Province, because
it appears to me that he was comparing
matters that were not comparable, and that
no relationship whatever exists between the

every country must be judged by its own
conditions. But a paper was put into my
hands during the last few minutes and I
think it is worth while referring to it, because it gives rather a different colouring
from the point of view of expenditure to a
very important Dominion referred to by the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Sir Robert
Lynn). In the first place Members of
Parliament in Canada are paid £800 each,
and I doubt very much whether a Resolution
of that kind would be received even in this
House with the same unanimity as is
secured in the Canadian Parliament.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Might I ask the
right hon. Gentleman is he quoting the
Federal or the Provincial Parliaments?
Mr. POLLOCK: For the moment I am
quoting the Federal Parliament, but I propose to deal with the Provincial Parliaments
now. The Provincial arrangements are rather
comparable to our own, but only in a very
few cases are the populations equal to ours
here. British Columbia has a population of
524,000, and there are seven Ministers.
Saskatchewan has seven
Ministers with a
population of 750,000 odd. Those are Provinces which we all know are comparable
and
to
occupy positions somewhat analagous
our own in its relation to the
British Empire. New Brunswick, with a
population of 300,000, has seven Ministers,
Nova Scotia, with a population of 387,000,
has nine Ministers, and Quebec eleven
Ministers, and so on, with an average of
probably ten over the whole range of the
Provinces of Canada. From my knowledge
of the conditions existing in Canada-and I
have some knowledge--I can say that the cost
of Parliamentary Government there is very considerably higher than anything we could have
ambition to in this modest Province of Ulster.
That is all I can say in regard to the comparisons that have been made, because I think
hon. Members could with difficulty follow the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Sir Robert
Lynn) in regard to these comparisons.
I come now to a matter for which, perhaps, I have to claim some measure of
responsibility, and that is the cost of administration in Northern Ireland. My hon.
Friend (Sir Robert Lynn) submitted an

Comment was made upon the cost of Parliament, and my hon. Friend the Member for
West Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn) interjected,
if I rightly interpret his statement, that if
these charges were limited one would be able
to pay the addition to the old-age pensions
that was suggested by an earlier amendment.
The cost of all Parliamentary work amounts
to £21,000, and I submit that that would go
a very small way in providing for the £350,000
which would be required for the purpose of
putting the old-age pension scheme in exact
line with the British position. I am concerned
to defend the cost of the Administration, and
I remind the House of something that perhaps they forget, and which, possibly, our
new Members do not know, that is, that on
the institution of this Province and the
transfer of its services we were bound by
the principal Act to take over such civil servants as were required for Northern Ireland,
and we were bound also to take them over on
the basis of the emoluments which they received. The alternative to that naturally was
that if we refused to take these servants over
we should have had to pay out an enormous
sum in pensions. We selected the very best
men we could from the Civil Service then existing in Dublin, and gave them the option

[Mr. Pollock]
of coming here on the same basis as obtained
under the Imperial authority, so that so far
as the costs of the salaries of these servantsand they form a very large proportion indeed of the Civil Service of Northern Ireland
-is concerned their rates of remuneration
were determined by authorities entirely
outside of ourselves. Whether they are paid
too much or too little it was not possible for
us to make any changes.
I submit that statement because it forms
the basis of the whole cost of the administration of Northern Ireland. The question
then arises: Have we too many servants administering the different departments of
Northern Ireland? Logically the charges of
my hon. Friend must lead up to this either
that the servants are overpaid or that the
Departments are overmanned.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Both.
Mr. POLLOCK: I submit that the hon.
Member is not in any position to judge of that
factor. If I offered the House some information in regard to my own Department perhaps it would enlighten hon. Members as to
what the amount which is charged against
that Department really covers. The Ministry
of Finance sounds very simple if you use that
expression alone, but let us see for a moment
what is the work that is performed by the
Ministry of Finance, then possibly hon.
Members may in their minds picture the
number of servants that are required for
the carrying out of these functions. All the
revenue service, which is the collection of
the revenue that accrues to the Province
with the exception of the reserved services,
the cost of which is included in the
figures I have given; all the Valuation
Department; all the registration, all the loan
services; the carrying out of public works,
and I doubt whether my hon. Friend has any
conception of the vast amount of construction in public works going on at the present
time in Northern Ireland.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I have.
the
Mr. POLLOCK: Charity funds; the stationery office, which has to supply the stationery
to all the Departments; teachers' pensions;
the Civil Service Commission-not an unimportant matter by any means; the Ulster
Savings Certificates, with all the administration; the Loans Guarantee Act;
collection of land purchase annuities, that
is the collection of £650,000 distributed
over the entire Province; and the tithe
rent charges. Now, if my hon. Friend will
take the list of the services that are perperformed by the Ministry of Finance-and
that, of course, is only typical-and if he will
examine the figures of the cost of the administration of all these services I think
he will admit that there is no commercial
undertaking in Belfast which is run more
economically than the Ministry of Finance.
But it is my prerogative not only to survey
the Ministry of Finance but also to be responsible for the cost of the administration of the
different Departments, and I think I can say
that where any saving can be effected no
opportunity is ever lost. In the institution
of all the services of Northern Ireland it was
very difficult for the head of any Department to know exactly the number of the staff
that would be necessary, but now that we
have had four years' experience I can give
this assurance that the Ministry of Finance
has let no opportunity pass by of criticising
the appointments in all these different
branches. I do certainly protest, and protest
most strongly, against any statement like
that of my hon. Friend (Sir Robert Lynn)
conveying to the Province a general charge of
extravagance without indicating any particular item which could be either reduced or
saved, and therefore creating the impression
among the people of this Province that the
services of Northern Ireland are being run
on extravagant lines.
I repeat what my right hon. Friend (the
Prime Minister) read to this House yesterday, when he informed hon. Members that on
the very best and highest testimony, that is
the Imperial Treasury, the services of Northern Ireland were run on economical lines.
Obviously it was the business of the Imperial
Treasury to discover whether they were or
were not carried out on economical lines, because every pound they were able to save in
the cost of our services accrued to the
Imperial Government. We want no higher
testimony than that. If there was any show
of extravagance in any Department those
very able men in the Imperial Treasury who
have vastly more experience than my hon.
Friend (Sir Robert Lynn) in these matters,
or than I have, or any member of this Parliament has, would have pointed it out and
yet here we have the testimony of those men
that they could not find one item in the
whole of our expenditure they could criticise.
Let us also remind the House that this
is not confined to a survey of our operations
from Whitehall, but Civil Servants of experience have come here and investigated our
conditions and they have over and over again
admitted their admiration of the manner in
which the services of Northern Ireland are
carried on. I have nothing more to say except that if my hon. Friend can put his
finger upon any special item and show where
a saving in that item can be made, I am
here to listen to him, and I will undertake
if there is any extravagance shown to have
that extravagance removed. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)

Oral Answers to Questions.
ASSISTANT PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY, MINISTRY OF FINANCE.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether he has yet received the
resignation of the Assistant Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Finance, and if
so, is it the intention of the Government to
appoint a successor.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I will reply to the hon. Member's question.
The answer to the first part of his inquiry
is in the affirmative, and as regards the
second part the matter is still under
consideration.
IRISH SAILORS AND SOLDIERS' LAND
TRUST.
2. Colonel WOODS: asked the Minister of
Finance, whether he can state what rents
will be charged to the tenants of the ex-
Service men's houses constructed in the
Belfast district under the Sailors' and
Soldiers' Land Trust Fund?
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): The honourable
and gallant Member is no doubt aware that
while the Ministry of Finance acts as the
agent of the Irish Sailors' and Soldiers' Land
Trust for the purpose of building the houses
for ex-Service men in somewhat the same way
as it acts for Imperial Departments, it has
no responsibility for the policy of the Trust
which is an Imperial Service administered
by trustees under Regulations made by the
Imperial Treasury. Under these Regulations the amount of rent to be charged to the
tenants of the houses in the Belfast district
and elsewhere is a matter for the trustees.
I understand that in the case of the houses
at Cregagh which are approaching completion, the trustees propose to fix the rent at
10s a week.
Colonel WOODS: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman whether he, as the agent for the
Imperial Government, considers that that is
a fair rent for these particular houses?
Mr. SPEAKER: I think that is really a
question which ought to be put in the
Imperial Parliament. Of course, as I have
stated before, this is one of those questions
which are entirely reserved.

SERVICE.
asked the

Mr. BARBOUR: The number of ex-

Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Oral Answers
UNEMPLOYMENT BENEFIT.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Labour whether he can state the
total number of people disqualified from
receiving unemployment benefit since the
commencement of the present year through
the operation of the condition making it
obligatory on a person to have contributed
six stamps in non-sheltered trades during the
preceding two insurance years, and if, in
view of the suffering caused to the people so
disqualified, he will consider the advisability
of removing the clause and restoring all
those to benefit who have been disqualified.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The number of persons disqualified from receiving extended benefit since
the 1st January, 1925, through the operation
of the condition requiring a person to have
contributed at least six stamps in the trades
to which the hon. Member refers during the
two years preceding the date of the application for benefit is 1,777.
Before framing the condition I gave very
careful consideration to all the circumstances, including the state of employment
in the various trades carried on in Northern
Ireland. The condition was brought into
force in each Employment Exchange area
with the concurrence of the Local Employment Committees and, in the general
interests of all the contributors to the
Fund, it does not appear advisable to withdraw it.
Mr. McMULLEN: I desire to inquire what
the Minister of Labour expects these people
to do who have been unable to obtain employment for two years, and who are denied
benefit?
Mr. ANDREWS: I am glad to be able to
say that a proportion of them are obtaining
employment at the present time, and I think
I am justified in saying that many of them
are more energetically looking for employment than heretofore. But I would remind
my hon. Friend that this is an insurance
fund, and that I am in no way justified in
giving compassionate gifts at the expense
of the fund.
UNEMPLOYMENT BENEFIT-NEW
CONDITIONS.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Labour
whether he can state how many applicants
for unemployment benefit have been refused
benefit since January 1st, 1925, when the new
regulations came into force?
Mr. ANDREWS: The number of applicants
who have been unable to qualify for unemployment benefit since the 1st January,
1925, on account of their failure to satisfy the
new conditions which came into force on that
date is 2,351.
UNEMPLOYMENT FUND.
6. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Labour
whether he can state when the Unemployment Fund in Northern Ireland became
separate from the corresponding fund in
Great Britain?
Mr. ANDREWS: The Northern Ireland
Unemployment Fund became separate from
the corresponding Fund in Great Britain on
the 1st January, 1922.
Mr. KYLE: Would the Minister of
Labour ask the Prime Minister to correct a
statement he made in this House implying
that the Labour Government were responsible for this division, and further will
the Minister tell this House what answer the
Conservative Minister of Labour gave to his
request for the amalgamation of the funds?
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps it
might clear the mind of the hon. Member if
I were to say that it was only after the
division took place that either the British
Government or the Northern Government
was able to realise that it was an uneconomical separation of the funds. What I referred
to the other day-I know that my hon.
Friend is referring to it now-was that we
have been endeavouring ever since to have
the funds amalgamated. What I said was
I thought it was a very unfortunate thing
that we could not get the Labour Government, when they were in power and knew
the details, to assist us in having the funds
amalgamated.
Mr. KYLE: Would the Minister of Labour
please answer the second part of the question,
as to what answer the Conservative Minister
of Labour gave when he was asked to amalgamate the funds?
The PRIME MINISTER: I think I can
answer that. We are at present in negotiations with the Imperial Government to have
the funds amalgamated, and I am hopeful of
a satisfactory result.
Mr. KYLE: I think my question could be
answered.
Mr. SPEAKER: I do not suppose it is
exactly out of order, but I think it is undesirable to deal with the British Government as regards parties. So far as this
Parliament is concerned, we really only know
the British Government no matter what it
is composed of.
SUMMER TIME IN SCHOOLS.
7. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
Debate on Address-
Unemployment
21 APRIL 1925
whether there would be any objection on the
part of his Department to schools in rural
areas observing Greenwich time instead of
Summer time, until the expiration of the
operation of the Summer Time Act.
Mr. BARBOUR: On behalf of my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Education, I
beg to answer this question.
The Ministry has continued the concession
made by the Commissioners of National
Education when "Summer Time" was first
introduced, whereby managers are authorised
to arrange for the marking of the rolls and
commencement of school business half an
hour later than during the observance of
Greenwich time. It is believed that this
arrangement has proved satisfactory to the
schools in the rural districts and the
Ministry does not consider that any further
change is necessary.

Order read for resuming adjourned Debate
on Question 16th April,
"That an humble Address be presented to
His Grace the Governor as followeth :-
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern
Ireland, in Parliament assembled, beg
leave to offer our humble thanks to your
Grace for the Speech which your Grace
has addressed to both Houses of Parliament." (Dr. Morrison).
Question again proposed.
Unemployment.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I desire to
move at the end of the Address to add the
words-
"But regret that in view of the serious
distress consequent upon the unemployment of 48,600 persons in Northern Ireland,
the Government has not thought fit to include in the gracious speech from the
Throne any mention of legislation recognizing the right of the unemployed to work or
maintenance."
I think it is to be regretted that no definite
proposal has emanated from the Government
as to how they intend to solve the question
of unemployment. The attitude that has
been taken up by this and by every other
Government up to the moment has been
that of ameliorative reform. This Government has worked through the medium of
the Loans Guarantee Act, and it has
assisted local administrative bodies by granting 60 per cent. of the wages cost in connection with schemes that have the approbation
of the Minister of Labour. But I want to
suggest that that is only treating with
effects instead of causes, and unless the
Government are prepared to tackle the
question fundamentally it means that
the problem of unemployment is going
to be with us for a considerable period.
During the course of the debate the Prime
Minister reproached hon. Members of the
House for making wild and extravagant
statements and allowing themselves to be
carried away by the plaudits of the multitude during the recent elections. He also
deprecated the idea of people making extravagant promises which it would be extremely
difficult to implement without legislation in
this House. I take it, therefore, that when
the Prime Minister gives a definite undertaking it is his intention to give effect to it
at the earliest possible moment. I recall that
in a speech delivered by the Prime Minister
in the month of November, 1923, a definite
undertaking was given that he and those
associated with him would solve the problem
of unemployment, whether it was solved by
Mr. Baldwin and his associates or not. Not
only have the Prime Minister and the
Government not solved unemployment
but I discover that the situation is slowly
and gradually becoming worse. When that
statement was made by the Prime Minister
we had 37,000 people unemployed in the area
over which this Parliament has jurisdiction.
I now observe that we have 48,600 unemployed
in the Six Counties, and, unfortunately, this
does not fully show the facts of the situation.
I elicited from the Minister of Labour this
afternoon the information that 1,777 people
have been disqualified from obtaining unemployment benefit from the start of the
present year. Through the operation of a
clause for which the Prime Minister and his
Government were responsible these people
have been disqualified from receiving unemployment benefit unless they have made six
contributions to the fund during the preceding two insurance years. These people
realising the hopelessness of obtaining
employment through the medium of the
Labour Exchange, have lost contact with the
Labour Exchange, and, consequently, numbers of people in the Six Counties are now
unemployed, and the Minister of Labour has
no record of them at all. That is the un-
Unemployment 112
Debate on Address-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. McMullen]
fortunate state of affairs that exists. That
briefly and clearly sums up the present
situation.
We have now to ask what the position is
in regard to the future-what the future
holds out in the way of stopping unemployment. I submit that neither the immediate
nor the distant future holds very much in
store for the people who are unemployed at
present. I regret that the feeling of
optimism which prevailed with the advent of
the Conservative Government in October
last has not been justified. That feeling of
optimism has given place to a feeling of
despair and hopelessness. It was felt that
people with money to invest who might be
suspicious of the character of legislation
introduced by a Labour Government
would with the return of the Conservative Government to power allow
their capital or money to slowly precolate through the usual channels of trade,
and that as a result the wheels of industry
would commence to rotate and that there
would be a return to general prosperity. But
I discover from the last figures available for
February, that 40,000 more people are unemployed in Great Britain and Ireland now
than when the Conservative
Government
came into power. Not only that but without
any protest from this House there has been
an unjustifiable increase in the bank rate.
Anybody with a minor acquaintance of
finance and I do not claim to know much
about it-knows full well that the increase
in the bank rate is going to make money
dearer and people who contemplated embarking on schemes which would have
undoubtedly provided people with employment will now hesitate and be retarded from
doing so owing to money becoming dearer.
There is the further fact that prices as a
result of the bank rate being increased will
also undoubtedly advance. As the wages of
the workers generally are not likely to increase and the purchasing power being
limited, it will mean that with the demand
falling off for commodities whose prices will
increase, unemployment will be even
than at the present moment. I believe these
two factors justify me in suggesting that
neither the immediate nor the distant future
holds any better times in store for the working classes of these six counties.
worse
I do not think any discussion on this
question would be complete without some
reference to the effect that machine production is having on the situation generally.
In my capacity as a City Councillor I had
recently an opportunity of visiting our
electric station, and I would like to say,
parenthetically, that the electric station is
in keeping with the best traditions of Belfast. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I
observed several hundred tons of coal being
put into the electric station without the aid
of human hands. The coal was discharged
out of the vessel which was alongside the
quay by means of a grab. That grab was
operated by a crane, and it deposited
the coal on to overhead elevators. These
overhead elevators conveyed the coal a
distance of 200 yards, and slowly fed the
boilers of the electric station. Not only that,
but when the coal was consumed the ashes
were taken away by means of a mechanical
process and were deposited on a rubbish heap
without human hands touching the whole of
the operations. I want to suggest that what
is taking place in the electric station is also
taking place in all our industries not only
in this city but throughout the length and
breadth of the civilised world. I have taken
the trouble to secure statistics relative to
the position in which firms find themselves
at the present time in consequence of the conversion of the fuel for steamers from coal
to oil. The five vessels which I propose to
take for this purpose are the "Franconia,"
Andania," Mauretania," Aquitania,"
..
and "Empress of India." I find that on
the "Franconia," before the ship was converted to oil fuel, 68 firemen were employed;
now 20 are employed. In the Andania' 44
were employed, now 25; "Mauretania" 335
were employed, now 88; "Aquitania," 309
were employed, now 80; "Empress of India,"
110 were employed, now 30. I find that on
the conversion of these ships from coal burning to oil fuel burning there has been a
saving of 623 men. I suggest that that is a
serious state of affairs not only for the working classes of Great Britain, but for the
working classes generally throughout the
length and breadth of the civilised world.
It is possible to go further, but I do not
want to weary the House. I want to try to
do justice, however, to this question with
which I am dealing, because I believe it is
one of the most serious concerning this or
any other Government. I want briefly to
refer to the home of the cotton industry in
Preston-Messrs Horrocks, Crewdson and
Co. From an advertisement that appeared in
the papers recently I learned that this firm
has 6,500 employees. The firm has got 7,500
looms and 330,000 spindles. The annual output is 1,500,000 pieces of cloth, equal to 34,000
miles in range. The point I want the House
to observe, as a matter of comparison, is that
it is possible for these 6,500 employees to
produce four times more than the 43,000
operatives engaged in the cotton industry in
the year 1760, which you will remember was
about the year in which steam was applied to
machinery. Let me put it in different
words. 6,500 workers are producing as much
as 172,000 workers produced in 1760, or to use
a further comparison, each worker is now producing twenty-six and a-half times as much as
Debate on Address-
Unemployment
21 APRIL 1925
a worker produced in 1760. This means that
commodities are being produced at a much
greater rate than the people can purchase
them, with the result that we have chronic
periods of unemployment.
I have gone back over the industrial
history of the last century to discover when
industrial crises occurred, and I find that
in the early days of the last century we
had an industrial crisis in 1803, followed by
others in 1810, 1815, 1825, 1830, 1836, 1847, 1857,
1864, 1873, 1882, and 1890. The last available
figure I have is 1907, which shows that we
are having a recurring period of trade
depression on an average about every seven
years. I believe it will be extremely difficult
for us to get back to normal times. If we do
get back to normal times these periods of
unemployment are going to recur much more
frequently than in the past. The tragic
feature of the situation as it appeals to me is
that young men and young women who are
now reaching the age of adolescence are going
to have few opportunities, if any, of acquiring
a skilled occupation. When I was a young
man I had an opportunity of becoming proficient in a certain direction in the local
shipyards, but it is not possible for a young
man at the present time to become skilled or
efficient in any of these trades owing to the
acute economic situation which we are in at
the present time.
I am going to suggest that there are ways
in which the Government can tackle this
problem. It does appear to be an anomalous
position that a person on going through the
main thoroughfares of Belfast will find our
shops and warerooms stocked with all the
commodities that the people who are in
poverty and are unemployed require. I
met a tailor, for instance, the other day, and
I asked him if he was unemployed. His
clothes were threadbare, and he suggested
that he was unemployed because there were
too many suits of clothes produced. The
same thing applies to shoemakers. Shoemakers are practically barefoot, because
under the present system of society too many
pairs of boots have been produced. Agricultural labourers
are unemployed, and in
poverty, at the moment, presumably because
there is too much foodstuff produced in this
country, and cannot be profitably employed.
(Laughter.) Han. Members can afford to
laugh because they are in comfortable
circumstances. They can jeer and sneer
when certain statements are made
the floor of this House. I want to suggest
that there is any quantity of land idle, any
amount of industrial capital in the way of
machinery idle, and any number of workers
idle. We have got 48,600 unemployed.

So far as I have been able with a limited
intelligence to observe these are largely the
things required in order to produce wealth.
We had a very profitable discussion the
other day on the question of economy. I
observed from the Ministry of Labour
Gazette that for the month of February a
sum of £3,712,000 was paid in Great Britain
and Ireland in unemployment benefit. If
you multiply that by twelve it reaches an
alarming total, and I suggest that the community should not be saddled with the
responsibility of providing this money,
month by month, and year by year. There
are many other ways of dealing with it. I
do not know whether this Government has
got the courage to deal with it or not. We
will probably be told as we were a day or
two ago when discussing old-age pensions that
it is absolutely impossible to provide the
money. My hon. Friend, the Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Kyle) suggested on that
occasion that when it became a question of
finding money it could be got from where
it was.
I observe that two-thirds of the
national capital is now held by less
than two per cent. of the people,
and that the value of the estates subject to
Estate Duty has risen from
£373,000,000 in 1920 and 1921 to £442,000,000
in 1923 and 1924. This does not indicate
poverty by any means. I also observe that
in 1923 and 1924 there were 10,000 more
super-tax payers-excluding the Free State,
whose figures were formerly included-than
there were in 1920 and 1921. That does not
suggest any great degree of poverty amongst
certain classes of the community.

I want to put it up definitely to the Prime
Minister and the Government to implement
the promises the Prime Minister gave. I
know of course the difficulty of solving the
unemployment problem. I know it would be
extremely difficult for this Government on
its own to do it, inasmuch as they are dependent to a great extent on other factors
outside the control of the Government. Our
shipbuilding industry is in an exceptionally
bad way at the moment, and the chances
are that we will have great difficulty in
getting back, if ever we do get back, to
the state of affairs which existed prewar owing to the many competitors we
have now who were formerly customers
of ours. The same thing would apply
to the linen industry, and as far as I
am able to visualise the situation it is an
extremely dark and doleful one for many of
the working classes in this area over which
we have jurisdiction I could visualise a
change taking place in affairs with the
electrification of industry or with a further
great revolution so far as our methods of
production are concerned, and I would like
if possible to get the Prime Minister into
the frame of mind of Mr. Baldwin. It is a
remarkable thing I believe when you get a
Conservative Prime Minister to speak of "the
next stage in industrial evolution." I can
recall the time when the Prime Minister of

and I believe that if the Government have

Mr. KYLE: In the absence of the hon.
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie) I desire to second the Amendment proposed by
the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
William McMullen). In doing so I would ask
what has the Government done for the workers of Northern Ireland? They had an
opportunity of making unemployment
national charge-what it ought to be-when
the Imperial Government granted £500,000
under what was known as the Craig-Collins
Pact. They had the opportunity then of making
unemployment a national charge and devising schemes in themselves to absorb the unemployed. Despite that opportunity £167,000
out of that £500,000 was not used. Owing to
the failure of the Government to realise the
terrible position of our working men and
working women all they did was to make
grants to local authorities, which have had
the result in Belfast of the tenants getting
notice of an increase in their rents following
an increase in the rates. The Belfast City
Council have mortgaged their people- and in
my opinion quite rightly-in an attempt to
deal with this problem of unemployment.
So far as the Government are concerned
they have done very little indeed, and in addition to that the unemployed of Belfast are
denied equal treatment with the unemployed
of Great Britain largely owing to the cruel
and inhuman treatment of the unemployed
by the Poor Law Guardians in refusing outdoor relief to the sufferers, and that despite
the fact that the Minister of Home Affairs
(Sir Dawson Bates) and the Minister of
Labour (Mr. Andrews) have told the Poor
Law Guardians of this city that they have
the power when they have the will to use the
rates of Belfast to relieve unemployment and
the unemployed sufferers. We have been told
in this House more than once that it is the
desire of the Government to give to the
people of the Six Counties equal treatment
with the people of Great Britain. In England it is recognised that a worker cannot
support a family on 18s. per week with 2s.
per child per week. The Belfast Guardians
refused any relief to any person who is, or
has been, in receipt of Unemployment Insurance benefits. We hold that that is a deplorable state of affairs. A friend of mine who
is a local Guardian told me of homes he has
visited in the East end of the city. In one
of these houses, a mother, who has gone
blind, her two sons, both unemployed, and
three other persons occupy a single upper
room, and this in the constituency of the
right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates).
There would not be a single word of protest
from these benches if the Government abolished the Guardians altogether, and substituted a Commissioner who knew the law and
was prepared to administer it. On top of
this iniquitous treatment of the workers the
Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews), in
answer to a question to-day, has doomed a
considerable number-2,357 to be exact-of
the work people to slow starvation by the
stringency of the new regulations governing
the granting of benefits. These are some facts
about unemployment in Belfast.
What is wrong with society to-day that,
despite the unquestionable fact that labour
allied to land can produce the food, can build
the houses, can make the clothes, can make
the boots, can produce the finest ships, weave
the finest linen the world has ever seen, that,
despite our productive powers being practically unlimited, thousands of our fellow
citizens are hungry, naked, and homeless? Is
it not that speculators gamble in the people's
food, that usurers take two-thirds of the
wealth that is created to swell their ill-gotten
gains, thus depriving honest toilers of the
bulk of the wealth they create? And in
taking such an inordinate share the moneylenders deprive many of us work people even
of the opportunity to make further profits
for them. Is it not that rings, trusts, and
combines throttle that competition which is
supposed to control the commercial world?
117 Debate on Address-

21 APRIL 1925
Take the fact that builders of houses have
got to pay 200 or 300 per cent. more for their
light castings to-day than before the Light
Castings Association had got their stranglehold on the light-casting trade, and this
despite the fact that wages in the lightcasting trade are only twenty to twenty-five
per cent. above what they were in 1914, with
the cost of living, as it is to-day, seventy-five
per cent. above pre-war.
What do the Government intend to do to
prevent this wholesale robbery of the people?
Set up a Commission, as our friends the
British Government have done on the other
side, which will talk for five months and
then tell us the price that goods are? As if
we needed a Commission to tell us what the
prices of goods are. Our wives could tell
us, or our mothers and sisters who keep
house for us could tell us that without
setting up a Commission to sit for five
months. This whitewashing of persons who
deliberately and with malice aforethought
have robbed the people we hope the
Government here will not follow that
lead from the other side.
We on these
benches propose that there ought to be a
general increase of workers' wages to enable
them to buy more, and so improve our home
markets. The sum of £700,000,000 has been
taken from the workers of Great Britain
and Northern Ireland over a period of two
years in wage reductions. Can anyone doubt
that if this sum had been in circulation the
fearful state of our unemployed workers
would not have been mitigated? We have
got to realise that these men and women,
these boys and girls who are striving to get
work, walking the boots off their feet in the
hopeless task of finding work, we have got
to realise that these men and women are
our brothers and sisters.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Hear, hear.
Mr. KYLE: Let hon. Members go to the
Queen's Road at eight o'clock in the morning
and see the numbers of men earnestly beseeching for work; as Burns puts it:-
See yonder poor, o'er-labour'd wight
So abject, mean, and vile,
Who begs a brother of the earth
To give him leave to toil."
Does this House realise what is happening?
The best blood, brain, and brawn of these
Six Counties of ours, are being banished to
the U.S.A., to Canada, Australia, to the farflang outposts of the British Empire. These
men are going all over the world in an endeavour to get work, and then, if they
happen to fail to find it after spending all
the money they have earned during a lifetime, if they have stayed more than two
years in the United States, or Canada, or
elsewhere, the Minister of Labour will deny
them their benefits, despite the fact that they
may have worked for ten or twelve years in
an insured trade in this country. There was
one case brought to my notice yesterday of a
man who worked for ten years in Combe
Barbour's after serving an apprenticeship in
Mackie's Foundry. This man goes to the
U.S.A. and comes back at the end of two
years and finds that, despite the fact that
he had paid for those ten years-from 1912 he
was in an insured trade-he is denied his
Unemployment Benefit to-day. These are
some of the factors of the unemployment
situation as we see it from these benches.
We had the right hon. Gentleman the
Minister of Finance the other day tell us we
had a higher percentage of men over 70 in
the Northern Counties than in England. He
did not tell us the reason. I will attempt to
tell you.
It is because our young men are
denied the right to work in their own land.
Hundreds if not thousands of most highly
skilled men have left these shores. That results in our workshops being denuded of men
when the occasion demands them.
If you
take the engineers away, if you take the
joiners away, if you take these men away in
the numbers in which they have been departing from these shores during the last
three years, and supposing that next year or
the year following there is a spurt in the
engineering trade, we shall not have got the
men to man the machines. We need to keep
these men while they are here. If the
modern system of society cannot keep these
men employed, it ought to keep them while
they are unemployed. They ought to either
get work or maintenance. That is the programme, as I say, we have to advocate from
these benches here. We hope and pray and
trust that the Government will bear these
things in mind when they are making new
regulations or considering fresh regulations
for the administration of the Unemployment
Insurance Fund.
And now hon. Members might ask what do
we propose. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I will give you eight proposals which, we
think, might help.
First and most important, increased wages
to bring consumption up to something more
like equilibrium with production.
Second, the raising of the school-leaving
age and maintenance grants for young persons.
Third, the maintenance of widows with dependent children to take them out of industry altogether.
Fourth, the prevention of overtime.
Fifth, the ratification of the Washington
Convention on the hours of labour. I do not
think that that question should need any
stress a forty-eight hour week by law.

Dr. MORRISON: I intervene in this debate with considerable hesitation
should like in the first instance to congratulate the Members who represent Labour in
this House on the able way in which they
have put their case to-day and on the able
way in which they put their case on Thursday. Their presence here has made gaps in

to see these Labour men here. They present
Labour to me in a comparatively new
I
aspect, and all my life I have been identified
with trying to help Labour and I am free
from any entanglements either of capital or
of labour, so that I can approach this question with an unbiassed mind.
I was impressed with the example that the
mover of the Amendment gave of how
machinery was displacing labour. I may tell
my Labour colleague across the House that
there is an
old recognised principle in
medicine that if you get bacteria introduced
into your system they produce toxin, and it

very serious and very dangerous and in some

and antibody is the cure. The bacteria produce the disease, and they produce also the
remedy.

the present moment Dutch potatoes and
being

Now when you come to this question of
saddling the boards of guardians or the ratepayers with supplementing the unemployment dole you introduce a very serious
question. Up to 1898 in the Northern Area,
and indeed in Ireland, the landlord paid
half the county cess and half the poor-rate.
By the Local Government Act of 1898 the
State took this charge, that is, the State
would relieve the landlord and undertake
the liability for the half of the rates and
half of the county cess. But the State did
more. In 1903 it fixed the standard year.
The grant they would give in relief of rates
and in relief of county cess or poor-rate
would be fixed by the rate that ruled in
1903, and after that any increase in expenditure would come wholly off the rates. This
means that since 1902 any increase in the
rates-and I may tell the House and those
men who pay rates whether they pay rates
for a house in Belfast or a house and land
in the country that those rates have quadrupled, and the rent in the country is not now
the serious matter which it used to be. The
question is rates. And you now propose,
that is, the Labour Members propose, to put

raises the question of the incidence of

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Dr. Morrison]
I was a dispensary doctor for twenty-eight
years. I moved through a very wide, industrious area, and I found that in nearly
every house where there were young girls
and women the industry of shirt-making was
being carried on. I became aware that
Labour, whether it came from Belfast or the
textile industry, generally demanded that
that should be stopped. Although it was the
means of spending two millions of money all
over our country districts, and perhaps
among the home workers in Belfast, it was
crushed out without scruple. The destruction of that industry, I maintain, was entirely due to the trade unions and their evil
influence on rural Ulster. Close to where I
live was an industry which employed, probably, 100 men. It had been working for
200 years.
In an evil hour these workers
called in an organiser, and that trade union
organiser told them they were not getting
enough wages. The result was that the wages
were increased, and since then-it was only
a couple of years ago that industry, which
had gone on for 200 years, has been closed,
unemployment has been produced, and distress and suffering caused in my district
amongst people who were earning not perhaps a wage the Labour Members think
necessary but a wage that kept them in comfort, and under the conditions that prevailed
in the country, they were prosperous, and
contented, and happy. The wheels of industry
are stopped, the machinery is scrapped, and
the place is definitely closed.
On my way to this House I pass at Ballymoney a big mill that had been running
perhaps for 100 years. That mill has a large
amount of water power. It met with an
accident, part of it was burred, and rather
than rebuild they gave up the water power,
and the centre of the business now is in
Belfast. I could take you, in connection
with this textile industry, to houses in Limavady which are closed. The people have lost
their employment, and have gone to Jerry
and other centres. For every three houses
that were in my district when I went to it
there are only two now. Where are these
people? They have gone, as the Labour
Leader (Mr. Kyle) said, some to the United
States. I know that. They have gone there
because under the conditions the Labour
Party in Belfast insist on they were denied
a living in their own place. That is how the
thing works out. They have been sent up
here to Belfast in hundreds, increasing the
housing problem, increasing unemployment,
and increasing misery and the number of
deaths in Belfast. You have all these things
existing in Belfast. It is a desperate condition of things. I have looked at the number
of deaths from tuberculosis in Belfast, and I
may tell you that the Belfast Corporation is
doing more to combat tuberculosis than any
other corporation or county committee, and
are doing it in a generous, scientific way
that redounds to their credit. In Belfast, in
1923, you had 687 deaths from tuberculosis,
and if you calculate that for every one who
dies you have ten ill, you have 6,780 people
suffering from the disease. I maintain that
that is due to the policy of Labour in driving
people from the country into the town, and
producing overcrowding and other unsatis
factory social conditions to such an extent
that disease is developed, and these evil results are produced.
With regard to disabled soldiers, there has
not been a word said by my hon. Friend
across the House. In no part of His Majesty's
dominions has Labour done such magnificent
work as in Belfast on behalf of the Empire.
You have these returned soldiers walking the
streets, some of them wounded, not able to
get a job, and you have the trade unions in
many instances refusing to allow them to
come in. You have a Government willing to
spend any amount of money in training these
people. I have gone into some of the Government offices, and there have been pointed out
to me the wonderful things these men make
in the way of carpentry. Yet when one of
them goes to a trade union they will not
allow him to get employment. A man came
six miles to me to con.plain about the position he was in. He was a wood polisher, who
was trained by the Government, and he
thought, poor simple man that he was, he
could go up to Belfast and get a job.
went to a friend, and when he went to the

Sir ROBERT LYNN: Profoundly as I
disagree with the arguments put forward by
my colleague in the representation of West
Belfast (Mr. William McMullen), I can, I
think, in all sincerity congratulate him on
his maiden speech. It was as graceful to
listen to as his arguments were unconvincing.
In the course of that speech he dealt with
the haunting sense of insecurity that the
unemployed suffer from, and with the terrible
conditions of those who are vainly in search
of work. I would like to remind him of this,
that after all a great deal of the social unrest
that exists in our country is due to the
political propaganda that has been carried on
by Socialists. The head of the Socialist order,
at least in modern times, Karl Marx, has laid
it down that it was his deliberate intention
to create industrial unrest, to prevent social
harmony, to embitter class feeling, to make
economic reform impossible, and to hurry
on revolution. Socialism, with its perverted
philosophy, its false history, and its equally
false economics, has created a feeling of unrest, and what we want really in the industrial world-and we want it to-day more than
ever-is peace-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)
- peace to develop our industries and
without that peace there can be no possible
progress either in the economic or in any
other world.
My hon. Friends need not think that they
can improve an engine by throwing handfuls
of sand in amongst the machinery. That is,
unfortunately, what has been done for a long
time. We want peace. We want goodwill,
and I agree with the hon. Member for North
Belfast (Mr. Kyle) that we want to remember
that we are all members of one family, and
that what hurts one branch of the family
also hurts another. I do not stand here to
say that unrest in itself is a bad thing. Why,
complete contentment only means a state that
is as bad as death. But if complete contentment is bad, surely incessant discontent is
something worse, and therefore we should try
to get rid of it. If we believe the
arguments that have been put forward, if
I may say so, with great force and I am sure

outside the creed of Socialism. I am not
ashamed to stand up in this House or anywhere else and say that I believe that private
enterprise has done a thousand times more
for the world than Socialism could do under
any conditions whatever.

But, Sir, the problem of unemployment is
not quite so easy of solution as my two hon.
Friends suggest. I remember-and I have
a great respect for him personally-the
Socialist Labour Minister, Mr. Shaw, a very
able and a genial Minister, telling us in the
House one night that it was impossible to
bring rabbits out of a hat. I do not know
whether my two hon. Friends have got the
rabbits in the hat or not, but I am sorry
to say that in the course of the speeches
the rabbits have not been produced, and the
Labour Minister has not been told how he
could improve on what he has done. I suggest to my hon. Friends that there are quite
a number of factors to be taken into consideration, every one of which has a direct
bearing on this question of unemployment.
First of all, there is the decrease of our
foreign trade. Do not let us forget this, that
without foreign trade Our country and
when I speak of our country of course I
mean Great Britain as well as Northern Ireland-would not be able to support more than
one-half of its present population. Now, as
the result of poverty caused by the war, our
former customers are unable to buy from us
to the same extent as they did before. How
are my hon. Friends going to meet that? Are
they going to meet that by passing an Amendment-work or maintenance? Then there is
the instability of the foreign exchanges.

the weather. Personally I think it is a blessing, because the Bank Rate would always be
going up if the Government manipulated it.
The moderate rise in the Bank Rate has had
an effect that my hon. Friend has overlooked,
and that is that it has reduced the prices of
the necessaries of life. If he goes into the
financial figures he will discover that what
I say is true. I am not going to labour that.
Then there are the traffic barriers. How is
my hon. Friend going to get rid of these?
These barriers are not only put up against
us by foreign countries, but are actually put
up by our own colonies. In what way is he
going to get these barriers wiped away?
Personally, as a Free Trader, I would like
to see every barrier removed. I do not see
any disposition on the part of the Third
Internationale to remove these tariff barriers
in the slightest. Then there is the successful
competition of other industrial countries.
England was the greatest industrial country
in the world for, I suppose, half a century,
but England has now very serious competitors, and surely you cannot suggest that
you are going to get rid of that competition
by establishing a Socialistic State. Then
there is the other question of the high cost
of production, and that has a direct bearing
on the whole argument of my hon. Friend.
Our productions must compete with foreign
productions. If you are going to increase
the cost of production will any sane man
tell me how you are going to compete in the
markets of the world with those other people
who produce much more cheaply than we do?
Then what really, I think, is equally bad
is the unrest that we have had in the labour
world for some years. I remember in the
year 1919 discussing this whole question with
Sir Auckland Geddes, who was then a member of the Cabinet of the Imperial Government. I remember his saying-and it stuck
in my mind ever since-" If we only get our
people to settle down to work for five years,
I think we will be able to wipe out the
whole debt that has been caused by the
war." But a short time after that we got
into a whole series of industrial troubles
and industrial strife, and a great deal of
our trouble to-day is directly due to the
strikes we had in 1920 and 1921, and
from then on, because, unfortunately, since
the war there has been so much unrest, and
just when we seemed to be getting into a
pleasing, easy country something crops up
and destroys the whole prospect.
As to the restriction of output, I say you
are up against a most important factor,
because I for one stand, and I express it
publicly-I have always done so for high
wages. I believe high wages are good, but
high wages must be linked up with high production, and it is just because the American
is producing three times as much per man as
we are doing that the American is able to
beat us in competition.
There is also the burden of taxation. I am
not going to deal with that now, but the
burden of taxation is undoubtedly restricting
employment. Work or maintenance will
never solve this problem of unemployment. I go a
and

say

Let me in conclusion say this, if the

I end as I began by saying that if we want
to get rid of unemployment we must drop
all talk about revolution. We must cease
restricting the output of our work. We
must cease our opposition to improved
methods of production. We must encourage
able men and pay them according to the
amount of work they do. I say it, and say
it with all respect, that the Socialistic
policy is all wrong because it would destroy
enterprise and discourage ability; it would
stop invention, penalize thrift, and rob service of its due reward. Because of these
things I have no hesitation in voting against
the Amendment.
