of unemployment, and they are world wide.
First of all there was the war with all its
waste of life, property, munitions and money.
And after the war was over old markets
had been lost and old business connections
had ceased to exist, and we in Northern
Ireland were particularly hard hit in that
way, because before the war our shipyards
had some of the best connections for their
output possible. As the result of the peace
settlement ships were actually taken in the
form of reparations and some of the best
customers of our Belfast yards got a considerable number of ships supplied to them
in this way. The result has been that those
concerns have not been able to order a
single ship since the war ended. That is a
most serious matter, but sooner or later, I
think, it is reasonable to expect it will right
itself.
Then, again, the linen trade. It is known
to all hon. Members that during the war
linen for domestic purposes ceased to be
produced, and to our undying credit
Northern Ireland produced in its mills and
factories with the aid of both employers and
workers the wings not only of the British
aeroplanes, but also of the aeroplanes of
practically all our Allies. Then when the
war ended a considerable quantity of this
linen was left on the hands of the then
existing British Government and, rather
foolishly and cruelly I think, they threw
that upon the market which was not willing
to accept it except at a price much less than
the cost of production.
When you take these things into consideration you cannot help but feel that bad
and all as things are it is really somewhat
wonderful that they are not worse. And,
remember, Northern Ireland is not the only
place in the world that is suffering from
unemployment. Great Britain is suffering
to a serious extent, and almost every country
in Europe is suffering through unemployment

opposite have no cause for complaint against

sympathy with our unemployed persons?

Debate on Address-

21 APRIL 1925
maintain it is quite wrong to call unemployment benefit the dole. I have always maintained, long before my hon. Friends came into
this House at all, or had an opportunity of
coming, that it should not be called a dole,
because it was not a dole; in other words,
that it was an insurance system to which our
workers contributed in order that when they
got out of employment and were seeking work
and were anxious to get it they would have
something to fall back upon. But if you were to
give it to them in perpetuity without regulations it would become a dole, and it
would be unfair to the contributors who remain
in work year after year, and who pay contributions, that a section of the community
should be permitted to remain out of work
and draw unemployment benefit in perpetuity. What are these regulations to which
my hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle) has so graphically
referred to-day? Simply, in the first place,
the test of a man being an insured person
is that he has paid twelve contributions at
some time to the Fund, and, further, that
as an earnest of his desire to work he will
have done some insurable work during the
last two years in each of six weeks, not necessarily consecutive. That regulation applies
only to those trades where the opportunities
for obtaining work have become greater and
not less than they were during that period.
Therefore, I think it is scarcely fair of
hon. Members to come here and describe
regulations as harsh, and cruel, and unfair,
which are, in my opinion, really reasonable
and only intended to safeguard the interests
of all the contributors to the Fund. I again
say to my hon. Friends, because, after all,
this is the marrow of the whole story, let
them come here with practical suggestions,
and let them tell us how this problem really
can be solved, not with wildcat schemes like
Socialism, but recognising the land we live
in and the difficulties with which we have
got to deal, and the Government will be very
glad to receive their suggestions.

Debate on Address-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Main Question again proposed.
Proportional Representation.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I beg to move, at
the end of the Address, to add the words:
"But humbly regret that no proposal is
made to give effect to the pledges to abolish
Proportional Representation and establish
single-member constituencies, and call
upon the Government to proceed at as early
a date as possible in the present Session
with the promised reform."
I will not detain the House for more than
a few minutes. Let me say that this is an
Amendment on a subject regarding which
divisions are not on party lines. Divisions
with regard to Proportional Representation
cut through all parties, even the smallest of
parties. If I may say so, two of the finest
speeches that I ever heard made against
Proportional Representation were made in
the Imperial Parliament by two right hon.
Members who were poles apart. The first
one was made by my right hon. Friend, the
Member for South Belfast (Mr. Moles), the
Deputy Speaker of this House, and the
second one was made by Mr. Ramsay
MacDonald, and having listened to those two
speeches, and having re-read them, I have
been strongly confirmed in my faith against
the folly of Proportional Representation. The
friends of Proportional Representation allege
that it will prevent anomalies, that it will
promote efficiency, that it will make for
economy. Well, even those of us who in
earlier stages had an academic liking for it.
and who thought it looked delightful on
paper, as it does, have discovered by painful experience that it is an exceedingly
costly, clumsy and inefficient system of representation. It is not necessary, I think,
that I should keep the House at any length
in dealing with the pros and cons of Proportional Representation.
The second part of the Amendment deals
with the attitude of the Government with
regard to this matter. We were told again
and again that Proportional Representation
would be abolished before the last General
Election. New Members of the House.
or those who have not taken an
interest in it, may not know that when the
Government of Ireland Act was being passed,
the Imperial Government wanted to make the
period six years in which we could not change,
but as a result of a very hard and strenuous
fight that was carried on by the Ulster party
under the leadership of Lord Carson, we succeeded in getting it reduced to three years,
and some of us were very hopeful that at the
end of three years the first thing the Parliament would do would be to abolish Propor
tional Representation. Then the last election
came, and came suddenly, and the result was
that we had our election on Proportional
Representation again. Well, if there is any
Member of this House who thinks that Proportional Representation should remain, he is
just as fully entitled to that opinion as I am
to the contrary, and I do not object in the
slightest to his holding that opinion; but 1
do say that if the majority of the Members
of this House still hold to the views expressed
so often in this House in the last four years.
then we should proceed at once to revert to
single-member constituencies.
Let me meet fairly and squarely the arguments that I know will be brought against me,
and that is, that electoral reforms are never
passed except by a dying Parliament. That
argument I am prepared to meet, because two
very important electoral reforms, even in
recent times, have been passed without waiting for a dying Parliament. The first was
with regard to the election of 1918. Remember
that was a real revolution in electoral reform,
because it introduced for the first time the
women's vote. That was passed a considerable time before the Parliament ended. The
second-and I would like Members, and especially Members of the Government to note
this fact-was contained in our own Act of
1920, because in that Act of 1920 it was laid
down that the number of Imperial representatives would be reduced from, I think, 23,
or whatever the number was, to 13, and in
order to do that it was necessary that the
then existing constituencies should be enlarged. For example, I represent a constituency that was then represented by three
-Woodvale, Falls and St. Anne's. We had to
wait for nearly three years before that provision in the Act of 1920 came into operation.
Remember we are not going to add to the
number of electors. We are not going to add
to or decrease the number of Members in this
House, because we are prevented from doing
that. All we are going to do is to take, say,
a unit like West Belfast with its four Members, and instead of having one unit make
four out of one. So that you are not increasing the membership of the House; you
are not interfering with the number of
electors, and I say it does not hold good to
the same extent as when you are adding
several millions to the old franchise. Therefore we should start to do this thing at once.
It is either necessary, or it is not necessary.
If the House says it is not necessary to change
from Proportional Representation, well, I
disagree, but I will be satisfied; but if it is
necessary, let us do the work at once, and I
will tell you why.
Who can tell when the next election is going
to come? Is the Government or any Member of this House going to give a guarantee
that there will be no election in Northern
Ireland for two, three, four or even five
years? The thing is impossible. No one
knows when an election is coming, and there-

fore if we want to get back to the single seat
constituencies I say our business is to set

Colonel WOODS: On rising to second this
amendment I, like my colleague, do not wish

P.R. system. I do not suppose that will

I would like to point out that under the P.R.

You are voting much as they do in America,

end to a man who is not at all popular and
who does not really represent the views of
the people who have put him in, not by their
own volition but by the surplus votes of the

As to the last election, my own view is that
it was most unnecessary and expensive, but
after all it was worth while if you take into

night in West Belfast. The hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin),
who is not in the House, went
up the Springfield Road with 5,000 or
6,000 of his followers, who were carrying all

them. We came down in the opposite
direction with about 5,000 or 6,000 followers
with Union Jacks and Orange flags flying,
and both parties passed on a narrow portion
of the road, but there was nothing but
hearty salutations on both sides. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) When such a situation arises in Belfast after many years of
disturbances, I think if nothing else accrued
from the election that that was a good thing.
It did much to cheer me for all the trouble
I had. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I do
not want to lay any particular stress on

done that before. It seems to me that promises
are made without any serious intention of
carrying them out. (Hon. Members: No,
no.) As regards my own peculiar situation
in being returned for two seats under P.R.,
I would like to say that although I have had
to relinquish that for South Belfast, I shall
always regard myself as the moral representative of that division in this House.
appreciate the honour done me in South
Belfast. I hope the Government will do
away with this clumsy and very expensive

The PRIME MINISTER: I do not think
anyone in the House has made more speeches
or more vigorous speeches against the system
of P.R. than I have made myself both here
and elsewhere. Therefore, it does not
require any argument on the part of any
Member in any part of the House to convince
me that P.R. is most unsuitable to British
institutions and to Northern Ireland. (Hon
Members: Hear, hear). At the same time
the difficulty here is that this amendment is
calling upon the Government to immediately
carry out a change. I wish we could have
carried out the change prior to the last
General Election, but there are certain very
grave considerations that I am not at liberty
to announce in the House, that made it
necessary to carry out the last election under
P.R., much as I object to the system.
However, the intention of the Government
stands fully as it did before. When the
opportune moment arrives a scheme of singlemember constituencies shall be devised and
I hope sincerely that the next General
Election in Ulster will come under the good
old fashioned British system and not under
the system of P.R. I am very sorry I cannot
go further to-day. I merely say that it is a
matter of choosing the opportune moment to
bring it in. I agree with my hon. Friend
one of the Members for West Belfast (Sir
Robert Lynn) that there is no necessity to
wait to the very end of an administration be
fore bringing in a change of that kind, but
at the same time it is customary that when
either the franchise is altered or a Redistribution Bill is brought in, the House goes to
the country under the new system as speedily
as possible. I believe myself that there might
be some difficulty, were a by-election to take
place, if the members of the House as a
whole were elected under one system and a
Member was returned at the by-election
under another system, but this and other
matters connected with it will be very carefully considered by my colleagues and myself,
and I hope to be able within a reasonable
time at all events to produce a Bill embodying the old-fashioned system. I am sorry
that is as far as it is possible to meet my
hon. Friends to-day.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Can the Prime

The PRIME MINISTER: I am willing to

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON : I rise to

HOUSE OF COMMONS Proportional Representation 148
Debate on Address-
[Mr. George Henderson]
say that while P.R. may not be ideal in some
respects it is a great improvement on the old
system of single constituencies, because I
think it not only secures majority rule, but, to
some extent, it is a safeguard for minorities.
It does give minorities a chance of having
something like fair and just representation in
this House.
The fundamental principle of a representative institution is that it should reflect as
far as possible the views of the different
parties and sections in the State in proportion to their voting capacity. That is one
thing which Proportional Representation
does to some extent. Now if we go back to
the old system of single constituencies in this
area it is very possible that very substantial
minorities will be left without representation
in this House, and I think that is not a position that would create confidence and good
will between the different sections of the
people in this community. If I might be
permitted to use it as an example, I think
the result of the election through which we
have just passed is really in favour of the
Proportional Representation system, because
it will be admitted on all sides that there is
not any considerable body of opinion in this
area that has not a spokesman in this House
at the present fime, and I think that is very
desirable.
Not only that but I think you will find,
if you compare the representation of the
different parties with the amount of first
preference votes they got, that Proportional
Representation has worked out very fairly.
If you take the figures for Belfast, I have
been informed that the Unionist first preferences were 67,911, and these secured eight
seats in the contested constituencies in
Belfast. Independent Unionists polled 38,036
first preference votes, and they secured four
seats, so that you will observe that the proportion is very accurate. Labour polled 18,114
and secured three seats. The Nationalists
polled 17,558 and secured one seat.
The probability is that the Labour
Party gained a little from the Nationalist
second preference vote, but if you add
the two together you will find that
they secured four seats, and the proportion
is accurate again. If you take the whole of
the contested seats in Ulster you will find,
according to the figures I have got, that
Government candidates received 211,662 first
preference votes, non-Government received
173,088. Government candidates secured 22
seats, and non-Government candidates
secured 18, in exact proportion again to the
votes cast by the different scetions of the
community. When an electoral system produces a result like that why do you want to
scrap it or change it? I say that this House
could not hope under any system to give a
more accurate reflex of the opinions of the
different parties and sections in our area
than it does at the present time.
There is just one other point I want to
make. I have said previously that our representative institution, to command confidence and respect, must be representative of
all classes. Now confidence is a plant that
is a bit hard to cultivate, especially, shall I
say, in Ireland. It is a plant that is very
easily blighted. Confidence between the
different sections of this community is hard
to build up and very easily shattered, and
at the present time I believe there are in this
community signs of a growing confidence
between minority and majority and between
the different sections of this community, and
I feel that no action that the Government
could take at the present time would be more
liable to shatter that growing confidence
than to abolish Proportional Representation
and go back to the old system. It would
necessitate a redistribution of seats with all
the discussion which that would be liable to
bring about, all the charges of jerrymandering and other things. I do feel that this
election has proved that Proportional Representation is a workable, fair electioneering
scheme, and I am very pleased that the
Prime Minister was wise enough not
to give an undertaking that the next election
would be fought under the old system.
hope the next election, whoever lives to see
it, will again be a Proportional Representation election, because I feel that it is the
most fair election, and gives the truest reflex of the wishes of the electors.

The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): The Bill
which hon. Members have now had in their
hands for some days is a very simple one,
and needs very little comment by way of
recommendation. Its object is to make
available annually
small
a
sum of
money to be utilized for purposes corresponding to those which fall under
Class V of the Imperial Civil List Act-I
refer to the pensions paid from the Civil List
to men distinguished in the domain of literature and art, or to their widows, who at
times, by reason of their very devotion to
their art, find themselves through illness or
age in circumstances of want. While here in
Northern Ireland such people are not debarred from being placed on the Imperial
Civil List, the amount available from British
funds for the whole of the United Kingdom
is so small that the probability of any grants
from that source to deserving cases
Northern Ireland may be anticipated as very
remote. In these circumstances the Government has deemed it desirable to introduce
the present Bill, the general intention of
which is to enable small pensions or gratuities to be granted to Ulstermen and Ulster
women who, having by their efforts in cultured or scientific pursuits shed lustre on
the Province, find themselves in old age, or
have left dependants who find themselves
faced with penury.
in
From the terms of the Bill it will be seen
that it is proposed to empower the Minister
of Finance to grant a pension or gratuity
on account of meritorious public service, in
the first instance, where such services have
been rendered in any public office in Northern
Ireland, and where the recipient is not
entitled to a pension under any of the
Superannuation Acts, and, in the second
place, where such services have been performed on behalf of science, literature, the
fine arts, or social work and progress in
Northern Ireland. The conditions, generally,
as regards the individual pensioner, are that
the recipient must have attained the age of
70 years or be totally incapacitated for his
work. It is also proposed that the private
means of the recipient or his dependants
shall be considered in awarding any such
pension, and that in any event the pension
shall cease, either after a specified period. or
on the death of the person to whom it is
awarded. The amount of any such pension
will not be taken into acount for purposes of
the Old Age Pensions Acts.
There is also the following limit proposed
to be placed on the amount available under
the Bill, and that is that the total cumulative amount in any one year of both gratuities and pensions shall not exceed £500, so
that I think hon. Members will recognise at
once the very limited scope of this Bill. The
total annual amount to be granted in respect
of any one pension is not to exceed £100, or,
in the case of a gratuity, a single payment of
£100. The total aggregate yearly amount
payable to any widow, children or dependants of any such persons is not to exceed
£200 by way of pension, or in case of a
gratuity a single payment of £200.
I am confident that hon. Members will be
in sympathy with the principle of this Bill
and, while we regret that anyone having
rendered such meritorious service or service
of such a distinguished character as to
qualify him in respect of this grant should
in his latter days find himself in want, and
while it is sad to think that the small sum
which it is proposed to make available
should really be a sum of moment to enable
him to support existence, I think hon.
Members will agree that there is a general
principle underlying such ex-gratia payments from public funds, and that is that
in discretionary payments of this sort the
limits should be severely set. Hon. Members will be aware that one of the most
fruitful sources of corruption in public
administration in the past was the grant of
unfettered discretion to the Government of
the day to award pensions from the Exchequer a power which was only too often
used for the purpose of political rewards.
This is the real ground for limiting the
amount that can be paid annually, for re-
Civil Pensions Bill-

quiring this House to vote such sum
annually, and for giving power to the House
at any time to require a full explanation of
the grounds on which any pension has been
granted. I beg to move.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I rise to say that, as
far as I am concerned, I am in cordial

or literature have given their services to the

may be useful in the construction of the Act
afterwards. As far as I am concerned I
think the Bill is a very modest one, and
have no hesitation whatever in giving it my
wholehearted support.

with the Bill as outlined by the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Barbour), but I would like
to know whether in its aspect regarding

case I have in mind. I have in mind the

remember that on one occasion he wrote to

clothed his offer in the most beautiful and

One supports the principle of the Measure,
and one can only wish that the principle

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James

starting in a very modest way purposely,
and I feel sure that the Measure will be of
great benefit to certain classes of the community who are found, after rendering meritorious services in many directions, without
any means at all. Although the maximum is

County Officers and Courts Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed, "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
Mr. BARBOUR: In this case also an explanatory note accompanies the Bill, which I
hope will enable hon. Members to understand
exactly what is arrived at under the Bill.
I should also like to state that in passing
this Bill we are merely following the procedure that has taken place in England,
which has preceded us by nearly six months
in passing an Act similar to if not identical
with what is now before the House. Our
County Court services, as hon. Members are
aware, rest upon very great antiquity, and
they have been built up piecemeal for a great
number of years. There have been some disabilities and hardships which seem anomalous
when viewed under present day conditions,
and the object of this Bill is to endeavour to
arrive at an agreed settlement of those
hardships or grievances of the class of officials who are administering these services,
and on the whole I hope hon. Members will
consider the terms at least equitable and
reasonably generous.
These reforms have for some time past beer.
the subject of careful deliberation, both by
the Imperial Government and, since its establishment, by our own Government, and
they are based generally on the findings of
the Viceregal Committee of Inquiry which
was instituted in October, 1919, under, the
chairmanship of Judge Wakely, K.C. A
161 County Officers and Courts Bill-

22 APRIL 1925
Second Reading.
corresponding Committee was set up about
the same time by the Imperial Government
to inquire into the English County Court
Service. Its findings were on the same lines
as those of the Irish Committee and these
English Reforms have already been affected
by the Imperial County Courts Act passed
last session.
In the first place in order to enable hon.
Members to understand the conditions under
which these public servants discharge their
duties and the disadvantages connected with
County Courts I may say that the character
of the work carried on in this service falls
into three divisions, and in each case the
Clerk of the Crown and Peace is
the officer responsible for the due performance of the work. The first division
is the duties of the Clerk in connection
with Crown and Peace work. This is a
purely Northern Ireland service. The one
difficulty in dealing with this matter is that
the nature of the services performed by the
officers for whom we propose to legislate is
of a three-fold character. One is a purely
Northern Ireland service; the second a reserved service, and the third is partly an
Imperial service and partly a Northern Ireland service. The reserved service consists of
the duties of the Clerk as Local Registrar of
Title, and then the service which is partly
Northern Ireland and partly Imperial is the
revision of the Voters' Lists in each county.
I need hardly say that under the Clauses
of this Bill we are only concerned with the
Northern Ireland functions. Under existing
arrangements the Clerk of the Crown and
Peace is granted an allowance from voted
moneys to provide for the salaries of his
clerical assistants, and these assistants are
accordingly in no sense the employees of the
State. Their rates of pay have been fixed
individually at the volition of the Clerks of
the Crown and Peace, and they are not entitled to pension or gratuity on retirement.
This system was probably adopted on account
of the lack of administrative machinery in
the county towns; but with the great development of the county courts and the increase
in the duties of the Clerks of the Crown and
Peace, it has been found to be unsuitable to
modern conditions. Nevertheless the duties
discharged by these officers are of a purely
public character, and by this Bill it is proposed to treat them as public servants by
altering their status to that of established
Civil Servants.
Besides the Clerk of the Crown and Peace
himself and his personal staff there is
another type of officer connected with county
courts, namely, the Registrars of the Civil
Bill Courts. With one exception they are,
however, merely part-time officers, and have
been excluded from the operation of the
scheme. The one exception is in the case of
the Registrar to the Recorder of Belfast, who
for a number of years has been regarded as
a full-time officer, and it will be seen that
the Bill makes special provision for this particular post.
The disadvantages under which the clerical
staffs labour under the present system will
be obvious, but I will deal for a few moments
with some of the most outstanding. Firstly,
as the clerical assistants are employed by the
Clerk of the Crown and Peace personally,
they have no security of tenure. They can
be dismissed at any time, and on the office of
the Clerk of the Crown and Peace becoming
vacant they cannot count on being retained
in the service by his successor, although it
has almost invariably happened in the past
that the incoming Clerk of the Crown and
Peace has been glad to avail himself of the
skill and experience of his predecessor's
appointees. Secondly, they are not entitled
to receive any pension. In consequence, they
cannot afford to retire at the normal retiring
age applicable to their brethren in similar
services, and this aspect of their case is
aggravated owing to the fact that the clerical
allowance from which they are paid, although
augmented by cost-of-living bonus, has not
been re-cast for many years, and in some
cases has become inadequate for the purpose.
Such are the conditions under which this
branch of the Public Service has been performed, and in my view it is surprising this
service has been so efficiently run under
circumstances not by any means conducive
to efficient work.
The Bill proposes, therefore, to convert the
staff of the Crown and Peace offices into an
established body to be called the County
Court Service, the members of which will
duly become established Civil Servants under
conditions comparable as regards pay, pensions, etc., to the Civil Servants of Northern
Ireland generally. Each Crown and Peace
Office instead of being a self-contained entity
becomes part of a system, and there will
result a consequent improvement in the prospects of the various staffs, who will be capable of being transferred from one district
to another, and who, in the past, have had
only a small field for promotion under the
present local limitations. Another very
important matter is that the system of
private patronage in filling the posts will
disappear. In short, the haphazard system
now in force will give place to a service
under central control.
It will be noted that Clause 7 of the Bill
-it will be found on page 6, line 22-excludes
persons with less than seven years' service,
and such persons will be required to satisfy
the Civil Service Commission as to their fitness before they can become established

officers, and generally their terms of admission to the Service will be prescribed by the
Ministry of Finance.
It will be noticed that the Bill contains no
provisions regarding existing clerks of the
Crown and Peace. There are two reasons for
this omission-firstly, because they have
special privileges under the Government of
Ireland Act, and, secondly, because as Local
Registrars of Title and Registration Officers
for Voters' Lists they are also Imperial servants. This latter circumstance also applies
in the case of future holders of the office of
the Clerk of the Crown and Peace, but some
mutual arrangement will be made between
the Imperial Government and our own which
will obviate any difficulty arising out of that.
I should like further to add that there is no
compulsion proposed to be put on any member of the staffs for whose benefit this Bill
is being introduced that he shall become a
member of the new service. It is purely
optional on his part whether he does so or
not. On the other hand, he will not
be accepted into the service unless
the Lord Chief Justice of Northern
Ireland certifies that he is a fit and
proper person to be SO accepted.
In order, however, to induce existing
officers to enter the new service, provision is
made in certain cases for an extension of the
age limits laid down in the Superannuation
Acts; provision is also made to enable a
gratuity to be awarded in the event of an
existing officer being required to retire by
reason of age or infirmity whilst being
ineligible for a pension. By a departmental
arrangement with the Treasury it is intended
that facilities for entering the Service will be
equally given to those clerks who are solely
employed on the reserved service of registration of title. Such clerks, while continuing to be members of the County Court Service, would, therefore, be regarded as on loan
to the registration of title side of the office.
I have explained that existing Clerks of
the Crown and Peace find no place in this
Bill, and accordingly as regards superannuation they continue to serve under their existing conditions. The Bill provides, however, that future Clerks of the Crown and
Peace shall be appointed by the Governor on
the recommendation of the Minister of Home
Affairs and shall be removable only by order
of the Governor made after consultation
with the Lord Chief Justice. As regards
superannuation, the Schedule to the Bill prescribes certain modifications of the Superannuation Acts for these officers. Briefly,
under the Bill the Clerk of the Crown and
Peace will receive a pension based on 1-45th
of salary and emoluments in respect of each
year of service in lieu of 1-60th as at present,
No pension is payable unless more than seven
years' service is involved. I should here explain that in agreeing to this concession due
regard has been paid to the fact that the
post of Clerk of the Crown and Peace is
normally filled by competent solicitors with
lengthy experience whose normal age at date
of entry must inevitably be far higher than
that of the normal entrant to the Civil Service. That is the reason for shortening the
period, in other words granting 1-45th
for each year's service instead of 1-60th
by way of retiring allowance. A similar
privilege applies under existing Statutes to
High Court Judges, County Court Judges
and to Registrars of County Courts in
England where similar considerations have
had to be taken into account. A further
modification has been introduced limiting
the retiring age of future appointees both to
the post of Clerk of the Crown and Peace
and to the Registrarship of Belfast to 72
years instead of holding the post till death
or voluntary retirement as is the case at the
present.
Turning now to the miscellaneous provisions contained in Part III of the Bill it
will be seen that Clause 10, which deals
with the making of Rules and Orders governing the County Court Service, amends the
County Court Officers and Courts (Ireland)
Act, 1877, by reducing from five to two the
number of County Court Judges whose concurrence is required in connection with the
making of such Orders. Hon. Members will
understand that while Ireland was all one
country the stipulation of the concurrence of
five county court judges was not unreasonable in any change of the rules which was
required to be made, but now with a much
smaller area it is thought two judges should
be qualified to give such concurrence. It is
reducing the number of the quorum in proportion to the reduction in the area and the
number of judges we have.
In Clause 12, which appears in italics--in
other words it is a money matter-provision
is made for the payment of travelling and
other expenses incurred by County Court
Criers. These officers are paid by County
Councils a very small annual allowance,
only running from £12 to £18, under an Act
of nearly one hundred years ago, and the
Clause has been introduced to remedy what
is considered to be a hardship, that is to say,
to provide them with a small allowance towards their out-of-pocket expenses. I trust
I have made it clear to hon. Members what
is intended to be enacted under this Bill. I
beg to move.

Oral Answers to Questions.
BANK OVERDRAFTS AND UNEMPLOY-
MENT.
of
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister
Finance what effect the higher charges on
overdrafts in Northern Ireland have on
unemployment, and what he proposes to do
to obtain for our business men the same
advantages as business men have in England.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Before attempting to reply to this
question, I propose to deal with the implication underlying it, namely, that charges on
overdrafts by banks operating in Northern
Ireland are higher than the charges for overdrafts in England. Considerable misunderstanding exists in regard to this matter,
which I am glad to have the opportunity of
clearing up. Comparison is usually effected
between the Bank of England Rate for Bills
and the Irish Banks' rate for overdrafts, but
this is misleading for the English Bank rate
for overdrafts is in excess of the published
official rate for bills. Assuming, however,
that the English Overdraft Rate-though
higher than the English Bill Rate-is less
than the Irish Overdraft Rate, it will be
found that, owing to variation in banking
practice in the two countries, the difference
is not appreciable. In England a
customer seeking an overdraft is nominally required to open a fixed Loan
Account for (say) a period of six months, and
he is charged at a fixed rate of interest on the
total sum throughout the entire period. In
Ireland no such separate Overdraft Account
exists or is presumed. It is an overdraft of
the customer's ordinary account, and the
interest charged is levied only on the actual
amount by which his account is overdrawn
from day to day. Any sums credited to his
account during the period of the overdraft
automatically reduce the amount on which
he pays interest, and this is not the case
under the English practice.
In regard to the two points actually raised
in the question, it would clearly not be
practicable to determine by way of question
and answer how far the present Bank Ratewhether Irish or English-affects unemployment, but it appears to me that employment is mainly affected by the price at which
goods can be produced and sold and in the
elements that make up price, the item in
respect of bank interest, or rather in
respect of the variation thereof, is inconsiderable. With regard to the last part of
the question, I cannot agree that any slight
advantage which the English business community may have over the business community in Northern Ireland in respect of
charges on overdrafts seriously hampers the
trade of this area, and it is quite evident
that it would be impracticable (quite
apart from its being ultra vires under the
Government of Ireland Act) for the Northern
Government to take any steps in the direction
indicated by the hon. Member.
Mr. KYLE: Will the Minister of Finance
make inquries as to the success of the
Municipal Bank in Birmingham, and if he
finds it is a success will he introduce legislation in this House to enable our Municipalities to have the same opportunities as
Birmingham has to-day?
Mr. POLLOCK: I have said in my answer
that any action on our part relating to banking arrangements would be ultra vires, and
although I have no objection to making the
inquiries my hon. Friend wishes, I can
assure him they will not achieve that result
which is in his mind.
Mr. KYLE: Do I understand from the
Minister of Finance that our Northern
Parliament would not have power to enable
Belfast to establish a Municipal Bank?
Mr. POLLOCK: That is so.
TRAINING OF ROMAN CATHOLIC
TEACHERS.
2. Sir ROBERT LYNN asked the Minister
of Finance whether the Northern Government has agreed to arrangements whereby
Roman Catholic National teachers must be
trained in St. Mary's Training College,
Hammersmith, London, instead of in the
Stranmillis Training College, Belfast, and
whether he can state what financial contribuition will be made to these students in
future.
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
23 APRIL 1925
of
Mr. POLLOCK: The Ministry
Education, acting in consultation with the
Ministry of Finance, has approached the
English Board of Education and the authorities of St. Mary's Roman Catholic Training
College, Hammersmith, with a view to an
arrangement under which Roman Catholic
men students may be trained in that college
for the position of teacher in Public Elementary Schools in Northern Ireland. It is
proposed that the arrangement with the
English Board of Education should take the
form of an Agency Service under Section 63
of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, and
that that Board should, on behalf of the
Ministry of Education, exercise the same
supervision over the training of students
from Northern Ireland as it does over the
training of teachers for service in schools
under the Board.
St. Mary's Roman Catholic Training
College, Hammersmith, is one of the training
colleges recognised by the English Board of
Education for the training of elementary
school teachers, and it is proposed that the
Northern Ireland students should be trained
therein, under the supervision of the Board
of Education, on a programme approved by
the Ministry of Education for Northern
Ireland. In conducting the tests at the termination of the course, on which depends the
certification of the students for employment
as teachers, the inspectors of the Ministry
would be associated with those of the Board
of Education.
It is proposed that the payment in respect
of Northern Ireland students who may be
trained at the Hammersmith Training
College, should be made by the Ministry of
Education to the English Board of
Education in the form of a capitation grant
equal in amount to that paid by the latter
Board-that is the English Board-to the
training colleges recognised by it for all
students resident therein. The amount of
this grant is at present fixed at £76 13s 4d
per annum for each student.
The corresponding capitation grant payable
out of the Parliamentary Vote in respect of
men students in Stranmillis Training
College is £75 per annum, excluding charges
in respect of capital expenditure. As the
large capital outlay for the provision and
equipment of an additional Hostel for proriding residential accommodation for the
students proposed to be sent to Hammersmith would under the proposed scheme be
avoided, it will be seen that the arrangement
would be an advantageous one from a financial point of view.
It it proposed that the scheme should
operate in the first instance for a period not
exceeding five years.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: May I ask my right
hon. Friend whether the teachers of other
denominations, Presbyterian or Church of
Ireland, would have the same privileges of
taking their courses in England or in Scotland?
Mr. POLLOCK: No. There is no difference
of opinion between the heads of the other
denominations to which my hon. Friend has
referred in regard to the training of teachers
for elementary schools. As a matter of fact
provision is being made at Stranmillis for
undertaking all the work in connection with
the training of these students.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Has my right hon.
Friend convinced himself that this does not
impinge on Section 5 of the Act of 1920?
Mr. POLLOCK: I am not prepared here
to offer any legal opinion on that subject,
but the Ministry is satisfied that they are
quite within their rights in adopting this
course in regard to these students.
SPECIAL CONSTABULARY AND
INSURANCE ACTS.
3. Sir ROBERT LYNN asked the Minister
of Finance whether the total loss to the
public owing to the delay on the part of the
Government in applying the provisions of the
Insurance Acts to the Special Constabulary
amounts to over £15,000, and whether he can
state what steps have been taken to prevent
similar losses in future?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I have been asked to reply
to this question. No delay on the part of
the Government such as suggested by the
hon. Member took place.
A ruling had been given by the Imperial
Government that the Special Constabulary
were exempt from insurance, and this ruling
was naturally accepted on the taking over
of the Special Constabulary from that
Government.
In March, 1922, the ruling of the Imperial
Government was challenged, and the
Ministry thereupon, in consultation with the
Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of
Labour, went into the whole question of the
application of the Insurance Acts to the
different ranks of the Special Constabulary.
As soon as the question could be authoritatively settled-and this was at a time when
the Ministry was actively engaged in
suppressing the widespread disturbances in
Northern Ireland, which were then at their
height-definite instructions were issued to
the Constabulary Authorities. The Ministry
was advised that it was liable under the
Statutes for the unpaid contributions
amounting approximately to the figure
mentioned by the hon. Member.
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
The instructions which have been issued
will obviate the necessity for such payments
in future.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Has my right hon.
Friend read the Report of the Auditor-
General, which states definitely that the loss
was due to the delay on the part of a
Government Department?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have read it, and
I have tried to explain the cause of it.
NUMBER OF NORTHERN IRELAND
CIVIL SERVANTS.
4. Sir ROBERT LYNN asked the Minister
of Finance, whether he can state the number
of Civil Servants now employed in Northern
Ireland; also the number of Civil Servants
the Government was compelled to take over
from Dublin under the provisions of the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920?
Mr. POLLOCK: The number of Civil
Servants employed in a permanent capacity
in the various Departments of the Government of Northern Ireland is, according to
the latest available figures, 1,051. In
addition to this number about 750 officers are
employed in an unestablished or temporary
capacity, more than one-half of whom are
connected with the administration of Unemployment Insurance whose salaries form a
charge on the Fund.
The hon. Member will, of course, appreciate that a considerable proportion of the
whole staff is engaged upon work for the
Imperial Government, the cost of which is
recouped by the Imperial Departments.
In consequence of the suspended operations
of the Civil Service Committee, which was
originally set up for the purpose, the allocation of staff was not completely carried out,
and although it was estimated that the staff
required to undertake the various duties
transferred to Northern Ireland would be
considerable, only 380 Civil Servants were
transferred to Belfast from Dublin, under
the provisions of the Government of Ireland
Act, 1920.
CONSTABULARY AS OFFICERS'
SERVANTS.
5. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of men of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, including the C1 Division, who are
engaged as private motor drivers, gardeners,
servants, and dog grooms by officers.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): No members of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary or Special Constabulary are employed as private
motor drivers, gardeners, or dog grooms.
Officers who are serving at the Constabulary
Depot and platoon officers in the Special Constabulary are permitted the part use of a
man to act as batman. All these are drawn
from the Special Constabulary. In the
Depot, and where gardens are attached to
barracks, the gardens are kept in a proper
state by fatigue parties or by voluntary
labour of the men.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask the right hon. Gentleman
is he aware that some of the Special Constabulary are used during the day for the care
of bulldogs and for driving private persons about?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, I am not aware
of it, and I think if the hon. Member would
give me any specific cases, and also give me
the names, instead of making general charges
against the Force, it would be more satisfactory.

GRANT FOR UPKEEP OF UNIFORM.
7. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether the Government contemplate giving volunteer officers of the C1
Special Constabulary a further grant for
the upkeep of uniform.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Officers of the C1
Constabulary receive an initial grant of £25
for the purchase of the necessary uniform
and equipment.
Officers who are employed full-time, and
who must necessarily make constant use of
their uniform, are entitled to a maintenance
allowance of £5 per annum. In the case of
other officers, however, as the occasions upon
which uniform is worn are limited to brief
periods of training and to occasional parades,
etc., the necessity for renewal of uniform
cannot arise for some time, and the question
of any additional grant in respect of uniform
does not, therefore, arise at present.

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I beg to move:
That an Independent Commission be set
up to investigate the whole question of
staffing of Government Departments and
expenditure in Northern Ireland.
I will not detain the House more than a
few moments in moving this motion that
stands in my name on the Paper, because
all the relevant facts dealing with this
question were discussed at great length a
week ago, and I am quite sure that if I spent
an hour or two hours of the House I would
find myself just much in the same position
as I was in a week ago, and that is, I would
not be able to convince my right hon.
Friends opposite, and my hon. Friends on
this side of the House would only be more
confirmed in their faith than they are.
Therefore it is not necessary for me to go into
details. I say this, and I say it to my right
hon. Friends opposite, if I have got no case
they should be as ready as I am to have it
investigated and have it discussed. I am
not going to express any opinion on the

and if that is done I do not see how anyone
can be prejudiced. Therefore, without going
into any details I beg to move.

Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I think the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Sir Robert
Lynn) deserves credit for bringing this forward. I may say that the citizens are very
anxious that this matter should be settled
up. Certain individuals outside are of the
opinion that things are not going the way
they ought to do. If this Commission were

is taking place. I would like to ask the

Spender is an expert in finance? This man
has been made Secretary of the Ministry of
Finance, and I question has he the ability
to hold that very high position. Charges are
also being made outside that certain friends
of hon. Members of this House hold very

The PRIME MINISTER: I shall be very
glad to answer the two points raised by the
hon. Member. I would like to explain to
the House and to those who trouble to read
our debates that in consequence of the resignation of our late permanent Secretary to
the Ministry of Finance I was faced, in consultation with my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Pollock), with the delicate task of appointing a successor, and I had to bear in mind
first of all the high qualifications necessary
for the head of the Civil Service in Ulster,
and in the second instance I had to bear in
mind how my right hon. Friend could best
be served with expert financial knowledge.
Now the Civil Service is a considerable body,
and the head of the Civil Service is not
necessarily the chief financial adviser to the
Ministry of Finance. In other words the
function of the head of the Civil Service is
to control, to guide, and advise the whole
Civil Service, to organise it department by
department, to secure the utmost efficiency
with the utmost economy. All this can be
done by a person who may not himself be
actually an expert on finance.
For a number of years I have been in constant touch with the British Treasury, and
I cannot recall one single instance when I
was interviewing the Chancellor of the Exchequer where the head of the Treasury was
brought in to advise on higher financial
matters. The head of the Treasury in Great
Britain occupies the position of controlling
and undertaking the duties which I have
just adumbrated with regard to the whole
of the Civil Service in Great Britain. The
real financial advisers are a different party,
and when I was considering the whole matter
I was most desirous not to bring in fresh
blood from outside but to appoint and if possible to promote inside our own Civil Service. I looked round and after considerable
and anxious consideration my right hon.
Friend and I settled upon the gallant Gentleman who has been mentioned by the right
hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. Henderson), and I am satisfied from my knowledge
that he is the right man in the right place.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) After all,
Colonel Spender's services to Ulster cannot
be valued. No one knows, except our late
leader, Lord Carson, and myself, the gallant
services that gallant gentleman has performed in the interests of the Ulster people.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) But I am
not for one moment suggesting that, because
of his services, or because of the great sacrifices he made on behalf of Ulster, sacrifices
almost costing him his whole position in the
British Army-I am not going back to those
days he is the proper man for this position,
but on pure merit alone. After all a man
cannot have passed the schools, cannot have
passed through the Staff College and been
graded G.S.O.1, cannot have been very high
in the ranks of the Artillery, and
cannot have won the D.S.O. during
the Great War without having been recog-
Supply-
Committee.
23 APRIL 1925
nised by others as having special ability for
organising and for the command of men.
That branch of the Treasury is exactly the
branch with which Colonel Spender is best
fitted to deal. Honourable, upright, anxious
to serve his country, always straining every
nerve and working hard and long hours in
order that everything may go smoothly with
the machinery that carries Ulster along-we
could not have made a better appointment,
and I feel confident that in time hon. Members will be thankful that we have at the
head of the Civil Service in Ulster such a
distinguished gentleman, and one who is so
able in himself to fill the office.
Then I turn to the second point which the
hon. Member (Mr. T. Henderson) raised.
He said it would allay the feeling throughout Ulster, and especially in Belfast, if some
form of inquiry were instituted and a report
made in order to show the outside public that
there was no extravagance in the running of
the Government Departments. The House
has learned from my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Pollock) that the Government are prepared
to take the steps which he has announced
to the House, but I think I might point out
that the city of Belfast has not yet grasped
the great advantage it is to it to have the
Civil Service in its midst instead of at a distance. I know quite well that certain people
run up against a bunch-I call them that in
no offensive term-of Civil Servants with
their heads together, or having lunch somewhere, and people point and say "Oh! look
at those Civil Servants in the corner there."
I know. All this sort of thing reaches me.
All those Civil Servants were in Dublin.
They earned their salaries there, the Income
Tax was deducted from their salaries there,
and went to other sources. the rents they
paid for their houses went to Dublin people,
the shopkeepers of Dublin all gained from
their spending their salaries and everything
in that city. Now what has happened is that
these Civil Servants have been moved in a
body from Dublin and their numbers made
up to what is considered necessary to carry
on the Departments, with the consequence
that practically the whole of the salaries of
Civil Servants are spent in the city of Belfast and the surrounding neighbourhood,
Northern Ireland collects the Income Tax on
their salaries, the shopkeepers get all the
money they have to spend for household
necessities, and also the rents they pay go
to the Belfast landlords instead of elsewhere.
In other words the city should be thankful
to have the Civil Service living in its midst,
spending its money rather than in some
distant town where Belfast could not get any
gain from it.
I think there has been a considerable
amount of misunderstanding and misconception; in other words, that people thought
that these Civil Servants in the North here
were in addition to, and that the cost of
maintaining them was in addition to what
was the normal fact before the separation of
Northern and Southern Ireland, and before
Home Rule was granted to us here. It may
be that the people can complain about ever
having the Government established here at
all. That is a different question, but once
having a Parliament and Government set
up in Ulster then Parliament and Ulster
have to carry on, and, in order to carry on,
the numbers, pay and everything else pertaining to the Civil Service are on as close
as possible parallel lines with the Departments across the water. I do not object, and

With regard to the question of an assistant

quite aware of the situation. The Cabinet

I can conscientiously say to the House that
I do not believe any Department could be

had an inside view of some of the work that
goes on they would think these Estimates

at all events we could not make a bigger cut

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I beg to move that
this amount be reduced by a sum of £5,000.
You will notice that the nett cost of this
House is £26,172. If Members will go through
the different Departments carefully they will
see that this is a very costly item. There
was a small decrease in the last Vote as the
Prime Minister pointed out, but there is a
nett increase in this Vote of £588. I do submit to Members that the cost of this Parliament is much higher than it ought to be.
I have objected all along, as my hon. Friends
know, to the scale on which we have been
running this Parliament. After all, we forget that we are a small provincial assembly,
very important no doubt for the work that
we have to do, but still we cannot afford to
run this Parliament of ours on the same
scale as the Imperial Parliament, with all
the wealth, tradition and history that it has
got behind it. I suggest in this Amendment
a reduction of 25 per cent. I think in these
times a reduction of 25 per cent. is not too
much to ask the House to make. We hear
a good deal in Parliament and other places
about making gestures on this, that and the
other. Would not it be a nice thing for us to
make a good, fine gesture of this sort to the
public who sent us here by reducing this
Estimate by 25 per cent. as I propose? I beg
to move.

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move the reduction of
the Estimate for the Ministry of Agriculture
by £100. I do so in order to call attention to
the refusal of the Minister of Agriculture
to have adequate representation of labourers
on the various consultative and advisory
committees established by the Ministry and
also to call attention to his refusal to set
up wages boards for the governance of the
wages of agricultural labourers.
In moving this reduction in the Estimate
for the Ministry of Agriculture, I do so in
no narrow pettifogging spirit, because I recognise, as everybody must, that agriculture
is the vital industry of our land, employing
more workers than our linen and shipbuilding trades combined, and I realise that the
desired end is to have the maximum number
of acres under tillage possible in order that
more of the foodstuffs necessary for Great
Britain might be grown in our land. It is
Supply-
Committee.
23 APRIL

said we have the most fertile soil in the
world. but I do not see any proposals in the
Estimate to follow the lead given by the Free
State so far as the development of the sugarbeet industry is concerned. They there
propose to establish a factory and to
subsidise this particular industry. I think
our Ministry ought to follow that very
admirable example, particularly in view of
the cheap foodstuffs such as potatoes that
are being imported from the Continent and
Canada, that is, unless the Ministry discover
another way of preventing them from coming
in. These imports are not remunerative to
our farming community, and, consequently,
I think the Ministry should take the
necessary steps to establish this sugar beet
industry.
The agricultural labourer, whom I referred
to a moment or two ago, is the hardest
worked man in any industry. He works
from daylight to dark, and very often after
dark. He has no protection from unscrupulous employers as his union, the hon.
Member for the University (Dr. Morrison)
will be pleased to learn, is not as strong as
We would like to see it. Therefore, he is not
protected from unscrupulous employers. He
gets no holidays except in rare instances,
nothing but hard, grinding toil from year's
end to year's end with low, inadequate wages.
The small farmer is also a very hard-worked
man, but he has the advantage of feeling
that he is working for himself, and he has
also the advantage of a day at the market
town with all the jollification that may
mean. These are relaxations the agricultural
labourers seldom have. I am glad to have
this opportunity of rising to express the regret that we on these benches feel for the
grave lack of consideration that is so constantly shown by the Government-probably
I should confine myself to the Minister of
Agriculture for the agricultural workers in
Ulster. Each year when the Estimates for
agriculture are presented a tremendous
amount of time is spent, no doubt very
wisely, in discussing potatoes, poultry, pigs,
fax, etc., but not one word is said about the
agricultural labourer and his position. When
I mention flax I may say it seems to me we
have not altered in the last hundred years
in our methods, and surely in these days of
science and scientific research we should be
able to make more perfect the production of
fax which is so essential in our linen
industry.
In making myself familiar with all that
took place in regard to the Estimates for
Agriculture I read in Hansard for the last
four years the debates on the Estimates so
far as agriculture was concerned, and I find
that everyone is prepared to pay high tribute
to the importance of agriculture in our
national life. So they spent this time discussing breeds of cattle, whether they like
goats or not, and other matters of firstclass importance no doubt, but they have
never yet discussed the importance of the
men who work on the land and who bring
all these schemes to fruition. They never so

and Holland proves it, that the labourer, the

at first, but he has the knowledge, and in

whole problem of agriculture and a very
limited point of view in regard to the

Committees, and we denounce that attitude
as vehemently as possible.
Next, I want to refer to the refusal of
the Ministry of Agriculture to set up Wages
Boards for the governance of the wages of
agricultural labourers. As this House is
aware, such Wages Boards were first set
up in Great Britain in 1917 by the Coalition
Government, and they were scrapped in
direct violation of the pledges of the Government. They were not re-established until the
Labour Government came into power in
1924. It is true that owing to the fact that
Labour was a minority Government they
were not able to pass the kind of Act they
had hoped for, but at any rate Wages Committees were again established and workers
wages are fixed by this means, and
workers themselves have equal representation
on the Boards with the farmers. Everyone
is prepared to admit that the wage of the
agricultural labourer is a scandal, that it is
impossible for him and his family to live
decently on it, but apparently the Government are prepared to simply sit in idle
fashion, and do nothing. We insist that the
only way to tackle this question, and the only
way to secure anything like a bare existence
the

23 APRIL 1925
CLASS V. No. 2.
AGRICULTURAL SERVICES.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £57,162 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st of March, 1926, to defray
the expenses of the Ministry of Agriculture
in respect of Agricultural Education and Research, Improvement of Live Stock, Agricultural Development, Agricultural Statistics.
and Afforestation, including sundry Grants
in Aid and special capital expenditure under
14 and 15 Geo. V, c. 13, s. 1 (N.I.).”
Mr. ARCHDALE: Agricultural Research
is divided into three divisions, and I have
to thank the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Sir Robert Lynn) for the many excellent
articles which have appeared in his paper
helping research. I believe myself that
nothing can be done without research, and
plenty of research, and those articles show
clearly the advantages to be gained by research. I must apologise for not answering
the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
William McMullen) on the last Vote. I
would just like to say that the Wages Boards
about which he spoke were established when
there was a fixed price in England for
farmers' produce. The Wages Boards were
established in fulfilment of the Prime
Minister's promise that the labourers should
get a proper wage while the farmer got a
proper price for his produce. Then they did
away with the prices in England and also
with the Wages Boards at the same time. I
quite agree that they have been established
again in England since, but I was four
years a member of a Wages Board in Dublin,
and my experience of them is that they do
not help the labourer at all. As regards
labourers coming to our consultative committees, with every due regard for the
labourer 1 cannot see how he can get away
from his farm and come up to these towns
and be of use to us as much as the farmer
who has the whole control of the land and
the cattle and everything else. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I am afraid unless some
things change very much we will not be able
to have labourers on our consultative committees.
As regards flax, we have done a considerable amount. Linen research has produced
flax which is about 40 per cent. higher in its
produce, and so have we in our Ministry
also. As regards £1,000 to the Farmers'
Union we find that the Farmers' Union are
our best friends all round the country. The
Organisation Society is a good helper too, but
it is not able to get together meetings to hear
lectures as the Farmers' Union do. We did
propose to give some help to the Ulster Agricultural Organisation Society, but when you
have only a certain amount it is like splitting
cloth when you have only enough to make a
pair of trousers and making trousers with
one leg and taking the rest for a coat, so we
gave it to the society which is the most use to
us.
Sugar beet requires an enormous amount
of capital. We have gone carefully into all
matters in connection with sugar beet. Only
this morning I met a Dutchman and had a
long conversation with him about starting a
factory to manufacture sugar beet in this
country. Sugar beet is not nearly as profitable as potatoes. Practically nowhere except
in the best lands of Northern Ireland could
sugar beet be grown. I believe sugar beet
cannot be, in fact, profitably started
in Northern Ireland. First of all about
a quarter of a million would be required
capital to build
a factory and
get the work going. What is to be
done in a short time when the subsidy
is done away with at the end of ten years?
At the present time there are 45,000,000
centals of sugar in foreign countries over and
above the quantity required for this country.
If that goes on what is to be done? I do not
think that sugar beet offers any possible way
of making money or helping the labourers or
anything else in Northern Ireland.

many experiments to improve the position

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Archdale]
farmer doing that. In my county they are
up as long as they have daylight working
They are all small farmers there and certainly they work about three times as hard as
any labourer. I may say that I have never
yet had any bother at all with the labourers
in my county.
As regards research, we are going in for
chemical nutrition. Dr. Robertson is the
head of it and he is one of the best scientists,
I suppose, in Ireland. He has saved enormous sums of money to the farmers by giving
them properly balanced food for their cattle.
He has also encouraged the production of
baby beef, which has been of great help. We
find there has been a tremendous expansion
in that among the farmers and dairies in
all parts of the country. Instead of keeping
on cattle until they are three years old, they
sell them now at about 18 months. We also
go in for analytical work to see that they get
pure seed and pure food. We dealt last year
with 2,200 samples of agricultural food and
seeds. In flax diseases our seed testing is
useful. The seed sent to our seed testing
division has more than doubled in the last
year, and 50 per cent. of this is sent by the
farmers, and in fact all the seedsmen in
Northern Ireland send their seed up to be
tested.
a
We have a place for animal diseases at
Stormont, where the hon. Member for West
Belfast can come and see the eggs being laid
in fact. We have increased the production
of eggs from 110 per head to 185, and that
means an enormous sum of money-a million
practically of money to the people of this
country. The animal research is there also.
In that Stormont division we have established three world's records for hens. We
have beaten the whole world. We established
a record for a pen of six White Wyandotte
pullets; we established record for one
White Wyandotte pullet and we established
a record of eggs per bird for a whole
section of 138 birds, beating America and
all other countries. Experiments are going
on for costing and quantities. Cambridge
University has just had an experiment of
that sort. They had very interesting experiments during last year. They tried it on 14
farms and they proved that heavy land lost.
Medium farms were fairly satisfactory.
Light lands also gave a profit. Heavy land
lost 4.6 per cent. of the capital invested.
They tried dairying to show whether it
gained or lost. Feeding cattle lost 16.3 per
cent of the capital invested. Dairy farms
gained 25.3 per cent.; pig feeding lost 24.8
per cent.; sheep gained 16 per cent. and
poultry gained 118.8 per cent, so it shows
what the ladies of this country can do if they
tackle it in the various districts.
We are going in for agricultural education
as much as we can. We have the North-
West School at Strabane where we hope to
grow all the new varieties of seed we raise
at Stormont-grow them there until they are
in bulk enough to be issued to the farmers
in the country. There also is the housewives
division. The numbers are full up and there
is a long waiting list. In the Ulster Dairy
School at Cookstown where the girls are
taught housewife work we are full up and
have a waiting list there also. In the Greenmount School which is in place of the agricultural school at Glasnevin, Dublin, we have
made every improvement. We are making
it into an agricultural college and establishing a horticultural place there. There are
30 students there now and we have accommodation for 50.
As regards the improvement of livestock
we urge on the farmers milk-recording as
much as possible, and certainly I am glad
to say farmers are taking to it. In 1921
when we began there were only six
associations and 1,244 cows. In 1925 there
are 42 associations and over 9,000 cows. To
show the advantage of that I happened to
come upon a report in a paper where it was
stated at a meeting of the Omagh Society
the other day that they had increased the
average per cow 138 gallons in four years.
A great many societies have increased very
much more. It shows the advantages of milkrecording. In the old way people were not
able to tell that their cows were properly
used.
We are bringing in black-faced rams to
put in mountain districts. We have placed
84 rams among the farmers, and they are
getting about double the prices for wool in
those districts that they had been getting.
There was great talk during my election
about bulls. We have got 6,100 bulls licensed
now for the various counties.
As to the poultry industry which I spoke
about before, the value of it to this country
is a great deal more than people think. Last
year we exported 300,000,000 eggs, that is,
£1,900,000 worth. We exported £542,000
worth of poultry, while the home consumption amounted to £613,400 worth of
eggs and £500,000 worth of chickens. That
means £3,555,400 in one year for all poultry
products. That could be nearly doubled if we
got a proper amount of attention paid to
the poultry instructress whom, we send over
the country. We got a temporary experiment
grant of £54,000, to be spent in temporary
work during the next four years. Of
course we have got extra bulls and rams,
we have additional instructors, and we are
paying more for helpers than we did before.
We are also providing £250 for experiments.
There has been a trial in England of a

Agriculture in establishing a record of the

being familiar with their wants and their

neat cottages. The House generally does not
know that we have scattered over every
Union perhaps three or four hundred houses
built under the old regime, whereby labourers
have half an acre of ground and four rooms
in their dwellings for 2s. 6d. a week,
and the improvement in their status since
they got those houses has been
I have always been impressing on these people the importance of
cleanliness and cheerfulness. It is amazing
to see how scrupulously clean these new and
modern houses are in many cases. They
have their little plots and gardens, with
rambler roses climbing over the windows and
on the gates and hedges. It is a delightful
thing. Now, in order to encourage those
people we gave prizes, and so far as I know
those prizes have all been stopped. I do not
see why when we are giving prizes for agricultural shows and things like that, in
which the farmer is deeply interested, we
should not also give prizes for the best
cottage in every union, substantial prizes
that would help and encourage the occupiers,
and I think these people should have a voice
in this matter.
With regard to the farmers, there are
many questions that they have got to determine. They want to know how to apply the
discoveries of science to farming. The farming industry is faced with foreign competition that is killing it, and that is the real
cause of all the poverty and suffering that
the agricultural classes are enduring at the
present time. Free Trade-everybody knows
it-and you know who are the supporters of
Free Trade in this country. I will not go into
that matter now, but it is necessary for the
farmer to take advantage of every discovery
that science has made and to apply it to his
farm. It is necessary for the labourer to get
a decent house and to be encouraged to
brighten it, and to bring about better times
when the labourer will have decent wages
and a decent house, and be a prosperous and
happy member of the community. That is
what we all desire to see. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).

who have any experience of agricultural
work,
from
apart altogther
the Wages
Board, realise that unscrupulous farmers

I should like to impress upon the Ministry

had got more time at his disposal than the

him. The hon. Member for the University
Supply-

to receive at the end of the week for his

I regret to say that the agricultural
labourers in Ireland, both in Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland, have been driven
to Canada, the United States, Australia, and
indeed all parts of the world, simply because
they are unable to obtain at home sufficient
to induce them to remain in this country.
That is a very serious state of affairs. While
we are making all these experiments in connection with hens, sheep, and cattle of all
kinds, I think it would be advisable to give
some consideration to the question of
the
agricultural labourer. Take him
into consideration in regard to the
fixing of wages. Agricultural wages
are very low in Northern Ireland at the
moment. Experience in Great Britain
showed that the standard of living amongst
agricultural labourers fell so low that it
became absolutely essential to restore the
Wages Board there. If any consideration is
going to be given to the agricultural
labourers, who form the largest part of the
community in Northern Ireland, I believe
that some regard should be had to the conditions under which they work as much as
in the case of the town workers.
From my knowledge of Irish history, 1
know that nearly all improvements that
have come to the countryside through the
British Parliament-I do not know a great
deal about agriculture, but I am speaking of
workers generally-principally came through
physical force movements of one kind or
another. I would not like to see the standard
of the agricultural labourer in Northern
Ireland fall so low that he would have to
resort to measures that were not constitutional. Simply because attention was not
given in time to the grievances of the people
in the past resort was had to physical force.
I do not suggest that in Northern Ireland,
or even in Southern Ireland, the agricultural labourer is likely to resort to physical
violence at the present time. We have
heard from an hon. Member behind that
they are not prepared to go on strike; they

attention to the position of the agricultural
labourer. Let us give him decent wages.
The housing conditions have improved

the Wages Board, in order to give the
labourer a higher wage and a better standard of living than he enjoys at the present
time.
I think the fewer of these people that
come to overcrowd the towns the better.
The situation in that respect is already
bad enough. If the countryside were
made more attractive for the agricultural labourer, we would probably
have less unemployment in the towns.
The Minister of Labour and those who form
the Cabinet know what that would mean; it
would mean that the people would be kept in
the countryside, on the farms. If that had
been done the industrial situation would not
be so bad as it is at the present moment.
You would have less unemployment, you
would have fewer people drawing the unemployment benefit, and you would save
from the point of view that a person, instead

on the Minister of Agriculture the advisability of having consultations with the
labourers on all questions affecting his conditions and on agriculture generally, and to
ask him, if he possibly can, to restore the
Wages Board, in order that the agricultural
labourer may have a higher standard of
living than he enjoys at the present time.

There are three specific heads under which

to be fixed on a permanent basis. Their
salaries will be paid direct instead of through
the medium of a lump sum allowance to the
Clerk of the Crown and Peace. One proper
question which was asked was as to what
would be the probable extra cost to the State
under the provisions of this Bill. The resultant immediate increase to be met by the
State on the basis of the proposals which
are embodied in the Estimate for the County
Court Service is approximately £800 per
annum, but the fact that many of the officers
will be placed on the minimum of the scale
means that the full increase will not be felt
for some years to come. It is thought that
by means of a gradual increasing charge, the
financial effect of the increments will ultimately amount to not more than £1,000
annually.
In addition, these officers will, of course,
now be entitled to receive pensions and gratuities on retirement, but a charge under this
head will not be felt for some years to come.
This explanation will meet some of the comments made by hon. Members during the
Second reading of this Bill and will I hope
satisfy them that the net cost is not excessive having regard to the rather unsatisfactory conditions of service which prevailed
before. It will now offer a prospect of a
career to these men, instead of being, as they
were in the past, underpaid and really in a
blind alley so to speak.
Before passing on to the second head I

criticism raised yesterday, and I beg to move

The PRIME MINISTER : Tuesday, the
28th, will be occupied with the consideration
of the remaining stages of the three Bills at
present before the House, namely the Civil
Pensions Bill, the Administrative Provisions
Bill, and the County Officers and Courts
Bill. It is hoped that the two Bills at present in the Senate-the Public Health (Milk
Regulations) Bill and the Charitable Loan
Societies Bill-will then be available for introduction in this House. On Wednesday the

of the Pharmacy and Poisons Bill, and to
devote the remainder of the day, if necessary,

for the Ministry of Commerce on this day.
