Committee.
30 APRIL 1925
(Mr.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR
Andrews): I feel that it is only when introducing the annual Estimates of the Ministry
of Labour that I have the opportunity of
making a general statement as regards the
work which the Department exists to perform. On this occasion we have with us
several new Members, and I think I shall,
therefore, as carefully as possible explain to
hon. Members how wide the ramifications of
the Ministry of Labour are and how closely
they are associated with the well-being of our
people. We administer all those great Acts
of Parliament which safeguard the interests
of our working classes from the day that they
enter employment until they leave it. These
Acts are first of all the Unemployment
Insurance Acts, which apply to and affect
over 260,000 persons; our Health Insurance
Act, which affects over 330,000 persons; the
Trade Boards Act, which affects rather over
62,000 persons, and our Factory Acts,
Truck Acts, and Workmen's Compensation
Acts, which really affect our entire community. In addition to that the Department
administers our relief schemes throughout
the whole of Northern Ireland, and the importance of these works is well known to the
Committee.
But the most important duty, I think, that
we are called upon to perform is to endeavour
to preserve industrial peace, so far as is
possible, by encouraging friendly co-opera-.
tion between our employers and their
workers. For convenience the Department
is divided into four branches. First of all,
there is the industrial relations section
which deals with labour disputes, administers our Trade Boards Acts, our
Factory and Truck Acts, and Workmen's
Compensation Acts. Secondly, we have our
Insurance Department which deals with the
two Insurance Acts, to which I have already
referred, and which so closely affect the
interests of the workers of Northern Ireland.
Then we have the Inspection branch, the
importance of which I am sure will be readily
recognised, because there is no use in this
Parliament or any other Parliament passing
Acts if they are to become a dead letter, and
our Inspection branch exists to see that Acts
of Parliament in Northern Ireland are complied with by all those who are called upon
by those Acts to do so. Then we have the
Finance branch which is responsible for disbursing the large sum of somewhat over
£3,000,000 a year and doing all the accounting work in connection with those
disbursements, which hon. Members know
are mainly in small sums, and therefore
require to be dealt with with very great
care.
If hon. Members will refer to Sub-head A
of this Vote which is on page 79 they will see
the sum set cut for salaries, wages and
allowances is £161,780.
That sum at first
sight, I admit, looks substantial. It is satisfactory to note that there is a small reduction of £1,470 as compared with last year, but
it is quite easy to calculate that after all it
is only five per cent. of the total sum disbursed by the Department, and from that
viewpoint I think it can be looked upon as
very reasonable as an administrative charge.
After all, the sum which the Exchequer is
called upon to bear is a comparatively small
one, because if hon. Members refer to Subhead V they will see that receipts appropriated in aid which are paid almost entirely
by our Unemployment Fund amount to
£117,405, so as I have said the difference is,
comparatively speaking, a small sum which
the Exchequer bears. This Estimate at first
sight would appear to show an increase for
the year of £25,085, but I think it is fair to
deduct from that sum the increase in nonrecurring capital expenditure of £10,200,
which is the increased sum provided this
year over last year for our new Centra!
Employment Exchange. In addition to that,
hon. Members will observe that the
appropriation in aid amounts to £18,150 less
than last year. Of course, that figure is
really settled by statute. It is the contribution towards administrative expenses from
the income derived from the contributions
paid by workers, employers and the State,
and is a matter over which the Department
has really no control. If these two sums are
added together it will be found that they
amount to £28,350, and if the £25,085 increase is deducted from that it will show
that there really is an actual saving on the
year of £3,265 in connection with this Vote.
I think hon. Members will be interested to
know that 90 per cent. of our administrative
expenditure is due to our insurance schemes.
For all the other services which we administer there is only an expenditure of ten
per cent., so that if the suggestion is made
that there is extravagance of any kind, which
I do not admit, it will have to be looked for
in my opinion in connection with these
insurance schemes. I would, however, like
to inform the Committee at the same time
that our Unemployment Insurance Acts
actually absorb rather over 74 per cent of the
total cost. I have had a comparison made
between the cost here and the cost in Great
Britain, and I venture to think that it is
highly satisfactory, because while the
administrative cost in Great Britain is 8.1
per cent., in Northern Ireland it is 8.6 per
cent. The trifling difference, of course, is
due to the fact that we are a smaller unit,
and necessarily the percentage of expenditure is somewhat more, but after all, as I
have stated, it is really only trifling.
I have no hesitation in saying that my
opinion, for what it is worth, is that the
Ministry of Labour is run as a business
undertaking and along business lines, and I
can assure hon, Members that we are con-
Supply-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Andrews]
tinually keeping before us economy coupled
with efficiency. There is no use in beginning.
I think, to cheesepare unduly in connection with the administration of Acts of
Parliament which so closely affect the wellbeing of our people as do the Acts of Parliaments which the Ministry of Labour
administers, because it is all-important
that those who are depending on
Unemployment benefit or Health Insurance
benefit for their very existence when
they are out of employment, either through
depression in trade or through ill-health,
should get what the law entitles them to get
as expeditiously as possible. Therefore, an
efficient, able and sufficient staff is necessary
to ensure that that shall be so, and it is gratifying to me to feel that complaints as regards
delay in the payment of benefit, no matter
what kind that benefit may be, are very much
fewer than they were when this Parliament
came into existence.
I say that an important State Department
such as this is run by many willing and able
workers, some of them greater and some of
them lesser, but each of them entitled to feel
that he is part of a great machine and provided he does his allotted duty faithfully
and well is entitled to claim his share of
any credit that may be earned. On the other
hand, charges to be made as regards extravagance or inefficiency should be levelled against
the man who for the time being is the
political head of the Department and who is
alone answerable to Parliament.
In conclusion, I would just like to say that
my Department continues to be deeply
indebted to those public-spirited persons
throughout the whole of Northern Ireland
who are co-operating with us and helping us
to carry on the work of the Department.
I would not like to end without saying that
it is very gratifying to me and to my
associates at the Ministry of Labour to feel
that the employers and workers in Northern
Ireland are taking more advantage of our
Employment Exchanges than ever they did
before, and that both sections of our
industrial community are co-operating in
the most friendly and helpful way with my
Department in every possible line of our
work. I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move a reduction
of £2,000 in the Estimate as presented. I do
so to call the attention of this Committee to
a fund that needs the protection of this
Committee. It is a fund established for the
benefit of the industrial classes. It is contributed to by employer, by employee, and
by the State, and for that reason I think
there should be no burden placed upon this
fund that it is very well able to do without.
After hearing the Minister of Labour's outline of the work of the various Departments
I do not wish to say one word against him as
the head of his Department, but I do want
to counsel him-if I am able enough to advise him-in regard to certain units of his
Department wherein economy can be brought
about. I find on going over the Estimate
that the rent of the various Exchanges when
they are combined total a very decent rum.
At the time when the Minister of Labour
(Mr. Andrews) was looking out for Exchanges the profiteers were on the warpath
and were claiming the highest possible
figures for the buildings the Minister wanted
to get to carry on his work. I refer to one
case with which I am quite conversant,
namely the Mountpottinger Y.M.C.A. The
Mountpottinger Y.M.C.A. has done very well
out of the Unemployment Fund in regard to
rent. I believe that not very long ago the
Minister was compelled to have a new entrance to that Exchange, and there was a
very large sum put on to the rent. I believe
anything from £7 10s. to £10 per week was
put on the rent for that entrance or outlet
for applicants to sign at the Y.M.C.A. Of
course, the figures I give you are not accurate, but anything from £7 10s. to £10 was
the cost of the new entrance to the Y.M.C.A.
I agree that it was necessary, but I do not
think the figure the Y.M.C.A. is charging
the Government is a decent one.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Sure you
wanted a new Exchange there the other day.
Mr. BEATTIE: Yes, I was asking for an
Exchange in Ballymacarrett, and I think it
is more necessary to-day than ever it was,
but I am not asking to go to the class of
landlord to whom the Minister of Labour
has gone in the past so that he may be robbed
and have every drop of blood sucked out of
him. I believe it is the duty of the landlord
class to let their buildings at decent rents
and not at the exorbitant figures they are
charging for the buildings we are in. Turning over the Estimate I find employees who
are contributors to this fund, and I am surprised that in this Department employees
are not treated on an equality with other Departments. I would have been the first to
say that the best treatment would have been
accorded to employees in the Minister of
Labour's Department, but I am sorry and
surprised on looking over the Estimate to
find that they are not.
Some hon. Members opposite always tackle
the big fellows first, and go for the high
figures, but I, being a layman and a working
class representative, am coming right down
to bedrock. I ask the Minister of Labour, and
I hope he will answer, why the cleaners in
the Exchanges are not entitled to the same
consideration as the cleaners in other Departments. Is a Labour Exchange not

If justice were meted out to the contributors to the fund I would have no complaint to-day. Just to give the Minister of
Labour (Mr. Andrews) a little inside knowledge let me quote a case of which I am aware,
and which only happened last week. A lady

continuously became unemployed. She was
two weeks unemployed when she was disallowed benefit for not genuinely seeking
work. After twenty-one years' continuous
work she becomes unemployed for two weeks,
and is turned down for not genuinely seeking work. By whom? Not by the Rota
Committee, but by the Minister's representative, who is being paid at the rate of
two guineas per hour and a quarter out of

Minister of Labour may be surprised, but

haps every day if I were there to see.
happened to be there on this occasion and

I am not raising any question about the

problem, as those who live in the country
districts especially know. Take the scutching
trade as an example. There you have got
an industry which certainly does not give
employment, except in very rare instances,
for more than six months in the year. When
workers are in this particular seasonal
occupation they are insured persons, liable
to pay contributions, but probably when they
cease to be employed in that seasonal trade,
unless they get into another seasonal trade
they are not liable to pay contributions.
Would I be justified as a trustee of the fund
to give exactly the same benefits to those
who are contributors to the fund only part
of the year as to those who contribute every
week of the fifty-two that they are employed?
But I may say this: In these seasonal trades
the workers get standard benefit to the extent to which they are entitled by
their contributions just the same as
the workers in any other branch of industry
do, and it is only s regards extended, or
free benefit, as it is called, that they are
dealt with at all differently. If my hon.
Friend will come some day to the Ministry
of Labour I am prepared to lay all the cards
on the table, and explain the position to him
from both standpoints, and I think I may be
able to satisfy him.

That raised a very interesting question as

is. We always advocate the telling of the

There is just one other matter that I want
to draw the Minister's attention to-the fees
for certifying surgeons. I would like to see
that item eliminated, in consequence of this
fact. A friend of mine, another trade union
official, the secretary of the National Union
of Vehicle Builders in Belfast, wrote to the
Ministry of Labour asking for a copy of the
certificate of one of these certifying surgeons.
He made that application because one of the
members of his society was suffering from
lead poisoning incurred in the course of his
employment. He was refused a copy of the
certificate; for what reason I do not know.
I think it is rather hard lines that a workman should be denied compensation on the
ground that he cannot get that certificate
from the Ministry of Labour, despite the
fact that the Minister of Labour pays the
certifying surgeons £25 for giving those
certificates. This worker cannot get his
certificate.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Why?
Mr. KYLE: I have been informed that
those certificates are of a confidential nature,
but I cannot for the life of me see why it
should be refused in the case of a workman
who contracts lead poisoning in the course
of his employment. He goes to his own
doctor who certifies that he is suffering from
lead poisoning. When he goes before another
surgeon he cannot get a certificate, with the
result that the man's compensation is held
up. I think the hon, and right hon. Members opposite will agree. I would just like
to finish by paying a compliment to the
Minister of Labour, because of this fact,

Andrews) knows quite well I am not in the
habit of flattering-but on the ground that
he has adopted a very desirable practice, and
I hope that the other Ministers in turn will
follow it.

(Mr. Kyle) and West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen).

his text, that no unnecessary burden should

a great many cases of fraud in connection
with these funds and the receipt of the unemployment dole. I think it is obvious to any
man who looks at the figures, where a sum
of £45,000 weekly is distributed to workers,
that there must be a serious number of cases
of fraud. With the object of satisfying
myself about this matter, which I think is
important, I went to the Minister of Labour,
and I find that he has had 70 or 80 cases of
prosecutions for fraud. What I want to
point out is that a worker in getting the
unemployment dole by fraud is injuring
honest labour in the first instance. The man
who is shirking and slacking and getting the
Idole when he is not entitled to it is an imposition on his class. He is living as a
parasite on the contributions paid by his
fellow workers. He is disloyal to his employer and he is disloyal to the State.

Mr. KYLE: Would the hon. Member state,
if the man is not employed, how is he wronging his employer.
Dr. MORRISON: He is injuring his class.
So far as I see that point is pointless. I would
like to mention a case that came before me.
I like these concrete cases. I happen to be

I believe I am not justified in stating what

Grand Jury had dealt with this case, which
amazed me, and amazed every member of
the Grand Jury, I went into Court to hear

a man who confessed to having defrauded

was in receipt of a pension of 16s. a week,

refused the

and ungrudgingly is also taken into consideration. I have sat with the Chairmen of

found them doing difficult work, in my judgment, honestly and fairly in nine cases out
of ten. I would go further and say that in
99 cases out of 100 both the employers and
representatives of Labour agreed with the
Chairman. Cases may happen from time to
time, such as those mentioned by the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle), where

eriticism, but to say that they are wilfully
done or done because the Chairman belongs to
a particular class of the community is a remark hardly worthy of the hon. Member,
and I do not think it is fair or just criticism.
These trained lawyers, I find, can sift evidence and can explain the regulations and
Acts of Parliament in a way that makes
them entitled to whatever little fee they
receive for their work from time to time.
It has been stated by the hon. Member for the
University (Dr. Morrison) that in connection
with this fund three parties contribute, namely,
the State, the employer, and the worker.
That is perfectly true, but what is the State?
The State only gets the money from the taxpayer, and the fact of the matter is that,
if you make the comparison, two-thirds
the money comes from the taxpayers, who
of
will include the employer, who is already

the representative of a class that is sometimes greatly abused-the employer class
Mr. KYLE: They look well on it.

other folk look thriving too, very vigorous

as a whole-here and there I have found exceptions-when I have come into contact with

the majority of them, although doing their

ST. MARY'S HALL, BELFAST.
1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs when he proposes to vacate
possession of St. Mary's Hall.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): This matter has been under
consideration for some time, and it is hoped
to vacate the premises at an early date.
Mr. DEVLIN: Will the right hon. Gentleman say what he means by that?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I mean what I have
tried to convey in my answer.
Mr. DEVLIN: In view of the unsatisfactory answer given by the right hon. Gentleman, I will raise this question on the
Adjournment.
SCALES OF OUT-DOOR RELIEF.
2. Mr. McMULLEN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that recipients of Poor-law relief in Northern Ireland are not given relief on the same scale
as in Great Britain, and whether he is prepared to consider the advisability of giving
equal treatment to recipients in Northern
Ireland pending the report of the Poor-law
Commission.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware that in
some Unions in Great Britain the Guardians
have in force scales of outdoor relief different
from those adopted by Boards of Guardians
in Northern Ireland. The question of the
granting of outdoor relief in any particular
Union is one primarily for the consideration
of the elected representatives of the ratepayers, i.e.The Board of Guardians concerned, and there is no authority vested in
the Minister of Home Affairs to over-ride the
Guardians or to prescribe scales in excess of
those considered appropriate by the Guardians.
I have received no representations from
the Boards of Guardians in Northern Ireland
as to the necessity for investing them with
fuller powers, and in the circumstances the
suggestion in the latter part of the hon.
Member's question does not arise,
FURNISHING OF THE GOVERNOR'S
RESIDENCE.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs, whether it is the fact that the
furnishing of the residence of the Governor
of Northern Ireland is to be given to Cross-
Channel firms.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I propose to answer this question.
The furnishing of the Governor's residence
is being carried out entirely by the Imperial
Government, and this Government has no
responsibility in the matter.
Mr. DEVLIN: Can the right hon. Gentleman not make representations to the
Imperial Parliament, that in view of the state
of trade in Ulster and the desirability of
having this work more economically done,
they should give this labour to local men?
Mr. POLLOCK: We have made frequent
representations not only in regard to the
specific case that my hon. Friend mentions,
but in many other similar cases. We act as
agent for the Imperial authority-that is the
Imperial Office of Works-in connection with
all the structural alterations and repairs in
this building. The furnishing, however, has
been retained by the Office of Works in its
own hands, and we have absolutely no responsibility for it; but practically the whole
of the structural work is being carried out
by local labour.
Mr. DEVLIN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman has the Board of Works an office
here in Northern Ireland ?
Mr. POLLOCK: No, sir; it has not any
office in Northern Ireland. As I have just
stated, we act as agent for the Imperial
Office of Works when they require any work
done.
Mr. KYLE: Does the Minister realise that
there is a considerable number of furnishing
tradesmen out of employment, and does he
not consider it a slur on their industry that
they are being deprived of the right of living
in their own town, and particularly when
they think it is their own money that is being
spent, whether it is Imperial Government
money or not?
Mr. POLLOCK: The Government quite
realise all that the hon. Member has said,

APPROVAL OF NORTHERN IRELAND
LAND BILL.
4. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Prime Minister, whether the Government of
Northern Ireland had a draft copy of the
Northern Ireland Land Bill sent to them before it was introduced by the Labour Government in the Imperial Parliament; if they gave
their approval to that Measure, and returned
the Bill to the Imperial Parliament as an
agreed Measure, although no section of
tenants was consulted or gave its approval.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have been asked by my
righ hon. Friend, the Prime Minister, to reply
to this question. A draft copy of the Bill
was transmitted to the Government of
Northern Ireland by Mr. Baldwin's administration in October, 1923, and on 2nd
November, 1923, in view of the decision that
had been made by the Imperial Government
that the Northern Government was to bear
the financial burden imposed by the Bill, a
reply was sent concurring in its general
principles. Subsequently, a revised draft of
the Bill containing no material alterations
was received from Mr. Ramsay M'Donald's
administration in July, 1924. The question
whether the Bill was or was not an agreed
Measure did not arise on this correspondence.
It will be remembered that subsequent action
on the part of this Government led to inproved terms being granted.
I may add that the interests of the tenants
were represented both before the Percy
Committee and the British Government.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Pharmacy and Poisons Bill,
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The main object of
this Bill is to establish a Pharmaceutical
Society of Northern Ireland which will have
the same powers of prescribing the qualifications of persons desirous of becoming Pharaceutical Chemists in Northern Ireland, and
of making regulations in connection therewith, as the Pharmaceutical Society of
Ireland had in Ireland generally, before the
passing of the Government of Ireland Act of
1920. Some persons may have regretted the
necessity for establishing a Northern
Ireland Society distinct from the Pharmaceutical Society of Ireland, but I may point
out that whatever view may be taken of this
aspect of the case we are bound now that the
matter is within the jurisdiction of this
Government to set up our own Society. A
body which has its headquarters in Dublin,
and whose regulations are subject to the
approval of the authorities of the Free State,
cannot legally exercise any jurisdiction in
Northern Ireland, and the qualifications
granted by such a body to persons in Northern Ireland might be open to question.
The Bill is not, however, confined to the
establishment of a Pharmaceutical Society of
Northern Ireland as the opportunity has been
taken of consolidating and revising the former Acts and introducing certain changes
Pharmacy and Poisons Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Second Reading.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
which will, I hope, be found beneficial to the
chemists and to the public who are deeply
interested in having the sale of poisons and
the compounding and dispensing of prescriptions entrusted to persons whose competence
is beyond question.
The Acts which governed this matter were
the Pharmacy Act of 1875, and the Amendment Act of 1890. Under the former Act there
were two grades-Pharmaceutical Chemists,
and secondly a grade known as Chemists and
Druggists. The 1890 Act put an end to the
creation of any further Chemists and Druggists, but established instead the grade of
Registered Druggists. We have, therefore,
now two large classes, Pharmaceutical
Chemists and Registered Druggists, and a
small and expiring class composed of the
Chemists and Druggists who were qualified
before the passing of the 1890 Act. The only
real distinction between these classes is that
a pharmaceutical chemist alone can
pound and dispense prescriptions, the others
are not entitled to do this. As regards the
sale of poisons, they are all on the same footing. We propose to do away in future with
these different grades, leaving the rights of
existing druggists untouched, and ultimately
to have only one grade, that of pharmaceutical chemists. This will ensure that in
future those who wish to sell poisons by retail or dispense prescriptions will have to
undergo a lengthy practical training and pass
the severe examination required for the
certificate of pharmaceutical chemist.
com-
This might inflict a certain amount of
hardship on the existing druggists, as they
will be an expiring body, and will find it
hard to get apprentices or assistants to enter
what is really a blind alley, and to mitigate
this we propose to allow the existing druggists to become pharmaceutical chemists on
passing a modified examination, which
should not present any great difficulty to men
with their training and experience, and
which will be held by a special board of
examiners representing the various interests
involved and the Ministry.
The conduct of the Society and the primary
power to make regulations will be in the
hands of the Council of the Society. As the
Council will have to be constituted
immediately after the passing of the Act, the
majority of the members in the first instance
will be nominated by the Minister of Home
Affairs, after consultation with the pharmaceutical chemists and the druggists, but two
members will be nominated by Queen's
University, and one by the joint committee
of the Ulster Medical Society and Ulster
Division of the British Medical Association.
When the members of Council, nominated by
the Minister of Home Affairs, go out of
office-one-third retiring each year-the members and associates of the Society will fill
their places by election, so that after the
first three years all the members of the Council, except the three nominated by the
Queen's University and the Medical profession, will be elected by the Society itself.
I think hon. Members will agree with me
that it is very desirable that Queen's University should be represented on the Council-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)—especially
as I hope some arrangement may be made
between the Society and the University for
the holding of examinations by the latter. It
is, of course, also necessary that the doctors
who are in such close relations with
Pharmaceutical Chemists should also have a
representative on the Council.
The successful working of the Act will depend to a great extent on the regulations
made by the first Council. They will be subject to the approval of the Minister of Home
Affairs, but I need hardly say that in a
technical matter of this nature the Minister
must rely largely on the experience and
knowledge of the members of the Council.
The regulations will also have to be laid
before Parliament, so that Parliament will
have an opportunity of criticising and revising any regulations which it is thought
should be modified.
One important innovation is the introduction of a system of annual licences.
Portion of the fees for these licencesnot exceeding one-half-will be paid
into the Exchequer, and the remainder
will go to the Society. In order to enable
the Society to meet the necessary initial expenditure the Government proposes to forego
its share during the first two years, so that
the Society will receive the whole amount of
these fees during these two years. It is also
proposed that the Registrar and Inspector
appointed under the Bill shall be Government
officials, their salaries and any other expenses
incurred by Government under the Bill
being defrayed as far as possible out of the
Government's share of the licence fees. It
is felt that the Registrar and Inspector who
will have duties to discharge which might
possibly bring them into conflict occasionally with members of the Society will be in
a better position to discharge those duties if
they are Government officials than if they are
officials of the Society. Power has been taken
to fix the fees after consultation with the
Society at such figure as may be thought
equitable.
The opportunity has also been taken to
settle the long vexed question of companies
carrying on business as Pharmaceutical
Chemists. We are now placing them in the
same position as individuals, subject to stringent safeguards as to the control of the
business being in the hands of a superintendent who is a fully qualified Pharmaceu-
365 Pharmacy and Poisons Bill-

5 MAY 1925
Second Reading.
tical Chemist, and the manager on each
premises being also a fully qualified Pharmaceutical Chemist. This will enable a
Company to take apprentices which up to this
they were unable to do. A similar provision
is made in the case of a Company carrying on
business as a Druggist.
We have also brought the Schedule to the
Poisons Act up to date and brought it into
line, save for one or two slight modifications,
with the English Schedule.
I may pass lightly over the remaining
points. As there may be cases where the Act
would entail hardship on individuals, we
have given the Council power, subject to the
approval of the Minister of Home Affairs to
deal with such cases exceptionally during a
period of two years from the date of passing
of the Act, and this should remove any
ground of complaint. We require every person carrying on business as a Pharmaceutical
Chemist or Druggist to exhibit his annual
licence and his certificate of qualification so
that the public will know what his qualifications are.
We also propose to allow anyone who was
engaged in Pharmacy and who served in the
Great War to add his service in H.M. Forces
up to a maximum of two years to his period
of apprenticeship or assistantship for the
purpose of the Act.
I should like before sitting down to refer
to the great assistance I received from both
the druggists and the pharmaceutical
chemists. I have had a great many negotiations with them. I have tried to bring both
wings of the profession together, and while
it has not been possible to meet all their
requests, I think I have gone a good distance.
I desire to express my appreciation to the
members of the profession for the way they
have assisted me. I believe the Act will be
a great improvement, and confer a benefit
not only on the profession, but also on the
public. I beg to move.
Mr. T. W. McMULLAN: This is a Bill in
which I am very much interested, and I
have followed its development as closely as 1
could. It is an important Bill which has
been rendered necessary by the political
changes in Ireland. The Ministry of Home
Affairs, as has been indicated by the Minister,
has spent much time on, and given a great
deal of consideration to, the points in this
Measure, more especially the former Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Home
Affairs, Mr. Megaw, whose absence from this
House I very much regret. They have had
a great deal of trouble over this Bill as the
interest of the traders involved have differed,
and in some respects, were even antagonistic. I think the Ministry have done their
best to reconcile these interests, and in many
ways they have succeeded.
The traders, however, who are interestedthe pharmaceutical chemists and the regi
stered druggists, and chemists and druggists
who are really one class-are not quite
satisfied. There are some points on which
they do not agree. Under the old Irish
Pharmaceutical Society there was some
antagonism between these interests. The
chemist and druggist, or registered druggist
felt that he was not treated very generously
in the old Irish Pharmaceutical Society, and
perhaps a little of that acerbity which
developed in those days may still exist, but
I think the effect of this new Act will be to
reconcile the different interests and make
them one happy family in the future. The
Bill proposes gradually to amalgamate these
trades. The object is most desirable, and I
believe that all traders who are interested,
will welcome this amalgamation as something
that will not only help them, but be very
much in the public interest.
Another point in the Bill I would like to
commend is the standard of education which
will be necessary before a boy can enter on
his apprenticeship. A general standard of
English education in the various examinations is insisted on. That is all to the good.
It will improve the standing of the Pharmaceutical chemist when he comes through his

are differences of opinion as to the methods

Public Health (Milk Regulations)
Bill (8).
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of this
Bill is to enable the Ministry of Home
Affairs to make Regulations, first of all in
regard to the labelling of tins and other
receptacles for condensed or dried milk exposed for sale in Northern Ireland, and also
for prescribing the minimum percentages
of milk fats and milk solids in these
foods. The necessity for introducing this
legislation in Northern Ireland arises from
the fact that similar legislation was
introduced and passed in England,
regulations have been issued under that
legislation. Unless similar power is conferred on the Ministry of Home Affairs here
I feel that a great deal of unsatisfactory
milk products will be dumped into Northern
Ireland.
and
It is proposed to make regulations which
will be divided into two main classes. First
of all you have what is known as full cream
and secondly you have skimmed milk. Each
of these classes is again sub-divided under
the heads of sweetened and unsweetened
milk. These regulations will provide what
the percentage of milk fats and milk solids
must be in these various products. Regulations will also be made dealing with dried
milk and prescribing the amounts of milk
solids that it must contain. But I think
perthe most important regulation is with regard
to the labelling of these tins. The label
must first of all set out the character of the
product whether it is dried or condensed
milk, it must set out distinctly the
centage of milk fats or solids, and it must
bear the name and address of the vendor.
It must also indicate what I think is one
of the most important of the regulations,
and that is that if it is skimmed milk it
must contain a warning that this skimmed
milk is not fit for babies. Although it is a
very simple Bill I think it will do a great
deal of good, because it is very necessary to
try to stamp out the importation and sale
of these very undesirable milk products. I
beg to move the Second Reading of the Bill.

I
Mr. T. W. MCMULLAN: This is a Bill in
which I am somewhat interested, and which
I welcome very gladly. Similar regulations
were introduced in Great Britain some six
months ago, and owing to the fact that
Northern Ireland did not adopt them the
trade here has been in a somewhat difficult
position. The trouble was that skimmed
milk, in which a very large trade is done,
and which is tinned in Holland and Den
mark, had been manufactured under conditions which did not comply with the regulations passed in Great Britain, and there was
a tendency to dump it into Northern Ireland. Just after the regulations came into
force in Great Britain I personally received
an offer of quite large quantities of tinned
milk at a very low price, which apparently
did not conform with the regulations.
came to the conclusion that we in Northern
Ireland should as quickly as possible adopt
similar regulations. I took the offer I had
received to the Ministry of Home Affairs,
and I pressed them to come into line
with the legislation passed in Great Britain
as quickly as possible. Partly as a result
of the cheap offers then made and partly
as a result of the tendency of the dealers
to show that they were not profiteering,
the price of skimmed milk to-day. in 15
ounce-weight tins works out at 13s per 4 doz.
cases; retail, two tins, 6d. The import price
to-day of any first-rate tinned milk is 12s 6d
per 4-doz cases. That is, the importer has to
pay 12s 6d cash, or, after trading charges,
the cost delivered is 12s 10 d. The retail
price over the counter works out at 13s., and
I believe that price, which shows no profit
to the dealer, is due to our slowness in adopting these English regulations. Therefore the
sooner they are in force in Northern Ireland
the better, and I cordially welcome the Bill.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I would like
to ask the Minister of Home Affairs if this
Bill enables the Government to compel railway companies to provide proper facilities
for the people who go to the railway stations
to collect milk. Milk in large quantities comes
from the country districts to this great industrial city, and there are no facilities at the
stations for people to receive the milk. It
is turned out of one can into another when
dust is flying about. This matter has given
the Public Health Committee of the Belfast
Corporation much concern. The railway
companies will not take any action in the
matter, with the result that the people of
Belfast are getting very impure milk through
the neglect of the railway companies to provide proper facilities at the receiving
stations, so that the milk can be put into
cans without coming in contact with dust
and other dirt. Is there anything in this
Bill to compel the railway companies to provide such facilities?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid that
this question does not arise out of the Bill
before the House, although the matter is very
important. Personally I am surprised that
the Corporation itself has not brought in
Regulations to prevent the contamination of
milk, but the point raised by the hon.
Member does not concern this Bill at all.

Canal (Continuance of Charging
Powers) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): The purpose of the Measure now
submitted to the House is to renew the
powers of charging higher tolls granted to
certain Canals Companies by the Canals
(Continuance of Charging Powers) Act,
Northern Ireland, 1923. The powers of the
Canal Companies to levy tolls and dues were
fixed by statute many years ago and the
charges then fixed have during recent years
proved utterly inadequate to meet the recently increased cost of maintenance and
operations of these canals owing to the
higher cost of labour and materials. In 1919
the Minister of Transport was empowered to
take over possession of canals and order an
increase of their tolls and also their dues
and charges. He exercised his powers in
Northern Ireland with respect to the Newry
canal and the Lagan canal and in each case
ordered an increase in tolls.
His control of the canals ceased in August.
1921, but the increased charges remained in
force for a further period of eighteen months,
after which they were renewed by the Northern Ireland Act of 1923. It is now necessary
to extend by a further enactment the power
to levy increased charges. Under the Bill
now before the House the Minister of Commerce will continue to have certain powers
of revision of the maximum charges authorised by the Minister of Transport, but he
will have no power as such to sanction any
increased charges in addition to those the
undertakers were entitled to make at 15th
February, 1923. I beg to move that the Bill
be read a Second time.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
whole House for Tuesday.

371 Charitable Loan Societies Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Second Reading.
The
Mr. POLLOCK: The preamble of this Bill
Nets out the object for which it is introduced.
It is for the purpose of ensuring the better
administration of the Loan Fund Societies in
Northern Ireland, and also for amending the
existing law in relation to the disposal of
the surplus funds of these Societies.
history of the existence of these institutions
is a somewhat long one. They were established in the year 1843, and the original Act
consolidated a law that had been apparently
then in existence, and which at that time
governed the Charitable Loan Societies. The
functions of the Loan Fund Board controlling
these objects were in 1915 transferred to the
Department of Agriculture and Technical
Instruction, and this body continued to be
the governing authority until the transfer to the Ministry of Finance. The
Loan Fund Societies were originally formed
for the purpose of lending money to the
industrious classes, and probably to the
agricultural classes, and in order to do that
they received gifts from different people,
some charitably disposed, and also issued
debentures on whatever assets they held.
Under the Act of 1843 the management of
the Societies was governed by certain rules
and regulations. These regulations must be
approved by the central authority, which
was previously the Local Fund Board, and
is at present the Ministry of Finance. These
Societies were never very numerous in Ireland, and at present, owing to the increase
of banking facilities, they are comparatively
little used. On the 1st January, 1922, there
were only seven Societies existing in Northern Ireland. The distribution of these
Societies is as follows:-
1 in County Antrim.

i


Fermanagh.
Tyrone.
Londonderry.
1 in the City of Londonderry.
Of late the facilities offered by these Societies
were practically, with one very marked
exception, that of Londonderry City, only
taken advantage of by the agricultural community, and the maximum loan in each case
was fixed at £10. At the present time only
three of these societies are in active operation, namely,
Kilrea, Co. Londonderry.
Coalisland, Co. Tyrone,
Crichton, Co. Fermanagh.
With regard to the four other Societies
which were in existence at the 1st January,
1922. three are in course of voluntary dissolution and one is being compulsory wound
up under the provisions of the Act of 1843.
At present there is a sum of £498 in the
hands of the Ministry..
This is a brief historical résumé of the Loan
Fund system and of its present position.
Now, under this Measure the Government are
seeking powers to strengthen the control of
the Ministry of Finance over the operations
of the existing Societies, and also, which is
perhaps more important, to make the necessary provision in regard to the disposal of
the surplus funds which may be in the hands
of the Societies themselves. With regard to
the first object, I not not propose to weary
hon. Members, but as to the second feature,
to which I have made reference, that is the
disposal of surplus funds, I would like to
take this opportunity of explaining to the
House that under the existing Act the annual
profits of a Society can be paid over to local
charities without any consultation with the
Government Authority. I wish to emphasise
that fact, that only the income of the Societies
can be used for the purpose of granting indiscriminate charity. But this power is
limited by provisions in the regulations
which were the rules governing the Societies
in former days and which still govern them.
The surplus funds, as distinct from the income, which may be available on the dissolution of a Society can also be handed over
to local charities, but in these circumstances
the consent of the central authority, that is
now the Ministry of Finance, must be
secured. Under this Bill it is proposed to
make the consent a statutory necessity in all
cases so that it may be ensured that the perwho
sons in agricultural districts
availed themselves of the facilities offered by
the Societies and from whom in consequence
the profits and surplus funds have been derived shall obtain the benefit. Hon. Members
are aware that certain surplus funds are, by
the operation of the Act of 1843, at present
in the hands of the Ministry of Finance-I
have stated the amount, £498-and further
sums will probably accrue on the dissolution
and winding up of these Societies that are at
present in a state of voluntary liquidation.
The Bill, therefore, proposes to give to the
Ministry of Finance a larger discretion in
the employment of such funds in order that
the persons or classes of persons from whom
the funds were originally derived may obtain
the maximum benefit from the accumulation
of these funds. I think this sufficiently explains the objects of the Measure. It is
rather small and deals with amounts that are
not of very great importance, and I hope the
House will see the necessity for it. I beg to
move.

Mrs. CHICHESTER: I rise to refer particularly to one paragraph in this Bill, that
is paragraph (c) of Clause 2 where it states

"The object to which the funds of a Loan

I have in my mind at the moment the case

whose salary has been reduced from £90, as it
was originally, to a mere pittance of £20, for
which sum he has had to work every Wednesday and Thursday for the past 43 years.
During the whole of that period the office
has never been closed for those two days in
the week. He is now nearly 70 years of age.
The house he lives in is the property of the
Society, to which he has paid rent for 43 years.

be imperative that the Ministry should consult the local wishes and see whether something could not be done to assist a man who

upon the

Northern Ireland at present,"
and he further said:
"I can assure hon. Members that they
(the Government) are not failing in their
duty so far as giving attention to this
matter is concerned." (OFFICIAL REPORT,
15th April, 1925, col. 54, Vol. 6.)
Previously to that he had indicated his entire
sympathy with this question. But that only
goes a certain way. It does not go far enough.
We really want more than words and more
than sympathy. We want action-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-and to feel that a
start has been made in this vitally important
matter. I think that probably the Minister
of Finance himself knows more about the
difficulties of the farmers of the Bann Valley
than, I may say, almost any other Member
of the Government, but he cannot, I am
convinced, feel and understand as those of us
who actually live in the affected areas, and
who daily and constantly see the havoc caused
by these waters, feel and understand. It is
our duty, therefore, to try to make hon.
Members and right hon. Members realise the
necessity and the difficulties of our situation.
I can speak to you to-day about the flooding
caused by the Lower Bann. Probably my
hon, and gallant Friend (Major Shillington)
on my left will be able to speak to you more
particularly of the difficulties of the Upper
Bann. As far as the Lower Bann is concerned and I speak of the country from
Lough Neagh to the sea-it has been recorded,
I believe, in ancient chronicles as "O'Cahan's
beautiful country." I wish the chronicler
could see to-day, as I have seen, thousands of acres of good farm land lying
submerged under those waters of the Bann,
and could have seen, as I saw at the end of
last season, acres of good potatoes lying
rotting in the fields, and the ruined crops.
If he had seen all that, I am confident he
would not have used that expression, but
would have depicted it in a very different
way.
We are dealing with what is one of the
main arteries of the Six Counties, and I
think it is superfluous to point out that if
the main artery of the body becomes blocked
death is the result. If a main drain becomes
choked and ceases to function, the minor
drains, such as in this case, the Main, the
Blackwater, the Ballinderry, and the Moyola,
will also become blocked and cease to function.
Because there is no proper outlet for the
waters of Lough Neagh at Toome those waters
are being dammed back, and the waters in
the rivers are being dammed back, and consequently bars are forming across the mouths
of those rivers with disastrous and widespread havoc to the surrounding country as
the result. The people of Ulster are surely
not going to be defeated by a problem because it is an old problem, they are not going
to give up the struggle merely because of
mistakes and admittedly mistakes have
been made in the past in dealing with this
question-they are not going to give up
attempting to find a solution because
no solution has been found in the
last 100 years. I am going to suggest
that Sir Alexander Binnie found the
solution in his report of 1906, but because
Westminster was a long cry from Lough
Neagh the plight of the Ulster farmers did
not appeal to the sympathy of the Imperial
House of Commons as it should, and as it
must do to a Legislature sittting in Ulster.
The plight of the farmers is really intolerable. It becomes worse with the succeeding
years, until it is not the last straw but the
last drop of water that would prove too much
for the long-suffering camel's back.
I want to make one point particularly. I
do not think that it is just a question of
material prosperity. I am quite convinced it
will be found that the health of the whole
community is affected by this excessive flooding. I think that statement is borne out by
the Allport Report, and I found a report of
Professor Johnson's which states:
Drainage is equivalent to a change of
climate in reference to the growth and
ripening of flowers, and also in reference
to the general health of the people.
In another report the injury through stagnant water is referred to, and it states that

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

It means more evaporation, more clouds,
less sunshine and above all less heat radiating from the earth, and that cannot be good
for the health of any community.
And yet we allow thousands of acres to be
waterlogged, and we take no steps to remedy
the evil. The remedy for the evil is, I suggest, for the Government to determine in consultation with the best engineering brains of
the day. It has been suggested that a Commission should be set up. It has been suggested that the present Commission dealing
with the development of our industrial resources should deal with this question in
particular. It has also been suggested that
Sir Alexander Binnie's Report of 1906 should
be adopted as it stands, and in this connection I would point out that the figure he
gives as the cost of his scheme is about
£76,000. Even allowing for a possibly greatly
increased cost now, I would suggest that it
has been found possible for grants to be given
to various counties for relief schemes.
would like to mention the grant which we
discussed here a few days ago, the grant given
to the County of Fermanagh for the building
of bridges; and I think I am correct in stating that a very large grant is being given
to the City of Derry for the purpose of a
bridge. I do not think it would be out of
place to suggest that here is a matter which
is affecting not one county but practically
the whole of the Six Counties, and to ask
that a grant might be given for an important
purpose like this.

Moreover, I would suggest that we migh
be justly entitled to claim a grant from the
Imperial authorities, for after all, in this
connection, it was the Board of Works which
carried out a scheme many years ago, a
scheme which was certainly meant to benefit
the people, but which resulted in increased
flooding, and which was never completely and
properly carried out. In 1889, I believe, a
Bill was introduced dealing with this subject, and it was suggested in that Bill that a
grant of £20,000 should be made for the purposes of a scheme of this kind. In 1904 the
then Chief Secretary, Mr. Wyndham, brought
in a Bill by which we were to receive a grant
of £50,000, provided that the Counties of
Antrim, Down, Derry, Armagh and Tyrone
raised a like amount. The principal point
in Sir Alexander Binnie's scheme is the entire abandonment of the navigation of the
Lower Bann, the abolition of some of the
existing weirs, the blasting away and excavating of some of the rocks, particularly in
the stretch between Toome and Portna, and
the rebuilding of the weir at Toome. I am
given to understand in connection with the
weir at Portna that the crest of the weir
there is 7 feet higher than the bed of the
river channel at the exit of the lake, and I
believe the same, or somewhat the same-I
cannot give the exact figures--applies to the
weir at the Cutts. Sir Alexander Binnie
.considers that if the course of action indicated were pursued instead of harming the
salmon fisheries they would be improved by
the removal of the obstructions which to a
certain extent prevent the fish passing out of
the river. The eel fisheries at Toome and
Portna would not be materially interfered
with, and I think that is a very important
point.
With regard to navigation he states that
he spent seven weeks in 1906 on the banks
of the Bann, near Portglenone, and that
during that whole time he never saw any
traffic. I may say, and I am quite sure my
statement will be corroborated by some of the
hon. Members, that so far as I know there
is practically no traffic on the Lower Bann
to-day-less certainly than there was in 1906.
I would also point out that in addition to
railways as a method of transport there is
now the motor traffic on the roads which
was not dreamt of at the time of the Bînnie
Report. This, of course, further eliminates
the necessity for navigation-navigation
which has been maintained by the loss of
thousands of acres of the best farming land,
by the ruin of many small farmers, and by
the penalising through a heavy annual
drainage rate of many larger farmers-men
who are an asset to the State and who should
be protected and encouraged and helped by
the State. I would like to explain that the
Lower Bann Navigation Trustees do not
appear to have carried out their duties even
then, because in 1906 they did not maintain
the Channels as they are bound to do. The
bed was silting up, the whole river was becoming choked, and increased flooding was
the result. In spite of that, the unfortunate
farmers have had to pay a heavy annual
drainage rate to the trustees, and if the
House will allow me I would like to give a
few figures in this connection.
I have here particulars of one farmer who
has 58 acres of land; his drainage rate is £3 18s
in addition to his ordinary rates. Another
man with 101 acres has a drainage rate of
£7 9s 2d, and a third with 36 acres has a
drainage rate of £2 12s 0d. At a public
meeting one of these men of whom I have
been speaking said that during the season
he had lost 70 tons of potatoes as well as hay
and corn. The biggest farmer mentioned
said that his loss amounted to about £300,
and that 15 of his cattle had died a few days
previously. I really think we must feel
sympathy with these men, and in this particular connection I would like to ask the
Government if they could find out and let
us know the amount of receipts and expenditure on navigation on the River Bann
in the past five years. It has been suggested
---and I would like to answer this point-

that when these men or their fathers were

I would like, however, to answer another
point which has been raised. According to
Sir Alexander Binnie's Report there is a
vertical fall of from 46 to 48 feet from Lough
Neagh to the sea, and I cannot conceive that it is impossible to find a solution
of some kind. The state of these farmers
was bad enough with the excessive rains
from which we have suffered in past seasons.
The hand of God has lain heavily on these
people. Is it right that the hand of man
should lie heavily on them too. They
have appealed for help year after
year; they have hoped against hope.
We have now a Parliament of Our
own sitting in our midst to redress Our
wrongs, to right our grievances, to protect
our own flesh and blood and to preserve our
chief industry from extinction. We have
now a chance of assisting the farmers to carry
out the great, useful work of providing food
for the whole community. I would suggest
that this matter does not affect only the Six
Counties but affects Belfast too, because
Belfast is the heart of the Counties, and if
any organ of the body goes wrong the heart
eventually becomes affected. Another point
is that this scheme, or a scheme, if carried
out would provide employment for hundreds
of the unemployed who are now walking
the streets. I would be the first
to acknowledge the debt of gratitude
which agriculture and farmers owe
to the Government. There is the £128,000
in relief of rates, and there are numerous
other ways in which they have assisted,
ways which perhaps they will not realise
until years have elapsed, but this is, I would
impress upon the Government, a calamity
which has been brought about by nature and
helped on by man, and I would implore
them to look upon it sympathetically and to
deal with it, or at any rate to start matters
going and try to find some solution.

waters of Lough Neagh lies a submerged
village, and on beautiful day or in
good clear weather if you gaze deep down
you will see the church spires and the houses
in the waters of that lake and the waters

Major SHILLINGTON: I should like in
seconding the Motion which has been so ably
and eloquently put before the House by the
hon. Member for Derry to state that no
question has been the subject of so many
Commissions, Reports and Inquiries as the
subject at present before this hon. House.
The county which I have the honour
to represent suffers unfortunately to the
extent of having 17,000 acres of the
best pasture and agricultural land submerged for many months each year owing to
this drainage problem. It is not only a local
problem. Each of our Six Counties, possibly
with the exception of Fermanagh, is affected
in a greater or less extent, and those of our
counties which are not affected to any great
extent contribute unfortunately to the disabilities which the several counties are subject to from this problem.
With the risk of wearying the House 1
would like to go back a bit. I understand
that in the year 1845 owing to representations
which were made by the people affected the
Board of Works instructed Mr. John
McMahon to prepare plans and formulate
a scheme to try to remedy this grievance.
That scheme was formulated, and the work
was proceeded with. At the outset it was
only supposed to cost £179,000 and was to be
completed in some three years time. The
final result was that the cost ran to over
£260,000 and it took some twelve years to
complete the operations. Many years after
that scheme was completed the complaints
were quite as bad as ever, and I think one
of the reasons for that was possibly due to
the fact that Mr. John McMahon in addition
to a drainage scheme tried to run a navigation scheme at the same time, and from
the Reports of Commissioners which were
formulated since it has been clearly demonstrated that it is impossible for a navigation
scheme and a drainage scheme to be combined.
We had the Monck Commission in 1882,
the Alport Commission in 1887, and finally
the Viceregal Commission on Arterial
Drainage which was presided over by Sir
Alexander Binnie, and of which the Right
Hon. Thomas Andrews, father of our present Minister of Labour was a member, their
Report being issued in 1907. In the meantime Sir Alexander Binnie had issued the
engineering report referred to by my

colleague (Mrs. Chichester.) In all these

that the navigation question in the Lower
Bann should be left out of the picture
altogether. It appears that in 1906-I think
Sir Alexander Binnie was then making inquiries-the upkeep of the navigation works
was costing over £1,000 a year whereas there
was a revenue of well under £100, which
certainly was not an economic proposition.
Our farmers have been paying this drainage
rate for a long number of years, and they
do not know on what system it is assessed.
I would be glad if some Member of the
Government would tell
us whether the
different Drainage Boards are subject to any
higher authority. I had different cases put
to me from which it would
appear that
they were not even carrying out the work
they were supposed to do.
It has been clearly demonstrated for a
number of years that after the works were
handed over in 1859 the Navigation Trustees
thought they had only to look after the
navigation operations, whereas it was proved
in 1887 that their duty was to look after the
drainage of the river. Things, however, had
got so bad in that time it was impossible
for them to overtake the work which should
have been carried on from year to year from
the time the works were handed over.
I am
aware that the Drainage Trustees to whom
parts of the works were handed over are only
able to strike a maintenance rate. They are
supposed to keep the works in the good order
and condition in which they were handed
over. The works were handed over in 1859,
and the trustees are not capable of performing the duties required of them.
This is a matter which must be taken up
by the Government and dealt with. It is
impossible for the local authorities to deal
with it, as was so ably pointed out by the
hon. Member (Mrs. Chichester), because it
is too big a thing altogether. The present
Drainage Trustees undertook a certain
amount of work, but the whole of the work
does not appear to be satisfactorily performed. I am continually having cases
brought to my notice. I had one inside the
last few weeks, in which it was pointed out
that a certain amount of drainage was two
or three feet higher than the tributary into
which it was supposed to fall. I understand
that attention was drawn to the matter, and
that after a few hours' work the water in
that particular drain went down two or three
feet in twelve hours. That work should have
been done months before.
I would like to know if these Drainage
Trustees are under the control of any higher
authority. There is no doubt that the whole
matter of drainage must be co-ordinated
under one Ministry, and I think from the
Reports issued it is the only satisfactory way
to deal with the question. There is another
point I would like to stress. In addition to
the drainage of thousands of acres of land for
cultivation the flooding that has taken place
in the last number of years has been very
detrimental to the health of the people. For
many years these flooded areas, I know, have
simply been nurseries for consumption and
other diseases. I appeal to the Government
most strongly to give this matter careful,
early and sympathetic consideration. I know
that the matter has been considered by the
Government, and I would like to pay tribute
to the personal interest taken in the subject
by the Minister of Finance, who visited the
flooded areas, not once, but several times this
year. It is a matter that does not brook any
delay, and if any Act is to be brought in
in reference to arterial drainage I say it will
be of no benefit unless the main question is
tackled also.
I agree with the mover of the Resolution
that Sir Alexander Binnie's report certainly
does show a way out of the difficulty. We
have, as has been stated, a fall of over 40
feet between Toome and the sea. Unfortunately there was only a fall of four feet between Toome and Portna, a distance of fifteen miles. The first real trouble is the
block at Portna, the water not being able to
get away. Sir Alexander Binnies report
suggested the lowering of the weir at the
Cutts at Coleraine, the removal of the weirs
at Carnroe, Portna and Toome, together with
the removal of other obstructions in the bed
of the river. I think that would certainly
go a long way to get rid of the difficulty.
I was surprised to find the other day that
certain bodies claim rights over the River
Bann as far as Lough Neagh, and yet those
rights do not seem to carry any obligations
as to the way the river should be kept. I
do not think that is a state of affairs that
should exist. A body claiming rights over a
stretch of water of any sort should have obligations cast on them as to the way in which
that stretch of water should be kept. I join
with my colleague in strongly urging the
Government to give the matter early consideration.

An inter-Departmental Committee has sat
quite recently to endeavour to discover how
the problem of arterial drainage in the
country can be solved, and although the
question of arterial drainage is not under
discussion at this moment, at the same time,
as the hon. Member (Major Shillington) has
reminded, us, it has a very material bearing
indeed on the whole problem of the central
drainage in the country. As has been mentioned,
a Bill will be introduced in this House very
shortly dealing with the question of arterial
drainage, and I do not mean to anticipate
any statement on the subject, but the problem shortly is this. A catchment area of
865 square miles drains into Lough Neagh
and the Lough itself is an inland water of
150 square miles area. It is fed by four main
rivers, the Upper Bann, Ballinderry, Blackwater, and Main. To carry off this great
volume of water is the great problem which
crystalises the whole subject. From all the
reports that have been made it has been
found that under no system, no matter what
might be attained, will it be possible to
render lands which are dry in summer absolutely immune from the inundations that
will take place from conditions that will
arise after floods in the winter.
It has been stated by the hon. Member for
Armagh (Major Shillington) that after the
arterial drainage-that is the clearance of
all the rivers and tributaries that flow into
Lough Neagh-has been effected it
would
only accentuate the one great problem of the

The only reason I suggest that this word be put

I would like to point out that one of the

A question was asked by one hon. Member
if there was any authority over the present
Drainage Boards. My right hon. Friend (Mr.
Pollock) has made inquiry and the reply he
gets is that the Drainage Boards are not at
present subject to any higher authority. No
Government Department or local authority
exercises any actual control over expenditure,
et cetera, and, therefore, these drainage au-
..thorities that at present exist have it all to
themselves and are not influenced or in any
way governed by any action of any Gevernment Department.
Another very important point I would like
to raise is that in helping my hon. Friend
(Mrs. Chichester), who moved this Motion,
we may be doing great damage to those who
are represented by the seconder of the
Motion, or, on the other hand, what possibly
may suit the Upper Bann may cause very
grave and serious flooding and difficulty to
those upon the Lower Bann. It happened
before that some hundreds of thousands of
pounds were sunk, not only without any
result, but with bad results, and so this
Government is most anxious not to gamble
with a great scheme costing hundreds of
thousands of pounds which might have no
result but to waste money, to waste Ulster's
money, and which might, perhaps, have the
further effect of creating an even worse condition of affairs than exists to-day. However,
as I have said, we have for some time past
been going into this thing in a quiet, and,
I hope, efficient way. I purposely, when I
issued my manifesto to the people at the last
election, pointed out it was in order to give
us time to deal with just such local important matters we were desirous of having as
little provocative or contentious legislation
as possible. It was with an eye to this particular big problem, the drainage of the Bann,
that that was inserted in my appeal to the
people. If the House support the Motion, as
amended by me, I can promise that every
effort will be thrown into doing our utmost
to serve the people in that part of the
country.

I claim to have a special knowledge of a
portion of the Bann, and that is why I speak
on this question of the Bann drainage. The
district in which I have lived and worked
for thirty years has been described as "the
garden of Ulster." It is situated in the
Bann Valley-the celebrated Bann Valley--
and for eight or ten miles the Bann forms
the eastern boundary of my dispensary district. The Cutts in Coleraine are in it. I
have been in every house along the Bann
shore for those eight or ten miles, and I
know more about the flooding, perhaps, as
it affects that part of the river than anybody
in this House. We have had for thirty years
in this district a Bann Drainage Association.
I have a letter here from the secretary of
that Association-and may I tell the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) that

it to the House before I sit down, and to try
to impress upon the House the moderate,
reasonable, and gentlemanly tone he adopts
in dealing with this question, probably as a
result of the wise attitude of his neighbours.
I think we should face the facts when we
come to deal with this question, and the first
fact is that you have a Navigation Board
upon the Bann. Now that Navigation
Board functions. It gets the drainage rate,
and this drainage rate is a very important
item on these people. The area along the
border of the Bann is called "the benefited
area," a phrase that, if I were allowed to

think the general opinion is that if you

not benefited.
In my district for thirty or forty years
they have had a Bann Drainage Association,
and I know of no other Bann Drainage Association except this one. Here is a letter I
have had. It will not take me long to read
it.
"I wrote to the Irish Society which owns
the salmon fishing at the Cutts, Castleroe,
and told them of what losses I have had
from flooding due entirely to the salmon
fishing. We have lost about £400 in crop in
general, and now since February we have
lost sixteen head of cattle and a valuable
cow with her time in to calve. To-day
while I am writing the Bann is up to the
house and every field covered with water.
If the gates were thrown open the Bann
would be in its banks inside twenty-four
hours, so that will let you see the amount
of water that is dammed back. Our cattle
got fluke as the result of grazing on the
flooded grass, which will mean a further
loss of £150.
If it were not for the
Cutts we would never have a flood, and
they know that too well."

I have been in that man's house a hundred
times, and know his farm, his circumstances,
and all about him, and what he says is absolutely true. Now this next letter is from
the secretary of the Association, one of the

"Dear Dr. Morrison,
I enclose plans (marked) of Cutts
Weir and Mill Race.
You can point out to the Rt. Hon. H. M.
Pollock on the plans the grievance we complain of, and what is chiefly the cause of
so much destruction on upwards of 1,100
acres in Derry and Antrim.
It is my oponion that this could be
remedied at a very moderate outlay and not
interfere with any of the vested rights. Of
course, I do not mean that the opening of
this mill race would be quite sufficient.
There must be a drainage surveillance and
the lessees of the fisheries must be kept
strictly within their rights.
I would suggest that the crests of the
two weirs be lowered one foot, or patent
sluices inserted in the lock gates as recommended in Binnie's report.
There is one other factor which contributes largely towards the flooding in our
district. The arch on the Derry side of the
Agivey Bann Bridge is completely silted up.
This together with the jutting out shoulder
between the bridge and the mouth of the
Agivey river causes the flood in the Agivey

PHARMACY AND POISONS (MONEY).
Resolved: Committee to consider of authorising the payment out of moneys provided
by Parliament of the salaries and other sums
which may become payable under any Act
of the present Session to establish a Pharmaceutical Society of Northern Ireland, and to
regulate the qualifications and provide for
the annual licensing of Pharmaceutical
Chemists, Chemists and Druggists, and
Druggists, in Northern Ireland, and to
amend and extend the law with respect to
the sale of poisons, and for other purposes
incidental thereto.-(Governor's recommendation signified.)-To-morrow.-(Mr. Pollock.)

POSSESSION OF ST. MARY'S HALL.
Motion made, and Question proposed, "That

Mr. DEVLIN: I have been reading in the
Press for the last four years that if those
whom I more specifically represent wanted
their grievances redressed and their wrongs
righted the proper place in which I should
operate for the righting of those wrongs
and the redressing of those grievances was
in this House. I recognise that there was
some force in that argument, and in that
spirit I have come to this House. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) And I would have
expected on the matter which I propose to
raise on the adjournment that I would have
been met in a real, genuine friendly spirit.
I do not propose to raise anything in this
House of this character unless I cannot get
satisfaction outside. I have risen for the
purpose of calling attention to the enforced
possession by the Government of St. Mary's
Hall. When I came here I think the
Government had possession of St. Mary's
Hall for four years, at least 3 years. When
I came here I made representations to the
right hon. Gentleman the Home Secretary,
and I asked him to restore St. Mary's Hall to
the rightful owners. He explained to me
that it was difficult in view of the fact that
it was occupied by the police. It has been
occupied now for 3 years or the greater
portion of that time, and all other institutions and buildings that have been compulsorily taken over by the Government for
purposes of this character have all been
vacated, and this remains as far as I know
the only building which has been retained
by the Government, and the use of which is
denied to those who used it and for whose
purpose it was brought into existence.
The Home Secretary told me that there
were two difficulties-the difficulty of finance
and the difficulty of housing the police who
are in St. Mary's Hall. I saw the Minister
of Finance about it, and I must say he was
most courteous and recognised the reasonable nature of the demand that I made on
behalf of those who required St. Mary's Hall.
I thought having made representations to the
right hon. Gentleman the Home Secretary,
and to the right hon. Gentleman the Minister
of Finance that the right hon. Gentleman
the Home Secretary would have risen to-day
in response to the interrogation I made to
him and said "Yes, St. Mary's Hall would
be restored to the rightful owners," but instead of that I get the same answer that
we were accustomed to get in the British
House of Commons-"the matter was under
consideration," as if the right hon. Gentleman had not time enough to consider this
demand during the last three and a half
years. He said the Hall would be vacated,
and when I asked when, he said sometime.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would remind the
hon. Member that my answer is a perfectly
plain one.
Mr. DEVLIN: How is it plain?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I stated at an early
date.
Mr. DEVLIN: At an early date? I know
what Ministerial answers are. You are copying bigger men than yourself when giving
an answer like that. We want St. Mary's
Hall for reasons I will state in a moment.
I wanted some definite answer from the
right hon. Gentleman as to when we were
going to get our property restored to us.
This is not an ordinary hall; it is an
institution. It is an institution used
for charitable and beneficent purposes
in the public interest.
It is the
centre of the home of the greatest
Catholic charitable organisation in Ulster,
the St. Vincent de Paul Society, where unselfish men devote their nights after laborious
days to serve the poor. It is the centre for
the Ladies' Charitable Association, where
equally beneficent work is done by publicspirited ladies on behalf of the poor of their
sex. It is also a social club.
The right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of
Home Affairs does not know what a favour
he conferred upon me by closing that hall.
I used to make speeches in that hall, and I
used to get a majority of only 300 or 400. I
was driven out of that hall, and I went to
the people and I got a majority of 17,000. I
am therefore not speaking in any selfish
spirit when I speak of the advantages I have
gained by being taken away from the congested atmosphere of St. Mary's Hall to the
pure air of large open spaces. The right hon.
Gentleman will see that I speak in an unselfish spirit in regard to this matter. To
give this hall back in a friendly way to its
rightful owners would have been a friendly.
St. Mary's Hall.

[Mr. Devlin]
gesture on the part of the Government, and
it would have been so regarded, and it is
proof of that that I did not raise this matter
in the House at all until I went to the right

given him the chance which he has rejected.
These are, from my own point of view, the
