Minister of Home Affairs cannot tell us
definitely when he is going to give this hall
back to the proper owners.
I come now to another consideration. If
I were one of the men behind the right hon.
Gentleman I would object to this hall being
used for this purpose. It is no more fitted
to house the police than would this gathering
here be fitted to be turned into a cabaret
show. It has not a single qualification for
a police barracks. I am amazed that an
epidemic of ill-health has not broken out
long ago, because the place is not at all
suited for habitation either structurally or
in any other way. I have no doubt the
answer the Minister of Home Affairs will
give is that he has no other accommodation.
I told him on Thursday last where he could
get suitable accommodation, far better than
he has got at St. Mary's Hall. There is the
Grand Central Hotel, which contains 260 bedrooms, and it has large dining halls and
drawing rooms which could be used as mess
rooms for the police. You can have all that
accommodation, and much more, for the
police at your door, and, therefore, I cannot
understand that there can be any other
reason in continuing to hold this building
unless for the purpose of further humiliating
those people who have been humiliated
before. I cannot account for it in any other
way, and therefore I hope the right hon.
Gentleman will really give to this House—
and I will speak beyond the right hon.
Gentleman to the great body of men in this
House the reason St. Mary's Hall is not
returned to its owners. What are we to
think of the consideration that is to be given
to the essential claims we may put forward
of a biggar character when in a twopencehalfpenny transaction of this sort you refuse
to give up the hall you hold, and when
private representations are unavailing you
compel private Members to raise the matter
in this House.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I desire to
associate myself with the protest so ably
made by the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin). I do so without having the
special interest in the matter that the hon.
Member has, but I do so as a representative
of West Belfast, and I hope the other representative of West Belfast will also make a
protest. The point that struck me particularly in the speech of the hon. Member for
West Belfast was that one would have expected that this hall would have been handed
back before it was necessary to make a protest in this House. The Government have
been asking the Onposition to take their
place in this House so that a better spirit
and a better feeling might prevail in Belfast
and throughout the Six Counties. The
Opposition have now taken their seats in
this House, but no gesture has come from the
Government to attempt to reconcile the
differences between conflicting elements.
I hold there is absolutely no justification for
continuing the occupation of this hall, and I
believe that most of the halls that were
occupied by the police have been surrendered.
If it is a question of lack of accommodation
I believe there are halls in Belfast that could
be used without depriving the Catholic community of the only hall available to them
for charitable, social, and political purposes.
For that reason I want to enter my protest
against the continued occupation of this
hall.
If the Government want the peace that is
existing at present to continue this gesture
of goodwill from the Government is essential.
I do not want to go into questions that one
might be tempted to go into when discussing
this matter, because no one wants to touch
on contentious matters that might promote
bad feeling. For that reason I hesitate to
enter upon matters that I otherwise might
have done, and I hope that after this protest
the Government will see the wisdom of handing back this hall to its rightful owners, so
that this section of the community may enjoy
those charitable and educational facilities
which they have been deprived of for the last
four years. If the Government do not do
that at an early date it will be essential that
we should go fully into those matters that
we have carefully refrained from going into
to-day.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Personally I regret

I told him in my answer to his question that

and I deny the charge emphatically.
I feel certain that my hon. Friend (Mr.

years, and particularly during the year 1922,
the hon. Member (Mr. Devlin) chose to remain away from Belfast, and therefore he
is not perhaps aware of the circumstances
under which the Government took possession
of the Hall. The Government did not com-

workers sat on the streets for a period of

ESTIMATES, 1925-6.
CLASS IV. No. J.
MINISTRY OF EDUCATION.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £54,717 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st March, 1926, to defray the
Salaries and Expenses of the Ministry of
Education."-(Note:-£18,000 has been voted
on account.)
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY, OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): The members of the Committee will
see that down on the Order Paper to-day
there are two classes of Votes in respect of
education. The first one, which we
are
taking
now, is for the administrative
expenses of the Ministry itself. Upon this
head there is a nett increase altogether this
year of £1,698. That arises mainlyactually altogether-from the normal increase
in salaries payable to the various employees
of the Ministry of Education in the administration of the Department. The number of
persons employed has been increased by two,
but only by two, and that arises in this way.
One of them is a messenger, and one a caretaker. The Department which has charge
of Public Elementary Education was until
during the course of the past year housed in
huts in the centre of this building. They
were found to be not only inconvenient but
too small and unhealthy, and accordingly
during the course of the year the Ministry
acquired, through the Ministry of Finance, a
house in Queen's Elms, and to that house the
Department dealing with Public Elementary
Education has been transferred. The rent of
the building is payable, of course, by the
Imperial Government, but the rates, which
account for the small increase in rates on
this Vote, have to be paid by us. In connection with the working of the Department,
it was found necessary to employ a caretaker
for that building, and an extra messenger,
who is an ex-Service man. That accounts for
the two increases in the personnel of the
staff.
There is one increase under sub-head B
which I might mention, and that is an increase in the travelling and subsistence
expenses of members of the Advisory Council. As the Committee is aware, the
Advisory Council was provided for by the
Act of 1923. It has now been set up, and will
be functioning during the coming year. This
sum is brought into the Estimates in order
to provide for the expenses of attendance at
the meetings. By its operation the Ministry
hopes to get in close touch with the best
educational opinion in the Province, and it
will greatly help during the coming year in
the carrying out of this work. Those represent the items of increase in this Vote,
and accordingly I beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: I desire to move a reduction
in this Vote if I cannot discuss the question
I wish to raise otherwise. I have not anything to say so far as the various items
mentioned by the Parliamentary Secretary of
the Ministry of Education are concerned, and

slip, and that Members of this Committee
might not realise how important education is
to the community of Northern Ireland. It
is from that point of view that I wish to make
a few remarks on this Vote. I will move a

Mr. ROBB: This is the Vote dealing with
the various Services that are carried out by
the Ministry of Education. Upon the whole
Vote there is a nett increase of £11,178.
That is accounted for in great measure—
altogether in fact-by the increases that are
proposed in respect of the Estimates of the
salaries of elementary school teachers. The
Committee will find this Vote on page 97,
and I think perhaps the most convenient way
to deal with it is to go through the subheads as they are set out on that and the
following pages.
The first sub-head is in respect of Training
Colleges. We have, as the Committee is
aware, a hostel at Stranmillis, established
for the reception of students in training as
elementary teachers. At that hostel there
are 314 students, and sub-head A1 deals with
the grants that are made in respect of the
training of those students. There is only
one item that calls for comment, and that is
the third item under this sub-head. The Members of the Committee will notice in respect
of diploma bonuses and certain grants to, or
in respect of ex-King's Scholars a reduced
amount of £1,100 as against £4,000 last year.
The explanation of that is this. The £4,000
set down in the Estimate last year included
arrears that this Government expected to be
called upon to pay-arrears payable in
respect of teachers employed in schools
in Northern Ireland, but who had
in fact been trained in colleges outside Northern Ireland. The claims for these
arrears were not formulated during the year,
and, accordingly, the Ministry thought it
fairer to the Committee to set down the
amount which they expected they would
actually be called upon to pay during the
coming year,and leave this question of the
arrears over until it does arise to be dealt
with by a supplementary Vote or in some
other way.

Sub-head A2 deals with model schools, and
no comment is necessary on that. The Committee will see in regard to the next item,
the salaries of teachers in public elementary
schools, there is an increase from £1,317,000
to £1,338,000. The Ministry anticipate an increase because they expect that with a more

authorities set up, there will be an increase
in the attendance of scholars in the schools

2,000, and this has necessitated the employment of fifty additional teachers. It is also

figures only deal with Belfast, but the

£1,300,000. Accordingly instead of £12,402
the sum which falls to paid by the Government of Northern Ireland to this Fund is
only £7,800. I may say that the effect of
that upon the Teacher's Pension Fund has
not been lost sight of and the efficiency of
this Fund to meet its liability as it falls
due will be carefully watched and attended
to by the Government.

On page 100 we have technical instruction,

The problem is to get an educated democracy

may be better able to take our place and

maintain it in the march onward in the

Now we have got a Government here, and
we have a fair start made with the Education Act put through this House a year ago.
I think it is important that the Ministry of
Education should pay attention to all the
details necessary to get us a healthy, happy
and contented people. I would strongly urge
on the Ministry to set about stirring up the
local authorities to have these nursery
schools, particularly in places like Belfast.
In the division where I live there are some
10,000 working mothers. These mothers
have got to work in the mills, factories and
warehouses of our city. Very often there is
a lack of care taken of the children during
the time the mother is making profits for
some employer of a mill, factory or warehouse, and very often the children contract
a disease and do not get the attention which
is necessary to build up healthy citizens.
I say the Ministry of Education can do this
thing if they stir up the local authorities in
that direction.
There is also the question of schools for
deficient children, for blind and deaf and
dumb children to which I think the Ministry
ought to pay some attention in the year that
lies ahead of us. When the Parliamentary
Secretary (Mr. Robb) speaks of the extra
2,000 children who have been attending school

Act came into force, I would remind him
of what Lord Carson, then Sir Edward, said:
two years ago in the British House of Commons. He said that there
were some
16,000 children in Belfast for whom no school
accommodation was available. In the district of the city which I represent I think it
is high time that we had a decent public
elementary school-I refer to the area of
North Belfast.
There is also another very important question which the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr.
Robb) did not mention, and that is the feeding of necessitous school children. I know
we are empowered to do that under the 1923
Act, but it was stated quite freely during
the election that when the Belfast Corporation wanted to feed a certain number of
children in the city the Ministry stepped in
the way and said they could only feed a certain number, which was less than the number the Corporation wanted to feed. These
on
things, may be, do not affect hon. Members
opposite to the same degree or the same extent as they affect those of us
these
benches, who live and have our being amongst

the necessity of immediately putting into

children.
Then there is another matter to which the
Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Robb) did not
refer, namely the question of medical inspection. I think the grant in aid of that

not sufficient. There is also the question

three out of every five children attending our

in the same way as Charles Trevelyan did

You cannot expect the County Councils in
Fermanagh and Tyrone, where the people are
more concerned about border lines, and more
concerned about words, words, words, than
they are about the health, and the life, and

Then there is another very vital question
which affects a tremendous number of chil-

dren, particularly in the city of Belfast.
refer to the youngsters between the age of
fourteen and sixteen. I think everybody in
this Committee will agree that it is a wrong
system of society that compels children, from
any cause whatsoever, to have to leave school
at fourteen years of age, and that the age
should be extended to sixteen. Try to think
of what a child has got to do, to go to the
mill or the factory, to run messages, sell
papers, or do this, that, or the other thing
on the public streets, at
the age of fourteen.
I think the Committee will agree that the
years between fourteen and sixteen are tremendously important and do a tremendous
lot to make a person, in the later years of
that person's life, either something worth
while in society or perhaps not so good. It
is to that end that we would strongly urge
that the school leaving age should be raised.
age
In addition to that school leaving
being raised there ought to be maintenance
grants to enable those people who are hard
put to keep their children at school for a
longer period than they otherwise would. I
think the Committee will agree that if that
were so, if all our children, whether they
be the sons of lords, dukes, or capitalists of
any sort, got attending school until they
were sixteen years of age, it would benefit
this Province enormously. I am quite certain that there would be far less trouble
about things that do not matter and far
more concern taken about things that really
do matter if this very desirable reform were
brought about.
Then there is the question of adult
education, to which the Parliamentary
Secretary (Mr. Robb) did not refer, but it is
very important. There are associations of
people in this city of ours who are concerned
about adult education, some in connection
with the University, and some in connection
with the trade unions. I refer to the
Workers' Educational Association and the
National Council of Labour Colleges, which
both carry on adult education. I do not see
any reference at all in these Estimates to
any grant which may be had by either of
these two organisations to enable them to
give to adults that education which is very
necessary in any subject which the adults
themselves in class assembled may desire to
take up. On this point I would just like
to say that I believe that if £1,000 were
allocated to adult education it would be of
ever so much more service to the community
than the £1,000 that is allocated on other
estimates to another source. I think it
would be of great advantage to the community in Belfast if adults, young men and
young women after sixteen years of age, and
perhaps as old as twenty-one, belonging to
the trade union movement or some other
movement, had opportunities for this education. It would help to broaden their viewpoint and make them see things more clearly
than they do to-day. From that point of
view I would strongly urge the Ministry to
make it easy, make it possible for grants for
adult education to be had by any body of
people who are agreeable to give that
education.
There is only one other question to which

£2,000 in respect of evening elementary
schools It is not true that the Ministry
have done nothing with regard to these, because there are 13 elementary evening schools
with an approximate attendance of 1,286
pupils in existence and financed by the
Ministry. However, it was not exactly to
that that the hon. Member referred. As I
understood he wanted a different sort of education. I would point out that the education
authorities have ample power to supply what
he wants under Section 22 of the Act of 1923.
Not only have they the power but the Act
lays on the education authorities the duty
for it reads as follows:
It shall be the duty of the education
authority, acting either alone or in combination with other education authorities
or educational institutions, to make provision, in accordance with a scheme approved by the Ministry, for affording to
persons resident in the education area, by
means of day or evening continuation
schools or classes or otherwise technical instruction
In the second sub-section technical instruction is defined as including:-
instruction in the principles of science and
art applicable to industries, and in the
application of special branches of science
and art to specific industries or employments. lt does not include instruction
given in elementary schools, but, save as
aforesaid, includes instruction in the
branches of science and art with respect
to which grants are for the time being
made out of moneys provided by Parliament and any other form of instruction
(including modern languages and commercial subjects) which may for the time
being be sanctioned by the Ministry . .
Under that Section it seems to me that the
local education authority has ample power
to provide what the hon. Member wants, and
any proposals from any education authority
to do what he wants would, I can assure him,
be very sympathetically considered by the
Ministry.
With regard to the pensions of secondary
school teachers, the hon. Member has some
complaints to make. Those Members of
Committee who were also Members of the
last Parliament may think when we come
to this that possibly my chickens are coming
home to roost,, for I may say that I advocated the cause of the secondary school
teachers in regard to pensions as well as 1
could and as efficiently as any other Member
of the House. His complaint, as I understand, is that the pension scheme does not
go as far as the teachers would have liked.
The explanation or view of the Government
is that all pension schemes for teachers have
been framed on a contributory basis. With
regard to the scheme of pensions for secondary teachers up to the present there have
been no contributions. The complaint has
been that existing teachers who are now for
the first time brought under this scheme did
not get credit for the whole of past service.
The Government was faced with this fact in
starting a scheme now that if we were to
give pensions at the full rate to teachers
437 Supply-

6 MAY
Educational Services.

coming in now who had never contributed
before we must supply that in one or two
ways. First of all, we might do so by increasing the contributions of the present
teachers who would be in that way compelled
to pay largely increased contributions for a
large number of years in order to pay pensions for back service for people who had
never contributed at all. On the other hand
the money might be supplied by the Government.
The view the Government took was that
it would be unfair to call upon young
teachers now during the whole of their
teaching career to pay largely increased contributions in order to provide pensions at
the full rate for people who had never contributed anything at all, and accordingly
that branch of the possibilities was excluded.
Then the Government had to consider to
what extent the funds at their disposal
would enable them to provide pensions for
secondary teachers in competition with other
claims upon the bounty of the Government,
and the Government decided that to the
extent of one year in three out of the funds
at their disposal they could supply the
pensions in respect of back service for
secondary teachers. They regret that they
could not go further, but the financial claims
were such that they did not feel in a position
to go any further. That is the way the
matter arose and the way in which it stands.
*
With regard to school books, may I point
out that local authorities have the power if
they are willing to supply these books for
school children who cannot supply them
themselves. No obstacle in the way of
doing so will be put in their way by the
Ministry. The hon. Member for the University (Dr. Morrison) and the hon. Member
for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) pressed upon
the Ministry the provision of better teaching in hygienics. May I say with regard to
such a claim and advocating such a course
it would have my hearty sympathy, but I
may also say quite frankly that I do not
know at the moment the position in which
that stands. Possibly I should know and the
Committee will perhaps excuse me in that
connection. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It is a matter that will not be lost sight
of. If there is anything that ought to be
remedied with regard to that I hope it will
be remedied in the near future. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)
Mr. KYLE: I want to refer to one thing.
Will schools that are being transferred to
the Ministry of Education be on the same
basis as in England? During election
times in England all parties can get the
hire of a school in which to hold meetings.
Will that be possible under our administration here? We of the Labour Party
have to hold our meetings in the open air,
and as the elections are generally held in the
winter time it is very troublesome. If the
Prime Minister were to hold a meeting one
night, the Member for West Belfast another
night and a member of the Labour Party
the next night it would be interesting and
good for the community.
Mr. ROBB: Again I have to say that I do
not know, but if the hon. Member would
put down a Question with reasonable notice
I will find out the position.
Mr. DEVLIN: I did not quite catch
whether the hon. Gentleman gave an answer
to the allegation made by the hon. Member
for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle) that the Ministry interfered with the Belfast Corporation
in regard to the number of necessitous
pupils?
The
Mr. ROBB: Perhaps the hon. Member
would put down a question with regard to
that. I have not got the full details.
Ministry did sanction an expenditure of
£6,000 last year for the Belfast Corporation,
but no part of it was spent. What the
position is at the moment I do not know, but
perhaps the hon. Member would put down
a question, and I may be able to give the
exact facts.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I want to
refer to one thing. It is a countryman's view
and is probably different from the city man's.
With regard to the limiting of the school
age, there are two times in the year when
farmer's sons and daughters from 14 to 16
years are necessary at home, and when they
help to increase food production. They are
not displacing any labour from any other
source. If they were not used there would
not be as much food production, and the
crops would not be safely harvested. I think
the conditions in the country are somewhat
different to city conditions. I do not suppose
there is any serious intention at present of
making a change, but if it were carried out
it would militate against the production of
food. With regard to the books, I think the
education authorities should try to cheapen
the books. There is no mistake but the present cost of school books is a serious drain,
especially on labourers' families in the
country. It is an important question, which
should receive the attention of the Ministry.

Mr. KYLE: I beg leave to withdraw the

439 Pharmacy and Poisons (Money)- HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Committee.
Pharmacy and Poisons (Money)
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session to establish a Pharmaceutical Society in Northern Ireland, and to
regulate the qualifications and provide for
the annual licensing of Pharmaceutical
Chemists, Chemists and Druggists, and
Druggists in Northern Ireland, and to amend
and extend the Law with respect to the sale
of poisons, and for other purposes incidental
thereto, it is expedient to authorise a charge
upon moneys provided by Parliament in respect of the salary of the Registrar and the
Inspector to be appointed under any such
Act, and any expenses of either of those
officers and of the Minister of Home Affairs
and Ministry of Home Affairs under any
such Act, to such amount as may be approved
by the Ministry of Finance,
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY OF THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): The only
financial point requiring the consideration of
this Committee will be found in Clause 26
(1) of the Pharmacy and Poisons Bill, which
provides for a charge on Votes of the salaries
of two officers, viz., the Registrar and the
Inspector who are to be appointed under
Section 8 of the Bill. These officers will be
officers of the Ministry of Home Affairs and
not officers of the Society. The Resolution
also refers to expenses of the Minister of
Home Affairs and the Ministry of Home
Affairs, and in this connection I need only
explain that as the service falls within the
province of my right hon. Friend it is
necessary to include any small cost of
administration which may be incurred. Such
expense will be inconsiderable.
As regards the two officers to whom I have
referred, under Section 8 of the Bill the
power is given to the Minister of Home
Affairs to appoint fit and proper persons to
these posts and to prescribe, subject to the
consent of the Ministry of Finance, the
salaries which shall attach to such posts.
As the salaries have not yet been fixed, it is
not possible for me to state accurately in
terms of cash what is involved, nor can 1
yet say whether it will be possible to utilise
part of the time of existing officials to carry
qut these services in lieu of creating fresh
posts. I would, however, draw the attention
of the Committee to sub-section (2) of Clause
26 which provides for a contribution from
the proceeds of the Licence Duties leviable
under the Bill towards these salaries up to a
maximum of one-half of the total amount of
the duty collected.
The net annual cost to the State is thereby
limited to the difference between the amount
of this contribution and the salaries which
will be paid, and as it is estimated that the
licence fees will produce an annual sum of
approximately £900, the appropriation in aid
from this source will almost if not altogether
recoup the Vote in respect of these salaries.
Attention has already been drawn in connection with the Second Reading of this Bill,
to the provision contained in sub-section (2)
of the Clause now under consideration to the
fact that the Government propose to waive
any claim to part of the licence duties for
the first two years. This concession will
leave at the disposal of the Society the whole
amount of licence duties during this period
and will lighten the burden which they will
have to bear in the initial years in connection with certain capital expenditure to be
incurred in the provision of accommodation
and in the equipment of a laboratory.
I would further remind the Committee that
the only power the Government has taken to
levy any contribution from this Society in
subsequent years is restricted to a maximum
of one half of the total amount of the licences
collected. It will be quite within ther power
to vary that sum so as to leave further sums
at the disposal of the Society as the Minister
of Finance and the Minister of Home Affairs
may consider necessary for carrying out the
inauguration and the duties laid upon them
under this Act.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolution reported, and agreed to.
The remaining Order was read and postponed.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 7th May, 1925.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
LOUGH ERNE FISHERIES.
1. Mr. GRANT (for Mr. COOPER) asked
the Prime Minister, whether the question of
establishing a hatchery in the Ballycassidy,
or some other suitable river, is being considered in connection with the proposal to
improve the Fisheries in Lough Erne?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have been asked by my right hon.
Friend (the Prime Minister) to reply to this
question. Under the Government of Ireland
Act, as modified by the Irish Free State (Consequential Provisions) Act, the service in connection with fisheries is at present reserved
to the Imperial Government, and consequently the Northern Government has no
jurisdiction in the matter. The representative of the Imperial Government in Northern
Ireland dealing with the question of fisheries
is the Imperial Secretary, with whom it is
suggested that the hon. Member should
communicate.
TEACHERS
AMALGAMATED
IN
SCHOOLS.
2. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education, whether, in cases of the amalgamation of two or more schools to form one
public elementary school, the Ministry
proposes to take steps to insure that all the
teachers employed in the schools which are
amalgamated shall be appointed to situations
in the new school, and guaranteed against
financial loss; or, in the alternative, shall
receive adequate compensation for loss of
office.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): In all amalgamations of schools the
interests of the existing teachers, as regards
employment and remuneration, are safeguarded.
POSITION OF JUNIOR ASSISTANT
MISTRESSES.
3. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education, if he could state the number of
Junior Assistant Mistresses in the service of
the Ministry, and if it is proposed to retain
the services of these teachers in the event of
the schools in which they are employed being
amalgamated or superseded by provided
schools; and, if the services of these teachers
be dispensed with, what compensation is it
proposed to award.
Mr. ROBB: There are about 600 Junior
Assistant Mistresses employed in Public
Elementary Schools.
Their interests, financial and other, are
safeguarded where amalgamations are carried
through by the Ministry or where a school
is transferred to an education authority.
Teachers in provided schools are appointed
by the Local Education Authorities, and the
Ministry has no reason to suppose that the
claims of existing teachers will be overlooked
by these authorities.
SALARIES OF TEACHERS IN
TECHNICAL SCHOOLS.
4. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education, how
the proposed revised scale of salaries for
teachers in technical schools was arrived at,
and whether any steps were taken by the
Ministry before putting the proposed scale
in operation to consult either the county or
local technical committees, and whether, in
view of the fact that these increased salaries
are causing a great deal of dissatisfaction
throughout the Northern area, he will consider the advisability of having the whole
question of these salaries inquired into again.
Mr. ROBB: The salary scales referred to
were framed by the Ministry of Education
after consultation with the Ministry of
Finance and were issued in draft to local
technical committees several months before
they were presented to Parliament and became operative.
The Ministry is not aware that the scales
are causing dissatisfaction and it does not
propose to re-open the question.
PENSIONED ARMY TEACHERS.
5. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education,
whether it is a fact that a principal teacher
in a public elementary school who has served
eighteen years in the Army, and receives
from the British Government a pension for
services rendered, is penalised by the Ministry of Education for Northern Ireland to
the extent that he does not receive the same
salary as a principal in such school who has
had no army service.

school managers or trustees. I have dealt
with the second part of the question in my
answer to question number 6.
Mr. ROBB: I assume this question refers
to army teachers, Pensioned army teachers
who take up teaching in Public Elementary
Schools are not treated as new entrants.
One-half of their Army service is credited
to them for incremental purposes.
It is not considered that it would be proper to allow any more liberal treatment in
the matter of the amount of incremental
grant to be awarded in the commencing
salary in respect of army service, in view of
the fact that the persons concerned continue
to receive the pensions granted to them on
account of this service in addition to their
emoluments as Elementary School teachers.
TEACHERS IN SMALL SCHOOLS.
6. Mr. GRANT asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education,
whether teachers formerly employed in a
number of small schools for which a Regional Committee has substituted one large
school, will receive a preference when the
staff of the latter is being appointed.
Mr. ROBB: The appointment of teachers
in provided schools is in the hands of the
Education Authorities, and the Ministry has
no reason for supposing that full consideration will not be given by these authorities to
the claims of teachers employed in schools
which have been superseded.
I may add that it is anticipated that the
enforcement of compulsory attendance will
result in employment for an increased number of teachers, and that, having regard to
the fact that the number of trained teachers
is strictly limited, teachers should have little
difficuly in obtaining employment.

to retain control of the buildings for other

in regard to the teachers in such schools if
the Regional Committees replace them by

Mr. ROBB: The question whether a voluntary school should be transferred to an
Education Authority is a matter for the
TEACHERS' PENSION SCHEME.
8. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Finance, if it is proposed, in
the new Pension Scheme, for teachers of
public elementary schools to make provision for (a) compensation to every teacher
who shall lose his employment owing to the
closing of his school or depletion of attendance occasioned by the opening of a new
provided school in his neighbourhood, and
who is unable to find another teaching
appointment; (b) the addition of a certain
number of years to the service of a teacher
who is not less than 45 years of age, so that
such a teacher may be superannuated in the
event of his school being closed.
Mr. POLLOCK: It is not proposed at
present to make any provision of the kind
suggested by the hon. Member. The information in my possession does not indicate
that any such loss of employment will occur

HOUSING IN RURAL AREAS.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir

PURCHASE OF CROSSLEY TENDERS.
10. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether it is a fact that twelve
Crossley tenders of the latest type have been
recently purchased, and whether it is not a
fact that there are at present at Prince's
Dock between forty and fifty such vehicles,
and that the mileage per car has not exceeded
100 miles since they were purchased.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is a fact that
twelve Crossley tenders have been purchased
to replace 16 tenders which were cast as unfit for further service and sold.
The number of vehicles at present in the
Depot, including 14 under and awaiting repair, is approximately as stated in the
question. A reserve of vehicles is kept to
replace old and worn out cars as they are

Sir Dawson Bates]
cast, and also temporarily for issue in place
of those which are from time to time brought
in for repair.
I am unable without special inquiry, which

be in the Depot at any particular time.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is it not a fact that before
the last purchase there were more than

Gentleman go on to state the mileage travelled

LABOURERS' COTTAGES IN KILLINCHY
DISTRICT.
11. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs, whether it is a fact that the
land bought for the erection of agricultural
labourers' cottages in the Killinchy district
of County Down, under the Downpatrick
Rural Council, was sold by the Commissioner
appointed by him.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is a fact that
certain lands which had been acquired by the
Rural District Council under a scheme confirmed in 1913, and which had never been
built on by the Rural District Council, were
sold by the Commissioner in accordance with
the terms of Section 16 of the Labourers'
Act of 1883.
Mr. KYLE: Would the Minister of Home
Affairs tell us was it by his authority that
this land was sold?
Mr. DAWSON BATES: It was sold by the

was stated at Downpatrick Rural Council on
Saturday last, there are twenty-eight applications for cottages in the Killinchy district,
and, in view of the widespread need for these
cottages, would the Minister of Home Affairs
give us some assurance that such action as

Sir DAWSON BATES: Of course my hon.
Friend must understand that this scheme

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
THE BUDGET.
Statement by Minister of inance
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House approves the proposals of
the Government for meeting the financial
requirements of the year."
Mr. POLLOCK: (who was received with
general cheers): In submitting a statement
of the probable revenue and expenditure of
the Province for the year on which we have
just entered, I would remind the House that
the present is the fourth successive year in
which it has been my privilege to ask
Parliament to approve of the financial proposals of the Government for meeting the
requirements of the Province.
I have often reminded the House of the
difficulties facing anyone placed in the
position of controller of the finances of a new
State, established under such abnormal and
novel conditions. During the passage of the
1920 Act, I foresaw those difficulties, and it
may interest the House if I read a few lines
from the report of our Ulster Committee
which was commissioned to negotiate with the
British Government the financial relations of
the two areas:-
"It cannot be questioned that there are
many unascertained liabilities (invisible
to-day) which will be discovered when new
The Budget.
The Budget.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
.. Parliaments and new forms of Government
have been established in Ireland. In view
of these probabilities, it will be necessary
to provide a considerable margin for such
contingencies. We have come to the conclusion that it would not be safe for the
Irish Parliaments to undertake their new
responsibilities with a present annual
burden of obligations to the Imperial Exchequer of more than five million pounds,
representing about two millions for Ulster.
If Ireland is to be raised to the standard
of Great Britain in many departments of
her social and economic life, large initial
expenditure will necessarily be required, and
our considered opinion is that the period
during which the nominal contribution is
-made should be agreed upon as five years
from the appointed day. The probationary
period of two years provided in the Bill is,
in our judgment, entirely insufficient for
the establishment of the new Parliamentary institution on a solid foundation."
Sir, had this view carried any weight with
the Government, we should not have had the
long and irritating controversies with the
Treasury on new situations arising from time
to time. These controversies culminated at
the end of 1922, when the Chancellor of the
day, Mr. Baldwin, offered to submit outstanding financial questions to arbitration,
reserving certain subjects for direct discussion with the Government, such as the
cost of the Special Constabulary. This was
agreed to by our Government, and a Committee was constituted with Lord Colwyn as
Chairman.
This Committee has functioned for a
period of almost two years, and as the House
is aware, has published two reports, the final
one being now in the hands of hon. Members.
The Interim Report which was issued towards the end of 1923 dealt with the contribution of Northern Ireland to Imperial
Services for the first two complete financial
years of her autonomous existence whilst the
Final Report has laid down the general lines
on which the contribution for further
period of five years should be determined.
a
I am pleased at this point to assure the
House that apart from the obligations of the
two great burdens of Unemployment Insurance and Special Constabulary, which are
now in process of solution, the general
finances of the Province are in a perfectly
sound condition. (Hon. Members: Hear.
hear)
The House will no doubt expect from me
an interpretation of the main principles
governing the findings of the Committee,
whose report has been 80 long and 80
anxiously awaited. Let me say, by way of
preface, that the report as it stands gives
no idea of the extended arguments which
took place before the Committee. The
Treasury was represented by its very ablest
advocates, and certainly that is saying a
good deal. I am delighted to say that the
formula set out on Page 5 of the report is
virtually word for word that which was subnitted by Northern Ireland.
With this preface, let me endeavour to
rake clear in simple language the effect
of the Committee's findings.
The principle underlying the decision of
the Committee is that Northern Ireland's
total expenditure on local services should
be admitted to keep pace with the
total expenditure of Britain on an equivalent basis per head of the population, that
is, if Great Britain increased her local
expenditure by 10s. per head of her population, we in Northern Ireland can do the
same.
This basis of calculation on our relative
populations tends very greatly to simplicity
and gives us much greater flexibility in our
administration, but when applied to individual cases it proves sometimes to our
advantage and sometimes much to the contrary. For example, we have, owing to
emigration of young Ulster people in the
latter part of the last century, been left
with a number of old people out of all
proportion to those in Great Britain, so
that legislation in regard to Old Age Pensions becomes relatively far more burdensome when applied to Northern Ireland.
On the other hand, the formula proves to
our advantage in many cases and, on the
whole, I am satisfied that it is to the
benefit of Northern Ireland that its Parliament should get the freedom which is conferred by a general basis of calculation and
which it would not secure if it were feasible, which I doubt, to make a separate
equitable calculation in each particular
case.
But in order to give this principle practical effect, it is necessary to have a starting
point, from a normal revenue and expenditure basis. For this purpose,
the year
1923-24 was agreed as suitable, this being
the second complete year of our financial
existence.
I do not wish to labour my explanation
too much and therefore a practical example
of the working of the principle may convey
more clearly to the House its effect on our
accounts.

With regard to the relief schemes, the
recommendation of the Committee is that
consideration be given to the expenditure
or this service in Great Britain, and the
Joint Exchequer Board will determine our
allowance accordingly. I am quite satisfied
to leave this matter in the hands of the
Joint Exchequer Board, which is a fairly
constituted and equitable body. The last
item, namely, Grants in Relief of Agricultural Rates, has been calculated on a
population basis relative to the concurrent
expenditure in Great Britain.
It will be seen from these results that the
Northern Government has succeeded not only
in the establishment of a principle which
will govern the future general financial relations of the two areas for the coming five
years, but has determined our position in
regard to special services of a temporary
character, which could not appropriately
be dealt with in the general formula.
With regard to the net financial result
for the past year, I cannot with propriety
state with any definiteness what the actual
outcome will be. This matter is at present
under consideration by the Joint Exchequer
Board, and I am hopeful of results that will
not be regarded as unsatisfactory.
Having endeavoured to explain the results
accruing from the labours of the Colwyn
Committee, I now turn to consideration of
our balance sheet for last year.

RESERVED REVENUE, 1925-26.
I now leave the year that has gone by with
all its cares and anxieties-and they were
great-and I turn to the present year with
perhaps something more of hope and anticipation. The House will understand that
I must rely on the officers of the Imperial
Treasury to supply me with all the estimates of reserved revenue, as well as the
amounts to be expended on its collection.
The Imperial Chancellor has introduced
changes in the taxation of the country
which have an important bearing on our
revenues. The results are as follow:-
In the domain of Customs and Excise, possibly hon. Members may have noticed that
the Imperial Chancellor has introduced an
increased Imperial preference on sugar,
tobacco, dried fruits, etc., from the
Dominions. The loss resulting from that
concession to the Dominions amounts in our
case this year that we have entered upon
to £29,000, and in a full year we shall suffer
to the extent of £34,000.
On the other hand, the re-imposition of
the M'Kenna duties, which have been greatly
in the public eye for some considerable
time means an addition to our revenue
estimated for this year at £24,000, and in a
full year they should produce £40,000.
It is proposed by the Chancellor to impose a tax on silk and artificial silk. That
is expected to produce in our Province a
sum of £60,000 this year, and if we were
dealing with a full year it is expected that
it would amount to £105,000.
A duty on hops has also been imposed by
the Chancellor of the Exchequer, from which
we expect to obtain a revenue of £5,000 this
year and £9,000 in a full year.
The totals of the increases and decreases
in Customs and Excise show that cur reve
nue will benefit this year to the extent of
£60,000, while in a full year the result would
be an increase of £120,000.

TRANSFERRED REVENUE, 1925-26.
I come now to the revenue which is imposed and collected by our own Government
in our own area. In addition to the Budget
changes which are expected to reduce our
revenue in the current year by a sum of
£205,000, and in a full year by £455,000, the

a certain class of Death Duties, the effect of
which, if applied locally, would, it is

and £55,000 in a full year.
our
As the House knows, the control of Death
Duties is reserved to our own Parliament,
but in this case I propose to follow the
British precedent for this very important
reason, that if we decided to strike out on
our own line, and thereby reduce
revenue by £25,000, such reduction would
not be reflected in our Imperial contribution,
and would therefore become a charge on
the resources of Northern Ireland. For that
important reason I propose that we should
follow the precedent set by the Imperial
Chancellor in regard to this matter of Death
Duties.
ESTATE DUTIES.-Basing my estimate of
revenue on the expected results of this
change, I reckon that Estate Duties should
produce a sum of £495,000, a decrease of
£133,000 on the actual yield of last year.
During that period, as I have explained, we
had two exceptional windfalls of large
estates, which gave us a return of about
£140,000, so that the decrease I have mentioned almost exactly balances the amount
of these rather exceptional windfalls. I am
not justified in assuming that any such
accidental fortune will accrue two years in
succession, and, therefore, I must base my
forecast on conservative lines.
STAMPS.-I estimate that Stamp Duties will
produce £270,000-a reduction of £45,000 on
last year's yield. I feel it more prudent to
estimate a reduction from these duties
during the year owing to the windfall last
year from the registration of a large stock
flotation, which is not likely to be reproduced
in the current year.
EXCISE DUTIES.-Excise Duties, expected to
realise £163,000 are £5,200 less than last
year. These duties comprise Spirit Licences,
Entertainments Tax and general small
licences.
MOTOR DUTIES.-Motor Vehicle Duties are
estimated by our Home Affairs Department
as likely to produce £305,000, which is
£21,000 more than the actual yield of last
year. I presume that the expected increase
in this Department arises from the constant
increase of motor-car traffic. This revenue,
as possibly some of the hon. Members know, is
applied to maintenance of Roads, and therefore does not affect our general account.
Adding all the various items of revenue
over which we exercise control, I estimate

It has been the custom for the enemies of
Ulster to decry these contributions to
Britain's services, on the ground that socalled grants from the Imperial Treasury
have largely neutralized their values. We
claim that these grants have not been made
for Ulster services. They are the outcome of
Imperial policy, for which we are in no wise
responsible, and we repudiate the constantly
reiterated charge that we were mendicants
on Britain's bounty. If we are to be burdened
with the defence of the Province, then we
should be able to command Ulster's revenues
for this purpose.
(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
If, as is unthinkable, we had consented
to surrender our British citizenship as so
many of Britain's enemies hoped and desired,
we should have had ample means for all our
requirements and Britain would have received no contribution for the past four
years, and therefore no assistance for her
financial burdens.

7 MAY 1925
HOUSING.
turn now to a subject which has been
exercising the minds of the Government for
some time. I refer to the important question
of housing. In speaking at this table on my
Budget Statement last year I stated
that "a very acute shortage of houses,
principally of the class suitable for the wage
earners still exists." As hon. Members are
aware, two Housing Acts in the years 1923
and 1924, which gave the Government
authority to make a payment of £60 to local
authorities and private builders for each
house built according to the specified
standard offered a considerable stimulus to
those who were willing to resume building
operations.
The Government has no reason, I venture
to say, to be ashamed of the efforts which
it has put forward towards a solution of this
problem. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Under these recent Acts, up to the present
time, 885 houses have been approved by the
Ministry of Home Affairs in connection with
schemes formulated by local authorities, and
of this number about 100 have been completed. In addition to this, however, the
records of the Ministry of Home Affairs
indicate that schemes are in contemplation
involving the erection of an additional 1,156
houses. Moreover, in Belfast alone, 1,129
houses have been completed during the past
two or three years by the local authority
under the unemployment relief schemes, as
distinct from the Housing Acts to which I
have referred.
I think, therefore, that as far as the local
authorities are concerned, a very considerable advance has been made in the provision
of houses since the introduction of the two
Acts I have mentioned.
The Government regard it as a matter of
paramount importance, however, that the
private builder should be encouraged to make
some contribution to the housing question.
Certificates have already been issued and
approved by the Ministry of Home Affairs
in respect of 2,106 houses, of which 890 have
been completed by these private builders.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) In addition
to this, I am informed that a considerable
number of plans have been lodged with that
Department for further houses, and it would
appear that the rate of progress of building
is on the increase. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
I should like to remind the House, however, that the Housing Acts only apply to
Urban areas and to certain industrial centres in Rural areas, seven of which in the
Counties of Antrim, Down, Londonderry and
Tyrone, have been approved by the Ministry
of Home Affairs.
Over and above the operation of the
Housing Acts, the Rural District Councils
are empowered to carry out Housing
Schemes for the labourers in their districts,
and there are at present before the Ministry
of Home Affairs 13 schemes involving the
erection of 1,100 cottages in the Province.
Some of my hon. Friends from the country
will realise the beneficial results that are
likely to accrue from the figures I have
mentioned. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Notwithstanding the great improvement
which has been made in the matter of housebuilding within the last two or three years,
the Government feel that much remains to
be done if the present housing shortage is
to be substantially met. We have not yet
by a long way reached the time, I am afraid,
when the supply of houses will meet the
demand which is likely to be made...
As a measure of their interest in this subject, I may say that the Government propose
to introduce legislation before the adjourn,
ment which will have the effect of expediting
building not only in urban, but, I am glad
to say, also in rural districts. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Mr. Pollock]
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE.
Unemployment Insurance is still causing
the Government grave concern. The liability
is continuing to mount up at a high rate,
and we are awaiting with some anxiety the
decision of the British Cabinet Committee,
which is considering the question of the
amalgamation of the British and Ulster
Funds. I don't think it is necessary to
enter any more fully into the question, as
the circumstances are well known to hon.
Members.
But closely allied with this subject is the
question of other forms of public relief which
has recently come very prominently to the
front.
PENSION SCHEMES.
As to the proposal which has been made
in the Imperial Parliament regarding the
now Pension Scheme, it has not been possible
to forecast what the cost would be for Northern Ireland, since the British scheme is not
yet fixed, and from the discussions which
are taking place in Westminster it would
seem as if amendments may be anticipated.
It would be wholly beyond my province,
therefore, to attempt to estimate the cost of
carrying out the full scheme in Northern
Ireland, but I am reasonably certain that,
unless some extraordinary charge is thrown
on the Exchequer other than that which it
now bears in regard to pensions and insurances, we shall be able to meet the cost by
our own resources. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I am fortified in this by the statement
of Mr. Churchill that in the first few years
the scheme would show a slight profit, so that
by the time the additional charge comes to
fall on the Government we shall have been
able to stabilise our expenditure more than
is possible at present.
With regard to Old Age Pensions, our only
hope of expansion is that the temporary
items of expenditure, such as Special Con
stabulary, should be eliminated from our
Budget, freeing the necessary cash, or by

extremity. It must be evident that vast

to reassure the House and the country, however, by stating that the Government is
hopeful that when the Joint Exchequer

near parallel as our financial resources will
permit, with Great Britain, in respect to
these two ameliorative reforms.
Sir, that is the statement I have to make
in regard to the finances of the Province,
and, as I said before, apart altogether from
the extraordinary liability which has been
thrown upon the Northern Government in
respect of services for which we feel that we
are not responsible, I see no reason whatever
why Northern Ireland, when prosperity
comes, should not be able to take advantage
to the very fullest of the opportunities that
will arise. I beg to move. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)

I was much struck with the reference the

of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
This is a question which I think many Members of this House will have to think a good
deal about. It is owing to the action of the

two Funds were separated in the first

Ireland are going to suffer, because the

When the Devolution Scheme was proposed

Imperial or United Kingdom basis. I think

the wider the area the less the risk.
Members: Hear, hear.) Therefore, I think

amalgamation of the two Funds.

In regard to the very vital question of
housing, a great deal has been said about the

in this connection. (Hon. Members: Hear,

far as the building of houses is concerned,
has absolutely failed. Our Government now
makes a grant of £60 of public money to
every jerry builder who sets about building
houses. I have got to subscribe my quota to
that £60 of public money, and industrial
and other workers have also to subscribe
their share, to bolster up private enterprise
despite the fact that if these people had been
keen for building houses for the people there
was nothing to hinder them doing so in prewar days, but they did not. Now they come
cringing to the State and to the local authorities asking them for God's sake to bolster
their system up so as to enable the people to
get houses to live in. Unfortunately, we have
got to bolster them up to enable our people to
get houses. The housing problem was never
tackled in Great Britain or this country in
any effective way until John Wheatley,
the Minister of Health under the Labour
administration on the other side, did so.
You will remember he pointed out that one
of the main reasons why we could not get
houses is because of the financial sharks who
take two-thirds of the wealth created for
doing no useful service. He also pointed
out that the rent of a house that would cost
£500 would be 9s 9d per week, and that
68 9d out of that 9s 9d went to those people
who neither toiled nor spun but simply lent
their money. Even if the bricklayers worked
for nothing, even if all the labour was done
for nothing it would not make a reduction
of three half-pence in the rent.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Kyle) has,
in my opinion, failed in one respect. He has
not followed the general custom in replying
to a Chancellor after he has introduced his
Budget for the year. He has not congratulated my right hon. Friend as he deserves
to be congratulated on the bold way in which
he has dealt with so many of those very
difficult and complicated questions that are
applicable entirely to the working classes in
our midst. He blamed, first of all, my right
hon. Friend for paying any contribution at
all to Great Britain which means that in a
certain number of years

The PRIME MINISTER : I have no desire whatever to misrepresent the hon. Member, but I think all the same that when those

this contribution without any refusal on our

ceivable. It is gradually melting away, as

£8,000,000 from Northern Ireland is, owing
to the reduction of taxation, gradually
going down and down, until it has come
to about two and a half millions. It is
conceivable that sixpence or a shilling more
off the income tax or a reduction in the tea
and other duties may produce the effect
that the contribution instead of being paid
by Northern Ireland to Great Britain may
be paid by Great Britain to Northern Ireland in order to preserve the same standard
of living amongst the population as prevails
on the other side. And, of course, all this
money is in Ulster.
That is the long view, and that is the
view which my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Pollock) and his colleagues take. Although
it may appear to be a good electioneering cry
-and I think it has been used for that purpose--it is not in the best interests of the
Ulster people on patriotic grounds that we
should demur to paying our fair share for
these services. It is not in her material
interest to introduce a system which would
prevent us from getting our just and proper
dues supposing taxation was reduced to the
extent I have named. I hope I have satisfied
the hon. Member (Mr. Kyle) that he will be
doing no service whatever to the people of
Ulster, except, perhaps, for the next twelve
months or the next couple of years, if he
tries to cut off from us the responsibility
of contributing what is just and fair to our
Imperial connection. The next point I would
like to deal with-it is a very important
one is the statement that this was a rich
man's Budget.
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
The PRIME MINISTER: It is nothing of
the kind. I think my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Pollock) has picked out some super-tax
payers, certainly some of those wealthy
citizens in our midst, so that when they pass
away their estates will have to pay a much
higher scale of death duties than under the
old system. That is not taxing the poor.
It is really ridiculous that one should endeavour to split up into compartments what is
helping the rich and what is helping the poor.
If you take sixpence off the income tax imposed on men who are conducting our great
industries in Ulster, does it not obviously
follow that it will help those industries to
compete with foreign countries and to secure
more work to help the working classes in
our midst? It is appalling to see not only
shipping going to foreign countries to be
repaired, but orders for the building of
ships. That was a thing which in past days
was utterly impossible, because no foreign
country could compete with the great yards
in Belfast, the Clyde. the Tyneside, and
other parts. The reason of that to a large
extent is that taxation is heavier per head
of the population in Great Britain and
Northern Ireland than it is in these foreign
countries, and that is because we have faced
manfully the paying-off of our war debt and
intend to get rid of that heavy liability in
as few years as possible. Some foreign
countries have chosen to delav tackling that
question with the result that the taxation of
their people is much lower than it is in this
country and they are able to get-that is
what it amounts to-the orders that should
be coming to Belfast and the other shipbuilding centres. This is a loss to our
working men who are strolling about our
streets drawing unemployment benefit instead of doing what they would like to do,
using the hammer and working. I think
that is an answer to the statement that this
is a Budget in favour of the richer classes.
It is a Budget which in my opinion deserves
the encomiums not only of this House but
of the whole of Ulster. My right hon.
Friend after four strenuous years is once
more able to assure us-and any assurance
he gives carries weight not only in Ulster
but elsewhere-that the financial position of
Ulster is sound, and we are proud of the
results he has produced to-day.
There is another point. The hon. Member
(Mr. Kyle) said that our representatives, referring to the representatives in the Imperial
Parliament, during the past number of
years were to blame for the fact that there
is a lower standard here than in Great
Britain. Long before the hon. Member or
any of his Party came into this House we
laid it down at this Table that our whole
ideal was that the standard amongst all
classes in Ulster should be the same as in
Great Britain, and I challenge anyone to
pick out in any quarter of the Six Counties
of Ulster where we have failed to secure
that except in the delayed action, for this is
what it amounts to, with regard to pensions
which my right hon. Friend is hoping to be
able to carry out in the autumn of this year.
With that exception-and the minute subject
of the Entertainments Tax-I think those
are the only two points-there has been no
deviation in four years from the standard
which has been set up in the British House
of Commons. I cannot think at the moment
of any other thing in which there has
been the slightest difference between a man
living here and one on the other side.
Mr. KYLE: The educational services.
The PRIME MINISTER: The hon. Member says the educational services,

Motion made, and Question proposed,

Minister if he can tell me the order of
business for next week.
Mr. POLLOCK: The Budget discussion will
continue on Tuesday, and there will be three
Resolutions arising out of the Budget, the
Committee Stage of the Canals (Continuance
of Charging Powers) Bill, Charitable Loan
Societies Bill, and Public Health (Milk
Regulations) Bill. If time permits there will

Stage of the Pharmacy and Poisons Bill

of the Rent and Mortgage Interest Restrictions Bill. On Thursday Estimates will be
considered.

HILLSBOROUGH PARK.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether he can state if several families were turned out of their' homes
in Hillsborough' Park, i.e., Samuel Ginn and
family, John Ginn and family, John Herdman and family, Mr. Maddison and family,
and others; and are these homes still lying
idle and what alternative accommodation
was provided for those turned out,
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): I am informed that none of the persons mentioned in the question were turned
out of their homes in Hillsborough Park.
Arrangements were made between these persons and the previous owner of the Park,
and these arrangements were, I am informed, satisfactory to all parties. The question of providing alternative accommodation
did not arise, as I understand that each of
the persons mentioned obtained satisfactory
accommodation.
As I informed the hon. Member on the 30th
ultimo, the question of the future use of the
Park is at present under consideration by
the Government..
Mr. BEATTIE: Could the Minister inform me whether or not it is true to say
that one family received £100 compensation?
Mr. POLLOCK: I am not in a position to
make that statement, as all the arrangements.
were made by the previous owners of the
property, and they did not come under, our
cognizance in any way.
OLD AGE PENSION-JAMES DOHERTY,
KILREA.

3. Mr. MCALLISTER asked the Minister
for Home Affairs, whether the Local
Pensions Committee recommended James
Doherty, of Coleraine Street, Kilrea, for an
Old Age Pension on four separate occasions,
and if on appeal by the Pensions Officer, the
findings of the Local Committee were overruled on each of the four occasions on the
evidence of James Doherty's marriage, certificate, wherein he was stated to be then 27
years of age, and his wife's age 25 years; and
whether the baptismal certificate of James
Doherty's wife, who has for some time been
receiving a pension certifies that she was
72 years of age on the 8th May, 1925, and
whether affidavits had been produced to show
that James Doherty is now 77 years of age.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The statement in the first
part of the question is not correct as the
Local Old Age Pension Committee on the
occasions when the successive claims of the '
applicant were before them gave conflicting
decisions.
It is the fact that the marriage certificate
of this applicant gives the
age of the
claimant as 27 years, and his wife as 25 years
at the time of their marriage, and according
to that certificate the claimant would now be
only 67 years of age. When the latest claim
of the applicant was before the Ministry,
there was submitted for the first time the
Baptismal Certificate of the wife, showing
that she is now 72 years of age. On the
strength of this certificate which has only
now been submitted and as the result of
special investigations which were concluded
on the 5th instant, the Ministry, on the 7th
instant, decided to allow the claim,
ELECTION MEETINGS AND TRANS-
FERRED SCHOOLS.
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Education,
whether transferred schools will be available
for all election meetings at the next and
subsequent elections in Northern Ireland?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): Under the existing regulations no
political meetings may be held in schoolhouses, nor may any political business whatso-ever be transacted therein. The Ministry
does not at present contemplate any amendment of this regulation.
Mr. KYLE: Would the Ministry consider
the alterations of those regulations at as
early a date as is possible, so as to enable
election meetings to be held in those schools?
Mr. ROBB: The Minister does not at
present contemplate any amendment to these
regulations. The House will understand
that schools are vested in authorities, and
that the wishes of those authorities would
have to receive consideration before any
amendment is made. Until that is done I'
do not think the Ministry "would be in a
position to consider any amendment.

Local Bills.
AMENDMENT TO STANDING ORDERS.
The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND MEANS
(Mr Moles): I beg to move that the Standing
Orders of this House be amended by the addition of the following Orders:-
PART XIII.
DIVORCE BILLS.
174. A Bill for the dissolution of a marriage
between persons domiciled in Northern Ireland shall not be introduced into Parliament
except upon a petition to bring in such Bill.
Such petition shall be signed by the party to
the said marriage who desires the dissolution
thereof (hereinafter in these Orders called
"the Petitioner'); and there shall be
annexed to such petition a printed copy of
the proposed Bill, which shall be deemed to
form part thereof.
175. Every such petition shall be lodged in
the office of the Clerk of the Parliaments,
together with the following documents:-
(a) an official copy of the proceedings taken
or had in the Court having jurisdiction
over matrimonial causes at the place of
his or her domicile or residence, or in
some other Court having jurisdiction in
that behalf, at the suit of the Petitioner;
(b) in any case in which any trial at nisi
prius has been had, or any writ of
inquiry executed within the United
Kingdom, wherein the petition has been
party, a report of the proceedings upon
such trial or writ of inquiry.
The accuracy of the said reports shall
be verified by the affidavit of the
Petitioner.
176. A copy of such Petition and Bill shall
be delivered to the other party to the said
marriage (hereinafter in these Orders called
"the Respondent") within seven days of the
lodgment of such Petition, in the office of the
Clerk of the Parliaments; and in case of
infancy, such copy shall be delivered to the
guardian, or next relation of full age, not
concerned in the consequences of the Bill.
177. Every such Petition and Bill shall
thereupon be referred to the Examiner of
Petitions for Local Bills, who shall certify
to both Houses whether or not the Standing
Orders have been complied with in respect
of them.
If the Examiner is satisfied that it is im.
possible for the Petitioner to deliver a copy
of the Petition and Bill to the Respondent,
he may accept proof of substituted service.
178 If the Examiner shall certify that
Standing Orders have been complied with,
the Certificate shall be laid upon the Table
of the House of Commons, whereupon the Bill
shall be deemed to have been read a First
Time, and shall be recorded in the Votes as
having been so read.
179. The Respondent, if desirous of being
heard upon the merits against any such Bill
shall enter an appearance in the office of the
Clerk of the Parliaments on or before the
seventh day after the day on which the Bill
has been read a First Time in the House of
Commons.
180. No such Bill shall be read a Second
Time in the House of Commons earlier than
the third, or later than the fifth, day on
which the House shall sit after the day
upon which such Bill has been read a First
Time.
181. Every such Bill, after having been
read a Second Time in the House of Commons, shall be sent to the Senate, and shall
be laid upon the Table of that House, and
when so laid shall be deemed to have been
read a First Time, and shall be recorded in
the Minutes as having been so read.
182. No such Bill shall be read a Second
Time in the Senate earlier than the third,
or later than the fifth, day on which the
House shall sit after the first reading thereof.
183. Every such Bill, after having been
read a Second Time in the Senate shall
(whether the appearance mentioned in Section 6 of these Orders has or has not been
entered) be referred to a Joint Standing
Committee of both Houses, to be called the
Joint Committee on Divorce Bills."
184. The Joint Committee on Divorce Bills
shall be appointed at the commencement of
each Session, and shall consist of the Speaker
of the Senate, four Members of the House
of Commons appointed by that House, and
three other Members of the Senate appointed
by the Senate. The Speaker of the Senate
shall be the Chairman of such Committee,
and in his absence the Chair shall be taken
by such Member thereof as the Joint Committee may choose. Three Members (of
whom the Chairman shall be one) shall form
the quorum.
185. The said Joint Committee shall inquire upon lawful evidence as to whether
the averments in the Preamble are proved
to the satisfaction of the Committee or not.
The Petitioner shall attend the Committee,
in order to his being examined, if the Committee think fit, whether there has or has
not been any collusion directly or indirectly
on his part, relative to any act of adultery
that may have been committed by his wife,
or whether there be any collusion directly or
indirectly between the Petitioner and the
Respondent, or any other person or persons
touching such Divorce Bill, or touching any
proceedings or sentence of divorce had in

B to the Standing Orders relative to Local
Bills, shall apply to Divorce Bills, unless
otherwise directly stated in the said Appendix, as if in such Table the words
Petitioner" were substituted for the words

As the House would desire me to say a
few words, it has now become necessary to
set up machinery for dealing with Divorce
Bills in Northern Ireland. Prior to the
1920 Act, under which this House was established, Divorce Bills in Ireland were dealt
with at Westminster. Recently a Divorce
Bill from Northern Ireland was presented
at Westminster, and the Law Lords
having there carefully deliberated upon the
question, reached the conclusion that a Bill
ought to be promoted in this Parliament for
our jurisdiction, and not at Westminster.
It, therefore, becomes necessary to set up
Standing Orders to regulate the procedure
in reference to such business. The Standing
Orders as they appear on the Paper are taken
almost word for word from the Standing
Orders applicable to such Bills at Westininster, with all such verbal changes and
adaptations as will suit our conditions, and
the law relating to divorce in this country.

We are told that the people are bearing the

standing, up to the war debt and paying it
off. It is a very familiar saying, "Be honourable and pay your debts," but when you are
told of £20 a head and £5 a head you wonder
which of the two nations is best off in regard
to the late war. I want to draw the Prime
Minister's attention to a statement which I
am going to make and one that he can rest
assured is quite accurate. In regard to the
shipbuilding industry, and the deplorable
position that it is in to-day, I find on inquiry that the order was first and foremost
for only two ships. It is true that the firm
concerned is so well pleased with that order
that it is going to order a further three
ships at the same price. It has been said
that the specifications of the German firm
are different from the British firms, and that
the ships will not be equal to British ships
-that we are assured of either in material,
workmanship, finish or equipment. I have
bad experience and know that the workmanship of a foreign ship is not equal to
that of a British built ship. The same
class of ship that was built by British workmen during the war is still sailing the seas,
but some of the foreign ships of the same
type are 'in the scrap heap.
*
But let us see the German firm which is
building the ships and the method by
which it is able to build them. This German
firm, I learn from inquiries, is a great
capitalist combine of shipping,
shipping, shipbuilding, engineering, steel working and
mine owning interests. That is the
combine that has got the order for
the building of British ships. How are
they able to build these ships? I will try
to tell you. This firm got the sum of
700,000,000 gold marks which was paid to
German capitalists as an indemnity for their
supposed losses through the illegal occupation of the Ruhr. It is just a few months
since and I am sure hon. Members here will
remember it well-a public loan of £40,000,000
was sent to Germany. I am sure hon. Menibers will remember that quite well. If they
were in London they saw the queues waiting
to deposit their money to send to Germany.
I think the £40,000,000 was collected in about
twenty minutes, and the British financiers
were offering about fifty times more than the
Germans were asking for. That £40,000,000
also went to assist this German combine to
compete against British shipbuilders. But
that was not all that this firm got from the
Government of Germany. They got another
loan, and this loan was all to themselves. It
was a loan of 10,000,000 dollars from America.
What else they got I do not know, but it is
quite evident that this firm is now cutting us
out with the aid of British capital.
In addition to all the indemnities and
private loans all the German shipbuilders are

Mr. BEATTIE: Yes.

and being assisted by British financiers to

I would call a tax on foreign-built ships.
Of course, perhaps, I will be told that that
is not feasible or practicable, but it is the
only way in which we are going to safeguard the shipbuilding industry if we continue to proceed along the lines which British
financiers are following to-day. At the same

than she can use and here is a very important point-the British Chamber of Shipping
has petitioned the Government not to give
loans to British shipbuilders. And why?
