[Mr. Beattie]
Because they say if more ships are built there
will be less trade for the ships already built.
Yet the very same people are ordering ships
from Germany. This may seem paradoxical,
but after all the explanation is simple.
The German loans guarantee eight per cent.
Capital knows no country, and capitalist
companies, as is well known, have neither
soul to be saved nor body to be kicked. Trade
does not follow the flag. It follows the
capital, and one of the most deplorable facts
about the position of the British working
man to-day is that one of the very articles
in the manufacture of which he has been
brought up to serve his time is being handed
to a foreign country, and that foreign country
is being financed by British money. I say
that if anything can be done towards bringing that to an end the sooner it is done the
better for the British workpeople as a whole.
Now there were five ships given over in the
month of March. These ships were fabricated
ships. The cost of the five ships was about
£150,000. The Diesel engines in these ships
are patented in Germany-another loss to
British trade owing to negligence on the part
of the people responsible. British ship owners
could not, under present circumstances,
have competed for these ships. If the British
workman could have had an opportunity to
build these ships with Government assistance
similar to what is given to German shipbuilders we could have built them as cheaply
if not more cheaply. But there is one thing
about the whole affair which seems strange
to my mind, and that is that when the estimates were given for these ships the steel to
be used in the building was estimated by the
British shipbuilders at from £23 to £27 per
ton. Now the estimate shown by the German
shipbuilder was £19 per ton. Surely something was wrong from that point of view.
British manufactured steel, £23 to £27 per
ton, and German steel, £19 per ton. That assisted the shipbuilders to meet the requirements of the order.
I only want to speak on one other matter
before sitting down. It was contended
through the Press, and the Belfast Press in
particular, that the Germans were employing
unskilled labour at low wages and long hours,
and that this helped them to take this order
from the British firms. I want to say it was
nothing of the sort. In the shipbuilding
yards in Germany there are only one-fourth
of their employees unskilled. Three-fourths
are skilled. Those figures are taken from
the returns of my trade union journal.
As I was saying the whole five ships totalled
£150,000 £153,000 to be exact-but here is the
point; the very week after that order was
sent to Germany the Clyde booked an order
from the Australian Government to the extent of £4,500,000 for two cruisers. Surely if
there was a cheaper market than the British
market for cruisers Australia would also
have taken it the same as any other commercial concern. These cruisers have been
taken at so much less than they would have
cost in Australia that the Australian Government are able to build an air cruiser ship in
their country out of the difference between
the prices there and the prices in this
country. No capitalist newspaper has ever
said "Cheep" about the low price at which
we are able to build a thirty-knot vessel in
this country.
It comes back to this, that we have had the
old bogey of foreign competition thrown at
us. Since I was an apprentice I have heard
that bogey sounded throughout the industrial world. The cry always was "Competition is going to ruin us We will have to
get longer hours and less wages." Only last
year with all our poverty-and I speak now
for British shipyards, that is including the
Ulster shipyards, seeing that the Ulster shipyards are inside the British area-we built
about twice the tonnage of all the rest of
the world. Germany only built about oneeighth of our total. When this began we had
about four times more work in hands than
Germany. There are no workmen in the
world to touch the British workmen, but we
are being slowly strangled by the war debt
of £1,000,000 a day, by bankers, financiers,
and the present Tory Government, who,
whilst they refuse a starvation minimum
wage to the workers, have increased the bank
rate, thus increasing the unearned inof the idle millions, and correspondingly decreasing the opportunity of
trade and employment generally. The
engines of these five ships are a very
important factor, but I will be very brief in
dealing with this question. I would like it
to be well known that owing to the patent
rights having gone to Germany the engines
of these five ships cost £153,000, while they
would have cost the British shipbuilder
£60,000. That was because the patent rights
were taken from this country to Germany.

Government of
Northern Ireland have discharged their

materially in dealing with the housing shortage, they have also paid their contribution

There is another matter that I want to

Constabulary. He has taunted the Prime

The Ministry of Finance was able to assure
us that our finances were in a healthy and
sound condition, and that we are not mendicants but paying our way and paying our fair
share, if not more, to the Imperial Exchequer.
I was rather sorry, however, that the Prime
Minister a short time afterwards gave us a
cold douche when in reply to the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle) he visualised
the time two or three years hence when it
was just possible if we objected to pay our

Instead of contributing to the Imperial Exchequer we should be getting money from the

of Northern Ireland will not have much difficulty in getting the services transferred.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It will not be
hard to get liberty from the Imperial Parliament to collect and expend our own taxes.
I remember the late Mr. T. W. Russell when
somebody asked "What about the British taxpayer?" saying "Do not mind the British taxpayer; I am not scared that you are going to
diddle him." If and when that time comes
things will be simplified with regard to the
transfer of services.
I have no objection to our Imperial contribution at all, in fact I am proud of it, but
I do feel that before we contribute to the
Imperial Parliament our people should, at
least, be put on a level with the English
people. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I am
glad to say with regard to agriculture we are
not mendicants, because the Northern Government is in receipt of land purchase annuities amounting to £661,000 a year. I think
agriculture contributes more than it draws.
Agricultural land is not relieved to the same
extent here as it is in England. I am informed that in England the Government pays
three-fourths of the rates. I was across in
England last year and visited some farms.
Since then I have been in touch with a good
many agents and have got particulars of their
farms. I was struck with the low rate on
agricultural land as compared with the rate
we pay in Northern Ireland. I feel that before we make an Imperial contribution we
should put our farmers on a level with the
English farmers. If we gave them another
£100,000 in relief of rates it would be money
kept in this area. They would not be put on
a level with the English farmers, but as I
say it would be money kept in this area and

it would be for the financial stability of this

These are items that we should be perfectly

wrong. I see the Chancellor of the
Exchequer smiling. We have a just
claim on these items before we contribute to
Imperial expenditure. We are told that
our Imperial connections are a valuable asset.
I do not say they are not of some value,
but the men, who sent me here to represent
them fail to see the value of the Imperial
connection with regard to land purchase.
There have been comparisons made between
Northern Ireland and the Irish Free State,
and I am free to make further comparisons.
The Imperial Parliament has reserved to
itself this question of land purchase. I am
dealing with the question of the benefit we
get from Imperial connections. They have
kept us waiting since 1918 for a scheme of
land purchase, and have offered our farmers
a Bill which is at present before the Imperial Houses which gives the unbought
tenants a reduction of 3s. 10d. in the £ as
compared with a reduction of 7s. in the Free
State. It may be possible that under this
scheme the farmers will not get immediate
benefit for four years because the appointed
day is four years hence. In the Free State
the farmer gets an immediate reduction of
5s. from the gale day immediately preceding the date of the passing of the Act.
You cannot blame these unbought tenants
for their attitude. They are not men opposed
to the Government in ordinary policy, but
they feel that in this matter they have been
let down by their friends. They feel very
sore at being let down by people whom they
supported. The Chancellor said that the
Government could not give a grant without
an Amendment to the Government of Ireland
Act. There are a great many points that
need discussion and have not yet been discussed. I appeal for the holding of another
conference, at which the Imperial Government, the Northern Government, the
tenants and the landlords should be represented with an independent chairman, to
discuss these financial questions which have
not been discussed. I do think that the
Government of Northern Ireland should
give immediate relief to these men.
With regard to the £661,000 that the
Government get annually from land purchase annuities, I would like that point
cleared up. Is that an offset to the pledges
that the Imperial Government have given
to bear the expenses involved in carrying
through a scheme of land purchase?

There is just one other thing I want to
say in regard to the financial relations of the
two countries. I understand the Irish Free
State have set up as a counter-claim to their
contribution to the Imperial Parliament the
over-taxation of Ireland in the past. The
Imperial Parliament has so far recognised
that claim that they have consented to leave
it to arbitration. Hon. Members will remember that a Commission was appointed,
I think by Mr. Gladstone, in the year
1894, which was presided over by Mr.
Childers, to inquire into the financial relations of Great Britain and Ireland, taking
into account their taxable capacity. There
were on this Commission seven members representing Ireland and eight representing
Great Britain. That Commission produced
a Report which was signed by thirteen out
of the fifteen members, and that Report
stated that in the opinion of the Commission
Ireland had been overtaxed to the extent of
two and three-quarter million pounds.
I think the hon. Member for Tyrone and
Fermanagh (Mr. Elliott) probably made a
mistake about the Irish Free State denying
the Imperial contribution. I understand the
position is that they have set up a counterclaim to the Imperial contribution in regard
to the matter of over-taxation. Northern Ire

wish to detain the House after the speeches

We have got to-day a promise from the

ENTERTAINMENT TAX.
Mr. KYLE: I beg to move at the end of
the Question to add the words, "provided
that the Government intends to place the
Entertainment Tax in Northern Ireland on
the same footing as in Great Britain."
I think after the discussion this afternoon,
and in view of the fact that the majority of
hon. Members on the opposite side have
already pledged their words that, so far as
they are concerned, they are going to see
that this Entertainment Tax is placed on
the same footing in Northern Ireland as it
is on the other side. I need not stress this
particular injustice at any great length. I
am assured that the majority of hon. Members on the other side of the House have
given a definite promise that they are going
to see to it that this tax on entertainments
in Northern Ireland is abolished, or put on
the same level as in Great Britain. I have
been told that the Minister of Finance (Mr.
Pollock) gave a definite pledge to a deputation
that he would see that the Entertainments
Tax was placed in the same position as it
is on the other side. In view of that I think
it is hardly necessary to put up very many
arguments for my proposition, but I think
it is necessary, for the information of
those hon. Members who have not promised
to support this particular Amendment, to let
them know just how the matter stands.
The tax imposed in England, Scotland, and
Wales on entertainments to which the charge
for admission is 24d. is nil; in the Northern
counties of Ireland it is d.; from 3d. to 4d.
it is nil in England and 1d. in the Northern
counties; from 44d. to 6d. it is nil in England
and 1d. in Northern Ireland; from 7d. to is.
there is 2d. of a tax in England and 3d. in
Northern Ireland; from 1s. to 1s. 3d. the
tax is 3d. in England and in the Six Counties
it is 4d. Hon. Members will thus see that
in Northern Ireland the people who provide
these amusements for the public are at a
distinct disadvantage as compared with the
people on the other side. If and when the
Minister of Finance gets up and accepts this
Amendment I hope these caterers for amusements will see that this remission is returned to the people who patronise either the
picture houses or the football matches. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) But, whether they
do or not, in regard to the picture houses,
I would like to point out that if we are not
to be put on the same lines as in England
there is the tendency that these people will
not be able to carry on in the summer
time as they do in the winter-a
picture house is not as attractive in
the summer as it is in the winter
--with the result that many of the picture
houses in Belfast whose wage bills amount
to three figures are going to be compelled
to dispense with the services of some of their
staff. We will then have a new form of
seasonal occupation, and the Minister of
Labour (Mr. Andrews) will have to meet
deputation after deputation from the trade
unions wanting to have his blood, because
he is putting these people down as
seasonal workers. I think it is in the best
interests of the Unemployment Insurance
Fund, which is in a bad way, that there
should be as few people unemployed as
possible.
Mr. ANDREWS: Hear, hear.
Mr. KYLE: If it is going to help and I
am assured by the people who run this par-

ticular form of amusement in the city of

bigger ideas than ever I had when I played

Tax. I am just afraid that in some of these

with the need for the abolition of this tax.
In another part of this country football is
looked upon in a different light from up
here. We look upon it as a sport. The
other part of the country looks upon it

tremendous lot to be said for it. If it is

I rise to supplement the observations which
have been made by my hon. Friend (Mr.
Kyle) and to support him in the claim he has
made. I do so, first of all, because I want
everybody in this city and in these Six
Counties to be placed in a position
equality with everybody else in Great Britain.
If things go on as they are going the song
"Britons never, never shall be slaves" will
be changed to "Britons never shall be slaves
except Belfast Britons," because whilst in
Manchester, Liverpool, Bradford, Glasgow
and in all the other great centres of population there is a tax upon entertainments of
an extremely moderate character we
compelled to pay a larger impost here.
are
Take. for instance, the case of football. I
quite agree with what my hon. Friend (Mr.
Kyle) has said, that it is the sport of the
The Budget-
Resumed Debate.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Devlin]
working classes. I am sorry that more
people who attend football matches do not
play football. I wish everybody could play
football instead of standing watching
matches. It would be better for the moral
strength and character of the people if we
had more football clubs, so that the young
people of our country could participate in
the game. My hon. Friend has pointed out
in what way they can be encouraged.
Juvenile football clubs have been started
lately. The leaders of sports can foster and
encourage the spirit of sport amongst the
youths, and any encouragement given to sport
is pre-eminently a service the moral
stamina of the nation.
to
As a rule sportsmen, even when they are
Government whips, are exceedingly decent
fellows when they are divorced from politics.
For a considerable time there had been no
racing in Ireland and the right hon. and
gallant Gentleman (Captain Dixon) went to
Derry and made a very strong speech. I would
suggest to him as one who admires his sporting proclivities that before he mounts the
forum in the Guildhall again he will attend
some sporting meetings and temper his
violence with his better love for the things
we are discussing now. These young football
associations are holding competitions-I
heard of this a minute or two ago-to encourage the younger members of the community to start football clubs. Every boy
who entered these football matches had to
pay a tax of 1d upon his 4d entrance. The
State took that penny and 3d was allowed
for the expense of fostering the sport, paying
for the ground, and meeting all the other
expenditure incidental to this highly desirable work. I think that is not fair at all.
I come now to the next question, the entertainment tax on picture houses. I have a
sneaking regard for picture houses. During
my enforced absence from public life, to
which so many eloquent and not altogether
generous references have been made here, 1
frequented picture houses. I used to go to
them two or three times a week, Unfortunately, I cannot go any longer, as I come here
instead. Therefore, as "one touch of nature
makes the whole world kin" I have a sneaking regard for these picture houses and I am
anxious to see them encouraged. As football is the sport of the working classes so
the picture houses are the centres of joy and
amusement for the poorer classes. I see
women with shawls, who would not for the
world go to the centre of the city to attend
a theatre, going to them, and I see little barefooted children getting in for 2d or 3d, and
sometimes for 1d. In their grey and grim
lives they witness very little joy and for this
reason some of them go to these places and
enjoy a couple of hours seeing a good story.
Some of the pictures might be condemnedyou cannot get perfection in anything-but
they give a good story told in the most vivid
form which impresses these young people.
They see colour and beauty and representations of all those higher and sweeter things
of life. Many of these picture houses are
centres of a very educative character, educative in the sense that those who go there
see foreign countries and witness representations of scenes that would never otherwise
come before their eyes. The pictures lift
them, as I say, out of the grim and grey
existence which they are called upon to live
in the squalid and wretched homes which are
so blighting an influence upon the character
and virtue of otherwise good and kindly
people. What sort of mean taxation is it
that makes these people out of their inadequate wage, out of their dole, pay this penny
upon an entrance fee of 4d? I do not think
it can be justified. I am not interested in
the slightest degree in the owners of these
picture houses.
In regard to sporting associations no profits
are made out of them at all, and so that
question does not arise. I am not interested
in the profits of the owners of picture houses
or of the theatres, though I do think the
incidence of taxation in these matters is
all wrong. Let me take a case in point. Supposing a theatrical company of a very highly
efficient character brings a very inspiring
play little known and little advertised. They
come and have an empty theatre for a week.
They may lose £100 on the week, and yet
they have to pay taxation upon every ticket
that is bought in that theatre. I do not
think that is fair. If there is a tax at all it
ought to be a tax upon the profits and not a
tax upon entrances. I would think that would
be the wiser course, though I confess I have
not given very much thought to it because 1
am not interested in the least degree in the
owners.
Finally I come to what is my strongest
argument. I am getting this in in a
side way.
I want to say to the right hon.
Gentleman the Minister of Finance that
my hon. Friend the Member for North
Belfast (Mr. Kyle) was wrong. He was
putting a far too generous interpretation
upon the speech of the right hon. Gentleman when he said we had extracted a promise from him. We tried to extract a
promise by our combined rhetorical
violence. We tried to "draw" the right
hon. Gentleman, but we did not succeed,
and the right hon. Gentleman has not
given us any promise at all. The hon. Member said that the Chancellor of the Exchequer has promised that in the sweet
by-and-by we will get all these things done
for us, but he did not say that at all. The
right hon. Gentleman said that if our

generous, then Belfast Britons would be put

That is what the Minister of Finance said.

Let me say in conclusion that in a
historic speech which I made not long ago
I stated I was going to come to this House
to offer constructive criticism. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) And that I propose to do.
You must forgive me if my method
offering it does not commend itself to the
Chairman of Committees, because he has
dual advantages in these controversies
which others do not possess. I would be
prepared if the Speaker would waive the
Rules of the House, which he will not do,
or if other opportunities are extended to me,
to offer to the right hon. Gentleman the
Minister of Finance some constructive
suggestions, I can see the whole reason for
the right hon. Gentleman's trepidation in
making us all Britons in equality of value
as well as Britons in equality of responsibility. I would be prepared to make many
suggestions to the right hon. Gentleman as
to where great savings might be brought
about even in this Northern Administration
without reference to the grant to the Imperial Government at all-I would be
prepared either publicly or in this House if I
get the opportunity or else privately. My
whole feeling about this Government is that
they would like to make contemptible little
economies when they ought to cast their
minds to the task of the bigger economies,
because that is where real economy lies. Why
keep up a tremendously swollen military
force under those peaceful conditions that
have been so eloquently depicted by various
speakers, including the hon. Member for
Antrim (Mr. G. Henderson) who tells us
that peace has been proclaimed and who
congratulated the Government on peace
having been proclaimed? The Prime
Minister tells us that peace has not only
been proclaimed but established, and the
hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh
(Mr. Elliott) tells us that peace and order
prevail in Ulster. Under these peaceful
conditions why spend these large sums of
money expended upon the maintenance of a
military force? In a population of one
million you are spending £2,000,000 upon
the police. I would say reduce that expenditure and take off the entertainments
tax, remove the thrift disqualification
clauses, reduce the age for pensions to 60
years, and give pensions at anyrate to
widows and orphans. Then you will have no
Opposition at all, because we will so rejoice
at this marvellous achievement, such a
splendid vindication of the Government,
that we will shower upon you even greater
congratulations than the Prime Minister
wanted for you.
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not think I have any
reason to complain of the character of the
debate that has resulted from the presentation of my annual statement of
accounts. But I suppose I am only concerned at this moment in the defence
with that part of my Budget which pertains
to the limitation which is down in the
Amendment now before the House. I am
greatly obliged to my hon. Friend for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin), who has spoken, for
offering such valuable advice, and I cannot
fail to appreciate the offer he has made.
Whether in public or in private I will be
very glad to hear of those constructive
measures which the hon. Gentleman has in
mind, and which will contribute SO
greatly to the wealth and prosperity of
Ulster.
But I am not hear to discuss the ethics of
sport either in respect of the entertainment
tax or the football clubs to which my hon.
Friend from the West referred in such
touching terms, No doubt these picture
houses are centres of enjoyment and amusement. Indeed the pictures which the hon.
Member presented of those places were so
appealing that it is very difficult, if the
ethics of the matter were being discussed,
to resist such an appeal. But I am afraid
that I have to descend to the practical
and utilitarian basis of life.
I may preliminarise any further remarks
by saying that I at no time gave any
definite undertaking to conform to the
practice in Great Britain in respect of the
entertainment tax. If I ever made any remark to deputations on this subject I said
I was perfectly willingly to place all our
services on the basis of Britain's arrangements within the limits of our financial
resources. I believe that qualification was
invariably made by the Prime Minister. If
I may say so, I am just as anxious as the
hon. Members opposite that all our services,
whether social or otherwise, should be on the
same basis as Great Britain. But I have to
remind the House that we are not on the
same basis, apart altogether from this
question we are discussing. We are not on
the same basis, and if we were we would
be in very bad shape indeed. Are hon Members opposite aware that in Great Britain
one half the cost of education-in our case
£1,000,000, the half of £2,00,000-is paid out
of rates? And if we followed Great Britain
in that we should have to impose on the
The Budget-
Resumed Debate.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
community of Northern Ireland a rating
equal to £1,000,000 in order to maintain the
education service. And further, we would
have to pay one million pounds more by way
of contribution to Great Britain. That is one
instance in which we are not on equal terms,
but it happens to suit us. As someone remarked in colloquial if not perhaps in eloquent language, the boot is on the other foot.
In the matter of property valuation-I do
not want to enlarge on these matters-we
have an advantage which is equal to £500,000
as compared with Great Britain. The boot
is on the other foot, I think, in that case also.
In the case of our police service, if it were
placed on the same basis or if Great Britain
insisted that we should be placed on the same
basis we should have to pay Great Britain
an amount of something like three to four
hundred thousand pounds additional contribution. Therefore to insist, as my hon.
Friend from the East Division (Mr. Beattie)
said that as loyal Britons we should insist,
that in every case we should be on the same
basis as Great Britain we would have been
ourselves in a very parlous state in connection with some of our services.
But in regard to what is known as social
services I am not behind any hon. Members,
whether behind me or facing me, in my demands on Great Britain that we should, in
respect of the standard of living, be placed
in the same position as in Great Britain,
and I have emphasized that fact in every
conference in which I have been present and
in every discussion in which I have taken
part.
Now I come down to practicalities in this
matter. As I say, if we had money to spare
upon social services up to the standard 1
would like, and if we had not such tremendous obligations apart from the normal
condition of finance, I should be the first to
say that in every respect where taxation was
concerned, that we should be on all fours
with Great Britain. But I am sorry to say
that the obligations which we have undertaken under very great stress, the obligations
to feed so many people in Northern Ireland,
to prevent starvation and misery and despair
perhaps, from ensuing-if we were not in
that position I should be the very first to
argue that it was necessary that we should
in all matters of taxation agree with Great
Britain.
In regard to the entertainment tax which
has not been remitted on all entrances under
6d the amount in question is £22,000. The other
concessions bring the total to £45,000. Now
the owners of these picture houses make no
pretence whatever that they propose to
give the benefits of part of this
£45,000
fectly
to the people. They are perhonest, and perfectly straightforward in that matter. They say their
business is in a parlous condition. There
are too many picture houses and they
are not making money. They say, "We want
this £45,000 in order to make profits." Now
when that Act was passed in Great Britain
it was represented that this relief would pass
to the people, but it has been found in
practice that the relief has not passed to the
people, and therefore it has resolved itself
into a subsidy to picture-house owners. That
in effect is what we are asked to do now. We
are asked, not to give relief to the peoplethose people that the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) has spoken of in such

Mr. DEVLIN: Would the right hon.
Gentleman say the British Government were

The British can do no wrong.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have just said the British
Government when they gave relief to the
extent we are now discussing were under the

No relief is given to the people who attend

I am not blaming the people who endeavour
to save these picture houses-the picture
house owners who endeavour to save themselves in that way. I am merely stating the
facts. I am not making excuses because
necessarily we cannot follow Great Britain,
but I am stating that, by comparison with

fimited, there can be no question as to which

We have unemployed people to the extent

the problem facing the Northern Government

not

My right hon. Friend the Prime Minister

That is the position that we are in now,

aspect that I want to deal with is this. If as

before the Committee at the moment is as

be in order.

Friend (Mr. Devlin) realises that in the
Question which I am now asked to rule I

Mr. BARBOUR : We had before

which constituted the County Officers into a
Civil Service of their own, and during the

Officers worked, and necessarily the only way
of improving their status would involve some
slight extra charge on the Estimates. It is
estimated the immediate effect of the change
will be about £417 in the course of the first
year, and that the increase will eventually
rise perhaps to the sum of £1,000. But the
changes in the status of these officials are so
very desirable and equitable, that I feel hon.
Members will have no difficulty in accepting
the results of the Bill, which has already
passed this House, and in accordance with
which this Estimate has been framed. I beg
to move.

CONSTITUTION OF JOINT UNOPPOSED
COMMITTEES.
Mr. SPEAKER: Before the adjournment
of the House is moved I should like to call
attention to an earlier proceeding to-day
when we were considering a Motion by the
Chairman of Ways and Means with regard
to the Joint Unopposed Committee on the
Belfast Corporation Bill and the London
Midland and Scottish Railway Co. Bill. Since
the addition of the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) to that Committee was
carried by the House the Standing Order
dealing with the matter has been brought to
my notice. It appears that under it, two
Members of this House, consisting of the
Chairman of Ways and Means and one other
Member, can be appointed by this House to
sit on a Joint Unopposed Committee, so that
the part of the Resolution which includes the
third Member is I am afraid void, being contrary to the Standing Orders.
Mr. DEVLIN: When I raised this
question I did. not intend that I should be
the Member selected, in fact, if I had known
that by the unanimous wish of the House I
should be the honoured person I should not
have raised the question at all. I do not
want the position as it would take a lot of
time which I cannot afford, but I think that
subsequent to this we really ought to have
an understanding with the Government with
regard to this, because, not only have the
Opposition no representative but the two
Senators who will be consulted with regard
to these Private Bills are also supporters of
the Government. I think it would be desireable that there should be at least one Member of the Opposition on the Committee.
The PRIME MINISTER: I readily
acquiesce with what the hon. Member (Mr.
Devlin) says. My right hon. Friend the
Chief Whip (Captain Dixon) will keep in
close touch with the hon. Members opposite,
and when these Committees have to be set
up will see that the Opposition gets proper
representation.

DEATH OF THE PREMIER OF NEV
ZEALAND.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Captain Mulholland).
The PRIME MINISTER: I think it would
be the desire of the House before we part,
that I should, on behalf of the Members of
all parts, offer our sincere sympathy to those
who are sorrowing in New Zealand on
account of the sudden and tragic death of
their Prime Minister. I know well that ali
sections of thought and feeling in Ulster
looked upon the late Mr. Massey as one of
our most distinguished sons in any part of
the globe. Our Province may be proud of
those it has sent forth to all corners to uphold British traditions, and in that long roll
of names none stands more honoured
in our hearts than that of the late Prime
Minister of New Zealand.. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). He was born and
spent his early life in the County of Derry.
From time to time it was his duty in the
interests of the Province-in the interests of
Great New Zealand to come to this country
on various duties. I therefore came into
545 Flax Trade Dispute.

12 MAY 1925
Flax Trade Dispute.
contact with him and formed a high opinion,
not only of his sterling character and worth,
but of his statesmanship, his Imperial feeling
towards all parts of Great Britain and the
Empire, and his extraordinary religious
feeling, if I may touch up on that solemn
subject.
His whole soul was centred upon the
people whom he had the honour to represent
in New Zealand, but throughout all there
was a warm place in his heart for his own
native heath, and over and over again when
I was talking with him he has shown undying affection for his native cou. ty and for
his native Ulster. There are few 1. ho could
say that they were Prime Minister for
thirteen years in succession, and none
amongst Imperial Prime Ministers of this
country who could show an unbroken record
from before the war up to the present dat.
That was the unique position filled by Mr.
Massey alone. When he was last here revisiting us he was full of vigour and
strength, and those who will remember him
when Queen's University honoured him so
signally will have been struck by the
brightness, the cheerfulness, the looking forward with hope and optimism beyond
ordinary to the future of that great country.
Now within these few months he is laid to
rest. I would like it to go out to New Zealand-to Auckland, which after all is
capital of what used to be called New
Ulster-to go out to Nev Ulster from old
Ulster that as they are mourning for their
Prime Minister, we here re joining sincerely
in mourning for a distinguished Ulsterman
whom we all loved.

Mr. KYLE: As intimated earlier, in conof the
sequence
reply the Minister
of Labour
me to a question
I had down on the Paper as to whether
he is aware of the practice of the Flax
Spinners' Association instituting a boycott
of men who leave any of their firms and find
employment in other places. I desire to raise
the matter at this stage. The Flax Spinners
have the practice when a man, or a number
of men, fall out with a particular management and leave that firm, the Association
send word to all the members of the Association to see that these men do not get employment. Recently we had a dispute in
County Armagh, the Armagh Spinning
Company, regarding flax dressers; and these
men who quit their work there or some of
them came to Belfast. One of them
found employment-a number of them have,
by the way, found employment. One of them
in particular found employment three weeks
ago, but he was approached last Tuesday, and
told that in consequence of the fact that he
had left Mr. Wilson's place in Armagh the
firm would not engage him any longer, and he
would have to leave the employment he was
in. I think this House will agree that that
is an unsocial practice. Had it been committed by trade unionists or any body of
workpeople here, or when it was committed
earlier in the last century in other parts of
the
country there were no people who
denounced it so strongly as members of the
Party who sit opposite. It was called boycott in those days. It is just the same
whether it is done by employers or workpeople.
The employers in this case, in my opinion, are
uilty of that unsocial practice, and I think
it should meet with the disapproval of this
House. This man was employed in the York
Street Flax-spinning Company up to last
'Tuesday when he got this letter or rather
tre got it:
"We have to inform you that as we had
a letter from the Armagh Spinning Company stating that this man was on strike
we had no alternative but to let him go."
In other words if any body of workpeople
leave job so far as the Spinners' Association
is concerned, they are going to keep them out
of work for the rest of their lives. I think
this is a reprehensible practice.
A'r. ANDREWS: It will be in the recol.
letion of the House that the answer I gave

real, and which applies to a particular firm.
is cuite in orde.. I would point out, however,

con erned are not satisfied about this matter.
the best course oper: for them would be to take

please tell us the business for next week or
the rest of this week?
The PRIME MINISTER: The announcement made on Thursday last by my right hon.
Friend, regarding this week's business holds.
The business for to-morrow, Wednesday, will
be the Committee stage of the Pharmacy
Bill, the Second Reading of the Rent Restrictions Bill and the Second Reading of the Rules
Publication Bill will appear on the Order
Paper, but will be taken only if time permits.
Otherwise the consideration of these Measures
will be deferred to Tuesday of next week.
On Thursday the following Estimates will be
taken: Class I, No. 3, Ministry of Finance;
Class I. No. 10, Secret Service; Class I, No.
11. Record Office. Class III, No. 4 Unemploy.
ment Grant. The Budget resolutions will be
reported to the House. Then we shall have
Committee of Ways and Means, and the
Finance Bill will be read a First time.
Mr. DEVLIN: Can the right hon. Gentleman say when the House will rise for Whitsuntide? Maybe I had better put that
question later on?
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps later on.
PRICE OF OFFICIAL DEBATES.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I rise to
suggest to this House, but especially to the
Minister of Finance, a method whereby he
could increase the revenue of this Government. I have been looking at a copy of the
Parliamentary Debates in this House and I
see the price is sixpence, for this which I hold
here in my hand. Were any newsagent to
publish a book and to charge sixpence for
something in similar form to this. he would
be entitled to six months for profiteering.
(Laughter). Is the charge of sixpence for
this book made for the purpose of putting
it out of the reach of the workers of the
Province of Ulster? I understand that the
Imperial Parliament has reduced the price
of Hansard to three pence, and I would
suggest to the Minister of Finance that he
should charge twopence for this publication,
and let the newsboys have it at three halfpence, so that they would have a halfpenny
on every copy of Hansard they sell. Then
the citizens of Ulster will get the truth and
nothing but the truth. (Laughter.) Right
hon. Members opposite may laugh, but
according to the reports in the Press the
Opposition are a poor lot. I am sure that
when this book gets into circulation it will
assist the Government, even if we are a poor
lot.
an
It is up to the Government to support this
suggestion of mine, and thus enable the
working men and working women of Ulster to
read what is taking place in this Parliament. I know that some of the hon. Members opposite will say it is a deplorable
thing and a horrible thing that I, as
Orangeman, should go out and vote with
the hon. Member for West Belfast, but I am
very proud to take a copy of Hansard into
the Orange Halls and to show it to the
Orangemen. I need not go so far as to
suggest that some of the hon. Members opposite should take it into the Unionist Clubs.
Take it anywhere, broadcast it anywhere.
I believe the Minister of Finance would be
able to raise a large sum of money in the way
I have suggested. and I believe the circulation of this book, if it were published at a
reasonable price, would beat the "Telegraph”
or the "News-Letter." It would also be the
means of giving the little fellows who bring
the papers to our doors an opportunity of
earning a better livelihood, because I believe
that this book would be bought more than
any newspaper circulating in Ulster. 1
would suggest that the Minister of Finance
should take into consideration at an early
date the reduction of the price of Hansard
to twopence, and that he should give it to
the newsboys at three halfpence.
Mr. POLLOCK: I was under the impression that some rearrangement was made last
Session in order that Hansard should be
circulated at a low price to those who are
interested in it and did not feel disposed to
pay the price charged. I presume, however,
that in the interest of that economy with
which the whole atmosphere seems to be
saturated at the present time, that the price
has been increased. However. I will undertake that the whole matter will be reconsidered.
Question, "That this House do now adjourn," put, and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at Twentyfive minutes after Six o'clock.

Wednesday, 13th May, 1925.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.

Private Business.
BELFAST CORPORATION BILL.
The Chairman of Ways and Means reported
from the Joint Committee on the Belfast
Corporation Bill as follows:-That they had
considered the said Bill, and examined the
allegations thereof, which were found to be
true, and that the Committee had gone
through the Bill, and made some Amendments thereto.
LONDON, MIDLAND AND SCOTTISH
RAILWAY BILL.
The Chairman of Ways and Means reported
from the Joint Committee on the London,
Midland and Scottish Railway Bill as
follows:-That they had considered the said
Bill, and examined the allegations thereof,
which were found to be true, and that the
Committee had gone through the Bill, and
made an Amendment thereto.
Papers Presented to Parliament.
Revised Estimate, Class VI, No. 2, Harbour
and Commercial Services. (By Command.)
Ordered to lie on the Table and to be printed.
Ministry of Finance :-Statement of Guarantees which the Ministry of Finance have
undertaken to give up to March 31st, 1925.

"(7) Notwithstanding anything in the
foregoing provisions of this section, the
Council shall have power, if it thinks fit,

chemist;

as may be prescribed."
The original Sub-clause (7) has been, as
hon. Members will observe, deleted. This
new sub-clause sets out in some detail the
conditions upon which members of pharmaceutical societies elsewhere may be registered. It also provides the conditions on
which other societies can be recognized by
the new Society to be formed in Northern
Ireland. This is I think the simplest way of
ensuring reciprocity between the new Society
and the other pharmaceutical societies in
England, Scotland and elsewhere.
Amendment agreed to.
Clause as amended to stand part of the
Bill.

Sir DAWSON BATES: There has been so
much misunderstanding in regard to law on
the subject of Rent Restriction that it will,
I think, be a convenience to the House, and
enable hon. Members to understand better
the effect of the Bill, if I briefly refer to the
existing legislation dealing with that subject. There have been altogether three Acts,
one passed in 1915, one in 1919, and one in
1920.
With regard to the 1915 Act, that Act first
established the principle of control. It only
applied to houses of a valuation of £26 and
under, and it laid down that the rent
charged on this class of house on 3rd August,
1924, was to be regarded as a standard rent,
and that no increase could be made thereon.
It also gave security of tenure. This Act
remained in force until the 1919 Act was
passed. Owing to the increase of prices, it
was felt that an injustice had been done to
the landlord, and, under the 1919 Act, in
addition to extending the valuation at which
restrictions should apply to houses of a
valuation of £52 and under, the landlord was
allowed to charge an additional 10 per cent.
over the standard rent. This was to cover
the addition to general costs and repairs.
The third Act was passed in 1920, and
prices at that time had increased materially.
That particular Act, I might tell hon. Members, is referred to in the present Bill as
"the principal Act." It may help them to
follow some of the Clauses in the Bill. Under
this Act houses up to a valuation of £78 were
brought within the scope of the Acts. As it
was felt that at that time conditions had
become so accentuated the landlord was empowered to charge 15 per cent. on the net
rent, and a further 25 per cent. as representing the difference between the cost of
repairs as in August, 1914 and 1920, in cases
where the landlord was liable for repairs.
In addition, the landlord became entitled to
charge any additional increase in rates over
those payable in 1914. This Act, however,
excluded from its provisions houses that were
erected after or were in course of erection in
April, 1919. I would like to remind hon.
Members that where houses were built between 1914 and 1919 the standard rent was
the rent at which the house was first let.
It was provided that that Act of 1920 should
terminate in June, 1923, as it was thought
by the authors of the Act that by the time
1923 arrived there would be a sufficient
number of houses, and that it would be
possible then to do away with the principle
of control. It was found, however, that owing
to the shortage in the supply of houses it
was impossible to allow the Act to lapse, and,
accordingly, the Acts have been continued
up to the present time. We are, therefore,
working under the 1920 Act. I think everybody will agree with me when I say that
State control, as opposed to private enterprise, has always ended in disaster.
Mr. KYLE: No, no.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The effect of the
Rent Restriction Acts, so far as the provision
of houses is concerned, has been disastrous,
and I think if those responsible for the introduction of the principle laid down in these
laws could have visualised the effect they
have had in the development of housing they
would have hesitated to introduce such a
far-reaching principle.
One of the obstacles to the development of
housing is uncertainty as to future legislation. Persons are not going to erect houses
if they fear the State is going to step in and
control them as to how these houses are to
be used. We must get back to normal conditions, and leave it to private enterprise
to meet the necessities of the case, aided, if
necessary, with the financial help, but without the control, of the State. You must
either do that or let the State take over the
whole question of housing.
T
Rent Restrictions Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mir. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: But, as I said
before, intervention by the State in business
has always had disastrous results.
Mr. KYLE indicated dissent.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: What about
shipping during the war?
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend
will get an opportunity of developing all these
points later on, and I do not expect that we
will agree.
The chief object of the Bill before the
House is gradually to do away with all restrictions. By this Bill we desire to remove
any possible fears that prospective builders
may have
as to the possibility of future
State control. It is impossible, without
disastrous results, to effect immediate decontrol; it must be done by stages.
We propose in effect to reverse the process under which these artificial restrictions were imposed. As has been explained, houses with a lower valuation
were first brought within the ambit of the
Act, and gradually the limiting valuation
was increased.
With regard to the £78 valuation, the Bill
provides that the restriction on the higher
valuation which was first imposed under
the Act of 1920, is to be the first to disappear.
We propose that decontrol on houses of
£52 to £78 valuation should take effect on
the 1st November, 1926. There will be a
breathing space for this class of tenant for
another 18 months, during which time I
hope the occupiers will find ample opportunity to make their own arrangements.
£52 Valuation:-The next stage will be
decontrol of houses between £26 and £52
valuation; that is, those houses which were
brought under the Act of 1919. This class
of house comes out of control on the first
of May, 1928, that is a period of 3 years.
£26 Valuation:-Lastly we are giving a
long period to the houses which do not exceed
a £26 valuation, and which were brought
in under the 1915 Act. We are extending
their period of control to 1st May, 1930-a
period of 5 years from the present date.
I do not think that anyone can accuse us
We
of adopting hasty or harsh measures.
have deliberately specified fixed dates for
this reason that one of the greatest difficulties which are agitating the minds of the
private builders and the public generally,
is the uncertainty of the Government's intentions in the future. I believe that it will
be to the good not alone of the landlord,
but of the tenant to know exactly how they
will stand in the future. Decontrol must be
faced sooner or later, and I believe we have
adopted the policy which will be the easiest
for the landlord and the easiest for the
tenant.
a
I want to say a word about Contracting
out. There can be no doubt but that
tenants of houses which are about to be decontrolled may want to make arrangements
with their landlords for new leases before
the date of decontrol, and we are making
express provision for that purpose in Subsections 2 and 3 of Section 2, under which
a lease can be made for a period of not
less than two years, but terminating subsequent to the date of decontrol. Once
valid lease is granted the principal Act will
no longer apply. I might mention, however,
that this will not only apply to houses of
a valuation of over £26. We have deliberately omitted houses under a £26
valuation from this Clause. They will not
be decontrolled for 5 years hence, and it is
quite an unusual thing to make long leases
for this class of house. Therefore occupiers
of houses of this type will not be able to
contract themselves out of the Act any more
than in the past.
With regard to the question of Decontrol
of Vacant Houses. We also provide that by
Clause 2 (1) where the landlord comes into
possession of a house over £8 in valuation,
that control shall cease to apply to such
house, but houses of £8 valuation and under
will remain subject to control, even if they
become vacant prior to the appointed day
for decontrol.
Now I come to the question of the one
house owner, which is agitating the minds
of many people. There are many cases in
which an individual purchases a house for
himself or herself with the intention of
occupying it. We believe that it is only
an act of justice that such persons should be
allowed to obtain possession, and that no conditions should be imposed which would prevent them from getting into their own
homes. We, therefore, propose that where
a dwelling house to which the Act applies
has been purchased by the landlord for
occupation as a residence for himself on or
before 1st May, 1923, that the landlord shall be
entitled to get possession on giving six months'
notice, without being obliged to provide
alternative accommodation. We also propose, regardless of the date when the
house was purchased, where the house is
required by the landlord for occupation as a
residence either for himself or his father or his
mother, or any son or daughter, or any
person residing with him or in his employment, to give possession provided the
landlord finds alternative accommodation,
that is substantially equivalent,
and pro-

vided the Court is satisfied that the granting of a decree would cause less hardship
than the with-holding of it, or where the
Court is satisfied that the premises are required for any purpose which in the opinion
of the Court is in the public interest.
Mr. DEVLIN: What does the right hon.
Gentleman mean by the words "Any person
residing with him"? That has a very broad
interpretation.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think if the hon.
Member will refer to the Clause itself he
will find that the exact expression is "residing with." My hon. Friend knows perfectly well that in many cases persons who
are not relatives live with people for many
years and are treated as members of the
family.
Mr. DEVLIN: But he may be brought in
specifically for the purposes of this Act.
Sir DAWSON BATES: If the hon. Member
will have a little patience I will explain
the whole thing to him. I think he is jumping to conclusions, as he is rather inclined
to do.
Hon. Members will observe that in the
alternative accommodation defined in Clause
4 "5 (1) (e)" the accommodation to be provided must be substantially equivalent. The
old definition of "alternative accommodation"
was identical in all respects.
To meet the case that my hon. Friend, the
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin), has
raised, I would inform him that if he looks
at Clause 4, sub-section 6, he will find that
with the object of dealing with persons who
make fraudulent representations to the judge
with a view to obtaining possession of a
house, provision has been inserted under
which such persons will render themselves
liable to criminal proceedings and to very
heavy penalties.
I now come to a provision which I am
quite satisfied will be criticised by hon.
Members opposite, that is the question of
repairs and the allowance to landlord for
repairs under the 1920 Act.
Under that Act, the landlord was authorised to charge an additional 25 per cent. on
the nett rent in cases where he was responsible for carrying out the repairs of the
house. This 25 per cent. increase has been
the subject of some misapprehension. It is a
common but fallacious idea that this 25 per
cent. was given by way of covering the whole
cost of repairs. This 25 per cent. was made
to cover the difference in the cost of repairs
between that existing in 1914 and 1920. The
facts are that in practically all tenancies
made in Belfast, and in other cases in Northern Ireland, especially in regard to the
smaller houses, it has been the custom for
the landlord to carry out the repairs, even
though under Deasy's Act, which I shall
refer to hereafter, the obligation of carryout the repairs was imposed on the tenant
in the absence of anything to the contrary.
Mr. KYLE: They generally do it.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The 25 per cent.
allowed to the landlord was therefore in
respect only of the additional cost of repairs,
and was not intended to cover the entire cost
of repairs, and a landlord in fixing his rent
in the pre-control period always had regard
to the liability he had for repairs, and I
think I am correct in saying that the amount
that a prudent landlord would set aside for
repairs would be in the neighbourhood of
15 per cent. of the rent he received.
The cost of wages and materials has fallen
appreciably since 1920. I have obtained some
figures, and I find that between May 1920
and May 1925 the wages paid to bricklayers
and joiners have fallen from 2s 3d to 1s 9d
per hour, and that there have been similar
cuts in the wages of glaziers, plasterers,
plumbers and slaters. As regards the price
of material, in the case of bricks and timber
the cost has fallen as much as 50 per cent.
since 1920, while the cost of slates has fallen
by almost 30 per cent. I cannot but think,
therefore, that I am reasonable in assuming
that in the next five years the cost will not
be any higher and possibly will be lower.
The Government is satisfied that it would
be unjustifiable to impose on the tenants
the continuance of the full charge of 25 per
cent. which is fixed rightly or wrongly as
being the appropriate figure representing
the difference in the cost between 1914 and
1920, and while it is not proposed to disturb
the 15 per cent. that is added in respect of
rent which was imposed under the Act of
1920, we propose that on and after the 1st
day of November, 1925, the 25 per cent. on
foot of repairs is to be reduced to 15 per
cent, making a total of 30 per cent, as against
40 per cent. imposed under the Act of 1920.
Reference has been made to what is known
as Deasy's Act, more properly known as
the Landlord and Tenants Act, 1860. Under
this Act the tenant, in the absence of an
express agreement to the contrary, is responsible for repairs. The framers of the 1920
Act appear not to have had this Act in mind,
and while the view and indeed the custom of
the landlords in Belfast, and I think in other
parts of the Six Counties, has always been
that they are liable for repairs in the absence
of a specific contract, and while some people
have held that Deasy's Act has been overridden by the Rent Restriction Act of 1920,
the matter is not free from doubt and we
have made it clear in this Bill that, in any
case where the rent has been increased under
Section 2 of the Act of 1920, the landlord
Rent Restrictions Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
shall be deemed to be responsible for the repairs. We also provide that any claim arising under the Act by a tenant against a landlord must be made within a period of six
months after such claim has arisen. That is
to prevent a lot of old claims being
made at some future date. As a corollary
to this principle of liability, the Bill provides machinery by a clause whereby the
tenant can be relieved of additional rent on
foot of repairs where the landlord neglects
to keep the premises in a reasonable state of
repair.
Before I sit down I would like-because
I think this has a certain amount of bearing
on the whole subject-to give hon. Members
some statistics in regard to housing operations in Northern Ireland since the time
the Rent Act of 1920 was introduced. At
that period substantial assistance was
afforded by the Imperial Government both to
private builders and local authorities erecting working-class houses, but up to the year
1922, when this assistance lapsed, only 533
houses were provided in Northern Ireland
by private builders, and 502 by local authorities, the numbers for Belfast, where the
greater proportion was built, being 279 and
459 respectively. Since then over 1,100
houses have been built with the aid of unemployment grants, most of these houses being
erected in the city of Belfast, where the
shortage is estimated to be at least 10,000
houses. In addition to these houses further
houses have been erected or are contemplated
under the provisions of the Housing Act.
passed by this Parliament in November, 1923,
under which a grant of £60 is paid out of
Government funds in respect of each
house erected complying with the prescribed
conditions, and local authorities are also
empowered to make a grant of £40.
At the moment over 2,100 houses to be
erected by private builders have been
approved, and of these over 900 have been
completed. The number of houses being
erected or contemplated by local authorities
under this Act is nearly 2,000, of which
approximately 200 have been completed.
These figures indicate a considerable improvement in housing operations of local
authorities, who, between the years 1890 and
1919, only provided a total of 664 houses, and
further that private enterprise is gradually
coming back into the field of the housing
industry. There is every reason to hope that
this progress will be maintained, and that
the housing shortage will be considerably
ameliorated in the course of the next few
years. I might also add that the approximate number of dwelling houses in the city
of Belfast two years ago was 82,000, of which
52,000, or 63 per cent., are rated at £8 and
under, 25,000, or 30 per cent., between £8 and
£20, and the remaining 5,000 at over £20. By
the end of the current year it is expected
that the total will approach 87,000 houses.
It is the intention of the Government to
introduce a measure extending the operations
of the Housing Acts to Rural Districts-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear) — and otherwise
amending the Acts with the object of accelerating building. The figures which I have
given show that there is a steady and substantial progress being made towards making
good the large deficit in housing accommodation. As shown, I believe it is only by
increased private enterprise and removing
restrictions of all kinds that the difficult
question of housing can be solved. We
believe this Act is a fair and just measure,
to both the landlords and the tenants, and
in that view I beg to move the Second
Reading.
Mr. BEATTIE: I rise to move the rejection

Sir DAWSON BATES: You will have an

Mr. BEATTIE: We may have. We never

most important; it is the most pressing of

about social reform, surely you ought to
listen to the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Grant)
who does claim to represent the working
classes. He can find nothing good in the
Bill, but, of course, according to his ancient
custom, though not believing in the Bill he
will vote for it. I have no doubt he will
produce amendments by the dozen and make
eloquent speeches on the amendments, but
he will vote against them.
Mr. GRANT: Question.
Mr. DEVLIN: I see he is converted. He
has come round to my view, that if you
want anything from Governments you do not
get it by making plausible speeches to the
electorate, but by going into the Lobby and
voting against them. I invite the hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Grant) to do that. The hon.
lady Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester) in
her very charming speech yesterday, told me
she would vote with me-and that was a great
concession-only for the fact that she thought
she might defeat the Government, and, of
course, she loves the Government more than
she loves other things. But may I point out
to the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Grant) that there is not the slightest chance
of his defeating the Government? In serried
array behind the Prime Minister are all the
agents of privilege. They will see that property is well protected and defended. Surely
from the place where the hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Grant) sits be may be able to come
along with us and for once shake the Government, frighten them at all events, if not convince them, influence them to do some of
those things which he thinks are eminently
desirable in the interest of the working
classes if this Bill is to be carried through.
So far as I am concerned I think it is a
contemptible Bill. I will vote against it, and
then after we have voted against it it will be
carried with the vote of the hon. Gentleman
opposite and others. Then he will come forward with his amendments and I will come
forward with mine. If he stands pat, so will
I, and together in alliance, holy or otherwise,
we may be able perhaps so to influence the
subsequent solution of this problem through
this Bill, as to offer something to the public
that will be acceptable to them.
Question put, "That the word 'now' stand
part of the Question."

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 14th May, 1925.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is prepared to pay Unemployment Benefit to workers resident in
Border counties, who, while residing in the
Free State, have Northern Ireland Unemployment cards, and pay contributions to
the Northern Ireland Unemployment Insurance Fund; and whether he is prepared
to take any further steps to a reciprocal
arrangement between the Free State and
the Northern counties with reference to the
availability of either's contributions.
The PARLIAMENTARY
SECRETARY
OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): As the answer to the hon.
Member's question is necessarily somewhat
lengthy I will, with his permission, circulate the answer in the Official Report.
The answer is as follows:
In accordance with the statutory provisions governing the Unemployment Insurance scheme in Northern Ireland an
insured contributor is disqualified from
receiving unemployment benefit while he
is resident, whether temporarily or permanently outside Northern Ireland. In the
face of this statutory disqualification my
Department cannot, as the hon. Member
will appreciate, pay benefit to insured
contributors while they are resident in the
Irish Free State.
In regard to the second part of the hon.
Member's question, when the Government
of Northern Ireland was made responsible
for unemployment insurance on the 1st
January, 1922, the provisions of the unemployment scheme were uniform throughout
the United Kingdom, and it was the
practice to treat contributions paid in any
part of the United Kingdom as valid for
the payment of benefit in any other part.
The establishment of the Government of
Northern Ireland involved no departure
from either this uniform scheme or
practice, and, the Imperial authorities
being at that time responsible for the administration of unemployment insurance in
what is now the Free State, as well as in
Great Britain, the practice was automatically continued in the Free State area also.
In April, 1922, the Provisional Government assumed control of the Free State
area, and they were at once informed by
the Ministry of Labour for Northern
Ireland that the continuance of the existing
practice, in so far as the Free State area
was concerned, was conditional entirely
(pending the completion of a reciprocity
agreement) on the maintenance of the
hitherto uniform insurance scheme.
Meantime, in order that the position
might be regularised, and the Northern
Ireland Unemployment Fund protected, the
Ministry pressed for a reciprocity agreement which would include Great Britain,
Northern Ireland, and the Free State.
Up to the summer of 1923 no progress had
been made in that direction. About that
time the Free State Parliament passed an
Unemployment Insurance Act, which made
a fundamental departure from the hitherto
uniform insurance schemes, and created the
precise position which, as the Free State
authorities had been informed at the outset,
necessarily prevented the Ministry from
continuing the practice above described for
the following amongst other reasons.
As trustees of the Unemployment Fund of
Northern Ireland the Department had no
option but to suspend a practice which in
consequence of the less favourable benefit
provisions prevailing in the Free State
following on the new legislation, would have
involved the Northern Ireland Fund in a
financial liability out of all proportion to
that which was likely to fall on the Free
State. Moreover, this "breakaway" by the
Free State Government from the common
scheme coincided with the making of claims
in Northern Ireland by men beginning to
be demobilised by the Free State Forces,
which threatened to cause a serious drain on
the resources of the Fund.
The Ministry immediately called for a conference to be held of representatives of the
appropriate Imperial, Northern Ireland and
Free State Departments to discuss these
important questions and to see whether, notwithstanding the divergence of the Free
State scheme, some form of tripartite reciprocity scheme could not be reached.
A special arrangement was made to meet
the case of certain classes of ex-members of
the Free State Forces who had previously
been insured persons in Northern Ireland,
but as regards general reciprocity the
divergence between the unemployment
insurance schemes instead of diminishing increased as time went on, and towards the end
of 1923 the Free State Department intimated
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
14 MAY 1925
that the provisions of their Unemployment
Insurance Scheme had become so different
from those of the scheme common to both
Great Britain and Northern Ireland that
any system of reciprocity was impracticable.
The latest stage was reached in July, 1923,
when a conference was held in London
between representatives of the three Departments to adjust the consequences of this
decision of the Free State Government.
Taking the situation as it is to-day, no reciprocity arrangement, even on a contribution basis, would be feasible as between the
several Unemployment Funds, for the
schemes are now on lines so divergent that
the contributions possess a much greater
benefit value in Great Britain and Northern
Ireland, both as regards rates and extent of
benefit, than in the Free State.
In viewing the foregoing I cannot see what
further steps can be taken to arrive at an
equitable arrangement which would be truly
reciprocal and consistent with our relations
to the scheme in Great Britain.
INSURANCE OF AGRICULTURAL
WORKERS.
2. Mr. KYLE: asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that the Imperial Government has set up a Departmental Committee with the following terms
of reference:-"To consider and report
whether it is desirable that workers in
agriculture should be compulsorily insureu
against the risks of unemployment, and, if
so, on what terms and conditions and in
what manner the insurance of agricultural
workers can be most effectively provided
either by the inclusion of agriculture within the scope of existing legislation;" or by
means of new legislation, and will the
Minister consider the advisability of following the lead given by the Imperial
Government.
Mr. GORDON: Yes, Sir, I am aware
that it has been decided to set up such a
Committee, and when it has reported due
consideration will be paid to its findings by
the Government.
Mr KYLE: Is the Minister of Labour not
prepared to set up a Committee, in view of
the somewhat different circumstances which
obtain in Northern Ireland, in order to get
first-hand evidence as to the desirability
of taking this step?
Mr. GORDON: I can add nothing to the
answer I have given to the hon. Member.
When the findings of the Committee are
reached, undoubtedly the Government will
consider the whole situation. I can nake
no more definite answer than I have already
given to the hon. Member.
Mr. KYLE: The conditions of agriculture
across the water are somewhat different
from those in Northern Ireland, and my
point is that we want a Committee set up
in Northern Ireland. What I want to
know from the Minister is this, is he prepared to set up a Committee in Northern
Ireland?
Mr GORDON: Not just at present.

RELIGION OF TEACHERS.

TRAVELLING FARES OF SCHOOL
CHILDREN.
6. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Commerce whether he will approach the various
railway and shipping companies with a view
to their allowing school children to travel
at half fares up to fourteen years of age,
instead of twelve years as at present, in view
of the fact that the school-leaving age is
now fourteen.
Mr. BARBOUR: The three principal railway companies in Northern Ireland issue
season tickets to persons under 18 years of
age at half the ordinary rates, and at twothirds the ordinary rates to persons of 18
and under 21 years.
The same companies
and the shipping companies charge half fares
for children of three and under 12 years in
the case of ordinary single and return
tickets, and, as their practice in this respect
corresponds to that of the companies in
Great Britain, I do not consider that I would
be justified in approaching them in the sense
which the honourable Member suggests.
Mr. KYLE: Does the Minister of Commerce appreciate the burden that is cast on
persons who wish to send their children to
schools at a distance, and will he not consider the advisability of making representations to the companies
ULSTER PAVILION, WEMBLEY.
7. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Commerce whether any Member of this
House is employed at the Ulster Pavilion
at Wembley; if so, in what capacity; and
whether the whole or any part of his salary
is chargeable against public funds.
Mr. BARBOUR: In answer to the first
part of my hon. Friend's question, there
is no Member of this House in the employment of my Ministry at the Ulster Pavilion
at Wembley; consequently the latter two
parts of the question do not arise. I should
explain that my Ministry has no official
cognizance of any appointments which

Mr. DEVLIN: On this Motion I would like
to suggest that some communication ought
to be made to Members of this House as to
the business of the House. I notice that the
Committee stage of the Rent Restrictions
Bill is down for to-day, and I think that is
rather forcing the pace.
Captain DIXON : It will not be taken
to-day.
Mr. DEVLIN: My hon. and gallant Friend
says he does not propose to take it to-day;
but that does not in any way influence me
in suggesting that before matters of very
great importance are placed upon the Paper
the question of the convenience of the
Business of the House.
Supply.

Members ought to be consulted. It is in the
interests of public business that we should
not be compelled to rush into the consideration of this important question without
having time to consider it. Really if this
Rent Restrictions Bill came on to-day we
would have practically no time to draft those
essential Amendments, which will, no doubt,
be accepted, and which will so conspicuously
improve the Measure when it is passing
through the House.
Captain DIXON: In answer to my hon.
Friend, I may say that we are only too happy
to meet the convenience of himself or any of
the other Members of the Opposition in this
matter. It is the custom for the Leader of
the Opposition to get up and ask what
the business of the House is, and
we are prepared to give it to the Opposition. In this particular case I quite agree
that it is too soon to move the Committee
stage of the Rent Restrictions Bill, and we
do not propose to take it to-day.
Mr. SPEAKER: Perhaps I may point out
to the hon. Member (Mr. Devlin), who ought
to know this, that really it is for the Government to settle the business and they often
put a large number of items down which are
often postponed till to-morrow. It does not
mean because business is down for a particular day it is going to be taken that day.
The point is that it is the business of the
Whips to inform Members of their own party
after consultation with the Government
Whips what business is really going to be
taken. The fact that certain business appears among the Orders of the day does not
mean that it will be taken.
Mr. DEVLIN: I am glad you made that
statement because that is just the point I
want to raise. When these orders are
placed on the Paper the Government ought
to let us know whether they propose to take
these Bills or not, because if they put these
Bills down and do not inform us as to what
they propose to do then we may think they
are going on with them and we may come in
with unconsidered opinions. Nothing is so
wrong in Parliamentary life as unconsidered
opinions expressed, as my right hon, Friend
recognises. We want to come with our
minds developed, our opinions well thought
out and our suggestions so fruitful of wisdom
that we may be able to contribute something
to the debate. So I would suggest to my
right hon, and gallant Friend that he will
these
inform the Opposition as regards Go
Orders placed on the paper whether the Government propose to take them on the day
on which they are placed on the Order
paper? I am sure with his usual courtesy
he will do so.
Mr. SPEAKER: Perhaps I may also add
that as a matter of Parliamentary procedure
it is really the duty of the Whip of the hon.
Member's party to ascertain the business.
Mr. DEVLIN: I have no Whip. I have to
do the whole thing myself.
Mr. SPEAKER: The sooner the hon. Member appoints a Whip the better.
Mr. DEVLIN: I shall have two, I hope,
soon.
Captain DIXON: Hon. Members must know
that the Whip puts as much business on the
Paper as he can, and it largely depends on
the eloquence of hon. Members on both sides
of the House if we can carry through that
business. It is rather impossible, therefore,
to meet the hon. Member's request and say
the exact business, but in so far as I can
I shall meet him and let him know what I
think will probably be taken on each day
the House meets.
Question put and agreed to.
