ending on the 31st of March, 1926, for grants
to local authorities, etc., in Northern Ireland
for assistance in carrying out approved
chemes to relieve unemployment."
(Note.-£50,000 has been voted on account).
Mr. GORDON: In moving this Estimate
I do not think I need say anything by way
of recommending it to hon. Members of this
Committee. The Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews) has brought before the Committee
so often the necessity for providing schemes
of relief with a view to absorbing the unemployed that it is not necessary for me to
cover the ground that he has covered so frequently, more than to move the Vote that is
in the Estimates toward Unemployment
Grants.
Mr. KYLE: I was wondering if the Minister of Labour, in making application to
this Committee for £150,000 for grants to
local authorities for the relief of unemployment, has taken into account the fact that
the Belfast Corporation, to enable them to
take advantage of the grants in the past,
have burdened their ratepayers to a tremendous extent, and if it would be possible
for the Government to give the Corporation,
or any other public body which have availed
themselves in the past of the opportunity of
getting fifty or sixty per cent. of the wages
on these various schemes which they have
put forward, somewhat better terms and
better conditions than they have been getting
in the past, so as to enable the Corporation
at the least cost to the ratepayers to put
into force any schemes which they may have
contemplated for the relief of unemployment.
It seems to me that the trouble of unemployment, in Belfast at least, is getting
more and more acute, and unless something
very big is attempted we are going to be
faced this winter with an army of unemployed numbering round about 50,000. That
is enough to give anyone cause to pause and
wonder what is going to happen if nothing
is done to provide for the winter that lies
ahead of us. I think the Minister of Labour
will find that this Vote is too small, and he
may have to apply to the Committee for a
Supplementary Estimate. I am sure if he
does so this Committee will give him a ready
response, as it always has done in a case of
this nature. I implore the Committee to try
to realise what the position will be during
the coming winter with the unemployed
numbering 48,000 now at the beginning of the
summer. What it is likely to be this winter
we cannot at all say, but unless numerous
orders are secured by the shipbuilding yards,
and unless the linen trade shows better signs
than it does at the moment we are going to
be face to face with a worse situation than
we have ever had before.
I respectfully suggest to the Minister of
Labour that something might be done in the
way of offering local authorities who have
already done something to prove that they
are interested in this problem still easier
terms than those already offered to them.
When you reckon that the Corporation of
Belfast have had to borrow something like
two millions of money for the purpose of
Unemployment Grants. 616
Supply--
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Kyle]
getting 100,000 under the last grant it immediately springs to one's mind that the
Corporation of Belfast cannot go on doing
things like that.
Mr. POLLOCK: What about the taxpayers?
Mr. KYLE: In our opinion this problem
of unemployment is a national problem and
ought to be borne by the whole community
as it is in the interests of the whole community that unemployment should be as well
met by the Government as possible. On that
score we hold that the entire problem should
be tackled by this Parliament, but on this

if the Ministry of Labour could see their
way to offer easier terms to those bodies
which have already taken advantage of the
schemes afforded by the Ministry I think it
would be a jolly good thing for the community of Belfast at least.
Mr. GRANT: I would like to support the
claim put forward by the hon. Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Kyle) that the Ministry
should seriously consider the advisability of
giving those local authorities who have been
public-spirited enough to come forward and

terms than they have been getting. It has
been pointed out that it is the ratepayers
and the taxpayers who will have to bear
the greater part of the burden, but when
we recollect that a few days ago the taxpayers of Belfast, through their representatives on this Committee, agreed to a Vote
of £128,000 to assist agriculture it is only
right that the agriculturists should assist
the townspeople, or any other people, in this
particular way. I do hope the Minister of
Labour (Mr. Andrews) will be able to make
the terms somewhat easier, because the coming winter is going to be a bad one for all
the people, and if the shipyards remain the
way they are, the prospect is going to be
very little brighter. I hope it will be possible to devise some schemes whereby we will
be able to get some more money to carry on
these particular works. I just wish again
to emphasise the claims put forward by the
hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle).
Mr. CRAWFORD: I would like to put in
a word for the urban and rural districts to
the Minister of Labour. In the urban and
rural districts we have as much unemployment in proportion to our numbers as in the
city. We have also been doing our best to
relieve unemployment in the past, and if
anything extra is to be done in that way for
the Corporation of Belfast I hope the Minister of Labour will be kind enough to extend it to the rural and urban districts also.
The farmers have been mentioned, but I
would remind hon. Members for the city that
the farmers here are not receiving the same
grants in relief of rates as the farmers in
England, Scotland, Wales or the Free State,
so that I think no exception need be taken
to anything that has been done in the past
for the farming community.
Dr. MORRISON: There is one aspect of
this question that appeals to me, and it is
that you are asking a man to work and you
are using State money to provide him with
work when he cannot get it otherwise. Now
I think that is a very valuable proposition
to make, but in the past we have been largely
giving men money for not working. We have
been encouraging people not to work and
have been giving them money that properly
should be used in encouraging them to work.
In my own district I know large numbers of
people who come under this category. I
have in my mind the mill workers who could
get farming work but prefer unemployment.
They get the dole and, therefore, they are
not willing to take the average work that is
going amongst the farm labourers.
It has been suggested by the Ballymoney
Chamber of Commerce that all men who are
getting the unemployment dole should be
compelled to work at works of public utility.
Now I think that is a very fair proposition,
and, while I would be in favour of providing
work such as the hon. Member (Mr.
Kyle) has suggested through loans to enable
local authorities, I think the people who
have had that opportunity should be compelled to come in and work, and that the
dole which they are now extracting from the
public taxpayers should be utilised and saved
in that respect by making them do some useful work.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: While I
recognise the serious state of unemploymen
in the city of Belfast and the amount of
taxation which has been undertaken by the
Belfast Corporation in order to provide work
for the unemployed I think in comparison
there has been just as large a rise in rural
rates as there has been in the city of Belfast,
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) If the agricultural industry were in a prosperous condition I would not object to one part of the
community, if they were able to do so, helping to shoulder the burdens of the other,
because we are told we should bear each
others' burdens. But I am afraid at the
present time the agricultural community is
not in such a state as to be able to shoulder
any more burdens than they are bearing.
We have to look at this thing comparatively,
because when we are asked to make a grant
in relief of agricultural rates of £128,000 and
are comparing that with a grant of £200,000to relieve unemployment we are talking
about an industry that produces more wealth
in this community than all the other industries put together. We have got to face
the fact that this Government up to the
present time has not been able to relieve the
rates on agricultural land to the same ex-

tent as in England. I have no objection, if

(Mr.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR
Andrews): There are one or two aspects
of this case which I would like to put before the Committee. In the first place I
would again like to express my indebtedness
to all our local authorities in Northern Ireland, and especially to the Belfast Corporation, for the way in which they have cooperated with the Government in promoting schemes of public utility in order to find
as much employment as possible for our unemployed. I am not in a position to promise
a higher percentage grant than that which
we are giving at present, and for this
reason: At the present time we are giving
sixty per cent. of the labour costs on condition that unemployed persons are engaged
for the work. If I were to give a larger
grant to the city of Belfast in all fairness
I would be obliged to extend the advantages
of that larger grant to our country districts
as well. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). Besides, hon. Members opposite are frequently
appealing to the Government to keep on
parallel lines with Great Britain, which has
been the policy of the Government since it
was formed and since this Parliament was
established some four years ago. To give a
larger percentage than sixty per cent. of the
labour costs would be going beyond what
is given in Great Britain.
There was one remark made by the hon.
Member for the University (Dr. Morrison)
to which I would like to refer. He mentioned that certain of our Chambers of Commerce have been suggesting that unemployment benefit should be used for the purpose
of paying wages to men working rather
than be given to men who were unemployed.
Legislation as it stands at the present time
is a bar to the Government doing anything
of the kind. In the second place, I would
point out that if we once admitted the
principle of subsidising wages I fear there
would be very few people for whom employers
would not ask for a subsidy. Another
argument which I think I am justified
is that where the Unusing
employment Fund is strained as it is at
large
the present time to keep such a
number of people from going into absolutely
dire want, the money is not available to provide work for them. To keep them working.
would involve at the present time an expenditure of about £8,000,000, because you have
not only, in the first place, to pay a living
wage, but in the second place, you would
have to provide the materials which these
in
men
would absorb while working, and
which cost about three times as much as the
actual wages that they would be paid.
These are some of the difficulties which the
Government are faced with in dealing with
this great problem. It is our wish to find
employment for as many of our people as
possible, and that is the reason why we are
asking for this sum of £200,000 to enable us
to co-operate with our local authorities
during the present financial year in the same
way as we have been doing in the past. Some
hon. Members may no doubt desire that this
sum should be larger than £200,000, but I
would point out that after all we are largely,
if not entirely, in the hands of our local
authorities. It is they who promote the
schemes, and as the hon. Member for North
Belfast (Mr. Kyle) very well knows all the
Government can do is to encourage local
authorities by means of this Grant to put
up as many schemes as possible. I may add,
on behalf of the Government, that if this
£200,000 should be absorbed by the local
authorities before the end of the financial
year, the Government would sympathetically
consider asking for a Supplementary Estimate
to allow us to continue the same work.

It is from a very strong
into this House.
supporter of the Government, who lives in

letter that most of the farmers in his parish
are at present in a very miserable condition,
that the farmer living next to him has lost
sixteen cattle, including his best springing
cows, and that their position is hopeless. I
know from several applications and letters I
have received during the past few days that
a great number of the farmers, as well as a
great number of people connected with
labour are in a very pitiable condition. As
I said before, they have lost beast after beast
with fluke, and from all parts of my
constituency I am receiving appeals asking
me to request the Government to defer the
annuities in some way for some period, say
twelve months, as a great many of these
people have lost every beast on their lands
through the ravages of fluke. Only last night
one of the most loyal men I know, a man
from Letterbreen, told me he had lost every
solitary beast he had in the world. He said
he was not able to pay his rent. Anyone
who goes through County Fermanagh will
hear the same thing every day. I would,
therefore, ask the Government not to promise
too much money, as the farmers feel that as
they are contributing £700,000 a year by way
of annuity in addition to other taxes-they
pay taxes of every sort-some of that
£700,000 should be used to assist them to
tide over bad times.

BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
Mr. KYLE: Would the Prime Minister
please tell us what the business will be for
next week?
The PRIME MINISTER: On Tuesday
next we propose to take in Committee of
Supply the Estimates for Harbours and
Commercial Services, Class IV, No. 2; the
Estimate for Home Affairs, Class II, No.
I, after which the Second Reading of the
Rules Publication Bill, and the Finance
Bill will be taken, and if time permits the
Committee stage of the Rent Restrictions
Bill. Wednesday and Thursday wifi be
mainly devoted to Estimates, and further
progress with Bills now before the House.
On Wednesday we propose to take the Vote
for the Royal Ulster Constabulary, Class
II. No. 2; the Vote for Special Constabulary, Class I, No. 3; on Thursday, Public
Works and Building, Class I, No. 5;
Stationery and Printing, Class I, No. 6,
and National Health Insurance, Class 3,
No. 2.

RAILWAY ROLLING STOCK.
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Labour
whether he could make representations to
the London, Midland and Scottish Railway
Company to the end that the rolling stock
required on the Northern Counties Committee be built in their own workshops,
York Road, Belfast.
5. The following question also stood in the
Order Paper in the name of Mr. KYLE:
To ask the Minister of Labour whether he
has made any representation to the Railway
Companies in Northern Ireland to use some
of the money received from the British
Government, on decontrol, to renew their
rolling stock, with the object of keeping their
shopmen employed.
Mr. ANDREWS: As this question and the
following one addressed to me by the hon.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers.
19 MAY 1925
Member for North Belfast are inter-related,
I propose with his concurrence to reply to
both together.
I have frequently approached the Railway
Companies operating in Northern Ireland
with a view to inducing them not only to
build their rolling stock here but also to undertake works of maintenance and construction in connection with their permanent way
and stations which would afford additional
employment. I have been informed that,
having regard to the difficult times which,
admittedly, the companies are experiencing,
they have in every direction endeavoured to
give as much employment as possible, and
but for the sums received from the Imperial
Government on the decontrol of the railways
much of this employment could not have been
given.
Mr. KYLE: Is the Minister aware it is
freely stated amongst the operatives in these
sheds for the manufacture of rolling stock
that coaches can be manufactured at a considerably less cost here than in Derby?
Mr. ANDREWS: I understand that the
Belfast and County Down Railway Company
build all their own carriages and wagons,
and that the Great Northern Railway
Company do
the same. The G.N.R.,
however build them in Dundalk, which
is unfortunately not in our area. The Midland Railway build all their wagons in Beliast. They are at the present time building
one carriage as an experiment, and if the
costs here compare reasonably and favourably with the cost of building them at Derby,
I may say that the company will sympathetically consider doing more of the work
here in the future than they have done in
the past. Of course the Derby works are
most important works where there is mass
production, and the prices must be taken
into consideration.
THE HOUSING PROBLEM.
7. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether any estimate has been made
by his Department as to the number of
houses that would require to be built in (1)
Belfast, and (2) the Six Counties, to meet the
present shortage.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): According to the report of
the Departmental Committee on Rent Restriction, the shortage of houses in Belfast
then amounted to 10,000 houses. The Committee gave no precise estimate of the shortage outside Belfast, but it is believed that it
is not generally so acute as in the City of
Belfast,

asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether
it is the intention of the Government to

Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer is in

BALLYMENA CHAMBER OF COMMERCE
AND "B" SPECIALS.
10. Mr. KYLE (for Mr. DEVLIN) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether his
attention had been called to the statements
made at the meeting of the Ballymena
Chamber of Commerce on the 11th May,
to the effect that the "B" Specials were in
the habit of stopping motorists at night with
pointed guns and in a provocative manner,
and why, now that Curfew has been
removed, the "B" Specials were still allowed
to go about the different roads with loaded
revolvers and at their pleasure hold up
peaceful citizens at any hour of the day or
night, and what steps the Minister proposes
to take to prevent a repetition of the
conduct complained of.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have received
a resolution from the Ballymena Chamber of
Commerce in the sense stated in the Question.
The question of the steps which may be
taken by the Police Force to ensure compliance with the law is one which depends on
the circumstances of each case, and on the
information before me I am not prepared
to admit the allegation against the Police
Force generally contained in the honourable
Member's Question. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear").

Mr. SPEAKER: I might say that this

Written Answer.
BELLEEK POTTERIES.-UNEMPLOY-
MENT INSURANCE.
Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of Labour,
whether his attention has been called to the
fact that those employees of the Belleek
Potteries, Limited, Belleek, resident in the
Free State, must have their cards stamped
with Northern Ireland unemployment
stamps; whether some of these employees,
resident in the Free State, were unemployed
from the 9th March until the 14th April last,
and have been refused unemployment benefit
for that period, both in the Free State and
Northern Ireland, though, until recently,
that benefit had been allowed to them by the
Free State; and what is proposed to be done
by the Minister in the matter?
Mr. ANDREWS: Every person employed
in insurable employment in Northern Ireland
is required to pay contributions to the
Unemployment Fund of Northern Ireland as
long as he is so employed. All insurable
workers in the Belleek Potteries, Limited,
are, therefore, required to have their books
stamped with Northern Ireland Unemployment stamps.
Several workers of that firm were suspended
from employment about the time that the
hon. Member mentions. Unemployment
benefit was paid to all those who complied
with the statutory requirements for the
receipt of benefit; but, as a claimant is disqualified from receiving benefit while resident either temporarily or permanently outside Northern Ireland, my Department was
unable to pay benefit to any of those workers
who, when unemployed, resided in the Irish
Free State. I am unable to say whether or
not the workers to which the hon. Member
refers were refused benefit by the Irish Free
State authorities.
As such cases can only be met by reciprocal arrangements between the two Governments, I refer the hon. Member to the
answer which I gave on the 14th inst. to the
hon. Member for North Belfast.

[Mr. Barbour]
The second item is a provision for a Grantin-Aid of £1,000 to Northern Air Lines,
Limited, in connection with the establishment of an Air Mail Service between Great
Britain and Northern Ireland. This air
service will connect both Londonderry and
Belfast with Stranraer, and on the outward
journey with Carlisle. A very considerable
saving of time in the transit of mails is
hoped to be effected. The distance
between Stranraer and Belfast will be
covered in a little less than one
hour
as compared with three hours
under present conditions, and the journey
between Belfast and Londonderry, which by
rail occupies two and three-quarter hours,
will be accomplished in normal weather
conditions in forty-five minutes. On the outward journey Carlisle will be reached in one
and a quarter hours from Belfast, as against
six hours and seventeen minutes by sea and
rail.
Under the conditions attached to the proposed grant the Company will ectablish and
maintain a regular Air Service for the conveyance of mails, passengers and goods.
During the past few years endeavours have
been made to have cross-channel mails so
accelerated that business men in Northern
Ireland may have a reasonable time within
which to attend to correspondence reaching
them from the other side. The proposed
Air Mail Service will undoubtedly help
towards that end, but in the meantime we
are not relaxing our efforts to secure
acceleration by the existing routes.

The expense of keeping the Line open is

effects the closing of this Line would h...
upon the city and port of Londonderry, d
cided to recommend that a grant be made f

Rules Publication Bill (S).
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. BARBOUR: In moving the Second
Reading of this Bill I feel that I need not
point out to hon. Members that the subject-
Rules Publication Bill-
Second Reading.
19 MAY 1925
"
matter dealt with, although, I fear, of a
highly technical character, concerns what
is one of the most marked Perliamentary
developments of modern times, and that is
a tendency in modern legislation to provide
by the drawing up of Rules and Orders
for the fulfilment of the purpose of a particular Statute. Half the Acts of Parliament
of recent years have delegated the right to
make Rules and Orders to different Government Departments acting either directly by
Orders in Council or through Authorities such
as the Lord Chancellor, the Electricity Commissioners and statutory bodies of a similar
character. Generally speaking, however,
Parliament keeps the final authority in its
own hands by laying down provisions by
which such Rules and Orders must be laid
before the two Houses, for a certain period
before they come into actual operation, and
such Rules and Orders shall be amended by
an address carried in both Houses of
Parliament. Further important safeguards
exist under the existing law which requires
the publication of sets of Rules when made
and the production of an annual volume of
the Rules when made. I do wish to impress
on hon. Members that the subject of this
Bill is not to confer any additional or bureaucratic powers on public Departments, but
to protect the public by requiring those
Departments to give due publicity to all the
Rules and Regulations as and when they
may be made.
Before dealing with the details of the
Measure I should explain what are the two
main reasons for the promotion of this Bill.
In the first place the provisions governing
the procedure in relation to these Rules and
Orders are contained in the Rules Publication
Act of 1893, and having regard to the increasing tendency in modern legislation to
which I have referred, it has become increasingly important that the machinery
governing the whole procedure in regard to
the publication and editing of Rules and
Orders should be brought up to date and
made as effective as possible. It is, therefore,
proposed to amend the law to this extent in
the light of the experience which has been
gained during the more than thirty years
under the system established by the Act
of 1893, and in addition the Bill is designed
to remove certain legal and technical difficulties which have arisen in the application
of the Act of 1893 to Northern Ireland.
Again, difficulties have arisen owing to the
fact that the distribution of administrative
services in the newly established Government
of Northern Ireland does not correspond exactly to the various Departments by which
these laws were administered at Westminster.
Another vital ground for amending the existing law is the comparative shortness of our
Parliament's sittings as compared with those
of the Imperial House. Hitherto Northern
Ireland Departments have, as far as practicable, carried out the provisions of the Act
of 1893, but I think it is clear that the observance of this Act in every particular is out of
the question. The various clauses, I think,
are fairly self-explanatory, and they really
consist of the substituting of Northern Ireland equivalents in the different departments and officials of our Northern Government for those more familiar titles by which
the same officials and departments are known
in the English administration.
A new Regulating Authority and Authority for determining particular questions is
specified in Clause 1 (4) in place of the
Treasury acting with the concurrence of the
Lord Chancellor and the Speaker of the
House of Commons. It is considered that
the Lord Chief Justice who is already
chairman of the Statute Law Committee
should take the place of the Lord Chancellor, and provision is made accordingly,
the Ministry of Finance also taking the place
of the Treasury.
The
Clause 2 defines in general terms the expression "Statutory Rules" and may be compared with section 4 of the Act of 1893.
definition of the Rule-Making Authority in
sub-section (2) of this Clause, that is to say
the department or authority which administers the service, has been widened and words
have been inserted to make it clear that the
Bill applies only to rules dealing with
matters which are within the jurisdiction of
the Parliament of Northern Ireland. As
regards the Act of 1893, I have already
pointed out that not a single one of the
references to existing authorities holds good.
In sub-section (2) of this Clause, various
authorities are cited, the exercise of whose
rule-making powers is covered by this Bill.
As showing the variety of such authorities
and, if I may use the term, the different
facets which they possess, I propose to cite
a few examples. The Governor of Northern
Ireland, acting alone, is a Rule-Making
Authority as regards Petty Sessions matters
and Fees, but the Governor in Council is the
Rule-Making Authority in respect of Registration Forms for Local Government
franchise. Again, the Lord Chief Justice
acting alone prescribes rules of procedure
in compensation cases under the Civil
Authorities Act, but he must act with the
concurrence of the County Court Judges in
prescribing County Court Rules, or again
the Minister of Home Affairs is a Rule-
Making Authority in respect of Police
Regulations and in the case of Orders dealing with the preservation of the peace. By
illustrating these I think I have conveyed to
hon. Members the nature of the legislation
comprised in this Bill.
635 Finance (Estate Duty) Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Second Reading.
[Mr. Barbour]
In this House we have recently passed
Acts in which we have constituted certain
Rule-making Authorities. For instance,
there is the Joint Nursing and Midwives
Act that was passed in the year 1922.
The Incorporated Law Society of Northern
Ireland also has the power and authority to
make certain rules, and under the Bill now
before Parliament the Pharmaceutical Society
of Northern Ireland has also certain powers
to make rules and regulations.
As will be seen in the Schedule to the Bill
the object of the Measure is to provide that
all rules as made by these Rule-Making
Authorities should receive the publicity that
their importance requires, that they should be
brought to the attention of this House and
that they should also be brought to the attention of the public. The public should
have an opportunity of acquainting themselves with the provisions, and a sufficient
time should elapse so that before they come
into force suitable representation could be
made if any objection is taken to any of
them.
There is also in Clause 3 another matter
to which I may direct the attention of hon.
Members, that is the Documentary Evidence
Acts. These Acts provide that prima facie
evidence of certain documents may be given
either by the production of the "Gazette"
containing the document, by the production
of a copy of the document purporting to be
printed by authority of the Government, or
by the production of an officially certified
copy. These Acts already apply to some of
the Rule-Making Authorities enumerated in
this Bill, but not all, and this Clause enables
every Rule-Making Authority to make use of
the convenient method of proof supplied by
the Documentary Evidence Acts.
The period of time specified for Rules
and Orders to lie on the Table of the
Imperial House is ten days, but it
is proposed under this Bill that the
number of days should not be less than
ten, but of these only five require to be
actual sitting days of this Parliament, and
then again the five days need not all be in
one Session. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
whole House for to-morrow.
Finance (Estate Duty) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
Mr. POLLOCK: It is rather a common
practice to defer the introduction of the
general Finance Bill until the Autumn
Session, but it is necessary that I should
submit to the House this short Measure in
order to enable the Government to assess the
estate duties upon the higher scale provided
for in our Budget. The changes in regard
to customs and excise became operative on
the adoption of the Budget Resolution, but
in the case of estate duties it is necessary
that we should by a special Bill provide for
the enforcement of the estate duties fore
shadowed by the Budget before they can
become effective. Consequently, the postponement of the Bill until the Autumn might
possibly have resulted in a considerable loss
of revenue. There is another reason why the
Measure should be introduced now and
passed this Session.
double
Section 28 of the Government of Ireland
Act, 1920, which provides against
death duties, necessitates a very close connection between our Estate Duty Office and
Somerset House. If we propose to adopt any
changes made in Great Britain in the rates
of estate duty it naturally results in very
great simplification of the work if the
changes here have the force of law on the
same date as the corresponding changes on
the other side. Clause 2 of this Bill enables
this to be done by Order in Council.
or
I do not think it is necessary that I should
say very much to the House in regard to
the changes in question. They do not
affect small estates under £12,000, nor do
they affect large estates of £1,000,000
over, of which I am sorry to say there are far
too few in this Province. I could wish there
were many more. The rates of duty for the
intermediate estates are proposed to be increased by from 1 per cent. to 6 per cent. As
I have already indicated to the House in my
earlier statement we expect the new scale
to result in an increased revenue of about
£55,000 in a full year and about £25,000 this
year. These estimates must, of course, be
regarded as purely speculative, because
clearly a single large estate coming under
assessment for duty purposes would affect
the results of the calculation very materially.
The proviso to Clause 1 is inserted merely
to protect the interests of persons who,
having purchased or lent money on an interest in expectancy after computing their
liability to death duties at a certain rate
would, if this safeguard were not provided,
be compelled to pay duty at the higher rate
and would therefore incur a financial loss.
The date inserted is the date of the financial
resolution which preceded the Bill, and we
must take it for granted that any persons
dealing in such interests after that date are
fully aware of their future liability. I
beg to move.

The reason I have for moving this Amendment is that I think the control of all houses,

and that is that restrictions remain on all

and 1930, will not be sufficient to provide

rather singular that the hon. Member for

would allow me to call attention to a matter

must follow on the Amendment we are now

you have made. I also understand that if
we carry this Amendment, "until there are

to second the proposition to insert the words

Rent Restrictions Bill-
Committee.
19 MAY 1925
has been devised in the interests of the landlords, and that unless the working people get
protection in regard to their houses they are
going to be placed in very dire straits. I do
not think anything I can say will add one
jot or tittle to the Amendment. If it is not
passed it will be broadcast to the people outside that this Committee does not care what
is going to happen to the common people who
are living in these houses.
Mr. GYLE: I have great pleasure in supporting this Amendment, that we insert
"until there are sufficient houses for the
people." I have given notice of another
Amendment to leave out "twenty-six" and
insert "thirty-six," but if we carry this
Amendment, as I hope we will, then, of
course, my Amendment will go by the board.
Is the Government really in earnest when
they propose to bring about decontrol of this
class of property in the year 1926? I would
like to know how many houses of this class
have been built since the conclusion of the
war. Is there any prospect whatever of
having a sufficient number of houses for
tenants of this class in 1926? I am afraid
if this Clause is carried, and the Government
insist on it we are going to have an enormous
number of people who will certainly be put
to a considerable amount of inconvenience.
The class of people living in houses of this
sort are very heavily hit at the present time
owing to bad trade. They are mostly shopkeepers and people in a fairly reasonable
way of living, but I think they are the very
class of people most heavily hit under present
circumstances, and I appeal to the Government to agree to this Amendment, and thus
protect a very deserving class of tenants.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am very glad
that you have also permitted a slight discussion on the other Amendments which are tending in the same direction, because I would like
to point out to my hon. Friend, the Member
for North Belfast, that this Bill has been
drafted with the greatest possible care by
the Government, with a view to dealing in
the best possible way with the various classes
of houses which up to the present time have
been controlled. The hon. Member (Mr.
Kyle) said that this was a landlords' measure.
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
The PRIME MINISTER: I only wish that
he had been present at some of the meetings
I have had with the landlords' representatives, and he would hardly have used that
description. The truth of the matter is that
one can hardly touch this puzzling problem
without having criticism either from the
landlords or from the tenants, and the
Government have endeavoured to the best
of their ability to hold the scales as evenly
as possible between the various interests
affected. After all, we are going step by step
towards decontrol, which, I think, the whole
community is looking forward to.
Mr. KYLE: No.
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps not for
the moment, because there is a shortage of
houses, but in a few days the Government
will introduce a measure, which, we hope,
will still further help to ease that situation,
and, consequently, before the six years are
up, to which other Clauses refer, we hope
that there will be sufficient houses to meet
all requirements and all classes. I do not
know whether the hon. Member moves about
the city as much as I do, but he will
know that the very class of houses that this
particular Amendment refers to is being
built in large numbers in all quarters of the
city. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) What
the Government are very anxious to
prevent is having decontrol of all houses
taking place on the same day. We would
prefer to take the thing in stages, and it
will be observed that the more expensively
rented houses, to which this sub-section refers the £52 houses-come first. Even in
that case the Government are allowing a year
and a half before they take any steps in the
matter, in regard to the next one three years,
and in regard to those which do not exceed
£26 five years.
This is going beyond what they have done
in Great Britain. It is taking what I consider the long view, and I hope the view
which will prove to be correct, that by the
time decontrol takes place there will be a
sufficiency of dwelling houses for the working
classes in Belfast and elsewhere. At the same
time this stabilises matters for a considerable
time, which is for the advantage not only
of the owners but of the tenants. Everyone
throughout the Six Counties will know
exactly where they stand in regard to the
letting and the renting of houses for the next
five years. It is of very great importance to
have a continuity of policy instead of carrying
on as we have been doing from year to year
under the Expiring Laws Continuance Act,
which I always think is a very haphazard way
of doing business and not satisfactory from
the point of view either of the owners or of
the tenants. I am sorry to have to inform
the hon. Member (Mr. Grant) that for these
very weighty reasons the Government cannot
accept his Amendment.
Mr. KYLE: Might I point out that in

there was a shortage of 10,000 houses in

ago, and since then 2,000 or 3,000 houses have
been built which still leaves a shortage of
7,000 houses.

a manner in which my hon. Friends op-
There is one important point which

It is only an aspect of the wider question of

not by dealing with the symptoms of the

payment of any agreed sum as part of the
consideration for such lease or agreement:
Provided that, where part of the dwellinghouse is lawfully sub-let at the commencement of the term, and is a dwelling-house
to which the principal Act applies, that
part shall, notwithstanding anything in the
foregoing provisions of this sub-section,
continue to be a dwelling-house to which
the principal Act applies.
(3) For the purposes of this section, the
expression" possession" shall be construed
as meaning actual possession, and a landlord shall not be deemed to have come into
possession by reason only of a change of
tenancy made with his consent.

of which the rateable value exceeds eight
pounds") and insert instead thereof the word
"twenty-six."
This Bill has been described by some of
my hon. Friends as being a landlords' Bill.
If there is any portion of the Bill which
could be described as a landlords' portion
of the Bill I think that portion is Clause 2.
Clause 2 states t".t
"Where the landlord of a dwelling-house
to which the principal Act applies, and of

or comes into possession of the whole of the

dwelling-house."
At the present moment in the city of Belfast
there are almost 500 vacant houses of a rateable valuation of £8 and upwards. The landlord has tried to sell those houses, but has
been unable to do so, and so he comes to the
Government and asks them to insert in this
Bill the word "eight." so that if houses of
that rateable valuation are in his possession

Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government
cannot accept this Amendment. Personally
I do not think there is such a great hardship
as my hon. Friend (Mr. Gyle) infers. The
total number of houses of a valuation of £8
or under comes to something like sixty-five
per cent. of the total number of houses in
Belfast. Now we are only dealing with houses
of over £8 valuation. We do not propose to
deal with houses of £8 or under. They remain subject to control, but my hon. Friend
(Mr. Gyle) suggests that we should raise that
to houses of £26 valuation. After all these
houses become vacant, and surely the man
who has the best right to such a house is
the owner of it. What happens is that when
that house becomes vacant the representatives
of the old tenants, who are probably leaving
the house and going to live elsewhere, sell
the right to that house for what is known as
"key money," one of the greatest evils in
the city of Belfast.
Mr. GYLE: How possibly can a house become vacant if the tenant sells his right for
key money? Sure it is an impossibility for
that house to become vacant. I am referring
to houses which are lying vacant in Belfast
to-day. There are a considerable number of
people who are living two and three families
in one house. The landlords, because they
cannot sell at enormous prices, refuse to let
those people have the houses, but instead
keep them cooped up three and four families
in one house, and the Government is giving
them the right now to charge any rent at
all they please.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend

leave it? He left his house to let it at £55

In regard to that
The CHAIRMAN: We are just taking the
first-named Amendment. The second part

Mr. KYLE: The Clause, as amended, or
as we suggest it should be amended, will
read:
"On and after the first day of November,

This is one of the Clauses of the Bill which
give something to the tenants, and what we
are asking for on these benches is that the
generosity of the Government in this particular Clause should be extended just a little
bit further than it is at present. We are
proposing to leave out fifteen and insert five,
which would mean, roughly, a reduction of
20 per cent. in the rent of the houses on
which this Act operates. I think the justice
of that will readily be seen, particularly in
view of the statements on the Second Reading
of this Bill, and particularly in view of the
fact that repairs on these houses are conspicuous by their absence. In fact no repairs
have been done at all practically. In regard
to that point I think it would meet the case
quite well if instead of paying 15 per cent.,
5 per cent. should be substituted. That would
be 20 per cent. reduction so far as the
tenants of these houses are concerned. When
you remember that wages have been reduced
by something like 100 per cent. in some cases,
and 50 per cent. in other cases, I think it
will readily be seen and appreciated by hon.
Members opposite that it would be something
to the tenants if we were permitted to have
this Amendment put into this Act. It would
also, so far as hon. Members opposite are
concerned, be an act of generosity if they
would say they would accept this Amendment.
I think if they agree to accept this Amendment it will save them another walk of a

do not carry out repairs.

will come in later on is already in operation.
I want to say this. The Public Health Committee working under the jurisdiction of the
Belfast Corporation serve a notice on the
landlords. The landlords are brought into
Court, but fortunately for the landlords, and
unfortunately for the tenants, the Minister
of Home Affairs has made nearly every
estate agent in the city of Belfast a magistrate, with the result that when the case
comes before the Court-I am sure the
Minister has seen it himself repeatedly-and
the responsible officers of the Corporation
endeavour to compel the owner to put the

landlord can afford to pay half-a-crown if

to roofs, sewers, etc., for eight or nine months.
The members of the Public Health Committee know how hard it is to compel the
agents throughout the city to spend the 25
per cent. They do not spend it; that is the

sooner this amount is reduced to 5 per cent.

that this figure should be reduced.

has
The great difficulty we have in the houses
in which we live is to get the landlord to
agree to do any repairs at all. It has been
stated that we could appeal to the court or
the Corporation to have the agent or landlord
brought into court. The difficulty always has
been that we of the working class have not
the money to employ lawyers. It is invariably
the agents who employ these lawyers to draft
Bills of this nature. I think it is a desirable thing that the landlord will not only
have to do the repairs but also must give an
account for these repairs to the tenant. Very
often the tenant is not aware that the landlord is endeavouring to put a spout on the
roof. He may be out at his work or, as
happens in many cases in North Belfast
where the women work in the mills and
factories they are out at their work all day.
I think it is a desirable thing that the landlords should be compelled to write down
what repairs they are undertaking to the
property. I feel it is extremely difficult to
carry on with all the conversation that is
going on on the other side.

Mr. KYLE: The purport of this Amendment is so eminently fair that I have no
doubt the Government will be able to see
their way to accept it. The landlord up to
now has been receiving 25 per cent for the
cost of repairs; after this Bill becomes an
Act he will receive 15 per cent, and the object
of this Amendment is only to see that he
carries out repairs to that extent, and that
if he does not carry out those repairs the
tenant will not be liable for the increased
rent due for repairs. I think when the case
is looked at like that, the fairness of this
Amendment ought to be apparent to every
Member of this Committee-not only to the
Members of the Committee, for they after all
are not so important as the people outside.
They may be more important just for the
moment, but they are not more important in
the long run. I think this Amendment is of
such a character that the Government would
be very well advised to accept it, as it only
ensures that the repairs will be carried out,
and if the repairs are not carried out that the
tenant shall not be asked to pay the increase
of rent on account of repairs.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government
cannot accept this Amendment for the simple
reason that they do not consider it at all
necessary. In Clause 7, which occurs later
in the Bill, he will see, I think, that the tenant gets ample protection against the landlord
who does not carry out repairs. There is,
however, a fallacy in the argument of the

of the landlords as I have had he might
change his views. The mere fact that we are
reducing that twenty-five per cent. by ten per
cent. shows that we are only too anxious to
meet the tenants. In regard to the question of
these repairs, if the hon. Member (Mr. Kyle)
had studied his Bill he would find there a
far more satisfactory Clause than he proposes. He will find in the Bill that if the
landlord does not keep the house in a tenantable and reasonable state of repair the tenant
can refuse to pay the rent in respect of those
repairs, and can go to the sanitary authority.
not the sanitary officer. And I would remind
the hon. Member for West Belfast. (Mr.
William McMullen) that he himself is a
member of one of those sanitary authorities,
namely the Belfast Corporation, and I am
sure he will take every opportunity of seeing that the Corporation issues the necessary
certificates where the landlords do not keep
these premises in repair.
Mr. HANNA: I want to say just one word
in answer to the hon. Member (Mr. William
McMullen) who spoke immediately before the
Minister of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson
Bates). He rather suggested that an attempt
was being made to withdraw from the
tenants certain of their rights by the Government refusing to accept this Amendment.
No such thing is contemplated. As a matter
of fact, this section only refers to those
landlords who are under obligation to do repairs, and if the landlord does not keep the
place in a reasonable state of repair, without introducing clumsy sanitary authorities
or anybody else it is open to the tenant to
come into court and sue the landlord to
carry out his contract. Why should there
be a multiplying of the causes of action such
as are suggested in this Amendment? Yon
have two causes of action, the cause against
the landlord for an account and the return
of the money on the one side, and he is also
taken to the police court and fined there.
I cannot see that that would be in the
tenant's interest, and I think it should be
ventilated that the tenants' rights, such as
they are at common law, are still protected
by the Government in their Bill.

Mr. DEVLIN: I beg to move in Clause
4, page 6, line 31, after "is" ("dwelling-house
is required") to insert "reasonably."
This word "reasonably" is used in the
English Act of 1923, and the sub-section
dealing with the same subject. I would
like an explanation from the Minister as to
why this word has been omitted from the
proposals he has now submitted to the House.
It may be said that in every case where
possession may be resumed the court must
consider it reasonable to decree possession.
But the English Act says this in addition,
and provides that the house must be
reasonably required by the landlord. I think
al! landlords are alike, and I do not see why
it should have been considered desirable
and even necessary to insert the word
"reasonably" in the one case, and that it
should have been omitted from this Bill
which the right hon. Gentleman is
presenting.
It comes back to this that once again
wo are getting all forms of legislation that
are in the interests of the privileged classes
in this House, and where there is any advantage for the working classes these advantages are denied to the working classes.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I would like
the right hon Gentleman to explain why it
is that this word has been taken out of his
proposal and whether he proposes to have
this word re-inserted or accepted by Amendment as in the case of the English Act.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think my hon.
Friend will probably agree with me that
most of the one-house owners are people who
belong to what might be called the working
classes. This is not a Measure on behalf of
what is sometimes referred to as the landlords' class at all. It is for the purpose of
meeting very hard cases where a workingman has saved money and bought his house
and is unable to get possession of it. I have
numerous letters, some of them very pathetic
letters, from owners of these houses and I
would like to read one. I think it is simply
a typical example of the hardship that exists
at the present time, caused by these onehouse owners not being able to get possession.
This one is written by a man who says:-
"My 'one-owner' house was paid for by my
son who was out in France. It was bought
purely for own occupation and that before
the Rent Restriction Act was passed at all.
I trust you will not allow any alterations
of the provisions you have detailed regarding such houses. It is only right that after
so many years' exclusion we should after six
months' notice get our own house for our
personal use. The occupant has no children,
his mother-in-law lives near by in a large
house with say one or two attendants, and he
and his like would probably wish to feel by
and by that they had acquired ownership by
length of residence."
Another person writes:-
"As an ex-Service man, one who purchased
a house over five years ago on the understanding that I would get occupying same in
order to get more comfortable accommodation for wife and family. This house I at
present reside in consists of two small bedrooms. My family is mixed and consists of
three boys and three girls, ages ranging from
23 years to 2 years. The house that I seek
possession of contains four bedrooms. The
occupier's family consists of three. She sublets two rooms. I have offered her several
houses and she would not accept them.”
I have got numerous letters of that type.
and I would like to remove from the mind
of the hon. Member the idea that these
houses are owned by rich landlords. The
vast majority of these one-house owners are
people of the working classes, very often men
who have saved money and bought the house
for the occupation of their own family.
For years past they have had very great
hardships and have had to take lodgings
while the tenant would not give up possession. It only applies to houses purchased
before May, 1923. In the case of houses purchased subsequent to that date the owner

Mr. BEATTIE: The position is that there

Mr. BEATTIE: I said I was going to presume something was meant by the Minister
of Home Affairs other than what he presented to this Committee because the Bill
says:-
"The dwelling-house is required by the
landlord for occupation as a residence for
himself."
I would prefer to see it read as follows:-
"The dwelling-house is reasonably required."
I cannot see any objection to that word being
inserted unless, as I said before, there is
some other motive in the minds of the Government. I would not be prepared to withhold the house of the one-house owner unreasonably. If he could show me just reasons
for wanting possession and that the hardship was greater upon him than upon the
tenant he wished to put out, then I would
say it was a reasonable requirement. The
Government's attitude on this Bill is something I cannot understand. They are taking
up a position which I do not think any
reasonable Government would adopt. They
take the attitude of holding fast to agreements arrived at between Government representatives and the landlord classes. I do not
mean working class landlords because you
will find that working class landlords are
men who will not ask their houses to be
handed over unreasonably. I refer to the
landlords to whom this Bill will give greater
scope in taking the homes of some of the
working class. I hold that there should be
no objection to this word "reasonably" being
introduced. By inserting it you would show
to the people that you are protecting their
interest in a small way.

It has been charged against the Government that this is a landlord's Bill, and it
has been suggested on more occasions than
one that the Government are interested
particularly in the rich section of the community. If we take it on this particular
case alone the Government are attempting to
do something for the person who is in a
position to buy a house. I know that a person does not require to be desperately rich
to purchase a house, but such a person is
in a very much better position than the unfortunate tenant who has been paying rent
for fourteen or fifteen years and who is not
in a position to buy his house. The Government are not giving protection to the very
people who require protection most. I think
the Government would be justified in leaving
these words out. Some consideration should
be given to the father or mother of the owner
of the house, but when it comes to the son,
daughter, or some person bona fide residing
with him I think it is going too far.
I should point out that probably one of the
most important drawbacks to this sub-section
is that a good deal of litigation might take
place. I know the legal fraternity always
like that sort of thing, and probably on that
account they will welcome this wording. The
tenant I suppose will have to employ a
solicitor or counsel to determine whether a
person is bona fide residing with the landlord or not.
That is open to grave abuse.
It is open to many misconstructions, and the
poor unfortunate tenant will be forced to go
into the law courts for the purpose of determining that some person is not bona fide
residing with the landlord. The landlord
might take a person in for three or four
months and argue that that person is bona
fide residing with him and if that person
cannot get that particular house he or she intends to reside with him.
It has been pointed out that judges and
other people who adjudicate are so hopelessly out of touch with the working classes
that they are apt to decide on some technical
point of law and to lose sight altogether of
the humanitarian aspect of the question. It
is just possible that in such a case the
technical or judicial point of view may operate
against the tenant. I know there is supposed
to be such a thing as the protection of the
Court, but the tenant does not always get it.

and Workmen's Compensation

on the street." I said "What particular
reason has he given for doing this?" "Well,"
he says, "for non-fulfilment of the payment of
rent." "Why did you fail to pay your rent?"
I asked. He replied "Some person or persons
were kind enough to write an anonymous
letter to the Minister of Labour about something that I was doing, and my claim was
held up for an indefinite period, and owing
to getting behind I could not fulfil my obligations to the landlord. The rent got that
far behind that, with the lesser amount
coming into the home, I could not meet my
obligation as it totalled up to such an
amount." By the way, I do not want to
carry this on with regard to the stoppage of
benefit. The benefit was paid. £9 was due,
and out of the benefit when it was paid the
man offered £3, but the landlord refused to
take it. That was an industrious working
man when he could get work to do. That was
a man who went during the war to serve in
his Majesty's forces. The working classes
also did their little part, although a number
of them stopped at home.
This new section is to give protection to the
unemployed workers in times of depression
such as that of which we are now in the
midst. I hope the Government will not tell
us the old repeated story that they cannot
see their way to accept this new Section, and
that is the last of it. The facts perhaps to
some of the Government representatives are
not convincing. I do not know what would
be convincing to the Government this past
few days. I wonder would some of the facts

with which I came in contact during my short

No order or judgment for the recovery

the passing of this Act be executed after

who has been unemployed for a period of
three months before the passing of this Act,
and unless and until the circumstances of
the person concerned have received the consideration of the local poor-law authority."

21 MAY 1925
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 21st May, 1925.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
SECONDARY TEACHERS' PENSION
SCHEME.
1. Mr. GYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Minister of Education,
whether it is the fact that within the past
eighteen months secondary teachers in
Northern Ireland were required to furnish
their birth certificates and particulars of service to the Education Department in
connection with the Pensions Scheme; is it
the fact that they have been recently put to
the unnecessary trouble of furnishing the
same particulars a second time; and if this
is the result of incompetency on the part of
the staff or only an effort to find work for an
overstaffed department.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I propose to take this question.
Birth Certificates or other evidence of age
and particulars of service were required
some time ago from secondary teachers in
connection with the salary regulations. The
documents bearing on age when examined in
the Ministry were returned to the teachers.
The Pension Scheme came later, and it has
been decided that, for the purpose of that
scheme evidence of age should be deposited
with the Ministry of Finance, to be retained
by that Ministry for reference when the
superannuation claims mature. No further
evidence of past service has been asked for
in connection with the Pension Scheme.
POLICE BARRACKS IN LISBURN.
2. Mr. GYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs, whether it is the intention of the
Government to erect new Police Barracks in
Lisburn, and if so, why is it necessary to
build and equip a large and expensive building for police at the present time when two
barracks already exist and a third one has
recently been dispensed with as unnecessary.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The suggestion that a new
barracks should be erected in Lisburn in
place of the two existing barracks, which are
not very suitable, is under consideration,
but no final decision has yet been come to.
TOMB STREET, BELFAST.
3. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. WILLIAM
MCMULLEN) asked the Minister of Home
Affairs, whether he is aware that complaints
have been made to the police regarding the
conduct of people who appear to visit Tomb
Street, Belfast, for unlawful purposes; and
whether he is prepared to have inquiries
made into the complaints made by residents
in that street?
Sir DAWSON BATES: A complaint has
been received from a resident in this street,
but so far the inquiries made by the police
do not confirm the allegations made.
The police are at all times ready to
investigate complaints.
BALLY MENA HEALTH VISITOR.
4. Mr. McALLISTER asked the Minister
of Home Affairs, whether the Ministry has
refused to approve of the appointment of
Miss M. J. Gillespie, as health visitor, under
the Child Welfare Scheme of the Ballymena
Urban Council, although the Council had on
two occasions nominated her for the appointment; what are the essential qualifications
for the appointment, and which of these
qualifications do the Ministry allege Miss
Gillespie does not possess.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer to the
first part of the question is in the affirmative.
As regards the remainder of the question
the essential qualifications for this position
as embodied in the advertisement issued by
the Council were:-
That the person to be appointed should be
fully trained,
Should possess the registration certificato
of the Joint Nursing and Midwives'
Council for Northern Ireland, and
Should have experience in maternity and
child-welfare work.
Although Miss Gillespie was a fully-trained
nurse and registered with the Nursing
Council, she had no experience of maternity
and child-welfare work, and as this is an
essential requisite in connection with the
important and valuable Child-Welfare
Scheme which has been in operation in
Ballymena Urban District, the Ministry was
unable to sanction her appointment.
Mr. MCALLISTER: My question was not
as to what the requirements were according
to the advertisement, but what are the requirements according to the regulations of
the Ministry of Home Affairs for this
appointment; and have those requirements
been complied with by Miss Gillespie?
Sir DAWSON BATES: When a vacancy
of this sort occurs the authority issues an

DOWNPATRICK LABOUR EXCHANGE.
BRANCH MANAGER.
5. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Labour whether it is a fact that
the person in charge of the Downpatrick
Labour Exchange holds a number of other
paid positions, and as a consequence claims
to benefit are rushed through the meetings
of the Local Employment Committee without
due regard being had to the circumstances
of the cases; whether it is a fact that workers
with genuine claims are being turned down
because the Branch Manager has not the
time to devote to a proper consideration of
each case; if it is a fact that documentary
evidence is still insisted on, and whether he
is satisfied that the insured workers in Downpatrick are being properly treated.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr. Andrews): Yes, sir, the Branch Manager at
Downpatrick is employed only for part of his
time by the Ministry of Labour, and I believe
that in the remainder of his time he has
other paid employment. I am not aware that
claims to unemployment benefit are dealt
with improperly, but if the hon. Member
can give me details of any cases in which, in
his view, injustice seems to have been done,
I will inquire into them at once.
The Department does not insist in general
on the production of written evidence from
employers as proof that an applicant is
making reasonable efforts to find work, but
it is quite within the province of any Local
Committee to require this evidence in a particular case if they consider that it would
assist them in coming to a just decision on
the claim.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I would like to ask
the Minister of Labour whether he thinks
that a person who holds jobs as Petty
Sessions Clerk, Clerk of the Urban District
Council, Commissioner for Oaths, Registrar
of Marriages, Insurance Agent, Executive
Sanitary Officer, Collector under the recent
Act passed for Affiliation Orders, and Secretary of the School Board, could discharge
his duties as Branch Manager of the Labour
Exchange, and whether he thinks it
desirable under the circumstances that a person who holds so many jobs should act in the
capacity of Branch Manager of the Labour
Exchange?
Mr. ANDREWS: I am glad to say that
there are at the present time 54 men and 12
women attending this Branch Exchange. It
is true that there are some other postal
claims to be considered, but I am of opinion
that this Branch Manager is doing his work
very thoroughly, and in the public interest,
on the ground of economy, I do not think I
would be justified in employing a full time
man for the work. So long as the work is
properly done I think that is all that the
public desire.
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: Would the Minister
of Labour kindly answer this, if it is a fact

the Act?

SUGAR BEET INDUSTRY.
10. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Agriculture, what action, if any, he has
taken to explore the possibilities of growing
sugar beet in Northern Ireland, and whether
the Minister does not think that this would
provide farmers with an additional valuable
crop and more work for men in agricultural
districts.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): Experiments carried out by the
Department of Agriculture and Technical
Instruction in 1911, 1912 and 1913 have shown
that sugar beet of a high sugar content can
be grown in Northern Ireland.
The reply to the second part of the question
is in the negative because if land were devoted to beet culture a corresponding decline
in the potato acreage might be expected, the
area placed under root crops being limited
by the quantity of manure available. The
Ministry is convinced that at present the
growing of potatoes is more profitable than
the beet culture.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is it not a fact that the
Ministry has definitely decided not to do anything in this matter on the ground that they
cannot afford to lose the sugar tax?
Mr. ARCHDALE: I am afraid that matter
has not been before the Ministry. I never
heard of that before. The only question is that
an acre of potatoes is value for £60, and an
acre of sugar beet is only value for £22. It
would be a very bad thing to improve one and
put out the other.
Mr. KYLE: In view of the unemployment
existing here, is it not a desirable thing to
have the sugar beet industry started in
Northern Ireland? Is it not a fact that a
Dutch gentleman is over here and is going
about telling the people in the country that
he is prepared to establish this particular industry in Northern Ireland if the Northern
Government gives a subsidy the same as is
given by the Imperial Government on the
other side?
Mr. ARCHDALE: We are already of the
opinion that the establishment of a sugar
beet factory would not be an economical
thing for Northern Ireland. It would not
employ more men, and would put those
engaged on potato growing out of employment. There is only a certain amount of
manure available. The Dutch gentleman
has certainly offered to give money, but that
is subject to a very large subsidy from our
Northern Government.

whole question will be reconsidered.

of the person who owes money to his grocer
or his tailor. It is not on all fours, and the
people in the various constituencies will not
be easily fooled with an argument of that
kind. It is not an argument. There is no
argument in it, and no person will be able to
discriminate more keenly than the person
who has been unemployed for three months.
Such a person is not likely to accept an argument of that kind, and if that is the best

that no better argument has come from the
Government Benches, and, if that is the best
apology--for it is nothing short of an apology

how to deal with you and the people who
occupy the Government Benches.

(1) The county court, if satisfied that
any error or omission in a notice of intention to increase rent, whether served before
or after the passing of this Act, is due to a
bona fide mistake on the part of the landlord, shall have power to amend such
notice, by correcting any errors and
supplying any omissions therein, which, if
not corrected or supplied, would render the
notice invalid, on such terms and conditions as respects arrears of rent or otherwise as appear to the court to be just and
reasonable, and, if the court so directs, the
notice as so amended shall have effect and
be deemed to have had effect as a valid
notice.

Mr. BLACK: I beg to move in page 13,

or
This is an Amendment of a somewhat
technical nature, as will be appreciated from
reading the Clause and the proposed Amendment. The Amendment is merely intended to
carry into effect what I conceive to be the
object of the Clause, which I do not think is
quite clearly set out in the Clause as printed
here. The object of the Clause is this:
Under the general law in Ireland, when a
tenant has entered into a tenancy agreement,
and in that agreement there is no express
condition as to whether the landlord or the
tenant is to do the repairs to the house, under
the general law, since the Landlord and
Tenant Act of 1860 the tenant is bound to do
the repairs. This Sub-section (4) as I understand it, is drafted with the intention of providing that, where the landlord has increased
the rent by the service of a notice, including
in the increase the amount of the permitted
increase which is applicable to the landlord's
liability to do the repairs, the landlord can
be considered to be under a liability to do
the repairs, and the tenant shall
not continue under the liability which is
already existing on him under the
general law. Under the Clause here, without
the words which I propose should be inserted,
it is provided that if such notice of increase
has been served the landlord shall be responsible for keeping the dwelling-house in a
reasonable state of repair as if he had
entered into an express covenant on that behalf. My reading of that Clause is that it
only implies an express covenant on the part
of the landlord, but it does not do away with
the Covenant which is implied by law on the
part of the tenant by Deasy's Act. The
words which I suggest should be inserted to

I beg to move.

Clause be inserted immediately preceding

the present time there is a considerable
amount of hardship existing amongst the
business community in 80 far as their
premises have now become decontrolled.
know of one block of buildings in the centre

I think the logical argument to use here today would be this; that all those people who
occupy these premises are traders and they
have goods to sell, and the cost of living today is about 80 per cent over pre-war. Quite

do object to these business tenants being left

pay rates on vacant houses they would be all
the more inclined to see these houses let

but I do know something about Belfast. Is

The overcrowding that takes place in some
of the working-class districts of Belfast is
scandalous. As you know, that is responsible
for a great deal of disease and disease is
costing the ratepayers of Belfast a very considerable sum.
Now it is ridiculous the state of affairs that
exists. The National Health Insurance Act
and your sanatoriums give a respite to the
worker for the purpose of recovering his
health. The workers contract tuberculosis
and other diseases and they are sent to a
sanatorium for the purpose of recovering
their health, and whatever result there is
from the sanatorium treatment is absolutely
nullified for the person who has got to go
back to a district that is overcrowded. The
Government propose to do nothing to mitigate
this evil at all. They are not prepared to
frame legislation for the purpose of compelling the landlord, if the house has been vacant
for six weeks, ether to let or sell the house.
The intention of this new Clause is to see
that these houses will not be held up in order
that the landlord may get an enhanced price
for them. I think it is only fair; it is not
penalising the landlord to any undue degree
or extent. It is simply asking that when a
house is vacant the Government should take
this step, and that there should be no abatement of rates-that the landlord should
have to pay the rates during the time the
house is vacant. I think it is a very reasonable new Clause. It is neither Socialism nor

in lucid moments are very sensible
people. I hope

NEW CLAUSE (Increase of rent in case
of sub-letting).
(1) Where part of a dwelling-house to
which the principal Act applies is lawfully
sub-let, and the part as sub-let is also a
dwelling-house to which the principal Act
applies, then, in addition to any increases
permitted by this Act or the principal Act,
an amount not exceeding ten per cent. of
the net rent of the dwelling-house comprised in the sub-tenancy shall be deemed
to be a permitted increase in the case of
that dwelling-house, and an amount equivalent to five per cent, of the net rent of the
dwelling-house comprised in the subtenancy shall be deemed to be a permitted
increase in the case of the dwelling-house
comprised in the tenancy.

Mr. BLACK: I have great difficulty in

In other words what change will
this Amendment make in the existing laws?
We will be left, if this Bill is passed into law,
with the Act of 1920, plus the alterations
made by this Bill. Accordingly, the first
thing we have to apply our minds to is, what
is the position under the Act of 1920? In the
first place the Act of 1920 does not apply to
furnished houses. They are specifically
exempted. Nothing is inserted in this
Amendment to provide for that. It has
nothing to do with the letting of furnished
apartments, so, in so far as the hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie) complains
of injustices done in the letting of furnished
apartments in the way of exorbitant rent
being charged this does not help that in any
way.
Mr. DEVLIN: It does not deal with furnished apartments.
a
Mr. BLACK: No, it does not deal with
furnished apartments. It only deals with the
letting of unfurnished rooms in house.
What is the present position? Take a house
which is a dwelling-house within the protection of the Act; there is a standard rent
fixed by law for that house, and the
landlord can only charge for that house that
standard rent plus a certain permitted increase. Now it is not the law that the tenant
can get out of that, or that the landlord can
get out of that, by putting in a dummy
tenant and sub-letting at an increased rent.
because the standard rent does not apply to
any particular letting of the house but to the
house itself, and by no device can you let
that house at a greater rent than the
standard rent plus the permitted increase.
It is also provided in the 1920 Act that
when you come to let any part of the house
it is to be treated as the dwelling-house for
the purposes of the Act, and, accordingly, you
cannot let any part of the house at a rent
greater than the maximum you can have for
the whole premises, that is to say the standard rent plus the permitted increase. There
is a specific Section of the Act of 1920 directed to this particular point, providing
that when you have let part of the house
and, have in fact a standard rent fixed for
the whole house, the sub-tenant of that part
of the house can come into the County Court
and have the standard rent applicable to
that part of the house ascertained, and the
standard rent applicable to that part of the
house, of course, must be smaller than the
standard rent applicable to the whole house.
The Section of the 1920 Act applicable to
this point is Section 12, sub-Section (3), and
with your permission I will read it. It
says:
"Where for the purpose of determining
the standard rent or rateable valuation of
any dwelling-house to which this Act
applies,❞—
Now it is provided in the Act that part of
an existing dwelling-house to which the Act
applies shall be deemed to be the dwellinghouse, so that this sub-Section applies to
part of the dwelling-house,—
"it is necessary to apportion the rent at
the date in relation to which the standard
rent is to be fixed, or the rateable value
of the property in which that dwellinghouse is comprised, the county court may.
on application by either party, make such
apportionment as seems just, and the decision of the court as to the amount to be
apportioned to the dwelling-house shall be
final and conclusive."
Accordingly, when you have a sub-letting of
part of an unfurnished dwelling-house, either
the landlord or the tenant is entitled to
come into the County Court to have the
standard rent of the whole dwelling-house
apportioned to that part of the dwellinghouse which is sub-let. Accordingly the
landlord is only entitled to let that portion
of the dwelling house at the apportioned
part of the standard rent plus the apportioned part of the permitted increase.
In my view the only effect this new Clause
would have would be to put into the landlord's pocket an extra five per cent. of the
apportioned part of the standard rent, apportioned upon the part of the premises sublet, and to put into the immediate tenant's
pocket another five per cent. of the same
apportioned part of the standard rent. So
far as I can read it that is the only effect
this proposed Clause would have. As far
as I can see the only effect is that the head
landlord is to get five per cent. more of the
sub-tenant's rent into his pocket, and the
immediate tenant is to get five per cent.
more. That is the only effect this Clause
could possibly have as I read it

the Bill and to try to bring before the people

in view of the fact that these protective

the debates on the Rent Restrictions Bill.
we would find absolute unanimity between

Committee.
