be now read a Second time. The rean 1
move is that at the present time where the
rent of a house exceeds 4s 7d per week and
there is a claim for arrears of rent to be
heard, it has got to be heard by the
Recorder's Court. When that Act, empowering a man to take the case, was placed on
the Statute Book the rents were much lower
than they are to-day. The result is that a
house which was 3s 6d before the war has
been raised so that it comes before the Record
Court, which, I think, is against the principle of the original Act that laid it down
that this particular figure of 4s 7d should be
the limit. I think that is against the principle of the Act. Therefore, I think it would
be in the best interests of the country and of
the tenants if this particular Amendment was
accepted by the Government.
There is also the fact that the minimum
cost to the tenant is £3 14s 3d for a case
heard in the Recorder's Court. It may be up
to any amount, but that is the minimum cost
to the tenant. I think it is a hardship to
the tenant to have to pay that, whereas if
it were dealt with by the ordinary petty sessions or lower court the cost would be much
less to the tenant and a lesser burden for him
to pay. For these reasons I think the Government would be well advised to accept this
particular Amendment, and I would be very
pleased to hear from the Government that
that was their intention. I am sure they do
not want to penalise the tenants in any way,
nor do they want to clutter up the Record
Court with a tremendous amount of business.
I am quite certain that as far as Belfast is
concerned these cases could be dealt with very
adequately and well by the lower court and
with less expense to the tenant, and it would
expedite business for the Government even
under this Act. I hope the Government will
see their way to accept this Amendment.

Written Answer.
DOWNPATRICK LOCAL EMPLOYMENT
COMMITTEE.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Labour, whether it is a fact that
an employer who sits on the Downpatrick Local
Employment Committee has a man employed
at twelve shillings a week lighting the street
lamps; whether the man in question is in
receipt of eighteen shillings a week unemployment benefit; whether the employer is
always on the Committee when the case
comes up for reconsideration; and if he will
state what steps he proposes to take in the
matter.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I understand that the duty of
maintaining the lighting of the streets in
Downpatrick falls on the Local Authority
and not on a private employer, and in these
circumstances the answer to the first part of
the hon. Member's question is in the
negative.
I am, however, informed that a claimant
at the Downpatrick office was employed during the winter by the Local Authority as a
lamp-lighter at a wage of 12s weekly while
in receipt of unemployment benefit at the
rate of 18s per week.
The unemployment Insurance Acts provide
that a claimant for benefit may be regarded
as "unemployed" although at the time of
claiming he is following an occupation which
he ordinarily followed in addition to his
usual employment and outside the working
hours of that employment, if the remuneration which he derives from this subsidiary
occupation does not exceed one pound per
week.
This test will be applied to the claim of
the applicant to whom I have referred; but
I am unable to say whether he was or was
not entitled to benefit. The matter is onein this instance-for determination by the
Insurance Officer, Court of Referees and
Umpire, and not by the Local Employment
Committee, as the satisfaction of one of the
statutory conditions is in question.

Mr. McALLISTER rose.
Mr. SPEAKER: Does the hon. Member
move a reduction?
Mr. MCALLISTER: I rise to move a reduction in respect of the Vote for the Royal
Ulster Constabulary. I do so in the first
place for the purpose of discussion. Let me
say there is no person in this House or out of
it who appreciates more or realises more the
necessity for a thoroughly efficient Police
Force that is to say, a regular Police Force
-than I do. I speak entirely with regard to
the Regular Police Force, the Royal Ulster
Constabulary, differentiating between the
Special Police Forces and that Constabulary.
I must say that I am entitled to judge a force,
or a set of men, as I find them, and with regard to the Regular Force I have always in
my experience found them courteous, obliging, and very efficient, especially considering
the short time they have been established. I
was particularly struck with the influence
of the local officers, the district-inspectors,
and their subordinates, on the
file of the Regular Constabulary.
and
rank
I have noticed that in districts where you
have a district-inspector and his immediate
subordinates, men of fair and equitable
minds and a high sense of public duty, that
that spirit seems to permeate throughout the
rank and file of the entire men under his
command, whether it be a district or a
barracks. Therefore, I would impress upon
the Government the immediate necessity of
taking every means in their power and of
exhausting every effort to secure districtinspectors and local officers of the highest
sense of public duty. If they do that I
believe they will go a long way towards
establishing a police force which will command the confidence of all sections of the
community of Northern Ireland.
But while I am in favour of a very
efficient police force, I say that for a fraction
of the amount of the total Votes for the
different sections of Constabulary in Ulster
a highly efficient police force, and one that
would be consistent with the financial
resources of Northern Ireland, could be
established and maintained. When you contrast the collective sums estimated for the
policing of Northern Ireland with the Votes
for the other Services it condemns the whole
system of government in Northern Ireland.
When you consider that you have a sum or
£2,600,000 for the police force of Northern
Ireland, and contrast with that the fact that
for the education of the future men and

rote practically a sum equivalent and

it was no arrangement of mine with the late
Mr. Collins whereby one-third of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary were to be Roman
Catholics and two-thirds Protestants.
That was an arrangement come to by a
Committee of this House. This House at
that time, without any representatives of
the hon. Members' side, came to the conclusion that it would be fair to the population of Northern Ireland if two-thirds were
to be of the Protestant persuasion and onethird of the Roman Catholic persuasion. Up
to the present time the Government has
most anxiously endeavoured to carry out the
recommendations of that Committee. With
regard to the appointment of officers that
has been carried out. So far as men coming
forward are concerned, I understand from
my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates)
that only some 500 Roman Catholics have
come forward to fill the 1,000 vacancies they
were entitled to. However, as to that the
Government have got nothing more to say except that the places were kept open for them
but the recruits did not come forward. It
was necessary to raise 3,000 men not only
in accordance with the recommendations of
the Committee of this House but in accordance with the recommendations of the Government in the first instance when the Act
of 1921 was passed, and later the Colwyn
Committee recommended, I think, within a
few men of 3,000 as the proper quota for
Northern Ireland. Therefore, we have not
only kept our-I will not say promise-we
have kept our intentions in regard to the
proportion of the two religions in the Force.
Out of six county inspectors the county inspectors of both Tyrone and Fermanagh are
Roman Catholics, that is to say, they have
two out of six, which is, if anything, over
the proportion to which I have referred.
Mr. DEVLIN: And the proportion in the
other counties?
The PRIME MINISTER: Of course, if you
have two out of six it is exactly one-third,
and that is in accordance with the recommendations of this House. Leaving to one
side, as I say, the Royal Ulster Constabulary-we have dealt with it fully, I hope,
now-let us come to the Special Constabulary, and let me remind the House that up
to to-day the Special Constabulary have

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I have no
desire to prolong unduly this Debate upon
this very interesting subject, but there are
one or two points on which I feel I would
like to make a passing reference. There
seems to be general agreement in the House
in regard to the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
No finer tribute has been paid to it in this
House or outside of it than the tribute that
has been paid to-day by the Members of the
Opposition, and especially by the Member
for the West Division of Belfast (Mr. Devlin), so that so far as the Force is concerned
it may be eliminated at once from the discussion in which we are at present engaged.
The controversy seems to have settled
round the Special Constabulary, and some
things have been said that I think the facts
did not fully warrant. Some people have
very short memories. We all know of the
terrible and trying times that we have
passed through during the past three or
four years, when our territory was invaded
from outside, when men were kidnapped and
taken away from their homes, when scenes
of destruction were witnessed in very many
districts, and when the Government really
found themselves in extreme difficulty as to
how law and order were going to be established and secured. I think those who have
studied the events of these trying times, and

As far as the Special Constabulary of all
classes are concerned I think they did their
work under extreme difficulty faithfully and
well, and the result up to the present has
been that peace has been established, and we
can go about our duties from day to day,
none daring to make us afraid. A question
has been raised in regard to the sectarian
character of the Special Constabulary.
Whose fault is that? It is certainly not the
fault of the authorities that the force has
been largely recruited from one particular
section of the community. The hon. Member
for Antrim (Mr. M'Allister) who sits
opposite has denounced in unmeasured terms
the Special Constabulary and the work they
have been doing, and he has told us that
one of the reasons why he and his friends
object to the Special Constabulary is that
they bear a sectarian colour. But every
citizen of Northern Ireland, when the trouble
was on, whether Catholic or Protestant, was
invited to enter this force and to do his
part in securing the safety of the State.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) If only one
section of the community responded to that
call why now is abuse being heaped upon
them? So far as the sectarian cry is concerned there is absolutely no foundation for
it. The ranks of the Special Constabulary
were open then to all classes of the community; they are open to-day, just as they
were in the very early stages when they were
established.
No question can arise in regard to the
Royal Ulster Constabulary. The hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) laid down
a very good principle that the forces which
have to do with law and order ought to be
recruited from all ranks and all classes in
the community. I am in thorough agreement with that. I sat upon the Police Committee which had to do with the establishment of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, and
the late Michael Collins had nothing
whatever to do with what the members
of that Committee laid down. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) They laid it
down clearly as a recommendation to
the Government that on the basis of
population the men who had to do
with the safety and the security of the State
should be reoruited from all sections of the
community. Although a great many did not
like the idea of putting into the report a
religious or sectarian division, they laid it
down on the basis of population, which meant
that the Catholic community of Northern
Ireland should be represented in the Royal
Ulster Constabulary, according to their
population, which was about one-third. I
think that was a fair and a reasonable proposition.

Order for Second Reading read.

"That the Bill be now read a Second Time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of this
Bill is to enable the local authorities to assist
financially Queen's University by making
direct grants. At the present time they have
power to make grants by way of providing
scholarships under the Education Act. They
have no right at all to contribute. The Bill
only follows the precedent which exists in
England and Scotland where the local
authorities have power to assist the various
provincial universities. There is a general
desire on the part of the local authorities to
assist Queen's University.
I would like to point out to hon. Members

Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of this
Bill is to encourage still further the building
of working-class houses in Northern Ireland.
Under the existing Acts, the 1923 Act and
the subsequent Act, the Government contribute £60 per house of certain dimensions.
that is to say, houses of a maximum of 950
superficial feet and a minimum of 600 superficial feet, and in addition local authorities
at the present time have power to contribute
up to the sum of £40 as an additional grant
to such houses, or, if they so prefer, they
can make a free loan of £100 for a period of
twenty-five years. The area within which
these houses were to be built was confined
to urban districts and industrial areas inside
rural areas. Having regard to the comparatively short time in which these Acts
have been in operation, I regard them as
being very successful, but at the same time
we think there are many matters which
could be improved upon. As a result of our
Housing Acts I find that no fewer than 885
houses have been approved of for erection by
local authorities themselves, and these local
authorities have also further schemes in
hand to the extent of 1,156 houses, while as
regards private owners, no fewer than 2.106
houses have been either built or arranged
for.
We intend to extend the scope of these
Acts not only to rural centres but to the
entire of the rural areas. There is another
way in which we propose to amend the Acts.
We feel that while the existing Acts have
been successful, a certain amount can be
done to accelerate the building.
I have taken out figures, and out of 300
houses I find that
19% have taken 4 months to build.

75%


"


I think there is a tendency on the part of
some of the builders to procrastinate in the
knowledge that the Act remains in force
until 1st April, 1926, and we propose under
this Bill to increase the subsidy of £60 by an
additional sum of £20 on every house that is
erected within four months after its commencement. We think four months is a
reasonable period for the construction of
houses of this type. When 19 per cent. of
300 houses can be built within four months.
we do not see any reason why a great many
more houses cannot be built within the same
period.
We also propose to give power to the local
authorities, if they so desire, to remit the
rates on these houses for a period of 10 years.
That is entirely a matter for themselves, and
I hope they will fall in with the suggestion,
but this Bill does not in any sense impose
any liability upon them to do so. I beg to
move.

Another result that will follow on

This Bill does not seem to me to be as
good a measure as the Chamberlain Act.
Under that Act £6 a year for twenty years
was granted by the Imperial Government,

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: What would

Mr. KYLE: Pre-war rents. That is what
I suggest to you. I know quite well the
difficulty any body is in who desires to build
a house at the present time. We all appreciate their position, but I am trying to get
you to realise that it is the duty of any
Government to see that the people who are
living under the jurisdiction of that Government are properly housed. So far as
this Bill is concerned it does not provide
houses to let but only houses for sale, as the
Chamberlain Act did. About 75 per cent of
the houses built under the Chamberlain Act
were sold. That is not what we want. We
want houses to let.
Further, to obviate any possibility of this
£80 subsidy being taken by those who are in
the building trade for private profit I think
some Clause should be inserted in the Bill
such as the Minister of Labour introduced
into his scheme for the relief of unemployment several years ago.
You will remember
that a sum of £500,000 was granted for the
relief of unemployment under certain conditions. A proportion of that money was
used in Belfast, and the Minister of Labour
laid it down as one of the conditions that this
money could only be given to Corporations,
Utility Societies, or some body that did not
primarily exist for making profit. That was
to ensure that the fund would be used in the
best interests of the people of Belfast.
This is public money, and I think a provision should be inserted in the Bill to the
effect that the subsidy would only be granted
to Corporations or Utility Societies or
Societies that did not primarily exist for
making profit. Some Clause to that effect
would strengthen the Bill very materially and
tend to promote its useful administration.
In my opinion the subsidy should not be given

officers of that Ministry had expressed their

charged for the erection of the houses, and
that the Fair Wages Clause had been observed
in every detail. I think a Clause of that
nature, or some strengthening of the Bill in
that direction would have a very beneficial
effect.
There is another point I would like to
mention in connection with the Unemployment
Relief Scheme of the Minister of Labour that
is well worth the consideration of the
Minister of Home Affairs. That is, he did
not give a grant to any public body unless
they were going to erect houses costing not
more than £500. That ensured that this
money would be used for the working classes,
and for them alone. I do not think that any
subsidy should be given in respect of any
house that will cost more than £500 to build.
If the Minister of Home Affairs would give

paid on houses costing more than £500 it
would show to the country that his Department was really interested in the erection of
houses for the ordinary working man and
woman. I will conclude as I started by say
ing how extremely sorry I am that the
Minister of Home Affairs has not thought fit
to introduce a Bill that would give us houses
to let rather than houses to sell.

I hold that what has been done in the
way of building 4,000 houses during the last
one and a half years has not made up the
leeway in regard to housing accommodation.
While you have had a growth in population
you have had a depreciation in houses, with
the result that there are a number of
buildings not habitable. I suggest that the
4,000 houses built have not made up the
leeway to allow for the growth of population and for the number of houses that have
become uninhabitable during the last couple
of years. I believe the attitude adopted by
the Government is not going to solve this

It may be information to hon. Members to

24d, and the total cost of the operatives concerned in the building of that house with a
life of 60 years would be 1s 3d per week.
You will realize, therefore, that that forms
a very inconsiderable part of the rent of the

Mr. BEATTIE: Pursuing the arguments
of yesterday, I would like to draw the
attention of this House to the Clauses of the

produce the results that we desire. Perhaps
it would be futile for me to take upon myself the title of prophet, and to say that it
will not meet the ends that we of the
Opposition have in view. The sum of £80 is
being substituted for the £60 grant towards
the building of each house. That amount is
provided with the object of expediting the
erection of houses. While it may, perhaps,
encourage the building employers to strike
out in order to get the £80, plus the amount
granted by the Local Authorities, I do not
think there is any guarantee that we are
going to get working-class houses.
Principal Act applies to a certain class of

house the class of house that we on this

built.
We believe that houses for the workingmen
of to-day should have bathrooms and the
latest labour-saving appliances, with the

was given yesterday as 950 superficial feet.
If you direct your mind to that space, and
if you are persons with reasonable consideration for the comfort of the working-classes, I
think you will find that that is not sufficient.
We desire to see homes with three bedrooms,
and I would like the Minister of Home
Affairs to pay particular attention to this
item-bathrooms. I do not mean
a bath
placed inside the scullery or in a small

thing for the working-class people. We have
been lacking in the past in the matter of
placing baths in homes, but I hope that in

I think the Bill should provide some

canny or slow motion principle, and not laying a sufficient number of bricks each day to
bring about a reduction in the cost of the

Correspondence went on in the Belfast Press

added 14d per week to the rent, labour, 1s
3d, and the cost of materials and profit, 1s
104d. A very substantial item that increases

call the money lender. The money lender
has always a finger in the pie, and he sees

this does not come directly through the

I would just like to refer to Section 3 of
the Bill, that is that local authorities may.
in pursuance of a general resolution, grant
relief from rates for ten years. I would
ask the Minister of Home Affairs what his
business friends think of that proposition.
Some of the great industries and some of the
business people who have been in such a depressing condition during the past number
of years will likely jib against this being
given out to a council that is unsympathetic,

week thrown off his rent, so that the regulation may be conformed with, but I predict

something should be done to safeguard the
tenants under that section. I do not think
the community at large would stand up and
allow it to pass. Broader shoulders than
the tenants should be made to bear this.
Broader shoulders are able to bear it. I do
not see why a privilege should be given to
any one individual whereby he will get something that the rest of the community has to
bear. If you take the broader way, you will
do the thing properly.
The Act as it stands will not, I suppose,
be altered. If this is the suggestion of the
Government to expedite house building I
am rather afraid they are just as far off as

way to tackle the question the better. It is
only playing with the question, which is a
very serious one in Northern Ireland to-day.
The Government are only tinkering with it.
They are not endeavouring to relieve the congestion caused by the shortage of houses.
If they find they can do it perhaps they will
let us know. I may be asked: "Give us your
suggestions?" Perhaps if I were on the

The PRIME MINISTER
Craig): I would like to wind up this debate,

nothing the Government can do is done

Measures, and we can discount it in advance.
The truth of the matter is that this Bill has
been brought forward by the Government
with the intention of meeting the demand
for working-class houses throughout Ulster-
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and it only is
applicable to the class of houses that you
would call working-class houses. Up to the
present time, entirely due to our limited

financial resources, we have been unable to

Grants under this Section shall be made
only in respect of houses-(a) which are
of such type and size as is specified in this
Section, and satisfy the Ministry as to
structural stability and proper sanitation;
(b) which are certified under this Section to
have been completed in a proper and workmanlike manner;
Then in regard to the bath accommodation
to which the hon. Member refers I will go on
to the portion dealing with that. It comes
under Schedule 2, Part I.
A house for which a sufficient water supply
is available must be provided as a rule with
a bath. The local authority may dispense
with the fitting of a bath if space for its
future installation is provided.
I think that meets the hon. Member's
criticism on this point. The only other one
I would like to deal with is regarding the
foregoing by the local authorities of the rates
for anything up to ten years-a maximum
of ten years. I myself, personally, believe
that that is one of the most important parts
of the Bill, and I hope that the local authorities throughout our Six Counties will take
full advantage of being able to excuse the
rates on the new houses that are being
built. It appears to me that what is wanted
is to place in our Counties more property of
a rateable value; in other words, that there
should be shifted from the burden on the
farmers' backs the payment of a certain
proportion of the rates in all the rural
districts on to the houses which are erected.
For example, if a couple of thousand houses
were erected in any one county in Ulster
under this scheme it means that
at the expiration of 10 years there
a couple of thousand houses
which will have a rateable value in
order to contribute to the rates of the
county for the time that these houses last
afterwards. From the point of view of the
county itself it seems to me to be a good inare
vestment to have spread over the county
more devlopment with a view to being able
to collect more rates from these houses when
they are built.
In addition to that we have the option
of contributing £40 which added to the £80
under this Bill, making a total of £120, is
an inducement to people to come
forward and erect more and more houses
for the working classes. Unfortunately
in some of our villages especially one cannot
but note with pain and sorrow that a great
many of these labourers cottages and other
houses of that type are falling down and
getting into disrepair. They require to be
replaced by modern up-to-date houses such
as can be erected under this Bill. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). Therefore, it will
be of great assistance to the Counties, and
great assistance to the working classes and
to the community as a whole if this Bill is
taken advantage of as we all sincerely
trust it will. We have had results to go on--
the results that have accrued from our last
Bill of 1923. It is not altogether guess-work.
It is something like a proportion sum. If
with only a £60 grant from the Gevernment
we have been able to get 2,000 houses either
constructed or in course of construction or
in the way to be constructed, surely it can
be assumed that at all events we cannot fall
short of 2,000 more houses. I hope it will
be more like 4,000 or 5,000 houses when we
increase the grant from £60 to £80, and open
the doors to County Councils and other local
authorities to allow the foregoing of the
rates up to a limit of ten years.

The question of the laying of bricks illustrates fairly well what I have to say. Despite what the hon. Member for East Belfast
(Mr. Beattie) has told us, you have here a

men are laying 700 bricks

Sir Crawford McCullagh told me and he

were asked to lay these bricks they

But I do think that there is one other

is one of the greatest deterrents to development about small towns. You take some
parcel of ground about a small town or
rural area and probably its value is 10s
or 12s. A man wants to build a house
and comes to the ground landlord and says
"I want that ground." The landlord probably says "I will give it to you at £5."
Housing Bill.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. George Henderson]
Probably up to that time it was worth 10s.
Then the lease falls out, and is it fair that
this man who puts his capital into this
property on which the ground landlord
never spent a shilling should be entirely
at the mercy of the landlord? I have in
my mind's eye at the present time a small
town not ten miles away where one of those
short term leases fell out. The rent was
£5. The landlord never spent a shilling
to increase the letting value, and yet to
get that lease renewed the owner had got
to pay a rent of £25 a year. As long as
things like that exist you cannot expect
development. It is not possible without
security. I think something should be
done to encourage the building of houses,
and we must give men who are willing to
spend money some security. I do not see
how this can be done unless some justice
is done on short term leases falling out.
There should be some machinery set up to
fix something like a fair rent on short term
leases. Not only are dwelling-houses hit
very hard, but I think at the present time
in the city of Belfast a great many leases
are falling out. If we want to encourage
houses we must give some security of
tenure.

of the House consistently malign the

Hear, hear, and other hon. Members: No,
no.) They persistently make statements that
they do not work as they ought to work. (Hon.
Members: No, no). They persistently make
the statement that they only do about onethird of a day's work in a day. They persistently make the statement that they only lay
from 200 to 250 bricks per day. They
never take into consideration at all the
class of work that these men may be engaged upon. I had occasion recently to
question the hon. Member for Fermanagh
and Tyrone's statement on this subject,

contracts. I asked him how many bricks

Members persistently lay it down that this

Mr. KYLE: They do not know.
Mr. GYLE: Do you think you

solve this most important problem of the
housing of the working classes. I can scarcely understand why only £20 per house is

an increase of £20, from £60 to £80. I do
not think that is going to induce the builder

will listen to some of the suggestions that
come from this side of the House we will
make this Bill a little better. At any rate
we will try. I welcome it because we must

and so far as we are concerned we will give

in the general

to the poor by not suspending this Urban

I object altogether to the right hon.
Gentleman setting his opinion against the

this aspersion on Nurse Gillespie he seems to
be absolutely unheedful of the magnificent

whose names have been recited by my hon.

There were a number of candidates who
applied for this position. They all stood in
a position of equality. None of them had
this experience to which he refers.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Several of the candidates came up to the qualifications laid
'down by the Ballymena Urban District

My point is that Nurse Gillespie had no

Mr. DEVLIN: That is not my point at
all. My point is that none of the candidates had this experience. The right hon.
Gentleman will not question that.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I deny it.
Mr. DEVLIN: The papers are here and
I can produce them to the right hon. Gentleman. None of the candidates had any experience at all in this work. Therefore, the
only course open to the Urban Council was
to proceed with the appointment of this lady
in view of the splendid references that were

Gentleman, whose duties are SO manifold

right hon. Gentleman will not deny that
the desire of the Urban District Council,

Sir DAWSON BATES: I do deny it.
Mr. DEVLIN: Then the right hon. Gentleman asserts that for some devious purpose,
with some sinister object in view, for some
indefensible purpose, this responsible public
body stooped to so mean a subterfuge in the
interest of a single candidate as to appoint
some incompetent person to discharge a most
elementary duty in regard to the administration of our public health. That is a most
serious allegation for the right hon. Gentleman to make. The election of this lady was
carried on 17th February. The right hon.
Gentleman waited until 8th April before he
wrote a letter refusing to sanction the appointment of Miss Gillespie. I would like to
know what was the meaning of this delay in
the decision which the right hon. Gentleman
gave?
I have watched the peculiar methods of
the Minister of Home Affairs in controversy
in this House. It will be far better for him,

transaction of this character, if he will
simply get up and let the House know what
the real reasons were that inspired him to

prevent him sanctioning the appointment of
this nurse.
Sir DAWSON BATES: May I correct the
hon. Member? No influences at all were
brought to bear on me.

Most of those rules and regulations have now

Sir DAWSON BATES: Several questions

The hon. Member (Mr. Johnstone) behind

The hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
William McMullen) has raised a question
as to why a certain candidate was not

Constabulary. My reply to that is that the
authorities did not consider the applicant a
suitable man to make an efficient policeman.
Hon. Members will quite agree with me that
it would be a most improper thing and
against public policy if I were to go into
details of each case and say why a man was
or was not accepted as a constable. I think
hon. Members will also realise that a very
great responsibility is imposed on the authorities to secure the best men as policemen,
and the fact that we have got such an
efficient police force as the Royal Ulster
Constabulary is really due to the great care
that is taken in the selection of candidates.
My hon. Friend (Mr. William McMullen)
also raised the question of why the Belfast
Board of Guardians do not contribute outdoor relief in money, but distribute it in
kind. I think there is a great deal to be

My hon. Friend the Member for North

They are only too anxious that an applicant

Mr. ANDREWS: My hon. Friend, the
Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle) raised
two questions affecting my Department. One

In the first class there are those who while

Northern Ireland.
Mr. KYLE: Why in Northern Ireland.
Mr. ANDREWS: Their cards were stamped
in the usual way and when they became unemployed they received Unemployment Benefit through one of our own Labour Exchanges, just in the same way as other
workers in Northern Ireland do. But there
was the other class who, while working in
Northern Ireland really came from the Free
State, whose homes are in the Free State,
and who are now residing in the Free State.
Of course a different position arises in
reference to those workers, because, in the
application of the Government of Ireland
Act to the Unemployment Insurance Acts,
a person is disqualified for benefit if he lives
outside Northern Ireland, and I have no
authority under these Acts to pay benefit to
those persons who are living in the Free
State.
I may say that the question of having a
reciprocity arrangement with the Free State
has been frequently discussed between the
Free State Minister and myself. We have
had a great deal of correspondence in reference to the matter, but so far we have been
unable to come to any agreement, and the
reasons that prevent that agreement are as
follows: The first is that the Free State
have refused to have a similar reciprocity
arrangement with Great Britain, and as we
have a reciprocity arrangement with Great
Britain the matter is complicated from that
standpoint. Then again an arrangement of
the kind should mean that equal benefit
would be payable under equal conditions in
the two areas, in other words that contributions paid in Northern Ireland should
have the same benefit value as contributions
paid in the Free State. My Ministry warned
the Free State Ministry of Labour that if they
departed from legislation similar to Great
Britain's legislation and to our legislation
in connection with this matter they would
produce a very impossible position.
Mr. KYLE: I would like to ask the right
hon. Gentleman if he could say that he would

would be easy enough.
Mr. ANDREWS: The answer to the question is in the negative, because I have no
power to do so, nor would it be fair to our
Northern Ireland workers, of whom the hon.
Member (Mr. Kyle) is a representative,
and for this reason: It would encourage employers, perhaps, along the boundary to employ workers from the Free State-because if
these workers were not insurable, and human
nature being what it is, employers would
escape an obligation which they are under
in reference to workers resident in Northern
Ireland. When my hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle)

equal benefits. As my hon. Friend knows
the contributions in the Free State are

much less generous manner. For instance,

is no longer payable in the Free State, and

to those existing in the Free State I am
quite sure hon. Members will appreciate

Now my hon. Friend, the Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Beattie), referred to what he
called the new regulations under our Unemployment Insurance Acts, and he asked
me if I was prepared to alter these new regulations, because of the fact that the linen
trade unfortunately has had a relapse of a
serious character, and that therefore the opportunities for obtaining employment in the
linen trade are not what they were some
months ago. I would point out to my hon.
Friend what these new regulations really
amount to. The first regulation provides
that the employed person shall have paid
twelve contributions at some time to the
Fund, and that regulation does not apply to
ex-Service men. Now the reason for that
regulation is quite apparent to everyone. It
is to prove the claimant for benefit is
really an insured person. And surely it is
not a difficult fence to get over, if the person
is an insured person at all, that he shall
show that he at some time paid or had paid
on his behalf twelve contributions.
The second provision is that there shall
be a reasonable period of insurable employment in those trades that are scheduled as
good trades where the opportunities during
the last two years for obtaining employment
have become better. Now here is the point,
six weeks' work or some work done in each
of six weeks, not necessarily in consecutive
weeks, shall be shown. Surely it is not
an unreasonable thing to ask that in those
trades where the opportunities for obtaining
employment have become greater the worker
will have done some work in two years. It is
true that the opportunities for obtaining
employment in the linen trade have lessened
during the last few months. But remember
it is not to the last few months alone that
these regulations are applied; it is for a
period of two years.

Now as regards these other trades where
the opportunities for obtaining employment
have not become better in the last two years
the old conditions still apply. Therefore
under the circumstances I do not feel i
would be justified in making an alteration
as my hon. Friend suggests, especially as I
feel that it is absolutely necessary in matters
of this kind that we should keep in step as
far as possible with Great Britain. Hon.
Members opposite are frequently appealing
to the Government to keep on parallel lines
with Great Britain. Well, they cannot have
it both ways. They cannot come here one
day and make that appeal to us and then
come another day and ask us to go out of
step.

Mr. ANDREWS: After all, this Bill to
which I have the honour to ask the House
to give a Second Reading to-day, is a very
simple little Measure. In my opinion it is
drafted in such a way that even those who
have not the advantage of being connected
with the legal profession can see at a glance
exactly what is intended. It empowers His
Grace the Governor of Northern Ireland to
make temporary provision by Order in
Council for the amendment of the Unemployment Insurance Acts, as was done in similar
circumstances last year, in order that the
considered policy of the Government and of
this Parliament may be adhered to, namely
that our Northern Ireland unemployment
insurance provisions should be similar to
those in force in Great Britain.
Under the Unemployment Insurance (No.
2) Act, passed in Great Britain in 1924, a new
statutory condition for the receipt of benefit
was introduced, which required that the
claimant must prove that not less than 30
contributions had been paid in respect of him
since the beginning of the first of the two
insurance years preceding the beginning of
the benefit year in which his claim was made.
901 Unemployment Insurance Bill-

27 MAY 1925
Second Reading.
The same provision was included in the corresponding Northern Ireland Measure. But
it was recognised both in Great Britain and
here that that condition would have been
'difficult to comply with owing to the depressed state of the industries at that time,
and power was given by those Acts to both the
Minister of Labour in Great Britain and to
myself to waive the operation of this first
statutory condition until the 1st of October,
1925. The Imperial Minister of Labour has
already stated that he proposes to introduce
a new Unemployment Insurance Bill during
the summer months, for the purpose of extending these powers of waiver and for other
matters possibly as well. These new conditions may be brought into force in Great
Britain while our Parliament is not sitting,
and therefore this Measure is introduced for
the purposes of giving me power here to continue to follow along similar lines with Great
Britain in reference to unemployment insurance matters. I think that that will appeal
to my hon. Friends. I would point out, however, that this is only a temporary Measure,
and that it only gives me power to do this
until such time as Parliament again
reassembles, and has an opportunity of dealing with the matter-but in no case after the
31st December next. So that it will be
necessary between this and then to introduce
a new Unemployment Bill here, and I will
undertake, on behalf of the Government, that
ample time will be given to permit of the
very fullest discussion in connection with the
matter.
Some hon. Members may say that this is
Well,
rather giving me a blank cheque.
really I would not have any wish to receive
a blank cheque which would involve so much

Hon. Members may raise the point about
our sadly overburdened Insurance Fund.
Well, as far as I see, with the information at
my disposal, this will not put a heavier
weekly burden upon the Fund than it is
being at the present time subjected to, and
even if it did we cannot help it. But I may
say that I am quite hopeful that in this
matter all will come right, provided our
employers and our workers play fair by each
other, fair by the community of which they
form such an important part, and fair by the
Fund itself. I cannot help but think that
everyone recognises that unemployment as
we know it to-day is a National problem
brought about by National and International
conditions beyond the reach of this Parliament to grapple with or to solve. Therefore
I feel that it should be dealt with in no
local way but in a National way, and that
the burden should be shared equally
throughout the whole United Kingdom.

ambit of Great Britain and Northern Ireland they should be exactly on the same
terms, whether they are working on the
Clyde or in Belfast.
Mr. DEVLIN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman, before he finally commits himself to proposals of that character, whether
the control of these services will be in the
hands of this Parliament, because that is a
very important thing. We should not allow
any powers we have to pass out of our hands.
The PRIME MINISTER: That is a matter
that is engaging the earnest consideration
of the Government. That is one of the
difficult questions we have to settle, as to
whether it is of more andyantage to us
to have the control of certain services
or whether it would be better that they
should be controlled by one central body.
That depends to a large extent upon
our own financial resources. It nearly
all comes back to that. The point I want to
make is that these are really most crucial
and difficult questions for the British
Cabinet and for ourselves to come together
about. Therefore what I am anxious to do
is to adjourn the House, after these two
Bills have got through their remaining stages,
until some nominal date in October, retaining to ourselves the right to call the House
together again if it appears to be necessary
to deal with anything of an extraordinarily
difficult character.
That is the best we can do at the moment,
because we have no idea how long it will take
us to have these protracted matters made
right, or how long it will take the Imperial
Parliament to pass through their Bill, which
is a very intricate one and the details of
which they are not yet certain about. If we
adjourn until the first Tuesday in October,
and reserve to ourselves the right to summon Mr. Speaker to call the House together.
again in the meantime, if it is necessary, I
think it will meet the convenience of Members on all sides of the House.
There is no use our meeting on 1st August
if there is no business immediately before
us, because the Government is not necessarily going to make business for this House
to deal with. We want to be businesslike
and only to come here to deal with business
that is of importance to the community.
Therefore, if we adjourn until 6th October,
and anything crops up which makes it
necessary for the House to meet earlier, the
Government will reserve the power to summon the Speaker to call the House together.
Mr KYLE: I am sorry this debate has
taken the course it has by developing into a

important than any of the matters raised by
either the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin) or the Prime Minister. As I have
already hinted, we are going to be faced with
an unemployment situation that is unpar-

Northern Ireland.

We are not opposed to unemployment insurance and we are not opposed to making
provision for the unemployed, but we are
opposed to the particular method that is
being adopted in regard to this matter. As
a matter of fact I do not know where the
Minister of Labour gets his authority to introduce a Bill giving the Governor of
Northern Ireland power, by Order in Council,
to adopt similar regulations to those passed
in Great Britain. Surely this is the proper,
place to do that, or the Minister of Labour
could do it by his own intelligence and his
own wisdom, and we all know he has no
small amount of that. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) There is no reason in the world
why he should not introduce in this House
a Measure to deal with the unemployment
situation as he finds it in Northern Ireland.
We agree to a large extent with the observations made by the senior Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) that we should enjoy
the same advantages as the citizens of Great
Britain, but that does not mean that we
should not deal here with our own unemployment problem as we find it. We will have
to do so sooner or later. Sooner or later we,
in Northern Ireland, will be compelled to
accept the position, whether hon. Members
opposite like it or not, and we will have to
face our own problems and settle them ourselves. It is for the Government to make a
start now. It was from that point of view
that my hon. Friend (Mr. William McMullen)
said we were opposed to the method by
which it is proposed to carry out the objects
of this Bill.
f
+
It appears to me that if the statement that
has been made is true, to the effect that the
present unemployment figure is going to be
reduced to 800,000 by the end of this year,
the Minister of Labour, when this Bill becomes an Act, will have power to cut off the
benefit of many hundreds, if not thousands,
of people in Northern Ireland who would.
otherwise be entitled to it. We know that
will be done by the large Tory majority on
the other side. Unemployment has increased
by over 100,000 since the Tory Government
came into office, and instead of helping
industry they are now going to put a
further burden on it.
I agree that pensions should be a National
charge just as Unemployment Insurance is,
but it is not a National charge at present; it
is a charge on industry. What we understand by a National charge is something that the Chancellor of the Exchequer
would put on the Income Tax. We noticed
that when the British Chancellor of the
Exchequer decided that there should be a re
duction of 6d in the Income Tax the
Northern Government very quickly decided
to follow on parallel lines, although in
Great Britain the people who are getting the
advantage of that 6d off the Income Tax will
be compelled to contribute towards this
Insurance Scheme, whereas in Northern Ireland a Bill is not going to be introduced
until October. The result is that hon. Members opposite who are in the proud position
of being able to pay this Income Tax will
get the benefit of the rebate up to October,
and will not be called upon to contribute
anything to this Insurance Scheme up to
that date. Therefore we are justified in saying
that so far as the Northern Government is
concerned they take particular pains to look
after the welfare of the wealthy people.
I do not want the Minister of Labour, or
any other person in this House or out of it,
to think that we on the Labour Benches are
opposed to Unemployment Insurance. We
are not. We have been in favour of it all
our lives. For twenty years before it was
attempted, the Trades' Union Congress
passed resolutions in favour of Unemployment Insurance and National Health
Insurance. We wanted a non-contributory
scheme. Of course we did; it would have
been much better for us, but seeing that the
workers create all the wealth, I am not so
sure of that.

Mr. JOHNSTONE: I wish to speak to
this Bill, and to express the hope that it will
not become a dead letter. It is an enabling
Bill, and I sincerely hope that the various
authorities who are empowered to raise rates
for the benefit of Queen's University will
take advantage of it. I have here some
figures which I think may interest the House
in regard to the amount of rate aid given to
some of the British Universities. We in
Belfast have no rate aid whatever. I find
that in Birmingham almost 9.9 per cent of
the total income of the University comes
from rate aid. In Bristol, 17.6 per cent. of
the total income comes from the rates.
Armstrong College, Newcastle, gets 7.9 per
cent. of its total income from the rates.
In Aberystwyth, 17.1 per cent. of the total income of the University comes from the rates.
Belfast, unfortunately, gets nothing at all. I
think that is really a very great pity. It is
a great pity that the very fine University of
Belfast should not be supported by rates as
these Universities across the water are. Of
the Universities that I have mentioned,
Birmingham, Bristol, Newcastle, and Aberystwyth, the majority are situated in large
industrial centres. The people who have
charge of those large industrial centres not
only realise what an important thing it is that
they should have a University in their midst,
but also that that University should be well
supported by the cities themselves in order
that they may have the benefit of the skilled
brains and the training and education which
are given in a University. I hope that this
enabling Bill will enable the people of Belfast
and the local authorities throughout the
Northern area to do something for the only
University that we have in Northern Ireland.

28 MAY 1925
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 28th May, 1925.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
LABOURERS' COTTAGES-LISBURN
DISTRICT.
1. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs if he will state the
grounds on which the application of Robert
Higgins for a cottage in connection with a
scheme promoted by the Lisburn Rural
District Council was struck out by the
Inspector; if he is aware that the house in
which Robert Higgins is living consists of
one small bedroom and kitchen; that his
family numbers nine, and that the house has
been condemned by three doctors; that a few
weeks ago a cottage became vacant, and that
Robert Higgins, though recommended by the
doctor for the cottage, was passed over, and
the cottage given to a man who deals in
cattle and owns a horse; and if he will also
state on what grounds the application of
Bernard Mulholland was struck out at the
same inquiry.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): It is a matter for the
Inspector to decide the number and sites of
the cottages to be erected, but I am unable
to give information on these points as I have
not yet received the Inspector's report.
As regards the remainder of the question,
the selection of tenants of the cottages
erected or to be erected by the Rural District
Council is a matter for the Council themselves, and I am not empowered to interfere
with their discretion in making such
selection.
INTOXICATING LIQUOR ACT, 1923.
2. Mr. GYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs, whether the Intoxicating Liquor Act
(Northern Ireland), 1923, in Section 3, provides that the holder of an on-licence who is
unable to comply with the requirements of
the Act with respect to the structural separation of the part of his premises in which the
sale of intoxicating liquor is carried on
from the part of those premises in which
any other business is carried on, is entitled
to compensation if the licence is not by
reason of such inability renewed at the
annual licensing sessions held next after the
date when such requirements came into
operation, viz., the sessions in September and
October, 1925; whether Section 6 provides
that intoxicating liquor shall not be sold or
offered for sale after 1st October, 1924, in
licensed premises where such separation
cannot be effected; whether the inability referred to must exist at the date of the holding of the sessions or when; and whether if
the effect of the two sections is to imperil the
licence-holder's right to compensation given
by the Act, what steps the Government
intend to take to remove this anomaly in the
Act.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As regards the
first part of the question, I have no jurisdiction to express an authoritative opinion
as the matter can only be finally settled by a
Court of competent jurisdiction. I may say,
however, that I am advised that the answer
to this part of the question is in the
affirmative.
The hon. Member does not correctly state
the effect of Section 6 (1) of the Act in the
second part of his question, and I would
refer him to the express provisions of that
section.
The remainder of the question raises
points for the consideration of the Claims
Tribunal, and it would be improper for me
to anticipate their decision thereon.
DANGEROUS CORNER IN BALLY-
GAWLEY.
3. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether his attention has
been directed to the suggestion made at the
Ballygawley Petty Sessions, on the 19th inst.
that a police pointsman be placed at a
dangerous corner on the Dungannon Road
in the centre of the town, where several
people nearly lost their lives owing to being
run over by motors; and whether the Minister has also had his attention drawn to the
statement of District Inspector Martin
admitting the dangerous nature of the corner,
but declaring that the local police force
would require to be considerably augmented
if point duty was to be done.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My attention has
been directed to this matter, but I may point
out that while some of the Magistrates were
in favour of the proposal to place a constable
on point duty at this corner, others were not.
The Police Officer who was present at the
Petty Sessions Court pointed out that the
roadway was wide at this spot, and that if
a danger sign were erected it would probably
meet the case.
This suggestion was adopted by the Bench,
who have communicated with the local
authority in the matter.

4. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of

that perforated bricks cost £5 7s 6d per 1,000
in Belfast as against £4 17s 0d in, London;
solid bricks £5 0s 0d per 1,000 in Belfast
against £4 5s 0d in London, and stock bricks
£3 5s Od in Belfast against £2 17s Od in
London; and what steps the Minister proposes to take to remove this serious obstacle
to the building of houses in Belfast.
(Mr.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
Barbour): I have been asked by my right

From the information available in my Ministry the prices of bricks in Belfast appear

MALONE REFORMATORY-WM.
COCHRANE.
5. Mr. DEVLIN, asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether a boy named William
Cochrane was in January, 1924, ordered by
the Belfast Magistrates to be detained in the
Malone Reformatory for three years; whether
the boy has been subjected to ill-treatment
at the hands of certain officials of the institution; whether as a result of this treatment
the boy lost the sight of one eye whilst the
sight of the other is threatened; whether he
has been a patient in the Royal Victoria
Hospital since 2nd April, 1925; whether the
remainder of his term of detention will be
remitted, and what redress the Minister
proposes to offer.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The reply to the
first part of the question is in the affirmative.
As regards the second part, a complaint has
been received from the boy's mother as to
his treatment in the Reformatory, but the
inquiries which have been made do not disclose any grounds for this complaint. Examination of the boy's eyes at the Belfast
Ophthalmic Hospital some months before the
alleged ill-treatment is supposed to have
taken place revealed the fact that he was
practically blind of one eye, and that the
sight of the other, though fair, was not quite
perfect. The oculists at the hospital consider
that the conditions in both eyes are probably
congenital. A report from the Royal Victoria
Hospital indicates that the sight at present
is practically unchanged.
The boy was sent to the hospital for treatment for seizures, to which he is reported to
have been subject for the last four or five
years, and he is about to be discharged
from hospital, Further inquiries are being
made, and I, will consider all the circumstances of the case.

"
Mr. DEVLIN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman what will happen to this boy
when he is discharged from the hospital? Is
he be sent back to the reformatory?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
stated to my hon,, Friend that I will take
the whole circumstances of the case into consideration to see whether the boy should be
discharged from the reformatory?

Ulster
fact that three members of the Royal

9. Mr. GYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to,, the Ministry of Education.
whether he has agreed to pay travelling and
lunch allowance to secondary teachers attending the compulsory course in geography at
Queen's University during July, 1925, provided they travel by train, and has refused
to meet similar expenses incurred by
teachers who travel from remote suburbs by
tram or bus and must also have lunch from
home; and, if the Ministry extended those
allowances to teachers who took a voluntary
course in 1923, what reason there is for refusing recognition of necessary expenditure
to teachers who are compelled to attend
lectures in 1925.
Mr. BARBOUR: On behalf of my hon.
Friend, the Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Education, I will reply to this
question.
It is the case that such allowances will be
payable this year to certain teachers, but
these allowances are not payable to teachers
resident within the City of Belfast or within
two miles thereof.
In 1923 no allowances were paid to teachers
whose home addresses were in Belfast.
Mr. GYLE: Is it not a fact that teachers
residing within two miles of Belfast pay
practically the same amount--they must
have luncheon down town-as people coming
from, say, Bangor?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Is my right hon.
Friend aware that it is alleged that some
teachers in Belfast have been paid, while
others have not?
Mr. BARBOUR: I will communicate that
to the Minister. My information is that in
1923 no allowances were paid to such teachers
and we are following the practice then set.

The
repayment
of
Mr. POLLOCK:
annuities is in the nature of a statutory contract between the tenant and the State, and

I do so because it has been generally aocepted in this Committee and elsewhere that
the question of housing should be a national
responsibility. I want to see that national
responsibility worked out through the local
authorities rather than depend upon private
enterprise in regard to the erection of houses.
Private enterprise has so lamentably failed
in the past to provide us with homes, to provide us with houses, that it seems to me that
to work out this national responsibility
through our local bodies would be very much
more efficacious than to subsidise private
enterprise to erect these houses. It is from
that point of view that I want the Commitee to approach this question.
It seems to me that, housing being a national
responsibility, it is but right that we as a
Committee should not allow profitering to
come in, that we should have these houses
erected at the cheapest possible price in the
most efficient way by our local authorities,
to the end that there may be no profitering
for individuals so far as this national charge
is concerned. During the war we had to
limit very seriously indeed the prices and
profits in respect of the making of shells and
munitions. We had to control that industry.
We had to take it over as a matter of fact
and had to do these things for the good of
the nation in the nation's peril. We contend

given from the Government side for extending this time. But can any man in the Government or any body of men say it would
take longer than four months to erect a
house of 950 superficial feet. The thing has
only to be stated to show the absurdity of
it. As a matter of fact the thing can be
done in two months instead of four months
and one wants to know why that has been
extended.

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I beg to
move in page 2, line 22, at the end of Clause
2. to add as a new Sub-section: "The cost of
houses to which Grants under this Section
may be made, must not exceed £500."
It will be perfectly obvious that
intention of this Amendment is to
try to ensure that the subsidy will
be given towards the erection of workingclass houses, and the hon. Members who sit
on these Benches are of the opinion it would
be possible for people who would not come
in under that category to benefit by these
grants. It will be agreed that most of the
houses that are being built to-day are being
built for the purpose of sale. There would
be a fairly big tendency if subsidies are to
be given to houses that will cost more than
£500 for that state of affairs to continue, and
we think there would be a greater possibility
of houses being built to be let if the subsidy
was confined to houses that will cost £500
and under. That is the principal reason
why we are attempting to limit the amount
to £500. A question that will enter very
largely is whether we will succeed in
getting any working-class dwellings erected.
The previous arguments put forward were
that the subsidy would not influence the
position to a great extent. We hold that
is not the state of affairs at all. I do not
think it is necessary to labour this question
unduly. Our principal contention is that
subsidies should be granted to essential
working-class houses, and that the cost of
them should not exceed £500. For that
reason I beg to move this Amendment.

the
middle
middle and the lower

the houses they are living in at the moment.
or the lodgings they are in, would be given

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: The reason
We move this Amendment is to try to
ensure that houses will be built as cheaply
as possible. We are of opinion that
an excessive charge is being made for most
building materials at the present time. A
question on the Order Paper to-day indicates
that we are being charged in Belfast a rate

by 10s. a ton. So far as my information goes,
that increase is still retained on the price

The Government profess themselves to be
exceptionally keen on getting houses for the
people. I presume the Government also want
the houses let at an economic rent. If houses
are going to be let at economic rents in
the near future it will be necessary to get
houses built as cheaply as possible. We
have had frequent discussions here as
whether the bricklayers are laying enough
bricks a day or not. The attention of the
Government benches seemed to be concentrated on that aspect of the question. We
are not asking that the bricklayers here
should lay as few bricks as they can. We
suggest that hon. Members are wasting their
eloquence on a subject which they know absolutely nothing about. The hon. Member for
West Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn), whether he
wanted to do it or not, confessed his ignorance of the whole question. He does not attempt to differentiate as to the question of
laying bricks. We get a tremendous number
of general charges preferred without any attempt being made to let us know exactly
what hon. Members are speaking about. The
hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr. Gyle)
gave a fairly clear explanation as to the
laying of bricks, and pointed out that while
in one particular aspect of building you
may succeed in getting 1,000 bricks a day
laid in another aspect you would not probably succeed in getting more than from 200
to 250 laid. It would be much better if hon.
Members on the Government benches instead
of wasting the time of the House on a discussion of this kind would try and concentrate on the question of building material.
We have had many points of view put forward in the discussion, but we want to try
and ensure that it will be possible to have
some of the houses that are going to be built
let at economic rents. If an excessive
charge is going to be made for the houses
it will be extremely difficult to do that.
I do not want to go too closely into the
question, but I have a decent idea of the
amount at which a kitchen house can be
built. I have a clear idea also of the amount
a parlour house can be built for at the
present time, and I am of opinion that
notwithstanding the Government subsidy it
will be extremely difficult to let the houses
at economic rents unless the present excessive charges are going to be reduced in
some particular direction. It is all very
well for hon. Members on the Government
benches to laugh when a proposal of this
kind comes along. I take it that the Government are really serious in their attempt to
get houses for the members of the working
classes. If that is the object, and we are
wrong in suggesting that excessive charges
are being made for building materials, why
do we have discussion on the matter at all?
Why not give the Ministry of Home Affairs
these powers? I do not think it is necessary for me at this stage to say anything
further. I would like to hear the arguments
that hon. Members opposite have to offer
to this Amendment, if they attempt to adduce any arguments at all. My experience
in this House is that many Members of the
Government take the opportunity of remaining
silent rather than attempt to put forward
an argument. I believe Members on the
Government benches will have great difficulty in putting forward an argument as
to why this proposal should not be adopted,
because I believe it is reasonable in every
way. If the Government's intentions are
what they profess them to be there is absolutely no reason why this proposal should
not be accepted. Let us know exactly where
we stand in connection with the matter of
building materials. If you prove that no
excessive charge is being made that will discount any argument advanced up to the
moment. There are many reasons why the
Government should lend a ready ear to this
proposal that is being made now and to
accept and embody it in the Bill.

who knows SO much about conditions
governing the building of ships and shipowning it is a most important pronouncement. It should receive the careful attention
of everybody who is interested in our industrial life. Personally, I cannot agree
with it in many respects because, as my hon.
Friend has said, he seems to think that the
root of the trouble is due to the fact that
our local authorities are paying wages
higher than those which are paid in
ordinary industrial firms where there is
a very fierce not only national but international competition. I see by the speech
that he also refers to the wages which are
being paid on relief schemes by the Ministry
of Labour in Northern Ireland. As regards
the Corporation side of the problem, the
members of the Corporation are quite able
to deal with the matter from their own standpoint, but I may say that so far as I know
the Belfast Corporation are not paying
higher wages than are being paid in comparable cities in Great Britain.
As regards the relief schemes, I would
have thought they would have been looked
upon with more sympathy by the gentleman
who made the speech that has been referred
to, because, after all, it is very largely
shipyard unemployed men who are getting
work on these schemes. Although the
weekly wage for full time is specified
at 46s. week,
a
owing to the irregularity of the employment, due to weather
conditions and other causes, the actual wage
received by the workers each week is very
much less. Again, the persons who are employed on these schemes are very often
tradesmen, who never expected that they
would be driven by force of circumstances to
accept work of this kind.
I
If I may say so, I think Mr. Strahan, in
his remarks, was a little severe both on
Governments and on local authorities.
think he was especially severe on Governments, for he referred to the Imperial
Government as well as to this Government.
I think he might have remembered that both
Governments, by means of guaranteeing
loans to encourage the building of ships, are
doing everything they possibly can to further
the shipbuilding industry. The real causes
of the depression in the shipbuilding industry are three in number. The first is,
that our naval programme has been greatly
reduced in recent years. Second, reparations
were accepted in the form of ships from
Germany, and those ships were handed over
to some of the best clients of our Belfast
yards, who have never been able to order a
ship from our local yards since. That may
have been a right policy or a wrong policy,
it is not for me to say; but the fact is there,
and it has undoubtedly been one of the
causes of the depression in the shipbuilding
industry, by which we have suffered to such
a severe extent. Third, not only here in
Northern Ireland and in Great Britain, but
throughout the world, ordinary trade has
been depressed since the war, or shortly after
the war, and there has not been the flow of
trade between nations which there was in
pre-war days. The result of that is that so
many ships are not really required to carry
the traffic which is available, and thousands
of ships are lying in harbours at the present
time for which goods cannot be found. Those
are some of the causes that have brought the
slump into the shipbuilding industry, and
I think they should be known. Mr. Strahan
says matters should be dealt with perfectly
frankly and perfectly candidly. I think so,
too, and in these few remarks I have tried
to do so.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I am glad
that the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Grant) has brought this matter to the notice
of the House. As a Member of this Parliament and of one of the local bodies against
whom the charge has been brought of paying
very high wages, I am glad that the Minister
of Labour is in the House to-night. While
we know that 46s. is not a living wage, we
remember that that is the wage paid on the
relief works sanctioned by the Minister of
Labour. Belfast Corporation pay £2 8s. Od.
or £2 9s. Od., but they are not paying more
than the Bangor Urban Council, and I think
it is a very serious thing indeed for any man
holding a responsible position to bring a
charge against the Government of paying
more wages than they should be paying. My
opinion is this, that any man who brings a
charge of this nature should first of all know
what the cost of living is, and should get
at the people who are really responsible for
the high cost of living. Take a man with
five children.
Mr. SPEAKER: I was considering whether
I ought to rise or not. It is rather difficult
to say to what extent we are entitled to discuss in this House speeches of private
individuals outside. I let the matter go as
far as it has gone, because so far as it concerns any Government Department, or any
action they are taking, it is quite in order;
but I do not think it is for this House on
the Motion for the Adjournment to discuss in
an academic way speeches of private individuals outside.

Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: What I was
going to say was this, as a Member of this
Parliament, which is responsible for paying
£2 6s. Od. a week, I want to prove to outsiders
that the Government is not paying more
wages than it is entitled to pay. I am going
to illustrate what it takes to keep a home
for a married man with five of a family. No
people realise what it takes to keep a family
more than some of us in the Opposition. I
know that some of the hon. Members opposite
have other people to lay out their money for
them and to purchase the necessities of life.
I am speaking as one who knows exactly
what it takes to keep a home, not, Mr.
Speaker, that I keep the purse. (Laughter.)
Take the case of a married man with five
of family, and
a
assume that he is
a labourer in the employment of the Belfast
Corporation. Provided that he works 5 days
a week he received £2 10s. Od. Allow 6s. for
each child, 10s. for the mother, and 10s. for
the father. May I ask the gentleman who
made these charges if he could keep himself
on 10s. a week, or a child on 6s. a week? I
will not detain you any longer, because 1
know you would rather not listen to Members
getting up and making charges against people
who are not here to defend themselves. I
think, however, that gentlemen who make
speeches like this should come forward at
election time, stand as candidates for
Parliamentary honours, and try to remedy
the state of affairs that they think exists.
I believe the Government and the Corporation
are only paying a living wage.
Mr. BEATTIE: In reference to the matter
raised by the hon. Member for North Belfast,
I think I am justified in getting up to speak
in view of the statements I made in this
House some time ago. The statement made
by a person outside this House concerning
wages is not in conformity with the statement made by me in this House, and I would
appeal to that gentleman, whom I know personally, to refer in his remarks more to the
British financiers who enabled German shipbuilding to become a menace to British shipbuilding. In view of the menace of foreign
competition I would like to know is this
Government prepared to take over all available land in the Six Counties, and set it out
in plots for the unemployed, so that they
can get the necessaries of life a little cheaper
than they are doing at the present time. I
believe that at the present time our imports
of food stuffs alone are increasing rapidly.
While we should be producing the essentials
of life ourselves, we are going for them to
foreign countries and paying them. Instead
of a decrease in our imports there is an increase. If we cannot get work for the shipbuilding industry I think the Government
should see that the unemployed are placed on
all the available land to produce the
essentials of life for the working people of
the Six Counties.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I would feel
obliged if you would permit me to make one
observation. I would like to congratulate the
Minister of Labour
on the very excellent
statement he has made. 1 believe the
statement of the Minister of Labour
is the most sensible statement in
this connection that I have heard coming from the lips of a responsible
statesman for quite a considerable time.
People are very prone to attribute all our
commercial and industrial depression at the
moment to the wages that obtain in industry.
There is one aspect of this question that
would briefly like to direct attention to. As
a member of the Corporation I was forced
some time ago without the opportunity of
saying a word to listen to a deputation that
came there. One of the deputation was
from one of the largest shipbuilding firms
probably in the world. I was not able to
discuss the matter with the gentleman I
refer to. We were asked to accept the statement that the wages paid to the Corporation
and other workers in the transport trades
were responsible for the great depression
that has taken place in the shipbuilding industry.
There is one aspect of the question I would
fail in my duty if I did not call attention to,
That is the question of the ver-capitalisation
of industry. There is one particular
illustration I would like to give: I take the
firm of Harland and Wolff. During the war
they established a new yard, known as the
East Yard, and which was built out of money
which I believe should have gone to the
Government by way of excess profits. These
gentlemen are now complaining about the
overhead charges, and the point I want to
direct attention to is, that while their old
yard is lying idle they brought into being a
new yard whereby the overhead charges of
the firm were considerably increased. We
are asked now that the wages of the Corporation and other employees should be reduced
in order to facilitate these shipyards to get
orders. I believe that a large portion of the
blame can be attributed more to the way in
which these firms were managed or mismanaged during the war than any question
of the wages of the workers in sheltered
trades or any other industry. I am obliged
for the opportunity of making my point of
view clear so far as this particular matte:
is concerned.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I will answer both the hon. Member's questions together.
If he will refer to my
message to the electors of Northern Ireland
before the last General Election, he will find
that I then undertook that no further licensing Measure would be considered during the
lifetime of this Parliament, and no further
Amendment of the existing Act would be
entertained unless, after a fair and reasonable trial, the original intention of Parliament when it was placed upon the Statute
Book is not being faithfully fulfilled. In
accordance with this statement, therefore,
the Government will not introduce licensing
legislation unless it appears that the original
intentions of Parliament have not been
given effect to by the Act of 1923. I am not
aware that there is any ground for apprehension as to the rights of the licensees referred to being adequately secured. Should
the necessity arise, however, the Government will give the question the fullest
consideration.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am obliged to the
hon. Member for the opportunity which he

I have received a resolution from the
Urban District Council of Ballymena asking

I made to the effect "that the casting vote
of the Chairman had to be resorted to to
perpetrate this job."
If the House will permit me I would like
to make a somewhat detailed statement of
the facts of this case.
According to the Minutes of the Urban
District Council of the 2nd February, the
Council considered applications for the post
of Health Visitor and Maternity and Child
Welfare Nurse, and decided to refer the
matter to the Public Health Committee to
recommend a suitable applicant.
The Public Health Committee met on the
12th February, and according to the Minutes
which I have now been able to obtain, the
following decision was arrived at, and I
