SHORT TERM LOANS FOR FARMERS.
Mr. CRAWFORD (by private notice) asked
the Prime Minister whether arrangements
have yet been made for the issue of shortterm loans to farmers in necessitous circumstances, as foreshadowed in this House on
28th May.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Since the hon. Member for Tyrone
and Fermanagh first questioned the Government on this subject, we decided, in order to
ensure the earliest possible relief, to ask the
banks who operate in the Province to allow
the Government to utilise their machinery
for distributing the Government loans to
farmers, and I am glad to announce their
willingness to co-operate. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) These loans will be issued to
those farmers who have been so unfortunate
as to suffer loss of stock during the past inclement weather of winter and spring, and
are intended to be utilised for replacing such
stock. It is proposed that forms of application be stocked by the banks, and obtained
from them by applicants, and, after completion, sent by the applicants to the Ministry
of Agriculture. Should that Ministry approve
the loan, it will be issued through the bank
selected by the applicant in the form of a
bill discounted at 24 per cent. free of stamp
duty. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Α
further intimation will be published when
the forms are available.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: May I ask
the right hon. Gentleman are these loans to
be confined to farmers who have lost stock?
There are farmers who lost practically their
all in crops last season. Will these loans not
be available for men who lost their crops,
and so tide them over the present time?
Mr. POLLOCK: It will be a very difficult
matter to estimate the losses based upon the
facts to which my hon. Friend has drawn
attention. In the meantime it is not proposed by the Government that these loans
should extend to farmers under such conditions, but will be limited to those who have
suffered such severe losses as is well known
from death of stock such as sheep, cattle, &c.
Mr. CRAWFORD: May I ask my right
hon. Friend if those necessitous farmers who
require money to buy seeds would not be included in this scheme?
Mr. POLLOCK: The provision of such a
thing as referred to by my hon. Friend is
determined by the Ministry of Agriculture,
and this House has voted a certain amount
for this purpose. I am quite sure my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Archdale) who presides over
this Ministry, will take care of that department.
Mr. GYLE: Will these loans that are supposed to be for farmers be extended to any
person who has lost his all through the operation of the Intoxicating Liquor Act, 1923?
Mr. SPEAKER: That does not arise out of
the question.

in the said Amendment." This is really an

Act or the tenancy agreement, shall, where
if he has served notice claiming an increase

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move,

:

Mr. Kyle]
which has caused hon. Gentlemen opposite to
sit up and take notice. The unemployment
problem cannot be solved under the present
system of society. We have got to face the
fact that, whether we like it or not, a new
system of society is going to come, because
it seems to me that a quarter of the people
of this Province are not going to perpetuate
and put up with the insecurity which the
capitalist system has caused.
What is life for us? We start work at
thirteen years of age. We serve our times
as shipwrights or mechanics. After five or
six years we come out of our time and are
generally paid off, because no firm will employ
an apprentice who has served his time in that
firm. We go to work in the yard for a year
or two, and are more than likely paid off.
Then we come come back to the firm with
which we served our apprenticeship, or we
may walk the streets. During all the time
we are only in receipt of sufficient wages to
enable us to keep our homes. You have only
got to reckon it up yourselves. £2 11s 6d is
the wage of an engineer to-day. Town shops
pay £3 1s 6d I know, and the
wage is a
little better in other places, but that is the
sort of wage on which the working classes
have got to live. Ask yourselves what position you would be in if you were out of work
for three out of the twelve months in the
year. Taking it in that way we are in a
state of insecurity practically all the days of
our lives, and do not know what is going
to happen.
Do you mean to tell me that with your
Education Act in force in Northern Ireland,
remembering the education the working
classes have received since 1879, and considering the benefit we are getting under the
1923 Act-you believe that the working
people-any sort of people, whether working
people or not-are going to put up with a
system that compels so many of us to live
on the border-line of poverty and not know
when we are going to get security. It is
quite true that we have got Unemployment
Insurance, National Health Insurance, and
Old-Age Pensions, but these are merely little
reforms brought in to try to appease that
growing feeling amongst the bulk of
humanity that they want security.
I do not fear the words "Socialism,"
"Communism," and those other "isms."
All these "isms" do not matter at all. It is
security we want. We want the same
security as the upper classes have at the
present time. We want to feel that if we
are strong and willing and able to work
there should be work for us to do, or that if
the State and the private employers cannot
give us that work to do, we should not be
compelled to starve, to see our children
starving, to see our women go without
clothes. This is the sort of thing that is
happening in Belfast at the present moment
This is the thing we are up against, and
it is this growing feeling of discontent with
the present system which makes me say that
the day will come--it may not be in my day,
though I hope it will, but, whether it comes
in my day or in the lifetime of any hon.
Member here, it will come-when
this
system of society that keeps us down will be
abolished and we will have a cleaner system
of society; you can call it whatever system
you like.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 9th June, 1925.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
BALLYMONEY POLICE BARRACKS.-
LABOURERS' WAGES.
1. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Finance, whether, in view of the
fact that labourers employed at the police
barracks, Ballymoney, only receive 84d per
hour as against 9d per hour paid to all other
labourers employed at similar work in the
same town, the Minister will be prepared to
submit the matter to an independent person
to arbitrate upon.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollack: My information as to the rates of
wages paid in Ballymoney district does not
agree with the statement of the hon. Member,
and as I informed him, in reply to a previous
question, the Architect to whom the matter
was referred, as provided by the contract,
found that the contractor had reasonably
observed the Fair Wages Clause. This
finding is under Clause 27 (b) of the contract
final and binding upon the contractor and the
Ministry.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I would like to inquire, in view of the fact that the Minister of
Finance does not seem to have any definite
information regarding these rates of wages,
whether he is prepared to enter into negotiation with the trades' union officials who are
responsible for the settling of wages in Ballymoney and district?
Mr. POLLOCK: No, sir; but I may say
that at present we are considering the question of the revision of the form of contract,
with the object, amongst other things, of
providing for the appointment of an independent arbitrator in cases of this kind. I
hope that this will solve any problem of this
kind that will arise in future.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Can we have an undertaking from the Minister of Finance that
this will be one of the first things to be dealt
with as soon as this impartial person is
appointed?
Mr. POLLOCK: I cannot give any undertaking in regard to that. I think I have
answered the question fully, and I hope I
have satisfied the hon. Member.
SPEAKER'S HOUSE, STORMONT.
2. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Finance, whether it is a fact that
the carving work connected with the
Speaker's House, now being erected at Stormont, is being done in London, and, if so,
having regard to the number of unemployed
carvers in Northern Ireland, the Minister
will take steps to have the work done locally.
Mr. POLLOCK: As the honourable Member
is no doubt aware, this is a matter for the
Imperial Government. I understand that
the contract for the building has been given
to a local firm, but that some carving work
required is not being done locally owing to
difficulties connected with the supervision of
the work.
CHEAP LOANS TO FARMERS.
3. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Finance whether the Government
would reconsider the restrictions placed on
the cheap loans to farmers who have lost
stock, and whether he is aware that many
farmers who lost practically all their crops
last year are in urgent need of such assistance until another crop is taken out.
Mr. POLLOCK: I am aware that the bad
harvests of last year have resulted in a large
amount of distress in the agricultural community generally. But I must refer the hon.
Member to the Estimates for Agricultural
Services, where he will see that provision has
been made to supply seed at the cheapest
possible rates in certain necessitous areas,
payment being spread over a period of time.
In these circumstances the Government
cannot see its way to extend the new scheme
for making short term loans to include the
provision of seed.
Mr. G. HENDERSON: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the number of cases
that can be relieved by the amount voted
in the Estimate referred to will be very small
in proportion to the number of cases that
will need assistance, and, therefore, I ask if
the Government can see their way to extend
these short term loans?
Mr. POLLOCK: I think I can assure my
hon. Friend and the House that my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Agriculture, if
necessitous circumstances develop, will, in
addition to the Estimate passed, not disregard the cases as they arise. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Mr. KYLE: Will the Minister of Finance
recommend the Government to give the same
terms to business men who are in distress at
the present time?
Mr. POLLOCK: No, sir; I do not think
that is quite a relevant question.

EX-SERVICE MEN'S HOUSES, BALLY-
CLARE.
4. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he is aware that
seventy applications for ex-Service men's
houses were sent in by the Ballyclare branch;
that only two have been erected, and in view
of the acute shortage of houses in this district
will he approach the proper authorities in
order that more of these houses may be
allotted to this district.
Mr. POLLOCK: I understand that the
question of the allotment of the houses remaining to be erected is at present before the
Land Trust, and that careful consideration
is being given to the matter with the object
of ensuring the most equitable distribution of
the houses. I will see that my honourable
Friend's representations with regard to the
Ballyclare district are communicated to the
Trustees.

RURAL DISTRICT.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether the Ballymoney Rural District Council provisionally approved of a
scheme of labourers' cottages, which included
eighteen for the division of Enagh; whether
subsequently this number was reduced to
nine, and no account of the reduction appeared in the newspaper report of the proceedings of the meeting of Council at which
the reduction was made; whether the reporters present were asked to suppress this
information; whether an application has
been made to the Council for the names of
the applicants whose representations were
rejected and the cause of rejection; whether
the majority of the members of the Council
are unaware as to what constitutes eligibility
for a cottage under the Labourers Acts;
whether he would consider the propriety of
issuing an explanatory memorandum on the
subject, and whether he will give the information sought for, or ask the Council to give
it.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The Ministry of Home
Affairs has no right to interfere with the
discretion of the Council when the Council
is formulating a scheme under the Labourers
Acts. The functions of the Ministry only
arise when the scheme is submitted for confirmation. The scheme to which the hon.

me.
TEMPORARY TEACHERS OF SCHOOLS.
6. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he could state the number
of temporary teachers of national schools who
were in the service of the Commissioners of
National Education in Northern Ireland at
the date of the formation of the Northern
Ministry of Education; how many such
teachers are now employed by the Ministry;
whether it is proposed, when schools are
transferred or amalgamated, to take over
these temporary teachers, and if not,
whether compensation will be paid, and at
what rate.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): Excluding locum tenens teachers,
who are employed for periods not exceeding
three months, and substitutes employed for
teachers who are absent owing to illness or
for the purpose of attending training colleges,
the number of teachers in Northern Ireland
temporarily recognised at the date of the
transfer of the Educational Services to this
Ministry was 9, and is at present 15.
With regard to the position of such teachers
in the event of the transfer to Education
Authorities of the schools in which they are
employed, I would refer the honourable
Member to Section 14 (4) of the Education
Act.
As the teachers referred to are employed
in a temporary capacity, pending inquiry by
the Ministry into the necessity for the continuance of the schools in which they are
serving, they cannot be regarded as having
any valid claim for compensation in the event
of the schools in which they are employed
being amalgamated or closed.

TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Mr. W. McMullen
Mr. KYLE: We feel that the Government
are not realising their responsibilities to the
unemployed of Belfast and the Six Counties.
Unless the Government are prepared to take
more steps than it is apparently their intention of doing at the moment, the question
of unemployment will, before this House meets
again, reach such a state that it will be impossible to avoid serious trouble in Belfast
and the country at large. It seems to me to
be perfectly obvious that if the people of
Belfast begin to think that the Government,
who are responsible for the maintenance of
order and of everything that goes to make a
happy community, are not paying sufficient
attention to this question of unemployment,
there may be serious trouble in the city. We
are going to have an army of something like
50,000 unemployed, who will be walking about
the streets with nothing to do-all owing to
the Government's apparent inertia in this
matter. Unless the Government can give us
some assurance that they are going to extend
to the business people the assistance that they
are giving to the farming community in the
way of lending money on easy terms to
enable them to develop their businesses, we
will have a very serious state of affairs. The
working people are in a bad plight at present,
but their condition will be accentuated if the
Government have no intention of doing anything further than is proposed up to the
present. That is the reason I raise the question on the Adjournment.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.

Friend did not give me notice that he proposed to raise this important question to-day,
because if he had done so I could obviously

The position of hon. Members is that the
House is now going to adjourn, and we are
not even getting an undertaking from the
Government that, in the event of any representations or recommendations coming from
that conference, the House will be summoned.
That will lie in the judgment of right hon.
Gentlemen opposite, and I want to suggest
that they do not realize the seriousness of the
situation. One hon. Gentleman (Dr. Morrison) was talking about the French Revolution
the other day. The powers that were in existence then under-estimated the seriousness
of the situation that led up to the French
Revolution. I am rather inclined to think
that all Governments are largely shortsighted. Owing to lack of touch with the
people they do not understand their problems
or how the people are situated. It is not my
duty to advise the Government. Probably
in days to come as a result of the industrial
unrest our numbers may be increased, but we
are not studying it from that point of view
but from the point of view of the welfare of
the community.
I want to suggest that the Government are
belittling this whole question. They do not
seem to understand. They are trifling with
it, and are most hopelessly out of touch with
the people. The responsibility for that will
be yours, and I suggest that it is a serious
responsibility, but you do not seem to be
alive to the whole question. During the time
this House is adjourned numbers of people
will be disqualified because two years will
have elapsed since they have contributed
stamps. Before I came to this House to-day
I heard of the case of a man with a long industrial record- unfortunately for himself
he is not the most fit physically-whose son
has been disqualified because he has been
two years unemployed. Unless before the 4th
August next his father can get six stamps
and God knows how he is going to get themhe is going to be disqualified too, and there is
nothing for them but the workhouse. Yet
this House is going to adjourn until October
without knowing definitely what the Government are going to do. I have entered my protest, and that is the only thing I am concerned about. I suggest that the Government
are not handling this question in the way in
which it should be handled. It is a serious
question both for hon. Members on these
benches and on the Government benches, but
the responsibility for the whole thing will lie
upon the Government if they do not act
differently to what they are doing at the
moment.

satisfy my hon. Friend (Mr. G. Henderson)
that our Government will not relax their
interest in this Measure, and I am quite sure
that even if they did we have a sufficient
number of Members around us here who will
keep the Government informed from time to
time of any weaknesses that may arise.
In regard to the question of loans to farmers for the replacement of stock, may I
say that the Government have taken such
measures already as will ensure that there
will be no delay in providing any farmers
who are necessitous from that cause with the
means to purchase additional stock? A conference with bankers has already been held
and all details of the matter have been
settled so that without an hour's delay I
hope the circumstances in which so many
unfortunate farmers find themselves will be
to that extent relieved.
As to undertaking the work contemplated
by my hon. Friend (Mr. G. Henderson), that
is to say, either to lend money to or to
compensate farmers for loss of crops, I
wonder does he realize the character of such
an adventure. A picture arises in my mind
of all the farmers in the North of Ireland
who have unfortunately through weather conditions lost crops or had crops which were
bad or of poor character, and of all the grades
of trouble that would arise too terrible to
contemplate even if the financial considerations underlying it had not a very important
influence on the matter. Therefore, I can
hold out no hope at all that such an undertaking could be given by the Government or
that such an adventure could be undertaken
to discover all the losses sustained by poor
crops in the North of Ireland and to lend
money to or compensate farmers for their
losses.
I do not think that my hon. Friend gives
this Government credit for all they have
done in this matter. He refers to the condition of those farmers who have not bought
out since 1918, but let me remind him that
the condition of many of those farmers is
the result of either their own inertia
or their own indisposition or their own
hope that they would get better terms
Government Grants.
Belfast Corporation Loans.
9 JUNE 1925
than those who had voluntarily purchased their land. To some extent at
least the fault lies not with the landlords or
the Government but in a large measure with
the tenants themselves. I can only say
finally, if any repetition is necessary, that
the Government will take care there will be
no unnecessary delay in bringing the whole
terms of this Measure into operation, and I
hope that when we meet again in October
the hon. Member will be gracious enough to
stand up in his place and admit that the
Government, at any rate, has tried to do its
duty.
On the other subjects that have been raised
I do not propose to touch. My right hon.
Friend (Mr. Andrews) is quite able to deal
with all matters relating to Labour. I do
not think the hon. Members opposite who
have discussed this subject have dealt fairly
with the Government. They have not had
the graciousness to admit what the Government has done in regard to Labour. They
do not realise that there are 200,000 people
in this small Province who are dependent
upon the Government grants for their living.
There are 200,000 out of a population of a
million and a quarter. If that alone were
not proof of what the Government is attempting to do in this matter I think my hon.
Friends on the opposite side are very hard
to please. My right hon. Friend has dealt
exhaustively with the matter, and he has
given the assurance that the conference
which is being called will be a real conference, and if it is in a position to make certain
recommendations which will ameliorate the
condition of unemployment in this Province
the Government will go a long way to carry
them out, but obviously at this moment it
would be quite futile and impossible for them
to give any undertaking as to the methods
hat will be adopted, because whatever
methods are suggested must be practical
methods, and must be methods that are
within the resources of the Province.
Hon. Members opposite do not seem to
realise that all the money provided for this
work comes from the pockets of the people of
Northern Ireland. I cannot create money.
I am not an alchemist. I cannot transmute
crude metal into gold. I can only find the
money from the pockets of the people, and
there are limits to that. I think the Govel nment has gone even beyond the limits of the
rapabilities of the people of Northern Ireiand, and if it had not been for the success
of our arrangements with the Imperial
Government, and the fact that we secured
the adhesion of the Committee that was
charged with this business to the principles
we laid down, we should have been in a very
parlous condition in regard to our finances,
and we would have been quite unable to do
ven as much as we have done in respect of
these great matters which face us to-day. At
any rate I can give an assurance that the
Government is not indifferent or callous, as
some hon. Member opposite said, to these
great matters. They will have our constant
attention. Therefore, if any additional grave
circumstances arise that do call for the meeting of our Parliament at an earlier date than
that which is contemplated, there will be no
difficulty whatever in having Parliament
called together. I do not think I am going
beyond my powers when I say I may give the
assurance that if any conditions of an extraordinary character should arise the Government will have no hesitation in calling
Parliament together.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): The hon. Member opposite (Mr.
G. Henderson) spoke about the pork industry.
I can assure him that we are fully alive to
the necessity of keeping a careful eye upon
it. We have a Pig Breeders' Advisory Committee, and several times we have had meetings of the curers and feeders with a view
to stabilizing the pork industry. Anything
that we can do to stabilize it we will do.

are attending the Labour Exchanges day

DANGEROUS DRUGS BILL,
"to amend the Dangerous Drugs Act, 1920,
and the Dangerous Drugs and Poisons
(Amendment) Act (Northern Ireland), 1924, so
far as is necessary to assimilate the law in
Northern Ireland to the law in force in
Great Britain in relation to certain
dangerous drugs, and for purposes connected
therewith,” presented by the Minister of
Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates), supported
by the Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Home Affairs (Mr. Hanna) to
be read a Second time to-morrow, and to be
printed.
Mr. DEVLIN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman, on a point of order, what is the
meaning of introducing this Dangerous
Drugs Bill now. I understood from the notification which was given in the Press-the
only notification given to the Members of this
House that this House was to reassemble--
that it was distinctly stated that the business
of the House just now was to deal with one
precise and vital matter, and I want to know
why this Dangerous Drugs Bill is being introduced now.
The PRIME MINISTER: I think the hon.
Member is justified in calling attention to
the fact that when we asked you, Sir, to call
the House together it was for one specific
purpose, and one specific purpose only. But
since we did that we have received a
communication from the Imperial Government notifying us of the fact that at the
Geneva Conference arrangements were made
in connection with Dangerous Drugs that
necessitated them having legislation passed
through their House prior to the 30th
When they came
September of this year.
to look into the matter they discovered that
in order to comply with the international arrangements entered into at Geneva it was
necessary for Northern Ireland to pass a Bill
to bring into line its legislation with the
legislation passed in the Imperial Parliament. I understand, and I am sure hon.
Members who have the Bill in their hands
will see, that there is very little in the Bill;
but the British Government have requested
us to be kind enough to pass the measure so
that it may be on the Statute Book before
the 30th September, in order that they can
carry out the obligations imposed upon them
at Geneva. I am sure the House will desire
to meet the Imperial Government in this
matter, which does not make very much difference to the regulations in the existing
Bill.
Mr. DEVLIN: Has the British Parliament
passed legislation?
The PRIME MINISTER: Yes.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Senate Election.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That in the opinion of this House the
decision of the Returning Officer at the
recent election for the Senate not to count
the ballot papers which reached him after
the close of the poll should be reviewed,
because such papers, though posted in ample
time, were subjected to an unreasonable
delay; and in view of these special circumstances this House directs the Returning
Officer to undertake a recount of the votes,
such recount to include the ballot papers
which were not received in time."-(Mr.
McAllister).
Mr. MCALLISTER: Before I address myself to the facts of this case may I be allowed
to place on record my appreciation of the
impartiality, the conspicuous fairness, and
the unfailing courtesy which I have always
received from you, Mr. Speaker, since I
entered this House. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). But from your experience-and it is
a wide experience-as a public representative
you will recognise that public representatives on many occasions are called upon to
undertake irksome, troublesome and
pleasant duties. That is the position I am
in to-day, and you will further recognise, I
am quite sure, that in the discharge of a
public duty personal esteem and all other
concerns must be subordinated to the discharge of that duty.
un-
I was particularly struck on opening the
paper this morning to see a reply of yours
to a question by the right hon. Gentleman
the Prime Minister. You stated in reply to
him that the election for the Senate had been
carried through in a strictly legal manner and
in accordance with the regulations guiding
that election. May I illustrate the result of
that answer by drawing a parallel case?
Suppose that you, Sir, or the right hon. Gentleman were a candidate at an ordinary election
and the Presiding Officer at that election
closed the polling booths four hours before
the appointed time, with the result that you
each lost 300 votes and turned a certain victory into defeat, would you say that that
election had been carried through in a legal
and satisfactory manner, or in the way it
should be? The only difference I can see
between that case and the present is that to
all intents and purposes-side-track the
issue as you will, draw any red herring
across it, use all the subtleties of debate at
your command, the one fact remains, the
real fact--the poll was closed not four
hours but four days before the appointed
time.
Now may I refer to a short regulation
that is germane to this question? It says:
A Member of the House of Commons
shall vote by filling up his voting paper
in the manner directed by the Election of
Senators (Northern Ireland) Order, 1921,

Post Office at 7-30 on the Saturday evening.

I was greatly struck yesterday by the

bitterest opponents of the Government.

Unemployment Fund- 2 SEPTEMBER 1925
Resolved: "That in the opinion of this
House the recent election for the Senate was
carried out in strict accordance with the
Regulations laid down by Mr. Speaker, and
that any demand for a recount is, therefore,
under the circumstances unjustifiable."-
(The Prime Minister).
Jnemployment Fund (Money).
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That it is expedient to authorise a
charge upon the Consolidated Fund in
respect of any further sums required to be
advanced by the Ministry of Finance, not
exceeding in the whole £750,000, under
powers to be conferred by an Act of this
Session, for the purpose of discharging the
liabilities of the Unemployment Fund of
Northern Ireland."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): It is my duty to move this Resolution and I think it is expedient I should explain it as shortly as possible to the Committee. Hon. Members will recall that in the
month of March last-in the last Session of
Parliament-my right hon. Friend who sits
beside me (Mr. Barbour) presented a resolution of a similar character. That Resolution
was directed to making provision for advances to the Unemployment Insurance Fund
to enable it to carry along its functions in
respect of benefits conferred on those who are
insured. The amount of that Vote was
£750,000. Having regard to the figures of
unemployment it was calculated that that
grant of £750,000 would have been sufficient
to have carried the fund along until 1st
November next, but it is within the knowledge of hon. Members that the conditions of industry in the Province in the intervening period reached a deplorable state
of depression and, therefore, the numbers
registered as claimants on the unemployment fund were greatly increased. This is,
of course, very well understood not only by
hon. Members but by the community. In the
month of March, when the House gave the
necessary authority to advance an additional
£750,000 to the Fund, the figures of unemployment stood at an average figure of, roughly,
46,000 totally unemployed and about 10,000
on systematic short time. To-day, as nearly
as can be computed, the corresponding figures
are 56,000 wholly unemployed and 6,000
partially out of work.
It will thus be seen that our calculations
as to the sufficiency of the last Vote to carry
us on until the 1st November were
very
seriously disturbed. That is to say, our calculations were that the money so provided
would have carried the fund till the month
of November next, but as a fact the money
that was then provided is now practically exhausted, and in order that payment of benefits
to the beneficiaries may be continued it was
necessary that Mr. Speaker should be asked
to call this special meeting of Parliament in
order that the necessary amount be provided
to carry the Insurance Fund on for a further
period. It is now asked under this Resolution
that the Ministry of Finance should be
authorised to advance to the Unemployment
Insurance Fund a further sum of £750,000.
Should this amount be required, as seems
most likely, the total liability of the Unemployment Insurance Fund to the Exchequer
will amount to a sum of £4,250,000. It is
possible that I may be asked how long it is
expected that the sum of £750,000 will bridge
the gulf and carry on the fund in a state of
solvency, or, should I say, in a position to
make advances to the beneficiaries, but,
really, it is most difficult reliably to forecast
the length of time that this present authorisation will provide for.
The position as we see it to-day is very bad
from the industrial point of view, and it is
especially bad in one of our industries, as is
common knowledge, that is, the textile industry. It may be possible to predicate that
as things are perhaps at their worst any
change is likely to be for the better, and
therefore, this amount which is asked for today will carry on the fund for some very considerable time at any rate. Having dealt then
very shortly with the necessity and with the
amount to be provided, I may go on to say
that it will be within the knowledge of the
Committee that negotiations have been proceeding for a considerable period not alone
with the present Government in Great
Britain but also with former Governments
with a view to remedying the situation
created by the long continued period of aggravated unemployment. These negotiations,
in which the Prime Minister, my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Labour, and myself
have been engaged, have not yet reached a
final stage, but I hope before this House
rises in the Autumn to be in a position to
state that an arrangement has been reached.
The guiding principle of my colleagues and
myself is that exactly the same standard of
benefits granted in Great Britain should be
extended to those who are suffering in our
area from similar unavoidable privations by
reason of the continued adverse conditions of
industry. None of us can ever be satisfied
that the relations of the Province to the Imperial authority have been placed upon a
sound and permanent basis until the necessary adjustments have been made to enable
us to maintain our social standards at a level
fully comparable with that of the rest of the
United Kingdom.

Dangerous Drugs Bill.
[Mr. Pollock]
I think I should also at this point state
that the solution of several collateral
questions is dependent upon the result of our
negotiations in respect of the Unemployment
Insurance deficit. Such matters as the
Widows, Orphans and Old Age Contributory
Pensions Scheme, the removal of the thrift
disqualification clause from the present Old
Age Pension Act and the Entertainment Tax
are all being carefully considered, and the
Government hope before the end of the
present Parliamentary Session to be able to
introduce legislation to deal comprehensively with all these social problems. 1
beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: I would like to have had an
assurance from the Minister of Finance that
this sum of money for which he is asking today would be sufficient to see that the recipients of Unemployment Insurance will get
benefits at the same level as at present and
under the same conditions. These conditions
may seem to be foreign to Members of the
Committee, but I assure them they are of
vital and tremendous interest to the people
who are unemployed. We will have our say
to-morrow on the Second Reading of the Bill,
but I would like to have had some assurance
from the Minister of Finance that this sum
is sufficient to cope with the number which
he states have been unemployed and on short
time and to pay them according to the regulations which were in force prior to the
passing of the Amending Insurance Act on
the other side of the water.
Mr. POLLOCK: I could not give that assurance. I am quite sure my right hon. Friend
the Minister of Labour will give an assurance
that the benefits will be given on all fours
with those existing in Great Britain.
Possibly that is the position my right hon.
Friend intends to occupy. I hope that will
be a sufficient answer to my hon. Friend on
the other side.

Dangerous Drugs Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
That the Bill be now read a Second time.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): This Bill, which is mainly
of a technical character, is based on the
Imperial Act which was passed on the seventh
of last month. The Imperial Act applies to
Northern Ireland only to the extent that it
deals with matters with which our Parliament have no power to deal, that is, matters
affecting export and import. Therefore, it
is necessary in order that the law relating to
dangerous drugs should be the same on this
side of the Channel as on the other side that
the remaining provisions should be embodied
in this present Bill. I do not think it is
necessary for me to say anything as to the
necessity for the Drugs Act to be similar
both in Great Britain and this country. The
regulation of the trade has been the subject
of a convention at Geneva, and following the
decision arrived at the British Government
undertook to bring in an Act, and thereupon
requested this Government to bring in a
similar Act. The urgency of the case arises
from the fact that the British Government
undertook that the Act should be brought
in before the 30th September. The main
clauses of importance in the Bill are as follows: Under Clause I coca leaves and
Indian hemp are brought within the scope
of Part I of the Act of 1920, which deals with
raw material. Indian hemp has hitherto
been outside the scope of the Dangerous
Drugs Act, and although it is little used in
this country, it has been brought within the
Act at the request of the Egyptian Government. With regard to Clause 2, in future it
will be impossible to sell heroin and Indian
hemp without a prescription from a doctor.
Clause 3 contains an improved definition of
medicinal opium, and involves no substantial change. Clause 4 provides for a relaxation of the existing requirements in the case
of preparations containing the drugs which
may be reported by the Health Committee
of the League after inquiry not to be capable
of abuse. I beg to move.
Mr. T. W. McMULLAN: This Bill might
also be called a sample of hasty legislation.
Hon. Members of this House feel somewhat
rushed. I, perhaps as an interested party,
was only able to get a copy of the Bill
immediately before the House sat, and I
have been too much interested in the proceedings of the House to be able to give it
any close attention. I expect that our
Minister of Home Affairs has been somewhat
rushed over this matter also, but we had an
explanation from the Prime Minister
yesterday as to the reasons for this legislation, and that explanation to me is per-
2 SEPTEMBER 1925
Dangerous Drugs Bill.
Adjournment.

The
I have no doubt that if this legislation goes
through as it will some substitute can be
found for the extract of Indian hemp. The
merit of the extract is that it is very soothing to the patient. I should be very sorry
indeed if the hon. Members of this House
through any hasty legislation on their part
should subject themselves to trouble and discomfort in the future. I hope that it will not
be long until the chemists find some substitute
for extract of Indian hemp. I would
suggest that chemists generally hold stocks
of these Collodion Corn Cures, and it may
be necessary-I only suggest it to the
Minister of Home Affairs-to give some time
in which these stocks can be cleared away.
fectly satisfactory. I am glad to say I
can corroborate so far as my knowledge goes
what the Minister of Home Affairs has said,
that there has not been a good deal of abuse
of drugs in Northern Ireland, but we must
recognise that the drug habit is a terrible
and a growing evil elsewhere, and it is
right that it should be combatted.
question is how best to combat it? It is a
long time now since England went to war
in order to compel China to allow its subjects to dope themselves with opium. The
feeling of our people is greatly changed since
those days, and I think we are all unanimous
in feeling that we should do all we can to
help those countries which are more unfortunately placed than we are in connection
with this terrible drug habit.
We are going to make a law. The chemists
of the country who are law-abiding and
honourable men will do their best to carry
out that law and to carry out the regulations
formed under that law to the very best of
their ability, but I think that the real
trouble lies in wealthy syndicates and unscrupulous adventurers who are making
themselves rich by breaking the law as it
stands and who will continue to break the
law by every means in their power. I
believe there is no other way to stop this
traffic in drugs except by very stringent
punishment. I think nothing but the fear of
punishment will induce these men who are
fattening on this nefarious traffic to cease
tempting our young people to acquire this
drug habit. I think the habit has been
very largely increased by tempting young
people to try the effects of these narcotics.
As to the Clauses of the Bill, Indian hemp
is mentioned. It is very little known in this
country. I have the authority of a literary
gentleman who bases his opinion on a wellknown book, "The Count of Monte Christo,"
that the inhaling of the fumes of hashish
has a very delightful effect and the patient is
transported into the seventh Heaven of
delight. We know nothing of that, I am
glad to say here. I believe that in Egypt it
is very largely used. In our own prosaic
way we have ailments, and among the
ailments to which humanity is liable there is
one humble and troublesome one. It is not
necessarily fatal. I do not think it is ever
fatal, but those who suffer from it find it
very pressing in its attentions and very uncomfortable and irritating to the sufferer.
I refer to the humble and irritating corn.
I understand that extract of Indian hemp
is used in small quantities in corn cures-in
what is known as the Collodion Corn Cures.
Another point I notice is the reference to
heroin. Up to now a certain proportion of
heroin could be used without it being necessary to register, but under this new
regulation it will be necessary for every
medical prescription containing heroin,
which is largely prescribed for chest
troubles, to be registered with the chemists,
and it will also be necessary to have a fresh
doctor's prescription for each bottle. I can
see that would be of advantage to the
chemists financially, but it will not be
an advantage financially to the patient. The
chemists will be put to a considerable
amount of trouble, but the chemists will be
willing to put up with the extra trouble
in order to help the Government. Generally,
I think that Members of this House will
approve any effort to reduce the traffic in
dangerous drugs, and help our young people
especially to get away from this terrible
habit, which is undermining the health of
a great many people in other countries than
ours, and I suppose to some extent in our
own. I have great pleasure in supporting
the Second Reading of the Bill.

SHORT TERM LOANS.-LIVE STOCK.
1. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Agriculture if he can state the
number of loans applied for by farmers
under the scheme of Short Loans to replace
loss in stock and the amount of money lent
on these applications up to date?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): Applications under the scheme
of Short Term Loans for the replacement
of live stock have been received from 588
farmers. The total amount of the loans
granted up to the 2nd instant is £12,062.
Mr. G. HENDERSON: May I ask the
Minister of Agriculture whether the Government would not reconsider the question of
extending these short loans, say, for
another year, and of granting these loans
to farmers who are in difficulties from other
causes than the loss of stock?
Mr. ARCHDALE: The Government are
considering the question of extending these
loans, and anyone in very bad circumstances
will get a renewal for another year. As regards the other question, I would like notice
of it.

ROAD TRAFFIC ACCIDENTS.
4. Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether in view

due to motor, equestrian, and pedestrian

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Hanna): There is a Statutory Committee,
i.e. The Roads Advisory Committee for
Northern Ireland- appointed under Section

ing to increase the rents of the labourers'

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
IRON
ORE MINES, COUNTY ANTRIM.
11. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that his Department has set aside the recommendation
of the Ballymena Local Employment Committee to allow miners formerly employed at
the Iron Ore Mines, County Antrim, the advantage of being scheduled along with
workers in the engineering trade; whether
he is aware that some of these
men have
worked in the Iron Ore Mines for 40 years;
and whether he is prepared to issue instructions that these men should receive their
unemployment benefit.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr. Andrews): I am aware that a number of persons have obtained intermittent employment
in the Iron Ore Mines, of County Antrim,
for a considerable time, and unemployed
miners claiming benefit after they have exhausted their insurance contributions are
called upon to show that they have had insured employment in each of six weeks during the two years preceding the date of
claim.
The claims of 54 miners were considered
having regard to this consideration in
January, 1925, and only seven of the
claimants failed to satisfy the condition.
As a result of representations by the
Trade Union to which the seven men belonged the Ballymena Local Employment
Committee, in which area the men reside,
was asked by the Department to consider
whether there was any reason why this condition should not be applied, and reported
that in their opinion there was not.
On a subsequent occasion the Committee
expressed a contrary opinion on the grounds
that it was not reasonable in the circumstances to ask for proof of employment in
so many weeks as six in two years.
In my view the first thoughts of the Committee were correct, and I regret, therefore,
that the men are not entitled to benefit
until they satisfy the conditions.

Bill
of

now, let me just state

is to enable the payment of Unemployment Insurance benefits to be continued by
renewing the statutory powers of the
Ministry of Finance, which are now almost
exhausted, to continue advancing moneys to
the Fund. The amount by which the lending
powers are being increased is three-quarters
of a million, and it is confidently anticipated
that this sum will be sufficient to finance the
deficit on the Fund up to the end of the
current calendar year. Of course, hon.
Members will realise that it is difficult to
form any close estimate of the amount that
may be actually required, seeing that the
factors on which the calculation is made are
of so uncertain a character, depending as
they do on the amount of unemployment and
the conditions of trade and industry. I beg
to move.

regulations laid down by the Minister of

Mr. KYLE: If hon. Members of this House
tried to put themselves into the positions of
the unemployed people who are walking the
streets of Belfast and the streets of the other
towns of this Province I think they would be
amazed at the calm manner in which
many of their purported friends are prepared
to allow these regulations to be put into
force without ever seeing those regulations,
and without knowing what they were going
to mean. We have had a statement from
the Minister of Labour to-day that since
April last there have been from 200 to 300
persons turned down for unemployment
benefit, and that up to that date 2,371 had
been turned down. In addition there are
the few hundreds mentioned by the Minister
of Labour as having been turned down under
the new regulations introduced on the 1st
January last.
These regulations, which are introduced
now, or are in operation now, are a set of
the most mean and contemptible devices
that ever came from the brains of man.
They are born in ignorance of the position
of the working classes and are conceived
in contempt for their intelligence. Take the
shipyard workers. I am pleased that the
hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. Grant)
is present, because in the case I am going
to mention the gentleman followed the same
occupation as he did. He was a shipwright,
and was turned off three years ago because
there was no work in the yards. He turned
round on his unemployment benefit, because
he could not get work to do. Let any hon.
Member on the opposite side of the House,
or on this side, try to get into the shoes of
a man who goes to the shipyard, who goes
to the Queen's Road at half-past seven in
the morning to waylay the foreman, to
"touch" him, as we call it in the vernacular, for a job every morning of the week.
Because he cannot get evidence to prove that
he was looking for work he is turned down
from unemployment benefit, despite the fact
that it is a physical impossibility for a man
to get these things.
Take the case of the textile workers. How
many hon. Members opposite have ever been
unemployed, have ever known what it is to
go home after tramping the streets looking
for work? There may be one, but that is about
all. I am afraid that, unless you have had
that experience, and unless you have a great
deal more human kindness in you than you
have shown up to now, you will not be
able to appreciate the position. Human
kindness! If you only had the intelligence,
if you only had a heart to see the sufferings
of these people-60,000 of them in the North
of Ireland-not able to get food to eat,
unemployed. You have these extra 3,000 or
4,000 who are not signing the register, unable
to get work, and the Minister, in his wisdom,
in his cunning malignity, to deprive these
already starving people of their food, introduces the inquisition which the Labour
Government abolished-" What does your
father earn? What does your mother earn?
What do your sisters earn?" And according
to the family income it is to be determined
whether or not these people are going to
get Unemployment Benefit. Did ever anybody hear of such a scandalous procedure? A
man or boy who has worked in a mill, in
a factory, in the shipyard, or in an engineering shop is to be asked what does his father
earn, what does his mother earn, what do
his sisters earn when half of them are
working in a factory. Surely these things
have only got to be stated for hon. Members
to realise that the people of this Province
more independently-minded than that
they are going to tolerate such a state of
affairs.

The day before yesterday, or on Monday

the Irish Spinners' Association employing

We want also to see if the Government
would inquire as to the effect of assisting the
linen trade at the present time-what effect
it would have on the trade itself. Would it
help? Would it not be better if this money
which is being spent in unemployment

paying wages of people who were producing

not know whether any of the Members on
this side of the House are stick-in-the-mud
free traders or tariff reformers. Certainly
so far as we are concerned we are not. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) We want to do anything that can be done no matter by what
name you call it, which will get our people
back to work and restore their moral. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) We want to try to
get these people back to healthy work, work
under decent conditions, so that they can
bring up their children in a way that you
and I as citizens of the Six Counties may not
be ashamed of them. We want this and you
want it. Therefore we want an inquiry as
to the effect of a subvention or subsidy or
whatever you like to call it in aid of one of
our staple trades-whether it would not be
better to assist the manufacturers, to assist
the spinners, to pay the level I have
mentioned, and to get these people restored
to work. I think it would be better in the
end. How many millions have the British
Government and have our Government expended in this way in regard to the payment
of unemployment benefit?
One thinks that if sufficient interest were
taken in the industrial situation, if
sufficient attention were paid to trade
unionists and capitalists that surely
something could be devised that would
assist the situation. We all know of
course that the introduction of the gold
standard a few weeks ago made exports 10
per cent. dearer in foreign countries. That
has crippled the linen industry. It is crippling our export trade and yet we sit idly by
and allow these things to be done simply to
spite some other country. We think that
much might be done, and whether it can be
done or not we believe that it is the first
duty of the Government of the Province to
see that the people are fed and clothed and
housed. You can call that Socialism; you can

horse sense. It should be the first duty of
our Government to see that these people are
fed and clothed and housed. Instead of recognising that to be their first duty they
introduce these regulations simply because
they are brought in in England. Simply
because they are brought in in London they
introduce these regulations here which are
going to penalise, going to make it more
difficult for a huge number of their colleagues, their mates, members of the same
lodges as they are, and they are doing that
or they get it done by getting the Duke to
put them in Order in Council. They
have not the courage; they have not the
decency, they have not the honesty to put
them on the Table. They do not want their
friends in the city to realise how they are
duped.

Why is this condition imposed at all? I
would remind the House that this is an insurance fund. It is only for the purpose of
ensuring that those who get benefit are insured persons. If I had the power and the
means to give compassionate grants to all
our unemployed I would be quite pleased
personally, but this House has never given
me that power, and it would be wrong of this
House to give me that power from this fund.
I pass from that to the other condition to
which my hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle) has referred, and that is called the family income
test. This is not a new condition; it is only
re-imposing an old condition. And what does
it really mean? It does not apply to covenanted or standard benefit. When a claimant
has exhausted all the benefit that his stamp
contributions entitle him to and when he
goes along and says "I want what is really
an overdraft" certain inquiries are made as
to his position, just in the same way as if
hon. Members or if I go to a bank and ask
for an overdraft. Bankers do not give us
overdrafts until they inquire into our position and see if there is a possibility of our
being able to pay the debt which we incur.
I do not think personally it is unreasonable
when a claimant has exhausted the benefit
to which his stamps entitle him that an
inquiry should be made to see if the
family can support that member without imposing hardship upon the household (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
In other words, is it unreasonable to think
that if the head of the household, the
husband, is earning a substantial sum he
should support his wife who happens to be
unemployed? Is it an unreasonable thing if
the father is earning and the mother is perhaps earning also a reasonable sum that
they should supply maintenance for their
own child? I do not think so.
And remember this. It is my duty to see
that the fund is conserved for those who
need it most. My hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle)

doing.

Unemployment Fund Bill- 3 SEPTEMBER 1925

This is not a question of voting, or argument, or anything of the sort. It is simply
a Money Bill to provide money for the people
of Northern Ireland who are unemployed to
prevent them from starving. It is the direct
opposite to what hon. Members opposite say
it is. We are really voting to save the people
from starvation, and I can only say that
when the time does arrive I shall have no
hesitation in going into the Lobby and voting
to prevent the people of Northern Ireland
from being starved.

dole. I was looking into some figures the

find that all the money paid out of the
Unemployment Fund-this is a thing I would
like the public to remember, because I hear

thing called the Treasury, and lifting money

weeks ended June 27, this year, 39 per cent.
was contributed by the employers, 35 per
cent. by the workers, and 25 per cent. by the

Mr. BLACK: One concrete suggestion has
come from hon. Members opposite. It was
that men should be put back upon the land.
The suggestion was put forward in a double
phase as I understood. First that men
should be put back upon the land in Ulster,
secondly that men should be brought from
Ulster and put on the land in the colonies.
Now with regard to Ulster what opportunity
is there for men to make their living on the
land in Ulster at the present time? I think
the whole cry of those men who represent
Ulster agricultural communities is that
there is no possible living for men in the
country now. The country needs to be
helped. The country needs more assistance
than the city does. Would it be any solution
to take the people out of the city and put
them in the country where there is no more
work apparently than there is in the city?
The second suggestion is to take men to the
Colonies. That is a surprising suggestion in
view of the attitude taken up by the Labour
Party in some of the Colonies. We read that
the Labour Mayor of Sydney has set
his face strongly against allowing any immigration in Australia. Here you have the
Labour Party saying send men to the
Colonies and there you have the Labour
Party saying they will not admit them. How
is that going to be a solution?
To-day the one result of the debate' seems
to be to add nothing whatever, I submit, by
way of concrete or helpful suggestion to
assist the Government in the measures they
have already taken. They have not solved
the problem, but they have done something,
and if there is anything more that can be
done it is the duty of every Member of the

whether the Members of this House sit on

person has any concrete suggestion to make to
supplement what has been done by the
Government it is his duty to make that
suggestion, and I am sure the Minister of
Labour will gladly welcome any practical
suggestion that is made in view of the
terrible condition-

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: We
been treated to a rather happy speech in
some respects by the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) in very unhappy
circumstances, because we all recognise the
very unhappy circumstances we are met to
discuss here to-day, that is the great
difficulty of providing a real and
efficient remedy for our unemployment.
I think the speech by the hon.
Member for West Belfast will help
operation between people in the Six County
area who differ in religion and politics with
regard to a solution for these very intricate
and difficult matters. I just got to my feet
for a minute or two to say that it should be
the first and foremost duty of the Government of Northern Ireland to do all that is
possible to encourage and develop our basic
industry, that is agriculture. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I do not know that I am
entirely enamoured of a slavish following of
everything that is done in England, either
in legislation or in administration, becanse
conditions in Northern Ireland are somewhat different from the conditions in
England.
the
England is largely an industrial country,
we are largely an agricultural country.
Therefore, I feel it might not be a safe policy
for the Government of this country to be
tied in every respect to following slavishly
legislation and administration in
England. The Government's first duty
should be in every way to encourage and develop the agricultural industry. I say that
for many reasons. One reason that would
be sufficient is that a people rooted in the
soil and contented in the soil makes the
most stable community and makes for stability in Government. Up to the present time
the Government, in my opinion, have not encouraged that industry as much as they might
have done. They have approved of an Act
to complete land purchase in Ulster which
puts the unbought tenants of the Six
Counties at a great disadvantage as compared
with the men in the Twenty-six Counties.
They have approved of an Act which was
passed without discussion and which gives
the tenants of this area a reduction of only
about 3s 6d as compared with a reduction
of about 7s.
I see the Government of the Free State
have appointed a conference to deal with
grain prices, and while it is not law they
have recommended, in order to encourage the
agricultural industry,
Short term loans for farmers,
Reduce railway freights for Irishgrown
farm produce,
Subsidy for tillage farming,
No income-tax where 25 per cent. of
holding is cultivated.
Import duty on imported malting barley,
and fixed minimum prices on barley for
malting or brewing, and
Tariffs on foreign flour and foreign oats.
I have not the figures before me at the present time, but I think the statistics recently
published by the Department of Agriculture
should give us cause to think owing to the
amount of the reduction in tillage there has
been in the Six-County area. I do think the
Government should have some policy to encourage tillage farming in this country, and
that the encouraging of farming and the
keeping of people on the land as far as
possible will to some extent help eventually
to solve the unemployment problem.
In connection with the Northern Ireland
Land Act it is a pity there was not a sum

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr. Gordon):
I do not know that I would have intervened
in the discussion had not an invitation been
issued to me by the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin). He suggested that if
the Minister of Labour spoke at that particular time the “luminary” sitting beside him
would probably reply to any of the arguments
put forward by Members of the House. There
are only two points I would like to refer to,
for no arguments have been advanced by any
of the Members on the Opposition Benches.
The whole argument of my hon. Friend, the
junior Member for West Belfast (Mr.
William McMullen) was that the Government
was tinkering with unemployment. The
senior Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin)
also expressed himself in similar language—
that to some extent we were tinkering with
the problem of unemployment.
A conference was formed some time ago and
representatives of all the Trades Unions and
representatives from this House were invited
to attend that conference. Some important
proposals were put forward by the Member
for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin), but I want to
tell this House that unemployment is not a
local or a national question. It is an international question, and until the wheels of industry begin to revolve throughout the whole
world it is absolutely impossible that the
problem can be settled in any particular
centre or in any particular part of the
country.
The hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Kyle) made one or two suggestions. One was
that the school age should be raised, and
another was that money should be taken from
the Insurance Fund for the purpose of assisting industry. It is such a debatable point
that I think it would be unfair to weary the
House by examining the proposal to take the
contributions of the workers, the contributions of the employers, and the contributions
of the State for the purpose of subsidising
any particular industry. I now come to the
two points I want particularly to refer to.
The first is that the Bill which has been
brought before the House to-day is a Money
Bill for the express purpose of finding money
to continue to pay to unemployed persons
their unemployment insurance. If the Opposition refuses to agree to the Second Reading, and in the event of the Government
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Unemployment Fund Bill—
Second Reading.
[Mr. Gordon]
being out-voted, the result would be that the
Opposition in their professed endeavour to
better the conditions of the unemployed,
would really be doing considerable injury to
the unemployed.

Mr. GORDON: I will come now to the
second point to which I desire to draw the
attention of the House. Members of the
Labour Party have suggested that the regulations that have been adopted should be
abolished and that we should go on as at
present. I would like to tell the House what
the result would be if the conditions in force
at present were allowed to continue. When
the recent Bill was introduced in the Imperial House of Commons the Minister of
Labour was given power to waive until the 1st
October or 3rd October, 1925, and he accordingly made Regulations that were much
easier for the unemployed than the 30 contributions over a period of two years provided
for in the Bill. If we allow the latter condition to operate, instead of an unemployed
person having to show eight contributions
a period of two years he will be
required to show 30 contributions over the
same period. Therefore the House will see
that the Regulations we are making are infinitely better than the conditions originally
inserted in the Bill that was passed by the
Party represented by hon. Members opposite.
It is all very well to suggest that the
Government should resign. Let me tell hon.
Members opposite that on another occasion it
was suggested that a Government should resign and it did so. Prior to the resignation
of that Government certain Members of the
Opposition said they were in a position to
solve the great problem with which the
country was faced, the problem of unemployment, and one Member of that Opposition
had issued a booklet of 41 pages showing how
his particular Party could solve that problem when they came into power. That Party
came into office and subsequently an important Member of the Cabinet, when he was
questioned in the House of Commons regarding the matter, said that any Government
that remained in power and allowed its
people to live on the Insurance Fund should
be scouted out of office. His Party was afterwards scouted out of office.
It is easy for the Opposition to ask what
the Government has done, what it is doing,
and what it is going to do. Several Members
of the Opposition are members of the Conference that has been called for the purpose
of probing deep down to the root of the problem and they have put forward no proposals
that the Government could act upon or that
would have been of service to the unemployed
who to-day are marching about the country.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: On a point of
order, would the hon. Member inform the

The public would then see that several suggestions were made. They were not solutions
of the problem, but they were palliatives.

I would like to deal with the complaint
made by the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin). I regret the incident he refers
to and I will investigate it if he will give me
some details. The hon. Member may rest assured that as long as the present Minister is
connected with the Ministry of Labour, and
as long as I am associated with it, the
interests of the working classes will be looked
after and they will suffer no disability so far
as we are concerned. One of the reasons why
these incidents arise is this. We invite
people to come to the Amelia Street Exchange
at certain times. We invite a batch at 10
o'clock, another batch at 11 o'clock, another
at 12 o'clock, another at 2 o'clock, and another
at 3 o'clock for the purpose of paying them.
Very often an applicant we invite to come at
12 o'clock comes at 10 o'clock, another person
who is invited to be there at 2 o'clock arrives
at 12 o'clock, and so on, and then they have
to stand in a queue.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is there any method by
which these women can be housed or sit in a
room and not made to stand in a queue during the winter months?
Mr. GORDON: There is a room provided,
and that is the reason we ask them to come
in batches so that we can accommodate the
number we invite to be there at a particular
hour. Very often a person comes out of his
or her turn and they remain standing outside
for a period of two hours. When we have
completed the new Labour Exchange which is
being erected at a cost of £50,000 we hope that
the conditions which at present exist will be
done away with.

they have been at the shipyard.

got a letter?" "No." "Go back and get

SHORT LOANS TO FARMERS.
3. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Agriculture if the Government
would reconsider the scheme of short loans
to farmers, with a view to further extending
the duration of the loans, and also of making
them available for all farmers in financial
difficulties, owing to the bad season through
which the industry has passed?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In the absence of my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Archdale) I propose to reply to
this Question.
As already announced the period for the
repayment of all short term loans for the
replacement of live stock losses has been
extended to 31st December, 1926. At present
the Government is not prepared to consider
a further extension of the duration of these
loans.
The suggestion that these loans should be
made available for all farmers in financial
difficulties, other than those arising from
the loss of live stock, would, if conceded,
open the door to claims of all kinds on the
Government, and is not one that could be
entertained.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: In view of
this unsatisfactory answer I will raise this
matter on the adjournment.

THE BOUNDARY.
Motion made and Question proposed: ""That

Mr. KYLE: I put down a question on the
Paper to-day so that the Prime Minister
might make a statement with regard to the
position of the Government in regard to this
very important question, and what steps he
proposes to take if and when the Boundary
Commission reports. I think it is the Prime
Minister's duty, or rather I thought it was
the Prime Minister's duty to inform public
opinion in the Six Counties as to what steps
he was prepared to take in certain
eventualities, and I do think that it is a
public service to allay the feelings of the
people regarding this very important
question, because it has been stated in the
Press that conversations are contemplated
between Mr. Cosgrave and the Prime
Minister. I think, therefore, that the
House and the country should know what
position the Government are prepared to
take up, and they also should know something of the state of mind of the people in
regard to this all-important question.
As far as Labour is concerned, we desire
to make our position quite clear. Housing,
wages, unemployment insurance, national
health insurance, old-age pensions, education, these are the important things to us.
As far as Labour is concerned we are not
going to agree to any worsening of our
position in regard to these all-important
matters, governing as they do the lives and
well-being of the great body of the working
people.
We believe also that there is common
ground for agreement between North and
South in, for example, the administration of
railways, in, for example, a common policy
regarding agriculture, and we respectfully
suggest to the Government that in any conversations the position of Labour, the
position of the working people, should not be
overlooked, and that bodies might be
created-you can call them by whatever name
you like to discuss common action in regard
to agriculture, fisheries; and there is one
other verv important thing amongst the
etceteras, and that is reciprocal labour
arrangements. The Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews) knows how hard it is on the people
who live, for example, in Belleek, and who,
because they live in the Free State while
they work in Northern Ireland, if they
happen to be unemployed-as there are some
of them unemployed to-day--are not entitled
to benefit from the Free State because they
work in Northern Ireland and their cards
are stamped in Northern Ireland. Surely it
should not be outside the wit of man to devise a reciprocal arrangement of some sort so
that the common people at least should not
be penalised.
This matter of the Boundary, so far as I
am concerned, is not a matter of very much
importance in comparison with the things I
have mentioned. We recognise, of course,
the position the Government are in, and,
therefore I think it is as little as we can
expect to hear the considered opinion of the
Prime Minister on
He
this question.
knows, and we all know, how much the
people of Belfast and of the Six Counties
value his opinion, value his considered judgment, and that being the case, it is not in
my opinion good enough merely to say that
he has nothing to state. In affairs of
Government it seems to me that there must
of necessity be a good deal of negotiation, a
good deal of arrangement, and I think it is
our duty here to get the Government to state
their position to the country.
I would also like to say that no good at all
can be done by arousing passion either in
North or South. It does not pay, to put it
in a very crude way, either for the North or
South to rouse bad feeling. We have had
here in the North some little trouble, very
great trouble. In the South there has been
tremendous trouble also with destruction of
property and loss of life. Nothing can be
gained by doing anything to arouse once
more those passions which, when aroused,
speedily become masters of the situation, no
matter where they may be. Trouble, either
civil or any other sort, has never served any
useful purpose so far as the country is concerned. It is much too costly. It dislocates
trade. We are now in the aftermath of the
huge world war which means that there is
tremendous unemployment in our land and
a tremendous number of people who are
suffering, so that so far as arousing bad
feeling is concerned or doing anything that
may precipitate trouble in our own land is
concerned, we should all be very careful and
do everything we can to allay bad feeling
and promote good feeling.
Ministers sitting opposite have wished
Ministers in the South well, and Ministers

Government in this matter, then it should

Mr. DEVLIN: I would be the very last to
stand here as a defender of the Boundary
Commission, but I think the right hon.
Gentleman is wrong in his assumption that
the responsibility rests with the Boundary
Commission. The final responsibility must
be borne by those who first assumed responsibility, that is the British Government.
The British Government appointed this
Boundary Commission. We have had no
responsibility for it. It was part of the
Treaty arrived at between Southern Ireland
and the British Government, and the British
Government naturally will take up the
decision that may be come to-at least, I
would expect so if they are men of honour,
which they are not always, which they very
rarely are. That is my experience of them
in dealing with Irish public affairs. But if
they are faithful to their responsibility they
will, of course, assume full power and full
responsibility for anything the Boundary
Commission does. Therefore, the right hon.
Gentleman is not altogether right in placing
the whole responsibility upon the shoulders
of the Boundary Commission.
I would like to say as far as I am concerned that I too regret the raising of this
question at the moment, because until the
Boundary Commission reports, I think it is
highly desirable that all of us who have any
love for our native land and any desire to
avoid the opening up of the old passions and
bitterness which brought such a curse on the
community North and South ought not to
encourage or foster had feeling, especially
in Ulster. For a responsible statesman like
the Minister of Labour, for whom I have
very high respect, to go out as he did in
recent weeks and make wild and inflammatory speeches is a very serious thing. I
think the holding of these heated meetings
in this somewhat warm atmosphere is
altogether unjustifiable. I could not trust
myself to make speeches during the last few
months, and, therefore, I have remained
silent. When speeches are made on public
platforms to audiences easily aroused and
amongst whom it is easy to create and foster
bitter passion, the fewer of these meetings
that are held the better.
I really do not know what the fighting
speeches of the right hon. Gentleman mean.
There is no one who wants to fight
hon.
the right
Gentleman. The Fron
