HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Devlin]
State Government and their representatives have all stated that they will
accept the report of the Boundary
Commission. The Boundary Commission is
the creation of the British Government.
Therefore, if you refuse to accept the judgment of the Boundary Commission, it will
not be the Free State you will have to fight,
but the British Government, and I wonder
that sane and sensible men would encourage
a spirit among their own people that they
would have to face a situation in which
the battalions of Ulster would be organised
against the battalions of the British Empire.
I have also to say that I recently noticed
a speech of a prominent member of the
Ulster Party, Mr. Charles Craig, in which
he suggested a conference. I am quite sure
that Mr. Charles Craig, freed from the
passions of Ulster, was very anxious to see
something done to promote peace, but no
sooner had he made that speech than out
on the ramparts rushed the Attorney-General,
the custodian in Ulster of law and order,
and the man who would be called upon if
any trouble arose to take criminal proceedings against revolutionaries in revolt
against Britain. It is a most unwise thing
for any man in his position to repudiate the
peaceful postulate of the Prime Minister's
brother, because I take it that is what was
in the mind of Mr. Charles Craig when he
made the speech suggesting some method by
which peace could be obtained. That speech
was repudiated not by some serious politician
or responsible statesman but by the Attorney-
General, who is more noted for the
enthusiasm of his own unthought oratory
than for the cold, decisive, legal methods
by which he should elucidate dangerous
points of law.
In my opinion if there are to be negotiations-the right hon. Gentleman (The Prime
Minister) says there are none, and that he
has heard of none-I would say this, let
them be negotiations along the lines of Irish
unity. I am not laying down any policy
by which that unity should be brought about,
but I suggest it should be along the
lines of Irish unity, and that these negotiations should suggest not a further subdivision of the country or a narrowing of
areas, but rather the bringing closer and
closer together, by whatever process judg
ment and patriotism can suggest, of the
people of Ulster and the people of the South
of Ireland. This is a very small island. It
is face to face both North and South economically and industrially with very serious
difficulties, and it strikes me that instead
of cold and rigid views expressed in inflammatory form upon the platforms we should
have men on both sides prepared to make
sacrifices for the ultimate unity which is
bound to come; I do not say by one Parliament, because the Treaty laid down that
two Parliaments would be perfectly acceptable to the South of Ireland.
It is not for me to suggest the methods
by which unity can be brought about. I
have never been consulted either by North
or South in regard to these matters. I am
only giving my opinion as an Irish citizen
and as one living here in Ulster and to some
extent responsible for a section of the population who have been rather neglected by
one side and rather badly treated by the
other. So far as I can speak for them their
one hope and desire is to live in peace-(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-and in a spirit of
amity with their fellow citizens. They hate
blood and outrage, and passion and hatred,
and all the things that have done so much to
disfigure this Northern Province and to
create bad feeling all over the country. We
are anxious that peace should be promoted
in whatever way it can be promoted.
In my judgment the man or men who think
that now or at any time you are going to
adjust these difficulties or that you are going
to destroy these evils by bloodshed were
never more mistaken in their lives. The
people will not have it. The people are sick
of it, both North and South. Not only are
the people North and South sick of bloodshed, but the world is sick of war. Look at
the tremendous tangle of the European
situation to-day. Look at the labour and
thought that are being given to try to disentangle things and to create peace in Europe
upon the foundation on which alone there
can be contentment and commercial power
and a renewal of industrial activities. I
care not whether they live in the North
or in the South, the man or men who try
to solve this problem in any other way than
by wisdom and by mutual sacrifice will be
regarded as a danger to Ireland and a
danger to the peace of the whole nation.
SHORT LOANS TO FARMERS.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: In raising
the question of short loans to farmers, I
want to do so in no controversial spirit. I
do so in the hope that the Government may
be induced to extend the scope of these loans
and to relax somewhat the conditions so that
needy farmers may have the opportunity of
taking advantage of the loans inaugurated
by the Government. When the conditions
attaching to these loans were first published,
I think they were such that they were of
very little use to our farmers, and the fact
that 588 farmers in the Six County area have
applied for them under these conditions is
an index of the financial state in which
farmers find themselves. When the con-

to 1926. I am sure we are all most thankful

more than £12,000 to farmers. It was said
by one of the hon. Members representing
division in Belfast that the country
needed more help from the towns than the
towns needed from the country. I am impressed with the fact that whatever the
country needed the country has not got it.
Up to the present time the only grant that
farming has got is the £128,000 in relief of
agricultural rates. If I am rightly informed
that grant is given as an equivalent to the
grant given to relieve agricultural rates in
England, and that grant is deducted from
our Imperial contribution. I speak subject
to correction by the Minister of Finance, but
my opinion is that this grant is deducted
from our Imperial contribution, and, therefore, directly is not a charge on the taxpayers
of Northern Ireland. Even supposing leans
were applied for up to half a million pounds on
behalf of farmers-and I can conceive loans
to that extent being applied for at the present time by the farmers in the Six County
area-that would be a great boon to the
agricultural community. The Government
could borrow the money at 4 per cent, and
it would only mean a burden of about £10,000
on the ratepayers of Northern Ireland.
It may be said that it is not consistent
for me to advocate a further burden on the
ratepayers of Northern Ireland, inasmuch as I
have been talking about economy. The Government have again and again said that agriculture is the premier industry of the Province, and I want a fair share of the money
expended. A loan of four million pounds
was given to shipbuilders, and three million
pounds to relief schemes-that is seven
million pounds granted by the Government,
largely for the benefit of the industrial
classes. I do not object to that, but I do
say that if the Government want the scheme
of short loans to be a real benefit to farmers
they ought to make them available for needy
farmers. If any Member of the House looks
at the conditions governing these loans he
will find that before a farmer gets the loan he
has to disclose his full financial position. He
has to disclose the amount of his rent and
everything else. I quote that as proving
that the farmers who are in need and in
straitened circumstanes have no chance of
getting the loans.
I would urge upon the Government these
two points, first, the extension of these short
loans to December, 1927, and secondly, widening the scope of loans, so that all farmers
who are in financial straits will be eligible
for them. I think we want to encourage
tillage farming. I do not know whether it
would be in order at this point or not, but
I claim the urgency and importance of the
question as the excuse for mentioning it. I
think the Government ought to institute some
scheme to encourage tillage farming in this

UNEMPLOYMENT.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I believe
that the subject introduced to-day is a very
serious matter for the people of Ulster who
have returned us to this Parliament. We met
here during the past week, and to my mind
very little has been done to try to assist
the unemployed in Ulster at the present
time. I hope that during the time this
House stands adjourned the responsible
Ministers of this Government will sit down
and have a conference and see if something
cannot be done that will receive the support
not only of Members opposite but of the
Members of the Opposition. The people
to-day are in a state of starvation. We
meet them every day of the week. Men
who are getting no unemployment money,
have three and four little children
to keep. They and their wives and
children are starving to-day. To my
mind the Government have not grappled
with this matter in the way they ought. It
is a very important question, and if something is not done I believe serious consequences may arise in Ulster. We may have
trouble about the Boundary, but there is a
greater trouble than that if you raise bother
with the starving men and women of Ulster.
That is what is likely to happen if something is not done.
I suggest to hon. Members opposite that
they take a run in a motor-car round the
different roads throughout the length and
breadth of Ulster, and they will find room
for great improvement. Everyone of us
wants to see Ulster one of the brightest
spots in the world. I hope and trust they
will start and try to make it a
bright spot by seeing that the roads
on which there is such heavy traffic are
properly constructed. They are a disgrace
to Ulster at the present time. It would give
employment to thousands of men and take
many off the dole which they are now receiving. I suggest that Ministers during the
time the House is on holidays should try to
prepare a scheme so that when we meet
again on the 6th October something will be
done for the unemployed of Ulster who are
Suffering great hardships.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I would like
to say a few words in support of the contention put forward by the hon. Member for
North Belt.st (Mr. Kyle.) With him I want
to say that I do not believe the Government
appreciate the unemployed situation at all.
It has been my privilege to, put before the
Government on two or three occasions the
state of affairs which I know exists so far as
Belfast and this Northern Province are
concerned. Hon Members opposite may not
attach much importance to my judgment.
I do not suppose they do, but still I would
not like to allow them without warning to
permit the situation to develop and become
more serious than it is at the moment. The
situation is extremely serious, and it is for
that reason that I would try to impress the
Government with a sense of their responsibility so that they may do something. So
far they have been absolutely bankrupt as
far as ideas are concerned. They have no
concrete proposals to put forward at all.
We have been told repeatedly in this House
that the people of Ulster are satisfied to go
on parallel lines with the people of Great
Britain. I want to suggest that we should
follow that course. In Great Britain the
people are not asked to exist purely on unemployment benefit. Fairly liberal schemes
of relief are given through Bcards of
Guardians, and similar relief is not being
given in Northern Ireland. The Minister of
Labour may smile, and if there is any
implication in that smile it is probably that
the Government have no responsibility. I
have been privileged to speak about this
matter at the Board of Guardians, the Corporation, and in this House, and generally
I find one body throwing the responsibility
on the other. Some one has got to accept
responsibility, and I do not think there is

anybody who can better accept it than the

A serious situation will ensue unless somebody takes the initiative. Plans are on foot
at the present time for a fairly serious
demonstration of the unemployed, and I want
to warn the Government. If the Government is going to turn a deaf ear to the
warnings it is receiving then the responsibility will be theirs. I am not concerned
with speeches made on the Boundary question. I believe the feeling of the people of
Northern Ireland at the moment is such
that all inflammatory speeches will fall on
deaf ears and will have no effect. You can
make all the inflammatory speeches about the
Boundary you care to make. The people are
not thinking in terms of the Boundary but
in terms of bread and butter, and I want
to suggest that between now and the official
opening of Parliament some Department of
the Government should accept the responsibility of easing the situation and seeing if
they cannot do something concrete. They
might follow the suggestion made by the
Member for Antrim (Mr. George Henderson)
for getting the people back on the land.
This Government has no responsibility for
foreign policy because if it had I would
suggest the opening up of trade with Russia.
You have no scruples of conscience, but I
have. You are probably too much interested
in the form of Government that obtains in
Russia at the moment. This glorified Parish
Council has no responsibility for foreign
policy, otherwise I should suggest that trade
relations with Russia should be opened up
immediately, and that credits should be
advanced so that Russia might be able to
buy the machinery she needs, and we might
get flax cheaper than we are getting it at
the moment. But there is no use making
this suggestion, because you are not responsible for foreign policy.
I am glad the Prime Minister has come
back, and he will probably lend a ready ear
to the suggestion I have made. We have had
statements from him and other Ministers
that they want to keep on parallel lines with
Great Britain, and that is all we are asking
at the moment. We are asking that the
initiative should be taken by the Government to see that the unemployment benefit
that the people receive should be supplemented to the extent that is given in Poor-
Law relief in Great Britain. We are not
asking you to do anything revolutionary, but
simply to keep on parallel lines with legislation in Great Britain.
In conclusion, I want to warn the Government that a serious situation is developing.
I accept full responsibility for my statement
when I say that whatever assistance I can
lend, even if it takes revolutionary form, 1
am going to render until the people get
justice.

Drainage Bill.
STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF
FINANCE.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): In view of the assurances that were
given on the general expectation that this
great and important Measure would be proceeded with at an early period of our sittings
I think it is only due to the House that I
should explain in a few sentences the
reasons which govern our decision to ask the
House to postpone consideration of the
Second Reading until the 21st of this month.
The full text of the Measure has been in
the hands of hon. Members since our last
Parliamentary sittings, and I take it for
granted, therefore, that they are fully aware
of the great responsibility that the Measure
would throw upon the public bodies of the
Province in respect of the general drainage
of the land of Ulster. That being so it
appears to the Government that it is very
essential that there should be agreement-full
agreement between the County Councils and
the Government in respect of this Measure;
in other words it would be very undesirable
if these public bodies laboured under the
impression that we are forcing something
upon them that they perhaps were not in full
agreement with. Be that as it may, however, my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates), has had
conferences with the County Councils on the
subject of this Bill. The result of these
conferences has been a general agreement, or
rather I should say an agreement on the
Loans to Farmers.
Adjournment.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Mr. POLLOCK: There are a great many
items of expenditure to be paid by the
English farmer. He has to pay tithes, but
apart from that factre-
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I was
ferring to the question of the relief of rates.
Mr. POLLOCK: It does not matter whether
he has to pay it in the form of tithes or
in rates to his Council, it is money out of
the pocket of the farmer-that is what I am
concerned about-as compared with similar
conditions in Northern Ireland. My experience and my knowledge do not conform to
the opinion of the hon. Member in regard
to the question of valuation, a subject I do
not intend to pursue further.
There is no comparison whatever in respect to the guarantees given to shipbuilders
and others. In the first place the Government does not advance money to shipbuilders
and others. What it does is to guarantee
certain loans in order that industry may be
encouraged in shipbuilding and in other
ways. But my hon. Friend is under a misapprehension when he assumes that no disclosures have got to be made in regard to
the position of borrowers under such circumstances. He made a point of the fact
that the farmer would have to disclose his
financial affairs to the banker or persons
from whom he borrowed money, but in every
case where a Government guarantee is given
a full disclosure of the financial position.
and the security offered, must be given by
those who ask for these large sums of money
guaranteed by the Government. I wish to
emphasise that fact.
The Government has also in respect of its
general agricultural policy done a great deal
more than the average citizen has any
apprehension of. Not only is it establishing,
and has established, as a matter of fact,
farms for training young farmers, but a
great deal of money has been sent at Greenmount, Strabane, and elsewhere, and this
Parliament has also voted £50,000 to be devoted to the improvement of agriculture
generally. All the farmers get the benefit or
this; not only those who are in poor circumstances, but also those in better circumstances. Therefore if von aggregate all the
money that has been sent, and is being
spent from time to time in the interests of
agriculture, you will find that by comparison
with what has taken place in Great Britain
we are ahead of anything done there up to
the present.
I offer no opinion as to what the British
Government or the Free State Government
propose to do. I am dealing with facts and
matters that have been dealt with by this
Parliament, and I say that as between the
British agricultural position and our own
position in the North of Ireland, we can
claim that the Government and Parliament
have done their duty to the farmers of
Ulster. It does not follow that because we
have undertaken certain improvements in
the conditions governing agriculture here we
are at the end of our resources in regard to
that. The right hon. Gentleman who
presides over the Ministry of Agriculture is
very much interested in agriculture, and
will watch all the developments of the
industry, and I can say this: that when any
great necessity arises for any particular
venture or policy the Government will not
fail to take note of it. But to follow the
suggestion of my hon. Friend and assume
that the Government is going to open the
door to 130,000 farmers in Northern Ireland
to ask for loans--
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: They are not
all in need of loans.
Mr. POLLOCK: I am glad to say they are
not. A great many of them do not require
assistance, but if they opened the door to
applications on the part of those 130,000
farmers who may want money for any other
purpose the Government would be embarking on an adventure which would not only
be reprehensible in itself but exceedingly improper as regards the interests of the general
taxpayers.
I have no more to say on that subject, but
if I again ask hon. Members to reflect on
what the hon. Member for Antrim desires
they will see that such a policy is quite out
of harmony with prudence, and as the
Minister responsible for finance I certainly
cannot favour any adventure in the direction
which the hon. Member has outlined. That
is all I have got to say on this subject of agriculture. As regards the remarks of the hon.
Members who have taken up the subject of
nemployment, I leave them to the Minister
more directly responsible.
Question, "That this House do now
adjourn," put, and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at One o'clock
till Tuesday, 6th October, pursuant
to the Resolution of the House of
this day.
Oral Answer.
Drainage Bill.

Drainage Bill.
STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF
FINANCE.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): In view of the assurances that were
given on the general expectation that this
great and important Measure would be proceeded with at an early period of our sittings
I think it is only due to the House that I
should explain in a few sentences the
reasons which govern our decision to ask the
House to postpone consideration of the
Second Reading until the 21st of this month.
The full text of the Measure has been in
the hands of hon. Members since our last
Parliamentary sittings, and I take it for
granted, therefore, that they are fully aware
of the great responsibility that the Measure
would throw upon the public bodies of the
Province in respect of the general drainage
of the land of Ulster. That being so it
appears to the Government that it is very
essential that there should be agreement--full
agreement-between the County Councils and
the Government in respect of this Measure;
in other words it would be very undesirable
if these public bodies laboured under the
impression that we are forcing something
upon them that they perhaps were not in full
agreement with. Be that as it may, however, my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates), has had
conferences with the County Councils on the
subject of this Bill. The result of these
conferences has been a general agreement, or
rather I should say an agreement on the
1131 The Proclaimed Demonstration. HOUSE OF COMMONS The Proclaimed Demonstration. 1132
[Mr. Pollock]
general principle of the Bill, leaving one or
two very important measures of detail for
future settlement. As these matters of
detail have not yet been fully considered I
am here to-day to ask the postponement of
the Second Reading of this Measure for a
fortnight in order that one or two meetings
which we propose to have with these bodies
shall be held in the intervening period. I have
no doubt at all from the general feeling that
exists in the Province as to the necessity for
passing this important Measure, that there
should not be any great difficulty in reaching
a full agreement, not only in regard to the
principle, but also to the general details of
the working of the Measure. I therefore
move that the Second Reading consideration
of this Bill be postponed until the 21st
October.
Mr. KYLE rose.
Mr. SPEAKER: There is no motion
equired. I allowed the right hon. Gentleman
to make the statement, and I am afraid no

THE PROCLAIMED LABOUR
DEMONSTRATION.
Motion made, and Question proposed:

Mr. KYLE: As intimated earlier, I want
to draw the attention of the House to what
I conceive to be an unwarranted interference
with the liberties of the citizens of Belfast
by the Minister of Home Affairs. He says
he accepts full responsibility for the action
of the Inspector-General in proclaiming a
peaceful demonstration. Demonstrations
have taken place in this city at various
times, some of which have been legal and
some of which have been illegal. I refer to
one when troops or men marched through
the city of Belfast with rifles. That, according to the law of the land at that date, was
an illegal demonstration.
the
We in the Labour movement have always
been Constitutionalists. We have held
demonstrations in this city to try to focus
the attention of the City Council, of the
Poor-Law Guardians, and of Parliament on
the numbers of people in Belfast who are
suffering from unemployment-suffering
hunger and starvation through unemployment. We have demonstrated to
Guardians, who have informed us that they
have no responsibility, that they have gone
as far as they can go, and that we should go
to the Government. We have demonstrated
to the City Council, and the City Council
have informed us that they have put the responsibility on the Guardians for giving outdoor relief, and that they have mortgaged
the ratepayers of the City of Belfast as far
as they can see fit to do. And still there is
that tremendous volume of unemployment
in Belfast; still there is that tremendous
number of 38,000 people--our own brothers
and sisters--walking the streets of Belfast
who cannot get work to do.
We proposed to hold a demonstration to
let Members of Parliament see the full
numbers of these people who were prepared
to go out and demonstrate. Many
of our trades unions--and we all know the
trades unions are constitutional associations
-very kindly volunteered to lend their banners. Many of them-some of them at
least, guaranteed to provide music, without
which no demonstration in Belfast is very
successful. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
We did all that. We intended to hold a
demonstration to let Members of Parliament see the numbers of unemployed, because we believe that hon. Members of this
House do not realise the depth and the
extent of the unemployment situation in
Northern Ireland and in Belfast in particular. We wanted to show you something
of the effects of the Regulations which the
Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews) got this
House to agree to some time ago. These
Regulations are condemning the people to
want and misery.
Hon. MEMBERS: No, no.
1138 The Proclaimed Demonstration. 6 OCTOBER 1925 The Proclaimed Demonstration. 1134
Mr. KYLE: Some hon. Members say no,
but officials of the Ministry have stated in
spite of the Regulations that a man may
have 300 contributions and if he has not
eight paid within the last couple of years
he does not qualify. Other officials have
decided that if he has paid thirty contributions at any time he is entitled to benefit.
We would, therefore, be obliged to the
Minister of Labour if he would make these
things clear to us in the course of this
debate on the adjournment. I want to say
deliberately that the action of the Home
Secretary was entirely unwarrantable. In
my opinion it was done deliberately to try
to provoke disorder in this loyal city of
Belfast. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We
have been carrying on these things constitutionally. We have been holding meetings
here and there in the city of Belfast. We
have had demonstrations and nothing has
ever taken place. No one has lost his life.
Nothing has been interfered with in any
shape or form, and yet we have the Minister
of Home Affairs interfering with 30,000
men, who are desperate for want of
employment. He sets himself to ban this
lawful demonstration and denies them the
liberties that the defenders of civil and
religious liberty prate so much about.
When we want to exercise those civil liberties the Home Secretary denies us that
right.
These are the things that breed rebels.
that breed dissension, that breed trouble,
and I accuse the Home Secretary of
trying to provoke disorder SO that he
may divert the attention of the people of
Belfast from the things that really matter---
from the unemployment situation so that
he may get the Catholics and Protestants
at each other's throats, and so that he may
be able to do as he did before; get all the
forces of the Crown in order, as he would
say, to bring about peace and harmony in
our city. We have had peace in our city
for quite a considerable time-and we are
all glad of peace. We do not want anything
but peace, but we do not want to give up
our civil liberties. Therefore we are taking
the constitutional way of raising this matter in the place where it ought to be
raised rather than have a demonstration
to-day with perhaps 100 or 200 members of
the working classes lying in the hospitals
or Union Infirmary of Belfast or in jail.
It would have been quite easy to provoke a
row if we had been unconstitutional people
who did not believe in law and order.
We believed in law and order in 1912
when hon. Members opposite stated they
did not care whether they were called rebels
or not. When hon. Members opposite set
themselves up against the authority of the
British Crown we were Constitutionalists
and we are Constitutionalists, I am proud
to say, to-day, despite the effort many of us
had to make, despite the fact we had to risk
our whole constitutional position in the
Labour movement by appealing to our members to refrain from demonstrating-to refrain from giving the authorities any
opportunity of worsening their already bad
condition. So I think the Home Secretary
deserves the censure of this House for his
action in depriving these people of their
civil liberty, in prohibiting this demonstration of the unemployed.
Who are these unemployed? Hon. Members
opposite may be fortunate in that some of
their brothers or sisters or friends are not
unemployed, but I think hon. Members on
this side of the House, not excluding any,
know something of the depth and the extent of unemployment.
Mr. GRANT: And on this side, too.
Mr. KYLE: I quite agree the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. Grant) does
know something about unemployment.
Mr. GRANT: I know more about it than
you do.
Mr. KYLE: But I am not satisfied that
the hon. Member for North Belfast is in the
right camp in his defence of the Regulations
that were issued by the Minister of Labour,
for his trade union, equally with all trade
unions, are opposed to them. Here are the
unemployment figures as compared with the
British. In Great Britain they have 11 per
cent; here we have 17 per cent., and yet you
enforce the same Regulations as they do in
Britain. The hon. Member for North
Belfast would be well advised to speak from
the trade union point of view and leave the
Unionist point of view to others.
I think that this House should mark its
disapproval, but I am at a loss to know how
on the adjournment of the House we can
give an opportunity to Members of the
House to express their disapproval of the
suppression of the liberties of the people.
Hon. Members who have long experience in
Parliament, either here or elsewhere, may
be able to devise ways and means, but so far
as we are concerned we feel as strongly as
hon. Members opposite ever felt at any time
in their lives about anything. We feel on this
unemployment question that it is a scandal
and a shame to try to impose Regulations
that are having the effect of starving
hundreds, if not thousands, of unemployed
in Belfast.

been referred to is simply this. It is dealt

representatives of Labour. And as a rule

I want to take this opportunity of pointing

Gentleman the Minister of Home Affairs is
responsible to this House for the maintenance
of law in Northern Ireland. This is the law.
The definition of an unlawful assembly is:-
"An unlawful assembly at common law is
an assembly of three or more persons with
intent to carry out any common purpose,
lawful or unlawful, in such a manner as
to endanger the public peace, or to give
firm and courageous persons in the
neighbourhood of such assembly reasonable
grounds to apprehend a breach of the peace
in consequence of it.
by

statute as unlawful assemblies or unlawful

intimidate the Executive or Parliament;
meetings for the purpose of spreading
sedition or listening to seditious speeches."
Now I want to tell hon. Members opposite
what seditious speeches are so that they will
not be able to say they do not know.

Carson in 1920?

connected with the State"

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Government Loans and Exchequer
Provisions [Money.]
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That it is expedient to authorise, under
powers to be conferred by an Act of this
Session-
(1) the establishment of a Government
Loans Fund, and the creation of Ulster
Loans Stock, with a guarantee for the payment of the dividends thereon and the
repayment of the principal from the Consolidated Fund;
(2) the issue out of the Consolidated
Fund, by way of advance, of any deficiency
of income of the Government Loans Fund
Account in any year, including any
deficiency caused by payments to any Sinking Fund that may be created by virtue of
any such Act, and the repayment out of
moneys to be provided by Parliament of
such advances;
(3) the payment out of
moneys to be
provided by Parliament of any amount
hereafter directed to be written off as
lost on account of any Government Loan;
(4) the amendment of the law relating to
the Exchequer and Consolidated Fund.”
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The Financial Resolution now before the Committee requires some explanation from me having regard to the necessarily technical language in which it is
framed. The Resolution is, of course, the
forerunner of a Money Bill, and in order
that the Committee may know exactly what
machinery is contemplated in the Bill it is
necessary that I should recall to your
memory some of the provisions of the Exchequer Borrowing and Local Loans Act. 1922,
which empowered the Ministry of Finance
to issue from the Consolidated Fund
loans to Local Authorities and enabled the
Ministry to borrow to place the Exchequer
in funds for this purpose by the issue of
Ulster Savings Certificates or by the issue
of other kinds of securities. On that occasion reference was made to the fact that in
Great Britain a special Loans Stock and a
separate Local Loans Fund were in existence, the needs of Local Authorities in Great
Britain being met by direct issues from that
for
Government Loans-
Committee.
7 OCTOBER 1925
Fund. Having regard to Northern Ireland's
then more limited requirements Parliament
readily appreciated how unnecessary it was
to set up similar machinery in Northern
Ireland at that time, and authority was
accordingly given to the Ministry of Finance
to conduct all lending operations through
the Exchequer, thereby obviating the necessity for the issue of a separate stock for this
purpose.
This was in 1922 and during the period
which has elapsed since that date the Exchequer has carried out extensive lending
operations not only in financing Local
Authorities but in certain other analogous
directions, one of the most important of
which has been the making of advances to
the Intoxicating Liquor Claims Fund. These
lending operations have yearly increased in
volume and it will perhaps be of interest to
mention some of the purposes for which
loans have been made:-
Housing Subsidies made by Local Authorities and housing construction undertaken
directly by the Authorities.
Small Dwellings Acquisition.
Water Supply.
Sanitation Works.
Gas and Electric Lighting.
Establishment of Markets.
Workhouse Hospitals.
Road Reconstruction.
Building of Technical Schools and Town
Halls.
Cemeteries.
Open Spaces.
In addition, Acts of Parliament have
authorised expenditure in the nature of
capital expenditure, e.g., Housing Subsidies
and Police Barrack Reconstruction Schemes.
In view of the magnitude of its present-day
lending operations it is now the view of the
Government that the time has arrived when
we should revert to the British system of
setting up a separate Fund to be fed from
the proceeds of a special Loans Stock. The
many advantages of such a system can be
dealt with at a later stage when the text
of the Bill is available.
There is, however, one point of some importance to which reference might be made
at this stage, and it is this. In the majority
of cases the loans are repayable over a
long period of years, and I need hardly point
out that the system, if it is to be satisfactory
in all respects, should have as an essential
part of it a form of borrowing which more
nearly coincides with the average period of
repayment, which, in this case, means a form
of borrowing by long-dated securities.
The passing of this Financial Resolution
will enable the Ministry of Finance to
bring in a Bill providing for the issue of
the long-dated Loan Stock and the setting
up of a separate Loans Fund, and as the
Government are desirous of obtaining powers
for these purposes at the earliest possible
date I trust that the Committee will give
us both stages of this Resolution to-day.
Turning to the text of the different parts
of the Resolutions themselves. The first part
which you have read, Mr. Chairman, is selfexplanatory. Paragraph 2 gives the security
of the Consolidated Fund, that is to say,
the credit of the whole Province is to be
pledged for the benefit of the investor in any
public issue. Paragraph 3 provides for a
charge on votes in respect of any bad debt
which can, of course, only be written off with
the consent of Parliament to be obtained by
separate statute. Paragraph 4 contains
certain miscellaneous provisions amending
the existing law as to the Exchequer and
finance operations, and calls for no detailed
observations from me at this stage. I beg
to move.

UNEMPLOYED BECOMING
UNEMPLOYABLE.
8. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister
whether he is aware that there is a
constantly increasing number of young men
and women who, through the failure of the
capitalistic system of production for profit.
to provide employment for them, are rapidly
becoming unemployable, and what steps he
is prepared to take to remedy this state of
affairs.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have been asked by the
Prime Minister to reply to this question.
I am glad to say that there is no evidence
of a constantly increasing number of young
men and women becoming rapidly unemployable. The unemployment that prevails
generally is due to the upheaval in world
conditions consequent on the Great War and
not, in my opinion, to the capitalist system
as suggested by the hon. Member, who is no
doubt familiar with the deplorable results
that have followed the substitution of
Socialism in Soviet Russia.
I feel I ought to add that I strongly deprecate attacks on capital, as any sense of
insecurity is bound to prevent industrial development and increase unemployment. The
most practical way of dealing with the
situation is, I think, by friendly co-operation between capital and labour to achieve
the common end in which they are both
vitally concerned.
Mr. KYLE: I would like to ask the
Minister of Labour what security he thinks
there is for this constantly increasing number of young men and women who are
becoming unemployed in our midst under the
capitalist system?
Mr. ANDREWS: 1 am surprised that my
hon. Friend should suggest that an increasing
number of our young people are becoming
unemployed. I do not admit that contention
at all. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
9. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister
whether, in view of the numbers of starving
men and women in Belfast consequent upon
unemployment, he is prepared to declare a
state of emergency, and to compel the Board
of Guardians to administer out-door relief on
the scale laid down by the Ministry of Health
in Great Britain.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I have been asked by the
Prime Minister to reply to this question.
I have consulted the Board of Guardians
in Belfast, and I am assured that the Guardians give every case of distress which comes
to their knowledge careful consideration. So
far back as October, 1923, the Guardians
impressed upon the Relieving Officers the
importance of giving their earnest attention
to all cases which may come under their
notice as Relieving Officer, or which may be
brought to their notice indirectly through
any other source or agency.
Each case
is
relieved according as necessity is shown.
The Ministry of Home Affairs in response to
representations made by the Board of Guardians and the Belfast Corporation, specially
augmented, in February, 1924, the ordinary
powers of granting out-door relief by an
Order under section 13 of the Local Gevernment (Ireland) Act, 1896. The Order under
that Section removes restrictions in the
ordinary law and extends the Guardians'
powers by authorising them to give out-door
relief, at their discretion, to heads of
families in distress. I am informed that the
term "heads of families" is interpreted in the
'widest possible sense.
The Government have no power to compel
the Board of Guardians, who are the duly
elected representatives of the ratepayers, to
give relief indiscriminately according to a
fixed scale, nor can I find that the Ministry
of Health in England or the Scottish Board
of Health have any such compulsory power.
I am informed that the Ministry of Health
have not approved of any scale upon which
Boards of Guardians should give out-door
relief, though that Department has taken
action when a Board of Guardians has exceeded its legal powers in this direction. No
such action has been necessary in Belfast.
The discretion as to the amount of relief to
meet the necessities of each case must be left
to the Board of Guardians, who are the
responsible authority under Statute for the
purpose.

What is the object of these Regulations?
They were made simply for the purpose of
conserving the money that is available for
the payment of benefit to those genuinely
unemployed insured persons who need
it most. Against that principle is
there a single hon. Member in this
House, no matter what side of it he
sits upon, going to lift up his voice? We are
simply keeping on parallel lines with Great
Britain, and, believe me, that the man, no
matter who he is, who suggests that we
should get off parallel lines with Great Britain
would be doing the greatest disservice to the
working people of this community of ours
that it would be possible to do to them. Our
great safeguard is to remain in as close
association in all matters, but especially in
connection with these social services, with
Great Britain as it is in our power to be.
I shall have other opportunities of dealing
with this matter when the Bill itself is introduced, but I do ask my hon. Friends to

the working classes, especially to

Bates) quoted speeches made by members of
the Labour Party. I have not got a band
of secretaries behind me to keep me supplied
with the speeches of the Members of the
front Government bench, and I have to depend, unfortunately, on my memory. I have
not got the manuscript here, but if I am
wrong I can be corrected. The right hon.
Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) quoted a
speech made by a member of the Labour
Party as likely to incite a breach of the
peace. I think that was the idea. There is
an old proverb very prevalent in County
Antrim, and I am sure it is well known in
Belfast, too, that people who live in glass
houses should refrain from throwing stones.
It is not
many months since the
right hon. Gentleman the Chief Whip (Capt.
Dixon) went to the city of Derry. He was
reported in the Press of Belfast as saying
in the Guildhall there something like the
following-I have not got the speech here,
but he was talking about the Border, about
probable resistance on the Border, and about
a disease that the voters have in the city
of Belfast that when the Government nut
out their bogey men there is a bit of apathy
in regard to them now-and he said that
when a "wheen" of shots were fired along
the Border it would cure the disease of the
voters of Belfast. If that was not a suggestion for some fanatic along the Border to
fire a few shots I do not know what it was.
In my opinion that speech was more likely to
incite a breach of the peace than any speech
which the Minister of Home Affairs (Sir
Dawson Bates) has quoted here to-day. That
is not the only speech; there are dozens of
others, but that one is fresh in my memory.
I do not think there has been a scintilla
of evidence put up by the Government to
show that this demonstration was likely to
lead to a breach of the peace, or that it
would be other than a peaceful demonstration of people who rightly or wrongly
believed they had a grievance. I think that
the Government were ill-advised to take the
drastic action that was taken in closing
down this safety-valve of expression.
Mr. MCALLISTER: After listening to the
speeches of the Members of the Government
in answer to the protest made against the
proclamation of this meeting, I rise to
associate myself with the members of the
Labour Party in the protest which they have
made. It is a serious thing to deprive peopl
ot their rightful liberties of freedom of
speech. It requires, in my judgment, great
justification on the evidence and facts put
before this House before we can condone the
action of the Government in proclaiming
the lawful right of the people to a demonstration here to bring home to the Members of the House the state of affairs with
regard to unemployment in Northern Ireland. These people believe that it is the
only means they have of furthering their
interests and safeguarding themselves from
hunger, poverty, and distress. It is a serious
thing to deprive them of that right, and
it casts a great responsibility on those
responsible for leading them. It tends to
lead these people from constitutional and
legal methods of reform into much more
serious unconstitutional methods. The
Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Kyle) has
opened this debate to-day in a constitutional
and exceedingly moderate manner. His
speech is a lesson in constitutional methods
to right hon. Gentlemen on the benches
opposite.
I was interested to see that the Home
Secretary at this stage has become a convert
to constitutional speeches and constitutional
methods. I hope he will practice what he
preaches, and that in future when he gets
any intimation that the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews),
or the Chief Whip (Captain Dixon) intend
to visit Armagh or Derry he will take the
opportunity of proclaiming the meetings
which they intend to address, because he
had more justification from the speeches they
have delivered within the last few weeks
for proclaiming their meetings than he ever
had for proclaiming meetings of the Labour
Party, which, so far as I have been able
to ascertain, have been constitutionally,
legally and moderately conducted in the
enunciation of their grievances. The
Minister of Labour has asked the representatives of Labour in this House to realise
their responsibility. As representing another
branch of the Opposition in this House. I
would ask him to realise his responsibility.
I note that the notice proclaiming this
meeting states-
"there is fear that it will lead to
disaffection."
The only grounds which by any means the
Government could have in their minds for
proclaiming this meeting would be that they
must conclude that promoting disaffection
means the criticism of the methods, speeches
and actions of the Government. If that is
what they mean by disaffection they would
have the jails filled with 90 per cent. of the
people of Northern Ireland. In the interests
of freedom of speech and in the interests of
constitutional agitation I whole-heartedly
support the protest which has been made
by the representatives of Labour in this
House.
1165 The Proclaimed Demonstration. 6 OCTOBER 1925 The Proclaimed Demonstration.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Hanna): I would have been very glad had it
been possible to close this debate at the end
of the speech of the right hon. Gentleman
the Minister of Labour, because I think, as
he indicated, if these people believed this
was the only way in which they could display their position, that has been entirely
shattered by the attitude of the right hon.
Gentleman when he invited them through
their representatives to come and see him any
time with regard to these matters. The hon.
Member who shares with me in the representation of County Antrim is not even yet
convinced that there was some danger here.
I want to take this opportunity of pointing
out to the House for the benefit of hon.
Members opposite what the law is. I will ask
the House to remember that the right hon.
Gentleman the Minister of Home Affairs is
responsible to this House for the maintenance
of law in Northern Ireland. This is the law.
The definition of an unlawful assembly is:-
"An unlawful assembly at common law is
an assembly of three or more persons with
intent to carry out any common purpose,
lawful or unlawful, in such a manner as
to endanger the public peace, or to give
firm and courageous persons in the
neighbourhood of such assembly reasonable
grounds to apprehend a breach of the peace
in consequence of it.
"It includes meetings forbidden by
statute as unlawful assemblies or unlawful
combinations or associations; meetings to
intimidate the Executive or Parliament;
meetings for the purpose of spreading
sedition or listening to seditious speeches."
Now I want to tell hon. Members opposite
what seditious speeches are so that they will
not be able to say they do not know.
Mr. KYLE: What about Sir Edward
Carson in 1920?
Mr. HANNA: I am not concerned with
what anybody else said or anybody else did.
I do say this that while I am associated
with the right hon. Gentleman in the maintenance of law and order in Northern Ireland
this thing will not go on. I am going to give
the House the meaning of seditious speeches.
"Sedition whether by words spoken or
written or by conduct is a misdemeanour
punishable by fine and imprisonment. It
embraces all those practices whether by
deed, word or writing which fall short of
High Treason, but tend directly or have
for their object to incite discontent or
disaffection-to incite ill-will between
different classes of the King's subjects-to
create public disturbance, and generally all
endeavours to promote public disorder, or
to incite unlawful assemblies or to use any
form of physical force in any public matter
connected with the State"
We are told here to-day that all that was
intended was a very peaceful, orderly procession. It reminds me of a little hymn we
used to sing in Sunday school long ago:
Lord, a little band and lowly,
Humbly now we come to Thee.
To-day and here, in these circumstances and
atmosphere! But what was intended? We
can only look at the speeches they made.
We can only watch their conduct so that we
may form some idea of what was intended.
It was intended that there should be a
demonstration early in September to this
House. The hon. Member opposite says there
never was any such intention, and Mr.
Gemmell, who has been referred to, also said
it was nothing but a rumour, but on the day
that the demonstration was to be held Mr.
John McWade, who resides at 61 Sultan
Street, Belfast, speaking at the spot where
the meeting had been summoned to attend
and discussing the fact that none of the
leaders who had promised to be there were
there, said:-
"It seems many of them (the leaders)
are suffering from funk and fear of the
R.U.C. Cossacks
They were not there.
"the only party that is represented here
to-day is the West Belfast Labour Party.
I am a member of the West Belfast Labour
Party and we are going to organise a
demonstration to the Parliament House on
the 2nd October when it is being opened
officially and we will go there whether permission is granted or not."
That was the first intimation we got about
it. We had sent police to warn them about
that meeting and we sent police back to
them to warn them about this meeting. I do
not want to take up very much of the time
of the House by reading speeches but I want
to draw your attention again to the speech
of the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
William McMullen) in reference to this
matter. He is all constitutional to-day, except that he has just suggested that if be
does not get everything he wants he will put
himself at the head of a band and be unconstitutional. This is what he said speaking
at Library Street:
"He has told the Government in the
Northern Parliament that something constitutional would have to be done, and if
something constitutional was not done
something unconstitutional would happen,
and if unconstitutional means had to be
resorted to he was prepared to place himself at the head of the unemployed in the
effort."
He then announced that the demonstration
had been arranged for 6th October to bring
an orderly, peaceful procession up to the

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Government Loans and Exchequer
Provisions [Money.]
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
Motion made, and Question proposed :
"That it is expedient to authorise, under
powers to be conferred by an Act of this
Session-
(1) the establishment of a Government
Loans Fund, and the creation of Ulster
Loans Stock, with a guarantee for the payment of the dividends thereon and the
repayment of the principal from the Consolidated Fund;
(2) the issue out of the Consolidated
Fund, by way of advance, of any deficiency
of income of the Government Loans Fund
Account in any year, including any
deficiency caused by payments to any Sinking Fund that may be created by virtue of
any such Act, and the repayment out of
moneys to be provided by Parliament of
such advances;
(3) the payment out of moneys to be
provided by Parliament of any amount
hereafter directed to be written off as
lost on account of any Government Loan;
(4) the amendment of the law relating to
the Exchequer and Consolidated Fund."
The MINISTER
OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The Financial Resolution now before the Committee requires some explanation from me having regard to the necessarily technical language in which it is
framed. The Resolution is, of course, the
forerunner of a Money Bill, and in order
that the Committee may know exactly what
machinery is contemplated in the Bill it is
necessary that I should recall to your
memory some of the provisions of the Exchequer Borrowing and Local Loans Act. 1922,
which empowered the Ministry of Finance
to issue from the Consolidated Fund for
loans to Local Authorities and enabled the
Ministry to borrow to place the Exchequer
in funds for this purpose by the issue of
Ulster Savings Certificates or by the issue
of other kinds of securities. On that occasion reference was made to the fact that in
Great Britain a special Loans Stock and a
separate Local Loans Fund were in existence, the needs of Local Authorities in Great
Britain being met by direct issues from that
Government Loans-
Committee.
7 OCTOBER 1925
Fund. Having regard to Northern Ireland's
then more limited requirements Parliament
readily appreciated how unnecessary it was
to set up similar machinery in Northern
Ireland at that time, and authority was
accordingly given to the Ministry of Finance
to conduct all lending operations through
the Exchequer, thereby obviating the necessity for the issue of a separate stock for this
purpose.
This was in 1922 and during the period
which has elapsed since that date the Exchequer has carried out extensive lending
operations not only in financing Local
Authorities but in certain other analogous
directions, one of the most important of
which has been the making of advances to
the Intoxicating Liquor Claims Fund. These
lending operations have yearly increased in
volume and it will perhaps be of interest to
mention some of the purposes for which
loans have been made :-
Housing Subsidies made by Local Authorities and housing construction undertaken
directly by the Authorities.
Small Dwellings Acquisition.
Water Supply.
Sanitation Works.
Gas and Electric Lighting.
Establishment of Markets.
Workhouse Hospitals.
Road Reconstruction.
Building of Technical Schools and Town
Halls.
Cemeteries.
Open Spaces.
In addition, Acts of Parliament have
authorised expenditure in the nature of
capital expenditure, e.g., Housing Subsidies
and Police Barrack Reconstruction Schemes.
In view of the magnitude of its present-day
lending operations it is now the view of the
Government that the time has arrived when
we should revert to the British system of
setting up a separate Fund to be fed from
the proceeds of a special Loans Stock. The
many advantages of such a system can be
dealt with at a later stage when the text
of the Bill is available.
There is, however, one point of some importance to which reference might be made
at this stage, and it is this. In the majority
of cases the loans are repayable over a
long period of years, and I need hardly point
out that the system, if it is to be satisfactory
in all respects, should have as an essential
part of it a form of borrowing which more
nearly coincides with the average period of
repayment, which, in this case, means a form
of borrowing by long-dated securities.
The passing of this Financial Resolution
will enable the Ministry of Finance to
bring in a Bill providing for the issue of
the long-dated Loan Stock and the setting
up of a separate Loans Fund, and as the
Government are desirous of obtaining powers
for these purposes at the earliest possible
date I trust that the Committee will give
us both stages of this Resolution to-day.
Turning to the text of the different parts
of the Resolutions themselves. The first part
which you have read, Mr. Chairman, is selfexplanatory. Paragraph 2 gives the security
of the Consolidated Fund, that is to say,
the credit of the whole Province is to be
pledged for the benefit of the investor in any
public issue. Paragraph 3 provides for a
charge on votes in respect of any bad debt
which can, of course, only be written off with
the consent of Parliament to be obtained by
separate statute. Paragraph 4 contains
certain miscellaneous provisions amending
the existing law as to the Exchequer and
finance operations, and calls for no detailed
observations from me at this stage. I beg
to move.
Question put and agreed to.
Resolution reported.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House doth agree with the Committee in
the said Resolution."

it stands sufficiently high to get within
measurable distance at any rate of the
British terms.

The function of each of these Committees is

of agriculture in connection with which the

Mr. ANDREWS: During the twelve
months from 1st October, 1924, to 30th
September, 1925, 7,834 of the 226,000 applications for extended benefit dealt with by the
Local Employment Committees were rejected
on the ground that the applicants were not
making reasonable efforts to obtain employment. During the same period, the Courts
of Referees disallowed 1,116 claims on the
statutory ground that they were not

carefully examining the facts in each case.
were satisfied that the applicant was not

UNEMPLOYED BECOMING
UNEMPLOYABLE.
8. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister
whether he is aware that there is a
constantly increasing number of young men
and women who, through the failure of the
capitalistic system of production for profit,
to provide employment for them, are rapidly
becoming unemployable, and what steps he
is prepared to take to remedy this state of
affairs.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have been asked by the
Prime Minister to reply to this question.
I am glad to say that there is no evidence
of a constantly increasing number of young
men and women becoming rapidly unemployable. The unemployment that prevails
generally is due to the upheaval in world
conditions consequent on the Great War and
not, in my opinion, to the capitalist system
as suggested by the hon. Member, who is no
doubt familiar with the deplorable results
that have followed the substitution of
Socialism in Soviet Russia.
I feel I ought to add that I strongly deprecate attacks on capital, as any sense of
insecurity is bound to prevent industrial development and increase unemployment. The
most practical way of dealing with the
situation is, I think, by friendly co-operation between capital and labour to achieve
the common end in which they are both
vitally concerned.
Mr. KYLE: I would like to ask the
Minister of Labour what security he thinks
there is for this constantly increasing number of young men and women who are
becoming unemployed in our midst under the
capitalist system?
Mr. ANDREWS: 1 am surprised that my
hon. Friend should suggest that an increasing
number of our young people are becoming
unemployed. I do not admit that contention
at all. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Mr. DEVLIN: Can the right hon. Gentleman say how long there will be any capital
at all in Ulster if the Government of Ulster
is carried on on the present lines?
OUT-DOOR RELIEF FOR UNEMPLOYED.
9. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister
whether, in view of the numbers of starving
men and women in Belfast consequent upon
unemployment, he is prepared to declare a
state of emergency, and to compel the Board
of Guardians to administer out-door relief on
the scale laid down by the Ministry of Health
in Great Britain.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I have been asked by the
Prime Minister to reply to this question.
I have consulted the Board of Guardians
in Belfast, and I am assured that the Guardians give every case of distress which comes
to their knowledge careful consideration. So
far back as October, 1923, the Guardians
impressed upon the Relieving Officers the
importance of giving their earnest attention
to all cases which may come under their
notice as Relieving Officer, or which may be
brought to their notice indirectly through
any other source or agency. Each case is
relieved according as necessity is shown.
The Ministry of Home Affairs in response to
representations made by the Board of Guardians and the Belfast Corporation, specially
augmented, in February, 1924, the ordinary
powers of granting out-door relief by an
Order under section 13 of the Local Gevernment (Ireland) Act, 1896. The Order under
that Section removes restrictions in the
ordinary law and extends the Guardians'
powers by authorising them to give out-door
relief, at their discretion, to heads of
families in distress. I am informed that the
term "heads of families" is interpreted in the
'widest possible sense.
The Government have no power to compel
the Board of Guardians, who are the duly
elected representatives of the ratepayers, to
give relief indiscriminately according to a
fixed scale, nor can I find that the Ministry
of Health in England or the Scottish Board
of Health have any such compulsory power.
I am informed that the Ministry of Health
have not approved of any scale upon which
Boards of Guardians should give out-door
relief, though that Department has taken
action when a Board of Guardians has exceeded its legal powers in this direction. No
such action has been necessary in Belfast.
The discretion as to the amount of relief to
meet the necessities of each case must be left
to the Board of Guardians, who are the
responsible authority under Statute for the
purpose.

PENALISING APPLICANTS FOR UN-
EMPLOYMENT BENEFIT.
11. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that applicants
for unemployment insurance benefit are
penalised more than once for the same
offence.
Mr. ANDREWS: It is the case-and in
my opinion it is essential in order to protect
the Fund and the interest of the contributors-that, when a claimant has refused an
offer of employment in a particular vacancy,
and has in consequence been disqualified for
benefit for a period, the Department should
be free to test his continued willingness to
take employment by offering him another
vacancy, and, if necessary, the same one;
and, if he again unreasonably refuses to
take the employment, to impose a further
period of disallowance. The applicant has
always the right to appeal to the Court of
Referees against this disallowance.
ANTRIM LOCAL EMPLOYMENT
COMMITTEE.
12. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether the decision of the Antrim
Local Employment Committee on the 16th
September, 1925, laying down a scale under
the Local Employment Committee Scheme
fixing a family income for the Exchange area
as follows:-man, 25s per week; wife, 20s
per week; each child under 18 years of age,
5s per week; each adult over 18 years of age,
20s per week, has been carried into effect.
and, if not, for what reason has the decision
of the Antrim Local Employment Committee
been set aside.
Mr. ANDREWS: The Antrim Local Employment Committee submitted to the
Ministry for approval certain scales of
family income which they provisionally suggested should be applied when applications
were being considered for the grants of
extended benefit by persons who have drawn
all the benefit to which they may be en
titled on their contributions.
The suggested scales were considerably in
excess of those previously observed by the
Local Employment Committees at Antrim
and elsewhere in Northern Ireland. The
Antrim Committee, in which I have full
confidence, has, therefore, been requested to
give further consideration to the question
at its next meeting, and it has been suggested that in proposing scales the
Committee should have regard to the rates
of wages generally prevailing in the district.

FREE COPIES OF ACTS OF
PARLIAMENT.
15. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs on what grounds he has discontinued the old practice of sending free
copies of Acts of Parliament, etc., to Local
Authorities, and seeing that the administering of these Acts rests on the Local
Authorities, will he resume the former
practice.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This action has
been taken by the Ministry of Home Affairs
in consequence of a general decision of the
Government curtailing on the grounds of
economy the free issue of Stationery Office
publications by Government Departments.
(Mr.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
Pollock): Perhaps I should supplement the
answer given by the Minister of Home
Affairs. At the beginning of this year an
investigation was made by my Department
into the cost of the publication and circulation of Government Papers on the ground
that it seemed to me that the cost was excessively heavy. It was found that a great
many free copies were distributed where, in
the opinion of the Ministry and the Government, it was desirable that they should be
bought in the ordinary way.
Administrative action was taken by my
Ministry to ensure that in future no Government publications of any sort would be distributed free without the specific sanction
of the Ministry to those bodies or persons
who might reasonably be expected to bear
the cost themselves. This action follows on
the lines adopted by the Stationery Office
of the Imperial Government. The results,
I may say are quite satisfactory, as the instructions have resulted in a very large increase in the circulation of Government
Papers.
I see no reason why Public Authorities
should receive Government Bills free to any
greater extent than private individuals, and
as the cost has been in our opinion excessively heavy, I see no reason to depart from
the arrangement made.
Mr. MCALLISTER: Has any arrangement
been made at all to notify local authorities
of the various changes made in the laws they
are called upon to administer?
Mr. POLLOCK: I think the changes in
the laws must be a matter of public notoriety
in view of the fact that the proceedings of
this Parliament are published in the Press
the morning after our meeting.

Sir DAWSON BATES: It is a fact that
I have received repeated applications from

the sense indicated in the question. The
existing prison officers were transferred to
this Government under the provisions of the
Government of Ireland Act. 1920, the conditions of transfer being laid down in the
Act, viz.: that after the appointed day transferred officers should continue to hold their
offices by the same tenure and upon the same
terms and conditions (including conditions
as to salary and superannuation) as heretofore. It will be noted that the conditions
in the Act are not identical with those suggested by the hon. Member. Provision is
made in the Act whereby any question affecting the rights of transferred officers can
be finally determined by the Civil Service
Committee, and the prison warders, relying
on this section, applied to the Civil Service
Committee for a decision on the point but
were notified that the matter was not one in
which the Committee could intervene. The
Ministry of Home Affairs, after consultation
with the Ministry of Finance, thereupon decided that the application of the prison warders
could not be entertained, on the ground that
the existing rate of pay and emoluments are
adequate for the duties discharged.
As regards the third part of the question,
I accept responsibility for the decision conveyed to the prison officers, a decision which
I may say was taken after consultation with
the Prime Minister.
The question of the pensions of transferred
officers and the mode of calculation, including the amount of cost of living bonus to
be reckoned for pension, is one for the Civil
Service Committee and not for the Government of Northern Ireland.

Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer to the
first part of the question is in the affirmative.
I understand that there were six prosecutions against milk vendors on the date referred to. In two cases the magistrates convicted and imposed fines, the other cases being
dismissed. The resident magistrate dissented
in one case in which he was not prepared to
accept the defence.
I am advised that the Courts have sufficient powers to impose adequate penalties
on persons for selling impure or adulterated
foods, where the circumstances warrant conviction.
It would, of course, be improper for me to
attempt to influence the decisions of the
Courts in individual cases.

SAILORS' AND SOLDIERS' LAND TRUST.
Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Finance whether he can state how many houses
have been built under the Sailors' and
Soldiers' Land Trust Scheme in Northern
Ireland; what conditions govern applications for the tenancy of these houses; what
recommendation is required; what was the
duration of the service of applicants who
have secured houses, and what number were
allocated to soldiers and sailors.
Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Finance whether he can state the cause of the
delay in building the 313 ex-Servicemen's
houses which have been authorised by the
Imperial Government.
Mr. POLLOCK: I will answer this question and that put by the hon. Member (Mr.
Kyle) regarding the delay in the building
of the ex-Servicemen's houses together.
As I have already pointed out, my
Ministry merely acts as the agent of the
Irish Sailors' and Soldiers' Land Trust,
which is an Imperial Service, but, as a
matter of courtesy to the hon. Gentleman,
I have obtained the following information :--
The number of ex-Servicemen's houses in
Northern Ireland completed to date is 678,
and 55 are at present in course of construction.
The delay that has taken place in proceeding with the remainder of the houses
was due to differences between the Trust and
the Imperial Treasury regarding the amount
required for the completion of the scheme,
but I am glad to be able to state that the
Trust has, within the past few days, sanctioned the erection of a further 134 houses,
and the work will be commenced as soon
as the necessary plans, specifications and
bills of quantities have been prepared.
Any ex-Serviceman who desires to obtain
ex-Serviceman's house, and has not
already submitted an application, should
an
apply to the Ministry of Finance for the
requisite form, which affords him an opportunity of giving particulars of his service,
etc. When houses are ready for occupation
or become vacant the applications are considered by the trustees, who select the prospective tenants.
The only condition which the applicants
are required to fulfil for consideration for
the tenancy of Trust houses is that they
must be "men who have served in any of
His Majesty's Naval, Military or Air Forces
in the Great War," and no special recommendation is required.
I am further informed that the duration
of the service of applicants who have secured
houses varies from six months to six years,
and that there is no specific distribution of
such houses as between soldier and sailor
candidates.

a
It seems to me rather strange that in this

for Great Britain, and this Bill which I have
the privilege to bring before the House today is intended in a similar way to right the
wrong here. It is a great Measure in my
opinion. I can say that because it has been
designed and given existence to in Great
Britain by British statesmen who alone

claim to any extent. At the same time I do
feel it a privilege to bring this Bill before the

I do feel that through the provisions of this
Bill we are truly visiting the fatherless and
the widows in their affliction. (Hon. Mem-
(bers: Hear, hear). It is not necessary that
I should deal, as I said, with each particular
Clause in the Measure, because the Bill
itself has been in the hands of hon. Members
for about a week, and the Government has
issued an explanatory memorandum which
deals, I think, in the clearest way possible
with all the important Clauses which the
Bill contains. But at the same time I would
like to say that when you come to give
pensions of necessity there must be some test.
Of course, I know that tests are not particularly popular. The only way to avoid tests is
to say you are going to give pensions to all.

connection with war pensions the test has
been military service, and the dependants
of those who were killed or who died on
active service received pensions as a consequence, and then when there was disability
attributable to the war disability pensions
were given on a generous scale. As regards
old-age pensions, the test has been different.
It has been the test of income, and up to
the present in Northern Ireland the test of
income has been income derived from savings
as well as income derived from earnings. I
know that my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Finance looks forward in a few
days to bringing in a Measure to remove
the thrift disqualification clause, and put us
in step with Great Britain in that connection. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The test in this instance is a different
test. This Bill is being in a measure linked
up with our Health Insurance Acts, so that
those who are entitled to be insured persons
and receive benefits under our Health Insurance Acts will be entitled to receive benefits
under this Act. In addition to that there
are certain exempted persons and certain
excepted industries and voluntary contributors who will be brought into the orbit
of the Measure as well. At the present time
we have 325,000 insured persons in Northern
Ireland. It is estimated that this figure
will be increased to about 350,000, and when
you take the children into account it will
mean that in Northern Ireland about 700,000
of our people will directly or indirectly be
eligible for benefits under the Act. That
really makes the scheme one of the widest
character. I should like to say that one
card and one stamp will be sufficient to
deal with both national health insurance
and with the benefits which will be given
and obtained under this Measure.
The most important provision in the Bill,
of course, is that which gives benefit to the
widow. The widow of an insured man who
dies after the date of the commencement of
this scheme, namely, 4th January next, and
who was under 70 years of age at that date
will be entitled to receive for herself 10s a
week pension so long as she lives or until
she re-marries or becomes 70 years of age,
in which case she will become without
further tests entitled to a pension
under our Old Age Non-Contributory Acts,
In addition to that the widow will be entitled
to receive 5s of an allowance for her eldest
or only child and 3s for the other children
whom she may have until they become 14
years of age, or if they remain full time at
a day school, 16 years of age. Now that
means that although the children's allowances are terminable the widow's pension still
goes on, which, I think, no hon. Member
can say is otherwise than a generous
arrangement. But then, unfortunately,
there are children who are orphans, having
lost both parents, and to these an orphan's
pension will be given of 7s 6d a week until
the orphan becomes 14 years of age, or if remaining full time at a day school 16 years
of age.
But we have to deal with a real difficulty.
and that is the existing widow. The diffculty which the existing widow presents is
this, that although her husband may have
been an insured person under our National
Health Insurance Acts, if he is dead now,
or dies before the 4th January next, he will
not have contributed anything to the pensions' benefits under this particular Act.
The same applies to the existing orphan. At
the same time it has been considered that.
it will involve great hardship to leave existing widows and orphans out of the
Measure altogether, and so it is provided in
the Bill that existing widows-that is those
who are widows to-day or become widows before the 4th January next-will receive a
pension at the rate of 10s per week provided
they have one or more children, and they
will also receive an allowance for those
children notwithstanding the fact that no
contributions have been paid. Again I cannot but think that that is a generous arrangement. Of course, hon. Members may ask
"Why does the widow who has no children
not get a pension?" (Hon. Members: Hear.
hear.) Well, the reason is because, as I have
said, no contributions will have been paid by
her husband on her behalf, and it is considered that while the duty of the mother
is to look after her children the widow who
has no children is not in a greater difficulty
to provide for herself than the girl who has
never been married. I think that is a complete answer. In reality you will see that
existing widows and orphans will get a
non-contributory pension. But the Bill does
not stop here. It goes further still, and it
provides on a contributory basis old-age
pensions at the rate of 10s a week to insured
men and insured women between the ages of
65 and 70 years, and also to the wives of insured men between these ages, notwithstanding the fact that such wives may not have
been insured themselves. These pensions, I
want to make it perfectly clear, do not become available until the 2nd January, 1928,
just in the same way as they will not be
available until that date in Great Britain.
