so doing he is providing in a measure for
his wife and for his children after he has
gone? (Hon Members: Hear, hear.) I know
a little of our working classes in Northern
Ireland, and I do not think they will object
in any degree to pay this small contribution
when they know the vast benefits that it will
bring to their wives and their children in
case they are taken, and when they fully
realize that it means the removal
of the burden of anxiety which at the
present time they are obliged to carry due
to the fact that at any time they may be cut
off and their wives and children left in a
hopeless position.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear
Mr. ANDREWS: therefore i say that the
contributory system is the only system
which we can adopt here-(Hon. Members:
Hear, hear) and, therefore, it is take it or
leave it on that understanding.
Now may I give just two examples of what
this Bill means? A few weeks ago 1 was
privileged with a few friends to spend eight
days in Scotland. One afternoon we stopped
at the side of a beautiful lake surrounded by
majestic mountains. We thought we would
have a cup of afternoon tea, and that we
would make a fire in order to boil the kettle.
I happened to notice some little way off a
small crofter's house, and I thought I could
get the kettle boiled more quickly there. I
went to the house and asked the good woman
would she boil it, and she said "Certainly."
While it was being boiled, of course, we had
a little talk. She told me that her husband
had died a year ago, and said "Sir, if it had
not been for the generosity of his employer,
Captain So-and-so" I forget the exact
name "and what we got from our Health
Insurance Benefit I do not know how we
could have carried on, and we are having a
heavy struggle now." I could see it from the
surroundings; I could see it with my own
own eyes. I said to her, "But, after all luck is
coming your way, because, as your husband
was an insured person, and as you evidently
have children"--I could see them in the
room; there were only two rooms in the
house; the bed was in the kitchen, one of
them at any rate-"you will be getting a
pension." She said "Yes. They tell me I
will be entitled to a pension," and she went
to the cupboard, brought some papers out,
showed them to me, and said "Could you
give me any help as to how it should be
filled in?" After we had talked for a little
the kettle was boiled, and as I was going
away she said, with the tears running out of
her eyes, "This in some way will bring my
husband nearer to me again, because I see
I really owe that pension to him, and it will
be a great help." I do not believe there is
'an hon. Member, no matter where he sits,
who does not desire that this Bill should be
1201 Widows' Pensions Bill-
Second Reading. 1202
13 OCTOBER 1925
passed as soon as possible, and that our
widows and orphans in Northern Ireland
shall enjoy the same benefits as the widows
and orphans in Great Britain. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Again, look at the old man aged sixty years
or so, worn out by industry, wondering how
he is going to carry on. He sees a bright
light, and that light is that, when he becomes
sixty-five, at any rate he will not be entirely
a burden on his own people but will have ten
shillings a week given to him by this
Measure. I am sure there is no hon. Member who would want to put out that light. I
do not say for one minute that this Bill is
the last word. I believe that, after all,
"through the ages one increasing purpose
runs," but I say it is a long step in the right
direction-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-it
is another bit of a foundation laid upon the
road of progress along which the men and
women of Northern Ireland will march-I
hope and pray-to greater happiness and
prosperity in the days that are to come.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I desire to
move as an Amendment to delete all the
words after That," and substitute the
following:--
"this House, while willing to pass a noncontributory Measure, which would confer
generous pensions on our widows and
orphans and aged, and reduce the age
limit to sixty-five years, while removing
the Thrift Disqualification Clauses of the
previous Acts, declines to give a Second
Reading to a Bill which imposes an
additional contribution on our lowly-paid
wage-earners, and on our industries, which
are in a precarious state, making no provision for many widows, orphans, and
aged, and families where the father is
incapacitated, and provides only to those
qualified to become recipients allowances
which are wholly inadequate."
In moving this Amendment, I desire at
the outset to return my thanks to the right
hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) for the very
clear exposition he has given us of those
provisions of the Bill upon which he touched.
I was rather sorry he did not deal with
more provisions of the Bill, because he dealt
with those which, to my mind, appear fairly
simple, and left untouched those which one
would have some difficulty in understanding. As I have pointed out to the House
before, to one unused to the language employed by Civil Servants and the legal
fraternity there is a certain amount of
difficulty in extracting commonsense from
the very involved and redundant language
which they employ for the purpose of drawing up Acts of Parliament. From that point
of view, while expressing my unstinted
tribute to the right hon. Gentleman, I rather
regret that he did not go more fully into
this Bill and explain some of those provisions which we have a little difficulty in
understanding.
It was but natural, I suppose, for the
right hon. Gentleman in introducing a
Measure of this sort to paint the bright side.
He did, undoubtedly, touch on some of the
dark features of the Bill, but he was not
quite so eulogistic as one of the pioneers of
the Old Age Pensions Acts. For example, I
have cut a quotation from a speech which
Mr. Asquith delivered a few days previously
to the introduction of the first Old Age
Pension Act, and Mr. Asquith even flattered that Measure more than the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) did this Measure
when introducing it here to-day. The words
Mr. Asquith used were:-
"It will, without any offence to their
self-respect, or to their proper pride, without any feeling of humiliation, put at least
half a million of old folk, the veterans of
our industrial army, entirely beyond the
reach of pecuniary anxiety and care."
I do not know if that could in all fairness
be claimed for an Act which started by
giving an old-age pensioner five shillings a
week, and half-a-crown to his wife, and I
do not believe that the Bill introduced to-day
is going to be sufficient.
We want to join issue 1ight at the outset
with the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andnews) on the question of the Bill being con-
(ributory. We want to suggest, and suggest
very definitely, that, instead of laying a
Foundation this afternoon, you have broken
a foundation. I want to contend, and I believe that we will be able to put forward
with a large amount of truth the argument
that is incontrovertible that the foundation
was laid in the 1908 Act, and that succeeding
Parliaments and Governments stood upon
that foundation, which was a non-contributory foundation. This afternoon you are
smashing that foundation when you are
bringing in one of the most mean and
contemptible Bills which have been introduced either in the British legislature or in
this legislature within the past quarter of
a century. It can be said that the founders
of the original Act gave very full consideration to the question of whether the Old Age
Pension Act should be contributory or noncontributory, and if the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) had taken the trouble
to read the debates that took place on the
original 1908 Act he would have found that
Mr. Lloyd George quite clearly and unambiguously stated that they had very carefully
considered the rival merits of contributory
and non-contributory schemes, and had come
to the conclusion that the only feasible and
practicable basis for the Old-Age Pension

has investments such as the War Loans.

for the purpose of removing the thrift disqualification. I want to suggest that the
burden should be spread over a larger
The right hon. Gentleman, the Minister
of Labour, and his followers will probably
say that we have no knowledge of industry,
and that we care less. That is not so, because we realise that up to a point-I am
sure this will appeal to the two hon. and
learned Members for the University, and
particularly to the hon. Gentleman on my
right (Dr. Morrison)-there is a common
identity of interest between employer and
employed. All Socialist economists, including
the great Karl Marx, adınit that. Take the

they employ 10,000 people. You want to
suggest that £4,000 is of no consideration
to Harland & Wolff.

Mr. W. MCMULLEN: You suggested that it
is a mere trifle.
Mr. ANDREWS: Comparatively speaking.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: It is not a question
of £4,000. It is a matter of 41d per week to
employer and employee, and not 2d as you
suggest. You are taking advantage of the
Health Insurance Acts for the purpose of
coating this pill, and you have no right to
take advantage of them, because a reduction
in contributions was due at any time owing
to the accumulated funds in the coffers of the
State and in the coffers of the Approved
Societies. While a reduction in health contributions is absolutely inevitable you want
to take advantage of that for the purpose
of introducing a contributory scheme. I
want to suggest that you have no right to
do that.

Mr. W. McMULLEN: I beg your pardon.
It is habit from which I find it very difficult
to break, but I am sure you and the right hon.
Gentlemen opposite know the attitude I want
to take up. The point I want to make is that
the figure is not £4,000, but £8,000, and 1

and his colleagues to examine the logic of

this argument, and to find out whether the

was absolutely inevitable. That reduction
had got to take place, and the employing
classes, the capitalists, should have had the
advantage of that for the purpose of allowing
them to compete with their international
competitors. Instead of giving our employers
that opportunity you are putting an additional burden upon industry.
Apart from that, what is the exact position?
It has often been pointed out in the columns
of the "Belfast Telegraph," particularly in
the leading articles, that our two main industries, linen and shipbuilding, are dependent upon exports. The home market
does not count so far as those two main industries are concerned. I think no one will
attempt to dispute the statement in any way
that during the war, when our factories were
manufacturing linen for war purposes, fo
aeroplanes and other purposes, certain substitutes got into the market that people got
inured to, and that they still use. I refer to
cotton, for example. The right hon. Gentleman may apply the test of reason to that,
and may say that the cotton manufacturer in
Great Britain will be liable to exactly the
same tax, and that the relative position of
the cotton industry and of the linen industry
will be exactly the same. I admit that, but
I suggest to him that if he had departed from
the legislation that has been adopted in
England, and had made this scheme a noncontributory one, he would have been giving
the linen merchants a better chance in the
international markets than they have at the
present time. We have many competitors on
the Continent who were formerly customers
of ours. I understand that France is manufacturing linen. I know they are in Czecko
Slovakia. I understand that that country is
entering into competition with us in the international markets, and in these proposals
you are hampering the linen industry of this
country.
By introducing this Measure to-day, you
are striking a blow at the linen industry
and at the shipbuilding industry. I propose
to tell you how. In the shipbuilding industry,
the firms concerned are dependent for the
whole of their raw material on Great Britain.
Their chief essential is coal, and the coal
employers in Great Britain are going
to be asked to pay this contribution,
inasmuch as a similar Bill has been
passed by the British Parliament. It
cannot be gainsaid that the price of coal,
apart from the value of coal-the hon. Member for the University (Dr. Morrison) will
recognize the distinction between value and
price is determined by the amount of competition there is in the international market.
I do not think that any Member opposite will
attempt to controvert the argument that it
is impossible to increase the price of coal in
the international market at the present time,
and the only way this impost can be borne
is by increasing the cost of the commodity in
the home market. If that takes place, Harland
& Wolff are going to pay more for their
ccal. Steamers are going to pay more for
their coal. Steel merchants are going to pay
more for their coal. What, then, is the
position of Harland & Wolff and Workman,
Clark & Co. for competing in the international market? I think I have said
sufficient to point out the effect of the impost
upon industry, while you are allowing a
large number of people in the community to
escape the Prime Minister, for example,
without any personal reference, who receives
a salary with no interest in industry. He is
only paying in an infinitesimal degree, whereas if the scheme were non-contributory he
would pay in a larger degree. He could
afford to pay much better than the lowly
individual worker or the employer in industry at the present time.
I have given one instance where it will
probably be difficult, if not impossible, to
pass the tax on to the consumer. It will
not be possible so far as the coal trade is
concerned, but in other trades it will be
possible to pass the tax on to the consumers
and the employees, making the position this,
that the employee will be paying his direct
contribution and he will also be paying as a
consumer. The obligation of the employer
will be passed on to the consumer, so that
the unfortunate worker will pay the direct
contribution and will also pay a higher price
for his commodities as a consumer. For
these reasons I want to suggest that a wrong
basis entirely has been taken. I want to
contend that the people who promoted the
original Act could see much more clearly

position? If I may deal with old-age
pensions for a moment, you are going to
have a contributory old-age pension scheme.
From 65 to 70 you will have a contributory
scheme, and from 70 onwards a non-contributory scheme. Where is the sensible Legislature or the sensible politician that is going
to have old-age pensions contributory from
65 to 70, and non-contributory from 70 onwards? From the point of view of legislation, the thing is absolutely ridiculous, and
the working out of the Act will be absolutely ridiculous. You make proposals about

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I have no desire this afternoon to enter into any lengthened criticism of the provisions of this Bill
which has been placed before the House in
such a very lucid and clear manner by the
Minister of Labour. He has put before the
House in the clearest possible way the main
provisions of the Bill, and at the same time
has displayed a kindly and generous spirit
which he always shows in connection with
matters of a similar character. I hold a
certain view-point in regard to this particular Measure that I would like in a few
minutes to put before the House. A good
deal has been said here to-day-indeed it has
been said often in this House-about following exactly on parallel lines with Great
Britain.
On many occasions I have stated that I
could not in its entirety subscribe to that
particular formulæ. While in the main one
may be able to accept it, yet I think the
proper view-point is to examine all these
measures that are dealt with by the Imperial
Parliament, and if they are suitable for our
conditions here accept them, and if there are
modifications necessary bring in those modifications. For instance, take the Health Insurance Act, which was passed through the
Imperial House. When it was applied to
Ireland the question of panel doctors was left
out because we have somewhat different conditions to deal with in Ireland. So on the
broad question of legislation the attitude I
have always taken is that while in the main
it may be possible for us to follow what takes
place in the Imperial Parliament, all questions ought to be considered on their merits,
and if amendments are necessary make them
if they are considered to be improvements.
I wish to make my position clear in regard
to that particular matter.
As far as I am personally concerned I am
going to support the Bill that has been introduced this afternoon. I am only sorry
that a Measure of this character had not
been introduced in the Imperial House many
years ago. I think that when the country
was very prosperous and the trade outlook
was good, and when the financial condition
of the British Exchequer was such as it was,
it was a pity that a great ameliorative
Measure of this character was not introduced then. The only thing that troubles
me, and it has troubled me since this Bill
passed through the Imperial House, is
whether this is exactly the right time to
introduce a Bill of such far-reaching importance, implying as it does a huge burden
upon the financial resources of the country.
May I just state briefly how I look upon
that particular aspect of this subject. The
Minister of Labour has told us what it is
going to involve, a charge upon the employer
of labour of 2d for a man and 1d for a
woman, and a similar charge upon the employee. I think provision is made that that
is to be increased in ten years by 50 per cent.
and in 20 years from now that is to be
doubled. It has been calculated by experts
on the other side that the immediate charge
involved in connection with the industries of
the country, the direct charge involved, will
mean something like £12,000,000 per annum,
a very serious thing at the present moment,
and that in ten years from now it will mean
another £6,000,000, and in 20 years another
£24,000,000.

In addition to that the Minister of Labour
has told us what the direct contribution is
going to be, but he has not told us all. He
has tried to make it as attractive as possible.
The Minister of Health in Great Britain has
told us that it is eventually going to involve a charge of £760,000,000 upon the State,
a capital charge of £760,000,000, a larger sum
than the National Debt in 1913, and that at a
time when industry is struggling for its very
existence, and at a time when the outlook
in regard to employment is not at all rosy.
It is certainly not bright in Great Britain,
and I am sorry to say that the numbers of
unemployed in Ulster are larger in proportion to the population than in Great Britain,
due to the fact that the two main industries,
linen and shipbuilding, are in a somewhat
parlous condition at the moment. I may be
wrong in that, but I can be corrected if I
am. I will support the Bill, and will pay
any contributions as far as I am concerned,
believing in the great injunction that we
should all try to bear each others' burdens if
we can and help those who cannot help themselves, but at the same time it is well for us
to know exactly the obligations we have to
face.
We in Northern Ireland will have to pay
our share of the £760,000,000, because it is
well for this House to remember that it is
the Imperial Parliament that imposes and
collects 90 per cent. of all the taxes we have
to pay in Northern Ireland, so that we have
to pay our share of the £760,000,000. There
is only one compensation, and that is that if
we did not adopt the Act in Northern Ireland
on somewhat similar lines to the Act passed
in Great Britain, we would make a present
of our share of Imperial contribution which
would be spent on the other side. In our
financial relationships with Great Britain,
when we are adjusting our contribution we
will get some reduction to balance our contribution under the Imperial Act.
I want to remind the House of an observation I made as an interruption in the speech
of the Minister of Labour, and to which the
Member for West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen) referred. Contributions in respect of National Health Insurance and
Unemployment Insurance, and now the contribution that has to be paid for this most
admirable purpose, have got to be paid by
industry whether industry makes a profit or
not. Let that never be lost sight of. It is
all very well for the Minister of Labour to
tell the House that in the linen trade, with a
wages bill of so much per week, the contributions will only amount to £150 a year.
That is a dividend of 5 per cent. on £3,000,
and how many firms are in the happy position
to-day of being able to pay a dividend? That
is why I am timid about the financial proposals we propose to adopt in conformity
with what is being done on the other side. I
only hope that when they work out we will
find that things will not be as black as one
might expect, and I hope that the trade outlook may improve, and that the burden that
is being placed both on the employer and the
workman will be such that both will be able
to bear it and carry on.
I want again in a few sentences to show
exactly what Great Britain has done-and
we are following in line with them-in regard to social reform during the past few
years. If you take what may be called
Social Services-and here I am quoting one
of the finest financial experts in Great
Britain who himself was Chancellor of the
Exchequer including the Poor Rate, Local
'Rate, Health Insurance, Unemployment Insurance, Workmen's Compensation and Old-
Age Pensions, in 1911 the charges covering
these different items came to the sum
of £30,000,000. What are they to-day?
£169,000,000. Our friends on the Opposition
Benches sometimes criticise the Government
for not being sympathetic enough, but these
contributions to the social services mean a
contribution of £3 18s. Od. per head of the
population. How does that compare with
the other countries throughout the world?
In Germany for similar services the contribution per head of the pepulation is
£1 12s. Od., in France 16s., in Belgium 48.,
and in Italy 3s. These countries have free
access to our markets and are competing
with the manufacturers and merchants of
(Great Britain and Ireland, and the industries of our country contribute to the
extent of £3 18s. Od. per head while these
other countries are paying only a trifle. They
have free access to our markets and take away
a large share of our trade, while we on the
other hand are precluded from entering into
their markets except we get over a very
high tariff wall. That is one of the thoughts
that trouble me in regard to the future of
the industries of this country.
Then, again, take the question of local
rates, a very important element to deal with
when we are considering a matter of this
kind. I have only got the figures for
England and Wales, but the ratio will be
probably somewhat similar, though I hope it
will not be quite as much in Northern Ireland. Twenty years ago-in 1904-the amount
raised locally was £56,000,000. If we take the
financial year 1924-25 we find the local tax-
'payer had to pay the huge sum of
£142,000,000. A very significant thing in connection with this increase is that in the
first thirteen years of the twenty it was
£19,000,000, while during the last seven
years it has been £67,000,000. I have given
the House in rough outline these figures to
show what the Government of Great Britain
has been doing during the last twenty years.
I have also given them to show the heavy
burden that both the ratepayers and the tax-
Widows' Pensions Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Second Reading.
[Sir Robert Anderson]
payers of Great Britain and Northern Ireland have to face at the present moment.
With that huge burden I cannot see how we
can expect the prosperity we would like.
To my mind one of the greatest questions
we have got to face to-day is that of unemployment, and anything that will act as a
barrier to finding work for our people is to
be deprecated. Some of my hon. Friends on
the Opposition Benches may ask me "What
is your remedy?" My remedy can be put
into a sentence or two-Harder work by the
employer, less time spent on the golf links
and in recreation and pleasure, more time
spent in the office and in going round the
various details of the works to see where
greater efficiency can be brought about and
where economy can be secured. That may be
an unpleasant truth to state, but I am acting
up to it myself in my own works. There is
nothing else for it if you are going to carry
on.
But there must also be harder workand I know my hon. Friends will not deprecate my making this statement-on the part
of the workers and the employees, because
when everything is said and done both employer and employee either stand or fall together. Without the co-operation of both in
these critical times I cannot see how anything can be accomplished effectively. Then
there must be greater production. My hon.
Friends may disagree with me in this respect, but unless there is greater productionand I speak as one who has some knowledge
of the markets of the world-and we have
cheaper goods to place upon those markets
we are going to be left behind in the race.
It is only an economic commonplace when
I say that we can only pay for the food
supplies we have to exist on by what we
export, and if our exports decrease and our
imports increase then we are living upon
our capital, and capital is a thing that cannot continue for ever.
Another thing is that unless taxation comes
down in this country and in Great Britain
from the height to which it has soared, in my
judgment you will not have the revival of
trade which we all hope for and pray for and
look forward to. I am sorry if I have exhausted the patience of hon. Members in
trying to put before them some of these
economic truths, as I hope my hon. Friends
opposite will think them, and the viewpoint
I take in regard to legislation of this
character. There is no Member of this
House more sympathetic towards social reform than I am. The Measure now before
this House is a great act of faith on the
part of this Government, and I sincerely hope
that the faith they have will be justified
in the coming years, that the optimism they
must have that trade is going to revive, and
that unemployment is going to be lessened
will be amply fulfilled.

I remember one formidable orator, the late

"Poverty: a Study of City Life."
years ago I got that book, and I know something, therefore, of the conditions that prevail in the city. I cannot go into these
points, but everybody admits that up to now

Dr. MORRISON: The second and third
classes, namely the distributor and the consumer, are able, in my opinion, to look after

through all the remedial social legislation

the State aiding in Land Purchase, in

Certificates, the building of schools, and

Church to which I belong, and it has been

years that no widow or orphan of that

that he should become a contributor to the
Orphan Society, under which for a contribution of 1d per week he was guaranteed a
pension for his widow and children. He did
that. Two years after that time I had the
experience of delivering that woman of her
seventh child in a corner of a double-roomed
cottage with the dead body of her husband
in the opposite corner. That woman and her
seven children were provided for. We on
this side are often charged with being unsympathetic and with having done nothing.
The hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin) has stated that twenty years ago he

--and I could count perhaps a dozen hon.

There is another case that illustrates the

I knew of another case where a

and

This Bill is on a contributory basis, and
for that very reason, to my mind at any rate,
is a great achievement, because it will foster
and encourage self-respect. By these weekly
payments a man will be securing his own
fortune. He will be securing the fortune of
his family. He will be helping to secure his
own fortune and the fortune of his family.
He will be helped to do it by his employer.
He will be helped to do it by the State, and
it will be due to his own exertions and largely
his own responsibility, and it will not be
due to charity. I am convinced that
nothing could possibly sap our pride and
independence as a nation more quickly, more
thoroughly, and more completely than the
thought that the workingman was to contribute nothing, and that the State and the
charitable sentimental public would do all.
That has been too much the tendency in the
past. There has been too much sentimentality
of the wrong kind. You turn people into
paupers. You do not allow them and do not
expect them to help themselves at all. You
do away with their self-respect, and eventually will do away with their capacity to help
themselves. This wrapping up in cotton
wool renders the limbs incapable of movement, and renders the brain incapable of
working. I do not believe in that, but I do
believe in this Bill. I do believe that in this
we have a right thing, and so I congratulate
the Government on having followed the
English lines.
There is one point I would just like to
mention before I sit down. Although to the
industrial worker and his employer this ill
is going to mean an increase of 2d each, the

Mr. BEATTIE: 1 rise to
attention of this House to the
which I placed on the Order Paper and the

question was in my opinion a violation of the
principle laid down by the Imperial Parliament in connection with the transfer of
prison officials from the Imperial Authorities to the Northern Ireland Authorities.
Under Section 55 of the Government
of Ireland Act, 1920, you
will find
provision made whereby the conditions
of Civil Servants must not be worsened
in any way by their transfer. I will
quote you the Section of the Act which
I think is all-sufficient to warrant the
Minister of Home Affairs granting the same
remuneration to his prison officials as is at
present paid to the prison officials in Great
Britain. Section 55 (i) of the Government of
Ireland Act 1920, definitely states:-
Subject to the provisions of this Act, all
existing Irish officers in the civil service
of the Crown who are not provided for
under the last preceding Section, and are
at the appointed day serving as Irish
officers shall, after that day, continue to
hold their offices by the same tenure and
upon the same terms and conditions (including conditions as to salaries and superannuation) as heretofore and shall be
liable to perform the same duties as theretofore,-
I think that Section is sufficient to warrant
the Civil Servants in the Prisons Service in
claiming justice in regard to their conditions.
I have here the scales of wages paid to the
English prison officials. Take chief warders,
second class. The pay in the English prisons
is £3 15s per week with a bonus calculated
on the cost of living figures of £2 0s 10d,
making a total wage of £5 15s 10d. Then we
come
Sir DAWSON BATES: Does my hon.

The re-grading scheme took place in 1920.

55.
We come to the principal warders, another
class of warder employed in prisons. In
England the pay of a principal warder is
216s per week and the bonus is £1 13s 9d,
making a total wage of £4 9s 9d. In the
Free State the principal warders are paid
£2 13s and the bonus is £2 1s 2d, making a
total wage of £4 14s 2d. Now take Northern
Ireland, which is supposed to be on parallel
lines with Great Britain. The wage of a
principal warder is £2 13s, and the bonus
£1 12s 9d, making a total wage of £4 5s 9d,
or a reduction of 4s per week.
Next we have the clerk-schoolmaster grade.
We find a reduction there also. In the case
of warders we find their pay is £2 5s per
week in England plus £1 9s 9d bonus, making
a total wage of £3 14s 9d. In the Free State
the pay is £2 3s and the bonus £1 16s 9d,
making a total of £3 19s 9d. In Northern
Ireland the wage is £2 3s and the bonus
£1 9s, making a total of £3 12s, a reduction
for Northern Ireland of 2s 9d per week.
The reductions in the wages of these
warders have been in operation since
October, 1923. We might naturally ask why
the Home Office has not conformed to the
regulations in regard to the transferred
officers of the prisons and placed them upon
the same footing as the present warders, but
we find

The Act of 1920 expressly protects all existing
Civil Servants against any alteration in their
terms of employment, rates of pay, or anything affecting those matters. It also provides that in case the Government which they
may elect to serve do anything which they
think unjust or unfair they have the right
to go to the Civil Service Committee. I may
remind my hon. Friend that the rate of pay
in England and Ireland at the time of the
passing of the Home Rule Act was the same,
and it was not until 1923 that the British
Government saw fit to make a slight increase.
I think the increase was something like 2s
to a man after he had served fifteen years.
The Prison Warders applied to the Government for an increase, and, after consultation
with my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, and having regard to the financial
resources of Northern Ireland, it was decided
that the increase could not be granted.
Accordingly the Prison Warders took the

Oral Answers to Questions.
TRAINING SETTLEMENTS FOR
UNEMPLOYED.
1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Labour whether he proposes to establish in
Northern Ireland training settlements for
unemployed young men; whether he has
asked the British Minister of Labour to
take into the settlements established in
England a number of young men from
Northern Ireland, and whether he does not
think that this work should be done at
home.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The Imperial Minister of Labour
has decided to open, as an experiment, two
centres in England for giving general workshop instruction to a limited number of unemployed young men and also an agricultural course for a few selected men who
have been accepted for emigration under the
Empire Settlement Act.
I have not asked the Imperial Minister of
Labour to take into any of his centres young
men from Northern Ireland, but I am in
close touch with the Imperial Authorities in
order to secure in the most practicable
manner similar advantages for our young
men here.

Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of

beet in Northern Ireland; whether he is
aware of the fact that the Development

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): The reply that I gave yesterday
to the question addressed to me on this
subject by the hon. Member for North
Belfast (Mr. Kyle) covers the first part of

As regards the second part, though no
officially aware of the Commissioner's

defer this visit pending the receipt of a
report from a Dutch expert who was then
conducting an independent examination of
the possibilities of Northern Ireland in relation to the establishment of a sugar beet
industry.
It is not competent for me to say when a
deputation will investigate the industry in
England. That, of course, is purely a matter
for the Commission.

MILK INSPECTION POWERS IN

6. Mr. KYLE (for Mr. William McMullen)

right to inspect these dairies.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is a fact that
the Public Health Officers of the Belfast
Corporation have no general authority to
inspect dairies outside the city boundary.
Those dairies are, however, subject to inspection by the officials of the districts in
which they are situated, and it is understood that the Local Government Authorities
of those outside areas are prepared to afford
facilities to the officials of the Belfast Corporation to inspect the dairies in conjunction
with their own officers.
It was proposed in a recent Bill brought
before Parliament by the Belfast Corporation to obtain powers from Parliament
to inspect dairies outside the city boundary,
but this clause was dropped in view of the
anticipated opposition from the representatives of the outside local authorities.
This particular difficulty has already been
brought under the notice of the Commission
which has been set up to examine into
Local Government services, and pending the
Report of that Commission it is not proposed
to take any action in this respect.

Government Loans and Exchequer

Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr Pollock): A few days ago I had the privilege of
submitting to the Committee a Money Resolution as a
necessary prelude and forerunner to the Bill which is now about
to be considered by the House. In the statement that I made I entered with some detail
into the circumstances which render the
present Measure necessary. I am quite aware
that financial matters are not exactly exhilarating in their character, and I hope that I
will not try the patience of the House too
much if I recapitulate some of the statements I then made and enter with some detail
into the various questions that arise out of
this Bill, copies of which I presume are in
the hands of hon. Members.
When we entered upon our career in 1921
as an autonomous State, our financial circumstances, and especially our financial relations
with Great Britain, were necessarily in a
very nebulous state. We had no experience
1253 Government Loans Bill-

14 OCTOBER 1925
Second Reading.
whatever to guide us in many of the paths on
which we were required to enter. An additional complication arose from the disturbed
condition of the country, due to the incursions of Southern malcontents.
It will also be apparent even to a superficial observer, that the commerce and industry of the country during the four initial
years of our separate existence could not fail
to be prejudiced by the extraordinary
economic world paralysis following the war.
From the commercial point of view, indeed,
no more unfavourable period could have been
selected to establish a small State with
federal relations to the Kingdom.
The commercial relations of Ulster are
world-wide, and as our two great staple
industries--shipbuilding and linen-are especially sensitive and vulnerable to worldconditions-it was hardly to be expected that
the revenue of the Province could fail to be
prejudically affected in a like degree to that
of Great Britain.
During these four years an additional burden was thrown on the Province, by reason of
the acute unemployment, consequent on the
general industrial depression, which unhappily has not yet been abated by the only
possible solvent, viz., a return to normal
trading conditions. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
But yet notwithstanding these undoubted
disadvantages, it is surely something to the
credit of our Government and to the people.
of our Province that we have succeeded in
maintaining the essential cervices of the Province on the basis of British standards, and
at the same time have been able to contribute
a sum of about 18 millions to the upkeep of
the Army and Navy, and the payment of the
interest of the National Debt.
It is also worthy of note-and I think it
necessary to mention these things in view of
the financial step that we propose to takethat apart from such provision as I have
mentioned our annual surpluses in revenue
and expenditure account during the four
years have amounted to a considerable sum.
In the year 1921-22 we had a surplus of
£30,917; in 1922-23, £32,042; in 1923-24
£46,778, and in 1924-25, £150,740, making a
total of £260,477 of an accumulated fund
under this head.
Our Sinking Funds have also been fully
maintained, the total amount laid aside for
ensuring a permanent return from all our
capital funds, such as land purchase
annuities, etc., being £117,000.
There are also other factors which are not
unworthy of mention, when we are asking
Parliamentary authority for the first time
to borrow in the open market such sums
as we require to lend to the local authorities
throughout the Province for their capital
expenditure.
There is no better barometer of a country's
economic and financial strength than the
relation which its export trade bears to
its imports. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Bearing this in mind, therefore, it is surely
a matter of no little satisfaction-apart altogether from our people it must be a matter
of satisfaction to Members of this House,
as it is to the Government, to find that on
investigation of the latest trade statistics
available, i.e., those for the last calendar
year, that notwithstanding the unparalleled
depression in our two great staple industries,
we have succeeded in maintaining a favourable trade balance. Such a result, emphasising as it does the energy and industry of
our trading community, augurs well for the
future prosperity of our Province, when the
world has emerged from its present conditions of inertia.
Before I enter upon a categorical investigation of the import of the different clauses
of the Measure, I should like to advert for
a few moments to the circumstances which
render this Measure necessary.
The practice of the British Government
in regard to financing local loans-that
is to say for the provision of money to lend
to local authorities for these schemes-has
been to establish a special fund, which is
known popularly in the market as "Local
Loans Fund," and the Stock which is issued
is known as Local Loans Stock. This fund
has been fed from time to time by the
issue of this Local Loans Stock, which is
quoted every day in the market, and is then
dealt with on the Stock Exchange from time
to time.
Up to now we have not found it necessary
to adopt the British practice for this reason,
that during the four years of our autonomous existence the amounts which we had to
deal with have not been of a very important
character, and in addition we have out of
our own resources and by our temporary
borrowings sufficient funds to enable us to
provide for the necessities of local authorities
and others.
our
There is no doubt whatever that
method has two serious defects. The most
important defect is that it is not legitimate
finance to borrow money temporarily as we
have done, and which is subject to repayment at any time, and at the same time
lend that money to other people, who will
only repay that money after a long term
of years, generally 60 years. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) That is too dangerous finance.
Another defect in our system is that it did
not lend itself to suitable accountancy. It
mixed up all our loans with our ordinary
accounts, and it is very undesirable from
the point of view of the information which
Parliament naturally desires in connection
with the loans which from time to time we
issued to local authorities.
1255 Government Loans Bill-
Second Reading. 1256
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Pollock]
It did not matter very much so long as
our loans were of a negligible character as
they have been, and were confined to comparatively small amounts, but when these
operations assume greater magnitude the
system does not lend itself to a satisfactory
method of accounts and the submission to
Parliament of the financial results of loan
legislation.
We have, therefore, decided by the introduction of this Measure to follow the British
practice of providing a separate and distinct
fund, which we call the Local Loans Fund.
From that fund will be issued all moneys
required by local authorities and other outside parties, which will be found in the
Schedule to the Bill on page 13, and also
all sums received by way of income from
the local authorities shall be lodged to that
specific account. I do not think I need
argue the advantage of that, because it
retains in a water-tight compartment, as it
were, all the loans operations which we
undertake, and, therefore, Parliament can be
informed from time to time as we go on
of the nature and volume of all these transactions.
In order to provide the money to establish
this fund, to endow it, to enable it to lend
these moneys, we propose to issue an Ulster
Loan Stock, almost corresponding with the
British Local Loan Stock, of which we have
heard so much for many years.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: The price?
Mr. POLLOCK: That is not arranged, but
I think it will be satisfactory when we reach
that point. The dividends on that stock
will be met from the returns which we receive from the local authorities who borrow
the money from us, that is to say, the one
presumably almost will balance the other.
It will be seen from the Measure that its
scope extends beyond that of the British
Local Loans Fund by bringing within its
operations certain loans and advances in
addition to those which may be strictly
described as "Local Loans." These additional
purposes are set out in the Schedule to the
Bill. They include certain agricultural and
educational loans which are described in
the Schedule as 'development loans," a
small item in the shape of Housing Loans to
Civil Servants; also advances to the Claims
Fund set up under the Intoxicating Liquor
Act, 1923. The latter is repaid over a term
of years by the trade.
"
It has also been thought desirable to take
power for dealing in a similar manner with
any future capital schemes which Parliament may authorise.
I would point out, however, that the term
"Government Loans," which is used in the
Bill, does not mean that the Fund will
become the medium for all classes of Exchequer advances. For example, advances
to the Unemployment Fund would continue
to be made from the Exchequer as in the
past on the ground that this is a very substantial account, and it is desirable to keep
it a section by itself.
The Loans Fund provided by this Measure
will be administered as a separate and inpendent Budget for the solvency of which
full provision is made, and will remain
independent of the State Budget except in
so far as the State liability exists to meet
any deficiency of income or losses by bad
debts. There can be no question that the
establishment of the Fund and the methods
of its operations will inevitably tend to a
greater efficiency in the administration of
the loan system.
The first Clause provides for the repayment of outstanding Exchequer advances
from the Government Loans Fund to the Exchequer and for all powers of the Exchequer
in regard to such Loans being for the
future transferred to the Fund. During the
four years that have passed we have made
large advances to public authorities and
others of moneys out of our own resources,
and in order that the whole of the liability
in respect of these Loans be consolidated into
one amount we must claim repayment of
these moneys from the Loans in order to
square our finances.

a limit of £375,000. This opening Clause
provides for an annual limit in respect of
Local Loans inclusive of Civil Service Housing Loans and Development Loans, and a
second limit in respect of the remaining purposes described in the Schedule. Authority
for these limits will be sought each year by

Clause 3 provides for the constitution of
Ulster Loans Stock. The Stock will be redeemable at the expiration of fifty years
from the date of its creation. This Clause
imposes a charge upon the Consolidated
Fund, that is, upon the credit of the Province
in respect of the payment of dividends and in
respect of the ultimate redemption of the
Loan. These provisions are necessary in
order to insure the due payment of dividends
and the redemption of the Loan at the proper
time no matter what contingency may arise.
The fixing of a redemption date for the
Stock does not follow the British system,
where the Local Stock is irredeemable, but it
is thought that with a new venture such as
this, a redeemable Stock is more attractive to
the investor.
Under this Clause it would also be
optional to Government to redeem Stock
before the final redemption date on giving
due notice to the holders.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: What is the
redemption period?
Mr. POLLOCK: That is a matter which I
do not think should be discussed in this
House prior to the circulation and publication of our prospectus, I do not think

Clause 5 deals with the Income Account
as apart from the Capital Account. In an

within the Fund. Clause 5 deals with the
Income Account and provides for payment to
this account of all interest due by the borrowers and for payment out of the account
of the dividends due on the Stock, Sinking
Fund payments, and expense of management
and administration. Any temporary deficiency in the Income Account will be met
in the first instance, from the Exchequer,
but if the Income Account for any year
should prove insufficient for the charges made
upon it, then the deficiency must be voted
by Parliament. In this way, provision is
made for the solvency of the Fund, and
Parliament will be kept in close touch with
the progress of loan transactions. Where
there is an excess of income, power is given
to the Ministry to transfer such sum as they
may think fit to the Exchequer as an alternative to allowing it to accumulate in the Fund.
Clause 6 deals with the Capital Account.
This account will receive the repayments
from borrowings of the principal of loans
which have been made, and in addition sums
will be transferred to it from time to time
out of the Income Account to make good the
deficiency arising from the issue of Ulster
Loans Stock at a discount, and to cover the
expenses of the issue of the Stock. The
issue expenses will thus be met, in the first
instance, from the Capital Account, which
will be recouped over a period of years out
of the Income Account. No separate Sinking
Fund Account will be opened, but the moneys
will form part of the Capital Account and
will be available for re-issue as Local Loans
in the ordinary way.
Clause 7 indicates that there will be one
Cash Balance in respect of the Fund out
of which all demands will be paid. It further
provides for the temporary investment in

I come now to Clause 8. This Clause is
designed to ensure the solvency of the Fund
by providing for a Vote from Parliament
to make good any bad debt. A bad debt can
only occur when a loan is advanced upon
insufficient security or when circumstances
have so altered as to render the payment of
a loan impracticable. A bad debt cannot be
written off except by express permission of
Parliament. It must be returned to Parliament and the authority of Parliament for the
wiping out or writing off-to use commercial
language of the bad debt, that is, a case of
default of the borrower. Should there be
subsequently any return of that money that
money must, of course, be lodged in the Exchequer as an extra receipt, because of the
fact that the Exchequer must make up the
bad debt and therefore if there is any repayment-
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Any composition.
Mr. POLLOCK-Any composition-my hon.
Friend is familiar with business operationsthat composition will go to the credit of the
Exchequer Account.
Clause 9 merely relates to the presentation
of accounts and the laying before Parliament
of a statement of all losses incurred under
the system.
I now propose to deal with the second part

Clause 10 allows for the countersignature of warrants for Treasury Bills by
a Principal Officer in the Comptroller and
Auditor-General's Department. Under the
law as it stands no provision is made for a
substitute in the case of illness or absence
of the Comptroller. The section also amends
the Clause of the Treasury Bills Act, 1877,
in its application to Northern Ireland, in the
sense of authorising the Ministry of Finance
instead of the Exchequer Bank to prepare
Treasury Bills. The actual practice in
Northern Ireland differs from that in
England where the Treasury Bills are prepared by the Bank of England.
Clause 11 (1) The alteration in the date of
presentation of the Consolidated Fund
Account is made so that it may coincide with
that for the annual Appropriation Accounts.
'As most of the information has already
appeared in the Public Income and Expenditure Account published each June, no
inconvenience will be caused to Members of
Parliament or the public.
Clause 11 (2) amends the Exchequer and
Audit Act of 1921 by giving the Comptroller
and Auditor-General discretion in the matter
of the class of audit he shall carry out. As
the Northern Ireland Act stands at present,
his audit must be a detailed audit including
a full arithmetical check, and he can only
be absolved from it in the case of any expenditure if the Ministry of Finance lay a
'Minute before Parliament empowering him
to a apply a test check. That was the
British system, but it was altered in 1921
so as to provide for a test check being the
Rule, and a full check is only required if
the Treasury ask for it. The effect of this
provision will be to give the Comptroller
and Auditor-General powers identical to
those which are possessed by the Imperial
Comptroller and Auditor-General. The
Ministry of Finance is satisfied that this
change should now be made, and in any case
the Public Accounts Committee expressed
their views in its favour in May last.

I now come to Clause 14. This section has
been inserted following representations made
by the Comptroller and Auditor-General to
the effect that statutory authority is necessary
to cover an economical arrangement made by
the Minister of Finance whereby money is
borrowed temporarily by means of an overdraft at the Exchequer Bank. The Comptroller and Auditor-General, while satisfied
that the practice of borrowing by overdraft
is sound and ought not to be disturbed, has
pointed out that the existing law does not
cover this method of borrowing, because
such overdrafts are not temporary borrowings in a technical sense, in that moneys are
not actually credited to the Exchequer by
the Bank. This does not accord with the
1-rovisions of the Appropriation Acts whereby
all borrowings, whether by Treasury Bills or
otherwise, must be paid into the Exchequer.
The Ministry is advised that there is substance in the point raised by the Comptroller
and Auditor-General, and this, the earliest
opportunity, is taken to obtain authority for
this method of borrowing. I should indicate
that though special statutory power has to be
obtained for this purpose, the overdraft must,
for all statutory purposes, be treated as a
normal borrowing; it cannot be utilised for
the purpose of raising money beyond the
amounts authorised by Statute.
I have endeavoured to explain the main
provisions of this Measure as well as the

operations, and I am grateful for the
patience with which the House has listened

I have only now to add a few sentences by

the financial centre of the world, and I have
a feeling that this subject opens up a fresh

desired it, that the Treasury would have.
fagreed to give its guarantee for the present
public issue.

Mr. KYLE: This very important Measure
has been introduced in an excellent speech
by the Minister of Labour. In the debate
which followed that speech some very strange
things have happened in this House. Practically all the speeches delivered have been
in criticism of the Bill. Members on the

very hard things about the Bill, about its
finances and about the burden it is going
to place on industry, but because the
Measure happens to have been introduced
by the Minister of Labour in the Northern
Parliament they are going to support it. I
think the most surprising thing of all has
been the statement that it is because the
Minister of Labour has said that it was
either this Bill or nothing that other hon.
Members of this House are going to support
it.
It has been made clear in the speech of the
Minister of Labour in this House that the
intention of the Tory Party is to do away
with pensions and substitute insurance. In
the speech of the Minister yesterday he made
that quite clear. I think that those Members of the House who have taken the trouble
to read the Bill will be bound to admit that
it deliberately sets out to take away the
present basis of Old Age Pensions and to
substitute an insurance scheme. One hon.
Member in the course of his speech stated
that this inability of the State in Ireland to
deal with widows and orphans was a stigma

Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester), when
she made that statement, realised that we
in Northern Ireland are going to follow the
example of Great Britain, the only country
in the world that has made a Widows'
Pension scheme or a Mothers' Pension scheme
a contributory scheme. New Zealand in 1912,
Denmark in 1914, 40 States and 2 Territories
in the United States of America, 5 out of 9
Canadian Provinces, Mothers' Pensions in
the Union of South Africa, 4 out of 5 States

in Australia-all these places have non-contributory widows' and mothers' pensions.

up this

Lloyd George laid a contribution on the employer and he advanced a very strong argument in favour of doing that. He said the
employer was being asked to pay because he
was going to get very much better service
than he would get without the National
Health Insurance Act. His employees were
not going to be out of work so long. They
were going to be returned to him much more
quickly, and were going to be kept in much
better health as they were going to have
adequate medical attendance. That, I think,
was a reasonable argument, but there is no
such argument in connection with this. If
a workman dies it is not usual to consider
his employer ought to provide for his wife
and children.
Mr. ANDREWS: Many of them do to a
certain extent.
Mr. JOHNSTONE: They may do, but, in
any case, it is not usual for an employer
to provide for a man's wife and children.
1 think if he is very generous he may give
them some assistance, but he is very seldom
saddled with them altogether. If he does
give them assistance it is purely a matter of
charity-exactly the same charity that leads
some of us to give a beggar a penny in the
street. Exactly the same thing happens in
regard to a man of 65 years of age. An employer does not as a rule pension a man at
65. He may keep him on to do odd jobs.
That is a different thing to giving him a
regular settled State pension.
The people who are going to benefit by
this Bill are the ratepayers. At the present
time it is the duty of the ratepayers to look
after a man when he becomes 65 if he is not
fit for work-to look after him until he be
comes eligible for the Old-Age Pension. It
is the duty of the ratepayers also to look
after widows and children who are left unprovided for, and it should be the duty of
the whole community and not of the employers to pay the contribution. I maintain
that it is very wrong indeed that the employer should be asked to pay for these, because there is no justification for it. He is
being saddled now with an extra charge for
which he gets no return except in so far as
he may be a ratepayer.

I would like also to refer to some places
away from home. Perhaps we think we are
glorifying ourselves in presenting this Bill in
England and Scotland and Northern Ireland,
but have hon. Members ever studied out
what is being done in the Dominions as far
as pensions are concerned? Pensions are
a very old thing in the Dominions. Take
the case of Canada-Alberta or Manitobaand New Zealand. Those places pay
pensions, and they are provided by the
municipalities. We do not come in with a
Bill of that description; we come in with a
Bill with a price on it. Those who do not
pay do not benefit. I may quote this
statement:--
The Act passed in Manitoba is most
thoroughgoing in its provisions, for it
makes allowances to any mother of a
neglected or dependant child or children,
whenever such mother is a widow or her
husband is an inmate of a penal institute
or an insane asylum, or because of
physical disability, or unable to support
the family, provided that the mother lacks
adequate means of properly caring for
such children, and provided that the
mother does not go into industry.
We do not want the mother to go into industry. We in the Labour movement believe
that widowed mothers should be taken out of
industry and that the State should give her
sufficient to maintain her in her own home.
The amount provided in this Bill will not
enable that to be done. I find that in
Australia and in British Columbia all
pensions for widows are derived from the
State, and there is none of them, so far as I
know, contributory; they are all noncontributory. If we are going to remain
thirty years behind the times I regret it. I
would like to see Ulster, which is a small
State, leading the Dominions and every other
country under the sun; but if it is going to
conduct its business as it has been doing,
taking what it gets from the Imperial Parliament, it is going to remain thirty years
behind the times.
Take West Australia, for example. They
have a State Children's Department, which
pays 9/- per week in respect of all children.
It has a scale for widows of £9 per month.
Those seem to be very decent sums, and are
adequate to keep widows out of industry. I
could quote other instances. In no case are
the pensions contributory. We in the
North of Ireland are going to be foolish
enough to fall into the invidious position of
adopting something which is obsolete,
and which does not meet the requirenients of the widows and orphans.

passing the Bill as it stands.

said, on the lines suggested by the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin), in order
that industry may get a fillip and get on its
feet. Was he sincere? Does he mean to suggest to this House that we should stop asking
industry to contribute, stop asking the employed contributor to contribute, and that
we should stop paying benefit? We can only
pay out benefit if we receive contributions.
The Minister of Labour made it perfectly
clear that we are not living in a land flowing
with milk and honey, that there was no tap
he could turn on that would pour gold into
the coffers of the Government.
Mr. KYLE: Then it is an Insurance Bill.
Mr. GORDON: It is an Insurance Bill,
and we have admitted that it is an Insurance
Bill.
Mr. KYLE: And not a Pensions Bill at all.
Mr. GORDON: It is a Pensions Bill, but
it is on a contributory basis. However, I
pass from that suggestion. I do not think
my hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle) was sincere when
he suggested that we should stop paying contributions, because when he stated that the
workers were the producers of all things-
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Mr. GORDON: If he meant that, if he
'were sincere why did he speak as if the
workers were the producers of all things and
demand that the workers should receive the
full fruits of their labours—
Mr. KYLE: Give us that and we will be
Fatisfied.
Mr. GORDON: And why then did the hon.
Gentleman (Mr. William McMullen) who
opened the debate say "Do not crush industry?" He said that an impost in the shape
of an increased contribution would crush in-
'dustry. Does he mean to tell this House,
does he mean to suggest that if an employer
who employs six men, say, is called upon to
pay an increased contribution of 1s per week
for those six men it will crush that industry?
My hon. Friend (Mr. William McMullen)
opened his speech by entering the domain
of economics. I am not going to contend with
him, but it is plain to an average man like
myself, who would not attempt to enter into
the domain of Socialistic economics in the
manner in which the hon. Member entered.
that an industry that is able to employ six
men and yet cannot pay an impost of 1s per
'week is in a peculiar position.
I think I have gone fairly widely over the
various arguments that have been put forward by hon. Members of this House. Some
have been most complimentary to my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Labour, and
Come have criticised with a blandness that has
amazed me, but at the same time have expressed their approval of the provisions of the
Bill and are determined to give all the help
they possibly can in order that the Bill may
be carried to a successful issue. I do not
think I need refer to anything that has been
said by the hon. Member from the East where
all the wisdom comes from.
Mr. BEATTIE: The wise men.
we
Mr. GORDON: Yes, the wise men from the
East. I make no reference to what he said.
If I did I would place him in an exceedingly
awkward position with respect to his
colleagues. I am not going to do it, but I
will say one thing. One of his colleagues.
the Member for West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen) suggested that this is an impost
on industry, and said were going to
destroy industry. What does the Leader of
the Opposition (Mr. Kyle) say? He says "Stop
asking the work people to pay arrears for a
period of time until industry gets on its
feet." When you stop asking contributions
it means you stop giving benefits to the people.
The hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Beattie) said quite different. I know these
hon. Members will be quite amazed when they
read their speeches and compare one with
the other. They will compare notes and be
more anxious in the future to get together
before coming to discuss and criticise a Bill
of this character. The Member for East

Did he mean that industry should give a

Mr. BEATTIE: I said that the State was

Seed Potatoes Supply Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of this
Bill is to ratify arrangements which were
entered into by the Minister of Finance, the
Minister of Commerce and myself with certain Boards of Guardians, with the object of
supplying seed potatoes to small farmers and
labourers occupying a small portion of
ground who would otherwise, owing to the
bad season, have been unable to get seed.
Hon. Members will remember what a bad
season 1924 was. The result was that seed in
certain districts, particularly in County Fermanagh, was extremely scarce, and unless
something was done by the Government for
these farmers and small occupiers they
would have had the greatest possible diffi
culty in getting seed, and possibly in some
cases they could not have got any, but in any
case they could not have got the proper
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Mr. Beattle.
variety. Steps were taken by the Government to invite the co-operation of Boards of
Guardians, and as a result the Boards of
Guardians of Enniskillen and Irvinestown
were satisfied as to the need for a scheme of
this character and offered to co-operate with
the Government. In these cases the Boards
of Guardians invited applications from small
farmers who held land not exceeding £15
valuation and labourers occupying a small
portion of ground. The farmer received up
to 5 cwt, and the labourer 2 cwt.
The Minister of Agriculture purchased the
seed and distributed it. The total cost to the
Government was £10 a ton, and the price
charged by the Government to the farmer
was £7 a ton. The money is recovered from
the county councils and they in turn levy a
rate on the applicants. The rate is spread
over a period of two years, 1926-1927. The
total cost to the Government is £3 a ton. The
amount distributed in the case of Enniskillen
was 80 tons and in the case of Irvinestown
69 tons. I am glad to say the scheme turned
out a great success, and from the reports I
have received I believe the potato crop all
over the County Fermanagh this season is
going to be very satisfactory.

question from the right hon. Gentleman in

COST OF GOVERNMENT PUBLICATIONS.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Finance if he can state the actual cost of
Government publications issued during the
preceding year to local authorities in the Six
Counties.
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): On behalf of
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) I have
been asked to answer this question. It
would require considerable research to obtain any reliable estimate of the actual cost
of publications issued by the various Government Departments to Local Authorities as
distinct from the cost of free issues in
general.
I am satisfied, however, that the amount
involved would be in excess of £300, although
the total cost of all Government publications issued gratuitously during last year
exceeded £950.
BRITISH EMPIRE UNION CARNIVAL.
2. Mr. GYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether the Committee of the British
Empire Union Carnival recently applied for
an occasional licence to sell wines, spirits and
beer for consumption in the carnival
grounds; whether the licence was refused,
and if so on what grounds was the refusal
based.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): An occasional licence as indicated was applied for, but its grant was not
recommended.
Occasional licences are only granted when
it is considered, as laid down by the Statute
(25 and 26 Vie., cap. 22) "conducive to public
convenience, comfort and order" to do so. In
this case there were no fewer than nine
licensed houses in the immediate vicinity of
the Old Potato Market where the carnival
was held.
In these circumstances it did not appear
that the statutory conditions geverning the
grant of licences were fulfilled, and the issue
of a licence could not therefore be recommended.
Mr. GYLE: Arising out of that answer
would the Minister say was there any influence brought to bear on him or his Department through any Member of this House of
through any member of the licensed trade?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Certainly not.
Mr. DEVLIN: Are you sure?

Question of Procedure.
Mr. CRAWFORD: On a point of order, I
would like some information from the
Minister as to what happens in case questions
which appear on the Order paper are not
reached in the proper time? I had an
important question on the paper recently, as
I thought important, and I received a written
answer with respect to it. I was therefore
precluded from asking any supplementary
questions.
Mr. SPEAKER: The position is really
governed by our Standing Orders-Standing
Order 8, sub-section 5, where it lays down that
if a question is not reached at half-past three
o'clock the Minister to whom it is addressed
shall cause the answer to be printed in the
Official Report of the Parliamentary Debates
unless the Member has signified his desire
to postpone the question. Of course where
there is a considerable number of questions
down, an hon. Member would be wise to signify to me and to the Minister, before his
question is taken, if he desires to postpone it
in which case it will appear the next day,
but where a question is not answered owing
to not being reached, the answer is circulated
in the Parliamentary Reports, and I think
it is also the custom of the Government
Departments concerned to issue to each Member the answer to his question. Of course,
from that moment it is public property and
available to the Press. A Member is, of course,
not able to ask supplementary questions, and
the only cure for that is to ask fewer supplementaries on the earlier questions.
Mr. JOHNSTONE: In connection with
that I should like your ruling. Supposing a
question is not answered orally in the House
but a typewritten answer is given, as is the
custom I understand, is it then open for a
Member in case he is not satisfied with the
answer to raise the matter on the Motion for
Adjournment?
Mr. SPEAKER: Oh, yes, certainly.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is it not within the competence of a Member who puts a question
down on the Paper and when that question
is not answered in the House to put it down
again on a subsequent day? It is very important as supplementary questions are the
only methods by which he can get the truth
out of Ministers.
Mr. SPEAKER: No, I do not think he
would be in order in putting down the identical question, but he could put down for a
subsequent day as a question points which
he wished to raise as a supplementary question. On the matter of questions, I should
perhaps mention to the House with regard
to questions taken on Wednesdays, if they
are sent either by post or handed in to the
Clerk of the House in time before Four
o'clock on Mondays it will be quite possible
for them to appear on the Paper for answer
on Wednesdays.

Mr. BARBOUR: My right hon. Friend
(Mr. Pollock) yesterday made a comprehensive statement on the various provisions
of the important Measure entitled the
Widows, Orphans and Old-Age Contributory Pensions Bill. He touched on certain of the financial aspects, and in view of
this it is only necessary for me at the present time to make a very short statement
on this Money Resolution. The Resolution as usual provides the requisite
authority for charging upon Votes the
additional expenditure to be met by the State
under the Scheme, and it is divided into
three parts.
The first provides for the payment
annually into the Ministry of Finance
Pensions Account to be set up under Clause
11 (2) of the Act of a sum of £145,000 or
such lesser sum as the Ministry of Finance
may annually determine in each of the ten
years commencing on 1st April, 1926, to be
sufficient, having regard to the state of that
account and of the Pensions Account (N.I.)
from time to time. The maximum figure of
£145,000 represents the equated annual
charge in respect of the total cost of the
scheme for the ten-year period as nearly
as this can be estimated; according to the
calculations there is actually a surplus of
contributions from employers and employees
on the first three years after which the
Pensions after age 65 come into operation,
and, consequently, the expenditure rises.
This scheme of equalising payments over the
ten-vear period follows the practice in Great
Britain in the similar Act recently passed,
their corresponding figure being the fixed
annual payment of four million pounds.
After the ten-year period has expired, it
is left open for Parliament to re-assess the
contribution required from Government
sources to render the scheme solvent. The
expenditure in each year will depend
naturally on the number of widows and
orphans and the number of old-age
pensioners who benefit from the scheme. It
is estimated that the peak of the net expenditure will be in 1945-46, after which date
the contributions are expected to increase at
a slightly greater rate than the benefits on
account of the population becoming more
industrial.
on

the expenditure the Old Age Pensions
which become payable to insured persons
over 70 as from 1st July, 1926, by virtue of
this Bill. Provision for this is not included
in the maximum sum of £145,000 to which I
have referred, but will be met from an Old-
Age Pensions Vote in the ordinary way. It

Pensions of approximately £1,050,000 will
probably rise on the existing basis after a
period of about thirty years to approxi
mately £1,400,000, apart from the increased
cost resulting from this Bill. This large
additional cost is due to two causes. One is
the decrease in emigration from 1850
onwards, and the second the increase
in the duration of life or, as it is generally
called, the decline in the death rate.
As regards the third part of the Resolution, I trust hon. Members will not look
for any estimate even of an approximate
nature in regard to the cost of administration
which will arise in carrying out this Bill.
It is impossible to pass legislation of this
character without adding to the Departmental charges, but in this case there is the
advantage that the administration of the
Scheme will fall to a large extent under the
National Health Insurance Scheme, and the
machinery and procedure required to carry
it out are already in existence. Further, it
is also intended where possible to take advantage of the machinery of the Ministry of
Labour in connection with its other
activities. It is not expected that any considerable addition to the existing staff of the
Ministry of Labour will be required. Payments will, of course, have to be made to the
Post Office, which agency will be required for
the distribution of the pensions, but here
again it is too early at this stage to make any
close estimate of the extra cost of such
service. I should like to draw the attention
of hon. Members to the fact that the principle
of making the scheme self-dependent has been
introduced, and the Government may recoup from the Pensions Fund a portion or
the whole of the cost of administration as it
thinks fit. I beg to move.

"
Old Age Pensions Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
