Mr. BARBOUR: During the course of the
discussion on the Old Age Pensions Estimate
in May last, I think it was apparent that
the question of modifying the disability imposed under the law as it stands on people
who have saved a moderate sum in respect
of old age was one which was engaging
seriously the minds of honourable Members
of all parties in the House. The difficulty
in the way of granting such a concession is,
of course, a financial one, but the Government have decided to undertake the responsibility of shouldering the additional burden
on their finances, though it is impossible to
do so in the current financial year. I now
rise to move the Second Reading of this Bill,
the main provision of which will take effect
as from 1st April, 1926.
As honourable Members are aware, on the
existing basis of calculation of means for the
purpose of determining whether an Old Age
Pension is payable, all means, whether from
carnings or savings or otherwise, are taken
into account. The main provision of the
Bill (Section 1 (1)) which follows the wording of the main Clause in the Old Age Pensions Act enacted by the Imperial Parliament last year, provides that the existing
basis of calculation of means shall be continued, but that it shall be made subject
to the proviso that means derived from any
source other than earnings shall be excluded
from calculation in so far as they do not
exceed 15s a week in the case of a single person or 30s a week in the case of a married
couple. If honourable Members will refer to
the examples given in the explanatory memorandum which has been circulated, they will
appreciate the full purport of the proposal.
To show how amply the Bill meets the grievance which it is designed to remedy, I need
only draw attention to the case mentioned in
example (d) in the appendix to the memorandum. Here, a married couple with a joint
income of £2 10s 0d a week will be entitled
to draw pension at the full rate amounting
to £1 a week if both are pensioners; that is
of course the extreme case. The Bill gives
no additional inducement to old people to
continue in employment after they have
reached the age of seventy. On the contrary,
it is a direct encouragement to be thrifty
during the earlier years of life, so that later
there may be no necessity for them to work.
In introducing this Measure, the Government have to take into cognisance our close
proximity to the Free State and that the
effect of these proposals will be to accentuate
still further and to a substantial degree, the
difference between the conditions under
which Old Age Pensions are granted here
and in the Free State. The Free State Old
Age Pensions Act of last year had already
made the pension conditions there less
favourable than ours, by reducing the maximum rate of pension to 9s a week. The
effect of this reduction in increasing the
total number of pensioners in Northern
Ireland was not, however, very great. But
we are now concerned not merely with the
difference of a shilling per week in the pension rates; the memorandum makes it clear
that in many cases the effect of the Bill will
be to entitle persons to pensions at the full
rate of 10s per week who previously had not
been entitled to a pension at all, or only to
pension at reduced rates. There will
consequently be a great temptation to persons resident in the Free State to migrate to
Northern Ireland merely for the purpose of
taking advantage of the more generous conditions here.
The existing law, I may remind hon. Members, prescribes a period of twelve years'
residence in the United Kingdom after
attaining the age of fifty as an essential
qualification for pension in the case of
British-born British subjects, and the Order
in Council to which the Schedule to this Bill
refers, provides further that residence in
Southern Ireland before the establishment of
the Irish Free State may be counted as residence in the United Kingdom for this
purpose. As the law now stands, therefore.
many persons in the Free State could come
to Northern Ireland and obtain a pension
under the new conditions without having
previously resided in Northern Ireland at
all.
I need hardly say the additional
financial burden resulting from this immigration might be very considerable. The
effect of the proviso to Section 1 (1), together
with the Schedule, is that persons coming
here from the Free State after the 7th
instant-the date of the introduction of the
Bill-will not be entitled to the benefit of the
new provisions until they have completed a
full twelve years' residence, in which
residence in Southern Ireland will not be
taken into consideration, that is, as regards
pensions on the new basis, they will be in
exactly the same position as persons coming
from any of the Dominions. They will still,
however, be allowed to count pre-Free State
residence in Southern Ireland for the
purpose of obtaining pensions under the old
conditions.
Section 2 is one to prevent fraud in the
case of persons applying for old-age pensions
who are not properly entitled or make false
or inaccurate statements. Under the existing Old Age Pensions Acts, proceedings
against persons who make false declarations
as to means for the purpose of obtaining a
pension must be taken within a period
1313 Old Age Pensions Bill-

15 OCTOBER 1925
Second Reading.
of six months from the time when the
offence was committed. It will, I think,
be obvious that in many cases a pensions
officer could not become aware of the fraud in
sufficient time to enable proceedings to be
taken within that period. The Clause provides, therefore, that proceedings may be commenced either within six months from the
date of the commission of the offence or
within three months from the time when
evidence sufficient to justify a prosecution
shall have come to the knowledge of the
Ministry of Finance.
Hon. Members will see that this Bill
really consists of three parts. There is one
modifying the disqualification on the ground
of thrift. The second one is the residence
qualification, and the third part refers to
this prevention of fraud. These are the three
main principles of the Bill and I am sure
they will recommend themselves to hon.
Members in view of the very sympathetic
attitude they have always shown towards the
extension to Northern Ireland of these
privileges that have been prevalent across
the water.

I rose for the special purpose of saying a
word for the poor farmer, because I believe
that in the matter of the calculation of their
incomes they are very badly treated. Take
the case of a farmer with a small farm in
some remote place in the country, where,
perhaps, from morning till night he sees
hardly anyone passing his place one man
pf that type told me that he had only seen
two seagulls passing in one day-when the
Pensions Officer goes to make up the amount
that man makes on that farm he puts it at
a value that is tremendous. One man told
me yesterday that he could show that he had
lost money farming 200 acres and over, but in
the case of another man I know, who farms
eleven acres, the Pensions Officer put down
£80 as the revenue he earned from that farm,
and the man did not get a pension. I hope
the Pensions Officers will not put excessive
values upon the earnings of poor farmers,
and that they will not be precluded from
getting pensions because they own a few
acres of land.
I have always spoken on behalf of the poor

Strange as it may appear to Members of
the Opposition, I have given considerable

always seemed to me strange and wrong that
thrift and economy should be a disqualification, that the savings of a hard long life,
the savings of these old people, who have
perhaps denied themselves many pleasures

The State in the past did not always

by the State. That wrong is now about to
be righted by this Measure.

it is possible that sometimes the neighbours

makes stupid statements which only make
his O w n case worse. I speak with

statements taken down. I realise fully

this Measure. I do not suggest that any
serious complaint has been made, but in so
far as there is anything that savours of the

considered, I think it is only right that I

down from the Home Office to make inquiries
they are asked to perform their work in
the most sympathetic fashion. I am practically the final arbiter in this branch of
appeals, and I have always found that the
cases have been sympathetically considered.
It is true that a great deal of the work in
connection with the matter is done by those
who have been described as clerks in the
office; but they are Civil Servants, men of
integrity and men of great ability, and they
approach all these matters with the greatest
sympathy.
Indeed, when I took up my duties as Parliamentary Secretary, and this matter was

Mr. MCALLISTER: I should like to intervene for a few moments at this stage, to
add my voice to the appeals that have been
made with regard to the system of administering the Old Age Pension Acts. I have
always held the opinion that the administration of an Act of Parliament is at least
of equal importance to the passing of the
Act, because if it is not properly and
generously administered it would have been
better not to have passed it at all. I think
there is something radically wrong with the
system by which appeals come to the Home
Office from the Old-Age Pension Committees.
I think those who appeal should be put in
such a position that they would know how the
report is worded and sent forward to the
official in the Home Office.
As far as I understand, the system is this.
The Pension Officer sends forward a statement of the facts, and it is on that statement of the facts that the ruling is made.
At all events I think I am right in saying
that the applicant for the Old Age Pension
never has an opportunity of seeing how the
evidence is summarised, and how it is submitted to the official on appeal. I think
that is entirely wrong and is a great injustice
to the applicant for the pension. I should
also like to support the suggestion made by
the hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Beattie) that the abolition of the thrift disqualification clause should be made retrospective, because these people were either
entitled to the pension or they were not.
They were told when they accepted this
Parliament that they would be put on the
same social status in every respect as their
brothers and sisters in Great Britain. Now
it is sought to deprive these people of two
years' benefit of the Old Age Pension.
Whether it was because the State was unable
to carry it through sooner or not, it is unjust that these people should be at that loss,
when they were assured that they would
benefit in the manner I have described.
With regard to the references by the Member for the University (Dr. Morrison) to the
neglect of my hon. Friend in not advocating
a certain social Measure which was passed
here recently, I would retort that the representatives of his party in the Imperial Parliament should have seen that the Bill passed
in England was made operative in Northern
Ireland.
In reference to the claim as to who is
responsible for this Bill being passed to-day,
I would add my voice to the Opposition and
say that if we had not been here I am perfectly confident there would have been no
Contributory Pensions Bill and no Old Age
Pensions Bill. The Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford) has stated that he drew the attention of the Government three years ago
to the existing state of affairs, and failed
to move them. That is entirely to the discredit of the Government, and justifies the
contention that we put forward. We raised
the question in May last, and the Minister
of Finance then refused to make any promise
that these Bills would be introduced. I see
the Minister making a note of my remark,
and for that reason I will refer him to the
statement he made when he was asked for a
definite promise, Yes or No. The statement
was typewritten, and was obviously submitted to the Cabinet. It was very carefully
prepared, and he read it to this House. He
said:-
I wish to reassure the House and the
country, however, by stating that the
Government is hopeful that when the Joint
Exchequer Board has interpreted the findings of the Colwyn Committee, we may
benot we will
in a position to introduce the necessary
legislation in the autumn to put us on
lines parallel, or as near parallel as our
financial resources will permitnot even parallel-——
with Great Britain in respect of these two
ameliorative reforms.
That statement summarised simply amounts
to this: there was no definite promise, but
he was hopeful of bringing in a Measure on
as near to parallel lines as possible. Since
that, owing to the incessant demands of the
Opposition, in six months, not in three years,
we have seen this Measure, though not a
complete one, passing here to-day.

take next week?

20th, the main business will be the Committee
stage of the Widows', Orphans and
Old Age Contributory Pensions Bill. In
addition it is proposed to take the financial
resolution in connection with the Old-Age
Pensions Bill. On Wednesday, the 21st, the
Second Reading of the Drainage Bill will

still under consideration by the House. On
Thursday, 22nd, the Supplemantary Estimates will be considered in Supply, and if

Second Reading of the Finance Bill and consider any Bills which may reach this House
from another place.

further borings for the purpose of locating

(Mr.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
Barbour): The Commission to which the hon.
Member refers have presented several Reports embodying recommendations involving

POST OFFICE APPOINTMENTS.
3. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Commerce whether it is a fact
that all appointments as postmasters, subpostmasters, supervisors, and medical officers
in the Post Office in Northern Ireland are
submitted to his Department for approval
before being finally ratified by the Post Office
authorities, and can he state what is the ob
ject of this procedure and by whose authority it was introduced.
Mr. BARBOUR: By arrangement with the

in the postal service are notified in advance
to my Ministry. The object of such action
is that steps may be taken to ensure that persons appointed to responsible positions in the
postal service are of unquestionable loyalty
to the established constitution of Northern
Ireland.

promotion?
Mr. BARBOUR: Of course, the hon.
Member will be aware that the postal service

SUMMER DAY MAIL SERVICE.
4. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Commerce whether he is aware
that the summer day mail service to and
from Great Britain and Northern Ireland
via Larne and Stranraer ceased on Saturday,
the 3rd inst.; whether it is a fact that the
Post Office authorities, prior to the cessation
of the service, submitted proposals to his department for a continuance of similar
facilities by the Holyhead route, and that the
offer was rejected, and if so will he give the
reason; whether he is aware that correspondence now posted in London after 6-15 p.m.
for provincial towns in Northern Ireland
suffers from 12 to 18 hours' delay in delivery
by being held over for dispatch by the
Ardrossan route; and in view of the present
inadequate postal facilities, whether he will
now reconsider his rejection of the Post Office
proposals if made.
Mr. BARBOUR: The reply to the first part
of the question is in the affirmative. In regard to the second part, it is the fact that,
prior to the cessation of the summer day service between Larne and Stranraer, the Post
Office Authorities submitted for my views a
proposal to utilise the Holyhead route for
the conveyance of mails intended for the
eastern portion of Northern Ireland and
posted in London too late for conveyance by
the night mail train to Stranraer. This proposal, if carried into effect, would, as the hon.
Member implies, enable earlier deliveries to
be made in certain districts. Before expressing an opinion on it, however, I considered
it desirable to ascertain the views of the
several Chambers of Commerce in the areas
affected. Replies from all the Chambers
have not yet been received. As the hon.
Member will have gathered from what I have
said, the proposed changes are still under
consideration, and he is, therefore, incorrect
in assuming that I have rejected the Post
Office proposal.

Sir DAWSON BATES: It is not quite
clear whether the hon. and learned Member
refers to the appointment of school medical
officers by education authorities, or to the
appointment of medical inspectors by the
Ministry of Home Affairs.
In the former case the qualifications for
such appointments are prescribed by Order
made by the Ministry, with the concurrence
of the Ministry of Education, on the 24th
November, 1924, and the qualifications are
that "all such medical officers shall be registered in the Medical Register in respect
of a diploma in sanitary, science, public
health, or State medicine, or shall have such
qualification or experience of public health
work or school inspection work as the
Ministry may approve."
In the case of the appointment of a medical
inspector by the Ministry for the purpose of
supervising the operations of local education
authorities and their officers in connection
with the medical inspection and treatment
of school children, the following qualifications have been prescribed and embodied
in the advertisement inviting applications
for the appointment:-
"Candidates must have at least seven
years' experience as practising physicians
or surgeons, and should have at least five
years' working experience in the medical
inspection of school children and child
welfare generally. The candidates should
be between 30 and 40 years of age."

It would be contrary to the public interest, and to long-established practice, to

I have read the report of the case which

Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
"That it is expedient in connection with
pensions payable to persons to whom the
Old Age Pensions Acts, 1908 to 1919, apply,
to authorise the provision out of moneys
provided by Parliament of such further
sums as will become payable as a consequence of providing by any Act of the
present Session that, for the purpose of determining the weekly rate of pension to
which a person is entitled, there shall, subject to the provisions of any such Act, be
deducted from his means as calculated
under the said Acts such part, if any, of
the means, but not exceeding in any case
thirty-nine pounds, as is derived from any

Mr. BARBOUR: In submitting this Resolution for the approval of the House, I think
it is my duty to make it clear, lest there may
be any misapprehension on the point, that
the figure of £143,000 mentioned in the explanatory Memorandum is the estimated
immediate addition to the annual cost of
old-age pensions in consequence of the adoption of this Measure. This figure takes no
cognisance of the increases in the number
of old-age pensions which can be anticipated
in the next thirty or forty years arising from
the natural decrease in the death rate.
Hon. Members will appreciate that since no
census has been taken in Northern Ireland
since 1911, it is a matter of considerable difficulty to make estimates of population on
which to calculate the additional cost involved by the modification of the means condition, and it will be remembered that when
this matter was discussed in the House last
session, it was estimated that the additional
cost might ultimately amount to £350,000 per
annum. The whole question has, however,
recently been investigated afresh by the
Government Actuary in connection with this
Bill and the Contributory Pensions Scheme.
There are at present 41,000 old-age pensioners in Northern Ireland, of whom 3,500
draw pensions at less than the maximum rate
of 10s per week. The total present cost of pensions alone, exclusive of the cost of administration, is £1,047,000, and it is now estimated
that after making allowance for persons who
will still be disqualified on the ground of
means for pensions under the Old Age Pensions Acts, approximately 5,500 persons will
become entitled to pensions in the next
financial year as a result of the operation of
this Bill, while most of the existing pensioners at less than the maximum rate of 10s
will now become entitled to pensions at the
maximum rate. That is the immediate result which is anticipated. The total cost on
this account in the year 1926-7 is not expected to exceed the figure of £143,000 mentioned in the Memorandum, but the Government is advised that, having regard to the

for

CLAUSE 1. (Contributory
Widows, Orphans, and Persons between the
Ages of 65 and 70).
(1) Subject to the provisions of this Act
relating to the payment of contributions
(including payments out of moneys provided by Parliament) and otherwise,
pensions shall be payable as follows, that
is to say-
(a) to the widow of an insured man a
pension at the rate of ten shillings per
week, with an additional allowance in
respect of children while under the age
hereinafter specified, at the rate of five
shillings per week for the eldest or only
such child, and three shillings per week
for each other such child (in this Act
called a "widow's pension");
(b) in respect of the orphan children
while under the age hereinafter specified
of an insured man or of an insured widow,
a pension at the rate of seven shillings
and sixpence per week for each such child
(in this Act called an "orphan's pension");
or
(c) to an insured man an insured
woman who has attained the age of sixtyfive but has not attained the age of
seventy, and to the wife of an insured
man who has attained the age of sixtyfive (such wife having attained the age
of sixty-five but not having attained the
age of seventy) a pension at the rate of
ten shillings per week (in this Act called
an "old age pension").
(2) The specified age in relation to any
child shall be the age of fourteen or the
age not exceeding sixteen up to which the
child remains under full-time instruction
in a day school.
(3) By way of contribution towards the
cost of carrying this Act into effect there
shall be paid such contributions as are
hereinafter in this Act provided.
Mr. KYLE: I beg to move in Clause 1, page
1, line 7, to leave out "the payment of contributions" ("relating to the payment of
contributions (including payments out of
moneys provided by Parliament)").
In moving this Amendment I want to
point out to the Committee that in Northern
Ireland we are adopting the principle laid
down in Britain. Now Great Britain is the
only country in the world that has adopted
a scheme of widows' or mothers' pensions and
In
made that scheme a contributory one.
New Zealand in 1912 a pension scheme was
brought into being which was a non-contributory one. In Denmark in January, 1914, a
non-contributory scheme was brought into
being in that country.
In forty States and two territories in the
United States of America there are noncontributory schemes, and I think the whole
movement is in favour of non-contributory
widows' and mothers' pensions. We owe a
lot to Judge Neil, of the United States. He
visited Belfast in 1912 and in the Co-operative
Hall gave us an outline of the proposals in
operation at that time in the United States
of America. Subsequent to that he went to
London and had a committee room provided
for him in which to meet Members of both
the House of Lords and the House of Commons, and as a result of that visit and that
outline of a mothers' pension scheme which
he had got put into force in so many States
in America, a great volume of opinion was
created in Great Britain and also in
Belfast to have non-contributory widows'
pensions brought into being. As I said, we
owe a tremendous lot to Judge Neil, of the
United States of America, for his advocacy
of this cause.

employment insurance scheme such as we

As this Bill is drafted the contribution
which our Exchequer will be called upon to
pay will be £145,000 a year on the average

million out of our own resources, which we
cannot do. I feel that the contributory
system is not placing the burden upon industry which my hon. Friend seems to think
it will. I quoted figures to prove that in my
Second Reading speech, and I need not repeat those figures to-day. I will put it in
other words. The increased contributions
which employers will have to pay for their
male employees will be only 2d per week, and
the employee himself will only pay 2d; for
the female worker the employer is only
asked to pay 1d and the female worker herself 1d. That really amounts to less than
one half per cent. of the total wages paid by
the firms in which the workers are employed.
Again, to show how trifling the contributions really are I would remind the Committee that for the last 4 years I have been
engaged very frequently in connection with
labour negotiations where there was a
difference of opinion between workers and
employers as to what wages should be paid
and received. When these negotiations take
place it is almost invariably a question of
whether 2s, 3s, 4s, 5s, 6s, 7s, 8s, 9s, or 10s is
to be given or not. I never heard of negotiations of the kind where only a question
of a 1d or 2d was in dispute. Obviously it
would be absurd, and therefore I think I
am justified in arguing that really this 1d
and 2d would amount to such a small thing
that they are not worth considering in connection with a matter of this kind. The
important thing is that these small contributions which the employers and workers
are asked to pay will give better benefits to
the insured person than any ordinary
insurance company is able to give, because,
of course, of the State grant which is added.
Therefore, I do feel that this is a proper

undoubtedly the Bill would have to be withdrawn, and they alone would be depriving

is made clear that the effect of any particular Amendment is in contravention of our
rules of procedure I am bound to rule. It
affords me no pleasure, but it is my duty.

ment cannot accept this Amendment.

Mr. ANDREWS: This Amendment

Mr. KYLE: Does the Government think
that 7s 6d can keep an orphan child? Hon.
Members know very well that it takes more
than 7s 6d to maintain a child in the poorhouse; it takes more than 7s 6d to keep a
child in a detention home or an orphans'
home of any sort or description. Therefore,
it is because these children ought to be
looked after that we want the sum of 12s
to be paid to the people looking after them
so that the children may be brought up as
decent citizens. It is from that point of view
that we seek to have the sum increased.
Right hon. Gentlemen know well the reason
why we want this sum to be increased to 12s.
I say that no child can be kept under the sum
of 12s, and it is because we desire these
orphan children to be brought up as healthy
citizens we want that sum to be paid to the
people looking after them.
Mr. ANDREWS: The Government do not
take the view that 7s 6d is in itself a sufficiency, but the Government are aware of the
fact that a great many organizations of a
charitable description exist at the present
time, many of them being associated with
our Churches. I am quite sure that those
charitable organizations do not intend to
cease operating. For instance, a society of the
kind communicated with me only a day or so
ago to say that they had an income of from
£13,000 to £14,000 a year and asked for my
opinion as to what their position would be
under this Bill. I said, "I do not think you
should be affected by this Bill at all; this
is a foundation which the Government is
laying, upon which you and other organizations such as yours will be able to build a
sufficiency in the future."
Mr. BEATTIE: The Minister seems to
complain that I moved the Amendment without an explanation being given. I thought

knowledge and the information he had at
his command with regard to the upkeep of
orphan children he would grasp why we
desire the alteration from 7s. 6d. to 12s.
That was why I did not explain the matter.

the Affiliation Bill to enable the relatives of
a child left in that position to seek for an
Affiliation Order against the father and it
'was accepted by this House. It went to the
Senate and an Amendment was introduced
there deleting the Clause. It came back here
and owing to the fact that the House was
going to adjourn the following day I did not
see my way to move the insertion of the
Clause. The one blot on our Bill, which
was a most necessary Bill, to remove the
stigma and stain that have remained on
Ireland for fifty years, was that the Senate
introduced an Amendment that left out the
child of an unmarried mother who had died
in her confinement or through diseases
incidental to pregnancy. The child has been
shut out of this Bill, and I suggest by my
'Amendment that this child should have the
same claim as if it were the child of a
married mother. The mother must be insured. That makes it clear that she must
be a contributor to these funds and that she
would come in were it not for the fact that
she had not been married. I think the
general humanity which animates all hon.
'Members, that social conscience about which
the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin) spoke, which has been roused by him,
should prompt us all to assist in this Amendment to the Bill in order to try to do something for this most helpless of all the helpless
creatures in the community. I beg to move.
Mr. ANDREWS: If my hon. Friend will
refer to Clause 4, sub-section (1) he will
find there that the illegitimate child of a
man or of his wife, who was living with him
at the time of his death-

That the child of an insured unmarried mother who dies as a result of

Dr. MORRISON: No, sir. I appreciate the

(Mr. Andrews) has met this question. In

and in only two cases did the

Amendment, by leave, withdrawn.
Mr. KYLE: I beg to move in Clause 1,
page 2, line 21, to leave out the word " fourteen"
("shall be the age of fourteen "), and
to insert instead thereof the word "sixteen."
With the development of that social
conscience, of which the hon. and learned
Member for the University (Dr. Morrison)
spoke just recently, it is becoming more and
more apparent that we are going to have
to increase the school-leaving age to sixteen,
and we want to see that these pensions are
paid to the widow, or to the guardian, until
the child is sixteen. That is the main purport of the Amendment. It is because of the
growing feeling that sixteen is to be the
school-leaving age and that it will be illegal
to employ people before they reach that
age that we want this inserted here. We
want to be in the van of progress in the
Six Counties, and it is from that point of
view that we want "sixteen" inserted here
instead of "fourteen."

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I would
point out to the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Andrews) that there is a very important
principle involved in connection with this
Amendment. The right hon. Gentleman will
remember that last week I addressed a question to him as to the number of people who
are in industry at the present time at fourteen years of age. This has a very important
bearing on the unemployment problem. At
the present time there are a large number
of boys employed at fourteen years of age,
and in many cases they are cutting out male
members of the community from getting employment. From that point of view I would
ask the right hon. Gentleman to give his very
careful and serious consideration to this
proposal, because, if it is agreed to, it would
be a direct inducement to the parents to keep
these children at school until they are sixteen instead of fourteen. The children would
thus get more benefit from the education
provided for them and it would relieve the
market to a great extent, and give some of
the adults an opportunity of getting employment which they cannot get at the present
time. From that point of view the Amendment is exceptionally important, and I would
ask the right hon. Gentleman to give it very
careful consideration in view of the very
grave industrial problems connected with it.
Mr. ANDREWS: I fully appreciate the
arguments brought forward by the two hon.
Members (Mr. Kyle and Mr. William
McMullen), but they will appreciate that we
cannot in a Bill of this kind make it illegal
for employers to employ people over fourteen years of age, or illegal for workers over
that age to accept employment. If they
will refer to Clause 1, sub-clause (2) they will
see it set out quite clearly that the age limit
is to be fourteen unless the child remains
full time at a day school. If the child does
that then the allowance to the widow will
be paid, so that I really think the hon.
Members' point is met.
The CHAIRMAN: Does the hon. Member
press the Amendment?
Mr. KYLE: I beg leave to withdraw.
Amendment by leave withdrawn.

Mr. DEVLIN: I must at this stage enter
a very strong protest against the methods by
which this Clause has been discussed. I have
been reading for the purpose of information
the discussions on this Bill in Committee in
the British Parliament, and I find that it was
perfectly within the province of the Members
of the British Parliament to discuss these
proposed increases in the amounts given to
widows and orphans. As in my judgment
this is the most vital part of the Measure,
namely whether the widows' and orphans'
pensions are adequate or not, this Committee
and the Members who hold the views I do are
placed in an extremely awkward position.
I have already stated that I think this
Measure loses a great deal of its value in
view of the inadequacy of these contributions,
and I cannot see why hon. Members were permitted in the British Parliament to move
Amendments increasing the amount of the
pensions while we are not permitted to do the
same here in this Committee. I think it,
therefore, my duty to register my protest
against the refusal to allow us to discuss
this matter and move these Amendments.
The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Member (Mr.
Devlin) was not in the Committee during part
of the period when this matter was under
review and, therefore, I hope the Committee
will indulge me while I explain to him what
was the basis of my ruling. The hon. Member
has quite correctly stated the fact that on
the Committee Stage on the other side Questions were submitted to the Committee, and
even put to the vote, but upon their being
re-submitted on the Report Stage Mr. Speaker
ruled and I read four successive rulings
upon Amendments of exactly the same terms
as those submitted to me-that, as these involved an increased charge upon the Exchequer, they were out of order, and he declined to permit them to be discussed. The
hon. Member, I am sure, sees my dilemma,
whether I am to follow the ruling of what
in no disrespectful sense I may describe as
a subordinate authority or whether I am to
follow the ruling of what is really the final
and absolute court of appeal, namely the
Speaker of the Imperial Parliament. I am
sure hon. Members are quite satisfied in their
own minds that, unpleasant as was the duty I
had to perform, I had no course open to me
but to follow the ruling which Mr. Speaker
gave in the Imperial House of Commons, and
I am also sure that the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) appreciates the
difficulty in which I find myself.
Question, "That Clause 1 stand part of

(1) In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, the expression "insured”
means insured under the National Health
Insurance Act, 1924 (in this Act referred to
as "the Insurance Act') or the Acts repealed by that Act, and in relation to any
person who is deemed to be insured for the
purposes of this Act, includes such a person; and the expression "insurance" in relation to a person so deemed to be insured
shall be construed accordingly.
(2) For the purposes of this Act, but not
for any other purpose, a person insured
under the Insurance Act shall be deemed
to continue to be so insured during any
period during which he is by virtue of subsection (4) of section twelve of the Insurance Act entitled to sanatorium benefit.
(3) An exempt person and a person engaged in an excepted employment shall be
deemed to be insured for the purposes of
this Act in the circumstances and to the
extent mentioned in this Act.

I would like the intention of this Amendment to be perfectly clear. It is an attempt
to do a little justice to a woman who, we

that she is in even a more difficult position

and whatever chance there might be for a

little chance for the wife of an incapacitated
husband to do so when she has got to attend
her husband in addition to looking after him
and the children.

After all,

the importance of this pension to the child

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: The Amendment before the Committee deals with the
contributions of those engaged in agriculture,
and I bring it forward in the name of charity.
I think they are entitled to what we ask for

life and there are not ordinarily so many
applying for benefit under the Health Insurance Acts as those engaged in other industries. We feel that the contributions paid
by those engaged in the agricultural industry under the Health Insurance Acts
would be quite sufficient to meet the demands
that would be made by these people under
this Bill. The Minister may, in this conto prove
nection, give statistics that go
that sickness is just as prevalent in the

make here, that agricultural labourers are
entitled to the benefit of this Bill without
paying any more contributions than they are
at present paying.

Mr. ANDREWS: If the Government were
to agree to this Amendment it would simply
mean giving non-contributory pensions to
those engaged in farming. Obviously that
would be unfair to our industrial workers in
our cities. The hon. Member for Antrim
(Mr. George Henderson) has pointed out that
in his opinion this will put a serious burden
upon agriculture, on the farmers and on the
labourers. I really cannot think that it will.
Take a small farmer, such as those for whom
the hon. Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester)
has appealed; he is a man probably with ten
or twenty acres. It would be a very exceptional case where such a farmer employs any
labourers at all, and, therefore, he is not
really affected by this Measure. Take the
farmer, again, who has fifty or sixty acres;
he will probably be employing three men to
help him to do the work of that farm. If he
employs the members of his own family, and
if he pays them any financial remuneration
at all, he can insure them, and then the
members of his own family will receive the
benefits of the Bill. If, on the other hand,
he has to employ labour from, as it were,
outside his own family he will have to pay
the contributions for them, but it really will
not amount to anything of importance. If he
has the three labourers to whom I have
referred it will only amount to 18
per week. I do not think any
farmer would like for the sake of 1s
per week to deny to his workers all those
advantages which this Bill gives to other
industrial workers, especially those in our
cities.
I think that really meets the point, but the
hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. George Henderson) has also referred to the fact that it
is rather unfair to the agricultural worker,
because he enjoys better health than the
worker in our cities. I very much question
if that is so. The returns of several of our
approved societies in this neighbourhood do
not point in that direction, but, if additional
proof is necessary, it is to be found in the
fact that in the Free State a Commission
was set up to investigate this and other
matters under the Health Insurance Acts
and to see if agricultural workers did not
get to the same extent the benefits which
those Acts brought within the reach of the
workers in the cities. The decision of that
Free State Commission was that, in Southern
Ireland at any rate, the workers in agricultural districts got fully the amount of benefits under the Insurance Acts that the
workers in the cities got, and for this
reason: Our city people suffer, as a
rule, from diseases that are of short duration. They suffer from pneumonia or a complaint of that kind where the illness lasts a
very short time. In the agricultural districts
a tremendous number of agricultural workers
suffer from complaints such as rheumatism,
bronchitis, asthma, and diseases of that kind,
where the illnesses extend for a very long
period, and where the sick person is not only
drawing sickness benefit but for a very long
period draws disablement benefit intermittently after the sickness benefit has been
stopped.
But, even if I admitted the hon. Member's
point, I would answer in reply to his criticism that. after all, if they do not draw so
much as regards sickness benefit and disablement benefit, the fact, I think, is undeniable
that, generally speaking, farm workers live
longer than the workers in our cities, and,
therefore, what they lose on the merry-gorounds they make up on the swing-boats, and
gain as regards the Old-Age Pensions provisions of the Bill. I think for these reasons,
and for many others which I could advance,
my hon. Friends would be justified in not
pressing the Amendment. I think it better
that this Amendment should not be agreed
to. because having contributory pensions for
our industrial workers in the city and noncontributory pensions for the workers in our
farming areas could not be justified.

it.

21 OCTOBER 1925
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 21st October, 1925.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
SHIPMENT OF CATTLE.
Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he will make any statement as to what steps he is taking with
regard to the shipment of cattle from Ulster.
in view of the allegations recently appearing
in the Press as to their condition in transit.
and on arrival, and whether any representations are being made by his Department to
the Imperial Authorities on this matter.
AGRICULTURE:
The MINISTER OF
(Mr. Archdale): As the honourable Member
appears to be aware, my Ministry has no
statutory responsibility regarding the shipment of cattle. I fully realize, however, the
importance of the matter from the point of
view of the farming community, and correspondence on the subject has taken place
between my Ministry and the Imperial
Authorities who, I am satisfied, are giving
this question their earnest and constant
attention.
ARDGLASS AND KILLOUGH HARBOURS:
2. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether, during the herringfishing season recently closed at Ardglass,
boats were frequently delayed owing to the
lack of accommodation at that port, and
whether he proposes to take steps before next
season to provide additional accommodation
either at Ardglass or Killough.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr Barbour): I have been asked by my right hon.
Friend to reply to this question. I
understand that, owing to the exceptionally
good season enjoyed by the herring fishing
industry in local waters this year, there was
at times considerable congestion at Ardglass
Harbour, and possibly consequential delay to
some of the vessels using the port. As the
honourable Member is doubtless aware, the
improvement of Ardglass Harbour or, alternatively, the provision of a suitable fishery
harbour at Killough formed the subject of
recommendations by the Commission on the
Natural and Industrial Resources of Northern Ireland. That Report is still the subject
of discussion, but I would remind the hon.
Member that, as pointed out in
reply given to him yesterday, recommendations involving considerable expenditure
from public funds require to be considered
a
"
adin the light of existing commitments and
financial resources available. In any event I
am afraid it will not be practicable to provide in time for next fishing season
ditional accommodation at either port on the
scale contemplated by the Report of the
Development Commission.
Mr. DEVLIN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman what is his idea of appointing
these Commissions if none of their recommendations, especially recommendations
dealing with matters of immediate utility,
are put into operation? Are these Commissions to be, like those in England, a pure
farce for the purpose of putting these things
off?
Mr. BARBOUR: I can assure the hon.
Member that these recommendations have not
been neglected. They have received our consideration, and a certain amount of action
has already been taken in regard to some of
them, but as to which of them will be proceeded with is a matter that will require to be submitted to the Cabinet for
further consideration of the order of
priority to which we consider they commend
themselves to public attention.
ENGLISH MAILS IN SOUTH DERRY.
3. Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he is aware of the
great delay in the receipt of English mails
in South Derry, and the consequent commercial loss involved, and, as this is due to
the fact that the Larne and Stranraer boat
train which carries these mails frequently
misses the connection at Belfast; whether
he has made representations to the proper
authorities with a view to having the mails
transferred to the South Derry train at
Greenisland.
Mr. BARBOUR: Following representations
made to me by the hon. Member, I
approached the Post Office Authorities on
this matter. I am glad to be able to inform the hon. Member that an arrangement
has now been made between the Post Office
and the Railway Company under which, on
occasions when the boat train is liable to
miss connection with the Belfast-Coleraine
train leaving Belfast at 10 p.m., all correspondence intended for the latter train, including that destined for South Derry, will
be transferred at Greenisland. This
arrangement came into force permanently
as from the 14th instant.

lodgment of documents in connection with

EX-SERVICEMEN'S HOUSES IN
BELFAST.
5. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state what steps,
if any, have been taken to acelerate the
building of the remaining three hundred and
thirteen ex-servicemen's houses in Belfast to
complete the schemes in Northern Ireland.
Mr. POLLOCK: I would refer the hon.
Member to the reply which I gave to the
hon. Member for North Belfast on the 13th
instant, from which he will see that plans,
specifications, etc., are now in course of preparation for the erection of 134 houses. With
regard to the remaining 179 houses the allocation thereof to various districts is at present under consideration.
I might add that the 313 houses are to be
spread over Northern Ireland and are not
confined to Belfast.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is it not a fact that those
houses are already allocated by a Committee
sitting in Belfast?
Mr. POLLOCK: No, sir. The allocation
of these houses is in the hands of the Trust,
which was established by the Imperial
Authority to determine all these details with
regard to the erection of houses.
Mr. DEVLIN: Can the right hon. Gentleman say how it comes that houses are given
to tenants of Corporation houses, when other
ex-service men, with families of three, four,
or five, are compelled to huddle together in
one or two rooms?
Mr. POLLOCK: am not responsible for
the allocation of houses by the Belfast Corporation.
Mr. DEVLIN: Has not the right hon.
Gentleman control over this matter? Does
he sanction the handing over of these houses
to persons who are not entitled to them?
Mr. POLLOCK: No, sir. I have repeated
on many occasions that the Trust which has
been established by the Imperial Authorities
has this matter in its own hands, and we only
carry out matters as agents in respect of the
details.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the Minister inform me whether the Committee of the Land
Trust, when considering the handing over of
these houses to ex-servicemen, take into consideration whether the applicants are employed or unemployed? If the applicant is
unemployed the Trust will not accept him as
a suitable tenant.
Mr. POLLOCK: I am convinced that all
relevant matters are taken into consideration
by the Trust-not the Committee of the
Trust; the Trust itself is really a small body.
But so far as the allocation of the houses is

HEAVY MOTOR TRAFFIC ON ROADS.
6. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Prime Minister
whether legislation will be introduced at an
early date to relieve the ratepayers of the
excessive burden of taxation due to the increase of heavy motor traffic on roads which
were never intended for such traffic.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I am glad to be able to announce that I hope for next year to increase
the Road Fund Grants on Class 1 Roads 50
per cent to 60 per cent, and on Class 2 Roads
'from 25 per cent to 30 per cent, and further
to make grants of 15 per cent of approved
expenditure on Class 3 Roads.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman if there is no possibility of the
Government introducing legislation to take
the control of the roads out of the ratepayers'
hands, and making the motor traffic pay for
their upkeep?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think that is a
very big question involving the control not
alone of motors but also of roads.

PRICE OF BREAD IN BELFAST.
8. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether, in view of the fact that the
quartern loaf is sold in Belfast for 10d when
the Food Council of Great Britain has stated
that there is no justification for a higher
price than 9d, he is prepared to take steps
to see that this essential commodity is reduced in price on parallel lines with Great
Britain.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates) to
reply. As the hon. Member is no doubt
aware the price of the quartern loaf in Belfast

understand, moreover, that it is the practice

of reducing the price of the loaf approximately to the latter figure mentioned by the
hon. Member.

Mr. SPEAKER: Does the hon. Member

Mr. DEVLIN: Yes. I was
taken by surprise by the ruling which you
have given on this matter. I handed in this
question which is as follows:
Whether in view of the fact that the
Catholics of Northern Ireland constitute
about one-third of the entire population,
he proposes to fill up one of the vacancies
in the Judiciary consequent on the death
of Sir Denis Henry by the appointment of
a Catholic, and so follow the precedent established by the Government when the
Northern Judiciary was set up.
Now you have ruled-
Mr. SPEAKER: I have not ruled publicly
yet-if the hon. Member will give me the
opportunity. With regard to this question,
in my view it is not a competent question to
put in this House for the reason that the appointment to which the hon. Member refers
is an appointment by His Majesty, and not
by the Governor of Northern Ireland. Consequently the responsibility for that appointment rests with His Majesty's Ministers in
London and not with the Ministers of this
Government.
Mr. DEVLIN: On that point of order you
have already permitted to-day, and not only
to-day but on other occasions, questions dealing with reserved services, and one of these
questions is on the Paper to-day. In fact,
the right hon. Gentleman the Minister of
Finance has already disclaimed responsibility
for these matters because they are matters
reserved. I am somewhat surprised to learn
that the appointments of judges in
Northern Ireland is in the hands of His
Majesty's Ministers in England, because I
understood that these appointments were
made by the Prime Minister, and if I mistake not a statement to that effect was made
in to-day's papers. If these appointments are
made by the Prime Minister of England or
by His Majesty on the recommendation of
the Prime Minister of England it is a very
important consideration. I intend to raise
this question on the adjournment if I do not
get a satisfactory answer, but probably if the
right hon. Gentleman has a satisfactory
answer it will save Mr. Speaker a constitutional question and further confroversy. If
he has not a satisfactory answer I propose
to raise it on the adjournment, and of course
I would like to know if your ruling with
regard to my question applies also to my
right to discuss this matter on the adjournment?
Mr. SPEAKER: My view, and the hon.
Member very well knows the position, is that
Parliament-all Parliaments-have to be very
careful indeed in any matter which may possibly amount to any criticism of the
Judiciary. Even supposing the matter was
entirely within the hands of this Government
I think it would be very undesirable to raise
it in this form, but quite beyond that I am
clear that the matter is a reserved service
of a type which it is not competent, in my
view, to raise in this form in this House.
Mr. DEVLIN: With all respect it is not
really a discussion of the judges. I do not
want to discuss the judges in this House or
outside it. This is a question of the appointment of judges which is an entirely different
thing. It is certainly news to me and it
must be information to many people that the
appointment of these judges does not rest
with the Prime Minister and Ministers of
Northern Ireland, but rests with the Imperial authority. It is quite a revelation to
me.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member, I
think, should know that under the Government of Ireland Act the Judiciary was one
of the services reserved to the Imperial Government and Parliament, and the Estimates
for the Northern Ireland Judiciary come up
and are discussed in the Imperial Parliament and not here.
Mr. DEVLIN: Then do I understand that
these judges are paid out of the Northern
Exchequer?
Hon. MEMBERS: No, no.
Mr. DEVLIN: Who pays them?
Mr. SPEAKER: I think I can inform the
hon. Member. The salaries of the judges
in Northern Ireland are a direct charge
upon the Consolidated Fund of the United
Kingdom. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I would
like to inquire whether His Majesty would

if that be so is it not within the province
of this Parliament to discuss the matter?
Mr. SPEAKER: That is a question I may
say I cannot answer from any knowledge,
but I assume that His Majesty's Government would probably consult some authorities here-whether the Government or
legal authorities I do not know. Very
likely they would, but that in my view
does not mean we are entitled to criticise
the action of His Majesty's Government in
this Parliament.

any sanitary authority whose area is

for the execution and performance by that
sanitary authority of any of the powers
and duties of the county council under
this Act.

this Act may delegate their powers and
duties under this Act to the education
committee or regional education committees of the authority, or to the maternity
and child welfare committee of the
authority, or partly to one such class of
committee and partly to the other, as they
think fit; and such delegation may be made
subject to such restrictions and conditions,
if any, as the authority think fit.
A sanitary authority with which a county
council have made arangements under the
last preceding sub-section may in like
manner delegate their powers and duties
under this Act to the maternity and child
welfare committee of the authority.

sanitary authority for the purposes of
sections two and three of the Notification
of Births (Extension) Act, 1915, as
amended by section four of the Maternity
and Child Welfare Act, 1918.

call a judge a pensioner. These people are
compelled to pay and, therefore, we ought to
call things by their proper names, and this
is really an Insurance Bill. By calling it

regard as a stigma, because the poor do not

That is why I am in favour of the Bill. It

the child has died, to some extent through
his action: and in addition to that the fact
that the child is deprived of its mother puts
it up doubly to the man in my opinion to
support the child.

Unemployment Insurance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr
Gordon): I beg to move the Second Reading
of the Unemployment Insurance Bill. I would
like to say at the outset that this Bill contains four main provisions with which I
purpose dealing. It alters three main principles in the interests of the contributor, and
finally I may say that it might be regarded
as a very generous Bill containing generous
provisions.
The object of this Bill is not to provide
employment, but it is to make it easy for
those who are unable to find it. If we continue the first statutory condition of the 30
contributions it will be impossible for a
great number of people to obtain unemployment benefit, and, consequently, we are
bringing forward this Bill with a view of
making their pathway in that direction easy.
The House will remember that in June, prior
to our Adjournment, a Bill was passed called
the Unemployment Temporary Provision Bill,
which gave power to the Governor to apply
by Order in Council so much as he thought
fit of a Bill which was to come on later in
the Imperial Parliament, and which was
finally passed. This power that enabled
the Governor to bring in certain provisions by Order in Council became effective,
and this Bill is now being introduced to
enact the various provisions and at the same
time to bring into being a new provision
not brought in by Order in Council.
Having given that explanation, I will proceed to explain what I said at the outset
of my speech, that there were four main
provisions in the Bill. The first provision is
the power given to the Minister to waive
the first statutory condition. I think I should
explain to the House what is meant by the
first statutory condition. It was necessary
under the previous Act that the applicant for
benefit should have thirty contributions in
the two years prior to the benefit year.
I may make it plain by saying that if
an applicant makes application for benefit in
October we would go over his record to July
1923, and we would examine whether he had
30 contributions to his credit. If it was
found he had not 30 contributions to his
credit then according to that Act he was not
entitled to benefit. And if hon. Members refuse to give a Second Reading to this Bill
here this evening they will place great numbers of unemployed people who have not 30
contributions to their credit in the peculiar
position that they will be outside the pale
of making application for benefit, because
they would not be entitled to it. The Bill
we are introducing here gives power to the
Minister to waive this particular clause from
1431 Unemployment Insurance Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS. Second Reading.
[Mr. Gordon]
the first October until June, 1926. His power
to waive came to an end at the end of
September and we purpose asking the House
again to give him power in order that he may
come to the rescue, if I may use the expression, of the victims of industrial depression
who have been unable to find employment,
and consequently are unable to provide themselves with the necessary contributions to
obtain benefit under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I think it would be well that I should
explain the conditions under which men can
obtain benefit by virtue of the waiver of the
Minister. He has decided that instead of the
Act requiring 30 contributions over two years
the Act shall require eight contributions
over two years. Furthermore where a man
has been unable to obtain employment in
order to have the eight contributions to his
credit over a period of two years, the Minister under his power to waive expects that
that man will have had 30 contributions to
his credit at some period of his life as he
was passing through Insurance.
Now, lest hon. Members on the Front
Bench opposite and other hon. Members of
this House should be of the opinion that if
a man has 30 contributions to his credit that
entitles him to benefit, I want to disabuse
their minds of that. I think that impression
has got abroad, and I want to disabuse the
mind of the general public. That is a wrong
impression. It is merely a step in the
right direction. A man may have 30
contributions to his credit, but from the
year 1918 he may not have been in any insurable employment. Consequently though
the man may have 30 contributions to
his credit there are other hurdles that he
must cross in order to reach the Insurance
Fund and in order to obtain benefit. I think
that it would be well I should explain that
because I know perfectly well that Members
of the Opposition here are likely to raise
that point. I want to show the Members of
the House that notwithstanding a man
having fulfilled the condition now laid down
by the Minister of 30 contributions he must
go further. He must also prove that he is
normally employed in such employment as
would make him an employed person within
the meaning of the principal Act, that in
normal times insurable employment suited
to his capacities would be likely to be available for him, but most important of all-I
want hon. Members to remember this-that
he has during the past two years immediately
preceding the date of application for benefit
been employed in an insurable employment
to such an extent as was reasonable, having
regard to all the circumstances of the case
in particular to the opportunities for obtaining insurable employment during that period.

for the guidance of Members of this House

a
I think 1 will pass on to what might be
termed the second provision of the Act
-the restoration of the waiting period.
I should explain to hon. Members who
mav not be aware what the waiting
period is. Some hon. Members may be
of the opinion that the waiting period is
gap. It is not a gap. There was
a time when we imposed gaps-say a certain
number of weeks. A man was entitled to
benefit for 10 or 15 weeks, and then we imposed a gap. When a man becomes unemployed he goes on the unemployment register,
and for the first six days he is unemployed
he is not entitled to any benefit, which means
that we are increasing the waiting period
to what it formerly was-six days.
There is no use in my attempting to
explain to the House that we have no
ulterior motive in restoring the waiting
period from three to six days. The Minister
within the past fortnight delivered a speech
in this House in which he explained the
state of the Unemployment Fund, and how
necessary it was in bringing in the new conditions to conserve the benefit for those who
were entitled to it most. Consequently,
certain conditions were brought in precluding certain people who, the Minister
thought, were not entitled to receive benefit
by reason of the fact that they could look
to their relatives for means of support. Those
people are not now entitled to receive benefit, because we think they can reasonably
look to their friends for support. When a man
becomes unemployed it is easier to stand
out at the beginning of his unemployment
than in the middle of a lengthy period or at

Second Reading.
the end. That is the only reason why we
have introduced what was formerly in operation, a waiting period of six days, so that
we may effect some saving and that the fund
may not run riot, as it were.
I should like to say, more especially to the
Leader of the Opposition and his party here,
that when we are introducing a waiting
period we are doing so on lines similar to
those adopted by trade unions. I think the
hon. Members will agree with that. Trade
unions have waiting periods as a rule, and
before any man becomes entitled to benefit
he must sign a "vacant book" for three days,
and in some cases, like the union of which
the Leader of the Opposition is a member, it
is six days. We consequently feel we are
imposing no unnecessary hardship on any of
the unemployed because we are merely conforming to conditions that obtain in the
trade union world.

propose on 4th January to reduce the contributions of the work people and employers
by 2d. I thought I would have had a
"hear, hear" from the Members of the
Opposition, who were so persistent in
making application to the Minister of
Labour this afternoon for a reduction
of the contributions in the Widows'
Pensions Bill, I think some observations were made during the course of the
discussions here to-day that our social
schemes were interwoven with each other to
some extent. That is so. Though we purpose
reducing the contribution of the workpeople
and of the employer, we hope to effect some
savings through the reduction of these contributions, and here is how we hope to effect
them. When a man becomes 65 years of age
he is no longer entitled to unemployment insurance benefit after the year 1928, and consequently the employer must continue while
he employs that man to bear his own proportion of that man's stamps. He will continue to pay his contribution.
I want to impress upon this House that
when a man passes 65 years of age we are
not relieving the employer of his responsibility. It has been thought that the probability was that when a man attained the age
of 65 though he received no benefit we would
ask no contribution for him, we felt, however, that that might place that man in a
better position than the ordinary workman
who was seeking employment, by virtue of
the fact that no contributions would be paid
for him. Therefore we decided that while
the man was employed, no matter what his
age was, contributions for him would have
to be paid by his employer. There are other
matters which are linked up with the reduction of contributions. There are the Exchequer grants which I am not going to
touch on at the moment but which may be
dealt with later on in Committee. Probably
the question may be raised by hon. Members
present, and I have no doubt it will be
answered by the Minister of Labour.
There is a final provision which I desire to
refer to. Hon. Members will remember that
the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1920 retained the principle laid down in the Act of
1911, to enter into agreement with associations. Some Members of this House may not
be aware what it means to enter into an
agreement with an association. The association to all intents and purposes means the
trade union. Members of trade unions made
application to the Minister of Labour at the
inception of unemployment insurance and he
permitted them to pay unemployment benefit
through their trade union, and so the agreement was entered into. Hon. Members will
see that it is necessary that some sort of
agreement should be entered into for the
reason that trade unions are responsible for
paying out the money of the unemployment
insurance fund. We require associations to
pay out of their funds a certain amount per
week for a certain period. We endeavoured
to meet them in this respect and only required them to pay 5/- a week for a period
of thirteen weeks. That gives them a
privilege, and I may say it is a
privilege because I know many men prefer
going to their association to receive their
combined benefits, the benefit paid by their
trade association and the unemployment insurance benefit paid through their association
We have determined to continue that relationship with the trade unions.
We know perfectly well that there has been
a considerable strain upon the funds of the
trade unions and that they have not been
able to pay as they formerly did. We realise
the great work which the trade unions have
done during the past four or five years, and
.we know that much of the funds formerly at
their disposal are not now available. Those
Funds were used in the interests of the unemployed over a certain number of years.
The unions are not able now to conform to
what was in the previous Acts, and so I say
we have reasonably met them in this regard.
I think I am safe in saying that the Bill
contains three provisions which are generous
to the unemployed and to the work people
and one provision which may to some extent
mitigate against them, that is the waiting
period at the beginning of their unemployment. But it is better that we should make
a gap at the beginning of the unemployment
rather than later on.
I have much pleasure in submitting this
Bill to the House, and I am sure that after
this explanation hon. Members will recognise
the fact that a refusal to pass it would place
