Mr. ELLIOTT: While I rise to support
the Amendment proposed by the Minister of
Agriculture I am sorry in one way I cannot
encourage private enterprise and support the
hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle),
because I think it would be a good thing if

I support the Amendment proposed by
the right hon. Gentleman, not because
the Bill has been introduced by the
hon. Member opposite, but because I believe
that if this Bill became law it would have a
disastrous effect on our premier industry.
Agriculture has passed like most other industries through a most depressing time, and
I regret to say that the outlook at present
for agriculture is not any brighter. T would
say to the hon. Member as I would even to
the Government, "If you cannot do anything
to encourage and foster our agricultural
industry, for any sake leave us alone and do
not make it any more difficult for us to
carry on."
The hon. Member who introduced this Bill
claims to have the interest of the workers,
even the agricultural workers, very much at
heart. One wonders if this is really so when
he introduces such a Measure as this which,
if passed into law, would have in my opinion
the effect of driving many more of our agricultural workers out of employment, and as
agricultural workers are not qualified to receive unemployment benefit it would mean
for them privation and want. If the hon.
Member really wishes to improve the conditions of the agricultural labourer-and we
on this side of the House would be perfectly
willing to do so if we could-he must really
begin by doing something to stabilise the
agricultural industry, and make it an industry in something more than name. I
have listened to the hon. Member with a great
deal of patience and was expecting to hear
that this would put us on parallel lines with
Great Britain. It is only a short time
since in this House the hon. Member and
those who sit with him voted against a
Measure because it was on parallel lines, so
that the parallel line argument is only
trotted out to us when it would appear to
suit the purpose of the hon. Members
opposite. In this case, however, would we
be going on parallel lines with Great Britain?
I say no, because the circumstances are entirely different. The farmer across the water
has not sunk his capital in his farm but is
only a tenant during his tenancy whether it
is for a year or a number of years, and
at the end of his tenancy can rise up and go
if the farm is not a paying proposition and
turn his attention to some other industry,
Agricultural Wages Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Second Reading.
[Mr. Elliott]
and after all even where conditions are
different to what they are in Northern Ireland has the setting up of agricultural Wages
Board been a success from any point of view.
I noticed in the "Daily Mail" a short time
ago a report which reads as follows:-
"Farmers at a meeting at Cambridge on
Saturday warned the Government and the
nation of the crisis in arable farming, due
to the increased cost of production and to
falling prices.
It was stated that 50 per cent. of the
farmers on arable lands were faced with
ruin, and it would be accomplished in the
next twelve months unless the Government
reduced the burdens on the industry.
Protests were made against a system of
wages fixed irrespective of the economic
position of the industry and without regard
to prices."
This goes to show that where Agricultural
Wages Boards have been tried they have not
been, to say the least of it, a success, nor
have they encouraged or helped in any way
the agricultural industry.
Hon. Members on the opposition Benches
must surely know that the interests of both
the agriculturist and the agricultural worker
are bound together so closely that by legislating for the worker without first of all
doing something to put the industry itself
on its feet is like putting the cart before
the horse.
Prior to the passing of the 1920 Act, under
which we are functioning here, we had in
Northern Ireland agricultural Wages Boards.
I myself sat on this Board for years, and
I could never find out any good that either
my colleagues or myself, either representing
labour or capital, ever did for either the
employer or employee. As far as I can
see this Bill would only be useful for setting
up another crowd of officials, and of these,
as far as the agricultural industry is concerned, I would say we have quite enough.
Instead of doing so the hon. Member would,
I think, be far better employed in trying
to help the farmers to secure remunerative
prices at least for their produce, and so
make it possible for the farmers to improve
the conditions of their agricultural labourers.
I may be told, as I was told in this House
not long ago, that I never spoke on behalf
of the agricultural labourer in this House
or in any other place, and lest I may be
taken as being in a false position to-day,
I state here publicly that I have advocated the
cause of the agricultural labourer, and maintain that in the attitude I am taking up
to-day I am advocating his cause.
Something has already been done to improve the lot of the agricultural labourer—
much more remains to be done, but if we
proceed on the lines laid down by this Bill
we would, I think, be going very much on
the lines of the man who killed the goose
which laid the golden eggs. I have already
said that something has been done for the
agricultural labourer-his housing conditions
have been improved, and we are glad of
that, and at present in almost, if not, indeed,
in all, our rural districts further labourers'
cottage schemes have been or are being put
in operation. We have been told here that
the wages of the agricultural labourers in
County Tyrone are only 22s 6d a week.
Representing the counties of Tyrone and
Fermanagh, but knowing much more about
the County Tyrone than I do about County
Fermanagh, I may say that I do not know
any farmer in County Tyrone who is paying
his labourers only 22s 6d a week. Labourers'
wages are at least 100 per cent. more than
pre-war wages, and by the Widows' and
Orphans' Contributory Pensions Bill, which
I hope will soon become law, a great deal
more has been done for him in arranging for
his old age and providing for his dependants.
But what has been done for the farmer? He
is at present paying at least 100 per cent.
more than pre-war wages-the shoeing of his
horses, which before the war cost him 2s 6d
each, cost him now 8s; his rates are three
to four times what they formerly were, and
to-day we find him offered, if indeed he can
get sale for them at all, 2s per cwt., or
probably £2 10s per ton for his potatoes.
The right hon. Gentleman in front (Mr.
Pollock) tells me that in County Down,
where the wages, according to the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle), are
higher than in any other county, potatoes
are only 1s 9d per cwt.
Mr. KYLE: They are 8d a stone in the
shops to-day.

In other countries not supposed to be as
much advanced as Great Britain and Ireland they have done things for agriculture.
Does the right hon. Gentleman know that in
Czecho-Slovakia for example, following the
Washington conference they have introduced
a universal 48 hours' week? It may be thought
they could not do that in agriculture. It has
been done, and if the right hon. Gentleman
does not know that he should know. It has

with industry as the Bill suggests.
We have got this so far as industry in
the City is concerned. The same opposition
was offered to these Boards at the outset as

is the experience there? It is not due to the
operation there of the Wages Boards that we

industry is concerned. You do not have that

articles in the Belfast Press in particular

Speaking from memory, I have not seen one

of wages fixed by the Trade Board. If that

harm at the same time to the farmer at all.
We would try to get the agricultural
labourer a decent wage, but we do not want
to injure the position of the farmer, because
we know that the farmer is having a great
enough struggle under the conditions in
which he has to live.
I had an opportunity quite recently, as
some hon. Members know, of touring a considerable portion of the Continent. I
travelled from the Hook of Holland right
through to Berlin, and most of the way I
was lying half out of the carriage window
for the purpose of seeing as much as possible
of the country. I paid particular attention
to Germany, and right throughout Germany
-the agricultural district of Germany-I was
struck by one thought, by one fact that was
continually coming up against me. It was
this, that there was not one poor, dilapidated

The wages being paid to the workers in the
shipyards, engineering shops, textile mills,
and factories, or in any insured occupation
are so small that the workers are unable to
save any money at all to enable them to live
during the time they are unemployed. From
that point of view the State has thought it
fit to set up an insurance scheme called Unemployment Insurance, and to that every
worker is compelled to contribute by law,
as is his employer. We say that as we are
compelled to pay for this insurance we should
get the insurance from the first day we are
unemployed, and not after we have been six
days out of work.
This is a Measure which should appeal to
every member of the Committee, at least it
should appeal to every member who understands what unemployment means to the
ordinary man and ordinary worker. At the
end of the first week there is no money, and
at the end of the first week there is no benefit
from the Unemployment Insurance Fund,
with the result that these people get into
arrears with their rent, with their grocer,
and with whoever they deal with to obtain the
necessaries of life. It makes it extremely
difficult for them to carry on. As it is the
intention of the Government and of every
member of this Committee that the people
of Ulster should be as well provided for as
possible, we have now the opportunity of
seeing that Unemployment Insurance should
be paid as and from the first day of unemployment. I hope hon. Members will
pass this Amendment, which will give some
little measure of justice to the unemployed.

sympathetic with these unemployed workers.

Mr. DEVLIN: I am sure the House may
congratulate itself that it has now reached
the final stage of this Measure. I now rise
to ask the Prime Minister and the Members
of the Government what precisely is their
attitude in regard to the whole question of
unemployment, apart altogether from the
question of the payment of these unemployment grants. The Government have boasted
and they have made claims, many of which
are perfectly justified, that they have not
been ungenerous in the way in which they
have financially treated this question; but I
think that every Member of the House will
agree in fact it has been stated over and
over again by men belonging to all political
parties, in Ulster and elsewhere-that this
method of dealing with the vital and urgent
question of unemployment is not the most
satisfactory way of dealing with it, and it
certainly is not the last word in grappling
with a problem so tremendous as this problem is. Now at the end of the Session, after
a waiting period of six months, in fact of
nearly nine months, I would have thought the
Government would have had some policy in
regard to unemployment, and that they would
have been able to tell the House what is being
done to deal with the ever-decreasing trade
of Ulster. They may tell us that we are only
suffering as they are suffering in Great
Britain, but then when one considers that
there is no unemployment in France, that
there is no unemployment in Italy, and that
there is no unemployment. in Switzerland,
one wonders whether all has been done that
might have been done to deal with this
problem.
The right hon. Gentleman (the Prime
Minister) has stated that he and his Government have made no claims or offered themselves no bouquets. That is not altogether
my recollection of their attitude in relation
to themselves, because I have been reading
their speeches with very great interest, and
when they deign to get away from the purely
political question, and when they divorce
themselves from the purely passionate
aspects of our public life, they are never able
to tell us whether they have coldly as a
Cabinet sat down to think out for themselves
if there is any method by which this difficulty could be met. I have stated before, and
I repeat it now, that I am altogether opposed
to this slavish copying of everything English,
not because it is English, but because we are
now placed in the position of having a set
Government for ourselves-

Oral Answer to Question.
RATES ON AGRICULTURAL LAND.
1. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Finance what proportion of the
rates on agricultural land in Northern Ireland are paid from Government Grants, and
what proportion is raised from rates levied
on the occupiers.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): According to statements
furnished by the County Councils in
Northern Ireland the total amount of
Government Grants received by the County
Councils during the year ending 31st March,
1925, was £619,990. Of this amount, which
was applied in reduction of local expenditure, £257,288 was applied exclusively to the
relief of rates on agricultural land, but
agricultural land shared in addition, in the
same way as other rateable property, in
the reduction of local expenditure effected
by the remainder of the Government Grant.
A calculation on the basis of these figures
shows that the reduction in local expenditure effected by the Government Grant by
which agricultural land benefited amounts to
£515,000, and it has been ascertained that
the net amount raised by rates on agricultural land for the year in question was
£476,045, or in the proportion of 52 per cent.
from Government Grants to 48 per cent. from
ates on agricultural land.

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"
That it is expedient to authorise the
payment out of moneys provided by Parliament, to such amount as may be sanctioned
by the Ministry of Finance, of the expenses
of the Drainage Advisory Committee which
may be established by virtue of any Act
of the present Session, empowering County
Councils to carry out schemes for the
drainage, and improvement by drainage, of
lands, and for other purposes connected with
drainage."
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): This resolution which the Committee is asked to pass will be the statutory
authority for charging on Voted Moneys the
expenses of the Advisory Committee, which
is being set up under sub-Section (1) of
Section 18 of the Act. The expenses in
question will, so far as can be foreseen,
consist merely of the travelling and other
out-of-pocket expenses of the members of the
Committee, but as the meetings will, for the
most part, be held in Belfast, the only expenses will be those of country members, i.e.,
the County Council representatives, who, in
deference to the views of the County Councils,
are being added to the Committee. The annual total of these expenses cannot, of course,
'be definitely laid down dependent as it is
on the number of meetings held and the
amount of travelling done, but it is hardly
likely that a sum of more than £200 a year
will be required. It is anticipated that the
duties of secretary of the Committee and of
any other officers who may be required will
be carried out by the existing staff of the
Ministry of Finance, no extra charge being
involved. I beg to move.

Census Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): In moving the Second Reading of this
Measure I would remind the House that the
last census was taken in Ireland in 1911, and
in Great Britain in 1921. In 1921 it was
impossible to have a census in Ireland for
reasons with which the House is quite familiar. Therefore all the particulars which
the census ordinarily supplies are very much
out of date. As it is nearly fifteen years since
this census was taken in Ireland it must be
apparent that a great deal of data which will
he supplied in the papers will notify a very
1569 Drainage (Money)—

28 OCTOBER 1925
Committee.
considerable change in the conditions resulting from the movements of the people from
various causes, such as the Great War,
full particulars. The practice in this census
factors which perhaps are not present to the
minds of many people, such as the very
serious influenza epidemic that took place in
the year 1918-19, in which it is stated that
5,000 people died in Northern Ireland. All
these factors, as I say, have created such a
possible change in the population of the
North of Ireland that it is additionally incumbent upon the Government to carry out
the census programme outlined in this Measure.
The need for a census extends to every
part of the Administration, and, while a
simple record of the number of people living
in each administrative division of the country is of great value, this accurate information needs to be supplemented by particulars
of age, of sex, of marital conditions, conditions as to orphanhood, and the occupation or
industry in which the persons making the
return are engaged; also the collection of
this information covering the whole country
and showing the number of rooms that are
occupied by the inhabitants will have
very direct bearing upon that very important
subject the housing question.
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
a
Mr. POLLOCK: The Government regards
this, apart from other considerations, as an
opportune time for proceeding with the work
of the census, because the country is in a perfectly peaceful condition, and therefore it is
not desirable that Northern Ireland should
lag behind other progressive countries in the
tabulation of the material that it is necessary to introduce into the census return.
This Measure has received considerable
attention in another place, and its details
have been discussed at very considerable
length. The Measure itself is largely selfexplanatory, the language used being so
simple that any ordinary reader can understand it. It is probable, however, that attention should be drawn to the points at which
this Bill departs in some of its essential
features from the censuses that have been
undertaken in the past, and also that attention should be drawn to matters in which
changes have been made to introduce features
corresponding to those in Great Britain. I
do not propose to go over all the Clauses
item by item, but I intend to bring out, if
I may, some of the salient features as they
appear, and which will probably be most interesting to the House.
In Section 4 (2), which in general cortesponds with the legislation prevailing in
Great Britain, the duty of setting out the
Schedule is imposed upon the head of the
household. In each previous census in Ireland this duty was imposed on the enumerator, that is the person who supplies the
paper and collects it. In practice, however,
the head of the household has been called
upon to fill up the Schedule to the best of
his ability, and the enumerator is placed
in the position of furnishing any information
that may be necessary in order that the
head of the household may be able to give
fuli particulars. The practice in this census
will remain the same, and the legislation has
been framed to give statutory effect and sup
port to the method. In the same Section and
sub-Section provision with regard to seperate
returns is made, and this is mainly introduced in order to suit persons living in
hotels who may have some delicacy about
giving information to the owner of the hotel
as to the particulars required in the census
paper. In such cases, therefore, the Bil
provides that the occupants of hotels on
the day on which the census is taken may at
their discretion furnish separate papers. It
is not expected that this will be a matter of
great importance, the probability being that
on Sunday evening the general body of the
population will be in their own homes, but
we think it necessary to make that provision lest any difficulty should arise on that
head.
Section 6 (2) is a new Section, that is new
to Ireland, but it corresponds with the provision made in Great Britain. In practice
all information which would normally be
required will be included in the census
abstracts, but it will be costly to tabulate
all conceivable information which could be
tabulated possibly from the census returns
in every minute detail. It is provided in
the Section that if any person or body of
persons desire any additional information
to that contained in the census returns this
information will only be secured at the individual's or body's own expense.
Section 9, which is more specific than was
contained in previous Acts relating to census
returns in Ireland, prevents the use of the
returns for proof of age in claims for oldage pension; that is to say, the family returns cannot be used for the purpose of
establishing the age of an old-age pensioner.
The practice which has existed in the past
of using Census Schedules for this purpose
has undoubtedly encouraged misstatements
in regard to the age for the purpose of
coming within the terms and conditions
of the Old Age Pensions Act, and therefore
in order that absolute accuracy may be
secured in this matter the Government think
it necessary that abstracts should not be
used and cannot be used for the purpose
of establishing the age in the case of an
old-age pensioner. I need hardly say that
the general purpose of this is to ensure

absolute privacy on everything returned in
the paper, and that therefore there will be
no hesitancy on the part of any person to
furnish the abstracts or give all information
which is called for in the return. I think
that this protection which the community
will have under the conditions which are
outlined in the Bill should enable us to secure
a very definite and very accurate return of
the inhabitants of Northern Ireland.
Now I turn to Section 11 which is the only
other Section which I will bring out into
relief, leaving other matters of greater detail
to the Committee stage which will come along
to-morrow. Section 11 corresponds to a
similar Section which exists in Great
Britain. It provides for the compiling
of a return based upon the need for the
periodical publication-a short compendium
relating to statistics in respect of Northern
Ireland. No burden is placed on the public
for the supply of additional statistics, and
the intention is to produce an official year
book for Northern Ireland much upon the
lines of that produced for many years by
almost every progressive community. These
are the outstanding features of the Measure.
I can ouly again emphasise the features of
the Bill to which I have referred, that is
to say that every head of a house or every
person who makes a return can be absolutely assured of the most complete privacy
in regard to the sacredness of the return
which will be made. I beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: I want, if I may, to welcome
this Measure. It seems to me to be absolutely essential for those of us who are interested in the Government of Northern Ireland to have absolutely accurate information
regarding our population. I was gratified to
note that the Minister of Finance in his

to act promptly in regard to the various
matters that arise through overcrowding, if
there is any. Without the accurate information contained in the census it will be impossible for any governing body, or any
authority speaking generally, to ascertain
the facts regarding not only the number of
people but also the number of young people
between 14 and 18 years of age. This is interesting to those who are concerned in the
problem mentioned yesterday by the Prime
Minister, the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin) and the Minister of Labourthe problem of what provision is to be made
for boys between 14 and 18 years of age. It
is difficult for a Government Department or
anybody else to make suggestions when they
do not know exactly the number of people
between these ages resident either in Belfast
or the Six Counties. Therefore, I think this
Measure should meet with the approval of
the whole population of the Six Counties,
and I hope that when the information is
obtained if it is found, for example, that
there is overcrowding definite action
will be taken by the Government to see that
this state of affairs will be made right. I
welcome the Measure.

CLASS II. No. 3.
SPECIAL CONSTABULARY.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£95,000 be granted to his Majesty for the
service of the year ending 31st March, 1926,
to defray the salaries and expenses of the
Special Constabulary (12 and 13 Geo. V.,
(N.1.) ).
C.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): In introducing this Estimate
I may perhaps save the time of the Committee, and narrow the discussion down if I
emphasise the fact that the Supplementary
Estimate, which I ask this House to approve
of, relates solely to the "A" Special Constabulary, that is, the whole-time Specials.
Hon. Members are aware that in the organisation of this Force, these "A" Specials act
either as barrack supernumeraries or in
mobile platoons, and in many ways they are
indistinguishable from the Royal Ulster Constabulary. As regards the "B" and "C"
Constabulary we do not ask for any further
money. Indeed, during this year we have
been able to effect substantial economies in
regard to these Forces.
When the original Estimate in regard to
the "A" Special Constabulary was framed we
had in mind the possibility of making a reduction in the Force over and above that
which would follow ordinary wastage. The
wastage has not been so great as was anticipated, and this is largely due to the fact that
as the Force gets smaller those who were left
are generally the pick, both as regards health
and character, and, as a result, the wastage
is a good deal slower. But apart from this
aspect of the question the Government found
that they could not make any drastic reduction in the Force. The Prime Minister,
speaking on this question in connection with
the introduction of the original Estimate,
stated that the Government must be the sole
judge as to the time when reduction can be
made with safety to the community, and as
regards myself and other Members of the
Government we adhere to that statement.
We have found that it has been impossible to
effect any reduction this year by demobilisation, apart altogether from wastage. The
reduction that we have been able to make
in regard to this Force, which numbers
round about 3,700 men, has only been 200 in
regard to wastage.
I do not think it is necessary to lay stress
in this Committee on the magnificent service
rendered by this Special Constabulary Force,
particularly by the "A" branch. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Some of us have
short memories, but I do not think any of
us who remained in Ulster during that period
could fail to contrast the present condition
of affairs with that which existed two or
three years ago.
I recollect that in one
year alone malicious damage amounted to no
less a sum than £3,000,000. To-day, I
am glad to say, the figure is practically nil.
May I say, looking at it from purely a business or an insurance point of view, that what
we receive for the premium we pay by way of
the pay of these "A" Specials is certainly
good value?
A very great responsibility rests on the
Government in this matter. We have to
consider many things. We nave to consider
'what the effect will be on the lawless sections of the community. For my own part
I believe the time is approaching when w
will be able to effect further economies by
means of a reduction in the "A" Special
Constabulary, but that time is not yet. In
putting this Supplementary Estimate before
the Committee I would like hon. Members
to look at it in the broadest possible way,
and for the moment to get rid of partisanship and to consider what is best for the
community at large. Whether or not this
Supplementary Estimate is to be granted I
I would like them to have regard to the feelings and fears of a large section of the community throughout Ulster who, for months
and in some cases for a very much longer
time, have learned to know what it is to live
without the protection of the law.
I suggest to this Committee that the
Government who brought about the peace
are, perhaps, the best judges as to when
those Measures which they adopted to bring
it about should be relaxed.
I am convinced that in the action which
the Government are taking in maintaining
this "A" Force they will have the support
of all law-abiding sections of the community,
regardless of creed or class. In that spirit
I ask the Committee to pass this Supplementary Estimate.
Mr. DEVLIN: I rejoice that the opportunity has at last arrived when we can
respond to the invitations given us from
the Government Benches as to what suggestions we
can make as to the best means
of augmenting and making adequate and

Members of this House who ventured to

Tyrone to come in here and assist the Government in maintaining law and order, have
not taken their seats in this House, but are
still actively resisting the Government of
Northern Ireland, and are doing their utmost
by their example to make government in
Northern Ireland impossible. I ask myself
have we reached such a stage that we can
afford to beat our swords into plough shares
and our spears into pruning hooks. I assert
that we have not, and so I say to the Government, who are responsible for maintaining
law and order, that we in the Border
counties, in Fermanagh and Tyrone particularly, put on them the responsibility of maintaining that peace which we are glad to say
they have been able to establish. While the
Government with a very firm hand have established law and order, I think they will
not dispute this statement of mine, that it
would have been impossible for the Government to have established that peace which
we are all enjoying at the present time had
it not been for the people of the Six Counties
as well as of the City of Belfast joining the
Special Constabularly.
The PRIME MINISTER: Hear, hear.
Mr. ELLIOTT: The hon. Member for
Antrim (Mr. McAllister) has stated more
than once in this House than the Special
Constabulary is a sectarian Force, but I
am here to state that in County Tyrone
several Roman Catholics joined the Special
Constabulary, and they were compelled by
people of their own side of the House, their
Roman Catholic brethren, to desist, and to
refrain from giving any assistance to the
Government of Northern Ireland in establishing peace and maintaining law and order,
so that if the Special Constabulary to-day
is composed of Protestant people it is simply
because the Roman Catholics up to this
point have refused to come in themselves
to assist the Government, and to take their
fair share of the responsibility of government. So, I say to the Government, you
have established peace in our midst. We
want you to maintain that peace which you
established, and, as far as I am concerned, I am perfectly satisfied to give the
Government this additional grant that they
may require believing, as I do, that the
Government are determined to keep the
police force in Ulster at such a pitch that
they can say that peace will be maintained.
At the same time I am delighted to know
that they are economising, and that this
year's Estimates, compared with those of
last year, show a big reduction as far as
the police force is concerned.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
McAllister) has also said that this is not
Supplementary Estimates. 1592
Supply--
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Elliott]
a disciplined Force, but I have not heard
one word from the hon. Member for Antrim
in support of that statement. I am quite
prepared to admit that a part of this Force
comprises only very ordinary men, but I am
prepared to state that they are loyal men-
(hon. Members: hear, hear)-and that they
are men who are prepared to stand for law
and order. If we had all men in Northern
Ireland of the same way of thinking as the
men of the Special Constabulary the time
would come when we could afford to dispense
with the Force. As long as we have an
element, however, in Northern Ireland out
for the purpose of wrecking our Northern
Constitution, and out to make Government
as far as they possibly can impossible, I say
to the Government, "Whatever money is
a
necessary to maintain our Force at such
a high pitch and at such level that
loyal people are able to go about their
I will
avocations peaceably, carry on."
support the Government in any demand they
make on this House to carry out and maintain that object.
It is all very good to say that we have
peace. We are delighted to have peace, but
surely there is an old saying that if we
want to maintain peace we must be prepared
for war. The time has not come yet to
dispense with the Force. I am delighted to
be here to-day as a representative of the
Border counties to give my meed of praise
to the brave men of the Special Constabulary
of all grades who have done their bit and
earned the respect and esteem of all Loyalists
and right-thinking men. I heartily support
the Government's Motion on this matter. I
shall have the greatest possible pleasure in
going into the Lobby to support a further
sum for the maintenance of the Special
Constabulary.
Mr. KYLE: I gave a pledge during my
election that I was willing to support rigid
economy so far as the administration of
the Northern area was concerned. When
one is faced with a Vote for £95,000 as an
additional sum for the Special Constabulary,
a sum which brings up the total to £1,220,000
for that Force, or £1 a head for every man,
woman and child in the Six Counties, it
seems to me to be asking too much. One
would like to say, as the Prime Minister
has said, how much we appreciate the services of the Special Constabulary during the
terrible times we came through, particularly
in this city. Those are the times I know
about best. I do not know about the Border
counties and cannot speak for what happened
there. I know, however, what happened here.
I know the Special Constabulary did render
very valiant services to the whole community
during that time. Are we to be told because
the Constabulary gave us that service and
assisted the Government in bringing about
the peace that has prevailed for the last
year and a half or two years-a peace that
we all desire and all want to see maintained
--are we to be told that because the Specials
helped us during that trouble, we, as a Parliament, are to continue spending that money
that is raised out of the taxpayers' pockets?
It seems to me that it would be a regrettable
thing if a body such as ours should come to
a decision like that. It is from that point of
view, while rendering all the credit due to
the services of the Specials and rendering
all the credit that is even due to the Government for bringing about peace, that we desire to see that this Vote of £95,000 should
not meet with the approval of the House and
should be reduced.
Mr. GRANT: I would like as one who
knows something about the troubles in this
city to rise to support the Government in
connection with this Vote. I wonder if
the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin) remembers that when the Crown
forces failed to protect the citizens of this
city the only people we had to stand between
us and his co-religionists who entered the
Province of Northern Ireland determined to
break down law and order, were the members
of the "A" Force and those associated with
them. They were the only men on whom the
Loyalists of Northern Ireland had to depend
for protection. During his speech the hon.
Member (Mr. Devlin) said that he was not
familiar with the terms of the Special Constabulary, that is the "A" and "B" classes.
I suppose the reason he is not familiar with
the terms is that during the time of the
trouble in Belfast he was not in the country,
or else he was lying very low. He was not
running the same risks as other Members
of this Committee who were elected at the
same time as he was, and who realised their
responsibilities and the duties that they owed
to those who sent them here. They came to
this House and had to run certain risks, and
they were only able to carry on their duties
through the protection afforded them by the
Special Constabulary. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) He certainly missed his chances at
that time. We all know that the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin), whatever
failings he may have, has great powers of
persuasion. He did not, however, avail himself of the opportunity at that time of using
his great powers of persuasion with the
people to try to assist the Government in the
restoration of law and order.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
McAllister) says that it is ridiculous to think
that we should have one policeman for every
six families. I well remember the time that
it would have taken six policemen for each
family, but we were not able to afford it at
that time. I also remember our Prime

Supply-

Minister stating in this House that should
he bankrupt Ulster he would restore law
and order. Every Member of the House
applauded that statement and supported the
Prime Minister, and we are here to support
him still in that attitude. Although I quite
agree with a great deal of what the Leader
of the Opposition (Mr. Kyle) has said, I would
like to remind him of the fact that in the
British House of Commons they had a discussion on similar lines to this. There was
a great cry-out for the Government to reduce
the strength of the Navy. They said that they
were spending too much money on the, Navy.
The Government listened to the persuasions of
the Labour Party and Opposition in the
Imperial House, and immediately issued
orders to close down two dockyards and to
suspend a considerable number of men who
would be thrown into the list of unemployed.
Within forty-eight hours of that outcry for
a reduction in the Navy there was a protest
against the great injustice that the Government were inflicting in closing down two
dockyards and suspending these men.
Mr. KYLE: I protest against any injustice
being done to any section, but it is not from
that point of view that we object to the
Vote.
Mr. GRANT: I would like to assure the
hon. Member that I am not trying to attack
the Labour Party. I only want to remind the
Committee that we must not get into the same
position as they did on the other side, and
that is throw these men out on the street.
I am sure if we do that we would have the
Opposition coming in and asking the Government what they were going to do with the
men they disbanded. I want to impress on
hon. Members on both sides that we must
not run into the same position as Great
Britain by listening to the appeals of people
to reduce the strength of the Navy, or, in our
case, the strength of the Special Constabulary,
If the Government do give way to these
appeals the very people who made them will
be the first to come into this House and ask
the Government to provide something for those
men thrown out on account of the position
they had taken up. I would like to say, in
conclusion, that I am satisfied that the
Government are doing the right thing. We
are not yet out of the wood, and we have
nothing to depend on except the splendid
men of the Special Constabulary, to whom
everybody on both sides of the House owes
so much.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I am one
of the Opposition referred to here, but let
me say that I was not returned to reduce
Government expenditure at the cost of
putting many of the Specials on the dole.
There have been repeated arguments put
forward, especially by the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Devlin), during the last
two or three weeks why the unemployment
money should be increased. What does this
mean? It may mean, as one hon. Member
said, a saving of £5,000, but we would be
putting a number of men on the street, and
there is the possibility that the same plea
would be put up as regards them, that
they were not genuinely seeking for work.
The result would be that their families
would suffer. The Force, as constituted
to-day, is composed of skilled craftsmen and
labouring men. This Force is the most
efficient Force, as the Prime Minister has
said, that we have got in the world. It is
most essential that Ulster, like every other
country, should have a Force, no matter
whether you call that Force "A" Specials
or soldiers. It is essential that every
country should have a force to protect it
and maintain law and order.
I am going to support the Government.
If the Government think it fit and necessary
that this amount of money should be granted
to keep the Force at the present time, I
agree. The Government know more about
it than I do. There is another matter I
would like to refer to-that is item E
(clothing). There is an additional sum of
£4,000 required for that. I would like the
Minister of Home Affairs to let me know
if the clothing, etc., for the Force are
purchased across the water?
The PRIME MINISTER: The Caledon
Mills make the most of it.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: When we
have woollen mills in Ulster all the cloth
to make the clothing should be bought in
Ulster. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Let
us keep the money in Ulster. I do not
believe that the question of religion should
be introduced. I believe that any citizen
who had the qualifications to become a
Special could have become a member of the
Force this "luxury Force," as the hon.
Member for Antrim (Mr. McAllister) called
it. All had equal opportunities to become
members of the Force. There was nothing
put in the way of citizens to become members of the Force, provided they were up
to the standard as far as height, age, etc.,
were concerned. I believe the Special Constabulary are performing a great public
duty. I would be the last man to suggest
that any saving should be effected at the
expense of the Special Constabulary, and I
am going to support the Government on this
occasion.
Question put, "That a sum not exceeding
£90,000 be granted for such service."

Original Question put and agreed to.
CLASS V. No. 2.
AGRICULTURAL SERVICES.
Motion made and Question proposed:
That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£2,760 be granted to his Majesty for the service of the year ending 31st March, 1926,
to defray the expenses of the. Ministry of
Agriculture in respect of Agriculture, Education and Research, Improvement of Live
Stock, Agricultural Development, Agricultural Statistics and Afforestation, including
sundry Grants in Aid and certain Capital
Expenditure under 14 and 15 Geo. V., c. 13.
s. I (N.I.).
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): Nearly every inhabitant of
Northern Ireland can remember the bad
weather of the last three years, but very
few people except those interested in agriculture understood the great losses that were
incurred by the farmers in a great many of
the counties through the loss of cattle by bad
feeding and the destruction of hay. It got
so bad in some of the counties that last May
the Government decided to give Short Term
Loans to those who had lost cattle through
disease. In May last they gave intimation
of that decision to this House, and notices
were issued all over the Six Counties that
applications would be received from May up
to the end of September. The idea was to
lend money through the banks, the applicant to pay 21 per cent, interest, and the
Government 3 per cent. to make up the
balance, the Short Term Loans to be repaid
on 31st December, 1926.
Altogether 1,209 applications have been received, and of those 942 have up to the
present been approved, representing a total
of £43,960. 149 applications are still being
considered and will be dealt with, I hope,
in the course of a week. The loans averaged
£56, ranging from as low as £5. The sum
of £2,200 in the Vote is the balance of the
interest paid to the banks by the Government, and it represents the discount over the
24 per cent. the borrowers are paying.
Miller, William Thomas
Morrison, Hugh Smith
Mulholland, The Hon. Henry George Hill
Pollock, Right Hon. Hugh MacDowell
Robb, John Hanna
Shillington, Major David Graham
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Capt. Mulholland.
With regard to the sum of £500 for temporary additional staff, we were obliged to
appoint three additional inspectors to inquire into the circumstances of the borrowers, although most of the work is done
by officials of the Ministry. We also had
to engage two temporary clerks. The sum of
£60 is for stamp duty on the Promissory
Notes.
Mr. JOHNSTONE: May I ask if the sum
of £2.200 represents the difference between
the interest payable by the borrower and the
interest payable to the bank?
Mr. ARCHDALE: Yes. 3 per cent. is payable by the Government and 2 per cent.
by the borrower.
Mr. KYLE: I want to say a word about
this Supplementary Estimate and I do so
largely because of the unsatisfactory answer
the Minister of Agriculture gave me the other
day in response to a question I put to him.
In my opinion it cast a reflection on the
workers in the agricultural industry. I
asked that representatives of the workers
should be put on the various Committees
that have been set up from time to time
during the existence of the Ministry of
Agriculture to advise the Ministry upon
certain matters. He said these Committees
were not connected with wages, and he did
not think labour men should be appointed
on them.
I would draw the right hon. Gentleman's
attention to the fact that during the time
he served on a Committee in Dublin there
was also on that Committee a man called
Frank from Lisburn, and I think the
Minister of Agriculture will agree that that
man did give efficient and useful service to
the Board at that time. I want to move a
reduction in this Estimate of £100, because I
do not think the Minister of Agriculture
has any right to deliberately and in a calculated way insult the people I have the
honour to represent in this House. The
people who are interested in agriculture are
not confined to the employing class as alleged.
The workers are just as much interested in
agriculture as any of the people the right
hon. Gentleman has appointed on these Committees.

The CHAIRMAN: I think I must point
out to the hon. Member that he is put in the
same difficulty here as arose in the course of
the discussion on the last Estimate. The one
head of this Supplementary Estimate is Replacement of Live Stock, and I find a
difficulty in seeing how the particular
question he is discussing now is related to
that point.
Mr. KYLE: The Estimate says. "to defray
the expenses of the Ministry of Agriculture
in respect of Agricultural Education and Research, Improvement of Live Stock," etc.
There is a Committee on Research.
The CHAIRMAN: I pointed out at some
length a little time ago that the whole
question of policy is open for discussion
when the original Estimate is introduced,
but that when a Supplementary Estimateand this is a Supplementary Estimate-is
presented discussion must not range at
large upon policy, but must be restricted to
the specific matter for which the sum is
asked to be voted. It is a technical difficulty.
Mr. KYLE: All I want to say is that I
desire to move a reduction of £100 in this
Estimate in consequence of the unsatisfactory
answer the Minister of Agriculture gave me
and which seemed to me to cast a reflection
on the people I represent in this House-the
'working classes. They are just as competent
to give assistance to the Ministry of Agriculture as they are to any other Ministry,
and if the Minister of Agriculture will pay
attention to what is happening in Denmark,
a country whose agricultural methods he is
opposed to. he will find that their labour
people are looked upon as being just as competent to give advice as the gentlemen the
Minister has appointed on these Committees.
Mr. ARCHDALE: The hon. Member has
stated that in my answer to him a few days
ago I unnecessarily insulted the labourers
of Northern Ireland. Nothing was further
from my mind. The answer I gave him was
that these were Consultative Committees,
each consisting of five or six members who
'were experts representing each of the
counties, and I do not think the labourers
would be qualified to give advice on the
various subjects dealt with. Nothing was
further from my mind than to insult these
workers.
Mr. KYLE: That is the insult, but the
right hon. Gentleman does not seem to
realise it.
The CHAIRMAN: I do not think this is
germane to the point.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: The only
comment I want to pass on this Estimate
is that it is not big enough. It seems to me
that the administrative charges are very
heavy. £500 is for staff expenses in connection with a total vote of £2,760.
As the Minister of Agriculture said,
anyone who has any acquaintance at all
with the agricultural industry knows that
during the past two years we have been
passing through a very trying time owing
to the inclement seasons, and the position
I took up in this House when the Government produced its scheme of Short Term
Loans has been entirely justified. While
farmers suffered severely through loss of
stock, a great many more suffered through
loss of crop, and I cannot see why the
Government confined these Loans to farmers
financially handicapped through loss of stock.
The Government should have allowed these
loans to be obtained by farmers who were
in financial straits owing to the generally
bad season through which we have passed,
and if this Estimate had been for £20,000 or
£30,000 or £40,000 we could have done no
better in the Six County area than to give
credit on easy terms to farmers, so that they
might be given a chance to repair their
broken finances.
I do not criticise the Estimate. We have
passed an Estimate for £95,000 extra for
special police, and I say that if agriculture
occupies the position that the Government
pretends it occupies, the primary position,
they should have extended this scheme to all
farmers in need of it. I said at that time
that I could assure the Government that
they would not be overburdened by farmers
coming in and asking for loans because the
farmer is a man averse to borrowing money,
and it is only in a case of dire necessity he
will borrow it.
I hope, owing to the financial position of
many farmers, the Government will in the
near future devise some scheme of easy credit
to help our agriculturists through what has
been recognised as one of the worst periods
through which we have passed. We have had
in the latter part of this year a very much
better summer, for which we are all deeply
thankful. The extra sunshine and better
weather have put a little moral and heart
into the agricultural community once more,
and if the Government can only be induced
to come to their aid now by some similar
scheme of easy credit, they would, I think,
be doing a service to the Six County area
that could not be over-estimated.
I want to say another thing. I do not
expect the Minister of Agriculture to answer,
because it would not be fair to ask him. I
have had numerous communications from

without the Ministry giving any reason for
their refusal. They think the Ministry should
have at least the courtesy to say on what

Oral Answers to Questions.
EGG INSPECTION IN OMAGH DISTRICT.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he has received any
complaints about the manner in which the
Egg Inspector for Omagh district carries
out his duties, and whether this man, who is
an Englishman, and seems not to understand the Irish egg trade, will be allowed
to continue to make it practically impossible
for egg merchants (who are willing and
anxious to comply with the law) to carry
on their trade.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): A few such complaints have been
received and have formed the subject of investigation by the Ministry. Some of the
merchants do not apparently appreciate the
duties of the marketing inspection staff. It
is the function of these officers to visit stores
and markets and to report to the Ministry
the facts that come under their notice.
Their standing instructions are that, at the
same time, they are to explain, when necessary, the requirements of the Marketing
of Eggs Act and the Rules thereunder, and
generally to give all practicable assistance
to licensed wholesale dealers to enable them
to comply with the Regulations. The
Ministry is quite satisfied that the officer
in question has a wide knowledge and experience of the egg trade, and that he is
not alone fully qualified to carry out the
duties allotted to him, but that he is actually
discharging his duties in an efficient
manner.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of that answer
by the right hon. Gentleman, may I ask him,
as complaints have been made about the way
in which this man carries out his duties, if
steps will be taken to ensure that he will
discharge them in a less obnoxious way in
future?
MARKETING OF EGGS ACT-APPOINT-
MENT OF LADY INSPECTORS.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether it would not be possible
in future to appoint Lady Inspectors under
the Marketing of Eggs Act, seeing that many
of these young ladies are properly qualified,
having been trained in the Dairy School
under the Department of Agriculture.
Mr. ARCHDALE: It is not proposed to
appoint women to any vacancies that may
arise in the Marketing Inspection staff. The
Ministry is satisfied that having regard to
the nature of the duties, a male staff is
calculated to achieve more satisfactory results. My hon. Friend will, no doubt, recollect that positions in the counties as
Instructors in Poultry Keeping and Buttermaking are open to women students who
have undergone a course of instruction at the
Ulster Dairy School, but the training at that
school would not in itself fit a student to
undertake inspection duties in connection
with the Marketing of Eggs Act. For such
work the honourable Member will appreciate
that a practical business experience is
essential.
DEPARTMENTAL
APPOINTMENTS-
CLAIMS OF ULSTERMEN.
3. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether, when appointing inspectors under the Marketing of Eggs Act,
it was not possible in Northern Ireland to
obtain Ulstermen properly qualified to perform these duties.

tioned in my reply in the House on the 22nd

BLACK SCAB IN COUNTY LONDON-
DERRY.
Mrs. CHICHESTER (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Agriculture whether
he is in a position to state, with regard to
the Black Scab area in County Londonderry,
that the area to be scheduled will be limited
as far as possible consistently with controlling the disease. Further, what steps has
he taken to find markets in Great Britain
for the potatoes which have been grown in
this area.
Mr. ARCHDALE: The Ministry has given
this matter its most careful consideration,
and has already come to a decision in the
direction mentioned by the hon. Member,
viz., to restrict the area to be scheduled to
the smallest extent consistent with control
of the spread of the disease.
With regard to the second part of the
question, the Ministry is, through its Chief
Marketing Inspector, making inquiries as to
the possibility of securing markets in Great
Britain for the varieties of potatoes grown
in the district to which the hon. Member
refers.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: Arising out of the
first part of the answer, will the Minister
state when it is proposed to confer with the
representatives appointed by the Derry
County Council in regard to the scheduling
of this area?
Mr. ARCHDALE: I have arranged to meet
a deputation from the County Derry Committee of Agriculture at 11 a.m. on Tuesday
next at my office.

ALLEGED POLICE RAID IN CO. DERRY.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is aware
that the police raided the house of Mr.
James Mallon, of Swateragh, Co. Derry, a
former member of the Derry County Council
and Magherafelt Rural District Council,
Census (Money).
Drainage Bill.
29 OCTOBER 1925
four times between the 26th September and
the 21st October, 1925, invariably at midnight, causing such annoyance to the family
that Mrs. Mallon was compelled to place herself under the doctor's care; whether he will
state if Mr. James Mallon has violated the
law; and if so, whether he will take suitable
action; and if not, whether he will give an
undertaking that these nocturnal visits shall
cease.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): No raid was made on the
house of Mr. Mallon, but visits by the police
were made on the dates mentioned in consequence of a complaint made by a neighbour
of molestation on the part of Mr. James
Mallon. The visits were made by a night
patrol in the course of their ordinary duty
owing to the difficulty of finding Mallon at
his home during the day time. The police
are unable to confirm the statement that
Mrs. Mallon has been compelled to place herself under the doctor's care as a result of
the visits of the police.
I may add that Mallon's conduct in the
past has given cause for complaint by the
police, and I am not prepared to give any
undertaking to restrain the police from the
legitimate performance of their duties.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Census (Money.)
Considered in Committee.
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair.)
Motion made, and Question proposed:-
"That it is expedient to authorise a charge
upon moneys provided by Parliament in respect of the expenses incurred, with the
approval of the Ministry of Finance, in connection with the taking of the Census for
Northern Ireland in the year nineteen
hundred and twenty-six, and for otherwise
collecting statistical information, under
powers to be conferred by an Act of the
present Session."
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINANCIAL
SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): Yesterday the
House gave a Second Reading to the Bill
authorising the taking of a Census of
Northern Ireland in 1926. A certain amount
of expenditure will obviously become
necessary in the taking of this Census, and
this Financial Resolution is, as the Committee is aware, the statutory authority for
charging such expenses on the yearly
Estimates. In point of fact, a Supplementary
Estimate for the expenses to be incurred in
the current financial year has already been
presented to the House and will be moved in
Committee of Supply either this evening or
at an early date.
The taking of a Census and the subsequent
tabulation of the information collected, in
order to make such information as useful as
possible for the various purposes for which
statistics of this kind are required,
necessarily involves considerable administrative expenditure. It is difficult at the
present moment to state with any degree of
accuracy what the total charge will eventually be, but it is safe to say that, in round
figures, a sum of £20,000 will be required.
Of this amount, the sum of £2,500 will be
required this year, and this is the amount
which the House will be asked to vote-the
balance of £17,500 being left over until the
following years 1926 and 1927 in which the
expenditure will be incurred.
This sum may seem high, but I can assure
the House that even with the use of up-todate tabulating machinery the amount of
detailed work that arises out of the questionnaire outlined in the Second Schedule to the
Bill will be of a most exacting character.
In addition to that we have been guided by
precedent of the recent British Census and
the former Census taken in Ireland. I beg
to move.
Question put and agreed to.
Resolution reported and agreed to.

CLAUSE 1 (Preparation, confirmation,
and carrying out of schemes for drainage
works).
1.-(1) The council of each county in
Northern Ireland other than a county
borough (in this Act referred to as "the
county council") shall be a drainage
authority for the purposes of draining any
lands within their county which are liable
to be flooded or injured by water, or whose
drainage is capable of being improved; and,
subject to the provisions of this Act, the
county council shall have power-

for the purpose of preparing any schemes

I think I am in order in reading this:--
I have read your speech about the Bann

water power on this river, when as you

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Hear, hear.
Dr. MORRISON: I am glad to hear the
"Hear, hear" of the hon. Member for Derry.
The letter goes on:-
I have had about forty years' experience
with water power and I am positive that
a few flood gates would let away more
water than the lower stretches of the river
could carry off . . . I am sure that at
some date some energetic person will develop the 10,500 h.p. that could be so easily
got on the Bann without raising the river
one hair's breadth. It is very rare to find
a river like the Bann supplied by a lough
like Lough Neagh, containing such a vast
supply of water, standing 52 feet above sea
level, and I consider it a crime of the first
magnitude to let people who do not realise
the value of cheap power destroy such
a magnificent asset to Ulster.
In taking the line that I have done in regard to this Measure, I am actuated by a desire to do justice to the people who live in
my district, and whom I have known intimately for forty years. I have suggested two
plans, the putting in of these flood gates,
and that until that is done the Government
would undertake the liability for the tax.
If you put flood gates in here they would
open and drain off the Bann between the
rainfalls, and you would have a storage
capacity in the lough itself, and a storage
capacity in the Bann itself, to accommodate two or three weeks' rain. Coming
up in the train to-day i read the speech
of the Minister of Finance, and I
agree in the main with it. I also
read the speech of the Prime Minister, and
I wholly agree with it. The Minister of
Finance pointed out that even now after
the heavy rain of the last fortnight the
level of the water in the river and the lough
is practically no higher than in summer
time. I cross the Bann every day I come
to this House, and I can see whether it
is in flood or not. We have had tremendously
heavy rain this last fortnight, and the water
is not over its banks yet. My point is that
if the closed mill race at Castleroe were
opened, and kept open, and automatic locks
inserted, as I am told is done in County
Fermanagh, during the interval between the
floods, you will get a steady amount of water
set free and allowed to pass on to the sea.
You will have the lough and the river at
summer level, and then you could stand a
fortnight's rain. There is no vast engineering scheme in connection with this, as far
as I can see.
Evidently the Minister of Finance is still
dreaming that he is going to do wonderful
things by draining the lough. But I am
glad to see that the Prime Minister sees
considerably further, and sees the danger.
If we are going to rush into a scheme like
this, that has already burnt the fingers of
many people, and that has involved huge
expenditure without producing appreciable
results, I think with our limited resources
we should count the cost before we undertake it. It was a totally different matter
when we were associated with the Empire,
and the Empire paid these bills. What I
want to do is to educate public opinion. I
want to educate this Committee on the
fact that there is an alternative-this
simple plan of drainage for draining
off the surplus water and keeping the Bann
and the lough at summer level. Then when
the flooding comes it will not flood the
district.
I have had dreams about the prosperity
of Ulster. I agree with my friend who says
that it would be a crime of the first magnitude to destroy the commercial advantages
that the Bann gives us as a channel leading
into the heart of Ulster. I dream and think
that some time we may have along the Bann

Mr. BARBOUR: If hon. Members will
glance at the Estimate which has been circulated, they will see that there are two
items covered by the total amount of £500.
The first item is for £100, and the provision is a nominal amount to meet any payments which may be authorised by my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Finance, under
the Civil Pensions Act, which was passed
by the House last May. Sub-Section (1) of
Section 3 of that Act lays down that any
pensions or gratuities payable under the
Act shall be paid out of moneys provided by
Parliament, that is, from Voted Moneys:
hence the necessity for this provision, although in point of fact no actual payment
is at the present time under consideration.
The second item is for an ex gratia payment of £400 to the widow of a Resident
Magistrate, the late Mr. Roche, who died
suddenly last Spring while still serving as a
Magistrate for Belfast. This Estimate is introduced in order to fulfil an undertaking
given by the Prime Minister in reply to a
Question in this House on 3rd September
last. The payment is an exceptional one and
is outside the scope of the Superannuation
Acts, but is warranted owing to the special
conditions attaching to the duties of Resident
Magistrate in this City during the years
1920 to 1922, and may be regarded as a
special tribute to his faithfulness to duty
during that period. I think the House will
not grudge this small grant to his widow and
six young children, which is additional to
the statutory gratuity which the widow has
already received under the Superannuation
Acts on the Award of the Civil Service Committee. I beg to move.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I only want
to intervene for a moment in connection with
the Vote now before the Committee. An
allowance is going to be made to the widow
of the late Mr. Roche, who was a
Resident Magistrate for the City of Belfast
for a number of years, and especially during
a very trying period in the history of the
city. I am not going to take the slightest

seen fit to propose it, but I want to refer to

allowance of this character, and when an
allowance of this nature is given I think
it ought to be given in every case where the
circumstances are somewhat similiar to
those in the case of Mr Roche.

has been presented to the Committee I feel
that when things of this kind are given the
Government ought equally to consider other
cases where a similar condition of affairs
exists. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. Sparrow's services were rendered as a
police officer for a good many years throughout the length and breadth of Ireland, and
then he passed through the difficult years
that Mr. Roche passed through in Counties
Donegal and Derry. He had to carry his life
in his hand equally with Mr. Roche. I would
appeal to the Government to consider his
case as sympathetically as they have done
Mr. Roche's. I am not raising the slightest
objection in Mr. Roche's case. I gladly vote
for the amount, and would have voted for a
larger sum, but I appeal to the Minister
of Finance and the Government to consider
the widow of the late Mr. Sparrow, the only
other Resident Magistrate, I think, who has
passed to his reward having served through
those difficult and trying years and leaving
his widow and family in such a position
that they find it extremely difficult to carry
on and have the children educated. I make
this appeal on their behalf, believing that the
Government when they understand the full
facts of the case will be as sympathetic as
they have been with the family of the late
Mr. Roche.
Mr. MARK: I would like in a few words

Mr. WM. McMULLEN: The answer I have

No raid was made on the house of Mr.
Mallon, but visits by the police were made
on the dates mentioned in consequence of
a complaint made by a neighbour of molestation on the part of Mr. James Mallon.
The visits were made by a night patrol
in the course of their ordinary duty owing
to the difficulty of finding Mallon at his
home during the day time. The police
are unable to confirm the statement that
Mrs. Mallon has been compelled to place
herself under the doctor's care as a result

Mallon's conduct in the past has given
cause for complaint by the police, and I
am not prepared to give any undertaking
to restrain the police from the legitimate
performance of their duties.
Raiding the house of a person at midnight
is not a legitimate part of police duties, and
I regret that the right hon. Gentleman (Sir
Dawson Bates) has evaded the direct question put to him, because a citizen of Northern Ireland, no matter what his political
opinions may have been in the past, is entitled to the protection of the law. All I
was asking in the question was that if this
gentleman has violated the law you should
take suitable action, but if he has not violated the law he should be freed from these
midnight visits from the police.
Now there has been a little bit of a dispute,
I understand, between this gentleman and
his next-door neighbour, and the police have
interested themselves in a way in which I
believe they are not justified at all. I had
better give some extracts from a letter I
have received from this gentleman to show
the way he has been treated by the police.
I believe these statements to be absolutely
correct, and if they are they are an absolute
disgrace to the police force. The letter is as
follows:-
"On the night of September 26 between
ten and eleven o'clock a knock came to my
door, and on opening it I found it was
two policemen. They asked me about a
dispute between the tenant next door and
myself."
Now I should like to inquire what a dispute
between this gentleman and the tenant next
door had to do with the police. I think it
is a matter for the law courts, and I would
suggest that the police in this district, or in
any other district in Northern Ireland,
should leave questions of this kind to the
Courts to decide rather than interest themselves in the matter and take sides. Law
proceedings were pending, this gentleman
had briefed a lawyer to represent him, and
the police were very much interested to know
the name of the lawyer he had briefed in
connection with the case. The letter states
"They inquired who the lawyer was and
where was his place of abode."
I would like to inquire as to whether it is
any part of the legitimate duties of the police
force that if a citizen of Northern Ireland
briefs a lawyer they should come to his
house at midnight for the purpose of inquiring who the lawyer is and where his place of
abode is. It seems to be an extraordinary
state of affairs altogether and much outside the duties of a police force. The letter
proceeds:

it was two policemen. They stepped inside. I noticed at once they were the
worse of drink. I asked them if they were
coming to arrest me. They said not."

Mr. KYLE: I would like to ask the
Minister of Finance does that Amendment
which he has put in to-day meet the case

Mr. POLLOCK: I am glad my hon. Friend
(Mr. Kyle) has made reference to that,
because it gives me an opportunity of making
an explanation which, I think, is very necessary under the circumstances. I think out
of courtesy to my hon. Friend, the Member
for Antrim (Mr. Crawford) it is right that
I should explain that the Amendment, as
suggested by him, would have had a most
damaging effect, and would have given
powers to an authority which no Government on earth that I know of, except perhaps
Russia, would have delegated to any body,
that is, to expropriate property without compensation. It is quite conceivable that
the river which my hon. Friend
had in his mind, and which has a
large number of factories and mills on
its banks, under the Amendment outlined
by him, the county council, or whatever
body had the necessary authority, could
have gone without any restraint and have
interfered with the working of these mills
or factories by the loosening of the water
that was impounded for the purpose of providing them with the necessary power. Of
course, that is inconceivable. I am sure my
hon. Friend the Member for Antrim did not
realise the full extent of the authority proposed to be given to the county councils.
in
A conference was held with the hon. Member afterwards, and this danger was
explained, and our technical officer, the
Parliamentary Draughtsman, had his
attention called to this matter. The result
of our conference was a modus vivendi, if I
may describe it so, by the change made in
the fifth paragraph of the First Schedule to
the Bill. I hope, however, that my hon.
Friend the Member for Antrim, who, I am
sorry to say, is not present, when he hears
the result of this will be satisfied. I have no
doubt he will, because it will enable the
county authority to deal with many matters
which were in his mind, but it did impose the
responsibility on the County Council, if they
be the authority, of giving compensation for
whatever injury was done to any person
who came under the scheme. I hope that
will satisfy my hon. Friend opposite (Mr.
Kyle).

I hardly think that the right hon. Gentleman, the Prime Minister, and the Chancellor
