SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES, 1925-26.
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
CLASS VI. No. 2.
HARBOUR AND COMMERCIAL
SERVICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£18,000 be granted to His Majesty for the
services of the year ending 31st March, 1926,
to, defray the Expenses of Harbours (1 Geo.
IV., c. 113, 39 and 40 Vic., c. 236) and Commercial Services, including certain Grants
in Aid, payments under Section 6 of 13 and
14 Geo. V., c. 6 (N.I.), and a Subvention in
Aid of Wages in the Coal Mining Industry.”
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): In introducing the Supplementary
Estimate for Harbour and Commercial
Services, I do not think that it is necessary
for me to dwell in any detail upon the
circumstances which have moved the
Government to seek the sanction of
this House for the expenditure outlined in the Estimate in connection
with the Government assistance to the linen
industry. The prevailing depression in that
industry, affecting as it does so large a
proportion of the wage-earners of Northern
Ireland, has convinced the Government that
the efforts which are now being made to
improve conditions are deserving of support
from public funds.
The scheme, towards the cost of which
it is proposed that Government financial
assistance shall be afforded may be divided
into two categories, namely (a) the bulking
of improved strains of flax seed, and (b)
intensive advertising campaign in the
United States of America in support of
British damask linen.
an
As indicated under sub-head J1, on page 2
of the Supplementary Estimate, the proposed
grant in aid of flax development falls into
two parts, the first of which is a supplementary grant of £1,000 to the Linen Industry
Research Association, Lambeg. In order to
avoid any possibility of confusion, I would
point out to the Committee that this supplementary grant is absolutely separate and distinct from the grant in aid of £10,000 to the
Linen Industry Research Association, of
which a first instalment of £3,000 has already
been voted in the current financial year.
The supplementary grant of £1,000 now before
the Committee provides for the recoupment
to the Association of part of the loss incurred by it in connection with the sowing,
at the request of the Imperial and Northern
Supply-
30 OCTOBER 1925
Supplementary Estimates.
Governments of a quantity of J.W.S.
pedigree flax seed in 1924. This seed had
been evolved and accumulated by the
Association until a quantity of some 16 tons
was available, and as the further bulking
of the seed lay outside the normal scope
of the Association's activities, a danger then
existed that the seed might be dispersed
or become otherwise unavailable for further
bulking..
As experiments over a period of years had
shown that the J.W.S. strain gave not only
an increased yield of fibre, but also produced
a better grade of fibre, the Northern
Government was anxious that the seed which
the Association had accumulated should
be made available for bulking operations
conducted over a period of several years.
Negotiations had already been instituted
between the Imperial and the Northern
Governments with the view to the creation
of a suitable body to undertake further
systematic bulking operations.
Pending the outcome of these negotiations,
however, and in order to secure continuity
in the sowing and bulking operations, it was
decided that the Linen Industry Research
Association should arrange for the sowing
of as much of the available seed as was
possible during the 1924 season on the understanding that, in the event of any loss
accruing in the conduct of the operations,
the Association would be indemnified, up to
a total of £1,250, by the Imperial and
Northern Governments. Of this total of
£1,250 it was agreed that the Northern
Government and Imperial Government
should guarantee £1,000 and £250 respectively.
In pursuance of this arrangement, some
10 tons of the J.W.S. seed were sown during
the 1924 season in the Yeovil district of
Somerset. This district was selected by
reason of the immunity from contamination
locally, or cross-fertilisation, and from other
seeds, and also because there were available
in the proximity suitable facilities for
de-seeding, which had been previously
used by the Association for its earlier
bulking operations. It had been hoped
that it would have been possible to
sow 300 acres, but, owing to unavoidable
delays, the operations began so late in the
season that only approximately 200 acres
of land could be secured, and this acreage
required, as I have already mentioned, some
10 tons of the seed that had been
accumulated.
Two types of agreements were entered into
with the growers, firstly, for undeseeded
crop, payment at the rate of £6 per ton;
and, secondly, for dressed seed, payment
based upon the price ruling in Belfast on
1st March, 1925, for Dutch seed. The pedigree
seed produced excellent crops, but unfortunately heavy rain in the latter part of the
season caused great delay and difficulty in
harvesting. In consequence of these adverse
factors a loss, slightly in excess of £1,250,
was incurred by the Association, and authority is, therefore, sought for the payment of
£1,000 in respect of Northern Ireland's proportion of the total guarantee of £1,250, from
both the Imperial and Northern Governments.
The second part of Sub-head J1 provides
for the continuance on a factory scale of the
systematic bulking of the J.W.S. seed to
which I have already referred. Following
the negotiations to which I have previously
alluded, between the Imperial and Northern
Governments, and arising out of the recent
Interim Report of the Board of Trade Flax-
Growing Committee, on which Committee
Northern Ireland was represented, the Flax
Industry Development Society, Limited, has
been formed for the purpose of the further
bulking of "pure line" seed. This new Society has taken over from the Linen Industry
Research Association the latter's interest in
contracts for the sowing of between 450 and
500 acres during the 1925 season. The Imperial Government having signified its willingness to assist in financing this Society
provided that the Northern Government
undertook a proportionate share of the financial liability involved, the Government of
Northern Ireland now proposes to contribute,
up to a total maximum of £10,000, one-fourth
of the total outlay on the purchase, repair,
and adaptation of two suitable factories in
Somersetshire, in addition to one-fourth of
the total advances to be made to the Society
in respect of working capital from Imperial
and Northern Ireland funds.
Under the arrangement contemplated the
Imperial and Northern Governments will become joint owners of the property and
equipment of both factories to the extent
of three-fourths and one-fourth respectively.
It has been laid down that the advances
made to the Society in respect of working
capital will rank pari passu as loans constituting a first charge on the assets of the
Society and will carry interest at current
Bank rate. It has further been stipulated
that if, at any time, the Society has a balance in hand substantially in excess of its
immediate requirements, a part of such
balance proportionate to the Government of
Northern Ireland's claim shall be repaid to
that Government.
It is estimated that the total outlay incurred by both Governments during the current financial year will amount to £26,500,
of which sum £18,000 is in respect of advances for working capital; £5,000 in respect
of the purchase price of the factories, and
£3,500 in respect of repairs and equipment.
Supplementary Estimates. 1676
Supply-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
The Imperial Government has undertaken to
contribute 75 per cent. of this total amount,
and provision has, therefore, been made in
the Supplementary Estimate new before the
Committee for the payment to the Flax Industry Development Society from Northern
Ireland funds of the remaining 25 per cent.,
namely, £6,625.
Hon. Members will, of course, realise the
very great importance of this experiment, not
only from its agricultural interest but from
its supreme interest to the flax spinning industry in Northern Ireland. It is also of
wider interest, as is shown by the large share
the Imperial Government is, taking in prosecuting the development of this "pure line"
seed.
Turning to Sub-head J2, which is a grant
in aid of Linen Publicity Campaign, I wish
to state that the view is strongly held within the linen trade that the time is ripe for
an intensive advertising campaign in favour
of Irish and Scottish damask linen in the
United States of America. It is considered
that, in order to be really effective, it will
be necessary to carry on this campaign over a
period of at least two years at an approximate
annual cost of £35,000. Towards this sum
the damask manufacturers and allied interests in Northern Ireland have guaranteed
a yearly contribution of £18,646, which sum,
it is hoped, may be augmented to £20,000,
while the Scottish linen manufacturers have
undertaken to contribute £4,000 in each of
the two years.
The Government has decided to contribute towards the same purpose 10s for every
£1 contributed by the linen trade and allied
interests in Northern Ireland during the
years 1925 and 1926, subject, however, to a
maximum Government contribution of
£10,000 in either year. It is proposed to
place the advertising scheme in the hands
of a thoroughly informed Committee in New
York, and it is hoped that, as a result of
this effort, the demand for Irish and Scottish
linens in their most important market will
be revived and strengthened. As I have already indicated, the Government contribution in the calendar year 1925 is subject to
a maximum of £10,000. It is estimated that
only £5,000 of this sum will fall due for payment in the current financial year and provision has therefore been made for that
amount.
a
The remaining item in the Supplementary
Estimate is a novel item in Northern Ireland and makes provision for the meeting of
situation which has only
The
recently arisen.
Committee
very
are no doubt conversant with the action
which was taken by the Imperial Government early in August to meet the crisis
in the Coal Mining Industry in Great
Britain, but it may not be out of place to
recapitulate briefly the principal events of
the past few months in the light of their
bearing upon the Estimate now under consideration.
In June 1924 an agreement was made between the mine owners and mine operatives
in Great Britain under which the proceeds
of the industry, after deduction of the costs
of production other than wages, were allocated in a certain proportion between wages
on the one hand and profits and capital
charges on the other. The agreement provided, however, that certain minimum wage
rates should be paid to the operatives even
should the proportion of the proceeds normally allocated to this purpose be insufficient
to meet it.
By June, 1925, the condition of the coal
mining industry was such that in practically
all the collieries in Great Britain the minimum wage was being paid only at the expense
of the share of the proceeds from the sale of
coal allocated to meet other costs, and the mine
owners, seeing no hope of relief from this
burden so long as the then existing conditions
continued, exercised their right to give "
month's notice of the termination of the 1924
agreement. They submitted for the consideration of the miners proposals which they
stated would enable them to continue to
operate the mines. These proposals would
have eliminated the minimum wage clause
of the 1924 agreement, and further suggested
an extension of the working hours from 7 to
8 hours per day.
The miners refused to accept either of these
proposals, and a complete stoppage of the
whole industry was threatened on the 31st
July. Notwithstanding an attempt at arbitration by the Government, no compromise
could be effected, and in order to avoid a
disastrous industrial stoppage the Government decided to set up a Commission to investigate the whole state of the industry, in
order to discover, if possible, some means of
securing economies in operation which would
offset the necessity of paying to the operatives the minimum wage which they demanded. Pending the receipt of the report
of the proposed Commission the Government
decided to preserve the status quo by agreeing to grant a temporary subvention in aid
of miners' wages. The intended effect of the
subsidy was theoretically that the workers
would continue to receive 1924 wages while,
at the same time, the owners would be able
to work under the conditions which they had
formulated in their 1925 proposals.
It is evident, I think, to hon. Members that
any colliery which did not receive this assistance would inevitably be working at a serious
disadvantage as compared with its competi-

tors, and this is the condition in which,
failing action upon the part of the Government of Northern Ireland, the only colliery
in our area would be situated, since the

I may say that this colliery, situated as
it is in Northern Ireland, represents an

we hope will be of very considerable benefit

cannot regard with equanimity the exposure

created by subsidy conditions on the other
side of the Channel.
I propose, accordingly, should the Committee agree, to pay to this Northern Ireland
Colliery a subsidy on lines parallel, but subject to such local modifications as may be

The Committee will, of course, understand
that in developing a new enterprise of this

the subsidy will be required during the remainder of our financial year, but I may say
that, on the basis of the returns already furnished to my Ministry in respect of the
months of August and September, it is hoped
that the amount which is provided will be
sufficient to meet the demands that may actually be made upon us.
Now as to the total figure required by the
Estimate submitted, I would like to sum up

of £2,625, which is the saving effected in
carrying on the Ulster exhibit at Wembley.
I should like to explain that these savings
are largely attributable to the fact that it
was found possible in the course of the
adaptation and extension of the section occupied by the Ulster Pavilion to effect considerable economies in construction, thus bringing
the total expenditure considerably below
that estimated in the first instance by the
architect. Moreover, there were certain
rentals due for payment by exhibitors in the
preceding year and not actually received during that year, which fall into credit in the
current financial year, and are, therefore,
available to be applied, in the usual way,
towards the reduction of the cost of the
exhibit. This estimated saving of £2,625 has,
accordingly, been deducted from the gross
total of £20,625 of the Supplementary Estimate, leaving a net sum of £18,000 now to be
voted. I beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: I think the Minister of Commerce (Mr. Barbour) is to be congratulated
on the very excellent statement he has made
this afternoon in regard to this Supplementary Estimate. I am very pleased that
our Northern Government are realising how
much private enterprise has failed in regard to our basic industry-or rather one
of our basic industries-namely the linen
trade. Private enterprise has absolutely
failed to make arrangements for the development of this industry, and now our Government have to step in to assist private enterprise in the development of the flax industry.
I think the quotation I made the other day
from Sir William Harcourt in 1893-"We are
all Socialists nowadays"-is very true, and I
am very pleased to welcome the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Barbour) and his colleagues
on the Front Bench into the ranks of the
Socialist Party now that they are taking on
themselves the job of developing this Flax
Association in conjunction with the Imperial Government.
It is very necessary. Without it the trade
and commerce of our country will go down.
Without it the development of the linen
trade itself will be hampered, and so I welcome the action of the Government in
stepping into line with the Imperial Government and instituting a factory for the bulking of this seed which is going to improve
the linen trade.
In regard to the other item of £5,000 in
aid of the linen publicity campaign, I
heartily endorse it. I was a member of the
sub-committee of the Unemployment Committee which recommended in the first instance that something along these lines should
be done I think it was following on a suggestion made by the hon. Member for West

I think it is necessary that our linen should
be more widely advertised in the United
States, and I am sure the granting of this

In regard to the subvention in aid of wages,

Coalisland. I was very much astonished to

Mr. DEVLIN: I rise as one who has not

kind that is proposed by the right hon.
Gentleman for the development of our trade

I should like, however, to say that it is a
somewhat dangerous principle to vote public
moneys out of the Exchequer without having
some say in the manner in which that money
is to be administered. These are comparatively small sums and one need not perhaps too strongly advance that objection,
but this may be the commencement of a
policy of voting large sums of money, and
I look with suspicion on the voting of such
sums out of the national Exchequer without
some control over and some power to influence the manner in which those funds
are administered.
I would like to say in regard to one of
these items, namely the subvention in aid
of the linen publicity campaign, that I was
one of those who supported that at the meeting of the Unemployment Committee, a most
excellent body that did very good work. It
was a true manifestation, that Committee, as
far as I could see, as one who never had
much opportunity of associating with
political opponents before in purely practical
work, it was a true manifestation of
how much can be done by union and
by the recognition of each others' right to
co-operate in what concerns the commercial
and industrial progress of the community.
This was the only suggestion as far as I
could see that could be made by the leaders
of the linen industry in Ulster, namely that
the Government should vote this sum. I am
not quite sure that the answers they gave
at that Committee as to whether their
methods of advertising were the most effective to produce the results they desired were
very satisfactory. It may be that this
money is just being thrown into a reservoir
and will disappear, It may be that they are
following out ancient methods of advertising, and that there is a lack of that
precious spirit of enterprise or of those more
picturesque methods by which an article like
linen could be advertised.
I venture now to suggest that I thought
it would be a good thing if the Government,
or the Association with the assistance of
the Government, could appoint some representative men to organise exhibitions, and
to bring those exhibits to all large centres
of industry in every part of America, because I think, from the artistic point of
view, apart altogether from the selfish aspect
from which we largely view it here in
Ulster where we are interested, an article
like Irish linen only requires to be
thoroughly known in order that it may
attract the public. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I am rather inclined to think from
what I have seen of the decline of the
linen industry-I do not want to cast any

slack. They have allowed their trade

Oral Answers to Questions.
WAGES OF AGRICULTURAL
LABOURERS.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Agriculture whether, in view of the conflicting
statements made in this House as to the
prevailing rates of wages of agricultural
labourers in the various counties of Northern
Ireland, he will have inquiries made as to
the wages paid by farmers to their employees
in Co. Antrim, Co. Down, Co. Derry, Co.
Fermanagh, Co. Tyrone, Co. Armagh, and
further, can he state what steps he is prepared to take to see that agricultural
labourers are adequately remunerated.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): In regard to the second part of
the Member's question. I think I made my
position clear to him when, on the 27th
ultimo, I moved the postponement of the
Second Reading of his Agricultural Wages
Bill. On that occasion I said that there was
an alternative to his Bill and the Boards it
proposed to establish; that alternative,
which would not require a Government Bill,
was Conciliation Boards, such as are in
operation in England. This machinery
could be established in the several counties
of Northern Ireland by the farmers and
labourers if they so desired.
As to the first part of the question, in
the circumstances the hon. Member will
recognise that the results of the inquiries
which he asks me to undertake would not
materially influence the views that I have
already expressed on this matter. If, however, the hon. Member still wishes me to
make inquiries as to wages I shall be happy
to do so.
Mr. KYLE: I do wish very much that the
Minister would make those inquiries as to
the rates of wages in the various counties,
because of certain statements that have been
made in this House. I said the wages in
Fermanagh were 25s and in other counties
22s 6d, and certain hon. Gentlemen said those
figures were wrong by something about 6s. I
think it is in the public interests that the
Minister of Agriculture should make these
inquiries and give the results to the House.
Mr. ARCHDALE: I will make the inquiries.
LIABILITY FOR ACCIDENTS TO
TEACHERS AND PUPILS.
3. Mr. CRAWFORD (for Dr. Morrison)
asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the
Ministry of Education whether there is now
a greater liability for accidents to teachers
and pupils than previously existed; whether
managers were warned of their liability
prior to the circular dated October, 1925; if
he will state how the liability was met in the
past for Acts in existence since 1846 and
1880; and what is the general object of this
warning circular at the present time.
SECRETARY
The PARLIAMENTARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): The Ministry has no reason to suppose that liabilities of the kind referred to
by the hon. Member are increasing.
I am not aware that any general warning
on the subject was issued to managers of
schools by the late Commissioners of National Education, but I understand that it
was the practice of the Commissioners to inform managers of their liability whenever
information was sought in regard to the
legal position. So far as can be ascertained,
this liability has been met in the past by
school managers.
Certain inquiries addressed to the Ministry
seemed to show that some uncertainty existed, and it was accordingly considered desirable in the general interest to bring the
matter more fully to the notice of education
authorities, managers and others concerned.
PURDYSBURN FEVER HOSPITAL.
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether, in view of the statements in
the public Press that Purdysburn Infectious Diseases Hospital is overcrowded, he
is satisfied that there is sufficient accommodation to provide for the isolation of
scarlet fever patients, and if he is not
satisfied that there is sufficient accommodation, can he state what steps he is
prepared to take to remedy this shortage.
Oral Answers.
Written Answer.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates):) While the accommodation for scarlet fever cases at Purdysburn Infectious Diseases Hospital is fully
occupied, there is no general overcrowding at
the Institution.
Arrangements have been made with the
Belfast Board of Guardians similar to those
made on previous occasions under which
accommodation will be made available at the
Workhouse Fever Hospital for all new cases
of scarlet fever, chargeable to the Union.
It is understood that under this arrangement at least 200 beds could be made available.
The Ministry is satisfied that the accommodation available is ample and that no
special steps are necessary at present.
HOURS OF CHEMISTS' APPRENTICES.
5. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether there are
any regulations prescribing the weekly hours
of duty for chemists' apprentices; if they
are expected to take duty on Sundays, and
if chemists' stores are open to inspection,
will he see that fixed hours are adhered to,
in order that apprentices may be allowed
reasonable time for recreation and study, in
view of the fact that they have to pass
an examination at the end of their
apprenticeship.
Sir DAWSON BATES: There are, I understand, no regulations at the moment prescribing the weekly hours of duty of
chemists' apprentices. The hours of duty
are a matter of arrangement between the
employer and apprentice, subject of course
to the general limitation under the Shops
Act, which provides that persons under 18
cannot be employed for more than 74 hours
per week, including meal times
It is possible that in some instances
apprentices may be asked to take duty
occasionally on Sunday, but so far as I am
aware this is not a general practice.
Chemists' stores are subject to inspection
under the provisions of Section 26 of the
Pharmacy and Poisons Act, 1925.
The conditions of employment of chemists'
apprentices is a matter with which, no doubt,
the Council of the Pharmaceutical Society
will deal when framing regulations under
Section 3 (1) (1) of the Pharmacy and
Poisons Act which empowers the Council
to make regulations with respect to the conditions upon which persons may be
apprenticed to Pharmaceutical Chemists, Registered Chemists and Druggists, or Registered Druggists, and the considerations to
which reference is made in this question
will, I am sure, be carefully borne in mind
by the Council in framing any such
regulations.
Written Answer.
MISS ISABELLA HARREN, LISDEAD
NATIONAL SCHOOL.
Mr. COOPER asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether he is aware that Miss Isabella
Harren, formerly of Lisdead National School,
County Fermanagh, in addition to being a
work-mistress taught reading, writing, spelling, and arithmetic, and was engaged daily
from 11 o'clock to 3, and whether, if these
facts are correct, she is entitled to a pension.
Mr. ROBB: The School Returns show that
Miss Harren taught "Infants and 1st
Standard children occasionally," but the
Ministry has no information as to the actual
time given by her to that work.
The Rule is that-
"Work-mistresses are required to attend
for only 2 hours a day, and, if competent,
they must assist the teachers generally in
conducting the school during the time
they are not employed in giving instruction
in needlework."
These teachers are paid a small salary
by the State for part-time service, and
neither the Commissioners of National
Education nor the Ministry ever possessed
any authority for awarding them a retiring
allowance.

Mr. DEVLIN: I understood when the hon.
and gallant Gentleman, the chief Whip
(Captain Dixon), rose in his place that it was
for the purpose of explaining to the House
the meaning of the absence of the Prime
Minister and the Minister of Finance--(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-because I should
have at once recognised that that was not
only an essential duty on the part of the
Chief Whip but that in the interest of the
Government, and of the Prime Minister and
of the Minister of Finance-
Captain DIXON: If I might interrupt the
hon. Member for a moment, I shall be glad
to give the information required. The Prime
Minister has been called to London on very
urgent business with reference to the affairs
of Ulster, particularly with reference to our
financial affairs. Therefore, he much regrets he had to go and could not be present
at this meeting of Parliament or at one or
two functions which he had to attend.
Mr. DEVLIN: There is no business so
important in my judgment as the business
which we were called upon to decide here today. This debate or the proceedings of this
day were neither invited nor initiated by
me. I ventured in the course of my
observations and address to the House last
week to introduce what in my opinion is the
most imperious of all questions that even a
Parliament of this character should be
called upon to discuss at this stage in the
economic and commercial life of the community. The right hon. Gentleman, the
Prime Minister, rose in his place, and
recognising, as he must have recognised, that
this was too important a question to be dealt
with at the tail end of a debate, he suggested
that a day should be taken for the purpose
of discussing it. I accepted that invitation
at once, because my earnest desire is that
we may be able, if we can ever get down to
the realities-and I have not much faith
that we ever can-the sooner we grapple
with this urgent and pressing problem in its
most practical form the better. Then I saw
in the papers the announcement this morning that the Prime Minister and the
Minister of Finance had gone to London on
the evening before the debate. Well, I consider that to be not only a grave dereliction
of public duty but a most contemptuous way
for two of the chief Ministers of this Ulster
Parliament to treat this important question
and the House itself.
Now what is the mission of the Prime
Minister and the Minister of Finance? It
is for discussing the desirability of proceeding with the building of the Ulster Parliament at Stormont, at least that is the purpose which is stated in the semi-official paragraph which appears in all the morning
papers. If ever there was anything more
grotesque it is this performance. Everybody
knows that the chief depression from which
Unemployment.
Unemployment.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Devlin]
industry and commerce suffer is not in the
building trade. The right hon. Gentleman
the Minister of Labour has admitted that
himself, not only in public speeches delivered to the Unemployment Committee, but
at subsequent meetings of the Unemployment Sub-Committees. It is not the building trade that is suffering at all, but other
more important and more vital industries,
and yet the Prime Minister feels it his duty
on an occasion of so paramount importance
as this to leave his duties in Parliament, to
treat this most imperative question in the
most contemptuous way, and to believe it to
be his duty not to remain at home to solve
the problem of unemployment and the depression of industry but to endeavour to secure a palace for politicians.
What are sane and sensible men to think
of a Government that proceeds on
a mission of this character for the purpose of
securing funds for the building of Parliament when, according to a discussion in the
City Hall yesterday Sir Crawford M'Cullagh
declared in SO many words that 10,003
people were hungering for houses, and that
is was impossible to satisfy the clamant
and irresistible demands of these poor
people for housing accommodation. If I
could gather anything from his observations
I found the chief difficulty was that they
could not get workers for the purpose of
building these houses, and if you cannot get
workers for the purpose of building houses
for the people-which next to the question
of our industries and unemployment is the
most vital and most humane and the most
Christian of all the ideas that should animate and inspire statesmanship-in spite of
all this your Prime Minister absents himself on this mission while, as I have said,
10,000 people are hungering for houses in
the city of Belfast.
I decline to discuss this question in the
absence of the Prime Minister. You yourselves repeatedly said in your Press that
the Opposition would be welcomed in this
House if it came forward with constructive
criticism. Our criticism has been largely
constructive. It is our function and our
purpose to criticise, whether constructive or
not. We were invited to divorce ourselves
from partisanship, and we did it in the
interests of the community as a whole, and
at this very time when the whole energies
of the Ministry and the Government, and of
the camp followers of the Government,
should be concentrated upon this colossal
question, that is so complex as to seem to
shake all minds in a belief of its solution,
you yourselves are making the atmosphere
of Belfast reek from political partisanship,
with vituperation and abuse of those who
differ from you on essential political and
public questions.
The first function one would think of
a Government would be to try to create a
better and kindlier atmosphere, and in that
all of us would be willing to co-operate. I
myself, when I came to this House, made
up my mind to be a constructive critic if
I could. I have added nothing to the
passions of our politics. I have often declined to address political meetings. I felt
that it was my duty, as it should be the
duty of all public-spirited men to be loyal,
not to shibboleths, but to the public
interests. And yet, in what way has that
co-operation been received? We have been
treated here as helots, regarded as enemies
within the camp to which we have been
elected. No attention has been paid to our
representations. You have distrusted us,
and tried to dispise us, but you are not
going to treat me with the contempt with
which the Prime Minister has treated this
Parliament.
I myself intended to-day to devote whatever time was given to me to the work of
putting forward a number of constructive
proposals to the Government for solving this
problem of unemployment. I will not do so
here. Why should I have any respect for
this House, and the Prime Minister? Look
at these Benches, half-empty. There are

commercial prosperity.
I think there has never been in the history

Gentleman the Minister of Finance, thought
so little of this problem of the 64,000 unemployed in the Six Counties they imme
diately trip off-whether to ensure the Parliament House being built at Stormont or

moving that Motion on the next day of
meeting.

I am throwing this out so that possibly he

an unemployment crisis in Sweden. Unemployment increased enormously until it
reached something like twenty or twenty-five
per cent, I understand, of the working-class
population. The Government in Sweden did
exactly what the Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews) is doing now. They encouraged

to undertake relief works, but, in spite of
that encouragement, and in spite of the relief works being undertaken, the unemployment still continued.

3 NOVEMBER 1925
The Swedish Government then decided that
they would have to tackle the problem themselves, and they started works so as to provide for unemployment. I do not think their
rules in Sweden or the lines on which they
laid down those works would altogether meet
with the approval of the Labour Party here,
because, in the first place, they made the
work of the manual labour type, and of the
hard ordinary manual labour type. It was
not skilled in any way, so that even a shipyard worker had to handle a pick and shovel
the same as anyone else. Then it was poorly
paid work. The calculation was made so
that a man in a day could just about make
as much as would keep him comfortably,
and it was piece work, so that it depended
altogether on how much a man did how
much he received.
I do not know whether that was a good
plan or not, but they were able to shut off
those works in June last, because unemployment had been reduced to normal dimensions. I do not say that that is the ideal
system by which to carry out unemployment relief, but it at least has this great
benefit that it does provide employment for
men, and they are not put in the position
of drawing what after all is a charitable
wage from the State, because, although this
is called Unemployment Insurance, in the
vast majority of cases it is no longer insurance at all. It is simply what has been
called over and over and over again-a dole.
It is exactly the same as Poor Relief except
that it is given by the State instead of by
the Board of Guardians from the rates, and
to my mind it is just as demoralising in that
way as any Poor Relief handed out by the
Relieving Officer. The sooner it can be done
away with and a man can feel that he is
doing some work for the money he is receiving the better it will be for the community.
I quite accept at its face value all that
has been said about the earnest desire of
every unemployed man to find work. I am
quite sure that every unemployed man is
anxious to find work, and no longer to draw
what is after all a charitable contribution from the State, but I should like to
put this point up to the Government and to
the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews). It
is a point about which I feel very strongly.
I was very sorry to see he had taken powers
under the last Unemployment Insurance
Act, which we passed a few days ago, to
give unemployment benefit to young boys
and young men under the age of twenty-one.
When a man is over twenty-one, when he
has been trained to labour, and trained to
understand how important it is that he
should do his day's work in order to get his
day's pay, he may be able to stand the moral
consequences of being without work for some
years, as many of these men have been.
We have heard of men who have been out
of work for two or three years. A man may
be out of work for two or three years and
still retain the desire and ability to work,
but what are you going to do with the young
lad who has not been at work for more than
a few months and who then comes on to the
dole and receives this weekly amount of
money? He has no work to do; he has never
been trained to work; he is being trained
really to believe that it is the duty of the
State to give him a subsistence wage whether
he does work or whether he does not.
In the case of the older men they may be
a drag on the community, but in the
case of these young men and boys they are
being trained up as idlers and wasters.
They are not going to be a benefit to the community but rather a direct and serious danger to the community for the rest of their
lives. They are going to be turned into
wasters, and will be a perpetual drag on
the community besides providing the raw
material from which revolutionists are
made. The sooner the Minister of Labour
is able to provide means by which these
young men will not get anything at all unless they do a certain amount of work,
whether it be in trained or manual labour,
the better it will be for us. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)

HOUSE OF COMMONS

there is one Member of the Government, at

In the city of Belfast we build steamers,

That would only amount to something less

we have given as a subsidy to the agricultural

able, as a matter of book-keeping, to make a

subsidy of £250,000, and, on the other hand,

We all know that at the present time, at the
rate we are driving, with the golden stream
flowing in this way, and nothing being returned for it, we are leading straight to national bankruptcy. What I want to do is to
see that some of this money that is being
poured down the sink at the present time
is directed into channels that will return

I will leave that point and go on to another
point. I find that to-day there are over 10.000
families in Belfast who are living in
one and two rooms. In some cases we
find that we have two, three, four, five
and even six people living in one room.
I receive letters day after day from people
who are asking for houses to be built. I
had a letter one day last week from an ex-
Serviceman who lost a foot in the war. He
tells me that he has been looking for a
house but cannot get it. He is living with
his wife and two children in two rooms. His
wife had only been discharged from hospital
having been ailing for eight weeks, and the
doctor says it is due to the conditions under
which they are living. There are thousands
of cases like that in Belfast, and I say that
the Government are neglecting their duty
in not putting forward every effort to see
that houses are provided for the people.
I believe the Minister of Labour knows
that houses can be provided. I can tell you
of one contractor in Belfast-not a very
large contractor-who has produced on an
average over three years one house in every
twenty-one hours with fourteen bricklayers
and a hundred men. He quarried the stone,
carted it to the site, built the houses, made
the streets, made the sewers, and turned
out five houses per week. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) It is a very simple matter.
After all, you know that if you multiply
fourteen bricklayers by ten you get 140. It
you multiply 100 working men by ten you
have 1,000, and if you multiply five houses
by ten you have 50. There you have 140
bricklayers, 1,000 working labourers, and 50
houses per week. Double it and you get 280
bricklayers, 2,000 working men, and 100
houses per week. Ten thousand houses are
required. In two years you would solve this
problem if the Government put their back
and brains into it. That is what we demand
from them. That is what the Government
is for. We insist on the Government putting their back into this. The contractors
are here. We are not going to change the
system. We are not going to have any nationalisation or the means of production or
distribution of exchange to solve this problem. This is a simple matter. We have the
unemployed walking our streets, and if the
Government put their back into this matter
it can be solved almost immediately.
There are two concrete suggestions I make.
I ask you to take these matters into consideration. Take the people off the streets of
Belfast and find them work. Do something
for them. I meet them day in and day out.
They are on my doorstep from early morning, and they are continually asking, "What
can I do to find work?" Do not run away

not find a better class of workmen in the

lem and which he intended to put forward if
the Prime Minister had only been here.

sav frankly and honest'v that I have never

little

May I say this, that this problem of unemployment with which we are dealing is
produced by many causes, some of which we
may have a little control over in this Parliament, but many of which are beyond our
reach altogether. Unemployment has undoubtedly been created by the war, and the
tremendous amount of wealth spent in the

our export trade has been injured to a very
serious degree. Therefore, over these consequences we. in this Parliament, have no
control whatever, but unemployment has
also been created in this city. in this Province and in Great Britain by the attacks

which the Socialist Party are ever making

and Northern Ireland used to be looked upon
as the workshops of the world, but foreign
nations have found the way to produce in

and England, are at the present time
putting up a case to the Imperial Government to have the Safeguarding of Industries Act applied to the linen trade,
and I am hopeful if this is done that

that some of the nine mills-very large
concerns which are at present stopped in
Northern Ireland will be started again. In

systematic short time to a very large degree
indeed. It is not because the employers

There is another matter in this connection
to which I would like to refer. Our trade
in Northern Ireland has been injured, and
is still being injured, by the action of
Southern Ireland. First of all, we had the
boycott, and when the boycott was removed
a tariff was very quickly imposed on goods
not only from Northern Ireland but from
Great Britain as well. That has injured
many trades here to a very considerable
extent, and it is remarkable, in my opinion,
that that tariff should have been imposed,
for this reason. Those persons in Southern
Ireland are always professing to be anti-
Partitionists, and yet nearly every legislative and administrative action that they
take is of a Partitionist character and helps
to build up a wall which we in Northern
Ireland find it difficult to scale. I was going
to ask the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin), if he had remained here
to-day, to use his influence with those in
Southern Ireland to have taken away those
tariffs which are injuring the trade of
Northern Ireland and producing a considerable amount of unemployment in our midst.

that in all 8,452 houses have been or are

Mr. ANDREWS-but, at any rate, it has
been my best, and in discharging a responsible duty I do think I have the right to
get the support of this community of ours
instead of being misrepresented in the way
I am at the present time. One example I
will give to-day. A prominent member of the
Labour Party, an intimate friend and colleague of the three Labour Gentlemen who
sit opposite to me, stated the other night that
in January last I had knocked off 10,000 persons from benefit under the new regulations.
As a matter of fact, in January last only
1,886 persons were deprived of benefit under
the new regulations referred to. Again, the
same gentleman stated that in September I
had knocked off 10,000 men under these new
regulations and under the Order in Council
we have heard so much about. As a matter
of fact, only 1,000 have been knocked off. It
is these gross exaggerations that are naturally creating a spirit of unrest in our midst.
and I think that those who are guilty of
practices of this kind are indeed incurring a
serious personal responsibility. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Let them tell the truth
in connection with the work that my Department is doing. I do not care who knows it.
After all, what is it that I am doing?
I am simply carrying on on parallel lines
with Great Britain. Hon. Members may remember that very shortly after I became responsible for the Labour Department I
brought into existence a Committee presided
over by my hon. and gallant Friend the
Member for Armagh (Major Shillington).
On that Committee were many Socialists,
because I have always thought that on Committees of the kind all sections of the community should be represented. They brought
in a unanimous report and I am going to
read to the House one or two of their suggestions. One was to this effect:
on
We are satisfied as to the desirability of
continuing unemployment insurance
parallel lines with Great Britain, inasmuch as the present abnormal industrial
depression and the movement of workpeople between the two countries leaves
no reasonable alternative.
That is just exactly what I am doing both
as regards legislation and as regards administration with the full consent and approval of
my colleagues. That Committee made
another suggestion, and that was that local
employment committees should be established
in our midst in order to help in the administration of unemployment benefit. That also
I have done. I say, as I have frequently said
before, that these committees have rendered
invaluable public services. I believe they are
absolutely impartial, and as proof of that I
will speak for a moment of the personnel of
the Belfast Committee. In the first place
there are on that Committee leading trade
unionists and leading employers and representatives of the community. The chairman
of that Committee is the hon. and gallant
Member for Armagh (Major Shillington).
One of the vice-chairmen is the Leader of
the Labour group in this House (Mr. Kyle),
and the second vice-chairman-and there are
only two-is an intimate friend and supporter
of the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin). What body could be more impartial
than a body presided over by these three
gentlemen?
When people talk about thousands of men
being cut off from benefit and the hardships
being imposed in consequence, I would like
to say that the instructions which my Department give to these committees are, that provided a man is seeking work, and genuinely
seeking work, and is really, according to the
tests laid down, an insured man, and provided they are satisfied that the taking from
him of his benefit would cause hardship
to the family, they are not to do it under
the family income test or any other test.
Really, it is absurd to say that this fund is
not being administered in the most reasonable and considerate way possible. The whole
idea underlying all our conditions and all
our regulations is to preserve the money for
those who need it most. Is there a man in
this House or out of this House who will
say that that is not as it ought to be? No.
I am sorry the hon. Gentleman ran away
to-day because I have been to some extent
placed in a difficulty. I intended not exactly

We have carried on this debate helpfully to-day without them. The
choice is theirs, whether they serve or

I would like to say, and I feel strongly on

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I rise to say
a word or two to correct the false impression given to the House by the Hon.
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Gyle). He
says this House gave a subsidy to agriculture
of £128,000. That is not correct. That
£128,000 was something agriculture was entitled to. It was the equivalent of the grant
given in England in relief of agricultural
rates. The only matter this House was concerned in with regard to that £128,000 was
how it should be spent and in what way it
should be spent. I think the House very
wisely decided to spend it in relief of agricultural rates. To speak of that grant
as a subsidy to agriculture is creating
rather a false impression.
I said in the House some time ago that
even with this grant all that the Government
had given for the relief of rates on agricultural land in Northern Ireland was nothing
like the amount given in England. On the
day I made that statement it was contradicted by some Member sitting on the front
Bench, but since that time I have made inquiries and I find that the Government in
. England relieved agricultural land of 75 per
cent. of the rates I wish to thank the right
hon. Gentleman the Minister of Home Affairs
publicly for the very full answer he gave to
a very delicate and intricate question the
other day in the House, that was the extent
to which agricultural land was relieved of
rates in Northern Ireland. The information
was that, taking into account all the grantsin-aid, agricultural land is relieved of rates
to the amount of 52 per cent. Therefore. I
think I have proved I was right in saying
agricultural land was not relieved to the
same extent here as in England.
I deplore the absence of the Prime Minister
and the Minister of Finance from this House
to-day, but as I am not in a position to judge
the relative importance of whether they
should be here or in London I am not going
to go into that matter. However, I think
it is unfortunate that during such an important discussion they should have found it
necessary to be absent.
With regard to this question of unemployment, the Minister of Labour has just said
that up to the present you have paid away
in unemployment benefit the sum of
£6,500,000 and that the Fund is in debt to
the extent of something like £3,750.000. The
problem is, what value has this country got
for that money paid away? The money question, after all, is very important, but there
is the even more important question of the
demoralisation of our people that is occurring
through their being unable to find employment and who have to get doles or money
for which they give no equivalent,
Mr. ANDREWS: They pay contributions.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: The Minister of Labour says they pay contributions,
but at the same time we are running up a
debt for which there is no contribution, and
in the Widows' and Orphans' Pensions Bill
those very contributions on behalf of unemployment have been reduced when the fund
is running into debt.
Mr. ANDREWS: The Government contribution is increased.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: Where does
the Government contribution come from?
Mr. ANDREWS: The taxpayers.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: Is that
being defrayed out of ordinary taxation or is
it being borrowed? Where does that money
come from? Is it provided for in the Estimates? If it is coming from the taxpayers
and is not provided for in the Estimates it
must be borrowed. The question, and
it may be a difficult question, for the
Government and the House to face is, how
can this amount of money be put into some
remunerative employment? I feel, as I have
said before, that one way out may be
that as the prosperity of this Six County area
is so much bound up with the prosperity of
agriculture it is to there we must look for
some means of helping to alleviate the question of unemployment.
The most pressing need at the present time
is that there should be some system of cheap
credit to farmers, because after three or
four very bad agricultural seasons their
finances are so depleted that they are not
in a position to extend their industry. I
think that a little help for the farmers in
the shape of some form of cheap credit is
one of the ways in which unemployment
might be helped. I do hope that the Government will in the near future propound some
scheme of cheap credit for farmers.
I do not know whether it would be possible
or not, but there is a great amount of land
in the Six County area from which we are

I rather think the Minister of Labour (Mr.

our unemployment was due to Socialism. He
said he thought a good deal of it was due to
Socialistic propaganda. I am not a Socialist,
and I am not going to defend them, but we
have in England at the present time
Government with a very big majority behind
them a Conservative Government. We have
the same here, and, therefore, I think that
proves that if there was any political remedy
for unemployment the problem would soon
disappear. How could we have according to
the Minister of Labour's position any more

with the complexions of our parties what

panaceas to cure unemployment protection
on stuffs such as linen yarn coming in here.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I am not going
to express any opinion with regard to that,
but I think if the Minister of Labour
approves of protection in the Six County
area you cannot blame the Government of
the twenty-six county area for applying protection to help their unemployment and to
encourage their industries. If the Minister
of Labour was right in saying that protection would help unemployment here he
should not in the same breath have blamed
the Government of the twenty-six counties
for trying protection to help unemployment
and to encourage the industries in their
area.

Oral Answers to Questions.
BELFAST WORKHOUSE CHAPLAIN.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state under
what powers he claims to be in a position
to make an appointment to the Belfast
Union of a clergyman to attend to the
spiritual needs of the inmates, without any
consultation with the Board of Guardians;
and if the Board of Guardians was consulted in the recent appointment of a
Church of Ireland clergyman.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Under Section 48 of
the Irish Poor Relief Act, 1838, the responsibility for appointing chaplains to workhouses devolves on the Ministry, and not
on the Guardians. In making such appointments it is the custom of the Ministry to
consult the head of the Church concerned,
who usually recommends a clergyman
officiating in the parish in which the workhouse is situated.
In the case of the Church of Ireland
chaplain to the Belfast workhouse, it has
been the practice for years past, with the
knowledge of the Guardians, to appoint the
Rector of St. Andrew's Church, in which
parish the workhouse is situated.
The present Rector is, however, unable to
assume duty at present as chaplain of the
workhouse, and, pending his formal appointment to the office, the Ministry has, on the
recommendation of the Bishop of the
Diocese, authorised an arrangement under
which the duties will be performed
temporarily by another clergyman.
As the Guardians are aware of the system
in operation, and as the present arrangement is merely one of emergency, there was
no necessity to refer it formally to the
Board of Guardians.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister of Home
Affairs willing to assure this House that in
future appointments, either temporary or
permanent, he will consult the various
public Boards in connection with which the
appointment is to be made, and that he
will not take upon himself the onus of
appointing a gentleman to a position at a
salary of £169 odd, which the Guardians
have to toe the line for? I hope that in
future the Minister will not take upon himself the responsibility.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
pointed out to my hon. Friend that it
devolves upon the Ministry to make the
appointment.
OLD-AGE PENSION COMMITTEE
QUALIFICATIONS.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the qualifications required for acting as a ward representative on the Old-Age Pension Committee.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No specific qualifications are prescribed in the case of members of Old-Age Pension Committees. These
Committees are appointed by the Councils
of Boroughs and Urban Districts with populations of 20,000 and over, and also by County
Councils, and the Councils when appointing
such Committees are not required to restrict
the members of the Committees to members
of the Council appointing them.
The Local Pension Committees in their
turn are authorised to appoint Sub-Committees and to delegate either absolutely or
subject to conditions any of their powers or
duties.
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
6 NOVEMBER 1925
POLICE EXAMINATION OF MOTOR
LICENCES.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the total
number of officers and men of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary employed on

Saturday,
31st October, 1925, in holding up the motor
traffic on roads leading from the city; the
total cost of the number so employed; the
total revenue derived from the defaulting
motorists; and whether in future the
Minister is prepared to select a more suitable
day than Saturday, owing to the dislocation
of traffic caused by this practice.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Inspector-
General informs me that 83 members of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary were, as part of
their ordinary duty, employed in the City
of Belfast, on Saturday, the 31st ultimo, in
checking whether licences had been duly
taken out in accordance with the requirements of Statute.
No extra expenditure was incurred for this
purpose. I regret that I have been unable,
within the time available, to ascertain the
precise extent to which, as the result of the
examination, it was found that licences had
not been taken out, but I am satisfied that
the examination on the date in question
fully fulfilled its object.
I have not been able to confirm that there
was any undue or avoidable inconvenience
caused to the motorists, and I am not prepared to give any general direction, such
as is suggested by the hon. Member, which
would exempt motorists from examination
on a particular day of the week.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of that answer,
which is not satisfactory, would the Minister
give a guarantee to this House that in
future he will try to protect the money of
the Six Counties instead of throwing it away
in the manner in which I saw it done on
Saturday morning last, when twelve policemen were engaged on roads through which
I have to pass in the morning? Then we
are told there is no extra staff employed. I
believe this is the only city in Great Britain
which has adopted this method-
Mr. SPEAKER: Order, order. The hon.
Member is only allowed to ask a question.
SAILORS' AND SOLDIERS' HOUSING
TRUST.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if the following condition is accepted by him as one of
the conditions laid down by the Soldiers' and
Sailors' Housing Trust as to the allocation
of houses built under the Trust; that an
unemployed ex-Serviceman, who has not any
financial assistance other than his unemployed benefit, has been refused a house on
the ground that he is not in a position to
meet the requirements of the Trust, although
living in rooms with his wife and family;
whether he can state the reason for refusing
an applicant who lives in two rooms, with a
family of eight, to one of these houses unless
he boards out some of his children. Whether
it is the fact that although the Trust may
accept tenants with whom it is satisfied, the
agent has the right to refuse any so recommended; and whether he can state if English
and Scotch ex-officers, who did not reside in
Northern Ireland prior to 1914, are in possession of any of these houses.
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock)
to reply on his behalf.
I have explained to the House on previous
occasions that the Sailors' and Soldiers' Land
Trust is an Imperial Service, and I have no
responsibility for, or control over, the allocation of the tenancies of these cottages by
the Trustees. I am prepared, however, to
give to the hon. Member such information
as is at my disposal, and I think that this
will meet most of the points raised by the
hon. Member. The Trustees have frequently
intimated that the main considerations which
are recognised in dealing with the allocation
of cottages are as follows:-
(1) Amount and nature of active service
at the Front, taking into consideration
any personal distinction gained.
(2) Disability arising out of such active
service, e.g., loss of limb, sight,
disease, etc.
(3) Married men to have priority over
single men, taking into account the number of children and the circumstances of
present accommodation.
(4) Satisfactory references as to character
and prospects of punctual payment of
rent.
I may add that the agent's duties are confined to installing those tenants who have
been approved by the Trust and to the collection of rents.
I am sure that the Trustees, with an extremely difficult duty to discharge, endeavour
to select as tenants for these cottages those
applicants who are regarded as possessing,
from all those points of view which the
Trustees have to take into account, the
strongest claims to consideration.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman try to influence the Trust to let
these houses according to the plans laid
down by the Imperial Government? Will he
also see that the right persons-and not, as
has already been the case, persons who are

SAILORS' AND SOLDIERS' HOUSING
TRUST.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if the following condition is accepted by him as one of
the conditions laid down by the Soldiers' and
Sailors' Housing Trust as to the allocation
of houses built under the Trust; that an
unemployed ex-Serviceman, who has not any
financial assistance other than his unemployed benefit, has been refused a house on
the ground that he is not in a position to
meet the requirements of the Trust, although
living in rooms with his wife and family;
whether he can state the reason for refusing
an applicant who lives in two rooms, with a
family of eight, to one of these houses unless
he boards out some of his children. Whether
it is the fact that although the Trust may
accept tenants with whom it is satisfied, the
agent has the right to refuse any so recommended; and whether he can state if English
and Scotch ex-officers, who did not reside in
Northern Ireland prior to 1914, are in possession of any of these houses.
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock)
to reply on his behalf.
I have explained to the House on previous
occasions that the Sailors' and Soldiers' Land
Trust is an Imperial Service, and I have no
responsibility for, or control over, the allocation of the tenancies of these cottages by
the Trustees. I am prepared, however, to
give to the hon. Member such information
as is at my disposal, and I think that this
will meet most of the points raised by the
hon. Member. The Trustees have frequently
intimated that the main considerations which
are recognised in dealing with the allocation
of cottages are as follows:-
(1) Amount and nature of active service
at the Front, taking into consideration
any personal distinction gained.
(2) Disability arising out of such active
service, e.g., loss of limb, sight,
disease, etc.
(3) Married men to have priority over
single men, taking into account the number of children and the circumstances of
present accommodation.
(4) Satisfactory references as to character
and prospects of punctual payment of
rent.
I may add that the agent's duties are confined to installing those tenants who have
been approved by the Trust and to the collection of rents.
I am sure that the Trustees, with an extremely difficult duty to discharge, endeavour
to select as tenants for these cottages those
applicants who are regarded as possessing,
from all those points of view which the
Trustees have to take into account, the
strongest claims to consideration.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman try to influence the Trust to let
these houses according to the plans laid
down by the Imperial Government? Will he
also see that the right persons--and not, as
has already been the case, persons who are

Mr. DEVLIN: On a point of Order. This
is really a most important matter, a highly
important matter. I do not think that in
the history of the most contemptible Board
of Guardians in Europe there were ever
proceedings of this character. This Bill
from the very beginning has been rushed.
Mr. KYLE: They talk about Russia.
Mr. DEVLIN: It is not the Bill that was
introduced at all. The Government subsequently brought forward a series of Amendments containing far more proposals than
the Bill itself, and now when we come to

at all. How any body of sane men or intelligent men-we are sane; we may not be

Mr. DEVLIN: I was prepared to offer
the most warm congratulations to the right
hon. Gentleman on what I would have regarded as marvellous lucidity and Parliamentary skill in submitting this Clause to
the House. Because, what is this Clause?
It is a Clause which was proposed in the
Senate yesterday. It was proposed by a
number of very experienced and representative Senators, who have given great attention and study to this question of drainage.
They made out what they conceived to be
an irresistible case in favour of it, and,
indeed, so strongly did they feel in their
own convictions in favour of this Amendment that, notwithstanding the repeated
appeals of the Leader of the Senate to them
to withdraw the Amendment, they declined
to do so. A vote was taken, and the Government was defeated by a substantial majority.
Now what do we find here? We find that
while Lord Londonderry, speaking for the
Government in the Upper House, declined
to accept this Clause, and proceeded to give
not very cogent, but, at all events, fairly
intelligent Government reasons for not
accepting it-he went so far as to say that
nothing on earth would make him accept
this Amendment. He declared that he was
prepared to be defeated rather than accept
this Amendment. And the valiant men in
the Senate, who believed in their principles
on the question of drainage, not like the
Members of this House, who carried out
the characteristic occupation we have been
engaged in for the last few days of running
away-
Mr. ANDREWS: Not all.
Mr. DEVLIN: Except the Minister of
Labour, who would have been better employed running along with the rest than
describing how rabbits ran and flags were
hoisted. Now, the Leader of the Senate,
Lord Londonderry, absolutely refused to
accept this Amendment. The Government
were defeated, and what ordinarily a
Drainage Bill-

Senate's Amendments.
Government would do under these circumstances would be to go down to the House,
now that the Prime Minister has triumphantly returned from London, and proclaim
that in view of the circumstances he would
resign or drop the Bill.
The PRIME MINISTER: Not on a question of drainage.
Mr. DEVLIN: But may I point out to the
right hon. Gentleman that this Drainage
Bill is their one great card.
Mr. ANDREWS: What about widows'
pensions?
Mr. DEVLIN: We dragged that out of
you. That is not your Bill at all; it is our
Bill. I think we have discussed that sufficiently. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I
think we had better stick to this. We have
had so much of the Boyne in the last few
nights' election meetings that I will stick
to the Bann now. No; the right hon.
Gentleman does a grave injustice to himself
and to the Government in saying that this
drainage question does not count.
The PRIME MINISTER: I did not say
that at all. What I said was that it was
not political.
Mr. DEVLIN: Neither do I say it is
political. I do not say it is political at all.
That is why I am so profoundly interested.
But this Bill, in my judgment, will not be of
the slightest use to anybody. I have that on
the authority of men who are more competent to discuss it than I am.
Apart altogether from that consideration,
if this Clause was a clause that was acceptable why was it not accepted by Lord Londonderry on behalf of the Government in the
Senate? Why does the representative of the
Government in this House come down to
commend to us the Clause that the Marquess
of Londonderry rejected in the Senate yesterday? That is what I cannot understand, unless it is that there was no alternative
for the Government except to resign, and the
right hon. Gentleman (the Prime Minister)
says that that is the last thing he will do.
I really cannot follow this method of Parliamentary procedure on the part of the Government in saying, "The thing is so bad that
we are prepared to stake our reputation and
the position of the Government on it before
we accept it," and then a few hours afterwards they send down a gentleman who is,
in my judgment, selected to do all the nasty
jobs because he is a very respectable and
very tactful Minister, but he is too honest to
say anything good about it. He could not
say anything good in this House to-day about
what was so bad in the Senate yesterday,
and, therefore, with a smile he presents to
us, not with the irresistible logic that ought
to be offered in the advancement of the great
cause which is incorporated in this Clause,
but with a smile he comes down here and
says, "Gentlemen of the Lower House, or
the Higher House, or whatever House you
belong to, here is a Clause that was so bad
yesterday that we were prepared to take defeat rather than carry it, and seeing it was
so bad yesterday we ask you to pass it to-day
because it is so good."
That, in my opinion, is a position which.
is perfectly unprecedented in the history of
Parliaments. But I come back to a point
I have already made. I suggested on the last
day that you ought to drop this Bill and
give it graver consideration. This Bill has
been ill thought out. No grave consideration
has been given to it. It has been rushed,
and, of course, we all know why it has been
rushed. I do not want to repeat it again,
but I would like to remind the right hon.
Gentleman, the Prime Minister, that for years,
and years, and years, when we were in the
Imperial House of Commons together, and
before either of us were born, there were
gallant men in Ulster fighting for the drainage of the Bann in the Imperial Parliament,
who were told that if ever there was a
claim on the part of Ulster--
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid the hon.
Member (Mr. Devlin) must confine himself to
the particular Amendment. We cannot go
again into the question of the Bill as a whole.
Mr. DEVLIN: But I want the Bill withdrawn, and it is on that point-
Mr. SPEAKER: It is too late to go into
that now, I am afraid.
Mr. DEVLIN: Very well, I will not pursue
the matter any further except to this extent,
and I think I am entitled to say this: When
this Bill was introduced here a few days ago
no one said a word about it except the hon.
lady Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester),
and she got up and blessed it. She poured
Bann water on it. (Laughter). She blessed
it with Bann water, but that was not because
it was a good Bill, but because it was a
good Government. When she sat down I expected to hear words of wisdom from the hon.
Members for Armagh and the hon. Members
for Antrim. I thought we might have their
views, and I waited, but they showed no
manifestation of any desire to intervene, to
give us the benefit of their local knowledge,
and to say what they thought of this Bill.
Then I intervened, and, as a consequence, a
discussion took place in which these gentlemen took part.
One of the things the Minister of Finance
stated was that he was backed in this Bill by
all the County Councils. I challenged him
on that point repeatedly and he said "Yes,"
and again I challenged him and he said

"Yes," and yet we have, within the past

and the representative of the Government

All I have to say is that most of the Members on the other side of the House are
businessmen. That is the reputation they
have got; whether they deserve it or not is
not for me to say. Was there ever a more
unbusinesslike transaction than this? The
Minister of Finance tells us that the County
Councils were in favour of this Measure, and
upon the strength of that-
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Mr. DEVLIN: The right hon. Gentleman
says, "Hear, hear." Here are copies of the
resolutions-
Mr. SPEAKER: I am very sorry, but I
cannot allow the hon. Member (Mr. Devlin)
to enter on a general discussion of the Bill.
It would set up an impossible precedent if,
when a Bill came back from the Senate, we
were again allowed to go into the merits of
the Bill as a whole. We can only deal with
the particular amendments passed by the
Senate, now before the House.
Mr. DEVLIN: I have finished.
The PRIME MINISTER: A great deal of
heat has been engendered in this debate
quite unnecessarily. The Bill, as a Bill, has
passed both Houses without a division. The
Amendment we are speaking upon at the
present moment is a Government Amendment, put forward by the Government in the
Senate, and accepted by the Senate, in lieu
of one put forward by a private Member
yesterday. There is no difference between
the Government Amendment put forward in
this House and the Amendment put forward
by the Government in the other House.
There is nothing extraordinary about what
has occurred, except that we have, after
careful consideration, decided to put forward
a Clause giving the public extra protection,
if necessary, as explained in this particular
Amendment. We did not think, however,
it was necessary before, in fact, we thought
the first arrangement was probably cheaper
to the public, as a whole, but in consequence
of a conference and general agreement all
round, it was thought this would probably
be the best way. When the Government put
it forward in the Senate, the Senate carried
it, and passed the Bill without any other
serious Amendment. They passed it unanimously, the same as this House. It seems to
me that really a great pother has been made
over a very small matter.
Mr. KYLE: The Government have made
the Amendment passed in the Senate their
own Amendment. I take it that is what
the Prime Minister means when he
says this Amendment is the Government's
Amendment, and that it is the Government's Clause they are putting into
the Bill. The Government did not think it
necessary to put this into the Bill in the
first instance. Is there any reason in the
world why the Government should accept the
Amendment sent down from the Senate?
Mr. POLLOCK: It is not acceptance.
Mr. KYLE: The Senate proposed to put
this in. The Government do not think it
necessary, and yet the Government to save
their own faces insert this and ask us to pass
it. I think we on the Opposition side are
acting in a perfectly constitutional way--we
are really acting on behalf of the Government-in asking this House to refuse to accept this Amendment of the Senate. As a.
matter of fact, the Amendment which the
Government are asking the House to accept
is putting into the hands of private persons
power which the County Council itself should
have, and from that point of view I think
we are acting in the best interests of the
citizens of the Six Counties in asking the
House to refuse to allow the Government to
accept the Amendment the Senate has sent
to us.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN : A very
strong case has been made out as to why
the Government should give further consideration to this whole question. The Prime
Minister and those who sit beside and behind
him are not in a terrible hurry to discuss
a very burning question, but we find they are
in an exceptionally great hurry so far as the
drainage of the Bann and Lough Neagh is
concerned. There does not seem to be any
great unanimity on this question. I do not
profess to know a great deal, or indeed anything at all, about this matter, but I have
followed the controversy in the Press. If I
can judge by the controversy that is taking
place in the Press by people who, I believe,
are political supporters of the Government,
the Government Measure does not reflect the
opinions of those people who live in close
proximity to where the flooding takes place.
It is on the cards that this House is likely
to adjourn on Tuesday, and this Bill is only
an instalment of what the Government propose to do. In view of the fact that there is
