Mr. BEATTIE: I wish to draw the
attention of the House to the very grave
situation which now prevails amongst the
unemployed in the City of Belfast. I may
say that upwards of 14,000 people are unemployed and in a state of starvation, and
some are dying by their own hands through
being driven to desperation through lack of
assistance. I hope this House will agree either
to suspend or amend the regulations which
the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews), with
his small Committee, is applying to the
class of worker to whom I refer, that is the
single men and women and the youths of our
city. You have heard, or if you have read
your papers you have read of the case of the
ex-Navy man who committed suicide. That
is only one case of many who are dying as
the
result of the regulations which
Minister of Labour has applied to Unemployment Insurance Benefit.
a
I can speak personally of the poor chap
who was buried this morning. There are
four sons in that family who joined up in
1914, and went to the war. One of them at
present is disabled by gunshot wounds, the
other brother has returned home and is dying
of consumption, and there is an old woman,
the old mother, of eighty years of age who
was dependent on the little assistance that
was coming into the home from the source
of extended benefit. The regulations denied
that poor soul the right to extended benefit
and brought upon him in a weak moment
his own hand to shorten his life, as you have
perhaps seen in last night's paper.
What do I ask the Minister to do, or what
does the Minister propose to do? I will
tell you.
The Minister of Labour has had
repeated requests from the Opposition
benches to increase the standard of the
family income from the minimum of 36s for a
man and woman. We have repeatedly asked
him to increase that, but we find that he has
refused the request on the recommendation
of the small Committee which he appointed.
They have reduced the family income for a
man, his wife, and three children by 6s per
week. The ultimate result of that is something most serious, and I am rather afraid,
if those regulations are put into operation,
of what the outcome may be for these distressed people, who are going to suffer
similarly to the case I have already referred
to and be struck off altogether.
I ask the Minister to suspend these regulations and to restore the benefits to
between 13,000 and 14,000 persons to whom
he has denied benefit. Failing the restoration of benefit to these people it will be very
hard to know what the end of it will be.
We have 7,825 people denied the right to
benefit for not genuinely seeking work; we
have 2,886 denied the right to benefit through
other causes; and then we have 1,116 denied
the right to benefit by the Courts of Referees.
That is not taking into account the number
of persons turned down by headquarters
themselves, which is the most serious point
in the regulations under which we are now
suffering. I do not say that, perhaps, some
of the cases that have been turned down
have not been turned down justly, but I do
say that to many of these people a very grave
injustice has been done.
We will take what the Minister proposes
to do. I have the names of the Committee,
and, just in passing, I would have preferred
if the Minister had got a city man or a local
man, who understood the conditions prevailing in the working-class homes, to
sit on that Committee with him. Perhaps
he would have been able to give good advice
and counsel and we might have had different
regulations to what we have. But another
serious problem in the regulations for me
is that the Minister is going to deny every
married woman the right to benefit if her
husband is working and earning 40s per
week, although she is an industrial worker
and will always have to continue at industrial work owing to the nature of her man's
employment. I think that is a grave scandal
that a contributor, who has contributed for
years, after she exceeds her standard benefit
is not going to be given the right to
extended benefit for which she would be
expected to pay whilst in employment.
The old scale of family income for a man
and wife was 36s. What do the Minister
and the Committee recommend? They recommend that the scale of family income
for husband and wife and three children
should be 40s. I do not know, but I would
ask the Minister (Mr. Andrews) and his
colleague (Mr. Gordon) to try and keep their
wives and three children on 40s. Let them see
if they can keep their homes on 40s. If they
do that on a month's trial, perhaps they will
come to a different conclusion to the one
they have arrived at, and which they are
putting into operation against the poor, unfortunates out of work through no fault of
their own. That is one case. But take the
case of a man who has had the opportunity
of serving his time to a trade. This tradesman has perhaps £3 per week. He has a son
of 18 or 20 years of age. Because that man
has £3 a week, the son who was drawing the
Bureau, is going to be struck off, with the
result that his father is expected to keep
him.
Dr. MORRISON: Quite right.

That these scales should not apply to single

it down to 22, but there is a condition

That the claims of married women living

Here is the funny part about it. We think
we have all the wisdom in this House. We
think we can carry out the ideals that would
be carried out in a perfect State, but the
fact is, as we have often accused you, that
you are copying methods that will lead you
to destruction. There is now a prescribed
form to be sent to the applicant for the purpose of getting a return of the family income.
The prescribed form in operation in Northern Ireland to-day is all sufficient. Why
under the sun they are going to Liverpool
to get another prescribed form for this area
I do not know and cannot understand.
That a form of declaration regarding family
income on the lines of the form in use in
Liverpool, but modified to meet local requirements, should be substituted for the
form at present in use.
May I deliberately say that the new form is
intentionally meant to implicate honest
people or innocent people who do not actually
know the amount of earnings coming into
the home. If they make a false declaration
on the new form they will be brought before
a magistrate and fined severely. I do not
see that there is anything in the Regulations
which will tend towards doing any good. If
this is the result of the appeal from the
Opposition, it would have been far better to
have declared at the last election that you
wanted no Opposition. You have men here
who live among the people, who know their
conditions, and who could give you an idea
of what happens in the workers' homes, and
yet this is the reply that you send us. It
looks as if you thought we were talking
tommy rot.
Let me give you an instance of one member
of the Committee who is a working man and
who knows what it is to keep a home-I refer
to Councillor Harry Midgley. He protested
against the Regulations and left your meeting; but before that he tabled an Amendment providing for a family scale which was
just, but not too generous. Why the Committee could not accept that Amendment in-

Before sitting down let me say that the

operation by the Minister of Labour in the

and now that if you do not remove these
stringent Regulations, and if you dare to put

bring about. That is all I have to say.

Is there a man in this House who thinks
for a moment that that unfortunate man
committed suicide because he lost his unemployment insurance. I have seen many
cases of people suffering from insanity. The
great majority who do suffer in that way
have an obsession. They may have the
illusion that no matter how wealthy they
are and I have known people with thonsands of pounds suffer in this way-they
will end up in destitution and poverty. You
may point out to them their possession of
obvious wealth, you may satisfy them, and
they become assured for the moment, but
as soon as your back is turned they return
to the old thing. There is some terrible
calamity hanging over them in the shape
of poverty, injury to their families, or their
spiritual welfare, with the result that even
with everything favourable around them they
commit suicide. That is an unfortunate
thing, but for us to say that because this
man lost his unemployment benefit he took
his life, and that, consequently, the Minister
of Labour is responsibie for his death, is
ridiculous. I do not doubt what the hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Beattie) has said, but I
think it is an extraordinary thing that the

because the contributions are as high as

Of course you may say, as you have said

influence, no prestige, and I cannot understand, if you accept that as being true, how
any person is prepared to listen to us, or

who is likely to put money into industry.
If we represent nobody, if we have got no
influence, if we have got no prestige, nobody
is going to be influenced by anything we say,
and, consequently, even if we make the
wildest speeches, we cannot be responsible in
any way, or to any extent, for unemployment. There is little or nothing in that
argument.
These regulations in force at the mo
ment want to be relaxed, and we do not
want any intriguing behind the scenes to
make even worse regulations than were in
force before the Labour Party in Great
Britain improved the Unemployment Acts,
or to make the scale worse than it is at the
moment. We do not want people to be
starved, because of what may be said about
finding money. It is the duty of
the Government to find the money.
Notwithstanding what hon. Members
Say in this House, there are many
ways to find the money if there is the will
to do so. It can be quite easily found. We
have all the justification in the world for
asking that there should be a relaxation, as
far as these regulations are concerned, and
that the people should get a larger measure
of justice than they are getting at the present time.

were
I come now to two points raised by the hon.
Member for West Belfast. One was, how are
we to determine when a man is not looking
for work. A perfectly reasonable question
and an exceedingly difficult question for me
to answer, inasmuch as all claims for unemployed benefit are placed before committees.
Statutory claims are dealt with by the superintendent of the exchange or an officer in
the Department. When a man's claim is perfectly straight, when he has contributions to
his credit his claim is looked upon as a perfectly legitimate claim and is granted. But
if the man has exhausted all his right to what
is known as statutory benefit then his case,
with the history of his claim, is submitted
to what has been termed in the House here
this afternoon as the Rota Committee. This
Rota Committee is representative of the
various trade union organisations in the city,
represented by the employers and represented
by public bodies, and when the claim comes
before the Committee, it is examined by this
particular Committee, and every committee
determines from their particular standpoint
whether that man or woman is entitled to
benefit.
For instance, I have even come across committees who demanded that the applicants
for benefit must show by documentary evidence that they have been making reasonable
efforts to obtain employment. Other committees are perfectly satisfied with the statement that the appliant makes before the
Committee, and if they are satisfied grant
benefit. But it is entirely outside the province
of the Minister of Labour or myself to interfere directly with the work of the Rota Committee by suggesting to them what they should
do.
Mr. KYLE: If the Parliamentary Secretary would tell us that these committees have
the right to recommend, he would be saying
what is absolutely correct. It is not correct
to say they grant benefit, because that is
where we have great trouble.

the junior hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. W. McMullen), I would say to him that
many cases that have been turned down by

Ministry of Labour and have been granted.
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: I never heard tell of
them.
Mr. GORDON: Furthermore, if the hon.
Member challenges. my statement I can produce them.
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: The same as you did
Hansard.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 10th November, 1925.
The House met at Twelve of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Paper Presented to Parliament.
Ministry of Home Affairs:
The Northern Ireland Winter Assize
Order, 1925.
Oral Answers to Questions.
SINN FEIN FLAG AT HILLSBOROUGH.
1. Mr. T. W. McMULLAN asked the Minister
of Home Affairs what information the police
have gathered with regard to the Sinn Fein
flag which was placed in a tree at the residence of Mr. McGiffard, Crumlin Lodge, Hillsborough, on the occasion of His Grace the
Governor's official entrance into residence at
Hillsborough Castle, and what steps the
authorities have taken, or propose to take,
against the perpetrators.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The facts of the incident referred to in this question are as follow:—
Information was conveyed to the police on
the morning of the 10th ultimo that a Sinn
Fein flag was flying from a tree in the avenue
of the residence referred to, and the police
had the flag immediately removed.
Every effort is being made to make the
persons who were responsible for this outrage
amenable. It would, however, be contrary
to the public interest to indicate what steps
have been, or may be, taken by the authorities in the case.
Mr. DEVLIN: Hurrah!
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Would the
Minister of Home Affairs state whether it is
a fact that a white blackbird was observed
on the same occasion?
Mr. DEVLIN: Or a rebellion?
LISBURN URBAN COUNCIL AND FAIR
WAGES CLAUSE.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he will take action to prevent
the Lisburn Urban Council giving a contract
to the "Herald" Office, Lisburn, as this
firm does not comply with the Fair Wages
Clause in the payment of the employees.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As already pointed
out in this House on the 15th May of last
year, instructions were issued to all local
authorities recommending the inclusion of
"Fair Wages Clauses" in contracts entered
into by local authorities.
The Lisburn Urban District Council are
well aware of these recommendations, which
are still in operation, but the Ministry of
Home Affairs has no power to compel them
to adopt them.
Mr. KYLE: In view of the fact that this
Urban Council refuses to put into operation
the Fair Wages Clause, would the Home
Secretary not take power to compel them to
observe it in their contracts?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not aware
that the Lisburn Urban District Council
have refused to do so, but it is a matter
entirely for themselves.
Mr. KYLE: I can tell the right hon.
Gentleman that the Urban District Council
of Lisburn have refused to put the
Fair Wages Clause into operation 80
far as the payment of the employees
in their establishment is concerned.
Will the Minister now, on this assurance from me, or if he does not like my
assurance, will he ask the Urban District
Council, and if they have done as I said, will
he take steps to compel the Council to carry
out the Fair Wages Clause?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am quite prepared to recommend the Urban Council to
do so, and to draw their attention to the
previous circular, but beyond that I am not
prepared to go.
SALARY OF ATTORNEY-GENERAL.
3. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Prime
Minister whether, in the interests of public
economy, he can introduce legislation so that
the salary of the incoming Attorney-General
shall be at least £1,000 less than that paid to
his predecessor.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I will take this question for my
right hon. Friend.
The reply to my hon. Friend's question is
in the negative. In view of the fact that this
House so recently as 1923 unanimously gave
legislative sanction to the increase of the
salary of the Attorney-General, the Government do not propose to make any change.
The House will not need to be reminded that
the gentlemen who from time to time fulfil
the duties of Attorney-General have all
attained to a position of high eminence in
their profession, and that their acceptance
of office deprives them of a large part of a
lucrative practice at the Bar.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I would like
to inquire, in view of a more recent utterance of the Prime Minister that it was
necessary in the interests of Ulster that all
the people should tighten their belts, whether
he is now prepared to show an example, or
does the tightening of belts refer to poor
working people only, and not to a prospective
Attorney-General?

put down a substantive motion dealing with
the matter.
Mr. DEVLIN: But as this can only be

-would they judicially consider the new

relevant matters, and would the right hon.

salaries in the House in relation to this most
extravagant Government?
Mr. SPEAKER: The position is that all
other salaries, or practically all other
salaries, certainly the salaries of all
Ministers, come up for discussion on the
annual Estimates, and that is the proper
time for their discussion. The question of
this particular salary is one which involves
legislation, because it is governed by Act of
Parliament. Therefore, the hon. Member
must put down a motion if he desires it to
be discussed.
Mr. DEVLIN: I invite my hon. Friend,
the Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford), to
enter into an alliance with me, and by our
mutual co-operation we may carry out the
purpose he has in view.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I would like
to know whether I am going to get a reply
to the query I addressed to the Prime
Minister as to whether this tightening of
belts is only intended for working people, or
whether it applies to the prospective
Attorney-General and other people who are
paid by the Northern Government?
Mr. SPEAKER: That is a type of question
that does not always receive an answer in
Parliament. It is really up to the Minister
whether he cares to answer a question of that
sort or not.

Mr. SPEAKER: I think it is very unfortunate and regrettable that any incident
such as the hon. Member mentions should

These incidents have been known to occur
in other Parliaments, and I am afraid sometimes will occur. They are very regrettable
and should be avoided as much as possible.
With regard to the hon. Member's point as
to whether or not he made a charge of murder
against anybody in debate, I have read fairly
carefully the debate which took place and I
think that in the heat of the discussion-in

Many people are dying and will die-yes.
the Government murdered a man yesterday.
A man died as a result of the Government

THE PROBLEM OF UNEMPLOYMENT.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That this House, at its rising this day, do
adjourn until Tuesday, December 8th, provided always that if it appears to the
satisfaction of Mr. Speaker, after consultation with the Government, that the public
interest requires that the House should meet
at an earlier time during the Adjournment,
Mr. Speaker may give notice that he is so
satisfied, and thereupon the House shall
meet at the time stated in such notice, and
shall transact its business as if it had been
duly adjourned to that time."-(Mr. Barbour.)
Mr. DEVLIN: On a point of order, can we
discuss this Motion?
Mr. SPEAKER: Yes.
Mr. DEVLIN: I venture to say that it is
entirely wrong for this Parliament to adjourn for a period of four weeks. I think in
view of the present condition of trade and
commerce it is eminently desirable that this
House should remain in Session. We have
made repeated attempts in the House to
have a full and adequate discussion on the
question of unemployment, but that privilege, or rather I should say that right, has
been denied to us by the refusal of the
Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance
to attend in their places when that most imperatively urgent question came before the
House for consideration.
I would call the attention of the House to
the discussion we had on the Unemployment
Bill. I ventured then to state that I would
be very glad indeed if I could offer some
humble contribution to this most vital
problem in the life of our community, and
the Prime Minister interrupted me and
stated that he thought it was undesirable
and inconvenient, I think, to discuss the matter at that stage in all its bearings. I at
once ceased to discuss the matter in that
aspect of it, and the Prime Minister suggested that a day should be found for the
discussion of it. I at once acquiesced in
the suggestion. I thought it a reasonable
suggestion for him to make, and I thought
the occasion would be infinitely more
adequate to deal with a subject so important
when the day was selected. I left it to the
Prime Minister to suit his own convenience
selected
and the right hon. Gentleman
Tuesday. I came to the House on Tuesday

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment.
VOTE OF CENSURE PROPOSED.
Mr. KYLE: I beg to move:
"That this House has no confidence in the
Government owing to its failure to deal
with the unemployment problem, or to recognise the urgency and importance of a
menace which has been getting more and
more out of hand, owing to the ineptitude,
dilatoriness, and incapacity of the Government to institute large and well-considered
schemes of employment, and to take steps
to restore the economic and commercial
prosperity of Northern Ireland."
In moving the Motion which stands in my
name I quite realise that in this happy and
contented House, where there so many happy
and contented people, it may be thought
rather amazing that a Motion of no confidence
in the Government on this question of unemployment should be put down. But I want
to assure hon. Members opposite that there
are some 62,000 to 64,000 people unemployed
Unemployment.
Unemployment.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Kyle]
in Northern Ireland, people who are suffering dire want and starvation, and, though the
right hon. Gentleman the Prime Minister and
his colleagues opposite may be happy and contented, these people in Belfast are not so
happy and contented-nor are the people in
the Six Counties who are suffering the pangs
of unemployment owing to the ineptitude and
dilatoriness of our Government-and we want
to express from these benches at least our
opinions of the actions of the Government so
far as unemployment is concerned.
We feel that in doing this we are voicing
the opinions of a great many people in the Six
Counties when we say that the Government
have not attempted to deal with this question
in the manner in which it ought to be dealt
with. It is of such importance thaf
it will eventually bring down this Government, with all their good majority, unless
they are prepared to deal with it. To prove
that this question is important I have only
to refer to the King's Speech of the 15th
April, in which it was stated:
'My Government recognises that the most
important and urgent subjects with which
it is faced are the state of our Industries
and the problem of Unemployment. Every
effort will be made to encourage agriculture, to aid industry and
through the operation of the Loans Guarantee Acts, and, in association with Local
Authorities, through schemes of public
utility, to find useful employment for our
people.
commerce
In the speech of the Prime Minister that
followed he certainly gave no indication as
to what he, as head of the Government, was
prepared to do in this particular matter of
unemployment. We were moved to table
this Resolution and everybody in this
House knows the history of how this
Resolution came to be tabled-by the feeling
of desperation and exasperation at the
inefficient way in which the Government
have attempted to deal with the terrible
problem of unemployment, despite the
admission in the King's Speech that it is a
most important and urgent subject. Our
desperation as Labour Members in this
House is nothing to the desperation of those
62,000 people who are unemployed to-day.
During the seven or eight months since this
House first met after the General Election
the numbers have increased to the alarming
total of 62,000. This is despite the fact that
the regulations are stricter. The numbers
given are probably smaller in proportion to
the total of unemployed than when the regulations were less strict. In other words, the
regulations which have been brought in by
the Minister of Labour have been such that
huge numbers of people have been denied
benefit and have been told that it is no use
signing at the Unemployment Exchanges as
there is no work for them. The result is
that the figure of 62,000 which is shown in
the Board of Trade Gazette for November, is
not the total number of unemployed so far
as the Six Counties are concerned.
What is the Government's record? They
point to a few road and housing schemes, all
useful in their way, but everyone of them is
mortgaging the future of the councils which
have brought them forward. The Government have shown in my opinion no real conception of government in the modern sense.
An instance of this may be taken and should
be mentioned-something that took place
during the Drainage Bill debate, when the
right hon. Gentleman opposite (Mr.
Andrews), compared the views held
by the County Council of Antrim with
some views held by some people in Russia.
They may have put certain schemes into
operation, many of which would have to be
carried out anyhow. After all roads have
got to be repaired and constructed to some
extent. Houses have got to be built for the
people no matter whether we are suffering
from this great evil of unemployment or not.
People must have some place in which to
live in this climate of ours.
Against this
can be put down the despicable way the
Government have tried to rob the unemployed by depriving them of the right to
benefit; secondly by lengthening the waiting
period, and thirdly, by re-instituting
inquisition. We have had something to say
about these things on a previous occasion.
I have already referred in this House to how
the Minister of Labour attempted to mislead
this House in regard to the Regulations. He
stated that as I was vice-chairman of the
Committee, I was responsible for those
Regulations. The Belfast Local Employment
Committee, of which I am vice-chairman,
passed a resolution at the September meeting
condemning these Regulations. I think the
Minister of Labour might have mentioned
that particular fact. I am not saying he did
it deliberately, but he did mislead a considerable number of people, and I think he
owes it to me to state that the Belfast
Employment Committee passed the resolution I have referred to. Therefore it is
hardly correct to say that I as vice-chairman
of the Belfast Employment Committee, or
that any member of that committee was responsible for those Regulations for which he
(the Minister of Labour) is solely responsible.
In once more discussing this problem of unemployment I suppose the Government
imagine that they are going to make capital

out of this debate by saying: "Look at the

After all, it is not discussing this question
that will relieve anything or achieve anything, but doing something that will set the
ball rolling for a revival of trade. Take the
eight points I made so long ago as the 21st
April, 1925.
The first of these eight points was
Increased wages to bring consumption
up to something more like equilibrium with
production.
Second, the raising of the school-leaving
age and maintenance grants for young persons.
If the Government like, we will agree to
take everybody over 65 years of age out of
industry.
Third, the maintenance of widows with
dependent children to take them out. of industry altogether.
Fourth, the prevention of overtime.
Fifth, the ratification of the Washington
Convention on the hours of labour. I do
not think that that question should need
any stress-a forty-eight hour week by law.
It would help some industries in our Northern province.
Sixth, the immediate starting of the proposal in the King's Speech for electrification
and drainage.
Seventh, the building of schools that are
necessary in Belfast and the country districts.
Eighth, an index of production.
All these points I made so long ago as the 21st
never been
April. Many of these have
thought of seriously by the Government much
less put into operation. We on this side admit that unemployment is a big and difficult

Labour in his speech on September 3rd. That

an adequate maintainance, we on these
Benches have alwavs maintained that we
prefer work. The Minister of Labour himmen
self has said we must mainly look to our

loth to say this, but it is possible that
the palmy days of the linen trade are over.
Just as the manufacture of coaches has
gone out of existence and been superseded by motor cars, and just as the
employed formerly in harness
making and other forms of industry have
been superseded so it may be that our linen
trade has
seen its palmiest days. Our
Government ought to look around for other

trade may never be able to secure the demand it once had. Ships though they will
be required may not be required in such
numbers if the world is poor and trade decreased, and if more countries are becoming
industrial and able to produce goods for
themselves.
What new industry can be developed in
Belfast and the Six Counties? This is to
some extent a problem for the specialists,
but we wish to see some sign that the
Government are really thinking seriously
along these lines. The Government set up a
Commission to inquire into the natural and
industrial resources of Northern Ireland. Is
the Government in earnest about that Commission and that Commission's findings? Is
the Government getting that Commission to
hurry up that work as though an emergency
existed? Is the Government prepared to
start any of the schemes that the Commission have proposed? It would be amusing
if it were not so tragic to compare the glib

out. This in itself is in my opinion enough
to justify a Vote of Censure on the Government for dilatoriness in tackling unemployment or economic development, duties for
which they are responsible.
The Prime Minister said in the King's

Those are suggestions made by the Government's own Commission. They are not highfalutin fantastic schemes of Labour men, but
we will take it that they are the sound and
safe proposals of the Government's own
Commission. And yet the Government does
nothing to put them into operation. Therefore, what use is there in wasting your
breath on the more drastic proposal that we
as Labour men should like to make, and
that we advocate as the only solution for the

little good indeed for a Socialist to put

Then there is the question of developing
the sugar beet industry, on which there have
been some very interesting questions in this
House. Everybody knows that the sugar
beet industry has been developed in Great
Britain, and that the friends of the right
hon. Gentleman (The Prime Minister) in the
Free State have also developed the sugar
beet industry. I think it would be very
fitting indeed if the Government could see
its way to assist the Ulster farmers in this
particular direction. If Ulster farmers are
anxious to partake in the new movement,
some of the big sugar groups in England,
with the assistance of Belfast financiers,
might be glad to take the matter up,
provided that the Farmer's Union would
give a guarantee of a sufficient area of beet.
Something like 5,000 acres are required to
keep a moderate sized factory going as a
paying concern, and the yield in the
Northern Counties, judging by the comparative return from roots, should be well
above the English average. I am not
a farmer. I do not represent farmers.
I do not make the pretence that
I know very much about farming. But
the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister
of Agriculture, has stated in this House that
potatoes pay better than sugar beet. Again
I do not think that that statement is in
consonance with the facts as outlined in the

from time to time in the public Press of the
City of Belfast. We would like the Government to tackle this question seriously,
because it means employment not only for
engineers but for a considerable number of
people for whom there is no employment at
the particular season of the year when the
sugar beet factories would be going.
If it is a wise and sensible proposal for the
Imperial Government to make in Great
Britain, and if our neighbours in the Free
State think it is a good proposition for them,
surely the Government of Northern Ireland
would be well advised at least to attempt to
establish a sugar beet factory in the
Northern area. These things have got to be
done, not talked about. The Government
are the only people who are in a position to
do these things, and it seems to me that they
lack initiative, despite the fact that many of

and despite the fact that they are in that
stimulating atmosphere of private enterprise
and competition. They are imbued with the
spirit of hesitation to spend money, which
holds industry up, and keeps this huge army

The Minister of Labour is fond of referring to financial questions and especially
to the question of foreign exchanges, and
how they affect employment. We know that,

Despite their promises, despite the statement

Another factor, generous unemployment

If necessary special powers of taxation

Government to enable us to impose some

I have suggested myself that the bank rate
ought to be lowered, and that we should
start a bank of our own, not the Ulster Bank
to which the Prime Minister referred when
he interrupted me on a former occasion, but
a national bank of our own, the same as in
some of the States in Australia. They have
found it a paying proposition. If we are
going to be a Dominion, as probably we shall

that are now living, why should we not make
the attempt now? That, at least, is the cry
from the Labour Benches. I have also
advocated that the rate of interest should
be limited, and that high profits and dividends should be curtailed. All these things
are burdens on industry. Is there any need
for me, when there are 62,000 persons unemployed in the Six Counties, to show that a
state of emergency exists, and to suggest
that a state of emergency should be declared
by the Government, just as a state of emergency had been declared in the past to deal
with other serious matters. The fact that
the volume of unemployment is not showing
any material decrease is tremendously serious
to the unemployed, and it should be serious
to every Member of this House. It seems to
me there is no need to prove this state of
emergency. The Minister of Labour told us
on September 3 that 29.5 per cent. of the
shipyard workers were idle, and that 21.9 per
cent. of the linen workers were idle.
Ministry of Labour Gazette in October says
64,000, and in November says 62,000 people
were unemployed in the Northern area. These
are the reasons why we want this House to
express its disapproval of the action of the
Government so far as unemployment is concerned.

Mr. POLLOCK: When did I say that?

There is one hon. Member of this House

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
At the request of my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Andrews) I intervene now in this debate for
what I hope will be only a few moments,
in order to assure the House that far from
this charge which is levelled against us by
the Socialist Members here to-day having any
foundation in fact, there is up to the present
to my certain knowledge no Government
throughout the whole world that has done
more for the unemployed than the Ulster
Government has done. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I was not able to be here for
reasons which are well known in all quarters
of the House the last time a debate on
similar lines was instituted by hon. Members
opposite, but I read what they had to say
then, and I have listened to the mover of
this Resolution again to-day, not in the hope
that he would deliver himself into my hands
or the hands of the Government, not because
I hoped it would have been possible for us
to have made some great party advantage
of it, but simply and solely because I welcome
from any man whether he be an opponent
in this House or outside this House, and my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) also welcomes from any man any suggestion or any
germ of a suggestion which would enable us
to do even something more than we have
done in order to alleviate the unemployment
in our midst. Therefore, it is with great
sorrow, I say advisedly, that I find so far no
concrete proposition has fallen from the
Benches opposite that any Government could
catch hold of and say, There is a sane and
proper manner in which we can do a little
more to alleviate unemployment.”

First of all, the charge has been made
against us that we have not taken advantage
of the Report of the Development Commission. Each Government Department has
gone most cautiously into the recommendations of that very valuable Commission and
its preliminary reports, and action has been
taken upon them. I am not going into
details, but I wish to assert at once that the
various Departments have been active in considering the recommendations of the Com
mission and carrying out a considerable
number of those propositions which they
recommended.
Another charge made against us is that
we have not increased the benefits under the
unemployment scheme over those which exist
in Great Britain. As my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Pollock) has intimated over and over
again, it is impossible for a small State like
Ulster, circumscribed in its financial relations
with Great Britain, and naturally circumscribed by the nature of its size-it is impossible for it to go beyond the regulations
laid down for the distribution of unemployment relief in Great Britain. It is well
known to all that while unemployment has
been to a large extent existent in our area
we have not flinched from borrowing the
necessary funds in order that not one of the
unemployed shall feel he is at a disadvantage
as compared with anyone unemployed in
Great Britain. That is an accomplishment
which, I may say, has exercised the
attention of my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Finance and the other Members
of the Government ever since we took office,
as has the question of keeping on not only
Unemployment.
Unemployment.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[The Prime Minister].
the same benefits but also of exacting only
the same contributions. We stand perfectly
clean with regard to that, and we took all
these steps long before the hon. Members
opposite entered the House.
Having made these remarks, I want to
treat this matter on as wide a basis as I
possibly can. In all that the Commission
on Development has reported so far, I think
the House and Ulster generally will agree
that no hidden mine of wealth has been revealed, and in my opinion they must
inevitably draw the conclusion that our
three industries, agriculture, linen, and
shipbuilding, must be fostered and assisted
in every way, because it is upon those three
industries Ulster has made her name, and it
is on those industries she must rely to renew
that name and maintain it for years to come.
With regard to agriculture, I think my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Archdale) has done
all that any white man can do to help that
industry throughout Ulster -(Hon. Members:
Hear, hear) and I think he will agree that
he has met not only a sympathetic Cabinet
but a sympathetic House when he has come to
ask for grants, loans, and legislation to help
the great industry over which he so ably
presides.
Linen, of course, is the staple industry of
the North. It is what gave Ulster the name
of Linenopolis. Its goods have up to the
present held the markets of the world, and
everyone is filled with sorrow to think that
it is passing through such an unfortunate
time as at the moment. When I was recently
in London I was approached by representatives of the linen industry, and I am glad to
be able to inform the House to-day that the
British Government undertake to facilitate
the safeguarding of the linen industry provided a case is established under existing
procedure. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I believe, as I believed when I first entered
politics in the year 1904, that the safety of
our industries can only be assured by some
measure of protection keeping out foreign
goods and supplying the working classes with
work here in our midst which keeps this
great industry going. I do not propose to-day
to enter into a long discussion on the subject
of Tariff Reform, but I am delighted to know
that the Safeguarding of Industries Act.
which is now being made use of by various
trades in Great Britain, will be sufficient to
help us here in Ulster to cover the linen industry and to give it the help which, I trust,
will bring back the prosperity which it used
to enjoy.
Then we come to the question of the shipyards, which are of equal importance to the
people of the great city of Belfast. I took
the opportunity of calling with Lord Kylsant
and having another earnest talk with him on
the whole subject, and he very kindly authorised me to say that he is deeply conscious
of the magnitude of the problem which faces
us in Northern Ireland of obtaining employment for the highly-skilled and competent
workmen of the shipbuilding industry at
Belfast, which has produced ships famous
throughout the world, and that he is most
anxious to do everything in his power to
assist in finding a solution of this difficulty.
When we consider the severe and universal
character of the depression in the shipbuilding industry, we may congratulate ourselves
that, during the past year, our city has been
more fortunate than others in the matter of
shipbuilding orders.
In this connnection, a helpful stimulus has
been afforded to the industry in Belfast by
the aid granted by the British Trade Facilities Scheme, in conjunction with the
Northern Ireland Loans Guarantee Act.
under which there are at present under construction in the port three of the largest and
most up-to-date motor vessels in the world.
Moreover, much benefit to employment has
arisen in the past few months through several
large vessels having undergone extensive repairs in the port.
The company of which Lord Kylsant is
chairman is at present providing employment in Northern Ireland for over 10,000
workers, the number of men engaged being
about 2,000 more than at this time last year.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) At the same
time no one appreciates more fully than
Lord Kylsant the fact that a considerable
proportion of the firm's extensive facilities
are not being utilised, and he has assured
me that, whilst he cannot at the moment
say when further orders for ships will come
to Belfast, he is hopeful that before long
some of the vacant slips may again be
occupied. Progressive shipowners, if they are
to maintain their positions, must keep their
fleets up-to-date by replacing older tonnage
with modern vessels, but shipowners have
had and are still having a most trying
time on account of the very heavy running
expenses of their steamers, low freights and
the diminished volume of world trade.
Lord Kylsant informs me that, in his
view, business generally is slowly improving,
and affirms his belief that shipowners who
cannot at present see their way to place
orders for new vessels will not hesitate to
do so when they can look with more assured
confidence to the future. Previous experiences of depressions in the shipping trade show
that it takes very little movement in the
right direction to cause a marked improvement all round, and it may not be long before
many of our slips are again the scene of
activity.
Unemployment.
Unemployment.
8 DECEMBER 1925
I think that that coming from Lord
Kylsant is some assurance to this House
that although the outlook has been black
and is still not clear he, as one of the
greatest shipping magnates in the world, is
hoping at all events that the worst is past
and that in the near future there may be
just that turn which will bring back prosperity to our yards.
Having dealt with these three main industries, and when I tell you that my right
hon. Friend here (Mr. Pollock) is exercising
his whole time in helping where he can
under the Facilities Act which we passed in
this House, I can say that no Government
can do more. But these trades must be
managed by those who are in control of
them. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) No
Government dare interfere with the workings
of a linen firm any more than with a shipyard except to assist them by loans where
they possibly can. But when it comes to
what a Government can do to tide over
bad times, to fill up gaps, and supplement
in some way what is being done under the
unemployment benefit system, then I say
again we have exhausted ourselves in every
way in our power. The local authorities who
have been so kind to us in helping in the
past are still invited by my right hon.
Friend and myself to put forward still
further schemes on the same scale as before
to provide employment for the out-of-work,
and we trust that even at considerable
sacrifice this offer will be taken advantage
of so that during the severe winter months
that lie ahead we may be able to do something to take these men off the streets that
are so anxious once more to find implements
in their hands and to be doing an honest
day's work for a day's pay.
We come to another point. These matters
are all done between the Government and
the local authorities. They are all done for
the purpose of helping to tide over bad times
until normal trade returns and until the
men are absorbed in the occupations for
which they are so well skilled and fitted.
But I have to announce to the House, and
perhaps they will pardon me making a
rather long statement-I have to announce
to the House that as a result of several conferences with the British Government a
modification of the original plan of
Parliamentary and administrative buildings
is to be adopted.
Our
I should explain that in the first instance,
in accordance with the terms of the Act of
1920, His Majesty's Office of Works submitted
sketches to us of how they proposed to carry
out their obligations of supplying us with
suitable buildings in order to start our new
Government. We had practically no option
but to gratefully accept the offer which was
made to us in fulfilment of the obligation of
the British Government under the Act of 1920.
Since then the suggestion has been thrown
out that greater efficiency and economy could
be secured by doing away with the two wing
buildings and housing the Senate and the
Commons as well as the bulk of our Civil
Service in one comprehensive building situate
upon the foundations already completed at
Stormont. This modification has been welcomed by us, so that instead of having a large
building lying empty a great part of the year,
the enlarged building will be a busy hive of
industry throughout the whole time.
Whilst we are perfectly satisfied with the
new arrangement we cannot help feeling a
certain disappointment that we are not to
have an example of Mr. Knot's architecture
in Ulster. As the House is aware, he sprang
into prominence and fame by the design of
the magnificent administrative buildings of
the London County Council. He was, I was
informed, chosen by the British Government
to design the two wing buildings which, of
course, now disappear, depriving us here in
Ulster of the benefit and advantage of his
magnificent architecture.
This leads me to explain that in order to
provide work for the unemployed class-that
is to say distinguishing the class which can
be employed suitably on manual labour of a
temporary character from the skilled workers
for whom I understand there is no shortage
of work at the present moment-we pressed
the Office of Works to economise in the new
comprehensive building to an extent sufficient
to provide funds to complete the long
approach from Newtownards Road to the
main entrance of the building, and I am
hopeful that early in the new year a large
number will be absorbed in this manner without adding to the estimate originally laid
down for the completion of the work.
I mention that because it is only one of the
many instances of the activity of my two
right hon. Friends here to find every possible
channel to absorb the unemployed in these
trying times. And before I close I would
just like to say this, that it would be easy
for any Government to come forward and
say we will raise a large sum of money, and
in this way get rid of the unemployed
problem. It is easy to say it, but the futility
of that can be exposed in a few moments.
If Ulster were to float a loan for the purpose of raising money in order to tide over
the exceptional unemployment at this
moment, it simply means that we are binding
our successors to pay off the interest and
sinking fund upon that loan which therefore
would practically prevent and Government in
the future from being able to deal with a
serious question of unemployment which

happened in their day. I believe the

Mr. BEATTIE: In rising to support the

is one thing they have done and done very

or come in contact with. We are told by the

perhaps he would be well advised if he would

believe his time would have been well spent

how to get out of the ruck that the shipbuilding industry is presently in, through
certain maladministrations of Governments
of the past.
I would like to say that shipbuilding is a
thing that is essential to the well-being of
Belfast as well as the linen. I agree that
linen is the staple industry, but I do not
think that in the past there has been so
much boasting about linen as there has been
by the Government in regard to the ocean
liners that sail the Atlantic. The people who
put these ocean liners on the Atlantic are
now very nearly forgotten. They can either
lie down and starve or commit suicide. I
would like the Minister of Labour to listen
as I believe he is partly interested in this.
I was rather surprised when the Prime
Minister said to the House that we were
going to curtail the building at Stormont.
Of course if they had taken our advice they
would have had no building there at all.
They would have taken the money and built
the homes that the people require.
The PRIME MINISTER: I think perhaps
I might correct the hon. Member. Members
must not go away with the impression that
we are erecting those buildings. That is
not so. Under the Act of 1920 the British
Government is pledged to supply Northern
Ireland with Parliamentary and administrative buildings. That is all found by
Great Britain and not out of the revenues
of Northern Ireland.
Mr. BEATTIE: Then I take it from the
correction of the Prime Minister that another
object has been found to which to put part
of the money that was going to be sent over
by the Imperial Parliament to build our
Parliament House. That being so I should
think that where the other part of that
money is going should be told to this House.
I do not believe that the Prime Minister or
his Cabinet went to London to submit to any
dictation or curtailment of their rights under
the Treaty in regard to the establishment of
Government buildings where the British Exchequer had to pay for them. If they did-well,
I am greatly surprised. I heard it stated not
very long ago in this House that any sort of
place would do for fifty-two gossipers to meet
to do the business of the Six Counties. I
would not go so far as to say that any sort
of place would do, because I am the kind of
chap who likes a decent place all the time-
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)—and if I were in
a position I would place all the working
classes in the highest position in the land,
because I believe they deserve it. I happened
to be speaking at an open-air meeting not
very long ago and I heard the remark passed
that the Government were a mutual admiration society. Whether that is correct or not
I will leave to the Government themselves.
Sometimes I think it is correct when I hear
this one getting up and admiring the other
for what his great speech was worth, while
it was worth nothing at the latter end to the
people most concerned.
Now, if the Prime Minister allows me, I
will give him some of Mr. Hill's opinions.
Mr. Hill as a working man, a riveter, who
has gone through the shipbuilding industry,
took upon himself to write to the Prime
Minister of England. At one time a working
man would nearly be put in gaol for daring
to do such a thing, but to-day, through the
efforts of the working classes and their
organisations, we are demanding equal consideration with the classes who control the
means of production. I am reading now from
the report, and if the Prime Minister wants
a copy I will give it to him, and when Mr.
Hill is speaking he is including Northern
Ireland in his figures because he is affected
in Northern Ireland as well. He says:-
"For the last five years we have had an
average of one-third of the men of the shipbuilding trade walking the streets in idle-

ness, and drawing unemployment benefit.

What do we find? We are told that the

What
do we find? In shipbuilding it takes four
tons of coal to make a ton of steel, and on
that coal there is a certain figure set aside
for idle drones to draw-anything ranging
from 3s. to 5s. a ton on coal for royalties. In
some cases it goes up the length of 7s. 9d. a
ton for royalties. There is a good way to
economise. The first thing to do is to cut
off all the drones that are on the material
for the shipbuilding industry, cut them off
completely, and allow them a few short
months to earn an honest living. That is one
way in which that gentleman could devote
his time to seeing what economies could be

inquire into the profits of the shipbuilders.
Although the industry is at a very low ebb
they are getting, in some cases, very decent
profits. Then we have watered capital in
shipbuilding, which I call another drone upon
the industry, and the sooner we awaken to
our own interests in this area and assist the
shipbuilding industry the better it will be
for all concerned in the Six Counties.
I leave that industry for the moment and

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Grant]
Coming back to the question of the Vote
of no confidence, I would like to congratulate
the Leader of the Opposition on the very
reasonable speech that he made here this
afternoon-a speech we have all heard many
times before. I must say that I agree with
some of the things he said. I am quite sure
that if some of us who are sitting on this
side of the House were on the Opposition
Benches we would make similar speeches,
because it is the duty of the Opposition to
make such speeches and to criticise the
Government. That is their job. I think the
Leader of the Opposition has done very well
this afternoon. I would be prepared to vote
with the Opposition on this Motion of no
confidence if they could assure me that by
doing so they would be able to find work for
the people, but I cannot see how this Motion
is going to provide employment for those who
are unemployed. On those grounds, therefore, I am bound to vote against this Motion.
Reading the Motion on the Order Paper,
I take it that this Vote of no confidence is
proposed because the Government has failed
to deal with the menace of unemployment,
and yet the Leader of the Opposition has
dragged in the name of the Member for
Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Elliott), and
says that he surely will vote with the Opposition because the South African farmers
arrived in Northern Ireland on a Sunday, and
because there was a parade of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary on a Sunday. I cannot
see what that has to do with the unemployment question. I hold very strong views
myself on the observance of Sunday, but I
do not think this will help us to solve the
problem of unemployment.
I think it was
altogether beside the point.
The Leader of the Opposition also mentioned
the findings of the different Royal Commissions that have sat from time to time,
and stated that the Government had failed
to put those findings into operation. We all
agree that Royal Commissions are very useful
bodies, and they are bound to bring in the
result of their investigations, but the Government is not bound to put their findings into
operation. I am absolutely certain that our
Prime Minister and his Cabinet would put
the findings in question into operation if they
had the money, but they have not got the
money and, therefore, they are not able to
give effect to the recommendations made. The
last speaker (Mr. Beattie) mentioned that the
Labour Party could solve the problem of
unemployment, but that, rather than satisfy

not do so. That is a very peculiar attitude
for a representative of the people to take up.
I entirely disagree with that attitude, and I
am absolutely certain that the hon. Member
who made that statement did not mean what
he said.

1898 the Government fixed a standard here
under which they would not contribute more
than half the county cess and poor rate.
The House will grasp what this really means
when I say that the rates are to-day three
times what they were in 1898. If a man paid
10s rates in that year it was standardised at
10s. The Government paid half and he paid
the other half. Since 1898 he has 30s to pay.
The Government pays half the first 10s, and
the man has to pay the other two sums of
10s each himself. It is an act of injustice
that the worker who owns his own house
has to pay this increased rate. He is already
contributing by his work and by stamping
his insurance card to this insurance fund,
and here is a special tax put upon him. In
the country every occupier of a labourer's
cottage has now to pay his rates. You would
put a tax upon him. You are already
putting that tax upon him because he has
to pay his rates, and it quite different from
the time the landlord or the farmer paid
them. We have in Coleraine Union 300
labourers' cottages. We have five unions in

The second is a little industry in my district that has been in existence for 200 years.
It employed 50 people. These people were
perfectly happy. They were living in comfort. They had probably more money to their
credit than the same number of people in
Belfast. They got turf in a neighbouring
bog. They had houses at a shilling a week.
They had a garden. They had advantages
that enabled them to educate their children
and live happy, comfortable lives far and
away superior to what is done in Belfast.
The trades' union organiser came round and
got them to join. He pictured a land of
Canaan flowing with milk and honey if they
would only subscribe to his union. They did
it. The result was they got one fortnight's
pay and then the bleach green closed. Now
the bleach green was running at a very small
profit. It was old-200 years old. It was not
up to modern conditions-I mean in the
shape of machinery, but it was carrying on
probably with advantage, until this Labour
organiser, not knowing these things-because
I do not imagine for a moment that any
man on that side of the House, or in this
House at all would take upon himself knowingly to injure even a family, let alone a
whole district. But I should like them to
remember that "evil is wrought by want of
thought as well as want of heart." For two
years these people were supporting themselves on unemployment benefit. Now I see
some of them working as surfacemen on the
roads, the last stage to which a working man
is deposed-working on the roads. The place
is closed and will be closed for all time as
far as that industry is concerned.
I want to take the example of the Lough
Swilly Railway, that is the railway running
from Derry to Carndonagh. I have been over
that line.

If you know anything at all about industry

machine method of production has gradually

It has gone through various forms.
evolution of industry still goes on. We have

The problem that awaits solution is the
problem of distribution, and you are not
tackling the problem of distribution at all.
I have stood in one of the main arteries in
Northern Ireland-near Groomsport-and it
was scarcely possible for my daughter to go
on the road in case she should be killed by
some of the motor-cars going through. I
can stand and watch the Daimlers and Rolls-
Royces and other makes of cars on the roads,
Sunday after Sunday. Apart altogether from
the question of violating the Sabbath-I am
not concerned with that at the moment-but
I can watch thousands of cars on the main
roads and I see no indications of poverty. I
may walk up to a house in Donegall Place
and see fur coats priced at 30 guineas and
50 guineas. These coats are not kept for
show purposes. Someone is able to purchase
them.
In order to try to solve the problem we have
got to have more equitable distribution of the
wealth produced at the present time, and if
we had, although it may not be an entirely
satisfactory state of affairs, I honestly believe
we would be able to provide a decent standard
of existence for every member of the community. I do suggest that if the wealth that is
exhausted on society at the moment was more
equitably distributed we would have less of
the extreme poverty that we have got at present. A lot of idle talk has been indulged

That is a serious position. We

so far as Great Britain is concerned. But I

The point I want to make is this, that your
system of society is entirely breaking down.
Countries that have been backward up till
the present century are being industrially
developed. Those peoples are now taking
their places, and are capturing a certain
portion of the world's market and of international trade, and we are never likely to
occupy the pre-eminent position that We
formerly did. It will probably be necessary
for us to concentrate much more attention on
the immediate development of the home
market to satisfy the needs and requirements
of our people, giving our people a higher purchasing power. We would probably find, if
that was started in one or two industries,
that the greater purchasing power of the
people would give a great fillip to industry,
and would take you some distance towards a
solution of the problems which appear to be
very vexatious at the moment, and which are
baffling the Government, for the reason that
the Government have made no attempt to
grapple with those problems in a scientific
fashion, and are simply resting on their oars,
hoping that the time is coming when trade is
going to revive. From that point of view
the Government deserve an exceptionally
severe censure, because they are penalising
some 60,000 people in Northern Ireland with
poverty and starvation.
If you are keen about the problem, if you
are serious about the problem, you should
have regard and give consideration to the
people who are suffering so much, and see
what is standing between them and the decent
livelihood that they might get, even with the
production of the present time, speaking
generally, of the two countries. If the
Government want to attempt to solve the
problem they have got to look at it in a big
way, and they have got to realise that
remedies that would have suited the last industrial depression will not suit this one,
because we have an industrial depression now
that is absolutely unparalleled in the history

I have also had the pleasure on behalf of

and that, it is estimated, will cost a sum of

As regards housing, I would like to say
that under our relief schemes 1,170 houses
have been built, and ex-servicemen's houses
to the number of 867 built or sanctioned.
Under our Housing Acts administered by the
Home Office 1,905 houses have been put in
hand by local authorities and 3,215 by private
builders with the assistance of the Government subsidy. Labourers' cottages are being
built in our country districts to the number
of 1,500; making 8,675 houses in all. I do not
think hon. Members, no matter how critical
they may be, can say the Government have
done nothing in this respect either.
The PRIME MINISTER: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: Again, the Ministry of
Home Affairs have sanctioned loans to local

quarter millions for the execution of works
of various kinds, very largely for the purpose of creating employment.
As regards roads, which have also been
referred to, I would point out that from the
Road Fund the Government have contributed
since December, 1921, £807,038. For firstclass roads the Ministry of Home Affairs
and the Ministry of Labour are jointly giving
for improvement purposes no less a sum
than 72 per cent. of the total cost, and for

51 per cent. of the total cost. Again, for
maintenance grants the Ministry of Home
Affairs have increased the grant formerly
given from 50 per cent. to 60 per cent, on firstclass roads, and on second-class roads from
25 per cent. to 30 per cent., and for the first
time they are giving a grant of 15 per cent.
in connection with third-class roads which
are used to a considerable extent for motor
traffic. I think, therefore, the Government
have been doing what is possible in order to
help our local authorities to make our roads
suitable for the traffic which they are now
called upon to bear, and that in this respect
also we have not neglected our duty either
to the unemployed or to the general public.

Motion made and Question proposed:

between the Governments of Great Britain,
the Irish Free State and Northern Ireland.
The PRIME MINISTER: For the convenience of the House and also in order to
have a record in the Reports of our Debates
I think it would be well if I read the

"Agreement amending and supplementing
the Articles of Agreement for a Treaty between Great Britain and Ireland, to which
the force of law was given by the Irish Free
State Agreement Act and by the Constitution of the Irish Free State Act, 1922.
"Whereas, on 6th December, 1921, Articles
of Agreement for a Treaty between Great
Britain and Ireland were entered into;

of law by the Irish Free State (Agreement)

respective peoples, make it desirable to

of Northern Ireland for the purposes of

of the said articles of agreement shall be

mentioned.

1 rise with feelings of deep thankfulness and
relief to move the Resolution that stands in
my name, and in doing so I wish earnestly
to impress upon the whole people of Ulster
that in connection with the Agreement that
has been arrived at I have no desire whatever
to stand in any special limelight or to be
made a great deal of. The truth of the
the
matter is that the credit SO far as
Northern Government is concerned
having carried through this Agreement rests
upon my colleagues in the Cabinet, the Members of the Government, the Members of this
and the other House, and the people of
Ulster generally. Had it not been for the
spade work of my colleagues and of our
representatives in the Imperial Parliament
I doubt very much if a final Agreement
should have been reached. They are entitled
to, and I am confident will receive in all
quarters, the praise that is due to men who
have stuck to their colours, who have clung
on to the old traditions, and who have
allowed us this day to lay our signatures, or
at least to signify by our votes that we have
accomplished what we set out to do. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
I must express the hope at this early stage
that as the first step has been taken by the
British Government in passing through
the necessary legislation with the maximum of
and

the minimum
of opposition--in fact none at allthis House will equally unanimously agree
to these terms, which I confidently believe
will start a new era not only in Ulster and
in the Free State, not only in the whole of
Ireland, but in the whole world where Irish
affairs have been so troublesome in past
generations. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I must apologise to the House if I am
naturally cautious in the language that I use
to-day, because everyone will agree that the
least said on these occasions is sometimes
soonest mended. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) and that injudicious statements or
remarks that may be construed differently to
what they are intended may, even at the last
moment, cause difficulty if not here in
Ulster in other parts of Ireland. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
From the beginning of the Boundary
controversy the Cabinet, the Government,
and the people of Ulster have been absolutely
united on a policy which to-day is being
consecrated by the Agreement which I have
just read to the House. It is a policy which.
was pressed upon the various British Gevernments and upon representatives of Southern
Ireland from time to time. On the 21st

At that time I impressed upon
Collins the fact that there never could be a
really harmonious working between the two
areas unless the Governments were placed
upon an equality regarding all services, and
that the statesmanlike policy was for the
executives to meet and, having equal powers
and an equal say in the affairs involved,

The British Government have already

When legislative effect has been given to the
instrument and when feeling has died down,
I believe that a new era will be opened in
Irish history-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)—–
and that there is a possibility that not
only may useful consultations take place
between individual Ministers, but by meetings of the Executive much may be accomplished to smooth over those small but
irritating difficulties that are bound to arise
from time to time between two neighbouring
States. If, as I believe, cordial relations
have been established, there are many points
which could be amicably arranged, such, for
instance, as easing the present Customs
Barrier Regulations; promoting a mutual,
more humane method of handling and
exporting live stock to Great Britain, combining to produce the evidence in our joint
possession that the country is absolutely
free from Foot and Mouth Disease, and thus
convincing our largest markets that they
need have no fear in accepting our cattle;
and further, in regard to the development of
our fisheries, in which connection I feel that
much more could be done to secure a market
in the great centres across the channel.
Further, I hope that the effect of all this
will be to open up a great business between
North and South, that we will be able to
take more freely of the products which they
can supply, and that, on the other hand, our
wholesale merchants will re-establish their
old business with the Free State to the
mutual advantage of both peoples. There is
no question but that for certain counties of
the Free State, Belfast, Derry, Enniskillen,
and Strabane are the natural distributing
centres, and the terms upon which business
is carried out undoubtedly tend to lower the
cost of living by those who purchase from
firms long accustomed to the practice of
trading in every part of Ireland. Other
matters doubtless will arise from time to
time. I have only adumbrated a few that
have occurred to me as being possible of
friendly settlement, and that friendly settlement could not come too soon to ease many
of those rough corners which at present do
aggravate people on both sides of the
Border.
During the negotiations Mr. Baldwin asked
me would it be possible, as an act of grace,
to deal leniently with our prisoners, and in

benefit of all, I agreed-
"that the cases of prisoners convicted in
Northern Ireland in respect of offences
during the period of disturbance shall be
reviewed by the British Government, whose
decision in each case shall be accepted by
the Government of Northern Ireland."
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) May I take it

The PRIME MINISTER: I now pass to
another subject. If, as everyone in Northern
Ireland earnestly hopes, peace is assured, it
necessarily follows that we would no longer
be justified in continuing to undertake, in its
entirety, the heavy financial burden of maintaining those gallant forces, which for now
almost six years have proved a rock of
strength to our native Province.
I have always maintained that the Cabinet
must be the judge as to when the Special
Constabulary should be disbanded. I regret
that the time has now come when financial
considerations have forced upon us an unpleasant decision. For several years the
British Government have recognised the
special claims of Ulster and have generously
given us grants each year to assist us in
defraying the cost of our Special Constabulary.
During each of these years we have had to
contribute from our own funds part of the
cost, but the expense of keeping on the A's "
and "C1's" out of our own money would
impose an overwhelming burden upon our
finances, and would either paralyse our other
activities or place such an accumulation of
debt upon our shoulders as would lead inevitably to bankruptcy. When I explain that the
cost of the Specials for the past five years
has amounted to the total sum of £7,426,000,

To me personally it is a matter of unspeakable regret to have to part with these men,
who from the earliest days of their formation
and during the dark periods of 1922 and 1923
never faltered in their devotion to duty and
never hesitated to face danger. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). The people of Ulster will
retain in their memories an undying gratitude
to these men who did so much to save our
Province in the hour of trial. I hesitate to
think what would have been the fate of Ulster
without these gallant men.
You will have observed by this morning's
Press that Mr. Winston Churchill referred
to the grant-in-aid of £1,200,000 towards winding up the Force and liquidating the very
heavy liabilities which we have incurred
since the 1st April last. I would like to explain how this figure was arrived at: I was
most anxious to retain the whole force till
the 30th September, 1926, which would have
involved a sum of £2,225,000. Towards this
sum the Chancellor of the Exchequer stated
that he could only contribute £500,000.
Negotiations on the subject were continued
for over a fortnight, and it was only on the
eve of the general Agreement being signed
that he consented to the larger figure of
£1,200,000, and, as a compromise, I, for my
part, consented to a more speedy demobilisation of the Force. In addition to this our
responsibility for equipment and stores to
the amount of £700,000 has been generously
waived. There will, still, however, be a considerable expenditure to be borne out of
Northern Ireland funds.
I should like to stress the point that this
is the last grant, unfortunately, we are to
receive from the Imperial Government.
Every penny of expenditure, therefore, over
and above this grant, must be defrayed out
of our own funds, and, with the already
great strain imposed upon our own Exchequer by the heavy deficit in the Unemployment Fund, to which I will refer later, hon.
Members will appreciate that generosity must
be measured by the means at our disposal.
No one would be foolish enough to disband
the whole of the Special Constabulary in one
day--even if such a course were desirable it
would be physically impossible-but, of
course, we must make a beginning at once.
We have throughout their period of service
paid each member of the "A" force a bounty
I regret that disbandment should be forced
upon us at a period of severe trade depression, but I feel sure that employers in Ulster
will recognise their moral responsibilities towards these gallant men who have protected
the trade of Ulster and have enabled them
to carry on their business by giving them
a preference and absorb them into civil employment on the termination of their engagement.
Doubtless some members of the Force may
desire to take up new occupation in the
Overseas Dominions, and I am in consultation with my colleagues as to the best way
in which I can be of assistance in this
respect.
I now come to the B's, which the House is
aware is to all intents a voluntary Force.
We have publicly, in season and out of
season, testified to the great services which
our B's have rendered to the Province.
Night after night they have patrolled the
roads and guarded the lives and liberties of
our people without regard to class or creed.
While we have not yet perfected our plans, a
scheme will be speedily devised for the retention of this branch of the Constabulary
in a modified form and at a cost which will
be within our own resources. There will be
less work for them to do, and we will not
have to call upon them to devote so much of
their time in future to police duties. In the
opinion of the Government it would be unwise to disband this Force, as it will in the
new circumstances be the only Force upon
which we can rely to support the permanent
Constabulary.
And now I come to a question, mentioned

have maintained silence since last July regarding the agreement that Mr. Churchill
referred to, by which the British Government have arranged to bear-I will not say
a satisfactory share-because I am very hard
to satisfy, but at all events a generous share
