HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. McGuffin]
I regret we are not able at the present
time to congratulate the Minister of Labour
(Mr. Andrews) on the improved condition of
trade. That is really the outstanding feature
in connection with the matter of dissolution
at the present moment. But we cannot
hasten that. They have exactly the same
difficulty to contend with across the water.
They have one and a quarter millions of
people out of employment there, and they
find the question is more than they are capable of dealing with. Even experts admit
that the solution is not apparent to them.
Here in this area we have 45,000 unemployed.
It is very regrettable. We have seen the
figure much lower, and we hope to see it
much lower in the near future. The people
would be well advised to remember that the
Government have assisted local authorities
so as to enable them to expend £3,000,000
on works and give employment to those who
would otherwise be unemployed. They have
also secured the employment of 17,000 people
in situations, and have contributed to the
Insurance Fund in support of the people to
the tune of £4,600,000. I would ask the
House how the industrialists of this city and
in the Six Counties would have fared if such
provision had not been made. Does it not
redound to the credit of the Government
that by their foresight they were enabled to
provide the ways and means by which these
people have become employed?
There is one thing on which I can congratulate the Government and that is on
having solved the difficulty associated with
the education question. It was a very
serious difficulty. After all the difference between one party and the other was of a
trifling character. I think it only amounted
to an ambiguity in the way two clauses were
phrased, one clause in particular at any
rate. I am glad a solution has been effected.
I took up a particular attitude with regard
to the discussion on this question. Although
I have adopted the attitude of a secularist
with regard to education I may say that I
am not opposed to an absolutely essential
arrangement being made with respect to the
provision of religious education in schools.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). It is not ourselves we are here to please; it is the people,
and the voice and mandate of the people
must be observed and recognised. They have
given expression to their opinion with no uncertain sound, and the Government have
been wise in effecting a solution of this
matter. I feel we can go forward to the
electors at the present time with confidence.
We as a Parliament have discharged our
duty not only with regard to political
matters generally but with regard to the
industrial interests of all concerned. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
I congratulate the Prime Minister upon the
degree of success he has achieved during the
four years and stormy years, too-through
which he has led this Parliament. His name
will be handed down to history as one of
the most successful Prime Ministers ever
connected with the affairs of any Parliament. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). He has
led us through crucial times in a wise way.
I am sure it is a matter of regret to some
of us that the Session has been abruptly
brought to a close. There were one or two
items with respect to which we were forecasting legislation, but we cannot order
these things otherwise now. I am quite
satisfied with what has been done.
I am
very sorry to think that this is the shortest
Session on record in connection with any
Parliament-introduced and almost dissolved on the same day.
Mr. COOPER: I would not like this occasion to pass without joining in the references to the death of my colleague, Mr.
William Coote. I remember four years ago
when we were going forward for election how
faithful Mr. Coote was to all his colleagues.
And after he came to this House he was
always the same. Sometimes, perhaps, I did
not agree with him, but his heart was
always in the right place so far as Ulster
was concerned. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
I would like on this occasion also to thank
the Prime Minister for the promise he has
given us that immediately Parliament
reassembles he will introduce a Drainage
Bill.
In my county, as most people know,
there is a tremendous amount of water, and
although my hon. Friend from Londonderry
(Sir Robert Anderson) is very fond of it we
want to get rid of the whole lot of it.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: It is not my
fault it is not dry.
Mr. COOPER: I may say that the lands
of a number of the most loyal supporters of
this Government have been flooded during
the greater part of last year I, myself, unfortunately have a farm on which I could
not walk without going down. That is
caused by several rivers being SO flooded
owing to the wet season that they are overflowing the whole country. The cry of the
farmers in all directions is for a drainage
scheme, and I am glad that we are going to
get it.
I would also like to congratulate the Prime
Minister and the Minister of Home Affairs
on the way they have re-established law and
order along the Border. Four years ago
when we started off on our election campaign
we did so under very trying conditions.
Every minute we heard that somebody had
been shot somewhere and every minute we

heard of another outrage along the Border.
But now, and for a considerable time past,
Ithe whole Border has been in a state of
absolute peace, and I think the people should

Imperial Parliament. The farmers
Northern Ireland have been very hard hit
in this respect. They have waited twenty
years for a Land Purchase Bill, and owing
to land purchase being one of the reserved
services, we in this House had very little
power to bring it to the attention of the
Imperial Parliament. Now, through the
good work put in by our Prime Minister, he
has at last succeeded in getting this Bill
almost placed on the Statute Book.
Some differences of opinion arose and
many debates took place on different platforms throughout the country. Undoubtedly the farmers who had waited
longest had suffered most, and many had
bitter feelings in regard to the delay.
Several questions were debated and no
solution seemed likely to be found, but at
last the farmers and landlords had an interview with the Prime Minister at Stormont,
and they went away good friends with all
their disputes settled. I cannot speak too
highly of the action the Prime Minister
took on that occasion in bringing us
together. I feel the farmers of Northern
Ireland are satisfied with the work
the Prime Minister has done on
their behalf. I feel confident he will be
back as our Prime Minister, and I look
forward with satisfaction to seeing the good
work that has been carried on during the
past four years carried on in the next Parliament under the supervision of the present
Government and our Prime Minister.
Mr. DONALD: As the debate will close
to-day, I will not detain the House very long,
but I think it is right that when one wants
to say anything he should embrace the opportunity that affords itself to him. I would
join in the chorus of approbation from all

Members I would like to refer to one point
raised by the seconder (Mr. Lavery), in regard to rent restrictions. I entirely disagree with the way in which he put it. He
said the restrictions should be wiped
out.
I do not agree with that
The only solution, if there is
a solution to this all-important questionthe Prime Minister said quite truly it was
a question that was not so easily solvedis to build more houses and to build them
cheaply. I would like to see more speedingup with regard to building, in order to
relieve distress and to relieve the strain on
the minds of the people with regard to the
high cost of the houses which are being
built at present. That, to my mind, is the
only solution, and as to the Rent Restriction
Act, we will be compelled to legislate on
lines parallel to the Imperial Government,
that is, not to remove the restrictions, but to
go easy.
I agree with the Prime Minister on the
point my hon. Friend who spoke last (Mr.
Mark) dealt with, that is the question of the
one-house owner. To my mind a very great
hardship is inflicted on those people. Many
people earned good wages during the war
and saved some money. They purchased
houses, but they naturally did so on the
understanding that legislation would
be brought in to relieve them and
that they would become the occupiers.
Owing to the way the matter has been
adjourned from time to time, the one-house
holder has not been able up to the present
time to become the occupier. If the Prime
Minister is returned to power, as I know he
will be, I think he will be doing the right
thing if he will at all events modify that
clause, so that these people may become the
occupiers, and thus be relieved of very
great hardships.
My hon. Friend said something with regard
to debt. We are not in debt. The imperial
authorities were just under the same liabilities as we were with regard to Unemployment Insurance. Ever since legislation was
introduced with regard to Unemployment
Insurance, it has been affected by the
state of the trade of the country. If the
money paid out to the unemployed overbalanced the income, there was nothing
left for the Government but to borrow
money in order to meet the demands of the
unemployed for the period, and when the
time came that the workers got into employ
ment again the money was paid back and the
loan was paid off. We are in the unfortunate position that we have not yet arrived
at that period when we are able to pay off
our loan, but I agree with the measures the
Government are adopting, I do not believe
it is right or proper for us to be cut off as
a small area, depending on two or three

You passed a Bill here in 1923, giving a

from the Government and £40 from the

Then it has been said that the production is
not what it should be. I agree, but if
those people would just look at the economic
side and say, "We are prepared to do
without this subsidy," it would make a
wonderful difference. This is a national
question, and I wish to point out that the
buyer of the house is deprived of even a
solitary farthing out of the £100. The man
who builds the house gets the £100, but the
person who buys the house gets nothing.
That is an injustice to the buyer in my
judgment.

judgment that is one of the most important

again that I do not think it is a right thing

are able to subsidise the house

What is the position to-day? The shipbuilding trades are unsheltered trades. The
sheltered trades are in receipt of very much
higher wages than the unsheltered trades, and
the unsheltered trades are clamouring now for
an increase of 18/- or £1 a week. Instead
of giving 18/- a week for nothing, could our
Government not go to the shipbuilder and
give him a subsidy to the extent that it is

Insurance? Offer the shipbuilder 18/- a
week to be added to the wages of
every man that is employed, and in my
judgment you will see a revival of trade
throughout the country. Naturally the
reply is, "Oh, that is too big a question,"
but we will have to get away from our old
ideas, for we are living in an entirely new
world. The war has altered the whole condition of things, and we are confronted
with a state of affairs entirely without
parallel in the history of the Province. I
regret to state that the shipbuilding outlook is not as bright as it was this time
last year.
The outlook is gloomy.
We
got an order the other day, but it would

this revival to be brought about?
It is a
world-wide question. We have probably

I offer this solution to our Government

nothing they should try the solution I am

there work longer hours, probably for

problem of unemployment at home, and it
will not be solved until you attempt something on the lines I have suggested here.
The most deplorable effect of all is that
young fellows are leaving school without
any prospects of getting into industries, in

I congratulate the Prime Minister on the

strange about what has been done. We
have heard of complaints across the water
that they have had four elections within
five years. Our Government has been going

am prepared, and I am going to offer myself to my constituency. Believe me, if

THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): The net amount of this Estimate is
£2,000, and the items which go to make it
up are two in number, viz., (1) Travelling,
Subsistence and Removal Expenses, and (2)
Agency Services. As regards the first, the
Committee will be aware that the Colwyn
Committee has been sitting throughout the
past year. In point of fact, the number and
duration of the meetings of this Committee
have proved greater than was originally anticipated, with the result that an excess
travelling and subsistence expenditure has
been incurred by officials of the Ministry to
the extent of about £200. The excess sum of
£300 for Removal Expenses of officers appointed to the Ministry of Finance has been
incurred in respect of officers who have been
in the Ministry of Finance for some years
but who, owing to difficulties in the way of
obtaining housing accommodation, had not
been able to arrange for the removal of their
household effects at an earlier date.
As regards the gross item of £2,800 required
for payment to Imperial Departments for
services performed as agent of this Ministry,
an explanation is already given on the face
of this Estimate. That is to say, on the
original estimate we had to depend on figures
provided by the Imperial Treasury. They
have revised this estimate with the result
that the charge to us has been increased to
the figure here. Savings, however, are likely
to be available to the extent of £1,300 on the
Salaries subhead, with the result that the
House is only asked to vote a net sum of
£2,000.
Colonel WOODS. I would like to ask if
the £300 for removal expenses would not

here?

to officers who had been transferred to the

effects to Belfast.

Mr. BARBOUR: I would like notice of

Estimate is £12,050 which is made up of the

works services carried out on behalf of
specific Departments, and this is offset by an
equivalent credit drawn from the appropriate departmental votes, thereby leaving
the net total of the Vote unaffected.
I propose to deal first of all with the
items which go to make up the sum of
£12,050. The largest item is the sum provided under Subhead EE for the purchase of

is in part settlement of a heavy claim for
malicious injuries for premises in May
Street which were forcibly entered and
partially destroyed by gunmen during the
disturbances in 1921-22.
I may say the
claim for reconditioning was of such a
serious character that the Government decided to buy out the property as the most
economical method of procedure and at the
same time to remove this very objectionable
slum area in the City of Belfast.
The second item of £1,500. under Subhead
FF is required to meet the cost of insuring
Government property. The estimate of

The Estimate is prepared in a form similar
to that of the Estimate for last year, save
that certain items have been reclassified
to other subheads where it is considered
they are more properly shown. The net
total, I am glad to say, is less by £7,763
than the 1923-24 provision. This reduction
has been made possible chiefly by the disappearance under Subhead A of the provision for the payment of the Assistant
Recorder in Belfast consequent upon the
completion of work arising out of claims
for compensation under the Criminal Injuries Acts and also by a reduction of two
in the number of Resident Magistrates to
be provided for. The other large item which
now disappears is the grant in aid of the
Bar Council of Northern Ireland, which
was given as a non-recurrent grant.
Other variations in the Estimate which
are worthy of mention will be found under
the heading of "Remuneration to Registrars"
which is reduced consequent upon the completion of the compensation work by the
Assistant Recorder; while under Subhead E,
Law Reporting, the sum of £150 provided
is the normal annual grant in aid. Last
year's provision of £300 was in respect of a
two years period. Owing to the shortness of
the present Session it will not be found
practicable to re-introduce the Bill which
was not proceeded with last Session, but
I am satisfied that any future Government
will regard the measure as so eminently
equitable that the failure to reintroduce the
Bill only means a postponement. I beg
to move.
Question put and agreed to.

Supplementary Estimates. 56

are deposited from time to time in the

Record Office was opened in 1923, records

material.

receipts from the fees which are charged for

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The necessity for the present
supplementary estimate of £350 which is reduced to £10 by savings which will be
affected by this Vote has arisen from the
decision of the Government after consultation with the Tuberculosis Committee of
the Belfast Corporation to send a deputation of experts to the Continent to
specially investigate certain new systems that
are in vogue there. Hon. Members are aware
that the Government at the present time contribute very considerable sums from time to
time annually to the local authorities to help
them in combating this terrible disease.
While the Government is not satisfied with
the progress that has been made at the same
time they think a great deal of good might
be done by sending these experts over to the
Continent to study certain of these systems
of treatment. One particular treatment
that has attracted much discussion
these
in the Press is the Dr. Spahlinger
treatment, and another is the new "Gold"
treatment. This committee of experts, who
include Dr. Houston, one of the best experts
on the subject, intend to visit
laboratories, and while it is impossible to
say what the result will be it is hoped that
their report will be extremely helpful. I
beg to move.

EDUCATIONAL SERVICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£10 be granted to His Majesty for the
service of the year ending 31st March, 1925,
to provide for Educational Services, including Grants in Aid of the Teachers' Pension
Fund, Northern Ireland."
Mr. McKEOWN: The circumstances in
which the House is now being asked to
sanction the payment of non-recurrent grants
toward the salaries of teachers employed in
technical schools are briefly set forth in
the explanatory note appended to the Supplementary Estimate, but it is perhaps desirable that I should make a somewhat fuller
statement on the subject.
As hon. Members are aware, new Regu
lations dealing with the recognition, employment and payment of teachers of technical schools, under which it is proposed
that certain scales of salary shall have
retrospective effect from 1st August, 1923, in
the case of all existing full time teachers,
were laid before Parliament in the Autumn
Session and at the beginning of the present
Session. These Regulations-which, I may
say, were framed by the Ministry of Education after careful consideration of the
recommendations of a Departmental Committee appointed by the Minister to report
on the subject-prescribe minimum scales
of salaries for all full time teachers, the
basic portion of each salary to be paid by
the Committee or Manager and the incremental portion by the Ministry. They also
prescribe minimum rates of remuneration for
part-time teachers, who will be paid entirely out of the funds at the disposal of
the Committees and Managers.
The operation of these new Regulations
will place a considerable burden on the
financial resources of the Committees and
Managers. The new basic salaries which
they will be required to pay to the teachers
will, in most cases, be substantially greater
than the salaries which they have had to
pay in the past, and, as the scales will
have retrospective effect from 1st August,
1923, they will have to pay to existing
teachers any arrears of basic salary which
may have accumulated from that date. Some
Committees and Managers will be in the
fortunate position of having sufficient funds
at their disposal to enable them to pay these
arrears, and in their cases no difficulty arises.
Others, however, will be less fortunately
circumstanced, and will have insufficient
funds or none at all, and in these cases
the Ministry and the Government have decided that it is necessary that assistance
shall be given from Parliamentary funds
to such extent as will enable the Committees and Managers to meet the financial obligations imposed upon them in the current
financial year by the new regulations.
desire to emphasise the point that a payment from the Special Grant now before the
House will be made only where the Ministry is satisfied that the total funds at
the disposal of the Committee or Manager
are insufficient to meet the financial obligations referred to, and that the payment
will be strictly limited to the sum required
to discharge these obligations.
Certain

committees have funds which
have accumulated from local rates contrihuted specially for the purpose of erecting
technical schools, but it is not proposed to
take such funds into account when determining whether or not the Committee is in
need of assistance from the special grant.
It is estimated that these special grants
will amount to the sum of £6,000. There
will, however, be savings available sufficient
to cover this expenditure, and, consequently,
the net sum which the House is now being
asked to vote is only the token figure of £10.
I feel sure from the questions asked from
time to time by hon. Members that they
will be only too pleased to sanction this
Vote. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.

ESTIMATES, 1925-1926.
VOTE ON ACCOUNT.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £1,766,000 be
granted to His Majesty, on account, for or
towards defraying the charges of the several
services for which a Vote on Account is required, for the year ending the 31st March,
1926."
Mr. POLLOCK: This is the fourth
annual occasion on which a Vote of this
kind has been submitted to the Committee.
Hon. Members may therefore be assumed to
be familiar with its objects. In the earlier
years of our Parliamentary procedure it was
my practice to enter at some length into the
various features of the principal services on
account of which this Vote is asked. The
object of this elaboration was to give the
fullest possible explanation of the circumstances of the different important services at
the moment. I do not, however, regard this
as necessary at present, as hon. Members I
assume are quite as well able to understand
its object as I am myself.
Shortly, all the balances of money in the
hands of the Departments must be handed
into the Exchequer at the end of the
financial year, and, therefore, in order to
provide for the continuity and payment of
the different services of the State it will be
necessary for the Committee to vote such
sums as will accomplish this purpose. Later
examination of course of all the Estimates
when they are submitted will enable hon.
Members either to commend or criticise the
different charges as they may think best at
the time.
It will be observed from the slips which
are in the hands of hon. Members that the
total estimate for the coming year is lower
by the sum of about £800,000 than that of the
present year. This reduction, however, is
largely explained by the fact that a sum of
£500,000 for criminal injuries will disappear.
This money, as hon. Members know, was distributed to the public authorities to assist
them in claims for malicious injuries. I
should also note that there is a drop of about
£275,000 in the provision for the Special Constabulary. This of course hon. Members will
understand is a conjectural amount as it is
impossible at this moment to foresee what the
necessities may be.
It will also be observed that the grants to
local authorities have increased by £120,000,
but this is explained by the fact that the
total includes an amount of £128,000 for an
agricultural grant, which will be made this
year.
Taking the services as a whole, the estiuated cost of each does not materially differ
from that of the previous year. The principal item on the sheet is the Education
Vote of £1,900,000. This does not greatly
differ from that of last year, but is a
very heavy drain on the resources of the
Province. I reckon that £250,000 of this
sum will have to be provided out of our
Land Purchase Annuities, as the Imperial
Government consider that the State should
not be expected to bear such a heavy charge
in respect of this service. I do not think
there is any other amount in the Vote that
calls for special comment, and, therefore,
I beg to move.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: The Minister of
Finance mentioned that any unexpended
balances are handed back at the end of the
year. I would like to ask him whether there
is not a practice in some Departments of
making savings on one branch and spending
them on another when Parliament has voted
the money distinctly for a certain branch,
and whether this is a matter that will have
his attention.
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not think it would
be regular that that course should be followed. It is not only very desirable, but,
as the Comptroller and Auditor-General has
a survey of all this expenditure, it is very
necessary that moneys voted by Parliament
for a specific object should be expended
upon that object.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I have been reading
his report for the year 1924, and I see he has
been dealing with that very question.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolution to be reported To-morrow.
Committee to sit again To-morrow.

Loans Guarantee Acts.
Loans Guarantee (Money).
Motion made, and Question proposed:

Guarantee Acts (Northern Ireland), 1922-24
(1) By increasing from £5,000,000 to
£6,000,000 the limit on the aggregate capital
amount of the loans in respect of which
guarantees under those Acts may be given;
and
(2) By extending by one year the period
within such guarantees may be given."
Mr. BARBOUR: This resolution is, of
course, merely a preliminary to the Bill,
but as it is in effect the Bill itself it will
be more convenient if any short statement
which I may have to make is made at this
stage. The policy which this Resolution recommends is the extension of the limit of the
amount of the guarantees which may be
given under the Loans Guarantee Acts
from £5,000,000 to £6,000,000, and of the
period during which such guarantees may
be given by one year. The position at the
present time is that guarantees have been
given amounting to £4,590,500, leaving
available a balance of £409,500. The
additional amount for which Parliamentary
approval is now sought will make available
for issue in the period ending 31st March,
1926, guarantees amounting to an aggregate
sum of £1,409,500.
I need not repeat what these facilities
consist of, nor need I remind you that this
machinery has proved a valuable agent in
the alleviation of unemployment in our
great shipbuilding industry. I am sorry to
say, however, that that industry is still
going through difficult times, and the
Government are of opinion that the time
has not yet arrived when these facilities
should be withdrawn.
Members will be aware that considerable
discussion has taken place in the Imperial
Parliament regarding trade facilities for
shipbuilding, and that the conditions prevailing during their tenure of office made
it necessary for the late Government to
discourage the granting of guarantees to
this industry. I am glad to see from recent
announcements that this embargo on trade
facilities for shipbuilding has been removed,
and that, accordingly, we may expect the
ready co-operation of the British Trade
Facilities Committee in connection with
future shipbuilding undertakings
affect our own ship yards.
which
The Committee will be aware of the very
material benefits which are afforded, both
by the State and municipalities in competing
countries, and it is, I think, quite sound
that we should use our State credit to
countervail these advantages if by so doing
we can prevent business being lost to this
country.
Mr. McGUFFIN: On a former occasion,
when a Motion of this kind was under discussion by the House, I thought it pertinent
to suggest to the Minister that some sympathy should be extended to industries which,
if assisted, might increase employment in
the city. I think the difficulty that confronted the Minister of Finance under the

several struggling firms of good reputation,
the proprietors of which have assured me
that they would be prepared to employ
thirty or forty extra hands if they could
only get a little guarantee from the Government, so as to enable them to tide over a
difficult time. They have abundance of
orders, but they have not the facilities without a guarantee, and they are limited in the

handicap. I quite realise that the guarantees have stimulated business in the Island,
and we are thankful for it, but we would
be glad to see the scheme further developed. For my part, I would not be prepared
to oppose a motion to extend the facilities
given in this connection.
I see that the Imperial Parliament is raising the amount available from £60,000,000 to

the benefit of the scheme on the other side
of the water. There is one particular in

of which assure me that a guarantee would

in the city. That would be on the capital
account. It would be for the adding of
machinery in order to meet the demands
that are made upon them at the present
time. They cannot cope with the demands,

very important one. I do not say that I

who could take advantage of a Government guarantee in a very profitable way,
and employ a greater number of hands than
they are able to employ at the present time.
This matter has been put to me on several
occasions by men who would be facilitated

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: This is one of
the most serious Votes that this House could
possibly give. We voted last year, I think, a
similar sum of £750,000 and I would like to
know if that money has already been used
up, or what part of it has been used up.
Mr. ANDREWS: As to the direct question
asked I am glad to be able to give the information which my hon. Friend desires.
It will be used up about the middle of April
of this year, that is, right at the beginning
of the new financial year, and this Vote is

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I am obliged
to the Minister for his reply. That means
that we will have borrowed by the first of
April about £2,750,000 roughly, and, as far
as the outlook is concerned, we have got
to borrow another £750,000 which is going to
be exhausted by the first of November next,
unless some extraordinary thing happens in
the meantime in the way of increased prosperity in the Northern area. The burden
is a very heavy one that we are called upon
to bear.. As far as I am concerned I have
reluctantly come to the conclusion that
whether we have an increase of prosperity
or not the area that we have control over
is not capable of paying the amount that is
necessary in order to keep us on a level with
Great Britain. And our people here will not
be prepared to submit to have their
allowance cut down in one of the ways it
must be cut down unless my right hon.
Friend can get a favourable settlement on the
other side. The working people here will not
submit to a lower standard of living than
what their comrades have in Great Britain,
and they certainly will not submit to a lower
out-of-work allowances than what their
comrades will have on the other side. I
think that is a principle which my right
hon. Friend has pressed for all he is worth
with the Imperial Treasury. This is not a
case where the Northern Government is
begging or looking for charity. I do not
look on it in that light at all. They are
only asking for fair play and justice in connection with this fund. We took over unwillingly the responsibilities of Government
here, and the authorities on the other side
must bear in mind that if we took over
certain responsibilities reluctantly from
them, that does not exonerate them from
certain responsibilities they owe to us. It is
all very well for us to say that we are contributing and we are contributing. As I
pointed out yesterday we have contributed
during the four years fifteen or sixteen
millions-probably more. I think these are
roughly the figures, so that it does not rest
with our critics on the other side to say
that we are not fulfilling our duty to them
and our responsibilities of citizenship of the
British Empire, when those that are
bordering on us in another territory up to
the present moment have not contributed
one penny piece. There is no question today that I think is so serious as this one
affecting the Unemployment Fund. To have
borrowed and to be going on borrowing and
reaching a borrowing in November of close
on four millions is a very serious thing to
contemplate. Even if we have a return of
prosperity it is an impossibility to expect
this little bit of territory that has been
lopped off from the larger territory with

time to continue to pay and make good also
the deficiency that exists at the present
moment. I can only hope that the pressure
being used and the arguments being used by
the Minister of Labour and those associated
with him will bear good results and that we
may have a favourable report at an early
date. Some decision must be arrived at by
this Government after they have heard the

Only this week a young man came to mehe had only arrived here from America-and
wanted to know was there any prospect of
getting employment. I said "None whatever." As a matter of fact he is not entitled to unemployment insurance. That is
another side to the question. Over and above
the people registered that my hon. Friend
knows about I would go so far as to say
there are upwards of 2,000 people that my
hon. Friend has not the naines of or any
record of at all who are not entitled to
benefit. Then we have the young generation
coming on without any outlook. Now there
has been a very useful discussion here today with regard to what is going to be done
to revive industries and there have been
very useful suggestions indeed. The Loans
Guarantee Act is playing an important part
in our main industries. But what I would
like to see is some ray of hope arising soon
of the development of new industries to absorb the artificial numbers I have quoted
into these industries. Then it has occurred
to me that when we were beginning here
we were all very keen about relief schemes,
but I have not heard a solitary word about
new proposals only from the Prime Minister
when he told us that when the next Government comes back the question of drainage is
likely to be taken up. There is no doubt that
that would give very useful employment to a
very large numebr of these people, but there
again that would not do anything like absorb
the very large number of skilled men who are
to-day on our Unemployment Fund.
Believe me this is a very serious question
for us, and I agree with my hon. Friend
(Sir Robert Anderson) that this Government
should not be saddled with the total responsibility with regard to the financial end of
this question. If the Imperial authorities are
prepared to co-operate with us in regard to
the loan for which we are asking all will be
well. We are on the wrong side to a very
large extent now, but I am delighted to
know that there is a prospect of co-operation
between the two Governments to relieve us
of a just responsibility resting upon the
Imperial authorities, seeing that we were not
responsible and that we would be no worse
off in my judgment than we have been in
ordinary depressions were it not for the number artificially created as a result of the
war. That is my opinion on going into the
figures. I do not see any hope of us arriving
at the deficiency period. As my hon. Friend
(Sir Robert Anderson) says there may be a
time arrive when the income will meet the
expenditure, but in my judgment we would
need to place upward of 20,000 people in employment in the very near future to relieve us to that extent. I do say again that
there is a responsibility on the shoulders of
the Imperial Exchequer in regard to this
Fund.

11 MARCH 1925
There is the point to be considered which
my hon. Friend (Mr. Donald) has mentioned
as regards relief schemes. I would like to
say he is under a slight misapprehension in
that connection. These schemes are being
carried on here just as they were before. My
right hon. Friend the Minister of Finance
(Mr. Pollock) and I have rarely, if ever,
turned down a scheme which has been put
before us by any of our local authorities
throughout Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Through these schemes
more than 17,000 positions have been
found for men who would otherwise
have been unemployed. My right hon.
Friend (Mr. Pollock) and I are still
sanctioning schemes, and only yesterday
sanctioned quite a number.
Again there is the question of the tradesman, with whom we have all the greatest
possible sympathy, who naturally does not
like to accept work on relief schemes if he
can get work at his own trade. On the
other hand it is only right I should say that
of the jobs that have been offered on
ordinary relief schemes to tradesmen and
others not one-half per cent. of those who
have been offered work have refused.
Remember, we are not forgetful as a Government of our tradesmen, because through
our Loans Guarantee Act
have
obtained work, as I think I have
already said to-day, in the building of about
twelve ships for tradesmen who otherwise
would not have had work to do. I hope the
House will be satisfied that the Government
have done all in their power to mitigate
the hardships associated with unemployment, and to lessen distress. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).

Oral Answers to Questions.
SECONDARY TEACHERS' PENSION
SCHEME.
1. Mr. McGUFFIN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state how many
existing Secondary Teachers there are in
the Northern area whose years of service
up to August 1st, 1932, would entitle them
to retire with pensions at that date under
the proposed Pension Scheme; also what is
the difference between the amount required
to pay to such Teachers pensions on the
proposed basis of one-third of their years of
service prior to August 1st, 1922, and the
amount which would be required to pay
them pensions on the English basis of full
recognition of Back Services?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): It would take longer research
than the time available admits to extract
the particulars which would enable a reply
to be made to the hon. Member's question.
Accurate statistics will, in fact, only be
secured when the Pension Scheme becomes
statutorily established. It may, however,
meet the point if I say that the Departmental Committee which considered the
establishment of a Pension Scheme for
Secondary Teachers were satisfied that the
cost to Government of granting one-third
of back service for superannuation purposes
for teachers as at 1st August, 1922, might
roughly be regarded as involving a capital
sum of £100,000. The cost of recognition of
back service in full would be three times
that figure.

Education Board and allotted to that Board
by the Imperial Parliament, has been earmarked for the Pension Fund of Secondary
Teachers in Northern Ireland.

EX-SERVICE TEMPORARY CIVIL
SERVANTS.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether he will give to the ex-
Service Temporary Civil Servants in the employment of the Government the same
advantages as those enjoyed by the same class
of Civil Servants under the Imperial Government.
Mr. POLLOCK: The Northern Government
has already afforded to the ex-Service
Temporary Clerks recruited by it much more
favourable recognition in making appointments to clerical posts than the Imperial
Government. Of the total clerical posts in
Northern Ireland, 60 per cent have already
been assigned to ex-Service Temporary Clerks
and without the imposition of competitive
examination. This percentage compares very
favourably with the corresponding English
proposals. In addition, all the Northern
Ireland appointees are pensionable, while
nearly half of those for whom provision is
at present contemplated in England will be
non-pensionable and the other half have been
required to undergo competitive tests.

GOVERNMENT MESSENGERS'
UNIFORMS.
4. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether he considers that the
Government Messengers employed in the
various Ministeries of the Government of
Northern Ireland are entitled to have two
uniforms per annum provided by the Government, and whether he will consider the
question of compensating these messengers for
such clothing hitherto provided from their
own private resources and expended in the
service of the Government.
Mr. POLLOCK: The supply of official uniform to the messengers employed in the
Service of the Government of Northern
has previously been under consideration,
but in consequence of a lack of unanimity
in the matter on the part of the Messengers
themselves the question has been postponed,
The matter will, however, be further considered, but I can hold out no hope of compensation for the use of private clothes as
an alternative to the supply of official
uniforms. The Messengers are already
afforded official protective clothing for use
out-of-doors when engaged upon their official
duties,
TAXATION OF MOTOR VEHICLES.
5. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether it is his intention to introduce legislation having for its object an
increase of the duties payable by Motor
Omnibuses.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I have been asked to answer
this question.
I have the whole question of the basis of
taxation of motor vehicles under careful
consideration at present, in consultation with
the Imperial Government.
It is generally recognised that the heavier
classes of motor vehicles, including motor
omnibuses and char-a-bancs, inflict greater
injury to the roads in proportion to the
licences payable by them.
A Commission, on which this Government
has representation, was appointed by the
Imperial Government to inquire into this
subject. The Government is following up
the recommendations of the Commission
with the view of ascertaining what will be
the best and most equitable scheme of taxation for all classes of motor vehicles in
substitution for the existing basis.
Colonel WOODS: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman when he is considering the new
scheme of taxation not to forget that, as he
himself has stated in public speeches, the
omnibus is the poor man's motor?
R.U.C.-SERGEANT L. H. M. BELL.
6. Mr. COOPER asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether Sergeant Leonard H.
M. Bell, a native of County Derry, served
for eight years and three months in County
Fermanagh in the Royal Irish Constabulary;
whether he had a good record, and was an
exceptionally fine type of policeman. Was
he refused admission into the Royal Ulster
Constabulary, although still under thirty
years of age. Would the Minister be prepared to reconsider Bell's application if, on
inquiries, he considers him a suitable
applicant for admission into the Force.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The facts stated
in the first part of the question are substantially correct.

I am informed by the Inspector-General
that this man refused to join the Royal
Ulster Constabulary on its formation, and in
fact was disbanded from the Royal Irish
Constabulary in April, 1922. He applied in
August, 1923, for permission to join the
Royal Ulster Constabulary, but the Inspector-
General did not feel justified in entertaining his application in the circumstances.
Mr. COOPER: May I ask on what date this
sergeant refused to join the R.U.C., and also
how many men there were in the barracks
in Enniskillen who refused to join.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think the hon.
Member misunderstands the matter. It is
not a question of refusing to join; it is a
question of a man not applying to join the
R.U.C. until August, 1923. As regards the
latter part of the hon. Member's question.
if he will give me the particulars I will
make inquiries into the matter.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Is it not a fact that
quite a number of men who refused to join
when the R.U.C. was being formed have since
been allowed to join, are exceptions being
made; and are some being allowed to come
in and others not? Is the right hon. Gentleman sure that there is no differentiation in
this case?
Mr. DONALD: I wish to supplement that
by asking my right hon. Friend, is not he
aware that owing to the state of the country
quite a number of men refused to join at
first, but later made application and were
accepted? This sergeant is in the same
category?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am quite aware
that unfortunately a very large number of
men of the R.I.C. declined to join during
the disturbed period, when their services
would have been most useful to the Government.
Mr. COOPER: May I ask if this man went
to Canada immediately when he was disbanded, and came home a short time after-

DISTRIBUTION OF AGRICULTURAL
'GRANT.
7. Mr. COOPER asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether the Government will consider the advisability of a more equitable
distribution of the agricultural grant as relief is granted on the basis of the poor rate
which existed in 1897, and whether it is not
the fact that rural districts which had a
low poor rate in 1897 have not been paying
heavily ever since for their economy in that
year.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The distribution of
the Agricultural grant is governed by Section
10 of the Local Government Act (Northern
Ireland), 1923, and it would require new
legislation to amend the basis of distribution.
While there might possibly be some cases of
hardship as suggested by the hon. Member,
I would remind him that there is at present
a Commission investigating the whole scheme
of Local Government Administration in
Northern Ireland.
Accordingly, the further consideration of
the basis of the distribution of this particular grant must stand over pending any
changes consequent on the report of the
Local Government Commission which may
ensue, both in relation to Local Government
machinery as well as in connection with the
general question of State subsidies to Local
Authorities as a whole.
FUTURE OF ROYAL ULSTER SPECIAL
CONSTABULARY.
8. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the intentions of the Government regarding the
future of the Royal Ulster Special Constabulary; whether it will be disbanded,
partially or wholly, in the near future, and
what period of notice will be given to
individuals to be disbanded, and what compensation, if any, will be granted.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is not proposed
to make any material alterations in the
Special Constabulary during the present
financial year, and a detailed statement will
be made when the Special Constabulary Vote
for the coming financial year is introduced.
SENIOR CIVIL SERVANTS.
9. Colonel WOODS asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state the number
of Senior Civil Servants on the staff of the
Ministry of Home Affairs, who have tendered
their resignations since 1st November, 1921,
and whether he can state the cause or
causes leading to such action.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been asked
to take this question. Two of the permanent
staff applied to the Civil Service Committee
for leave to retire under paragraph 3 of the
8th Schedule of the Government of Ireland
Act, 1920.
Colonel WOODS: May I ask the reason
why?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would refer the
hon, and gallant Member to the 1920 Act.
I think he will find there the conditions
under which transferred Civil Servants can
retire if they so desire.
Colonel WOODS: I would like to ask was
there not some powerful motive that induced two Senior Civil Servants to tender
their resignations?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think if the hon.
and gallant Member will study the beneficent incidence of the 1920 Act he will find
that very large pensions are given to transferred Civil Servants. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Education Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
(The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown)).
The MARQUESS OF LONDONDERRY (who
was received with general cheers): I would
once again claim the privilege, which is accorded to Ministers to address either House, of
saying a few words in connection with the
Motion which has just been made by the
hon. Member (Mr. McKeown).
Strictly speaking, the object of this Bill
is not to make further enactments in regard to education in Northern Ireland. It
is rather for the purpose of removing certain
misapprehensions which have arisen in regard
to the meaning and also the intention of the
Education Act of 1923, and which have caused
much anxiety to many persons deeply int
terested in the question of religious instruction in the public elementary schools throughout tho Province.
The Government believe that the Education Act, as it stands, would not have the
effect of introducing what is regarded-and
perhaps rightly regarded-with much concern
by many of our people, namely, an element
of a secularizing tendency into the work of the
schools. Nevertheless, we feel that, if by the
amendment of certain clauses doubts can be
removed and the smooth working of the Act
secured, it is only right and reasonable that
this improvement should be effected in that
way. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I am
sure that every Member of this
House fully appreciates the constitutional
limitations imposed upon the Parliament of
Northern Ireland by the Government of Ireland Act of 1920. We could not, even if we
would, pass any measure that would be at
variance with the letter or the spirit of that
Act-at least such a measure would not have
the force of law or any legal significance
whatever. We are, however, advised that the
proposals embodied in the Bill now before
the House are within our competence and
do not in any respect conflict with the articles
of our Constitution, that is the Act of 1920,
to which I have referred.
are
With those proposals I will deal quite
shortly. They perfectly simple and
straightforward. Let me begin with the two
additions which we make to the law, as it
stands.
In the first place, by the specific mention
of voluntary religious instruction in the
title, we shall make it plain that that form
Education Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Marquess of Londonderry]
of instruction has lost none of its importance under the new system, but is as much
part of our system of public education as
ever it was.
In the second place, the addition of words
specifically permitting the grant to local
schools' committees of advisory functions in
the appointment of teachers in transferred
schools, before the education authority
makes teaching appointments, will remove
doubts of the legality of a condition of transfer which has already been imposed and
accepted in the transfer of several schools.
Those are our proposed additions. I now
come to the two omissions which we propose
to make in the principal act. The first
provision relates to the proviso to Clause 26,
and it is proposed that this proviso should
drop out, the effect being simply, that, while
the prohibition definitely imposed by the
Government of Ireland Act remains undisturbed, the impression-apparently, a very
general, though a very mistaken impression
-that religious instruction will not be permitted in provided and transferred schools
under the Education Act will be immediately,
and for all time, removed. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
The second omission is of a similar nature.
We leave out words in the sub-section of
Section 66, to which objection has been
taken, apparently as placing some additional
and extra Constitutional limitation upon the
powers of the education authority. We will
remain limited by the words of the Government of Ireland Act, instead of by words
founded upon that Act and inserted in the
statute, in order to guide our education
authorities in their exercise of the power of
appointment and dismissal of teachers and
to safeguard the religious liberties of the
subject.
There is nothing which the Government
desires more than the maintenance of a
voluntary religious element in our public
education. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
We have no hesitation, therefore, in commending to hon. Members the adoption of
the measure before the House to-day,
because, as it itself truly declares, its sole
object and effect is the maintenance of a
principle already recognised and universally
accepted in Ulster, a principle upon which
all parties have agreed for generations,
namely, that the basis of our system of
public education is compulsory united
secular and voluntary separate religious
instruction. I have great pleasure in supporting the Bill. (Hon. Members:
hear.)
Hear,
Sir ROBERT LYNN: As one Member of
the House who has taken a share in bringing about this settlement last week, I rise
to support most heartily the views that have
been expressed by the noble Marquess. It
is not necessary to go into the controversy
that has gone on for eighteen months regarding this matter. The principal thing
for us now is to realise that we have got a
settlement that meets with the hearty and
cordial approval of everyone in Northern
Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) And
on that point we have got to concentrate. As
the noble Marquess has said, this Amending
Bill makes it plain and clear to everyone
that Bible teaching will go on in the schools
as Bible teaching has gone on for generations, and that, I think, was all that the
Churches and others asked for, and now
they have got it. We will go on exactly as
we have done for nearly a century. I rise,
not only to support the Second Reading of
this Bill, but, as far as one Member can,
to ask that all controversy on the religious
aspect of education should now cease, and
that the people of Northern Ireland should
unite their forces in making this Bill and
this system what it ought to be one of the
best in the Empire. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
It is very easy to get up a controversy,
especially with regard to religion. We have
now reached a stage when we are all agreed,
and our business is to see that whatever
controversy, whatever bitterness, and whatever hard words were used on either side
are all forgotten, and concentrate on making
this Act, as it will be, I hope, before the
week is out, a huge success. I think everyone is agreed that there is no reason why
one need take up time debating the subject,
but let us get on with the essential work of
educating the people.
Mr. CRAWFORD: As one of those who
in this House, on public platforms, and in
ordinary conversation expressed dissatisfaction with some Clauses of the Education
Act, I wish to take this opportunity to
congratulate the Prime Minister and his
colleagues, including the Minister of Education, on having composed the difference in
the ranks of the Government's supporters
on the Education Act and its provisions in
respect of religious instruction. The
Government did well to realise the strength
of the feeling that was abroad on this question, a feeling that was growing every hour
more pronounced and dangerous.
The representatives of those who have pressed for
this Amending Bill, and who met the Prime
Minister in conference, are to be congratulated not less than the Government on
their moderation and reasonableness and
helpfulness. Two or three things have
emerged from the public controversy that
has taken place, which I feel ought to be,
and I am sure will be, noted carefully,
89€
Committee.
Education Bill—
12 MARCH 1925
especially by those who will have to do
with the future administration of the Act.
In the first place no privilege, no preference
and no advantage is sought over anybody in
respect of religious belief. The Protestant
people of Northern Ireland are not asking,
and have never asked, anything for themselves that they are not prepared to concede
to their Roman Catholic fellow country-men.
They have been desiring only in respect of
religious instruction a continuance, as the
noble Marquess has said, of the status quo
as it existed under the Commissioners of
National Education. Then in the second
place it has been made clear beyond any
possibility of doubt that the Protestant
people of Northern Ireland wish their
children to be given Bible instruction by the
teaching staff as heretofore, and are prepared
if need be, to insist that the teachers
appointed to teach their children be teachers
who profess the Protestant faith. It will be
agreed on all sides that these are reasonable
demands. But that the spirit of criticism has
been stilled, occasion could no doubt be found
to criticise this Amending Bill.
nature of the case it must have in it something of compromise, and for myself I think it
meets the case admirably so long as it is
administered in the spirit and intention of
those who have put it forward and those who
have accepted it in settlement of the points
at issue.
In the
If, on the other hand, there should appear
now or at any future time another spirit on
the part of the administrators which would
render uncertain the giving of Bible
instruction by the teaching staff as heretofore to Protestant children, then we shall
have all this trouble over again and perhaps
even in a more aggravated form. That is a
contingency, however, which I sincerely hope
is not likely to arise. I prefer to place
confidence in the Ministry and teachers, and
Regional and District Committees, and so I
look forward with great optimism that all
will be well and that from to-day we shall
start out as one body to realise to the full
the high hopes and ambitions of the Minister
of Education, and the Government that the
education of the youth of Northern Ireland,
as my hon. Friend (Sir Robert Lynn) has
said, will excel in every respect that of any
other portion of the King's Dominions. There
is only one other observation I would make
and I hope it will not be misunderstood in
any way. There have been some changes since
the original Act was passed and I hope that
any arrangement made since will not stand
in the way of everyone receiving absolute
fair play. I trust this Education Act and
the Amending Bill will be of immense
advantage to the youth of Northern Ireland.
Dr. MORRISON: I have had occasion to
speak so often against the Education Act
that I am delighted to have an opportunity
now of speaking in its favour. I had only to
find exception to these two Clauses that are
now being altered, and while I am in agreement with what the hon. Member for
Antrim (Mr. Crawford) has said, I myself
think it is an agreed compromise, a settlement that should meet with the wishes of
everybody in Ulster. I believe that with
sympathetic and reasonable administration
the Amending Bill will secure everything
that the Party for whom I speak desire. I
congratulate the Government, and I congratulate especially the Prime Minister, on
the success of the conference, and, if I may
be allowed to say it, I would like to congratulate the Noble Marquess on the
sportsmanlike spirit with which he has
come into this House and supported the
Second Reading of the Bill. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Admittedly in passing
the Education Act we made a mistake, but
I find that Governments and individuals
who make no mistakes never make any.
thing. We have now through these slight
changes a great Measure of reform which
in my opinion will give satisfaction to every
reasonable person in Ulster, and when you
meet the wishes of the reasonable people in
any community you need not worry about
the unreasonable.

King's Speech.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
King's Speech.
THE GOVERNOR'S ANSWER TO THE
ADDRESS.
The PRIME MINISTER (at the Bar)
reported the Answer to the Address from his
Grace the Governor of Northern Ireland as
followeth :
I have received with great satisfaction
the expression of your thanks for the
Speech with which I have opened the present Session of Parliament.
PROROGATION.
Message from the Senate.
A Message was delivered by the Gentleman
Usher of the Black Rod as followeth :-
I am commanded by the Senate to inform this Honourable House that the
Speech of His Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland proroguing this present
Parliament is to be communicated in the
Senate forthwith, and, further, I am
commanded to invite this 'Honourable
House to attend in the Senate in order to
hear the said Speech.
The House went, and having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in the Clerk's
place at the Table): I have to acquaint the
House that the House has this day been
to the Senate, where the Speaker of the
Senate communicated His Grace's Speech to
both Houses of Parliament as follows:
KING'S SPEECH.
MEMBERS OF THE SENATE AND OF
THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
I thank you for passing the legislative
measures foreshadowed in my Speech at
the opening of Parliament upon Tuesday
last.
MEMBERS OF THE HOUSE OF
COMMONS.
I thank you for the provision of supplies
for the Public Services.
MEMBERS OF THE SENATE AND OF
THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
In bidding you farewell, I pray that the
blessing of Almighty God may rest upon
your labours.
After which the Proclamation proroguing
Parliament was read as follows:
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION FOR PROROGUING
THE PRESENT PARLIAMENT
OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
WHEREAS it is provided by Section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said Act,
that the Governor of Northern Ireland shall
in His Majesty's name summon, prorogue
and dissolve the Parliament of Northern
Ireland;
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
Duke of Abercorn, Governor of Northern
Ireland, by this Proclamation do publish
and declare His Majesty's Pleasure that the
said Parliament be, as from the reading of
this Proclamation in the Parliament of
Northern Ireland, prorogued to Thursday,
the Second day of April, one thousand nine
hundred and twenty-five, to be then holden.
Given at Belfast, this 13th day of March,
1925.
(Signed) ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
End of the Fifth Session (opened

Tuesday,
10th March, 1925) of the First Parliament of
Northern Ireland, in the Fifteenth year of
the Reign of His Majesty King George the
Fifth.
A PROCLAMATION
FOR DISSOLVING THE FIRST PARLIA-
CRBI MOMENT OF NORTHERN IRELAND MUJOV
AND DECLARING THE CALLING
OF ANOTHER.
WHEREAS it is provided by section eleven
of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, as
modified by and in pursuance of certain
enactments amending the said Act, that the
Governor of Northern Ireland shall in His
Majesty's name summon, prorogue and dissolve the Parliament of Northern Ireland.
And whereas it is desirable that the present
Parliament of Northern Ireland, which
stands prorogued to Thursday the Second day
of April next, shall be dissolved and that a
new Parliament should be called:
Now therefore I, James Albert Edward,
Duke of Abercorn, Governor of Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation, do publish and
declare His Majesty's pleasure that the said
Parliament be, as from the date of this
Proclamation, dissolved, and that the Senators and Members of the House of Commons
be discharged from their Meeting and Attendance on the said Thursday, the Second day of
April next;
And I do hereby make known to all His
Majesty's loving subjects His Royal Will and
Pleasure to call a new Parliament of Northern Ireland, and do further declare that I
have taken Order that Writs shall be issued
forthwith in His Majesty's Name under the
Great Seal of Northern Ireland in due Form
and according to Law, for calling a Parliament of Northern Ireland to meet at the
City of Belfast on Tuesday, the Fourteenth
day of April next, and for causing the Senators and Commons who are to serve in the
said Parliament to be duly returned to and
give their Attendance in His Majesty's said
Parliament on Tuesday, the Fourteenth day
of April next, which Writs are to be returnable in due course of Law.
Given the Fourteenth day of March, in
the year of our Lord One Thousand Nine
Hundred and Twenty-five.
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
