moment. Experience in Great Britain
showed that the standard of living amongst
agricultural labourers fell so low that it
became absolutely essential to restore the
Wages Board there. If any consideration is
going to be given to the agricultural
labourers, who form the largest part of the
community in Northern Ireland, I believe
that some regard should be had to the conditions under which they work as much as
in the case of the town workers.
From my knowledge of Irish history, 1
know that nearly all improvements that
have come to the countryside through the
British Parliament-I do not know a great
deal about agriculture, but I am speaking of
workers generally-principally came through
physical force movements of one kind or
another. I would not like to see the standard
of the agricultural labourer in Northern
Ireland fall so low that he would have to
resort to measures that were not constitutional. Simply because attention was not
given in time to the grievances of the people
in the past resort was had to physical force.
I do not suggest that in Northern Ireland,
or even in Southern Ireland, the agricultural labourer is likely to resort to physical
violence at the present time. We have
heard from an hon. Member behind that
they are not prepared to go on strike; they
have not the courage to fight for a decent
living wage.
But when all these experiments are being made let us give some
attention to the position of the agricultural
labourer. Let us give him decent wages.
The housing conditions have improved
during the last half century, but I believe
there is room for considerable improvement
yet. The Ministry should consider in the
very near future the advisability of restoring
the Wages Board, in order to give the
labourer a higher wage and a better standard of living than he enjoys at the present
time.
I think the fewer of these people that
come to overcrowd the towns the better.
The situation in that respect is already
bad enough. If the countryside were
made more attractive for the agricultural labourer, we would probably
have less unemployment in the towns.
The Minister of Labour and those who form
the Cabinet know what that would mean; it
would mean that the people would be kept in
the countryside, on the farms. If that had
been done the industrial situation would not
be so bad as it is at the present moment.
You would have less unemployment, you
would have fewer people drawing, the unemployment benefit, and you would save
from the point of view that a person, instead
of being more or less of a parasite on the
community, would be producing food stuffs
to be consumed in Northern Ireland, or to
be exported to Great Britain and other
places. All I want to do is to try to impress
on the Minister of Agriculture the advisability of having consultations with the
labourers on all questions affecting his conditions and on agriculture generally, and to
ask him, if he possibly can, to restore the
Wages Board, in order that the agricultural
labourer may have a higher standard of
living than he enjoys at the present time.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I will not detain the

amount.

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I am sure there
are a great many Members who like myself
are ignorant of the work that is being done.
Could the right hon. Gentleman inform us
as to what work is being done?
some of these bacon-curing places are going
out of existence altogether, and the people are
going on the dole, as it is called. The trade
is going from the North of Ireland. Denmark has increased immensely its stock of
pigs. The trade is gradually being filched
away from Northern Ireland, and nothing is
being done to help the farmers in this
respect. I ask the Minister of Agriculture
can nothing be done? The Feeding Stuffs Act
is not administered as it ought to be. Some
steps should be taken to prevent the importation of deleterious feeding stuffs, and the
farmers should be educated in such a way
that they would not use those inferior
materials in time to come
Then, I think the Ministry of Agriculture
would be well advised if they would call a
meeting at an early date of representatives of
the farmers and curers and so get to know
the type of pig wanted in order to recapture
this trade which is rapidly leaving us and
going to Denmark. We should try to induce
the farmers to realise that they are losing
a valuable thing which is a great loss to them
and to Northern Ireland. There is another
way. Some education should be given to the
farmers so that they would not be compelled
to kill pigs and bring them to market and
be left at the dealers' and the curers' mercy.
If they could be educated to bring them on
foot they could then bring them home again
and not be compelled to sell them at a bad
price. An effort must be made in some way
to get the very best breed of pigs in Northern
Ireland, and we should try our level best to
recapture this industry. I hope the Minister
of Agriculture, in the interest of the farmers
and the labourers, will take steps at an early
date to get back this trade.

to be fixed on a permanent basis. Their
salaries will be paid direct instead of through

Clerk of the Crown and Peace. One proper
question which was asked was as to what
would be the probable extra cost to the State
under the provisions of this Bill. The resultant immediate increase to be met by the
State on the basis of the proposals which
are embodied in the Estimate for the County
Court Service is approximately £800 per
annum, but the fact that many of the officers
will be placed on the minimum of the scale
means that the full increase will not be felt
for some years to come. It is thought that
by means of a gradual increasing charge, the
financial effect of the increments will ultimately amount to not more than £1,000
annually.
In addition, these officers will, of course,
now be entitled to receive pensions and gratuities on retirement, but a charge under this
head will not be felt for some years to come.
This explanation will meet some of the comments made by hon. Members during the
Second reading of this Bill and will I hope
satisfy them that the net cost is not excessive having regard to the rather unsatisfactory conditions of service which prevailed
before. It will now offer a prospect of a
career to these men, instead of being, as they

Mr. KYLE: Might I ask the Prime
Minister what business he proposes to take
next week?
The PRIME MINISTER: Tuesday, the
28th, will be occupied with the consideration
of the remaining stages of the three Bills at
present before the House, namely the Civil
Pensions Bill, the Administrative Provisions
Bill, and the County Officers and Courts
Bill. It is hoped that the two Bills at present in the Senate-the Public Health (Milk
Regulations) Bill and the Charitable Loan
Societies Bill-will then be available for introduction in this House. On Wednesday the
29th it is proposed to take the Second Reading
of the Pharmacy and Poisons Bill, and to
devote the remainder of the day, if necessary,
to the consideration of Estimates. It is proposed to take, inter alia, the Estimate for
Grants to Local Authorities and the Estimate
for the Ministry of Commerce on this day.
Thursday, the 30th, will be devoted to the
consideration of Estimates, and those selected will be announced later.
C1 SPECIAL CONSTABULARY.
Colonel WOODS: I wish to raise the question of the C1 Special Constabulary. The cost
of this force is well known-it is down in
the Estimates-but how much is being wasted
is not shown there. I am not attacking the
Minister of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates)
or the Government. I am only putting up
what is well known. I have proof of anything I may say, and I can prove that the
Government are not getting the best value
for their money.
The way in which the force is constituted
provides for eight battalions in each district
in Belfast-North, South, East, and West.
Each battalion consists of men to the
strength of 750. That means that in each
district in Belfast there are 1,500 men-that
is on paper.
What is the truth of the
matter? The truth works out that there are
eighty men really to a battalion, that is 160
men to each district. Now the Minister of
of Home Affairs has his own regulations, and
they are carried out on paper. For instance,
there are weekly parades, and these parades
are returned as showing an average of somewhere about 200 men. As a matter of fact
there are twenty men on parade-twenty to
twenty-four is the average. I have proof of
this and if the right hon. Gentleman (Sir
Dawson Bates) will make further inquiries—
independent inquiries-himself he will find
that it is quite true. Each man is paid 1s.
6d. for his parades up to the amount of 7s.
per quarter. Now when men are shown as
being on parade when they are not actually
on parade their money must be paid out,
hence these numerous scandals about money
being paid to men who are sometimes in
America, or have severed their connection
with the force, but who certainly were not
on parades. I do not say this is the fault of
the officers. It is rather due to the instructions which they have received to show a
certain number of men on parade whether it
is right or wrong.
The men have been reduced in strength,
but the staff has not. We have still got a
highly paid, very expensive staff, and what
their particular duties would be now it would
be difficult to say. Might I say before I leave
the subject of the strength of this force that
that probably was the reason the Prime
Minister on the Border made a statement
which I am sure he thought was right, but
which actually was not right? The divisional
instructional staff is composed of three officers and three or more head constables. The
object of this highly paid staff is the instruction and supervision of the training of the
units, but they do not do anything like that
at all. There is an Adjutant, a Quarter
Master, a Regimental Sergeant-Major, and a
Regimental Quarter-Master Sergeant, and
they are paid an instructional allowance
though they do not come under the headquarters staff. They are still paid that
allowance, though they do not do anything
for it.
There was a charge made about the employment of Englishmen, and I have not heard
it absolutely refuted yet. I will just give you
one instance of which I have proof. There
were vacancies for three clerks at the police
depot at Newtownards, and the Commandant
sent a letter to the Royal Army Service Corps
Record Office-

Sir DAWSON BATES: May I say how much
I regret that any hon. Member of this House
should get up and make charges of fraud
against officers in the Special Constabulary?
I would have thought that the proper course
would have been for the hon, and gallant
Member to have submitted his facts to the
Attorney-General (Mr. Best) with a view to
the Attorney-General or taking proceedings
against those officers for fraud.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: No.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The charge is the
grave one of fraud-that these officers received payment on behalf of men who were in
America or elsewhere, and did not attend
parades. All I can say is that I deny that. I
deny it emphatically, and I challenge the hon.
and gallant Member (Colonel Woods) to submit
a statement of all the facts to the Attorney-
General, and I am sure the Attorney-General
will deal with it, as he always does, absolutely
impartially. I say, further, that I deprecate
very much than an hon. Member of this House
should take advantage of the privilege of this

it has been the constitutional practice that
where a force-if we argue on the analogy of
the Army, the Navy, or the Air Force-if
any Department is badly run, if the system
in regard to any of these services is not
efficient, and if the House of Commons is
discussing their estimates an hon. Member
can point these things out; he can put his
finger here or there and say that might be
improved. That is the proper scope of
Parliament. I have been a long time in the
Imperial Parliament and I have never heard
yet a charge of this sort made against a
gallant officer of the Army, Navy, or Air
Force inside the House of Commons.
This is a serious charge of fraud and I do
hold that there is nothing worse than hon.
Members using their position in this House
for the purpose of charging officer's with
fraud. How are we here on the spur of the
moment able to defend these gentlemen?
How is it possible for my right hon. Friend
(Sir Dawson Bates) to know what is going
to fall from the lips of the hon. Member
(Colonel Woods?)
May I point out also that there is the
grave danger of unsettling the minds of the
people by suggesting that our forces are not
what they ought to be, while as a matter of
fact the history behind this force would be
an honour to any force that ever had been
raised.
May I point out not only to the hon.
Member (Colonel Woods), but to other hon.
Members the extraordinarily difficult position
in which such charges put us. For four
years I have been able to convince the
British Government that it was right and
proper that the Special Constabularly should
be maintained. On the strength of that representation my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Pollock) and myself have been able to secure
such contributions towards the upkeep of this
magnificent force that we have been
excused practically any cost whatever
on the revenue of Northern Ireland.
Is it to be the same in future, or when
we go across and say, "We want a contribution towards the Special Constabulary,"
will speeches of this sort be handed to us? Is
the British Chancellor of the Exchequer to
say to us, "Set your own house in order before
you come over here?" I warn hon. Members,
not only one hon. Member for West Belfast,
but I am sorry to say, other hon. Members,
that this causing of unrest and suspicion,
this dropping of a little poison day by day
into our debates as to the spendthrift nature
of the Government, these charges against the
conduct of our Special Constabulary are going
to prejudice us very much in our finances of
this year.
These drops of poison from day to day from
persons whom we ought to consider friends
of Ulster are often dressed up with a little
eyewash to make it appear that those men are
still friends of the Government and of myself.
But they do no service to us whatever. On
the broader question of endeavouring to
establish the services in such a way that
Ulster can carry on without having this constant trafficking, in order to get our finances
settled, no more inappropriate moment could
have been chosen by these hon. Members for
making these statements. Just at the very
critical point when my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Pollock) has brought our finances upjust when the Colwyn Committee has reported, and just when the Treasury are fighting my right hon Friend as to the exact
meaning of certain phraseology in the report,
it is thrown to the world, it is broadcast,
that he and I and others are carrying on the
government of the country in such an extravagant manner that I doubt very much
what the result will be. But let it stand
on record in the Debates that if we are
prejudiced by this sort of thing-this cruel,
slanderous way in which these statements
are made the responsibility rests upon the
shoulders of those hon. Members who have
prejudiced our case. Do not let it be said
that it was the fault of the Government

here if we are not able to persuade the
British Government and the British House
of Commons that we have done our best for
the people here, and in doing so have done
our best for Great Britain and the Empire.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Colonel WOODS rose.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member has already addressed the House three times. He is
only entitled to address it once.
Question put, and agreed to.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 28th April, 1925.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
CENSORSHIP OF CORRESPONDENCE.
1. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether all correspondence passing through the post in
Northern Ireland is liable to censorship;
whether letters posted in Great Britain, the
Free State, and Northern Ireland are liable
to be opened and the contents perused;
whether this work is performed by two
officials attached to the staff of the Ministry
of Home Affairs and one Post Office official
of supervising rank, and whether he can state
what is the monthly expenditure of public
funds in connection with this work, and what
part is borne by the Government of Northern Ireland; and whether in view of the
peaceful state of Northern Ireland he will
consider the abolition of this censorship.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): As regards the first two
parts of the Question, correspondence for
delivery to, or emanating from, persons in
Northern Ireland suspected of engaging in
seditious activities is liable to censorship.
The reply to the third part is in the
affirmative. The total charge to the police
Votes is approximately £80 per month.
I regret that the time has not yet arrived
when this valuable precaution can be safely
abandoned.
Mr. McMULLEN: I would like to ask
whether or not this is in operation in Great
Britain and the Free State?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid I
cannot answer in regard to what is happening there.
TAXI-CAB OWNERS-QUESTION OF
COMPENSATION.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state what
compensation (if any) for loss of earnings he
is prepared to grant to the taxi owners who
ply for hire at the public stands at St.
George's Church, High Street, and Castle
Junction, and who were compelled by the
police to remove for four hours on the 15th
April.
Sir DAWSON BATES: On the date in
question the streets referred to were closed
to all traffic by order of the Belfast Corporation during the progress of His Grace the
Governor to open Parliament and on his
return.
The streets were closed to traffic for about
an hour and a quarter.
There are no funds at my disposal out of
which such compensation as is suggested by
the Hon. Member could be paid, nor has any
such compensation been hitherto paid.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the loss that
these men have sustained and the fact that
they require to earn their living, is the
Minister of Home Affairs prepared to make
a small grant out of funds set aside for purposes such as this?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
indicated to my hon. Friend that there are
no funds at my disposal for such a purpose.
TREATMENT OF CONSUMPTION.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is prepared to test
the latest discovery made by Mr. Newell, of
London, in his noble attempt to overcome the
great white plague of consumption.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Inquiries are being
made by the Ministry into this matter. If as
a result of the inquiries there seems to be
good reason to suppose that the remedy referred to would have useful results the
Ministry would be prepared to give the
matter the fullest possible consideration.
PROTECTION OF ANIMALS.

CHICHESTER:
To ask the Minister of Home Affairs, when
he proposes to make the Captive Birds Shooting Prohibition Act, 1921, and the Protection
of Animals (1911) Amendment Act, 1921,
applicable to Northern Ireland.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I beg leave to postpone this Question.
MR. DANIEL McDEVITT, BELFAST.

formerly carried on business at 5 Rosemary
Street, Belfast, if he was seen within the

of the fact that no charge has been preferred
against the person named, and having re-

Sir DAWSON BATES: The claim of
Catherine Campbell was disallowed by the
Ministry on appeal on the grounds that there
was not sufficient proof that she had
reached the age of 70 years.
The documents submitted in support of her
claim were mere statements of memory and
belief, and were not substantiated by any

Gardeners Insurance Society on the 29th
July, 1912, when he gave the date of birth as
the 12th August, 1855. There was no further
evidence submitted on his behalf.

Finance if he can state the approximate date

HOUSING IN RURAL AREAS.
9. Major SHILLINGTON asked the
Minister of Finance whether it would not be
possible to extend the subsidy now being
given for the erection of houses in urban
areas to all rural areas.
Mr. POLLOCK: The question of further
facilities for the construction of houses in
rural areas is engaging the attention of the
Government, and it is hoped that it will be
possible to make a pronouncement shortly on
the subject.
DRAINAGE BILL.
10. Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the Prime
Minister if he will state when the Bill foreshadowed in the King's Speech-providing
for the better administration of the Drainage Acts-will be introduced.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have been asked by the
Prime Minister to take this question. I
anticipate that the Bill for the better
administration of the Drainage Acts will be
ready for introduction in this House during
the coming month.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: Arising out of that
answer, I wonder if the right hon. Gentleman would not consider the advisability of
bringing in the Bill sooner. I would like to
ask him whether he realises the importance
of time in this matter, and whether by the
time the Bill will have passed through both
Houses it will be impossible for the local
authorities to carry out the necessary action
in the country in order to enable this
pressing question to be dealt with before the
end of the year?
Mr. POLLOCK: In reply to my hon. Friend,
the Government fully realize the necessity
for expedition in this matter. They have been
giving it very serious consideration for some
time, and have instructed the draughtsman
to expedite the preparation of the Bill as
much as could be possibly done in view of
the other work which is in hand. It is being
vigorously prosecuted at the present time,
and I can assure the hon. Member that every
effort is being made to facilitate the matter.
BRANCH LABOUR EXCHANGE IN EAST
:
BELFAST.
11. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is considering the advisability of opening a branch exchange in East
Belfast for women, girls and boys, owing to
the congestion that exists at Amelia Street.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr. Andrews) On the grounds of economy in administration I am not prepared to consent to
the opening of an additional Employment
Exchange at present. It is unfortunately
the fact that, owing to the recent increase of
unemployment among women the resources
of the Amelia Street Exchange have been
considerably taxed. Arrangements, however,
have been made for less frequent signatures
for the time being. This will have the
effect of reducing the number of women having to attend the Exchange each day by one
half, and it is, I think, the best way of
dealing with what I hope is a temporary
difficulty.
Mr. BEATTIE: Owing to the unsatisfactory answer given to my question, I desire
to give notice that I will raise this question
on the adjournment of the House to-day.

unemployed on Friday, 3rd April, was 262,

civilians.

Minister took to see that these unemployed
clerks, particularly ex-Service men,
engaged as presiding officers and poll clerks
on the counting of the votes?

Officers. They were approached and
asked to employ as many ex-Service.
men as possible, and in many instances the

Compel them to do so.

SUMMER TIME IN RURAL SCHOOLS.
15. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education,
whether, in view of the fact that there is a
general demand for ignoring Summer Time
in Schools in rural areas, he will take steps
to ascertain from the managers if any change
of hours would be desirable.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): No intimation has previously
reached the Ministry of the existence of any
general demand for ignoring Summer Time
in the schools in rural areas, and it is not
considered that any useful purpose would be
secured by an extension of the present rules
under which managers may arrange for the
school work to commence as late as 11 a.m.
In the circumstances, it is not proposed to
take the action suggested.

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Before this

Land purchase is a reserved service

We have always thought that while this is

was immediately, as far as we know, accepted

has been that they believe it is a fair

There is a general feeling held all

that outside bodies like the Chamber

I come to the first part of the Motion
which is with regard to the bonus, and I
stand to be corrected by the Minister of
Finance at the very start. I have looked
through the Report of the Colwyn Committee,
and as far as it is possible for a layman to
gather the facts out of it I have not found
that the Government of Northern Ireland
have been credited with this item by the
Imperial Parliament. I think it is clearly
an Imperial obligation. If we go back to the
year 1903 when the Imperial Parliament first
recognised its responsibilities for land purchase for this country, and when they had
to provide a bonus to bridge over the
difference between what the landlords could
afford to accept and the tenants could afford
to pay there was provided under the Act of
1903 a bonus of £12,000,000 for this purpose.
Owing to the finances of that Act breaking
down there was only £10,000,000 of the
£12,000,000 provided under the Act, used as
bonus, and therefore the Imperial Parliament
of that time had a saving of £2,000,000. To
come to more recent history, I find that in
the memorandum explaining the financial
resolution in connection with the Northern
Ireland Land Bill the third paragraph
says:-
"The purpose of the Bill is to provide for
of
the completion
land purchase in

Unbought Tenants.
28 APRIL 1925
Northern Ireland on the lines recommended by a
sub-committee of the Irish
Convention in 1918."
If you will bear with me I will read the
Recommendations of the Sub-Committee of
the Irish Convention with regard to the
bonus. It says this on page 95:
"It will be remembered that when the
payment of a bonus was first proposed in
1903 it was described as 'a free gift to
Ireland.' It has always been treated as a
payment to be made by the taxpayers, not
of Great Britain or Ireland, but of Ireland
and Great Britain. In other words, though
for an Irish service it has always been regarded as an Imperial obligation. We see
no reason why land not yet sold should be
differentiated in this respect from land already sold or agreed to be sold. Accordingly, we recommend that the annual
charge for the bonus payable in future
sales should, like the charges for bonus
and excess stock in completed and pending
sales, be in the first instance paid by the
Irish Government, but should, so far as
Great Britain's share thereof is concerned,
be regarded as a contribution by the Irish
Government to Imperial expenditure."
This is the point of view I want to put
before the House. It probably is not as
clearly expressed as I would like it to be
in the Motion, because as the Motion was
originally drafted it was found to
be rather cumbrous and the pruning
knife was somewhat severely applied to it.
I do not object to the Government of Northern Ireland in the first instance paying this
bonus, but I do object to the Imperial Parliament not carrying out its specific pledges,
obligations, and promises in this matter. We
should take from the Imperial Parliament
whatever sum is necessary to carry
out this scheme. It may be said that
the Imperial Parliament could not do
this, inasmuch as the Irish Free State
is paying the bonus out of its own
funds. I should like to point out that the
recommendation here is that this amount
should be deducted from the Imperial contribution. The Irish Free State occupies a
very different position from Northern Ireland in regard to this matter, because up to
the present time, I think, there has been no
Imperial contribution whatever from the
Irish Free State. I say this that we should
not consent on this matter to allow the Imperial Government to shirk its obligations,
and not to carry out the pledges that were
specifically given by the then Prime Minister. When this report was issued Mr.
Lloyd George was Prime Minister, and he
gave a specific pledge that the Imperial
Government would carry out the report, because it was the only unanimous finding that
the Irish Convention came to.
With regard to the general provisions of
the Measure, it has been said that it is only
a few disgruntled old-time Liberals who are
objecting to this Measure. Well, if the Government hold that view, I can tell them
they are entirely wrong, because in no ditrict that I have visited has the dissatisfaction been so strongly expressed as in districts where the Government have been very
strongly supported up to the present time.
These men really ask themselves this question: Is this the price that we are going to
have to pay for our loyalty? Are men across
the Border going to receive on the completion
of land purchase a reduction of 7s in the £,
whereas we are put off with 3s. 74d, about
half? Is that what our loyalty is going to
cost us? I tell the Government this, that if
they are clapping themselves on the back
and saying there is no dissatisfaction in regard to this matter except on the part of a
few old-time Liberals there will be an
awakening for them some day. It may be
said that these fellows are always growling;
they have always a grievance. It may be
said that there is an interested party in
every camp depending too much on their attitude. Burns, the Scottish poet, once said
very truly-
"If self the wavering balance shake,
It's rarely right adjusted!"
So I think we had better just look to see if
there is any real cause for dissatisfaction in
regard to the terms of purchase, and the
conditions of this Measure. We are told we
should be very glad of it, because it is based
on an agreement that was come to in Dublin
in 1918, when all parties were represented,
the landlords, the tenants, the taxpayers and
everybody else, that this Bill was built on
that agreement and therefore we should be
satisfied. I just want to say that, if anybody wanted to do it, the tenants are the
people who could justly claim that that
bargain be adhered to, because it was entered into when agriculture was prosperous,
and when the conditions were bound to
colour any bargain that was made at that
time. Further, we might justly ask for a revision on the other hand, that the landlords'
security in rent charge has depreciated considerably since then. It has been depreciated
on account of the passing of an Act in the
Free State in 1923. It has depreciated much
more on the present prospects and outlook
of agriculture. We realise that the landlords'
rent charge always occupies some such position as the preference shareholder in an
industrial concern, that is, he has got to be
paid first. But I tell you this, when the
ordinary shares in an industrial firm do not
earn a dividend, then the preference shares
come down in the market. I say this, that
there has been a very severe depreciation in
the landlords' rent charges since 1918. But we
waive that.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. George Henderson]
We come to another point that is causing
dissatisfaction, and it is this. Since that
bargain was entered into, that is now seven
years ago-1918-it is no fault of the unbought tenants that that bargain has not
been carried out. Sometimes we are told
that these men should have bought out under
the Act of 1903; that some of them had a
chance of doing so. I do not deny that. You
will meet unreasonable tenants just as you
meet unreasonable landlords, because human
nature is very much the same the world over.
It is very hard to get any correct data. We are
naturally inclined to fling names at the landlords, and to say that they are to blame, and
the landlords are naturally inclined to say
that we are the boys to blame; but we are
convinced that the blame is more on the
other side. However, since 1918 no tenants
have had an opportunity of buying. I think
the House will agree to that. Since that
bargain was entered into in 1918, no tenants
have had the opportunity of buying, and
they have in the interval been paying rents
that are in round figures about 20 per cent.
higher than they would have been paying if
the bargain had been carried out. Take a
£100 rental. On that the tenant has paid
since that bargain was entered into in Dublin in 1918 somewhere about £140. Not only
that, but he will have to continue to pay his
annuities for seven years longer. There is
no blinking the fact that the tenant is under
a tremendous loss because of the delay that
has occurred in carrying out land purchase.
How has the landlord fared? In the interval
he has collected his old rents, and he was
getting 12 per cent. more than he would have
got if the bargain had been carried out. If
you count 5 per cent to cover his overhead
charges, he was getting 7 per cent. more. I
want to say this to the House, that when the
tenants are asking that the whole loss should
not be put on them I think it is not an unreasonable request. If sacrifices are to be
made, they should be made generally, and the
tenants should get some consideration for the
losses that have been sustained by the delay
in carrying out land purchase.
But we have even a stronger ground than
that for dissatisfaction, because we hold that
this Bill does not carry out the 1918 bargain,
inasmuch as it adds 1 or 12 years to the
purchase money. By one stroke of the pen
it increased the purchase money of the unbought tenant in the Six Counties over half
a million, and one result of that is this, we
are told it will increase the duration of the
tenants's annuity for 4 years. You will find
that the estimate for the purchase of land
is £380,000. If you multiply that by 4 you
get a sum of £1,710,000. Nobody has ever
tried to challenge those figures. We hold
that this Bill, even as compared with the
bargain entered into in 1918, is going to cost
the unbought tenants £1,710,000 more before
I
the loans are redeemed. And the Government says that is fair. I want this House
to say that that, is not a fair Measure.
want this House to say this is our property,
and whoever is responsible for it is taking
what is ours. Of course, I admit this is
brought about by a reduction in the stock
position. In the 1918 scheme it was proposed to pay the landlord 5 per cent. stock.
In this Bill it is proposed to pay the landlord with 4 per cent. stock. The idea was
and is now to give the landlord stock at
something like its face value in the market.
We hold that the landlord receiving the
same amount of 4 per cent. stock now as he
would have received of 5 per cent. stock in
1918 is as well off.
I put that to two tests, and I want this
House to say they are both fair. If you
want to know the value of anything, where
is the best place to go? You go down to the
market and see how you can sell it. If the
landlord wanted to sell the 5 per cent. stock
in 1918 he could have got about £95 for it in
the market. If he wants to sell the 4 per cent.
stock to-day he will get £98 for it. That is
one test. The other is this. I say he is
not worse off, because £4 10s 0d has as much
spending value now aus £5 had in 1918.
Therefore, I hold that in asking that the
purchase money should not be increased in
this Bill, we are not asking the landlords
to suffer any hardship. If this one cou
clusion were granted it would have this
effect that instead of the tenants getting
a reduction of 3s 7 or 3s 8d they would
get a reduction of 5s, and that I hold is the
only way inside the covers of the Bill that
the tenants can be recouped for the tremendous loss that they have been at owing to
the delay in land purchase. I hold that on
all these grounds there is grave cause for
dissatisfaction, and I say further that our

a fair Bill to complete land purchase in

any tenant who bought out in 1903 would

We look on this as an important matter.
It is important for the community that
Our Government should insist that no
bonafide agricultural holding be left outside and that no holding on which a judicial
rent has been fixed should be omitted. That
provision was in the 1903 Act, and I do not
see why it should not be included in this
Bill. We hold that this Bill, if it is to do
anything, should give immediate relief. It
is possible under the Bill as it stands that
may be four years before a tenant would
get relief, because it may be four years
before the appointed day. If the Government
realise the present acute financial stress
which many of these men are suffering
under-and I question if they do with the

Mr. Archdale)-they should grant them
immediate relief. The Government are
going to give a grant of £40,000 to help in
carrying this through. They should give
this money now and not wait for four years.
Why is this four years mentioned in the
Bill? Under the Convention agreement
which I read, the time for the appointed
day was limited to three years, and they
said that the main reason for limiting the
day to that was because there were so many
pending cases that the Court would be engaged in. There are practically no pending
cases now. Why should it be four years,
and why should these men not get immediate
relief? We hold if there is to be a satisfactory settlement the number of years' purchase must not be increased, and the tenant
must get the benefit of the cheaper stock. We
hold that provision must be made for arrears.
Some of these people are two years in arrears,
and I must say that on the whole landlords
have not been too bad in waiting for the
rents. The situation is acute, and I say that
these claims are honest. I hold every one of
them is based on justice. We are only asking the barest justice. Even if these claims
are met the tenants under this Bill will only
be receiving a reduction of 5s as compared
with 7s in other parts of Ireland.
I appeal to this House to say that these
are fair and just demands that we set up on
behalf of the unbought tenants. I appeal to
the Government that even at this eleventh
hour we should have a settlement of this
question so that it will leave no bitterness
and rancour behind. I appeal to them to
use their influence with the Imperia!
Government to have this Bill amended along
the lines we have suggested. This Government is the only avenue through which we
can approach the Imperial Government.
The situation is desperate. Owing to the
economic situation these people need immediate relief. The £40,000 that the Government is going to give was never more needed
than at the present time. I may be asked
"Why not reject the Bill?" I have nothing
to do with the rejection of the Bill. My
object is to put before the country and before this House the amendments that we
think fair. I have done that, and it is for
this Government and for the Imperial
Government to accept these amendments and
incorporate them in the Bill, or take the responsibility of rejecting them.

The question this Government was then
faced with was whether Land Purchase in
Northern Ireland should be completed or
whether it should be deferred. We had to
make up our mind on the one side or the
other, and after the most serious consideration, although it severely tried the
finances of this Province, we agreed to
accept the liability, which amounted to
£45,000 a year, in order toyplace those
tenants who had not bought in the past, and
many of whom had opportunities of buying
in the past, in the position of their more
favoured brethren who had accepted the
terms of the Wyndham Act and had purchased their tenancies under that Act
voluntarily.
The argument of the Imperial Government
in respect of this liability which they imposed
upon us was this. We have transferred to you
the Land Purchase Annuities amounting to
£600,000 a year, which, however, unfortunately
are ear-marked for a great many liabilities
and all the charges arising from the transfer
of land must be borne by the Northern
Government from this source. That deals
with the first part of the subject embodied
in the Motion. I refer now to the second
part of the Motion which deals with the
general question; that is to say the advantages
on the one hand and the disadvantages on the
other which the hon. Member for Antrim
(Mr. G. Henderson) has gone into with so
much particularity. I do not propose to
follow the hon. Member in all the minute
calculations he has submitted. I doubt if
hon. Members who listened to him could
follow them, although I am bound to give
him this credit-that he is in full possession
of all the arguments that can be used pro
or con and has studied this question with an
assiduity with which so far as I know no
other inhabitant of Northern Ireland has
approached the subject.
Let me state the advantages on the one
hand and the disadvantages on the other
that arise to the farmer and to the landlord respectively. Before I do so I should
like to state the general principle on which
this Bill was passed. As the House is
aware, the Imperial Government, being hard
pressed by us from time to time to complete
land purchase in Northern Ireland, established a Committee with a view of considering the question and, if possible, bringing
it to an issue. In the Preamble to Lord
Eustace Percy's Committee's Report it states
the basis on which they proceeded, and it
may be for the information of the House if
I read very shortly indeed the entire basis
of the Bill.
Since all parties are agreed that land
purchase should be completed at the
earliest possible moment, compulsion is required as a means, not so much of coercion,
as of automatic adjustment. There is,
therefore, no reason why the introduction
of compulsion should materially alter the
basis of purchase. On the contrary, such
an alteration would be manifestly unfair,
as discriminating between estates sold before 1909 under the favourable financial
terms offered by the Wyndham Act and
estates where sale was arrested after that
date when less favourable terms were
substituted by the Birrell Act.
In other words, the Committee had made
up its mind that it would proceed to the
most favourable period when land was transferred from the landlord to the tenant-that
was under the Wyndham Act.
This was recognised by the Convention, and
we, in our turn, have confined ourselves to
the consideration how best the principles
of land purchase previously laid down and
unanimously accepted by the Convention
can be adapted to the circumstances of the
moment.
In view of what we have already said
about the nature of the compulsion which
it is now proposed to introduce, it is evident, that a compulsory scheme should, as
far as possible, be based on the general
assent of both landlords and tenants. Such
assent was secured by the agreement embodied in the Convention Report and we
believe that it would be contrary to the
interest of both parties to throw the whole
question of land purchase once more into
the melting pot. The effect of any such
action would necessarily be to postpone indefinitely a solution which, by common consent, is urgently required. We have, therefore, adopted the Convention Report as the
basis of our deliberations.
It must be clear from what I have read that
the whole basis of this Bill which is at
present before the Imperial Parliament is
the Report which was issued by Lord
MacDonnell's Committee in the Irish Convention. At that time landlord and tenant.
without a dissentient voice, agreed that that
was a fair and equitable settlement of the
entire question. It has been regarded so.
ever since, and until the Free State passed
its recent Act giving bonus terms out of
all proportion to the previous Acts of Parliament there never had been anv question
raised by tenant or by landlord that the
conditions which were embodied in the Convention Report were unfair, unjust, or inequitable.
But let us examine for a moment what the
results embodied in the Measure are in
respect of the tenant on the one hand and
the landlord on the other. The tenant gets

I honestly support this Motion because I
believe that the Bill is unjust, unfair, and
inequitable. In my opinion the best test of
legislation is does it satisfy the requirements
and the wishes of the people for whom that
legislation is passed. At the negotiation of
the Irish Treaty with the Free State and at
the passing of the Government of Ireland
Act of 1920 all the tenants in Ireland were in
exactly the same position. To-day we find the
tenant in the Free State with a reduction
of 7s. in the pound and the tenant in Northern Ireland with a reduction of 3s. 7d. in the
pound. But apart from all juggling with
figures the test of any legislation is how it
is received by the people for whom it is
passed. There has not been a dissentient
voice in the Free State. The tenants
in the Free State have accepted it as a just
and equitable answer to their claim, and I
know, particularly within this last few weeks,
and in the only county where this Bill was
put to the test. in the only county not
directly affected by the Border at the election, that county returned a representative
who stood on his opposition to this Bill and
on no other question. I know that the tenant
farmers of County Antrim and of the Six
Counties generally have received this Bill
with absolute disgust and contempt.

at a loss to know in which way I should vote.
I have heard my hon. Friend, the Member
for Antrim (Mr. Henderson) put before us
the case for the unbought tenants, and I
have heard the Prime Minister tell us that
if this Motion is carried the Bill in the
Imperial Parliament will be lost. That is
rather an awkward position for one who is
not very well experienced in agricultural
matters, but my position must be this, that
my hon. Friend, the Member for Antrim,
was the only candidate that went forward on
the ticket of the unbought tenants, and the
unbought tenants returned him to this Parliament. Therefore, I must take it that he has
a mandate from the unbought tenants, and I
must support the Motion. I must support
the Motion even although the Prime Minister
tells us that this Bill will be lost if the
Motion is carried. I must support the
Motion, because I believe that the unbought
tenants are suffering from a very serious
grievance in so far as they have not been put
on as good terms as their fellow-farmers in
the Free State. Those are the reasons why
I support the Motion that has been so very
ably moved by my hon. Friend, the Member
for Antrim.

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move a reduction in
this Vote of £100. I do so to call attention
to the anomalous position occupied by the
old-age pensioners in Northern Ireland.
During the debate on the Address in reply to
the King's speech, we on these benches did
our very best to get some assurance from the
Government that they would grant to the oldage pensioners here the same benefits as are
granted in Great Britain. During the progress of that debate the Minister of Finance
made a statement in the course of which he
said that, so far as the abolition of the thrift
disqualification Clause was concerned, to
carry out the policy that had been adopted
in Great Britain would involve an expenditure of £350,000 a year on this province. Since
then, in answer to a question, the right hon.
Gentleman has said that he was slightly in
error. Possibly I may be able to point out
how far he was in error in that connection.
You will remember that he said it would
cost this province £350,000 a year to abolish
the thrift disqualification Clause. In submitting his answer yesterday, he pointed out
that the number of pensioners in receipt of
a reduced rate of pension was 3,569 being
divided in the following way. People in
receipt of a pension of 8s per week, 1,259. To
give those people the full pension would
mean an addition of 2s each, which if you
work it out, you will find would involve an
expenditure of £6,546. There are 1,358
persons in receipt of a pension of 6s per week.
To add the 4s that those 1,358 persons should
get per week would cost us £14,123 per year.
There are three persons in receipt of 5s per
week; that would involve on the English basis
an expenditure of £39. There are 734 persons in receipt of a pension of 4s per week,
which upon the 10s per week basis would
involve an expenditure of £11,450. There are
178 persons in receipt of a pension of 2s per
week, which on the 10s per week basis, would
work out at £3,802 per annum. There are
37 persons in receipt of a pension of one
shilling per week, and if those persons were
in receipt of a pension of 10s per week it
would involve an expenditure of £872 per
annum. Add those totals together and you
will find that instead of the £350,000
mentioned by the right hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Pollock) it would involve an expenditure of £36,832. One wonders if the finances
of Northern Ireland are carried on in this
way for everything. For the right hon.
Gentleman to get up in this House and make
a statement-

The
PRIME MINISTER: I very readily
rise to answer the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin). The explanation I may
say has been given in this House on former
occasions when he was not present, but it
will be within the recollection of the House
that the whole matter resolved itself into
a question of our finances. When the Act of
1920 was passed it was understood and hoped
by everyone in Ulster that Ulstermen and
women would be able to maintain the same
level, the same standard of living as across
the water, and as I have frequently said I
felt quite confident that Ulster would never
have accepted the Act of 1920 had anything
otherwise been the intention. After granting
a different status to the Free State the complicated question of finance between Great
Britain and Northern Ireland became more
acute, and during the past four years my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) and my
colleagues and myself have been anxiously
pursuing with the British Government the
whole question of how it could be
standardised in such a way that each year
there should issue to Northern Ireland
sufficient funds to enable us to pay old age
pensioners, unemployment insurance, and
other matters on exactly the same scale as
prevails in Great Britain.
That has been our whole battle with the
Treasury across the Channel. Up to a few
days ago, when the Colwyn Committee
reported, we were in considerable doubt as
to our financial position, and at the present
moment the Colwyn Committee report has
been called in question as to certain phraseology, and until a determination of that
phraseology has been reached between the
representatives of the Treasury on the Joint
Exchequer Board and my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Pollock) and his advisers it is still impossible for this House to quite understand
how our financial position stands. But over
There is this heavy weight hanging upon
our finances, and I repeat again as soon as
the determination of the financial side between my right hon. Friend and the Treasury
Members on the Joint Exchequer Boardwhen these are settled up and we are able to
get down to bedrock with regard to our
finances the first consideration of my
colleagues and myself shall be to see how far
we can go to meet this question of the oldage pensions. We are most anxious that at
the first possible moment we shall be able to
assure the old people in our midst that
they are to be treated no worse than if they
lived in another part of Great Britain and
Northern Ireland. It is quite impossible to
go any further without plunging into something which we do not know how to meet
from the financial point of view. It is all
very well for the hon. Member
Belfast to come here
and
a plea of that .kind.

Certain queries have been drawn up, very
sympathetic queries, and ones which are certainly easier to answer than the queries have
been in the past. These are sent down to the
applicant, who is in many cases illiterate, in
many cases helpless and completely uneducated, very often unable to understand, and
unable, perhaps, to get the necessary advice
and the information that is needed. If these
sub-Committees are to continue in existence
I feel the only remedy for the present state
of affairs is that there should be in attendance at the meetings a representative of the
Ministry, in order that that representative
might hear the evidence as it is given, the
pros and the cons, and that he might get all
the local colour, and not merely have to read
the evidence submitted by the pensions
officer. At the present I feel that the old-age
pensioner who cannot produce a birth certificate is not getting fair play.
Then in the decision of these cases too much
consideration is given to the question of
whether an applicant is living with compassionate friends who have taken pity on him
or her, and too much consideration is given
to the amount of food given in that particular
house or cottage. The applicant is very often
decided against. He is penalised because he
has friends or relations, not necessarily near
relations, who happen to be compassionate.
Not only are the applicants penalised, but the
compassionate friend is also penalised, because the State will not help him, and he has
to continue to keep the poor man or woman,
or else see him or her starve. I would like
to emphasise this point about the Pensions
Committees, because I do hope that something
might be done to have representatives of the
Ministry at these local sub-committees. I feel
that that would give power to the sub-committees, or possibly to the sub-committees
and the Government, to deal satisfactorily
with the old-age pensioners.
There is another point I would like to raise
on these Estimates, and that is that where
there is difficulty of obtaining proof as to
age. When eventually, although the birth
certificate may not be available the

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): As I am the Minister
responsible for the administration of the
Old Age Pensions Act perhaps the Committee
will allow me to say a few words on some of
the points raised by hon. Members. If I may
say so, I think a certain amount of misunderstanding exists as to the working of the
Old Age Pensions Act. There are no fewer
than eighty Pension Committees of a most
democratic character established throughout
the Six Counties. Those are brought into
being and appointed by the local County
Councils, and they in turn appoint the Pensions Sub-Committees who investigate each
case. If an applicant thinks that he or she
is entitled to the old age pension they get
the necessary form and go to the pensions
officer, who is entitled and bound to give
them every help and assistance in filling upthat form. The case then comes before the
Committee and they adjudicate on it. Now
it has been sugested here that, unless an applicant produces a birth certificate, the application will be turned down on account of
want of proof. That is not so. Very, very
often it is difficult for these old people to
get a birth certificate, but if the birth certificate cannot be obtained they may fall back
upon other means. For instance, it may be
possible to get a marriage certificate, or very
often these old people have insured themselves in one or other of the different
societies from time to time. That is another
way in which proof of age can be supplied.

CLASS II. No. 7.
GRANTS TO LOCAL AUTHORITIES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £369,334 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during the
year ending on the 31st March, 1926, to
provide for grants to local authorities in
respect of Health, Housing, etc., and in
relief of local rates, including a Grant in
Aid (9 and 10 Geo. V., c. 45; 13 and 14 Geo.
V., cc. 30 and 31 (N.I.)) (Note.-£122,000
has been voted on account.)
Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I desire to
move a reduction of this Vote by £18,000.
I refer to page 78, paragraph "T."
I see
from the Estimates that the Government propose to vote a sum of £18,000 to assist the
Fermanagh County Council to erect two
bridges at Lough Erne. I have no desire to
recapitulate the arguments that have been
applied in various other directions. When
I was speaking in connection with old age
pensions I had this matter in my mind
when I stated that the Government was
spending money on other, purposes which
could very well be utilised for old age
pensions. I do suggest this is an extravagant
waste of public money. I have not had the
opportunity, as the Prime Minister had, of
touring the Border, but I believe there is no
justification for the erection of these two
bridges. I believe it would be possible by
entering the Free State to do all the Government propose to do with these two bridges.
One of the bridges proposed is from
Boa Island to the mainland, and the other
is at Rosscor.
The CHAIRMAN: Do I understand the
hon. Member proposes a reduction of the
Vote by £18,000 or to omit a particular item
amounting to £18,000?
Mr. W. McMULLEN: A reduction.
The CHAIRMAN: A reduction of the Vote.
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: The Border is in
the melting pot at the moment. As this
Committee is aware the Boundary Commission is now sitting. What the decision of
the Commission may be is in the lap of the
gods.
If the decision is to transfer Feriranagh into the Free State, I suggest it
would be an extravagant waste of public
money so far as this Government is concerned, and consequently there is no justification for the spending of this £18,000 in
view of the fact that we could profitably
use this £18,000 in Belfast for effecting reforms which are very inuch needed. Probably on the adjournment of the House, if
we have the opportunity this afternoon, we
shall be able to indicate ways by which this
sum of £18,000 could be more profitably spent
than in erecting two bridges over Lough
Erne. In my opinion, they are not required
at all, and I believe there is no justification
for them in view of the sittings of the
Boundary Commission at the moment, The
Commission may make alterations and if
they do recommend such changes and the
British Government give effect to them-I
believe they have no alternative but to give
effect to their decisions-it will mean that
money of the citizens of Northern Ireland
to the extent of £18,000 will be absolutely
wasted on the erection of two unnecessary
bridges.
I, therefore, want to condemn the Government for perpetuating the idea by the erection of these two bridges that the Border
is going to be in any way permanent. Even
if it is going to be permanent I do not believe it is a wise policy for the Government
to adopt. This Government should try to
encourage intercourse between the people of
Northern and Southern Ireland. It is not
in the interest of the people of Northern Ireland that we should have more bridges on
this artificial Boundary than ere in existence. If we give the people in the Free State
the impression that sooner than enter their
territory we are prepared to erect bridges for
the purpose of confining all our activities to
Northern Ireland the day of a better understanding with the people of the Free State
is going to be more remote than it is at the
present time. If for no other reason, the
Government deserve severe censure for not
attempting to cultivate a better feeling between the citizens of North and South. By
erecting these two bridges they are not only
wasting public money but alienating the
sympathies of the people.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: The Government, I dare say, has made a point of sending
their inspectors to see whether it is necessary that these bridges should be built,

Mr. DEVLIN: Might I ask a question before the Motion is put? Can the Chancellor
of the Exchequer inform the House when he
proposes to introduce his Budget, or has he
any statement to make in reference to the
Budget that was introduced in the British
House of Commons yesterday?
Mr. POLLOCK: Obviously it is impossible for me to make any definite arrangement as to the day on which I would present
the yearly Budget to this House. It would
appear to me that possibly that might be convenient towards the end of next week-possibly the last day of our sittings next week. In
regard to the second part of the question,
I have known for some time that the British
Government was instituting inquiries as to
the possibility of a consolidation of the
different forms of public relief in the country, but I have no knowledge of the details
except such as appeared in the public Press
this morning. I have ordered investigations
to be made to see how far the general outline of the scheme can be made applicable to
Northern Ireland. When the result of my
investigations is known possibly I may be
able to make some definite statement to the
House in regard to our position. In the
meantime, as the hon. Member (Mr. Devlin)
can no doubt realise, the position is too indefinite, and the explanation given by the
Chancellor is of such a character that no
definite answer can be given in respect of
the future position.

not see his way to open a branch Exchange

owing to the economy in administration being
carried out by him. To-day during the sitting of this House I asked the Members, both
on the Government side and the Opposition
side, if they had seen economy carried out.
We have not, and I have cast my vote against
the Estimates.
But here is a case in point where flesh and
blood are going to be made the victims of
economy. We have in the city of Belfast a
big army of unemployed. We have an army
of unemployed men, and we have an army of
unemployed women, girls and boys. We provide for the men five exchanges, and we provide for the women, girls and boys only one.
That Exchange was set up at the time the
Insurance Act brought in women workers.
I believe I speak correctly when I say—I
stand to be corrected if my figures are not
just right-that we have 23,500 odd men unemployed and registered at the five Exchanges. This means that a little over 4,000
are allocated to each Exchange. We have in
the women's section, which also includes girls
and boys, over 8,000 unemployed. We have
also to add to that short-time workers, and
from information I have received they total
well over 5,000, making a total of 13,000 unemployed persons depending on one Exchange against 29,500 men for five Exchanges. I do not know whether hon. Members opposite have ever had the experience
of attending the Amelia Street Exchange.
If they have not, I would advise them to go
there some Tuesday or Friday morning
and perhaps they
will
come back with a

have seen herded together in one flat where

have been compelled through no fault of their
own to sign on at the Labour Exchange and
attend there for payment packed like herrings
in a barrel-so close together that they could
not actually move. You would think to see
them standing they were cemented together,

experience I have seen women who fainted,

to attend this Exchange in order to get the

am sure the Minister of Labour will agree,

room. I know you cannot make this place

a serious matter, on a very wet morning,
for them to have to walk such an enormous
distance, through perhaps snow and rain. I
will not detain the House by going into the
matter as fully as my hon. Friends have done.
They have placed before you a considerable
number of facts and figures. I simply wish
to impress upon the Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews) that it is absolutely necessary that
these women should have a place where they
can go and register much more easily than
they are able to do at the present time.
have great pleasure in supporting my hon.
Friends.

THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
ANDREWS): I take it that the object of the
question asked me yesterday by the hon Member for East Belfast (Mr. Reattie) was with
a view to relieving the congestion at Amelia
Street. I think he forgets that in my answer
I very clearly stated that I felt that I had
taken the best means under the existing conditions of relieving that congestion by asking
these unemployed women only to sign once, at
the time they drew their benefit, instead of,
as previously, twice or even oftener in each
week. I quite admit that the Amelia Street
Exchange is not as I would like to see it. I
would point out to my hon. Friend the Member for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie) that at the
present time we are building, at a cost of over
£40,000, a central Exchange, on a site chosen
by the Site Committee of the Local Employment Committee in Belfast. I am glad to
think that my hon. Friend was a member of
that Site Committee, and, therefore, I am
certain that he thought that the site which
was chosen would be one which would
be most convenient not only for the
unemployed persons of East Belfast, but for
the workers of the whole City. For these
reasons I do not see that it is necessary
that I should comply with his request under
existing conditions, and so put the funds at
the disposal of the Department to the expense
of opening an Exchange for women in East
Belfast. If I did so I would no doubt be
faced with similar requests from other parts
of the City. (Hon. Members: Hear,hear.)
My hon. Friends all laid a good deal of
stress on the point that there were five
Exchanges for men and only one for women.
At first sight it would seem that there was
some point in that contention; but, on the
other hand, there are only about 8,000 women,
who are dealt with at Amelia Street, while
in the other Exchanges, taking them collectively, we are dealing with over 23,000 men.
But there is another great difficulty.
women are only being asked to sign at
present once in the week, while the men are
being asked to sign far more frequently-in
some cases every day, and in the case of
casual workers often more than once a day.

Oral Answers to Questions.
EARLY CLOSING ACTS IN SMALLER
TOWNS.
1. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs if the Rural
District Councils, as the administrative
authority, have powers to enforce the Early
Closing Acts in the smaller towns, and to
make compulsory the weekly half-holiday
where two-thirds of the shopkeepers in a
town are in favour of the proposal, and if
these authorities have not these powers would
he consider the advisability of granting them
at an early date.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): Rural District Councils have
no functions under the Shops Act of 1912. In
towns within rural districts which have
town commissioners, the commissioners may
make an order fixing a weekly half-holiday,
subject to the Order being confirmed by the
Minister of Home Affairs
The suggestion of the hon. Member as to
the extension of the Act will require careful
consideration, and so far there has been no
general demand for the extension of the Act
to rural districts.

Election of Senators.
SPEAKER'S
ANNOUNCEMENT.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have an announcement
to make to the House in regard to the
election of two Senators. This is the first
occasion upon which such an election has
been contested, and under the Order in
Council issued by His Majesty's Government
in 1921, it is laid down that an election of
such Senators shall be held in such manner
as may be provided by regulations or
directions made or given by the House of
Commons of Northern Ireland, or (in the
absence of or subject to regulations or
directions so made or given) by the Speaker.
I propose, therefore, with the approval of
the House, to conduct the voting on the same
system as is carried out in the case of Members elected by a university to Parliament.
That is to say, voting cards will be sent round
to every Member of this House, and he will
then mark his vote upon them, sign themthe signature will have to be witnessed-and
return them to my office at the specified
time.
If that meets with the approval of the
House, I propose to carry out the election on
that system.
The House signified its assent.

Supply-
Committee.
30 APRIL 1925
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I feel that it is only when introducing the annual Estimates of the Ministry
of Labour that I have the opportunity of
making a general statement as regards the
Work which the Department exists to perform. On this occasion we have with us
several new Members, and I think I shall,
therefore, as carefully as possible explain to
hon, Members how wide the ramifications of
the Ministry of Labour are and how closely
they are associated with the well-being of our
people. We administer all those great Acts
of Parliament which safeguard the interests
of our working classes from the day that they
enter employment until they leave it. These
Acts are first of all the Unemployment
Insurance Acts, which apply to and affect
aver 260,000 persons; our Health Insurance
Act, which affects over 330,000 persons; the
Trade Boards Act, which affects rather over
62,000 persons, and our Factory Acts,
Truck Acts, and Workmen's Compensation
Acts, which really affect our entire community. In addition to that the Department
administers our relief schemes throughout
the whole of Northern Ireland, and the importance of these works is well known to the
Committee.
But the most important duty, I think, that
we are called upon to perform is to endeavour
to preserve industrial peace, so far as is
possible, by encouraging friendly co-operation between our employers and their
workers. For convenience the Department
is divided into four branches. First of all,
there is the industrial relations section
which deals with labour disputes, administers our Trade Boards Acts, our
Factory and Truck Acts, and Workmen's
Compensation Acts. Secondly, we have our
Insurance Department which deals with the
two Insurance Acts, to which I have already
referred, and which so closely affect the
interests of the workers of Northern Ireland.
Then we have the Inspection branch, the
importance of which I am sure will be readily
recognised, because there is no use in this
Parliament or any other Parliament passing
Acts if they are to become a dead letter, and
our Inspection branch exists to see that Acts
of Parliament in Northern Ireland are complied with by all those who are called upon
by those Acts to do so. Then we have the
Finance branch which is responsible for disbursing the large sum of somewhat over
£3,000,000 a year and doing all the accounting work in connection with those
disbursements, which hon. Members know
are mainly in small sums, and therefore
require to be dealt with with very great
care.
If hon. Members will refer to Sub-head A
of this Vote which is on page 79 they will see
the sum set cut for salaries, wages and
allowances is £161,780. That sum at first
sight, I admit, looks substantial. It is satisfactory to note that there is a small reduction of £1,470 as compared with last year, but
it is quite easy to calculate that after all it
is only five per cent. of the total sum disbursed by the Department, and from that
viewpoint I think it can be looked upon as
very reasonable as an administrative charge.
After all, the sum which the Exchequer is
called upon to bear is a comparatively small
one, because if hon. Members refer to Subhead V they will see that receipts appropriated in aid which are paid almost entirely
by our Unemployment Fund amount to
£117,405, so as I have said the difference is,
comparatively speaking, a small sum which
the Exchequer bears. This Estimate at first
sight would appear to show an increase for
the year of £25,085, but I think it is fair to
deduct from that sum the increase in nonrecurring capital expenditure of £10,200,
which is the increased sum provided this
year over last year for our new Centra
Employment Exchange. In addition to that,
hon. Members will observe that the
appropriation in aid amounts to £18,150 less
than last year. Of course, that figure is
really settled by statute. It is the contribu
tion towards administrative expenses from
the income derived from the contributions
paid by workers, employers and the State,
and is a matter over which the Department
has really no control. If these two sums are
added together it will be found that they
amount to £28,350, and if the £25,085 increase is deducted from that it will show
that there really is an actual saving on the
year of £3,265 in connection with this Vote.
I think hon. Members will be interested to
know that 90 per cent. of our administrative
expenditure is due to our insurance schemes.
For all the other services which we administer there is only an expenditure of ten
per cent., so that if the suggestion is made
that there is extravagance of any kind, which
I do not admit, it will have to be looked for
in my opinion in connection with these
insurance schemes. I would, however, like
to inform the Committee at the same time
that our Unemployment Insurance Acts
actually absorb rather over 74 per cent of the
total cost. I have had a comparison made
between the cost here and the cost in Great
Britain, and I venture to think that it is
highly satisfactory, because while the
administrative cost in Great Britain is 8.1
per cent., in Northern Ireland it is 8.6 per
cent. The trifling difference, of course, is
due to the fact that we are a smaller unit,
and necessarily the percentage of expenditure is somewhat more, but after all, as I
have stated, it is really only trifling.
I have no hesitation in saying that my
opinion, for what it is worth, is that the
Ministry of Labour is run as a business
undertaking and along business lines, and I
can assure hon, Members that we are con-
Supply-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Andrews]
tinually keeping before us economy coupled
with efficiency. There is no use in beginning.
I think, to cheesepare unduly in connection with the administration of Acts of
Parliament which so closely affect the wellbeing of our people as do the Acts of Parliaments which the Ministry of Labour
administers, because it is all-important
that those who are depending on
Unemployment benefit or Health Insurance
benefit for their very existence when
they are out of employment, either through
depression in trade or through ill-health,
should get what the law entitles them to get
as expeditiously as possible. Therefore, an
efficient, able and sufficient staff is necessary
to ensure that that shall be so, and it is gratifying to me to feel that complaints as regards
delay in the payment of benefit, no matter
what kind that benefit may be, are very much
fewer than they were when this Parliament
came into existence.
I say that an important State Department
such as this is run by many willing and able
workers, some of them greater and some of
them lesser, but each of them entitled to feel
that he is part of a great machine and provided he does his allotted duty faithfully
and well is entitled to claim his share of
any credit that may be earned. On the other
hand, charges to be made as regards extravagance or inefficiency should be levelled against
the man who for the time being is the
political head of the Department and who is
alone answerable to Parliament.
In conclusion, I would just like to say that
my Department continues to be deeply
indebted to those public-spirited persons
throughout the whole of Northern Ireland
who are co-operating with us and helping us
to carry on the work of the Department.
I would not like to end without saying that
it is very gratifying to me and to my
associates at the Ministry of Labour to feel
that the employers and workers in Northern
Ireland are taking more advantage of our
Employment Exchanges than ever they did
before, and that both sections of our
industrial community are co-operating in
the most friendly and helpful way with my
Department in every possible line of our
work. I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move a reduction
of £2,000 in the Estimate as presented. I do
so to call the attention of this Committee to
a fund that needs the protection of this
Committee. It is a fund established for the
benefit of the industrial classes. It is contributed to by employer, by employee, and
by the State, and for that reason I think
there should be no burden placed upon this
fund that it is very well able to do without.
After hearing the Minister of Labour's outline of the work of the various Departments
I do not wish to say one word against him as
the head of his Department, but I do want
to counsel him-if I am able enough to advise him-in regard to certain units of his
Department wherein economy can be brought
about. I find on going over the Estimate
that the rent of the various Exchanges when
they are combined total a very decent rum.
At the time when the Minister of Labour
(Mr. Andrews) was looking out for Exchanges the profiteers were on the warpath
and were claiming the highest possible
figures for the buildings the Minister wanted
to get to carry on his work. I refer to one
case with which I am quite conversant,
namely the Mountpottinger Y.M.C.A. The
Mountpottinger Y.M.C.A. has done very well
out of the Unemployment Fund in regard to
rent. I believe that not very long ago the
Minister was compelled to have a new entrance to that Exchange, and there was a
very large sum put on to the rent. I believe
anything from £7 10s. to £10 per week was
put on the rent for that entrance or outlet
for applicants to sign at the Y.M.C.A. Of
course, the figures I give you are not accurate, but anything from £7 10s. to £10 was
the cost of the new entrance to the Y.M.C.A.
I agree that it was necessary, but I do not
think the figure the Y.M.C.A. is charging
the Government is a decent one.
Sure you
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON:
wanted a new Exchange there the other day.
Mr. BEATTIE: Yes, I was asking for an
Exchange in Ballymacarrett, and I think it
is more necessary to-day than ever it was,
but I am not asking to go to the class of
landlord to whom the Minister of Labour
has gone in the past so that he may be robbed

him. I believe it is the duty of the landlord

and not at the exorbitant figures they are
charging for the buildings we are in. Turning over the Estimate I find employees who
are contributors to this fund, and I am surprised that in this Department employees
are not treated on an equality with other Departments. I would have been the first to
say that the best treatment would have been
accorded to employees in the Minister of
Labour's Department, but I am sorry and
surprised on looking over the Estimate to
find that they are not.
Some hon. Members opposite always tackle
the big fellows first, and go for the high
figures, but I, being a layman and a working
class representative, am coming right down
to bedrock. I ask the Minister of Labour, and
I hope he will answer, why the cleaners in

consideration as the cleaners in other Departments. Is a Labour Exchange not
harder to clean out than an office? Is it not
more laborious work cleaning an Exchange
out after three or four thousand people
have tramped over it than cleaning out an

over it? I say that the work of the cleaners

the case of Mrs. Lynass, a winder, in the
