It was quite a common thing to
bring little children with their migrated
fathers and mothers from the country places
into this great industrial centre. and compel
them by the force of necessity and by our industrial and economic conditions to work in
our mills and factories on what was known as

women workers than any other Constituency of the British Parliament. It was my
duty to take an interest in them. They were
the most defenceless of the community. I used

Motion made, and Question proposed:
That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session to establish a Pharmaceutical Society in Northern Ireland, and to
regulate the qualifications and provide for
the annual licensing of Pharmaceutical
Chemists, Chemists and Druggists, and
Druggists in Northern Ireland, and to amend
and extend the Law with respect to the sale
of poisons, and for other purposes incidental
thereto, it is expedient to authorise a charge
upon moneys provided by Parliament in respect of the salary of the Registrar and the
Inspector to be appointed under any such
Act, and any expenses of either of those
officers and of the Minister of Home Affairs
and Ministry of Home Affairs under any
such Act, to such amount as may be approved
by the Ministry of Finance.
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN
CIAL SECRETARY OF THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): The only
financial point requiring the consideration of
this Committee will be found in Clause 26
(1) of the Pharmacy and Poisons Bill, which
provides for a charge on Votes of the salaries
of two officers, viz., the Registrar and the
Inspector who are to be appointed under
Section 8 of the Bill. These officers will be
officers of the Ministry of Home Affairs and
not officers of the Society. The Resolution
also refers to expenses of the Minister of
Home Affairs and the Ministry of Home
Affairs, and in this connection I need only
explain that as the service falls within the
province of my right hon. Friend it is
necessary to include any small cost of
administration which may be incurred. Such
expense will be inconsiderable.
As regards the two officers to whom I have
referred, under Section 8 of the Bill the
of Home
power is given to the Minister
Affairs to appoint fit and proper persons to
these posts and to prescribe, subject to the
the
consent of the Ministry of Finance,
salaries which shall attach to such posts.
As the salaries have not yet been fixed, it is
not possible for me to state accurately in
terms of cash what is involved, nor can 1
yet say whether it will be possible to utilise
part of the time of existing officials to carry
out these services in lieu of creating fresh
posts. I would, however, draw the attention
of the Committee to sub-section (2) of Clause
26 which provides for a contribution from
the proceeds of the Licence Duties leviable
under the Bill towards these salaries up to a
maximum of one-half of the total amount of
the duty collected.
The net annual cost to the State is thereby
limited to the difference between the amount
of this contribution and the salaries which
will be paid, and as it is estimated that the
licence fees will produce an annual sum of
approximately £900, the appropriation in aid
from this source will almost if not altogether
recoup the Vote in respect of these salaries.
Attention has already been drawn in connection with the Second Reading of this Bill,
to the provision contained in sub-section (2)
of the Clause now under consideration to the
fact that the Government propose to waive
any claim to part of the licence duties for
the first two years. This concession will
leave at the disposal of the Society the whole
amount of licence duties during this period
and will lighten the burden which they will
have to bear in the initial years in connec¹
tion with certain capital expenditure to be
incurred in the provision of accommodation
and in the equipment of a laboratory.
I would further remind the Committee that
the only power the Government has taken to
levy any contribution from this Society in
subsequent years is restricted to a maximum
of one half of the total amount of the licences
collected. It will be quite within ther power
to vary that sum so as to leave further sums
at the disposal of the Society as the Minister
of Finance and the Minister of Home Affairs
may consider necessary for carrying out the
inauguration and the duties laid upon them
under this Act.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 7th May, 1925.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
LOUGH ERNE FISHERIES.
1. Mr. GRANT (for Mr. COOPER) asked
the Prime Minister, whether the question of
establishing a hatchery in the Ballycassidy,
or some other suitable river, is being considered in connection with the proposal to
improve the Fisheries in Lough Erne?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have been asked by my right hon.
Friend (the Prime Minister) to reply to this
question. Under the Government of Ireland
Act, as modified by the Irish Free State (Consequential Provisions) Act, the service in connection with fisheries is at present reserved
to the Imperial Government, and consequently the Northern Government has no
jurisdiction in the matter. The representative of the Imperial Government in Northern
Ireland dealing with the question of fisheries
is the Imperial Secretary, with whom it is
suggested that the hon. Member should
communicate.
TEACHERS IN
AMALGAMATED
SCHOOLS.
2. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education, whether, in cases of the amalgamation of two or more schools to form one
public elementary school, the Ministry
proposes to take steps to insure that all the
teachers employed in the schools which are
amalgamated shall be appointed to situations
in the new school, and guaranteed against
financial loss; or, in the alternative, shall
receive adequate compensation for loss of
office.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): In all amalgamations of schools the
interests of the existing teachers, as regards
employment and remuneration, are safeguarded.
POSITION OF JUNIOR ASSISTANT
MISTRESSES.
3. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education, if he could state the number of
Junior Assistant Mistresses in the service of
the Ministry, and if it is proposed to retain
the services of these teachers in the event of,,
the schools in which they are employed being
amalgamated or superseded by provided
schools; and, if the services of these teachers
be dispensed with, what compensation is it
proposed to award.
Mr. ROBB: There are about 600 Junior
Assistant Mistresses employed in Public'
Elementary Schools...!
Their interests, financial and other, are
safeguarded where amalgamations are carried
through by the Ministry or where a ischool
is transferred to an education authority......?
Teachers in provided schools are appointed
by the Local Education Authorities, and the
Ministry has no reason to suppose that the
claims of existing teachers will be overlooked
by these authorities.
SALARIES OF TEACHERS IN
TECHNICAL SCHOOLS.
4. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education, how
the proposed revised scale of salaries for
teachers in technical schools was arrived at,
and whether any steps were taken by the
Ministry before putting the proposed scale
in operation to consult either the county or
local technical committees, and whether, in
view of the fact that these increased salaries
are causing a great deal of dissatisfaction
throughout the Northern area, he will consider the advisability of having the whole
question of these salaries inquired into again.
Mr. ROBB: The salary scales referred to
were framed by the Ministry of Education
after consultation with the Ministry of
Finance and were issued in draft to local
technical committees several months before
they were presented to Parliament and became operative.
The Ministry is not aware that the scales
are causing dissatisfaction and it does not
propose to re-open the question.

services rendered, is penalised by the Ministry of Education for Northern Ireland to
the extent that he does not receive the same
salary as a principal in such school who has
had no army service.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
THE BUDGET.
Statement by Minister of inance
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House approves the proposals of
the Government for meeting the financial
requirements of the year."
Mr. POLLOCK: (who was received with
general cheers): In submitting a statement
of the probable revenue and expenditure of
the Province for the year on which we have
just entered, I would remind the House that
the present is the fourth successive year in
which it has been my privilege to ask
Parliament to approve of the financial proposals of the Government for meeting the
requirements of the Province.
*
I have often reminded the House of the
difficulties facing anyone placed in the
position of controller of the finances of a new
State, established under such abnormal and
novel conditions. During the passage of the
1920 Act, I foresaw those difficulties, and it
may interest the House if I read a few lines
from the report of our Ulster Committee
which was commissioned to negotiate with the
British Government the financial relations of
the two areas:-
"It cannot be questioned that there are
many unascertained liabilities (invisible
to-day) which will be discovered when new
The Budget.
The Budget.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
་
[Mr. Pollock]
Parliaments and new forms of Government
have been established in Ireland, In view
of these probabilities, it will be necessary
to provide a considerable margin for such
contingencies. We have come to the conclusion that it would not be safe for the
Irish Parliaments to undertake their new
responsibilities with a present annual
burden of obligations to the Imperial Exchequer of more than five million pounds,
representing about two millions for Ulster.
If Ireland is to be raised to the standard
of Great Britain in many departments of
her social and economic life, large initial
expenditure will necessarily be required, and
our considered opinion is that the period
during which the nominal contribution is
made should be agreed upon as five years
from the appointed day. The probationary
period of two years provided in the Bill is,
in our judgment, entirely insufficient for
the establishment of the new Parliamentary institution on a solid foundation."
Sir, had this view carried any weight with
the Government, we should not have had the
long and irritating controversies with the
Treasury on new situations arising from time
to time. These controversies culminated at
the end of 1922, when the Chancellor of the
day, Mr. Baldwin, offered to submit outstanding financial questions to arbitration,
reserving certain subjects for direct discussion with the Government, such as the
cost of the Special Constabulary. This was
agreed to by our Government, and a Committee was constituted with Lord Colwyn as
Chairman.
.
This Committee has functioned for a
period of almost two years, and as the House
is aware, has published two reports, the final
one being now in the hands of hon. Members.
The Interim Report which was issued towards the end of 1923 dealt with the contribution of Northern Ireland to Imperial
Services for the first two complete financial
years of her autonomous existence whilst the
Final Report has laid down the general lines
on which the contribution for further
period of five years should be determined.
a
I am pleased at this point to assure the
House that apart from the obligations of the
two great burdens of Unemployment Insurance and Special Constabulary, which are
now in process of solution, the general
finances of the Province are in a perfectly
sound condition." (Hon. Members: Hear.
hear)
The House will no doubt expect from me
an interpretation of the main principles
governing the findings of the Committee,
whose report has been So long and 80
anxiously awaited. Let me say, by way of
preface, that the report as it stands gives
no idea of the extended arguments which
took place before the Committee. The
Treasury was represented by its very ablest
advocates, and certainly that is saying a
good deal. I am delighted to say that the
formula set out on Page 5 of the report is
virtually word for word that which was submitted by Northern Ireland.
With this preface, let me endeavour to
wake clear in simple language the effect
of the Committee's findings.
The principle underlying the decision of
the Committee is that Northern Ireland's
total expenditure on local services should
be admitted to keep pace with the
total expenditure of Britain on an equivalent basis per head of the population, that
is, if Great Britain increased her local
expenditure by 10s. per head of her poplation, we in Northern Ireland can do the
same.
This basis of calculation on our relative
populations tends very greatly to simplicity
and gives us much greater flexibility in our
administration, but when applied to individual cases it proves sometimes to our
advantage and sometimes much to the contrary. For example, we have, owing to
emigration of young Ulster people in the
latter part of the last century, been left
with a number of old people out of all
proportion to those in Great Britain, so
that legislation in regard to Old Age Pensions becomes relatively far more burdensome when applied to Northern Ireland.
On the other hand, the formula proves to
our advantage in many cases and, on the
whole, I am satisfied that it is to the
benefit of Northern Ireland that its Parliament should get the freedom which is conferred by a general basis of calculation and
which it would not secure if it were feasible, which I doubt, to make a separate
equitable calculation in each particular
case.
But in order to give this principle practical effect, it is necessary to have a starting
point, from a normal revenue and expenditure basis. For this purpose, the year
1923-24 was agreed as suitable, this being
the second complete year of our financial
existence.
I do not wish to labour my explanation
too much and therefore a practical example
of the working of the principle may convey
more clearly to the House its effect on our
accounts.

I now leave the year that has gone by with

I must rely on the officers of the Imperial

amounts to be expended on its collection.
The Imperial Chancellor has introduced
changes in the taxation of the country
which have an important bearing on our
revenues. The results are as follow:-
In the domain of Customs and Excise, possibly hon. Members may have noticed that
the Imperial Chancellor has introduced an
increased Imperial preference on sugar,
tobacco, dried fruits, etc., from the
Dominions. The loss resulting from that
concession to the Dominions amounts in our
caso this year that we have entered upon
to £29,000, and in a full year we shall suffer
to the extent of £34,000.
On the other hand, the re-imposition of
the M'Kenna duties, which have been greatly
in the public eye for some considerable
time means an addition to our revenue
estimated for this year at £24,000, and in a
full year they should produce £40,000.

It is proposed by the Chancellor to impose a tax on silk and artificial silk. That
is expected to produce in our Province a
sum of £60,000 this year, and if we were
dealing with a full year it is expected that
it would amount to £105,000.
A duty on hops has also been imposed by
the Chancellor of the Exchequer, from which
we expect to obtain a revenue of £5,000 this
year and £9,000 in a full year.
The totals of the increases and decreases
in Customs and Excise show that cur reve
nue will benefit this year to the extent of
£60,000, while in a full year the result would
be an increase of £120,000.
Now, I turn to the changes in Inland
Revenue. I am sure hon. Members know
that the Chancellor of the Exchequer has
proposed a reduction in the standard rate
of income tax of 6d in the £. That means
a loss to our revenue in this year of
£176,000, and in the full year we shall lose
£106,500. I hope hon. Members will appreciate therefore that every shilling of change
in income tax means a difference one way or
the other, according as it goes up or down,
of £800,000 a year.
In addition the Chancellor proposes an
increased allowance in respect of earned incomes, including an allowance to certain
taxpayers over 65 years of age in respect of
investment income. That means a loss to
us of £34,000 this year, and of £83,500 in
a full year.
The super tax reduction proposed in the
lower ranges means a loss to us of £55,000
this year, and of £85,000 in a full year.
Totalling these changes in Inland Revenue
matters, we find that we suffer this year
in our revenue from this source a loss of
£265,000, and in a full year, when they
become operative, we should lose £575,000.
Taking Customs and Excise and Inland
Revenue together, the decrease in all those
reserved taxes is £205,000 this year, with a
prospective loss in a full year of £455,000.

HOUSING.
: turn now to a subject which 'has been
exercising the minds of the Government for
some time. I refer to the important question
of housing. In speaking at this table on my
Budget Statement last year I stated
that a very acute shortage of houses,
principally of the class suitable for the wage
earners still exists." As hon. Members are
aware, two Housing Acts in the years 1923
and 1924, which gave the Government
authority to make a payment of £60 to local
authorities and private builders for each
house built according to the specified
standard offered a considerable stimulus to
those who were willing to resume building
operations.
The Government has no reason, I venture
to say, to be ashamed of the efforts which
it has put forward towards a solution of this
problem. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Under these recent Acts, up to the present
time, 885 houses, have been approved by the
Ministry of Home Affairs in connection with
schemes formulated by local authorities, and
of this number about 100, have been completed. In addition to this, however, the
records of the Ministry of Home Affairs
indicate that schemes are in
contemplation
involving the erection of an additional 1,156
houses. Moreover, in Belfast alone, 1,129
houses have been completed during the past
two or three years by the local authority
under the unemployment relief, schemes, as
distinct from the Housing Acts to which I
have referred.
I think, therefore, that as far as the local
authorities are concerned, a very considerable advance has been made in the provision
of houses since the introduction of the two
Acts I have mentioned.

The Government regard it as a matter of
paramount importance, however, that the
private builder should be encouraged to make
some contribution to the housing question.
Certificates have already been issued and
approved by the Ministry of Home Affairs
in respect of 2,106 houses, of which 890 have
been completed by these private builders.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) In addition
to this, I am informed that a considerable
number of plans have been lodged with that
Department for further houses, and it would
appear that the rate of progress of building
is on the increase. (Hon. Members: Hear.
hear.)
I should like to remind the House, however, that the Housing Acts only apply to
Urban areas and to certain industrial centres in Rural areas, seven of which in the
Counties of Antrim, Down, Londonderry and
Tyrone, have been approved by the Ministry
of Home Affairs.
Over and above the operation of the
Housing Acts, the Rural District Councils
are empowered to carry out Housing
Schemes for the labourers in their districts,
and there are at present before the Ministry
of Home Affairs 13 schemes, involving the
erection of 1,100 cottages in the Province.
Some of my hon. Friends from the country
will realise the beneficial results, that are
likely to accrue from the figures I have
mentioned. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Notwithstanding the great improvement
which has been made in the matter of housebuilding within the last two or three years,
the Government feel that much remains to
be done if the present housing shortage is
to be substantially met. We have not yet
by a long way reached the time, I am afraid,
when the supply of houses will meet the
demand which is likely to be made..
As a measure of their interest in this subject, I may say that the Government propose
to introduce legislation before the adjourṛnment which will have the effect of expediting
building not only in urban,, but, I am glad
to say, also in rural districts. (Hon, Members: Hear, hear.)

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE.
Unemployment Insurance is still causing
the Government grave concern. The liability
is continuing to mount up at a high rate,
and we are awaiting with some anxiety the
decision of the British Cabinet Committee,
which is considering the question of the
amalgamation of the British and Ulster
Funds. I don't think it is necessary to
enter any more fully into the question, as
the circumstances are well known to hon.
Members.
But closely allied with this subject is the
question of other forms of public relief which
has recently come very prominently to the
front.
鸞
PENSION SCHEMES.
As to the proposal which has been made
in the Imperial Parliament regarding the
new Pension Scheme, it has not been possible
to forecast what the cost would be for Northern Ireland, since the British scheme is not
yet fixed, and from the discussions which
are taking place in Westminster it would
seem as if amendments may be anticipated.
It would be wholly beyond my province,
therefore, to attempt to estimate the cost of
carrying out the full scheme in Northern
Ireland, but I am reasonably certain that,
unless some extraordinary charge is thrown
on the Exchequer other than that which it
now bears in regard to pensions and insurances, we shall be able to meet the cost by
our own resources. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I am fortified in this by the statement
of Mr. Churchill that in the first few years
the scheme would show a slight profit, so that
by the time the additional charge comes to
fall on the Government we shall have been
able to stabilise our expenditure more than
is possible at present.
With regard to Old Age Pensions, our only
hope of expansion is that the temporary
items of expenditure, such as Special Constabulary, should be eliminated from our
Budget, freeing the necessary cash, or by
resorting to borrowing. I can only say that
borrowing for expenditure of that kind is
very unsound finance, and can only be resorted to in some very extraordinary
extremity. It must be evident that vast
sums cannot be spent in two directions in
excess of our normal requirements. I wish

of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
This is a question which I think, many, Members of this House will have to think a good

two Funds were
re separated in the first

When the Devolution Scheme was proposed

that any scheme such as an unemployment insurance scheme should be kept on an
Imperial or United Kingdom basis. I think
our Government are very largely to blame

the wider the area the less the risk. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Therefore, I think
they are very much to blame in this connection.
I am sure, so far as the industrial

amalgamation of the two Funds.
In regard to the very vital question of

We want to point out to the Members of this House that private enterprise so
far as the building of houses is concerned,
has absolutely failed. Our Government now
makes a grant of £60 of public money to
every jerry builder who sets about building
houses. I have got to subscribe my quota to

You will remember he pointed out that one

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):

not followed the general custom in replying

to be congratulated on the bold way in which
he has dealt with so many of those very
difficult and complicated questions that are
applicable entirely to the working classes in
our midst. He blamed, first of all, my right
hon. Friend for paying any contribution at
all to Great Britain which means that in a

this contribution without any refusal on our

ceivable. It is gradually melting away, as

That is the long view, and that is the

Pollock) and his colleagues take. Although
it may appear to be a good electioneering cry
-and I think it has been used for that purpose it is not in the best interests of the
Ulster people on patriotic grounds that we
should demur to paying our fair share for
these services. It is not in her material
interest to introduce a system which would
prevent us from getting our just and proper

man's Budget.
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear,
The PRIME MINISTER: It is nothing of
the kind. I think my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Pollock) has picked out some super-tax
payers, certainly some of those wealthy
citizens in our midst, so that when they pass
away their estates will have to pay a much
higher scale of death duties than under the
old system. That is not taxing the poor.
It is really ridiculous that one should endeavour to split up into compartments what is
helping the rich and what is helping the poor.
If you take sixpence off the income tax imposed on men who are conducting our great
industries in Ulster, does it not obviously
follow that it will help those industries to
compete with foreign countries and to secure
more work to help the working classes in
our midst? It is appalling to see not only
chipping going to foreign countries to be
repaired, but orders 8 for the building of
ships. That was a thing which in past days
was utterly impossible, because no foreign
country could compete with the great yards
in Belfast, the Clyde, the Tyneside, and
other parts. The reason of that to a large
extent is that taxation is heavier per head
of the population in Great Britain and
Northern Ireland than it is in these foreign
countries, and that is because we have faced
manfully the paying-off of our war debt and
intend to get rid of that heavy liability in
as few years as possible. Some foreign
countries have chosen to delav tackling that
question with the result that the taxation of
their people is much lower than it is in this
country and they are able to get-that is
what it amounts to-the orders that should
be coming to Belfast and the other shipbuilding centres. This is a loss to our
working men who are strolling about our
streets drawing unemployment benefit instead of doing what they would like to do,
using the hammer and working. I think
that is an answer to the statement that this
is a Budget in favour of the richer classes.
It is a Budget which in my opinion deserves
the encomiums not only of this House but
of the whole of Ulster. My right hon.
Friend after four strenuous years is once
more able to assure us-and any assurance
he gives carries weight not only in Ulster
but elsewhere-that the financial position of
Ulster is sound, and we are proud of the
results he has produced to-day.
There is another point. The hon. Member
(Mr. Kyle) said that our representatives, referring to the representatives in the Imperial
Parliament, during the past number of
years were to blame for the fact that there
is a lower standard here than in Great
Britain. Long before the hon. Member or
any of his Party came into this House we
laid it down at this Table that our whole
ideal was that the standard amongst all
classes in Ulster should be the same as in
Great Britain, and I challenge anyone to
pick out in any quarter of the Six Counties
of Ulster where we have failed to secure
that except in the delayed action, for this is
what it amounts to, with regard to pensions
which my right hon. Friend is hoping to be
able to carry out in the autumn of this year.
With that exception-and the minute subject
of the Entertainments Tax-I think those
are the only two points-there has been no
deviation in four years from the standard
which has been set up in the British House
of Commons. I cannot think at the moment
of any other thing in which there has
been the slightest difference between a man
living here and one on the other side.

HILLSBOROUGH PARK.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether he can state if several families were turned out of their homes
in Hillsborough Park, i.e., Samuel Ginn and
family, John Ginn and family, John Herdman and family, Mr. Maddison and family,
and others; and are these homes still lying
idle and what alternative accommodation
was provided for those turned out,
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): I am informed that none of the persons mentioned in the question were turned
out of their homes in Hillsborough Park.
Arrangements were made between these persons and the previous owner of the Park,
and these arrangements were, I am informed, satisfactory to all parties. The question of providing alternative accommodation
did not arise, as I understand that each of
the persons mentioned obtained satisfactory
accommodation.
As I informed the hon. Member on the 30th
ultimo, the question of the future use of the
Park is at present under consideration by
the Government,
Mr. BEATTIE: Could the Minister inform me whether or not it is true to say
that one family received £100 compensation?
Mr. POLLOCK: I am not in a position to
make that statement, as all the arrangements
were made by the previous owners of the
property, and they did not come under our
cognizance in any way.
OLD AGE PENSION-JAMES DOHERTY,
KILREA.
3. Mr. MCALLISTER asked the Minister
for Home Affairs, whether the Local
Pensions Committec recommended James
Doherty, of Coleraine Street, Kilrea, for an
Old Age Pension on four separate occasions,
and if on appeal by the Pensions Officer, the
findings of the Local Committee were overruled on each of the four occasions on the
evidence of James Doherty's marriage certificate, wherein he was stated to be then 27
years of age, and his wife's age 25 years; and
whether the baptismal certificate of James
Doherty's wife, who has for some time been
receiving a pension certifies that she was
72 years of age on the 8th May, 1925, and
whether affidavits had been produced to show
that James Doherty is now 77 years of age.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The statement in the first
part of the question is not correct as the
Local Old Age Pension Committee on the
occasions when the successive claims of the
applicant were before them gave conflicting
decisions.
It is the fact that the marriage certificate
of this applicant gives the age of the
claimant as 27 years, and his wife as 25 years
at the time of their marriage, and according
to that certificate the claimant would now be
only 67 years of age. When the latest claim
of the applicant was before the Ministry,
there was submitted for the first time the
Baptismal Certificate of the wife, showing
that she is now 72 years of age. On the
strength of this certificate which has only
now been submitted and as the result of
special investigations which were concluded
on the 5th instant, the Ministry, on the 7th
instant, decided to allow the claim.
ELECTION MEETINGS AND TRANS-
FERRED SCHOOLS..
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Education,
whether transferred schools will be available
for all election meetings at the next and
subsequent elections in Northern Ireland?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): Under the existing regulations no
political meetings may be held in schoolhouses, nor may any political business whatso-ever be transacted therein. The Ministry
does not at present contemplate any amendment of this regulation.
Mr. KYLE: Would the Ministry consider
the alterations of those regulations at as
early a date as is possible, so as to enable
election meetings to be held in those schools?
Mr.. ROBB: The Minister does not at
present contemplate any amendment to these
regulations. The House will understand
that schools are vested in authorities, and
that the wishes of those authorities would
have to receive consideration before any
amendment is made. Until that is done I
do not think the Ministry would be in a
position to consider any amendment.

it will cost this Government in order to

AMENDMENT TO STANDING ORDERS.
The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND MEANS
(Mr Moles): I beg to move that the Standing
Orders of this House be amended by the addition of the following Orders:-
PART XIII.
DIVORCE BILLS.
174. A Bill for the dissolution of a marriage
between persons domiciled in Northern Ireland shall not be introduced into Parliament
except upon a petition to bring in such Bill.
Such petition shall be signed by the party to
the said marriage who desires the dissolution
thereof (hereinafter in these Orders called
"the Petitioner'); and there shall be
annexed to such petition a printed copy of
the proposed Bill, which shall be deemed to
form part thereof.
175. Every such petition shall be lodged in
the office of the Clerk of the Parliaments,
together with the following documents:-
-
(a) an official copy of the proceedings taken
or had in the Court having jurisdiction
over matrimonial causes at the place of
his or her domicile or residence, or in
some other Court having jurisdiction in
that behalf, at the suit of the Petitioner;
(b) in any case in which any trial at nisi
prius has been had, or any writ of
inquiry executed within the United
Kingdom, wherein the petition has been
party, a report of the proceedings upon
such trial or writ of inquiry.
The accuracy of the said reports shall
be verified by the affidavit of the
Petitioner.
176. A copy of such Petition and Bill shall
be delivered to the other party to the said
marriage (hereinafter in these Orders called
"the Respondent") within seven days of the
lodgment of such Petition, in the office of the
Clerk of the Parliaments; and in case of
infancy, such copy shall be delivered to the
guardian, or next relation of full age, not
concerned in the consequences of the Bill.
177. Every such Petition and Bill shall
thereupon be referred to the Examiner of
Petitions for Local Bills, who shall certify
to both Houses whether or not the Standing
Orders have been complied with in respect
of them.
If the Examiner is satisfied that it is impossible for the Petitioner to deliver a copy
of the Petition and Bill to the Respondent,
he may accept proof of substituted service.
178 If the Examiner shall certify that
Standing Orders have been complied with,
the Certificate shall be laid upon the Table
of the House of Commons, whereupon the Bill'
179. The Respondent, if desirous of being
heard upon the merits against any such Bill
shall enter an appearance in the office of the
Clerk of the Parliaments on or before the
seventh day after the day on which the Bill
has been read a First Time in the House of
Commons.
180. No such Bill shall be read a Second
Time in the House of Commons earlier than
the third, or later than the fifth, day on
which the House shall sit after the day
upon which such Bill has been read a First
Time.
181. Every such Bill, after having been
read a Second Time in the House of Commons, shall be sent to the Senate, and shall
be laid upon the Table of that House, and
when so laid shall be deemed to have been
read a First Time, and shall be recorded in
the Minutes as having been so read.
182. No such Bill shall be read a Second
Time in the Senate earlier than the third,
or later than the fifth, day on which the
House shall sit after the first reading thereof.
183. Every such Bill, after having been
read a Second Time in the Senate shall
(whether the appearance mentioned in Section 6 of these Orders has or has not been
entered) be referred to a Joint Standing
Committee of both Houses, to be called the
"Joint Committee on Divorce Bills.”
184. The Joint Committee on Divorce Bills
shall be appointed at the commencement of
each Session, and shall consist of the Speaker
of the Senate, four Members of the House
of Commons appointed by that House, and
three other Members of the Senate appointed
by the Senate. The Speaker of the Senate
shall be the Chairman of such Committee,
and in his absence the Chair shall be taken
by such Member thereof as the Joint Committee may choose. Three Members (of
whom the Chairman shall be one) shall form
the quorum.
185. The said Joint Committee shall inquire upon lawful evidence as to whether
the averments in the Preamble are proved
to the satisfaction of the Committee or not.
The Petitioner shall attend the Committee,
in order to his being examined, if the Committee think fit, whether there has or has
not been any collusion directly or indirectly
on his part, relative to any act of adultery
that may have been committed by his wife,
or whether there be any collusion directly or
indirectly between the Petitioner and the
Respondent, or any other person or person
touching such Divorce Bill, or touching any
proceedings or sentence of divorce had in

a Divorce Bill
As the House would desire me to say a
few words, it has now become necessary to
set up machinery for dealing with Divorce
Bills in Northern Ireland. Prior to the
1920 Act, under which this House was established, Divorce Bills in Ireland were dealt
with at Westminster. Recently a Divorce
Bill from Northern Ireland was presented
Law
at Westminster, and the
Lords
having there carefully deliberated upon the
question, reached the conclusion that a Bill
ought to be promoted in this Parliament for
our jurisdiction, and not at Westminster.
It, therefore, becomes necessary to set up
Standing Orders to regulate the procedure
in reference to such business. The Standing
Orders as they appear on the Paper are taken
almost word for word from the Standing
Orders applicable to such Bills at Westminster, with all such verbal changes and
adaptations as will suit our conditions, and
the law relating to divorce in this country.

class of ship that was built by British workmen during the war is still sailing the seas,
but some of the foreign ships of the same
type are in the scrap heap..
I have
But let us see the German firm which is
building the ships and the method by
which it is able to build them. This German
firm, I learn from inquiries, is a great
capitalist combine of shipping, shipbuilding, engineering, steel, working and
mine, owning interests. That is . the
combine that has got the order. . for
the building of British ships. How are
they able to build these ships? I will try
to tell you. This firm got the sum of
700,000,000 gold marks which was paid to
German capitalists as an indemnity for their
supposed losses through the illegal occupa
tion of the Ruhr. It is just a few months
since and I
sure hon. Members here will
remember it well-a public loan of £40,000,000
was sent to Germany. I am sure hon, Members will remember that quite well. If they
were in London they saw the queues waiting
to deposit their money to send to Germany.
I think, the £40,000,000 was collected in about
twenty minutes, and the British financiers
were offering about fifty times more than the
Germans were asking for. That £40,000,000
also went to assist this German combine to
compete against British shipbuilders. But
that was not all that this firm got from the
Government of Germany. They got another
loan, and this loan was all to themselves. It
was a loan of 10,000,000 dollars from America.
What else they got I do not know, but it is
quite evident that this firm is now cutting us
out with the aid of British capital.

and
In addition to all the indemnities
private loans all the German shipbuilders are
.
getting loans from their Government up tc
fifty per cent. of the total cost of the shipt
they build. They build in instalments.. I do
not think we have started the instalment
system here yet, but the German firms get
this loan in instalments. As the work proceeds, and up to the time the ships are
handed over for their first voyages, they get
this loan at the rate of a half of one per
cent. That is the interest on their loan.
Even when the ships are finished they are
not asked to hand back the loan. They
can keep it for a further five years, and then
at the end of that period, if they are not fit
to pay back the loan, they can ask for an
extension of a further five years. Of course
the interest is higher after the first five years
than it was before the ship was handed over.
It may be true to say that German workmen
work long hours for less wages than the
British workmen, and that they eat black
bread-aye without sausages now-but it is
not true to say that that is any reason why
an onslaught should be made on the shipbuilding and engineering workers' wages to
try to compete with a country far above our
equals as far as assistance is concerned.
Germany has gone out to assist industry and
has endeavoured to assist industrý

financiers are following to-day. At the same

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
Because they say if more ships are built there
will be less trade for the ships already built.
Yet the very same people are ordering ships
from Germany. This may seem paradoxical,
but after all the explanation is simple.
The German loans guarantee eight per cent.
Capital knows no country, and capitalist
companies, as is well known, have neither
soul to be saved nor body to be kicked. Trade
does not follow the flag. It follows the
capital, and one of the most deplorable facts
about the position of the British working
man to-day is that one of the very articles
in the manufacture of which he has been
brought up to serve his time is being handed
to a foreign country, and that foreign country
is being financed by British money.
I say
that if anything can be done towards bringing that to an end the sooner it is done the
better for the British workpeople as a whole.
Now there were five ships given over in the
month of March. These ships were fabricated
ships. The cost of the five ships was about
£150,000. The Diesel engines in these ships
to
are patented in Germany-another loss
British trade owing to negligence on the part
of the people responsible. British ship owners
could not, under present circumstances,
have competed for these ships. If the British
workman could have had an opportunity to
build these ships with Government assistance
similar to what is given to German shipbuilders we could have built them as cheaply
if not more cheaply. But there is one thing
about the whole affair which seems strange
to my mind, and that is that when the estimates were given for these ships the steel to
be used in the building was estimated by the
British shipbuilders at from £23 to £27 per
ton. Now the estimate shown by the German
shipbuilder was £19 per ton. Surely something was wrong from that point of view.
British manufactured steel, £23 to £27 per
ton, and German steel, £19 per ton. That assisted the shipbuilders to meet the requirements of the order.
I only want to speak on one other matter
before sitting down. It was contended
through the Press, and the Belfast Press in
particular, that the Germans were employing
unskilled labour at low wages and long hours,
and that this helped them to take this order
from the British firms. I want to say it was
nothing of the sort. In the shipbuilding
yards in Germany there are only one-fourth
of their employees unskilled. Three-fourths
, are skilled. Those figures are taken from
the returns of my trade union journal.
As I was saying the whole five ships totalled
£150,000 £153,000 to be exact-but here is the
point; the very week after that order was
sent to Germany the Clyde booked an order
from the Australian Government to the extent of £4,500,000 for two cruisers. Surely if
there was a cheaper market than the British
market for cruisers Australia would also
have taken it the same as any other commercial concern. These cruisers have been
taken at so much less than they would have
cost in Australia that the Australian Government are able to build an air cruiser ship in
their country out of the difference between
the prices there and the prices in this
country. No capitalist newspaper has ever
said "Cheep" about the low price at which
we are able to build a thirty-knot vessel in
this country.
It comes back to this, that we have had the
old bogey of foreign competition thrown at
us. Since I was an apprentice I have heard
that bogey sounded throughout the industrial world. The cry always was "Competition is going to ruin us. We will have to
get longer hours and less wages." Only last
year with all our poverty-and I speak now
for British shipyards, that is including the
Ulster shipyards, seeing that the Ulster shipyards are inside the British area-we built
about twice the tonnage of all the rest of
the world. Germany only built about oneeighth of our total. When this began we had
about four times more work in hands than
Germany. There are no workmen in the
world to touch the British workmen, but we
are being slowly strangled by the war debt
of £1,000,000 a day, by bankers, financiers,
and the present Tory Government, who,
whilst they refuse a starvation minimum
wage to the workers, have increased the bank
rate, thus increasing the unearned income of the idle millions, and correspondingly decreasing the opportunity of
trade and employment generally. The
engines of these five ships are a very
important factor, but I will be very brief in
dealing with this question. I would like it
to be well known that owing to the patent
rights having gone to Germany the engines
of these five ships cost £153,000, while they
would have cost the British shipbuilder
£60,000. That was because the patent rights
were taken from this country to Germany.

ing of houses, in millions." The people who

On the question of the Imperial contribution the Prime Minister has attempted to

that
where there are

Looking back for the last four years, and
taking a retrospective view, it is as well to
know exactly what the Northern Government have done. One would think, listening
to hon. Members on the benches opposite,
that the Northern Government had sat idly
by-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-had refused
to do anything at all for the relief of unemployment, to help to build houses, to help
agriculture, or to provide work for our
people. But when we look at the record of the
Government as set forth we find that the
Government have first of all justified their
existence, because they have paid and
discharged fully their liabilities. Some
of the hon. Members on the benches
opposite think it is proper to be generous
before you are just. I have learned that the
proper procedure is to be just before you are
generous,
and SO the Government of
Northern Ireland have discharged their
liabilities in full. They have relieved unemployment, they have helped very materially agriculture, they have assisted very
materially in dealing with the housing shortage, they have also paid their contribution
in full to the Imperial Exchequer, and after
having done all that, we find they have a
balance in hand, and we find it has not been
necessary for the Government to curtail even
the old-age pensions in order to have a clear
balance sheet.
If we contrast that with the state of affairs
that exists in the Irish Free State, which we
hear so much about, which is held up to us
as a kind of promised land which is literally
flowing with milk and honey, we find that the
first thing the Government of the Irish Free
State have done-
Mr. DEVLIN: Is to remove the tax on tea.
Mr. ELLIOTT:-is to deny their liability
to the Imperial Exchequer at all, and in
order to pay their administrative expenses
they have had to reduce the old age pensions.
I think the record of Northern Ireland,
standing out as it does pre-eminently as
compared with the record of the Irish Free
State, is one we have no reason to be
ashamed of.
I would like to reiterate what has been
said on more than one occasion by Members
sitting on the benches on this side of the
House, that the sympathy with the old-age
pensioners does not all lie in the bosoms
of the hon. Members on the benches opposite.
There are Members on this side of the

opposite.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Personally I do welcome

65, or even at 60. I want to see pensions for

I want to see the Entertainments Tax removed, but I want to be assured that when

I am particularly glad to have the

the same claim to a subsidy for helping to

reside in the city and urban areas. There

areas; but the housing shortage is

constituents residing
in the Border counties-I mention

I have no objection to our Imperial contribution at all, in fact I am proud of it, but
I do feel that before we contribute to the

Agricultural land is not relieved to the same
extent here as it is in England. I am informed that in England the Government pays
three-fourths of the rates. I was across in
England last year and visited some farms.
Since then I have been in touch with a good
many agents and have got particulars of their

we pay in Northern Ireland. I feel that before we make an Imperial contribution we

say it would be money kept in this area and

it would be for the financial stability of this

There have been comparisons made between

and I am free to make further comparisons.
The Imperial Parliament has reserved to
itself this question of land purchase. I am
dealing with the question of the benefit we
get from Imperial connections. They have
kept us waiting since 1918 for a scheme of
land purchase, and have offered our farmers
a Bill which is at present before the Imperial Houses which gives the unbought
tenants a reduction of 3s. 10d. in the as

scheme the farmers will not get immediate

the farmer gets an immediate reduction of
5s. from the gale day immediately preceding the date of the passing of the Act.
You cannot blame these unbought tenants
for their attitude. They are not men opposed
to the Government in ordinary policy, but

sore at being let down by people whom they
supported. The Chancellor said that the

British Parliament gave their word on that

I come now to the next question, the entertainment tax on picture houses. I have a
sneaking regard for picture houses. During

anxious to see them encouraged. As football is the sport of the working classes so
the picture houses are the centres of joy and
amusement for the poorer classes.
women with shawls, who would not for the

Some of the pictures might be condemnedyou cannot get perfection in anything-but
they give a good story told in the most vivid
form which impresses these young people.
They see colour and beauty and representations of all those higher and sweeter things
of life. Many of these picture houses are

see foreign countries and witness representations of scenes that would never otherwise
come before their eyes. The pictures lift

upon an entrance fee of 4d? I do not think
it can be justified. I am not interested in

picture houses.
In regard to sporting associations no profits
are made out of them at all, and so that
question does not arise. I am not interested
in the profits of the owners of picture houses
or of the theatres, though I do think the
incidence of taxation in these matters is
all wrong. Let me take a case in point. Supposing a theatrical company of a very highly
efficient character brings a very inspiring
play little known and little advertised. They
come and have an empty theatre for a week.
They may lose £100 on the week, and yet
they have to pay taxation upon every ticket
that is bought in that theatre. I do not
think that is fair. If there is a tax at all it
ought to be a tax upon the profits and not a
tax upon entrances. I would think that would
be the wiser course, though I confess I have
not given very much thought to it because 1
am not interested in the least degree in the
owners.

would like, and if we had not such tremendous obligations apart from the normal

6d the amount in question is £22,000. The other

£45,000 to the people.. They are perfectly honest and perfectly straightforward in that matter. They say their

this £45,000 in order to make profits." Now
when that Act was passed in Great Britain

Mr. SPEAKER: Before the adjournment
of the House is moved I should like to call
attention to an earlier proceeding to-day
when we were considering a Motion by the
Chairman of Ways and Means with regard
to the Joint Unopposed Committee on the
Belfast Corporation Bill and the London
Midland and Scottish Railway Co. Bill. Since
the addition of the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) to that Committee was
carried by the House the Standing Order
dealing with the matter has been brought to
my notice. It appears that under it, two
Members of this House, consisting of the
Chairman of Ways and Means and one other
Member, can be appointed by this House to
sit on a Joint Unopposed Committee, so that
the part of the Resolution which includes the
third Member is I am afraid void, being.contrary to the Standing Orders.
Mr. DEVLIN: When Ippraised this
question I did not intend that I should be
the Member selected, in fact, if I had known
that by the unanimous wish of the House I
should be the honoured person I should not

want the position as it would take a lot of

subsequent to this we really ought to have
an understanding with the Government with
regard to this, because, not only have the
Opposition no representative but the two
Senators who will be consulted with regard
to these Private Bills are also supporters of
the Government. I think it would be desireable that there should be at least one Member of the Opposition on the Committee.

DEATH OF THE PREMIER OF NEV.
ZEALAND.
Motion made, and Question proposed,

(Captain Mulholland).
The PRIME MINISTER: I think it would
be the desire of the House before we part,
that I should, on behalf of the Members of
all parts, offer our sincere sympathy to those
who are sorrowing in New Zealand on
account of the sudden and tragic death of
their Prime Minister. I know well that all
sections of thought and feeling in Ulster
looked upon the late Mr. Massey as one of
our most distinguished sons in any part of
the globe. Our Province may be proud of
those it has sent forth to all corners to uphold British traditions, and in that long roll
of names none stands more honoured
in our hearts than that of the late Prime
Minister of New Zealand. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). He was born and
spent his early life in the County of Derry.
From time to time it was his duty in the
interests of the Province-in the interests of
Great New Zealand to come to this country
on various duties. I therefore came into

His whole soul was centred upon the

A FLAX TRADE DISPUTE.
+
Mr. KYLE: As intimated earlier, in consequence of the reply the Minister
of Labour gave me to a question
I had down on the Paper as to whether
he is aware of the practice of the Flax
Spinners' Association instituting a boycott
of men who leave any of their firms and find
employment in other places. desire to raise
the matter at this stage. The Flax Spinners
have the practice when a man, or a number
of men, fall out with a particular management and leave that firm, the Association
send word to all the members of the Association to see that these men do not get employment. Recently we had a dispute in
County Armagh, the Armagh Spinning
Company, regarding flax dressers; and these
men who quit their work there-or some of
them-came to Belfast. One of them
found employment a number of them have,
by the way, found employment. One of them
in particular found employment three weeks
ago, but he was approached last Tuesday, and
told that in consequence of the fact that he
had left Mr. Wilson's place in Armagh the
firm would not engage him any longer, and he
would have to leave the employment he was
in. I think this House will agree that that
is an unsocial practice. Had it been committed by trade unionists or any body of
workpeople here, or when it was committed
earlier in the last century in other parts of
the country there were no people who
denounced it so strongly as members of the
Party who sit opposite. It was called boycott in those days. It is just the same
whether it is done by employers or workpeople.
The employers in this case, in my opinion, are
uilty of that unsocial practice, and I think
it should meet with the disapproval of this
House. This man was employed in the York
Street Flax-spinning Company up to last
'Tuesday when he got this letter or rather
we got it:
"We have to inform you that as we had
a letter from the Armagh Spinning Company stating that this man was on strike
we had no alternative but to let him go."
I. other words if any body of workpeople
leave job so far as the Spinners' Association
is concerned, they are going to keep them out
of work for the rest of their lives. I think
this is a reprehensible practice.
Ar. ANDREWS: It will be in the recolletion of the House that the answer I gave
was that I was not aware of the practice
referred to by the hon. Member. I am still
not aware that there is this practice, but I
have no doubt that the letter which he has
real, and which applies to a particular firm.
is cuite in orde. I would point out, however,
to my hon. Frit nd, that if the trade unions
concerned are not satisfied about this matter.
the best course oper: for them would be to take
the matter up with the Association, because
after all, I have no power to compel any
employer to give work to a man if he does not
desire to give work to him any more than I
have power to compel a workman to serve a
firm which he prefers not to serve.
The hon. Member referred to the fact that
I personally was a member of this Association.
I would like just to say exactly what my
position is in connection with the Association,
so that there may be no misunderstanding.
My firm are members of the Association. I
do not represent my firm upon the Association
for vry obvious reasons. I can only add
that as this dispute has arisen I think it
should be settled if possible Ietween the
parties concerned.

PRICE OF
OFFICIAL DEBATES.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I rise to
suggest to this House, but especially to the
Minister of Finance, a method whereby he
could increase the revenue of this Government. I have been looking at a copy of the
Parliamentary Debates in this House and I
see the price is sixpence, for this which I hold
here in my hand. Were any newsagent to
publish a book and to charge sixpence for
something in similar form to this. he would
be entitled to six months for profiteering.
(Laughter). Is the charge of sixpence for
this book made for the purpose of putting
it out of the reach of the workers of the
Province of Ulster? I understand that the
Imperial Parliament has reduced the price
of Hansard to three pence, and I would
suggest to the Minister of Finance that he
should charge twopence for this publication,
and let the newsboys have it at three halfpence, so that they would have a halfpenny
on every copy of Hansard they sell. Then
the citizens of Ulster will get the truth and
nothing but the truth. (Laughter.) Right
hon. Members opposite may laugh, but
according to the reports in the Press the
Opposition are a poor lot. I am sure that
when this book gets into circulation it will
assist the Government, even if we are a poor
lot.
It is up to the Government to support this
suggestion of mine, and thus enable the
working men and working women of Ulster to
read what is taking place in this Parliament. I know that some of the hon. Members opposite will say it is a deplorable
thing and a horrible thing that I, as an
Orangeman, should go out and vote with
the hon. Member for West Belfast, but I am
very proud to take a copy of Hansard into
the Orange Halls and to show it to the
Orangemen. I need not go so far as to
suggest that some of the hon. Members opposite should take it into the Unionist Clubs.
Take it anywhere, broadcast it anywhere.
I believe the Minister of Finance would be
able to raise a large sum of money in the way
I have suggested. and I believe the circulation of this book, if it were published at a
reasonable price, would beat the "Telegraph"
or the "News-Letter." It would also be the
means of giving the little fellows who bring
the papers to our doors an opportunity of
earning a better livelihood, because I believe
that this book would be bought more than
any newspaper circulating in Ulster. I
would suggest that the Minister of Finance
should take into consideration at an early
date the reduction of the price of Hansard
to twopence, and that he should give it to
the newsboys at three halfpence.
Mr. POLLOCK: I was under the impres
sion that some rearrangement was made last
Session in order that Hansard should be
circulated at a low price to those who are
interested in it and did not feel disposed to
pay the price charged. I presume, however.
that in the interest of that economy with
which the whole atmosphere seems to be
saturated at the present time, that the price
has been increased. However. I will undertake that the whole matter will be reconsidered.
Question, "That this House do now adjourn," put, and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at Twentyfive minutes after Six o'clock.

Mr. T. W. MCMULLAN: With your permission I would like to say a few words on
this Clause, not with any idea of criticising
it. but to make as clear as I can the expected
future position financially of this Pharmaceutical Society. This Clause deals with the
revenue to be derived from the licences
which will be granted to the trade, and it
deals with the application of that revenue.
Until all the licences have been issued to the
pharmicists and chemists and registered
druggists by the Ministry of Home Affairs it
is impossible to know exactly what the income will be, but assuming that such licences
should be arranged, as they very probably
will be arranged at three guineas for the
pharmacists; and two guineas for the other
trades concerned, it is expected that the
total revenue will be perhaps from £800 to
£900 per annum. The whole of the revenue
will go to this new Society for the first two
years. After the first two years it is proposed that at least half of the revenue should
be given to the Pharmaceutical Society for
their purposes, and the Government in their
discretion will take whatever proportion they
think is proper of the other fifty per cent.
Well, it is impossible until the Society is
formed, and the Council has discussed its
responsibility to estimate what the expenditure is likely to be. I think hon. Members
will agree with me when I say that the
Society is not likely to be unduly extravagant on an income of £400 to £500 a year.
It is a very important Society, embracing a
great many members, and £400 to £500 a
year is a very small income. The members
are very anxious that they should be housed.
They are very anxious that they should
have a boardroom and offices, and above all.
that they should have well-equipped laboratories, which are very necessary to them for
the purpose of holding examinations. The
inembers of this Society are under this Bill
compelled to resign their share of the headquarters in Dublin. These members helped
to install those headquarters in Dublin, and
they have helped to maintain them, and
they claim now they should have something
in exchange that they should be given
premises properly fitted up in our Own
capital.
With the resources they are expected to
have it seems to me it would be quite
impossible for the members of the Pharmaceutical Society to put up those premises.
The only alternative is to ask the Government. We have gone to the Government on
this question, and of course we were metvery properly met-with the position that as
we could not put forward exact figures of
revenue and exact figures of coming expenditure, it was quite impossible for them
to discuss a grant of a definite nature, but
they have drawn our attention to the way in
which sub-section 2 of this clause is worded.
You will find there that the Ministry can
exercise its own judgment after the second
year as to what proportion of the second
fifty per cent. of the revenue will be allocated
to Government Charges and what proportion
may be handed over to the Pharmaceutical
Society. The Parliamentary Secretary of
Finance (Mr. Barbour) when introducing
the Money Resolution of this Bill, very clearly
indicated this, and pointed out to us that it
would be within their power to be generous
if necessary with this second fifty per cent.
of the income accruing from licences after
the second year. It has now been arranged
that as soon as the Council of the Society
is prepared to put its estimate of expenditure before the Ministry of Finance, the
whole matter can be discussed, and I hope

Sir DAWSON BATES: There has been so
much misunderstanding in regard to law on
the subject of Rent Restriction that it will,
I think, be a convenience to the House, and
enable hon. Members to understand better
the effect of the Bill, if I briefly refer to the
existing legislation dealing with that subject. There have been altogether three Acts,
one passed in 1915, one in 1919, and one in
1920.
With regard to the 1915 Act, that Act first
established the principle of control. It only
applied to houses of a valuation of £26 and
under, and it laid down that the rent
charged on this class of house on 3rd August,
1924, was to be regarded as a standard rent,
and that no increase could be made thereon.
It also gave security of tenure. This Act
remained in force until the 1919 Act was
passed. Owing to the increase of prices, it
was felt that an injustice had been done to
the landlord, and, under the 1919 Act, in
addition to extending the valuation at which
restrictions should apply to houses of a
valuation of £52 and under, the landlord was
allowed to charge an additional 10 per cent.
over the standard rent. This was to cover
the addition to general costs and repairs.
The third Act was passed in 1920, and
prices at that time had increased materially.
That particular Act, I might tell hon. Members, is referred to in the present Bill as
"the principal Act." It may help them to
follow some of the Clauses in the Bill. Under
this Act houses up to a valuation of £78 were
brought within the scope of the Acts. As it
was felt that at that time conditions had
become so accentuated the landlord was empowered to charge 15 per cent. on the net
rent, and a further 25 per cent. as representing the difference between the cost of
repairs as in August, 1914 and 1920, in cases
where the landlord was liable for repairs.
In addition, the landlord became entitled to
charge any additional increase in rates over
those payable in 1914. This Act, however,
excluded from its provisions houses that were
erected after or were in course of erection in
April, 1919. I would like to remind hon.
Members that where houses were built between 1914 and 1919 the standard rent was
the rent at which the house was first let.
It was provided that that Act of 1920 should
terminate in June, 1923, as it was thought
by the authors of the Act that by the time
1923 arrived there would be a sufficient
number of houses, and that it would be
possible then to do away with the principle
of control. It was found, however, that owing
to the shortage in the supply of houses it
was impossible to allow the Act to lapse, and,
accordingly, the Acts have been continued
up to the present time. We are, therefore,
working under the 1920 Act. I think everybody will agree with me when I say that
State control, as opposed to private enterprise, has always ended in disaster.
Mr. KYLE: No, no.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The effect of the
Rent Restriction Acts, so far as the provision
of houses is concerned, has been disastrous,
and I think if those responsible for the introduction of the principle laid down in these
laws could have visualised the effect they
have had in the development of housing they
would have hesitated to introduce such a
far-reaching principle.
One of the obstacles to the development of
housing is uncertainty as to future legislation. Persons are not going to erect houses
if they fear the State is going to step in and
control them as to how these houses are to
be used. We must get back to normal conditions, and leave it to private enterprise
to meet the necessities of the case, aided, if
necessary, with the financial help, but without the control, of the State. You must
either do that or let the State take over the
whole question of housing.
T
Rent Restrictions Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: But, as I said
before, intervention by the State in business
has always had disastrous results.
Mr. KYLE indicated dissent.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: What about
shipping during the war?
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend
will get an opportunity of developing all these
points later on, and I do not expect that we
will agree.
The chief object of the Bill before the
House is gradually to do away with all restrictions. By this Bill we desire to remove
any possible fears that prospective builders
may have
as to the possibility of future
State control. It is impossible, without
disastrous results, to effect immediate decontrol; it must be done by stages.
re-
We propose in effect to reverse the process under which these artificial
strictions were imposed. As has been explained, houses with a lower valuation
were first brought within the ambit of the
Act, and gradually the limiting valuation
was increased.
With regard to the £78 valuation, the Bill
provides that the restriction on the higher
valuation which was first imposed under
the Act of 1920, is to be the first to disappear.
We propose that decontrol on houses of
£52 to £78 valuation should take effect on
the 1st November, 1926. There will be a
breathing space for this class of tenant for
another 18 months, during which time I
hope the occupiers will find ample opportunity to make their own arrangements.
£52 Valuation:-The next stage will be
decontrol of houses between £26 and £52
valuation; that is, those houses which were
brought under the Act of 1919. This class
of house comes out of control on the first
of May, 1928, that is a period of 3 years.
£26 Valuation:-Lastly we are giving a
long period to the houses which do not exceed
a £26 valuation, and which were brought
in under the 1915 Act. We are extending
their period of control to 1st May, 1930-a
period of 5 years from the present date.
I do not think that anyone can accuse us
of adopting hasty or harsh measures. We
have deliberately specified fixed dates for
this reason that one of the greatest difficulties which are agitating the minds of the
private builders and the public generally,
is the uncertainty of the Government's intentions in the future. I believe that it will
be to the good not alone of the landlord,
but of the tenant to know exactly how they
will stand in the future. Decontrol must be
faced sooner or later, and I believe we have
adopted the policy which will be the easiest
for the landlord and the easiest for the
tenant.
I want to say a word about Contracting
out. There can be no doubt but that
tenants of houses which are about to be decontrolled may want to make arrangements
with their landlords for new leases before
the date of decontrol, and we are making
express provision for that purpose in Subsections 2 and 3 of Section 2, under which
a lease can be made for a period of not
less than two years, but terminating subsequent to the date of decontrol. Once a
valid lease is granted the principal Act will
no longer apply. I might mention, however,
that this will not only apply to houses of
a valuation of over £26. We have deliberately omitted houses under a £26
valuation from this Clause. They will not
be decontrolled for 5 years hence, and it is
quite an unusual thing to make long leases
for this class of house. Therefore occupiers
of houses of this type will not be able to
contract themselves out of the Act any more
than in the past.
With regard to the question of Decontrol
of Vacant Houses. We also provide that by
Clause 2 (1) where the landlord comes into
possession of a house over £8 in valuation,
that control shall cease to apply to such
house, but houses of £8 valuation and under
will remain subject to control, even if they
become vacant prior to the appointed day
for decontrol.
Now I come to the question of the one
house owner, which is agitating the minds
of many people. There are many cases in
which an individual purchases a house for
himself or herself with the intention of
occupying it. We believe that it is only
an act of justice that such persons should be
allowed to obtain possession, and that no conditions should be imposed which would prevent them from getting into their own
homes. We, therefore, propose that where
a dwelling house to which the Act applies
has been purchased by the landlord for
occupation as a residence for himself on or
before 1st May, 1923, that the landlord shall be
entitled to get possession on giving six months'
notice, without being obliged to provide
alternative accommodation. We also prowhen the
pose, regardless of the date
house was purchased, where the house is
required by the landlord for occupation as a
residence either for himself or his father or his
mother, or any son or daughter, or any
person residing with him or in his employment, to give possession provided the
landlord finds alternative accommodation,
that is substantially equivalent, and pro-

vided the Court is satisfied that the granting of a decree would cause less hardship
than the with-holding of it, or where the

of the Court is in the public interest.
Mr. DEVLIN: What does the right hon.
Gentleman mean by the words "Any person
residing with him"? That has a very broad
interpretation.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think if the hon.
Member will refer to the Clause itself he
will find that the exact expression is "residing with." My hon. Friend knows perfectly well that in many cases persons who
are not relatives live with people for many
years and are treated as members of the
family.
Mr. DEVLIN: But he may be brought in
specifically for the purposes of this Act.
Sir DAWSON BATES: If the hon. Member
will have a little patience I will explain
the whole thing to him. I think he is jumping to conclusions, as he is rather inclined
to do.
Hon. Members will observe that in the
alternative accommodation defined in Clause
"5 (1) (e)" the accommodation to be prorided must be substantially equivalent. The
old definition of "alternative accommodation"
was identical in all respects.
To meet the case that my hon. Friend, the
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin), has
raised, I would inform him that if he looks
at Clause 4, sub-section 6, he will find that
with the object of dealing with persons who
make fraudulent representations to the judge
with a view to obtaining possession of a
house, provision has been inserted under
which such persons will render themselves
liable to criminal proceedings and to very
heavy penalties.
I now come to a provision which I am
quite satisfied will be criticised by hon.
Members opposite, that is the question of
repairs and the allowance to landlord for
repairs under the 1920 Act.
Under that Act, the landlord was authorised to charge an additional 25 per cent. on
the nett rent in cases where he was responsible for carrying out the repairs of the
house. This 25 per cent. increase has been
the subject of some misapprehension. It is a
common but fallacious idea that this 25 per
cent. was given by way of covering the whole
cost of repairs. This 25 per cent. was made
to cover the difference in the cost of repairs
between that existing in 1914 and 1920. The
facts are that in practically all tenancies
made in Belfast, and in other cases in Northern Ireland, especially in regard to the
smaller houses, it has been the custom for
the landlord to carry out the repairs, even
though under Deasy's Act, which I shall
refer to hereafter, the obligation of carryout the repairs was imposed on the tenant
in the absence of anything to the contrary.
Mr. KYLE: They generally do it.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The 25 per cent.
allowed to the landlord was therefore in
respect only of the additional cost of repairs,
and was not intended to cover the entire cost
of repairs, and a landlord in fixing his rent
in the pre-control period always had regard
to the liability he had for repairs, and I
think I am correçt in saying that the amount
that a prudent landlord would set aside for
repairs would be in the neighbourhood of
15 per cent. of the rent he received.
The cost of wages and materials has fallen
appreciably since 1920. I have obtained some
figures, and I find that between May 1920
and May 1925 the wages paid to bricklayers
and joiners have fallen from 2s 3d to 1s 9d
per hour, and that there have been similar
cuts in the wages of glaziers, plasterers,
plumbers and slaters. As regards the price
of material, in the case of bricks and timber
the cost has fallen as much as 50 per cent.
since 1920, while the cost of slates has fallen
by almost 30 per cent. I cannot but think,
therefore, that I am reasonable in assuming
that in the next five years the cost will not
be any higher and possibly will be lower.
The Government is satisfied that it would
be unjustifiable to impose on the tenants
the continuance of the full charge of 25 per
cent. which is fixed rightly or wrongly as
being the appropriate figure representing
the difference in the cost between 1914 and
1920, and while it is not proposed to disturb
the 15 per cent. that is added in respect of
rent which was imposed under the Act of
1920, we propose that on and after the 1st
day of November, 1925, the 25 per cent. on
foot of repairs is to be reduced to 15 per
cent, making a total of 30 per cent. as against
40 per cent. imposed under the Act of 1920.
Reference has been made to what is known
as Deasy's Act, more properly known as
the Landlord and Tenants Act, 1860. Under
this Act the tenant, in the absence of an
express agreement to the contrary, is responsible for repairs. The framers of the 1920
Act appear not to have had this Act in mind,
and while the view and indeed the custom of
the landlords in Belfast, and I think in other
parts of the Six Counties, has always been
that they are liable for repairs in the absence
of a specific contract, and while some people
have held that Deasy's Act has been overridden by the Rent Restriction Act of 1920,
the matter is not free from doubt and we
have made it clear in this Bill that, in any
case where the rent has been increased under
Section 2 of the Act of 1920, the landlord
