we had in the House that so deeply impressed me as when he said that industry
and trade were so over-burdened by overtaxation as to make them almost helpless.
Over taxation is the great and over-powering cause of so many of these evil resultants
of which we complain in our industry and
trade to-day. Well, here is an opportunity
-a magnificent opportunity for the right
hon. Gentleman to relieve that burden from
the backs of the people in trade and industry.
But there is another thing I would like
to say. I wish the right hon. Gentleman
would try-it may not be altogether germane to this discussion-I know he will not
have such a responsive hearing here-but
I wish the right hon. Gentleman would try
to bring about a better understanding with
Southern Ireland. If I mention union you
will all think there is such a dangerous and
sinister move at the back of it, but it is
possible, if you cannot have a union, to have
an understanding, and although declarations
of the most kindly and generous nature have
been made by Southern Ireland there has
been no direct response from the North to
these declarations. I myself never thought
it was desirable constantly to say "The
North must come in," but I am afraid if
you go on with this reckless extravagance
they will not let you in. (Laughter.) I think
if the cost of government goes on as it is
here in the North of Ireland this Northern
Province would not be an asset. even if you
were in. Your revenue is nearly
£11,000,000, and the revenue of the whole of
Ireland in 1913 was only £13,000,000, and yet
we have to go like beggarmen to the English
Parliament and Downing Street, and appeal
for our own money to the British Minister.
Again in that respect I want to raise an
objection here. We are sometimes told if we
saved this money in the police England.
would get it. England has no right to it at
all. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I do not
know, for I have not consulted any Gentleman on this side of the House as to what
their view is, but my view is that we ought
not to be paying a solitary penny to the
British Exchequer out of the revenue of
'Ulster unless what we choose to give of our
own volition.
You are a very loyal party. You love the
Empire. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) You
are very proud of the Empire. You have declared over and over again you would like
to assist the Empire. Why force you to do
it? Why not leave you to give of your own
volition out of the inexhaustible resources of
your loyalty? You will do it, and if it is
a legitimate contribution you will have our
support, but to give these vast sums to England and then to go over to the English
Parliament begging of the British Chancellor
of the Exchequer to restore you something
of your own is a humiliation that I for
one, as a representative of the people in
this Parliament, will not subject myself to without protest. I say, then, in
conclusion that this occasion affords all of
us an opportunity of exploring the whole
fiscal field and of suggesting within the
measure of our limited intellects and experience the methods by which economy combined with efficiency can be carried out. I,
therefore, support the Motion moved by my
hon. Friend (Mr. McAllister).

having earned the encomiums of all classes

Ulster Constabulary were to be Roman
Catholics and two-thirds Protestants.
That was an arrangement come to by a
Committee of this House. This House at
that time, without any representatives of
the hon. Members' side, came to the conclusion that it would be fair to the population of Northern Ireland if two-thirds were
to be of the Protestant persuasion and onethird of the Roman Catholic persuasion. Up
to the present time the Government has
most anxiously endeavoured to carry out the
recommendations of that Committee. With
regard to the appointment of officers that
has been carried out. So far as men coming
forward are concerned, I understand from
my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates)
that only some 500 Roman Catholics have
come forward to fill the 1,000 vacancies they
were entitled to. However, as to that the
Government have got nothing more to say except that the places were kept open for them
but the recruits did not come forward. It
was necessary to raise 3,000 men not only
in accordance with the recommendations of
the Committee of this House but in accordance with the recommendations of the Government in the first instance when the Act
of 1921 was passed, and later the Colwyn
Committee recommended, I think, within a
few men of 3,000 as the proper quota for
Northern Ireland. Therefore, we have not
only kept our-I will not say promise-we
have kept our intentions in regard to the
proportion of the two religions in the Force.
Out of six county inspectors the county inspectors of both Tyrone and Fermanagh are
Roman Catholics, that is to say, they have
two out of six, which is, if anything, over
the proportion to which I have referred.
Mr. DEVLIN: And the proportion in the
other counties?
The PRIME MINISTER: Of course, if you
have two out of six it is exactly one-third,
and that is in accordance with the recommendations of this House. Leaving to one
side, as I say, the Royal Ulster Constabulary-we have dealt with it fully, I hope,
now let us come to the Special Constabulary, and let me remind the House that up
to to-day the Special Constabulary have
cost Northern Ireland nothing.

We pay it to England and England gives

Mr. DEVLIN: Now that we have got it
we will keep it.
The PRIME MINISTER: Now that we

The PRIME MINISTER: The hon. Member (Mr. Devlin) once more gets off the line.

services of that practically voluntary body

Let me take, in conclusion, the state of

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I have no
desire to prolong unduly this Debate upon

one or two points on which I feel I would
like to make a passing reference. There
seems to be general agreement in the House
in regard to the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
No finer tribute has been paid to it in this
House or outside of it than the tribute that
has been paid to-day by the Members of the
Opposition, and especially by the Member
for the West Division of Belfast (Mr. Devlin), so that so far as the Force is concerned
it may be eliminated at once from the discussion in which we are at present engaged.
The controversy seems to have settled
round the Special Constabulary, and some
things have been said that I think the facts
did not fully warrant. Some people have
very short memories. We all know of the
terrible and trying times that we have
passed through during the past three or
four years, when our territory was invaded
from outside, when men were kidnapped and
taken away from their homes, when scenes
of destruction were witnessed in very many
districts, and when the Government really
found themselves in extreme difficulty as to
how law and order were going to be established and secured. I think those who have
studied the ovents of these trying times, and
the means that were adopted in order to bring
that unhappy state of affairs to an end.
must admit that it was the Special Constabulary that eventually brought peace to
our borders. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I think we owe a debt of gratitude that never
can be repaid to the men of the "B" Constabulary-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-
men who went on duty after having worked
all day. From the employer down to the

Local Authorities (University
Grants) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second Time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of this
Bill is to enable the local authorities to assist
financially Queen's University by making
direct grants. At the present time they have
power to make grants by way of providing
scholarships under the Education Act. They
have no right at all to contribute. The Bill
only follows the precedent which exists in
England and Scotland where the local
authorities have power to assist the various
provincial universities. There is a general
desire on the part of the local authorities to
assist Queen's University.
I would like to point out to hon. Members
that it is entirely an enabling Bill. If the
local authorities do not wish to contribute
they need not do so. To that extent it does
not impose any additional burden on the
rates. I beg to move.

Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:

Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of this
Bill is to encourage still further the building
of working-class houses in Northern Ireland.
Under the existing Acts, the 1923 Act and
the subsequent Act. the Government contribute £60 per house of certain dimensions.
that is to say, houses of a maximum of 950
superficial feet and a minimum of 600 superficial feet, and in addition local authorities
at the present time have power to contribute
up to the sum of £40 as an additional grant
to such houses, or, if they so prefer, they
can make a free loan of £100 for a period of
twenty-five years. The area within which
these houses were to be built was confined
to urban districts and industrial areas inside
rural areas. Having regard to the comparatively short time in which these Acts
have been in operation, I regard them as
being very successful. but at the same time
we think there are many matters which
could be improved upon. As a result of our
Housing Acts I find that no fewer than 885
houses have been approved of for erection by
local authorities themselves, and these local
authorities have also further schemes in
hand to the extent of 1,156 houses, while as
regards private owners, no fewer than 2.106
houses have been either built or arranged
for.
We intend to extend the scope of these
Acts not only to rural centres but to the
entire of the rural areas. There is another
way in which we propose to amend the Acts.
We feel that while the existing Acts have
been successful, a certain amount can be
done to accelerate the building.
I have taken out figures, and out of 300
houses I find that
19% have taken 4 months to build.

want houses to let.
Further, to obviate any possibility of this
£80 subsidy being taken by those who are in

some Clause should be inserted in the Bill
such as the Minister of Labour introduced

to ensure that the fund would be used in the
best interests of the people of Belfast.

This is public money, and I think a provision should be inserted in the Bill to the

to Corporations or Utility Societies or
Societies that did not primarily exist for
making profit. Some Clause to that effect
would strengthen the Bill very materially and
tend to promote its useful administration.

in every detail. I think a Clause of that

effect.

better Bill, in my opinion, than any Housing Bill that has been produced up to now.

we are only too happy to be able to offer

working-class inhabitants. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Dr. MORRISON: Although I am a representative of the University in this House I
also partly represent rural Ulster. I have
been engaged in farming for the greater part

the extreme satisfaction I feel at the policy
that has been outlined by the Prime Minister
here to-day. I think it probably is the result, to a slight extent, of the stress some
of us have laid upon the necessity for relieving the land of the undue burden of taxation
that has been placed upon it in the past. It
is quite evident that if you increase the
amount of rateable property in the country
you reduce the direct taxation on land, taxation which, in my opinion, is, and always
has been oppressive. Grants of £128,000 look
large, but in reality when you divide them
over all the tax-paying farmers of Ulster
they represent very small sums indeed, and
I think the policy outlined by the Prime
Minister will be received with gratitude by
the agricultural community.

The first is on the ground of public policy.

There is another matter I would like to
refer to which was mentioned briefly by
another Member, and that is the case of
appointments. The Home Office seems to
have taken up the attitude that the only
appointment they will make is one accepted
by their advisers. (Hon. Members: Hear,

times correct in their selection, and I am
going to prove as far as my ability will
allow me that they misinformed the Home
Secretary in regard to a particular appointment at the Belfast Board of Guardians.
We in the Belfast Board of Guardians by
a majority and by the advice of the medical
authorities there selected a candidate out of
six for an appointment as superintendent of
the Fever Hospital. The appointment was
forwarded to the Home Office, but the Home
Office turned down the girl because she did
not meet the requirements of the Nursing
and Midwives' Council; that was, she had
not been registered as a fever nurse although
she was asked to be superintendent of an
unregistered hospital. The fever section of
the Belfast Union, I would point out, is
not a registered fever hospital. That being
the case we do not think that the requirements of a registered fever nurse should
be one of the conditions set out for the
superintendent of that class of hospital.
While we try to give the best service to
the people we also demand justice regarding
the selections that the Guardians make. As
one of the Guardians I feel that my judgment
in the selection in this particular instance
was superior to the one made by the Home
Office. This girl has been 18 years in
the Belfast Infirmary. She went
through her probationary period and
the different branches of the nursing
profession. She also went through
a course of fever training. When this new
Council was set up there was no intimation
whatever given to the nurses that they had

after the new Council came into operation,

the British

I agree that nensions should be a National

think that is really a very great pity. It is

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 28th May, 1925,
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
LABOURERS' COTTAGES-LISBURN
DISTRICT.
1. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs if he will state the
grounds on which the application of Robert
Higgins for a cottage in connection with a
scheme promoted by the Lisburn Rural
District Council was struck out by the
Inspector; if he is aware that the house in
which Robert Higgins is living consists of
one small bedroom and kitchen; that his
family numbers nine, and that the house has
been condemned by three doctors; that a few
weeks ago a cottage became vacant, and that
Robert Higgins, though recommended by the
doctor for the cottage, was passed over, and
the cottage given to a man who deals in
cattle and owns a horse; and if he will also
state on what grounds the application of
Bernard Mulholland was struck out at the
same inquiry.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): It is a matter for the
Inspector to decide the number and sites of
the cottages to be erected, but I am unable
to give information on these points as I have
not yet received the Inspector's report.
As regards the remainder of the question,
the selection of tenants of the cottages
erected or to be erected by the Rural District
Council is a matter for the Council themselves, and I am not empowered to interfere
with their discretion in making such
selection.
INTOXICATING LIQUOR ACT, 1923.
2. Mr. GYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs, whether the Intoxicating Liquor Act
(Northern Ireland), 1923, in Section 3, provides that the holder of an on-licence who is
unable to comply with the requirements of
the Act with respect to the structural separation of the part of his premises in which the
sale of intoxicating liquor is carried on
from the part of those premises in which
any other business is carried on, is entitled
to compensation if the licence is not by
reason of such inability renewed at the
annual licensing sessions held next after the
date when such requirements came into
operation, viz., the sessions in September and
October, 1925; whether Section 6 provides
that intoxicating liquor shall not be sold or
offered for sale after 1st October, 1924, in
licensed premises where such separation
cannot be effected; whether the inability referred to must exist at the date of the holding of the sessions or when; and whether if
the effect of the two sections is to imperil the
licence-holder's right to compensation given
by the Act, what steps the Government
intend to take to remove this anomaly in the
Act.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As regards the
first part of the question, I have no jurisdiction to express an authoritative opinion
as the matter can only be finally settled by a
Court of competent jurisdiction. I may say,
however, that I am advised that the answer
to this part of the question is in the
affirmative.
The hon. Member does not correctly state
the effect of Section 6 (1) of the Act in the
second part of his question, and I would
refer him to the express provisions of that
section.
The remainder of the question raises
points for the consideration of the Claims
Tribunal, and it would be improper for me
to anticipate their decision thereon.
DANGEROUS CORNER IN BALLY-
GAWLEY.
3. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether his attention has
been directed to the suggestion made at the
Ballygawley Petty Sessions, on the 19th inst.
that a police pointsman be placed at a
dangerous corner on the Dungannon Road
in the centre of the town, where several
people nearly lost their lives owing to being
run over by motors; and whether the Minister has also had his attention drawn to the
statement of District Inspector Martin
admitting the dangerous nature of the corner,
but declaring that the local police force
would require to be considerably augmented
if point duty was to be done.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My attention has
been directed to this matter, but I may point
out that while some of the Magistrates were
in favour of the proposal to place a constable
on point duty at this corner, others were not.
The Police Officer who was present at the
Petty Sessions Court pointed out that the
roadway was wide at this spot, and that if
a danger sign were erected it would probably
meet the case.
This suggestion was adopted by the Bench,
who have communicated with the local
authority in the matter.

that perforated bricks cost £5 7s 6d per 1,000
in Belfast as against £4 17s 0d in London:
solid bricks £5 0s 0d per 1,000 in Belfast

to the building of houses in Belfast,
(Mr.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
Barbour): I have been asked by my right
Honourable Friend to reply to this question.
From the information available in my Ministry the prices of bricks in Belfast appear

MALONE REFORMATORY-WM.
COCHRANE.
5. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether a boy named William
Cochrane was in January, 1924, ordered by
the Belfast Magistrates to be detained in the
Malone Reformatory for three years; whether
the boy has been subjected to ill-treatment
at the hands of certain officials of the institution;
whether as a result of this treatment
the boy lost the sight of one eye whilst the
sight of the other is threatened; whether he
has been a patient in the Royal Victoria
Hospital since 2nd April, 1925; whether the
remainder of his term of detention will be
remitted, and what redress the Minister
proposes to offer.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The reply to the
first part of the question is in the affirmative.
As regards the second part, a complaint has
been received from the boy's mother as to
his treatment in the Reformatory, but the
inquiries which have been made do not disclose any grounds for this complaint. Examination of the boy's eyes at the Belfast
Ophthalmic Hospital some months before the
alleged ill-treatment is supposed to have
taken place revealed the fact that he was
practically blind of one eye, and that the
sight of the other, though fair, was not quite
perfect. The oculists at the hospital consider
that the conditions in both eyes are probably
congenital. A report from the Royal Victoria
Hospital indicates that the sight at present
is practically unchanged.
The boy was sent to the hospital for treatment for seizures, to which he is reported to
have been subject for the last four or five
years, and he is about to be discharged
from hospital. Further inquiries are being
made, and I will consider all the circumstances of the case.
Mr. DEVLIN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman what will happen to this boy
when he is discharged from the hospital? Is
he be sent back to the reformatory?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
stated to my hon. Friend that I will take
the whole circumstances of the case into consideration to see whether the boy should be
discharged from the reformatory?

The PRIME MINISTER: Yes, we are

which judicial rents are fixed presuppose
that the Government acts as an arbitrator between the landlord and tenant. The
proposal of the hon. Member is a direct
negation of this principle and it is not one
which this Government could entertain.
I have no cause to believe that landlords
generally are acting in an unreasonable
spirit where their tenants find themselves in
arrears by reason of the recent bad seasons.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: May I ask
the right hon. Gentleman is there not a
precedent for this seeing that after two or
three bad seasons some years ago the judicial
rents were reduced by three years under the
Land Act of 1887 by the Imperial Parliament?
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes, I believe in the past
the Imperial Parliament did deal with the
land question in the way touched upon by
my hon. Friend, but I cannot agree that the
circumstances now are identical with those
of the period to which he calls attention.
Mr. G. HENDERSON: Does the right hon.
Gentleman think that agriculture in this
Northern Province was ever in a worse condition than it is at present?
Mr. POLLOCK: No, but I understand the
rents are considerably lower now than they
were when the investigation was taken by
the Imperial Parliament at an earlier date.

as high as the rents?
ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURE.
Mr. COOPER (by private notice) asked the
Prime Minister whether in addition to the
£128,000 already granted in relief of agricultural rates the £10,000 spread over four
years for scientific research work, the grant
of £1,000 to the Ulster Farmers' Union, the
annual grants to County Committees, and the
scheme for assisting the easy purchase of
stock, &c., it is possible for the Government
to see its way further to assist agriculture
in view of the continued serious depression.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am glad to be
able to inform my hon. Friend that in response to representations made by the Ulster
Farmers' Union the Government is making
arrangements under which loans will be made
to local authorities at the low rate of interest
of 2 per cent. to allow them to make short
term advances in necessitous cases to tide
farmers over the present difficult times.
Mr. KYLE: Will the right hon. Gentleman
give such a grant to the unemployed workers
in Belfast during the present bad time?
Mr. DEVLIN: Does that mean an assurance
on the part of the right hon. Gentleman that
an equivalent grant will be given to the
towns?
The PRIME MINISTER: No, this is not
a grant; it is merely a loan at practically
nominal interest to help the farmers over the
present trying times. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Is the Farmers'
Union a local authority?

The PRIME MINISTER: No, the Farmers'
Union is the most representative agricultural
body in Northern Ireland, and it has
helped us very much in giving us advice as
to how to help the farmers during these present troublous times.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Can we get an
assurance from the Prime Minister that he
will be prepared to give a loan or grant to
an organisation representative of the industrial workers in, the same way as he has
given it to the Farmers' Union?
Mr. COOPER: I would like to thank the
Prime Minister for his reply which, I think,
will cause great gratification in the country.

I do so because it has been generally accepted in this Committee and elsewhere that
the question of housing should be a national
responsibility. I want to see that national
responsibility worked out through the local
authorities rather than depend upon private
enterprise in regard to the erection of houses.
Private enterprise has so lamentably failed
in the past to provide us with homes, to provide us with houses, that it seems to me that
to work out this national responsibility
through our local bodies would be very much
more efficacious than to subsidise private
enterprise to erect these houses. It is from
that point of view that I want the Commitee to approach this question.
It seems to me that, housing being a national
responsibility, it is but right that we as a
Committee should not allow profitering to
come in, that we should have these houses
erected at the cheapest possible price in the
most efficient way by our local authorities,
to the end that there may be no profitering
for individuals so far as this national charge
is concerned. During the war we had to
limit very seriously indeed the prices and
profits in respect of the making of shells and
munitions. We had to control that industry.
We had to take it over as a matter of fact
and had to do these things for the good of
the nation in the nation's peril. We contend

houses, and these houses were being let at
47 per cent. to 50 per cent. less than similar
houses built across the Channel. We discovered quite recently how impossible it is to
get any public body, no matter how
efficient it is, to build houses as cheaply as
they are built by private enterprise. I was
really surprised, in the interests of the class
my hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle) professes to speak
for, when he got up to propose the Amendment which stands on the Paper, because the
poorest amongst the working classes would
be the people who would suffer most if the
Amendment he has on the Paper were carried.
Mr. KYLE: Nonsense.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: My hon. Friend
says nonsense," but I believe an ounce of
fact is worth a ton of socialist argument.
Talk as you like, I say this, a public body
can never build houses as cheaply as private
enterprise. There is no question about it.
The thing has been settled, and settled in
this city of ours. There was a discussion
here yesterday with regard to the number
of bricks laid. Whereas Belfast Corporation
was getting less than 300 bricks, at the same
time I discovered that private builders got
1,000 to 1,100. The hon. Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Gyle) was quite right with regard to the thousand bricks, but they were
laid by private enterprise, and not by public
bodies.
There is another point in connection
with this Amendment to which I would
like to draw the attention of the
Committee. I was keenly interested,
as some of the other Members of this House
were, in the passing of the Housing Bill in
the Imperial Parliament. The hon. Member
for West Belfast and others were members
of that committee. In that committee I was
anxious to get the Government to offer the
same terms to private people that they were
giving to utility and other societies, because
I happened to know at that time that the
shipbuilding industry in this city was in a
prosperous condition, and the then leaders of
the shipbuilding industry were prepared to
put down a very large sum of money in order
to provide houses if they could get the Government to agree. And if they had I believe
there would have been no shortage of houses
in Belfast to-day. I do ask the Committee
not to be carried away even by the most eloquent Socialist arguments on this question
and to realise that if you are going to get
cheap houses and plenty of houses in this
Province there is only one way of doing it
and that is stimulating private enterprise.
(Hon. Members: Hear hear.) So far as 1
am concerned I have no hesitation in voting
against that Amendment.
The CHAIRMAN: I have carefully considered the original point to which I invited the attention of the Committee. I am
now clear as to what I ought to rule. 1
am all the clearer because of the debate that
has taken place. It will be observed that
the purpose of the Amendment is:
"Grants under this section shall be made
only in respect of houses which have been
erected by a local authority, a public utility society, or any society or corporation
not primarily established for the making
of profit."
Whereas the parent Act, the 1923 Act, contains in the first clause the following provision which is in distinct conflict with the
Amendment:
Subject to the provisions of this Section
the Ministry of Home Affairs of Northern
Ireland, in this Act referred to as "the
Ministry" may make grants to any persons
or bodies of persons constructing houses
and to local authorities carrying out
schemes for the provision of houses for the
working classes under the Housing of the
Working Classes Acts.
and so on. It will be clear, therefore, that
to admit this Amendment would be to admit
proposals in distinct conflict with the
cardinal clause of the parent Bill. I accordingly rule the Amendment out of order.
Mr. KYLE: I take it that the ruling means
that this House, a legislative assembly, have
no power to amend an Act passed before.
The CHAIRMAN: No; the hon. Member
puts a much too sweeping interpretation upon
a matter-of-fact ruling. What has been ruled
is that you cannot put in an amending Act
a provision which is in conflict with another
Act not the subject of consideration before
this Committee. To do that, I repeat, would
involve a glaring breach of order passing
two proposals in conflict with each otherwhich is one of the things I am here to
prevent.
Clause ordered to stand part of the Bill.
CLAUSE 2 (Increase of grant in respect
of construction of certain houses).
Eighty pounds shall be substituted for
sixty pounds in sub-section (2) of section
one of the principal Act as the amount
of the grant to be made under that section
in respect of a house which is commenced
after the passing of this Act and completed
within a period not exceeding four months
from the date of the commencement of
such house.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best): 1
beg to move in Clause 2, page 2, line 21. to

months") and insert "six."
The object of this amendment is to increase from four to six months the time
which may elapse between the commencement of a house and its completion so as to
qualify the builder of this house for the
subsidy. The Prime Minister yesterday in
answer to a request from all sides of the
House, particularly the hon. Member for
Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Elliott), who is
absent to-day, and the hon. Member
Antrim (Mr. George Henderson) below the
gangway, said he would see that this change
would be made. The effect would be that six
months would be given to the person building
a house within which to complete the house
in order to qualify for this increased subsidy. I beg to move.
for
Mr. KYLE: Is there no other reason except that the Prime Minister gave a pledge
that this time should be altered? Does the

Did the draftsman who drafted this Bill not

against the insignificant numbers
on this

take longer than four months to erect a

representations were made by the various

towns was considerable. The houses to
which the hon. Member referred were probably houses in the city of Belfast or close

that a farmer often builds his own house,

man.
Mr. COOPER: We often do it in

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I beg to
move in page 2, line 22, at the end of Clause
2, to add as a new Sub-section: "The cost of
houses to which Grants under this Section
may be made, must not exceed £500."
It will be perfectly obvious that the
intention of this Amendment is to
try to ensure that the subsidy will
be given towards the erection of workingclass houses, and the hon. Members who sit
on these Benches are of the opinion it would
be possible for people who would not come
in under that category to benefit by these
grants. It will be agreed that most of the
houses that are being built to-day are being
built for the purpose of sale. There would
be a fairly big tendency if subsidies are to
be given to houses that will cost more than.
£500 for that state of affairs to continue, and
we think there would be a greater possibility
of houses being built to be let if the subsidy
was confined to houses that will cost £500
and under. That is the principal reason
why we are attempting to limit the amount
to £500. A question that will enter very
largely is whether we will succeed in
getting any working-class dwellings erected.
The previous arguments put forward were
that the subsidy would not influence the
position to a great extent. We hold that
is not the state of affairs at all. I do not
think it is necessary to labour this question
unduly. Our principal contention is that
subsidies should be granted to essential
working-class houses, and that the cost of
them should not exceed £500. For that
reason I beg to move this Amendment.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: While I suppose the greatest need would be for houses
of the type just described by the hon.
Member (Mr. W. McMullen), there are also
other classes in the community that are
seriously effected by the housing shortage,
as well as what might commonly be
called the working classes. What about
the middle and the lower middle
classes; those who have been, perhaps,
the heaviest taxed in the community
considering their means, and who are
equally anxious to get houses to live in?
They are in just as difficult a position as
those who occupy the smaller houses described by my hon. Friend. I think it would
not be fair for Parliament to exclude that
class from benefiting under this Bill by
putting in a rigid Clause of this character
that the subsidy should be limited to houses
costing £500. That would be unwise and
extremely unfair. We owe a debt to that
class of the community, and if houses can
be erected for them, or if they can erect
houses themselves, that will also be relieving
the housing shortage considerably, because
the houses they are living in at the moment,
or the lodgings they are in, would be given
up, and there would be an incentive to them
to build houses, too. My hon. Friend (Mr.
W. McMullen) cannot have fully viewed
the possibilities that lie in the direction I
have indicated. I hope he will not press a
proposal of this kind to a vote, and thus
deprive another class in the community
which, after all, have suffered perhaps as
much as any class as a result of the war.
and who are feeling their position as
acutely, or perhaps more so, both from the
point of view of taxation and that of local
rates.

on the Order Paper presents somewhat the

guise from that on which I was obliged to

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: The reason
We move this Amendment is to try to
ensure that houses will be built as cheaply
as possible. We are of opinion that
an excessive charge is being made for most
building materials at the present time. A

to those who pay any attention to this industry that during a strike in 1923 the

that increase is still retained on the price

The Government profess themselves to be
exceptionally keen on getting houses for the
people. I presume the Government also want
the houses let at an economic rent. If houses
are going to be let at economic rents in
the near future it will be necessary to get
houses built as cheaply as possible. We
have had frequent discussions here as
whether the bricklayers are laying enough
bricks a day or not. The attention of the
Government benches seemed to be concentrated on that aspect of the question. We
are not asking that the bricklayers here
should lay as few bricks as they can. We
suggest that hon. Members are wasting their
eloquence on a subject which they know absolutely nothing about. The hon. Member for
West Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn), whether he
wanted to do it or not, confessed his ignorance of the whole question. He does not attempt to differentiate as to the question of
laying bricks. We get a tremendous number
of general charges preferred without any attempt being made to let us know exactly
what hon. Members are speaking about. The
hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr. Gyle)
gave a fairly clear explanation as to the
laying of bricks, and pointed out that while
in one particular aspect of building you
may succeed in getting 1,000 bricks a day
laid in another aspect you would not probably succeed in getting more than from 200
to 250 laid. It would be much better if hon.
Members on the Government benches instead
of wasting the time of the House on a discussion of this kind would try and concentrate on the question of building material.
We have had many points of view put forward in the discussion, but we want to try
and ensure that it will be possible to have
some of the houses that are going to be built
let at economic rents. If an excessive
charge is going to be made for the houses
it will be extremely difficult to do that.
I do not want to go too closely into the
question, but I have a decent idea of the
amount at which a kitchen house can be
built. I have a clear idea also of the amount
a parlour house can be built for at the
present time, and I am of opinion that
notwithstanding the Government subsidy it
will be extremely difficult to let the houses
at economic rents unless the present excessive charges are going to be reduced in
some particular direction. It is all very
well for hon. Members on the Government
benches to laugh when a proposal of this
kind comes along. I take it that the Government are really serious in their attempt to
get houses for the members of the working
classes. If that is the object, and we are
wrong in suggesting that excessive charges
are being made for building materials, why
do we have discussion on the matter at all?
Why not give the Ministry of Home Affairs
these powers? I do not think it is necessary for me at this stage to say anything
further. I would like to hear the arguments
that hon. Members opposite have to offer
to this Amendment, if they attempt to adduce any arguments at all. My experience
in this House is that many Members of the
Government take the opportunity of remaining
silent rather than attempt to put forward
an argument. I believe Members on the
Government benches will have great difficulty in putting forward an argument as
to why this proposal should not be adopted,
because I believe it is reasonable in every
way. If the Government's intentions are
what they profess them to be there is absolutely no reason why this proposal should
not be accepted. Let us know exactly where
we stand in connection with the matter of
building materials. If you prove that no
excessive charge is being made that will discount any argument advanced up to the
inoment. There are many reasons why the
Government should lend a ready ear to this
proposal that is being made now and to
accept and embody it in the Bill.

INDUSTRY.
Motion made, and Question proposed:

(Captain Mullholland.)
Mr. GRANT: I would like to ask the
Minister of Labour if he has read the speech
delivered yesterday by Mr. Strachan, director
of Messrs. Workman, Clark & Co., in connection with the depression in the shipbuilding industry. He there states that the root
of the trouble is to be found in the position
in which the sheltered trades have entrenched
themselves and in the rates of wages paid
by public bodies to unskilled labour.
view of the importance attached to this statement I would like to know if the Minister
is prepared to give the House his view on
In
957 Shipbuilding Industry.

28 MAY 1925
Shipbuilding Industry.
this question which is of such vital importance to all sections of the people.
Mr. ANDREWS: 1 have read the speech to
which my hon. Friend the Member for North
Belfast (Mr. Grant) has referred, and coming from a gentleman who occupies such a
high position in the shipbuilding world, and
who knows SO much about conditions
governing the building of ships and shipowning it is a most important pronouncement. It should receive the careful attention
of everybody who is interested in our industrial life. Personally, I cannot agree
with it in many respects because, as my hon.
Friend has said, he seems to think that the
root of the trouble is due to the fact that
our local authorities are paying wages
which
higher than those
are paid in
ordinary industrial firms where there is
a very fierce not only national but international competition. I see by the speech
that he also refers to the wages which are
being paid on relief schemes by the Ministry
of Labour in Northern Ireland. As regards
the Corporation side of the problem, the
members of the Corporation are quite able
to deal with the matter from their own standpoint, but I may say that so far as I know
the Belfast Corporation are not paying
higher wages than are being paid in comparable cities in Great Britain.
As regards the relief schemes, I would
have thought they would have been looked
upon with more sympathy by the gentleman
who made the speech that has been referred
to, because, after all, it is very largely
shipyard unemployed men who are getting
work on these schemes. Although the
weekly wage for full time is specified
at 469. a week, owing to the irregularity of the employment, due to weather
conditions and other causes, the actual wage
received by the workers each week is very
much less. Again, the persons who are employed on these schemes are very often
tradesmen, who never expected that they
would be driven by force of circumstances to
accept work of this kind.
If I may say so, I think Mr. Strahan, in
his remarks, was a little severe both on
Governments and on local authorities. I
think he was especially severe on Governments, for he referred to the Imperial
Government as well as to this Government.
I think he might have remembered that both
Governments, by means of guaranteeing
loans to encourage the building of ships, are
doing everything they possibly can to further
the shipbuilding industry. The real causes
of the depression in the shipbuilding industry are three in number. The first is,
that our naval programme has been greatly
reduced in recent years. Second, reparations
were accepted in the form of ships from
Germany, and those ships were handed over
to some of the best clients of our Belfast
yards, who have never been able to order a
ship from our local yards since. That may
have been a right policy or a wrong policy.
it is not for me to say; but the fact is there,
and it has undoubtedly been one of the
causes of the depression in the shipbuilding
industry, by which we have suffered to such
a severe extent. Third, not only here in
Northern Ireland and in Great Britain, but
throughout the world, ordinary trade has
been depressed since the war, or shortly after
the war, and there has not been the flow of
trade between nations which there was in
pre-war days. The result of that is that so
many ships are not really required to carry
the traffic which is available, and thousands
of ships are lying in harbours at the present
time for which goods cannot be found. Those
are some of the causes that have brought the
slump into the shipbuilding industry, and
I think they should be known. Mr. Strahan
says matters should be dealt with perfectly
frankly and perfectly candidly. I think so,
too, and in these few remarks I have tried
to do so.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I am glad
that the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Grant) has brought this matter to the notice
of the House. As a Member of this Parliament and of one of the local bodies against
whom the charge has been brought of paying
very high wages, I am glad that the Minister
of Labour is in the House to-night. While
we know that 46s. is not a living wage, we
remember that that is the wage paid on the
relief works sanctioned by the Minister of
Labour. Belfast Corporation pay £2 8s. Od.
or £2 9s. Od., but they are not paying more
than the Bangor Urban Council, and I think
it is a very serious thing indeed for any man
holding a responsible position to bring a
charge against the Government of paying
more wages than they should be paying. My
opinion is this, that any man who brings a
charge of this nature should first of all know
what the cost of living is, and should get
at the people who are really responsible for
the high cost of living. Take a man with
five children.
Mr. SPEAKER: I was considering whether
I ought to rise or not. It is rather difficult
to say to what extent we are entitled to discuss in this House speeches of private
individuals outside. I let the matter go as
far as it has gone, because so far as it concerns any Government Department, or any
action they are taking, it is quite in order;
but I do not think it is for this House on
the Motion for the Adjournment to discuss in
an academic way speeches of private individuals outside.

British financiers who enabled German shipbuilding to become a menace to British shipbuilding. In view of the menace of foreign
competition I would like to know is this

in plots for the unemployed, so that they

While we should be producing the essentials

should see that the unemployed are placed on

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I would feel
obliged if you would permit me to make one
observation. I would like to congratulate the
Minister of Labour on the very excellent
statement he has made. I believe the
statement of the Minister of Labour
is the most sensible statement in
this connection that I have heard coming from the lips of a responsible
statesman for quite a considerable time.
People are very prone to attribute all our
commercial and industrial depression at the
moment to the wages that obtain in industry.
There is one aspect of this question that I
would briefly like to direct attention to. As
a member of the Corporation I was forced
some time ago without the opportunity of
saying a word to listen to a deputation that
came there. One of the deputation was
from one of the largest shipbuilding firms
probably in the world. I was not able to

refer to. We were asked to accept the statement that the wages paid to the Corporation
and other workers in the transport trades
were responsible for the great depression
that has taken place in the shipbuilding industry.
There is one aspect of the question I would
fail in my duty if I did not call attention to.
That is the question of the over-capitalisation
of industry. There is one particular
illustration I would like to give: I take the
firm of Harland and Wolff. During the war
they established a new yard, known as the
East Yard, and which was built out of money
which I believe should have gone to the
Government by way of excess profits. These
gentlemen are now complaining about the
overhead charges, and the point I want to
direct attention to is, that while their old
yard is lying idle they brought into being a
new yard whereby the overhead charges of
the firm were considerably increased.
are asked now that the wages of the Corporation and other employees should be reduced
in order to facilitate these shipyards to get
orders. I believe that a large portion of the

which these firms were managed or mismanaged during the war than any question
of the wages of the workers in sheltered
trades or any other industry. I am obliged
for the opportunity of making my point of
view clear so far as this particular matter
is concerned.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I will answer both the hon. Member's questions together. If he will refer to my
message to the electors of Northern Ireland
before the last General Election, he will find
that I then undertook that no further licensing Measure would be considered during the
lifetime of this Parliament, and no further
Amendment of the existing Act would be
entertained unless, after a fair and reasonable trial, the original intention of Parliament when it was placed upon the Statute
Book is not being faithfully fulfilled. In
accordance with this statement, therefore,
the Government will not introduce licensing
legislation unless it appears that the original
intentions of Parliament have not been
given effect to by the Act of 1923. I am not
aware that there is any ground for apprehension as to the rights of the licensees referred to being adequately secured. Should
the necessity arise, however, the Government will give the question the fullest
consideration.

BALLYMENA HEALTH VISITOR.
Mr. T. W. McMULLAN (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs,
whether his attention has been called to a
recent resolution of the Ballymena Urban
District Council protesting against a statement made by him in this House on the 27th
ult., and whether he has any statement now
to make on the subject?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am obliged to the
hon. Member for the opportunity which he
has afforded me of making a statement on
this point.
I have received a resolution from the
Urban District Council of Ballymena asking
me publicly to withdraw the statement which
I made to the effect "that the casting vote
of the Chairman had to be resorted to to
perpetrate this job."
If the House will permit me I would like
to make a somewhat detailed statement of
the facts of this case.
According to the Minutes of the Urban
District Council of the 2nd February, the
Council considered applications for the post
of Health Visitor and Maternity and Child
Welfare Nurse, and decided to refer the
matter to the Public Health Committee to
recommend a suitable applicant.
The Public Health Committee met on the
12th February, and according to the Minutes
which I have now been able to obtain, the
following decision was arrived at, and I
quote the extract from the minutes
verbatim:-
:-
"After consultation with Dr. Currie, who
is the Council's own Medical Officer of
Health, and the ladies associated with him,
the Committee ascertained that while all
the candidates possessed the certificates required, only two of them (I will not mention
names, but neither of them was Miss
Gillespie) had the necessary district training and experience which they considered
essential." (The minutes are signed by Mr.
McClelland, the Chairman of the Committee,
and also Chairman of the Urban District
Council).
On the 17th February a meeting of the
Council in Committee was held, the Chairman of the Council being in the chair, when,
notwithstanding the recommendation of the
Committee specially appointed by the
Council to consider the qualifications of the
applicants, a motion was proposed that Miss
Mary J. Gillespie be appointed, the voting
of the ordinary members of the Council was
even, and the chairman thereupon gave his
vote, as he was entitled to do, in favour of
Miss Gillespie, thus deciding the appointment in her favour.
These minutes were confirmed at a meeting
of the Council on the 2nd March, on which
day a letter from the Ministry was considered drawing attention to the fact that the
qualifications of the person appointed did
not comply with the terms of the advertisement. A resolution was also passed at that
meeting to inform the Ministry that none
of the applicants had the experience asked
for by the advertisement outside hospital
training.
I need not weary the House recounting the
remainder of the proceedings, which have
already been discussed.
I express my regret that I used the
expresion "casting vote," which I stated was
given by the Chairman. It was not, in the
legal sense, "the casting vote," but as I have
stated, Mr. McClelland-after the voting of
the ordinary members of the Council showed
an equal number of votes for and against
Miss Gillespie-then exercised his right of
voting, which decided the appointment in
her favour.
I am sorry that I should have offended the
feelings of the members of the Council by
the use of the expression, "perpetrating a
job." but I may perhaps be permitted to
point out that it is deeply to be regretted
that the Council, having appointed a Committee to investigate the qualifications and
experience of the candidates, should override the finding of their own Committee on a
question of fact, as the Committee found
that while all the applicants had the
necessary certificates, only two possessed the
experience which they considered essential.
May I also repeat that the object of the
Ministry has been to secure a properly
qualified and properly experienced person for
this important job, affecting as it does the
health and welfare of children and expectant
mothers in the community, and I would express the earnest hope that the Council may
see their way to refrain from pressing the
claims of any candidate whom their own
specially appointed Committee could not recommend for appointment. The appointment, I may say, is a well-paid one, the salary
being £164 per year, half of which is paid
by the Ministry of Home Affairs, and I feel
sure that the Council will have no difficulty
in securing a properly qualified and properly
experienced person for the position.

collective judgment of the Urban Council of
Ballymena? Should he not accord to the
Urban Council the same privilege that he
himself claims?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The whole point
turns as to whether or not Miss Gillespie
had the experience which is essential for
this appointment. The Committee of the
Ballymena Urban Council decided that she
had not. I am confirmed in my opinion by
the reports and certificates which I myself
have received, and having regard to the fact
that the Government are paying part of the
salary, they decided it was absolutely
essential that the nurse should have had
actual experience in midwifery and child
welfare, which she had not.
Mr. MCALLISTER: As a matter of fact
does not the Council contend that this nurse
had all the qualifications set out in the
published regulations of the Ministry of
Home Affairs?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, they never
took up that contention; in fact, their own
medical officer reported to his Council that
Miss Gillespie had not this experience.
Mr. MCALLISTER: I did not ask had she
the experience. I asked had she the
qualifications laid down by the Ministry.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, she had not.
Mr. McALLISTER: In what particular?
Mr. SPEAKER: I think this should be
pursued on another occasion.
SHORT TERM LOANS FOR FARMERS.
Mr. CRAWFORD (by private notice) asked
the Prime Minister whether arrangements
have yet been made for the issue of shortterm loans to farmers in necessitous circumstances, as foreshadowed in this House on
28th May.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Since the hon. Member for Tyrone
and Fermanagh first questioned the Government on this subject, we decided, in order to
ensure the earliest possible relief, to ask the
banks who operate in the Province to allow
the Government to utilise their machinery
for distributing the Government loans to
farmers, and I am glad to announce their
willingness to co-operate. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) These loans will be issued to
those farmers who have been so unfortunate
as to suffer loss of stock during the past inclement weather of winter and spring, and
are intended to be utilised for replacing such
stock. It is proposed that forms of application be stocked by the banks, and obtained
from them by applicants, and, after completion, sent by the applicants to the Ministry
of Agriculture. Should that Ministry approve
the loan, it will be issued through the bank
selected by the applicant in the form of a
bill discounted at 2 per cent, free of stamp
duty. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) A
further intimation will be published when
the forms are available.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: May I ask
the right hon. Gentleman are these loans to
be confined to farmers who have lost stock?
There are farmers who lost practically their
all in crops last season. Will these loans not
be available for men who lost their crops,
and so tide them over the present time?
Mr. POLLOCK: It will be a very difficult
matter to estimate the losses based upon the
facts to which my hon. Friend has drawn
attention. In the meantime it is not proposed by the Government that these loans
should extend to farmers under such conditions, but will be limited to those who have
suffered such severe losses as is well known
from death of stock such as sheep, cattle, &c.
Mr. CRAWFORD: May I ask my right
hon. Friend if those necessitous farmers who
require money to buy seeds would not be in-
Icluded in this scheme?
Mr. POLLOCK: The provision of such a
thing as referred to by my hon. Friend is
determined by the Ministry of Agriculture,
and this House has voted a certain amount
for this purpose. I am quite sure my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Archdale) who presides over
this Ministry, will take care of that department.
Mr. GYLE: Will these loans that are supposed to be for farmers be extended to any
person who has lost his all through the operation of the Intoxicating Liquor Act, 1923 ?
Mr. SPEAKER: That does not arise out of
the question.

What is life for us? We start work at
thirteen years of age. We serve our times
as shipwrights or mechanics. After five or
six years we come out of our time and are
generally paid off, because no firm will employ
an apprentice who has served his time in that
firm. We go to work in the yard for a year
or two, and are more than likely paid off.
Then we come come back to the firm with
which we served our apprenticeship, or we
may walk the streets. During all the time
we are only in receipt of sufficient wages to
enable us to keep our homes. You have only
got to reckon it up yourselves. £2 11s 6d is
the wage of an engineer to-day. Town shops
pay £3 1s 6d I know, and the wage is a
little better in other places, but that is the
sort of wage on which the working classes
have got to live. Ask yourselves what position you would be in if you were out of work
for three out of the twelve months in the

state of insecurity practically all the days of

happening in Belfast at the present momen

it is this growing feeling of discontent wit
the present system which makes me say the
the day will come-it may not be in my da

in my day or in the lifetime of any ho

system of society that keeps us down will
abolished and we will have a cleaner syste

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 9th June, 1925.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
BALLYMONEY POLICE BARRACKS.—
LABOURERS' WAGES.
1. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Finance, whether, in view of the
fact that labourers employed at the police
barracks, Ballymoney, only receive 8d per
hour as against 9d per hour paid to all other
labourers employed at similar work in the
same town, the Minister will be prepared to
submit the matter to an independent person
to arbitrate upon.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): My information as to the rates of
wages paid in Ballymoney district does not
agree with the statement of the hon. Member,
and as I informed him, in reply to a previous
question, the Architect to whom the matter
was referred, as provided by the contract,
found that the contractor had reasonably
observed the Fair Wages Clause. This
finding is under Clause 27 (b) of the contract
final and binding upon the contractor and the
Ministry.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I would like to inquire, in view of the fact that the Minister of
Finance does not seem to have any definite
information regarding these rates of wages,
whether he is prepared to enter into negotiation with the trades' union officials who are
responsible for the settling of wages in Ballymoney and district?
Mr. POLLOCK: No, sir; but I may say
that at present we are considering the question of the revision of the form of contract,
with the object, amongst other things, of
providing for the appointment of an independent arbitrator in cases of this kind. I
hope that this will solve any problem of this
kind that will arise in future.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Can we have an undertaking from the Minister of Finance that
this will be one of the first things to be dealt
with as soon as this impartial person is
appointed?
Mr. POLLOCK: I cannot give any undertaking in regard to that. I think I have
answered the question fully, and I hope I
have satisfied the hon. Member.
SPEAKER'S HOUSE, STORMONT.
2. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Finance, whether it is a fact that
the carving work connected with the
Speaker's House, now being erected at Stormont, is being done in London, and, if so,
having regard to the number of unemployed
carvers in Northern Ireland, the Minister
will take steps to have the work done locally.
Mr. POLLOCK: As the honourable Member
is no doubt aware, this is a matter for the
Imperial Government. I understand that
the contract for the building has been given
to a local firm, but that some carving work
required is not being done locally owing to
difficulties connected with the supervision of
the work.
CHEAP LOANS TO FARMERS.
3. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Finance whether the Government
would reconsider the restrictions placed on
the cheap loans to farmers who have lost
stock, and whether he is aware that many
farmers who lost practically all their crops
last year are in urgent need of such assistance until another crop is taken out.
Mr. POLLOCK: I am aware that the bad
harvests of last year have resulted in a large
amount of distress in the agricultural community generally. But I must refer the hon.
Member to the Estimates for Agricultural
Services, where he will see that provision has
been made to supply seed at the cheapest
possible rates in certain necessitous areas,
payment being spread over a period of time.
In these circumstances the Government
cannot see its way to extend the new scheme
for making short term loans to include the
provision of seed.
Mr. G. HENDERSON: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the number of cases
that can be relieved by the amount voted
in the Estimate referred to will be very small
in proportion to the number of cases that
will need assistance, and, therefore, I ask if
the Government can see their way to extend
these short term loans?
Mr. POLLOCK: I think I can assure my
hon. Friend and the House that my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Agriculture, if
necessitous circumstances develop, will, in
addition to the Estimate passed, not disregard the cases as they arise. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Mr. KYLE: Will the Minister of Finance
recommend the Government to give the same
terms to business men who are in distress at
the present time?
Mr. POLLOCK: No, sir; I do not think
that is quite a relevant question."

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
EX-SERVICE MEN'S HOUSES, BALLY-
CLARE.
4. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he is aware that
seventy applications for ex-Service men's
houses were sent in by the Ballyclare branch;
that only two have been erected, and in view
of the acute shortage of houses in this district
will he approach the proper authorities in
order that more of these houses may be
allotted to this district.
Mr. POLLOCK: I understand that the
question of the allotment of the houses remaining to be erected is at present before the
Land Trust, and that careful consideration
is being given to the matter with the object
of ensuring the most equitable distribution of
the houses. I will see that my honourable
Friend's representations with regard to the
Ballyclare district are communicated to the
Trustees.
LABOURERS' COTTAGES.-BALLYMONEY
RURAL DISTRICT.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether the Ballymoney Rural District Council provisionally approved of a
scheme of labourers' cottages, which included
eighteen for the division of Enagh; whether
subsequently this number was reduced to
nine, and no account of the reduction appeared in the newspaper report of the proceedings of the meeting of Council at which
the reduction was made; whether the reporters present were asked to suppress this
information; whether an application has
been made to the Council for the names of
the applicants whose representations were
rejected and the cause of rejection; whether
the majority of the members of the Council
are unaware as to what constitutes eligibility
for a cottage under the Labourers Acts;
whether he would consider the propriety of
issuing an explanatory memorandum on the
subject, and whether he will give the information sought for, or ask the Council to give
it.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The Ministry of Home
Affairs has no right to interfere with the
discretion of the Council when the Council
is formulating a scheme under the Labourers
Acts. The functions of the Ministry only
arise when the scheme is submitted for confirmation. The scheme to which the hon.
Member refers has not yet been submitted to
me.
•
TEMPORARY TEACHERS OF SCHOOLS.
6. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he could state the number
of temporary teachers of national schools who
were in the service of the Commissioners of
National Education in Northern Ireland at
the date of the formation of the Northern
Ministry of Education; how many such
teachers are now employed by the Ministry;
whether it is proposed, when schools are
transferred or amalgamated, to take over
and
these temporary teachers,
if not,
whether compensation will be paid, and at
what rate.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): Excluding locum tenens teachers,
who are employed for periods not exceeding
three months, and substitutes employed for
teachers who are absent owing to illness or
for the purpose of attending training colleges,
the number of teachers in Northern Ireland
temporarily recognised at the date of the
transfer of the Educational Services to this
Ministry was 9, and is at present 15.
With regard to the position of such teachers
in the event of the transfer to Education
Authorities of the schools in which they are
employed, I would refer the honourable
Member to Section 14 (4) of the Education
Act.
As the teachers referred to are employed
in a temporary capacity, pending inquiry by
the Ministry into the necessity for the continuance of the schools in which they are
serving, they cannot be regarded as having
any valid claim for compensation in the event
of the schools in which they are employed
being amalgamated or closed.

THE UNEMPLOYMENT PROBLEM.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House do now adjourn."-Captain
Dixon.)
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Mr. W. McMullen
Mr. KYLE: We feel that the Government
are not realising their responsibilities to the
unemployed of Belfast and the Six Counties.
Unless the Government are prepared to take
more steps than it is apparently their intention of doing at the moment, the question
of unemployment will, before this House meets
again, reach such a state that it will be impossible to avoid serious trouble in Belfast
and the country at large. It seems to me to
he perfectly obvious that if the people of
Belfast begin to think that the Government,
who are responsible for the maintenance of
order and of everything that goes to make a
happy community, are not paying sufficient
attention to this question of unemployment,
there may be serious trouble in the city. We
are going to have an army of something like
50,000 unemployed, who will be walking about
the streets with nothing to do-all owing to
the Government's apparent inertia in this
matter. Unless the Government can give us
some assurance that they are going to extend
to the business people the assistance that they
are giving to the farming community in the
way of lending money on easy terms to
enable them to develop their businesses, we
will have a very serious state of affairs. The
working people are in a bad plight at present,
but their condition will be accentuated if the
Government have no intention of doing anything further than is proposed up to the
present. That is the reason I raise the question on the Adjournment.
:
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) I am rather sorry that my hon.
Friend did not give me notice that he proposed to raise this important question to-day.
because if he had done so I could obviously
have given a more considered reply after consultation with my colleagues than I am in a
987 The Unemployment Problem. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Unemployment Problem. 988

[Mr. Andrews]
position to do.
However, I think he is
perhaps, if I may say so, a little ungenerous
in his remarks-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)
-because he must realise, as every man who
wishes to look on this problem calmly and
from a reasonable standpoint does, that the
Government has been doing everything possible to deal with this matter. In the first
place we have, through our Loans Guarantee
Acts, been encouraging private enterprise,
encouraging orders to be placed which undoubtedly would not othewise have been
placed. We have agreed to give grants from
our Exchequer to local authorities for every
scheme, I think almost without exception,
that they have put forward, and in addition
to that we have given unemployment benefit
in step with Great Britain to those for whom
work could not be found.
Further, as my hon. Friend knows, on
behalf of the Government I have agreed, in
conjunction with the Lord Mayor, to call a
conference to consider this whole problem
from every viewpoint. I am glad to be able
to tell the House that the invitations to that
conference have already been issued by the
Lord Mayor and myself, and that it is proposed to hold the preliminary meeting on
Tuesday next, to consider how this matter
can best be approached. It is not for me
to-day even to indicate what course that
body when they meet will pursue, but I would
like to assure my hon. Friend that he is
obviously wrong in thinking that the Government are callous about this matter. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) The Government are
just as anxious as he or any member of the
community is to do everything possible, but
unfortunately we cannot do the impossible,
and I would remind my hon. Friend that this
trouble is not centred alone in the City of
Belfast or in the Six Counties for that matter.
There are large towns in Great Britain, and
there are large districts throughout the world
in a far more serious plight than Northern
Ireland is in.
I admit that the position is serious. No
one regrets it more than I do. No one, if I
may say so, carries a heavier burden than I
do-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and if my
hon. Friend or others can put forward
practical proposals to relieve the situation
no one will welcome those proposals more
than I will.
Mr. WM. MCMULLEN: I would like to ask
the Minister of Labour whether this conference, which I understand he, in conjunction
with the Lord Mayor, is summoning, to be
held in Belfast, is going to consider this
whole question, or whether the conference
will decide whether a Departmental Commission be set up.
Mr. ANDREWS: In this House the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin), who
I regret is not present to-day, suggested that
a conference should be held. The Belfast
Local Employment Committee also made
that suggestion to me, and the Corporation
unanimously made the same suggestion. That
conference has been approved I think by the
community at large, and purposely I do not
A want to say one single word that will fetter
that conference. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) It is to be composed of representative
men of all classes, of all parties, and of all
creeds. I want the community to put confidence in the members who form that conference, and above everything else, as I have
already said, I want to lift this whole matter
above party, above sect, and above class. I
do appeal to my hon. Friend to help me in
what I believe is fundamental to the success
of the conference, or any measure of success
which it is possible to achieve.
Mr. WM. McMULLEN: I regret that the
right hon. Gentleman has not answered my
question. What I want definite information
on is this-whether it is the intention of the
right hon. Gentleman to allow this conference
that he is summoning to deal with the whole
problem or whether he is going to ask the
conference to decide whether a Departmental
Commission should be set up or not?
Mr. ANDREWS: I thought I had made it
clear to my hon. Friend that I was not going
to be pressed into tying or fettering in any
way that conference. Therefore, I say that
I am going to leave the matter and all other
such matters to the conference to decide, and
I think that is a wise course to pursue.
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask the Minister
of Labour what proportion of Labour representation he is giving on this conference? I
would like to see the conference doing some
thing. I hope it is not going to meet and
indulge in talking, but that something

I would like to know what proportion of
representation Labour will have
conference?

Mr. WM. MCMULLEN: I regret very
much that I cannot agree with the statements

made by the right hon. Gentleman. If I
remember correctly the initiative in this matter was taken by the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin), and it was subsequently
taken up by the City Council. The Council,
I think, requested that Parliament should be

Parliament has not been taken into consideration at all. We had a preliminary discussion on this question. Certain suggestions
were thrown out by this House. The House
is now going to adjourn and we cannot get
any definite undertaking from the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) as to whether the
suggestions made by hon. Members of this
House are going to be acted upon or not.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): What suggestions?
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN : The
suggestion was thrown out by the hon.
Member for the University (Mr. Johnstone)
that a Departmental Committee should be set
up, and in the opinion of some of us that
would be much the better way to approach
this question. Instead the Government
apparently are going to be subordinated to the
City Council, or the General Purposes Committee of the Corporation, because the
Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews) does not
think fit to take the House into his confidence
and tell us what is going to be done. As one
hon. Member of this House I want to protest
strongly against that attitude being taken up
by the right hon. Gentleman and the
Government generally. As a representative
of a large industrial constituency I have a
right to know before the House adjourns what
attitude the Government is going to take up.
I do not believe, that the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) is attempting to
belittle this problem in any way at all, nor
do I question his sincerity or his sympathy.
I believe he has a large share of both those
qualities, but I do suggest that he is not
treating the House fairly or going the right
Iway about the matter. On the last occasion
on which I discussed this matter I suggested
that the whole conference is foredoomed to
failure. It is fairly obvious that orthodox
opinions and orthodox economics are not going
to solve this problem at all. We have been
acting on those orthodox opinions and ideas
all along and the problem is steadily and
gradually getting worse. My concern is this:
If we are going to have expressed at this conference only the stereotyped ideas and
orthodox opinions that have brought us to the
present impasse the situation is going to get
gradually worse. Of the opinions I have
heard expressed as to the lines along which
this problem should be solved by hon. Mem-
+
bers who have taken part in the discussions
up to the present I have no hope at all, and
until the Government are prepared to deal
with it in a way in which they have not dealt
with it up to the moment no good is going
to result from this conference.
The position of hon. Members is that the
House is now going to adjourn, and we are
not even getting an undertaking from the
Government that, in the event of any repre
sentations or recommendations coming from
that conference, the House will be summoned.
That will lie in the judgment of right hon.
Gentlemen opposite, and I want to suggest
that they do not realize the seriousness of the
situation. One hon. Gentleman (Dr. Morrison) was talking about the French Revolution
the other day. The powers that were in existence then under-estimated the seriousness
of the situation that led up to the French
Revolution. I am rather inclined to think
that all Governments are largely shortsighted. Owing to lack of touch with the
people they do not understand their problems
or how the people are situated. It is not my
duty to advise the Government. Probably
in days to come as a result of the industrial
unrest our numbers may be increased, but we
are not studying it from that point of view
but from the point of view of the welfare of
the community.
I want to suggest that the Government are
belittling this whole question. They do not
seem to understand. They are trifling with
it, and are most hopelessly out of touch with
the people. The responsibility for that will
be yours, and I suggest that it is a serious
responsibility, but you do not seem to he
alive to the whole question. During the time
this House is adjourned numbers of people
will be disqualified because two years will
have elapsed since they have contributed
stamps. Before I came to this House to-day
I heard of the case of a man with a long industrial record-unfortunately for himself
he is not the most fit physically-whose son
has been disqualified because he has been
two years unemployed. Unless before the 4th
August next his father can get six stampsand God knows how he is going to get themhe is going to be disqualified too, and there is
nothing for them but the workhouse. Yet
this House is going to adjourn until October
without knowing definitely what the Government are going to do. I have entered my protest, and that is the only thing I am concerned about. I suggest that the Government
are not handling this question in the way in
which it should be handled. It is a serious
question both for hon. Members on these
benches and on the Government benches, but
the responsibility for the whole thing will lie
upon the Government if they do not act
differently to what they are doing at the
moment.

Dr. MORRISON: I must confess that I
think the Labour hon. Members in this House
have a right to complain, and for this reason:
A question has been raised as to the constitution of this conference. I would think that
the people to whom the Minister of Labour
would most naturally send invitations, or
whom he would consult, would be the Labour
Members of this House. We have one on this
bench who I think correctly interprets
Labour. We have others on the other side
who also think they interpret the wishes of
Labour. In any event these people speak for
the working classes. They are sent here by
the large majority of workers. I would resent it myself if, when you proposed to deal
with some medical question you ignored the
medical profession in this House, and I think
the Labour Members in turn have a right to
object.
I do not see either why, with due care
against tying the hands of this conference,
the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews) should
not be able to say whether or not we are
going to have a Departmental Committee if
that conference approves of it. So far as I
can see the Government have done everything
they possibly could to meet this difficult situation, and everything that has been done has
been explained here in this House, so that in
that respect nobody has any right to complain. But admittedly the condition of
affairs in Belfast is very serious, and
hon. Members returned to represent the
people have a right to explain their views
before this House and to advocate them
strongly within reason. I think we are
all unanimously anxious, if it is at all
possible, to meet the serious state of affairs
that exists in Belfast, and I am sure no
more sympathetic person could be applied to
for that purpose than the Minister of Labour
(Mr. Andrews). (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
