for raising any point here to-day without
having given due notice to the Minister of
the Department concerned. However, Ministers seem to be in a fairly conciliatory mood
to-day and I will try to raise the point in
the least controversial manner possible under
the circumstances. The House will remember that some time ago I asked the
Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock) if the
Northern Government could not consent to
give the grant in aid that they promised in
connection with the Land Purchase Bill from
the first gale day preceding the passing of
the Act rather than from the appointed day.
That was that the unbought tenants should
have relief of a substantial character from
the passing of this Act rather than from the
appointed day, which under the Bill may be
four years ahead.
In reply to that question the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Pollock) said the Government
could not consider it because it would involve
an additional burden on the finances of
Ulster. He also said it would mean amending the Northern Ireland Land Bill, but I
think it would not have done the Northern
Ireland Land Bill any harm to have had it
amended in this respect. However, dealing
with the other point of its throwing an
additional burden on Ulster finances, the
Government have now consented to give small
loans. I thank the Government for that, and
I welcome it because I think it is very much
needed. But when they have done this thing
they should not have left the other undone,
and I claim for these men whom I am sent
here to represent and for those who have
been kept out of the benefits of land purchase
since 1918, that is seven years, with the prospect under this Act that it may be four
years before they get relief, should
receive the Ulster Government's first
consideration because their rents are 20
per cent. higher on the average than those
other men who are now paying of their
loans. I am personally very sorry the
Government did not at the time consent to
have at least some discussion on this point,
because it is no pleasure to me to come here
and criticise the Government. I would much
rather try to co-operate in producing a
scheme that would allow these men to settle
down, having been fairly treated. I do not
know how far I have succeeded, but I have
tried in discussing this question not to allow
my prejudices to affect it, but to discuss the
thing from a purely financial standpoint. I
do not wish to hold out any threats, but if
the Government thinks that because this
Act was slipped through the Imperial Parliament without discussion they have got
rid of the question they are mistaken, because I have had two communications from
different parts of Northern Ireland this week
asking me to assist at public meetings of protest against the terms of the Northern Ireland Land Act. I do hope that even at this
stage the Government will in their wisdom
and-I was going to use another word,
generosity, but it is not generosity, it is only
justice we are asking-meet us
on this
point, because if this Act is going to stand
as it is with a prospect of years before the
farmers get relief there is going to be
general disappointment and bitterness that
will not be beneficial to the Government of
this area.
There is another point which I think is
important that I raised when the Minister of
Agriculture was not present, that is the
question of our pork exports. There is probably no section of the agricultural industry
that is more capable of development than our
pork industry, and I suggest that the Ministry of Agriculture might with profit take
into consideration the setting up of an
Advisory Committee in connection with this
industry. It is rather a strange thing that
this branch of our industry, which has kept
a steady price, and which really, I suppose,
may be said to be remunerative to some
extent, should be declining. In face of this
the Department should take into consideration
the setting up of an Advisory Committee

[Mr. G. Henderson]
composed of representatives of
feeders, curers, and shippers to take into

as to how best to foster the breeding and

House, because I see hon. Members are all

simply mention it to-day to bring it under

Just before I sit down I want to say I am
Sorry that the Government have not seen
their way to find themselves short loans to
farmers who have suffered severe losses
through storm, and, as I said before, I feel
there are other farmers who have lost as
much, probably, and are in as bad a condition. I do not think there is any risk in
leaving this question to the farmers themselves as a farmer is a man who does not
ask for a loan unless he is in very great
need of it. I do not think there will be any
abuse if the Government leave these loans
open to needy farmers who require financial assistance. The House will agree that
the industrial condition of Northern Ireland
will largely depend on agriculture, and anything that can be done at the present time
to help agriculture to tide over its present
difficulties will eventually help every other
industry and trade.
Mr. POLLOCK: My hon. Friend (Mr. G.
Henderson) has raised a question which has
been considered by this House at an early
stage of its sittings, that is, the question of
expediting the appointed days. My hon.
Friend forgets that this matter is within the
determination of the Imperial Government.
To begin with, the Land Commission is a
reserved service, and the control of this
matter will lie in the hands of that
body; but I can give this assurance on
the part of our Government that so far as
we can bring any influence to bear upon the
British Treasury that influence will be exerted in order that the appointed days should
be expedited. It must be remembered that
the issue of stock by the British Treasury
must keep side by side with the appointed
days, and, therefore, when we analyze the
whole subject we get back to the fact that
the matter is largely determined by the
British Treasury by its action in regard to
the issue of the necessary stock in order to
provide for the payment of the interests concerned. Therefore, so far as the complaint
which the hon. Member has made to-day is
concerned, the Government of Northern Ireland, who are in a secondary sense responsible for the successful carrying out of this
scheme, will naturally from time to time, as
I have said before, exercise what influence
can be brought to bear in order that the
apprehensions of my hon. Friend may not
be realized-that is, that four years may
elapse before the farmers shall have the
benefit of the Act. I hardly think it conceivable that such a state of things will
materialize; certainly it will not materialize
if any action on the part of this Government
can avoid it. But to talk of amendments to
the Act or of any particular measure that
may be adopted by our Government or our
Parliament is entirely out of the question,
because we have got no standing whatever
with respect to the matter. I hope this will
satisfy my hon. Friend (Mr. G. Henderson)
that our Government will not relax their
interest in this Measure, and I am quite sure
that even if they did we have a sufficient
number of Members around us here who will
keep the Government informed from time to
time of any weaknesses that may arise.
.
In regard to the question of loans to farmers for the replacement of stock, may I
say that the Government have taken such
measures already as will ensure that there
will be no delay in providing any farmers
who are necessitous from that cause with the
means to purchase additional stock? A conference with bankers has already been held
and all details of the matter have been
settled so that without an hour's delay I
hope the circumstances in which so many
unfortunate farmers find themselves will be
to that extent relieved.
As to undertaking the work contemplated
by my hon. Friend (Mr. G. Henderson), that
is to say, either to lend money to or to
compensate farmers for loss of crops, I
wonder does he realize the character of such
an adventure. A picture arises in my mind
of all the farmers in the North of Ireland
who have unfortunately through weather conditions lost crops or had crops which were
bad or of poor character, and of all the grades
of trouble that would arise too terrible to
contemplate even if the financial considerations underlying it had not a very important
influence on the matter. Therefore, I can
hold out no hope at all that such an undertaking could be given by the Government or
that such an adventure could be undertaken
to discover all the losses sustained by poor
crops in the North of Ireland and to lend
money to or compensate farmers for their
losses.
I do not think that my hon. Friend gives
this Government credit for all they have
done in this matter. He refers to the condition of those farmers who have not bought
out since 1918, but let me remind him that
the condition of many of those farmers is
the result of either their Own inertia
or their own indisposition or their own
hope that they would get better terms
Government Grants.

ar
tis
than those who had voluntarily purchased their land. To some extent at
least the fault lies not with the landlords or
the Government but in a large measure with
the tenants themselves. I can only say
finally, if any repetition is necessary, that
the Government will take care there will be
no unnecessary delay in bringing the whole
terms of this Measure into operation, and I
hope that when we meet again in October
the hon. Member will be gracious enough to
stand up in his place and admit that the
Government, at any rate, has tried to do its
duty.
On the other subjects that have been raised
I do not propose to touch. My right hon.
Friend (Mr. Andrews) is quite able to deal
with all matters relating to Labour. I do
not think the hon. Members opposite who
have discussed this subject have dealt fairly
with the Government. They have not had
the graciousness to admit what the Government has done in regard to Labour. They
do not realise that there are 200,000 people
in this small Province who are dependent
upon the Government grants for their living.
There are 200,000 out of a population of a
million and a quarter. If that alone were
not proof of what the Government is attempting to do in this matter I think my hon.
Friends on the opposite side are very hard
to please. My right hon. Friend has dealt
exhaustively with the matter, and he has
given the assurance that the conference
which is being called will be a real conference, and if it is in a position to make certain
recommendations which will ameliorate the
condition of unemployment in this Province
the Government will go a long way to carry
them out, but obviously at this moment it
would be quite futile and impossible for them
to give any undertaking as to the methods
that will be adopted, because whatever
methods are suggested must be practical
methods, and must be methods that are
within the resources of the Province.
Hon. Members opposite do not seem to
realise that all the money provided for this
work comes from the pockets of the people of
Northern Ireland. I cannot create money.
I am not an alchemist. I cannot transmute
crude metal into gold. I can only find the
money from the pockets of the people, and
there are limits to that. I think the Government has gone even beyond the limits of the
capabilities of the people of Northern Ireland, and if it had not been for the success
of our arrangements with the Imperial
Government, and the fact that we secured
the adhesion of the Committee that was
charged with this business to the principles
we laid down, we should have been in a very
parlous condition in regard to our finances,
and we would have been quite unable to do
wen as much as we have done in respect of
these great matters which face us to-day. At
any rate I can give an assurance that the
Government is not indifferent or callous, as
some hon. Member opposite said, to these
great matters. They will have our constant
attention. Therefore, if any additional grave
circumstances arise that do call for the meeting of our Parliament at an earlier date than
that which is contemplated, there will be no
difficulty whatever in having Parliament
called together. I do not think I am going
beyond my powers when I say I may give the
assurance that if any conditions of an extraordinary character should arise the Government will have no hesitation in calling
Parliament together.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): The hon. Member opposite (Mr.
G. Henderson) spoke about the pork industry.
I can assure him that we are fully alive to
the necessity of keeping a careful eye upon
it. We have a Pig Breeders' Advisory Committee, and several times we have had meetings of the curers and feeders with a view
to stabilizing the pork industry. Anything
that we can do to stabilize it we will do.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: Before the
Minister of Home Affairs goes out, there is

Springfield Village.
I would like to ask the Minister of Home
Affairs what is the cause of the delay in
sanctioning the loan of £108,000 for the
Road Construction Scheme that the Belfast
Corporation intend to carry out in the

the cause of the delay. It is a wonder the

happy new year. In any case I think there

do not know what is the cause. The Corporation are very anxious to go ahead with

Home Affairs is blamed for the delay. I

I would like to ask the Minister of Home
Affairs if there is any possibility of his
granting this sanction at once, so that the
Corporation may be in a position next week
to start a few of the unemployed men who

Gentleman, the Prime Minister, what he
proposes to do in relation to the Motion
which stands in my name?
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James
Craig): Do I understand the hon. Member to
ask for time to discuss the Motion?
Mr. DEVLIN: Unless the right hon.
Gentleman is willing to accept it without
discussion. (A laugh.) I do not see that
there is any point in this initial humour.
The PRIME MINISTER: I think the
question is a little bit unexpected by the
House. If the hon. Member is asking for
time to discuss the Motion, I will suggest
that we might discuss it to-morrow.
Mr. DEVLIN: I assume the right
hon. Gentleman will state whether tomorrow is the day on which it
can be
discussed.
Whether the election was carried out
strictly according to law, and in accordance
with the regulations laid down by you; and
secondly,
Whether any instructions had been issued
by you, or by any person authorised by you,
to the Post Office authorities, to delay the
delivery of any registered letters?
Mr. SPEAKER: In regard to the first
question, the answer is in the affirmative.
The election was, I believe, carried out
strictly according to the law and according
to the regulations.
In regard to the second question, the
answer is in the negative. No instructions
were issued by me, or by anybody responsible to me in reference to delay in delivery
of registered letters.
Mr. DEVLIN: May I ask whether instructions were given by anybody, not by you,
but by any responsible person here in these
premises, that these registered letters were
only to be received according to what was
stated by the Postmaster-General in the
House of Commons?
Mr. SPEAKER: No. This of course, is
rather anticipating, perhaps, the discussion.
But no instructions were ever given by me,
or by anybody responsible to me in the Department of the Houses of Parliament, with
regard to any delay in the delivery of registered letters.
Mr. DEVLIN: May I ask the Prime
Minister whether in the discussion to-morrow
he will be prepared to state what precisely
has taken place between the Post Office and
the authorities here in regard to their re
ception of registered letters?
Mr. SPEAKER: Perhaps I may intervene
to point out to the hon. Member that I have
issued to day the correspondence which has
taken place up to the present time between
me and the Postmaster-General on this
matter, and I think it is available in the
Library at this moment.
Mr. DEVLIN: May I suggest also that the
correspondence which has taken place between yourself and me ought also to be
issued to the Members of the House, so that
they may have all the bearings of this case
before them when they come to consider it,
because I think it is equally vital to the
proper consideration of this question that
the Members of the House should be in
possession of all that is in that correspondence between you and me, as well as in
this correspondence between yourself and the
postal authorities.

"to amend the Dangerous Drugs Act, 1920,
and the Dangerous Drugs and Poisons
(Amendment) Act (Northern Ireland), 1924, so
far as is necessary to assimilate the law in
Northern Ireland to the law in force in
Great Britain in relation to certain
dangerous drugs, and for purposes connected
therewith," presented by the Minister of
Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates), supported
by the Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Home Affairs (Mr. Hanna) to
be read a Second time to-morrow, and to be
printed.
Mr. DEVLIN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman, on a point of order, what is the
meaning of introducing this Dangerous
Drugs Bill n
now. I understood from the notification which was given in the Press-the
only notification given to the Members of this
House that this House was to reassemblethat it was distinctly stated that the business
of the House just now was to deal with one
precise and vital matter, and I want to know
why this Dangerous Drugs Bill is being introduced now.
a
The PRIME MINISTER: I think the hon.
Member is justified in calling attention to
the fact that when we asked you, Sir, to call
the House together it was for one specific
purpose, and one specific purpose only. But
since we did that we have received
communication from the Imperial Government notifying us of the fact that at the
Geneva Conference arrangements were made
in connection with Dangerous Drugs that
necessitated them having legislation passed
through their House prior to the 30th
September of this year. When they came
to look into the matter they discovered that
in order to comply with the international arrangements entered into at Geneva it was
necessary for Northern Ireland to pass a Bill
to bring into line its legislation with the
legislation passed in the Imperial Parliament. I understand, and I am sure hon.
Members who have the Bill in their hands
will see, that there is very little in the Bill;
but the British Government have requested
us to be kind enough to pass the measure so
that it may be on the Statute Book before
the 30th September, in order that they can
carry out the obligations imposed upon them
at Geneva. I am sure the House will desire
to meet the Imperial Government in this
matter, which does not make very much difference to the regulations in the existing
Bill.
Mr. DEVLIN: Has the British Parliament
passed legislation?
The PRIME MINISTER: Yes.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Senate Election.
Motion made and Question proposed:
hat in the opinion of this House the
decision of the Returning Officer at the
recent election for the Senate not to count
the ballot papers which reached him after
the close of the poll should be reviewed,
because such papers, though posted in ample
time, were subjected to an unreasonable
delay; and in view of these special circumstances this House directs the Returning
Officer to undertake a recount of the votes,
such recount to include the ballot papers
which were not received in time."-(Mr.
McAllister).
Mr. MCALLISTER: Before I address myself to the facts of this case may I be allowed
to place on record my appreciation of the
impartiality, the conspicuous fairness, and
the unfailing courtesy which I have always
received from you, Mr. Speaker, since I
entered this House. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). But from your experience and it is
a wide experience as a public representative
you will recognise that public representatives on many occasions are called upon to
undertake irksome, troublesome and unpleasant duties. That is the position I am
in to-day, and you will further recognise, I
am quite sure, that in the discharge of a
public duty personal esteem and all other
concerns must be subordinated to the discharge of that duty.
I was particularly struck on opening the
paper this morning to see a reply of yours
to a question by the right hon. Gentleman
the Prime Minister. You stated in reply to
him that the election for the Senate had been
carried through in a strictly legal manner and
in accordance with the regulations guiding
that election. May I illustrate the result of
that answer by drawing a parallel case?
Suppose that you, Sir, or the right hon. Gentleman were a candidate at an ordinary election
and the Presiding Officer at that election
closed the polling booths four hours before
the appointed time, with the result that you
each lost 300 votes and turned a certain victory into defeat, would you say that that
election had been carried through in a legal
and satisfactory manner, or in the way it
should be? The only difference I can see
between that case and the present is that to
all intents and purposes-side-track the
issue as you will, draw any red herring
across it, use all the subtleties of debate at
your command, the one fact remains, the
real fact-the poll was closed not four
hours but four days before the appointed
time.
Now may I refer to a short regulation
that is germane to this question? It says:
""
A Member of the House of Commons
shall vote by filling up his voting paper
in the manner directed by the Election of
Senators (Northern Ireland) Order, 1921,
The Senate Election.
The Senate Election,
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. McAllister]
signing it in the presence of a witness, and
delivering the same by hand or sending
the same by post, so that it shall reach
my Office before the close of the poll, at
such time and on such day as I shall
notify. No voting paper received after
the close of the poll will be counted."
The facts in this case are that the voting
papers of my Friend, the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) and my own were
posted about noon on Saturday, the 11th
July. The voting paper of the hon. Member
for Antrim (Mr. George Henderson) was
posted some time that evening, and the envelopes bear the Post Office mark showing
that ours were received and handled by the
Post Office at 1-30 p.m., and that the hon. Member for Antrim's paper was handled by the
Post Office at 7-30 on the Saturday evening.
If I am correctly informed there
were four intervening posts between
the posting of our letters and what should
have been the close of the poll at ten o'clock
on July 14. Yet our letters were not received, with the result that one-third of the
community of Northern Ireland has been
prevented from having one representative
in the Senate to voice their interests, defend
their rights, and plead their cause.
I was greatly struck yesterday by the
publication of the correspondence between
Mr. Speaker and the Assistant Postmaster-
General of the Imperial Parliament, and,
while I very often take exception to the expenditure incurred by the Government, in
this case I must say that I think their
money was well spent and the expenditure
justified, because it places on record, in my
judgment, an inefficiency, a chaos, an official
confusion that are unparalleled and unconceivable either by the best friends or the
bitterest opponents of the Government.
Now you, Sir, asked a question in the
Imperial Parliament to the following effect.
You asked the Postmaster-General
"whether he is aware that three
registered letters addressed to the Speaker

Parliament Buildings, Belfast, until 11-45

the 11th July, and that the explanation of
the Postmaster of Belfast for such extraordinary delay is that it is not customary
to deliver registered letters to official or
business addresses until the second
delivery on any day; whether such
custom prevails generally or applies only
to Belfast; whether there was any postal
delivery in Belfast on the Saturday afternoon, Monday morning, and Tuesday

Now the significance of the reference to the
police being always on duty, in my
judgment, is that the only inference that
can be drawn from that question is that the
police are presumed and have been
structed to receive registered letters and to
sign the forms. In a subsequent letter it is
perfectly clear that notice of our voting papers
being contained in registered letters was
brought to the police on the 13th July-the
morning preceding the poll-and, therefore,
the Government cannot have it both ways.
Either the police had authority-which seems
to me strange-to sign a receipt for a registered letter or else they had not authority.
The reply of the Assistant Postmaster-
General to that question was this:
"It is the practice not to deliver registered letters unless there is a responsible
person in attendance to accept them, and
for this reason both in Belfast and elsewhere registered letters are in many
instances held over for the second
delivery, with the concurrence of
the Government Departments and firms
concerned. As the Speaker's Office
was closed from the afternoon of
Saturday, the 11th, to the morning of the
14th July, and it was known from inquiry
that no responsible official would be on
duty during this period, there was no alternative but to retain the registered packets until the second delivery on the 14th
July. If the hon. Member will designate
a responsible official who will be in attendance to accept and sign for registered
letters they can be delivered at the House
of Commons about 8 a.m. without
difficulty."
It is significant that after that letter an
official was appointed to receive those letters
on 16th July, two days after the election.

Jnemployment Fund (Money).
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That it is expedient to authorise a
charge upon the Consolidated Fund in
respect of any further sums required to be
advanced by the Ministry of Finance, not
exceeding in the whole £750,000, under
powers to be conferred by an Act of this
Session, for the purpose of discharging the
liabilities of the Unemployment Fund of
Northern Ireland."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): It is my duty to move this Resolution and I think it is expedient I should explain it as shortly as possible to the Committee. Hon. Members will recall that in the
month of March last-in the last Session of
Parliament-my right hon. Friend who sits
beside me (Mr. Barbour) presented a resolution of a similar character. That Resolution
was directed to making provision for advances to the Unemployment Insurance Fund
to enable it to carry along its functions in
respect of benefits conferred on those who are
insured. The amount of that Vote was
£750,000. Having regard to the figures of
unemployment it was calculated that that
grant of £750,000 would have been sufficient
to have carried the fund along until 1st
November next, but it is within the knowledge of hon. Members that the conditions of industry in the Province in the intervening period reached a deplorable state
of depression and, therefore, the numbers
registered as claimants on the unemployment fund were greatly increased. This is,
of course, very well understood not only by
hon. Members but by the community. In the
month of March, when the House gave the
necessary authority to advance an additional
£750,000 to the Fund, the figures of unemployment stood at an average figure of, roughly,
46,000 totally unemployed and about 10,000
on systematic short time. To-day, as nearly
as can be computed, the corresponding figures
are 56,000 wholly unemployed and 6,000
partially out of work.
It will thus be seen that our calculations
as to the sufficiency of the last Vote to carry
us on until the 1st November were very
seriously disturbed. That is to say, our calculations were that the money so provided
would have carried the fund till the month
of November next, but as a fact the money
that was then provided is now practically exhausted, and in order that payment of benefits
to the beneficiaries may be continued it was
necessary that Mr. Speaker should be asked
to call this special meeting of Parliament in
order that the necessary amount be provided
to carry the Insurance Fund on for a further
period. It is now asked under this Resolution
that the Ministry of Finance should be
authorised to advance to the Unemployment
Insurance Fund a further sum of £750,000.
Should this amount be required, as seems
most likely, the total liability of the Unemployment Insurance Fund to the Exchequer
will amount to a sum of £4,250,000. It is
possible that I may be asked how long it is
expected that the sum of £750,000 will bridge
the gulf and carry on the fund in a state of
solvency, or, should I say, in a position to
make advances to the beneficiaries, but,
really, it is most difficult reliably to forecast
the length of time that this present authorisation will provide for.
The position as we see it to-day is very bad
from the industrial point of view, and it is
especially bad in one of our industries, as is
common knowledge, that is, the textile industry. It may be possible to predicate that
as things are perhaps at their worst any
change is likely to be for the better, and
therefore, this amount which is asked for today will carry on the fund for some very considerable time at any rate. Having dealt then
very shortly with the necessity and with the
amount to be provided, I may go on to say
that it will be within the knowledge of the
Committee that negotiations have been proceeding for a considerable period not alone
with the present Government in Great
Britain but also with former Governments
with a view to remedying the situation
created by the long continued period of aggravated unemployment. These negotiations,
in which the Prime Minister, my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Labour, and myself
have been engaged, have not yet reached a
final stage, but I hope before this House
rises in the Autumn to be in a position to
state that an arrangement has been reached.
The guiding principle of my colleagues and
myself is that exactly the same standard of
benefits granted in Great Britain should be
extended to those who are suffering in our
area from similar unavoidable privations by
reason of the continued adverse conditions of
industry. None of us can ever be satisfied
that the relations of the Province to the Imperial authority have been placed upon a
sound and permanent basis until the necessary adjustments have been made to enable
us to maintain our social standards at a level
fully comparable with that of the rest of the
United Kingdom.

Dangerous Drugs Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
'That the Bill be now read a Second time.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): This Bill, which is mainly
of a technical character, is based on the
Imperial Act which was passed on the seventh
of last month. The Imperial Act applies to
Northern Ireland only to the extent that it
Ideals with matters with which our Parliament have no power to deal, that is, matters
affecting export and import. Therefore, it
is necessary in order that the law relating to
dangerous drugs should be the same on this
side of the Channel as on the other side that
the remaining provisions should be embodied
in this present Bill. I do not think it is
necessary for me to say anything as to the
. necessity for the Drugs Act to be similar
both in Great Britain and this country. The
regulation of the trade has been the subject
of a convention at Geneva, and following the
decision arrived at the British Government
undertook to bring in an Act, and thereupon
requested this Government to bring in a
similar Act. The urgency of the case arises
from the fact that the British Government
undertook that the Act should be brought
in before the 30th September. The main
clauses of importance in the Bill are as follows: Under Clause I coca leaves and
Indian hemp are brought within the scope
of Part I of the Act of 1920, which deals with
raw material. Indian hemp has hitherto
been outside the scope of the Dangerous
Drugs Act, and although it is little used in
this country, it has been brought within the
Act at the request of the Egyptian Government. With regard to Clause 2, in future it
will be impossible to sell heroin and Indian
hemp without a prescription from a doctor.
Clause 3 contains an improved definition of
medicinal opium, and involves no substantial change. Clause 4 provides for a relaxation of the existing requirements in the case
of preparations containing the drugs which
may be reported by the Health, Committee
of the League after inquiry not to be capable
of abuse. I beg to move.

We are going to make a law. The chemists
of the country who are law-abiding and
honourable men will do their best to carry
out that law and to carry out the regulations
formed under that law to the very best of

believe there is no other way to stop this

As to the Clauses of the Bill, Indian hemp
is mentioned. It is very little known in this
country. I have the authority of a literary
gentleman who bases his opinion on a wellknown book, "The Count of Monte Christo,"
that the inhaling of the fumes of hashish
has a very delightful effect and the patient is
transported into the seventh Heaven of
delight. We know nothing of that, I am
glad to say here. I believe that in Egypt it
is very largely used. In our own prosaic
way we have ailments, and among the
ailments to which humanity is liable there is
one humble and troublesome one. It is not
necessarily fatal. I do not think it is ever
fatal, but those who suffer from it find it
very pressing in its attentions and very uncomfortable and irritating to the sufferer.
I refer to the humble and irritating corn.
I understand that extract of Indian hemp
is used in small quantities in corn cures-in
what is known as the Collodion Corn Cures.
Another point I notice is the reference to
heroin. Up to now a certain proportion of
heroin could be used without it being necessary to register, but under this new
regulation it will be necessary for every
medical prescription containing heroin,
which is largely prescribed for chest
troubles, to be registered with the chemists,
and it will also be necessary to have a fresh
doctor's prescription for each bottle. I can
see that would be of advantage to the
chemists financially, but it will not be
an advantage financially to the patient. The
chemists will be put to a considerable
amount of trouble, but the chemists will be
willing to put up with the extra trouble
in order to help the Government. Generally,
I think that Members of this House will
approve any effort to reduce the traffic in
dangerous drugs, and help our young people
especially to get away from this terrible
habit, which is undermining the health of
a great many people in other countries than
ours, and I suppose to some extent in our
own. I have great pleasure in supporting
the Second Reading of the Bill.

Minister of Agriculture if he can state the

under the scheme of Short Loans to replace

on these applications up to date?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): Applications under the scheme
of Short Term Loans for the replacement
of live stock have been received from 588
farmers. The total amount of the loans
granted up to the 2nd instant is £12,062.

Minister of Agriculture whether the Government would not reconsider the question of

for

say,

ROAD TRAFFIC ACCIDENTS.-
4. Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether in view
of the many accidents which are occurring,
due to motor, equestrian, and pedestrian
traffic, he is willing to set up a Committee to
inquire into what measures should be taken
to prevent a continuance of such accidents.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Hanna): There is a Statutory Committee,
i.e. The Roads Advisory Committee for
Northern Ireland-appointed under Section
22 of the Ministry of Transport Act, 1919, to
advise the Ministry of Home Affairs in all
matters connected with road traffic.
This Committee comprises representatives
of road authorities as well as of users of
horse and mechanical road traffic, and has
kept the Ministry advised on the many
problems relating to traffic.
It is proposed to introduce at an early date
a Bill relating to road traffic, and the
assistance of the Roads Advisory Committee
will be invited in connection with it.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Arising out of the
answer, may I ask the Parliamentary Secretary whether the Committee applies to the

6. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he can give an assurance to
the House that, from the reports received
from his Inspectors, material of good
quality is being used in the houses under
construction by builders in receipt of the
Government subsidy.
Mr. HANNA: Before the subsidy is paid
in respect of any house, the Ministry requires to be satisfied from the reports of the
Ministry's Inspectors that the standard of
construction and the materials used are in
accordance with the specifications contained
in the Ministry's rules.
In addition to that in the case of houses
erected in urban centres, a further certificate to the like effect is required from the
Surveyors of the urban authorities.
Mr. KYLE: May I ask the Parliamentary
Secretary, in view of the agitation that exists
at present in Belfast about the rotten
material that is being used in the construction of houses, whether he will take steps to
prevent any private contractor from getting
this subsidy for houses which may, on investigation, be proved to have been built
with bad material?
Mr. HANNA: The Ministry will not
sanction the payment of the subsidy in any
case in which it has not got a certificate.

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE IRON
ORE MINES, COUNTY ANTRIM.
11. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that his Department has set aside the recommendation
of the Ballymena Local Employment Committee to allow miners formerly employed at
the Iron Ore Mines, County Antrim, the advantage of being scheduled along with
workers in the engineering trade; whether
he is aware that some of these men have
worked in the Iron Ore Mines for 40 years;
and whether he is prepared to issue instructions that these men should receive their
unemployment benefit.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr. Andrews): I am aware that a number of persons have obtained intermittent employment
in the Iron Ore Mines, of County Antrim,
for a considerable time, and unemployed
miners claiming benefit after they have exhausted their insurance contributions are
called upon to show that they have had insured employment in each of six weeks during the two years preceding the date of
claim.
The claims of 54 miners were considered
having regard to this consideration in
January, 1925, and only seven of the
claimants failed to satisfy the condition.
As a result of representations by the
Trade Union to which the seven men belonged the Ballymena Local Employment
Committee, in which area the men reside,
was asked by the Department to consider
whether there was any reason why this condition should not be applied, and reported
that in their opinion there was not.
On a subsequent occasion the Committee
expressed a contrary opinion on the grounds
that it was not reasonable in the circumstances to ask for proof of employment in
so many weeks as six in two years.
In my view the first thoughts of the Committee were correct, and I regret, therefore,
that the men are not entitled to benefit
until they satisfy the conditions.

BENEFIT.

Member desires information supplementary

question dated the 21st April, 1925.
The number of persons who have been disqualified for unemployment benefit between
the 21st April and the 24th August on
account of their failure to comply with the
requirements of the new conditions which
came into force on the 1st January, 1925,
is 435.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment Fund Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
Mr. BARBOUR: In moving yesterday the
Resolution which was the
necessary
preliminary to this Bill, my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) detailed the
circumstances which necessitated its introduction. In moving the Second Reading
of the Bill
now, let me just state
again that no new principle of any kind is
involved. The intention of the Bill, in fact,
is to enable the payment of Unemployment Insurance benefits to be continued by
renewing the statutory powers of the
Ministry of Finance, which are now almost
exhausted, to continue advancing moneys to
the Fund. The amount by which the lending
powers are being increased is three-quarters
of a million, and it is confidently anticipated
that this sum will be sufficient to finance the
deficit on the Fund up to the end of the
current calendar year. Of course, hon.
Members will realise that it is difficult to
form any close estimate of the amount that
may be actually required, seeing that the
factors on which the calculation is made are
of SO uncertain a character, depending as
they do on the amount of unemployment and
the conditions of trade and industry. I beg
to move.
Mr. KYLE: I want, if I may, to move that
this House refuses to agree to the Second
Reading of this Bill as a protest against the

In the Unemployment Conference we were
all asked to put forward suggestions of our
own and we did, perhaps not sufficiently
thought out, perhaps sudden suggestions that
sprung to our minds, perhaps the results of
our experience, perhaps ideas that we thought
might materialise to something. I think all
these reports of these conferences should be
published. I do not think the public have
any idea of the work that was done at these
conferences. I believe there are many suggestions made possibly by people who have
other occupations-nearly every Member of
this House has some other occupation. A
number of them must have, for they hardly
ever come here. Members of this conference
are public men and even when they put forward suggestions they did not have an opportunity of pressing them or explaining
them or trying to submit their values to those
who will ultimately be the arbitrators.
I think the report of all the proceedings
of this conference ought to be published.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The public
ought to know what was done at this conference, and if there are any suggestions, as I
think there are most valuable suggestionsin fact I think some of the most valuable
suggestions at this conference were made by
myself. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) But at
any rate I am unfortunately in this position
-I cannot put them into operation. Therefore they are not of much value. But if
they were of any value they might be considered by the Government. Several valuable
suggestions were made by many people. I
was only joking when I said that mine were
valuable suggestions. But this House ought
to have an opportunity of seeing what they
were, dissecting them, finding out if carried
into effect would they to some extent mitigate
the evils and solve the problem. If that were
done some advance might be made by some of
us who claim that we have, if not found a
solution, all done our best to contribute to
some satisfactory conclusion of the question
which doubly affects the whole community
and with which all are profoundly concerned.

Mr. BLACK: One concrete suggestion has
come from hon. Members opposite. It was
that men should be put back upon the land.
The suggestion was put forward in a double
phase as I understood. First that men
should be put back upon the land in Ulster,
secondly that men should be brought from
Ulster and put on the land in the colonies.
Now with regard to Ulster what opportunity
is there for men to make their living on the
land in Ulster at the present time? I think
the whole cry of those men who represent
Ulster agricultural communities is that
there is no possible living for men in the
country now. The country needs to be
helped. The country needs more assistance
than the city does. Would it be any solution
to take the people out of the city and put
them in the country where there is no more
work apparently than there is in the city?
The second suggestion is to take men to the
Colonies. That is a surprising suggestion in
view of the attitude taken up by the Labour
Party in some of the Colonies. We read that
the Labour Mayor of Sydney has set
his face strongly against allowing any immigration in Australia. Here you have the
Labour Party saying send men to the
Colonies and there you have the Labour
Party saying they will not admit them. How
is that going to be a solution?
To-day the one result of the debate seems
to be to add nothing whatever, I submit, by
way of concrete or helpful suggestion to
assist the Government in the measures they
have already taken. They have not solved
the problem, but they have done something,
and if there is anything more that can be
done it is the duty of every Member of the

whether the Members of this House sit on

Labour will gladly welcome any practical
suggestion that is made in view of the
terrible condition-

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: We have
been treated to a rather happy speech in
some respects by the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) in very unhappy
circumstances, because we all recognise the
very unhappy circumstances we are met to
discuss here to-day, that is the great
difficulty of providing a real and
efficient remedy for our unemployment.
I think the speech by the hon.
Member for West Belfast will help cooperation between people in the Six County
area who differ in religion and politics with
regard to a solution for these very intricate
and difficult matters. I just got to my feet
for a minute or two to say that it should be
the first and foremost duty of the Government of Northern Ireland to do all that is
possible to encourage and develop our basic
industry, that is agriculture. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I do not know that I am
entirely enamoured of a slavish following of
everything that is done in England, either
in legislation or in administration, becanse
conditions in Northern Ireland are somewhat different from the conditions in
England.
England is largely an industrial country,
we are largely an agricultural country.
Therefore, I feel it might not be a safe policy
for the Government of this country to be
tied in every respect to following slavishly
the legislation and administration in
England. The Government's first duty
should be in every way to encourage and develop the agricultural industry. I say that
for many reasons. One reason that would
be sufficient is that a people rooted in the
soil and contented in the soil makes the
most stable community and makes for stability in Government. Up to the present time
the Government, in my opinion, have not encouraged that industry as much as they might
have done. They have approved of an Act
to complete land purchase in Ulster which
puts the unbought tenants of the Six
Counties at a great disadvantage as compared
with the men in the Twenty-six Counties.
They have approved of an Act which was
passed without discussion and which gives
the tenants of this area a reduction of only
about 3s 6d as compared with a reduction
of about 7s.
I see the Government of the Free State
have appointed a conference to deal with
grain prices, and while it is not law they
have recommended, in order to encourage the
agricultural industry,
Short term loans for farmers,
Reduce railway freights for Irishgrown
farm produce,
Subsidy for tillage farming,
No income-tax where 25 per cent. of
holding is cultivated.
Import duty on imported malting barley,
and fixed minimum prices on barley for
malting or brewing, and
Tariffs on foreign flour and foreign oats.
I have not the figures before me at the present time, but I think the statistics recently
published by the Department of Agriculture
should give us cause to think owing to the
amount of the reduction in tillage there has
been in the Six-County area. I do think the
Government should have some policy to encourage tillage farming in this country, and
that the encouraging of farming and the
keeping of people on the land as far as
possible will to some extent help eventually
to solve the unemployment problem.
In connection with the Northern Ireland
Land Act it is a pity there was not a sum

I do not know that I would have intervened

would probably reply to any of the arguments

are only two points I would like to refer to,

The whole argument of my hon. Friend, the
junior Member for West Belfast (Mr.
William McMullen) was that the Government
was tinkering with unemployment. The
senior Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin)
also expressed himself in similar language—
that to some extent we were tinkering with
the problem of unemployment.
A conference was formed some time ago and
representatives of all the Trades Unions and
representatives from this House were invited
to attend that conference. Some important
proposals were put forward by the Member
for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin), but I want to
tell this House that unemployment is not a
local or a national question. It is an international question, and until the wheels of industry begin to revolve throughout the whole
world it is absolutely impossible that the
problem can be settled in any particular
centre or in any particular part of the
country.
The hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Kyle) made one or two suggestions. One was
that the school age should be raised, and
another was that money should be taken from
the Insurance Fund for the purpose of assisting industry. It is such a debatable point
that I think it would be unfair to weary the
House by examining the proposal to take the
contributions of the workers, the contributions of the employers, and the contributions
of the State for the purpose of subsidising
any particular industry. I now come to the
two points I want particularly to refer to.
The first is that the Bill which has been
brought before the House to-day is a Money
Bill for the express purpose of finding money
to continue to pay to unemployed persons
their unemployment insurance. If the Opposition refuses to agree to the Second Reading, and in the event of the Government

1920, which provides for controlling and restricting the production, possession, sale,
and distribution of raw opium. The Amendment carried out by the Clause is to apply
the provisions of Section 3 to coca leaves
and Indian hemp, and the preparations
made therefrom. Coca leaves are already
subject to the provisions of the Act, being
substances containing cocaine, and the
practical effect of the alteration in this
respect is of little importance, but the Convention desired that this substance should
be put on the same footing as raw opium.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Hanna): I have been asked by the right hon.
Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) to reply to
this Question.
From reliable information which was
received by the police, it was considered
expedient that an adequate force of police
should be stationed on duty in the vicinity
of the Parliament House, and along the
approaches thereto for the prevention or
obstruction or disturbance.

SHORT LOANS TO FARMERS.
3. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Agriculture if the Government
would reconsider the scheme of short loans
to farmers, with a view to further extending
the duration of the loans, and also of making
them available for all farmers in financial
difficulties, owing to the bad season through
which the industry has passed?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In the absence of my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Archdale) I propose to reply to
this Question.
As already announced the period for the
repayment of all short term loans for the
replacement of live stock losses has been
extended to 31st December, 1926. At present
the Government is not prepared to consider
a further extension of the duration of these
loans.
The suggestion that these loans should be
made available for all farmers in financial
difficulties, other than those arising from
the loss of live stock, would, if conceded,
open the door to claims of all kinds on the
Government, and is not one that could be
entertained.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: In view of
this unsatisfactory answer I will raise this
matter on the adjournment.

THE BOUNDARY.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House do now adjourn." (Captain
Dixon).
Mr. KYLE: I put down a question on the
Paper to-day so that the Prime Minister
might make a statement with regard to the
position of the Government in regard to this
very important question, and what steps he
proposes to take if and when the Boundary
Commission reports. I think it is the Prime
Minister's duty, or rather I thought it was
the Prime Minister's duty to inform public
opinion in the Six Counties as to what steps
he was prepared to take in certain
eventualities, and I do think that it is a
public service to allay the feelings of the
people regarding this very important
question, because it has been stated in the
Press that conversations are contemplated
between Mr. Cosgrave and the Prime
Minister. I think, therefore, that the
House and the country should know what
position the Government are prepared to
take up, and they also should know something of the state of mind of the people in
regard to this all-important question.
As far as Labour is concerned, we desire
to make our position quite clear. Housing,
wages, unemployment insurance, national
health insurance, old-age pensions, education, these are the important things to us.
As far as Labour is concerned we are not
going to agree to any worsening of our
position in regard to these all-important
matters, governing as they do the lives and
well-being of the great body of the working
people.
the
We believe also that there is common
ground for agreement between North and
South in, for example, the administration of
railways, in, for example, a common policy
regarding agriculture, and we respectfully
suggest to the Government that in any conversations the position of Labour,
position of the working people, should not be
overlooked, and that bodies might be
created-you can call them by whatever name
you like to discuss common action in regard
to agriculture, fisheries; and there is one
other very important thing amongst the
etceteras, and that is reciprocal labour
arrangements. The Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews) knows how hard it is on the people
who live, for example, in Belleek, and who,
because they live in the Free State while
they work in Northern Ireland, if they
happen to be unemployed-as there are some
of them unemployed to-day--are not entitled
to benefit from the Free State because they
work in Northern Ireland and their cards
are stamped in Northern Ireland. Surely it
should not be outside the wit of man to devise a reciprocal arrangement of some sort so
that the common people at least should not
be penalised.
This matter of the Boundary, so far as I
am concerned, is not a matter of very much
importance in comparison with the things I
have mentioned. We recognise, of course,
the position the Government are in, and,
therefore I think it is as little as we can
expect to hear the considered opinion of the
Prime Minister on this question. He
knows, and we all know, how much the
people of Belfast and of the Six Counties
value his opinion, value his considered judgment, and that being the case, it is not in
my opinion good enough merely to say that
he has nothing to state. In affairs of
Government it seems to me that there must
of necessity be a good deal of negotiation, a
good deal of arrangement, and I think it is
our duty here to get the Government to state
their position to the country.
I would also like to say that no good at all
can be done by arousing passion either in
North or South. It does not pay, to put it
in a very crude way, either for the North or
South to rouse bad feeling. We have had
here in the North some little trouble, very
great trouble. In the South there has been
tremendous trouble also with destruction of
property and loss of life. Nothing can be
gained by doing anything to arouse once
more those passions which, when aroused,
speedily become masters of the situation, no
matter where they may be. Trouble, either
civil or any other sort, has never served any
useful purpose so far as the country is concerned. It is much too costly. It dislocates
trade. We are now in the aftermath of the
huge world war which means that there is
tremendous unemployment in our land and
a tremendous number of people who are
suffering, so that so far as arousing bad
feeling is concerned or doing anything that
may precipitate trouble in our own land is
concerned, we should all be very careful and
do everything we can to allay bad feeling
and promote good feeling.
Ministers sitting opposite have wished
Ministers in the South well, and Ministers
in the South have wished Ministers in the
North well. If that is the case and that is
the true feeling, and I am sure it is, of the
Government in this matter, then it should

not be outside their wisdom to get some link
of connection in such vital matters as
agriculture and the railways which might

see it, and I do think we are entitled to have

here to-day, because if these conversations
take place it will enable him to state what

prepared to take, and I think it would be of

of the whole community in the Six Counties.
We ought to have some statement from
the Prime Minister on this all-important
question, and I would implore Ministers
and Members at their public meetings
not to do anything to arouse ill-feeling,
not, for example, to say if the Free
State wants territory let them come and
take it. It is all very well to win the
applause of a crowd by making statements
like that, but, after all, in a country like
ours, with a population of 1,250,000, we might
cause some of them to lose their lives, we
might cause the destruction of property, and
we might dislocate trade and commerce by
making statements like that. I would
suggest to Members opposite that when
making speeches in this connection they
should be made with the deliberate object
of creating good feeling rather than promoting bad feeling.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am afraid I
am not prepared to make any statement on
the subject of the Boundary. I do not think
it would serve any good end. The decision
of the Government and myself is well known
to the country, and from that we do not
intend to deviate in the slightest degree.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) But in order
that there may not go out to the public
the suggestion even that pourparlers have
been invited by either the British Government or the Free State Government, I would
like to say here that neither myself nor any
of my colleagues has received any invitation
in any quarter to meet and discuss this
matter. If anything is to be done at all
it will be done in this House openly, in
front of those who represent the constituences most affected, and, as I have said
before, unless the people who live in the
constituences that are affected are satisfied
with the decision arrived at, the
quences will no longer remain with this
Government, which has announced its intention and will carry out its intention.
conse-
With regard to the other matters to which
the hon. Member (Mr. Kyle) has referred,
of course we are all most anxious naturally
that having secured peace in the South and
in the North nothing should be done to
break that peace-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) but at the same time the matter is
out of our hands. The Boundary Commission are working behind closed doors. I
know nothing whatever of what is going on,
and I doubt if anybody else does. It is
they, and not ourselves, who have the responsibility for breaking or keeping the
peace.
Mr. DEVLIN: I would be the very last to
stand here as a defender of the Boundary
Commission, but I think the right hon.
Gentleman is wrong in his assumption that
the responsibility rests with the Boundary
Commission. The final responsibility must
be borne by those who first assumed responsibility, that is the British Government.
The British Government appointed this
Boundary Commission. We have had no
responsibility for it. It was part of the
Treaty arrived at between Southern Ireland
and the British Government, and the British
Government naturally will take up tho
decision that may be come to at least, I
would expect so if they are men of honour,
which they are not always, which they very
rarely are. That is my experience of them
in dealing with Irish public affairs. But if
they are faithful to their responsibility they
will, of course, assume full power and full
responsibility for anything the Boundary
Commission does. Therefore, the right hon.
Gentleman is not altogether right in placing
the whole responsibility upon the shoulders
of the Boundary Commission.
I would like to say as far as I am concerned that I too regret the raising of this
question at the moment, because until the
Boundary Commission reports, I think it is
highly desirable that all of us who have any
love for our native land and any desire to
avoid the opening up of the old passions and
bitterness which brought such a curse on the
community North and South ought not to
encourage or foster bad feeling, especially
in Ulster. For a responsible statesman like
the Minister of Labour, for whom I have
very high respect, to go out as he did in
recent weeks and make wild and inflammatory speeches is a very serious thing. I
think the holding of these heated meetings
in this somewhat warm atmosphere is
altogether unjustifiable. I could not trust
myself to make speeches during the last few
months, and, therefore, I have remained
silent. When speeches are made on public
platforms to audiences easily aroused and
amongst whom it is easy to create and foster
bitter passion, the fewer of these meetings
that are held the better.
I really do not know what the fighting
speeches of the right hon. Gentleman mean.
There is no one who wants to fight
the right hon. Gentleman. The Fron

The Boundary.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Devlin]
State Government and their representatives have all stated that they will
accept the report of the Boundary
Commission. The Boundary Commission is
the creation of the British Government.
Therefore, if you refuse to accept the judgment of the Boundary Commission, it will
not be the Free State you will have to fight,
but the British Government, and I wonder
that sane and sensible men would encourage
a spirit among their own people that they
would have to face a situation in which
the battalions of Ulster would be organised
against the battalions of the British Empire.
I have also to say that I recently noticed
a speech of a prominent member of the
Ulster Party, Mr. Charles Craig, in which
he suggested a conference. I am quite sure
that Mr. Charles Craig, freed from the
passions of Ulster, was very anxious to see
something done to promote peace, but no
sooner had he made that speech than out
on the ramparts rushed the Attorney-General,
the custodian in Ulster of law and order,
and the man who would be called upon if
any trouble arose to take criminal proceedings against revolutionaries in revolt
against Britain. It is a most unwise thing
for any man in his position to repudiate the
peaceful postulate of the Prime Minister's
brother, because I take it that is what was
in the mind of Mr. Charles Craig when he
made the speech suggesting some method by
which peace could be obtained. That speech
was repudiated not by some serious politician
or responsible statesman but by the Attorney-
General, who is more noted for the
enthusiasm of his own unthought oratory
than for the cold, decisive, legal methods
by which he should elucidate dangerous
points of law.
In my opinion if there are to be negotiations-the right hon. Gentleman (The Prime
Minister) says there are none, and that he
has heard of none-I would say this, let
them be negotiations along the lines of Irish
unity. I am not laying down any policy
by which that unity should be brought about,
but I suggest it should be along the
lines of Irish unity, and that these negotiations should suggest not a further subdivision of the country or a narrowing of
areas, but rather the bringing closer and
closer together, by whatever process judg
ment and patriotism can suggest, of the
people of Ulster and the people of the South
of Ireland. This is a very small island. It
is face to face both North and South economically and industrially with very serious
difficulties, and it strikes me that instead
of cold and rigid views expressed in inflammatory form upon the platforms we should
have men on both sides prepared to make
sacrifices for the ultimate unity which is
bound to come; I do not say by one Parliament, because the Treaty laid down that
two Parliaments would be perfectly acceptable to the South of Ireland.
It is not for me to suggest the methods
by which unity can be brought about. I
have never been consulted either by North
or South in regard to these matters. I am
only giving my opinion as an Irish citizen
and as one living here in Ulster and to some
extent responsible for a section of the population who have been rather neglected by
one side and rather badly treated by the
other. So far as I can speak for them their
one hope and desire is to live in peace-(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)—and in a spirit of
amity with their fellow citizens. They hate
blood and outrage, and passion and hatred,
and all the things that have done so much to
disfigure this Northern Province and to
create bad feeling all over the country. We
are anxious that peace should be promoted
in whatever way it can be promoted.
In my judgment the man or men who think
that now or at any time you are going to
adjust these difficulties or that you are going
to destroy these evils by bloodshed were
never more mistaken in their lives. The
people will not have it. The people are sick
of it, both North and South. Not only are
the people North and South sick of bloodshed, but the world is sick of war. Look at
the tremendous tangle of the European
situation to-day. Look at the labour and
thought that are being given to try to disentangle things and to create peace in Europe
upon the foundation on which alone there
can be contentment and commercial power
and a renewal of industrial activities. I
care not whether they live in the North
or in the South, the man or men who try
to solve this problem in any other way than
by wisdom and by mutual sacrifice will be
regarded as a danger to Ireland and a
danger to the peace of the whole nation.

from the financial aspect, which naturally concerns me. I think the hon. Member has perhaps not apprehended or given full consideration to all that the Government and Parliament have done in the interests of agriculture in Northern Ireland. I do not think
anyone can suggest that there has been any
lack of sympathy for agriculture. Indeed, I
have stated over and over again not only in
this House but elsewhere that I think money
ápplied in the interests of agriculture, the
premier industry of the country, could not
be better spent, but there are so many other

and Ulster farmers,

items of expenditure to be paid by the
English farmer. He has to pay tithes, but
apart from that fact-
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I was referring to the question of the relief of rates.
Mr. POLLOCK: It does not matter whether

concerned about-as compared with similar

There is no comparison whatever in respect to the guarantees given to shipbuilders
and others. In the first place the Government does not advance money to shipbuilders
and others. What it does is to guarantee
certain loans in order that industry may be
encouraged in shipbuilding and in other
ways. But my hon. Friend is under a misapprehension when he assumes that no disclosures have got to be made in regard to
the position of borrowers under such circumstances. He made a point of the fact
that the farmer would have to disclose his
financial affairs to the banker or persons
from whom he borrowed money, but in every
case where a Government guarantee is given
a full disclosure of the financial position.
and the security offered, must be given by
those who ask for these large sums of money
guaranteed by the Government. I wish to
emphasise that fact.
The Government has also in respect of its
general agricultural policy done a great deal
more than the average citizen has any
apprehension of. Not only is it establishing,
and has established, as a matter of fact,
farms for training young farmers, but a
great deal of money has been spent at Greenmount, Strabane, and elsewhere, and this
Parliament has also voted £50,000 to be devoted to the improvement of agriculture
generally. All the farmers get the benefit of
this; not only those who are in poor circumstances, but also those in better circumstances. Therefore if you aggregate all the
money that has been spent, and is being
spent from time to time in the interests of
agriculture, you will find that by comparison
with what has taken place in Great Britain
we are ahead of anything done there up to
the present.
I offer no opinion as to what the British
Government or the Free State Government
propose to do. I am dealing with facts and
matters that have been dealt with by this
Parliament, and I say that as between the
British agricultural position and our Own
position in the North of Ireland, we can
claim that the Government and Parliament
have done their duty to the farmers of
Ulster. It does not follow that because we
have undertaken certain improvements in
the conditions governing agriculture here we
are at the end of our resources in regard to
that. The right hon. Gentleman who
presides over the Ministry of Agriculture is
very much interested in agriculture, and
will watch all the developments of the
industry, and I can say this: that when any
great necessity arises for any particular
venture or policy the Government will not
fail to take note of it. But to follow the
suggestion of my hon. Friend and assume
that the Government is going to open the
door to 130,000 farmers in Northern Ireland
to ask for loans--
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: They are not
all in need of loans.
Mr. POLLOCK: I am glad to say they are
not. A great many of them do not require
assistance, but if they opened the door to
applications on the part of those 130,000
farmers who may want money for any other
purpose the Government would be embarking on an adventure which would not only
be reprehensible in itself but exceedingly improper as regards the interests of the general
taxpayers.
I have no more to say on that subject, but
if I again ask hon. Members to reflect on
what the hon. Member for Antrim desires
they will see that such a policy is quite out
of harmony with prudence, and as the
Minister responsible for finance I certainly
cannot favour any adventure in the direction
which the hon. Member has outlined. That
is all I have got to say on this subject of agriculture. As regards the remarks of the hon.
Members who have taken up the subject of
unemployment, I leave them to the Minister
more directly responsible.

PROCLAMATION OF LABOUR
DEMONSTRATION.
Mr. KYLE (by Private Notice) asked the
Minister of Home Affairs by whose authority the Inspector General proclaimed the
demonstration that was to be held under
the auspices of the Belfast Labour Party,
which proposed to demonstrate peacefully
to protest against the Regulations laid down
by the Ministry of Labour.
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I accept full responsibility for the action of the Inspector
General, which he took after consultation
with me.
I regret that in view of the public utterances of the organisers I cannot agree with
the hon. Member that this was intended to
be a peaceable demonstration. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. KYLE: The import of this to the
working classes of this city is so great that
I give notice that on the adjournment of the
House I will draw attention to the matter.

Drainage Bill.
STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF
FINANCE.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): In view of the assurances that were
given on the general expectation that this
great and important Measure would be proceeded with at an early period of our sittings
I think it is only due to the House that I
should explain in a few sentences the
reasons which govern our decision to ask the
House to postpone consideration of the
Second Reading until the 21st of this month.
The full text of the Measure has been in
the hands of hon. Members since our last
Parliamentary sittings, and I take it for
granted, therefore, that they are fully aware
of the great responsibility that the Measure
would throw upon the public bodies of the
Province in respect of the general drainage
of the land of Ulster. That being so it
appears to the Government that it is very
essential that there should be agreement-full
agreement-between the County Councils and
the Government in respect of this Measure;
in other words it would be very undesirable
if these public bodies laboured under the
impression that we are forcing something
upon them that they perhaps were not in full
agreement with. Be that as it may, however, my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates), has had
conferences with the County Councils on the
subject of this Bill. The result of these
conferences has been a general agreement, or
rather I should say an agreement on the
1131 The Proclaimed Demonstration. HOUSE OF COMMONS The Proclaimed Demonstration. 1132

[Mr. Pollock]
general principle of the Bill, leaving one or
two very important measures of detail for
future settlement. As these matters of
detail have not yet been fully considered I
am here to-day to ask the postponement of
the Second Reading of this Measure for a
fortnight in order that one or two meetings
which we propose to have with these bodies
shall be held in the intervening period. I have
no doubt at all from the general feeling that
exists in the Province as to the necessity for
passing this important Measure, that there
should not be any great difficulty in reaching
a full agreement, not only in regard to the
principle, but also to the general details of
the working of the Measure. I therefore
move that the Second Reading consideration
of this Bill be postponed until the 21st
October.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Government Loans and Exchequer
Provisions [Money.]
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That it is expedient to authorise, under
powers to be conferred by an Act of this
Session-
(1) the establishment of a Government
Loans Fund, and the creation of Ulster
Loans Stock, with a guarantee for the payment of the dividends thereon and the
repayment of the principal from the Consolidated Fund;
(2) the issue out of the Consolidated
Fund, by way of advance, of any deficiency
of income of the Government Loans Fund
Account in any year, including any
deficiency caused by payments to any Sinking Fund that may be created by virtue of
any such Act, and the repayment out of
moneys to be provided by Parliament of
such advances;
(3) the
payment out of moneys to be
provided by Parliament of any amount
hereafter directed to be written off as
lost on account of any Government Loan;
(4) the amendment of the law relating to
the Exchequer and Consolidated Fund."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The Financial Resolution now before the Committee requires some explanation from me having regard to the necesit
sarily technical language in which is
framed. The Resolution is, of course, the
forerunner of a Money Bill, and in order
that the Committee may know exactly what
machinery is contemplated in the Bill it is
necessary that I should recall to your
memory some of the provisions of the Exchequer Borrowing and Local Loans Act, 1922,
which empowered the Ministry of Finance
to issue from the Consolidated Fund for
loans to Local Authorities and enabled the
Ministry to borrow to place the Exchequer
in funds for this purpose by the issue of
Ulster Savings Certificates or by the issue
of other kinds of securities. On that occasion reference was made to the fact that in
Great Britain a special Loans Stock and a
separate Local Loans Fund were in existence, the needs of Local Authorities in Great
Britain being met by direct issues from that
Government Loans-
Committee.
7 OCTOBER 1925
Fund. Having regard to Northern Ireland's
then more limited requirements Parliament
readily appreciated how unnecessary it was
to set up similar machinery in Northern
Ireland at that time, and authority was
accordingly given to the Ministry of Finance
to conduct all lending operations through
the Exchequer, thereby obviating the necessity for the issue of a separate stock for this
purpose.
This was in 1922 and during the period
which has elapsed since that date the Exchequer has carried out extensive lending
operations not only in financing Local
Authorities but in certain other analogous
directions, one of the most important of
which has been the making of advances to
the Intoxicating Liquor Claims Fund. These
lending operations have yearly increased in
volume and it will perhaps be of interest to
mention some of the purposes for which
loans have been made:-
Housing Subsidies made by Local Authorities and housing construction undertaken
directly by the Authorities.
Small Dwellings Acquisition.
Water Supply.
Sanitation Works.
Gas and Electric Lighting.
Establishment of Markets.
Workhouse Hospitals.
Road Reconstruction.
Building of Technical Schools and Town
Halls.
Cemeteries.
Open Spaces.
In addition, Acts of Parliament have
authorised expenditure in the nature of
capital expenditure, e.g., Housing Subsidies
and Police Barrack Reconstruction Schemes.
In view of the magnitude of its present-day
lending operations it is now the view of the
Government that the time has arrived when
we should revert to the British system of
setting up a separate Fund to be fed from
the proceeds of a special Loans Stock. The
many advantages of such a system can be
dealt with at a later stage when the text
of the Bill is available.
There is, however, one point of some importance to which reference might be made
at this stage, and it is this. In the majority
of cases the loans are repayable over a
long period of years, and I need hardly point
out that the system, if it is to be satisfactory
in all respects, should have as an essential
part of it a form of borrowing which more
nearly coincides with the average period of
repayment, which, in this case, means a form
of borrowing by long-dated securities.
The passing of this Financial Resolution
will enable the Ministry of Finance to
bring in a Bill providing for the issue of
the long-dated Loan Stock and the setting
up of a separate Loans Fund, and as the
Government are desirous of obtaining powers
for these purposes at the earliest possible
date I trust that the Committee will give
us both stages of this Resolution to-day.
Turning to the text of the different parts
of the Resolutions themselves. The first part
which you have read, Mr. Chairman, is selfexplanatory. Paragraph 2 gives the security
of the Consolidated Fund, that is to say,
the credit of the whole Province is to be
pledged for the benefit of the investor in any
public issue. Paragraph 3 provides for a
charge on votes in respect of any bad debt
which can, of course, only be written off with
the consent of Parliament to be obtained by
separate statute. Paragraph 4 contains
certain miscellaneous provisions amending
the existing law as to the Exchequer and
finance operations, and calls for no detailed
observations from me at this stage. I beg
to move.
Question put and agreed to.
Resolution reported.
