UNEMPLOYED BECOMING
UNEMPLOYABLE.
8. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister
whether he is aware that there is રી
constantly increasing number of young men
and women who, through the failure of the
capitalistic system of production for profit,
to provide employment for them, are rapidly
becoming unemployable, and what steps he
is prepared to take to remedy this state of
affairs.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have been asked by the
Prime Minister to reply to this question.
I am glad to say that there is no evidence
of a constantly increasing number of young
men and women becoming rapidly unemployable. The unemployment that prevails
generally is due to the upheaval in world
conditions consequent on the Great War and
not, in my opinion, to the capitalist system
as suggested by the hon. Member, who is no
doubt familiar with the deplorable results
that have followed the substitution of
Socialism in Soviet Russia.
I feel I ought to add that I strongly deprecate attacks on capital, as any sense of
insecurity is bound to prevent industrial development and increase unemployment. The
most practical way of dealing with the
situation is, I think, by friendly co-operation between capital and labour to achieve
the common end in which they are both
vitally concerned.
Mr. KYLE: I would like to ask the
Minister of Labour what security he thinks
there is for this constantly increasing number of young men and women who are
becoming unemployed in our midst under the
capitalist system?
Mr. ANDREWS: I am surprised that my
hon. Friend should suggest that an increasing
number of our young people are becoming
unemployed. I do not admit that contention
at all. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
.
9. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister
whether, in view of the numbers of starving
men and women in Belfast consequent upon
unemployment, he is prepared to declare a
state of emergency, and to compel the Board
of Guardians to administer out-door relief on
the scale laid down by the Ministry of Health
in Great Britain.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I have been asked by the
Prime Minister to reply to this question.
I have consulted the Board of Guardians
in Belfast, and I am assured that the Guardians give every case of distress which comes
to their knowledge careful consideration. So
far back as October, 1923, the Guardians
impressed upon the Relieving Officers the
importance of giving their earnest attention
to all cases which may come under their
notice as Relieving Officer, or which may be
brought to their notice indirectly through
any other source or agency. Each case is
relieved according as necessity is shown.
The Ministry of Home Affairs in response to
representations made by the Board of Guardians and the Belfast Corporation, specially
augmented, in February, 1924, the ordinary
powers of granting out-door relief by an
Order under section 13 of the Local Government (Ireland) Act, 1896. The Order under
that Section removes restrictions in the
ordinary law and extends the Guardians'
powers by authorising them to give out-door
relief, at their discretion, to heads of
families in distress. I am informed that the
term "heads of families" is interpreted in the
'widest possible sense.
The Government have no power to compel
the Board of Guardians, who are the duly
elected representatives of the ratepayers, to
give relief indiscriminately according to a
fixed scale, nor can I find that the Ministry
of Health in England or the Scottish Board
of Health have any such compulsory power.
I am informed that the Ministry of Health
have not approved of any scale upon which
Boards of Guardians should give out-door
relief, though that Department has taken
action when a Board of Guardians has exceeded its legal powers in this direction. No
such action has been necessary in Belfast.
The discretion as to the amount of relief to
meet the necessities of each case must be left
to the Board of Guardians, who are the
responsible authority under Statute for the
purpose.

PENALISING APPLICANTS FOR UN-
EMPLOYMENT BENEFIT.
11. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that applicants
for unemployment insurance benefit are
penalised more than once for the same
offence.
Mr. ANDREWS: It is the case-and in
my opinion it is essential in order to protect
the Fund and the interest of the contributors-that, when a claimant has refused an
offer of employment in a particular vacancy,
and has in consequence been disqualified for
benefit for a period, the Department should
be free to test his continued willingness to
take employment by offering him another
vacancy, and, if necessary, the same one;
and, if he again unreasonably refuses to
take the employment, to impose a further
period of disallowance. The applicant has
always the right to appeal to the Court of
Referees against this disallowance.
ANTRIM LOCAL EMPLOYMENT
COMMITTEE.
12. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether the decision of the Antrim
Local Employment Committee on the 16th
September, 1925, laying down a scale under
the Local Employment Committee Scheme
fixing a family income for the Exchange area
as follows:-man, 25s per week; wife, 20s
per week; each child under 18 years of age,
5s per week; each adult over 18 years of age,
20s per week, has been carried into effect,
and, if not, for what reason has the decision
of the Antrim Local Employment Committee
been set aside.
Mr. ANDREWS: The Antrim Local Employment Committee submitted to the
Ministry for approval certain scales of
family income which they provisionally suggested should be applied when applications
were being considered for the grants of
extended benefit by persons who have drawn
all the benefit to which they may be en
titled on their contributions.
The suggested scales were considerably in
excess of those previously observed by the
Local Employment Committees at Antrim
and elsewhere in Northern Ireland. The
Antrim Committee, in which I have full
confidence, has, therefore, been requested to
give further consideration to the question
at its next meeting, and it has been suggested that in proposing scales the
Committee should have regard to the rates
of wages generally prevailing in the district.

FREE COPIES OF ACTS OF
PARLIAMENT.
15. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs on what grounds he has discontinued the old practice of sending free
copies of Acts of Parliament, etc., to Local
Authorities, and seeing that the administering of these Acts rests on the Local
Authorities, will he resume the former
practice.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This action has
been taken by the Ministry of Home Affairs
in consequence of a general decision of the
Government curtailing on the grounds of
economy the free issue of Stationery Office
publications by Government Departments.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Perhaps I should supplement the
answer given by the Minister of Home
Affairs. At the beginning of this year an
investigation was made by my Department
into the cost of the publication and circulation of Government Papers on the ground
that it seemed to me that the cost was excessively heavy. It was found that a great
many free copies were distributed where, in
the opinion of the Ministry and the Government, it was desirable that they should be
bought in the ordinary way.
Administrative action was taken by my
Ministry to ensure that in future no Government publications of any sort would be distributed free without the specific sanction
of the Ministry to those bodies or persons
who might reasonably be expected to bear
the cost themselves. This action follows on
the lines adopted by the Stationery Office
of the Imperial Government. The results,
I may say are quite satisfactory, as the instructions have resulted in a very large increase in the circulation of Government
Papers.
I see no reason why Public Authorities
should receive Government Bills free to any
greater extent than private individuals, and
as the cost has been in our opinion excessively heavy, I see no reason to depart from
the arrangement made.
Mr. MCALLISTER: Has any arrangement
been made at all to notify local authorities
of the various changes made in the laws they
are called upon to administer?
Mr. POLLOCK: I think the changes in
the laws must be a matter of public notoriety
in view of the fact that the proceedings of
this Parliament are published in the Press
the morning after our meeting.

SAILORS' AND SOLDIERS' LAND TRUST.
Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Finance whether he can state how many houses
have been built under the Sailors' and
Soldiers' Land Trust Scheme in Northern
Ireland; what conditions govern applications for the tenancy of these houses; what
recommendation is required; what was the
duration of the service of applicants who
have secured houses, and what number were
allocated to soldiers and sailors.
Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Finance whether he can state the cause of the
delay in building the 313 ex-Servicemen's
houses which have been authorised by the
Imperial Government.
Mr. POLLOCK: I will answer this question and that put by the hon. Member (Mr.
Kyle) regarding the delay in the building
of the ex-Servicemen's houses together.
As I have already pointed out, my
Ministry merely acts as the agent of the
Irish Sailors' and Soldiers' Land Trust,
which is an Imperial Service, but, as a
matter of courtesy to the hon. Gentleman,
I have obtained the following information :-
The number of ex-Servicemen's houses in
Northern Ireland completed to date is 678,
and 55 are at present in course of construction.
The delay that has taken place in proceeding with the remainder of the houses
was due to differences between the Trust and
the Imperial Treasury regarding the amount
required for the completion of the scheme,
but I am glad to be able to state that the
Trust has, within the past few days, sanctioned the erection of a further 134 houses,
and the work will be commenced as soon
as the necessary plans, specifications and
bills of quantities have been prepared.
Any ex-Serviceman who desires to obtain
an ex-Serviceman's house, and has not
already submitted an application, should
apply to the Ministry of Finance for the
requisite form, which affords him an opportunity of giving particulars of his service,
etc. When houses are ready for occupation
or become vacant the applications are considered by the trustees, who select the prospective tenants.

The only condition which the applicants
are required to fulfil for consideration for
the tenancy of Trust houses is that they
must be men who have served in any of
His Majesty's Naval, Military or Air Forces
in the Great War," and no special recommendation is required.
I am further informed that the duration
of the service of applicants who have secured
houses varies from six months to six years,
and that there is no specific distribution of
such houses as between soldier and sailor
candidates.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Widows', Orphans' and Old - Age
Contributory Pensions Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
That the Bill be now read a Second time."
Mr. ANDREWS: I am sure that every hon.
Member of this House will appreciate that
his is a Measure of outstanding importance,
ecause it affects the well-being of practially all our industrial classes in Northern
reland. On 4th January next it is estimated 5,600 widows will become entitled to
ensions, and in addition to that 16,000 dependent children will be entitled to benefits
nder this Measure. (Hon. Members: Hear,
ear.) Hon. Members will not expect me tolay to wade through all the various clauses
f this complicated Measure, which number
6, but I do feel it will be necessary for me
o draw upon the patience of hon. Members
For a longer time than I generally do, so that
I may endeavour, as far as I can, to explain
hose provisions, which in my mind are
Fundamental. If I did not do so I would be
eaving myself open to the charge that notwithstanding the importance of the Bill I did
not take the trouble to explain fully what its
various provisions involved. You, Sir, may
be aware of the fact that a distinguished
British statesman a few weeks ago said that
those who sought popularity ought not to
make themselves responsible for an In-
Surance Measure. As during the last four
years and a half I have been responsible for
no fewer than eleven such Measures, I am
afraid it follows that my reputation must be
at a rather low ebb.
However that may be, the difficulty
associated with a Measure of this kind is
that the human mind being what it is and
people's view-points being very different
there are bound to be those who will say that
the Measure goes too far, that it is pauperising in its effect, and that it really puts a
burden on the few which as it becomes unbearable is bound to re-act against the
many; while on the other hand there are
certain to be those who will take a different
view and say that the Measure does not go far
enough, that it gives an insufficiency to
those whom it professes to benefit, and that
it is in reality mean and contemptible and a
fraud. I have to endeavour to balance
between those two forces in my remarks today. Hon. Members are aware of the fact
that during the last thirty years, as a
reflection of the ever-growing social
conscience, Measure after Measure has been
passed at Westminster, the object of which
has been to help our industrial classes in
times of adversity. I refer, of course, to the
Old-Age Pensions Act, to our Health Insurance and Unemployment Acts, to our Workmen's Compensation Acts, and to other
Measures of a similar kind.
It seems to me rather strange that in this
great group of Measures of social reform
there is one gap, and that gap should be
associated with those with whom every one
of us in this House, I am sure, has the
greatest possible sympathy, namely, our
widows and orphans. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The Measure which was passed at Westminster in August last righted that wrong
for Great Britain, and this Bill which I have
the privilege to bring before the House today is intended in a similar way to right the
wrong here. It is a great Measure in my
opinion. I can say that because it has been
designed and given existence to in Great
Britain by British statesmen who alone
deserve the credit, a credit which I cannot
claim to any extent. At the same time I do
feel it a privilege to bring this Bill before the
House to-day because I know it will bring
hope and brightness into the homes of
thousands of our people where at the present
time there is nothing but darkness, care, and
distress.
I do feel that through the provisions of this
Bill we are truly visiting the fatherless and
the widows in their affliction. (Hon. Mem-
(bers: Hear, hear). It is not necessary that
I should deal, as I said, with each particular
Clause in the Measure, because the Bill
itself has been in the hands of hon. Members
for about a week, and the Government has
issued an explanatory memorandum which
deals, I think, in the clearest way possible
with all the important Clauses which the
Bill contains. But at the same time I would
like to say that when you come to give
pensions of necessity there must be some test.
Of course, I know that tests are not particularly popular. The only way to avoid tests is
to say you are going to give pensions to all.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Hear, hear.
Second Reading. 1196
Widows' Pensions Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Mr. ANDREWS: My hon. Friend says
"Hear, hear." That means he would give
pensions to those who do not need them
as well as to those who need them.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: No, those
who need them.
Mr. ANDREWS: My hon. Friend now says
to those who need them. It follows there
must be some test to find out who needs
them and who does not need them. In
connection with war pensions the test has
been military service, and the dependants
of those who were killed or who died on
active service received pensions as a consequence, and then when there was disability
attributable to the war disability pensions
were given on a generous scale. As regards
old-age pensions, the test has been different.
It has been the test of income, and up to
the present in Northern Ireland the test of
income has been income derived from savings
as well as income derived from earnings. I
know that my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Finance looks forward in a few
days to bringing in a Measure to remove
the thrift disqualification clause, and put us
in step with Great Britain in that connection. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The test in this instance is a different
test. This Bill is being in a measure linked
up with our Health Insurance Acts, so that
those who are entitled to be insured persons
and receive benefits under our Health Insurance. Acts will be entitled to receive benefits
under this Act. In addition to that there
are certain exempted persons and certain
excepted industries and voluntary contributors who will be brought into the orbit
of the Measure as well. At the present time
we have 325,000 insured persons in Northern
Ireland. It is estimated that this figure
will be increased to about 350,000, and when
you take the children into account it will
mean that in Northern Ireland about 700,000
of our people will directly or indirectly be
eligible for benefits under the Act. That
really makes the scheme one of the widest
character. I should like to say that one
card and one stamp will be sufficient to
deal with both national health insurance
and with the benefits which will be given
and obtained under this Measure.
The most important provision in the Bill,
of course, is that which gives benefit to the
widow. The widow of an insured man who
dies after the date of the commencement of
this scheme, namely, 4th January next, and
who was under 70 years of age at that date
will be entitled to receive for herself 10s a
week pension so long as she lives or until
she re-marries or becomes 70 years of age,
in which case she will become without
further tests entitled to a pension
under our Old Age Non-Contributory Acts,
In addition to that the widow will be entitled
to receive 5s of an allowance for her eldest
or only child and 3s for the other children
whom she may have until they become 14
years of age, or if they remain full time at
a day school, 16 years of age. Now that
means that although the children's allowances are terminable the widow's pension still
goes on, which, I think, no hon. Member
can say is otherwise than a generous
But
arrangement.
then, unfortunately,
there are children who are orphans, having
lost both parents, and to these an orphan's
pension will be given of 7s 6d a week until
the orphan becomes 14 years of age, or if remaining full time at a day school 16 years
of age.
But we have to deal with a real difficulty.
and that is the existing widow. The difficulty which the existing widow presents is
this, that although her husband may have
been an insured person under our National
Health Insurance Acts, if he is dead now,
or dies before the 4th January next, he will
not have contributed anything to the pensions' benefits under this particular Act.
The same applies to the existing orphan. At
the same time it has been considered that
it will involve great hardship to leave existing widows and orphans out of the
Measure altogether, and so it is provided in
the Bill that existing widows-that is those
who are widows to-day or become widows before the 4th January next-will receive a
pension at the rate of 10s per week provided
they have one or more children, and they
will also receive an allowance for those
children notwithstanding the fact that no
contributions have been paid. Again I cannot but think that that is a generous arrangement. Of course, hon. Members may ask
"Why does the widow who has no children
not get a pension?" (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Well, the reason is because, as I have
said, no contributions will have been paid by
her husband on her behalf, and it is considered that while the duty of the mother
is to look after her children the widow who
has no children is not in a greater difficulty
to provide for herself than the girl who has
never been married. I think that is a complete answer. In reality you will see that
existing widows and orphans will get a
non-contributory pension. But the Bill does
not stop here. It goes further still, and it
provides on a contributory basis old-age
pensions at the rate of 10s a week to insured
men and insured women between the ages of
65 and 70 years, and also to the wives of insured men between these ages, notwithstanding the fact that such wives may not have
been insured themselves. These pensions, 1
want to make it perfectly clear, do not become available until the 2nd January, 1928,
just in the same way as they will not be
available until that date in Great Britain.

thing. Unfortunately that is not
If it were the Members of the Government

by the workers and by the employers,

as is done in the case of health insurance and

involves are not very large. In the first
place the employer will have to pay for those
men whom he employs, 44d per week, and
the worker himself will have to pay
another 4d per week. For every woman
worker the employer will pay 24d and the
female worker will herself pay 2d. But that
is not the end of the story. Our Health
Insurance Fund will be relieved of certain
obligations which it is under at the
present time, and therefore speaking in round
figures the contributions to this fund will be
reduced to the extent of about a half-penny
in each instance. Then our Unemployment
Fund, I am very glad to feel, will also

to this fund will be reduced by 2d as far as

worker, and 2d for the worker himself; a
penny as far as the employer is concerned for
female worker, and a penny for the worker
herself. That means that the additional
contribution which this Measure will evolve
will be 2d from the employer for the male
worker, 2d from the worker himself; a penny
from the employer for the female worker and
a penny from the worker herself.

Now may I give just two examples of what
this Bill means? A few weeks ago 1 was
privileged with a few friends to spend eight

have a cup of afternoon tea. and that we

I happened to notice some little way off a

would she boil it, and she said "Certainly."
While it was being boiled, of course, we had

had died a year ago, and said "Sir, if it had
not been for the generosity of his employer,
Captain So-and-so"- I forget the exact
name-"and what we got from our Health
Insurance Benefit I do not know how we
could have carried on, and we are having a
heavy struggle now." I could see it from the

coming your way, because, as your husband
Iwas an insured person, and as you evidently

In addition to that the Minister of Labour
has told us what the direct contribution is
going to be, but he has not told us all. He
has tried to make it as attractive as possible.
The Minister of Health in Great Britain has
told us that it is eventually going to involve a charge of £760,000,000 upon the State,
a capital charge of £760,000,000, a larger sum
than the National Debt in 1913, and that at a
time when industry is struggling for its very
existence, and at a time when the outlook
in regard to employment is not at all rosy.
It is certainly not bright in Great Britain,
and I am sorry to say that the numbers of
unemployed in Ulster are larger in proportion to the population than in Great Britain,
due to the fact that the two main industries,
linen and shipbuilding, are in a somewhat
parlous condition at the moment. I may be
wrong in that, but I can be corrected if I
am. I will support the Bill, and will pay
any contributions as far as I am concerned,
believing in the great injunction that we
should all try to bear each others' burdens if
we can and help those who cannot help themselves, but at the same time it is well for us
to know exactly the obligations we have to
face.
We in Northern Ireland will have to pay
our share of the £760,000,000, because it is
well for this House to remember that it is
the Imperial Parliament that imposes and
collects 90 per cent. of all the taxes we have
to pay in Northern Ireland, so that we have
to pay our share of the £760,000,000.
There
is only one compensation, and that is that if
we did not adopt the Act in Northern Ireland
on somewhat similar lines to the Act passed
in Great Britain, we would make a present
of our share of Imperial contribution which
would be spent on the other side. In our
financial relationships with Great Britain,
when we are adjusting our contribution we
will get some reduction to balance our contribution under the Imperial Act.
I want to remind the House of an observation I made as an interruption in the speech
of the Minister of Labour, and to which the
Member for West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen) referred. Contributions in respect of National Health Insurance and
Unemployment Insurance, and now the contribution that has to be paid for this most
admirable purpose, have got to be paid by
industry whether industry makes a profit or
not. Let that never be lost sight of. It is
all very well for the Minister of Labour to
tell the House that in the linen trade, with a
wages bill of so much per week, the contributions will only amount to £150 a year.
That is a dividend of 5 per cent. on £3,000,
and how many firms are in the happy position
to-day of being able to pay a dividend? That
is why I am timid about the financial proposals we propose to adopt in conformity
with what is being done on the other side. I
only hope that when they work out we will
find that things will not be as black as one
might expect, and I hope that the trade outlook may improve, and that the burden that
is being placed both on the employer and the
workman will be such that both will be able
to bear it and carry on.
I want again in a few sentences to show
exactly what Great Britain has done-and
we are following in line with them-in regard to social reform during the past few
years. If you take what may be called
Social Services-and here I am quoting one
of the finest financial experts in Great
Britain who himself was Chancellor of the
Exchequer—including the Poor Rate, Local
Rate, Health Insurance, Unemployment Insurance, Workmen's Compensation and Old-
Age Pensions, in 1911 the charges covering
these different items came to the sum
of £30,000,000. What are they to-day?
£169,000,000. Our friends on the Opposition
Benches sometimes criticise the Government
for not being sympathetic enough, but these
contributions to the social services mean a
contribution of £3 18s. Od. per head of the
population. How does that compare with
the other countries throughout the world?
In Germany for similar services the contribution per head
is
of the pepulation
£1 12s. Od., in France 16s., in Belgium 48.,
and in Italy 3s. These countries have free
access to our markets and are competing
'with the manufacturers and merchants of
(Great Britain and Ireland, and the industries of our country contribute to the
extent of £3 18s. Od. per head while these
other countries are paying only a trifle. They
have free access to our markets and take away
a large share of our trade, while we on the

that trouble me in regard to the future of

Then, again, take the question of local
rates, a very important element to deal with

burden that both the ratepayers and the tax-

payers of Great Britain and Northern Ireland have to face at the present moment.
With that huge burden I cannot see how we
can expect the prosperity we would like.
To my mind one of the greatest questions
we have got to face to-day is that of unemployment, and anything that will act as a
barrier to finding work for our people is to
be deprecated. Some of my hon. Friends on
the Opposition Benches may ask me "What
is your remedy?" My remedy can be put
into a sentence or two-Harder work by the
employer, less time spent on the golf links
and in recreation and pleasure, more time
spent in the office and in going round the
various details of the works to see where
greater efficiency can be brought about and
where economy can be secured. That may be
an unpleasant truth to state, but I am acting
up to it myself in my own works. There is
nothing else for it if you are going to carry
on.
But there must also be harder workand I know my hon. Friends will not deprecate my making this statement-on the part
of the workers and the employees, because
when everything is said and done both employer and employee either stand or fall together. Without the co-operation of both in
these critical times I cannot see how anything can be accomplished effectively. Then
there must be greater production. My hon.
Friends may disagree with me in this respect, but unless there is greater production--
and I speak as one who has some knowledge
of the markets of the world-and we
cheaper goods to place upon those markets
we are going to be left behind in the race.
It is only an economic commonplace when
I say that we can only pay for the food
supplies we have to exist on by what we
export, and if our exports decrease and our
imports increase then we are living upon
our capital, and capital is a thing that cannot continue for ever.
have
Another thing is that unless taxation comes
down in this country and in Great Britain
from the height to which it has soared, in my
judgment you will not have the revival of
trade which we all hope for and pray for and
look forward to. I am sorry if I have exhausted the patience of hon. Members in
trying to put before them some of these
economic truths, as I hope my hon. Friends
opposite will think them, and the viewpoint
I take in regard to legislation of this
character. There is no Member of this
House more sympathetic towards social
form than I am. The Measure now before
this House is a great act of faith on the
part of this Government, and I sincerely hope
that the faith they have will be justified
in the coming years, that the optimism they
must have that trade is going to revive, and
that unemployment is going to be lessened
will be amply fulfilled.
re-
The Measure will involve a burden upon the
employing class and upon the worker. It
will also involve a burden on the general
taxpayer, because the general taxpayer is involved as well as the person who contributes
with the difference that the man who

I would like to see a great many people who

than it is.
But we
are limited in our financial re-
Sources and if we go beyond the limit of the

attention, and in parts with some sympathy,

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON indicated dissent.
Mr. DEVLIN: Perhaps he was too intelligent to be one of the hierarchy. He at
all events was one of the rank and file.
I look back during almost the last quarter
of a century when I was a Member of the

British House of Commons, and I cannot
forget that great trinity of social reforms
which have pressed forward with such power
during the last few years. First of all, there
were old age pensions, then unemployment,
then work or maintenance and now widows'
pensions. Many of us were preaching those
doctrines for nearly twenty years and they
were regarded as a gospel of Utopia. When
I first went into Parliament one of the first
votes I gave was in favour of old age pensions.
It was not a very magnificent measure as was
said by my hon. Friend (Mr. William
McMullen). It was a proposal to give 5s a
week to the aged workers who had given
nalf a century of their blood and service in
the army of industry, and I remember to
what a fury the Tory Party worked itself
when that proposal of a miserable pittance
of 5s a week was being given to these aged
poor in the winter of their lives.
I remember one formidable orator, the late
Lord Chaplin, declaring in the most passionate manner that a vast measure of that sort
owing to the financial position of England
meant the ruin of the Empire. That was a
proposal to spend £25,000,000 a year upon
those old people who had a burden of service
for half a century. Yet fifteen years afterwards this Empire, which was to be ruined
by the burden of £25,000,000 a year for old
age pensions, was able to bear the burden
of £7,000,000 a day for the Great War which
lasted five years. These islands were not
only able to bear this burden, but this
Empire was the only part of the world able
to bear adequately the financial burdens
which the war imposed.
Then the question of work or maintenance
was not one that should have been dealt
with at a moment of great industrial danger.
It should have been foreseen by statesmen.
They might have known that after the war,
if they had known anything about the aftermath of war in other periods, they would be
face to face with this reaction, but nothing
was done until the war was over. The fact
that the whole situation was mishandled by
those who have denied absolutely the right
of the working classes to the control of their
destinies is to a large degree the cause of
the present appalling condition of trade and
industry in these islands.
Now the question of widows' pensions comes
along. Why has this Bill been introduced
to-day? Is it not because you believe in it
at all. If the right hon, Gentlemen had believed the proposals for the creation of
pensions for widows and orphaned children
were a desirable thing they should have said
so in the King's Speech. Proposals of this
character were adumbrated in the King's
Speech in the English Parliament. A
definite promise was given by Mr. Baldwin and his party at the last election
that this was one of the fundamental"
principles of the Tory programme.
You never mentioned it at all, simply
because you never had the slightest intention of introducing a Widows' and Orphans'
Bill, even of the inadequate character of
this Measure. But you did it because there
was an Opposition in this House. (Hon.
Members: No, no.) You did it because
there were men in this House who, moved
by a spirit of social passion and anxious to
carry on the heritage of those working for
humane causes, were determined that you
would not sneak out of your responsibility
to the widows and orphans of Ulster as long
as we would be here. That was the reason
why the Prime Minister, I suppose, used
the violent language he did when addressing
a meeting the other night in Belfast. I
forget what the contemptuous references
were to myself. I pass that over.
As representing the minority branded to be eternal
outcasts in our own community, we may
suffer that insult mildly with the rest, but
hon. Gentlemen below me here are to be
wiped out at the next elections and utterly
despised, and hon. Gentlemen here are
traitors. I know why I am held up to
idicule and scorn, and denounced. That I
can understand, but these gentlemen are
elected by the votes of the people of Ulster,
by the votes of the working classes, and
these gentlemen are elected and sent here
as I am sent here, for the purpose of compelling the Government to pass democratic
legislation in a Parliament where that legislation has not been adumbrated in the
King's Speech.
Therefore, I say the heinousness of our
crime and the cause of this enmity to those
in the Opposition is because we
are here
to compel the Government to do those acts
of justice to the most lowly and most
defenceless of the community which this
Measure most inadequately proposes to do
here to-day. For twenty years we have been
waiting for these Measures, and we have got
them at last. I might say the same in
Iegard to the removal of the thrift disqualification. There never was a single promise
made that the thrift disqualification regarding old-age pensions would be removed until
we raised it in this House, until we continuously pressed for it. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Pollock) never voluntarily rose and said that
this disqualification would be removed. We
are a sort of gift Parliament.
Mr. POLLOCK: May I be allowed to intervene. I did state at this Table that the
thrift disqualification clause would be removed in the autumn of this year, following
upon the arrangements that were then pro

Poverty: a Study of City Life."
years ago I got that book, and I know something, therefore, of the conditions that prevail in the city. I cannot go into these
points, but everybody admits that up to now
these most unfortunate people, the widows
with their children, were left to the cold
charity of the Poor Law. I think everybody
-the majority of people at any rate-deplored that. It is the first duty of the State
to see to the prosperity, and happiness, and
health of the wealth producer, and the wealth
producer is the worker.
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Dr. MORRISON: The second and third
classes, namely the distributor and the consumer, are able, in my opinion, to look after
themselves. Contributory help from the
worker or the person helped, with the exception of the Old Age Pensions Acts, runs
through all the remedial social legislation
we have had for the last ten years. You get
the State aiding in Land Purchase, in
National Health Insurance, in War Savings
Certificates, the building of schools, and
other things, in order to help the people in
the things which are necessary and which
they cannot do for themselves. The necessity for this has long been recognised in the
Church to which I belong, and it has been
our proud, boast for the last ten or twenty
years that no
widow or orphan of that
Church is unprovided for. Let me give you
just one case. Probably about twenty years
ago a wife asked me to go and see her
husband. I knew that the man was doomed,
and the only advice I could give him was
that he should become a contributor to the
Orphan Society, under which for a contribution of 1d per week he was guaranteed a
pension for his widow and children. He did
that. Two years after that time I had the
experience of delivering that woman of her
seventh child in a corner of a double-roomed
cottage with the dead body of her husband
in the opposite corner. That woman and her
seven children were provided for. We on
this side are often charged with being unsympathetic and with having done nothing.
The hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin) has stated that twenty years ago he
was urging on Parliament the necessity of
making provisions for this and cases like it.
While he was urging it Members on this side
of the House were doing it as far as it was
in their power.
(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Mr. DEVLIN: Doing what?
Dr. MORRISON: Making provision for the
widows and for the orphans. One of the
things I noticed in connection with that was
that, while the great majority of our people
--and I could count perhaps a dozen hon.
Members of this House who are engaged on
that very laudable work-while the members
of our Communion were doing that, there
'were some who could well afford to do it
but did not do it. In this particular case
the woman to whom I have referred was provided with a free cottage for eight years. On
this side of the House we are not perhaps so
prone to speak of our own goods works. We
leave that to the other side.
There is another case that illustrates the
great necessity for help in cases of this kind.
I mention it to illustrate one or two points.
The second hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. William McMullen) put his case here

the case to which I am going to refer they

one of the men who were left stranded

to our Pension Fund, because we have also
a Pension Fund that will take a man on not

qualified and when he needs support.

and will think, it well worth it. I am convinced that his wife, when she understands
the meaning of this Bill, will look upon it as
a blessing and a ray of sunshine into her
life. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I do, however, wish to say a word for his
employer, the farmer. In many cases the
small farmers are poor--just as poor as their
Own labourers, and it certainly will
mean a burden to them. I am afraid at
first sight-I know that at first sight they
will say this is another monstrous burden
added to the burden they already have to
bear, and that they cannot pay. I wish if
it were possible for the Government to find
some way in which the agricultural labourer
and the farmer could be helped. I have a
resolution in my hand at the present moment
in which it is pointed out that the present
insurance contributions, having regard to the
low incidence of sickness amongst the rural
workers, are sufficient to secure for the latter
and their dependents all the benefits proposed by this new Bill. I am not going as
far as that. I am not going to endorse that
statement, but I wonder if it might not be
found possible to consider this question of
the agricultural labourer and his employer,
who is, as I have said, sometimes no richer
than the labourer. However, leaving the
question of the amount on one side, I do
believe that when the farmer has time to
reflect he will not grudge a certain contribution in order to effect the object of this
Bill. He is sorely pressed. He is heavily
over-rated. He has in the past never
hesitated to put his hand deeply into his
pocket in order to help widows and children
in his neighbourhood. Not only that, but
with the heavy rates which he pays there
is a large proportion for outdoor relief. I
believe that this Bill will do away with the
necessity for those collections which have
always been so generously responded to in

Mr. BEATTIE: I rise to draw the
attention of this House to the Question
which I placed on the Order Paper and the
answer which I received from the Minister
of Home Affairs and which I regard as unsatisfactory. The grievance embodied in my
question was in my opinion a violation of the
principle laid down by the Imperial Parliament in connection with the transfer of
prison officials from the Imperial Authorities to the Northern Ireland Authorities.
Under Section 55 of the
of Ireland Act, 1920, you
provision made whereby the
of Civil Servants must not be worsened
in any way by their transfer. I will
quote you the Section of the Act which
I think is all-sufficient to warrant the
Minister of Home Affairs granting the same
remuneration to his prison officials as is at
present paid to the prison officials in Great
Britain. Section 55 (i) of the Government of
Ireland Act 1920, definitely states:-

will find

Subject to the provisions of this Act, all

of the Crown who are not provided for
under the last preceding Section, and are
at the appointed day serving as Irish

liable to perform the same duties as thereto.
fore,-
I think that Section is sufficient to warrant
the Civil Servants in the Prisons Service in
claiming justice in regard to their conditions.
I have here the scales of wages paid to the
English prison officials. Take chief warders,
second class. The pay in the English prisons
is £3 15s per week with a bonus calculated
on the cost of living figures of £2 Os 10d,
making a total wage of £5 15s 10d. Then we
come-
Sir DAWSON BATES: Does my hon.
Friend refer to the chief warders or the
principal warders ?
Mr. BEATTIE: To chief warders, class 2.
The re-grading scheme took place in 1920.
I think the same categories now prevail in
Northern Ireland prisons as in English
prisons, although prior to assimilation there
were grades in England which did not exist
in Northern Ireland. Similar grades do
exist now. We come to Southern Ireland.
We are repeatedly asked by the Government
if we are prepared to accept the legislation
passed in Southern Ireland as far as Civil
Servants are concerned. We are told time
and again about old-age pensioners, school
teachers, post office officials, et cetera, but
here are the Southern Ireland prison officials'
conditions. The same class of warder has
£3 98. His bonus, based on the cost of living
is £2 Es 2d, making a total of £5 17s 2d, as
against the English wage of £5 15s 10d. Now
we come to the Northern Ireland Civil Servants in the prisons. Their conditions are
supposed to be similar to the English. The
same class of warder in Northern Ireland has
a wage of £3 9s. His bonus, based on the
English cost of living figure, runs to £1 18s 7d,
making a total wage of £5 7s 7d, or 8s 3d
below the recognised rate he should be receiving according to the Act of 1920, Section
55.
We come to the principal warders, another
class of warder employed in prisons. In
England the pay of a principal warder is
£2 16s per week and the bonus is £1 13s 9d,
making a total wage of £4 9s 9d. In the
Free State the principal warders are paid
£2 13s and the bonus is £2 1s 2d, making a
total wage of £4 14s 2d. Now take Northern
Ireland, which is supposed to be on parallel
lines with Great Britain. The wage of a
principal warder is £2 13s, and the bonus
£1 12s 9d, making a total wage of £4 5s 9d,
or a reduction of 4s per week.
Next we have the clerk-schoolmaster grade.
We find a reduction there also. In the case
of warders we find their pay is £2 5s per
week in England plus £1 9s 9d bonus, making
a total wage of £3 14s 9d. In the Free State
the pay is £2 3s and the bonus £1 16s 9d,
making a total of £3 19s 9d. In Northern
Ireland the wage is £2 3s and the bonus
£1 9s, making a total of £3 12s, a reduction
for Northern Ireland of 2s 9d per week.
The reductions in the wages of these
warders have been in operation since
October, 1923. We might naturally ask why
the Home Office has not conformed to the
regulations in regard to the transferred
officers of the prisons and placed them upon
the same footing as the present warders, but
we find---

The Act of 1920 expressly protects all existing
Civil Servants against any alteration in their
terms of employment, rates of pay, or anything affecting those matters. It also provides that in case the Government which they
may elect to serve do anything which they
think unjust or unfair they have the right
to go to the Civil Service Committee. I may
remind my hon. Friend that the rate of pay
in England and Ireland at the time of the
passing of the Home Rule Act was the same,
and it was not until 1923 that the British
Government saw fit to make a slight increase.
I think the increase was something like 2s
to a man after he had served fifteen years.

Section 55 (1) of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, provides that "Existing
Irish Officers shall after the appointed day
continue to hold their offices by the same
tenure and upon same terms and conditions (including conditions as to salaries
and superannuation) as heretofore.
and while performing the same or
analagous duties shall receive not less
salaries than they would have received if
the Act had not passed." The Committee
are of opinion that this Section does not
make it incumbent upon the Government
of Northern Ireland to vary the salaries
and other terms of service of existing
Irish officers in accordance with variations
which
may be made either to their
advantage or disadvantage in the case of
Officers in the Civil Service of the United
Kingdom, and does not therefore enable
existing Irish officers in the Prison Service
of Northern Ireland to claim as of right
the extension to them of any increase of
salary granted to Prison Officers in
England. It is for the Ministry of Finance
to decide whether any such increase should
in this particular instance be granted in
Northern Ireland, and the Committee are
unable to intervene in the matter.
The whole point is this: if my hon. Friend's
contention is correct it means that if the
British Government choose at any time to
increase existing salaries the Government
of Northern Ireland would have to do the
same. I would like to ask my hon. Friend
this question. Supposing the English Government, with ideas of economy, started to
reduce existing salaries, would he like to
have the salaries in Northern Ireland reduced
too? It would be entirely illegal on our part
to reduce the salaries existing at the date of
the passing of the 1920 Act.
Mr. BEATTIE: You have already done it.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think my hon.
Friend is deliberately misunderstanding the

Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
TRAINING SETTLEMENTS FOR
UNEMPLOYED.
1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Labour whether he proposes to establish in
Northern Ireland training settlements for
unemployed young men; whether he has
asked the British Minister of Labour to
take into the settlements established in
England a number
young men from
Northern Ireland, and whether he does not
think that this work should be done at
home.
of
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The Imperial Minister of Labour
has decided to open, as an experiment, two
centres in England for giving general workshop instruction to a limited number of unemployed young men and also an agricultural course for a few selected men who
have been accepted for emigration under the
Empire Settlement Act.
I have not asked the Imperial Minister of
Labour to take into any of his centres young
men from Northern Ireland, but I am in
close touch with the Imperial Authorities in
order to secure in the most practicable
manner similar advantages for our young
men here.

Government Loans and Exchequer

Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr Pollock): A few days ago I had the privilege of
submitting to the Committee a Money Resolution as a necessary prelude and forerunner to the Bill which is now about
to be considered by the House. In the statement that I made I entered with some detail
into the circumstances which render the
present Measure necessary. I am quite aware
that financial matters are not exactly exhilarating in their character, and I hope that I
will not try the patience of the House too
much if I recapitulate some of the statements I then made and enter with some detail
into the various questions that arise out of
this Bill, copies of which I presume are in
the hands of hon. Members.
When we entered upon our career in 1921
as an autonomous State, our financial circumstances, and especially our financial relations
with Great Britain, were necessarily in a
very nebulous state. We had no experience
1253 Government Loans Bill-

14 OCTOBER 1925
Second Reading.
D

whatever to guide us in many of the paths ou
which we were required to enter. An additional complication arose from the disturbed
condition of the country, due to the incursions of Southern malcontents."
It will also be apparent even to a superficial observer, that the commerce and industry of the country during the four initial
years of our separate existence could not fail
to be prejudiced by the extraordinary
economic world paralysis following the war.
From the commercial point of view, indeed,
no more unfavourable period could have been
selected to establish a small State with
federal relations to the Kingdom.
The commercial relations of Ulster are
world-wide, and as our two great staple
industries-shipbuilding and linen-are especially sensitive and vulnerable to worldconditions-it was hardly to be expected that
the revenue of the Province could fail to be
prejudically affected in a like degree to that
of Great Britain.
During these four years an additional burden was thrown on the Province, by reason of
the acute unemployment, consequent on the
general industrial depression. which unhappily has not yet been abated by the only
possible solvent, viz., a return to normal
trading conditions. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
But yet notwithstanding these undoubted
disadvantages, it is surely something to the
credit of our Government and to the people
of our Province that we have succeeded in
maintaining the essential services of the Province on the basis of British standards, and
at the same time have been able to contribute
a sum of about 18 millions to. the upkeep of
the Army and Navy, and the payment of the
interest of the National Debt.
It is also, worthy of note-and I think it
necessary to mention these things in view of
the financial step that we propose to takethat apart from such provision as I have
mentioned our annual surpluses in revenue
and expenditure account during the four
years have amounted to a considerable sum.
In the year 1921-22 we had a surplus of
£30,917; in 1922-23, £32,042; in 1923-24
£46,778, and in 1924-25, £150,740, making a
total of £260,477 of an accumulated fund
under this head.
Our Sinking Funds have also been fully
maintained, the total amount laid aside for
ensuring a permanent return from all our
capital funds, such as land purchase
annuities, etc., being £417,000.
There are also other factors which are not
unworthy of mention, when we are asking
Parliamentary authority for the first time
to borrow in the open market such sums
as we require to lend to the local authorities
throughout the Province for their capital
expenditure.
There is no better barometer of a country's
economic and financial strength than the
relation which its export trade bears to
its imports. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Bearing this in mind, therefore, it is surely
a matter of no little satisfaction-apart altogether from our people it must be a matter
of satisfaction to Members of this House,
as it is to the Government, to find that on
investigation of the latest trade statistics
available, i.e., those for the last calendar
year, that notwithstanding the unparalleled
depression in our two great staple industries,
we have succeeded in maintaining a favourable trade balance. Such a result, emphasising as it does the energy and industry of
our trading community, augurs well for the
future prosperity of our Province, when the
world has emerged from its present conditions of inertia.
Before I enter upon a categorical investigation of the import of the different clauses
of the Measure, I should like to advert for
a few moments to the circumstances which
render this Measure necessary.
The practice of the British Government
in regard to financing local loans-that
is to say for the provision of money to lend
to local authorities for these schemes-has
been to establish a special fund, which is
known popularly in the market as
"Local
Loans Fund," and the Stock which is issuedis known as Local Loans Stock. This fund
has been fed from time to time by the
issue of this Local Loans Stock, which is
quoted every day in the market, and is then
dealt with on the Stock Exchange from time
to time.
Up to now we have not found it necessary
to adopt the British practice for this reason,
that during the four years of our autonomous existence the amounts which we had to
deal with have not been of a very important
character, and in addition we have out of
our own resources and by our temporary
borrowings sufficient funds to enable us to
provide for the necessities of local authorities
and others.
that our
There is no doubt whatever
method has two serious defects. The most
important defect is that it is not legitimate
finance to borrow money temporarily as we
have done, and which is subject to repayment at any time, and at the same time
lend that money to other people, who will
only repay that money after a long term
of years, generally 60 years. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) That is too dangerous finance.
Another defect in our system is that it did
not lend itself to suitable accountancy. It
mixed up all our loans with our ordinary
accounts, and it is very undesirable from
the point of view of the information which
Parliament naturally desires in connection
with the loans which from time to time we
issued to local authorities.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Pollock]
It did not matter very much so long as
our loans were of a negligible character as
they have been, and were confined to comparatively small amounts, but when these
operations assume greater magnitude the
system does not lend itself to a satisfactory
method of accounts and the submission to
Parliament of the financial results of loan
legislation.
We have, therefore, decided by the introduction of this Measure to follow the British
practice of providing a separate and distinct
fund, which we call the Local Loans Fund.
From that fund will be issued all moneys
required by local authorities and other outside parties, which will be found in the
Schedule to the Bill on page 13, and also
all sums received by way of income from
the local authorities shall be lodged to that
specific account. I do not think I need
argue the advantage of that, because it
retains in a water-tight compartment, as it
were, all the loans operations which we
undertake, and, therefore, Parliament can be
informed from time to time as we go on
of the nature and volume of all these transactions.
In order to provide the money to establish
this fund, to endow it, to enable it to lend
these moneys, we propose to issue an Ulster
Loan Stock, almost corresponding with the
British Local Loan Stock, of which we have
heard so much for many years.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: The price?
Mr. POLLOCK: That is not arranged, but
I think it will be satisfactory when we reach
that point. The dividends on that stock
will be met from the returns which we receive from the local authorities who borrow
the money from us, that is to say, the one
presumably almost will balance the other.
It will be seen from the Measure that its
'scope extends beyond that of the British
Local Loans Fund bv bringing within its
operations certain loans and advances in
addition to those which may be strictly
described as "Local Loans." These additional
purposes are set out in the Schedule to the
Bill. They include certain agricultural and
educational loans which are described in
the Schedule as development loans," a
small item in the shape of Housing Loans to
Civil Servants; also advances to the Claims
Fund set up under the Intoxicating Liquor
Act, 1923. The latter is repaid over a term
of years by the trade.

It has also been thought desirable to take
power for dealing in a similar manner with
any future capital schemes which Parliament may authorise.
I would point out, however, that the term
"Government Loans," which is used in the
Bill, does not mean that the Fund will
become the medium for all classes of Exchequer advances. For example, advances
to the Unemployment Fund would continue
to be made from the Exchequer as in the
past on the ground that this is a very substantial account, and it is desirable to keep
it a section by itself.
The Loans Fund provided by this Measure
will be administered as a separate and inpendent Budget for the solvency of which
full provision is made, and will remain
independent of the State Budget except in
so far as the State liability exists to meet
any deficiency of income or losses by bad
debts. There can be no question that the
establishment of the Fund and the methods
of its operations will inevitably tend to a
greater efficiency in the administration of
the loan system.
The first Clause provides for the repayment of outstanding Exchequer advances
from the Government Loans Fund to the Exchequer and for all powers of the Exchequer
in regard to such Loans being for the
future transferred to the Fund. During the
four years that have passed we have made
large advances to public authorities and
others of moneys out of our own resources,
and in order that the whole of the liability
in respect of these Loans be consolidated into
one amount we must claim repayment of
these moneys from the Loans in order to
square our finances.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: What is the
average rate of interest?
Mr. POLLOCK: Do I understand the hon.
Member to ask for the average rate of
interest?
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Yes.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have not made up the
average, but I may say it has been very close
upon the cost of our own borrowing which
is not very far from five per cent. The
amounts outstanding which were issued during the four years under the heads in the
Schedule aggregate to £1,109,000. It also has
as its object the ensuring of greater Parliamentary control over Loans than exists at
the present time. In the Acts authorising
the issue of Loans, while the nature of the
purposes for which Loans may be made has
been defined, no limit has been imposed
upon the extent to which the Ministry of
Finance can lend save in the case of one
Act, viz., that authorising capital expenditure on police barrack reconstruction within
a limit of £375,000. This opening Clause
provides for an annual limit in respect of
Local Loans inclusive of Civil Service Housing Loans and Development Loans, and શ
second limit in respect of the remaining purposes described in the Schedule. Authority
for these limits will be sought each year by

borrowed?

carried out immediately as one of the first

Clause 3 provides for the constitution of
Ulster Loans Stock. The Stock will be redeemable at the expiration of fifty years
from the date of its creation. This Clause
imposes a charge upon the Consolidated
Fund, that is, upon the credit of the Province
in respect of the payment of dividends and in
respect of the ultimate redemption of the
Loan. These provisions are necessary in
order to insure the due payment of dividends
and the redemption of the Loan at the proper
time no matter what contingency may arise.
The fixing of a redemption date for the
Stock does not follow the British system,
where the Local Stock is irredeemable, but it
is thought that with a new venture such as
this, a redeemable Stock is more attractive to
the investor.
Under this Clause it would also be
optional to Government to redeem Stock
before the final redemption date on giving
due notice to the holders.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: What is the
redemption period?
Mr. POLLOCK: That is a matter which I
do not think should be discussed in this
House prior to the circulation and publication of our prospectus, I do not think
•
there is anything particularly provided about
that question, but possibly I may touch upon
it later.
Clause 4 deals with a matter already
referred to, namely, the repayment to the
Exchequer of the moneys owed to it by
local authorities and other borrowers. In
return for this payment, the Fund will, of
course, receive the repayments by local
authorities in respect of existing indebtedness. It is also provided that the expenses
of issuing the Stock shall be a charge to
capital, but this charge will be repaid over
a series of years from the Income Account by
means of a book Sinking Fund, which will
be found referred to in Clause 6.
Clause 5 deals with the Income Account
as apart from the Capital Account. In an
earlier Clause it was provided that separate
Capital and Income Accounts should be kept
within the Fund. Clause 5 deals with the
Income Account and provides for payment to
this account of all interest due by the borrowers and for payment out of the account
of the dividends due on the Stock, Sinking
Fund payments, and expense of management
and administration. Any temporary deficiency in the Income Account will be met
in the first instance, from the Exchequer,
but if the Income Account for any year
should prove insufficient for the charges made
upon it, then the deficiency must be voted
by Parliament. In this way, provision is
made for the solvency of the Fund, and
Parliament will be kept in close touch with
the progress of loan transactions. Where
there is an excess of income, power is given
to the Ministry to transfer such sum as they
may think fit to the Exchequer as an alternative to allowing it to accumulate in the Fund.
Clause 6 deals with the Capital Account.
This account will receive the repayments
from borrowings of the principal of loans
which have been made, and in addition sums
will be transferred to it from time to time
out of the Income Account to make good the
deficiency arising from the issue of Ulster
Loans Stock at a discount, and to cover the
expenses of the issue of the Stock. The
issue expenses will thus be met, in the first
instance, from the Capital Account, which
will be recouped over a period of years out
of the Income Account. No separate Sinking
Fund Account will be opened, but the moneys
will form part of the Capital Account and
will be available for re-issue as Local Loans
in the ordinary way.
Clause 7 indicates that there will be one
Cash Balance in respect of the Fund out
of which all demands will be paid. It further
provides for the temporary investment in

Trustee Securities of any capital moneys
that may accumulate in the coffers of the

I come now to Clause 8. This Clause is
designed to ensure the solvency of the Fund
by providing for a Vote from Parliament
to make good any bad debt. A bad debt can
only occur when a loan is advanced upon
insufficient security or when circumstances
have so altered as to render the payment of
a loan impracticable. A bad debt cannot be
written off except by express permission of
Parliament. It must be returned to Parliament and the authority of Parliament for the
wiping out or writing off-to use commercial
language of the bad debt, that is, a case of
default of the borrower. Should there be
subsequently any return of that money that
money must, of course, be lodged in the Exchequer as an extra receipt, because of the
fact that the Exchequer must make up the
bad debt and therefore if there is any repayment-
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Any composition.
Mr. POLLOCK-Any composition-my hon.
Friend is familiar with business operationsthat composition will go to the credit of the
Exchequer Account.
Clause 9 merely relates to the presentation
of accounts and the laying before Parliament
of a statement of all losses incurred under
the system.
I now propose to deal with the second part
of the Bill very shortly.
Clause 10 allows for the countersignature of warrants for Treasury Bills by
a Principal Officer in the Comptroller and
Auditor-General's Department. Under the
law as it stands no provision is made for a
substitute in the case of illness or absence
of the Comptroller. The section also amends
the Clause of the Treasury Bills Act, 1877,
in its application to Northern Ireland, in the
sense of authorising the Ministry of Finance
instead of the Exchequer Bank to prepare
Treasury Bills. The actual practice in
Northern Ireland differs from that in
England where the Treasury Bills are prepared by the Bank of England.
Clause 11 (1) The alteration in the date of
presentation of the Consolidated Fund
'Account is made so that it may coincide with
that for the annual Appropriation Accounts.
As most of the information has already
appeared in the Public Income and Expenditure Account published each June, no
inconvenience will be caused to Members of
Parliament or the public.
Clause 11 (2) amends the Exchequer and
Audit Act of 1921 by giving the Comptroller
and Auditor-General discretion in the matter
of the class of audit he shall carry out. As
the Northern Ireland Act stands at present,
his audit must be a detailed audit including
a full arithmetical check, and he can only
be absolved from it in the case of any expenditure if the Ministry of Finance lay a
Minute before Parliament empowering him
to a apply a test check. That was the
British system, but it was altered in 1921
so as to provide for a test check being the
Rule, and a full check is only required if
the Treasury ask for it. The effect of this
provision will be to give the Comptroller
and Auditor-General powers identical to
those which are possessed by the Imperial
Comptroller and Auditor-General. The
Ministry of Finance is satisfied that this
change should now be made, and in any case
the Public Accounts Committee expressed
their views in its favour in May last.
Clause 12 provides for the payment into
the Church Temporalities Sinking Fund of

(that is, Tithe Rentcharges, Perpetuity Rents, &c.); and
(b) redemptions of terminable Church
Revenue (that is, Tithe and Land
Annuities)
with a view to the provision of an income in perpetuity from the proceeds of
these sales of capital.
It is obvious that sales and redemptions by
extinguishing Church Temporalities Revenue
would, if not counteracted by transfer of the
capital to the Sinking Fund. have the effect
of decreasing the annual Sinking Fund provision. The Redemption payments have, in
fact, been credited to the Sinking Fund and
this provision is required to regularise the
'proceeding.
Clause 13 provides (a) for an increase from
£31.000 to £34,500 as the amount of the Grant
in Aid to Queen's University authorised by
the Exchequer and Financial Provisions Act,
1924. in respect of the Agricultural Faculty
Buildings at present in course of erection.
The original estimate, on which the statutory
provision of £31,000 was based, was made at
an early stage in the arrangements when
accurate estimating was difficult, and it has
since been found that the total cost of the
'work, which provides only for the minimum
accommodation necessary, will probably
reach £46,000 instead of £42,000. Both
'Government and the University are contributing proportionately to this increased
cost:
(b) for amending the Exchequer and
Financial Provisions Act of 1924, in relation

I now come to Clause 14. This section has
been inserted following representations made
by the Comptroller and Auditor-General to
the effect that statutory authority is necessary
to cover an economical arrangement made by
the Minister of Finance whereby money is
borrowed temporarily by means of an overdraft at the Exchequer Bank. The Comptroller and Auditor-General, while satisfied
that the practice of borrowing by overdraft
is sound and ought not to be disturbed, has
pointed out that the existing law does not
cover this method of borrowing, because
such overdrafts are not temporary borrowings in a technical sense, in that moneys are
not actually credited to the Exchequer by
the Bank. This does not accord with the
provisions of the Appropriation Acts whereby
all borrowings, whether by Treasury Bills or
otherwise, must be paid into the Exchequer.
The Ministry is advised that there is substance in the point raised by the Comptroller
and Auditor-General, and this, the earliest
opportunity, is taken to obtain authority for
this method of borrowing. I should indicate
that though special statutory power has to be
obtained for this purpose, the overdraft must,
for all statutory purposes, be treated as a
normal borrowing; it cannot be utilised for
the purpose of raising money beyond the
amounts authorised by Statute.

grateful for the

am
I have only now to add a few sentences by
way of summary. We are proposing by our
arrangements to test the credit of Ulster in
the financial centre of the world, and I have
a feeling that this subject opens up a fresh
chapter in the autonomous life of the Province. When we entered on our new career,
the British Government agreed to guarantee
our financial commitments to the extent of
£3,500,000, and I daresay they would have
guaranteed even a larger sum had we required it. We have only utilised a portion
of this guarantee for our Ulster Saving
Certificates. I think it is likely, had we so
desired it, that the Treasury would have
agreed to give its guarantee for the present
public issue.
But I felt that we had fully emerged from
our infantile stage, and had proved our
capacity for Government.
Mr. DEVLIN: No, no.
Mr. POLLOCK: During our career no part
of our policy-of the Government's policyhas really been seriously criticised at any
time, and I believed that the time had
arrived when we were able to stand upon our
own character and reputation.
The issue, therefore, will be made pledging
the credit of the Ulster people, and will form
a security in which a trustee in any part of
the Kingdom can invest his funds.
A few days ago, when I submited the
Money Resolution which preceded the introduction of this Rill, the hon. Member
opposite asked me a very pertinent question,
and one which was justified. As I interpreted the question of the hon. Member, he
inquired whether we would be able to borrow
on as good terms as the British Government
in order that we might be able to lend local
authorities on as favourable terms as
formerly. I could not pretend to the role
of prophet, but I replied that we expected to
come within measurable distance of the
terms secured for British issues.
We must remember in this connection that
British credit is world-established, and is
indeed world-embracing. It has become
almost a synonym for security. Its reputation has penetrated to the remotest corners
of the earth, and in this penetration Ulstermen have fully taken their part.
We claim also that Ulster is a part of
the Kingdom, indissolubly linked to it by
ties stronger than iron bands.
Half a
century ago Mr. Gladstone stated that it
would pass the wit of man to devise any
scheme which would disentangle the cords
which bound Great Britain and Ireland, and
the further we Ulster people go in our
separate career we discover the literal truth
of this aphorism. Therefore, as a Province,

has been introduced in an excellent speech
by the Minister of Labour. In the debate
which followed that speech some very strange
things have happened in this House. Practically all the speeches delivered have been
in criticism of the Bill. Members on the

to place on industry, but because the
Measure happens to have been introduced
by the Minister of Labour in the Northern
Parliament they are going to support it. I
think the most surprising thing of all has
been the statement that it is because the
Minister of Labour has said that it was
either this Bill or nothing that other hon.
Members of this House are going to support
it.
It has been made clear in the speech of the
Minister of Labour in this House that the
intention of the Tory Party is to do away
with pensions and substitute insurance. In
the speech of the Minister yesterday he made
that quite clear. I think that those Members of the House who have taken the trouble
to read the Bill will be bound to admit that
it deliberately sets out to take away the
present basis of Old Age Pensions and to
substitute an insurance scheme. One hon.
Member in the course of his speech stated
that this inability of the State in Ireland to
deal with widows and orphans was a stigma

Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester), when

in Northern Ireland are going to follow the
example of Great Britain, the only country
in the world that has made a Widows'
Pension scheme or a Mothers' Pension scheme
a contributory scheme. New Zealand in 1912,
Denmark in 1914, 40 States and 2 Territories
in the United States of America, 5 out of 9
Canadian Provinces, Mothers' Pensions in
the Union of South Africa, 4 out of 5 States

in Australia-all these places have non-contributory widows' and mothers' pensions.

There is another thing that might be inserted in the Bill to the advantage of a
certain section of the community. You will
remember that some years ago in the Imperial House the pension age for blind people
was reduced to fifty at the instance of Mr.

to reduce the age to forty-five in regard to

Much display has been made from the
opposite side, and even from this side, of
the fact that this contribution by employers
is going to put a heavier tax on industry.
It seems to me that the workers, being the
people who produce things, have got to pay
all the time. We could argue about that
I know.
Mr. ANDREWS: About most things.
Mr. KYLE: About most things, but it
seems to me that as the general taxpayer

our country to live, and seeing that these

it should be held that the workers should
have to pay for their pensions. The inadequacy of the amount that has been proposed has been stressed by the hon. Member
for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) and I think
rightly. During the war when the War Office
issued their pensions lists it was laid down
that a widow should receive a pension of
20s per week; if that widow was over forty
she was to receive a pension of 26s 8d per
week; for every orphaned child there was a
pension of 128 per week. It seems to me, and
particularly bearing in mind what the
Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews) said in
introducing this Measure, that there may
be an attempt being made at the present.
time to reduce the pensions that were given
to the widows and orphans of the men who
fell in the Great War.
Mr. ANDREWS: May I interrupt the
hon. Member to say that I really did not
say that?

generous scale. I am sorry if I am misquoting him.
Mr. ANDREWS: You are right now.
Mr. KYLE: The pensions were given on a

to imply does it not?-that when he is
offering a widow's pension of 10s, and saying

pension of 20s might be reduced, and then
it would not be a generous pension.

Mr. ANDREWS: I did not say 'too
generous."
Mr. KYLE: I did not say you did. I
said you said it was a generous pension.
I am not accusing the Minister of Labour
of wanting to reduce these war pensions. I

of the British Government, which our
