the Minister of Labour with a sinceritywhether it was a feigned sincerity or not I
cannot say, but he looked over with a sincerity-and he wanted the Minister of Labour
to ask industry to stop paying contributions.
Let there be no more contributions paid, he
said, on the lines suggested by the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin), in order
that industry may get a fillip and get on its
feet. Was he sincere? Does he mean to suggest to this House that we should stop asking
industry to contribute, stop asking the employed contributor to contribute, and that
we should stop paying benefit? We can only
pay out benefit if we receive contributions.
The Minister of Labour made it perfectly
clear that we are not living in a land flowing
with milk and honey, that there was no tap
he could turn on that would pour gold into
the coffers of the Government.
Mr. KYLE: Then it is an Insurance Bill.
Mr. GORDON: It is an Insurance Bill,
and we have admitted that it is an Insurance
Bill.
Mr. KYLE: And not a Pensions Bill at all.
Mr. GORDON: It is a Pensions Bill, but
it is on a contributory basis. However, I
pass from that suggestion. I do not think
my hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle) was sincere when
he suggested that we should stop paying contributions, because when he stated that the
'workers were the producers of all things—
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Mr. GORDON: If he meant that, if he
'were sincere why did he speak as if the
workers were the producers of all things and
demand that the workers should receive the
full fruits of their labours-
Mr. KYLE: Give us that and we will be
Fatisfied.
Mr. GORDON: And why then did the hon.
Gentleman (Mr. William McMullen) who
opened the debate say "Do not crush industry?" He said that an impost in the shape
of an increased contribution would crush in-
'dustry. Does he mean to tell this House,
does he mean to suggest that if an employer
(who employs six men, say, is called upon to
pay an increased contribution of 1s per week
for those six men it will crush that industry?
My hon. Friend (Mr. William McMullen)
opened his speech by entering the domain
of economics. I am not going to contend with
him, but it is plain to an average man like
myself, who would not attempt to enter into
the domain of Socialistic economics in the
manner in which the hon. Member entered.
that an industry that is able to employ six
men and yet cannot pay an impost of 1s per
'week is in a peculiar position.
I think I have gone fairly widely over the
various arguments that have been put forward by hon. Members of this House. Some
have been most complimentary to my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Labour, and
Come have criticised with a blandness that has
amazed me, but at the same time have expressed their approval of the provisions of the
Bill and are determined to give all the help
they possibly can in order that the Bill may
be carried to a successful issue. I do not
think I need refer to anything that has been
said by the hon. Member from the East where
all the wisdom comes from.
Mr. BEATTIE: The wise men.
Mr. GORDON: Yes, the wise men from the
East. I make no reference to what he said.
If I did I would place him in an exceedingly
awkward position with respect to his
colleagues. I am not going to do it, but I
will say one thing. One of his colleagues.
the Member for West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen) suggested that this is an impost
on industry, and said we were going to
destroy industry. What does the Leader of
the Opposition (Mr. Kyle) say? He says "Stop
asking the workpeople to pay arrears for a
period of time until industry gets on its
feet." When you stop asking contributions
it means you stop giving benefits to the people.
The hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Beattie) said quite different. I know these
hon. Members will be quite amazed when they
read their speeches and compare one with
the other. They will compare notes and be
more anxious in the future to get together
before coming to discuss and criticise a Bill
of this character. The Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Beattie) said industry should
give a pension to the soldier of industry.
Did he mean that industry should give a
pension to the soldier of industry?
Mr. BEATTIE: I said that the State was
under an obligation to give a pension to the
soldier of industry.

Seed Potatoes Supply Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of this
Bill is to ratify arrangements which were
entered into by the Minister of Finance, the
Minister of Commerce and myself with certain Boards of Guardians, with the object of
supplying seed potatoes to small farmers and
labourers occupying a small portion of
ground who would otherwise, owing to the
bad season, have been unable to get seed.
Hon. Members will remember what a bad
season 1924 was. The result was that seed in
certain districts, particularly in County Fermanagh, was extremely scarce, and unless
something was done by the Government for
these farmers and small occupiers they
would have had the greatest possible difficulty in getting seed, and possibly in some
cases they could not have got any, but in any
case they could not have got the proper
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Mr. Beattie.
variety. Steps were taken by the Government to invite the co-operation of Boards of
Guardians, and as a result the Boards of
Guardians of Enniskillen and Irvinestown
were satisfied as to the need for a scheme of
this character and offered to co-operate with
the Government. In these cases the Boards
of Guardians invited applications from small
farmers who held land not exceeding £15
valuation and labourers occupying a small
portion of ground. The farmer received up
to 5 cwt, and the labourer 2 cwt. .
The Minister of Agriculture purchased the
seed and distributed it. The total cost to the
Government was £10 a ton, and the price
charged by the Government to the farmer
'was £7 a ton. The money is recovered from
the county councils and they in turn levy a
rate on the applicants. The rate is spread
ver a period of two years, 1926-1927. The
total cost to the Government is £3 a ton. The
amount distributed in the case of Enniskillen
was 80 tons and in the case of Irvinestown
69 tons. I am glad to say the scheme turned
out a great success, and from the reports I
have received I believe the potato crop all
over the County Fermanagh this season is
going to be very satisfactory.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I only rise to ask a
question from the right hon. Gentleman in

This Bill only deals with what happened in

COST OF GOVERNMENT PUBLICATIONS.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Finance if he can state the actual cost of
Government publications issued during the
preceding year to local authorities in the Six
Counties.
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): On behalf of
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) I have
been asked to answer this question. It
would require considerable research to obtain any reliable estimate of the actual cost
of publications issued by the various Government Departments to Local Authorities as
distinct from the cost of free issues in
general.
I am satisfied, however, that the amount
involved would be in excess of £300, although
the total cost of all Government publications issued gratuitously during last year
exceeded £950.
BRITISH EMPIRE UNION CARNIVAL.
2. Mr. GYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether the Committee of the British
Empire Union Carnival recently applied for
an cocasional licence to sell wines, spirits and
beer for consumption in the carnival
grounds; whether the licence was refused,
and if so on what grounds was the refusal
based.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): An occasional licence as indicated was applied for, but its grant was not
recommended.
Occasional licences are only granted when
it is considered, as laid down by the Statute
(25 and 26 Vic., cap. 22) "conducive to public
convenience, comfort and order" to do so. In
this case there were no fewer than nine
licensed houses in the immediate vicinity of
the Old Potato Market where the carnival
was held.
In these circumstances it did not appear
that the statutory conditions geverning the
grant of licences were fulfilled, and the issue
of a licence could not therefore be recommended.
Mr. GYLE: Arising out of that answer
would the Minister say was there any influence brought to bear on him or his Department through any Member of this House o
through any member of the licensed trade?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Certainly not.
Mr. DEVLIN: Are you sure?

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session to make provision for pensions for widows, orphans, and persons between the ages of sixty-five and seventy,
and for the payment of contributions in

is expedient that there shall be paid out
of moneys provided by Parliament-
(a) into the Ministry of Finance Pensions Account as constituted by the said

day of March, nineteen hundred and
twenty-seven, and for each of the next
nine succeeding years, such sum not
exceeding one hundred and forty-five
thousand pounds, as the Ministry of
Finance may for each of the said years
determine, having regard to the assets
and liabilities of the said account and of
the Pensions Account (Northern Ireland), and thereafter such sums as
Parliament may hereafter determine;

under the Old Age Pensions Acts, 1908
to 1924, by virtue of the said Act;

said Act."-(Mr. Barbour.)

within the province of hon, Members of the

The CHAIRMAN: The point of order
which the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Devlin)
raises is not related to the Resolution strictly
speaking, but it is obviously a point of some
substance, and it is desirable that the procedure should be clear in respect of it. It is
not within the competence of a private Member to move Amendments which have the
effect of increasing the public charge. That
is the exact rule upon the matter. Of course,
I could not rule upon a hypothetical Amendment. I should have to look at the precise
terms of any Amendment before I gave a
definite ruling in respect of it.
Mr. DEVLIN: As this raises a very important point I would like further to press

The CHAIRMAN. What I hope I
have made clear, and what I desire to
make clear is that the specific ground upon
which the decision must repose is whether

The CHAIRMAN: When we reach a
specific Amendment put forward on the Committee Stage of the Bill I will look at that
particular Amendment in the light of the

Mr. BARBOUR: My right hon. Friend
(Mr. Pollock) yesterday made a comprehensive statement on the various provisions
of the important Measure entitled the
Widows, Orphans and Old-Age Contributory Pensions Bill. He touched on certain of the financial aspects, and in view of
this it is only necessary for me at the present time to make a very short statement
on this Money Resolution. The Resolution as usual provides the requisite
authority for charging upon Votes the
additional expenditure to be met by the State
under the Scheme, and it is divided into
three parts.
The first provides for the payment
annually into the Ministry of Finance
Pensions Account to be set up under Clause
11 (2) of the Act of a sum of £145,000 or
such lesser sum as the Ministry of Finance
may annually determine in each of the ten
years commencing on 1st April, 1926, to be
sufficient, having regard to the state of that
account and of the Pensions Account (N.I.)
from time to time. The maximum figure of
£145,000 represents the equated annual
charge in respect of the total cost of the
scheme for the ten-year period as nearly
as this can be estimated; according to the
calculations there is actually a surplus of
contributions from employers and employees
on the first three years after which the
Pensions after age 65 come into operation,
and, consequently, the expenditure rises.
This scheme of equalising payments over the
ten-vear period follows the practice in Great
Britain in the similar Act recently passed,
their corresponding figure being the fixed
annual payment of four million pounds.
After the ten-year period has expired, it
is left open for Parliament to re-assess the
contribution
Government
required from
sources to render the scheme solvent. The
expenditure in each year will depend
naturally on the number of widows and
orphans and
the number of old-age
pensioners who benefit from the scheme. It
is estimated that the peak of the net expenditure will be in 1945-46, after which date
the contributions are expected to increase at
a slightly greater rate than the benefits on
account of the population becoming more
industrial.
The second part of the Resolution covers
the expenditure on
the Old Age Pensions
which become payable to insured persons
over 70 as from 1st July, 1926, by virtue of
this Bill. Provision for this is not included
in the maximum sum of £145,000 to which I
have referred, but will be met from an Old-
Age Pensions Vote in the ordinary way. It

Now, after all the experience we have had

We need not continue either luridly to paint

widow who has lost the breadwinner as well
as the father of the family, or the plight

for being placed there without the slightest
hope or chance for the future. All these

these social reforms is not only to give some
relief but to lift from the recipients the
humiliation of poor-law relief, and I do not
think that 10s for a widow, 5s for the first
child, and 3s for the other children is ample.
On the contrary, I believe that these widows
and children will while getting the State

guardians. In my opinion no measure can
justify itself when dealing with a problem of
this sort unless it deals with it in such a
way as to lift this humiliation, from these
people and at the same time meet the adequate domestic necessities of the situation.

proposed:
Mr. BARBOUR: During the course of the
discussion on the Old Age Pensions Estimate
in May last, I think it was apparent that
the question of modifying the disability imposed under the law as it stands on people
who have saved a moderate sum in respect
of old age was one which was engaging
seriously the minds of honourable Members
of all parties in the House. The difficulty
in the way of granting such a concession is,
of course, a financial one, but the Government have decided to undertake the responsibility of shouldering the additional burden
on their finances, though it is impossible to
do so in the current financial year. I now
rise to move the Second Reading of this Bill,
the main provision of which will take effect
as from 1st April, 1926.
As honourable Members are aware, on the
existing basis of calculation of means for the
purpose of determining whether an Old Age
Pension is payable, all means, whether from
carnings or savings or otherwise, are taken
into account. The main provision of the
Bill (Section 1 (1)) which follows the wording of the main Clause in the Old Age Pensions Act enacted by the Imperial Parlianent last year, provides that the existing
basis of calculation of means shall be continued, but that it shall be made subject
to the proviso that means derived from any
source other than earnings shall be excluded
from calculation in so far as they do not
exceed 15s a week in the case of a single person or 30s a week in the case of a married
couple. If honourable Members will refer to
the examples given in the explanatory memorandum which has been circulated, they will
appreciate the full purport of the proposal.
To show how amply the Bill meets the grievance which it is designed to remedy, I need
only draw attention to the case mentioned in
example (d) in the appendix to the memorandum. Here, a married couple with a joint
income of £2 10s 0d a week will be entitled
to draw pension at the full rate amounting
to £1 a week if both are pensioners; that is
of course the extreme case. The Bill gives
no additional inducement to old people to
continue in employment after they have
reached the age of seventy. On the contrary,
it is a direct encouragement to be thrifty
during the earlier years of life, so that later
there may be no necessity for them to work.
In introducing this Measure, the Government have to take into cognisance our close
proximity to the Free State and that the
effect of these proposals will be to accentuate
still further and to a substantial degree, the
difference between the conditions under
which Old Age Pensions are granted her
and in the Free State. The Free State Ol
Age Pensions Act of last year had alread
made the pension conditions there les
favourable than ours, by reducing the max
mum rate of pension to 9s a week. Th
effect of this reduction in increasing th
total number of pensioners in Norther
Ireland was not, however, very great. Bu
we are now concerned not merely with th
difference of a shilling per week in the per
sion rates; the memorandum makes it clea
that in many cases the effect of the Bill wil
be to entitle persons to pensions at the ful
rate of 10s per week who previously had no
been entitled to a pension at all, or only t
pension at reduced rates. There wil
consequently be a great temptation to per
sons resident in the Free State to migrate t
Northern Ireland merely for the purpose o
taking advantage of the more generous con
ditions here.
The existing law, I may remind hon. Mem
bers, prescribes a period of twelve years
residence in the United Kingdom afte
attaining the age of fifty as an essentia
qualification for pension in the case o
British-born British subjects, and the Orde
in Council to which the Schedule to this Bi
refers, provides further that residence i
Southern Ireland before the establishment o
the Irish Free State may be counted as res
dence in the United Kingdom for thi
purpose. As the law now stands, therefore
many persons in the Free State could com
to Northern Ireland and obtain a pensio
under the new conditions without havin
previously resided in Northern Ireland a
all. I need hardly say the additiona
financial burden resulting from this immi
gration might be very considerable. Th
effect of the proviso to Section 1 (1), togethe
with the Schedule, is that persons coming
here from the Free State after the 7t
instant the date of the introduction of the
Bill-will not be entitled to the benefit of th
new provisions until they have completed
full twelve years' residence, in whic
residence in Southern Ireland will not b
taken into consideration, that is, as regard
pensions on the new basis, they will be
exactly the same position as persons coming
from any of the Dominions. They will still
however, be allowed to count pre-Free Stat
residence in Southern Ireland for the
purpose of obtaining pensions under the old
conditions.

COAL INDUSTRY IN SIX COUNTIES.
2. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Commerce what steps, if any, have been
taken to carry out the recommendations contained in pages 73 and 74 of the Report of
the Commission on the Natural and Industrial Resources of Northern Ireland to make
further borings for the purpose of locating
additional seams of coal in the Six Counties.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): The Commission to which the hon.
Member refers have presented several Reports embodying recommendations involving
a considerable outlay of public money. As
he will readily appreciate, such recommendations can only be considered in the light
of existing commitments and financial resources available. In view of these facts,
the Government have not yet made any de
cision upon the recommendations referred to
in the question, but I can assure the honourable Member that these recommendations will
receive the earnest consideration of the
Government at the earliest opportune
moment.
Mr. DEVLIN: Can the right hon. Gentleman give us any information as to the position of the new industry at Coalisland?
Mr. BARBOUR: I think that hardly
arises out of this question.
POST OFFICE APPOINTMENTS.
3. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Commerce whether it is a fact
that all appointments as postmasters, subpostmasters, supervisors, and medical officers
in the Post Office in Northern Ireland are
submitted to his Department for approval
before being finally ratified by the Post Office
authorities, and can he state what is the ob
ject of this procedure and by whose authority it was introduced.
Mr. BARBOUR: By arrangement with the
Post Office authorities certain appointments
in the postal service are notified in advance
to my Ministry. The object of such action
is that steps may be taken to ensure that persons appointed to responsible positions in the
postal service are of unquestionable loyalty
to the established constitution of Northern
Treland.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Arising out
of that answer I should like to inquire if
any cases have occurred in which recommendations by the Postal Authorities were rejected by the right hon. Gentleman's Department, and I would also like to know if recommended candidates were deprived of
promotion?
Mr. BARBOUR: Of course, the hon.
Member will be aware that the postal service
Oral Answers.

is a reserved service, and, consequently,
whether my Ministry might or might not influence any appointments taking place in
Northern Ireland would not interfere with

SUMMER DAY MAIL SERVICE.
4. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Commerce whether he is aware
that the summer day mail service to and
from Great Britain and Northern Ireland
via Larne and Stranraer ceased on Saturday,
the 3rd inst.; whether it is a fact that the
Post Office authorities, prior to the cessation
of the service, submitted proposals to his department for a continuance of similar
facilities by the Holyhead route, and that the
offer was rejected, and if so will he give the
reason; whether he is aware that correspondence now posted in London after 6-15 p.m.
for provincial towns in Northern Ireland
suffers from 12 to 18 hours' delay in delivery
by being held over for dispatch by the
Ardrossan route; and in view of the present
inadequate postal facilities, whether he will
now reconsider his rejection of the Post Office
proposals if made.
Mr. BARBOUR: The reply to the first part
of the question is in the affirmative. In regard to the second part, it is the fact that,
prior to the cessation of the summer day service between Larne and Stranraer, the Post
Office Authorities submitted for my views a
proposal to utilise the Holyhead route for
the conveyance of mails intended for the
eastern portion of Northern Ireland and
posted in London too late for conveyance by
the night mail train to Stranraer. This proposal, if carried into effect, would, as the hon.
Member implies, enable earlier deliveries to
be made in certain districts. Before expressing an opinion on it, however, I considered
it desirable to ascertain the views of the
several Chambers of Commerce in the areas
affected. Replies from all the Chambers
have not yet been received. As the hon.
Member will have gathered from what I have
said, the proposed changes are still under
consideration, and he is, therefore, incorrect
in assuming that I have rejected the Post
Office proposal.
ENTERTAINMENT TAX IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
5. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Finance when he proposes to readjust the
Entertainment Tax in Northern Ireland, in
order to make it uniform with the impost in
Great Britain.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I regret to have to inform the hon.
Member that owing to the heavy additional
expenditure which will result from the
social legislation now before the House, I
cannot foresee any immediate possibility of
a reduction in taxation. I have undertaken,
however, that if and when a reduction can
be made the claims of the amusement
caterers will receive my first consideration.
Mr. DEVLIN: Did not the right hon.
Gentleman on several occasions give a
promise to the House that in the readjustment of the financial relations between
Northern Ireland and the Imperial Authority he would place Northern Ireland in the
same position as England in this matter?
Mr. POLLOCK: No, I did not give any
such undertaking as my hon. Friend
suggests. What I believe I did say was that
in view of the fact that several collateral
questions were being discussed at the time
upon the result of which the Government
arrangements would be made, I hoped to be
able to promote legislation dealing with oldage pensions, the entertainment tax, and
other matters.
Mr. DEVLIN: Do I understand that the
Northern Government have departed from
the theory laid down universally and constantly announced in this House and that concessions made by the British authorities in
England are not to be made in Northern
Ireland? Do I understand that is the new
policy of the Government?
Oral Answers.

Mr. POLLOCK: There is not any new
policy. We are not bound to follow literally
the taxation policy of Great Britain, and in
this particular case it was found necessary
to continue the arrangement now in existence, because of the considerable expenditure
arising from the development of social questions, which I am glad to say have had the
blessing of my hon. Friend.
Mr. DEVLIN: I beg to give the right hon.
Gentleman notice in view of his speeches and
departure from the Government's declared
policy in this matter that I will raise this
question at the first opportunity.
STRABANE POST OFFICE-NEW
PREMISES.
6. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Finance whether any department
under his control has been consulted in
connection with the purchase of new premises for the Post Office in Strabane, and,
if so, whether he can say what is the reason
for the delay in completing the transaction.
Mr. POLLOCK: As the hon. Member is
aware, the Post Office is a Reserved Service.
I am, however, in a position to inform him
that my Ministry, in its capacity as agent
for the Imperial Office of Works, has from
time to time been consulted by that Department as to the suitability for Post Office
purposes of various building sites in Strabane, and very recently on the question of
premises which is at present under consideration. The hon. Member will appreciate
that the final decision in this matter will
rest with the Imperial Government.
HOUSING ACTS SUBSIDY-PERIOD FOR

of houses which will qualify for subsidy
under the Housing Acts, and a Bill with
this object will be brought before Parliament in due course.
Mr. KYLE: Would the Minister say why
he refused to accept an Amendment from
these benches to this very effect?

Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
"That it is expedient in connection with
pensions payable to persons to whom the
Old Age Pensions Acts, 1908 to 1919, apply,
to authorise the provision out of moneys
provided by Parliament of such further
sums as will become payable as a consequence of providing by any Act of the
present Session that, for the purpose of determining the weekly rate of pension to
which a person is entitled, there shall, subject to the provisions of any such Act, be
deducted from his means as calculated
under the said Acts such part, if any, of
the means, but not exceeding in any case
thirty-nine pounds, as is derived from any

Mr. BARBOUR: In submitting this Resolution for the approval of the House, I think
it is my duty to make it clear, lest there may
be any misapprehension on the point, that
the figure of £143,000 mentioned in the explanatory Memorandum is the estimated
immediate addition to the annual cost of
old-age pensions in consequence of the ȧdoption of this Measure. This figure takes no
cognisance of the increases in the number
of old-age pensions which can be anticipated
in the next thirty or forty years arising from
the natural decrease in the death rate.
Hon. Members will appreciate that since no
census has been taken in Northern Ireland
since 1911, it is a matter of considerable difficulty to make estimates of population on
which to calculate the additional cost involved by the modification of the means condition, and it will be remembered that when
this matter was discussed in the House last
session, it was estimated that the additional
cost might ultimately amount to £350,000 per
annum. The whole question has, however,
recently been investigated afresh by the
Government Actuary in connection with this
Bill and the Contributory Pensions Scheme.
There are at present 41,000 old-age pensioners in Northern Ireland, of whom 3,500
draw pensions at less than the maximum rate
of 10s per week. The total present cost of pensions alone, exclusive of the cost of administration, is £1,047,000, and it is now estimated
that after making allowance for persons who
will still be disqualified on the ground of
means for pensions under the Old Age Pensions Acts, approximately 5,500 persons will
become entitled to pensions in the next
financial year as a result of the operation of
this Bill, while most of the existing pensioners at less than the maximum rate of 10s
will now become entitled to pensions at the
maximum rate. That is the immediate result which is anticipated. The total cost on
this account in the year 1926-7 is not expected to exceed the figure of £143,000 mentioned in the Memorandum, but the Government is advised that, having regard to the

The CHAIRMAN: The Committee will
observe that there is a great variety of
Amendments to this Bill upon the Order
Paper. Some of them are bound up in each
other; some of them are alternative proposals, and obviously the only way in which
we can disentangle these will be by sticking
strictly to the rule of debate and by discussing one specific Amendment at one time, and
no other. I am sure the Committee will
forgive me for offering that suggestion in view
of the difficulties which this particular Bill
presents and which they will see develop
as we get on.
CLAUSE 1. (Contributory Pensions for
Widows, Orphans, and Persons between the
Ages of 65 and 70).
(1) Subject to the provisions of this Act
relating to the payment of contributions
(including payments out of moneys provided by Parliament) and otherwise,
pensions shall be payable as follows, that
is to say-
(a) to the widow of an insured man a
pension at the rate of ten shillings per
week, with an additional allowance in
respect of children while under the age
hereinafter specified, at the rate of five
shillings per week for the eldest or only
such child, and three shillings per week
for each other such child (in this Act
called a "widow's pension");
(b) in respect of the orphan children
while under the age hereinafter specified
of an insured man or of an insured widow,
a pension at the rate of seven shillings
and sixpence per week for each such child
(in this Act called an "orphan's pension");
(c) to an insured man or an insured
woman who has attained the age of sixtyfive but has not attained the age of
seventy, and to the wife of an insured
man who has attained the age of sixtyfive (such wife having attained the age
of sixty-five but not having attained the
age of seventy) a pension at the rate of
ten shillings per week (in this Act called
an "old age pension").
(2) The specified age in relation to any
child shall be the age of fourteen or the
age not exceeding sixteen up to which the
child remains under full-time instructioa
in a day school.
(3) By way of contribution towards the
cost of carrying this Act into effect ther
shall be paid such contributions as are
hereinafter in this Act provided.
Mr. KYLE: I beg to move in Clause 1, page
1, line 7, to leave out "the payment of contributions" ("relating to the payment of
contributions (including payments out of
moneys provided by Parliament)").
In moving this Amendment I want to
point out to the Committee that in Northern
Ireland we are adopting the principle laid
down in Britain. Now Great Britain is the
only country in the world that has adopted
a scheme of widows' or mothers' pensions and
made that scheme a contributory one. In
New Zealand in 1912 a pension scheme was
brought into being which was a non-contributory one. In Denmark in January, 1914, a
non-contributory scheme was brought into
being in that country.
In forty States and two territories in the
United States of America there are noncontributory schemes, and I think the whole
movement is in favour of non-contributory
widows' and mothers' pensions. We owe a
lot to Judge Neil, of the United States. He
visited Belfast in 1912 and in the Co-operative
Hall gave us an outline of the proposals in
operation at that time in the United States
of America. Subsequent to that he went to
London and had a committee room provided
for him in which to meet Members of both
the House of Lords and the House of Commons, and as a result of that visit and that
outline of a mothers' pension scheme which
he had got put into force in so many States
in America, a great volume of opinion was
created in Great Britain and also in
Belfast to have non-contributory widows'
pensions brought into being. As I said, we
owe a tremendous lot to Judge Neil, of the
United States of America, for his advocacy
of this cause.

In five out of the nine Canadian Provinces
there are non-contributory schemes. In the
Union of South Africa they have got a
scheme of mothers' pensions which is noncontributory. In four out of the five States
in Australia there are non-contributory
schemes. Therefore, as I said the other
day, we are taking a step in the wrong direction by having this widows'. orphans' and
old age pensions scheme on a contributory
basis. I think I am stating something that
should meet with the approval of every Member of this Committee. I want, Sir, to obey
strictly your ruling in regard to these
Amendments because I can quite see that if
once we get off the exact terms of the
Amendment we may land anywhere.
In this year of grace, 1925, the State itself
should be able to provide pensions on a noncontributory basis for the widows and
orphans of the men who have fallen in the
battle of industry. Just as pensions are noncontributory so far as soldiers and sailors
(and airmen are concerned so ought these
'widows to receive their pensions on a noncontributory basis. Just as pensions have not
to be paid for by ex-Cabinet Ministers or by
very important people in the State so, in
fact, much more, I think, the widows of the
veterans of industry, the widows of the men
who have fallen in the battle of industry,
should also be provided for by the State. It
is a very important matter, indeed, that
this Bill when it is an Act should be on a
non-contributory basis because of the fact
that during the advocacy of non-contributory
widows' pensions we have always made it a
point that these widows should be taken out
of industry in order that they might be able
to look after their homes and bring up their
children as healthy citizens by giving proper
attention to the matters that concern them.
That being the case, I think no words of mine
should be needed to impress upon the Committee the fact that, it is important and imperative that they should accept this Amendment that has been put down, that is, to
make this Measure a non-contributory
Measure instead of a contributory one.
Mr. DEVLIN: On the Second Reading I
assented to the principle of the Bill as proposed by the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Andrews) and I, therefore, committed myself
to the principle of a contributory' scheme,
but I think that the present may not be an
inopportune moment to point out that there
is only one justification for a contributory
scheme, and that is that the pensions should

giving a substantial contribution to the fund

are in favour of the Bill and who think
the only method by which this matter can be

I stated on the last occasion on which we

purposes of the pensions is to relieve those

10s is not ample for a widow and 5s is not

Gentleman, in view of the fact that he has
got some of his political opponents in this

ought to hold out some hope to those Members that while he will ask the workers and

called upon to make by this Measure the
grant ought to be of such a substantial character that it will meet the adequate demands
of the people whom it is intended to benefit.

However, this is an Amendment I am obliged to say that the Government cannot accept because the very foundation upon which
this Measure is built is a contributory system.
It is in practically all its provisions drafted
on parallel lines with Great Britain.
hon. Friend the Member for North Belfast
(Mr. Kyle) has referred to other countries
where there are systems of pensions which
non-contributory, but it is extraordinarily difficult to draw parallels between
countries in connection with social services,
and to isolate one social service and say because that country deals with it in a
particular way every country could do the
same thing. We spend a huge sum in connection with unemployment insurance. In
the United States, to which the hon. Member (Mr. Kyle) referred, they have no unare
Widows' Pensions Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Andrews]
employment insurance scheme such as we
have, and therefore what we here have got
to do, as I said on the Second Reading, is to
cut our coat according to our cloth.
As this Bill is drafted the contribution
which our Exchequer will be called upon to
pay will be £145,000 a year on the average
for the first ten years. We can, owing to our
financial arrangements with Great Britain,
recover the greater part of that from our
contribution, as we are quite entitled to, but
if we were to adopt the principle of non-contributory pensions instead of the charge
being £145,000 on the average, it would
amount to £630,000 a year, and we would
have to attempt to raise the other half
million out of our own resources, which we
cannot do. I feel that the contributory
system is not placing the burden upon industry which my hon. Friend seems to think
it will. I quoted figures to prove that in my
Second Reading speech, and I need not repeat those figures to-day. I will put it in
other words. The increased contributions
which employers will have to pay for their
male employees will be only 2d per week, and
the employee himself will only pay 2d; for
the female worker the employer is only
asked to pay 1d and the female worker herself 1d. That really amounts to less than
one half per cent. of the total wages paid by
the firms in which the workers are employed.
Again, to show how trifling the contributions really are I would remind the Committee that for the last 4 years I have been
engaged very frequently in connection with
labour negotiations where there was a
difference of opinion between workers and
employers as to what wages should be paid
and received. When these negotiations take
place it is almost invariably a question of
whether 2s, 3s, 4s, 5s, 6s, 7s, 8s, 9s, or 10s is
to be given or not. I never heard of negotiations of the kind where only a question
of a 1d or 2d was in dispute. Obviously it
would be absurd, and therefore I think I
am justified in arguing that really this 1d
and 2d would amount to such a small thing
that they are not worth considering in connection with a matter of this kind. The
important thing is that these small contributions which the employers and workers
are asked to pay will give better benefits to
the insured person than any ordinary
insurance company is able to give, because,
of course, of the State grant which is added.
Therefore, I do feel that this is a proper
system and, as I have already said, it is the
only system that can be adopted at the
present time. I would ask my hon. Friends
not to press this matter to a division, because if they do and if they were successful
undoubtedly the Bill would have to be withdrawn, and they alone would be depriving
our insured persons of these benefits. I am
sure they do not want to take up this
position, and I do appeal to them to join
with the Government in doing this great
thing for those in our community who require pensions.

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move in Clause 1,

age that we want this inserted here. We
want to be in the van of progress in the

view that we want "sixteen" inserted here
instead of "fourteen."

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I would
point out to the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Andrews) that there is a very important
principle involved in connection with this
Amendment. The right hon. Gentleman will
remember that last week I addressed a question to him as to the number of people who
are in industry at the present time at fourteen years of age. This has a very important
bearing on the unemployment problem. At
the present time there are a large number
of boys employed at fourteen years of age,
and in many cases they are cutting out male
members of the community from getting employment. From that point of view I would
ask the right hon. Gentleman to give his very
careful and serious consideration to this
proposal, because, if it is agreed to, it would
be a direct inducement to the parents to keep
these children at school until they are sixteen instead of fourteen. The children would
thus get more benefit from the education
provided for them and it would relieve the
market to a great extent, and give some of
the adults an opportunity of getting employment which they cannot get at the present
time. From that point of view the Amendment is exceptionally important, and I would
ask the right hon. Gentleman to give it very
careful consideration in view of the very
grave industrial problems connected with it.
Mr. ANDREWS: I fully appreciate the
arguments brought forward by the two hon.
Members (Mr. Kyle and Mr. William
McMullen), but they will appreciate that we
cannot in a Bill of this kind make it illegal

that age to accept employment. If they
will refer to Clause 1, sub-clause (2) they will
see it set out quite clearly that the age limit
is to be fourteen unless the child remains
full time at a day school. If the child does
that then the allowance to the widow will

Members' point is met.

I have already stated that I think this

and I cannot see why hon. Members were permitted in the British Parliament to move
Amendments increasing the amount of the
pensions while we are not permitted to do the

this matter and move these Amendments.

sions to
provisions as regards penwidows and orphans come

they were faced with this difficulty. They

iclaim, and so the Bill has been designed

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: The Amendment before the Committee deals with the
contributions of those engaged in agriculture,
and I bring it forward in the name of charity.
I think they are entitled to what we ask for
them. Men engaged in agriculture are, as
a rule, healthy men. They live an open air
life and there are not ordinarily so many
applying for benefit under the Health Insurance Acts as those engaged in other industries. We feel that the contributions paid
by those engaged in the agricultural industry under the Health Insurance Acts
would be quite sufficient to meet the demands
that would be made by these people under
this Bill. The Minister may, in this connection, give statistics that go to prove
that sickness is just as prevalent in the
country districts as in the urban districts,
and if he does, I would ask him would these
statistics apply to people engaged in the
agricultural industry alone; because in a
great many of our small rural towns where
the housing conditions are not good and the
sanitary conditions are not perfect there may
be a good deal of sickness and a higher rate
of mortality. We feel that if the statistics
were available they would prove the case I
make here, that agricultural labourers are
entitled to the benefit of this Bill without
paying any more contributions than they are
at present paying.
There is another point. I think that the
towns will have a slight advantage as compared with the country. Children who are
at school up to 16 years of age will receive
benefit under this Measure. It is more
likely that children in the towns will be
attending school up to 16 years than those
in the country. Therefore, I feel in this
respect that the towns will have an advantage under the Pensions Act. Furthermore,
we have people in the city and urban areas
marrying earlier in life than those in the
rural areas. I suppose that is to their credit
and they are probably to be commended for it.
There is more reason to believe that they
will be a bigger burden on the Pensions Bill
than those living in rural areas. I feel there
is a strong case made for special treatment
on behalf of the agricultural industry. The
Government should extend fair play and
abolish the contributions under this Bill so
far as the agricultural industry is concerned.
If they do not abolish them they should at
least give very liberal concessions in regard
to the contributions.
Mr. KYLE: I support this Amendment for
a different reason to that put forward by the
hon. Member. I support it because I
believe the agricultural labourer is not
sufficiently paid to enable him to pay the
contributions under the Bill. I think the
right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of
Labour, might very well consider this
Amendment. An agricultural labourer has
to pay sufficient when he pays under the
Health Insurance Acts, and those contributions should be enough to cover those under
the Pensions Scheme. It is from that point
of view that I desire to support the Amendment proposed by the hon. Member for
Antrim.
Mr. DEVLIN: I desire for both reasonsthe reasons stated by the hon. Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Kyle), and the hon.
Member for Antrim (Mr. George Henderson)
-to support this Amendment. I have
already an Amendment down, at least I have
given notice of an Amendment, if I am permitted-I do not know whether I will or not
-subsequently to propose it to the effect
that there be no contribution, either in
urban or rural districts, for four years, and
that no such demand be made upon industry,
whether it be agricultural or urban, until
business has stabilised itself in Northern
Ireland. I agree that the labourers are not
as well paid as they ought to be, and that
this burden ought not to be put upon them,
but I agree, too, that the farmers have passed
through a time of very great trial, have had
heavy burdens to bear in the shape of heavy
rating and bad seasons, that the burden is
one they are not very well able to bear. For
the reason that neither in our cities, in our
urban communities, nor in our agricultural
districts should this burden be put upon the
people while there is the present trade depression I shall support the Amendment.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I cannot let this
Amendment pass without saying a word or
two on the subject, because I was the first
Member to raise this question in the House
on the Second Reading of this Bill. Although
I do not-and I say so at once in order to
prevent any misunderstanding-intend to
vote against the Government on this Amendment, at the same time I would like to add
my appeal to those of hon. Members opposite
to the Government to consider the question
not only of the agricultural labourer but of
the small farmer in this connection. It is
true that the contribution which is demanded from the agricultural labourer and
from the farmer is the same as that which
will be paid by the industrial worker, but it
means an additional contribution of 4d in the
case of the farmer and the labourer from
what they are already paying, while to
the industrial worker it will only mean 2d.
-
-
I would like to speak for the small farmers especially the small struggling
farmers in the country of
whom
we have SO many, who are absolutely over-burdened by the rates they
have to pay, who in a great many instances
are quite as poor, or nearly as poor, as the
Widows' Pensions Bill-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mrs. Chichester]
labourers whom they employ, and who are in a
far worse condition financially than countless
numbers of the unemployed in the cities, who
are drawing the dole at the present moment.
I must speak on their behalf and ask the
Government if it would not be possible to
reconsider the case of the agricultural
labourer and farmer, and if this is not a
case where with advantage it might be
possible to a certain extent to provide for the
small farmers in the country who are
struggling against such enormous odds. I
would support what has been said by hon.
Members opposite, though, as I have already
stated. I do not intend to vote against the
Government.
Mr. ANDREWS: If the Government were
to agree to this Amendment it would simply
mean giving non-contributory pensions to
those engaged in farming.
Obviously that
.would be unfair to our industrial workers in
our cities. The hon. Member for Antrim
(Mr. George Henderson) has pointed out that
in his opinion this will put a serious burden
upon agriculture, on the farmers and on the
labourers. I really cannot think that it will.
Take a small farmer. such as those for whom
the hon. Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester)
has appealed; he is a man probably with ten
or twenty acres. It would be a very exceptional case where such a farmer employs any
labourers at all, and, therefore, he is not
really affected by this Measure. Take the
farmer, again, who has fifty or sixty acres;
he will probably be employing three men to
help him to do the work of that farm. If he
employs the members of his own family, and
if he pays them any financial remuneration
at all, he can insure them, and then the
members of his own family will receive the
benefits of the Bill. If, on the other hand,
he has to employ labour from, as it were,
outside his own family he will have to pay
the contributions for them, but it really will
not amount to anything of importance. If he
has the three labourers to whom I have
referred it will only amount to 1s
per week. I do not think any
farmer would like for the sake of 1s
per week to deny to his workers all those
advantages which this Bill gives to other
industrial workers, especially those in our
cities.
I think that really meets the point, but the
hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. George Henderson) has also referred to the fact that it
is rather unfair to the agricultural worker,
because he enjoys better health than the
worker in our cities. I very much question
if that is so. The returns of several of our
approved societies in this neighbourhood do
not point in that direction, but, if additional
proof is necessary, it is to be found in the
fact that in the Free State a Commission
was set up to investigate this and other
matters under the Health Insurance Acts
and to see if agricultural workers did not
get to the same extent the benefits which
those Acts brought within the reach of the
workers in the cities. The decision of that
Free State Commission was that, in Southern
Ireland at any rate, the workers in agricultural districts got fully the amount of benefits under the Insurance Acts that the
workers in the cities got, and for this
reason: Our city people suffer, as a
rule, from diseases that are of short duration. They suffer from pneumonia or a complaint of that kind where the illness lasts a
very short time. In the agricultural districts
a tremendous number of agricultural workers
suffer from complaints such as rheumatism,
bronchitis, asthma, and diseases of that kind.
where the illnesses extend for a very long
period. and where the sick person is not only
drawing sickness benefit but for a very long
period draws disablement benefit intermittently after the sickness benefit has been
stopped.
But, even if I admitted the hon. Member's
point, I would answer in reply to his criticism that. after all, if they do not draw so
much as regards sickness benefit and disablement benefit, the fact, I think, is undeniable
that, generally speaking, farm workers live
longer than the workers in our cities, and,
therefore, what they lose on the merry-gorounds they make up on the swing-boats, and
gain as regards the Old-Age Pensions provisions of the Bill. I think for these reasons,
and for many others which I could advance.
my hon. Friends would be justified in not
pressing the Amendment. I think it better
that this Amendment should not be agreed
to. because having contributory pensions for
our industrial workers in the city and noncontributory pensions for the workers in our
farming areas could not be justified.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: Would the
Minister give us an assurance that he will
reconsider the rates of contribution from
the agricultural industry?
Mr. ANDREWS: No; because that would
be preferential treatment, which I do not
think could be justified.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: We deserve
it.
Question put, "That those words be there
inserted."

have already settled that the Bill is to be on

ENGLISH MAILS IN SOUTH DERRY.
3. Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he is aware of the
great delay in the receipt of English mails
in South Derry, and the consequent commercial loss involved, and, as this is due to
the fact that the Larne and Stranraer boat
train which carries these mails frequently
misses the connection at Belfast; whether
he has made representations to the proper
authorities with a view to having the mails
transferred to the South Derry train at
Greenisland.
Mr. BARBOUR: Following representations
made to me by the hon. Member, I
approached the Post Office Authorities on
this matter. I am glad to be able to inform the hon. Member that an arrangement
has now been made between the Post Office
and the Railway Company under which, on
occasions when the boat train is liable to
miss connection with the Belfast-Coleraine
train leaving Belfast at 10 p.m., all correspondence intended for the latter train, including that destined for South Derry, will
be transferred at Greenisland. This
arrangement came into force permanently
as from the 14th instant.

5. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state what steps,
if any, have been taken to acelerate the
building of the remaining three hundred and

specifications, etc., are now in course of preparation for the erection of 134 houses. With

spread over Northern Ireland and are not
confined to Belfast.

which was established by the Imperial
Authority to determine all these details with
regard to the erection of houses.

HEAVY MOTOR TRAFFIC ON ROADS.
6. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Prime Minister
whether legislation will be introduced at an
early date to relieve the ratepayers of the
excessive burden of taxation due to the increase of heavy motor traffic on roads which
were never intended for such traffic.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I am glad to be able to announce that I hope for next year to increase
the Road Fund Grants on Class 1 Roads 50
per cent to 60 per cent, and on Class 2 Roads
'from 25 per cent to 30 per cent, and further
to make grants of 15 per cent of approved
expenditure on Class 3 Roads.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman if there is no possibility of the
Government introducing legislation to take
the control of the roads out of the ratepayers'
hands, and making the motor traffic pay for
their upkeep?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think that is a
very big question involving the control not
alone of motors but also of roads.

PRICE OF BREAD IN BELFAST.
8. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether, in view of the fact that the
quartern loaf is sold in Belfast for 10ld when
the Food Council of Great Britain has stated
that there is no justification for a higher
price than 9d, he is prepared to take steps
to see that this essential commodity is reduced in price on parallel lines with Great
Britain.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates) to
reply. As the hon. Member is no doubt
aware the price of the quartern loaf in Belfast
was reduced on the 15th instant to 93d. I
understand, moreover, that it is the practice
of the leading Belfast bakers to allow a discount for cash payment, which has the effect
of reducing the price of the loaf approximately to the latter figure mentioned by the
hon. Member.

CLAUSE 41 (Local Authorities)—
(1) The local authority for the purposes
of this Act shall be, in the case of a
county borough, the borough council, and
elsewhere, the county council.
(2) A county council may for the purposes of this Act make arrangements with
any sanitary authority whose area is
wholly or partly situate within the county
for the execution and performance by that
sanitary authority of any of the powers
and duties of the county council under
this Act.
(3) A local authority for the purpose of
this Act may delegate their powers and
duties under this Act to the education
committee or regional education committees of the authority, or to the maternity
and child welfare committee of the
authority, or partly to one such class of
committee and partly to the other, as they
think fit; and such delegation may be made
subject to such restrictions and conditions,
if any, as the authority think fit.
A sanitary authority with which a county
council have made arangements under the
last preceding sub-section may in like
manner delegate their powers and duties
under this Act to the maternity and child
welfare committee of the authority.
In this section the expression "maternity
and child welfare committee" means any
committee set up by a local authority or
sanitary authority for the purposes of
sections two and three of the Notification
of Births (Extension) Act, 1915, as
amended by section four of the Maternity
and Child Welfare Act, 1918.

page 47, line 17, to leave out "Contributory
Pensions" ("This Act may be cited as the
Widows', Orphans' and Old Age Contributory
Pensions Act (Northern Ireland 1925") and
to insert Insurance."

I have some difficulty in determining at
the moment whether this Amendment is
strictly in order, because the word "contributory" has occurred in a variety of places
in the various clauses with which we have
dealt, but I will allow the hon. Member
(Mr. Kyle) to develop his point, as I believe
in always giving a private Member the
benefit of any doubt there is.
Mr. KYLE: The reason I desire to change
the Title of this Bill to "Widows', Orphans'
and Old Age Insurance Act" is that the
Minister responsible for the Bill has made
it quite clear to the House, as also has the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Labour (Mr. Gordon) in his reply to the debate on the Second Reading, that this is an
insurance Measure and should not be called
a Pensions Act, either contributory or anything else. There is a definite meaning
attached to the word "Pensions" which
should not be used as a definition in the
Title of this Measure. It is, as I say, in
consequence of the fact that it has been
generally admitted on both sides of the Committee that this is an insurance Measure
that I move this Amendment, and I think
the admission which was made by the Minister in the introduction of this Bill, is borne
out when one reads the Measure itself. I
have tried before to point out that this is a
Measure consolidating National Health
Insurance and Old-Age Pensions as we knew
them, and changing the basis of Old-Age
Pensions to an insurance scheme. Therefore
I think the Committee for the sake of common honesty in regard to this Measure
ought to call it an Insurance Bill or Act,
rather than a Contributory Pensions Act.
For these reasons I beg to move.
Mr. DEVLIN: I would like to support
the Amendment moved by the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Kyle). This is really an insurance
Bill, because if you compel people to pay you
are not giving them pensions. For instance,
judges-if I may touch upon a subject which
is sacrosanct-do not contribute anything and
they get large pensions. Nobody would ever
call a judge a pensioner. These people are
compelled to pay and, therefore, we ought to
call things by their proper names, and this
is really an Insurance Bill. By calling it
insurance you will remove what people will
regard as a stigma, because the poor do not
like pensions unless they contribute to them.
That is why I am in favour of the Bill. It
is only people in high places who take pensions and contribute nothing. I cannot see
any possible objection to the Minister of
Labour accepting the proposal of the hon.
Member (Mr. Kyle).
Mr. ANDREWS: The Government cannot
accept this Amendment. The Committee has
already decided to accept the principle of
contributions, and, therefore, it is a contributory pension that the people are getting.
But it is only right that I should
add that the scheme is linked up
with our Health Insurance Act, and
that the test is a test of insurance. There
is nothing inconsistent in calling it a Contributory Pensions Bill and at the same time
saying that the test shall be one of insurance. The hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin) has raised a question relating
to judges and their pensions. I say there is
no analogy between the two forms of pensions
at all.
Mr. DEVLIN: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: This is a pension which
is given to widows. I would like to inform
the hon. Member (Mr. Devlin) that there is
no pension at all given to the widow in the
case of the death of a member of the
Judiciary.
Mr. DEVLIN: I know, but we are talking about pensions. What we are discussing
now is by what name we will call this Bill.
It is an insurance Measure, whether contritributory or not, because the people have
to pay into it, and if they did not pay they
would not get the pensions. Therefore, it
Widows' Pensions Bill-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Devlin]
is an insurance scheme. In the case of judges
they pay nothing into any fund. This is
true in the case of other high officials as
well, very highly-paid people who could well
save money out of their large salaries, and
who get pensions when they reach the age
to retire, though you never get a judge to
retire unless he is pushed into it by somebody who wants his job.
Mr. ANDREWS: A judge gets nothing unless he does retire.
Mr. DEVLIN: What we want to do is to
give the widow the same chance as the judge.
If she has no means she should be entitled
to a pension just as a judge is when he comes
to retire. I do not see why the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) should object to
accept the Amendment proposed by the hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Kyle). It is a much more
dignified way to express the terms of these
proposals than by calling it a Pensions Act,
because it is not really a Pensions Act; it
is an Insurance Act.
Mr. BEATTIE: I rise to support my colleague in his Amendment. I agree with the
sentiments that have been expressed by the
previous speakers. This is not really a pensions scheme at all. It is an insurance
scheme. I would like to point out to the
Minister that when in the past we have been
granting pensions we have never asked for
any contributions. The State does
not ask for a
contribution from
soldiers. When a soldier loses his
life on the battlefield or elsewhere
his widow gets a pension. We consider ourselves as being in the industrial army; we
are soldiers of industry, and if the State cannot consider it worth its while to grant pensions free of all contributions to the industrial soldiers it should not pretend to do
so under the institution of pensions on a contributory basis. Perhaps we are not very interesting, but we are so interested in this
Bill that we want to try to make it better
than we found it by changing the name of
it and placing it before the general public
as what it really is. In the near future I
expect to see health pensions, unemployment
pensions and all classes of things in that line
included as pensions when they are not pensions at all. I certainly do not agree with
the Bill being classified as a Pensions Bill,
and am in full sympathy with my colleagues
that it is an Insurance Bill, and by adopting
that we are clearing the way to bring in a
real Pensions Bill for the widows
orphans of the class which we on this side
of the House represent.
and
Mr. ANDREWS: Really, if I may say so,
it is merely a quibble what we call the Bill.
It will not affect a single widow, a single
orphan, or a single old person in the least
what we call the Bill, and my opinion is that
a rose by any other name would smell as
sweet-
Mr. KYLE:
ance Bill.
Therefore call it an Insur-
Mr. DEVLIN: Why not make a concession to the Opposition? You have not made
any up to the present.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I just wish to know if the
hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie)
wishes to convey to this side of the House
that a soldier who gives his life for his
country has not contributed to the pension.
Mr. BEATTIE: He has contributed by
service in the field, and the industrial soldier
has also contributed service.

Mr. W. McMULLEN: I would just like
to intimate to the right hon. Gentleman that
it is not a quibble at all. If he casts his
mind back over the Acts from 1908 to 1924
he will find out that the Old Age Pensions
Acts have not been harnessed to Unemployment and Health Insurance Acts. Now the
present Act is harnessed to Health Insurance
and Unemployment Insurance, and it is quite
right to argue that it is not a Pensions Act
at all; it is an Insurance Act. It is putting
it reasonably and sensibly. There is far
greater justification for calling it an Insurance Act than for calling it a Pensions Act.
It is not a quibble at all. It is a reasonable
request when you harness Unemployment Insurance and Health Insurance with it and
make contributions to these two schemes a
condition for benefits going to be paid under
this alleged Pensions Bill. There is far
greater justification for describing it as a
Contributory Insurance Act rather than a
Contributory Pensions Act. To-day I presume we will be discussing Unemployment
Insurance and we will be discussing the
changes we are going to make, proving quite
clearly and conclusively that the widows' and
orphans' and old-age pensions are contingent
on this Act. You have admitted that. (Hon.
Members: No, no.) Whether you have
agreed to admit it in so many words by legislation you have admitted it. Consequently
you have made a case for the change of name
from Contributory Pensions to Contributory
Insurance Act, and logically you are entitled
to do it too.
Question put, "That the words proposed to
be left out stand part of the Question."
The Committee divided: Ayes, 25; Noes, 5.

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move on page 48, line
13, column 4, to leave out "4d." and insert
"2d." The Amendment is in regard to contributions which are to my mind too heavy and
will impose an undue burden on the working
people.
I have no hope at this stage that the
Minister of Labour will relax anything of
the tight hold that he has on this particular
'Measure-one might really call it a stranglehold-despite the lesson he should have
learned from yesterday's proceedings when
the right hon. Gentleman the Minister of
Home Affairs, in reply to a question, fell into
line with an Amendment that was proposed
from these Benches some time ago when the
Rent Act was before this House. Despite
the fact that he thought no good could come
from the Opposition Benches he fell into line
yesterday at the request of the hon. Member
for Armagh. So I cannot say that the
Minister of Labour will give us anything in
this connection. It is only from a sense of
public duty that I rise to propose this. It
seems to me that it is absolutely hopeless to
approach the Government or to approach
those who sit behind them for any form of
mercy or decent treatment for the working
'people of the Six Counties. We are
here representing the workers of the various
constituencies-
The PRIME MINISTER: We all do that.
Mr. KYLE: We are doing that to the best

the working people in the Six Counties
would favour a reduction of these contributions, particularly those people whom the
hon. Gentleman the Member for Tyrone and

to the agricultural labourers. I think there

for these people it would mean some benefit,

I think that I can be quite fair in stating
that those of us who support this Amendment to reduce the contributions are more
in keeping with the wishes of the electors

Gentleman the Minister of Labour or the

of the electors when we say that the contributions under this Measure should be reduced
as we have outlined in this Amendment I
have pleasure in proposing.

Dr. MORRISON:
I throw myself on the
mercy of the Committee in order to bring
before them the matter which I am about to
raise. It is this. I labour under a disability
owing to the fact that in order to get here for
the opening of the House I have to get up at
6 o'clock and catch an early train, and then
in order to get a train home I have to leave
at half-past five. I raised this matter during
the passage of this Bill through Committee
and the Minister of Labour kindly consented
to consider it. I am afraid that the Report
Stage or the Third Reading may take place
in my absence and, therefore, I want to raise
this point now. I will raise it at every stage
and in all the public utterances I may make
in regard to social questions. The point I
want to make is clear and easily understood.
We were all united on it when we did not
all sit on these benches. We have a real
Opposition now. We had a semi-Opposition
then.

hon. Members, when we
were discussing this matter, said that the
Bill provides for them. I think the
Minister himself does not hold that that is
the case, but if he has not fully considered
the question his chief of staff thinks it is
not provided for, because I discussed the
matter with him. I would beg of the Committee to take the opportunity of remedying
this grave injustice that has been done to
these unfortunate children. I think there
would not be more than one or two per
cent., and I think the number will be
materially reduced by the Illegitimate
Children (Affiliation Order) Act which has
been passed by this House. We have 1,300 of
these cases happening in Northern Ireland
every year, and I feel myself that there would
not be more than one per cent. that would
benefit under the provision that I would like
to see made. I would appeal to the right
hon. Gentleman who has charge of this Bill,
and who I know possesses the inestimable
advantage of having a generous mind and a
sympathetic heart, not alone for the poor
helpless child but for the reputation of this
House, to try to remedy this, which every-
'body admits is a gross injustice.
Mr. ANDREWS: The glaring injustice
to which my hon. Friend has referred is not
an injustice created by this Measure, and I
do not think it is an injustice that can be
remedied in this Bill. The hon. Member
raised this question yesterday, and I think
what I said yesterday was quite correct. I
asked my hon. Friend to come and discuss
this matter with me to-morrow forenoon, but

my fault. But I did not know that the hon.
Member was going to raise this question

namely, that after all we have to consider
the paying of a pension to an orphan. We
are not justified in paying a pension to an
orphan until we know that the child is an
orphan, and the trouble is to discover the
father in cases of this kind. After all, I am
sure every hon. Member will admit that the
father of the child is doubly responsible
in this instance, because the poor mother of
the child has died, to some extent through
his action: and in addition to that the fact
that the child is deprived of its mother puts
it up doubly to the man in my opinion to
support the child.
I do feel that it would be putting a
premium on this sort of wrong-doing to allow
those fellows, whom no words are sufficient
to condem, the opportunity of escaping from
the responsibility which undoubtedly is
theirs. I feel, therefore, that it would not
be right of the Government to accept an
Amendment of this kind for the reasons I
have mentioned, notwithstanding the fact
that we have the greatest sympathy with the
poor child. If we could meet the case without incurring a very serious general liability,
I would be quite sympathetically disposed to
do it, and it was for that reason that I said
to my hon. Friend that I was prepared on
behalf of the Government to reconsider the
matter yesterday; but for so far I have not
been able to find any way out of the difficulty.

Committee in London appointed by the
British Government. That Committee was
made up of men of all parties-not all
Members of Parliament-representing humanitarian agencies, financiers and other
eminent authorities. They all-practically
unanimously-agreed that the old-age pension
should be universal, and they drafted a
scheme, which was forwarded to the Chancellor of the Exchequer. At the time, of
course, it was not accepted, because of the
financial exigencies which is the euphonious
way of meeting all difficulties-a way that
has been adopted from the English curriculum by the Minister of Labour here. That
is the reason that was given.
Some people might think it is rather an
outlandish proposal to come from any responsible person that every person should get the
old-age pension. I merely say for the information of the hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Johnstone) that the proposal was thought
out, carefully considered and subsequently
commended by this very large and representative body of men, who gave the deepest
thought and consideration to this question.
Question: "That the Bill be now read the
Third time," put, and agreed to.
Ordered: That the Clerk do carry the Bill
to the Senate, and desire their concurrence.
Unemployment Insurance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I beg to move the Second Reading
of the Unemployment Insurance Bill. I would
like to say at the outset that this Bill contains four main provisions with which I
purpose dealing. It alters three main principles in the interests of the contributor, and
finally I may say that it might be regarded
as a very generous Bill containing generous
provisions.
The object of this Bill is not to provide
employment, but it is to make it easy for
those who are unable to find it. If we continue the first statutory condition of the 30
contributions it will be impossible for a
great number of people to obtain unemployment benefit, and, consequently, we are
bringing forward this Bill with a view of
making their pathway in that direction easy.
The House will remember that in June, prior
to our Adjournment, a Bill was passed called
the Unemployment Temporary Provision Bill,
which gave power to the Governor to apply
by Order in Council so much as he thought
fit of a Bill which was to come on later in
the Imperial Parliament, and which was
finally passed. This power
that enabled
the Governor to bring in certain provisions by Order in Council became effective,
and this Bill is now being introduced to
enact the various provisions and at the same
time to bring into being a new provision
not brought in by Order in Council.
Having given that explanation, I will proceed to explain what I said at the outset
of my speech, that there were four main
provisions in the Bill. The first provision is
the power given to the Minister to waive
the first statutory condition. I think I should
explain to the House what is meant by the
first statutory condition. It was necessary
under the previous Act that the applicant for
benefit should have thirty contributions in
the two years prior to the benefit year.
I may make it plain by saying that if
an applicant makes application for benefit in
October we would go over his record to July
1923, and we would examine whether he had
30 contributions to his credit. If it was
found he had not 30 contributions to his
credit then according to that Act he was not
entitled to benefit. And if hon. Members refuse to give a Second Reading to this Bill
here this evening they will place great numbers of unemployed people who have not 30
contributions to their credit in the peculiar
position that they will be outside the pale
of making application for benefit, because
they would not be entitled to it. The Bill
we are introducing here gives power to the
Minister to waive this particular clause from
1431 Unemployment Insurance Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS. Second Reading.

[Mr. Gordon]
the first October until June, 1926. His power
to waive came to an end at the end of
September and we purpose asking the House
again to give him power in order that he may
come to the rescue, if I may use the expression, of the victims of industrial depression
who have been unable to find employment,
and consequently are unable to provide themselves with the necessary contributions to
obtain benefit under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I think it would be well that I should
explain the conditions under which men can
obtain benefit by virtue of the waiver of the
Minister. He has decided that instead of the
Act requiring 30 contributions over two years
the Act shall require eight contributions
over two years. Furthermore where a man
has been unable to obtain employment in
order to have the eight contributions to his
credit over a period of two years, the Minister under his power to waive expects that
that man will have had 30 contributions to
his credit at some period of his life as he
was passing through Insurance.
Now, lest hon. Members on the Front
Bench opposite and other hon. Members of
this House should be of the opinion that if
a man has 30 contributions to his credit that
entitles him to benefit, I want to disabuse
their minds of that. I think that impression
has got abroad, and I want to disabuse the
mind of the general public. That is a wrong
impression. It is merely a step in the
right direction. A man may have 30
contributions to his credit, but from the
year 1918 he may not have been in any insurable employment. Consequently though
the man may have 30 contributions to
his credit there are other hurdles that he
must cross in order to reach the Insurance
Fund and in order to obtain benefit. I think
that it would be well I should explain that
because I know perfectly well that Members
of the Opposition here are likely to raise
that point. I want to show the Members of
the House that notwithstanding a man
having fulfilled the condition now laid down
by the Minister of 30 contributions he must
go further. He must also prove that he is
normally employed in such employment as
would make him an employed person within
the meaning of the principal Act, that in
normal times insurable employment suited
to his capacities would be likely to be available for him, but most important of all-I
want hon. Members to remember this-that
he has during the past two years immediately
preceding the date of application for benefit
been employed in an insurable employment
to such an extent as was reasonable, having
regard to all the circumstances of the case
in particular to the opportunities for obtaining insurable employment during that period.
