Oral Answers to Questions.
RETIREMENT OF A WORKMISTRESS.
1. Mr. COOPER asked the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Education if
Miss Isabella Harren was employed for 25
years and 3 months in Lisdead School, County
Fermanagh, as a workmistress, at a salary
of £40 per annum, until compelled to retire
on attaining 60 years of age, and if he can
state why she has not received a pension.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): The facts are as stated by the hon.
Member, except that the retirement of the
teacher in question was due to the failure
of the school in which she was employed to
maintain the minimum average attendance
of girl pupils, as required by the regulations,
to warrant her further recognition. Miss
Harren's salary at the date of her retirement
was £39 per annum. Workmistresses are
required to devote only two hours daily to
the performance of their school duties, and,
being thus part-time employees, they are not
eligible for pensions or gratuities on retirement.
Mr. COOPER: May I ask if this lady had
been also teaching in the school and was a
full-time employee?
Mr. ROBB: As a result of inquiries which
I have made, I learn she was employed as a
part-time teacher of sewing and not in any
other capacity.
Mr. COOPER: I would ask the Parliamentary Secretary to ascertain if she did not
also teach scholars in the school.
Mr. SPEAKER: The proper course is for
the hon. Member to give notice of that question and to put it down for another day.
RELIEF WORKS AT BELFAST HARBOUR.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Labour whether any arrangements have been
made with the Belfast Harbour Commissioners to proceed with relief works such
as are being carried out in Glasgow and
Liverpool, in order to provide further dock
and shed accommodation, as well as badly
needed work for the unemployed.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR: (Mr.
Andrews): I have been in negotiation with
the Belfast Harbour Commissioners on the
subject of the construction of a new dock
and, whilst I regret that they do not feel
justified in proceeding at present with the
scheme, in view of the diminished revenue

g it very prominently to the front rank
ur local problems.

airment, and in many cases the destrucof farmers' crops and stocks have reted a movement amongst the affected

he second circumstance which has, not
aturally, added momentum to this agitais the closer proximity of our local

med will be more deeply interested in

than the more remote assembly at Westminster, and, therefore, more active in its endeavour to discover a remedy for the disease.
Whilst there are overwhelming arguments
for seriously attempting to tackle this gigantic problem, we must not lose our sense of
proportion and underrate the difficulties
ahead of us in our endeavour to effect a
radical cure of the periodical floodings which
cause such losses to the agricultural community. These difficulties can best be
apprehended if I submit a short sketch of
the efforts which have been made from time
to time during the past 150 years to counteract the effect of conditions which are largely
produced by the physical features of the
Province.
The disastrous results of three successive
years of excessive rainfall have contributed
to a belief in the theory that the climatic
conditions of the country have changed for
the worse. This impression has a tendency
to develop feelings almost of despair in the
minds of those who till the soil and who find
all their labours frustated from year to year
by the unkindness of Nature. But this impression has no foundation in fact.
Meteorological records prove beyond doubt
that in days long past weather disturbances
were quite as frequent as to-day, and often
more violent, and leading experts in this
domain of investigation are satisfied that
cycles of normal and abnormal weather conditions follow each other in succession. It
perhaps throws a light on this theory that
the past summer was one of unusual drought
and warmth, and the rivers are not yet flowing
at their autumn capacity, notwithstanding
the recent heavy rains, while the level of
Lough Neagh is not yet higher than its normal summer level. It may be, therefore,
that we have begun a new cycle of favourable
seasons.
As far back as the year 1748 agricultural
conditions appear to have been in a parlous
plight in Ulster, for we find from early records that about that period the flooding of
the country around Lough Neagh was the
subject of frequent reports from engineers.
In this connection it is interesting to note
that between the years 1750 and the present
no fewer than nineteen separate enquiries
were set up, and that on five of these investigations the subject was examined by Parliamentary or Royal Commissions.
I offer this information to the House in
order that hon. Members may realize the
importance attached to the subject of Irish
drainage in days gone by. As a result of
all these investigations, innumerable Acts of
Parliament were passed, many of which are
either now in abeyance or are actually
wiped off the Statute Book.
Drainage Bill—

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Pollock]
It would appear that the main purpose of
these Acts was to provide for the establishment of local Drainage Boards or Committees
to whom statutory authority was given to
carry out schemes of district drainage, and
levy a rate on the areas benefited for the cost
of same. There still remain in Northern Ireland ten of these Drainage Boards, of which
eight were set up under an Act of 1842, and
two under an Act of 1863.
With the exception, however, of the Lough
Erne and Lough Neagh Boards, the others
may be regarded as defunct. The existing
bodies are expected to deal with the levels of
waters in these two great central basins and
to keep, as far as possible, a free outlet to
the sea-rather than the general and more
or less local questions of arterial drainage.
I am afraid that the extent to which they
have justified their existence is open to
serious doubt. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
But without discussing this aspect of the
case, the problem facing us to-day is no less
serious and important than it appears to have
been 150 years ago, notwithstanding that vast
sums of money have been spent on drainage
schemes in the interval.
Under the Acts of 1842 and 1857 a total
of £2,400,000 approximately was expended on
attempts to ameliorate or cure the conditions
of land flooding. When we remember that
the value of money in those days in its
relation to commodities was at least three
times greater than to-day we begin to have
some glimmerings of the magnitude of the
financial problems which must be faced,
equally with those in the domain
engineering.
of
In discussing the general question of
drainage in Ulster, we must always bear
in mind that the problem naturally
divides itself into two separate branches,
although these are correlated So far
a3 their effects on the country as a
whole are concerned, and it is a question for
later decision, the extent to which suggested
remedies in the two branches of work would
require to be conducted concurrently-that
is to say, the development of arterial drainage concurrently with attempts to improve
the outlet to the sea.
The first part of the problem is concerned
with the cleaning and scouring of existing
water courses, the removal of disused weirs
and other obstructions in the beds of streams,
60 as to ensure that the general drainage
system of agricultural land may, under conditions of excessive rainfall, be permitted
freely to discharge into the rivers which
carry the waters into the central reservoirs.
The second branch of the work contemplates provision for relieving the central
basins of Lough Neagh and Lough Erne of
the increased volume of water which would
naturally follow active development of the
arterial drainage system under conditions of
excessive rainfall as set up under the first
part of the scheme, and conveying the surplus waters expeditiously to the sea.
In the case of Lough Neagh, the only outlet for its waters is the lower River Bann,
and the second branch of the scheme would,
therefore, largely concentrate on the effort to
increase the facilities for the volume of water
flowing through that river, by such engincering methods as can be devised.
As regards the first part of the scheme
which may be called, for easy description,
"arterial drainage," it is obvious that this
can only be carried out by a general supervision on the part of the local authorities.
It will be seen, therefore, that parts one
and two of the Bill give wide powers to
County Councils, not alone to compel attention to local drainage on the part of owners
or occupiers of land, but in addition to prosecute schemes of drainage themselves.
Furthermore, the County authorities will be
empowered, for the purpose of carrying out
the provisions of the scheme, to create local
drainage districts, and to establish Committees who will undertake schemes of local
drainage. This describes the first part of
the programme.
But when we come to the second branch
of the scheme, which concerns the authorities
named in Part Three of the Bill, that is to
say, the question of relieving the Central
Basins of the heavy volume of additional
floods caused by excessive rainfall we are met
with engineering difficulties, which cannot be
undertaken without serious thought as to the
efficacy of any proposed remedies. It would
I apprehend, be very imprudent on the
part of the Government to undertake schemes
involving heavy financial liability without
being assured that the expenditure of money
which must necessarily be large will accomplish the results which we have in view.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) These difficulties especially apply to Lough Neagh and
to the River Bann, which, as I have said, is
its only outlet to the sea.
The Lough Erne problem does not appear
to present such difficulties, and, with a little
patience can probably be satisfactorily solved.
But as regards Lough Neagh the size of
the Channel of the river, that is, the River
Bann-is quite unequal to the discharge of
the winter floods, and consequently the
higher level of the Lough has the effect of
banking up the rivers, which feed its waters,
and thereby causes widespread flooding and

serious loss.
It may interest the House and enable them
to realise something of the formidable nature

of this problem if I mention one or two
figures. I think figures do not always contain a realistic idea of the features of a
Measure such as this. The calculated catchment area of Lough Neagh is 1,860 square
miles. The waters of 1,860 square miles
empty into Lough Neagh, The daily flow

I do not know whether the communication
of these figures to the House will enable
them to realise the immensity of the problem, but at any rate the figures are sufficiently large to compel attention.
When I speak of the necessity for the exercise of care in the attempt to enlarge the outflow of the Bann I would recall this very important fact, that engineers
of the highest eminence have been from time
to time engaged in the attempt to grapple
with the trouble, and that vast sums of
money have been expended in the effort to
solve the exact same difficulty which faces
us to-day.
Is the problem then insoluble?
It may be assumed that all the distinguished men, who have been engaged in the
endeavour to solve it were not exactly fools,
and yet with apparently unlimited funds at
their command they have left the problem
where they found it.
The most noteworthy of these efforts to
enlarge the Bann is known as the McMahon
scheme, on which a sum of £264,000 was expended, without any permanent improvement
being effected on the conditions of flooding
caused by the congestion of the waters of the
River.
I am sure the House will not expect a
layman like myself to express a dogmatic
opinion on the subject, but we are fortunate
to have as head of our engineering staff an
officer of exceptional ability and long experience of flooded lands and their remedies.
This officer has explained that the difficulty lies not so much in putting forward a
scheme of works, which would cure flooding
troubles-although this is not entirely simple
of solution-but rather in evolving one, the
cost of the execution of which would not be
absolutely out of all proportion to the benefits
derived therefrom, and that this difficulty
has been appreciated by preceding engineers
who have reported can be deduced by implication when investigating their reports.
It is within the knowledge of the House
that we have had engineers engaged for
months on a complete survey of the Bann.
Our Chief Engineer very wisely decided to
approach the whole question de novo because of the great diversity of opinion held
by engineers in the past. In that, I think,
if I may offer an opinion, he was well advised.
He expected to have been in a position to
make a complete report and recommendations by this time, but, curiously enough,
the droughty summer, which in some respects
was ideal for outdoor survey work generally,
has militated against an important section
of the survey. It is a fact that owing to the
small rainfall the surface of the Lough is
still only at normal summer level, and as it
is necessary to take observations of the conditions of the Lough and River in times of
flood it is impossible to have the survey completed within the expected time.
The Government, however, having given
an undertaking that legislation would be
promoted at the earliest possible moment, decided to submit the present Measure as an
evidence of their good faith and as an instalment of the final project.
I am happy to say that the County Councils who are charged with the full responsibility of arterial drainage have not only
urged and encouraged the Government to
proceed with their legislative proposals with
as much expedition as possible, but are in
full accord with the provisions of the
Measure, although offering the opinion that
the authority of the existing Drainage
Boards should be changed and a central
scheme proceeded with as expeditiously as
possible as a national project. But the Councils are quite satisfied to have the assurance
that when a radical scheme is undertaken to
relieve the central waters of the Province,
the drainage administration under the existing Boards may be put upon a different basis
by further legislation. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
In the case of the Lough Erne Drainage
Board, it would have been impossible to interfere with its present powers, because
the Board operates in the Free State as well
as in Ulster, and, therefore, any legislative
step on our part might to some extent have
been ultra vires without the concurrence of
the Free State Government. I have no doubt
that given the necessary time some arrangement will be reached whereby this difficulty
may be solved.
But the Lough Neagh problem, lying as it
does within our own area, rests on a different basis. There is no use contesting the
fact that if the County Councils carry out
radical schemes of arterial drainage, it is
possible that the acceleration of the flow of
the tributary rivers might conceivably create
a serious condition of things in Lough Neagh
unless greater relief is given through the outlet of the Bann, but I am living in hope that
during the progress of the County Council
activities our plans may be so far developed
that concurrent remedial measures may be
undertaken in the outlet river, and as we shall
be in touch with the County Councils from
time to time regarding their operations, we

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Pollock]
can be guided in our treatment of the subject by the benefit which we shall derive
from their advice and assistance.
Summarised, Parts One and Two of the
Bill propose to empower County Councils
to carry out schemes of arterial drainage
and to establish subsidiary local bodies for
that purpose. Part three contemplates
schemes of central drainage, and continues
the existing drainage authorities in their
functions, until new development schemes
have been worked out in detail.
The Bill also provides in Part Four for
the establishment of a strong Advisory Committee on which all the County Councils
are represented. We attach importance to
this Committee,, as it ensures the interest
and sympathy of the County Councils in
this work. This body will act, at any rate
during what I may call the probationary
period as advisers in regard to the propriety or otherwise of prosecuting schemes
which might possibly be advantageous or,
on the other hand, might lead to difficulties.
The Committee will join with the Government
nominees, and this will give a sense of
security that no schemes are likely to be
undertaken without a full consideration of
the probable effect on the various interests
likely to be affected.
I should mention also that the Imperial
Government will be represented on the proposed Advisory Committee because of
fishery interests, which are a Council of
Ireland concern, and which may be affected
by drainage schemes proposed to be undertaken under this Measure.
Part Five is merely supplemental and
explanatory and requires no further elucidation until the period of the Committee
Stage.
The three schedules, as is usual, give detailed descriptions of the classes of work
and directions for carrying out the different projects.
I have now given a general outline of the
Bill which the House is asked to consider
to-day. I do not think hon. Members will
expect me to discuss the clauses item by
item, as these will be thoroughly examined
when the Bill is considered in Committee.
I have some minor Amendments to submit
when that stage is reached, but as these do
not affect the principle of the Measure, 1
will not touch upon them to-day.
con-
In conclusion let me remind the House
that the forces of nature seem to have combined for our discomfort in the
figuration of the Province, whose margin
is hounded by an enormous mountainous
catchment area, emptying its waters into
the centre of the country, without providing
a sufficient outlet to the sea. Therefore in
our effort we are endeavouring to combat
and if possible to defeat these natural forces,
always a difficult task. But modern science
has been able to accomplish amazing feats,
and it may be that we shall succeed when
so many others have failed. But our task
is not rendered easier by persons or bodies
engaging in uninformed criticism and
apparently ignorant of the complexities of
this vast problem. Unless close investigation is made of the complexities of this
vast problem, it is exceedingly difficult to
offer an intelligent opinion.
The Government needs the sympathy, and
assistance of every interest in the Province
in this enterprise, and we are willing to
hear and listen respectfully to any suggestions or advice from persons or bodies
competent to submit them.
If we succeed in reaching our goal, we can
comfort ourselves with the reflection that
success will spell such a great accretion of
agricultural wealth for the Province, as has
not been experienced in its history.
May I say finally that as the County Councils have approved the Bill possibly it may be
accepted by the House as an agreed Measure.
I beg to move. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I only wish in a few words to amplify what
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) has
already said regarding this Bill, and to clear
up what possibly may be a misunderstanding
in the House, as apparently there has been
a misunderstanding on the part of the Portadown Chamber of Commerce. The Government were faced with the larger problem as
well as the smaller, and had the choice, the
free choice, of postponing the introduction
of this Measure until our scheme was ripe
for the actual drainage of Lough Neagh
itself. My right hon. Friend at a meeting of
the various county councils concerned asked
on
the specific question whether they would
prefer that this Bill should be held up until
that Measure was ready or that we should
go ahead with the present Bill and then introduce the other one as soon as our experts
have concluded their survey of the whole
jarea.
The Councils were unanimous in saying,
"Please give us this first instalment of your
intentions," and the Bill is brought in with
a view to meeting the very point that the
hon. Lady Member for Derry (Mrs.
Chichester) raised just now, that is, that
they may under this Bill get on with the
schemes, which would necessarily take a long
time to prepare, so that the other schemes
would, as we hope, catch them up later on,
and the actual operation of both Acts, as
we hope they will then be, can be carried
out together without any intensifying of the
flooded area. We will thus be carrying out
the local arterial drainage which is so
necessary in many parts of Ulster. The
'Government felt that the county councils
were really the best authorities to decide
whether we should wait for the whole Bill
or take it in two instalments. We have
gone into all these details. We have considered all the points, and have been put
into possession, as far as possible, of what the
cxperts have been able to say up to the
present moment. Therefore, going on with
this Bill so far from prejudicing the prosecution of the second Measure will actually
nerve everyone concerned to go ahead more
rapidly in order that there may be no flooding by the effects of this Bill before the other
one has been introduced and carried into
effect.
I hope the House will realise that this is
perhaps one of the most serious problems
it has had to face. Certainly it is one that
the Government have entered into with no
misgiving-but with a certain trepidation in
this sense that where others have failed they
have got to make a success. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) But it is essential, as I stated
in this House on one occasion before, that
before we ask the taxpayers or the ratepayers, whoever they may be, to sanction
a scheme, necessarily a very costly one, we
should be absolutely assured that the money
'will not follow the millions already spent
Lough Neagh itself and therefore
we do feel that it is
to take even extra precautions before we
cut even a single sod in any new scheme
which may be devised. I may say that from
my experience of the engineer who is in
charge of our investigations and who, as my
right hon. Friend has said, has had wide
experience in problems of a similar character
I also have implicit faith in him. I believe
the lines along which he and his subordinates
are working at the present moment are the
right lines.

[The Prime Minister]
I think that without going into any further
details to-day the House may take it from
me that we are progressing and progressing
well towards a solution of this extremely
difficult problem. In the meantime I hope
the House will take exactly the same view
as the County Councils, and allow us to go
on with this Bill. It is entirely in the interests of all concerned in Ulster. There is
nothing political about it, and it is a matter
of supreme importance to some parts of the
country that it should be placed on the
Statute Book as quickly as possible. And
we, I hope, will take the same broad view
as the representatives of the County Councils
and go ahead with the Bill and get it on the
Statute Book at the earliest possible date.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I think this
Bill is like the curate's egg. It is good in
parts-very good in parts. I had a feeling
when I came to this House that a Bill which
specifically continued the power of such
bodies as the Lough Neagh Drainage and
Navigation Company and the Lower Bann
Navigation Trustees-not only continued
these powers but extended them and gave
those bodies power to promote drainage
schemes would have justified me in opposing
that Bill.
Mr. POLLOCK: May I interrupt the hon.
Member? They are not empowered to promote drainage schemes-at any rate to carry
them out or go on with them. The Minister
of Finance has complete control.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: Does that
not place them in exactly the same position
as the county councils? You are excluding
these drainage boards from any popular
control. (An hon. Member: They are not.)
Then I have misunderstood the wording of
Part 3 of the Bill if these drainage boards
are not excluded from popular control. They
are certainly under the Ministry in the same
way as the County Councils are. These are
drainage boards that have proved themselves
to be inefficient, expensive, and absolutely
useless as far as carrying out their functions
is concerned. And for a Bill not only to
maintain the privileges of these bodies but to
extend them is a thing I shall oppose. And
this House really has to face this question
that for years these drainage boards-these
inefficient boards-have been levying on the
farmer a rate-a rate for what? A rate for
drainage works that never drained anything.
In fact it may be said that only you are
dealing with one of the most law-abiding,
peace-loving communities of farmers around
the shores of Lough Neagh and along the
Lower Bann there would have been a revolt
long ago. It has been suggested by a drainage association, the Agivey Drainage Association, that the farmers as a protest against
these boards being allowed to levy a rate
should refuse to pay that rate.
the
Only for the assurance given by
Minister of Finance here to-day that the
County Councils have agreed to this Measure
or given a qualified agreement I certainly
would have felt justified in opposing this
Bill because it contains Part 3 and continues
the powers of these boards. Now the
Minister of Finance in his able speech in
introducing this Bill stated that drainage resolved itself into two parts, that is, arterial
drainage facilitating the flow of the waters
into the basin of Lough Neagh, and the other
part was the drainage of Lough Neagh, facilitating the waters on their way to the sea,
This Bill deals with the first portion, arterial
drainage, but in my opinion fails entirely to
deal with the second. There is, in my opinion,
no provision to remedy the biggest problem,
the problem on which any efficient drainage
system for the Six County area must depend,
that is, the drainage of Lough Neagh by the
Lower Bann, because that is admitted by the
Minister of Finance himself. He said when
we pass this Bill the County Councils will
have, under our control, to find an outlet for
the surplus waters brought down by the
drainage scheme. As the hon. Member for
Derry (Mrs. Chichester) said, this seems like
putting the horse before the cart with a
vengence (laughter)-the cart before the
horse.
I do feel that it would have been more to
the interests of the Six County area in general
if the Government had been in a position to
propound a schme for draining Lough Neagh
and so obviating the flooding that Occurs
there continually every year through the
channel of the Lower Bann being less or more
impeded. Now the right hon. Gentleman suggested that this question had been intensified by the three bad seasons through which
we had passed. But is it not a fact also that
even in normal times there is serious flooding
around the shores of Lough Neagh and the
Lower Bann? He said there were great natural
difficulties-there is no doubt about that-in
the way of making a means of conveying the
waters of Lough Neagh to the sea. I would
like to ask the Minister of Finance has that
river at the present time, even with its
natural difficulties, a free course from Lough
Neagh to the sea. Are there not artificial
barriers in the Lower Bann impeding the
natural flow of the waters from Lough Neagh
to the sea? Are these not maintained largely
for keeping in use a navigation scheme that
is useless and benefits scarcely anybody?
Now I think it is a pity that this Bill
should be impaired by these defects, because
in other respects I think it is important that
county councils should be given power to
carry out schemes to help arterial drainage. There is another objection to the Bill.

Libraries Act, and you put upon their

In one week I have attended thirteen committee meetings in connection with county
council work, and I think if this thing goes
on you will find it exceedingly difficult to

hands but still keeps it in the hands of the
Minister of Home Affairs. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I know it is not possible to do
that without having the authority of the
county councils behind. These committees
can do absolutely nothing without the consent of the Minister of Home Affairs, and if

by a certain amount of bravery they get past

that, the only thing it would do, so far as I
can see at present, would be to relieve the
difficulty in some counties that are under
the control of this Government. Take the
configuration of County Antrim. From
Greenisland round to Ballycastle there is a
range of hills, very often in close proximity
to the sea. The watershed of these hills
drains into the sea, and only one river, the
Bush, on the north-west coast of Antrim,
runs into the sea. The remainder of the
county is either directly or indirectly drained
into the Bann through the Maine and other
rivers. There is not one thing in this Bill
to enable us to take away the extra water
from the Bann. It certainly gives us power
to clear our watercourses and things of that
description, which will bring the water more
quickly down into the Maine, but our complaint is that we have too much water there
already. If this Bill is passed into law, it
will be of no service in the next ten years.
Mr. POLLOCK: What are we to do?
Mr. CRAWFORD: I would say to them
honestly we can do nothing.

one difficulty that has not been mentioned

difficulty that is one of our glories.
down our rivers, especially the Maine, we

Mr. COOPER: I welcome this Bill on
behalf of a number of farmers who live along
Lough Erne and along the banks of the
Sillies River. I have seen very great floods
in Upper Lough Erne; I have seen ricks of
hay in the middle of the water, and people

The
that, this Bill has a very bad defect so far
as Lough Erne and the County of Fermanagh
are concerned, and that is dual control. It
is proposed in the first part of the Bill to
vest in the County Council all drainage outside of the works at present carried on by
the Lough Erne Drainage Board, and to
my mind dual control will ruin the Bill.
I think you must give the whole of the
drainage in the County of Fermanagh to
the County Council or to the Drainage Board,
or at least that you must have a joint committee. One of the first things the County
Council would undertake would be the drainage of the Sillies River, and immediately
the County Council would undertake that
their interests would be in conflict with those
of the Lough Erne Drainage Board.
Sillies River would have to be drained into
the very part of Lough Erne which is flooded,
that is, into Upper Lough Erne. The
Minister of Finance, in introducing this Bill,
spoke of the torrents of water that would
come down certain rivers into Lough Neagh.
That is exactly what is going to happen in
my opinion in the County of Fermanagh. If
the County Council undertook to drain the
Sillies River, which needs to be drained,
which is crying out to be drained, there will
be a great rush of water right into Upper
Lough Erne, where the lake is already
flooded. At the same time as the County
Council want to get the water into Lough
Erne the Drainage Board will want to get
it out, and the two Boards will be in conflict
the very minute you undertake any such
scheme.
I would appeal to the Government, before
they go any further with this Bill, before
the Third Reading-and I hope it will pass
the Third Reading very soon-to have a
conference of some sort between the Drainage
Boards and the County Councils, and to
produce out of that conference some sort of
working arrangement between the two sets
of bodies. As far as I can see, the drainage
of the Sillies River is absolutely dependent
on the drainage of Lough Erne, and if the
water is not got away out of Lough Erne
the drainage of the Sillies River will be
useless. The water cannot be got out of
Lough Erne unless the Lough Erne Drainage
Board undertakes considerable work in the
way of dredging and opening of the channel
between Upper Lough Erne and Lower Lough
Erne. I think the Bill is an excellent one,
but the means of carrying it out will require
careful consideration, and will require all
the interests being brought together.

cent. of the cost of carrying through these

from the Employment Exchanges. I thought

Mr. BARBOUR: The provisions of the
Unemployment Insurance Bill were explained
in detail yesterday by my hon. Friend
the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Labour, and it must have been
clear to hon. Members from the
planation which he gave that the
financial provisions of the Measure depend
on uncertain or unknown considerations. In
short, the financial effect of this Bill will
be dependent upon the rate of unemployment
prevailing from time to time, and there is
no known factor on which we can base any
calculations with a view to arriving at the
actual cost to the State. All that can be
done is to make provision for certain
eventualities, and as this provision must
involve an additional State charge it is
necessary to obtain a Financial Resolution
from this Committee before the proposals
of the Bill can be passed. I propose to endeavour to explain what is the broad effect
of these financial proposals, and as one must
adopt some figure to go on, to simplify
matters I will assume that the existing high
rate of unemployment, namely, 25 per cent..
is the basis for all calculations.
One of the most important provisions of
the Bill is, of course, contained in Clause 1
and deals with the waiver of the "first
statutory condition." That condition requires thirty contributions to have been paid
in the two years prior to the benefit year.
This waiver has, of course, been in force
since the 1924 Act was passed so that no fresh
charge is added to the present weekly
expenditure of the Unemployment Fund,
but I need hardly point out that
its continuance will prevent the Fund
from
substantial
obtaining the very
relief estimated in Northern Ireland to
amount, under present conditions, to £10,000
per week, or at the rate of £500,000 a year,
which it would obtain if this extension were
not introduced into this Bill. Owing to the
continued serious state of unemployment,
the time has not yet arrived for the withdrawal of the waiver, which would effect this
saving, and I do do not propose to make any
further reference to this fact other than to
emphasise that the continued existence of
such a serious charge on the Fund, taken in
conjunction with the relief which it is proposed to give to employers and employees and
to which I will refer later on results in a
very substantial increase in the charges upon
the Fund.
I a
Turning now to a balance sheet of the finaucial proposals of the Bill, Clause 3 (1) (a)
proposes to reduce the contribution payable
by employers and employed as from the 4th
January next (this being the date on which
the contributions payable under the Widows,'
Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pensions
Bill begin to be payable), and this concession will cost the Fund, on the basis of a
25 per cent. rate of unemployment, an annual
amount estimated at £131,600 (or on a 20
per cent. basis a sum of £140,500). On the
other hand, the increase in the "waiting
period" from three days to six days-to
which effect is given by Clause 2-will save
the Fund on the same 25 per cent. basis
approximately £100,000 per annum (or on a
20 per cent. basis £80,000). So far, therefore,
leaving out of account the £500,000 charge to
which I have referred earlier on, the fund
will be £31,600 to the bad. It is proposed to
make good this £31,600, and in addition to
offset to some small extent the drain on the
fund by reason of the extension effected by
Clause 1, by providing additional sums from
the Exchequer, and the somewhat complicated financial resolution now before the
Committee proposes to effect this.
Part I lays down that as from the 5th April,
1926, there shall be an additional State contribution of 1d in the case of men and ad
in the case of women, and this (taking a 25
per cent. basis) will bring in an additional
£43,400 (or on a 20 per cent basis £46,300).
In addition, however, provision is made in
Part II of the resolution for a contingent
additional Exchequer contribution of 1d for
men and id for other cases which will operate
if at the end of any quarter the deficiency in
the fund is higher than it may be on the 31st
December next. This contingent contribution
will, it is estimated, bring into the fund an
annual sum of £31,300 (or on a 20 per cent.
basis £33,400). Assuming that this further
sum will become payable, the Committee will
observe that the total increase in the Exchequer contribution amounts in all to a sum of
1495 Unemployment Insurance (Money) HOUSE OF COMMONS. Widows' Pensions Bill.

[Mr. Barbour]
£74,700 per annum (or on a 20 per cent. basis,
to a sum of £79,709). Hon. Members are, of
course, aware that as unemployment decreases the State contribution has to increase
by reason of the fact that contributions from
employers and employees also increase. The
contingent contribution, however, provided
in this resolution is to some extent intended
to act as a corrective to the diminution of
State contribution by reason of widespread
unemployment, as it imposes a fresh Exchequer charge to meet serious deficits occasioned by such unemployment.
I would repeat that these figures are necessarily hypothetical, but I hope that I have
shown that if there were no Bill, and if we
took no action, we should have effected an
immediate saving at the rate of £500,000 per
annum, but that seeing that we were not
prepared to adopt this course, we have introduced provisions which will have the effect
of reducing to a slight extent the current
rate of deficit on the fund. while at the same
time conceding to the employer and the employee the relief to which they are entitled
by reason of the effect which the widows'
orphans' and old-age contributory pensions
scheme is likely to have on our unemployment
insurance scheme. I beg to move.

Mr. BEATTIE: I have listened
attentively to the right hon. Gentleman explaining the reason for asking the money
required. I had also in my mind a method
of saving which the Minister of Labour I
believe adopted on or about the first of
September, and I was feeling surprised that
money to this extent should be asked for the
Fund, because by the methods adopted under
the new regulations I think the Fund has
been saved a terrible amount of money and
the unemployed have been deprived of same.
But this money is asked for at the rate of
£10,000 per week, I believe, or £500,000 per
jannum. If we are going to turn off the
people that this money is for at the rate of
between two and three hundred per week I
do not see why the Minister should ask for
any financial assistance whatsoever.
I agree with the money resolution, and I
hope when the money is granted by the Government that the people whom it is voted for
will receive it, because in my experience since
the 1st September there has been a stand
taken by the Minister of Labour which has
been referred to as a bulwark by Members
of the Government, that is the family income.
Now a committee is at the present
time considering the family income, and I
want to say that that condition of affairs
should not be allowed to exist in our Six
Counties unless we raise the basis of the
family income to a living wage. To calculate a man's right to extended benefit on the
family income of 38s. plus the amounts
allowed for members of the family I say
is a shame and a disgrace, and it is a bulwark
that any man who is head of a house when
he is working cannot get over, to the extent
of more than one member of his family
getting unemployment benefit. For that
reason I hope when the family income is
being considered by the Committee the
Minister set up that the basis of the head
of the family will be increased and the
amounts put up for members of his family
.will also be added to and each member of
the family who has been out of employment
through no fault of his own will be allowed
to participate in the sums as asked here
to-day by the Minister of Finance, and not
be deprived by some other resource which
I believe the Minister has taken for
economising and trying to cut down that
£10,000 per week.

I think 5s is inadequate. It ought to be

been proposed before. I admit that is a

creeping along the road towards social reform. I think, with regard to the 5s, that
the same argument applies to it as applies
to the argument in favour of 20s for the
widow. I do not want to prolong the discussion and make it any more difficult. I
wish formally to move the Amendment.

rather surprising that no attempt has been
made by Members opposite to try to ex-

plain exactly how a child could be fed on
5s a week. We have got discrimination so
far as this Bill is concerned. An orphan
child has been given 7s 6d, a fatherless child
-the eldest or only child-is given 5s, and

no Member opposite has attempted to

Surely it is not suggested that a widow can

the Bill as to how they expect a child to live
on the figure given under this scheme.
I regret that we have not had the time nor

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 27th October, 1925.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Private Business.
Wright's Divorce Bill.
The following Report was made from the
Joint Committee on Divorce Bills:-
That they had considered Wright's
Divorce Bill, and that the averments in the
Preamble had been proved to their satisfaction, and that they had gone through the
Bill and made an Amendment thereto.
Oral Answers to Questions.
PURCHASE OF EGGS BY WEIGHT.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is aware that there
is a considerable body of agricultural opinion
in favour of the purchase of eggs by weight,
and whether he has considered the advisability of having this system made
compulsory.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): The question of the purchase of
eggs by weight was seriously considered by
the Ministry when the Marketing of Eggs
Act was being framed. It was felt, however,
that despite the advantages of the system
the time was not quite ripe for such a radical change in commercial practice. Since
then the Ministry has lost no opportunity of
impressing on licensees the advantages of
this method. It is based on equity, and
encourages the production and marketing of
larger eggs. Wholesale dealers who aim at
the maximum benefit from grading as specified in the Rules under the Act find that the
adoption of purchase by weight very materially assists their grading operations. Actual
experience of the system in some districts
has largely dissipated misapprehensions
which were entertained regarding it, and the
Ministry has kept in close touch with developments. The advantages have been
demonstrated by means of a special leaflet
issued by the Ministry, and one association
of egg merchants have agreed to conduct
their purchases on a weight basis. Many
other individual members of the trade have
also fallen into line, and the Ministry is
now satisfied that the time is approaching
when a Measure, making it compulsory for
any person who purchases eggs for resale to
make these purchases on a weight basis,
would be well received and would be in the
interests of the poultry industry as a whole.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of the answer
of the right hon. Gentleman, in view of the
importance of this matter, and having regard to the circumstances that every licensed wholesale dealer is obliged to grade to
specified weights, and that the adoption of
the weight system would admittedly be a
direct encouragement to the production and
marketing of larger eggs, can the Minister
give an assurance that he will take the
earliest opportunity of making purchase by
weight mandatory?
Mr. ARCHDALE: I have arranged to
place this important matter on the agenda
for the next meeting of the Advisory Committee, in connection with the Egg Industry, which will take place at an early date.
My hon. Friend will appreciate that a
change of this nature may require legislation and that even with the support of a
considerable volume of public opinion some
considerable time must elapse before effect
could be given to a proposal which would
so radically affect the trade.
PREVENTIBLE DISEASES IN NOR
THERN IRELAND.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether in view of the evidence
contained in the last report of his Department of the increase in typhoid fever during the past few years, and also in view
of the recent serious outbreak of scarlet
fever in Lisburn, Belfast, and other places
in Northern Ireland, he is prepared to issue a special circular to the various administrative bodies on the subject, and
institute a campaign to reduce the mortality from these preventible diseases.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The regrettable increase in the number of cases of scarlatina
and typhoid during the last few years has
been engaging the earnest and close attention of the Ministry. The question of the
issue of a special circular to local authorities was considered and it was thought that
probably better results would be gained by
personal visitation of the medical inspectors of the Ministry to those districts where
there is an excessive incidence of these
infectious diseases. It is only right that I
should point out that the apparent increase in the number of cases is probably
to a large extent due to the better system
of notification to the local sanitary authorities which is now being insisted upon,
and further the local authorities are
required to send in weekly returns to the
Ministry. It is also satisfactory to record
that the annual number of deaths in Nor-
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
thern Ireland from scarlatina and typhoid
shows a marked diminution, the rate for
the year 1923 being about one-third of the
average of the previous ten years.
I can assure the hon. Member that every
possible step which is likely to produce
useful results has been and is being taken,
and the Ministry's inspectors are keeping
in the closest touch with the responsible
local sanitary authorities.
PERSONS INELIGIBLE AS RELIEVING
OFFICERS.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether the proprietor of a retail
shop or an assistant therein is eligible for
the office of Relieving Officer of a Poor Law
Union.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Under Article 29
of the General Regulations governing the
proceedings of Boards of Guardians, no person who is engaged in retail trade of any
kind is eligible for appointment as Relieving
Officer.
Mr. KYLE: Would the Minister be surprised to learn that there is one appointed in
a certain country district, and will he take
action if I give him full particulars?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would be very
surprised, and I would be very glad indeed
if my hon. Friend would furnish me with
the particulars.
EMPLOYMENT OF YOUNG PERSONS.
4. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Labour whether his attention has been
called to the decision of the President of the
Board of Trade and the British Minister of
Labour to appoint a committee to inquire
into "the arrangements for enabling young
persons to enter into and retain suitable
employment," and whether he proposes to
appoint a similar committee.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr. Andrews): I assume that the hon. Member
refers to the committee which has been
appointed by the President of the Board of
Education-not the Board of Trade-jointly
with the Imperial Minister of Labour to
inquire into this matter.
The system of education in Northern Ireland is so different from that of England and
Wales that the administrative problems in
connection with the question are not therefore identical. I shall carefully watch, however, the work of the committee, and meantime I am glad to say that in many towns in
Northern Ireland there is a close and valuable co-operation between the Technical
Education Authorities and the Local Employment Committees with the direct object of
fitting young persons for entering into and
retaining suitable employment. Within the
last few days I have had an opportunity,
which I greatly appreciated, of seeing the
helpful co-operation that exists at Londonderry between these bodies and the excellent
work which is being carried on by the Technical School.
Mr. DEVLIN: Can the right hon. Gentle
man say what objection he can have to the
appointment of a Committee of this character, and in what respect there is any
difference between the methods-business
methods-in Northern Ireland and in
England? Surely this problem is as vital
and as pressing in Northern Ireland as in
'England, (Hon. Members: Order, order).
Mr. ANDREWS: I think I have informed
the hon. Member that I will carefully watch
the situation, and if I find it necessary or
desirable to appoint such a Committee it
will be done. At the moment, however, I am
not in a position to say that such a Com.
mittee will be appointed.
Mr. DEVLIN: Why is it necessary that
we can do nothing in this House or in the
conduct of government in Northern Ireland
without waiting to see what the Government
in another country does and how it works
out?
Mr. ANDREWS: I do not think that
arises out of this question.
Mr. DEVLIN: That is for Mr. Speaker.


INDUSTRIAL ASSURANCE COMPANIES
IN NORTHERN IRELAND.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he will state the number
of Industrial Insurance Companies operating
in Northern Ireland, the percentage of the
premium income of each spent in salaries
and other working expenses, and the number
of insured persons in each lapsed during the
past three years in Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have been asked by my right hon.
Friend to reply.
At the present time there are ten Joint
Stock Companies, one Industrial and Provident Society, and five Collecting Societies,
having their principal offices in Great
Britain, entitled to carry on, and in fact
carrying on Industrial Assurance business
in Northern Ireland. There are in addition
three Companies and Societies, incorporated
or registered in the Irish Free State,
engaged in this class of business, which have

PENSIONS OF RETIRED TEACHERS.

6. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he has receievd
memorandum from the Executive of the
Northern Retired Teachers' Union, setting
forth the case of the existing retired
teachers for further increases to their
pensions, and what steps he proposes to take
in the matter.
Mr.
POLLOCK: The memorandum
mentioned has been brought to my notice.
As the hon. Member is aware, a special
clause was introduced into the Education
Act, 1923, in order to alleviate hardship in
the case of those retired teachers whose
pensions, being calculated in relation to the
small salaries which prevailed until within
the last few years, were inadequate for their
support in the altered conditions of living.
The memorandum, to which the hon. Member refers, asks that in addition to these increases the benefits of a forthcoming scheme
be extended to all pensioned teachers. Some
misapprehension appears, however, to exist
in the minds of the pensioned teachers as
the Government has not in contemplation
any alteration in the basis of the pension
scheme for Public Elementary Teachers
generally.
COST OF LIVING IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
7. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Commerce whether in view of the opinion that
is widely held in Belfast that the cost of
food and clothing in Northern Ireland is
higher than in Great Britain, he is prepared to create machinery by which publicity and attention to the matter may be
given.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Barbour) to
reply. The hon. Member will appreciate
that this question raises 'verv wide issues.
The evidence at present available as to
relative conditions is not such as to
justify the Government in taking steps of
the nature indicated. I should add, how-
I
ever, for the information of the honourable
Member that the Government is keeping in
close touch with the deliberations of the
Imperial Food Council.
Mr. KYLE: Is the Government satisfied
that the implication of this question is
correct, namely that the cost of living is
higher in Belfast and Northern Ireland,
speaking generally, than it is in London
and big centres in England, and, in view of
the action of the British Government in
establishing the Food Council, could such
action not be taken in this Province ?
Mr. POLLOCK: I am not sure that I
can follow the hon. Member in his implication in regard to the relative cost of living
in Northern Ireland and Great Britain. It
would be a very difficult matter to probe
that and to answer the question with any
degree of accuracy. I can only repeat the
assurance I have given in my reply that
the Ministry of Commerce is in very close
touch, indeed, with the conditions in Great
Britain, and is especially keeping abreast
of the investigations of the Imperial Food
Council, which are being directed to matters analogous with that which the hon.
Member has mentioned.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Expiring Laws Continuance Bill (S).
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
Mr. POLLOCK: Hon. Members must be
familiar with the procedure in regard to
this Measure seeing that it has been repeated for the four years of our existence.
The Bill, of course, is a Measure which is
passed annually, and it is for the purpose
of continuing those Measures which are regarded as experimental or indeed for any
other reasons that may appear to have been
cogent to necessitate the renewal from year
to year of the Measures which are covered
by the Schedule attached to the Bill. The
Bill proposes to continue the operation of
these Measures in the Schedules until the
31st December, 1926. The Bill is in fact
similar to that which is passed from year
to year in the Imperial Parliament, and which
is connected with subjects that relate to
matters outside the powers of our Northern
Expiring Laws Bill.

Widows', Orphans', and Old Age
Contributory Pensions Bill.
Order read for resuming adjourned debate on consideration of Bill as amended in
Committee.
As amended again considered.
CLAUSE I (Contributory Pensions for
Widows, Orphans and Persons between the
ages of 65 and 70).
1-(1) Subject to the provisions of this Act
relating to the payment of contributions (including.payments out of moneys provided by
Parliament) and otherwise, pensions shall be
payable as follows, that is to say-
(a) to the widow of an insured man a
pension at the rate of ten shillings per
week, with an additional allowance in respect of children while under the age hereinafter specified, at the rate of five
shillings per week for the eldest or only
such child, and three shillings per week
for each other such child (in this Act
called a "widow's pension");
(b) in respect of the orphan children
while under the age hereinafter specified
of an insured man or of an insured widow,
a pension at the rate of seven shillings and
sixpence per week for each such child (in
this Act called an "orphan's pension");
(c) to an insured man or an insured
woman who has attained the age of sixtyfive but has not attained the age of seventy,
and to the wife of an insured man who
has attained the age of sixty-five (such
wife having attained the age of sixty-five
but not having attained the age of seventy)
a pension at the rate of ten shillings per
week (in this Act called an "old-age
pension").

Amendments are in order in conjunction with the Financial Resolution which
was passed after the Second Reading and
before the Committee Stage of this Bill.
Whether or not Amendments which might
impose or increase a charge on the Exchequer
are in order depends on the terms of the
Financial Resolution which governs the Committee Stage of the Bill, and in this Bill the
Financial Resolution provides for a certain
sum to be paid into the Fund from which
these benefits will be paid. In the case of
this Bill, although if the pensions were increased, there would be an ultimate charge
upon the Exchequer, nevertheless treating
this Bill as it stands, the money which was
granted by the Financial Resolution would
be sufficient to pay the increased benefits,

it would be necessary if the increased benefits were agreed upon, for the Government to

Financial Resolution had contained a sentence to the effect that the benefits were to

The PRIME MINISTER: With the consent
of my right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) who
is in charge of this Bill, I rise to make a few
remarks on this Amendment, remarks which
would really be applicable to many of the
'Amendments that have been put down by the
Opposition. The hon. Gentleman who has
moved this Amendment has done what is
tantamount to asking us to place a still
further proportion on the Government's
shoulders, on the Exchequer's shoulders, and
therefore on the taxpayers' shoulders, of the
benefits flowing from this great Measure.
God help Ulster the day that hon. Members
opposite have charge of the finances of this
Province. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Mr. DEVLIN: We will save Ulster when
we get hold of them.

I
The PRIME MINISTER: Of course
realise quite well the inconsequent feeling
that exists in the minds of those who are in
opposition to a Government. I have been in
opposition myself many a time, and I do not
hesitate to say that if the figures in the Bill
10s for the widow, 5s for the first child, and
3s for the second child, had been 15s, 7s 6d,
and 5s respectively, hon. Members would
have made exactly the same speeches, to the
effect that the amount should have been £1,
and so on in a higher scale. That, of course, is
Opposition work, and our work as a Government in opposition to that is first of all to
study what our finances will enable us to do.
Secondly in whatever we do we should not
make such a differentiation in the treatment
of the people over here as compared with
other parts of the United Kingdom that we
will not be upon parallel lines, with the
result that when it comes to the adjustment
by my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) of the
amount payable as an Imperial contribution
each year, we will find ourselves saddling
the Ulster taxpayers with something which
will run our Own Province into debt.
Temporary alleviation for a year or two on
any one of the points raised by hon. Members would necessitate borrowing, and would
simply mean that we here in this generation
would be prejudicing our children who would
come after us, because we would be making
it impossible for them to have the same
benefits that the poorer classes might enjoy
across the water.
Therefore my right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews), with that skill and caution which have
characterized him throughout his whole term
of office, has pointed out to us, and we are all
aware of it, that the Bill is really giving the
people in Ulster exactly the same rights and
privileges as are enjoyed by the working
and other classes across the water, and is
carrying out strictly the intentions of my
colleagues and of myself. Not since the
Opposition came into this House, but ever
since we took up the reins of office we determined that we would go consistently on the
same lines as Great Britain. Otherwise we
never would have accepted self-government
for Ulster. If it was intended for a moment
that we were to go backwards, that we were
to drop down to a different category of social
standards in this Province, I personally
would not have been a party to undertaking
the government of Ulster at all. That being
so, here we are to-day very rapidly putting
into operation a Bill, which had there been
no Home Rule in Ireland at all, would have
automatically covered Ulster the same as
the remainder of the United Kingdom. That
is the standard we have taken throughout.
and that is the standard we propose to
adhere to. The hon. Member, who is the
most able, if I may say so, at picking points
here and there in connection with the conduct of any Government, says this Bill was
never even mentioned in the King's Speech.
Mr. DEVLIN: Or anywhere else.
The PRIME MINISTER: Supposing we
had postponed this in order to refer to it in
the King's Speech, that would have meant
that it would have been impossible for my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews to have got
the whole of his machinery into order, so that
the benefits might fall into the hands of the
people on the 4th January when the Measure
comes into force. Therefore, the suggestion
of the hon. Member, far from helping the
people of Belfast and Ulster generally,
would have been detrimental to their
interests by postponing the benefits for a
still further period. I think I have shattered
that piece of cheap rhetoric which the hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Devlin) has indulged in.
Another point which I would like to make
is this. A suggestion which comes very
frequently from hon. Members opposite is
that the Government never had this in mind
at a certain time. I myself and my colleagues feel that it is not the duty of the
Government to take credit to themselves for
this, that, or the other thing if it can
possibly be avoided. After all, we are only
doing what is right for the people of Ulster.
We make no capital out of that. We are
only doing right for the people over whom
we have at the present moment the responsibility of government, and so long as I am
in this position I do not intend to point
here and there at these great Measures of
reform. I simply say these Measures of reform belong to the Ulster people by right,

Mr. KYLE: This Measure that I submit
to the House to-day proposes to bring a
somewhat belated justice to the agricultural
workers in Northern Ireland. It is based to
some extent on the fact that agriculture can
be said to be a sweated industry. Other
industries have had their Trades' Boards
Agricultural Wages Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Second Reading.
[Mr. Kyle]
and Wages' Boards, in which attention has
been given to the wages paid to the operatives. I have only to refer to the work
done by the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin) in 1906 and 1909 on the Government inquiry held at that date into some
sections of the linen trade, and also to the
establishment of Trades' Boards as a result
of investigations made by the British
Government. This Measure which I am
proposing to-day is to make machinery for
the regulation of the wages of agricultural
workers. I think we are quite safe in saying
that this is a sweated industry, particularly
when I refer to the wages being paid at
the present time. The wages paid in the
industry itself are, in my opinion, nothing
short of a public scandal. This Measure
proposes to establish machinery for their
Jegulation, and should have the support of
every right-thinking man. The wages in
Tyrone and Fermanagh are 22s 6d a week,
in Armagh and Derry 22s 6d a week, and in
Down and Antrim 25s a week. I am
strengthened in what I have to say of the
Measure by resolutions passed at meetings
of agricultural labourers, from as far north
as Bushmills to Killough in South Down.
From every constituency in the Province,
with the exception of Fermanagh, I have
had resolutions in favour of this Measure
which I am proposing this afternoon.
I would like to say before I go into the
Bill proper that we on the Opposition Benches
have a great deal to stand in the way of
obloquy, particularly from the Press. I
think it is the duty of those responsible for
the Press to keep public opinion informed.
In other countries it is recognised as a desirable state of affairs for an Opposition to
oppose and criticise the Measures produced
by the Government. Therefore, I think it
is the duty of those responsible for the
Press to keep public opinion informed. I am
not complaining. I do not want to be taken
as complaining of what appears in our Press,
but I think so far as this new Parliamentwhich is only in existence about five years
-is concerned that a great deal depends on
the newspapers of our Province to keep public opinion informed. In fact, it has been
stated that we on the Opposition benches
are traitors. If the Government is going to
be a real governing body it is necessary to
have criticism.
un-
As this Measure may be reckoned non-Party
I would urge the Government to withdraw
their Whips and permit a free and
fettered vote of the House, and if a majority
is in favour of this Measure that the Government might take it over and be responsible
for its further stages. I am fortified by
that in being informed that this is the first
occasion since Parliament was created that
a private Member has introduced a Bill. I,
therefore, would appeal to the Government,
and to every Member of the House, to give
this matter their earnest consideration before they vote on it at all to the end that
we may have, if it is possible, an agreed
Measure.
The legislation that I am proposing has a
history. It can be said to have started when
the Labour Party in the British House introduced a Wages and Hours Bill for agricultural labourers in May, 1913. Such an
impression was created by the discussion
that Mr. Lloyd George advocated a minimum
wage in October of the same year. The
Conservative party, not to be left behind, introduced a Bill on 14th April, 1914, which
was called the Agricultural Employment
Boards Bill. This, however, did not meet
with acceptance by the Liberal Government
of the day and was defeated. The Coalition
Government introduced the Corn Production
Act in 1917, which gave a minimum wage to
labourers and established committees in
London, Edinburgh, and Dublin. It was
there that the Minister of Agriculture served
his apprenticeship, the benefit of which we
are reaping to-day by his very able adminis
tration so far as the Ministry of Agriculture
is concerned. County Committees were set
up under the Corn Production Act to make
recommendations, which were fixed by the
Central Board and had the force of law.
I think it will be agreed that during the
period that the Corn Production Act was in
force agriculture, our country's basic industry, was never in a more flourishing condition. The Corn Production Act was repealed in 1921, and since then our agricultural
community has suffered to such an extent
that we have had to give relief in rates to
the tune of £128,000 these past two years, as
well as granting loans to farmers for loss
of their live stock.
This Bill is an attempt to allow the social
conscience to determine what rate of wages
should be paid to agricultural labourers,
with whom every Member of this House has
expressed their sympathy. I think we are all
agreed that agriculture is the most important
industry in any country-(Hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-as if it fails us we are ruined,
and without adequate protection for our
agricultural workers to enable them to take
advantage of the scientific development of
the industry with the intense interest that
is being shown by Denmark, Canada, and
Australia and other countries it cannot
compete with them in the English
market. By allowing our workers to be driven
to poverty we are enabling our competitors
to capture this our most important market.
Clause 1 of this Bill deals with the
establishment of an Agricultural Wages
Committee in each county or for the estab

lishment of a committee covering the area

Agricultural Wages Board for Northern
Ireland. Clause 2 defines the duties and
powers of the Committees in the matter of
fixing minimum rates of wages for workers
employed in agriculture on time and piece
work. It also lays it down in Sub-Section 4
that such wages are adequate to promote
efficiency and to enable a man in an ordinary case to maintain himself and his
family in a reasonable standard of comfort.
Clause 3 deals with the manner by which
rates are confirmed after being fixed by
County Committees, and determines the
action to be taken in certain eventualities
by the Wages Board. Clause specifies the
manner by which complaints are to be made
to the Committees in regard to piece work,
for which no rate has been laid down.
Clause 5 defines the power of the Agricultural Wages Board to request Committees
to fix, cancel, or vary minimum rates of
'wages. Clause 6 defines the power of the
Board to fix, cancel, or vary minimum rates
where Committees have failed to comply
with their notices. Clause 8 deals with
penalities for breach of the Act and the
manner in which proceedings may be taken.
Clause 9 deals with employers who victimise
their employees for action taken under this
Bill. Clause 10 gives the Minister power
to issue regulations and provides for their
annulment in certain circumstances.
The remainder of the Clauses are largely
detail and definitions, and do not require
explanation.
Agriculture, as I have said, is still the
country's basic industry, and has a special
place of its own in our national life in
contrast to either the linen or shipbuilding
trades. Some years ago Sir Horace Plunkett,
our greatest living agriculturist, crystallised
the needs of agriculture in the striking
words-better farming, better business,
better living. It is an excellent slogan and
if adopted by the farming community in the
North, would lead to striking development
of our premier industry. This is not the
occasion for dealing with better farming and
better business, but I have no doubt that
the Minister of Agriculture is paying
attention to these two fields of activity.
Better living, without which we cannot have
better farming and better business in the
countryside, requires drastic and immediate
attention. The wages of an agricultural
labourer which I have just mentioned are
lamentably insufficient to keep himself and
family and involves underfeeding which
breeds disease and leads to an enfeebled
people, and which must lead to the decline
and degeneration of our rural population.
The other day the Minister of Labour, in
reply to the hon. Member for Antrim who

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): I have to congratulate my hon.
Friend opposite (Mr. Kyle) on the speech
in which he moved the Second Reading of
this Bill. His history of the Wages Boards,
I think, is perfectly correct, but he left out
the very important fact that when the
original Wages Boards were established in
1917 there were also established guaranteed
prices to farmers and a restriction on the
raising of agricultural rents. The reason
that farmers were in a good position at that
time was because they were getting extra
prices for their stuff during war time. Therefore, it hardly follows that we should follow
the example of the Imperial Government at
the present time without any sort of fixed
prices or other conditions that were in the
original Act. I was for three years on the
head Wages' Board in Dublin, but I would
be very sorry to have another three years
on a head Wages Board anywhere, because
it is difficult work. I myself do not believe
it does
any good for the agricultural
labourer.
The Act of 1917 was repealed in 1921, and
in the autumn of that year-that is shortly
after the formation of the Northern Government-deputations were received by me as
Minister of Agriculture from the Workers'
Union, the National Union of Agricultural
Labourers and the Ulster Farmers' Union
in regard to this question. We carefully
considered it in the Ministry with regard
both to employers and employees, and we
came to the decision that it would not be for
the benefit of the country or of the labourer
or the farmer to have Wages Boards at that
time, and I see no reason yet to alter my
opinion on that point. We could not at
that time have fixed wages without a guaranteed price, and it was utterly impossible
at that time to give a guaranteed price.
There is an alternative, the Conciliation
Boards such as they have in England, but
they would not require a Government Bill,
and could be arranged in the various counties
if the farmers and labourers desired. Only
this morning I received a resolution passed
by the Farmers' Union, and I would like to
read one or two clauses of it. It says:
That we protest against the enactment
of any Measure proposing to establish
Wages Boards for the regulation of hours
and wages of agricultural labourers in
Northern Ireland, on the following
grounds:-
We have come to the conclusion, after
investigation, that there is no demand on
the part of any substantial section of
labourers for the establishment of such
Boards.
As regards that clause I think it is correct.
We have not had in the Ministry nor is
there as far as I can make out from inquiries
in the counties, any great demand by the
labourers for such a Board. The resolution
also says:
Without prejudice to the reasons stated
above, we contend that the corollary to
the standardisation and regulation of
wages and hours of labourers, is some form
of guaranteed prices to the farmer for his
produce.
Agriculture is one of the industries in
which it is impossible arbitrarily to fix
hours of work owing to its operation being
entirely dependent upon climatic conditions, and that any such attempt could
only result in the creation of unemploy
ment amongst labourers-where none now
exists-give an impetus to the reversion of
arable land to grass, and the further curtailment of tillage operations, with consequent deplorable effects
upon the community generally by the reduced production
of essential food stuffs.
To my mind a Wages Board in the present
depressed state of agriculture would be a
calamity for the labourer-(hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-as a standard wage could not
be fixed with prices as they are at present,
except an extraordinarily low one. If it were
fixed at the present time you would have
to take into account prices and the way the
farmers have to carry on owing to the great
depression. Therefore, skilful men could
not get the wages they get at the present
time, while the man who is not able to do
such work as thatching, ploughing, and
things of that sort would in many cases be
dispensed with and the land would go out
of cultivation, as the Farmers' Union say
in their resolution, and as it is in England.
In regard to what my hon. Friend (Mr.
Kyle) said about wages, I think his figures
are a good deal lower than they are in some
of the counties. I can only speak for Fermanagh, and certainly the wages I pay to
my labourers and the wages the men living

immediately round me pay are about 6s over

do not know about wages in Tyrone, but I
understand they are 25s, and that they are
considerably more in Down, Armagh and
Derry. Hon. Members who are not country
members hardly realise that a labourer in
the country getting perquisites—getting a
house, ground for potatoes, and in many
cases potatoes, milk, and a turf bog-is a
great deal better off on a small wage than
a working man in a town, and is able to
live in comfort, which a man in a town
cannot do. No woman in a town can go out
and take a stick for a fire. You will get
very few in Donegall Place or anywhere like
that.
Mr. KYLE: There are wooden blocks.
(Laughter.)
Mr. ARCHDALE: In the country if a
woman wants a stick for the fire she goes
to the nearest hedge. I find if you put a
stick suitable for firing in a hedge it is not
always there at the end of the week. It is
rather wonderful how a labourer in the
country can live on a wage on which a town
man could not live. I certainly am in sympathy with the agricultural labourer. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) We could not do
without them, but I say a skilled agricultural labourer nearly always gets a fair, good
wage, and a great many are kept on out of
kindness by the farmer who, if this Wages
Bill came into operation, would I am afraid,
be sent off, and they would have no dole to
fall back upon. I know there are some
farmers who do not pay sufficient wages, but
I believe the great majority of the farmers
of Northern Ireland pay a wage which is
as high as they can afford to pay and at
the same time carry on tillage operations. I
would be very sorry to do anything to prevent the agricultural labourer getting his
wages, but if Wages Boards came in at the
present time instead of doing what my hon.
Friend wishes and what we all wish it would
do the reverse. I beg to move that instead
of this Bill being read a Second time now
it be read a Second time this day six months.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I recognise that this is a
unique occasion, as it is the first time a
private Bill has been introduced since the
establishment of our Ulster Parliament. That
is not the only unique thing about this
occasion, because I think it rather unique
that the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Kyle) who supported the hon. Member for
'Antrim (Mr. George Henderson) so loyally
and well when he moved a Motion in favour
of the unbought tenants, has to stand alone.
The representative of the unbought tenants
is not here to support him when he brings
in a Bill on behalf of the agricultural
labourers.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: It is not
fair to attack the hon. Member when he is
not here.
Mr. ELLIOTT: While I rise to support
the Amendment proposed by the Minister of
Agriculture I am sorry in one way I cannot
encourage private enterprise and support the
hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle),
because I think it would be a good thing if
Members like myself would take every
opportunity of bringing in private Measures.
I support the Amendment proposed by
the right hon. Gentleman, not because
the Bill has been introduced by the
hon. Member opposite, but because I believe
that if this Bill became law it would have a
disastrous effect on our premier industry.
Agriculture has passed like most other industries through a most depressing time, and
I regret to say that the outlook at present
for agriculture is not any brighter. T would
say to the hon. Member as I would even to
the Government, "If you cannot do anything
to encourage and foster our agricultural
industry, for any sake leave us alone and do
not make it any more difficult for us to
carry on."
The hon. Member who introduced this Bill
claims to have the interest of the workers,
even the agricultural workers, very much at
heart. One wonders if this is really so when
he introduces such a Measure as this which,
if passed into law, would have in my opinion
the effect of driving many more of our agricultural workers out of employment, and as
agricultural workers are not qualified to receive unemployment benefit it would mean
for them privation and want. If the hon.
Member really wishes to improve the conditions of the agricultural labourer-and we
on this side of the House would be perfectly
willing to do so if we could-he must really
begin by doing something to stabilise the
agricultural industry, and make it an industry in something more than name. I
have listened to the hon. Member with a great
deal of patience and was expecting to hear
that this would put us on parallel lines with
Great Britain. It is only a short time
since in this House the hon. Member and
those who sit with him voted against a
Measure because it was on parallel lines, so
that the parallel line argument is only
trotted out to us when it would appear to
suit the purpose of the hon. Members
opposite. In this case, however, would we
be going on parallel lines with Great Britain?
I say no, because the circumstances are entirely different. The farmer across the water
has not sunk his capital in his farm but is
only a tenant during his tenancy whether it
is for a year or a number of years, and
at the end of his tenancy can rise up and go
if the farm is not a paying proposition and
turn his attention to some other industry,
