[Mr. Elliott]
and after all even where conditions are
different to what they are in Northern Ireland has the setting up of agricultural Wages
Board been a success from any point of view.
I noticed in the "Daily Mail" a short time
ago a report which reads as follows:-
"Farmers at a meeting at Cambridge on
Saturday warned the Government and the
nation of the crisis in arable farming, due
to the increased cost of production and to
falling prices.
It was stated that 50 per cent. of the
farmers on arable lands were faced with
ruin, and it would be accomplished in the
next twelve months unless the Government
reduced the burdens on the industry.
Protests were made against a system of
wages fixed irrespective of the economic
position of the industry and without regard
to prices."
This goes to show that where Agricultural
Wages Boards have been tried they have not
been, to say the least of it, a success, nor
have they encouraged or helped in any way
the agricultural industry.
Hon. Members on the opposition Benches
must surely know that the interests of both
the agriculturist and the agricultural worker
are bound together so closely that by legislating for the worker without first of all
doing something to put the industry itself
on its feet is like putting the cart before
the horse.
Prior to the passing of the 1920 Act, under
which we are functioning here, we had in
Northern Ireland agricultural Wages Boards.
I myself sat on this Board for years, and
I could never find out any good that either
my colleagues or myself, either representing
labour or capital, ever did for either the
employer or employee. As far as I can
see this Bill would only be useful for setting
up another crowd of officials, and of these,
as far as the agricultural industry is concerned, I would say we have quite enough.
Instead of doing so the hon. Member would,
I think, be far better employed in trying
to help the farmers to secure remunerative
prices at least for their produce, and so
make it possible for the farmers to improve
the conditions of their agricultural labourers.
I may be told, as I was told in this House
not long ago, that I never spoke on behalf
of the agricultural labourer in this House
or in any other place, and lest I may be
taken as being in a false position to-day,
I state here publicly that I have advocated the
cause of the agricultural labourer, and maintain that in the attitude I am taking up
to-day I am advocating his cause.
Something has already been done to improve the lot of the agricultural labourermuch more remains to be done, but if we
proceed on the lines laid down by this Bill
we would, I think, be going very much on
the lines of the man who killed the goose
which laid the golden eggs. I have already
said that something has been done for the
agricultural labourer-his housing conditions
have been improved, and we are glad of
that, and at present in almost, if not, indeed,
in all, our rural districts further labourers'
cottage schemes have been or are being put
in operation. We have been told here that
the wages of the agricultural labourers in
County Tyrone are only 22s 6d
a week.
Representing the counties of Tyrone and
Fermanagh, but knowing much more about
the County Tyrone than I do about County
Fermanagh, I may say that I do not know
any farmer in County Tyrone who is paying
his labourers only 22s 6d a week. Labourers'
wages are at least 100 per cent. more than
pre-war wages, and by the Widows' and
Orphans' Contributory Pensions Bill, which
I hope will soon become law, a great deal
more has been done for him in arranging for
his old age and providing for his dependants.
But what has been done for the farmer? He
is at present paying at least 100 per cent.
more than pre-war wages-the shoeing of his
horses, which before the war cost him 2s 6d
cach, cost him now Ss; his rates are three
to four times what they formerly were, and
to-day we find him offered, if indeed he can
get sale for them at all, 2s per cwt., or
probably £2 10s per ton for his potatoes.
The right hon. Gentleman in front (Mr.
Pollock) tells me that in County Down,
where the wages, according to the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle), are
higher than in any other county, potatoes
are only 1s 9d per cwt.
Mr. KYLE: They are Sd a stone in the

What is the state of industry at the
present time? We are told that scarcely any
one can get a living because you are driven
out of the British market. Even your present state is not satisfactory. Wages are
down to rock bottom. Your agricultural
labourers could not work for much less than
they are working for at the present time,
and still you cannot compete with
tinental countries. (An hon. Member: Why?)
It is not because the wages of the agricultural
labourers are high, but because your methods
are absolutely antiquated, and you want to
go on asking the agricultural labourer to
exist on a miserable pittance when, if you
displayed intelligence, if you trusted your
agricultural labourer, and came together
with the agricultural labourer to discuss
affairs of industry you might find perhaps
that some ignorant agricultural labourer

You have asked repeatedly for Labour and

I have listened to the hon. Member for
the University (Dr. Morrison). The first
speech I heard the hon. Member deliver was
one following my maiden speech on unemployment, when he talked at length about the
harm the trade union organiser did in certain parts of Northern Ireland. I see now

In that copy of the "Ulster Review" the hon.
Member has contributed an article on the

working a tremendous amount of havoc on

I observe in the course of that article, it

closed down the industry.

In other countries not supposed to be as
much advanced as Great Britain and Ireland they have done things for agriculture.
Does the right hon. Gentleman know that in
Czecho-Slovakia for example, following the
Washington conference they have introduced
a universal 48 hours' week? It may be thought
they could not do that in agriculture. It has
been done, and if the right hon. Gentleman
does not know that he should know. It has
not been found as impracticable as people
would suggest. They have found a way of
spreading these 48 hours per week over the
month, and they have produced a quite feas
ible scheme. If he paid more attention to
methods in operation on the Continent we
would not have the right hon. Gentleman
coming here and proposing the Second Reading of this Bill this day six months. You
would possibly get into the frame of mind
to have the Second Reading considered today and have agriculture brought into line
with industry as the Bill suggests.
We have got this so far as industry in
the City is concerned. The same opposition
was offered to these Boards at the outset as
has been offered by the farmers in connection
with this Agricultural Wages Board. What
is the experience there? It is not due to the
operation there of the Wages Boards that we
are losing our position so far as the linen
industry is concerned. You do not have that
argument at all. I read nearly all the
articles in the Belfast Press in particular
in connection with the linen industry. I
read one no later than last Saturday night.
Speaking from memory, I have not seen one
article appearing in any portion of the Press
of Belfast, whether Unionist or Nationalist,
no matter what it was, that attributed the
depression in the linen trade to the rate
of wages fixed by the Trade Board. If that
is the experience so far as the Trade Board
is concerned why could not the same thing
operate so far as the agricultural labourer is
concerned? Let us try to get some means
of insuring at least a livelihood to the
agricultural labourer without doing any
harm at the same time to the farmer at all.
We would try to get the agricultural
labourer a decent wage, but we do not want
to injure the position of the farmer, because
we know that the farmer is having a great
enough struggle under the conditions in
which he has to live.

The wages being paid to the workers in the
shipyards, engineering shops, textile mills,
and factories, or in any insured occupation
are so small that the workers are unable to
save any money at all to enable them to live
during the time they are unemployed. From
that point of view the State has thought it
fit to set up an insurance scheme called Unemployment Insurance, and to that every
worker is compelled to contribute by law,
as is his employer. We say that as we are
compelled to pay for this insurance we should
get the insurance from the first day we are
unemployed, and not after we have been six
days out of work.
This is a Measure which should appeal to
every member of the Committee, at least it
should appeal to every member who understands what unemployment means to the
ordinary man and ordinary worker. At the
end of the first week there is no money, and
at the end of the first week there is no benefit
from the Unemployment Insurance Fund,
with the result that these people get into
arrears with their rent, with their grocer,
and with whoever they deal with to obtain the
necessaries of life. It makes it extremely
difficult for them to carry on. As it is the
intention of the Government and of every
member of this Committee that the people
of Ulster should be as well provided for as
possible, we have now the opportunity of
seeing that Unemployment Insurance should
be paid as and from the first day of unemployment. I hope hon. Members will
pass this Amendment, which will give some
little measure of justice to the unemployed.

Mr. DEVLIN: I am sure the House may
congratulate itself that it has now reached
the final stage of this Measure. I now rise
to ask the Prime Minister and the Members
of the Government what precisely is their
attitude in regard to the whole question of
unemployment, apart altogether from the
question of the payment of these unemployment grants. The Government have boasted
and they have made claims, many of which
are perfectly justified, that they have not
been ungenerous in the way in which they
have financially treated this question; but I
think that every Member of the House will
agree-in fact it has been stated over and
over again by men belonging to all political
parties, in Ulster and elsewhere-that this
method of dealing with the vital and urgent
question of unemployment is not the most
satisfactory way of dealing with it, and it
certainly is not the last word in grappling
with a problem so tremendous as this problem is. Now at the end of the Session, after
a waiting period of six months, in fact of
nearly nine months, I would have thought the
Government would have had some policy in
regard to unemployment, and that they would
have been able to tell the House what is being
done to deal with the ever-decreasing trade
of Ulster. They may tell us that we are only
suffering as they are suffering in Great
Britain, but then when one considers that
there is no unemployment in France, that
there is no unemployment in Italy, and that
there is no unemployment in Switzerland,
one wonders whether all has been done that
might have been done to deal with this
problem.
The right hon. Gentleman (the Prime
Minister) has stated that he and his Government have made no claims or offered themselves no bouquets. That is not altogether
my recollection of their attitude in relation
to themselves, because I have been reading
their speeches with very great interest, and

political question, and when they divorce
themselves from the purely passionate
aspects of our public life, they are never able

Cabinet sat down to think out for themselves
if there is any method by which this difficulty could be met. I have stated before, and

to this slavish copying of everything English,

now placed in the position of having a set
Government for ourselves-

constituency I have the honour to represent
who, because of the depression in the linen
trade and the depression in the shipbuilding
trade, are absolutely down and out, absolutely up against poverty without knowing
where to go for relief. The guardians turned
them down; the Minister of Labour turned
them down. If the Minister issued some regulations to tell these people what they ought
to do under circumstances like these-they
cannot just die of starvation, they have to
do anything they possibly can to eke out a
miserable existence-if the Ministry would
issue regulations to inform them what they
are to do it would be much more valuable
than issuing regulations taking away benefit.
I am sure very few Members on this side
of the House or on the other side of the
House have not received from day to day

work. I have a bundle of documents, about

matters that should be attended to by the

I think it is a crying injustice that

higher rate than they otherwise
would if it were not for the fact that they get
extended benefit-it is a crying shame that
these people are denied the benefit for which
they will have to pay in subsequent years.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 28th October, 1925.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answer to Question.
RATES ON AGRICULTURAL LAND.
1. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Finance what proportion of the
rates on agricultural land in Northern Ireland are paid from Government Grants, and
what proportion is raised from rates levied
on the occupiers.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): According to statements
furnished
the County
by
Councils in
Northern Ireland the total amount of
Government Grants received by the County
Councils during the year ending 31st March,
1925, was £619,990. Of this amount, which
was applied in reduction of local expenditure, £257,288 was applied exclusively to the
relief of rates on agricultural land, but
agricultural land shared in addition, in the
same way as other rateable property, in
the reduction of local expenditure effected
by the remainder of the Government Grant.
A calculation on the basis of these figures
shows that the reduction in local expenditure effected by the Government Grant by
which agricultural land benefited amounts to
£515,000, and it has been ascertained that
the net amount raised by rates on agricultural land for the year in question was
£476,045, or in the proportion of 52 per cent.
from Government Grants to 48 per cent. from
rates on agricultural land.

question will, so far as can be foreseen,

- Section 4 (2), which in general corteds with the legislation prevailing in
at Britain, the duty of setting out the
edule is imposed upon the head of the
sehold. In each previous census in Ireland this duty was imposed on the enumerator, that is the person who supplies the
paper and collects it. In practice, however,

sub-Section provision with regard to seperate
returns is made, and this is mainly introduced in order to suit persons living in
hotels who may have some delicacy about
giving information to the owner of the hotel
as to the particulars required in the census
paper. In such cases, therefore, the Bill
provides that the occupants of hotels on
the day on which the census is taken may at
their discretion furnish separate papers. It
is not expected that this will be a matter of
great importance, the probability being that
on Sunday evening the general body of the
population will be in their own homes, but
we think it necessary to make that provision lest any difficulty should arise on that
head.
Section 6 (2) is a new Section, that is new
to Ireland, but it corresponds with the provision made in Great Britain. In practice
all information which would normally be
required will be included in the census
abstracts, but it will be costly to tabulate
all conceivable information which could be
tabulated possibly from the census returns
in every minute detail. It is provided in
the Section that if any person or body of
persons desire any additional information
to that contained in the census returns this
information will only be secured at the individual's or body's own expense.
Section 9, which is more specific than was
contained in previous Acts relating to census
returns in Ireland, prevents the use of the
returns for proof of age in claims for oldage pension; that is to say, the family returns cannot be used for the purpose of
establishing the age of an old-age pensioner.
The practice which has existed in the past
of using Census Schedules for this purpose
has undoubtedly encouraged misstatements
in regard to the age for the purpose of
coming within the terms and conditions
of the Old Age Pensions Act, and therefore
in order that absolute accuracy may be
secured in this matter the Government think
it necessary that abstracts should not be
used and cannot be used for the purpose
of establishing the age in the case of an
old-age pensioner. I need hardly say that
the general purpose of this is to ensure

the intention is to produce an official year

Mr. KYLE: I want, if I may, to welcome
this Measure. It seems to me to be absolutely essential for those of us who are interested in the Government of Northern Ireland to have absolutely accurate information
regarding our population. I was gratified to

like our own-Belfast. I think that is very

Minister, the hon. Member for West Belfast

and I hope that when the information is

will be taken by the Government to see that
this state of affairs will be made right. I
welcome the Measure.

SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES 1925-1926.
Considered in Committee.
Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
CLASS II. No. 3.
SPECIAL CONSTABULARY.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£95,000 be granted to his Majesty for the
service of the year ending 31st March, 1926,
to defray the salaries and expenses of the
Special Constabulary (12 and 13 Geo. V., c. 8
(N.1.) ).
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): In introducing this Estimate
I may perhaps save the time of the Committee, and narrow the discussion down if I
emphasise the fact that the Supplementary
Estimate, which I ask this House to approve
of, relates solely to the "A" Special Constabulary, that is, the whole-time Specials.
Hon. Members are aware that in the organisation of this Force, these "A" Specials act
either as barrack supernumeraries or in
mobile platoons, and in many ways they are
indistinguishable from the Royal Ulster Constabulary. As regards the "B" and "C"
Constabulary we do not ask for any further
money. Indeed, during this year we have
been able to effect substantial economies in
regard to these Forces.
When the original Estimate in regard to
the "A" Special Constabulary was framed we
had in mind the possibility of making a reduction in the Force over and above that
which would follow ordinary wastage. The
wastage has not been so great as was anticipated, and this is largely due to the fact that
as the Force gets smaller those who were left
are generally the pick, both as regards health
and character, and, as a result, the wastage
is a good deal slower. But apart from this
aspect of the question the Government found
that they could not make any drastic reduction in the Force. The Prime Minister,
speaking on this question in connection with
the introduction of the original Estimate,
stated that the Government must be the sole
judge as to the time when reduction can be
made with safety to the community, and as
regards myself and other Members of the
Government we adhere to that statement.
We have found that it has been impossible to
effect any reduction this year by demobilisation, apart altogether from wastage. The
reduction that we have been able to make
in regard to this Force, which numbers
round about 3,700 men, has only been 200 in
regard to wastage.
I do not think it is necessary to lay stress
in this Committee on the magnificent service
rendered by this Special Constabulary Force,
particularly by the "A" branch. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Some of us have
short memories, but I do not think any of
us who remained in Ulster during that period
could fail to contrast the present condition
of affairs with that which existed two or
three years ago.
I recollect that in one
year alone malicious damage amounted to no
less а sum than £3,000,000. To-day, I
am glad to say, the figure is practically nil.
May I say, looking at it from purely a business or an insurance point of view, that what

A very great responsibility rests on the
Government in this matter. We have to
consider many things. We nave to consider
'what the effect will be on the lawless sections of the community. For my own part
I believe the time is approaching when w

Government who brought about the peace
are, perhaps, the best judges as to when
those Measures which they adopted to bring
it about should be relaxed.
I am convinced that in the action which
the Government are taking in maintaining
this "A" Force they will have the support
of all law-abiding sections of the community,
regardless of creed or class. In that spirit
I ask the Committee to pass this Supplementary Estimate.

What are the facts? In spite of everything there has been a steady material
decrease in our expenditure upon our Special
Constabulary. If any Members care to look
up the Estimates for 1923-24 they will find
that since then we have been able to decrease
expenditure to the extent of £308,000, and if
they will look up the expenditure for 1924-25

with what is being asked for to-day, there

£180,000. So far from neglecting any opportunity to effect savings, where they may be
effected without in any way materially influencing the real value of the Force itself,
the Government are strictly exercising
economy to the end which I have just
mentioned, as is shown by the saving on
last year of no less than £180,000.
I cannot say how much we appreciate
what the Specials have done for us, and I
still maintain that they are the cheapest
Force of their sort in the world. The hon.

in any other part of the world? What

what would other parts of the world give to

Take Greece and Turkey, take the Mosul

'what would they think of a paltry £1,220,000

whole. This is the best investment that

We are told here from day to day that
one day we are clamouring for economy, and
the next day we are urging expenditure.
That is not a correct interpretation of our
work here. We say spend less, but spend
it wisely. Spend it in necessary legislation
and in necessary administration; do not
spend it on luxuries, do not spend thousands
of pounds on a police force in a peaceful
country. Our contention is that instead of
blowing off that two million pounds in
powder from policemen's revolvers, and
burning in in petrol in Crossley tenders, you
should expend the money in alleviating suffering and extending the benefits paid to
the unemployed, and in not depriving, as
you did yesterday, the child of an unmarried
mother who dies at the birth of the child
of the same benefits as are given to other
orphan children in the country. The last
mentioned would only cost you about £100 a
year, and yet you refused to receive an Amendment in this House to contribute to a deserving cause such as that. We resist this
Vote on the ground that Northern Ireland
cannot afford to have a policeman for every
six families. We resist it on the ground
that it is unnecessary, extravagant, and a
pure luxury in administration.

Original Question put and agreed to.
CLASS V. No. 2.
AGRICULTURAL SERVICES.
Motion made and Question proposed:
That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£2,760 be granted to his Majesty for the service of the year ending 31st March, 1926,
to defray the expenses of the Ministry of
Agriculture in respect of Agriculture, Education and Research, Improvement of Live
Stock, Agricultural Development, Agricultural Statistics and Afforestation, including
sundry Grants in Aid and certain Capital
Expenditure under 14 and 15 Geo. V., c. 13.
s. I (N.I.).
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): Nearly every inhabitant of
Northern Ireland can remember the bad
weather of the last three years, but very
few people except those interested in agriculture understood the great losses that were
incurred by the farmers in a great many of
the counties through the loss of cattle by bad
feeding and the destruction of hay. It got
so bad in some of the counties that last May
the Government decided to give Short Term
Loans to those who had lost cattle through
disease. In May last they gave intimation
of that decision to this House, and notices
were issued all over the Six Counties that
applications would be received from May up
to the end of September. The idea was to
lend money through the banks, the applicant to pay 24 per cent. interest, and the
Government 3 per cent. to make up the
balance, the Short Term Loans to be repaid
on 31st December, 1926.
Altogether 1,209 applications have been received, and of those 942 have up to the
present been approved, representing a total
of £43,960. 149 applications are still being
considered and will be dealt with, I hope,
in the course of a week. The loans averaged
256, ranging from as low as £5. The sum
of £2,200 in the Vote is the balance of the
interest paid to the banks by the Government, and it represents the discount over the
24 per cent. the borrowers are paying.
Miller, William Thomas
Morrison, Hugh Smith
Mulholland, The Hon. Henry George Hill
Pollock, Right Hon. Hugh MacDowell
Robb, John Hanna
Shillington, Major David Graham

appoint three additional inspectors to inquire into the circumstances of the bor
rowers, although most of the work is done
by officials of the Ministry. We also had
to engage two temporary clerks. The sum of
£60 is for stamp duty on the Promissory
Notes.

of £2.200 represents the difference between
the interest payable by the borrower and the
interest payable to the bank?

able by the Government and 2 per cent.
by the borrower.

Oral Answers to Questions.
EGG INSPECTION IN OMAGH DISTRICT.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he has received any
complaints about the manner in which the
Egg Inspector for Omagh district carries
out his duties, and whether this man, who is
an Englishman, and seems not to understand the Irish egg trade, will be allowed
to continue to make it practically impossible
for egg merchants (who are willing and
anxious to comply with the law) to carry
on their trade.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): A few such complaints have been
received and have formed the subject of investigation by the Ministry. Some of the
merchants do not apparently appreciate the
duties of the marketing inspection staff. It
is the function of these officers to visit stores
and markets and to report to the Ministry
the facts that come under their notice.
Their standing instructions are that, at the
same time, they are to explain, when necessary, the requirements of the Marketing
of Eggs Act and the Rules thereunder, and
generally to give all practicable assistance
to licensed wholesale dealers to enable them
to comply with the Regulations. The
Ministry is quite satisfied that the officer
in question has a wide knowledge and experience of the egg trade, and that he is
not alone fully qualified to carry out the
duties allotted to him, but that he is actually
discharging his duties in an efficient
manner.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of that answer
by the right hon. Gentleman, may I ask him,
as complaints have been made about the way
in which this man carries out his duties, if
steps will be taken to ensure that he will
discharge them in a less obnoxious way in
future?
Mr. ARCHDALE: I am quite satisfied that
this official is discharging his duties in a
proper manner, and I deprecate attacks on
officials who are not able to defend themselves.
MARKETING OF EGGS ACT-APPOINT-
MENT OF LADY INSPECTORS.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether it would not be possible
in future to appoint Lady Inspectors under
the Marketing of Eggs Act, seeing that many
of these young ladies are properly qualified,
having been trained in the Dairy School
under the Department of Agriculture.-
Mr. ARCHDALE: It is not proposed to
appoint women to any vacancies that may
arise in the Marketing Inspection staff. The
Ministry is satisfied that having regard to
the nature of the duties, a male staff is
calculated to achieve more satisfactory results. My hon. Friend will, no doubt, recollect that positions in the counties as
Instructors in Poultry Keeping and Buttermaking are open to women students who
have undergone a course of instruction at the
Ulster Dairy School, but the training at that
school would not in itself fit a student to
undertake inspection duties in connection
with the Marketing of Eggs Act. For such
work the honourable Member will appreciate
that a practical business experience is
essential.
DEPARTMENTAL
APPOINTMENTS—
CLAIMS OF ULSTERMEN.
3. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether, when appointing inspectors under the Marketing of Eggs Act,
it was not possible in Northern Ireland to
obtain Ulstermen properly qualified to perform these duties.
4. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is prepared in making future appointments in his Department
to give preference to properly qualified
Ulstermen.
Mr. ARCHDALE: With my hon. Friend's
permission I propose to answer questions 3
and 4 together. These questions come rather
within the province of the Minister of
Financo, whom I have consulted. When it
was found necessary to employ inspectors
under the Marketing of Eggs Act, applications were invited by advertisement in the
Northern Ireland Press. An examination
was held, as a result of which a short list
of qualified candidates was submitted to the
Selection Board by whom the final selections
were made. Of the four inspectors so recruited three were resident in Northern
Ireland.

BLACK SCAB IN COUNTY LONDON-
DERRY.
Mrs. CHICHESTER (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Agriculture whether
he is in a position to state, with regard to
the Black Scab area in County Londonderry,
that the area to be scheduled will be limited
as far as possible consistently with controlling the disease. Further, what steps has
he taken to find markets in Great Britain
for the potatoes which have been grown in
this area.
Mr. ARCHDALE: The Ministry has given
this matter its most careful consideration,
and has already come to a decision in the
direction mentioned by the hon. Member,
viz., to restrict the area to be scheduled to
the smallest extent consistent with control
of the spread of the disease.
With regard to the second part of the
question, the Ministry is, through its Chief
Marketing Inspector, making inquiries as to
the possibility of securing markets in Great
Britain for the varieties of potatoes grown
in the district to which the hon. Member
refers.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: Arising out of the
first part of the answer, will the Minister
state when it is proposed to confer with the
representatives appointed by the Derry
County Council in regard to the scheduling
of this area?
Mr. ARCHDALE: I have arranged to meet
a deputation from the County Derry Committee of Agriculture at 11 a.m. on Tuesday
next at my office.

ALLEGED POLICE RAID IN CO. DERRY.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is aware
that the police raided the house of Mr.
James Mallon, of Swateragh, Co. Derry, a
former member of the Derry County Council
and Magherafelt Rural District Council,
Census (Money).
Drainage Bill.
29 OCTOBER 1925
four times between the 26th September and
the 21st October, 1925, invariably at midnight, causing such annoyance to the family
that Mrs. Mallon was compelled to place herself under the doctor's care; whether he will
state if Mr. James Mallon has violated the
law;
and if so, whether he will take suitable
action; and if not, whether he will give an
undertaking that these nocturnal visits shall
cease.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): No raid was made on the
house of Mr. Mallon, but visits by the police
were made on the dates mentioned in consequence of a complaint made by a neighbour
of molestation on the part of Mr. James
Mallon. The visits were made by a night
patrol in the course of their ordinary duty
owing to the difficulty of finding Mallon at
his home during the day time. The police
are unable to confirm the statement that
Mrs. Mallon has been compelled to place herself under the doctor's care as a result of
the visits of the police.
I may add that Mallon's conduct in the
past has given cause for complaint by the
police, and I am not prepared to give any
undertaking to restrain the police from the
legitimate performance of their duties.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Census (Money.)
Considered in Committee.
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair.)
Motion made, and Question proposed:-
"That it is expedient to authorise a charge
upon moneys provided by Parliament in respect of the expenses incurred, with the
approval of the Ministry of Finance, in connection with the taking of the Census for
Northern Ireland in the year nineteen
hundred and twenty-six, and for otherwise
collecting statistical information, under
powers to be conferred by an Act of the
present Session."
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINANCIAL
SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): Yesterday the
House gave a Second Reading to the Bill
authorising the taking of a Census of
Northern Ireland in 1926. A certain amount
of expenditure will obviously become
necessary in the taking of this Census, and
this Financial Resolution is, as the Committee is aware, the statutory authority for
charging such expenses on the yearly
Estimates. In point of fact, a Supplementary
Estimate for the expenses to be incurred in
the current financial year has already been
presented to the House and will be moved in
Committee of Supply either this evening or
at an early date.
The taking of a Census and the subsequent
tabulation of the information collected, in
order to make such information as useful as
possible for the various purposes for which
statistics of this kind are required,
necessarily involves considerable administrative expenditure. It is difficult at the
present moment to state with any degree of
accuracy what the total charge will eventually be, but it is safe to say that, in round
figures, a sum of £20,000 will be required.
Of this amount, the sum of £2,500 will be
required this year, and this is the amount
which the House will be asked to vote-the
balance of £17,500 being left over until the
following years 1926 and 1927 in which the
expenditure will be incurred.
This sum may seem high, but I can assure
the House that even with the use of up-todate tabulating machinery the amount of
detailed work that arises out of the questionnaire outlined in the Second Schedule to the
Bill will be of a most exacting character.
In addition to that we have been guided by
precedent of the recent British Census and
the former Census taken in Ireland. I beg
to move.
Question put and agreed to.
Resolution reported and agreed to.

Dr. MORRISON: I beg to move, in page 11,

This opens up a very wide question. I

to point out to the Committee is that, while
we are helping the community generally, we
are doing a very serious injustice to the
people who for ten miles in my district live

fines. They are paying a drainage rate which
is divided into two sections, that which is
levied upon the benefited area, and that which
is placed upon the catchment area, up in the
mountains where the streams accumulate.
What I want the Government to do is this,
that in view of the fact that these industrial,

"We take the responsibility for this rate off."
It involves only something like £1,000.

gates in the existing weirs
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Hear, hear.

I have had about forty years' experience
with water power and I am positive that
a few flood gates would let away more
water than the lower stretches of the river
could carry off . . . I am sure that at
some date some energetic person will develop the 10,500 h.p. that could be so easily
got on the Bann without raising the river
one hair's breadth. It is very rare to find
a river like the Bann supplied by a lough
like Lough Neagh, containing such a vast
supply of water, standing 52 feet above sea
level, and I consider it a crime of the first

a magnificent asset to Ulster.
In taking the line that I have done in regard to this Measure, I am actuated by a desire to do justice to the people who live in
my district, and whom I have known intimately for forty years. I have suggested two
plans, the putting in of these flood gates,
and that until that is done the Government
would undertake the liability for the tax.
If you put flood gates in here they would
open and drain off the Bann between the
rainfalls, and you would have a storage
capacity in the lough itself, and a storage
capacity in the Bann itself, to accommodate two or three weeks' rain. Coming
up in the train to-day I read the speech
of the Minister of Finance, and I
agree in the main with it. I also
read the speech of the Prime Minister, and
I wholly agree with it. The Minister of
Finance pointed out that even now after
the heavy rain of the last fortnight the
level of the water in the river and the lough
is practically no higher than in summer
time. I cross the Bann every day I come
to this House, and I can see whether it
is in flood or not. We have had tremendously
heavy rain this last fortnight, and the water
is not over its banks yet. My point is that
if the closed mill race at Castleroe were
opened, and kept open, and automatic locks
inserted, as I am told is done in County
Fermanagh, during the interval between the
floods, you will get a steady amount of water
set free and allowed to pass on to the sea.
You will have the lough and the river at
summer level, and then you could stand a
fortnight's rain. There is no vast engineering scheme in connection with this, as far
as I can see.
Evidently the Minister of Finance is still
dreaming that he is going to do wonderful
things by draining the lough. But I am
glad to see that the Prime Minister sees
considerably further, and sees the danger.
If we are going to rush into a scheme like

many people, and that has involved huge
expenditure without producing appreciable
results, I think with our limited resources
we should count the cost before we undertake it. It was a totally different matter
when we were associated with the Empire,
and the Empire paid these bills. What I
want to do is to educate public opinion.
I
want to educate this Committee on the
fact that there is an alternative-this
simple plan of drainage for draining
off the surplus water and keeping the Bann
and the lough at summer level. Then when
the flooding comes it will not flood the
'district.

that the Bann gives us as a channel leading
into the heart of Ulster. I dream and think
that some time we may have along the Bann

from the drainage rate to the engineering

doubt at all about that. He is asking by this

to adopt any scheme of drainage until pro
vision has been made on the Lower Bann by

work can be done by way of remedial
measures, apart altogether from the Bann
or anything affecting the Bann, even in the
Lough Neagh catchment area; that is to say
even if the major scheme which we
are now investigating should take longer
than we anticipate. I hope it will not, but
I am advised that to carry out some of the
works suggested by the hon. Members in
their Amendment, that is to say, the opening
of the mill race at Castleroe, would probably
imply that it would be impossible to shut
these locks for an indefinite period of flooding and that the probability is that the
trouble would be accentuated by the suggestion rather than improved.
I have never suggested, as some of my hon.
Friends behind me said, that we would go
into this matter without exploring every
avenue. The Government are exploring every
avenue, but I think it would be the consensus of opinion of all the Members of this
Committee that it would be very improper
at this stage to interfere with any small
or minor remedial measures generally
over the Six Counties, which, without
affecting the great major schemes, might
result in considerable advantage to meadow
lands and other places that suffer from
flooding during the winter seasons. Therefore,
while it would be impossible to carry out
the suggestion contained in this Amendment,
let me say to my hon. Friends that the
general investigation of the subject is being
expedited as far as can be, but the extraordinary difficulty before the engineer is to
take the necessary measurements under
winter flooding conditions. These have not
been reached yet, but it will be a very
short time, I apprehend, if we have a number
of heavy rainfalls such as we are having
now, before he will be able to complete
bis report in regard to that work.
and it will then be for the Government,

Mr. BARBOUR: In moving the Money
resolution in connection with the Census
Bill, I referred to the expenditure which is

This is the amount of money which we
expect to expend during the present
Treasury year on the Census Bill which has

is
necessary to make arrangements in

CLASS I. No. 8.
SUPERANNUATION AND OTHER
ALLOWANCES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£500 be granted to His Majesty for the service of the year ending 31st March, 1926, to
pay Superannuation and additional allowances and gratuities under sundry statutes,
and Supplementary Pensions and Allowances
granted by the Ministry of Finance, and
in respect of Workmen's Compensation
Insurance."
Mr. BARBOUR: If hon. Members will
glance at the Estimate which has been circulated, they will see that there are two
items covered by the total amount of £500.
The first item is for £100, and the provision is a nominal amount to meet any payments which may be authorised by my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Finance, under
the Civil Pensions Act, which was passed
by the House last May. Sub-Section (1) of
Section 3 of that Act lays down that any
pensions or gratuities payable under the
Act shall be paid out of moneys provided by
Parliament, that is, from Voted Moneys:
hence the necessity for this provision, although in point of fact no actual payment
is at the present time under consideration.
The second item is for an ex gratia payment of £400 to the widow of a Resident
Magistrate, the late Mr. Roche, who died
suddenly last Spring while still serving as a
Magistrate for Belfast. This Estimate is introduced in order to fulfil an undertaking
given by the Prime Minister in reply to a
Question in this House on 3rd September
last. The payment is an exceptional one and
is outside the scope of the Superannuation
Acts, but is warranted owing to the special
conditions attaching to the duties of Resident
Magistrate in this City during the years
1920 to 1922, and may be regarded as a
special tribute to his faithfulness to duty
during that period. I think the House will
not grudge this small grant to his widow and
six young children, which is additional to
the statutory gratuity which the widow has
already received under the Superannuation
Acts on the Award of the Civil Service Committee. I beg to move.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I only want
to intervene for a moment in connection with
the Vote now before the Committee. An
allowance is going to be made to the widow
of the late Mr. Roche, who was a
Resident Magistrate for the City of Belfast
for a number of years, and especially during
a very trying period in the history of the
city. I am not going to take the slightest
objection to the Vote; in fact I would have
voted for a larger sum had the Government
seen fit to propose it, but I want to refer to
it for two reasons. First of all we are establishing a certain precedent by giving an
allowance of this character, and when an
allowance of this nature is given I think
it ought to be given in every case where the
circumstances are somewhat similiar to
those in the case of Mr Roche.

has been presented to the Committee I feel
that when things of this kind are given the
Government ought equally to consider other
cases where a similar condition of affairs
exists. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. Sparrow's services were rendered as a
police officer for a good many years throughout the length and breadth of Ireland, and
then he passed through the difficult years
that Mr. Roche passed through in Counties
Donegal and Derry. He had to carry his life
in his hand equally with Mr. Roche. I would
appeal to the Government to consider his
case as sympathetically as they have done
Mr. Roche's. I am not raising the slightest
objection in Mr. Roche's case. I gladly vote
for the amount, and would have voted for a
larger sum, but I appeal to the Minister
of Finance and the Government to consider
the widow of the late Mr. Sparrow, the only

Magherafelt Rural District Council. I made

Mr. SPEAKER: Would the hon. Member
read the answer? The House has not heard

Mr. WM. MCMULLEN: The answer I have
got is:
No raid was made on the house of Mr.
Mallon, but visits by the police were made
on the dates mentioned in consequence of
a complaint made by a neighbour of molestation on the part of Mr. James Mallon.
The visits were made by a night patrol
in the course of their ordinary duty owing
to the difficulty of finding Mallon at his
home during the day time. The police
are unable to confirm the statement that
Mrs. Mallon has been compelled to place
herself under the doctor's care as a result
of the visits of the police. I may add that
Mallon's conduct in the past has given
cause for complaint by the police, and I
am not prepared to give any undertaking
to restrain the police from the legitimate
performance of their duties.
Raiding the house of a person at midnight
is not a legitimate part of police duties, and
I regret that the right hon. Gentleman (Sir
Dawson Bates) has evaded the direct question put to him, because a citizen of Northern Ireland, no matter what his political
opinions may have been in the past, is entitled to the protection of the law. All I
was asking in the question was that if this
gentleman has violated the law you should
take suitable action, but if he has not violated the law he should be freed from these
midnight visits from the police.
Now there has been a little bit of a dispute,
I understand, between this gentleman and
his next-door neighbour, and the police have
interested themselves in a way in which I
believe they are not justified at all. I had
better give some extracts from a letter I
have received from this gentleman to show
the way he has been treated by the police.
I believe these statements to be absolutely
correct, and if they are they are an absolute
disgrace to the police force. The letter is as
follows:-
"On the night of September 26 between
ten and eleven o'clock a knock came to my
door, and on opening it I found it was
two policemen. They asked me about a
dispute between the tenant next door and
myself."
Now I should like to inquire what a dispute
between this gentleman and the tenant next
door had to do with the police. I think it
is a matter for the law courts, and I would
suggest that the police in this district, or in
any other district in Northern Ireland,
should leave questions of this kind to the
Courts to decide rather than interest themselves in the matter and take sides. Law
proceedings were pending, this gentleman
had briefed a lawyer to represent him, and
the police were very much interested to know
the name of the lawyer he had briefed in
connection with the case. The letter states
"They inquired who the lawyer was and
where was his place of abode."
I would like to inquire as to whether it is
any part of the legitimate duties of the police
force that if a citizen of Northern Ireland
briefs a lawyer they should come to his
house at midnight for the purpose of inquir
ing who the lawyer is and where his place of
abode is. It seems to be an extraordinary
state of affairs altogether and much outside the duties of a police force. The letter
proceeds:
"Again, on the night of the 16th October.
about twelve o'clock, a loud knocking
came to my door. I was then asleep.
Mrs. Mallon woke me up and I came downstairs, and on opening the door I found
it was two policemen. They stepped inside. I noticed at once they were the
worse of drink. I asked them if they were
coming to arrest me. They said not."
Sir DAWSON BATES: Is my hon. Friend
prepared to give me the
names of the

Mr. WILLIAM M'MULLEN: No; I am

my house at the hour of midnight. They
said they wanted a statement from me to
hear my side about this dispute with the
tenant. I said that litigation was pending
and that I did not think it prudent to
make any statement until the hearing of
the case, but they insisted. They kept me
about three-quarters of an hour standing

Minister of Finance does that Amendment

Mr. POLLOCK: I am glad my hon. Friend
(Mr. Kyle) has made reference to that,
because it gives me an opportunity of making
an explanation which, I think, is very necessary under the circumstances. I think out
of courtesy to my hon. Friend, the Member

J should explain that the Amendment, as

that is, to expropriate property without compensation. It is quite conceivable that
in the river which my
hon. Friend
had in his mind, and which has a

by him, the county council, or whatever

course, that is inconceivable. I am sure my
hon. Friend the Member for Antrim did not

A conference was held with the hon. Member afterwards, and this danger was

As experiments over a period of years had
shown that the J.W.S. strain gave not only
an increased yield of fibre, but also produced
a better grade of fibre, the Northern
Government was anxious that the seed which
the Association had accumulated should
be made available for bulking operations
conducted over a period of several years.
Negotiations had already been instituted
between the Imperial and the Northern
Governments with the view to the creation
of a suitable body to undertake further
systematic bulking operations.
Pending the outcome of these negotiations,
however, and in order to secure continuity
in the sowing and bulking operations, it was
decided that the Linen Industry Research
Association should arrange for the sowing
of as much of the available seed as was
possible during the 1924 season on the understanding that, in the event of
any loss
accruing in the conduct of the operations,
the Association would be indemnified, up to
a total of £1,250, by the Imperial and
Northern Governments. Of this total of
£1,250 it was agreed that the Northern
Government and Imperial Government
should guarantee £1,000 and £250 respectively.
In pursuance of this arrangement, some
10 tons of the J.W.S. seed were sown during
the 1924 season in the Yeovil district of
Somerset. This district was selected by
reason of the immunity from contamination
locally, or cross-fertilisation, and from other
seeds, and also because there were available
in the proximity suitable facilities for
de-seeding, which had been previously
used by the Association for its earlier
bulking operations. It had been hoped
that it would have been possible to
SOW 300 acres, but, owing to unavoidable
delays, the operations began so late in the
season that only approximately 200 acros
of land could be secured, and this acreage
required, as I have already mentioned, some
10 tons of the seed that had been
accumulated,
Two types of agreements were entered into
with the growers, firstly, for undeseeded
crop, payment at the rate of £6 per ton;
and, secondly, for dressed seed, payment
based upon the price ruling in Belfast on
1st March, 1925, for Dutch seed. The pedigree
seed produced excellent crops, but unfortunately heavy rain in the latter part of the
season caused great delay and difficulty in
harvesting. In consequence of these adverse
factors a loss, slightly in excess of £1,250,
was incurred by the Association, and authority is, therefore, sought for the payment of
£1,000 in respect of Northern Ireland's proportion of the total guarantee of £1,250, from
both the Imperial and Northern Governments.
The second part of Sub-head J1 provides

500 acres during the 1925 season. The Imperial Government having signified its willingness to assist in financing this Society
provided that the Northern Government
undertook a proportionate share of the financial liability involved, the Government of
Northern Ireland now proposes to contribute,
up to a total maximum of £10,000, one-fourth
of the total outlay on the purchase, repair,
and adaptation of two suitable factories in
Somersetshire, in addition to one-fourth of
the total advances to be made to the Society
in respect of working capital from Imperial
and Northern Ireland funds.
Under the arrangement contemplated the
Imperial and Northern Governments will become joint owners of the property and
equipment of both factories to the extent
of three-fourths and one-fourth respectively.
It has been laid down that the advances
made to the Society in respect of working
capital will rank pari passu as loans constituting a first charge on the assets of the
Society and will carry interest at current
Bank rate. It has further been stipulated
that if, at any time, the Society has a balance in hand substantially in excess of its
immediate requirements, a part of such
balance proportionate to the Government of
Northern Ireland's claim shall be repaid to
that Government.
It is estimated that the total outlay incurred by both Governments during the current financial year will amount to £26,500,
of which sum £18,000 is in respect of advances for working capital; £5,000 in respect
of the purchase price of the factories, and
£3,500 in respect of repairs and equipment.
Supplementary Estimates. 1676
Supply-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
The Imperial Government has undertaken to
contribute 75 per cent. of this total amount,
and provision has, therefore, been made in
the Supplementary Estimate new before the
Committee for the payment to the Flax Industry Development Society from Northern
Ireland funds of the remaining 25 per cent.,
namely, £6,625.
Hon. Members will, of course, realise the
very great importance of this experiment, not
only from its agricultural interest but from
its supreme interest to the flax spinning industry in Northern Ireland. It is also of
wider interest, as is shown by the large share
the Imperial Government is, taking in prosecuting the development of this "pure line"
seed.
Turning to Sub-head J2, which is a grant
in aid of Linen Publicity Campaign, I wish
to state that the view is strongly held within the linen trade that the time is ripe for
an intensive advertising campaign in favour
of Irish and Scottish damask linen in the
United States of America. It is considered
that, in order to be really effective, it will
be necessary to carry on this campaign over a
period of at least two years at an approximate
annual cost of £35,000. Towards this sum
the damask manufacturers and allied interests in Northern Ireland have guaranteed
a yearly contribution of £18,646, which sum,
it is hoped, may be augmented to £20,000,
while the Scottish linen manufacturers have
undertaken to contribute £4,000 in each of
the two years.
The Government has decided to contribute towards the same purpose 10s for every
£1 contributed by the linen trade and allied
interests in Northern Ireland during the
years 1925 and 1926, subject, however, to a
maximum Government contribution of
£10,000 in either year. It is proposed to
place the advertising scheme in the hands
of a thoroughly informed Committee in New
York, and it is hoped that, as a result of
this effort, the demand for Irish and Scottish
linens in their most important market will
be revived and strengthened. As I have already indicated, the Government contribution in the calendar year 1925 is subject to
a maximum of £10,000. It is estimated that
only £5,000 of this sum will fall due for payment in the current financial year and provision has therefore been made for that
amount.
The remaining item in the Supplementary
Estimate is a novel item in Northern Ireland and makes provision for the meeting of a situation which has only
very recently arisen. The Committee
are no doubt conversant with the action
which was taken by the Imperial Government early in August to meet the crisis
in the Coal Mining Industry in Great
Britain, but it may not be out of place to
recapitulate briefly the principal events of
the past few months in the light of their
bearing upon the Estimate now under consideration.
In June 1924 an agreement was made between the mine owners and mine operatives
in Great Britain under which the proceeds
of the industry, after deduction of the costs
of production other than wages, were allocated in a certain proportion between wages
on the one hand and profits and capital
charges on the other. The agreement provided, however, that certain minimum wage
rates should be paid to the operatives even
should the proportion of the proceeds normally allocated to this purpose be insufficient
to meet it.
By June, 1925, the condition of the coal
mining industry was such that in practically
all the collieries in Great Britain the minimum wage was being paid only at the expense
of the share of the proceeds from the sale of
coal allocated to meet other costs, and the mine
owners, seeing no hope of relief from this
burden so long as the then existing conditions
continued, exercised their right to give a
month's notice of the termination of the 1924
agreement. They submitted for the consideration of the miners proposals which they
stated would enable them to continue to
operate the mines. These proposals would
have eliminated the minimum wage clause
of the 1924 agreement, and further suggested
an extension of the working hours from 7 to
8 hours per day.

The miners refused to accept either of these
proposals, and a complete stoppage of the
whole industry was threatened on the 31st
July. Notwithstanding an attempt at arbitration by the Government, no compromise
could be effected, and in order to avoid a
disastrous industrial stoppage the Government decided to set up a Commission to investigate the whole state of the industry, in
order to discover, if possible, some means of
securing economies in operation which would
offset the necessity of paying to the operatives the minimum wage which they de
manded. Pending the receipt of the report
of the proposed Commission the Government
decided to preserve the status quo by agreeing to grant a temporary subvention in aid
of miners' wages. The intended effect of the
subsidy was theoretically that the workers
would continue to receive 1924 wages while,
at the same time, the owners would be able
to work under the conditions which they had
formulated in their 1925 proposals.
It is evident, I think, to hon. Members that
any colliery which did not receive this assistance would inevitably be working at a serious
disadvantage as compared with its competi-
Supplementary Estimates. 1678
Supply-
30 OCTOBER 1925
tors, and this is the condition in which,
failing action upon the part of the Government of Northern Ireland, the only colliery
in our area would be situated. since the
provisions of the Imperial Mines Department's subvention scheme relate only to
mines situated in Great Britain.
I may say that this colliery, situated as
it is in Northern Ireland, represents an
enterprise which I am sure everybody is
ardently desirous to have succeed, and which
we hope will be of very considerable benefit
to the industrial situation generally in
Northern Ireland. It has been undertaken
privately at considerable financial risk, and
I am sure the Committee will agree with me
that the Government of Northern Ireland
cannot regard with equanimity the exposure
in its initial stages of an enterprise of this
nature to wholly abnormal competition
created by subsidy conditions on the other
side of the Channel.
I propose, accordingly, should the Committee agree, to pay to this Northern Ireland
Colliery a subsidy on lines parallel, but subject to such local modifications as may be
found necessary, with those laid down in the
agreement between H.M. Government and the
Mining Association of Great Britain.
The Committee will, of course, understand
that in developing a new enterprise of this
nature it is extremely difficult to form any
accurate forecast as to the extent to which
the subsidy will be required during the remainder of our financial year, but I may say
that, on the basis of the returns already furnished to my Ministry in respect of the
months of August and September, it is hoped
that the amount which is provided will be
sufficient to meet the demands that may actually be made upon us.
Now as to the total figure required by the
Estimate submitted, I would like to sum up
by saying that the gross total of this Supplementary Estimate amounts to £20,625, to offset which it is hoped we can bring in a sum
of £2,625, which is the saving effected in
carrying on the Ulster exhibit at Wembley.
I should like to explain that these savings
are largely attributable to the fact that it
was found possible in the course of the
adaptation and extension of the section occupied by the Ulster Pavilion to effect considerable economies in construction, thus bringing
the total expenditure considerably below
that estimated in the first instance by the
architect. Moreover, there were certain
rentals due for payment by exhibitors in the
preceding year and not actually received during that year, which fall into credit in the
current financial year, and are, therefore,
available to be applied, in the usual way,
towards the reduction of the cost of the
exhibit. This estimated saving of £2,625 has,
accordingly, been deducted from the gross
total of £20,625 of the Supplementary Estimate, leaving a net sum of £18,000 now to be
voted. I beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: I think the Minister of Commerce (Mr. Barbour) is to be congratulated
on the very excellent statement he has made
this afternoon in regard to this Supplementary Estimate. I am very pleased that
our Northern Government are realising how
much private enterprise has failed in regard to our basic industry-or rather one
of our basic industries-namely the linen
trade. Private enterprise has absolutely
failed to make arrangements for the development of this industry, and now our Government have to step in to assist private enterprise in the development of the flax industry.
I think the quotation I made the other day
from Sir William Harcourt in 1893 "We are
all Socialists nowadays"-is very true, and I
am very pleased to welcome the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Barbour) and his colleagues
on the Front Bench into the ranks of the
Socialist Party now that they are taking on
themselves the job of developing this Flax
Association in conjunction with the Imperial Government.
It is very necessary. Without it the trade
and commerce of our country will go down.
Without it the development of the linen
trade itself will be hampered, and so I welcome the action of the Government in
stepping into line with the Imperial Government and instituting a factory for the bulking of this seed which is going to improve
the linen trade.
In regard to the other item of £5,000 in
aid of the linen publicity campaign, I
heartily endorse it. I was a member of the
sub-committee of the Unemployment Committee which recommended in the first instance that something along these lines should
be done I think it was following on a suggestion made by the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) at a former meeting.
I think it is necessary that our linen should
be more widely advertised in the United
States, and I am sure the granting of this
amount of £5,000 in aid of this will meet
with the approval of every citizen in the
Six Counties. But I hope, as well as that,
that the Government themselves will see to it
that they have some say as to how this
money is to be spent, because I think it
would be a wrong policy that the Government should merely vote money to private
enterprise without having a say in how the
money itself, which is raised from the taxpayers, should be spent.
In regard to the subvention in aid of wages,
I hope the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Barbour) will see that this £8,000, if it is
all required, will be paid to the miners at
Coalisland. I was very much astonished to

find that we in Northern Ireland are going

Mr. DEVLIN: I rise as one who has not
become a Socialist yet. (Laughter.) I do not
know whether I am a half Socialist like the
right hon. Gentleman opposite, but, whatever my views may be on those questions
that for the moment are largely abstract, I
would like to say that I am in entire accord
with the proposals which have been presented
here to-day. I am glad to be able to congratulate the Government upon the fact that
at last they have put forward a proposal
for the expenditure of public money that will
result in something productive. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Any expenditure of that
kind that is proposed by the right hon.
Gentleman for the development of our trade
will have my most hearty support.
I should like, however, to say that it is a
somewhat dangerous principle to vote public
moneys out of the Exchequer without having
some say in the manner in which that money
is to be administered. These are comparatively small sums and one need not perhaps too strongly advance that objection,
but this may be the commencement of a
policy of voting large sums of money, and
I look with suspicion on the voting of such
sums out of the national Exchequer without
some control over and some power to influence the manner in which those funds
are administered.
I would like to say in regard to one of
these items, namely the subvention in aid
of the linen publicity campaign, that I was
one of those who supported that at the meeting of the Unemployment Committee, a most
excellent body that did very good work. It
was a true manifestation, that Committee, as
far as I could see, as one who never had
much opportunity of associating with
political opponents before in purely practical
work, it was a true manifestation of
how much can be done by union and
by the recognition of each others' right to

and industrial progress of the community.
This was the only suggestion as far as I
could see that could be made by the leaders
of the linen industry in Ulster, namely that
the Government should vote this sum. I am
not quite sure that the answers they gave
at that Committee as to whether their
methods of advertising were the most effec
tive to produce the results they desired were
very satisfactory. It may be that this
money is just being thrown into a reservoir
and will disappear. It may be that they are
following out ancient methods of adver
tising, and that there is a lack of that
precious spirit of enterprise or of those more
picturesque methods by which an article like
linen could be advertised.

I venture now to suggest that I thought
it would be a good thing if the Government,
or the Association with the assistance of
the Government, could appoint some representative men to organise exhibitions, and
to bring those exhibits to all large centres
of industry in every part of America, be
cause I think, from the artistic point of
view, apart altogether from the selfish aspect
from which we largely view it here in
Ulster where we are interested, an article
like Irish linen only requires to be
thoroughly known in order that it may
attract the public. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I am rather inclined to think from
what I have seen of the decline of the
linen industry-I do not want to cast any
reflection upon the men engaged in that industry, but I think they have been rather
slack. They have allowed their trade

Mr. POLLOCK: As I have been in close
contact with this matter, I think it is right
that I should give some more detailed information than has been submitted in the
Estimate, although my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Barbour) did enter into the circumstances under which the grant has been submitted to Parliament. I can fully agree
with what the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin) has said as to the antiquated
method of advertising that has been pursued
to some extent in the past, and it is because
the trade felt that the results had not been
commensurate with the expenditure on the

in the trade papers which ordinary people
never saw, did not read, and knew nothing
about, and in consequence of which the
money was lost, that an advertising scheme
should be attempted for the whole country
by means of entrance into newspapers that
were read by the housewives of America,
that is, by the people who used the linen
and bought the linen. The trade papers,
which were used in the past for the purpose
of advertising in America, were not read by
this class, and never entered into the houses

that extent the money spent, in effect, was

But when it is borne in mind that if a
campaign of this kind only produces the
sale of sufficient linen to start 500 additional
looms in Belfast it would more than pay
the amount that the Government, at any
rate, will spend in advertising. And I would
assure my hon. Friend that the subsidy
which is suggested is not given to individuals
as he appeared to suggest; it is given to the
trade as a whole to endeavour to lift the
trade from the depths to which it has got
at the present time. Something must be
done to save the staple industry, or one of
the staple industries of Belfast, and the
Government, I submit, is not going very far
when it suggests that for every pound the
trade itself pays into this advertising
venture the Government will put up a sum
of 10s. The big responsibility, therefore, is
on the trade. That is the security that the
money will be profitably expended. It is
the best security. In addition to that, in
order that some supervision may be observed
in regard to this matter, the Government
from my right hon. Friend's Department will
get into close touch from time to time with
the methods that are adopted, and possibly
also with results when they have been attained. I am going to impress on the House
this fact, that even a very small result in the
starting of a comparatively very small
number of looms will more than pay all
the money put into this advertising scheme.
To that extent, therefore, I am sure the
Committee will agree that the Government
is fully justified in the step that has been
taken.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I would just

also in this advertising campaign which is

goods in America.
I am sure there will be some attention paid
to the admirable suggestion put forward by

Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I would like
to say that I am glad the Minister of Commerce, and also the Minister of Finance, have

ment deserve very great credit for tackling

Oral Answers to Questions.
WAGES OF AGRICULTURAL
LABOURERS.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Agriculture whether, in view of the conflicting
statements made in this House as to the
prevailing rates of wages of agricultural
labourers in the various counties of Northern
Ireland, he will have inquiries made as to
the wages paid by farmers to their employees
in Co. Antrim, Co. Down, Co. Derry, Co.
Fermanagh, Co. Tyrone, Co. Armagh, and
further, can he state what steps he is preto
pared to take
see that agricultural
labourers are adequately remunerated.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): In regard to the second part of
the Member's question, I think I made my
position clear to him when, on the 27th
ultimo, I moved the postponement of the
Second Reading of his Agricultural Wages
Bill. On that occasion I said that there was
an alternative to his Bill and the Boards it
proposed to establish; that alternative,
which would not require a Government Bill,
was Conciliation Boards, such as
are in
operation in England. This machinery
could be established in the several counties
of Northern Ireland by the farmers and
labourers if they so desired.
As to the first part of the question, in
the circumstances the hon. Member will
recognise that the results of the inquiries
which he asks me to undertake would not
materially influence the views that I have
already expressed on this matter. If, however, the hon. Member still wishes me to
make inquiries as to wages I shall be happy
to do so.
Mr. KYLE: I do wish very much that the
Minister would make those inquiries as to
the rates of wages in the various counties,
because of certain statements that have been
made in this House. I said the wages in
Fermanagh were 25s and in other counties
22s 6d, and certain hon. Gentlemen said those
figures were wrong by something about 6s. I
think it is in the public interests that the
Minister of Agriculture should make these
inquiries and give the results to the House.
Mr. ARCHDALE: I will make the inquiries.
LIABILITY FOR ACCIDENTS TO
TEACHERS AND PUPILS.
3. Mr. CRAWFORD (for Dr. Morrison)
asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the
Ministry of Education whether there is now
a greater liability for accidents to teachers
and pupils than previously existed; whether
managers were warned of their liability
prior to the circular dated October, 1925; if
he will state how the liability was met in the
past for Acts in existence since 1846 and
1880; and what is the general object of this
warning circular at the present time.
SECRETARY
The PARLIAMENTARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): The Ministry has no reason to suppose that liabilities of the kind referred to
by the hon. Member are increasing.
I am not aware that any general warning
on the subject was issued to managers of
schools by the late Commissioners of National Education, but I understand that it
was the practice of the Commissioners to inform managers of their liability whenever
information was sought in regard to the
legal position. So far as can be ascertained,
this liability has been met in the past by
school managers.
Certain inquiries addressed to the Ministry
scemed to show that some uncertainty existed, and it was accordingly considered desirable in the general interest to bring the
matter more fully to the notice of education
authorities, managers and others concerned.
PURDYSBURN FEVER HOSPITAL.
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether, in view of the statements in
the public Press that Purdysburn Infectious Diseases Hospital is overcrowded, he
is satisfied that there is sufficient accommodation to provide for the isolation of
scarlet fever patients, and if he is not
satisfied that there is sufficient accommodation, can he state what steps he is
prepared to take to remedy this shortage.
Oral Answers.
Written Answer.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates):) While the accommodation for scarlet fever cases at Purdysburn Infectious Diseases Hospital is fully
occupied, there is no general overcrowding at
the Institution.
Arrangements have been made with the
Belfast Board of Guardians similar to those
made on previous occasions under which
accommodation will be made available at the
Workhouse Fever Hospital for all new cases
of scarlet fever, chargeable to the Union.
It is understood that under this arrangement at least 200 beds could be made available.
The Ministry is satisfied that the accommodation available is ample and that no
special steps are necessary at present.
HOURS OF CHEMISTS' APPRENTICES.
5. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether there are
any regulations prescribing the weekly hours
of duty for chemists' apprentices; if they
are expected to take duty on Sundays, and
if chemists' stores are open to inspection,
will he see that fixed hours are adhered to,
in order that apprentices may be allowed
reasonable time for recreation and study, in
view of the fact that they have to pass
an examination at the end of their
apprenticeship.
Sir DAWSON BATES: There are, I understand, no regulations at the moment prescribing the weekly hours of duty of
chemists' apprentices. The hours of duty
are a matter of arrangement between the
employer and apprentice, subject of course
to the general limitation under the Shops
Act, which provides that persons under 18
cannot be employed for more than 74 hours
per week, including meal times.
It is possible that in some instances
apprentices may be asked to take duty
occasionally on Sunday, but so far as I am
aware this is not a general practice.
Chemists' stores are subject to inspection
under the provisions of Section 26 of the
Pharmacy and Poisons Act, 1925.
The conditions of employment of chemists'
apprentices is a matter with which, no doubt,
the Council of the Pharmaceutical Society
will deal when framing regulations under
Section 3 (1) (1) of the Pharmacy and
Poisons Act which empowers the Council
to make regulations with respect to the conditions upon which persons may be
apprenticed to Pharmaceutical Chemists, Registered Chemists and Druggists, or Registered Druggists, and the considerations to
which reference is made in this question
will, I am sure, be carefully borne in mind
by the Council in framing any such
regulations.
Written Answer.
MISS ISABELLA HARREN, LISDEAD
NATIONAL SCHOOL.
Mr. COOPER asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether he is aware that Miss Isabella
Harren, formerly of Lisdead National School,
County Fermanagh, in addition to being a
work-mistress taught reading, writing, spelling, and arithmetic, and was engaged daily
from 11 o'clock to 3, and whether, if these
facts are correct, she is entitled to a pension.

Mr. ROBB: The School Returns show that
Miss Harren taught 'Infants and 1st
Standard children occasionally," but the
Ministry has no information as to the actual
time given by her to that work.
The Rule is that-
"Work-mistresses are required to attend
for only 2 hours a day, and, if competent,
they must assist the teachers generally in
conducting the school during the time
they are not employed in giving instruction
in needlework."
These teachers are paid a small salary
by the State for part-time service, and
neither the Commissioners of National
Education nor the Ministry ever possessed
any authority for awarding them a retiring
allowance.

Mr. DEVLIN: I understood when the hon.
and gallant Gentleman, the chief Whip
Captain DIXON: If I might interrupt the
hon. Member for a moment, I shall be glad
to give the information required. The Prime
Minister has been called to London on very
urgent business with reference to the affairs
of Ulster, particularly with reference to our
