Mr. DEVLIN: There is no business so
important in my judgment as the business
which we were called upon to decide here today. This debate or the proceedings of this
day were neither invited nor initiated by
me. I ventured in the course of my
observations and address to the House last
week to introduce what in my opinion is the
most imperious of all questions that even a
Parliament of this character should be
called upon to discuss at this stage in the
economic and commercial life of the community. The right hon. Gentleman, the
Prime Minister, rose in his place, and
recognising, as he must have recognised, that
this was too important a question to be dealt
with at the tail end of a debate, he suggested
that a day should be taken for the purpose
of discussing it. I accepted that invitation
at once, because my earnest desire is that
we may be able, if we can ever get down to
the realities-and I have not much faith
that we ever can-the sooner we grapple
with this urgent and pressing problem in its
most practical form the better. Then I saw
in the papers the announcement this morning that the Prime Minister and the
Minister of Finance had gone to London on
the evening before the debate. Well, I consider that to be not only a grave dereliction
of public duty but a most contemptuous way
for two of the chief Ministers of this Ulster
Parliament to treat this important question
and the House itself.
Now what is the mission of the Prime
Minister and the Minister of Finance? It
is for discussing the desirability of proceeding with the building of the Ulster Parliament at Stormont, at least that is the purpose which is stated in the semi-official paragraph which appears in all the morning
papers. If ever there was anything more
grotesque it is this performance. Everybody
knows that the chief depression from which
Unemployment.
Unemployment.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Devlin]
industry and commerce suffer is not in the
building trade. The right hon. Gentleman
the Minister of Labour has admitted that
himself, not only in public speeches delivered to the Unemployment Committee, but
at subsequent meetings of the Unemployment Sub-Committees. It is not the building trade that is suffering at all, but other
more important and more vital industries,
and yet the Prime Minister feels it his duty
on an occasion of so paramount importance
as this to leave his duties in Parliament, to
treat this most imperative question in the
most contemptuous way, and to believe it to
be his duty not to remain at home to solve
the problem of unemployment and the depression of industry but to endeavour to secure a palace for politicians.
What are sane and sensible men to think
of a Government that proceeds on a mission of this character for the purpose of
securing funds for the building of Parliament when, according to a discussion in the
City Hall yesterday Sir Crawford M'Cullagh
declared in SO many words that 10,000
people were hungering for houses, and that
is was impossible to satisfy the clamant
and irresistible demands of these poor
people for housing accommodation. If I
could gather anything from his observations
I found the chief difficulty was that they
could not get workers for the purpose of
building these houses, and if you cannot get
workers for the purpose of building houses
for the people-which next to the question
of our industries and unemployment is the
most vital and most humane and the most
Christian of all the ideas that should animate and inspire statesmanship-in spite of
all this your Prime Minister absents himself on this mission while, as I have said,
10,000 people are hungering for houses in
the city of Belfast.
I decline to discuss this question in the
absence of the Prime Minister. You yourselves repeatedly said in your Press that
the Opposition would be welcomed in this
House if it came forward with constructive
criticism. Our criticism has been largely
constructive. It is our function and our
purpose to criticise, whether constructive or
not. We were invited to divorce ourselves
from partisanship, and we did it in the
interests of the community as a whole, and
at this very time when the whole energies
of the Ministry and the Government, and of
the camp followers of the Government,
should be concentrated upon this colossal
question, that is so complex as to seem to
shake all minds in a belief of its solution,
you yourselves are making the atmosphere
of Belfast reek from political partisanship,
with vituperation and abuse of those who
differ from you on essential political and
public questions.
The first function one would think of
a Government would be to try to create a
better and kindlier atmosphere, and in that
all of us would be willing to co-operate. I
myself, when I came to this House, made
up my mind to be a constructive critic if
I could. I have added nothing to the
passions of our politics. I have often declined to address political meetings. I felt
that it was my duty, as it should be the
duty of all public-spirited men to be loyal,
not to shibboleths, but to the public
interests. And yet, in what way has that
co-operation been received? We have been
treated here as helots, regarded as enemies
within the camp to which we have been
elected. No attention has been paid to our
representations. You have distrusted us,
and tried to dispise us, but you are not
going to treat me with the contempt with
which the Prime Minister has treated this
Parliament.
I myself intended to-day to devote whatever time was given to me to the work of
putting forward a number of constructive
proposals to the Government for solving this
problem of unemployment. I will not do so
here. Why should I have any respect for
this House, and the Prime Minister? Look
at these Benches, half-empty. There are
only fifty-two of us in this House. Everyone of us is paid for our work, and yet there
are only twenty-two of us in this House, and
the whole Parliament only consists of fiftytwo Members. Is this the interest they take
in the poor? Is this the readiness and
promptitude they show to deal with this
unemployment problem? Is this the way
they are to be elected to play fast and loose
with the greatest and most important and
most vital interests of the community at a
time when our industries are languishing,
when our commerce is dying and when we
are almost on the eve of industrial bankruptcy? The only thing we are offered is to
have soon an Ulster Parliament in which
the death and destruction of our industries
will be announced and Courts of Law in
which an inquest will be held on them after
their demise.
What did I propose to do? I proposed
to deal with the shipbuilding industry and
to make definite suggestions. I proposed to
deal with the linen industry and to make
definite suggestions. I proposed to deal with
the coal industry and to make definite suggestions. I proposed to deal with agriculture
and make definite suggestions. I proposed
to deal with afforestation and to make
definite suggestions, all of which would have
helped the industry and reduced the number
of unemployed. I proposed to deal with the
fishing industry, with electricity, and with
many other germane matters, but I will
not do it here. I am not going to address

The hon. Member for North Belfast, who
sits on the Opposition side of the House (Mr.
Thomas Henderson), asked a question of the
Prime Minister on the Motion for the Adjournment of the House the other day. He
wanted to know if anything was going to be
done in connection with the erection of the
Law Courts, and the Prime Minister replied
that the Government were doing all they possibly could to have the work pushed on.
The hon. Member for North Belfast was well
satisfied with the answer. To show the
straightforwardness of the Prime Minister,
and his interest in the matter, he has gone
across to London to try to push on this
particular work, and yet he is accused of
insulting this House, and of insulting hon.
Members who have left it, by going to do
the very thing he was asked to do by a
Member of the Opposition. Then we should
also remember that the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Devlin). even since he
came into this House, has not always attended to his duties. I read in the papers

For that reason I would have liked the Minister of Finance to have been here, because

Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL: I have been a
Member of this House now for a considerable
number of years, and I have often heard use
being made of the expressions "Parliamentary tactics," "old Parliamentary hand
and such like things, but I must confess that
to-day for the first time I have come across
what to my mind can only be Parliamentary
tactics, or, as my Colleague, the Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Grant), put it just now,
political expediency. I do not think I have
ever listened to a more treasonable, unchristian, and ungodly sentiment than that
expressed by the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) in this House to-day.
It was selfish in the extreme-even if
it was a personal insult to the hon. Member, which I do not acknowledge, on the
part of the Prime Minister in not being
here to-day to listen to his panacea for all
these ills. Out of his own mouth he stands
convicted that he will not do anything to
help in this problem of unemployment because the Prime Minister is not here. That
is as selfish a motive as was ever put forward
by any man.
I do not profess to put forward any cure
for this unemployment. I wish to God I
could, and so says every honest man in the
country. I am now speaking as an employer
of labour. Is there anyone with one ounce
- of sense who thinks for a moment that an
employer of labour will not do everything
humanly possible to get full employment for
himself, his works and his hands? (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I think it is most
unfair that it should be harped on that it is
the employer's fault. I know I can speak
not only for my own firm but for many other
firms which I know intimately.
We are
-moving heaven and earth to get work. We
bare working at less than a pittance. We are
working and losing money at the same time
in order that we may keep our places going.
I think, as my Colleague, the Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Grant), pointed out, this
is only a political move on the eve of an
election, and it should be made fully
known to the electors of South Belfast that
they are being fooled by words said in this
House. The truth is not being told to them.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I have too much
confidence in the good sense of the people of
South Belfast and the people of Ulster
generally to imagine for one moment that
they are going to be deceived by the
theatrical display to which we have been
subjected this afternoon-because it was no
more than a theatrical display with no
reality behind it. I hold no brief for the
Prime Minister or even for the Government,
but I say this, that it is very inconsistent
for the hon. Member who has left to charge
the Prime Minister and the Minister of
Finance with going away when the object
of their going is to bring large sums of
money to this city to be spent in giving
employment to the unemployed. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I could not think of anything more appropriate that the two right
hon. Gentlemen could have undertaken, and
there may be other important points to be
looked after on the other side that one does
not want to discuss.
Take simply the building of the Parliament House and the Law Courts. Both these
works, if they were started, would give an
enormous amount of employment to a large
number of people all over the Province, and
yet the Prime Minister is criticised. I have
criticised him myself, and I may criticise
him again, but I believe in being fair to
the Prime Minister, and I think he is doing
a great deal better service to Ulster in
spending his time in London to-day trying
to get money than if he had been sitting
here listening to platitudes that have been
repeated over and over again. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I say, and I say it in all sincerity, that I
think no man could have worked harder
for the unemployed in Ulster than the
Minister of Labour has done. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Every one of us knows
that the Minister of Labour has devoted the
last four and a half years to this work, and
that he has provided employment in many
cases where employment would not have
been provided, and that he has done service
for which every law-abiding, Ulster-loving
man feels grateful.
What is the remedy these people have got?
If I found I had any remedy for unemployment I would feel I was a traitor to my
Province if I did not produce it at once.
They have had opportunities during the past
four and a half years to put their schemes
before the public. I do not know what the
scheme of my hon. Friend, the Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Devlin), is. I am sure it
will be a very eloquent scheme, but it may
not be very substantial. I know what the

I have urged, over and over again, on the
Government that there are
schemes
that should be undertaken which might give

Most people, even the people my hon. Friend

Sooner or later we have got to re-model the

I do suggest in all sincerity to the

Then there are other schemes, such as the

House during the last two months has been
dealing with that subject, but I think in an
inverted way. I am not going to discuss that
now, but there is a lot of practical public
work of that character that might be undertaken. It is of no use coming here and
blaming the Government and saying the
Government should provide work for everyone. I deny the right of any man to claim
from a Government-no matter what Government it is the right either to work or
maintenance. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The duty of every man is to provide work
for himself. The duty of a Government is
to see, as far as possible, that no one is
allowed to starve, but beyond that I think
it is unfair to ask the Government to go.
Why, take our shipbuilding, which is more
depressed probably than any other industry
in the country. What do hon. Members who

wish it were possible to increase the trade

Mr. JOHNSTONE: I rise this afternoon
labouring under a great deal of disappointment. Ever since I was a boy nothing has
delighted me better than a conjurer, and this
afternoon I fully expected that I was going to
see the rabbit finally produced out of the
hat. We did get the length of seeing the
tip of one of its ears, but after that
unfortunately all we saw was the white scut
as it disappeared into its hole. I for one was
exceedingly sorry that we did not hear the
suggestions that were to be made from the
other side of the House.
Mr. GRANT: They would have been no
good.
Mr. JOHNSTONE: Perhaps not, but still
I would rather hear even a bad suggestion
than not hear any suggestion, because even
a bad suggestion may contain some germ of
truth which may be useful and which may
help to solve this terrible problem. This is
not a problem that affects Northern Ireland
alone. It affects the whole of Europe at
the present time with the exception of one
country. Like the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. William McMullen) I had a
journey on the Continent this year, and I
got the length of Sweden. I am not saying
this as a suggestion. I am simply going to
show the way they dealt with unemployment
in Sweden for the consideration of those who
have the duty of dealing with it here, and
I am glad to see that the Minister who has
the duty of looking after unemployment in
Northern Ireland is here and not in London.
I am throwing this out so that possibly he
may consider if. In 1920 and 1921 there was
an unemployment crisis in Sweden. Unemployment increased enormously until it
reached something like twenty or twenty-five
per cent, I understand, of the working-class
population. The Government in Sweden did
exactly what the Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews) is doing now. They encouraged
corporations and local bodies of every kind
to undertake relief works, but, in spite of
that encouragement, and in spite of the relief works being undertaken, the unemployment still continued.

The Swedish Government then decided that
they would have to tackle the problem themselves, and they started works so as to provide for unemployment. I do not think their
rules in Sweden or the lines on which they
laid down those works would altogether meet
with the approval of the Labour Party here,
because, in the first place, they made the
work of the manual labour type, and of the
hard ordinary manual labour type. It was
not skilled in any way, so that even a shipyard worker had to handle a pick and shovel
the same as anyone else. Then it was poorly
paid work. The calculation was made so
that a man in a day could just about make
as much as would keep him comfortably,
and it was piece work, so that it depended
altogether on how much a man did how
much he received.
I do not know whether that was a good
plan or not, but they were able to shut off
those works in June last, because unemployment had been reduced to normal dimensions. I do not say that that is the ideal
system by which to carry out unemployment relief, but it at least has this great
benefit that it does provide employment for
men, and they are not put in the position
of drawing what after all is a charitable
wage from the State, because, although this
is called Unemployment Insurance, in the
vast majority of cases it is no longer insurance at all. It is simply what has been
called over and over and over again-a dole.
It is exactly the same as Poor Relief except
that it is given by the State instead of by
the Board of Guardians from the rates, and
to my mind it is just as demoralising in that
way as any Poor Relief handed out by the
Relieving Officer. The sooner it can be done
away with and a man can feel that he is
doing some work for the money he is receiving the better it will be for the community.
I quite accept at its face value all that
has been said about the earnest desire of
every unemployed man to find work. I am
quite sure that every unemployed man is
anxious to find work, and no longer to draw
what is after all a charitable contribution from the State, but I should like to
put this point up to the Government and to
the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews). It
is a point about which I feel very strongly.
I was very sorry to see he had taken powers
under the last Unemployment Insurance
Act, which we passed a few days ago, to
give unemployment benefit to young boys
and young men under the age of twenty-one.
When a man is over twenty-one, when he
has been trained to labour, and trained to
understand how important it is that he
should do his day's work in order to get his
day's pay, he may be able to stand the moral
consequences of being without work for some
years, as many of these men have been.
We have heard of men who have been out
of work for two or three years. A man may
be out of work for two or three years and
still retain the desire and ability to work,
but what are you going to do with the young
lad who has not been at work for more than
a few months and who then comes on to the
dole and receives this weekly amount of
money? He has no work to do; he has never
been trained to work; he is being trained
really to believe that it is the duty of the
State to give him a subsistence wage whether
he does work or whether he does not.
In the case of the older men they may be
a drag on the community, but in the
case of these young men and boys they are
being trained up as idlers and wasters.
They are not going to be a benefit to the community but rather a direct and serious danger to the community for the rest of their
lives. They are going to be turned into
wasters, and will be a perpetual drag on
the community besides providing the raw
material from which revolutionists are
made. The sooner the Minister of Labour
is able to provide means by which these
young men will not get anything at all unless they do a certain amount of work,
whether it be in trained or manual labour,
the better it will be for us. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)

there is one Member of the Government, at

In the city of Belfast we build steamers,
large passenger steamers, different in many
respects from the steamers that are built
either on the Clyde or on the Tyne. We
build steamers such as the Olympic, and
those boats. I understand, cost something like
£3,000,000. I want to make a suggestion to
the Minister of Finance, or rather to the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Finance (Mr. Barbour). I want to make the
suggestion to him that if he could see his
way to give a subsidy to the shipbuilding industry, so that some members of the great
firm of Harland and Wolff might go across
the water and secure an order for a ship such
as the Olympic, that would give work for
three years to the artisans of Belfast. That
ship, if we could secure the order, would
provide employment for all classes of
men; it would provide employment not only
for the artisan and the skilled worker, but
for the unskilled worker. 2,500 men per week
for three years would be employed if we
could see our way to give a subsidy of, say,
£250,000 over three years.
That would only amount to something less
than £85,000 per year, less than the amount
we have given as a subsidy to the agricultural
community. In return for that we would be
able, as a matter of book-keeping, to make a
dead profit of something like £150,000 in the
three years. This is a matter than can
quite easily be tested by any of your actuaries. On the one hand you would have the
subsidy of £250,000, and, on the other hand,
you would find handed back to you a saving
in the dole or Unemployment Insurance of
something like £400,000. I think that is
something which our Northern Government
should take into consideration. There is no
question or doubt about this matter. I have
talked it over with many people, employers of
labour, and, as I have said before, leaders of
the workmen, and they all seem to think
that if something of that description is not
done immediately we are going to find ourselves in a very parlous condition indeed.
We all know that at the present time, at the
rate we are driving, with the golden stream
flowing in this way, and nothing being returned for it, we are leading straight to national bankruptcy. What I want to do is to
see that some of this money that is being
poured down the sink at the present time
is directed into channels that will return
something or other, so that we will get some
return for our money.
I will leave that point and go on to another
point. I find that to-day there are over 10,000
families in Belfast who are living in
one and two
rooms. In some cases we
find that we have two, three, four, five
and even six people living in one room.
I receive letters day after day from people
who are asking for houses to be built. I
had a letter one day last week from an ex-
Serviceman who lost a foot in the war. He
tells me that he has been looking for a
house but cannot get it. He is living with
his wife and two children in two rooms. His
wife had only been discharged from hospital
having been ailing for eight weeks, and the
doctor says it is due to the conditions under
which they are living. There are thousands
of cases like that in Belfast, and I say that
the Government are neglecting their duty
in not putting forward every effort to see
that houses are provided for the people.
I believe the Minister of Labour knows
that houses can be provided. I can tell you
of one contractor in Belfast-not a very
large contractor-who has produced on an
average over three years one house in every
twenty-one hours with fourteen bricklayers
and a hundred men. He quarried the stone,
carted it to the site, built the houses, made
the streets, made the sewers, and turned
out five houses per week. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) It is a very simple matter.
After all, you know that if you multiply
fourteen bricklayers by ten you get 140. If
you multiply 100 working men by ten you
have 1,000, and if you multiply five houses
by ten you have 50. There you have 140
bricklayers, 1,000 working labourers, and 50
houses per week. Double it and you get 250
bricklayers, 2,000 working men, and 100
houses per week. Ten thousand houses are
required. In two years you would solve this
problem if the Government put their back
and brains into it. That is what we demand
from them. That is what the Government
is for. We insist on the Government put
ting their back into this. The contractors
are here. We are not going to change the
system. We are not going to have any na
tionalisation or the means of production or
distribution of exchange to solve this prob
lem. This is a simple matter. We have the
unemployed walking our streets, and if the
Government put their back into this matter
it can be solved almost immediately.
There are two concrete suggestions I make.
I ask you to take these matters into consideration. Take the people off the streets of
Belfast and find them work. Do something
for them. I meet them day in and day out.
They are on my doorstep from early morn
ing, and they are continually asking, "What
can I do to find work?" Do not run away
with the idea that the Belfast working man
does not want work. He wants it. You will
not find a better class of workmen in the
whole world than you find in Northern Ire
land. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Al-

The MINISTER OF LABOUR: (Mr.
Andrews): When the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) suggested to the Prime
Minister that we should in this House discuss the unemployment problem in Northern
Ireland and when the Prime Minister agreed
to give to-day for a full discussion I did hope
sincerely that the hon. Member had got some
brain wave, and that he was going to produce
some scheme or schemes which would help
the Government over this great tragic difficulty. Instead of that he has come here today and has made a bitter attack upon the
Prime Minister. He has accused the Prime
Minister of being discourteous to him, and
he has run away notwithstanding the fact
that he said before he went that he had a
great many proposals which would go a long
way towards finding a solution of this prob
lem and which he intended to put forward if
the Prime Minister had only been here.
I accuse the hon. Member to-day of being
very discourteous indeed to my colleagues
and to me. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
After all my Department is charged with the
great responsibility of dealing or attempting
to deal as far as we can with this problem,
and therefore I think it would have been
only fair of him to tell me in this House
of these proposals which he has at the back
of his brain. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Instead of that he and the Labour Members
of the Opposition have bolted from this House
like rabbits, placing the White flag alongside
the Red flag. The Labour Members, and
those who belong to their party who are not
Members of this House, have for weeks and
weeks at street corners been abusing me,
misrepresenting me and maligning me in
every possible way that they can, and I
thought to-day they would have taken advantage of this opportunity to make the
charges face to face and give me the opportunity of answering them if I could. If I
could not, well, it would have been for them
a great and glorious victory. I say they can
claim no victory by running away to-day,
and I accuse them of, for party reasons,
adopting the course they have taken. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Now, since I became Minister of Labour I
say frankly and honestly that I have never
looked upon this as a party question-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear) or endeavoured to
make party capital out of it. I have frequently on public platforms and in this
House refrained from saying many things
that I could have said and would have been
justified in saying but for fear it might he
said that I was using our unemployed people
for party ends. On the contrary, the
Members of the Labour groun in this House
of ours have never ceased since they came
into this House, and before it, to endeavour
to raise up an agitation to misrepresent
the Government solely to gain a little
notoriety and to serve the party to
which they belong. I think I know something of the people of Ulster, and my opinion
is that tactics of that kind are a great deal
more likely to recoil against those who adopt
them than injure the Government at whom
they are levied.
May I say this, that this problem of unemployment with which we are dealing is
produced by many causes, some of which we
may have a little control over in this Parliament, but many of which are beyond our
reach altogether. Unemployment has undoubtedly been created by the war, and the
tremendous amount of wealth spent in the
furtherance of the war. Exchanges throughout the world have become absolutely abnormal, and irregular, with the result that
our export trade has been injured to a very
serious degree. Therefore, over these consequences we, in this Parliament, have no
control whatever, but unemployment has
also been created in this city, in this Province and in Great Britain by the attacks
Unemployment. 1712
Unemployment.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
which the Socialist Party are ever making
upon capital, and which are producing a
fatal want of confidence, which is preventing
the development of our industries in the
way they must develop if employment is to
be found for our ever-increasing population.
In other words, why should men with money
invest in bricks and mortar, in fixed
machinery, if they feel that there is a want of
security and that continual attacks will be
made upon them, in the first place, because
they happen to be employers and give employment, and in the second place, because
they are capitalists, and because it is said
their capital should not belong to them, but
to the nation as a whole. Really, it is no
wonder we are faced with unemployment,
no wonder that we have so many unemployed
people in our midst. It is a wonder really,
that things are not worse than they are.
Again, we all know quite well that another
thing has injured our trade. Great Britain
and Northern Ireland used to be looked upon
as the workshops of the world, but foreign
nations have found the way to produce in
just the same way as we can and they send
their goods here. We leave our markets
absolutely open to them while they, in large
measure, close their markets to us. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) The House may be
astonished to hear that if the linen yarns
and linen goods which are imported into the
United Kingdom were made here in Northern
Ireland, constant employment would be
found for over 6,000 people in our midst.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I am glad to
be able to say that linen employers here, in
co-operation with linen employers in Scotland
and England, are at the present time
putting up a case to the Imperial Government to have the Safeguarding of Industries Act applied to the linen trade,
and I am hopeful if this is done that
additional employment will be provided, and
that some of the nine mills-very large
concerns which are at present stopped in
Northern Ireland will be started again. In
addition to those nine mills which are completely stopped, there is not a mill in the
trade at present which is not working
systematic short time to a very large degree
indeed. It is not because the employers
want to work short time; it is because they
cannot help themselves, and I do feel that
it would be an advantage to this trade,
which is faced with such a fierce foreign
competition, if, at any rate to some extent,
it were protected against dumped goods from
foreign countries. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
There is another matter in this connection
to which I would like to refer. Our trade
in Northern Ireland has been injured, and
is still being injured, by the action of
Southern Ireland. First of all, we had the
boycott, and when the boycott was removed
a tariff was very quickly imposed on goods
not only from Northern Ireland but from
Great Britain as well. That has injured
many trades here to a very considerable
extent, and it is remarkable, in my opinion,
that that tariff should have been imposed,
for this reason. Those persons in Southern
Ireland are always professing to be anti-
Partitionists, and yet nearly every legis
lative and administrative action that they
take is of a Partitionist character and helps
to build up a wall which we in Northern
Ireland find it difficult to scale. I was going
to ask the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin), if he had remained here
to-day, to use his influence with those in
Southern Ireland to have taken away those
tariffs which are injuring the trade of
Northern Ireland and producing a consider
able amount of unemployment in our midst.
The hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Gyle), in the very interesting speech which
he made referred to quite a number of
matters, and made several suggestions, which
I feel are entitled to an answer. He said
that the Government had not done enough.
Well, I think I ought to take advantage of
this opportunity to tell the House and the
people of Northern Ireland
some of the
things which the Government have done.
In the first place, I will take housing, to
which the hon. Member for East Belfast
has referred. I would like him to know that
since the Housing Act came into force in
1923 our local authorities have built 1,905
houses. In addition to that, private builders
have built 3,010 houses, and labourers'
cottages have been built in the agricultural
districts to the number of 1,500. Through
our relief schemes in this city and else
where, 1,170 houses have been built, and
under the ex-Servicemen's scheme houses
have been built to the number of 867. So
that in all 8,452 houses have been or are
being built with Government assistance in
Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I think that is a record that the
Government has some right to be proud of.
The hon. Member for West Belfast (Sir
Robert Lynu), whom I am glad to see back
again, referred to roads, and said he thought
we might do more in that direction. I would
like to tell him that the local authorities
and the Government together have been
spending just over a million per annum on
roads in Northern Ireland, and that the
Government have been giving on the average
a little over £200,000 a year towards that
million. That, again, is a great deal, when
you take into consideration how many other
things the Government are doing, all involving considerable expenditure at the pre
sent time. On relief schemes, we, with the
local authorities, have spent £3,440,000. The

The whole difficulty, with our small financial
resources is to get the money. The money
that is spent from our Unemployment Fund
is provided by three contributors, but when
the Government begin to give subsidies, if
it were foolish enough to do it, it would mean
that the whole burden would have to be

practical difficulty. But we have
Government guaranteed loans for our shipbuilders, and through that medium five ships
have already been built in our local shipyards, and six are at present being built.
as a
Mr. GYLE: Two of them are still lying
outside the dock.
Mr. ANDREWS: What I say is quite true,
no matter where they are lying. Five have

day in life. That has been done without it

Then we come to the question of the payment of unemployment benefit. I know there
is room for the two things, but the fact
remains that since we took over the government of Northern Ireland we have spent six
and a half million pounds in paying unemployment benefit, and our fund at the present
time is overdrawn to the extent of three and
three-quarter millions, and we are paying
out each week about £35,000 more than we
are receiving. Of course that is a serious
state of affairs, but, after all, our people
cannot be allowed to starve, and if we cannot
get work for them we are bound to pay this
money out whether we like it or not.
It may be argued on one side that that is
an uneconomic thing to do, and it may be
suggested that we should have relief schemes
to employ everybody. That is really impossible. You cannot have relief schemes for
women, because obviously they cannot do
work like men in the middle of the street,
for example. Therefore, whether we like it
or not, unemployment benefit must continue
for the vast majority of our people, and we
cannot get away from it. But I would like
to point out to the House that in dealing
with this problem I have really endeavoured
to do all that is humanly possible. I have
asked hon. Members over and over again to
give me a remedy. I have said that I will
claim no credit for the remedy given to me
by another, and yet no remedy of a practical
kind has ever been suggested to me by the
Labour-Socialist group sitting opposite. The
only suggestion which they have ever made
was one to confiscate the property of somebody else. They actually suggested the confiscation of property belonging to two noblemen which the noblemen in question do not
own, because years and years ago it was sold
by those noblemen to their tenants, and the
land at the present time is occupied by those
tenant farmers who are really the owners of
the land, subject to an annuity, and they are
making excellent use of it. I wonder if
their suggestion is that we should throw out
those tenant farmers and put in men who
know nothing at all about tilling land.
Mr. McBRIDE: What about the property
some of them have bought themselves?
Mr. ANDREWS: As my hon. Friend
suggests, once you begin to confiscate property there is no end to it, and there is no
security for anybody. The result would be
that things would be even worse than they
are to-day. No, the only thing we can do in
Northern Ireland, in my opinion, is this,
to go on as we are doing, providing as much
employment as we possibly can, and encour-

No. I have never for a moment suggested

to this problem of my best. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) It may have been a poor

Sir ROBERT LYNN: No.
Mr. ANDREWS- -but, at any rate, it has
been my best, and in discharging a responsible duty I do think I have the right to
get the support of this community of ours
instead of being misrepresented in the way
I am at the present time. One example I
will give to-day. A prominent member of the
Labour Party, an intimate friend and colleague of the three Labour Gentlemen who
sit opposite to me, stated the other night that
in January last I had knocked off 10,000 persons from benefit under the new regulations.
As a matter of fact, in January last only
1,886 persons were deprived of benefit under
the new regulations referred to. Again, the
same gentleman stated that in September I
had knocked off 10,000 men under these new
regulations and under the Order in Council
we have heard so much about. As a matter
of fact, only 1,000 have been knocked off. It
is these gross exaggerations that are naturally creating a spirit of unrest in our midst,
and I think that those who are guilty of
practices of this kind are indeed incurring a
serious personal responsibility. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Let them tell the truth
in connection with the work that my Department is doing. I do not care who knows it.
After all, what is it that I am doing?
I am simply carrying on on parallel lines
with Great Britain. Hon. Members may remember that very shortly after I became responsible for the Labour Department I
brought into existence a Committee presided
over by my hon. and gallant Friend the
Member for Armagh (Major Shillington).
On that Committee were many Socialists,
because I have always thought that on Committees of the kind all sections of the community should be represented. They brought
in a unanimous report and I am going to
read to the House one or two of their suggestions. One was to this effect:
on
We are satisfied as to the desirability of
continuing unemployment insurance
parallel lines with Great Britain, inasmuch as the present abnormal industrial
depression and the movement of workpeople between the two countries leaves
no reasonable alternative.
That is just exactly what I am doing both
as regards legislation and as regards administration with the full consent and approval of
my colleagues. That Committee made
another suggestion, and that was that local
employment committees should be established
in our midst in order to help in the administration of unemployment benefit. That also
I have done. I say, as I have frequently said
before, that these committees have rendered
invaluable public services. I believe they are
absolutely impartial, and as proof of that I
will speak for a moment of the personnel of
the Belfast Committee. In the first place
there are on that Committee leading trade
unionists and leading employers and representatives of the community. The chairman
of that Committee is the hon. and gallant
Member for Armagh (Major Shillington).
One of the vice-chairmen is the Leader of
the Labour group in this House (Mr. Kyle),
and the second vice-chairman-and there are
only two-is an intimate friend and supporter
of the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin). What body could be more impartial
than a body presided over by these three
gentlemen ?
When people talk about thousands of men
being cut off from benefit and the hardships
being imposed in consequence, I would like
to say that the instructions which my Department give to these committees are, that provided a man is seeking work, and genuinely
seeking work, and is really, according to the
tests laid down, an insured man, and provided they are satisfied that the taking from
him of his benefit would cause hardship
to the family, they are not to do it under
the family income test or any other test.
Really, it is absurd to say that this fund is
not being administered in the most reasonable and considerate way possible. The whole
idea underlying all our conditions and all
our regulations is to preserve the money for
those who need it most. Is there a man in
this House or out of this House who will
say that that is not as it ought to be? No.
I am sorry the hon. Gentleman ran away
to-day because I have been to some extent
placed in a difficulty. I intended not exactly

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Under Section 48 of
the Irish Poor Relief Act, 1838, the responsibility for appointing chaplains to workhouses devolves on the Ministry, and not
on the Guardians. In making such appointments it is the custom of the Ministry to
consult the head of the Church concerned,
who usually recommends a clergyman
officiating in the parish in which the workhouse is situated.
In the case of the Church of Ireland
chaplain to the Belfast workhouse, it has
been the practice for years past, with the
knowledge of the Guardians, to appoint the
Rector of St. Andrew's Church, in which
parish the workhouse is situated.
The present Rector is, however, unable to
assume duty at present as chaplain of the
workhouse, and, pending his formal appointment to the office, the Ministry has, on the
recommendation of the Bishop of the
Diocese, authorised an arrangement under
which the duties will be performed
temporarily by another clergyman.
As the Guardians are aware of the system
in operation, and as the present arrangement is merely one of emergency, there was
no necessity to refer it formally to the
Board of Guardians.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister of Home
Affairs willing to assure this House that in
future appointments, either temporary or
permanent, he will consult the various
public Boards in connection with which the
appointment is to be made, and that he
will not take upon himself the onus of
appointing a gentleman to a position at a
salary of £169 odd, which the Guardians
have to toe the line for? I hope that in
future the Minister will not take upon himself the responsibility.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
pointed out to my hon. Friend that it
devolves upon the Ministry to make the
appointment.
OLD-AGE PENSION COMMITTEE
QUALIFICATIONS.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the qualifications required for acting as a ward representative on the Old-Age Pension Committee.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No specific qualifications are prescribed in the case of members of Old-Age Pension Committees. These
Committees are appointed by the Councils
of Boroughs and Urban Districts with populations of 20,000 and over, and also by County
Councils, and the Councils when appointing
such Committees are not required to restrict
the members of the Committees to members
of the Council appointing them.
The Local Pension Committees in their
turn are authorised to appoint Sub-Committees and to delegate either absolutely or
subject to conditions any of their powers or
duties.

Saturday,

Minister is prepared to select a more suitable

the
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Inspector-
General informs me that 83 members of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary were, as part of
their ordinary duty, employed in the City
of Belfast, on Saturday, the 31st ultimo, in
checking whether licences had been duly
taken out in accordance with the requirements of Statute.
No extra expenditure was incurred for this
purpose. I regret that I have been unable,
within the time available, to ascertain the
precise extent to which, as the result of the
examination, it was found that licences had
not been taken out, but I am satisfied that
the examination on the date in question
fully fulfilled its object.
I have not been able to confirm that there
was any undue or avoidable inconvenience
caused to the motorists, and I am not prepared to give any general direction, such
as is suggested by the hon. Member, which
would exempt motorists from examination
on a particular day of the week.

SAILORS' AND SOLDIERS' HOUSING
TRUST.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if the following condition is accepted by him as one of
the conditions laid down by the Soldiers' and
Sailors' Housing Trust as to the allocation
of houses built under the Trust; that an
unemployed ex-Serviceman, who has not any
financial assistance other than his unemployed benefit, has been refused a house on
the ground that he is not in a position to
meet the requirements of the Trust, although
living in rooms with his wife and family;
whether he can state the reason for refusing
an applicant who lives in two rooms, with a
family of eight, to one of these houses unless
he boards out some of his children. Whether
it is the fact that although the Trust may
accept tenants with whom it is satisfied, the
agent has the right to refuse any so recommended; and whether he can state if English
and Scotch ex-officers, who did not reside in
Northern Ireland prior to 1914, are in possession of any of these houses.
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock)
to reply on his behalf.
I have explained to the House on previous
occasions that the Sailors' and Soldiers' Land
Trust is an Imperial Service, and I have no
responsibility for, or control over, the allocation of the tenancies of these cottages by
the Trustees. I am prepared, however, to
give to the hon. Member such information
as is at my disposal, and I think that this
will meet most of the points raised by the
hon. Member. The Trustees have frequently
intimated that the main considerations which
are recognised in dealing with the allocation
of cottages are as follows:-
(1) Amount and nature of active service
at the Front, taking into consideration
any personal distinction gained.
(2) Disability arising out of such active
service, e.g., loss of limb, sight,
disease, etc.
(3) Married men to have priority over
single men, taking into account the number of children and the circumstances of
present accommodation.
(4) Satisfactory references as to character
and prospects of punctual payment of
rent.
I may add that the agent's duties are confined to installing those tenants who have
been approved by the Trust and to the collection of rents.
I am sure that the Trustees, with an extremely difficult duty to discharge, endeavour
to select as tenants for these cottages those
applicants who are regarded as possessing,
from all those points of view which the
Trustees have to take into account, the
strongest claims to consideration.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman try to influence the Trust to let
these houses according to the plans laid
down by the Imperial Government? Will he
also see that the right persons and not, as
has already been the case, persons who are

APPOINTMENT OF MUSIC INSPECTOR.
5. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Gyle) asked the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether the position of Inspector
of Schools (specially referring to music), as
advertised in the local newspapers in July
last, has yet been filled; if so, who was
appointed, at what salary, and how long he
has been resident in this city.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): The position in question has been
filled by the appointment of Mr. T. O. Corrin
on the salary scale as approved for other
inspectors of schools below the rank of
senior inspector. This salary commences at
£300 per year, and increases by annual incre
ments to a maximum of £550 per year, with
cost of living bonus at appropriate rates as
payable to all Civil Servants.
The Ministry is not in possession of information as to the precise duration of the
period for which Mr. Corrin has been resident
in Belfast, but he has been assistant musical
director in the Belfast station of the British
Broadcasting Company since August, 1924,
and for some time previously he was organist
and choir-master in one of the churches in
Portadown.

PRIME MINISTER'S VISITS TO LONDON.
Mr. GRANT (by Private Notice) asked the
Prime Minister whether he can inform the
House of the result of his three recent visits
to London to secure work for the unemployed.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James
Craig): Yes, sir. In pursuance of the
policy outlined by my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews) in his
admirable speech on Tuesday, I am glad to
be able to state that as a result of conversa
tions between my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock), and my
self and representatives of the British
Treasury and the Office of Works, we have
secured a promise of early prosecution of
fresh work on the site of the new Parliament
and Administrative Buildings for a large
number of men of the unskilled labour class.
None of the cost will fall on either our Exchequer or on local rates. I may add that
in addition I found a favourable opportunity
for pressing in private quarters for further
work for our shipyards, and I am hopeful
that good results will follow.

Mr. DEVLIN: I was prepared to offer
the most warm congratulations to the right
hon. Gentleman on what I would have regarded as marvellous lucidity and Parlia
mentary skill in submitting this Clause to
the House. Because, what is this Clause?
It is a Clause which was proposed in the
Senate yesterday. It was proposed by a
number of very experienced and representative Senators, who have given great attention and study to this question of drainage.
They made out what they conceived to be
an irresistible case in favour of it, and,
indeed, so strongly did they feel in their
own convictions in favour of this Amend
ment that, notwithstanding the repeated
appeals of the Leader of the Senate to them
to withdraw the Amendment, they declined
to do so. A vote was taken, and the Govern
ment was defeated by a substantial majority.
Now what do we find here? We find that
while Lord Londonderry, speaking for the
Government in the Upper House, declined
to accept this Clause, and proceeded to give
not very cogent, but, at all events, fairly
intelligent Government reasons for not
accepting it-he went so far as to say that
nothing on earth would make him accept
this Amendment. He declared that he was
prepared to be defeated rather than accept
this Amendment. And the valiant men in
the Senate, who believed in their principles
on the question of drainage, not like the
Members of this House, who carried out
the characteristic occupation we have been
engaged in for the last few days of running
away-
Mr. ANDREWS: Not all.
were
Mr. DEVLIN: Except the Minister
Labour, who would have been better employed running along with the rest than
describing how rabbits ran and flags
hoisted. Now, the Leader of the Senate,
Lord Londonderry, absolutely refused to
accept this Amendment. The Government
were defeated, and what ordinarily a

Apart altogether from that consideration,
if this Clause was a clause that was acceptable why was it not accepted by Lord Londonderry on behalf of the Government in the
Senate? Why does the representative of the
Government in this House come down to
commend to us the Clause that the Marquess
of Londonderry rejected in the Senate yesterday? That is what I cannot understand, unless it is that there was no alternative
for the Government except to resign, and the
right hon. Gentleman (the Prime Minister)
says that that is the last thing he will do.
I really cannot follow this method of Parliamentary procedure on the part of the Government in saying, "The thing is so bad that
we are prepared to stake our reputation and
the position of the Government on it before
we accept it," and then a few hours afterwards they send down a gentleman who is,
in my judgment, selected to do all the nasty
jobs because he is a very respectable and
very tactful Minister, but he is too honest to
say anything good about it. He could not
say anything good in this House to-day about
what was so bad in the Senate yesterday,
and, therefore, with a smile he presents to

us, not with the irresistible logic that ought
to be offered in the advancement of the great
cause which is incorporated in this Clause,
but with a smile he comes down here and
says, Gentlemen of the Lower House, or
the Higher House, or whatever House you
belong to, here is a Clause that was so bad
yesterday that we were prepared to take defeat rather than carry it, and seeing it was
so bad yesterday we ask you to pass it to-day
because it is so good."
That, in my opinion, is a position which
is perfectly unprecedented in the history of

I have already made. I suggested on the last

Mr. SPEAKER: I am very sorry, but I
cannot allow the hon. Member (Mr. Devlin)
to enter on a general discussion of the Bill.
It would set up an impossible precedent if,
when a Bill came back from the Senate, we

Mr. DEVLIN: I have finished.
The PRIME MINISTER: A great deal of
heat has been engendered in this debate
quite unnecessarily. The Bill, as a Bill, has
passed both Houses without a division. The
Amendment we are speaking upon at the
present moment is a Government Amendment, put forward by the Government in the
Senate, and accepted by the Senate, in lieu
of one put forward by a private Member
yesterday. There is no difference between
the Government Amendment put forward in
this House and the Amendment put forward
by the Government in the other House.
There is nothing extraordinary about what
has occurred, except that we have, after
careful consideration, decided to put forward
a Clause giving the public extra protection,
if necessary, as explained in this particular
Amendment. We did not think, however,
it was necessary before, in fact, we thought
the first arrangement was probably cheaper
to the public, as a whole, but in consequence
of a conference and general agreement all
round, it was thought this would probably
be the best way. When the Government put
it forward in the Senate, the Senate carried
it, and passed the Bill without any other
serious Amendment. They passed it unanimously, the same as this House. It seems to
me that really a great pother has been made
over a very small matter.

to us.

1751 Unemployment Benefit Regulations. HOUSE OF COMMONS Unemployment Benefit Regulations.1752

Unemployment Benefit Regulations.
MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Captain Mulholland).
Mr. BEATTIE: I wish to draw the
attention of the House to the very grave
situation which now prevails amongst the
unemployed in the City of Belfast. I may
say that upwards of 14,000 people are unemployed and in a state of starvation, and
some are dying by their own hands through
being driven to desperation through lack of
assistance. I hope this House will agree either
to suspend or amend the regulations which
the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews), with
his small Committee, is applying to the
class of worker to whom I refer, that is the
single men and women and the youths of our
city. You have heard, or if you have read
your papers you have read of the case of the
ex-Navy man who committed suicide. That
is only one case of many who are dying as
a result of the regulations which the
Minister of Labour has applied to Unemployment Insurance Benefit.
I can speak personally of the poor chap
who was buried this morning. There are
four sons in that family who joined up in
1914, and went to the war. One of them at
present is disabled by gunshot wounds, the
other brother has returned home and is dying
of consumption, and there is an old woman,
the old mother, of eighty years of age who
was dependent on the little assistance that
was coming into the home from the source
of extended benefit. The regulations denied
that poor soul the right to extended benefit
and brought upon him in a weak moment
his own hand to shorten his life, as you have
perhaps seen in last night's paper.
What do I ask the Minister to do, or what
does the Minister propose to do? I will
tell you.
The Minister of Labour has had
repeated requests from the Opposition
benches to increase the standard of the
family income from the minimum of 36s for a
man and woman. We have repeatedly asked
him to increase that, but we find that he has
refused the request on the recommendation
of the small Committee which he appointed.
They have reduced the family income for a
man, his wife, and three children by 68 per
week. The ultimate result of that is something most serious, and I am rather afraid,
if those regulations are put into operation,
of what the outcome may be for these distressed people, who are going to suffer
similarly to the case I have already referred
to and be struck off altogether.
I ask the Minister to suspend these regulations and to restore the benefits to
between 13,000 and 14,000 persons to whom
he has denied benefit. Failing the restoration of benefit to these people it will be very
hard to know what the end of it will be.
We have 7,825 people denied the right to
benefit for not genuinely seeking work; we
have 2,886 denied the right to benefit through
other causes; and then we have 1,116 denied
the right to benefit by the Courts of Referees.
That is not taking into account the number
of persons turned down by headquarters
themselves, which is the most serious point
in the regulations under which we are now
suffering. I do not say that, perhaps, some
of the cases that have been turned down
have not been turned down justly, but I do
say that to many of these people a very grave
injustice has been done.
We will take what the Minister proposes
to do. I have the names of the Committee,
and, just in passing, I would have preferred
if the Minister had got a city man or a local
man, who understood the conditions prevailing in the working-class homes, to
sit on that Committee with him. Perhaps
he would have been able to give good advice
and counsel and we might have had different
regulations to what we have. But another
serious problem in the regulations for me
is that the Minister is going to deny every
married woman the right to benefit if her
husband is working and earning 40s per
week, although she is an industrial worker
and will always have to continue at industrial work owing to the nature of her man's
employment. I think that is a grave scandal
that a contributor, who has contributed for
years, after she exceeds her standard benefit
is not going to be given the right to
extended benefit for which she would be
expected to pay whilst in employment.
The old scale of family income for a man
and wife was 36s. What do the Minister
and the Committee recommend? They recommend that the scale of family income
for husband and wife and three children
should be 40s. I do not know, but I would
ask the Minister (Mr. Andrews) and his
colleague (Mr. Gordon) to try and keep their
wives and three children on 40s. Let them see
if they can keep their homes on 40s. If they
do that on a month's trial, perhaps they will
come to a different conclusion to the one
they have arrived at, and which they are
putting into operation against the poor, unfortunates out of work through no fault of
their own. That is one case. But take the
case of a man who has had the opportunity
of serving his time to a trade. This tradesman has perhaps £3 per week. He has a son
of 18 or 20 years of age. Because that man
has £3 a week, the son, who was drawing the
Bureau, is going to be struck off, with the
result that his father is expected to keep
him.
Dr. MORRISON: Quite right.
1753 Unemployment Benefit Regulations 6 NOVEMBER 1925 Unemployment Benefit Regulations 1754
Mr. BEATTIE: How many of your sons do
you keep?
Dr. MORRISON: I kept them all.
Mr. BEATTIE: And you put them into
good jobs. I am only speaking about the
rights of the people. It is their money. The
Minister has only the distribution of it. It
does not belong to him. It belongs to the
people, and the people have the right to get
the money in time of need. We extend the
hand of generosity to the children. The
Minister has not only reduced the allowance
to heads of families, but he has taken for
the children the bare pittance that this House
granted under the Widows' and Orphans'
Pensions Bill. Three shillings per week is
the minimum he is going to allow. The
minimum prior to these regulations coming
in was 3s 4d. The minimum is now down to
3s. I thought that the little sum I suggested
to the Minister (Mr. Andrews) and the hon.
Member (Mr. Gordon) would have had some
weight with them, and that they would have
discovered 3s was not sufficient to keep a cat
let alone sufficient to keep a child.
Committee go further, and say:
The
That where the total income of a family
provides a sum for each member of the
family which does not exceed the sum laid
down in the mimimum scale, the claim
should be ordinarily allowed. Where such
sum exceeds the sum laid down in the
maximum scale, the claim to be disallowed
by the officers of the Department.
This means that there is no right of appeal
whatever. We had at one time to curtail
the activities of the officers of the Department in cutting off benefit, but this power
is going to be restored, and the officers of
the Department will have the right to turn
these people off extended benefit.
Cases between minimum and maximum
to be referred to the Rota Committee, and
dealt with on their merits, but in considering the sum to be provided for each
member of the family the mean scale
should not be exceeded, unless there are
in the opinion of the Committee exceptional circumstances, e.g., high rent, sickness.
They make provision for high rents, but I
do not know how much they allow for sickness. The doctors' fees at the present time
are very high.
Mr. KYLE: You have a good Trade Union.
Mr. BEATTIE: When you want to keep
your child from school for a day you pay
2s 6d for a "line," and 2s 6d for a bottle,
and that makes 5s.
Mr. KYLE: It is a shame.
Mr. BEATTIE: It is a shame, but we are
not in a position to stop it. The doctors are
like lawyers, they are well combined.
That these scales should not apply to single
persons of the age of 22 and upwards,
unless exceptional circumstances become
known.
That is the only redeeming thing I see the
Sub-Committee have done. I am pleased that
they have come very near the age suggested
by myself on the occasion that the last scale
was drawn up, that is 21 years. You extended that to 25, and now you have brought
it down to 22, but there is a condition
attached to it, and he will be a good man
who at 22 years of age gets the benefit.
That the claims of married women living
with their husbands who are in full time
employment should be disallowed unless in
exceptional circumstances.
Here is the funny part about it. We think
we have all the wisdom in this House. We
think we can carry out the ideals that would
be carried out in a perfect State, but the
fact is, as we have often accused you, that
you are copying methods that will lead you
to destruction. There is now a prescribed
form to be sent to the applicant for the purpose of getting a return of the family income.
The prescribed form in operation in Northern Ireland to-day is all sufficient. Why
under the sun they are going to Liverpool
to get another prescribed form for this area
I do not know and cannot understand.
That a form of declaration regarding family
income on the lines of the form in use in
Liverpool, but modified to meet local requirements, should be substituted for the
form at present in use.
May I deliberately say that the new form is
intentionally meant to implicate honest
people or innocent people who do not actually
know the amount of earnings coming into
the home. If they make a false declaration
on the new form they will be brought before
a magistrate and fined severely. I do not
see that there is anything in the Regulations
which will tend towards doing any good. If
this is the result of the appeal from the
Opposition, it would have been far better to
have declared at the last election that you
wanted no Opposition. You have men here
who live among the people, who know their
conditions, and who could give you an idea
of what happens in the workers' homes, and
yet this is the reply that you send us. It
looks as if you thought we were talking
tommy rot.
Let me give you an instance of one member
of the Committee who is a working man and
who knows what it is to keep a home--I refer
to Councillor Harry Midgley. He protested
against the Regulations and left your meeting; but before that he tabled an Amendment providing for a family scale which was
just, but not too generous. Why the Committee could not accept that Amendment in-
1755 Unemployment Benefit Regulations. HOUSE OF COMMONS. Unemployment Benefit Regulations.1756

[Mr. Beattie]
stead of adopting what they did I do not
know, and I was taken by surprise at the
attitude of the Committee.
Before sitting down let me say that the
outcome is going to be most serious to the
City of Belfast. I represent an industrial
constituency. I represent a large percentage
of these people who are being denied the
right of benefit, and I am not going to be
silent in this House or outside when I see
these people suffering and dying from starvation. The result of their deaths, although
certified to be from natural causes, is really
due to starvation caused through the stringent Regulations that have been put into
operation by the Minister of Labour in the
year 1925. We may be contradicted in the
numbers we give, but I would refer the
Minister of Labour to the answer he gave to
a question of mine on the 16th October
(Hansard, No. 20) as to how many were disallowed benefit. He gave the numbers then,
but since that date others have been added
to them. Many thousands more have been
turned down at headquarters. I say here
and now that if you do not remove these
stringent Regulations, and if you dare to put
them into operation, well you will have to
bear the result, and that result I hope to
bring about. That is all I have to say.

Is there a man in this House who thinks
for a moment that that unfortunate man
committed suicide because he lost his unemployment insurance. I have seen many
cases of people suffering from insanity. The
great majority who do suffer in that way
have an obsession. They may
have the
illusion that no matter how wealthy they

will end up in destitution and poverty. You

In conclusion, I would only add that in
pursuance of my duties as Minister of
Labour I have a most difficult task, and
what I mean to do to the end is to hold
the balance fairly in the interests of all
classes of the community. It is my duty
to care not only for those who are entitled
to benefit, and whom I always desire to
see getting benefit, but to protect the fund
against abuse, and hold the balance fairly
as between the beneficiaries and the contributors. As trustee of the fund I can adopt
no other course, and from it I am not going
to depart by one hair's breadth, no matter
what charges are levelled against me, true
or untrue.

I come now to two points raised by the hon.

we to determine when a man is not looking
for work. A perfectly reasonable question
and an exceedingly difficult question for me
to answer, inasmuch as all claims for unemployed benefit are placed before committees.
Statutory claims are dealt with by the superintendent of the exchange or an officer in
the Department. When a man's claim is perfectly straight, when he has contributions to
his credit his claim is looked upon as a perfectly legitimate claim and is granted. But
if the man has exhausted all his right to what
is known as statutory benefit then his case,
with the history of his claim, is submitted
to what has been termed in the House here
this afternoon as the Rota Committee. This
Rota Committee is representative of the
various trade union organisations in the city,
represented by the employers and represented
by public bodies, and when the claim comes
before the Committee, it is examined by this
particular Committee, and every committee
determines from their particular standpoint
whether that man or woman is entitled to
benefit.

For instance, I have even come across committees who demanded that the applicants

benefit. But it is entirely outside the province
of the Minister of Labour or myself to interfere directly with the work of the Rota Committee by suggesting to them what they should

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 10th November, 1925.
The House met at Twelve of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Paper Presented to Parliament.
Ministry of Home Affairs:
The Northern Ireland Winter Assize
Order, 1925.
Oral Answers to Questions.
SINN FEIN FLAG AT HILLSBOROUGH.
1. Mr. T. W. McMULLAN asked the Minister
of Home Affairs what information the police
have gathered with regard to the Sinn Fein
flag which was placed in a tree at the residence of Mr. McGiffard, Crumlin Lodge, Hillsborough, on the occasion of His Grace the
Governor's official entrance into residence at
Hillsborough Castle, and what steps the
authorities have taken, or propose to take,
against the perpetrators.
.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The facts of the incident referred to in this question are as follow:-
Information was conveyed to the police on
the morning of the 10th ultimo that a Sinn
Fein flag was flying from a tree in the avenue
of the residence referred to, and the police
had the flag immediately removed.
Every effort is being made to make the
persons who were responsible for this outrage
amenable. It would, however, be contrary
to the public interest to indicate what steps
have been, or may be, taken by the authorities in the case.
Mr. DEVLIN: Hurrah!
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Would the
Minister of Home Affairs state whether it is
a fact that a white blackbird was observed
on the same occasion?
Mr. DEVLIN: Or a rebellion?
LISBURN URBAN COUNCIL AND FAIR
WAGES CLAUSE.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he will take action to prevent
the Lisburn Urban Council giving a contract
to the "Herald " Office, Lisburn, as this
firm does not comply with the Fair Wages
Clause in the payment of the employees.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As already pointed
out in this House on the 15th May of last
year, instructions were issued to all local
authorities recommending the inclusion of
"Fair Wages Clauses" in contracts entered
into by local authorities.
The Lisburn Urban District Council are
well aware of these recommendations, which
are still in operation, but the Ministry of
Home Affairs has no power to compel them
to adopt them.
Mr. KYLE: In view of the fact that this
Urban Council refuses to put into operation
the Fair Wages Clause, would the Home
Secretary not take power to compel them to
observe it in their contracts?

SALARY OF ATTORNEY-GENERAL.
3. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Prime
Minister whether, in the interests of public
economy, he can introduce legislation so that
the salary of the incoming Attorney-General
shall be at least £1,000 less than that paid to
his predecessor.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I will take this question for my
right hon. Friend.
The reply to my hon. Friend's question is
in the negative. In view of the fact that this
House so recently as 1923 unanimously gave
legislative sanction to the increase of the
salary of the Attorney-General, the Government do not propose to make any change.
The House will not need to be reminded that
the gentlemen who from time to time fulfil
the duties of Attorney-General have all
attained to a position of high eminence in
their profession, and that their acceptance
of office deprives them of a large part of a
lucrative practice at the Bar.

the simple one of good taste and good order,
that if charges were made upon one side as

so charged was entitled to the courtesy of a
fair and patient hearing. That was the
only observation I made, and I put it, not
only to the good sense of the House as a
whole, but to the hon. Member for East

Motion made and Question proposed:

satisfaction of Mr. Speaker, after consultation with the Government, that the public
interest requires that the House should meet

Tuesday. I came to the House on Tuesday
