While the Council of Ireland has been
abolished we have put something far more
valuable in its place, because the House will
agree that,
matter how perfect the
machinery that might have been set upand I think nobody will claim for Clause 11
that the machinery was perfect-without
confidence and goodwill results could not
have been obtained. With the establishment of confidence and goodwill we can do
without very much machinery, and, therefore, I do earnestly hope that in the coming
days this arrangement that has been substituted for Clause 11, that is for the Council of Ireland, this arrangement whereby
provision has been made that the two Governments-the Government of the Free State
and the Government of Northern Irelandshould meet to discuss questions of common
interest and questions that are common to
both Governments, will bear very rich fruit,
and surely it will not be found impossible
to devise some system of unity in our
financial and commercial relations that will.
at least rob the present Boundary of some,
if not all, of the handicaps which it is imposing upon trade and commerce at the
present time.
One of our newspapers-the "Irish Times"
-stressed the position in regard to this
Agreement very well when it said that it
was not a triumph for astuteness and
diplomacy but for magnanimity and goodwill. I believe that it is along the lines of
magnanimity and goodwill that the future
hopes and future ambitions of this country'
lie, and along no other lines can they be
attained. Therefore, to-day I do welcome
this new Agreement between Dublin, Belfast,
and London. It has been entered into under
very happy auspices, and I hope it will be
fruitful and produce the results desired and
give us peace, confidence, and goodwill in
this land.
I do not know whether I would be wise
in touching upon the question of minorities.
Minorities in Ireland seem to be inevitable,
but I would like to deprecate, and I have
always deprecated, the extravagant language
that has been used in regard to the treatment of minorities both in North and South.
I think it is worthy of notice that very
often the most extravagant language that
has been used in both these cases has been
used by people who live outside the area
concerned. I do not know whether I would
be wise in making an appeal in the spirit
of this new Agreement to the minorities to
come in and take their part in the government and management of the affairs of the
State. It would be at least well worth a
trial, and I do feel that if the Governments,
both North and South, are approached in
this spirit they would be inclined to be fair
and generous to the minorities. I do deprecate, no matter from what quarter it
comes, Irishmen who differ in political outlook and views being described as enemies
of each other. At root bottom we are not
enemies. At root bottom we are all Irishmen, and I believe that according to our
lights we all love this land and desire to see
it prosperous. I deprecate at the present
time any extravagant language, and I appeal
to the minorities to come in and take their
part in establishing confidence and goodwill.
If there are-and I have no doubt that there
are-grievances surely this House, and the
Houses of Parliament, are the places to discuss, ventilate, and if possible remedy those
grievances.
With regard to the financial part of the
Agreement I, too, would like to impress
upon the Government the necessity of making known to this House at the earliest date
the new arrangement that has been entered
into with the Imperial Government with
regard to unemployment benefit. If this
arrangement was come to in July I do not
see what is to be gained by withholding
the information for two months longer, and
I hope the Government will see that this
House and the general public are put in
possession of all the facts with regard to
this new agreement at the very earliest possible date.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
•
[Mr. George Henderson]
With regard to the question of our Imperial contribution, I have never advocated,
and I have no wish to advocate, any repudiation of our Imperial contribution, but
if the Government do take up the stand that
the industrial population, the agricultural
community, the Old Age pensioners, and
Unemployment Insurance should not be on
a lower basis in this Province than in England, I think then we would be justified in
taking up the attitude that, before we pay
any contributions towards the Imperial Exchequer, we should at least defray all those
charges that are necessary to bring our own
people on to a level with the state of things
in England.
I may say also that I am less or more
disappointed that under this new Agreement
some of the services that have been reserved
to the Imperial Parliament have not been
handed over to be dealt with by the Ulster
Government and Parliament. For instance,
the question of the completion of land purchase is a reserved service. That has become, and is now, an entirely local matter,
affecting only the people in these Six
Counties, and I think that in any re-arrangement that has been made in regard to powers
being handed over to the Northern Parliament our Government should have insisted
that this, which is a reserved service, should
have been handed over to the Government
and Parliament of Northern Ireland to be
dealt with by them. The Imperial Parliament are not, as I understand, making any
contribution towards this scheme, and that
they should wish to retain a scheme that
they really have not time to discuss is beyond my comprehension. I am very sorry
this matter has not been transferred along
with the other powers to the Government
and Parliament of Northern Ireland. However, on the whole, I am pleased to be here
to-day to congratulate the Government and
the Prime Minister on this new Agreement,
because, as I said at the start, it is carrying out the policy for which I have stood as
long as I have been in political life.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I think all hon.
Members-at any rate those on this side of
the House, and I really think to-day I might
include a large number of those on the opposite side of the House-have come here
with thanksgiving and gratitude in their
hearts to subscribe to the Resolution which
has been put down by the Prime Minister.
It is with great diffidence that I rise to speak
here to-day, not because I have any doubt
as to the merits of that Resolution, which I
am about to support, but because I feel, as
has already been said, that this is a question
which affects everyone of us so vitally, which
affects our constituencies so tremendously,
that there is not a Member sitting on this
side of the House who would not wish to put
the seal of his approval to this Resolution.
As we have already listened to a considerable number of speeches I do not intend to
delay the House by any long speech on my
part, but I intend to endeavour to convey my
thoughts, my rejoicings, and, if I may say
so, my pride in our Prime Minister-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-in as few words as
possible.
In doing so may I be allowed for once to do
more than just attempt to voice the views
and the sentiments of my own constituents,
and to do what I rarely, if ever, attempt
to do in this House, and that is to speak on
behalf of the women of the Province. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Our anxiety in the
past few years has been just as great as the
men's anxiety, perhaps more so, because the
passive part, as is well known, is always the
very hard part, and it is more trying to sit at
home and wait than to go out and take action
and to dare. We have gone through the
troubled years of darkness and danger, and 1
firmly believe they now lie behind us. We
have waited and hoped, we have prayed, and
we have trusted. Our hopes have been fulfilled, our prayers have been answered, and
our trust has been justified.
The burden of anxiety has been lifted from
our shoulders, and although we have been
told here to-day that we must give credit
and thanks to all the Members of the Government for the solution which has been reached
in an equal manner to the credit and thanks
which we give to the Prime Minister, although
we are, I am convinced, prepared to acknowledge our debt and our gratitude to all the
Members of the Cabinet, there is one person
who stands out, and one person to whom 1
think in far greater measure than any other
we owe the feelings which are in our hearts
to-day. He has toiled and worked for us, he
has given of his best for us, he has fought
for us and stood by us, he has never spared
himself, and I am very glad that the Prime
Minister is not in the House at the moment,
because it is far easier to speak as I wish
to speak of the absent than it is of the present.
He alone knows what the strain has been for
him of the past few years, and of the past
few weeks, and he alone knows how heavy
was the burden which we placed upon his
shoulders and how it weighed him down. It
is not often that I quote verses in this House.
The senior Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin) who is not in his place to-day, and
the reason for whose absence we all regret-
(hon. Members: Hear, hear) said once on an
occasion when I had spoken in this House that
poetry was at a discount, or words to that
effect, in the Northern Parliament. Well, I
disagreed with him then; I disagree with him
now, and I disagree with him particularly in
this instance, because I believe that there
is not a Member of this House, even of the
Opposition, who will not say that the verses
which I am going to quote might have been

written for our own Prime Minister, and who
will not subscribe to them.
And since he was master and servant
in all that we asked him,
We leaned hard on his wisdom in all
things, knowing not how we tasked him.
For on him each new day laid command,
every tryannous hour,
To confront, or confirm, or make smooth
some dread issue of power.
To deliver true judgment aright, at the
instant unaided,
In the strict, level ultimate phrase
that allowed or dissuaded,
To foresee, or allay, to avert from us
perils unnumbered,
To stand guard on our gates, when he
guessed that the watchman had
slumbered.
The Prime Minister guarded our gates,
although the watchman never slumbered, but
he saw and he knew what was beyond their
vision and beyond their ken. He has stood
by us day and night untiringly, unceasing
in his vigilance, and I want to say hereand I believe that I voice the sentiments of
every Member on this side of the House-that
we owe him more than mere thanks. As a
people we owe him a place in our hearts for
all time-(hon Members: Hear, hear)—and 1
believe that he will hold that place in every
little cottage home along the Border which
he has kept. He has done more than merely
keep his word to the letter. He has fulfilled
every boast, every promise, every speech, and
there are few indeed of whom so much can
be said.
Having paid this tribute to the Prime
Minister on behalf of the women of Ulster,
I do want to add that with our feeling of
gratitude and thanksgiving we to-day combine
something else. There is a new feeling which
has been alluded to already. There is a wish
to co-operate, too, with the minority in our
midst, and with those other Irishmen across
our frontier, a wish for a better mutual understanding. There are new hopes before us,
new prospects waiting. Again it is our Prime
Minister who by his actions has brought us
nearer to our neighbours across that Border
which he has held, and who has enabled us
to reach out the hand of friendship as we
reach it out to-day. To-day the sun of peace
has risen above the darkest clouds, and we
earnestly pray that it may never set again.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I desire to
move the following Amendment, to leave out
from the word "House" to the end of the
Question, and to insert instead thereof the
words
While prepared to welcome any arrangement between Irishmen to settle the affairs
of their common country, regrets the

considers that the Agreement does not provide means whereby the unity of Ireland

I regret exceedingly on an occasion such as

in what way the people are going to benefit

to suggest that as a result of this arrangement the people are not going to benefit at
all. Our employers are groaning under the
burden of taxation, and the issue has not
been faced in the straightforward fashion in
which it should have been faced, because the
truth of the matter is that this country is
far too small and too poor for two Parliaments. The members of the Chamber of
Trade and of the Chamber of Commerce may

go out and state straightforwardly what a
good many of them believe, that this country
is absolutely too poor to maintain two Parliaments. I believe there are economic circumstances and exigencies that before very long
will force even the Members on the Government Benches to come to the conclusion that
I have arrived at already. I believe instinctively that I am right. Quite recently we
devoted a sum of about £10,000 to the purpose

Mr. ELLIOTT: I was rather sorry that

Tyrone, which I know particularly well, we
have no Nationalist members on the County
Council, simply because they have refused at
all times to take their seats. At our very

administrative work of the County Tyrone.
At a later stage, rather than have the people

fault of the Nationalist people and not the

With regard to the other hon. Member for

they ought to be treated, and I believe we can

I would conclude by just saying how much
I, as a Border representative, admire the

way in which he has led us in Ulster, admire
the way in which he has fulfilled every pledge
which he had given to us. We, as Ulstermen,
are proud of our Ulster leader, and we hope
he may live to realize the hope which he has
expressed here to-day that all Irishmen,
whether living in Northern Ireland or in
Southern Ireland, will work together for the
common good of Ireland, and will see to it
that Ireland is made one of the brightest spots
in all the King's Dominions. I congratulate

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): This is a small Bill brought in to provide for certain omissions that have been
discovered in the administration of the Education Act (Northern Ireland), 1923. The
first Clause deals with the powers of councils
of county boroughs to borrow money for cer
tain purposes. It was found, in the adminis
tration of the Act, that it had been omitted
to give the necessary specific powers to the
councils of county boroughs to borrow money
where, instead of undertaking works themselves, they propose to make contributions
towards the expense of those works where
they are undertaken by other people. The
first Clause of the Bill gives that power.
The second sub-Clause of Clause 1 is rendered necessary by the fact that certain
councils of county boroughs have peculiar
powers of their own under local Acts with
regard to the raising of money which it is
proposed to borrow. Accordingly sub-Clause
(2) provides that the borrowing powers of the
council of a county borough may be exercised
by that council in any manner, whether by
the creation of stock or otherwise; in which
Education Bill.
Second Reading.
9 DECEMBER 1925
they are authorised to borrow under any
local Act applicable to their county borough.
The third sub-Clause deals with another
quatter. It provides that the borrowing
powers of an education authority, being the
council of any county or county borough,
shall be deemed to include a power to borrow
money for the purpose of making contributions under the provisions of the principal
Act towards works, the cost of which, in the
opinion of the Ministry ought, by reason of
the permanent character of the works, to be
spread over a term of years. It was found in
working that it was not quite clear that the
borrowing powers of an education authority
extended to borrowing for this particular
purpose, and this sub-Clause is to make it
quite clear that the borrowing powers of an
education authority are extended to cover
that particular phase of their activities.
The next sub-Clause is rendered necessary
by reason of the fact that the education
anthorities which were set up were new bodies
without experience, and in budgeting for the
incoming year some of them found that they
had not provided sufficient money to defray
their day-to-day expenses under the Education Act. It was found, when they came to
supply those deficiencies by means of an
overdraft at the bank, or by anything of a
temporary nature, they had no power to do so,
and so the Section proposes that the Education
Authority should have power by means of
overdraft to put the Regional Committees or
the Education Committees in funds to
enable them to discharge their day-to-day
expenses for which, as a matter of fact, they
have no money in hand, owing to the shortness of the provision they have made, if that
shortness is due to their own inexperience.
It will be noticed that this power is strictly
limited. It is intended to cover only the
next two years, during which time, in the
opinion of the Government, the authorities
ought to have sufficient experience to enable
them to draw up their budget properly in the
beginning of the year. Those are the provisions of this Bill. It does not in any way
touch generally the policy of the Act of 1923.
Its objects is to enable the authorities to
make provision for certain omissions that
have been found to exist when the Act came
to be worked out. I beg to move.

Superannuation Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second Time."
Mr. BARBOUR: The object of this Bill is
to safeguard those of our Civil Servants
whose right of pension does not at present rest
on any definite statutory basis. Hon. Members will, of course, understand that owing
to the conditions which obtained at the time
that our Civil Service was started owing to
the transfer of Civil Servants from Dublin
and elsewhere there were necessarily some
officers not provided for by the former Acts
which governed the terms of pensions, and
not subsequently taken care of in the Superannuation Acts which have been passed by
this House. I should explain that one of the
conditions entitling a Civil Servant to a
pension is the receipt of a Civil Service
Certificate from the Civil Service Commission. The Civil Service Commission for
Northern Ireland was not set up until a
considerable time after the transfer of
functions, and, consequently, delay has
occurred in issuing Civil Service Certificates
to officers recruited in Northern Ireland.
Clause 1 provides that for superannuation
purposes the Ministry of Finance may
certify that the date of established service
begins at a date prior to the date when the
Civil Service Certificate will eventually be
issued.
Clause 2 refers to those persons who, although transferred Irish officers, did not at
the time of transfer hold established posts
in the Imperial Service, but have subsequently received established posts in the
Northern Ireland Civil Service, are at present not properly covered by the Superannuation Acts.
Clause 2, paragraph 2, refers to officials in
these Departments prior to the establishment
of the Government of Ireland Act, which
were financed by means of income derived
from endowment funds placed at the disposal
of the services in Ireland. It was the intention of the Government that out of those
endowment funds provision should be made
for the pensions of officers employed in administering those services. Now the endowment funds have been transferred to Northern Ireland and form part of our capital, the
income of which is paid into the Exchequer,
and the pensions of these officers require to
be paid out of the income received from the
Capital Fund. So this clause gives power to
the Ministry of Finance to admit for superannuation purposes those officers who were formerly employed by these services, which were
financed by these funds. Possibly I might
illustrate this, and make it more familiar to
Members of the House by allusion to the
Endowment Fund which was administered
by the Department of Agriculture.

The third Clause repeals Section 72 of the
Education Act and re-enacts it in another
form. This applies to officers who have
been employed in one capacity, and afterwards are appointed as Civil Servants in
another capacity. It is simply designed to
co-ordinate various services in accordance
with the purposes served in the capacity emploved, and in proportion to the time employed in each capacity.
Clause 4 provides that if any award is made
to a person under Clauses 2 and 3 by the Civil
Service Committee based on the rights which
the transferred Irish officer had at the date
of transfer, the supplemental amount to be
awarded by the Ministry of Finance, under
the terms of the present Act, shall be
reckoned after taking into consideration the
amount awarded by the Civil Service Com
mittee.
It is a technical administrative Bill altogether. It is simply to clear up the rights
of these Civil Servants who, at the present
time, were the Acts to stand unamended,
would run the risk of falling between two
stools so far as pension rights are concerned.
Mr. KYLE: Can the right hon. Gentle
man, the Minister of Commerce, give the
House the assurance before the Second Reading is passed that no Civil Servant in Nor
thern Ireland will suffer in consequence of
this Superannuation Bill. It is purely a
technical matter, but there may be some an
biguity or some doubt in the minds of those
of us who are interested in the maintenance
of our Civil Servants for the work they do
for the State. We would not want them to
suffer by allowing the Second Reading to
pass without discussion. If the right hon.
Gentleman can give the House this assurance
I am sure it will pass without discussion.

entirely with a view to protecting the interests of the Civil Servants.

Mr. ELLIOTT: On a point of Order. May
I ask why the order of the questions to-day
has been altered, so that my questions which

Numbers 1 to 6 now appear as 3 to 8. If

Mr. SPEAKER: The rule is that questions
appear on the Paper under the heading
"notices given on such and such a date" in
the order in which they are handed in at
the table. Presumably, that was the order in
which they appeared yesterday, namely, that
the hon. Member's questions were the first
ones received. Then, subsequently, when they
appear on the Paper for answer in the
House, as on the Paper to-day, they are rearranged in the order of the different Ministries in order to simplify matters. To-day
the Ministry of Agriculture come first.
While still in separate Ministries they
should remain under those Ministries in
the order in which they were handed in, so
that the hon. Member (Mr. Elliott) has certainly a grievance owing to the fact that they
have been altered by mistake. Obviously the
order got altered by mistake. The only thing
I can suggest now if the matter is one of
importance to him is that the hon. Lady the
Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester) might

which they appeared yesterday, after question No. 8, but without her concurrence I

appears on the Paper.

must assume the order in which they appeared on the Paper yesterday, was the order

cannot say.

markets for potatoes from the newlyscheduled area.
A very successful demonstration of the
desirable qualities of coloured potatoes,
such as are grown in the South Londonderry
area, was recently held on the premises of a
prominent firm of grocers in Liverpool.
Furthermore, with the object of bringing
the merits of these potatoes directly before
cross-Channel consumers a plan has been
put into operation whereby limited quantities of the potatoes have been placed
on sale in 7 and 14 lb. bags. I am glad to
say that at present potatoes are now moving
freely from the scheduled area to cross-
Channel destinations.

made for the supply to growers in the South
Londonderry scheduled area of limited quantities of immune varieties of seed potatoes
at reduced prices. Seed so supplied will, as
far as practicable, be of a type suited for the
export trade.

LICENCES UNDER MARKETING OF
EGGS ACT.
6. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture how many licences have been
suspended, cancelled, or revoked under the
Marketing of Eggs Act; whether he fully
appreciates the seriousness from the traders'
point of view of the withdrawal of a licence,
and what means he has taken to safeguard
the legitimate interests of the trading community from being endangered by the mere
ipse dixit of an inspector.
Mr. ARCHDALE: There have been six cases
where licences have been suspended, cancelled, or revoked under the Marketing of
Eggs Act. The Ministry fully appreciates
the seriousness of such action, and this course
is taken by it only when there is serious and
persistant disregard of the Rules. The
position as to the Ministry's Inspectors was
explained in my answer to the hon. Member's
question on the 29th October last.
MARKETING OF AGRICULTURAL
PRODUCE.
7. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he has any evidence that
the operations of the Marketing of Eggs Act
have resulted in enhanced prices for Ulster
eggs, and whether if this is so, he proposes
to seek powers to improve in a like manner
the marketing of other items of agricultural
produce, such as butter, bacon, poultry,
potatoes, and fruit.
Mr. ARCHDALE: The Ministry is satisfied
that the Marketing of Eggs Act has resulted
in enhanced prices. In fact, eggs from
Northern Ireland have for some time been
making higher prices than those from
Denmark. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The Ministry has in contemplation the introduction of legislation for improvement of
marketing of other articles of agricultural
produce, for example potatoes, butter, etc.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The Ministry, however, considers that it
is not advisable to take steps for obtaining
further legislation until the difficulties of
the present Act have been overcome.

INLAND REVENUE DEPARTMENT
EMPLOYMENT OF EX-POLICEMEN.
9. Mr. GYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether any arrangement-official,
semi-official, or private-exists between the
Department of Inland Revenue in Belfast and
the Inspector-General of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary, by which the latter provides
the Department of Inland Revenue with the
ex-members of the police force for work of a
clerical nature, and if such an arrangement
exists (or has existed), how many men have
been so supplied by the Inspector-General's
Department to the Inland Revenue, and how
many ex-Service
men were amongst the
number.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I am taking this question for my
right hon. Friend.
I find that in the early part of this year
the Inland Revenue Department invoked the
assistance of my Ministry to afford them help
of a temporary character, in order to deal
with the collection of considerable arrears of
Income Tax in Belfast. As an alternative to
the more expensive arrangement of bringing
over staff from London for the purpose it was
desired to obtain the services of Established
Civil Servants or in lieu Pensioned Constabulary officials. My Ministry suggested
the employment of ex-Servicemen, but the
Inland Revenue Department with whom the
responsibility rested decided that officials
with training were essential, and arrangements were accordingly made for bringing
under their notice the names of suitable
police pensioners. I understand that a selection of five officers was made, but I am not in
possession of any information as to whether
these five pensioners were also ex-Servicemen.
Mr. GYLE: Arising out of that answer,
I would like to know if the men who were
employed were not employed on the very
simplest clerical work, and if the work
they were employed on could have been as
well done by ex-Servicemen who were walking the streets of Belfast, as by the men that
were employed, pensioners, with a very large
rate of pension, some of them over £4 per
week. Ex-Servicemen walking the streets of
Belfast were quite capable of doing the work:
Mr. POLLOCK: In regard to those remarks,
I would remind the hon. Member that the
service in question is not under our control,
and we were bound to comply with the views
of the Department-the Inland Revenue
Department-in regard to the class of
labourers which they required at that time.
It was not for us to decide the character of
the employees.
Colonel WOODS: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman if a recommendation from
him would not be taken seriously by the
Department?
Mr. POLLOCK: I think no recommendation
from any Department would influence the
Inland Revenue with regard to the character
of the work or the character of the officials
who undertake the work. I think they would
regard it as unwarrantable interference.
Mr. GYLE: Does the right hon. Gentleman
suggest that the characters of these men were
not what they ought to be.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have made no such
suggestion.

partments in Northern Ireland.
Mr. POLLOCK: No contracts were entered
into with any tailoring firms in Belfast or
elsewhere for the supply of the uniforms re
ferred to by the hon. Member. Advantage
was taken of the existing machinery of the
Post Office Stores Department for the ex
peditious and economical supply of the uni
forms in question.

in view of the unemployment among tailoring
employees in this city he will assure this

EVIDENCE AT COURTS OF REFEREES.
11. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he will issue instructions to
the Courts of Referees, setting out that if
written statements from employers are
challenged by the applicant, said em
ployers will be notified and summoned to

in writing be ruled out.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I have been asked by the Minister
of Labour to reply.
I am unable to adopt the suggestion con
tained in the hon. Member's question.
Oral, Answers.
Oral Answers.
10 DECEMBER 1925
D
The statutory function of the Court of
Referees is to recommend whether or not,
in the light of all the ascertained facts, the
statutory conditions for the receipt of unemployment benefit are satisfied. I have no
authority to compel any person to attend a
Court, and, in the circumstances, I cannot
interfere with the Court's discretion and
direct it to ignore any evidence which in its
opinion has a bearing on the subject.
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask whether in
view of these statements that have been made
in the past by the employer, written or
otherwise, is the Minister not prepared to reconsider the answer given in this House.
Mr. GORDON: I will be glad if the hon.
Member can give me any further information
regarding the facts.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Is the hon. Member
aware that it is possible under this arrangement for employers to make any statement
they care to make. A number of these statements are not correct, to the prejudice of the
person claiming unemployment benefit. The
applicant has to be present, and is interrogated. There is no interrogation of the employer at all. In view of that unsatisfactory
state of affairs would the hon. Member recommend the Court not to give unduc
credence to any statement made by the
employers.
Mr. GORDON: In answer to the question
put forward by the hon. Member, I would
like to say that all the evidence that is sent
forward to the Court of Referees by the employers must be taken into consideration, inasmuch as if we refused to accept the information from the employers all the men who
are making claims for benefit would be refused, because we could not get any evidence
that they were making genuine application
for employment.

and 30th November, 980 men, 2,165 women (of

girls have not been admitted to extended
benefit having regard to the condition referred to by the hon. Member.

these applicants is the Minister not prepared
to consider the abolition of the family income altogether for people in Northern
Ireland?

been instituted by the various local employment committees, and so far as we can ascertain we know of no cases of grave hardship
or injustice that have been inflicted on any
particular family. In all areas where there

CHAIRMEN OF COURTS OF REFEREES.
16. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is prepared to consider
the abolition of paid Chairmen on Courts of
Referees, with a view to saving the moneys
of the insured contributors and the fund.
Mr. GORDON The panel of paid Chairmen of Courts of Referees consists of a small
number of persons with legal experience who
are not connected with representative interests either of employers or workers.
Having regard to the number of questions
involving interpretation of the Statutes with
which Courts of Referees have to deal, it is
necessary that the Courts should have the
benefit of Chairmen possessing legal qualific
tions, and I feel that it would not be in the
interests of the contributors to the Fund that
the present system should be altered.

PERSONAL EXPLANATION.
Mr. KYLE: I want to crave the indulgence
of the House in order to make a personal
explanation regarding something that took
place in this House on Tuesday last. It has
been widely reported that I myself did not
take part in the division on the Vote of no
confidence in the House on that day. The
Press of Belfast is notorious-the Telegraph'
is notorious for its scurrilous language. The
reason why I take notice of this is that I
had an important engagement in County
Antrim on that night, and I had to leave the
House before the division was taken. The
Chief Whip of the Unionist Party (Captain
Dixon) in this House knowing that
deliberately made a statement—at least if he
did not know it, the clerk in his office
knew it-at a meeting the other evening in East Belfast, and I think he ought
to withdraw that statement. I think it is
most unfair that-
Mr. SPEAKER: I gave the hon. Member
permission to raise a question on a personal
explanation, namely as to why he was not
present at the division, because I understood
from him that some publicity had been given
to the fact, but he is not entitled in giving
a personal explanation either to make attacks
on the Press outside or to deal in this House
with matters in speeches made outside the
House. That would be impossible obviously
and would give rise to a desire on the part
of other hon. Members to reply. A personal
explanation must simply be an explanation
on some personal matter by the Member concerned, and there can be no debate on it.
If the hon. Member would simply confine
himself to the reason why he did not take
part in the division I will allow him to
proceed, though of course one could not allow
every Member to explain in the House why
he was absent from a division.
Mr. KYLE: I quite appreciate your
position as guardian of the rights and
privileges of Members. I appreciate that,
but I think it is unfair for any Member of
the 'House to state outside what is untrue
about another Member of this House. After

take the opportunity of a personal explanation to raise controversial matters I really
could not allow-
Mr. SPEAKER: No. It is a controversy

THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): I believe that hon. Members of
this House are already so familiar with these
Consolidated Fund Bills that it is not necessary for me to do more than remind them
that it is a purely formal Measure in order
to give effect to Votes of Supply already
passed in Committee of Supply and Ways and
Means. They will see that the first Clause
authorises the issue from the Consolidated
Fund of the necessary moneys required to
meet the Votes which have been made. The
second provides the usual power which is
granted to the Ministry of Finance to borrow
sums in order to meet this expenditure, and
it also provides for the dates on which such
borrowing should be repaid. The third Clause
appropriates to each particular service the
sums of money voted for that purpose. I beg
to move.

Prime Minister in the event of any of these
men taking his advice seriously will they
get any gratuity to enable them to go overseas? It is important that these men should
be treated properly, because they have given
great services. Is it a fact that after leaving
the Special Constabulary they will not be
entitled to the dole? If it is so, it is going
to be very serious for these men and their
families. I think the Prime Minister
should think over this matter very carefully
before he starts disbanding these men who
have performed useful services to the
citizens of Ulster, and who in my opinion
ought not to be disbanded for a considerable
time.

I will consider that.

Mr. POLLOCK: I regret I have to ask the
House for the third time this year to make
further provision for those who are unemployed. The House must by this time have
become familiar with the character of the
Measure which I submit to the House, a
Measure which authorises the Minister of
Finance to make advances to the Unemploy
ment Insurance Fund in order that the Fund
may be put in a position to provide the
necessary relief for those who are on the
register. The amount which we ask the House
now to authorise the Ministry of Finance to
advance is £500,000. The period for which
this advance would suffice must naturally be
determined by the amount of unemployment,
and, therefore, I cannot speculate as
to

how far that will carry the Fund along.
I think from all the discussions that
this House hon.
have taken place in
Members will not be very optimistic in
regard to the limitation of the period,
but when this £500,000 is absorbed, whether
sooner or later, the total amount which will
then have been advanced to the Unemployment Fund will be £4,750,000, and if you add
to that sum the contribution from employers,
from employed, and from the State, amounting to a total of £3,670,000, the House will
have some idea of the vast sum of money
which has been expended on unemployment
during the period of responsibility of the
Northern Government. The £3,670,000, which
I have mentioned, added to the loans which
have been advanced of £4,000,000 odd will
reach a total of £7,670,000. This is a curious
commentary on the claim of hon. Members on
the opposite side of the House that the Government have done little or nothing for unemployment. Apart from all the other
measures that have been passed and the benefits that have accrued from the provision of
labour, if this stood alone practically
£7,000,000 of the money of the taxpayers of
Northern Ireland has been advanced or paid
for the purpose of affording relief to those
who, possibly through no fault of their own,
have been unemployed.
Under the circumstances it is natural that
one should consider if there is any remedy,
any specific for this disease, but I do not
propose to initiate a debate upon that part
of the subject because, as the House is aware,
even during this week we have had a full
day devoted to the discussion of this most
difficult problem with very inconclusive results. I am bound to say with some experience of this matter that I have not yet heard
any suggestion or any proposal made from
any part of the House, whether from the
opposite side or from our own side, that will
produce even a palliative for this trouble.
It is all very well to talk about increasing
the area of benefit, or of carrying out certain
proposals, but the whole thing resolves itself
into a question of finance, of the provision
of money-additional money-to be thrown
into what is apparently a pit without bottom.
In my judgment, if it is worth anything,
there is only one cure for this disease, and
that is work-work that will produce
materials that can be sold in the markets of
the world-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)—and
until that point is reached we need hope for
very little amelioration even of the trouble
with which we are faced to-day. However,
these are all purely speculative opinions.
The fact is we have got to meet the condition
of things here and the provision of money,
and the money we ask you to authorise the
Ministry of Finance to advance to the Unemployment Fund is £500,000. No further in
formation, I think, is required by hon. Members who, I repeat, are more familiar, or as
familiar with the subject as I am, and, therefore, I beg to move.

and a deplorable state of affairs that
should have an admission from the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) that he has never

people who set themselves up to form a
Government would be able to deal with all
these problems, and that at least from some
member of the Government Party, either
front Bench or back Bench, there should be
some suggestion or idea as to how to deal
with this problem.
On behalf of my colleagues I want to say
that we are not satisfied with the present
arrangement at all. We have asked that
justice should be done to the people. On
divers occasions we have suggested that the
amount of relief paid to the unfortunate unemployed is not sufficient, but we think that
the money that is being paid week after week
is being wasted except that it suffices to keep
a certain number of people alive. In the first
speech I made in this House I said we did not
want an indefinite continuance of Unemployment Benefit, because it was slowly and surely
sapping and draining the resources of this
small State, and that sooner or later this
small State of ours would find itself in a
very serious position as far as unemployment benefit was concerned.
I have given some thought to this question. Perhaps may be accused of taking
too serious a view of the matter, but I believe
it is a very serious question for this Government, and one that is likely to cause great
concern in the near future, and I regret that
the Government are not doing something to
provide work of some kind or other. I
accused the Government the day before yesterday of taking up a Micawber-like attitude,
and I do not think I could do better in the
way of a description than that, because we
have the Prime Minister turning to the head
of one Department and telling us that the
right hon. Gentleman is doing his best, and
then turning to the head of another Department and telling us that that right hon.
Gentleman also is doing his best. What we
want to know is if the best of these men is
good enough. We think it is not good enough,
because it is a most unsatisfactory state of
affairs to be paying away thousands of
pounds week after week to people who might
be usefully doing work and providing wealth
for the State when there is so much wealth
required, when there are men walking about
the streets idle and without food. We have
got land, we have got capital, and we have
got labour, and all the economists from the
days of Adam Smith downwards have told us
that that is all that is required for producing
wealth.
There is something radically wrong with
the present economic situation, and before
the Government attempt to spend these huge
sums of money on unemployment benefit they
should do something. The last thing they
attempted has proved quite a fiasco. The right
hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews), induced certain representative
people to attend a number of conferences for
the purpose of going into the whole question.
I think they went fairly fully into the question up to a point, but what has been the
result? Money has been spent on improving
the roads, relief schemes of one kind or
another have been undertaken, but I would
point out that at some stage or other those
things are coming to an end, and then your
position is exactly where you began.
I would like again to point out the seriousness of the situation and ask the Government
to give more thought and more consideration
to the problem. I know that many harsh
and unfair things are said about myself here
and in other places for my attitude. I do
not mind that. I am absolutely indifferent
and impervious to all the criticism that is
lovelled against me. I am endeavouring to
do my best, and this afternoon I want my
best to be to put it straightforwardly to the
Government that they are not making any
attempt to grapple with this problem. It is
a more serious matter for the Government
than for the occupants of these benches,
because the Government are likely to get
into a great deal of disfavour and discredit
for not making an attempt to grapple with
this trouble satisfactorily, and the chances
are that the people will become discontented
and will be inclined to try other people to
see if they have got a remedy or not.
We have got fairly clear ideas about the
whole problem, but of course it is quite futile
for any occupant of these benches to make
any suggestion. (Hon. Members: No, no.)
Yes, quite futile, because any of the sugges
tions put forward from these benches are
generally voted as being absolutely impracticable by the representatives of the
Government, and perhaps they would cost
money. That reminds me of a point I wanted
to make a few days ago, and I want to ask
some member of the Government to give
serious consideration to this proposal. We
have a large number of juveniles in employment in Belfast, and, I believe, in the Six
Counties, at the present time. I put a question to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews)
some time ago as to how many youths below
the age of eighteen were employed in industry
and how many people over sixty-five were
employed in industry. The Minister of
Labour on that occasion told me he had no
reliable information as far 88 those two
points were concerned. I would suggest to
the Minister of Labour that if he is sincerely
desirous of easing the situation he should
inquire into those two points.
I believe that it is true to say that in a
large number of factories in the city of
Belfast adult males have been discharged.

In Murray's tobacco factory-I do not want
to mention any names, but I believe it is
true of the tobacco factories in the city of
Belfast, and I suggest that it is not at all

and female adults are being discharged from

It would possibly be in the interests of the
State that an effort should be made to keep
those children at school longer than they
are kept at the present time. Of course I
will be told that that would cost money. I
quite realise that it would cost money, but
we are spending a great deal of money at
the present time, and our children of the
present time, if given a better education,
would become greater assets to the State
than they are now. Then, again, there are
the people of over sixty-five years of age.
Some attempt should perhaps be undertaken
with a view to getting the people of over
sixty-five and seventy years of age out of
industry. If we could hit upon a scheme
whereby we could give something like an
adequate pension to a person at sixty-five
years of age, even in a temporary way-
Mr. POLLOCK: That would be a dole.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I quite understand that—until such times as we might be
able to get out of the present economic
morass things might be more satisfactory.
The right hon. Gentleman suggests that that
would be a dole. I quite agree that it would
be a dole, but is not our present situation
this: that we are doling out thousands of
pounds each week and all to no purpose? I
have come now to the point that owing to
the Government having no policy it is not,
possible to stop that money. I was leading
up to that point. If it is true that the
Government have not got a policy and the
Government cannot provide work for the
people I suggest what I believe would be a
more satisfactory way than the one being
pursued by the Government at the present
time.
If we can give our children the education
denied to some of us-they can be kept at
Continuation Schools until they are eighteen
years of age-if they were given a technical
education it might ease the problem in the
future. In the main there is practically no
employment for our youths. Any employment there is will only lead to blind alley
occupations. There is practically no future
for our youths. Our shipyards cannot provide
the future that they formally did, say up to
1920. Most of our industries cannot provide
that opportunity for our young people. As a
result we have had more crime than we
should have had, and we have got more young
people taken to industrial schools and to
prisons.
This is all a very serious state of affairs.
I did not happen to know I was going to
speak this afternoon or I might have dealt
with other points of view. I have, I believe,
suggested two or three practical points that
the Government should give some attention
to, and I would like the information I asked
for earlier to be given so that the House
might be in possession of that information
before we attempt to pass this Bill. The Government should do what they consider satisfactory in the direction of trying to provide
work instead of doling out a certain amount
of money each week, because we are getting
further and further into debt, and even at
the end of six or twelve months we will have
spent perhaps some hundreds of thousands of
pounds, and our position then will be no
better than it is at the present time. That
is such an extremely serious and critical
situation that one feels that the Government
would be justified in giving the problem even
more serious consideration than they have
done up to the present.
Mr. POLLOCK: Perhaps I should have

hope it will afford such a measure of relief as

The hon. Member, in the course of his remarks, displayed some incongruity in his

Member suggests that work should be provided. A great deal of work has been provided, but there is not an unlimited outlet
for work here, and if you develop work that
has no useful object and is not work of utility
you are doing something almost worse than

when men feel they are engaged on Government work they are not producing the

experience. The hon. Member does not suggest that these men who are unemployed and
walking the streets should enter into employment on an equivalent of the dole as
wages? I am sure he will argue that it is
necessary that these men should be paid

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not object, and I am
not going to join issue on that. That is
where the main difficulty arises, because men
who are employed in works-though not in
works of utility-which are only provided for
the purpose of simply keeping them in
Occupations of some kind do not produce
material equal even to the money they get.
That is one of the difficulties among others,
about the provision of work.
But apart from that we have through the
public authorities and through other sources
been enabled to provide a great deal of work.
Let me say also I did not decry, and I am
sure the hon. Member will not decry, the
fact that this Government has entered into
liabilities guaranteeing not far short of
£5,000,000 in order that ships may be built
in Belfast and employment provided. Is that
nothing? That surely must stand to the
credit of the Government-that they explored that avenue of employment, and that
is the proper sort of employment, because it
brings an enormous sum of money into the
country.
The hon. Member has complained that
conferences have met here and that the
suggestions they made-as I apprehend him
-were perfectly futile. The Government cannot be charged with criminality or culp
ability in respect of that. The Government
cannot be responsible if the brains of the
best men in the community cannot devise
schemes whereby employment can be de
veloped, and submit them to the Govern
ment. Is there any responsibility to be
allotted to the Government for that? There
is another feature of the problem which the
hon. Member mentioned, and with which 1
have very great sympathy, I am bound to
say. That is when the adolescent stage is
reached, and when youths should, if possible,
be placed in employment in order that they
might be trained for some useful occupation-
I presume that was what was in his mindthat would enable them to earn a livelihood
here or elsewhere.
I am in full sympathy with any project
that has that object in view, and as a matter
of fact the Government have that subject
in their minds very much at the present
time. I am not in a position to develop it
because the consideration of it has not proceeded very far yet, but I suggest to the
hon. Member that there is a very large field
of opportunity in our Technical Classes in the
College of Technology which, although taken
advantage of to a very large extent by the
youth of the community, does not go suffi
ciently far. I think the Continuation School,
as the hon. Member suggests, would really
perform the functions which he has in mind;
that is that training in particular crafts or
trades should be given to young men from the
age of 14, 15, 16 up to 17 years, perhaps, to
enable them to engage in some useful
occupation.
I may say that I have been occupied my.
self in investigating a matter which is particularly related to that side of the question.
But I wish to remind the House that that
will not cure the unemployment problem.
That will only benefit the youth of the community who are coming on, and who, having
reached the adult stage, would obviously
otherwise become unemployed, and be in the
future a drain upon the fund and the taxpayers. That does not cure or relieve the
present condition of unemployment, and I
repeat what I said before, that I have heard
no suggestion from any part of the House
that the Government could adopt that will
relieve this Unemployment Insurance Fund
from the terrible drain upon it at present.

I go further, and I would remind these

I made a suggestion in this House regarding shipbuilding. The Minister of Finance

was absent on very much more important

if you can persuade the Government to give

Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I rise to-day
to suggest something to the Minister of Finance in regard to providing employment. I
view with alarm the action of the Cabinet
in allowing the Imperial Parliament, for
some reason best known to the Members on
the Government Bench, to reduce the size
of the Parliamentary Buildings at Stormont.
Pictures of this building, if I may say so,
have been spread broadcast throughout the
world. As I said yesterday, they are taking
the two wings off this building, and that to
my mind will affect a saving of almost a
million pounds. I want to know from the
Minister of Finance if this Government has
received anything in return for allowing the
Imperial Government to reduce the size of
the Government buildings? This building, if
it had been carried out as designed by the
architect, would have been a great asset to

Cabinet Ministers have neglected their duty
in allowing the Imperial authorities to go
back on their obligation to give to the citizens

the Province. The citizens of Ulster have
been the backbone of the Empire, and in

rendered they should be provided with proper
buildings at Stormont.

By the way, there is one thing the Government have done. They have provided employment, so far as motormen and conductors
are concerned, by erecting these buildings at
Stormont, because the people will have to
travel a great distance to get there. Whether
that site was selected for the purpose of
enabling someone to get rid of his land or
not I do not know. It is not a site for the
Parliament House at all. It is too far out
of the way. I believe the site was decided on
to prevent the workingmen of Belfast from
hearing the speeches of the hon. Members. I
am not at all satisfied with the action of
the right hon. Members opposite in allowing
the Imperial Parliament to act in this way,
and I, as one Member of this House, want
to know what is at the back of it. There is
something seriously wrong. We are not
going to talk about the Boundary now; that
is a thing of the past; I hope it is gone for
ever. We want to go on and prosper. What
I want to know is, has this Government got
anything in return for allowing the Imperial
Government to reduce the size of the proposed
building at Stormont, which means a saving
of about a million pounds. As one of the
Opposition, I suggest that the Minister of
Finance, together with the Prime Minister
and the other Members of the Cabinet, should
go back to the Imperial Government and tell
them that the citizens of Ulster are not prepared to take the skeleton offered to them,
but must have in its entirety the structure
first offered to them.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: No surrender!
Mr. T. HENDERSON: You have a good
opportunity of creating additional employment by urging the Imperial Government to
carry out their obligations to the citizens of
Ulster.
Mr. KYLE: I would not have taken part
in this discussion to-day but for the point
raised by the Minister of Finance that, in

Is it not the boast of the Government of

twenty millions to Imperial affairs since our
Parliament was established? Surely, if that
is 80,
we have a perfect right to know
whether or not we are going to get back
some of that twenty millions in the form,
perhaps, of the absorption of our Unemployment Fund. I hope the suggestion of the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen) is true, that the Imperial Government are going to take over our liabilities in
this connection. It would be as little as they
could do. After all, our Parliament was set
up at the beginning of very bad times, and
we have had very bad times in industry ever
since. From that point of view we would
not be asking a great deal. It would not
have been taking a great deal not to have
given the money in the first instance. I do
not think it is at all appropriate that the
Minister of Finance should calmly wave us
off by saying that not until this thing is
discussed in the Imperial Parliament will we
be in a position to ascertain how the Unemployment Fund is going to be situated.
It does seem strange that the representa.
tives of the University, of commercial houses,
of the Flax Spinners' Association, and of the
Weavers' Association in this House cannot
suggest to us any palliative or remedy for
unemployment. We have a representative of
the publicans, too, and it is strange that all
those people cannot put forward a scheme.
The only thing the Government can ask is,
what have the three Members on the Front
Opposition Bench to offer to the House and
to the country? Surely the Government does
not mean to suggest that these members of
the Chamber of Commerce, these responsible
directors of concerns, have nothing to offer
or to suggest whereby unemployment may be
modified. As the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. W. McMullen) said in the House
the other day, protection is not a vital
problem. It is said that one man with
adequate machinery can produce enough
cloth to do 300 people for a year, that one
man can produce woollen goods to do
hundreds of people, that five men with appropriate machinery can produce enough foodstuffs to do more than 1,000 people for a year.
What is wrong with modern society that
despite these facts-because they are factsthere are so many people hungry, naked, and
homeless, that our children are walking about
barefoot, that our women are not so well
clad as we should like to see them, and that
there are so many destitute people? What
is wrong? There must be something wrong
with society. There are 62,000 people unem.
ployed, and it seems to me a ludicrous
attitude for a responsible Government to
adopt, to say that they can do nothing, and
to ask the Opposition to produce their
schemes. After all, it is the Government
that is responsible for the health and happiness of the people, not the Opposition. I am
quite certain of this, that any suggestion that
we might make would be turned down by the
right hon. Gentlemen opposite.
My hon.
Friend (Mr. W. McMullen) spoke about the

The only other thing I have got to say is

That is the only solution the Government

system of society is wrong. You are entitled

Mr. KYLE: It is 150 years since the capitalist system came in. Roughly speaking, the
age of capitalism is about 150 years, and we
find 1,200,000 unemployed in Great Britain
and 62,000 in the North of Ireland, and all
you can do is to take public money to subsidise private employers. Some of us have even
agreed to it. We will agree to almost anything to get our people work, to bolster up
your system of society, to bolster up your
ideas, and yet, despite all that, this system
is crumbling and breaking down. Surely
there is something in the system we advocate,
which is that things ought to be produced
for use, that food ought to be produced because people are hungry, and not to enable
people to make a profit out of it, that houses
ought to be built for people to live in,
not to enable swindlers to swindle the Belfast
Corporation, but that people may live in comfort in their houses. That is what Socialism
means.
Socialism, in my opinion, is the only remedy
for this particular ill, because as the hon.
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie) said
during the debate the other day, it was not
employment so much that mattered, it was life'
that really mattered. That is what he was
getting at, that it was life that mattered and
that instead of living to work we should work
to live. Did Lord Leverhulme himself not
say that six hours a day would be enough if
everybody did his share? We have got to get
rid of the fellows who are sitting on our
backs and taking two-thirds of the national
wealth for doing nothing. Until we have got
rid of capitalism, there will be unemployment.
We on these benches are prepared to do
anything within bounds, even to approve of
the subsidies that you are providing for employers, to try to get our people work because
we realise the degradation that is going on.
Go down to Amelia Street or Frederick Street
or any of the Labour Exchanges and see the
poor people. I do not know whether that
would be better than listening to speeches
from the Opposition Benches to get you to
realise that your system has broken down so
badly. Something ought to be done to make
good to those people.

Mr. DAVISON: I am greatly indebted to
the Deputy Chairman for the generosity with
which he has permitted this Amendment to
be moved. The idea underlying the Amendment is that county councils for purposes of
borrowing should be put upon the same footing as county boroughs. County councils are
limited in their powers of borrowing by the
Application of Enactments Order of 1898. Up
to one-tenth they borrow with the approval of
the Local Government Board, now the Ministry of Home Affairs. When the money borrowed amounts to over one-tenth of the total
annual value of the county the Application
of Enactments Order requires the making of
a Provisional Order, and it is confirmed by
Parliament. This would be a very cumbersome procedure for the purpose of borrowing
the money required for the erection of schools
or any substantial capital expenditure, and I
suggest that this provision limiting the borrowing powers should be wiped out for the
purposes of borrowing by county councils.
The Amendment does no more, as I stated,
than to give the same privileges to county
councils that the Bill gives to county
boroughs.
And it further extends to the county councils the benefit of the removal of the necessity
for two approvals to the authorities before
the money can be borrowed. As the law
stands at present, or as amended by this proposed Bill, both the Ministry of Home Affairs
and the Ministry of Education have to give
their approval to the borrowing of any money
over one-tenth. The case of the county council is even stronger than that of the county
borough, because the borrowing power of the
county council is limited to the education
rate and does not extend to the whole county.
I beg to move.

Mr. CRAWFORD: I beg to move in Paragraph I (Section b) after line 8 ("as aforesaid"), add "Vehicles owned by farmers and
used exclusively by them for conveying farm
produce not exceeding 12 cwt. in weight unladen, £9." I move this for one or two
reasons. In the first place a trader can get
a lorry and use it every day of the week and
he pays exactly the same rate as farmers, who
get a lorry to bring their produce to town
once a week. There is another reason why
this should be granted. The roads are now
improved so much for motor people that
farmers can scarcely get their horses to go
over them, and they are compelled to hire
motors and convey their produce to the
various towns. The Labour Members who
are interested in getting cheaper food will
no doubt find that this adds considerably to
the cost of food. It may be said by those
in charge of this matter that farmers would
use these lorries for many other purposes.
That could be arranged by altering the lorries
in such a way that they could only be used
for the express purpose of bringing produce
into the markets and bringing necessaries
home. In the northern part of County
Antrim, in which I am particularly interested, petrol is paid for at a higher rate
than in the southern part of the county.
People living at remote distances from towns
and cities are harassed and hampered in
every degree. This House has always taken
up the position that agriculture is the principal industry in Northern Ireland.
Here
is a splendid opportunity for the Government
to make a concession of a small nature to
farmers, and that is that instead of paying
the ordinary trading rate of £12 farmers
should get a special rate of £9. I beg to
move.
Dr. MORRISON: I wish to express my
concurrence with what has been said by my
hon. Friend, the Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford). I think it would be a much
better plan if the tax were put on petrol.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) In that way
ascertaining
there could be no difficulty in
who was using the roads or injuring them.
It should be easily ascertained in this age of
scientific achievement whether power is de
rived from paraffin oil or steam. In the
meantime I think that this small concession
to the farmers should be made. I have said
repeatedly in this House that agriculture was
never before in the critical position it is in
to-day. In my opinion it never was so bad.
I think that a small concession like this
would be well received by farmers. They do
not own many lorries. They are not able to
afford buying them, and when they do use
them it is only once or twice a week, and
then it is only for an hour or so on the road.
Yet if this Amendment is not granted they
will have to pay the same tax as the man
who is driving a lorry on the road from early
morning till late at night. I hope the House
will accept the Amendment.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I rise to
support the Amendment. I think the hon.
Member (Mr. Crawford) might have well
asked as a matter of justice that the rate
should be reduced to £6, and in the case of
vehicles not exceeding 12 cwt. in weight,
unladen (£20), that the rate should be £10.
Taking the duty from the standpoint of
private cars or cars for conveying produce
to the markets, the farmers were badly hit
by the change in the basis of duty from
petrol to horse power. A car only being used
once or twice a week has to pay exactly the
same duty as the car which is being used
every day. The only fair basis of taxation
with regard to these vehicles should be on
the petrol, and it should be taken off the
horse power. With regard to the matter of
conveying produce to the market and taking
necessaries home, I am sure it is within the
knowledge of the House that there have been
lately strong protests from the farming community as to the very slippery state of the
roads, more especially the roads in the immediate vicinity of Belfast. The farming community is taxed in two ways. Notwithstanding the grants that have been made
road expenditure out of the Road Fund, the
rates on the agricultural community are year
after year being used for road maintenance.
The farmer is taxed to repair and keep up
the roads for increased road traffic, and he

Monday, 14th December, 1925.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
PREMIUM BULLS-CONSULTATIVE
COMMITTEE.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agiculture the names of those present at the
last meeting of the Consultative Committee,
the chairman on that occasion; whether the
application for the selection of premium
bulls at the annual sale in Cookstown was
dealt with at that meeting. and if a vote was
taken on the subject, and with what result.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): The hon. Member's reference to
voting seems to be based upon a misapprehension as to the constitution and functions
of the Consultative Committee. It is a nonstatutory and purely advisory committee without any administrative powers whatever,
and it is, therefore, not the practice to take
a vote at the meeting. For the same reasons,
and also because members give their services
voluntarily, I do not feel free to give the
names of those who attended at any particular meeting as to do so might be regarded as giving a record of attendance. I
may say, however, that the president at the
last meeting was the Permanent Secretary
to the Ministry, who always, in my absence,
takes the chair at meetings of these Committees, and that the attendance, which
was very satisfactory, included the following:-
--
1. The Chairman, Antrim County Committee of Agriculture.
2. Ex-Vice Chairman, Antrim County Committee of Agriculture.
3. Chairman, Down County Committee of
Agriculture.
4. The Chairman, Tyrone County Committee of Agriculture.
5. Ex-Vice Chairman, Londonderry County
Committee of Agriculture.
6. Member, Fermanagh County Committee
of Agriculture.
7. Member of Ministry's Advisory Cattle
Committee, who is also a member of this
Committee.
Although, as I have said, no vote is taken,
no difficulty occurs in ascertaining the
general feeling of members of this Commit
tee, each of whom is invited individually to
express his views on each matter that may
come under discussion.
In regard to the question of the establishment of Cookstown as a centre for the selec
tion of premium bulls, I may say that this
question was considered last year by both
the Cattle Advisory Committee and the Consultative Committee, when they both recom
mended that no change should be made in
the existing arrangements, which have been
in operation since 1903. Following a resolution received from the Tyrone County Com
mittee of Agriculture, this question was
raised again this year with the Cattle
Advisory Committee, and with the Consulta
tive Committee, at the meeting to which the
honourable Member refers. Again both
Committees recommended no change.
I might add that deputations to the
Ministry from the Ulster Farmers' Union,
the Royal Ulster Agricultural Society and
the North-West Agricultural Society also
urged that in the interests of the live stock
industry, no change should be made.
I wish to make it quite clear to the
honourable Member that the responsibility
for deciding what, if any, action should be
taken on a recommendation of any of these
Committees rests entirely with the
Ministry.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of that reply,
may I ask the right hon. Gentleman if he
is quite satisfied that his constituents and
mine, who are vitally interested in the selec
tion of premium bulls at the annual sale of
bulls at Cookstown, got a fair deal at the
committee meeting referred to, seeing that
the meeting was in charge of a Departmental
official, who, on more than one occasion, had
expressed his strong disapproval of the re
quest of the parties interested being granted,
and this in spite of the fact that the right
hon. Gentleman himself told these people
during the recent election campaign in that
constituency, that he was quite in sympathy
with the proposal, and whether he is any
longer going to allow the officials of his
Department to thwart him in carrying out
what he himself believes to be right?
Mr. ARCHDALE: I may say that I believe
my constituents, both in Tyrone and
Fermanagh, get perfectly fair dealing at the
Committee. As regards my opinion of the
Cookstown bulls, I certainly was in favour
of the proposal at the time referred to, and
had been for some time, but on the recom
mendation made to me since my return to the
Ministry I have changed
my opinion
altogether.

BLACK SCAB AREA IN TYRONE.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of Agriculture if he can give the total acreage of the
area in Co. Tyrone scheduled for Black Scab,
and whether he is prepared to reconsider his
decision to debar the residents in the Black
Scab area in Co. Tyrone from the provisions
he is making for the farmers in the
scheduled area in Co. Londonderry, and to
provide them with a supply of immune
variety seed potatoes on the same terms as
the farmers in Co. Londonderry.
Mr. ARCHDALE: I would crave the
indulgence of the House, as this is rather a
long question.
Mr. SPEAKER: When there are few
questions there is no objection to that course,
but when we have a good many questions on
the Paper I think if there are any specially
long answers they really ought to
circulated with the Official Report, or else
condensed. Otherwise it is not fair to other
Members who come on later.
be
Mr. ELLIOTT: If this answer is unduly
long I will take it if the right hon. Gentleman sends it by post.
Mr. ARCHDALE: I will give it to the hon.
Member when the sitting is over.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Can I not have it at once?
Mr. SPEAKER: The normal course is for
the hon. Gentleman to get his answer sometime during the afternoon.
The following is the answer :--
The total acreage of the Tyrone scheduled
area is approximately 2,800. I see no reason
to reconsider the decision regarding the
suggestion that special measures should now
be taken to introduce seed of immune
varieties to this area.
The Tyrone area was scheduled twelve
months ago, when potatoes were selling for
at least double the price they are now
realising, and the growers in this small
scheduled area had no difficulty last spring
in procuring the required quantity of seed of
immune varieties to plant this area. The
problem confronting the Ministry in South
Derry is on the the other hand quite
unprecedented.
There we have an intensively cultivated
district extending right into the mountains
between Londonderry and Tyrone, and much
larger than the Tyrone scheduled area. This
Londonderry area was scheduled only last
month.
This district specialized in the growing of
"Skerry" potatoes (a non-immune variety) of
excellent quality, chiefly for Dublin and Belfast markets, where they command the highest
price. These markets are now closed to
potatoes from this area, and they have to be
sold in England-the only market availableat considerably lower prices than could be
procured in Belfast or Dublin. The loss to
farmers in the South Derry scheduled area
is, therefore, very severe.
From the point of view both of the control
of disease within this area and the preservation of its valuable potato industry, the
Ministry was satisfied that Government aid
was not alone justified, but was imperatively
called for in the exceptional circumstances,
and particularly as the supplies in the
districts of seed of immune varieties were
quite inadequate. Accordingly, in order to
assist in expediting the introduction of fair
supplies of immune seed, the Ministry, on
strong representation from the Londonderry
County Committee of Agriculture and after
consultation with its Advisory Potato Committee and Consultative Committee, made the
special arrangement of which I gave particulars last week in reply to an inquiry from
the honourable Member for County Londonderry.
The Ministry feels that it could not justify,
in respect of the area which was scheduled
twelve months ago in County Tyrone, the
adoption of measures similar to those which
have been found to be absolutely essential for
the County Londonderry area which was
scheduled last month. The circumstances of
the two districts are not in any way
comparable.
THE ADJUSTMENTS IN PETROL PRICES.
3. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Commerce whether he will state
why the new prices fixed for petrol do not
apply to the whole area of Northern Ireland;
whether he is aware that many important
centres are excluded, and that there is grave
dissatisfaction in the excluded area, and will
he make fresh representations so that this
anomaly may be removed.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): As the hon. Member is doubtless
aware, the recent territorial adjustments in
petrol prices are the outcome of protracted
negotiations with the three principal petrol
distributing companies. These negotiations
culminated in a conference in London on
2nd instant, when the representatives of
Northern Ireland strongly urged the case for
a reduction in price throughout the whole of
the Northern Ireland area. The directors
of the companies, however, explained very
fully that the large mileage to be covered in
relation to the gallonage delivered involved
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS

•
[Mr. Barbour]
high costs of transport and distribution, thus
precluding them from granting a general reduction in price at this stage.
While my attention has been drawn to the
expressions of dissatisfaction to which the
hon. Member refers, 1 am satisfied that no
useful purpose would be served by re-opening the matter at this juncture. I would
add, however, for the information of the hon.
Member, that the companies have promised
to review from time to time the question of
a reduction of price in the area at present
excluded from the concession.
Mr. G. HENDERSON: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask the right hon. Gentleman
if this is entirely a question of transport, and
may I point out to him that there was no
difference in the prices of petrol in these
areas until the present arrangement was
made?
Mr. BARBOUR: The change arose entirely
out of very strong representations that were
made by the representatives of Northern
Ireland, and I can assure the hon. Member
that the interests of Ballymena did not escape
the attention of those who tried to represent
their interests over there. The directors met
us very fairly, and I was greatly impressed
with the arguments they put forward.
This was the only way in which they could
make a concession, as the prices are fixed
entirely in relation to the consumption of
petrol over a certain area, that is to say, the
number of gallons consumed per square
mile. In fact, we were able to get a greater
concession from them than they had at first
proposed to give us.
TAXATION OF MOTOR LORRIES.
4. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Finance whether he has received from the
Antrim County Council, and other bodies,
suggestions that motor lorries used by
farmers exclusively for marketing their produce should be partially exempted from
taxation, and whether, in the interests of
agriculture, he is prepared to grant some

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have received no representations
on the lines indicated by the hon. Member
and I regret I cannot see my way to make

I propose to deal exhaustively with this
matter on the Second Reading of the Finance
Bill later on.
