Mr. SPEAKER: Yes, that is so.
EX-SERVICEMEN'S HOUSES.-GILFORD
DISTRICT.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Finance what progress has been made with
the proposals to erect homes for ex-Servicemen in the Gilford district of Co. Down.
Mr. POLLOCK: The question of the
allocation of the remaining houses to be
erected in Northern Ireland by the Irish
Sailors' and Soldiers' Land Trust will, I am
informed, be dealt with very shortly, when
the claims of ex-Servicemen in the Gilford
district will receive careful consideration.
LAND PURCHASE ANNUITIES.
6. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Finance what amount of the
Land Purchase Annuities collected by the
Northern Ireland Government is paid into
the Sinking Fund; how this money is invested, and at what rate of interest.
Mr. POLLOCK:. The annual amount set
aside in accordance with Section 3 of the
Exchequer and Financial Provisions Act
(N.I.), 1925, for the purpose of securing
permanent revenues in perpetuity equivalent
to the varying terminable revenues in respect of Land Purchase Annuities is not a
fixed figure, but varies from time to time as
the result of actuarial valuations.
Up to date the sum of £280,612 has been
placed to credit of the Sinking Fund, and
invested in Trustee securities. The average
rate of interest naturally fluctuates with
each investment, but the present return is
approximately 4 per cent.
OPENING OF LETTERS IN TRANSIT.
7. Mr. W. MCMULLEN asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether his Department has
requested the Postal Authorities in Belfast
to open letters in course of transit, and
under what Act of Parliament he derives
his authority for the censoring of letters of
private individuals.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): As regards the first part of
the question, I would refer the hon. Member
to the answer given on the 28th April last
to his question concerning censorship.
As regards the second part of the question,
the authority is the Warrant of his Grace
the Governor granted under Section 56 (2)
of the Post Office Act, 1908.

DISMISSAL OF SPECIALS-MOUNT-
POTTINGER BARRACKS.
8. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
reasons for the dismissal of thirteen B
Specials and a sergeant, of the Mountpottinger Barracks, on or about 6th August,
1924, and whether in view of statements made
by some of the dismissed men he would
institute an inquiry into the working of this
division for this past two years.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The question asked
by the hon. Member apparently refers to a
matter which was raised in this House in
November last year by the hon. Member for
North Belfast, and which was fully discussed
at that time. I made full inquiries into the
matter, and ascertained from the responsible
police authorities that 7 members of the B
Class Special Constabulary in the Mountpottinger area (and not 14, as stated in the
question) had not had their contracts renewed at the termination of their quarterly
contract on 30th September, 1924. I see no
reason for the institution of any inquiry as
proposed.
PREVENTION OF PERSONATION AT
ELECTIONS.
9. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister
whether he will initiate legislation to
effectively prevent personation at Local
Government and Parliamentary elections.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The existing laws
relating to personation at Local Government
and Parliamentary Elections already provide
substantial penalties for breaches in this
connection, and provision is also made for
enabling agents of the candidates to be
present during the elections in order to
assist in the regular conduct of the elections.
Accordingly, it would appear that the evil
referred to in the hon. Member's question
could best be remedied by the activities of
the agents of the candidates in rendering
assistance to the Election Officers.
Mr. KYLE: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman is he going to bring in legislation
so that the Crown may prosecute when the
agents made an arrest? That is the whole
difficulty-the agents have at present to
carry on a private prosecution. Would the
right hon. Gentleman give the House an
assurance that the Crown will prosecute in
cases of personation ?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I see no reason to
alter the law at the present time. I think the
hon. Member is perfectly well aware that the
Crown do prosecute at Assizes.
ADMINISTRATION OF LAND
PURCHASE.
10. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Prime Minister whether the question of the
completion of Land Purchase and the administration of the Land Commission had been
handed over to the Government and Parliament of Northern Ireland in accordance with
his statement in introducing the resolution
regarding the Boundary Agreement, that
Ulster had been placed upon exactly the same
level with regard to all her services as
Southern Ireland.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have taken this
question for the Prime Minister. I think
that the hon. Member has probably misunderstood the statement made by my right
hon. Friend the Prime Minister on
Wednesday last. The negotiations which
took place in London affected only what have
been known as the Council of Ireland
Services. There are, of course, still in
Northern Ireland services which are
reserved to the Imperial Government, of
which the Land Commission is one.

Sir DAWSON BATES: Under Section 1

TREATMENT OF POLITICAL
PRISONERS.
13. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he is aware that in the
recent sentences on political prisoners in
Great Britain the prisoners were committed
to the second division; whether he has
power to recommend similar treatment in
Northern Ireland, and, if so, will he apply
the same in the case of Mr. Sam Patterson
(an ex-Service man) who is in ill-health, and
at present in hospital.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer to the
first part of the question is in the affirmative.
I am advised that the Irish Prison Acts
do not authorise me to put a prisoner undergoing a sentence of hard labour in the
second division.
I may add that the prisoner is reported
to be in good health. He is not and has not
been in the hospital whilst in prison.
GOVERNMENT OFFICIALS AND OUT-
SIDE WORK.
14. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he is aware that it is a
common complaint in the City of Belfast
that members of his staff are engaged in
doing the legitimate work of architects, who
are taxpayers; whether the chief architect
and assistant architect are carrying on a
private practice under the name of Smith
and Rippingham, architects, Eglantine
Avenue; and what steps he is prepared to
take to bring this reprehensible practice to
an end.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have been asked to
reply to this question, which is proper to my
Department. This matter has been discussed on previous occasions,and I would refer the hon. Member to the reply
given on the 22nd May, 1924, to a similar
question by the honourable Member for
Queen's University.
I have nothing to add to the information
then conveyed except to say
that the
Government sees nothing reprehensible in a
Civil Servant devoting his leisure time to
whatever work he may select so long as such
work neither infringes the regulations of the
Civil Service, nor interferes with the proper
and efficient discharge of his official duties.
If there had been any grounds for the complaint of the honourable Member, no doubt
the R.I.B.A.-of which Institute I understand higher officers in question are members
-would havo communicated with
Government on the matter.

RELEASE OF ARRESTED MEN.
18. Mr. W. MCMULLEN asked the Minister of Home Affairs if he can say when the
men who were arrested on the 22nd November, 1925, are to be released.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not prepared
to make any statement in regard to this
matter at present, but I would draw the
attention of the hon. Member to the answer
which I gave to a supplemental question
on the same subject which he addressed to
me on the 8th instant to the effect that these
men have the right to go before the Advisory
Committee, and that I was prepared to give
every consideration to any advice which I
might receive from that committee.

RULES OF THE HOUSE.
A QUESTION AS TO PROCEDURE.
Mr. SPEAKER: Before I call on the Clerk
to read the Orders of the Day there is just
one matter I want to refer to with regard
to what happened in the Committee Stage
of the Education (Administrative Provisions)
Bill on the last day that the House sat.
Owing to a misunderstanding an Amendment
was proposed for which leave to withdraw
was asked. Leave was refused and thereupon
the Question as to whether leave should be
granted or not was put to the House and a
division was taken. That, of course, was
against the Rules of the House. The proper
procedure is that where a Member asks to
withdraw an Amendment, if one Member
objects then that is enough and it cannot be
withdrawn. The Amendment must then be
put to the House. It is not competent to take a division on the Question
whether an Amendment should be withdrawn. Therefore as the division was
not properly taken, I propose that no record
of the division should appear in the Votes of
the House. When the Votes are published,
that division will not appear.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
Perhaps I may assure the hon. Member from
my recollection of the practice in the Imperial Parliament that if those Members who
have been chosen to fill the Chair from time
to time happen not to be present, it has
always been the practice to call on
competent Member to fill the place and carry
on the business. I am sure the whole House
will agree that Mr. Speaker's action in
calling on you, sir, could not be found fault
with in the slightest degree. Many times in
the Imperial Parliament I have been asked
to take the Chair on a sudden emergency in
order that the business may not be interrupted.

Mr. ROBB: Perhaps I should state to the
Committee the reasons why it has been found
convenient to have this Bill re-committed.
It arose in this way: As originally drafted
the Bill proposed to enable the County
Councils to borrow temporarily to discharge
the current debts of the Regional Committees. This provision is purely temporary
and is only intended to cover the next two
years. Since Thursday last when the Bill
was in Committee, and quite independently
of the Bill itself, it has come to the knowledge of the Ministry that certain urban
district councils, who under Section 23 of the
Education Act of 1923 may, if they so elect,
continue to act as Education Authorities for
Technical Education purposes, find themselves in the same difficulty as the Regional
Committees. Owing to their lack of experience they were not able to forecast
accurately the amount of money that, under
the new conditions, would be required in the
current year, and did not strike, or ask to
have struck. a high enough rate for
educational purposes, and, in order that they
may be able to pay their debts before the
end of the year, it is necessary that they
also should be given power to overdraw.
This proposal is, like the other proposal,
merely a temporary measure. It is intended only to keep things running and
enable payment to be made of the debts of
these urban district councils until, with
sufficient experience, they will be able to
forecast accurately their probable requirements for the year. As the Bill stood the
Title was:-
"To extend the powers of councils of
counties and county boroughs to borrow
money for the purposes of the Education
Act (Northern Ireland), 1923."
It did not touch urban district councils, and,
consequently, when it was proposed by this
Amendment to give extended powers also to
urban district councils, these urban district
councils not being within the words of the
Title, it became necessary to re-commit the
Bill and ask the Committee to pass this
Clause in Committee before it is reported to
the House, the Report Stage being on the
Order Paper for to-day. Consequently I
move, on page 2, at the end of line 32, to
add the Amendment that appears as number
5 on page 3 of the Order Paper to-day. It
is to extend to the urban district councils
the same power as is given to the Regional
Committees for educational purposes. It
reads as follows:-
"(5) Where, before the first day of April,
nineteen hundred and twenty-eight, an
Urban District Council in the exercise of
their powers under section three of the
Local Authorities (Financial Provisions)
Act, 1921.-
The Clause is in that form because,
although by the Financial Provisions Act of
1921 local authorities can overdraw, they
must repay within a year, and it was in
order to extend the time in which repayment
can be made that the Bill was originally
introduced. Accordingly, that is the form it
now takes, that where, before the 1st April,
1928, an Urban District Council exercises
these powers of borrowing by overdraft the
Ministry may allow them to repay that
money so borrowed within two years of the
date on which it was borrowed. I beg to
move.
Amendment agreed to.

My experience of the law is this that the
very best thing we did in Northern Ireland
was to pass that special Act enabling the

When the Civil Authorities Act was passed

passed. It has come up year after year-it

Oral Answer to Question.
DEMANDS OF "A" SPECIAL
CONSTABULARY.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN (by Private
Notice) asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he can state if it is a fact that members of the "A" Special Constabulary in
various parts of Northern Ireland who have
been served with notice of disbandment, have
commandeered their barracks, arrested their
officers, and have refused duty pending a
reply from the Prime Minister, to an ultimatum demanding repayment of 3s per week
from a date in November, 1922, and whether
he will make a statement on the situation?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): As the House will remember,
the Prime Minister on Wednesday of last
week made a comprehensive statement in
which, amongst other things, he indicated
that the disbandment of the "A" and "C1"
Forces of the Special Constabulary had now
become necessary.
In the intervening period the Government
have been giving their most anxious and
careful consideration to the terms which
should be granted to the members of these
Forces on disbandment.
I might explain that so far as the members
of the "A" Force are concerned, their engagements are on a purely temporary basis,
and if regard were paid to legal considerations only the Government could terminate
at once the services of each member of this
Force without any payment after the date
of termination. Further, since the inception
of the Force its members have received a
bounty in lieu of pension, which, at the special
request of the men, has been paid at the end
of each contractual period instead of being
reserved for payment as a lump sum on final
discharge.
The problem which has been confronting
the Government is how far they could proceed, by way of payment, over and above
their legal obligations.
It is right that I should emphasise that
the sum of £1,200,000, which we are promised
by the Imperial Government, has already
been mortgaged, except to a very slight extent. It follows, therefore, that whatever
special terms we have to give to the men on
dishandment must be met out of the pockets
of the taxpayer of Northern Ireland. The
Government, therefore, had, while endeavouring to deal generously with the members of
the Special Constabulary on the one hand, always to keep in mind the heavy burdens
which the taxpayer of Northern Ireland had
to bear.
Many conferences have been held on this
subject by the Government, and as a result
I am in a position to announce the following
conclusions which have been arrived at by
the Cabinet:-
Each member of the A. Special Constabulary, whether officer or man, will receive two months' leave on full pay,
counting the two months from the day on
which he receives leave. As some members
will receive leave during the current month
of December, and as these members will
suffer more comparatively than those
members whose disbandment is ordered
later, it has been decided as a concession to
those who receive notice during the current
month to begin to count the two months
as from the 1st January next.
I may mention that for this purpose the
allowances to which the individual is
entitled at the date he receives notice will
be counted in ascertaining the amount to
be paid on disbandment.
It will not be possible to. ascertain at once
the total amount to be paid to each mem
ber, and it is proposed to advance to each
officer or man a substantial sum, and the
balance will be paid at the end of the two
months' period.
I may also mention that each demobilised man will receive a free thirdclass railway warrant either to his home in

the British Islands, or to the place in
which he was recruited. First-class fare
will be allowed in the case of officers.
As regards the C.1 Force, full-time members of this Force whose engagements are
similar to those of Class A., will be granted
the same terms.
I feel confident that the Members of the
House and the public will realise that the
Government, in the
terms which they
have adopted here, dealt not only
fairly but generously with the members of these Forces. The Government
were in the position of arbiter between
the claims of the members of the Force on
the one hand and the taxpayers of Northern
Ireland on the other. It may be that we
have weighted the balance in favour of the
men, but I venture to hope that the public
will not object if we have strained their
generosity.
These terms have been adopted as the result of much care and deliberation, and I am
authorised to state, with the full concurrence
of every Member of the Cabinet, that they
are final and conclusive. In saying this I
have in mind the fact that some members of
the A. Force, and I am glad to say that the
number is not considerable, have during the
last 48 hours been adopting an attitude
which certainly is not in keeping with that
spirit of loyalty which they have hitherto
shown. The Government are willing to
attribute this improper attitude which they
have adopted to a want of consideration on
their part, or it may be to unwise advice, but,
to whatever cause it may be due, the Government now wish to make it plain that the
terms which have now been decided upon
cannot be augmented, and if after the
publication of these terms, which will be
circulated without delay to the respective
barracks, any officer or man displays any
indication of insubordination, he will thereby render himself liable to immediate dismissal, and will forfeit any of the benefits
which the Government's proposals offer.

Mr. ROBB: Perhaps it will be for the

dealt with the borrowing powers of councils
of county boroughs. It was proposed to enact,
firstly, that all such councils should be entitled to borrow for education purposes in
the manner in which they could borrow
under any local Act; secondly, that such
borrowing should not be subject to the
statutory limitations on borrowing; and,
thirdly, that the departmental consent necessary to such borrowing should be given by
the Ministry of Education, and not, as heretofore, by the Ministry of Home Affairs.
In Committee, as the House will remember,
the hon. and learned Member for County
Armagh proposed an Amendment, the object
of which was to put the councils of counties
on the same footing as the councils of county
boroughs to the extent of removing the limitation on borrowing. The Government promised to reconsider the matter and bring it
up on report. Since Thursday last the matter
has been further considered by the Ministries
concerned and the Amendments which have
been set down by the Government not only
meet the wishes of the hon. and learned
Member (Mr. Davison) but go further and
propose to put the councils of counties in
the same position as the councils of county
boroughs by removing the statutory limit of
borrowing, as he desires, and also by enabling the councils of counties to pledge for
their education borrowing the whole county
fund just as the councils of county boroughs
can do. This should enable the councils of
counties to borrow money much more cheaply
and advantageously than if they were
stricted, as they were restricted under the

the education rate.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The Bill which it is my privilege
now to submit to the House deals with an increase in the scales of contributions by the
trade towards the compensation which has
been given to those who were engaged in
what is known as the spirit grocers' business.
I think it would meet the convenience of the
House if I made a short explanation, or
rather submit something of a short history,
of the progress of this question. It will be
remembered in this House that a Claims
1997 Intoxicating Liquor Bill- 15 DECEMBER 1925

Second Reading.
Tribunal was set up statutorily by this
Parliament for the purpose of determining
the compensation which spirit grocers would
receive by reason of the extinction of their
business. We calculated at that time that
the aggregate amount which would be
sufficient to cover the claims of those who
were engaged in that end of the trade would
be between £150,000 and £200,000. From the
data in our possession at that time we
assumed that would possibly be a fair total
of the money that would be sufficient to meet
these payments.
The Tribunal began its operations, and
under the terms of reference by which it
was bound it was found that the amounts
that were required for the purpose of compensating these traders were individually
very considerably larger than anything we
had calculated upon in making our arrangements for the procedure. It may perhaps
surprise the House to learn that instead of
our £150,000 and £200,000 being sufficient for
the purpose for which the money was to be
applied, the sum has already amounted to a
total of £380,000, and there are still some
number of I was going to say some fewcountry claims not yet satisfied, so I think we
may make up our minds that possibly the
total will reach a sum not far from £450,000.
as
As the power of the Government to levy
trade (as it had undertaken
upon the
to do) a scale of charges regarded
sufficient to compensate the spirit grocers
proved inadequate, as I say it is necessary to
come to the House and ask for power to increase the levy so as to enable the interest on
the capital money which the Government has
advanced, and also a Sinking Fund, to be provided. We have had conferences with the
different members of the trade, and although
it would be wrong to say that every Member
is satisfied absolutely, still upon the whole I
think I
can assume that the general
trade is satisfied that the arrangements we
have made are fair and equitable. Now, if I
may say so, I have great sympathy with the
trade in this matter. While some part of the
responsibility is unmistakeably attachable to
themselves, because, although the Government
had contemplated that compensation based
on three years' profits would be adequate, the
trade were sufficiently generous to admit that
they were willing to pay a levy based upon a
five years' estimate of profits. To that extent
I say responsibility for the present position
rests with the trade.
We recognise now that their generosity has
imposed a very heavy burden on them, and it
is no part of the Government's policy to impose a heavy burden on any part of the community if that can be avoided. The arrangement that was made with the trade was that
this capital money, that is to say £450,000,
should be extinguished in a period of twenty
The House will realise that a comyears.
paratively short period of twenty years would
mean a very heavy burden upon the trade,
and in view of the representations that were
made by those who were competent to speak
for them, we agreed to relax that provision,
and agreed also to a 45 years' term. It will
be understood, that the 45 years' extension, instead of 20 years, naturally lowers the contribution very materially, and to that extent
I was very glad indeed to be able to meet
the trade, although it means that the
Government of the country has to carry a
large burden of debt over a very much longer
period.
There were also other little points that had
to be considered, and I considered them from
the point of view of making the burden, as
I have said before, as easily borne by those
who had to bear it as possible, and so after
some discussions with those who, as I say,
were entitled to speak for the trade, I
agreed that the Measure should not be
brought into operation for another year,
that is to say instead of imposing an
additional levy for the financial year
that we are now entering on the trade
will not be asked to start the larger levy,
the larger rate of contribution, until the year
following, that is the year 1927. I think that
the trade realises that we have-so far as it
was possible for
at any rate-dealt
generously with them in this matter. The
whole object that we had in view was to
carry the transaction-a very difficult and
burdensome transaction-through with as
little irritation to those who were concerned
as possible. For that reason I felt I was
justified in making the concessions which I
am now outlining. As the trade is in full
agreement with the Government I hope that
those Members who are listening to me now

move.

The

functions of the tribunal would thereupon be
transferred to the Ministry of Finance as
already provided in the original Act. The
reason for the change is twofold.
Firstly, when the Act was first drawn up,
it was not known within what period the
assessment of compensation would take place.
Accordingly, the ample margin of three
years was allowed. It is now quite clear
that compensation will have been finally
assessed and paid by the close of the present
Financial Year, and accordingly the transfer
of functions is arranged for an earlier date.
Secondly, the other function of the Claims
Tribunal has been to fix the annual levy.
That levy has now been fixed by the
Tribunal for a period of three Licensing
Years-the period contemplated by the
original Act-and now that no alteration is
going to be made in the current Licensing
Year, the opportunity has been taken, for
administrative convenience, to provide that
the transfer to the Ministry of Finance
shall take place at a reasonable period before the new levy has to be imposed in the
forthcoming year. Under the Act as it
stands, the transfer takes place at a period
which is administratively inconvenient.

Finance Bill.

Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. POLLOCK: I rise to move the Second
Reading of the Finance Bill. Within the
scope of this Measure there are included
three separate subjects, of which the first is
the amendment of the scales of taxation in
respect of mechanically propelled vehicles.
The second part of the Measure is an amendment of the law relating to succession duty
rendered necessary by a recent decision of
the House of Lords. The third part of the
Measure is a small but necessary change
in the law of inland revenue. I propose to
discuss these matters with as much brevity
as is possible consistent with the importance
of the matters I am about to submit to the
House.
It is not unnatural that any Measure which
has for its object the imposition of taxation
should be subject to an amount of criticism,
or, at anyrate, comment on the part of those
who are interested; and if the matter is of
general interest so much the greater is the
comment or criticism. For some time past
it has been borne in on the Government that
the revenue derived from the taxation of
heavy motor vehicles especially is not nearly
commensurate with the cost of the construction and upkeep of roads necessary for this
form of transport. We have, therefore, been
encouraged and, indeed, compelled by the
strength of public opinion to review the
conditions under which the services have
been conducted.
My right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Home Affairs, has received many resolutions
from public bodies on this subject. All the
County Councils of the Province have uttered
protests-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-
Chambers of Commerce passed resolutions,
Finance Bill-
Second Reading.
15 DECEMBER 1925
and the Farmers' Union have also pressed
the Government on this matter. These protests are not unnatural when the burden
borne by ratepayers is considered. So long
as the development of motor traffic was in
its initial stage of infancy the Government
had no desire at all to interfere to any
extent or to change any of the burdens borne
by it in view of the fact that it was contributing to the convenience of very large
portions of the community, and particularly
those who live in remote districts far away
from railway stations.
But in view of those representations which,
as I have said, we have received, we feel the
time has arrived when the trade should stand
on its own feet and become part of the
economic system of the country. We feel,
therefore, that it is entitled to bear its fair
share of the burden in order that the roads
of the Province may be maintained. Hitherto
the ratepayer has borne the major portion
of that burden. He has paid in many cases
very heavily in rates without receiving any
advantage in exchange. He has to pay for
the construction and maintenance of roads,
many of which are really prejudicial to
the interests of the ratepayers who were concerned. Some of these ratepayers, such as
the railways, were paying very heavy rates
for a service which in effect was tending to
their own undoing. To me, at anyrate, this
seems hardly just or equitable.
It has been suggested by those who criticise
this Measure that because the English
Government have not moved in this matter,
therefore we should disregard the necessities
of our own local conditions. But the conditions in Ulster are very different from those
obtaining in England. I wish to impress this
upon hon. Members perhaps as much as any
part of the statement I have to make.
Because the humidity of our climate is so
much greater than that of England the cost
is greater not only in the construction but in
maintenance of the roads. We have also much
longer stretches of bogland in Ulster, on
which unstable foundations it is difficult and
costly not only to construct but to maintain.
Any one who is familiar with the country
districts of Northern Ireland understands
the character of the roads which proceed
through these long stretches of bogland.
Furthermore, there is a considerably larger
mileage of roads in Ireland in proportion to
the population than in Great Britain. The
figures are that for every thousand of the
population of Great Britain there are 4
miles of roads. In Ulster there are ten
miles. That is to say, that to the inhabitants of Northern Ireland, if they intend to
maintain roads of the same character as
those existing in Britain, the cost per
thousand of the population would be 2 times
as great. All these factors suggest that our
local conditions and those of Great Britain
are not comparable, and that we must work
out our own salvation in our own way dependent upon and consistent with the conditions
under which we live.
The estimates of the expenditure on our
Ulster roads for the year in which we now
find ourselves-this present year-are about
£1,200,000, that is, for construction and
maintenance. Of this vast sum motor
taxation, this levy on the motor trade, only
raises £300,000 O'r thereabouts. Of this
£300,000 commercial motors over two tons,
that is to say, all large motors of two tons
weight-I mean unladen-actually only provide some £30,000, and it is estimated by
expert opinion that this class of motor does
far the largest damage to the roads. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) The balance of
revenue, roughly £270,000, is provided in the
main by private motors which it is not the
intention of the Government to touch in respect of taxes for reasons which I will explain, and also light vehicles which
admittedly do less damage to the roads.
en-
To be more definite, we have it on the
evidence of practical men that investigation
and experience prove that the heavy fiveton lorry 5 tons unladen-regularly
gaged, damages a road to the extent of £300
per annum, and yet this class of vehicle has
in the past escaped with a tax of £30. It
seems to me that it is difficult to defend the
position of the heavier lorry by any process
of logic or reason.
It was suggested on Thursday, when my
right hon. Friend submitted the Money
Resolution which necessarily preceded this
Bill, that the farming element were prejudiced because the Bill proposed to increase
the tax on the lighter class of motor wagon
by £2 per annum. That argument was submitted to us and I think that apart altogether from the farmers or any liability
that the Government are under to assist
them in any way, it must be admitted that
the lighter wagon of 12 cwt. and one ton do
infinitely less damage to the roads than the
heavy wagon to which I have referred. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). But nevertheless it
has been found on investigation that the
distribution of these small licences has not
been very great nor have their uses in the
country been very general.
In order that the House may realise the
position of farmers and their relation to the
use of lorries let me mention that there are
120,000 farmers in Northern Ireland and the
latest returns I have been able to get show
that there are only 50 12-cwt. lorries in
the whole of Ulster. The following is the
distribution of these lorries:-Antrim, 2;
Down, 2; Tyrone, 2; Fermanagh, 3; in Derry
County, 9; in Armagh, 17; and in Belfast

Let me deal in detail with the arguments
which have been submitted against the
changes. First, I will touch upon the railway argument. It has been suggested that
the Government are considering the interests
of the railways in these matters. I have no
interest in the railways, and 1 hold no brief
for them. I begin by saying that. But at
the same time it is not part of the business
of the Government to bear heavily or unjustly upon any portion of the community,
and the railways have just as great rights
as any section of the community, but no more.
It is evident that the heavy lorries which,
I am informed, do from 80 per cent. to 90.
per cent. of the road damage through the
country are receiving in effect a huge subsidy
out of the rates, and it has been calculated
that that subsidy in money value is not less
than £500,000 a year. If the same subsidy
were given to the railways it would mean
that all the goods traffic on the railways
could be carried for 40 per cent. less than
at the present time. I need not tell you
what the effect of that would be upon the
markets. I do not want to emphasise that
point, but I am dealing with arguments put
forward that for some reason or other we
were considering the railways. Hon. Members will realise that in commending the
proposed scale of motor taxation to the House
I am in reality merely advocating the interests of the whole of the ratepayers of
Northern Ireland, as they are the persons
affected. This consideration will, I am sure.
carry considerable weight with the hon.
Members who listen to me.
Now I come to the second argument, that is,
the benefits. Who benefits by the change?
It is the ratepayers who will benefit by the
increased scales, because all the money of
the Road Fund is ear-marked for the con
struction and maintenance of roads. It is
the ratepayers who will benefit because roads
must be constructed and maintained, and
who must maintain them if the users of
them do not contribute? Obviously the rate
payers. From the fact that in this year
£1,200,000 has been expended upon the roads
of Northern Ireland and the insufficiency,
in fact the negligibility of the contribution
from motor taxation, it must of necessity
be a burden which would be thrown upon
the ratepayers if the roads of the country
are to be maintained. Therefore, it is the
ratepayer who will benefit by any addition
to motor taxation.
Thirdly, passenger fares. Great play has
been made by some people that the passenger
fares of charabanes will have to be increased
because of this comparatively small additional
taxation which will be imposed upon chara
bancs. Perhaps it will interest hon. Members
to learn something of the calculation under
that head. Take a vehicle seating 32 pas
sengers. The increase in tax is £4. If you
take a very moderate mileage for a charabanc
of 15,000 miles a year, the additional cost per
mile is 1-15th of a penny, and if this is dis
tributed over an average load of only
passengers, the increase is 1-300th part of a
penny per mile. That would be the increase
each passenger would have to pay because
of the additional £4 of taxation levied on
the charabanc. I find there is not great
sympathy with those who have discussed the
matter of the charabancs.

Weighing all these arguments and in vier

their duty in the interests of the Province

who use the roads and in whose interest
they are maintained.

e has given to this House of the intention

position in which you are now placing the

Mr. GRANT: I rise to oppose the Second
Reading of the Bill, but before giving my
reasons for doing so I would like to compliment the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock)
on the very lucid explanation he gave us
in moving the Second Reading of the
Measure. I am bound, however, to confess
that I cannot compliment him on the tactics
he has adopted on behalf of the Government
in bringing the Opposition, who voted against
them on Thursday last, into the Lobby with
them this afternoon. They have made a compromise. Those who were disloyal to the
Government on Thursday last have got a
concession and they can now go into the
Lobby with the Government. We have been
often told and have read in the Press that
this is a Belfast Parliament. After what
has taken place we may call it a Farmers'
Parliament.
It is on behalf of Belfast people that I
rise to protest against this particular Bill.
I join with my Friends on the Opposition
benches, if I may call them my friends for
this afternoon, in pointing out that the
Minister in introducing the Intoxicating
Liquor Bill said that they brought in representatives of the trade and consulted with
them on that particular matter. In connection with the Pharmacy Bill recently passed
in the House we were also told that the
representatives of the trade were brought in
and consulted and the Bill drafted to suit
their requirements. We have this powerful
motor trade entirely ignored and a Bill is
brought in as drafted by some Civil Servant
in the Ministry of Finance. All the claims
I hold in my hand a statement from very
large firms in Belfast who are engaged in
bringing the necessaries of life from the
country-from the farmers who have been
spoon-fed by this Government. One particular firm that I know very well is going to
have to pav £944 extra in taxation at the
beginning of the year as a result of this Bill.
The Government have professed that they
are interested in bringing down the cost of
living. They point out to us that they are
doing everything they possibly can to reduce
the cost of living, and yet they are going to
put extra taxation on the necessaries of life
by increasing the taxation on heavy motors.
I am not foolish enough to think that the
consumer will not have to pay for this extra
taxation. I know very well that milk, bread,
and other food, for which the unemployed
and poor working people can hardly find
money, are bound to be increased in price
as a result of this taxation, and yet the
Government bring in this Bill, which will
have that effect. It is very easy for Members
of the Government, who do not know anything about the difficulties experienced by
working people even to exist at the moment,
to say that this will not mean anything
extra. I know from personal experience that
if there is only the slightest increase in the
cost of transport of any particular commodity
the price of that commodity immediately
jumps up.
The Minister pointed out in his speech this
afternoon one or two things that I cannot
agree with. He said it was the intention of
the Government to prevent motor lorries or
charabancs of too great length being used on
the roads. They object to the length of the
vehicles, and yet they are making provision
for the taxation of trailers at the end of
these lorries. The Government ought to be
consistent and abolish these vehicles off the
roads altogether if their argument is sound.
The Minister also said that these heavy
motors were responsible for destroying
the roads, and that they ought to be made
pay for them. I wonder has the Minister
taken into consideration the fact that some
very heavy lorries never go on the country
roads at all. People who own warehouses in
Belfast keep the lorries running to the steamship sheds and railway goods yards all the
time. They never travel a yard on country
roads. Yet they have got to pay an extra
tax for damage for which they are not really
responsible.
In connection with the Intoxicating
Liquor Bill, we find that those in the
country districts have only to pay compensation to the amount of damage done in
their own respective districts, but under this
particular Bill the compensation is spread

HOUSE OF COMMONS

over the Six Counties, no matter whether
the lorries are used on the roads or not. I
want to make a strong appeal to the Government to reconsider their action, though I
fear that I am appealing to deaf ears as a
result of the concessions made here this
afternoon. At anyrate I am taking this
opportunity to register my protest, and I
am determined to go into the Lobby and vote
against the Second Reading of this Bill.
Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL: I have listened
with great interest to the arguments put
forward by the Minister of Finance in moving the Second Reading of this Bill, and I
want to acknowledge straight away that I
think there is an absolute necessity for this
taxation. The roads have got to be kept up.
It is an old saying that the man who pays
the piper has the right to choose the tune.
and I think if you are going to choose the
tune-good roads-then you ought to see that
the persons who use the roads pay for them.
I am going to vote against this Amendment
to postpone the Second Reading of the Bill
for three months. My reason for that attitude is, I think it should be settled at once.
There are points in the Bill that I strongly
object to. The first and the main thing that
I object to is this, if I may be allowed to
put it in the form of a simile. A man bought
a large lorry, say, six months ago. He
bought it in perfect good faith, assuming
that the tax was going to remain the same.
On payment of that tax he was able to run
it economically. Suddenly he finds this thing
thrown at him, with the result that on the
1st January the lorry will become scrap from
an economic point of view. I think, therefore, that in fairness to that man he should
be given a fair warning that he is going to
be taxed, and that the tax should be imposed
upon him gradually, and not all in one year.
In other words, that the tax instead of being
imposed in full on the first day of next year.
should be spread over a period of five years.
beginning with 20 per cent., until it arrives
at the full figure as now suggested.
The Minister of Finance used a very strong
argument, and I acknowledge the absolute
necessity of having this money, but I do not.
think that the credit of Northern Ireland
has fallen so far that he could not raise
£50,000 for one year, or £250,000 for the five
years. I would go the length of suggesting
to the Government that instead of an increase
at the rate of 20 per cent. per annum for
five years they should put on the tax at the
rate of 20 per cent. of the proposed increase
for six or seven years. However, my proposal is that the Government saould borrow
more money than they are going to raise
from this tax, and form a sinking fund by
gradually increasing these taxes. Thereby,
at the end of five years, the man who has
bought a lorry within the past six months
knows what is coming forward. It is up to
him to say whether he will buy a new lorry
that size, or go for a one ton lorry that is
going to be let off cheaply. At the same time
it will have the tendency-and I fancy it is
the wish of most people--to reduce the traffic
of the really heavy lorry, and thereby save
the roads from a considerable amount of
damage. I put that forward to the Government. I do not profess to be a master of
finance or a financier at all, but I ask the
Minister of Finance to consider whether it
would be possible to put this tax on by steps,
and if he can see his way to that, so far as
the heavy lorries are concerned, I am perfectly willing to back him up in even
increasing that tax still further.
Colonel WOODS: I rise to support the
Amendment before the House. To my mind
this Bill is a curiosity in more than one
respect. I have been informed that it has
been the practice to bring in a Finance Bill
immediately after the Budget. This one has
been brought in as an afterthought. It is a
hastily designed affair, it is full of faults.
and shows want of thought. I agree entirely
with the hon. Member who said that this
Measure was brought in without any consultation with the people who are directly
interested in the taxation. Early in 1923,
there was a Departmental Committee on
Motor Transport and Road Vehicles set up
by the Imperial Government, and in May,
1923, I asked the right hon. Gentleman, the
Minister of Home Affairs, a question upon
the subject, and he was kind enought to give
me an answer. It was to this effect:-
I am aware that there is a desire for a
change in the existing law regarding the
system of taxation of motor vehicles.
The matter is at present engaging the
attention of a special Committee appointed
by the Minister of Transport, London.
Any change in the present system would
necessarily be made with close regard to
the system of Imperial taxation, and 1
have accordingly, in conjunction with my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance,
and with the kind permission of the Imperial authorities, appointed a small informal Committee to follow the proceedings
of the London Committee and to attend at
the private sittings of that Committee.
The conditions regarding the taxation of
motor vehicles in Northern Ireland are in
no way dissimilar to those in Great
Britain-
I want those particular words underlined.
-and, as the evidence tendered to the
London Committee is of the most comprehensive and exhaustive character, the
setting up of a special Committee to hear
evidence in Northern Ireland would involve unnecessary delay and the incurring
of unjustifiable expense.

The Members of this House are entitled to

Boundary Commission, for supressing a report? I would like to ask the right hon.
Gentleman if their recommendations were

I would like to ask the Minister of Finance,

planation of the Bill that he has given from

I do not know whether the House is aware

They pay for them over a period of a year

are they to do when the taxation is increased? I do not know whether the object

Mr. POLLOCK: No.
Colonel WOODS: If you are sufficiently

Mr. ARCHDALE: That would be a good
job, too.
Colonel WOODS: Perhaps the right hon.
Gentleman is right. I cannot speak with
his experience. Take it from the point of

country

Mr. POLLOCK: Oh, yes.
Colonel WOODS: Taking this taxation
from the commercial point of view, I can say
that business men all over regret that this

of safeguarding the commerce of Ulster. And
it is regarded by most business men that I
have spoken to on the subject as a blow at
commerce. What advantages do we get
from the commercial standpoint? I can tell
you what we will lose. The vans that deliver milk in this city from the country,
untapped by the railways-and I think they
have found it cheaper to bring milk even

certainly deliver milk in Belfast, and even
the bakeries in Belfast deliver bread throughout the whole of Ulster. These people
cannot carry on. With the increase of
taxation they cannot deliver these things—
Mr. POLLOCK: The three-hundredth part
of a penny.
Colonel WOODS: The three-hundredth part
of a penny if multiplied by two or three
millions will amount to enough money.
(Laughter.) Well, then, from the point of
view of the linen trade are there going to
be deliveries from the quays to the warehouses and from the warehouses to the shipping? Are we going to get our insurance at
the same figure? No; it will be increased.
It all adds to the price of the commodity to
be sold, and Heaven knows we are suffering

enough now with the freight that is added

Now 1 come to what the Prime Minister

the people of Ulster would not be taxed any

Mr. POLLOCK: We have worse roads.
Colonel WOODS: Worse roads! They were
never any good at any rate. You will never
make them like the English roads. There
was one point the right hon. Gentleman
brought up, and that was that this year we
were paying £1,200,000 for the upkeep of the

to be paid every year? I would like to ask,
is he basing his calculations on this year or
for ten years? I understand the life of a
concrete road is certainly something more
than one year, that is, of course, if it is
made right.
Well, regarding the railway influence, it
certainly seems to anyone looking at this
Bill for the first time or the second time,
that the railway influence had some bearing
on it. But I would point out to the Government and to those interested in the railways
that they must give way to progress. At one
time the railway was not, and we had a
magnificent service of coaches. We had a
reputation for horses; we had great breeding
stations for horses and many servants were
kept. Country inns were kept up, and it was
at one time a great industry. The railway
came along and wiped it clean out of existence. Now when we have this better prospect, and cheaper transport comes along I
think it is about time that the railways
should recognise that their function lies in
the long distances and not in the short ones,
and that they should make some compromise
with road transport and not try to put them
out of existence.
Finally I consider that this House has not
been treated fairly, and it has certainly not
been treated with any respect when this report that was submitted to the Government
by their experts-two Civil Servants, I daresay the best we can find in the country, and
one gentleman who is well known for his
sanity-this report was not given to the
House nor are we given any idea of what was
recommended to the Government. But at the
same time there are means of finding out
something, and we know that their recommendations were not as submitted in the
terms of the Bill to-day. I certainly will
oppose the Second Reading of this Bill.
Mr. COOPER: My name has been referred
to by the hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Beattie). Consequently I would just like to
say a few words to let him see our side of
this case. In County Fermanagh where these
words were spoken we are very glad to see
the motor cars and we are very glad to see
the motor buses provided they are not the
great big ones. We are glad to see the motor
'buses because they bring the railway rates
down. I think nearly everyone in the Province of Ulster knows that since the motor
'bus went to Armagh the railway rates have
been reduced by half. Now most of the people
hope that we will have a few light motor
'buses coming as far as Enniskillen, because
the railway companies continue to keep up
the old charge there. But I understand that
the rates in existence at the present time for
motor lorries were fixed about ten or fifteen
yars ago, and that no increase has been made
on these charges since. Now the position of
the ratepayers in the country, for instance
in my own county is that in 1913 our bill
for the upkeep of the roads was £14,000. This
year the bill for the upkeep of our roads
was £12,297. And that means that during
that period the cost to the ratepayers of
keeping up the roads has increased to three
times, while the cost of the motor licence has
not increased by a single farthing. And although the increase is so large at every meeting we get a letter from the Ministry of
Home Affairs in Belfast, and every letter
says we want you to make your roads better
still.
Now the hon. Member for East Belfast
(Mr. Beattie) stated that we had very bad
roads in County Fermanagh. But I would
like to tell him we have nearly as good roads
in Fermanagh as in any other county in the
Six, and we have our proportion and over
our proportion of both motor cars and lorries.
I am very glad to say we have. We nave
very large motor traffic and we have inoreasing motor traffic. There is no one more
pleased than I am to see it there. But if the
bill to the ratepayers is to go on increasing
at this tremendous rate, surely the people
who run these cars must contribute to the
bill? (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Now in that statement to which reference
was made the hon. Member will see that I
referred to heavy motor lorries-particularly
to heavy motor lorries, and I know that we in
Fermanagh have gone to considerable trouble
to put the roads in first class repair, and a
few days later we have had the trouble
of sending out the county surveyor to
dig a ten-tonner out of it. Some of the motor
lorries which have come down from Belfast
have been so big that they have actually gone
down into the road altogether. And it has
been asked why we have not made our roads
properly. But with the increasing expenditure we have never been able to overtake,

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I desire
also to associate myself with the congratulations to the Minister of Finance on his
clear statement here, and no part of that
statement pleased me better than the one
in which he said that the money which
would accrue from the motor tax would
every penny of it go to the upkeep of the
roads-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-because
we find that the Chancellor of the Exchequer
in England at the present time is turning
his eyes in the direction of making a raid
on the Road Fund. Therefore, it is
especially agreeable to me that the Minister
of Finance has made it clear that this money
would go to road upkeep.
Now I do not know where the Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Grant) conjured up the
picture of the Government spoon-feeding the
farmers with regard to this Bill. It must
be that the hon. Member has a lively imagination. I hardly thought of charging him
with that. Therefore, I cannot conceive how
he conjured up this vision except from his
lively imagination. I cannot see that there
is any special provision made for the farmer
with regard to this Bill. I do think that
in putting forward a claim in this House
that the farmer should receive special consideration in this new tax we were not asking that they should be given special favours.
We are simply saying that this system of
taxation which is at present proposed in
this Bill is an injustice to the farming community and should be modified, so that this
injustice should be to some extent done away
with.
Now when the basis of taxation was shifted
from petrol on to horsepower and carrying
capacity, no section of the community was
hit to the same extent as the farming community. No section of this new basis of
taxation applied with such injustice, because
I do say it is grossly unfair to the farmers
to tax on this flat rate the farmer that may
have his lorry out only once or twice a week
to exactly the same degree as the man whose
lorry is out every day of the week.
I say that the basis of taxation set out
in this Bill is grossly unfair to the farming
community and should be amended. I intend in the Committee Stage to ask that the
scale of charges with regard to the farming
community be amended. Like the hon.
Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr.
Cooper) I gladly admit that the passenger
charabancs which have come on our roads
have been a great benefit to rural Ulster and
have opened up the rural districts. This has
tended to soften the amenities of rural life
and I have no doubt will tend to keep the
people more in the rural districts and on the
land. I also freely admit that the lorries
conveying our produce have had a very good
effect in bringing down our transport
charges.
The Minister of Finance in his statement
said, if I heard him aright, that 40 per cent.
of our transport is carried by motor at the
present time and if that 40 per cent. went
on the railways they could afford to carry
it much cheaper. I would like to ask the
Minister of Finance had the railways not
this 40 per cent. at one time, and why did
they lose it? They lost it because they refused to reduce their charges to meet the
people of this country. I do not wish to
see either motor 'buses or motor lorries
taxed to such an extent that they will be
put off our roads, because I freely admit
that along these lines they are a great
benefit, but I do wish to say that these motor
'buses and motor lorries should pay rates
in accordance with the damage they do to our
roads.
The farming community have a perfect
right to, and in justice ask for, special rates
because they are hit in two ways.
It is a
well-known fact that owing to the present
slippery state of many of our roads farmers
are almost entirely unable to use the old
horse traction as it is a danger to put horses
on many of the roads that have been reconstructed. In the reconstruction there seems
to have been only one interest considered,
that of the motorists. Therefore, the farmer
cannot use his horse to convey his stuff to
the market and to bring home his necessities
in the same manner as he used to do. He is

I do think this House should face the fact
that we should do everything to encourage
tillage farming. If a duty is put on the
farmers' lorries it will be a tax on the
whole of tillage farming. We have got to
realise this fact that last year there were
were 27,000 acres less under the plough in

Of that 27,000 acres, 12,000 represented corn.
The first duty of the Government is to encourage tillage farming. Let the Government and this House think what those 27,000
acres would mean in extra employment, in
the present state of our employment market,

If that tax were put on the farmers' lorries

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I think I may
approach this subject this afternoon in a
somewhat detached manner. I was not present in the House the other day when a
debate took place on the matter under discussion this afternoon, and I have had no
person interviewing me in regard to the
question, so that I have had to come to my
own conclusions independently of any outside opinions. The position I take up in
regard to this question I can state in a
sentence or two.
The Bill as originally drafted and submitted to the House in the Money Resolution
was one I could not have supported in its
entirety without most of the modifications
which the Minister of Finance has indicated
to-day. I think he has understood public
opinion rightly, and he has indicated that
the Government are prepared on the first two
classes of motors to allow the taxation to remain exactly as it was without any increase.
"The greatest good of the greatest number,"
I presume, was in his mind. Therefore, the
masses of the, owners of these one-ton and
smaller lorries will not have to pay any
additional contribution towards the upkeep
of the roads, for, after all, they are not the
people who contribute to the wear and tear
of the surfaces of these roads throughout the
country. On these particular points I am
very glad the Government has consented to
make a concession.
We come now to the other classes that remain. There are the trucks from two tons
up to five tons, including the 'buses. Any
right-thinking person who has studied this
motor problem as it has developed, and is
likely to develop during the next few years,
must concede the fact that these very heavy
vehicles on the roads of rural Ulster are putting an undue strain upon them. It will be
conceded that it is hardly fair to the rural
community in the Six Counties to have the
roads cut up and made impassable by heavy
motor traffic. There may be a five-ton truck
carrying another five tons, with probably two
trailers. No road in the Six Counties is able
to stand such traffic. You are asking the
rural community-I do not mean merely the
farmers, but the whole rural community, the
ratepayers of the six different counties-to
put their hands in their pockets to keep up
these roads, and put them into first-class
order. I do not think it is reasonable to expect them to do it all. The people who are
receiving the main benefits from these
roads, the motorists, are not travelling for
pleasure. They charge a certain rate for the
goods or traffic they carry, and they ought to
be prepared to pay some additional taxation.
The County Councils have a grievance. I
do think an effort is being made in this Bili
to remedy an undoubted grievance. But the
question remains in regard to these motor
lorries, whether after all the proposals in
the Bill do not go a little bit too far. I am
not at all sure-I have not closely studied the
matter-that in some cases the increase of
350 per cent. upon the existing taxes is not
possibly a little bit excessive. There might
be room for compromise there, and some
little concession might be made. But I do
think the owners of heavy motor lorries, enjoying the privileges of going on the country
roads, ought to be, and are, I hope,
prepared to make an increased contribution
for the privileges they enjoy. That is only
fair and reasonable.
There is another side to this question:
How does that affect another class of the
community? You can never increase taxation upon any one class of the community
without considering how it is going to act
and re-act upon other interests as well. We
have heard that most of these heavy lorries
come out of the city of Belfast and the other
industrial centres and trade in various districts throughout the Six Counties. A point
has been made here to-day, and I would like
to emphasise it. It shows you how difficult
it is with the best intention in the world to
bring in remedial legislation without committing unwittingly or of necessity an
injustice upon someone else. Take the
merchants and manufacturers of, say a big
centre like the city of Belfast or the city of
Londonderry who use two-ton and four-ton
trucks for the conveyance of their merchandise to and from the railways and steamboats. There are hundreds of these vehicles

series of changes in the taxation and addtions to the taxation at the tail end of the
Session. You are putting a fresh tax upon
Ulster.

they were there, and I was there at the
childrens' treat given in Bangor to the
children of East Belfast.
I myself had something to do with the
organising of a treat for 5,000 children in
West Belfast. We took them to Bangor
where they could have a day from their
homes at the beautiful open space at Ballyholme, where the breezes of the sea came as
a fresh experience in their young lives. It
was a source of infinite delight to them and
even greater delight to those who participated. We were charged for that 6d for each
child. Some of the children had never
feasted their eyes upon a blade of grass,
hardly any of them had ever had a view of
the sea, and to them it was an infinite pleasure. The motor owners only charged 6d a
head for them.
I should be very sorry to cripple in the
slightest degree the great vehicular institutions that enable us to do these things. My
opinion is that this Bill ought to be withdrawn or postponed for three months. The
game is not worth the candle. It is not of
any value to the Treasury, but it would be
a matter of encouragement to this trade to
drop the tax altogether. I think that the

Oral Answers
16 DECEMBER 1925
I may perhaps state that my attention has
been drawn to statements which have appeared giving a misrepresentation of the
terms of service of the "A" Special Constabulary.
Members of the Special Constabulary have
no right to continuing employment, and, as
I mentioned yesterday, their engagements are
on a purely temporary basis, their contract
of service being renewed from month to
month.
Their basic rate of pay is seven shillings
per day, but, in addition, the following allowances may be drawn:-
(1) Rent Allowance (which is paid to 1,795
Constables) at an average of £20 per
annum.
(2) Medical Allowance at an average of
28 3d per month.
(3) Boot Allowance at the rate of 1s 6d
per week.
(4) Plain Clothes Allowance for 50 men-
58 per week.
(5) Pension Bounty £20 per annum.
(6) Uniform Allowance for County and
and Area Commandants and Adjutants,
£20 per annum.
(7) Uniform Upkeep Allowance to these
Officers at £5 per annum.
(8) Uniform Allowance to other Officers
at £10 per annum.
(9) Separation Allowance for 1,300 men at
2s per day.
There are further technical allowances to
wireless men and drivers at 2s per day, and
to fitters, at 48 per day.
The officers draw over and above their basic
pay of 78 per day, command allowance varying from 126 6d to 176 6d per day; head constables draw 4s per day, station sergeants,
28, and sergeants, 2s over and above their
basic pay.
The amount to which these allowances
reach in the whole may be gauged from the
fact that, according to this year's estimates,
the total allowances amount to £504,000, as
compared with £602,000 for the item of pay
alone.
I have thought it well to mention these
figures so as to remove any misconception
that may be in the minds, either of Members
of the House or of the public as to the conditions of service of these men, and as
to the pay and allowances which they
have been drawing, and also to indicate
the heavy burden which will be imposed on the taxpayer of Northern Ireland,
if the Government continue the maintenance
of the Force for a day longer than is absolutely necessary.

The CHAIRMAN: There are two manuscript Amendments to this Finance Bill in
addition to those which appear on the Order
Paper. The Amendment which I propose to
take first in order to preserve the sequence
of the Amendments is the one that stands
last on the Order Paper, and I propose to
take it on page 2, line 6, subject to certain
modifications to make it fit. The Amendment which the hon. Member (Mr. George
Henderson) will move will, therefore, be in
the following terms:-
Page 2, line 6, insert "Vehicles as described in the said Bill owned by farmers
and used exclusively for agricultural purposes shall be charged half the standard
duty.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I am sure I
am only expressing the mind of the Committee in congratulating you, Mr. Moles, on
being restored to health and being able once
more to take your wonted place as Chairman
of Committees. I am sure this Committee
will readily recognise the wonderful knowledge of Parliamentary procedure which you
have, and will always feel sure that in the
conduct of the business here you will keep
them right. Therefore, I congratulate you
on being restored to health and being in your
old place in this Committee. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
In moving the Amendment which stands
in my name I do not intend to occupy the
time of the Committee very long because I
spoke on this question yesterday. I thank
you, Mr. Moles, for allowing this Amendment
to come first, so preserving the other Amendments I have on the Paper if I should feel
disposed to move them. It has been suggested that the farming community is a community who would like to shove the burdens
they should shoulder themselves on to other
people and that they in this action and other
actions that have been taken on their behalf are asking other people to pay the rates
they should pay. I want to emphasise the
point that in putting forward this Amendment I am asking no special favour for
farmers. I am only asking that taxation
that is unjust in its incidence to them should
be modified to give them something like
fair play.
There is an inclination in some quarters
at the present time to sneer at farmers and
the farming community. It is not so very
long since those same people when during
the war we were getting down to the
foundations, realities, and essences, were
very loud in their praise of the farmers.
We are accused now of coming here to be
spoon-fed. If it had not been for the farming community at that time there might
not be so many spoons needed now in some
parts of the community. We were told at
that time that never again would farming
be allowed to slip back again into the bad
state it was in prior to the war, but at the
present time agriculture is really slipping
back and is, I think, probably in some respects in as bad if not worse condition than
it was previous to the war.
I wish to say this, and I think the Committee will agree with me, that as long as
the basis of taxation for these motors is
put on either horse-power or on unladen
weight that tax is an unjust tax on the
farming community and bears unequally on
them. I challenge any Member of this Committee to deny that assertion. As long as
taxation is based as it is at present on
either horse-power or carrying capacity, the
weights are loaded against the farming community. If the basis of taxation had been
changed from carrying capacity and put
on petrol then I would have no case because the user of a motor vehicle would be
taxed in accordance with how he uses the
roads. The Prime Minister says we have
not the power to touch or change the basis
of taxation. It seems to me rather strange if
there should be such unanimity of opinion
SU
Finance Bill-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

[Mr. G. Henderson]
in this House and apparently in the Press
and other places that the basis of taxation
should be changed there is not some attempt
made to do it. Is it officialdom? Is it
that the Excise officials are against a
change in the basis of taxation? But
since the Prime Minister has told us
that we have no power to change the basis of
taxation we can, in the manner in which this
amendment suggests, help at least to make
more just and more equitable to the farming
community the taxes paid on the unladen
weight of a lorry. It will be readily
admitted that, taking the farmers generally,
their lorries do not use the roads to anything
like the same extent as is done by lorries
owned by traders. A farmer's lorry may
only be on the road once, twice, or three
times, or, indeed, at some times of the year
when he is getting his hay and corn harvested,
it may not be once on the road. Therefore, I
say that from that standpoint we can claim,
and claim justly, exceptional treatment with
regard to this taxation. The farmer is taxed
undoubtedly on his car. if he owns a car, but
that is a class of motor on which he should
be taxed, because if he is not able to pay that
tax he should do without a car. But in the
present state of our roads it is becoming more
and more necessary for a farmer either to
have a lorry of his own or to pay somebody
else with a lorry for drawing his stuff to
market and for bringing home his necessities.
Therefore, I say that on that head he is
doubly taxed.
I just want to say this with regard to
taxation and the suggestion that has been
made that the farmers would like to shift
their liability for taxation on to other
people. Take the County of Antrim-my
Own county. In the year 1914 the taxes
raised in County Antrim were £79,000. In
the year 1918 that amount had gone up to
£100,540. In the year 1925 it had gone up
to £149,236, and for the present year, that
is 1925-26, the estimate is £176,816.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): You mean rates not taxes.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: Yes, rates.
Mr. POLLOCK: You said taxes.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: It is the
rates I mean. If you take the rates in
County Antrim last year and this year
there is a difference of £27,580. These rates,
the Committee must remember, are borne
largely by the farming community. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) In fact, the farming
community, instead of wanting to put their
share of this on to other people, are the
backbone and mainstay of the rates in the
Six County area.
Mr. KYLE: What about the £128,000?
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I do say this,
though it is probably not germane to this
debate, that the rate collectors at the present
time are having some difficulty in a great
many cases in getting the rates in, not on
account of any want of willingness to pay on
the farmers' part, but because they are not
able to pay. Some hon. Members opposite
may smile, but it is nothing to smile at. It
is a fact. It may not, again, be germane
to this debate, but I do suggest that, unless
some very substantial relief can be given
to the rates, the agricultural industry is.going
to be very severely handicapped and hampered. I think that disposes effectively of
the suggestion that the farmers would like
to put their responsibilities in regard to the
payment of rates on to other people.
Now I come to another point. Some concessions have been granted by the Government. I do not want to belittle those
concessions too much, but I think they do
not at all adequately meet the farmers' case.
With regard to the concessions given on
vehicles up to 12 cwt., unladen, we might
rule that out as far as any concession to
farmers is concerned. The figures quoted by
the Minister of Finance yesterday suggest
that that relief will not cover very many,
because there are only fifty vehicles of that
class in the Six Counties. With regard to
the other concession on vehicles up to one
ton, I do not know that that will bring relief
to a great many farmers, because I understand that a great many ton trucks used by
farmers, especially those of English manufacture, while they are nominally ton trucks,
weigh more than a ton, unladen, and that
will not bring them in under this concession
that has been granted under Number 2. I
think if the Government had wanted to give
a concession that would cover farmers they
should have taken in lorries of one ton weight
and under two tons. But, as I said before,
these concessions, to my mind, do not
adequately meet the farmers' case.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock), in
his very admirable speech in introducing
this Bill yesterday, quoted resolutions passed
by county councils and other bodies in
support of the Bill. I want to give you a
recommendation of the Finance and Law
Committee of the Antrim County Council to
their last quarterly meeting. The recommendation they made to the County Council
reads as follows:-
"That farmers be exempted from taxation
in respect of one ton motor lorries owned
by them, the definition of the word
farmer to include all persons residing
on agricultural land of a valuation of at
least £10, and not exceeding £100."
"
That was the recommendation of the Finance
Committee of the Antrim County Council.

"
We owe a great deal of our unemployment

the land, although I myself would never live

As I have said, I speak with complete ignorance of those matters. The difference be
tween me and most Members of this House

is that I always admit my ignorance. I speak

I have never heard the farmers complaining that they are starving. I do not think
farmers as a rule like to pay taxes. It is

Grant) who likes to pay taxes. It is only the

much like the farmers in every country in
the world. By the very nature of their occupation they take perhaps a rather rigid view
of their responsibilities, and they do not like
to pay because they are not so much accustomed to the interchange of small finance as
they are in the towns and cities. They do
not like to pay and they have got the reputation of being miserly, mean and near, and
perhaps to some extent that is true. That

be imposed on them. I know now that I

with the motor trade, some of them permanent officials of the Government, and
they sent those gentlemen over there for
the purpose of being present at the meetings
of this committee of which they were not
members. I take it the purpose of keeping
these three gentlemen there-perhaps six
gentlemen-at enormous cost to
Northern Government was so that these
gentlemen might bring back either recommendations or information for the benefit
and advantage of the Northern Government.
I think I have not overstated the case. Well,
the House was absolutely entitled to do
either one of two things either to adopt
the policy laid down by the Departmental
Committee or else submit here to this House
the proposals, recommendations, or experiences of the distinguished gentlemen,
both their own public servants and those
connected with the motor traffic. They were
entitled to take the House into their confidence as to what was the result of those
deliberations. But we remained in complete
and absolute ignorance as to what the fruits
of their work were, and until this moment
I am not aware of what the recommendations
of those gentlemen were.
I therefore say that either you were entirely wrong in imposing upon the taxpayers of Ulster the cost of sending these
men to London for two years or you were
entirely wrong in not letting the Northern
Parliament know what were the precise
results of the operations of these gentlemen
who were present at the Departmental Committee. The right hon. Gentleman has done
neither one thing nor the other.
I say here it is entirely wrong, and
I repeat what I said yesterday, that
it is entirely wrong for the Minister
of Finance to come here and introduce
a new fiscal Measure-because this is
a new fiscal Measure-to introduce new
taxes and burdens on a struggling trade
when these taxes are outside the period and
entirely divorced from the general fiscal
proposals that are submitted in the Budget.
Has it ever been done before? I do not
think so. I never remember a precedent.
But one of the things that rather intrigued
me in the speech was when he referred to
the desirability in the interests of the trade
of doing away with the large heavy motors.
I take it that refers to chars-a-bancs. No. I
am to a large extent interested in this-any
interest I have taken in these taxes apart
from the feeling I have that this would
be a blow to a most important industry which has been spoon-fed in England
and England is the home of all wisdom. It
is the fount from which you drink in inspiration. In England they are actually
spoon-feeding this industry. You come along
and the method you adopt in dealing with it
is to put fresh taxation on it. And what I

to get at is the chars-a-bancs. There was a
fundamental hostility manifested to the
chars-a-bancs in the speech of the right hon.
Gentleman.
