Mr. POLLOCK: Perhaps I can shorten the
proceedings if I outline a suggestion which
has been made by hon. Members in regard
to a question which has apparently disturbed
the minds of a number of people, and that
is the fact that many motors, or at least
some motors, say, of the nominal weight of
one ton or two tons, as the case may be,
weigh perhaps a few pounds over the nominal
weight, or a little at any rate. That may be
a hardship, because if you take the case of
a one-ton waggon, and it weighed 1 ton, 7 lbs.,
for example, it would mean, of course, that
the tax would be chargeable upon 2 tons. To
that extent it would be a hardship upon the
man who owned the waggon in question.
Therefore, reviewing the whole circumstances
and features of that part of the question, the
Government have come to the conclusion that
it would perhaps simplify the discussion here,
and at the same time remove a possible
source of grievance if, instead of, for example,
imposing the tax upon a 1-ton waggon, the
language expressing the tax was Exceeding
12 cwt., but not exceeding one ton and a
quarter." That would give a margin of
5 cwt. for those small irregularities by the
addition of gadgets or some other implement
that would increase the weight over the ton.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). If you carry
out that right down through the scale, the
principle applies to each. The next one is,
""
Exceeding one ton and a quarter, but not
exceeding two tons and a quarter." It will
give a concession which I am sure will be
appreciated. Therefore, the Government is
prepared to move as an Amendment in the
direction I have indicated, if hon. Members
are satisfied.

I have a note in respect of the following
line. There is some difficulty. The difficulty
is that the Amendment about £10 for each
trailer cannot be accepted, because the tax
is on the motor and not on the trailer. If
more than one trailer is used the motor
vehicle becomes a locomotive. That will
obviate the necessity for the change. The
hon. Member agrees?
Mr. T. W. McMULLAN indicated assent.
Mr. POLLOCK: The additional tax in that
case will be on the motor. If more than one
trailer is used it then becomes a road locomotive, in other words a train for the purpose of motor tax and speed. It will, therefore, be seen that it is not necessary to
change the original printed line in the Bill.
I beg to move.

This tax now proposed is proposed to be put

desire to divide the House on this question.
It we

upon that industry and commerce.
take the waggon that brings up goods from

diminished trade.

any extent and these vehicles are going to be

Every one of these firms, particularly the

that traverse the road from Banbridge to

people are going to be penalised by this extra

desire to protest against the proposals which
emanated from the Government Benches.
I tried earlier to-day to get the right hon.
Gentleman to refrain from putting this Bill
through its final stages, because one realises
that they are doing an injustice, and quite
apart from that there is the inconvenience to
Members. Even now I have not got the actual
proposals of the right hon. Gentleman before
me. I admit his difficulty in letting us know
these things. But it does show that the
Government had not made up their minds,
and they want to push it through whether
we like it or whether we do not like it. We
are not getting the opportunity of considering how this is going to effect us, nor is time
being allowed to these people.-I am not now
speaking about the people with lorries on hire
at all-to try to recast their business in the
light of this particular taxation. I think
from this point of view it is to be regretted
that the Government are determined to put
this penalty, this impost on industry, and I
desire to protest as strongly as it is possible
to protest.
We admit that the Government have made a
very considerable concession, in my opinion,
in regard to the lighter trucks, because the
lighter trucks, after all, belong to the oneman industry in Belfast-the express delivery
sort of business, one of which in Belfast is
run by ex-Service men, which the Government would have taxed considerably if they
had maintained their original proposals.
They have given way there but they have
not given way on the heavier lorries, and are
about to put a tax on these.
Mr. POLLOCK: May I say, not to prolong
the proceedings, that there is one newspaper
in Belfast which stated that the Government

dustry from our point of view has been established. It is now stabilised and become

so that I do not think the hon. Member's
charge that we have brought this thing
in suddenly will stand examination. We have
been discussing this for six months and 1
hope this Bill will now become law.
Mr. KYLE: Is that the reason we have
had so many amendments? It shows the
Government had not their minds made up
at all. They say they have their minds made
up and yet they are presenting manuscript
amendments which are amended by verbal
amendments. They have had it in their
minds for six months! Could anything be
more ridiculous? If you had had it we would
have had a thing that could not be altered
at all like the laws of the Medes and Persians.
You would not have been prepared to alter
a comma. You would never have been prepared to alter a dash. It seems to me to be

Government's minds for the past six months
and yet they have had to introduce amendments themselves as well as at the last
moment to introduce such substantial amendments as those introduced here.

Mr. MARK: There is just one matter I
would like to ask the Minister of Finance
to make clear to the House. That is in the
event of a motor lorry meeting with an
accident and the owner of the machine deciding not to put another lorry on the road
would there be a refund of these taxes?
Supposing £60 was paid on a lorry which
was only a month in use would a proportional
part of that tax be refunded if the owner
decided not to continue?
Mr. POLLOCK: Collections during the
year are divided into quarterly payments, so
that if the owner of the car that is in my
hon. Friend's mind met with an accident
he would only be penalised to the extent of
the quarterly payment he had made.
Mr. MARK: And if he had paid the
whole year?
Mr. POLLOCK: If a motor owner pays
the tax for the entire year and elects to
discontinue the use of the car he can re
cover the proportionate tax for the remainder of the year.

of which I have given private notice to the
Minister of Home Affairs. It is with regard
to what I look upon as a very important
matter. When this House passed the Education Bill one of the provisions put in that
Bill was a provision for the medical inspection of school children, and I think most of
the Members at that time-certainly all the
medical Members-looked forward to that
provision as being likely to be of great value
as regards the health of the community and
as regards the health of the children themselves. It is left to the Ministry of Home
Affairs to set this service up. It is not a
matter that comes under the Education
Authority. It comes directly under the
Ministry of Home Affairs,
The point that I wish to put this afternoon
is that this is an entirely new service, and
that there is not at present practising in
Northern Ireland practically anyone who has
had any experience of this service. It is not
purely and simply a matter of medical knowledge. It is a matter to a very large extent
of administration and organisation, and those
who know how much has been done in connection with this matter in England, where
medical inspection has been in force for a
large number of years, know it is a complicated matter. It is a matter that may
possibly in the future involve the ratepayers
in large sums of money. I do not wish to
frighten those who have been talking about
the rates here, but I know that in one particular borough in England the provision for
school medical inspection and protection of
children who have to be inspected amounts
to a sum on the rates that is equal to 178
per head for every child attending the school.
That is a pretty large sum, and taking in
a city like Belfast it would represent a very
large sum of money. I do not say that it
is the average amount of money to be spent
on children, but some amount will be spent
on them in connection with this Measure of
school medical inspection.
The point I want to make this afternoon
is that I noticed an advertisement appeared
in one of the papers not long ago for a school
medical inspection officer-a qualified doctor
-and the salary that was offered was a
matter of £400. It is utterly impossible to
get a man with any experience of this particular type of administration and work for
a sum of £400. The assistant school medical
inspectors in England have got very much
larger salaries than that. I think as a matter
of fact the salary at which they start is
something like £500 to £600, and it rises from
that to a considerably higher amount. The
much-maligned Belfast Corporation had the
sense when it was setting up this school
medical inspection to offer a salary of £750,
and they got an officer who has had several
years' experience of this particular type
of work, and who is an exceedingly
capable and exceedingly active and
energetic officer. (Hon. Members: Hear
hear.) I am perfectly certain that any expense the Belfast Corporation are going to
be put to in connection with school medical
inspection the school medical officer for
Belfast will see that they get full value for
their money.
It is losing the ship for the want of a
ha'porth of tar if the counties are going to
pursue an opposite line of policy, and if they
are going to offer small salaries which will
only attract men who have only been recently
qualified, and who have no experience whatever of this particular type of work. They
are going to have an officer who perhaps will
learn his work-because it is work that can
be learned-but he is going to cost a great
deal of money, and for the money they spend
they are not going to get good value. I would
like to suggest to the Minister of Home Affairs
that he should exercise his power of persuasion-I know he cannot order the County
Councils to do the duty-in the line of ensuring that these counties when setting up a
very important and absolutely new service
like this should take care that they get men
or women who have had experience with regard to this matter, and who really know
what they are doing.
I do not advocate an increase in the rates,
but this is an increase in the rates that is
bound to come, and I think a saving of £200
or £300 will be dearly paid for, not only in
the amount that officers' mistakes will cost
the county, but possibly in the effect it will
have in regard to the health of the school
children during the next few years. I know
that the Minister of Home Affairs has this
matter very much at heart, and I am not
speaking so much to him as to the counties
through the medium of the newspapers. I
hope they will take it from me-I have had
a fair amount of experience in medical inspection in one way or another-that the man
who does not know his job, no matter what
you pay him, is a very dear proposition.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. KYLE: I would like to ask the
Minister of Home Affairs if he has any report
to make to the House, in regard to the
demand that the Special constables have presented to the Government.
Medical Inspection.
Adjournment.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Sir DAWSON BATES: With regard to the
point raised by my hon. Friend, the Member
for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle), at the present
moment I have really little to add to what
I have already stated. The Government have
laid down what they consider generous terms,
and I am sufficiently optimistic to believe
that by the time those terms have been
ventilated in the Force scattered throughout
the Six Counties the men will realise the
generosity of the terms and I think, will
drop their agitation. I hope that in a few
days' time all our trouble will be past. Of
course I may be speaking in an optimistic
way, but I have great belief in the good
sense of the members of the "A" Constabulary.
With regard to the question raised by the
hon. Member for the University (Mr. Johnstone), I am sure the Members of this House
and of the various Education Authorities
will appreciate a great deal of what has been
said. But the hon. Member will also appreciate that, so far as the Government is concerned, so long as you have an authority
elected by the people, there is a limit to the
extent to which the Government can interfere. We can veto the appointment of a
particular officer. I may add that these
education schemes are at the present time in
a purely experimental stage, and I find that,
with the exception of Belfast, in the counties
where appointments have been made they are
only of a temporary character pending the
reorganisation of the services of the county.
With regard to the question of the salaries,
that is a rather difficult matter. I hope that
the suasion of the members of the medical
profession and of the British Medical Association will induce the local authorities to
see that the professional men are properly
paid. I think we all wish that they should
be properly paid, but at the same time the
་
hon. Member will appreciate the difficulty
that the Government would have to face in
laying down a certain salary for certain
work. After all, the appointments must rest
with the local authorities, and, so long as
the Government is satisfied that the persons
appointed have sufficient qualifications to
carry out the work, it is a little bit difficult
for us to interfere.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I must compliment the hon. Member for the University
upon raising this important question. We
all realise that it is absolutely absurd to propose to pay a medical man £400 a year. I,
for one, am not going to allow these inexperienced medical officers to practise upon
children. The hon. Member for the Univer
sity has pointed out very clearly the danger
of any county in Ulster appointing medical
men of this type. It is utterly impossible to
get men of ability to administer this Act
at a salary of £100. The Belfast Corporation
have a good officer. All appointments must
be confirmed by the Ministry of Home
Affairs. The Belfast Corporation give men
£1,000 to doctor the roads, and the human
frame is a bit more important than the supervision of roads. To offer £400 a year for the
position described is an insult to the medical
profession, and I would ask the Minister of
Home Affairs absolutely to refuse to confirm
any such appointment. We know quite well
that no medical man fit for the position
would apply when the remuneration offered
is the figure stated by the hon. Member for
the University. You will only get a quick
doctor for £400.

Oral Answers to Questions.
BURIAL CHARGES IN BELFAST.
2. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he will
inquire as to the rates charged by the undertakers for burials to cemeteries inside the
boundary of the City of Belfast, and whether
he will express an opinion as to the reasonableness or otherwise of these charges.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The Ministry of Home
Affairs has no functions whatsoever in connection with charges made by undertakers for carrying out burials, and it would
be wholly outside the province of the
Ministry to institute any inquiries as to the
scales of charges or to express any opinion
as to the reasonableness or otherwise of
these charges.
LABOURERS' COTTAGES-RENTS IN
LURGAN RURAL DISTRICT.
3. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that a resolution was passed by the
Lurgan Rural District Council at a meeting
held on Thursday, the 3rd December, 1925,
regretting the delay on the part of the
Ministry in settling the rents for the twentyone labourers' cottages built by the aforementioned Council, and which were ready
for occupation on the 1st of October last, and
whether, in view of the fact that some of the
prospective tenants are at present housed in
unsanitary dwellings, and that the Council
is losing rents, he will expedite a settlement
at the rent originally fixed by the Ministry,
viz., 4s per week, with the least possible
delay.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The delay in this
case has been due to the necessity for giving
careful consideration to the proposals
formulated by the Council in regard to the
rents of these new cottages, in order to
arrive at a satisfactory and equitable
solution in the interests of the ratepayers
and of the prospective tenants.
The Council originally proposed a rent of
8s a week for these new cottages, but on the
representations of the Ministry that such a
rent was excessive, and that the Council
should consider the propriety of reducing it,
the Council revised their proposals and fixed
a rent of 6s a week for the cottages within
three miles of the Urban Districts of Portadown and Lurgan, and rents of 5s a week for
cottages outside these limits.
After consideration of these proposals,
approval has been given to these revised
rates, which approval has already been communicated to the Rural District Council.
CONTRACTS IN LURGAN AND MOIRA
DISTRICTS.
4. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether it is a fact
that the Lurgan Board of Guardians has instructed the clerk and master respectively
to write to tradesmen inviting estimates for
contracts over the value of £10, and whether
this is in accordance with the regulations of
the Ministry.
The following question also stood on the
Paper in the name of Mr. WILLIAM
MCMULLEN :
5. To ask the Minister of Home Affairs
whether it is a fact that the Lurgan Rural
Council and the Moira Rural Council do not
invite tenders for contracts above the value
of £10, and whether this is in accordance
with the regulations of the Ministry?
Sir DAWSON BATES: With the hon.
Member's permission I will answer this
question and his question No. 5 together.
A Board of Guardians is required by the
general regulations to advertise for tenders
for supplies, etc., exceeding £10 in cost.
The law governing the procedure of Rural
District Councils in connection with accept-
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

[Sir Dawson Bates]
ance of contracts is laid down by Statute, and
not by regulations of the Ministry. The onus
rests on a Rural District Council or Board of
Guardians to satisfy the auditor that in
placing orders or entering into contracts they
have acted in conformity with law. I have
no information as to the procedure adopted
by the Lurgan Rural District Council and
the Moira Rural District Council, but I have
no doubt that these Councils will place themselves in a position to justify to the auditor
the procedure that may be adopted by them.
The attention of the clerk and master of the
Lurgan Board of Guardians has been drawn
to the regulations.
UNEMPLOYED IN NEWTOWNARDS
AREA.
6. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Labour whether he is aware that
seven hundred and seventy people are at
present unemployed in the area under the
control of the Newtownards Local Employment Committee, as compared with eigh
hundred and twenty-two a month ago, and i
he will state the number of claims that have
been disallowed during the same period, and
the reason for such disallowance.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The figures given by the hon.
Member are correct. I am glad to be able
to state, however, that out of 822 persons registered as unemployed at Newtownards on
the 2nd November, no fewer than 593 found
work in the course of the month.
The number of persons disallowed extended
benefit was 111; 56 on the ground that their
family income did not warrant a grant, 38
because they were unable to show that they
were making reasonable efforts to get work,
and the remainder for the reason that they
were not normally insured persons.
SPEED OF PNEUMATIC-TYRED
OMNIBUSES.
7. Mr. T. W. MCMULLAN (for Mr. Crawford) asked the Prime Minister whether he
is prepared to introduce legislation so that
motor omnibuses and charabancs having
pneumatic tyres should be allowed to travel
at a speed of 20 miles per hour.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have a recommendation from the Roads Advisory Committee of Northern Ireland to the effect that
the speed limit allowed for motor omnibuses
and charabancs wholly fitted with pneumatic
tyres, should be increased from 12 miles an
hour to 20 miles an hour, provided that the
axle weight does not exceed 4 tons, and to
15 miles an hour in cases where the axle
weight exceeds 4 tons but does not exceed
6 tons.
This recommendation is receiving careful
consideration at present, in conjunction with
other recommendations of a cognate character dealing with road traffic questions, which
will form the subject of a Road Traffic Bill,
which it is hoped will be introduced into this
House early next Session.

WHAN v. WALKER-DISTRICT
INSPECTOR'S REPORT.
Mr. KYLE (by Private Notice) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs if he would now
produce the report of District-Inspector Allen
in the case of Whan v. Walker, as the action
had been withdrawn in the High Court, and
is no longer sub judice.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would refer
the hon. Member to the statement I
made in my previous reply in this House
on the 20th October last, when I pointed out
that it would be contrary to the public interest and to long established practice, to
disclose a report made by the police of their
investigations of an alleged crime.
Mr. KYLE: This has been an infliction
upon this woman, the like of which has not
been known in Northern Ireland since the
Parliament of Northern Ireland had control,
and I think-
Mr. SPEAKER: That, I think, is a reflection upon the Judiciary of Northern
Ireland.
Mr. KYLE: I am not desirous of reflecting
upon the Judiciary, but this woman has
suffered, and I think it is in the public
interest and in the interest of the right hon.
Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) himself, that
this matter should be cleared up.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member must
just ask a supplementary question, and not
make a speech.
Mr. BEATTIE: Might I ask whether, as
the information asked for is a matter of
public interest, the Minister would be prepared to give the facts of the report to the
persons concerned for their information?
Sir DAWSON BATES: As I have already
stated, I think it is entirely against public
policy to disclose reports which the Government receive from police inspectors.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN. Is the right
hon. Gentleman aware that a large number
of people have come to the conclusion that
in this case there has been a grave miscarriage of justice.
Mr. GRANT: Supplementary to that question, is it not a fact that District-Inspector
Allen, who is a very efficient officer of police,
has furnished a report in connection with
this case that proves that this woman is
absolutely innocent, and is the Minister of

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): I fear that the hon. Member is confusing two Sinking Funds. The Sinking
Fund which is invested at a rate of approximately 4 per cent. is a Northern Ireland
Fund set up by an Act of this Parliament,
for the purpose of securing that when the
revenue from the Land Purchase Annuities
terminates, there will be a permanent revenue from investments to take its place.
This fund has no connection with the machinery of Land Purchase.
If the hon. Member wishes his question to
be taken as referring to the Sinking Fund
set up by the Imperial Government under the
Acts of 1903 and 1909, I would point out that,
being a Reserved Service, this Fund is under
the control of the Imperial Authorities, and
I am, therefore, not in a position to give any
definite information on the subject. So far
as can be ascertained from the published accounts, it would appear that the Sinking
Fund moneys have so far been utilised mainly
for the issue of fresh loans at the original
rate of interest, and it is probable, therefore,
that up to the present the operations on this
fund will not have materially affected the
term of the advances.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

PROROGATION.
Message from the Senate.
A message was delivered by the Gentleman
Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:-
Mr. Speaker, I am commanded to inform
this Honourable House that the Speech of
his Grace the Governor of Northern Ireland Proroguing this present Parliament is
to be communicated in the Senate forth-.
with, and further, I am commanded to
invite this Honourable House to attend in
the Senate to hear the said Speech.
The House went, and having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in the Clerk's
place at the Table): I have to report that
this House has this day attended in the
Senate where the Speaker of the Senate on
behalf of his Grace the Governor read the
Speech to both Houses of Parliament as
followeth :
KING'S SPEECH.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I have to congratulate you upon the
measures which have been placed on the
Statue Book during the first Session of
this present Parliament.
I regret that Northern Ireland still
continues to suffer from the general depression in trade which exists throughout the United Kingdom. The problem
of unemployment is the greatest that
confronts us at the moment in common
with Great Britain, and it is gratifying
that representatives of our manufactures
and commerce and the people of Northern
Ireland have freely responded to the
invitation of the Government to take
part in an Unemployment Conference
which is carefully exploring the postion
as it affects Northern Ireland. By means
of the Loans Guarantee Act continued
assistance has been rendered to the Shipbuilding Industry; while it is hoped that
the endeavour to hasten a revival of the
Linen Trade by the co-operation with
local manufacturers in a special advertising campaign in America will meet
with success. Financial assistance is also
being afforded to the Coal Industry in
Northern Ireland. In addition, the Local
Authorities are continuing to give their
valuable co-operation in the promotion
of schemes of public utility designed
expressly to give useful employment to
our people.
The results which have attended
Northern Ireland's participation in the
British Empire Exhibition this year are
most satisfactory. In organising a larger
and more fully representative exhibit of
Ulster products than was possible in
the previous year the Government and
exhibitors alike have again emphasised
Ulster's attachment to the Imperial connection.
An Act has been passed making
further provision for the payment of
Unemployment Benefit to those insured
persons who cannot obtain work and for
protecting the interests of those most in
need of the assistance of the Unemploy
ment Fund.
It is with great pleasure that I am
able to refer to the Widows', Orphans'
and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act.
The measure marks one more stage in
the great Social Insurance code which
has been built up in the last few years,
and guarantees for our insured workpeople the same provision against proverty
and distress which persons similarly
situated in the rest of the United Kingdom will be afforded in times of bereave
ment and old age.
It is satisfactory that, notwithstanding the severe industrial depression, the
thrifty habits of the people continue to
be demonstrated by the interest shown
in Ulster Savings Certificates, in which a
total of £2,000,000 has now been invested.
Your Drainage Act provides machinery
which will enable remedial measures to
be undertaken to prevent the flooding
our agricultural land.
Operations under the scheme of loans
to farmers for the replacement of live
stock lost owing to the recent unfavour.
able season have now been concluded. I
am satisfied that this scheme eased considerably a serious situation, particularly
in the poorer districts. More than £46,000
was spent on this work.
It is gratifying to learn that the
recent legislation passed by Parliament
granting additional financial inducements
to private individuals and local authorities
for the erection of houses has been at
tended with such success and that the
rate of building during the last few
months has been steadily increasing.
The Government Loans and Exchequer
Provisions Act has effected a number of
improvements in our financial system
and has provided an economically sound
method of financing the loans which are
made from time to time for capital pur
poses. The reception given to the issue
of Ulster Loan Stock has provided a
satisfactory indication of the credit of
Northern Ireland.
It gives me satisfaction to observe
continuance of peaceful conditions and the
2101 King's Speech.

22 DECEMBER 1925
End of Session.
1$
absence of abnormal crime in Northern
Ireland, and I am glad to note the restoration of that respect for the law which is
the foundation of Society. This happy
result has been attained by a firm and
impartial enforcement of the law and by
the vigilance of the Constabulary Forces,
and I earnestly pray that no untoward
event may occur to disturb the conditions
which now prevail.
Members of the House of Commons.
I thank
you for the provision of
supplies for the public services.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I am deeply moved and gratified at
the Agreement entered into between the
Governments of Great Britain, Northern
Ireland, and the Irish Free State. As a
result it is
earnest
my
prayer that
friendly relations between the Governments and peoples of Northern Ireland
and the Irish Free State may be promoted
and cemented by a spirit of goodwill
and friendship to the common advantage
of both.
Recent developments in the field of
world politics give ground for hope that
the new spirit of mutual confidence between nation and nation may bring in
its train the long-awaited revival in trade
which cannot fail to affect beneficially
the industries of Northern Ireland.
I pray that the blessing of Almighty
God may rest upon your labours.
After which the Proclamation Proroguing
Parliament was read as followeth :-
:-
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION
For Proroguing the present Parliament of
Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by Section eleven
of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, as
modified by and in pursuance of certain
enactments amending the said Act, that the
Governor of Northern Ireland shall in His
Majesty's name summon, prorogue and dissolve the Parliament of Northern Ireland.
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that this
present Parliament of Northern Ireland
should be prorogued to the ninth day of
March, One Thousand Nine Hundred and
Twenty-six.
ᎪᏞᏴᎬᎡᎢ ᎬᎠᎳᎪᎡᎠ,
NOW I, JAMES
DUKE OF ABERCORN, Governor of Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation do publish
and declare His Majesty's Pleasure that the
said Parliament be, as from the reading of
this Proclamation in the Parliament of
Northern Ireland, prorogued to the ninth day
of March, One Thousand Nine Hundred and
Twenty-six.
AND I do hereby further declare His
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to be that
the said Parliament shall on the said ninth
day of March, One Thousand Nine Hundred
and Twenty-six, assemble and be holden for
the dispatch of divers urgent and important
affairs, and the Senators and Members of the
House of Commons of Northern Ireland are
hereby required to give their attendance
accordingly..
Given at Government House, Hillsborough,
this Eighteenth day of December, One Thousand Nine Hundred and Twenty-five.
Signed by his own hand,
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
End of the First Session (opened

Tuesday,
14th April, 1925) of the Second Parliament of
Northern Ireland, in the Sixteenth year of
the Reign of His Majesty King George the
Fifth.

UNIVERSITY OF IOWA
3 1858 029 298 555

Tuesday, 10th March, 1925.
The Fifth Session of the First Parliament
of Northern Ireland, appointed to meet 10th
March, 1925, in the fifteenth year of the
Reign of King George V, was opened by the
Governor (His Grace the Duke of Abercorn,
K.P.) in person.
The House met at Ten Minutes before
Twelve of the Clock. Mr. Speaker (Right
Hon. Hugh O'Neill, D.L., M.P.) in the
Chair.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod
(Major T. D. H. Hackett, D.S.O.) was
announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman
Usher said: His Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland commands this Honourable House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Three of
the Clock, and then resumed.
Local Bills.
Mr. SPEAKER laid upon the Table
Report from the Examiner of Petitions for
Local Bills, that he has certified that the
Standing Orders have been complied with
on the following cases:
Belfast Corporation,
London, Midland and Scottish Railway.

SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are returned for two or more places in any part of
Northern Ireland do make their Election for
which of the places they will serve, within
one week after it shall appear that there is
no question upon the Return for that place;
and if anything shall come in question
touching the Return or Election of any
Member, he is to withdraw during the time
the matter is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath been elected or returned a Member of this House or endeavoured so to be,
by Bribery, or any other corrupt practices,
this House will proceed with the utmost
severity against all such persons as shall
have been wilfully concerned in such Bribery
or other corrupt practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath been tampering with any
Witness in respect of his evidence to be
given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any person
from appearing or giving evidence, the same
is declared to be a high crime or misdemeanour; and this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
King's Speech.
King's Speech.
10 MARCH 1925
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in any
case before this House, or any Committee
thereof, this House will proceed with the
utmost severity against such offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary do take care that,
during the Session of Parliament, the passages through the streets leading to this
House be kept free and open, and that no
obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members to and from this House,
and that no disorder be allowed in the precincts of or in the passages leading to this
House, during the Sitting of Parliament,
and that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant at Arms
attending this House do communicate this
Order to the Commissioner of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings and
Records of this House be printed, being first
perused by Mr. Speaker; and that he do
appoint the printing thereof; and that no
person but such as he shall appoint do presume to print the same.

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report to the
House that the House has this day attended
in the Senate to hear the Speech of his
Grace, the Governor, on behalf of the
Crown, to both Houses of Parliament; of
which I have for greater accuracy obtained
a copy. The Speech is as follows:-
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
A year ago I expressed satisfaction that
law and order had been re-established and
maintained throughout Northern Ireland,
and I am glad to learn that now it has
been found possible to relax the enforcement of the special powers granted by
Parliament for this purpose, and that all
interned persons have been released and
the Curfew restrictions have been entirely
removed.
It is a matter of great regret that
unemployment to such an extent still
continues in our midst; there was recently
welcome improvement in the linen industry, and although this has not been
maintained lately, I am aware that a
diminution in trade is unfortunately not
unusual in the winter months, and it is
hoped that a revival may take place in
the Spring.
The more settled conditions prevailing
on the Continent give hopes of an improvement in trade. It is anticipated
that the valuable recommendations made
by our Commission on Development,
which among other things is investigating
the possibility of electrical power for industrial purposes, may prove of benefit.
The legislation passed for the prevention of unfair competition in industry
and of sweating is working satisfactorily,
and improvements have been made in
the ventilation of our mills and factories
and in other conditions affecting the
welfare of employees.
The relief works initiated by my
Government since its establishment have
received the generous and sympathetic
co-operation of our Local Authorities and
involve a capital cost of £3,000,000. These
works include the construction of workers'
houses, improvements of roads and harbours, water supply, tramway reconstruction, and many other works of public
utility. By this means over 17,000
situations for unemployed persons have
been found which would not otherwise
have existed, and every effort will be made
to continue the promotion of schemes of
public utility to provide useful work. In
addition, the facilities afforded under the
Loans Guarantee Acts have contributed
materially to the reduction of unemployment, and you will be asked to extend
still further the provisions of these Acts.
Nevertheless, in spite of continued
efforts to increase the field of employment,
large numbers of insured workers have
had to rely on the resources of the
Unemployment Insurance Scheme, which
has been maintained on the same lines as
in Great Britain. Since the 1st January,
1922, the contributory Insurance Fund has
provided benefit for unemployed workers
to the extent of £4,600,000.

Ireland, and in the development of our
egg industry. There is no doubt that

confidence in British markets in the

dress): I beg to move,

"That an humble Address be presented

Your Grace,

I should like to be allowed to express the
pleasure I have in being allowed to move
this Address, and to say that I feel it a
great honour to be allowed to do so; an
honour not only to myself as a Member of
this House, but an honour also to the profession to which I belong, and to the
University which I have the privilege of
representing. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The fact that it can be said that law and
order have been re-established and maintained throughout Northern Ireland is one
which must afford gratification to everyone resident in the Six Counties. We
no longer go to our homes at night amid the
sounds of rifle and machine-gun fire. We
move about with security. We can travel
safely by night as well as by day. Interned
persons have been set free, and the irksome
Debate on Address.
10 MARCH 1925

Debate on Address.
The Poor-Law administration has been a
source of much trouble in the past. The
Commission now sitting gives every facility
for getting all grievances made public and
remedied.
restrictions of Curfew have been removed.
All this speaks volumes for the efficiency of
our Government, and tells of the wise and
thorough way in which the work has been
done. Our Government was faced with a
task of the utmost difficulty and anxiety.
The problem was dealt with firmly and
quietly in a way which should earn the undying gratitude of all loyal and law-abiding
men. Amid the cares of office and the manifold duties of various departments
Prime Minister (Sir James Craig) and his
colleagues have accomplished a gigantic task.
As a result we are now back again to the
peaceful conditions of ten years ago.
The
fabled labours of Hercules were small compared with those which our Government has
accomplished. We cannot praise them too
highly for what they have done for us.
our
While the terrible calamity of crime and
outrage has been succesfully grappled with,
we have still, unfortunately, a spectre of
another kind in our midst the problem of
unemployment. This affects us in our most
important trades, especially in the manufacture of linen and of ships. Much has been
done by the Government to provide work
for the unemployed and to improve the conditions under which the workers live. Large
sums have been spent on improvements.
Encouragement has been given to housebuilding, road and tramway construction,
harbour improvements, and water supplyall efforts, which, in time to come, will contribuie to the prosperity of the district.
Needless to say, the dislocation of trade and
commerce has been so widespread that the
best ameliorative measures fall short of
finding work for all. Those who are still
workless have to fall back upon the Unemployment Insurance Scheme. Fortunately
our people are enabled to participate in this
in the same way as the unemployed in Great
Britain. This is a very great advantage to
the unemployed.
Parliament is soon to be dissolved, and it
is a very satisfactory thing to think that
the first Parliament of Northern Ireland has
to its credit such a great and important
measure as the Education Act. This Act has
been the subject of much criticism, and the
critics have at times waxed very warm over
it. However, we are fortunate in having
now reached the stage of agreement in which
all parties are satisfied, and it is to be hoped
that the Act will now be put in force and
worked harmoniously for the good of the
children, The Education Committees of
Belfast and Londonderry have set a good
example in energy and enthusiasm.
Belfast our honourable colleague who presides over the Committee has shown commendable energy, and given his time and
ability unstintedly in his endeavours to effect
the much-needed improvements which the
city requires in regard to schools.
In
I desire to congratulate the Minister of
Agriculture (Mr. Archdale) on the success
of his endeavours to improve our most important industry. It is particularly gratifying to note that the breed of cattle is
being improved. From the point of view of
those interested in the health of the people
this is most important, because it gives them
reason to hope that the cow afflicted with
tubercle will be gradually eliminated. While
people naturally have their attention
directed to cures for this disease, the getting
rid of the causes of the disease are more
important. The families of the farmers are
themselves equally the victims of the diseased
cow with those in towns who consume the
milk and butter. An improvement in the
breed of the cows will in the end benefit
everyone. The quality of agricultural produce will improve the demand for it, and
increase the resources of the Province. I
beg to move.

We are pleased to find in the first paragraph of the King's Speech a delightfully
favourable reference to the orderly and
peaceful state of Northern Ireland whereby
many of the special powers in force during
the troublous times have been relaxed, interned prisoners released and Curfew restrictions removed. It is to the solid, steady
and persistent work of our Cabinet, loyally
backed up by our Ulster police of all
classes, from the Inspector-General to the
youngest recruit, that we are indebted for
this tranquillity. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Do we ever stop to think of or realize
the happy change from murder, burnings
and deeds of evil? I fear we are not
sufficiently grateful for this improvement.
In this connection we especially thank the
Minister of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson
Bates) for his undaunted courage and determination to suppress riot and bloodshed at
all costs, and congratulate him
on his

successful campaign and assure him of the

next paragraph makes reference to unemployment. Of all the public positions I
hold that on the Local Employment
Committee is the most irksome. I always
leave its meetings with a sore heart. Men.
and women attend there week after week
and are asked: "Can't you get work of some
kind?" while at the same time the questioner
knows it is next to impossible; many, very
many of these people would be glad of any
kind of employment, while some who are on
the lists would fear the sight of work. In
this connection if the right hon. Gentleman
the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews) can
inform me how we are to get clear of them
I should be very glad, indeed. This class
can be eliminated only through public
bodies finding work of utility, which in like
manner will be undertaken only if borrowings can be secured at a very low rate of
interest and spread over quite a long period
so that those then enjoying the improvements will have to pay at least a little of
this cost. This unemployment question is a
very sad one both for town and country.
It is up to the Government to find labour
for these people. It has not come
expected, and I am afraid it is not going to
come in the near future, at least to the
extent we hoped for. True, there is an improvement, but there is more or less of a
slump in some industries. We know there
is a slump in shipbuilding. We regret these
things. We regret that so many of these
people, our friends and neighbours, cannot
find work. We have every confidence in the
Minister of Labour. We can only hope that
the efforts of the right hon. Gentleman
who is deserving of all praise, may be as
successful in the future as they have been in
the past.
We have all the greatest confidence
in him, and if the difficulty can be solved,
he is the one for the task. (Hon. Members:

on the Statute Book. The Act has outlived
its usefulness and is doing a great injury
to the working class whom it is supposed to
benefit.
We all rejoice to know that a Bill for the
better administration of Drainage Acts is
shortly to be introduced. I can conceive of
nothing more useful and beneficial to the
farmers in general than some assistance in
this direction County canals in many parts
aro at present silted from bank to bank, and
main drains are practically full of vegetation, being more like the fields on either side
than a water course. This should be the
work of County Councils, who should have
the
power to strike a rate for
purpose.
Every farmer would have to contribute according to the poor law valuation and, in
general, every farmer would benefit-better
crops, more and richer quality of milk,
healthier cattle, all as the result of sweet
and health-producing graes versus
grass and other deleterious vegetation not
better than rushes. I have had personal
experience of this; hence my offering an
opinion.
Sour
Amongst other Measures to be brought
forward I notice we are promised a Bill
having for its object the preservation of
ancient monuments. I am more than
pleased with this promise, as our country
is rich in these and historical buildings fast
going to decay. We have been far too

high if they can only get the object of
their choice into the land of the Stars and
Stripes. Should we not learn from this

His Grace has informed us that local

Derry are moving along rapidly, and he

function. We are all pleased to hear of
the amicable arrangement that has been

10 MARCH 1925
come to within the last 48 or 60 hours.
Then we have the Local Government Commission sitting at the present time. There
again they are doing good work. They
have a rich harvest before them ready for
the sickle, and I am looking forward for
great usefulness in this connection. I hope
there will be very wise pruning done and a

has had some thirty years' experience of

I am quite satisfied that they have useful

May I in conclusion say that as a young
Parliament, launched in the most difficult
and trying times, we may well feel proud
of the progress made and success achieved,
and, being safely led by our Prime
Minister in whom we have implicit

and strongly supported as he is by the

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
My first pleasure is to congratulate very
heartily my hon. Friend, the Member for
the University (Sir John Campbell) and my
hon. Friend and Colleague in the representation of County Down (Mr. Lavery) on the
way in which they have discharged their
duties to-day. It is rather interesting to
look back upon my own Parliamentary
career and to recall how frequently in the
Imperial Parliament and now in this new
Parliament of our own I have heard speeches
on similar occasions, and I can only say
that my two hon. Friends have acquitted
themselves in accordance with the highest
traditions of those who have been charged
with the duty of proposing and seconding
the Address.
Before I make a few remarks
on the
subjects that have been touched upon, I
think it would be within the duty that
devolves upon me and in accordance with
the wishes of all the Members if I said how
sad it is not to see one familiar face opposite
to us here. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
From the time that our Northern Government was established the late Mr. Coote
threw himself so heartily into all our proceedings, and spoke with such vigour and
such sincerity in our debates that there is
not one here but feels a loss in our midst.
The Speech from the Throne, if I may use
the expression to-day, covered a certain
number of matters that have been referred
to, and my hon. Friend behind me who
seconded the Address (Mr. Lavery) referred
to one or two outstanding things which,
although it may be impossible to deal with
them during the week that lies ahead before
we again ask for the confidence of the
country, will be dealt with as speedily as
possible after our reassembly.
There are two outstanding matters to
which I would like to refer. One of these
is in connection with the very important
question of drainage, accentuated so much
by the very severe weather that has afflicted
us during the past year. The Government
are fully alive to the difficulties in connection with reorganizing the Boards, and my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance,
is hard at work endeavouring to get the
various Acts bearing upon the question
co-ordinated. He is at the same time busy
consulting those best able to judge in order
that we may tackle the problem in the way
in which it deserves.
My hon. Friend (Mr. Lavery) referred to
Housing, and suggested that we should, with
a sweep of the pen, do away with all
restrictions. It sounds very simple. My
hon. Friend is one of those benevolent
Members of the House in whose suggestions one would like to acquiesce, but I
think it is not quite such a simple problem
as he believes. Even the British Government have had to announce that they
propose to continue the restrictions for
another two years, and I have no doubt the
Government here will have to adopt a
similar proceeding. At the same time I
think it will be possible for us to remove
this grievance of the one-house owners, or
at all events to introduce terms similar to
those in the English Act, which the British
Government are about to continue.
There are several other outstanding
matters which will be dealt with by the new
Parliament but it is unnecessary for me today to say more than that they will receive
that energetic attention that has characterized the actions of all my colleagues
during the past four years. Whether
it is the Ministry of Home Affairs,
the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of
Education, the Ministry of Agriculture or
the Ministry of Labour, each of the particular problems that face the Ministers will be
dealt with as rapidly and as effectively as
possible.
The really interesting part of the Speech
refers to the Dissolution which is foretold,
and I would like to say that amongst the
many heavy responsibilities that rest upon
my shoulders is that of pronouncing when it
is considered proper once again to appeal to
the country and to advise the Governor on
that subject. The Governor has graciously
consented to my request. I am moved to do
Debate on Address.
Debate on Address.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
that for many reasons which it is not
necessary to mention in the House. At all
events we will not be charged with having
overstayed our welcome. I do not think that
that cry has been raised in the country, and
we are going for a fresh assurance from the
people that we represent them in this House
properly and carry on the Government
according to their desire. In addition to that
it will be most useful for them to be able
to say on the one hand that they are satisfied
with the progress that we have made during
the past four years, and to strengthen our
hands with regard to the heavy tasks that
lie ahead.
Of course, I admit frankly that besides
being Prime Minister in Ulster I am the
political head of the Loyalist Party-(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)—and I must safeguard the interests of the Loyalists throughout the length and breadth of the Ulster
area. It is, therefore, a privilege to me to be
able to say when I consider the decks have
been cleared and all those internal difficulties
that have been exercising the minds of all
classes and creeds have been satisfactorily
assuaged, that we may be able to go to the
country on what, after all, is the very life
blood of our existence-the question of what
is going to happen to us when the Boundary
Commission reports. He will be a courageous
man through the coming few weeks who will
attempt to divide the Loyalist Party when
that very stern and grim problem is facing
the people, and perplexing the minds of the
local authorities upon the Borderland. I
believe that a pronouncement by the people
while the Commission is sitting in their midst
will go a long way to assure them that the
feeling throughout the length and breadth of
Ulster is that they will remain steadfast inside the ambit of Great Britain and the
British Empire. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
Some time ago I issued a notice to
say that if individuals or local authorities
throughout the counties were desirous of
giving evidence before the Commission I had
no objection whatever, nor would it
cause the slightest embarrassment to
the Government. It left each
person and each local authority
to do what they thought was best in the
interests of the Ulster Loyalists amongst
whom they live. Even to-day there is a
desire that something more should be done
in order to reassure those who feel that
their homesteads are at stake, and I believe
there is no more constitutional or effective
way than saying we have appealed to the
people to say once more to us, "You represent us in the attitude that you adopt regarding the Boundary and regarding the
land that belongs to Ulster, the land that
Ulster will not part with." Therefore, I
justify the Government.
In this connection I wish to emphasize
most strongly that we are a united
Cabinet and a united Government in the
decision we have arrived at. There has
never been the slightest difference of
opinion as to the difficult problem of when
to go to the country. It is quite true that
we might have put it off for a month or
two. I can see no benefit from that to the
people as a whole. After all, one wishes to
cause as little disturbance amongst the
people as possible at election times. It is
better to get it over and done with without
having a long drawn-out contest, and there
is not a man or woman in Ulster who has
not already made up his or her mind as to
exactly how he or she is going to vote when
the election comes. Although I do not for
a moment desire to curtail the oratorical
ability of individual Members, I do not
believe one of them will turn a single vote
by the various meetings they will hold
throughout the constituencies-not one.
Therefore it seems to me foolish in
the extreme to cause an unnecessary
disturbance throughout the Northern
area when both political sides are
quite determined as to how they
will vote when the polling takes place.
This is not an appropriate time for me
to make an election speech in this House.
Our duty to-day is to tender our grateful
thanks, in accordance with the words that
you have read from the Chair, for the
Speech that was delivered by the Governor
this afternoon. But I do think that the
public outside would like to know exactly
the dates on which they will be expected
to do their duty. If we can get the
Address completed this afternoon, we
propose to take to-morrow the Estimates,
first of all the Supplementary Estimates,
and after that a Vote on Account in order
to carry us over the financial year, notice
being given that on Thursday we will take
those trifling Measures which have been
mentioned in the Speech. Then, when they
have gone to another place, we ought to be
able with any care on our part to wind up
the business of this short Session on
Friday next, when his Grace the Governor
is prepared to issue a Proclamation dissolv..
ing the Parliament on the Saturday
Following out the dates that we are
compelled to observe by statute, we shall
have the nominations on the 24th day of
this month, and be able to hold the elections
on Friday, 3rd April. That will compress
the election into the shortest possible time,
and therefore, as I say, cause as little
disturbance in the body politic as is
possible.

10 MARCH 1925

Before I resume my seat, I would like just
to comment on what my two hon. Friends
have said with regard to the Parliament
itself during the past four years. It was a
great experiment. When one looks back to
twenty or thirty years ago, and carries
one's mind to the controversy over Home
a
Rule, it is safe to say there was not a man
then living who would have ever dreamt of
foretelling that we would be sitting in the
City of Belfast, the capital of Ulster,
managing our own affairs in our own
Parliament. Judging by history, the
Members of this House and of the Senate
have accomplished a wonderful undertaking
in getting down to business so rapidly, in
appointing out of their own Members
Government which has carried on So
successfully, and in having surmounted
all the difficulties of the past four years.
We find Ulster emerging from it peaceful;
I am sorry to say not so prosperous as I
should wish, but at all events contented,
and with no outstanding grievance or
difficulty worth talking about. I think that
is a great accomplishment. I think that it
is almost true to say that it could not have
occurred in any other part of the world,
but such is the Ulster character that given
a task, given something definite to perform,
we are second to none in any part of the
world in carrying it out. (Hcn. Members:
Hear, hear.) This Parliament has gone
through these four years, and after all that
is the customary period, because in all Parliaments of the past a year was allowed before
the Government was compelled to go to the
country.
We have done nothing extraordinary,
nothing out of the common, in asking the
country for a renewal of confidence just at
this particular time; and hon. Members on
all sides will bear in mind that even when
the Boundary question is out of the way,
we, as a Government, have still got to face
several problems that require unity within
our own ranks and loyalty at our backs,
just as much as during the preceding period.
We still require to have analysed the Colwyn
Report. We still have on that Report to
make stable the financial relations between
Great Britain and ourselves. We still have
to surmount the great difficulty of the
Unemployment Fund, well-known and
thoroughly understood by Members in this
House; and we have also to face the difficult
problem of securing in our hands the
administration of those Services which, in
the original Act of 1920, were devolved upon
a Council of Ireland. That must be done
before the expiration of five years. These
and many other matters can be better
stated at a later date. I merely mention
that to show the absolute necessity of the
Ulster people backing up the Ulster Government to the very utmost of their power, in
order that we may be enabled to solve these
problems. And, Sir, I feel fit to solve them.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I feel fit to
tackle them as I have tackled the problems
of the past, and my colleagues are just
as firm in facing them as they were the
others which we have got over. I must
apologize to the House for going into matters
which, perhaps, are a little outside the
subject of our debates to-day, but my one
desire is that they should know everything
I know, and that I should carry them with
me in the policy that the Government proposes to pursue. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I would like in the

Mr. Coote was not only a regular attender,

He was a man of independent mind, a man

Having paid this tribute-a very weak

The PRIME MINISTER: Hear, hear.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: It is always a difficult thing to move or second the Address.

after all there is only one point in this
Address to-day. I am
am sorry for many

We are all of one mind on the subject.
Why ask us then to declare again that we
are of one mind? Less than five months
ago those of us who are members of the Imperial Parliament faced the country. The
only subject that we put before the electors
was the Boundary question; on that Boundary question we got a vote that certainly
has impressed the people of Great Britain,
and I for one would be satisfied to leave it
there. But after all the Prime Minister, as

but the Leader of the party, and if he says

the feeling that we should not have gone
to the country until after the Boundary
Commission had reported, but if the Prime
Minister in his wisdom thinks that there
are reasons why we should go then I bow
to his decision. I only hope that the result of the election will be to strengthen the
hands of the Government. But let me say
this, that no election that can take place
in Northern Ireland can make the determination of the people on the Boundary question more clear than it has been made in
the past months. There are many things
that one might enter into, but I doubt if it

myself with saying that I hope in the ap-
Leal the Government is going to make to

to serve to the best of his ability.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I have no desire to make anything in the nature of a
lengthened speech on what, after all, is a
very historic occasion. We are closing one
wonderful chapter in the history of the Six
Counties, and we are opening up another
one, and I can only express the hope that
the same success will be secured through the

up the reins of office after the election is
over as has been secured by the present
Government who are now about to appeal
to the grand inquest of the electors for a
decision. There are just a few outstanding
things that I want to make a passing reference to, not in any way of dealing exhaustively with them, but just by way of fastening
our thoughts upon a few matters that are
worthy of note in connection with the
various subjects that have been brought before us so effectively and efficiently by the
proposer and seconder of the Address and
by the Prime Minister himself in the very
informative speech with which he has
favoured the House. The first thing, I
think, that strikes us is the reference to
law and order. The foundation of all society is the recognition of law, and I think
there never was a territory subjected to so
many difficulties as the territory that we
live in was subjected to during the past
eventful four years. Never had a Government so many difficulties to overcome in
trying to defeat enemies from the outside
and enemies from within, and I must say
that they laboured so successfully that to-day
Northern Ireland is as peaceful, as contented, and as law-abiding as any part of
the British Empire. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) In this connection it is right and
fitting that a tribute should be paid to
those who by their efforts brought about
such a happy result. I know the Minister
of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates) has been
subjected from time to time to a great deal
of criticism. Some of it, I suppose, he
deserved possibly he welcomed it-and
some of it he did not deserve, but he and
the law officers of the Crown who have been
associated with him throughout this long,
trying, and difficult period have succeeded
in overcoming the forces of disorder, and
at the expiration of this Parliament have
placed Northern Ireland in the condition
I have just described. I think they are
to be heartily congratulated on this result.
and I am absolutely certain that those to
whom they may appeal in the coming days
will show by their actions that they
appreciate what has been accomplished.
Now the other subject is one of very great
importance, but I am only going to make a
passing reference to it. After law and order
comes finance, and without the wherewithal
to carry on no Government can efficiently
do its work. In this respect we have been
greatly hampered by the financial arrange-

In connection with finance may I just
refer to another subject that has come into
my mind? Some of us have been seriously
$0.
concerned about the position of the Unemployment Fund. The House has always
dealt with the greatest sympathy with the
proposals made to it by the Minister of
Finance in his efforts to help those who
have been down and out, as it were, and
have been struggling against poverty and
against unemployment. He has shown in
the most magnanimous manner his kindness
of heart, his large outlook, and his desire
ot do what was best for those who were
struggling under great difficulties, and this
Houso has always given him practically his
own way, although he does not always think
We have overdrawn, I think, at the
moment to the tune of over £2,500,000, and
possibly there are still further advances that
will have to be met. I would like in a
sentence or two to inform the House that I
never liked the arrangement whereby we
were being treated as a separate unit from
Great Britain in connection with this
matter. I know the British Government
borrowed originally something like £23,000,000
to help the unemployed. They have reduced that sum now to about £6,000,000,
while we, instead of having a reduction, are
increasing. But it is due to the fact-and
it is a very simple matter to explain-that
this particular patch of territory that was
separated from the main territory was a
place where unemployment had reached a
very serious state indeed, and especially so
from the fact that in Ulster we have the
industries that were hit most of all through
the slump. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Just as if Lancashire had come in for a
bad period of adversity in the cotton trade.
and had to depend entirely upon its own resources to finance its unemployment, so
Ulster was placed in the same position,
which I contend is a most unfair position
for us to occupy, and the sooner the Government that is going to come into office at
some future period presses, and presses
seriously, upon the British authorities that
in this question of the Unemployment Fund
we should come in along with the greater
unit of Great Britain the better. In all
fairness I think that is a proposal that
ought to be received with sympathy, and I
trust the result will be beneficial.
I do not think I need refer to any further
matters, except to congratulate the Minister

through which they have been passing. I am
glad the difficulties have been overcome and
that the education of the young people in
Ulster can now go ahead without any
serious difficulty. Those are the
things about which I would like to say a
few words here on this interesting afternoon

when we are all so happy and so cheerful

are like the old war horses who scent the

There is nothing to fear in that respect.
Their record is a good one, one upon which

during the past four years. I have criticised

It is to me a great joy and pleasure, and I

I say that I refer to the Prime
Minister. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I sincerely hope that the prosperity

Colonel WOODS: I would be very sorry to
interrupt the throwing of bouquets across the
floor of this House-verbal ones, of coursebut I would like first of all to pay my tribute to the man who in my opinion was one
of the most sincere gentleman it has been my
privilege to know-the late Mr. William
Coote. Of a truly modest, quiet,
and kindly disposition, never seeking
self-aggrandisement or publicity, but
only the betterment of his fellow
creatures, he had a heart which, as I

On behalf of such as these he spared himself not at all, and his memory will ever be
respected by men, women, and children as a
sincere and true friend whose aid was ever
at the service of the deserving. His loss to
the country and to this House is inestimable
at this time when his keenly discriminative
powers would have been of great assistance
to the electors to separate the chaff from the
wheat, and he would have been able to
place before the electorate a clear and clean
issue. There is nothing I can say too much
to emphasise the great loss this House and
the country have sustained through the untimely death of one of Ulster's foremost men,
a death which I know was hastened by his
unstinting zeal in the public cause. He
deserved better of his country.
the hon.
I would like to congratulate
Member for the University (Sir John
Campbell) who moved the Address and the
hon. Member for Down (Mr. Lavery) who
seconded it. I am only sorry that we have
not had more evidence of their powers of
oratory, because I was greatly struck by the
remarks of them both. But the seconder of
the Address (Mr. Lavery) referred to
various matters which I do not think were
in the Gracious Speech before the House, but
might have been in last year's, or last week's.
I would like to have further enlightenment as
to the preservation of ancient monuments
to which he referred. If the result of the
forthcoming election bears that out-well, all
of us will be pleased.
The Prime Minister in his speech referred
very often to what will happen when he returns. His speech had the tone of an electioneering speech because he asserted so
often that he was coming back. We will all
be glad to see him. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). At the same time he made in the
past a lot of promises that he has not
exactly fulfilled to the letter. With all due
respect to him might I mention a few?
There was one promise he made across the
floor of this House in regard to the Education Act. That is one promise which I am
very glad he broke. He said at that time he
would not move one inch in regard to the
Education Act, or bring in an amending
Bill. I am relieved to know that he has
done so, because he has saved me an awful
lot of trouble.
I was rather astonished at the Prime
Minister when he remarked that all internal
questions are settled and the decks clear. I
hope that things will never be worse. I
cannot speak exactly from his point of view,
or say what he thinks about the decks being
clear. I think the decks are very untidy
and there are a lot of loose ends lying about.
There are several questions which should
have been dealt with before this House dissolved that have not been dealt with. For instance, the Prime, Minister made a promise
that Proportional Representation would be
abolished before this House would go to the
country again. I speak with great feeling
on this matter, because it makes a vast
difference to an independent Member who
has got to fight a constituency. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). It amounts to somewhere
about three or four times the expense. That
to my mind is a drawback. It is not going
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
10 MARCH 1925
to be an inducement to anyone to put himself up as a candidate for Parliament when he
has got to pay electioneering expenses for a
whole county instead of for a single-member
constituency. I cannot speak with any degree of authority such as the Minister of
Labour (Mr. Andrews) may be able to do, as
I have not made a study of the thing, but
from what I know Proportional Representation is a clumsy and expensive machine.
The sooner it is abolished the better. It is
a pity it was not abolished before the coming
election. The Prime Minister says he is the
best judge of that. I daresay he is, but I do
not understand why there should be an election just now.
There was one thing the Prime Minister
said which I hope he did not mean exactly.
This has been said again and again on
various platforms. He said he dared any
man to create a split amongst Loyalists. A
Loyalist is a man who is loyal. A man is
not disloyal because he wears brown gloves
and goes to the same place as another man
who wears grey gloves. I think it is a crime
and a disgrace when a man is called disloyal
and a traitor because he disagrees in some
small particular with another person. There
is nothing disloyal in that. I hope the
Prime Minister does not mean that a man
is a traitor and a treacherous dog if he disagrees with him in regard to some particular
item. The Prime Minister said that there
are no grievances to speak of. He has announced that an amending Bill to the
Education Act will be introduced. He has
done this against a promise he made. He
gave a promise some. time ago that there
would not be any amending Bill brought in
to the Licensing Act. Will that promise
hold as well as other promises he has made
in the past? Will he again give an undertaking that there will be no change in that
particular Act? I would like a pronouncement from him as to what he will do under
these circumstances.
I agree entirely with my colleague the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Sir Robert
Lynn) when he pointed out that the last
election for the Imperial Parliament was
entirely upon the question of the Boundary,
and that the result could not have been
better. I cannot quite gather what is the
reason for this particular election just now.
The Prime Minister has said it is unnecesary to state the reasons in this House.
I do not know, but I fancy a great many of
the electors would like to know why the
country is being put to such a lot of expense and trouble, especially now when they
cannot afford it, and coming so soon after
the Imperial Elections. The matter of the
Border does not hold good if you take into
consideration the result of the Imperial
Election. Will the Prime Minister give one
of the real reasons why he chose this time
for the election? Will he give us one
reason So as to placate more or less the
people outside? It would be a rather good
thing if he did so. The Prime Minister has
promised to deal with many items for the
benefit of the country when he returns. I
hope to see him in his old seat again. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I also hope to see a
few friends sitting with me on this side, because at present it is very lonely and
draughty. I have nobody but a teetotaller
behind me, and another hon. Member who
is a questionable teetotaller. If you think
you are justified in going to the country
with hardly any excuse then I have nothing
further to say. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. McGUFFIN: I only want to make
two or three observations, and my first is
that what I am going to say is not to be
regarded in the nature of a valedictory
address. I expect we are all coming back
again. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The
Government by its performances of the last
four years is almost assured that it will.
The particular point raised in the course of
this debate is as to the wisdom of the Prime
Minister in particular and the Cabinet as
a whole selecting the present as a suitable
occasion for dissolution. All I can say with
respect to that matter is in line with what
Members of the Government have said on
many another occasion in this House when
I felt I had a difference with the Prime
Minister as regards a certain thing, namely,
that if we knew as much as he knew perhaps
we would act similarly. It is not possible
that we should know the
reasons that
operate in the Prime Minister's mind at the
present moment to induce him to take this
as the
proper opportunity to dissolve
Parliament. I assume there is sufficient
reason for it, and it is not necessary that
the House should be initiated into that
reason to justify the procedure. 1, therefore, find no fault with the Government in
the course they have taken in bringing off
an election at the present time.
The only thing I would like to say is as
to the way in which the Prime Minister has
fulfilled the two pledges he gave with respect to licensing reform and education. If
he had omitted to carry out either then
there might have been objection raised to
the dissolution, but, seeing that he has fulfilled his pledges in regard to these two important matters, I see no reason why the
occasion should not be made use of for
having a dissolution. The all-important
point in connection with the matter is that
we are satisfied with what we have done up
to the present, and we are going to give the
public an opportunity of declaring their
opinion as to what has been done in this
House.
